en: When about to enter upon the vow, standing between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires and facing eastward, he touches water. As to why he touches water: man is indeed impure in that he speaks untruth; by that he is foul within. Water, however, is pure; "Having become pure, may I enter upon the vow," he thinks. Water is a means of purification; "Purified by the means of purification, may I enter upon the vow," he intends. For this reason, he touches water.
Gazing toward the fire, he undertakes the vow, saying:

"O Agni, lord of vows, I shall perform the vow; may I accomplish it; may it be successful for me. Agni indeed is the lord of vows among the gods; it is to him that he says this: "I shall perform the vow; may I accomplish it; may it be successful for me. There is nothing hidden here.
Then, when the sacrifice has been completed, he releases his vows, saying:

"O Agni, Lord of Vows, I have performed the vow; I was able to do it; may that be successful for me. For he was indeed able, since he has reached the completion of the sacrifice; for one who has reached the completion of the sacrifice, it is indeed successful. Most people indeed enter upon the vow with this [formula], but one should rather enter upon it with this [other].
This world is indeed twofold; there is no third:
truth and untruth. The gods are truth, and humans are untruth. "I go from untruth to truth"—thus he goes from among humans to the gods.
He should indeed speak only the truth. For the gods observe this very vow, which is truth; therefore, they possess glory. Indeed, he who, knowing this, speaks the truth, becomes glorious.

Then, when the rite is concluded, he releases the vow, saying: "I am now who I truly am. For when one enters upon the vow, he becomes as it were non-human; it would not be appropriate for him to say, "I now pass from truth to untruth," because by that he would indeed become human again. Therefore, he should release the vow with these words: "I am now who I truly am."

Now, therefore, regarding eating and fasting. On this point, Āṣāḍha Sāvayasa considered fasting alone to be the vow. For the gods indeed perceive the mind of a human being; they know that he is about to undertake this vow, thinking, "Tomorrow morning he will sacrifice. Then all the gods come to his house, and they dwell in his house; that is the Upavasatha (the day of preparation).

That indeed is improper: for what man would eat before others among men who have not eaten, how much more so one who would eat before the gods who have not eaten? Therefore, he should certainly not eat.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "If he does not eat, he belongs to the ancestors; if he eats, he eats beyond the measure of the gods. Therefore, he should eat that which is both eaten and uneaten. For that of which no sacrificial oblation is taken is indeed both eaten and uneaten. When he eats that, he does not belong to the ancestors; and when he eats that of which no sacrificial oblation is taken, he does not eat beyond the measure of the gods.

He should indeed eat only forest food—either wild plants or the produce of trees. Regarding this, Barku Vārṣṇa used to say, "Cook for me month after month; they do not take the sacrificial oblation from these. But one should not do so; for this grain that grows in the field is the offspring of rice and barley, and by doing this, he makes rice and barley more abundant. Therefore, he should eat only forest food.

He should sleep that night either in the Āhavanīya fire-hall or in the Gārhapatya fire-hall. For he who undertakes a vow approaches the gods; he thus lies in the midst of those very gods whom he approaches. He should sleep on the ground, for the service toward one who is superior is as if from below.

In the morning, he indeed first attends to the waters; he leads forward the waters. For the waters are the sacrifice; thus, by this first act, he attends to the sacrifice. He leads them forward; he thereby extends the sacrifice.

He draws it forward with these undefined utterances (*vyāhṛti*): "Who yokes thee? He yokes thee. For whom does he yoke thee? For him he yokes thee. Prajāpati is indeed undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he yokes the sacrifice to Prajāpati.
And again, as to why he brings forward the waters:
by water indeed all this [universe] is pervaded; thus, by this very first rite, he obtains everything.
Or rather, whatever here the Hotṛ, or the Adhvaryu, or the Brahman, or the Āgnīdhra, or the sacrificer himself does not accomplish, all that becomes accomplished for him by this [rite].
Furthermore, as to why he brings forward the waters:
when the gods were sacrificing with the sacrifice, the Asuras and Rakṣases guarded them, saying, "You shall not sacrifice! Because they guarded (arakṣan) them, therefore they are called Rakṣases.

Then the gods beheld this thunderbolt: the waters are the thunderbolt, for the waters are indeed a thunderbolt. Therefore, wherever these [waters] flow, they make a hollow; wherever they settle, they burn up. Having raised this thunderbolt aloft, they performed the sacrifice in its safety, security, and freedom from wind. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now raises this thunderbolt aloft and performs the sacrifice in its safety, security, and freedom from wind. Therefore, he leads forward the waters.
Having poured them out, he places them to the north of the Gārhapatya fire.

Water is indeed female and fire is male; the Gārhapatya is the home. Thus, this procreative union is brought about right within the home. He who leads forward the waters raises up the thunderbolt. For if one who is not firmly established raises up the thunderbolt, he is unable to raise it, and it destroys him.
As to why he places it on the Gārhapatya fire-altar:
the Gārhapatya is indeed the house, and the house is a firm foundation; thus this thunderbolt does not injure him, and for that reason he places it on the Gārhapatya.
He leads them northward past the Āhavanīya fire.
Water is indeed female and Agni is male; thus a productive union is brought about. For a union is arranged in this very way: for the woman lies on the left side of the man.

They should not pass between them, lest they pass between a couple engaged in sexual intercourse. He should not set them down by moving them too far away, nor should he set them down without having reached their place. For if he were to set them down after moving them too far, since there is a certain rivalry between the fire and the waters, it would be as if that rivalry of the fire were increased wherever his waters touch it; he would thereby increase the rival in the fire. And if he were to set them down without having reached the place, he would not fulfill that purpose for which they are brought forward. Therefore, he brings them forward directly alongside the Āhavanīya fire.

Then he strews it with grass. He brings forward the vessels in pairs: the winnowing-basket and the Agnihotra-ladle, the wooden sword and the potsherds, the yoke-pin and the black antelope skin, and the mortar and pestle, and the lower and upper grinding stones—that makes ten. For the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the Virāj; thus he completes this sacrifice as the Virāj. Now, as to why they are in pairs: power indeed is in pairs; for when two join together, then there is power. A pair is indeed a productive union; thus a productive union is brought about.

Then he takes up the winnowing-basket and the Agnihotra-ladle with the formula: "For the work of you two, for the service of you two. Work is indeed the sacrifice, for it is for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "for the work of you two. "For the service of you two"—for he indeed serves the sacrifice.
Then he restrains his speech;

for the sacrifice is speech, and [he does so] thinking, "I shall extend the sacrifice undisturbed. Then he heats [the offering-ladle], either with the formula, "The Rakṣas is burnt up, the enemies are burnt up," or, "The Rakṣas is scorched, the enemies are scorched."

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakshasas; thus, right from the beginning of the sacrifice, he drives away the destructive spirits and Rakshasas from there.

Then he goes forth, saying, "I follow the wide atmosphere. For the Rakṣas roams through the atmosphere, rootless and severed on both sides, just as this man, rootless and severed on both sides, roams through the atmosphere; thus, by means of the Brahman, he makes that atmosphere free from fear and free from destruction.
Or rather, he should take it from the cart itself.

For in the beginning, this world was indeed like a cart; or rather, whatever here is capable of moving, that was like a cart. Thinking, "I shall do what was done in the beginning," he should therefore take it from the cart itself.
The cart is indeed abundance; for the cart is truly abundance.
Therefore, when something becomes much, they say, "It has become a cart-load. Thus, one attains that very abundance; therefore, one should take [the water] from a cart alone.

"The sacrifice does not dwell in a leather bag; the seers took [the ritual formulas] from a leather bag for Kauṣṭa, not from a pot or a bellows. Those sacrificial formulas (yajus) belonged to the leather bags for the sages; they are now common [formulas]. 'Let me fashion sacrifice after sacrifice,' [he thought]; therefore, one should take [the formulas] from a cart."
Moreover, one should take it from the vessel while it is still there; having pushed it aside, one should take it, for they unyoke from the very place where they yoke.

Of this very cart, Agni is indeed the pole, for Agni is the pole; and that part of it which they drive over becomes, as it were, scorched by Agni. And that which is behind the *kastambhī* (the central post) is its fore-part, the altar; the *nīḍa* (the seat) is indeed its *havirdhāna* (sacrificial oblation-holder).
He touches the pole with the formula:

"Thou art the pole; injure him who injures us; injure him whom we injure. For Agni is indeed this pole-horse, and he is about to pass beyond him as he is about to take the oblation; therefore, he propitiates him with these [words]. Thus, Agni, the pole-horse, does not harm him as he passes by.
Regarding this, Āruṇi indeed said:
"Verily, by means of unrighteousness, I shall strike down my rivals"—this is what he said with reference to that.
Then, having touched the pole behind the post, he mutters:

"Thou art the best carrier of the gods, the most liberal, the most fulfilling, the most beloved, the best invoker of the gods. Thou art the unswerving oblation-holder; stand firm, do not waver! He thus praises the very post so that, being praised, it may be well-disposed toward him as he takes the oblation. "May thy lord of the sacrifice not waver"—the lord of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer; thus he prays for the sacrificer's safety.

Then he steps upon it with the formula, "May Viṣṇu step upon thee! For Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride across these worlds for the sake of the gods—this very stride which belongs to them. With his first step he planted this [earth], with the second this intermediate space, and with the last the sky. Verily, this Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, strides this stride for him.
Then he gazes at it with the words, "Wide for the wind. The wind is indeed breath; thus, by means of the sacred word (brahman), he makes a wide passage for the breath, the wind.

Then he throws it away, saying, "The Rakṣas is struck down! If anything has been damaged there, or even if nothing has been touched, he thereby strikes down those destructive powers and Rakṣases from that place.
Then he takes hold of it, saying, "Let them restrain themselves. There are five fingers; the sacrifice is fivefold; thus he establishes the sacrifice here.
Then he takes [the Soma], saying:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee, acceptable to Agni. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it. "With the arms of the Aśvins"—the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryu priests. "With the hands of Pūṣan"—Pūṣan is the distributor of portions, the one who places food before men with his hands. The gods are truth and men are untruth; thus, by means of truth itself, he takes it.
Then he assigns [the portions] to the deities.

Indeed, all the deities attend upon the Adhvaryu when he is about to take the oblation, thinking, "He will utter my name; he will utter my name. He thus creates a lack of discord among them while they are together.
Furthermore, as to why he announces the deity:

for from as many deities as the oblations are taken, they consider him to be in debt; therefore, so that they may fulfill for him whatever desire he has for which he takes the oblation, he indeed announces the deity. Thus, having taken the oblations in the proper order as before—
Then he touches it with the formula:
"For the being, not for the non-being. Thus, he causes that very thing which he has taken up to swell again.
Then he looks toward the east, saying, "May I behold the light.

For this cart-pole becomes, as it were, encompassed; its eye, as it were, becomes seized by evil. The light is indeed the sacrifice, and the gods are the sun; thus, by means of the light, he beholds from here.

Then he descends with the words, "May the dwellings on earth be firm. The dwellings are indeed the house; for those houses of the sacrificer are liable to collapse after him when this Adhvaryu, who performs the sacrifice for him, departs. They are liable to cause his lineage to be shaken. He thus makes them firm upon this earth, so that they do not collapse and do not shake. Therefore he says, "May the dwellings on earth be firm. Then he steps forward with the words, "I follow the wide mid-air"; the significance of this is the same as before.
He is the one in whose Gārhapatya fire they cook the sacrificial oblations.

They set down his vessels near the Gārhapatya fire; he should then set them down behind the Gārhapatya for one who cooks the oblations on the Āhavanīya, for they set down his vessels near the Āhavanīya; he should then set them down behind the Āhavanīya. "I set thee down on the navel of the earth," he says; the navel is indeed the middle, and the middle is free from danger; therefore he says, "I set thee down on the navel of the earth. "In the lap of Aditi," he says; for they say that when they guard something well-guarded, they do so as if in a lap; therefore he says, "in the lap of Aditi. "O Agni, protect the offering! he says; he thus entrusts this oblation to Agni for protection and to this Earth; therefore he says, "O Agni, protect the offering."
He makes two strainers with the formula, "You two are strainers, belonging to Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "You two belong to the sacrifice."
These two indeed become [the strainers].

This one who blows here is indeed the purifier; he blows as if he were one alone, yet having entered within this person, he moves both forward and backward—these being the prāṇa and udāna breaths. Therefore, according to the measure of that very [breath], there are two.
Or there may even be three;
for the vyāna is the third. However, there are indeed only two: having purified these sprinkling waters (prokṣaṇī) with those two, he sprinkles with them. Now, as to why he purifies with those two.
Vṛtra indeed lay here having encompassed all this—that which is between heaven and earth. Because he lay there having encompassed all this, he is named Vṛtra.
Indra struck him down;

being struck, he flowed forth as a putrid mass toward the waters on all sides—for this ocean flows from every side—and therefore some of the waters were loathsome. They overflowed one over the other, and from them these Darbha grasses arose. These are waters that have not become putrid; yet there is something as if mixed with the others, because Vṛtra, being putrid, flowed over them. That very thing he removes from them by means of these two purifiers. Then he sprinkles with pure waters; therefore he purifies by means of these two.

He purifies it with the formula: "At the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he purifies it. "With a flawless strainer"—he thereby refers to this wind that blows, for this is the flawless strainer; by means of this he says, "with the rays of the sun. The rays of the sun are indeed the purifiers; therefore he says, "with the rays of the sun."

Having placed them in his left hand, he points them out with his right hand; he thereby praises them and magnifies them. "O divine waters, you who go first, you who drink first"—for the waters are indeed divine, therefore he says, "O divine waters. As for "you who go first," they are called "going first" because they go to the ocean; as for "you who drink first," they are called "drinking first" because they are the first to drink of King Soma. "Lead this sacrifice today to the front, lead the lord of the sacrifice to a good station, the lord of the sacrifice who seeks the gods"—by this he means, "lead the sacrifice well, lead the sacrificer well."
"Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra," he says.
For indeed, it was these [verses] that Indra chose when contending with Vṛtra; with them he struck him down. Therefore he says, "Indra chose you for the slaying of Vṛtra."
"You have chosen Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra," he says.
For these very [goddesses] chose Indra when he was contending with Vṛtra; it was by means of them that they struck him down. Therefore he says, "You have chosen Indra for the slaying of Vṛtra."
"Ye are sprinkled"—with these words he makes amends to these [goddesses]; then he sprinkles the oblation. Indeed, there is one single bond for the sprinkling: it is this that makes it pure.

He sprinkles it with the formula, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni"; thus he makes it pure for whichever deity the oblation belongs to. In this very manner, having sprinkled the sacrificial offerings one after another as before.

Then he sprinkles the sacrificial vessels with the formula: "Be purified for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods! For he purifies them for the divine rite, for the sacrifice to the gods. When he says, "Whatever impure thing has struck you, that I now purify for you," he means this: whatever impure thing—a carpenter or someone else—has here struck them, that he now makes pure for them by means of water. Therefore he says, "Whatever impure thing has struck you, that I now purify for you."

Then he takes up a black antelope skin for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice. Indeed, the Sacrifice fled from the gods; having become a black antelope, it wandered away. The gods, having discovered it, stripped off its hide and carried it away.

Of him, whatever hairs are white and black, those are the form of the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants: those that are white are the form of the Sāmans, and those that are black are the form of the Ṛg-verses; or alternatively, those that are black are the form of the Sāmans and those that are white are the form of the Ṛg-verses; and those that are brownish-yellow are the form of the Yajus-formulas.

This threefold knowledge is indeed the sacrifice. Its craft is this, its color is this: namely, that there is a black antelope skin. This is for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice; therefore they undergo consecration upon the black antelope skin for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice. Therefore there is pounding upon it and grinding upon it, so that the oblation may not be spilled. Whatever grain or flour might fall here, by that the sacrifice shall be established in the sacrifice. Therefore there is pounding upon it and grinding upon it.

Then he takes up the black antelope skin with the words, "Thou art a refuge. For this is indeed the skin of the black antelope; that is his human refuge, but among the gods it is a refuge (śarma); therefore he says, "Thou art a refuge. He shakes it out with the words, "Shaken off is the Rakṣas, shaken off are the enemies! By this he drives away the destructive Rakṣases from here. He shakes it over the vessels as they are being carried across; whatever impurity there was in them, that he shakes out of them.

He spreads that [skin] with its neck pointing westward, saying: "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may Aditi recognize thee! This earth, indeed, is Aditi; this is her skin, for whatever exists upon her is her skin. Therefore he says, "Thou art the skin of Aditi. "May Aditi recognize thee," he says, for she recognizes her own; thus he establishes a mutual recognition between himself and the black antelope skin so that they do not injure one another. It remains held down by his left hand.

Then he brings the mortar from the south, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (nāṣṭrā) and demons (rakṣas) enter here before [the sacrifice]. For the Brāhmaṇa is the repeller of demons; therefore, it remains held down by his left hand.
Then he places the mortar.

"You are a stone, you are a tree-born; you are a pressing-stone, broad-based"—this is what he says. Just as they press King Soma with the pressing-stones, so too does he press the Haviryajña sacrifice with the mortar and pestle and the large and small grinding stones. "Adrayaḥ" (the stones) is indeed one of their names; therefore he says, "You are a stone. "You are a tree-born," for it is indeed born from a tree. "You are a pressing-stone, broad-based," for it is indeed a pressing-stone and it is broad-based. "May the skin of Aditi recognize you"—he says this to create a mutual understanding between the black antelope skin and the stone, so that they do not injure each other.

Then he pours out the oblation-material with the words, "Thou art Agni's body, the release of speech. For the sacrifice is indeed Agni's body, and it is the release of speech. For when he restrains his speech while about to take the oblation-material, he releases it here; and because he releases this speech here, and because the sacrifice has established itself in the mortar and has spread forth, therefore he says, "the release of speech."

If he should here utter human speech before [the offering], he should mutter there either a verse or a sacrificial formula belonging to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he takes up the sacrifice again. This is his expiation: "I take thee for the feast of the gods," for the oblation is indeed taken while saying, "I call upon the gods."

Then he takes up the mallet with the formula, "Thou art the great stone, belonging to the trees. For this is indeed the great stone, and it belongs to the trees. He places it down with the words, "Prepare this oblation for the gods; prepare it well; prepare it! By this he means to say, "Fashion this oblation for the gods; fashion it well-fashioned; fashion it!"
Then he causes the preparer of the oblation to call out:

"O preparer of the oblation, come! O preparer of the oblation, come! For the preparer of the oblation is speech; it is speech that he thereby releases. Speech, indeed, is the sacrifice; it is the sacrifice that he thus calls back again.

Now, these are the four [forms of address] for speech: "Come! for a Brāhmaṇa; "Come hither! for a Vaiśya and a Rājanya; and "Run hither! for a Śūdra. Whatever he says for the Brāhmaṇa, that is indeed the most sacrificial; and this, indeed, is the most peaceful form of speech, namely, "Come! Therefore, one should say only "Come!"
In ancient times, indeed, it was the wife alone who used to rise as the preparer of the oblation;

even now, whoever rises for that purpose does so. When he causes the preparer of the oblation to respond, then one person strikes together the large and small grinding stones. This is why they cause her to respond with this speech here.
Manu, it is said, had a bull.

Into him had entered speech that slays Asuras and slays rivals; from his snorting and bellowing, the Asuras and Rakṣasas were crushed as they went along. Those Asuras said to one another, "Alas, this bull pursues us with evil! How might we overcome him? Now, Kilāta and Ākuli were two Asura-Brahmins.

The two of them said, "We do not indeed know Manu, for Śraddhādevī is [his wife]. They came and said, "Manu, let us sacrifice for you. He asked, "With what? "With this bull," they replied. "So be it. When that bull had been immolated, its speech departed.
She entered the body of Manāvī, the wife of Manu.

Whenever they listened to her as she spoke, from that very spot the Asuras and Rakṣases would flee, being crushed. Those Asuras said to one another, "Something worse than this is surely overtaking us, for the human voice speaks more. Kilāta and Ākuli both said, "Manu is indeed a believer in the gods; he surely knows us. They went to him and said, "O Manu, let us two sacrifice for you. He asked, "By what means? They replied, "By this very wife of yours. "So be it," he said. When she was seized for the sacrifice, that Speech departed from her.
She entered the sacrifice itself and the sacrificial vessels;

therefore, they were unable to drive her out. This very speech, which slays the Asuras, speaks aloud. For one who knows this, if they respond with this speech here, his rivals indeed become more wretched.

He strikes it, saying, "Thou art a cock, honey-tongued. For he was indeed honey-tongued for the gods and poison-tongued for the Asuras. "Be thou such as thou wast for the gods," this is what he says. "Proclaim food and strength; through thee may we conquer every host"—in this there is nothing obscure.
Then he takes up the winnowing basket with the formula,
"Thou art increased by rain," for it is indeed increased by rain— whether it be made of reeds, or of bamboos, or of grass-stalks— for rain alone causes these to grow.

Then he pours out the sacrificial food (havir), saying, "May that which has grown by rain recognize thee! For these [grains] have indeed grown by rain, whether they be rice or barley; for rain indeed causes them to grow. And thus he speaks to the winnowing basket for the sake of mutual recognition, so that they may not harm one another.

Then he winnows them, saying, "Winnowed away is the Rakṣas, winnowed away are the enemies. Then he threshes the husks, saying, "Struck away is the Rakṣas. Thus he strikes away these destructive Rakṣases from there.

Then he winnows them, saying, "May Vāyu winnow you! Now, this Vāyu who blows here is indeed that [Vāyu]; for he indeed winnows all this, whatever is winnowed here. Thus, it is he who now winnows these; when they reach that point where he winnows them over.

Then he consecrates it with the mantra: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand; may they be well-received. Then he husks them three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.

Now, some thresh [the grains] while saying, "Be pure for the gods! Be pure for the gods! But one should not do so; for this oblation has already been assigned to its specific deity, yet by saying "Be pure for the gods," he makes it belong to all the gods (vaiśvadeva). Therefore, he should thresh them silently.
One of them indeed lays down the potsherds alone;
the other lays down the large and small grinding stones. Now, these two things are performed together; and as for the fact that these two are performed together—

The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), indeed, is the head of the sacrifice; these other [potsherds] are just like the skull-bones of the head, and these flour-particles are its brain. Now, they think: "This is one limb and that is another; let us perform them together, let us make them the same. Therefore, both of these are performed together.

Now, he who lays down the potsherds takes up the fire-brander with the formula, "Thou art the bold one. Because he approaches the fire with it boldly, it is therefore called the *dhṛṣṭi* (the bold one). And because he censures the sacrifice with it, or rather, he as it were hates it with it, it is therefore called the *upaveṣa* (the hater).
With that [formula], he pushes forward the glowing coals:

"O Agni, drive away the raw-eating Agni; expel the flesh-eater! For that by which humans eat after cooking it is the raw-eater (āmāda), and that by which they burn a corpse is the flesh-eater (kravyād). It is these two that he thus drives away from here.
Then he heats the charcoal with the formula, "Bring hither the one who goes to the gods!
[The meaning is: "In him who goes to the gods, let us cook the oblations; in him let us extend the sacrifice. For this reason, he heats it.
He places it down upon the middle potsherd.

Indeed, while the gods were performing the sacrifice, they were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases, thinking, "Lest the destructive Rakṣases rise up against us from below. For Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; therefore he places it thus. And as to why it is this very [brick] and no other: for this one alone is consecrated by the Yajus-formula and is fit for the sacrifice; therefore he places it down upon the middle potsherd.
He lays it down.

"Thou art firm; make the earth firm"—by means of the very form of the earth he thus makes this [altar] firm, and by this very means he repels his hateful rival. "I set thee down, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility, winner of kinsmen, for the slaying of the rival"—for in the Yajus formulas there is much that is a prayer for blessing; thus he prays for both the priesthood and the nobility. By saying "winner of kinsmen," he prays for abundance, for kinsmen are indeed abundance; thus he prays for abundance when he says, "I set thee down for the slaying of the rival. If he does not intend to practice sorcery, he uses this formula; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he should say, "for the slaying of so-and-so. It remains pressed down by the finger of the left hand.

Then he throws a coal away [to the north], thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (nāṣṭrā) and demons (rakṣāṃsi) enter here. For the Brāhmaṇa is the repeller of demons; therefore, it remains pressed down by the finger of his left hand.

Then he scatters coals over it with the formula, "O Agni, grasp the sacred word (brahman)! [He does this] so that the destructive spirits and demons may not enter here before [the fire is established]; for Agni is the repeller of demons; therefore he scatters coals over it.
Then he lays down that which is behind [the western brick] with the formula:

"Thou art the support; make firm the atmosphere! By means of the very form of the atmosphere, he thus makes it firm; by this very act, he repels his hateful rival. "I lay thee down, winner of the priesthood, winner of the nobility, winner of kinsmen, for the destruction of the rival! Thus he says.
Then, as for that which he places in front:
"Thou art the support; make firm the sky!"—he makes this very thing firm by means of the form of the sky itself; [and with the words] "by this very [power]... bind it! //

Then he places that one on the south with the formula: "I place thee for all the quarters. Now, as to whether there is anything beyond these worlds or not, by that very act he repels his hateful rival. For that which is beyond these worlds—whether it exists or not—is uncertain; and "all the quarters" is likewise uncertain. Therefore he says, "I place thee for all the quarters. As for the other potsherds, he places them either silently, or with the formula: "Ye are piled, piled upwards."

Then he covers it with charcoal, saying: "Heat yourselves with the fervor of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases. For the most brilliant heat is that of the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases; thinking, "May these become well-heated," he therefore covers it with charcoal.

Now, he who lays down the two pressing-stones takes a black antelope skin with the formula, "Thou art a refuge. He shakes it out with the words, "Shaken off is the Rakṣas; shaken off are the enemies"—this is the same explanation as before. He spreads it with the neck pointing westward, saying, "Thou art the skin of Aditi; may Aditi recognize thee!"—this is the same explanation as before.
Then he places the lower millstone (dṛṣad):

"Thou art a bowl (dhiṣaṇā), a mountain; may the skin of Aditi recognize thee! For she is indeed a bowl and she is indeed a mountain; "may the skin of Aditi recognize thee"—he says this to establish a mutual recognition between the black antelope skin and the stone, so that they may not injure one another. This very earth is this [stone] in form.
Then he places a peg with its point directed northward, saying:

"Thou art the support of heaven. This is indeed the intermediate space by its own form; for by the intermediate space these two, heaven and earth, are supported. Therefore he says: "Thou art the support of heaven."

Then he places the lower millstone (upala), saying: "Thou art Dhiṣaṇā, daughter of the mountain; may the mountain recognize thee! For she is the younger one, like a daughter; therefore he says, "daughter of the mountain. "May the mountain recognize thee," he says, for it recognizes its own. He thus speaks with the large and small millstones to establish mutual recognition, so that they may not injure each other. This upper millstone (dṛṣad) is indeed the sky in form; the two millstones are the jaws, and the wooden pin (śamyā) is the tongue; therefore he strikes together with the pin, for one speaks with the tongue.
Then he pours out the sacrificial food with the formula, "Thou art grain; nourish the gods. For grain indeed nourishes the gods; thus it is that the sacrificial food is taken.
Then he grinds [the grain], saying:

"For out-breath thee, for in-breath thee, for diffused breath thee; may I bestow long extension for life. He pours it out, saying: "May the god Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand; for sight thee!"
Now, as to why he grinds in this manner:
the oblation of the gods is indeed living, and that of the immortals is immortal; yet here they slay the sacrificial oblation with the mortar and pestle, and with the large and small grinding stones.

When he says, "For out-breathing thee, for up-breathing thee," he thereby bestows the out-breathing and the up-breathing; when he says, "For through-breathing thee," he thereby bestows the through-breathing; when he says, "May I place you along a long extension for the sake of life," he thereby bestows life. With the words, "May the divine Savitṛ, the golden-handed, receive you with his flawless hand, so that they may be well-received," [he says] "For sight thee! and thereby bestows sight. These indeed belong to one who lives; thus, this very living thing becomes the oblation of the gods, the immortal of the immortals. Therefore, he grinds it in this manner; they grind it, and having ground it, they heat the potsherds over it.

Then one pours out the clarified butter (ājya). Whatever oblation is taken for a specified deity, it belongs to that deity; he takes it with another sacrificial formula (yajus), for in the case of clarified butter, he does not specify it as an oblation for any particular deity. Therefore, he takes it with an undefined formula: "Thou art the milk of the great ones. Some indeed say that "the great ones" (mahī) is the name of cows; this is their milk, therefore he says, "Thou art the milk of the great ones. Thus, indeed, it is taken by means of the formula itself; for this reason also he says, "Thou art the milk of the great ones."
He pours [the grain] together with the strainers;

having placed the two strainers in the vessel, he says: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour thee together. This is the very same explanation for this sacrificial formula.

Then he sits down within the altar-ground. Now one person comes with the secondary waters (upasarjanī); he brings them forward, and he receives them with the two strainers, saying: "The waters have united with the plants. For indeed, these waters unite here with those ground plants; "the plants have united with the sap. For indeed, these ground plants unite here with the water, for the water is their sap.

"May these wealthy ones be united with the moving ones," he says; for the "wealthy ones" are the waters and the "moving ones" are the plants, and it is these two together that are here being united. "May the honeyed ones be united with the honeyed ones," he says; by this he means, "May those full of sap be united with those full of sap."
Then he mixes it together with the formula, "I mix thee for generation. Just as something cut out from wood might be produced from fire, even so does he mix it.
Then he divides it into two parts.

If there are two oblations—as there are indeed two oblations at the full moon sacrifice—he touches them at that point when he intends not to mix them again, saying, "This is for Agni; this is for Agni and Soma. For originally they take the oblation separately; they pound it together and grind it together, but then he makes it separate again. Therefore, he touches it in this manner. He places the sacrificial cake upon the fire, and he places the clarified butter upon the fire.

Now, this is indeed done both together; for when these two things are performed together, that which is the clarified butter (ājya) is one half of the self of the sacrifice, and that which is the oblation (havis) here is the other half. [The thought is: "May we cause both that half and this half to go to Agni. Therefore, these two are performed together; in this way, indeed, this self of the sacrifice is joined together.

He places the clarified butter on the fire with the words, "For food, thee!"—by saying "for food, thee," he means for rain. He then takes it off the fire with the words, "For strength, thee!"—by saying "for strength, thee," he means for that vigorous sap which is produced from rain.

Then he spreads the sacrificial cake upon [the potsherds] with the words, "Thou art the Gharma. He thereby makes it the sacrifice itself; he spreads it just as one would prepare the Gharma. With the words, "All-life," he bestows life upon it.
He spreads it out with the words, "O wide-spreading one, spread yourself wide!"—he thus causes it to spread wide.
With the words, "May your lord of the sacrifice spread wide," the lord of the sacrifice is indeed the sacrificer; he thus invokes a blessing for the sacrificer.
One should not make it excessively wide;

for if one were to make it wide, one would make it human-like, and that which is human-like is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I make the sacrifice a failure," he should therefore not make it excessively wide.
"One should make it the size of a horse's hoof," so some indeed say.
"Who knows how large a horse's hoof is? One should make it however large one personally considers it to be in one's mind, provided it is not too broad."

He touches it with water, either once or thrice. Whatever of this [sacrificial food] they injure while threshing or grinding, or whatever they diminish or tear asunder—water being a means of pacification—he pacifies that with water, the means of pacification; he heals that with water. Therefore, he touches it with water.
He touches it, saying, "May Agni not harm thy skin! For he is about to heat it with fire; thus he says, "May this [fire] not harm thy skin."
He carries fire around it;
he thus encloses it with fire so that no destructive spirits or Rakṣases may touch it, for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; therefore he carries fire around it.

He cooks it with the formula, "May the god Savitṛ cook thee. For no human indeed is its cooker, since he is a god; thus, the god Savitṛ himself cooks it. With the words, "Upon the highest vault," he says this so that it may be in the divine realm when he says, "Upon the highest vault. He touches it with the formula, "I know thee as cooked"; for that reason, he touches it.
He touches it, saying, "Do not fear, do not tremble. By this he means: "Do not be afraid, do not tremble, since I, a human being, am touching you who are non-human."

When it has been cooked, he then covers it, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits and demons look down upon it from above," and also, "Lest he should lie as if naked or as if robbed. For this reason, he indeed covers it.
He covers it [with the cloth], thinking:

"May the sacrifice be unwearied; may the offspring of the sacrificer be unwearied. He does so thinking: "Lest either the sacrifice or the sacrificer should become weary because I am covering this [fire]. Therefore, he covers it in this manner.
Then he pours out the rinsing water from the vessel and the washings from his fingers for the Āptyas; as to why he pours it out for the Āptyas.

In the beginning, Agni was indeed established in four forms. The one whom they first chose for the office of Hotṛ ran away; the second one they chose ran away as well; the third one they chose ran away too. Then this Agni who exists here today hid himself out of fear; he entered the waters. The gods, having discovered him, brought him forth from the waters by force. He stood upon the waters, saying, "You are dripping off! You are without a place of refuge! They are carrying me away against my will! From that, the Āptyas were born: Trita, Dvita, and Ekata.

They moved about together with Indra, just as a Brahmin here follows after a king. When he (Indra) slew Viśvarūpa, the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ, they recognized these [breaths] of his even as he was being slain; indeed, Trita alone had slain him. Thus Indra was released from that, for he is a god.

They said, "Let those who have announced this victim come to us."—"Why?"—"So that the sacrifice may be cleansed upon them. Thus the sacrifice is cleansed upon them when they pour out for them the rinsing of the vessel and the washing of the fingers.

The Āptyas said to him: "We have indeed attained this; let us lead it beyond us."—"Beyond whom?"—"Beyond whoever should sacrifice with an oblation that is without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Therefore, one should not sacrifice with an oblation that is without a sacrificial fee. For the sacrifice is wiped away from the Āptyas, and the Āptyas wipe it away from him who sacrifices with an oblation that is without a sacrificial fee.

Then the gods assigned this as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the New and Full Moon sacrifices, namely the *anvāhārya* rice; [they did so] thinking, "Lest this oblation be without a sacrificial fee. He pours it out separately; thus he creates discord among them. He heats it over the fire; thus it becomes cooked for them. He pours it out with the words, "For Trita thee! For Dvita thee! For Ekata thee! For this sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), which is offered, is indeed an animal.

In the beginning, the gods indeed sacrificed a man as an animal. When he had been sacrificed, his vital essence (medha) departed; it entered a horse. They sacrificed the horse. When that had been sacrificed, its vital essence departed; it entered a cow. They sacrificed the cow... it entered a sheep. They sacrificed the sheep... it entered a goat. They sacrificed the goat. When that had been sacrificed, its vital essence departed.
He entered this earth;

they searched for him while digging and found him—these two, rice and barley. Therefore, even now, people find these two as if by digging. Indeed, as powerful as all these animals of his would have been if they had been sacrificed, so powerful does his oblation become for one who knows this. This is how it comes to be that they say, "The animal is fivefold."

When they are ground, then it becomes hair; when he pours water upon them, then it becomes skin; when he mixes them together, then it becomes flesh—for at that time it becomes continuous, and flesh is, as it were, continuous; when it is boiled, then it becomes bone—for at that time it becomes hard, and bone is hard; then, when he is about to take it off the fire and bastes it, he bestows marrow upon it. This is what constitutes the fivefold animal, as they say: "The animal is fivefold."

The man whom they sacrificed became a *kiṃpuruṣa*; the horse and the cow which they sacrificed became the *gaura* and the *gavaya* respectively; the sheep which they sacrificed became a camel; and the goat which they sacrificed became a *śarabha*. Therefore, one should not eat of these animals, for their sacrificial essence has departed.

When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, it shattered upon being struck and became fourfold: one-third—or as much as that—became the wooden sword (sphyá); one-third—or as much as that—the sacrificial post (yūpa); and one-third—or as much as that—the chariot (rátha). Then, where he struck him, the tip (cakála) shattered; falling down, it became the arrow (śará), and because it shattered (aśīryata), it is called "arrow" (śára). Thus did that thunderbolt become fourfold.

Then, by means of two [objects] the Brahmins proceed at the sacrifice; by means of two, the kinsmen of the Rājanya, in the act of piercing: the Brahmins with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the wooden sword (*sphya*), and the kinsmen of the Rājanya with the chariot (*ratha*) and the arrow (*śara*).

When he takes up the wooden sword (sphya), just as Indra then raised the thunderbolt against Vṛtra, even so does he now raise this thunderbolt against evil, against the hater, his rival; therefore, indeed, he takes up the wooden sword.
He takes it up with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee, the performer of the sacrifice, for the gods. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up. "With the arms of the Aśvins"—the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryus; thus he takes it up with their very arms, not with his own. For this [sacrificial post] is a thunderbolt, and no mortal man is its bearer; therefore, he takes it up with these deities.
"I take that which has been made for the gods by the sacrifice.

The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus he says, "I take that which has been made for the gods by the sacrifice. Having placed it in his left hand and stroked it with his right, he mutters; in that he mutters, he truly consecrates it.

He mutters: "Thou art the right arm of Indra. For that which is the right arm of Indra is indeed the most powerful; therefore he says, "Thou art the right arm of Indra. "A thousand-edged, hundred-fold-sharp"—for that thunderbolt was indeed thousand-edged and hundred-fold-sharp, which he hurled at Vṛtra; he thus makes it so once again.

"Thou art Vāyu, of sharp brilliance. This indeed is the sharpest brilliance, namely this one who blows here; for he blows across these worlds transversely. "He sharpens him [the sacrificer]—a weapon against his enemies," he says; if he does not intend to practice sorcery, he says, "a weapon against such-and-such"; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he says, "a weapon against so-and-so. With that sharpened [weapon], he does not touch himself nor the earth, thinking, "Lest by this sharpened thunderbolt I should harm either myself or the earth. Therefore, he neither touches himself nor the earth.
The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Whenever the gods defeated the Asuras, the Asuras would rise up against them once again.
Those gods said:
"We are indeed conquering the Asuras, but then they rise up against us again. How, then, might we conquer them in a way that is irreversible?"
That Agni said, "They escape by fleeing toward the north"; and indeed, they used to escape by fleeing toward the north.
Then that Fire said:

"I will search from the north, and then you shall hem them in from here. Having hemmed them in, we will confine them within these worlds; and whatever beyond these four worlds there may be, they shall not be gathered back again from there."

That Agni went around to the north. Then these [worlds] hemmed them in from here; having hemmed them in, they pressed them down with these worlds. And because they did not come together again after that fourth world which exceeds these worlds, that is the reason why there is the *stambayajus*.
He who goes around on the north side is that very Agnīdh;

he is Agni by his very nature. The Adhvaryu thus hemms them in from this side; having hemmed them in, he presses them down with these worlds. And because they do not rise up again from what is beyond these four worlds, therefore even now the Asuras do not rise up. For with that same power with which the gods hemmed them in, with that very Brahman-power they hem them in now at the sacrifice.

Whoever acts as an enemy toward the sacrificer, and whoever hates him—him he thus lays low with these worlds. And whatever exceeds these worlds, all that he takes away from this very earth, for on her all these worlds are established. For what would he take away if he were to take away the intermediate space, saying, "I take away the intermediate space," or "I take away the sky"? Therefore, he takes away everything from this very earth alone.
Then he strikes after placing a blade of grass in between, thinking, "Lest I should injure the earth with this sharpened thunderbolt"; therefore, he strikes after placing a blade of grass in between.
He strikes.

"O Earth, place of sacrifice to the gods, may I not harm your root with the plant"—by saying this, he makes it as if he were taking it up from its very root; "may I not harm your roots among the plants"—this he says while lifting it up. "Go to the fold, to the cow-pen"—even as he is about to set it down, he thus makes it one that will not stray away; for that which is within the fold does not stray, therefore he says, "Go to the fold, to the cow-pen. "May the sky rain for you"—for wherever they injure or strike her while digging, water is the pacification; thus he pacifies it with water, he unites it with water, therefore he says, "May the sky rain for you. "Bind him, O God Savitṛ, on the furthest earth"—he thus addresses the divine Savitṛ, saying, "Bind him in blind darkness," when he says, "on the furthest earth. "With sixty fetters"—he says this for the sake of binding; "him who hates us and whom we hate, do not release him from there"—if he should not intend to practice sorcery; but if he should intend to practice sorcery, he should say, "Do not release so-and-so from there."

Then he strikes a second time with the formula: "May I strike Araru away from the earth, the place of sacrifice to the gods. For Araru was indeed the name of an Asura-Rakṣasa; him the gods struck off from this earth, and so does this [sacrificer] now strike him off from it. "Go to the pen, to the cow-stall! May the sky rain for thee! Bind him, O god Savitṛ, on the furthest earth with a hundred fetters—him who hates us and whom we hate—do not release him from there!"

The Āgnīdhra places it down with the formula, "O Araru, do not fly up to heaven! For when the gods were striking down Araru, the Asura-Rakṣasa, he sought to fly up to heaven; Agni placed him down with the words, "O Araru, do not fly up to heaven! and so he did not fly up to heaven. In the same way, the Adhvaryu now separates him from this world, and the Āgnīdhra from heaven; therefore, he does it thus.
Then he strikes the third [time]:

"May your drop not spill over to heaven. This drop of hers is indeed this sap of hers upon which living beings subsist; "may it not fall to heaven," he thereby says. "Go to the cow-pen, O Gomatī! he says.
He indeed carries it three times with a Yajus formula.

For these worlds are three; he thus lays it down by means of these very worlds. Indeed, these worlds are manifest (addhā), and the Yajus is manifest; therefore, he carries it three times with a Yajus formula.
The fourth [layer] is done in silence.

For whether there is anything beyond these worlds or not, by that very fact he strikes down his hateful rival. Indeed, that which is beyond these worlds—whether it exists or not—is indeterminate; and that which is done in silence is indeterminate. Therefore, the fourth layer is performed in silence.
The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the gods were, as it were, inferior; but the Asuras thought, "This world belongs to us alone!"
They said, "Come, let us divide this earth; having divided it, let us live upon it. They went forth, dividing it from west to east with ox-hides.
The gods heard of that:

"The Asuras are indeed dividing this earth; come, let us go to where the Asuras are dividing it. What shall we become if we do not share in it? Taking Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, as their leader, they went there.
They said, "Grant us a share in this earth; let there indeed be a portion for us here as well. The Asuras, as if feeling resentment, replied, "We shall give you only as much as this Viṣṇu lies upon."
Vishnu was indeed a dwarf;
the gods were not displeased with that, for they thought, "A great thing has come to us, since they have given us what is commensurate with our sacrifice."

Having laid Viṣṇu facing eastward, they enclosed him on all sides with the meters: "With the Gāyatrī meter I enclose thee," [saying this] from the south; "With the Triṣṭubh meter I enclose thee," [saying this] from the west; "With the Jagatī meter I enclose thee," [saying this] from the north.

Having enclosed it on all sides with meters and having placed Agni in front, they moved about worshipping and toiling with him; by means of him, they found this entire earth. Because they found this entire [earth] by means of him, therefore it is called the *vedi* (altar). Therefore they say, "As large as the *vedi* is, so large is the earth," for by means of this they found this entire [earth]. Thus indeed he who knows this appropriates this entire [earth] from his rivals and excludes his rivals from it.
Thus, this Viṣṇu became ill;
surrounded on all sides by the meters, Agni did not depart from his front, and so he sank down right there into the roots of the plants.

Those gods said, "Where indeed has Viṣṇu been? Where has the sacrifice been? They replied, "Agni, surrounded on all sides by the meters, has not departed from the front; search for him right here. Digging as it were, they sought him and found him at a depth of three finger-breadths. Therefore, the altar (vedi) should be three finger-breadths deep; and so indeed did Pañci make the altar of the Soma-sacrifice exactly three finger-breadths deep.
One should not do it in that way.

He was indeed searching for the roots of the plants; therefore, one should tell him, "You must dig up the very roots of the plants. And because they found Viṣṇu there, it is called the *vedi* (the sacrificial altar).

They enclosed it with the subsequent enclosure, saying, "Thou art subtle and thou art auspicious," on the south; having thus found this very earth, they made it subtle and auspicious. Saying, "Thou art pleasant and thou art easy to sit upon," on the west; having thus found this very earth, they made it pleasant and easy to sit upon. Saying, "Thou art full of vigor and thou art full of milk," on the north; having thus found this very earth, they made it full of sap and fit for subsistence.

He indeed performs the first tracing around three times and the subsequent one three times; that makes six times. There are six seasons in the year, and the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. Thus, as great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, so much does he encompass by this.

With six *vyāhṛtis* he first encloses the enclosure, and with six [more] he encloses the latter; that makes twelve times. There are indeed twelve months in a year, and the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—just so much does he thus enclose.
"It should be one fathom long at the back," they say;

for man is indeed this much in size, and the three-cubit [length] is commensurate with man. The [front part] facing east is threefold, for the sacrifice is threefold; there is no fixed measure here other than whatever extent one may personally deem appropriate in one's mind—that much one should make it.
He raises the shoulder-blades on both sides of the fire.
The altar is indeed a woman and the fire is a man; for a woman lies embracing a man, and thus a productive union is brought about. Therefore, he raises the shoulder-blades on both sides of the fire.
It should indeed be wider at the back;

it is contracted in the middle and wide again in front, for they praise a woman in this very way: "broad-hipped, with well-rounded shoulders, and slender-waisted. Thus he makes it acceptable to the gods.

It should indeed slope toward the east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or it may slope toward the north, for the north is the direction of men. He throws up loose soil from the south, for that is the direction of the ancestors. If it were to slope toward the south, the sacrificer would quickly go to yonder world; thus, however, the sacrificer lives long. Therefore, he throws up loose soil from the south. He should make it full of loose soil; for loose soil is cattle, and he thereby makes it rich in cattle.
He wipes that [image].

The gods, indeed, when they were about to engage in battle, said: "Come now, let us place that immortal portion of this earth which is the sacrificial ground for the gods upon the moon; if the Asuras should conquer us here, then from there, praising and toiling, we may overcome them again. That immortal portion of this earth which was the sacrificial ground for the gods, they placed upon the moon; that is this black spot on the moon. Therefore they say, "In the moon is the sacrificial ground of this earth. And indeed, one's sacrifice becomes offered even on this [spot] of his; therefore he wipes it away.
He wipes it.

"Before the creeping of the cruel one, O Virapśin"—the "cruel" is indeed battle, for in battle the cruel is done; a man lies slain, a horse lies slain, for they deposited this [sacrificial ground] before the battles. Therefore he says, "Before the creeping of the cruel one, O Virapśin. "Having taken up the earth, the giver of life"—for what life there was of this earth, they took up and deposited in the moon. Therefore he says, "Having taken up the earth, the giver of life. "Which they placed in the moon with funeral offerings (svadhā)"—this he means by saying, "which they deposited in the moon through sacred power (brahman). "The wise, pointing her out, sacrifice"—by this very means they sacrifice, pointing her out. And indeed, for him who knows this, his sacrifice is performed even on that very sacrificial ground (devayajana).

Then he says, "Set down the sprinkling waters. The wooden sword (sphya) is indeed a thunderbolt, and the Brahmin protected this sacrifice from of old; and the waters are a thunderbolt—thus he sets them down for the sake of protection by means of that thunderbolt. While the sprinkling waters are being held directly above [the altar], he then lifts up the wooden sword. For if he were to set down the sprinkling waters while the wooden sword is still lying on the ground, the two thunderbolts would collide; thus they do not collide. Therefore, while the sprinkling waters are being held directly above, he then lifts up the wooden sword.

Then he utters this speech: "Set down the sprinkling waters; place the fuel and the sacrificial grass; cleanse the offering-spoons; gird the wife; bring the clarified butter!"—this is indeed the formal summons. If he should so desire, he may say this; but if he should not desire it, he need not pay attention to it, for he himself knows that "this work is to be performed from here."

Then he strikes the wooden sword (sphya) towards the north, saying, "I strike you, [Name], with the thunderbolt," if he should practice sorcery; for the wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt, and he surely lays him low with it.
Then he washes his hands;
for whatever of this [earth] was cruel, that he has taken away from her on this day; therefore he washes his hands.
Those who first sacrificed used to perform their sacrifices with a sense of touch (or hesitation).

They became worse off, while those who did not sacrifice became better off. Then lack of faith (Aśraddhā) entered among men, thinking: "Those who sacrifice become worse off, while those who do not sacrifice become better off. Consequently, the sacrificial oblation (havis) no longer went from here to the gods, for the gods subsist upon what is offered from here.

Those gods said to Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa: "Lack of faith indeed possesses men; teach them the sacrifice. He went to them and asked, "Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa, why do you not sacrifice? They replied, "With what desire should we sacrifice? Those who sacrifice become worse off, while those who do not sacrifice become better off."
He said:

"Bṛhaspati Āṅgirasa said: 'Whatever we have heard was approved by the gods, that indeed becomes this sacrifice—namely, when the oblations have been prepared and the altar arranged, you have touched them; therefore, you have become worse off. Sacrifice without touching, and thus you will become better.'—'How far [should one avoid touching]?'—'Until the spreading of the sacrificial grass (barhis). For indeed, by means of the sacrificial grass, this [altar] is appeased. If anything should happen before the spreading of the sacrificial grass, he should cast it away while spreading the grass itself. And when they spread the sacrificial grass, they even step upon it with their feet. He who, knowing this, sacrifices without touching, truly becomes better. Therefore, one should sacrifice without touching."

He indeed wipes the offering-spoons. Now, as for why he wipes the spoons: just as is the way of the gods, so too is the way of men; therefore, whenever the serving of food has been prepared for men, [they wipe the vessels].

Then he cleanses the vessels; having cleansed them with those [vessels], he serves the food. Indeed, this sacrifice of the gods consists of cooked oblations and a prepared altar; of these, the ladles are their very vessels.

When he wipes it, he indeed cleanses it; [he does so] thinking, "I shall proceed with them once they are cleansed. He cleanses it for the gods in a twofold manner, but for men in a single way: for the gods with both water and the sacred word (brahman), for the waters are the *kuśa* grass and the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is the sacred word; but for men in a single way, namely with water alone. Thus, in this way, it becomes distinct.
Then he takes up the *sruva* ladle;
he heats it, saying either: "The Rakṣas is burnt away; the enemies are burnt away," or "The Rakṣas is scorched; the enemies are scorched."

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases; therefore, right from the beginning of the sacrifice, he thus drives away the destructive spirits and Rakṣases.

He cleanses [the spoon] from the inside with its tips, saying, "Unsharpened art thou, the destroyer of rivals. He says this so that he may, without ceasing, destroy the rivals of the sacrificer; "I cleanse thee, the vigorous, for the sake of vigor," he says, which means, "I cleanse thee, the worthy of sacrifice, for the sake of the sacrifice. With this same formula he cleanses all the offering-spoons, saying, "Thee, the vigorous," and the *prāśitraharaṇa* (the vessel for the portion of the eater) silently.
"He cleanses it with the tips [of the grass] on the inside and with the roots on the outside.

This is as it were the *prāṇa* (out-breath) and as it were the *udāna* (up-breath); he thus bestows both the *prāṇa* and the *udāna*. Therefore, these hairs are as it were [the tips], and these are as it were [the roots].
He indeed hands it over after wiping it again and again and heating it again and again;
just as one might wash a garment by first rubbing it and then rinsing it thoroughly without further rubbing at the end, so too does he hand it over after heating it again and again.
He indeed cleanses the *sruva* ladle first, and then the other *sruca* spoons.

The *sruc* is female and the *sruva* is male; therefore, even when many women go along together, he who among them is like a young man—the male—goes there first, while the others follow behind him. That is why he cleanses the *sruva* first, and then the other *sruca* spoons.
He should indeed sweep it in such a way that he does not sprinkle over the fire;

for just as one would sprinkle with the rinsing of the vessel him to whom one is about to bring food, so it would be in this case. Therefore, he should sweep it in such a way that he does not sprinkle over the fire, having stepped out somewhat towards the east.
Now, some indeed throw the wiping-cords of the ladles into the fire, saying, "These were the Vedas;

with these they wiped the ladles clean. "This is something of the sacrifice; let us not cast it away"—thinking thus, they would bring some food and have him drink the rinsing-water of the vessels. But one should rather throw them away. Thus it is.
Then he girds the wife. The wife, indeed, is the hind part of the sacrifice; thinking, "May my sacrifice proceed eastward," he thus yokes her, so that she, being yoked, may sit beside his sacrifice.
He girds her with a girdle; for they yoke what is fit to be yoked with a girdle.

Now there is indeed something impure in the wife that is below the navel; and she is about to look at this clarified butter, so he interposes this girdle between them. Then she looks at the clarified butter with the pure upper part [of her body]. Therefore he girds the wife.
He girds her with a cloth.

The cloth, indeed, belongs to the plants, while the rope belongs to Varuṇa; thus he interposes the plants between her and it. In this way, that Varuṇic rope does not injure her. Therefore, he girds her with a cloth.
He girds himself with the words, "The girdle of Aditi.

Aditi is indeed this earth; she is the wife of the gods, and she becomes the wife of this [sacrificer]. Thus he makes for her this very girdle, not a rope; for the girdle (rāsnā) is indeed gold; it is that very thing he makes for her.
He indeed should not make a knot; for a knot belongs to Varuṇa, and Varuṇa would seize his wife if he were to make a knot. Therefore, he does not make a knot.

He pushes it upwards only; [with the words] "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seat. For she (the wife) does not sit behind, facing eastward, to attend upon the sacrifice of the gods. This earth indeed is Aditi, and she is the wife of the gods; she sits behind, facing eastward, to attend upon the sacrifice of the gods. If he were now to mount her, that wife would quickly go to yonder world. Thus, however, the wife lives long. He thereby makes amends to her; thus this earth does not harm her. Therefore, let her sit as if from the south.
Then he gazes at the clarified butter.
The wife is indeed female, and the clarified butter is seed; thus a productive union is brought about. Therefore, he gazes at the clarified butter.

He looks at it [with the formula]: "With unerring eye I gaze upon thee. By this he means to say, "With uninjured eye I gaze upon thee. "Thou art the tongue of Agni"—for when they offer into the fire, then tongues as it were rise up from the fire; therefore he says, "Thou art the tongue of Agni. "A good bringer to the gods"—by this he means to say, "One who is propitious to the gods. "Be for me for every station, for every sacrificial formula"—by this he means to say, "Be for me for the entire sacrifice."
Then, taking the clarified butter, he recites [the formula] facing eastward.

Then he places it over the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "May my entire sacrifice be cooked on the Āhavanīya," for they cook the oblations on the Āhavanīya. Now, as to why he first places it there [on the Gārhapatya]: it is because he intends to give space for the wife; for it would not be fitting if he were to pour [the butter] back prematurely while intending to give space for the wife. And if he were not to give space for the wife, he would exclude the wife from the sacrifice. Thus, he does not exclude the wife from the sacrifice. Therefore, having melted it together, he brings it forward to the east, having given space for the wife. But for one who has no wife, he places it over the Āhavanīya at the very beginning. He takes it from there and sets it down within the altar (antarvedi).

Regarding this they say: "One should not place [the butter] within the altar (antarvedi), for it is from here that they perform the joint sacrifice to the wives of the gods; he would thus make the wives of the gods like barren cows, and his wife would become one who has a husband other than him. To this Yājñavalkya said: "Let it be for the wife as prescribed. Who would care whether the wife has a husband other than him, or whether the altar is the sacrifice and the clarified butter is the sacrifice—[thinking], 'From the sacrifice, I shall fashion the sacrifice'? Therefore, one should place it only within the altar."
There are two strainers for the sprinkling water;
he takes them from there and purifies the clarified butter with them. Indeed, this is the single purpose of the purification: he thereby makes it pure.
He purifies it with the formula:
"At the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify thee with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun. Its significance is the same as that of the *sāvanīya* offering.
Then, with two strainers smeared with clarified butter, he purifies the sprinkling water with the formula:
"At the impulse of Savitṛ, I purify you... [and so on]. Now, as to why he purifies the sprinkling water with two strainers smeared with clarified butter:

he thereby places milk into the waters. This milk is placed within the waters; for when it rains here, then plants are born; having eaten the plants and drunk the waters, this essence (rasa) comes into being. Therefore, it is for the sake of the completeness of the essence.

Then he gazes at the clarified butter. Regarding this, some have the sacrificer gaze at it; but Yājñavalkya said: "How is it that the Adhvaryus do not themselves perform [the rites], and how is it that they do not themselves recite [the formulas], when so many blessings are being performed? How is it that faith remains with them right here? Whatever blessing the officiating priests invoke in the sacrifice belongs to the sacrificer alone; therefore, the Adhvaryu himself should gaze at it.
He reflects:

"The eye is indeed truth, for the eye is truth. Therefore, if two people were to come disputing, one saying 'I saw it' and the other 'I heard it,' we would believe the one who says 'I saw it. Thus, by means of truth itself, he makes this successful."
He gazes at it [with the words]:

"Thou art brilliance; thou art seed; thou art immortality. This mantra is indeed reality, for this is brilliance, this is seed, and this is immortality; thus he causes this very thing to prosper through reality itself.
The sacrifice is indeed man;
therefore the sacrifice is man, because man extends it. While it is being extended, it is ordained to be as large as a man; therefore the sacrifice is man.
Of this [sacrifice], this [right hand] is the *juhū* ladle;
this [left hand] is the *upabhṛt*; the self itself is the *dhruvā*. For from the self indeed all these limbs originate; therefore, from the *dhruvā* alone the entire sacrifice originates.
The breath itself is the dipping-spoon (sruva).
This very breath moves along all the limbs; therefore, the dipping-spoon moves along all the offering-spoons (sruc).

Of that [sacrifice], this very heaven is the *juhū* ladle; this intermediate space is the *upabhṛt*; and this earth is the *dhruvā*. Indeed, all these worlds originate from this very [earth]; therefore, the entire sacrifice originates from the *dhruvā* alone.
This very one who blows here is the sruva-spoon;
he blows along all these worlds, and therefore the sruva moves along after all the sruca-ladles.

This very sacrifice, as it is being performed, is performed for the gods, for the seasons, and for the meters. Whatever is the oblation (havis), that belongs to the gods; whatever is King Soma, and whatever is the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), that he takes by pointing it out, saying, "I take thee, acceptable to such-and-such one"—thus indeed is it for these.

Now, as for those portions of clarified butter (ājya) that are taken: they are taken for the sake of both the seasons and the meters; not specifying each one individually, he takes them merely in the form of clarified butter. He indeed takes four ladlings in the juhū-spoon and eight times in the upabhṛt-spoon.
When he takes [the butter] into the fourfold ladle, he takes it for the seasons;

for he takes it for the fore-offerings (prayāja), and the fore-offerings are indeed the seasons. He takes it without specifying [any particular season], merely in the form of clarified butter (ājya), to avoid repetition (ajāmitā). For he would commit a repetition if he were to take it saying, "For Spring thee! For Summer thee! Therefore, he takes it without specifying, merely in the form of clarified butter.

Now, when he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he takes it for the metres; for he takes it for the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s), and the after-offerings are indeed the metres. Taking it thus without specifying [the metre], he takes it in the form of clarified butter alone, to avoid repetition (*ajāmitā*). For he would commit a repetition if he were to take it saying, "For the Gāyatrī thee! For the Triṣṭubh thee! Therefore, he takes it without specifying, in the form of clarified butter alone.
Now, as for that which he takes four times into the *dhruvā* ladle:

he takes it for the sake of the entire sacrifice; and since he does not specify it for any particular purpose, he takes it merely in the form of clarified butter (*ājya*). For to whom indeed could he specify it, when he cuts off portions for all the deities? Therefore, he takes it without specification, merely in the form of clarified butter.
The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū*;

he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt*. Eating indeed follows the *juhū*; eating follows the *upabhṛt*. The *juhū* eats; the *upabhṛt* eats. He takes four portions in the *juhū* and eight times in the *upabhṛt*.

In that he takes four times in the *juhū* ladle, he thereby makes the eater more limited and smaller; and in that he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he thereby makes the one to be eaten more unlimited and greater—for that is successful where the eater is smaller and the one to be eaten is greater.
When taking [the butter] with the four-spoon ladle, he takes more clarified butter;
when taking it eight times with the upabhṛt ladle, he takes less clarified butter.
When he draws [the oblation] into the four-pronged ladle, it is as follows.

He takes more clarified butter; thus, making the eater (the sacrificer) more limited and weaker, he bestows vigor and strength upon him. Now, when he takes eight times in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he takes less clarified butter; thus, making the eater (the enemy) more unlimited and stronger, he renders him devoid of vigor and weak. Therefore, even after a king has settled among a foreign people, he overcomes them from a single dwelling, and they submit to him however he desires. It is by this very power that he takes more clarified butter in the *juhū* ladle: whatever he takes in the *juhū*, he offers with the *juhū*; whatever he takes in the *upabhṛt*, he offers with the *juhū*.
Regarding this, they say:

"Why, then, should one take [the butter] in the *upabhṛt* ladle, since one does not offer with the *upabhṛt*? He said: "If he were to offer with the *upabhṛt*, these creatures would indeed be separate; there would be neither an eater nor food. But because he offers after having brought it together from that [ladle], therefore these subjects remain under the control of the Kṣatriya, and the cattle attend upon the Vaiśya. And because he offers after having brought it together from that [ladle], therefore, whenever the Kṣatriya desires, he says, 'O Vaiśya, bring me that which is deposited beyond you! He overcomes him, and he follows him exactly as he desires—by this very power."

These very Ājya-offerings are drawn from the metres. When he draws four times into the Juhū-ladle, he draws for the Gāyatrī; and when he draws eight times into the Upabhṛt-ladle, he draws for the Triṣṭubh and Jagatī; and when he draws four times into the Dhruvā-ladle, he draws for the Anuṣṭubh. The Anuṣṭubh is indeed speech, and from speech all this universe originates; therefore, the entire sacrifice originates from the Dhruvā. This earth is indeed the Anuṣṭubh, and from her all this universe originates; therefore, the entire sacrifice originates from the Dhruvā.

He takes it up with the words, "Thou art the abode, dear to the gods. For clarified butter (ājya) is indeed the most beloved abode of the gods; therefore he says, "Thou art the abode, dear to the gods. With the words, "Thou art the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods," he speaks thus because clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra); therefore he says, "Thou art the inviolable place of sacrifice for the gods."

With this *yajus*, he takes [the butter] once in the *juhū* ladle, and three times silently; with this same *yajus*, he takes it once in the *upabhṛt* ladle, and seven times silently; with this same *yajus*, he takes it once in the *dhruvā* ladle, and three times silently. Regarding this, they say: "One should take it three times each with the *yajus*, for the sacrifice is threefold. But let him rather take it once each time; for in this way, what is taken three times in total is accomplished here.
The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters;
he first sprinkles the fuel itself with the formula, "Thou art black, dwelling in the dug-out place; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Agni. By this, he makes it pure for Agni.
Then he sprinkles the altar:
"Thou art the altar; I sprinkle thee, acceptable for the sacrificial grass (barhis). By this, he makes it pure for the sacrificial grass.
Then he hands him the sacrificial grass (barhis);

he places it down with its knot toward the east and sprinkles it, saying, "Thou art the sacrificial grass; I sprinkle thee, acceptable to the offering-spoons. By this, he makes it pure for the offering-spoons.

Then, with those sprinkling waters which remain, he pours them over the roots of the plants, saying, "Thou art Aditi’s moistening. For this earth is indeed Aditi; thus he moistens the roots of these very plants. Therefore, these plants have moist roots; hence, even though their tops become dry, their roots remain moist.

Then, having loosened the knot, he takes up the prastara-bunch from the front with the formula, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s tuft. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; this very crest-lock is his tuft; it is this that he thereby places in him. He takes it from the front, for this tuft is in the front; therefore he takes it from the front.

Then he loosens the girdle, thinking, "A woman will surely give birth for him in an orderly manner"; therefore he loosens the girdle. He places it on the right hip; this is indeed her *nīvi* (the tucked-in end of the garment), for this *nīvi* is as if on the right side; therefore he places it on the right hip. He covers it again, for this *nīvi* is indeed covered; therefore he covers it again.
