Then he strews the sacrificial grass (barhis). This prastara-bunch is indeed the top-knot; and those hairs of his which are directed downwards are this other sacrificial grass—this he thus bestows upon him. That is why he strews the sacrificial grass.
The altar is indeed a woman;

around her sit here both the gods and those Brahmins who have heard the sacred lore and are learned in the Vedas. While they are thus seated around her, he makes her unclothed, for the sake of her very state of being unclothed; therefore, he strews the sacrificial grass (barhis).

As great as the altar is, so great is the earth; the sacrificial grass (barhis) is the plants. Thus he places the plants upon this very earth, and these plants are established upon this earth; therefore he strews the sacrificial grass.

"One should indeed spread it thickly," they say; "for wherever its plants are thickest, that is what is most fit for its livelihood. Therefore one should spread it thickly. Now, he spreads it in three layers upon the gatherer himself, for the sacrifice is threefold; moreover, he may also spread it by pulling it out, for the verse has been recited: "They spread the sacrificial grass in rows. He spreads it with the roots downward, for these plants are established in this earth with their roots downward; therefore he spreads it with the roots downward.
He spreads [the grass] with the words:
"I spread thee, soft as wool, a good seat for the gods. By saying "soft as wool," he means "excellent for the gods"; by saying "a good seat for the gods," he means "a comfortable seat for the gods."
Then he prepares the fire-altar.

The Āhavanīya is indeed the head of the sacrifice, for the head is the front part; he thus prepares that front part of the sacrifice. Holding the prastara-bunch directly above it, he prepares it; for this prastara is the top-knot (stūpa), and he thereby restores that very knot to him. Therefore, he prepares it while holding the prastara directly above.

Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks (paridhis). As to why he lays down the enclosing-sticks: when the gods first chose Agni for the office of Hotṛ, he said, "I am indeed not able to do this—be your Hotṛ and carry your oblations—since you have chosen three others before me; they have fled from here, so provide them for me, and then I shall indeed be able to do this—be your Hotṛ and carry your oblations. They said, "So be it," and they provided these for him; these are the enclosing-sticks.

He said: "The thunderbolt, indeed, has hemmed them in with the *vaṣaṭ*-call. I am afraid of the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call; lest the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, should hem me in, surround me with these very [verses], so that the thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṣ*-call, shall not hem me in. "So be it," they said, and they surrounded him with these. The thunderbolt, the *vaṣaṭ*-call, did not hem him in. In that he surrounds [the fire] with these, he truly girds armor for Agni.
They indeed said this:
"If you employ us in this sacrifice, then let there also be a share for us in the sacrifice."

"So be it," said the gods. "Whatever shall fall outside the enclosing-sticks (paridhi), that will be offered into you; and whatever they shall offer over and above [the fire], that shall belong to you. Thus, when they offer into the fire, they satisfy them; and when they offer over and above [the fire], they satisfy them; and when it falls outside the enclosing-sticks, that is offered into these [gods]. Therefore, one should not think of what has fallen as lost, for these [gods] have entered this earth. Whatever here falls, all that finds its support in her alone.

He touches what has been spilled, saying: "To the Lord of the Earth, Svāhā! To the Lord of the World, Svāhā! To the Lord of Beings, Svāhā! These indeed are the names of those fires: the Lord of the Earth, the Lord of the World, and the Lord of Beings. Thus, as if it were offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, so does this become for him in these fires.

Now, some indeed lay these enclosing-sticks (paridhi) around as parts of the fuel-wood (idhma). But one should not do so; for those which he lays around as parts of the fuel-wood become unsuitable for him, since the fuel-wood is prepared solely for the purpose of being added to the fire. However, they become suitable for him who brings other sticks specifically for them, [thinking] "these are the enclosing-sticks. Therefore, one should bring others.
They should indeed be made of *palāśa* wood;
for the *palāśa* is the Brahman, and Agni is the Brahman, since the fires are the Brahman—therefore they should be made of *palāśa* wood.

If one should not find Palāśa wood, then there may be Vikaṅkata; if one should not find Vikaṅkata, then there may be Kārṣmarya; if one should not find Kārṣmarya, then there may be Bilva, or Khadira, or Udumbara. For these trees are sacrificial; therefore, they are made from these trees.
Or they should be moist;
for this is their life, by this they possess brilliance, and by this they possess vigor; therefore, they should be moist.
He first lays on the middle enclosing-stick with the formula:
"May the Gandharva Viśvāvasu lay thee around for the safety of all; thou art the enclosure of the sacrificer; Agni is praised as the object of praise."
Then he lays down the southern enclosing-stick with the formula:
"Thou art the right arm of Indra; for the safety of all, thou art the enclosure of the sacrificer; thou art Agni, the praised Iḍ."
Then he lays down the northern enclosing-stick with the formula:

"May Mitra and Varuna enclose thee from the north with a firm law for the safety of all; thou art the enclosure of the sacrificer; Agni is the praised Iḍ. For these are indeed fires; therefore he says, "Agni is the praised Iḍ."
Then he places the fuel-stick on the fire. He first touches the middle enclosing-stick; by that he first kindles them. Then he places it on the fire; by that he directly kindles the fire itself.
He places the fuel on the fire with this Gāyatrī verse:

"O Sage, we kindle thee, the enjoyer of the oblation, the radiant, the great one, O Agni, at the sacrifice. By means of this Gāyatrī, he thus kindles the Gāyatrī itself; and the Gāyatrī, being kindled, kindles the other meters. The meters, being kindled, carry the sacrifice to the gods.

Now, as for the second fuel-stick which he places upon the fire: by it he kindles the spring itself; that spring, being kindled, kindles the other seasons. The seasons, being kindled, cause offspring to be born and ripen the plants. He places it on with the words, "Thou art fuel," for the spring is indeed kindled.
Then, having placed the fuel on the fire, he mutters:

"May Sūrya protect thee from the east against any malevolent spell. This is for protection; for the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are on all sides, and thus he makes Sūrya himself the protector in the east so that no destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) or demons (*rakṣas*) may descend upon him from the front. For Sūrya is the repeller of destructive spirits and demons.
Now, as for that third fuel-stick which he places upon the fire during the after-offerings (*anuyāja*), by it he kindles the Brāhmaṇa; that Brāhmaṇa, being kindled, carries the sacrifice to the gods.

Then he approaches the strewn altar. Taking two blades of grass, he lays them down crosswise with the formula, "Ye are the two arms of Savitṛ. For this *stūpa* (the bunch of grass) is indeed the *prastara*; thus he places these two as its eyebrows, which is why these two eyebrows are placed crosswise. The *prastara* is the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is the common people (*viś*). He places them crosswise for the separation of the nobility and the common people; therefore he lays them down crosswise, and for that very reason they are called *vidhṛti*s (separators).
He spreads that sacrificial grass with the formula:

"I spread thee, soft as wool, a good seat for the gods. By saying "soft as wool," he means "good for the gods"; by saying "a good seat for the gods," he means "a comfortable resting place for the gods."
He places it down with the formula:

"May the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas sit upon thee! For these indeed are the three classes of gods—the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; thus he says, "May they sit upon thee. While it is being placed down, it remains held by his left hand.

Then he takes hold of the *juhū* ladle from the south with his right hand, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā-rakṣāṃsi*) enter here before [the sacrifice is complete]"; for the Brāhmaṇa is the repeller of the *rakṣases*. Therefore, it remains held down by his left hand.

Then he takes up the *juhū* ladle with the formula: "Thou art dripping with ghee (*ghṛtācī*), O *juhū* by name. For she is indeed dripping with ghee, and she is the *juhū* by name; [he says] "May she sit here on this dear seat with her dear abode. He takes up the *upabhṛt* with: "Thou art dripping with ghee, O *upabhṛt* by name. For she is indeed dripping with ghee, and she is the *upabhṛt* by name; [he says] "May she sit here on this dear seat with her dear abode. He takes up the *dhruvā* with: "Thou art dripping with ghee, O *dhruvā* by name. For she is indeed dripping with ghee, and she is the *dhruvā* by name; [he says] "May she sit here on this dear seat with her dear abode. With the words "May she sit here on this dear seat with her dear abode," he refers to whatever other sacrificial food (*havis*) there may be.
He places the *juhū* spoon above, and the other spoons below.

The *juhū* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other spoons are the common people (*viś*). He thus makes the nobility superior to the common people; therefore, the subjects wait upon the nobleman seated above while they themselves remain below. That is why he places the *juhū* above and the other spoons below.

He touches it, saying, "They have sat down firmly," for they have indeed sat down firmly; "in the womb of Truth," for the sacrifice is the womb of Truth, since they have sat down in the sacrifice. "O Viṣṇu, protect them! Protect the sacrifice! Protect the lord of the sacrifice!"—by this he says to the sacrificer, "Protect me, the leader of the sacrifice! and thus he does not exclude himself from the sacrifice. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; therefore, he entrusts all this to the sacrifice itself for its protection. That is why he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect them!"
The Adhvaryu indeed kindles this fire with the fuel;
therefore it is called *idhma*. The Hotṛ kindles it with the *sāmidhenī* verses; therefore they are called *sāmidhenīs*.
He said: "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled," for it is indeed for Agni as he is being kindled that he recites this.

Regarding this, some say: "O Hotṛ, recite for Agni as he is being kindled. But one should not speak thus; for previously he is not yet the Hotṛ—it is only when they choose him that he becomes the Hotṛ. Therefore, one should simply say: "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled."

He recites verses addressed to Agni; he thus kindles him by means of his own deity. He recites Gāyatrī verses; the Gāyatrī is indeed the metre of Agni; he thus kindles him by means of his own metre. The Gāyatrī is vigor, the Gāyatrī is the Brahman; he thus kindles him by means of vigor.
He recites eleven verses.
The Triṣṭubh indeed consists of eleven syllables; the Gāyatrī is the Brahman and the Triṣṭubh is the Kṣatra. By means of both these powers, he thus kindles him. Therefore, he recites eleven verses.
He indeed recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times;
for sacrifices have a threefold beginning and a threefold conclusion. Therefore, he recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times.

These amount to fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses. The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed fifteenfold; the thunderbolt is vigor. He thus brings these *sāmidhenīs* to completion as vigor. Therefore, while these are being recited, he should press down with his two thumbs upon whomsoever he hates, saying, "I press down this one, so-and-so! Thus, by means of this thunderbolt, he presses him down.
Or there are fifteen nights in a half-month;
for the year comes about by way of half-months, and thus he obtains those nights.
There are three hundred and sixty syllables in fifteen Gāyatrīs; and there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year. Thus he obtains the days, and thereby he obtains the year itself.
There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

One should recite the invitatory verse for the sacrifice in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). He sacrifices to that deity for whom he prepares the oblation. There are twelve months in a year and five seasons; this very [year] is Prajāpati as the seventeenfold [sacrifice]. Prajāpati is indeed everything; thus, by means of everything, he successfully fulfills without fail whatever desire for which he prepares the sacrifice. He sacrifices to the deity in a low voice; what is in a low voice is indeed undefined, and the undefined is everything. Thus, by means of everything, he successfully fulfills without fail whatever desire for which he prepares the sacrifice. This is the procedure for the sacrifice.

"One should recite twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses even at the New and Full Moon sacrifices," they say. "There are twelve months in a year, five seasons, and three worlds—that makes twenty. This one who shines yonder is the twenty-first; he is the goal and the foundation. Thus, he goes to that goal and finds that foundation. Therefore, one should recite twenty-one."

One should recite these very [verses] for one who has already attained his goal, for one who thinks, "May I become neither better nor worse. For indeed, whatever kind of person they recite them for, he becomes exactly that—either better or worse—for him to whom they recite these while knowing this. This is merely a deliberation; however, these [verses] are not actually recited.
One should recite the first verse three times and the last verse three times without taking breath;

for these worlds are three, and thus he extends these very worlds and sustains these worlds. There are three vital breaths in a person; he thereby establishes them in him as continuous and uninterrupted. This is the manner of recitation.

As long as his speech lasts, he should desire to speak in that very same way; one should explain this to him: "If, while desiring to speak, he speaks with equal breath and does not breathe out, his action would be interrupted; that is the censure."
If he should not desire this, he may recite each verse individually without taking breath;

by means of each single verse, he thus connects these worlds, and by means of each single verse, he gratifies these worlds. Now, as for the fact that he bestows breath: the Gāyatrī is indeed breath. In that he recites the entire Gāyatrī, he thereby bestows the entire breath. Therefore, he should recite each verse individually without taking breath.

He recites them continuously and without interruption. It is thus that he makes the days and nights of the year continuous; these very days and nights of the year revolve continuously and without interruption. Furthermore, he does not provide a standing place for his hateful rival; for were he to recite them without continuity, he would indeed provide a standing place. Therefore, he recites them continuously and without interruption.
He recites after uttering the *hiṃ* sound.

For they say, "There is no sacrifice without the *sāman*," and indeed, no *sāman* is sung without the *hiṃ* sound. When he utters *hiṃ*, the form of the *hiṃ*-sound is thereby produced; by means of the *praṇava* alone he approaches the form of the *sāman*. With this—"Oṃ oṃ oṃ"—his entire sacrifice becomes possessed of the *sāman*.

And as to why he utters the *hiṃ* sound: the *hiṃ* is indeed breath; for the *hiṃ* is truly breath. Therefore, one cannot utter the *hiṃ* while holding his nostrils closed. Or rather, he recites the verse with speech; for speech and breath are a couple. Thus, this couple is produced at the beginning of the *sāmidhenī* verses; therefore, he recites after having uttered the *hiṃ*.
He indeed utters the *hiṃ* sound in a low voice; for if he were to utter the *hiṃ* sound aloud, he would perform only one of the two [aspects]. Therefore, he utters the *hiṃ* sound in a low voice.
He recites both "coming" (eti) and "going forth" (preti).
Thus he yokes the Gāyatrī both hitherward and thitherward; thitherward it carries the sacrifice to the gods, and hitherward it protects men. Therefore, he recites both "coming" and "going forth."
And as to why he recites both "eti" (he comes) and "preti" (he goes):
"preti" is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa), and "eti" is the up-breath (udāna); it is these two, the out-breath and the up-breath, that he thereby bestows. Therefore, he recites both "eti" and "preti."
And as to why he recites both "forth" (pra) and "hither" (ā):

seed is indeed cast forth (pra), and it comes hither (ā) when it is born; cattle spread out (pra) and come together (ā) again; indeed, all this world moves both hither and forth. Therefore, he recites both "hither" and "forth."
He recites:
"Forward, O strengths, toward heaven..."—that is "pra" (forward). Then, "O Agni, come hither for the feast..."—that is "ā" (hither). Thus it becomes both "pra" and "ā".
Regarding this, some say:
"Both of these indeed become 'pra'. Thus, "pra vo vājā abhidyavaḥ" is like something beyond comprehension; "pra agna āyāhi vītaye" is likewise "pra. Therefore, it is "pra."

He recites: "Forward, O strengths (vāja), toward heaven... This [verse] begins with "forward" (pra). Now, "strengths" (vāja) is indeed food; thus, food is what is here spoken of. "Toward heaven" (abhidyava): the half-months are indeed "toward heaven"; thus, the half-months are what is here spoken of. "Possessing oblations" (haviṣmantaḥ): cattle are indeed "possessing oblations"; thus, cattle are what is here spoken of.

"O Ghṛtācī!"—Videgha Māthava was indeed carrying Agni Vaiśvānara in his mouth. Gotama Rāhūgaṇa was his seer-priest (purohita). When he was addressed, he would not respond, thinking, "Lest Agni Vaiśvānara should fall out from my mouth."
He resolved to invoke him with Ṛg-verses: "O Sage, we kindle you, the enjoyer of the oblation, the radiant and great Agni, at this sacrifice, O Videgha."
He did not respond:
"O Agni, your pure, bright, and shining flames rise up; your lights and rays—[O Videgha!]"
He did not respond at all; rather, he uttered only these words:

"We choose you, O one whose back is dripping with ghee. Thereupon, Agni Vaiśvānara blazed up from his mouth at the mere mention of "ghee. He was unable to hold him back, and he issued forth from his mouth and fell upon this earth. His footprints became footprints [of the gods].
At that time, Videgha Māthava was dwelling on the Sarasvatī.

From that very place, he proceeded eastward, burning along this earth; and Gotama Rāhūgaṇa and Videgha Māthava followed after him as he burned. He burnt all these rivers; [the river] which flows out from the northern mountain is called Sadānīrā—he did not burn across that one. Formerly, Brahmins did not cross it, thinking, "It has not been burnt across by Agni Vaiśvānara."
Therefore, even now, many Brahmins in the eastern regions consider that place to be more like a wilderness, as if it were not yet fully cultivated or tasted by the fire Vaiśvānara.

Now, however, at this time, the Brāhmaṇas have indeed become more like cultivated fields; for they have now gratified [the gods] with sacrifices even during the latest part of the summer. Consequently, it causes a slight irritation, for they have not been completely burnt away by the Vaiśvānara fire.

Videgha Māthava said: "Where shall I be in relation to you? He replied: "To the east of this very place shall be your realm. Even today, this remains the boundary of the Kosalas and Videhas, for they are indeed the Māthavas.
Then Gautama Rāhūgaṇa said: "Why did you not answer me when I addressed you? He replied: "Agni Vaiśvānara was in my mouth; he would have fallen out from my mouth, therefore I did not answer you."
"How did that happen? [he asked.

"At the very moment you uttered the words, 'We shall churn the butter-stream,' Agni Vaiśvānara blazed forth from my mouth as the fame of the clarified butter; I was unable to sustain him, and he fell away from my mouth."
In that he [recites] what contains "ghee" among the *sāmidhenī* verses, he thereby kindles him with the very *sāmidhenī*; he thus bestows vigor upon him.
"Then [he says], 'She goes to the gods, seeking favor, O Ghr̥tācī.

The sacrificer is indeed 'one seeking favor,' for he desires to win over the gods; he indeed wishes to reach the gods. Therefore he says, 'She goes to the gods, seeking favor. This verse, though addressed to Agni, is undefined; for everything that is undefined is everything, and thus he proceeds with everything."
"O Agni, come for the feast!"—thus it is said. "For the feast," he says; for these worlds were, as it were, close together at first. Having touched them, indeed, the sky was [separated] from them.

Those gods desired: "How indeed might these worlds become more distant from one another? How might this [universe] become more spacious? They separated them by means of these very three syllables: *vī-taya* (for expansion). Thus these worlds became far apart (*vi-ṭūram*). Consequently, it became more spacious for the gods. Indeed, it becomes more spacious for him who, knowing thus, recites this [verse] with the words *vī-taya*.

"Being praised, for the giver of the oblation"—the giver of the oblation is indeed the sacrificer; thus he says, "being praised, for the sacrificer. "Sit down as the Hotṛ on the sacrificial grass"—Agni is indeed the Hotṛ and this world is the sacrificial grass; he thus places Agni in this very world. This Agni is established in this world. This [verse] is recited in reference to this very world; he who knows this and for whom they recite this [verse] wins this very world.

"With fuel-sticks, O Aṅgiras, thee"—for with fuel-sticks the Aṅgirases kindled him; "O Aṅgiras"—for Agni is indeed Aṅgiras; "with ghee we make thee grow"—this is a *sāmidhenī* verse; with it he truly kindles him completely and bestows vigor upon him.

"Bṛhacchocā yaviṣṭhya" (O thou who shinest brightly, youngest one). For he indeed shines brightly when kindled; and "yaviṣṭhya" means "the youngest," for Agni is the youngest; therefore he says "yaviṣṭhya. This verse has been uttered in accordance with this very world—the intermediate space (antarikṣa) world alone. Therefore, although it belongs to Agni, it is undefined (anirukta), for this world is undefined; and he who knows this and for whom they recite this verse, wins that very world.

"He [has bestowed] upon us wide renown"—that which is wide is indeed that [heaven] wherein the gods are; "this renowned [place] wherein the gods are"—"O God, do thou cause us to dwell there," he thereby says. "Do thou cause us to dwell here"—that is to say, "do thou cause us to attain this."

"O Agni, great is thy heroic power"—this "great" (bṛhat) is indeed that [world] in which the gods dwell, and this "heroic power" (suvīrya) is that in which the gods dwell. This verse is recited in accordance with that very world; by means of this verse, he who knows thus and for whom they recite it conquers that very world, namely heaven.
Thus he says:

"Worthy of praise, worthy of homage"—for he is indeed worthy of praise and worthy of homage; "may he pierce through the darkness"—for once kindled, he is seen as if piercing through the darkness; "Agni is kindled, the bull"—for he is indeed kindled as a bull; "the bull Agni is kindled"—for he is indeed kindled.

"Like a horse, the bearer of the gods. For indeed, having become a horse, he carries the sacrifice to the gods. And as for "na" (not) in the verse, it is "om"; therefore he says, "like a horse, the bearer of the gods."
"Let those possessing oblations worship him," he says;
for men, possessing oblations, indeed worship him; therefore he says, "Let those possessing oblations worship him."
"We, the bulls, kindle you, the bull, O Bull"—for they indeed kindle him. "O Agni, shining mightily"—for he indeed shines mightily when fully kindled.
He recites that triplet containing the word *vṛṣan*.

For all these *sāmidhenī* verses belong to Agni; yet Indra is the deity of the sacrifice, and Indra is the bull (*vṛṣan*). Thus, by this means, his *sāmidhenīs* become possessed of Indra. Therefore, he recites that triplet containing the word *vṛṣan*.
He recites the invitatory verse.

"We choose Agni as the messenger."—The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. While they were thus contending, Gāyatrī stood between them. That which was Gāyatrī was indeed this earth; she stood right there between them. Both sides became aware of this, thinking: "To whichever side she turns, they shall be the victors, and the others shall be defeated. Both sides then made overtures to her. Agni was the messenger of the gods, and Saharakṣas—the demon of the Asuras—was that of the Asuras. She went over to Agni. Therefore, he recites: "We choose Agni as the messenger," for he was indeed the messenger of the gods. And: "The Hotṛ, the all-knowing."
Now, some indeed recite this [verse] as follows:

"He who is the Hotṛ, the all-knowing"—one might think, "I shall not say this, lest I speak of myself. But he should not speak thus; for they perform what is human at his sacrifice, and that which is human in the sacrifice is a failure. Thinking, "Lest I cause a failure in the sacrifice," the Hotṛ should recite exactly as it is stated in the Ṛg-verse: "the Hotṛ, the all-knowing. And [he says], "of this sacrifice, the skillful-minded one"; for Agni is indeed the skillful-minded one of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "of this sacrifice, the skillful-minded one. This [Agni] turned toward the gods; from that the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. Verily, he prospers in himself and his rivals are defeated, for whomsoever they recite this verse while he knows thus.
Or rather, one should recite that eighth [verse].
This [verse] is indeed a Gāyatrī by its very nature; for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. Therefore, one should recite the eighth [verse].

Now, some place the *dhāyyā* verses at the beginning, saying, "The *dhāyyās* are food; we thus place this food at the very start. But one should not do so, for it becomes ill-placed for him who places the *dhāyyās* at the beginning; for then either the tenth or the eleventh [verse] becomes the [actual] tenth. It is indeed well-placed for him to whom they recite this as the eighth. Therefore, one should place the *dhāyyās* only after [the first eight].
"Being kindled, O sacrifice... so [it is said].

The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; when he says, "Being kindled, O sacrifice," he thereby says, "O Agni, the purifier, worthy of praise. For he is indeed the purifier, and he is indeed worthy of praise. When he says, "We entreat him whose hair is flame," his hair, as it were, shines when he is kindled. When he says, "O Agni, being kindled, accept the oblation," from this point onward he should place all the fuel-wood that is other than the kindling-sticks (*samidh*). For he cuts off that which is other than the kindling-sticks; for what is redundant in the sacrifice, that is redundant for his enemy, and it overflows upon his hateful rival. Therefore, from this point onward he should place all the fuel-wood that is other than the kindling-sticks.
"Serve the gods at this well-performed sacrifice."

"The *adhvara* is indeed the sacrifice; 'I will worship the gods, O thou worthy of good sacrifice,' this is what he thereby says. 'For thou art the bearer of oblations,' for Agni is indeed the bearer of oblations; therefore he says, 'For thou art the bearer of oblations. 'Offer ye, serve ye Agni while the sacrifice proceeds; choose him as the bearer of oblations'—with this [verse] he gives the summons. By this he means: 'Offer and sacrifice for whatever desire you have kindled [him], do that! 'While the sacrifice proceeds, [serve] Agni'—the *adhvara* is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, 'While the sacrifice proceeds, [serve] Agni. 'Choose him as the bearer of oblations'—for Agni is indeed the bearer of oblations; therefore he says, 'Choose him as the bearer of oblations.'"

Now, he recites that triplet containing the word *adhvara*. For when the gods were sacrificing with the sacrifice, their rivals, the Asuras, desired to do them harm; though they sought to harm them, they were unable to do so and were utterly defeated. Therefore, the sacrifice is called *adhvara* (the unharmable). Indeed, an enemy who seeks to harm him perishes, for whomsoever, knowing this, they recite the triplet containing *adhvara*. And as much as one wins by performing the Soma-sacrifice (*saumya-adhvara*), so much does he win.

The gods indeed yoked Agni to the most important task when they said, "As Hotṛ, carry this oblation of ours. Having yoked him to that most important task, they encouraged him, saying, "Truly, you are powerful; truly, you are capable of this," thereby bestowing power upon him. Just as people nowadays encourage the one among their kinsmen whom they yoke to the most important task, saying, "Truly, you are powerful; truly, you are capable of this," thereby bestowing power upon him, so too does he now bestow power upon this very [Agni].
"O Agni, you are great, O Brāhmaṇa, O Bhārata!

For Agni is indeed the Brahman; therefore he says "Brāhmaṇa. He says "Bhārata," for he bears the oblation to the gods; therefore they say, "Agni is Bhārata. Moreover, having become the vital breath (prāṇa), he sustains these creatures; for that reason also he says "Bhārata."

Then he chooses the ancestral lineage (*ārṣeya*). He thereby announces him both to the *ṛṣis* and to the gods, saying, "This one is of great heroism who has reached the sacrifice. Therefore, he chooses the ancestral lineage.
He chooses [the name] from the further side toward the nearer side;

for offspring are born from the further side toward the nearer side, and he thus humbles him who is superior, for in this world the father comes first, then the son, then the grandson; therefore he chooses from the further side toward the nearer side.
Having stated his lineage, he says: "Kindled by the gods, kindled by Manu.
For the gods indeed kindled him first; therefore he says, "kindled by the gods. And "kindled by Manu," for Manu indeed kindled him first; therefore he says, "kindled by Manu."
"Chanted by the seers":
for the seers indeed chanted this first; therefore they call it "chanted by the seers."
"Rejoiced by the sages (vipra)":
these indeed are the sages, namely the ṛṣis; for they rejoiced in this [sacrifice], therefore he says, "rejoiced by the sages."
"Commended by the seers":
these indeed are the seers, namely the ṛṣis; for they praised him, therefore he says, "commended by the seers."
"He who is sharpened by prayer," for he is indeed sharpened by prayer; "he to whom ghee is offered," for he is indeed one to whom ghee is offered.

"The leader of sacrifices, the charioteer of rites"—with this [formula] they indeed lead forward all sacrifices, both those that are *pākayajñas* and those that are others; therefore he says, "the leader of sacrifices."
"He is the charioteer of the sacrifices.
Indeed, having become a chariot, he carries the sacrifice to the gods; therefore he says, "the charioteer of the sacrifices."

"The invincible Hotṛ, the swift carrier of oblations"—for the Rakṣases do not overcome him; therefore he says, "the invincible Hotṛ. "The swift carrier of oblations"—for he overcomes all evil; therefore he says, "the swift carrier of oblations."

"The vessel of the gods, the ladle of the gods"—for this Agni is indeed the vessel of the gods; therefore, they offer into the fire for all the gods, since he is the vessel of the gods. Indeed, one obtains the vessel of that person whose vessel one desires to obtain, provided one knows this thus.
"The cup, the drink of the gods.
For by means of this very cup, as it truly is, the gods consume; therefore he says, "the cup, the drink of the gods."
"O Agni, like the felly encompasses the spokes, you encompass the gods.
By this he means: "Just as the felly encompasses the spokes on all sides, so do you encompass the gods on all sides."

"Bring the gods for the sacrificer," he says; thus he has brought the gods for this sacrifice. "O Agni, bring Agni," he says; thus he has brought Agni for the butter-portion (ājyabhāga) dedicated to Agni. "Bring Soma," he says; thus he has brought Soma for the butter-portion dedicated to Soma. "Bring Agni," he says; thus he has brought Agni for that cake (puroḍāśa) which belongs to both [deities] and is never omitted, being dedicated to Agni. Thus he has brought Agni for it.

Then, according to the respective deities: "Bring the butter-drinking gods!"—by saying this, he has brought the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; for the butter-drinking gods are indeed the *prayāja* and *anuyāja*. "Bring Agni for the office of the Hotṛ!"—by saying this, he has brought Agni for the office of the Hotṛ. "Bring your own greatness!"—by saying this, he has brought his own greatness; for speech is his own greatness, and thus he has brought speech. "And bring them, O Jātavedas, and sacrifice with a good sacrifice!"—by saying this, he refers to those very deities whom he has brought; and when he says, "And sacrifice with a good sacrifice," he means: "Bring them hither and sacrifice with them immediately."
He indeed recites while standing; for this [verse] which he recites is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), and thus, having become that very thing, he recites it. Therefore, he recites while standing.

Sitting, he recites the *yājyā*; for this *yājyā* is this [earth]. Therefore, no one recites the *yājyā* while standing, because this *yājyā* is this [earth]; thus, having become this very thing, it offers the sacrifice. Therefore, sitting, he recites the *yājyā*.
Indeed, that fire which has been kindled with the *sāmidhenī* verses shines forth far more intensely than any other fire; for it becomes unassailable and unapproachable.

Just as the fire, when kindled by the *sāmidhenī* verses, blazes forth, even so does the Brāhmaṇa who knows the *sāmidhenīs* and recites them blaze forth; for he becomes unassailable and unassailable by touch.

He recites the invitatory verse: "Forward," for the forward-breath is indeed the *pravān*; by this [verse] he kindles the forward-breath. "O Agni, come hither for the feast," for the downward-breath is indeed the *etavān*; by this [verse] he kindles the downward-breath. "The great light, O youngest one," for the upward-breath is indeed the *bṛhacchocis*; by this [verse] he kindles the upward-breath.
"He [bestows] upon us wide renown"—wide renown is indeed the ear, for by means of the ear one hears this vast and wide world; with this [verse], he kindles the ear.
"Worthy of praise, worthy of homage"—speech indeed is worthy of praise, for speech praises all this; by speech all this is praised. By means of this [verse], he kindles speech itself.
"Like a horse, the bearer of the gods"—the mind, indeed, is the bearer of the gods, for it is the mind that carries most of this wise person about; with this [verse], he kindles the mind.
"O Agni, shine forth mightily!"—the eye indeed shines; with this [verse], he kindles the eye itself.

"We choose Agni as the messenger"—this refers to that very central breath; with this [verse], he kindles it. This one is indeed the intermediary among the vital breaths, for from it the other breaths go upward, and from it the others go downward. He becomes an intermediary, and they regard him as an intermediary who thus knows this intermediary among the vital breaths.
"We pray for him whose hair is flame. The penis, indeed, is "flame-haired," for this penis causes the greatest burning; with this [verse], he kindles the penis.

"O Agni, kindled with an oblation"—with this [verse], he kindles that very downward breath which is here; "offer and serve"—with this, he kindles his entire self, even unto the nails and the body hairs.

If he should recite [the formula] against him during the first *sāmidhenī* verse, he should say to him: "Verily, you have placed your own breath into the fire; through your own breath you shall meet with affliction. And so indeed it would come to pass.

If he should revile him while the second [sacrificial formula] is being recited, he should say to him: "Having placed the downward breath (apāna) of yourself into the fire, you will meet with affliction through that downward breath of yours"; and so indeed it shall come to pass.
If he should recite [the verse] over the third [layer], he should say to him: "The upward breath (udāna) indeed... by the upward breath... it would be."

If he should utter [a curse] on the fourth day, one should reply to him: "Verily, you have placed this hearing of yours in the fire; through the hearing of your self, you will meet with affliction; you will become deaf. And so indeed it shall come to pass.
If he should speak back on the fifth day, one should say to him: "Having placed speech into the fire from yourself, you will suffer injury to your own speech; you shall become mute."

If he should utter [the challenge] at the sixth [verse], one should say to him: "Verily, having placed this mind of yours into the fire, you will suffer injury to your mind; seized by the mind-stealer, you will wander about utterly bewildered. And so indeed it shall be.
If on the seventh [day]... [you eat], then that eye which is placed by you in the fire of the self—you will suffer injury to that eye of the self; you will become blind.

If [he were to eat] on the eighth day... or if he were to place that middle vital breath of his into the fire, [the seer would say]: "By placing the middle vital breath of your self into the fire, you will meet with affliction through that middle vital breath; you will die from suffocation. And so it would indeed happen.
If [you do so] on the ninth day... this is indeed a request for injury to yourself; you will suffer harm to yourself through the penis and will become impotent.

"If you were to breathe out on the tenth day... [he would say], 'Verily, by placing this downward-breathing of yours into the fire, you will meet with affliction through that downward-breathing of yours; you will die suffocated. And so indeed it would be."
"If [you do this] on the eleventh day...
[he would say], 'Since you have placed this entire self into the fire, you will suffer with your whole self; you will die and go quickly to that world. And so it would indeed come to pass."

Just as one who approaches a fire that has been kindled with the *sāmidhenī* verses meets with distress, even so does one meet with distress by reviling a Brāhmaṇa who, knowing the *sāmidhenīs*, is reciting them after him.

They indeed kindled this very fire, thinking, "When it is kindled, we shall offer to the gods. Upon it he offers these two first oblations: to Mind and to Speech. For Mind and Speech, when yoked together, carry the sacrifice to the gods.

In that it is performed silently, the mind carries the sacrifice to the gods; and in that it is performed with articulated speech, speech carries the sacrifice to the gods. Indeed, this twofold thing is performed here; thus he satisfies these two. When they are satisfied and pleased, they carry the sacrifice to the gods.
He pours that [libation] with the *sruva*-ladle;
he pours what belongs to the mind, for the mind is a bull and the *sruva* is a bull.
He pours that [libation] with the *sruc* ladle;
he pours it with speech, for speech is a woman, and the *sruc* is indeed a woman.
He offers that silently;
he offers it with the mind, not saying "svāhā," for the mind is undefined, and what is silent is indeed undefined.
He offers it with a mantra;
for that which one offers with speech is indeed articulated, and a mantra is indeed articulated.
He pours the libation while sitting; he pours that which is for the mind while standing.

For both mind and speech, when yoked together, carry the sacrifice to the gods. Of two things that are yoked, whichever is the weaker, for it, they provide support. Speech is indeed weaker than mind, for the mind is, as it were, more unlimited, whereas speech is more limited. Thus, he provides support for speech. These two, being yoked together, carry the sacrifice to the gods; therefore, he pours the libation for speech while standing.

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asura-Rakṣasas on the south. They raised up this [fire] on the south; for strength is, as it were, uplifted. Therefore, standing on the south, he pours the libation. In that he pours the libation on both sides, therefore this mind and speech, though being the same, are yet distinct. Indeed, of these two libations, one is the head of the sacrifice and the other is the root.
He pours that [libation] with the *sruva* ladle;
he who is the root of the sacrifice. He pours that with the *sruk* ladle; he who is the head of the sacrifice.
He offers that silently;
for that which is the root of the sacrifice is, as it were, silent, since here the voice does not speak.
He offers it with a mantra;
for the mantra is speech, and speech is indeed the head of the sacrifice, since it is from the head that speech speaks.

He pours the libation while sitting for that which is the root of the sacrifice, for this root stands as if seated; he pours the libation while standing for that which is the head of the sacrifice, for this head stands as if upright.

Having first poured the *āghāra* libation with the *sruva* ladle, he says, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire! This is just as one would place a yoke upon a draft-animal; for when he pours the first *āghāra*, it is like placing the yoke upon [the animal], for they yoke [the animal] after having placed the yoke upon it.
Then he cleanses it.

He thereby yokes it, thinking, "Being yoked, may it carry the sacrifice to the gods"; therefore he cleanses it. He cleanses it while moving around; for they yoke a draft animal by moving around it. He cleanses it thrice each time, for the sacrifice is threefold.

He cleanses [the fire] with the formula: "O Agni, winner of the prize, I cleanse thee who art about to win the prize; I cleanse thee, the winner of the prize. By this he means to say, "I cleanse thee, the worshipful one, who art about to carry the sacrifice. Then he cleanses it silently three times from above. This is just as if, having yoked [a horse], one were to urge it on, saying, "Go forward! Carry [the load]! In the same way, he strikes it with the whip, saying, "Go forward! Carry the sacrifice to the gods! That is why he cleanses it silently three times from above. Because this ritual action is performed between these two, therefore mind and speech, though being the same, are yet distinct.
When he is about to pour the second libation with the *sruva*-ladle, he places his joined palms (*añjali*) before the two ladles, saying, "Homage to the gods!

Svadhā to the fathers! Thus, being about to perform the priestly office for both the gods and the fathers, he pays homage to them. He takes up the two ladles, saying, "May you two be easy for me to control!"—by this he means, "May I be able to support you. "May I today collect the clarified butter for the gods without spilling"—by this he means, "May I today extend the sacrifice for the gods without agitation."

"With my foot, O Viṣṇu, may I not step upon you!"—Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; it is to him that he makes this plea: "May I not step upon you. "O Agni, I shall resort to your lap, which possesses wealth"—by this he means: "O Agni, I shall resort to your auspicious lap."

"Thou art Viṣṇu’s station," he says. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; for it stands near him, therefore he says, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s station. "From here Indra performed his heroic deed," he says; for from here, standing on the south, Indra drove away the destructive spirits and demons (nāṣṭrā rakṣāṃsi), therefore he says, "From here Indra performed his heroic deed. "The sacrifice has stood up erect," he says; the sacrifice is indeed the adhvara; thus he says, "The adhvara has stood up erect."

"O Agni, know the office of the Hotṛ; know the office of the messenger! For Agni is both of these among the gods: the Hotṛ and the messenger; thus he says, "Know both that which thou art of the gods. "May Heaven and Earth protect thee; protect thou Heaven and Earth"—in this there is nothing hidden, as it were. "As the maker of good offerings for the gods, O Indra, be present with the offering of ghee, Svāhā! Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "O Indra, with the ghee. Moreover, he pours this libation for Speech; and they say that Indra is Speech. For this reason also he says, "O Indra, with the ghee."
Then, having gone around without touching the two offering-spoons, he anoints them with the *dhruvā* spoon.

For the second libation (*uttara-āghāra*) is the head of the sacrifice, and the *dhruvā* is the body; thus he places the head back into the body. Indeed, the second libation is the head of the sacrifice, and the head is prosperity (*śrī*), for the head is indeed prosperity; therefore, when someone is the best in a region, they say, "He is the head of that region."
The sacrificer alone corresponds to the *dhruvā* [spoon].

He who acts with hostility toward him corresponds to the *upabhṛt* [spoon]. For if he were to smear [the butter] with the *upabhṛt*, he would place vigor in him who acts with hostility toward the sacrificer; thus, he places that vigor in the sacrificer himself. Therefore, he smears [the butter] with the *dhruvā*.

He anoints them together with the formula, "May light unite with light. For the clarified butter in one [ladle] is indeed light, and the [substance] in the other is light; thus these two lights meet together. Therefore, he anoints them in this manner.

Now, therefore, concerning the mind and the speech: "I am the auspicious one," thus the mind spoke; and "I am the auspicious one," thus the speech spoke. They both spoke thus: "I am the auspicious one."
Then the mind said:

"I am indeed superior to you; for there is nothing that you speak which has not been previously understood by me. You are merely one who imitates my actions and follows my path; I am indeed superior to you."
Then Speech said:
"I am indeed superior to you; for whatever you know, I make known, and I make understood."
They went to Prajāpati for a further inquiry.

Prajāpati spoke in favor of the mind alone: "The mind is indeed better than speech; for you, O Speech, are merely an imitator and a follower of the mind. Indeed, the worse becomes the imitator and follower of the better."
When she was spoken against, Vāk was astonished;

her fetus fell away, and Vāk said to Prajāpati, "May I become for you one who carries no oblation, since you have spoken against me. Therefore, whatever belongs to Prajāpati that is performed at the sacrifice is performed in a whisper, for Vāk had become a carrier of oblations for Prajāpati.

Now, this very seed the gods placed upon a hide or in something else, and they sought it out, saying, "It is surely here! From that, he came into being threefold; therefore, even a woman of the Ātreyī lineage is considered tainted, for these [beings] were born from that female deity, Vāc.
He indeed calls for the *pravara* (the choosing of the priests).
Now, as to why he calls for the *pravara*: the call (*āśrāvaṇa*) is the sacrifice; having thus proclaimed the sacrifice, he then chooses the Hotṛ. Therefore, he calls for the *pravara*.
Having taken hold of the faggot-bands themselves, he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*.
For if the Adhvaryu were to call for the *āśrāvaṇa* without having grasped the sacrifice, he would either tremble or meet with some other misfortune.

Regarding this, some say that one should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made while touching the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) that has been spread in the Veda, or while cutting off a chip from the fuel-wood (*idhma*) and touching it, saying, "This is indeed something of the sacrifice; by touching this, we shall cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made for the sacrifice. But one should not do so. That which constitutes something of the sacrifice is the fact that the fuel-wood is bound together and they sweep the fire; by that very act, he causes the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made for the sacrifice. Therefore, he should cause the *āśrāvaṇa* call to be made while touching only the bindings of the fuel-wood.

Having called for the Śrauṣaṭ, he chooses Agni first—him who is the Hotṛ of the gods. By this, he makes amends both to Agni and to the gods. In that he chooses Agni first, he makes amends to Agni; then, in that he chooses him who is the Hotṛ of the gods first, he makes amends to the gods.

He says, "Agni, the god, the divine Hotṛ. For Agni is indeed the Hotṛ of the gods; therefore he says, "Agni, the god, the divine Hotṛ. By this, he makes atonement both for Agni and for the gods. In that he first mentions Agni, he makes atonement for Agni; and in that he first mentions him who is the Hotṛ of the gods, he thereby makes atonement for the gods.
"May he, the knowing one, the wise one, sacrifice to the gods"—for Agni is indeed the one who knows the gods; by saying this, he means: "May he, knowing them, sacrifice to them in due order."
"Like Manu, like Bharata.

For in the beginning, Manu indeed sacrificed with the sacrifice; imitating him, these creatures now sacrifice. Therefore he says, "like Manu. They say, moreover, "the sacrifice of Manu"; for that very reason he says, "like Manu."
"Like Bharata.
For he bears the oblation to the gods; therefore they say, "Agni is Bharata. Moreover, having become the vital breath, he sustains these creatures; for that reason also they say, "Like Bharata."
Then he chooses the ancestral lineage (ārṣeya).
He thereby announces him to the seers and to the gods, saying, "He is one of great heroism who has reached the sacrifice. That is why he chooses the ancestral lineage.

He chooses from the further side towards the nearer side; for offspring are born from the further side towards the nearer side, and he thus humbles himself before the superior. For in this world, first comes the father, then the son, then the grandson; therefore he chooses from the further side towards the nearer side.

Having stated the *ārṣeya*, he says, "Accompanied by the Brahman. For Agni is indeed the Brahman; therefore he says, "Accompanied by the Brahman. And when he says, "And may he bring hither," he thereby refers to those very deities whom he has previously caused to bring [the oblation], saying, "And may they bring hither."
"The Brahmins are the promoters of this sacrifice.

Indeed, those Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) are the promoters of the sacrifice, for they extend it and they bring it forth; he makes amends to them, and therefore he says, "The Brahmins are the promoters of this sacrifice."
"He is a human being.
Therefore, he chooses this human one as the Hotṛ; for he was the Hotṛ in ancient times, and he is the Hotṛ even now.
Having stepped forward, he becomes the Hotṛ;

he mutters prayers, he hastens to the deities so that he may offer the *vaṣaṭ* call to the gods in due order, so that he may carry the oblation to the gods in due order, and so that he does not stumble—thus he hastens to the deities.

There he mutters this: "O God Savitṛ, choose this truth. Thus he approaches Savitṛ for impulsion, for he is the impeller of the gods. With the words, "Agni as Hotṛ," he makes amends both to Agni and to the gods; in that he mentions Agni first, he makes amends to Agni, and then in that he mentions him who is the Hotṛ of the gods, he makes amends to the gods.
"Together with his father Vaiśvānara.

The year, indeed, is the father Vaiśvānara Prajāpati; thus he makes amends to the year, to Prajāpati. "O Agni, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, speak forth and sacrifice!"—for he is about to recite and about to sacrifice; thus he makes amends to these very deities, saying, "Do you recite, do you sacrifice!"
"May we be in the bounty of the Vasus;

may we be in the wide expanse of the Rudras; O Ādityas, may we be in the care of Aditi, free from affliction"—by this he means: "May we be under the protection of these three classes of gods, namely the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas."
"May I utter today speech acceptable to the gods"—by this he means, "May I recite today what is acceptable to the gods"; for that is successful for one who recites what is acceptable to the gods.
"Accepted by the Brahmins," he says; this means, "May I recite today what is acceptable to the Brahmins. For that is successful for one who recites what is acceptable to the Brahmins.

"To Narāśaṃsa, the beloved"—"men" (naraḥ) are indeed offspring; thus he speaks for all offspring, for that is complete: both he who knows it and he who does not say, "Thou hast spoken well, thou hast spoken well," and so they are dismissed. With the words, "What crooked eye today has flown away at the choosing of the Hotṛ—may Agni Jātavedas, the far-seeing, bring that back again," he says this: "Just as those fires which they chose for the office of Hotṛ in the beginning fled away, even so, whatever of mine has been lost here through the choosing, may that be replenished for me. And so, indeed, this of his is replenished again.
Then he touches both the Adhvaryu and the Āgnīdhra;
for the Adhvaryu is Mind and the Hotṛ is Speech—thus he unites both Mind and Speech.
There he mutters:

"May the six wide expanses protect me from distress—Agni and the Earth, the Waters and Vāja, Day and Night. By this he means: "May these deities protect me from misfortune. For indeed, there is no stumbling for one whom these deities protect from misfortune.
Then he approaches the Hotṛ’s seat.
From the Hotṛ’s seat, he throws away a blade of grass, saying, "Expelled is Parāvasu! For the Hotṛ of the Asuras was indeed named Purāvasu; it is him that he thus expels from the Hotṛ’s seat.
Then he sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat with the formula:
"Here I sit in the seat of Arvāvasu. For Arvāvasu by name is the Hotṛ of the gods; it is in his very seat that he now sits.

There he mutters: "O Viśvakarman, you are the protector of the body; do not harm us, do not injure me; this world is yours. He moves northward between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires; for he stands there between these two, and thus he makes amends to them with the words, "Do not harm us, do not injure me," so that these two do not injure him.

Then, looking at the fire, he mutters: "O All-Gods, instruct me how I, being chosen as the Hotṛ here, shall think when seated; tell me clearly my portion, and by which path I shall carry the oblation to you. Just as one would say to those for whom food has been cooked, "Instruct me how I shall bring it to you, how I shall serve you," even so he seeks instruction from the gods. He says, "Instruct me how I may offer the Vaṣaṭ-call correctly, how I may carry the oblation correctly. Therefore, he mutters thus.

"Agni, the Hotṛ, let him know the office of the Hotṛ for Agni"—by this he means, "Let Agni here, as the Hotṛ, know it"; "the office of the Hotṛ for Agni," for his indeed is the office of the Hotṛ. "Let him know the Prāvitra"—the Prāvitra is the sacrifice; thus he means, "Let him know the sacrifice. "Propitious be the deity to thee, O sacrificer!"—by this he means, "Propitious be the deity to thee, O sacrificer, for whom Agni is the Hotṛ. "O Adhvaryu, bring forward the butter-sprinkling ladle!"—with these words he gives the impulse to the Adhvaryu; and as to why he says "one" [ladle]...

The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū* ladle; he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt* ladle. If he were to speak as if there were two [ladles], he would make his hateful rival rise up against the sacrificer. The eater indeed follows the *juhū* ladle; the food follows the *upabhṛt* ladle. If he were to speak as if there were two [ladles], he would make the eater rise up against the food. Therefore, he speaks as if there were only one.

"Seeking the gods, possessing all boons"—by saying this, he indeed praises her and magnifies her. "We shall praise the gods worthy of praise; we shall honor those worthy of honor; we shall sacrifice to those worthy of sacrifice"—by this he means: "We shall praise those gods who are worthy of praise; we shall honor those who are worthy of honor; we shall sacrifice to those who are worthy of sacrifice. For humans are worthy of praise, the ancestors are worthy of honor, and the gods are worthy of sacrifice.
Those creatures indeed that are not included in the sacrifice perish;

in this very way, he now causes these creatures that have not perished to participate in the sacrifice: after men come the domestic animals, after the gods come the birds, the plants, and the trees—whatever there is here, all that is thus made to participate in the sacrifice.
Now, these indeed are the nine utterances (vyāhṛtis); there are these nine vital breaths in a person; he thus places these very ones into him; therefore there are nine utterances.
Sacrifice indeed departed from the gods.

The gods addressed it, saying, "Hear us; turn back to us! It said, "So be it," and thus returned to the gods. With it having returned, the gods sacrificed; having sacrificed with it, they became that which these gods now are.

When he calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he thereby addresses the sacrifice with the words, "Hear us! Turn toward us! And when he responds with the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*, the sacrifice turns toward him with the words, "So be it. With that sacrifice having thus turned toward him as seed, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) proceed by handing it over to one another behind the back of the sacrificer. Just as they would proceed by handing over a full vessel, even so do the officiating priests proceed by handing it over through this [sacrifice]. They proceed by means of speech alone; for the sacrifice is speech, and seed is speech. Thus, by this very means, they proceed by handing it over.

Having said, "Recite after me," the Adhvaryu must not speak out of turn, nor indeed should the Hotṛ speak out of turn; the Adhvaryu then causes the announcement, and thus the sacrifice returns to the Āgnīdhra.
He should not speak out against Agni.
Until the call for the response, he causes the response; thus, O Agnīdh, that [speech] returns again to the Adhvaryu in the sacrifice.
That Adhvaryu must not speak out of turn;
when it is time to say "Recite the offering prayer," the Adhvaryu hands over the sacrifice to the Hotṛ by saying simply, "Recite."
The Hotṛ should not speak out until the *vaṣaṭ* call;

at that *vaṣaṭ* call, he pours it as seed into Agni himself as the womb. For Agni is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; from him it is born. This applies to the *haviryajña*; now, however, regarding the Soma sacrifice (*saumya adhvaryu*).
Having indeed taken up the cup, the Adhvaryu should not speak out until the commencement; rather, the Adhvaryu hands over the sacrifice to the Udgātṛs with the words, "Come hither! (upāvartadhvam).
Those Udgātṛ priests should not speak out of turn;
up to the final verse, saying "This is the last," the Udgātṛs hand over the sacrifice to the Hotṛ.
The Hotṛ priest must not speak out of turn until the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he pours that seed—which has become semen—into Agni as its very womb. For Agni is indeed the womb of the sacrifice; from him, the sacrifice is born.

If he were to speak out against him—against whomsoever the sacrifice turns back—it would be as if one were to pour out a full vessel; even so would he pour the sacrificer out. But where the officiating priests proceed with the sacrifice in mutual agreement, there everything is successful and nothing goes astray. Therefore, the sacrifice must be maintained in this very way.

Now, these indeed are the five Vyahrtis: "Oshravaya," "Astu Shraushat," "Yaja," "Ye Yajamahe," and "Vausat. The sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; this is one measure of the sacrifice, this is its perfection.
They have seventeen syllables. Prajāpati is indeed seventeenfold; the sacrifice is Prajāpati. This is one measure of the sacrifice; this is the perfection.

With "O, cause to hear! the gods released the east wind; with "Let there be hearing! they caused the clouds to overflow; with "Sacrifice! they [produced] lightning; and with "We who sacrifice," by means of the *vaṣaṭ* call itself, they caused it to rain.

If he should desire rain, whether he is performing an *iṣṭi* sacrifice or the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), he should say, "I am desirous of rain. Then he should say to the Adhvaryu, "Meditate mentally upon the east wind and lightning"; to the Āgnīdhra, "Meditate mentally upon the clouds"; to the Hotṛ, "Meditate mentally upon thunder and rain"; and to the Brahman, "Meditate mentally upon all these. Where the officiating priests proceed with the sacrifice in such mutual agreement, it indeed rains there.
"O, make them hear!"—with these words the gods invoked the Virāj.

"Let there be hearing!"—with this they released the calf. "Sacrifice!"—with this they won [the prize]. "We sacrifice!"—with this they drew near. With the *vaṣaṭ*-call, they milked the Virāj. This earth is indeed the Virāj; this is her milking. Verily, for him who knows this milking of the Virāj, this Virāj milks all desires.
The seasonal offerings (prayāja) are indeed the seasons;
therefore there are five of them, for there are five seasons.
The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice in their father Prajāpati, the year, saying, "This shall be ours; this shall be ours."

Then the gods, praising and toiling, wandered about; they saw these fore-offerings (prayāja) and sacrificed with them. By means of them, they drove forth the seasons and the year; from the seasons and from the year, they excluded their rivals. Therefore, they are called "fore-offerings" (prajā), for this very word "prajā" is indeed the same as "prayāja. And so, in like manner, he now drives forth the seasons and the year by means of these; from the seasons and from the year, he excludes his rivals. That is why he sacrifices with the fore-offerings.
These indeed have clarified butter as their oblation.

Clarified butter is a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, the clarified butter, the gods drove forth the seasons and the year, and from the seasons and the year they drove away their enemies. In the same way, this sacrificer now drives forth the seasons and the year by means of this thunderbolt, the clarified butter, and from the seasons and the year he drives away his enemies. Therefore, they have clarified butter as their oblation.

This ghee is indeed the own milk of the year; by means of that own milk, the gods made him their own. In the same way, this sacrificer now makes him his own by means of that own milk. Therefore, they have ghee as their sacrificial offering.
Wherever he may be standing, he should cause the announcement for the *prayāja* offerings;

from that very spot he must not move away. Indeed, a battle is imminent for him who sacrifices with the *prayājas*. Of two combatants engaged in conflict, whichever one is defeated, he retreats; whereas the victor advances further and further. Therefore, he should step forward further and further, and he should offer the oblations further and further.
One should not do it in that way.

One should not move away from the very spot where, while standing, one calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* for the *prayāja* offerings; rather, one should offer the oblations at the very place where one considers the fire to be most kindled, for by offering into a well-kindled fire, the oblations truly become successful.

Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *samidhs*. By this, he kindles the spring; the kindled spring kindles the other seasons. The seasons being kindled, creatures are brought forth and plants ripen. Indeed, he has thereby named all the seasons. Then he says, "Recite the offering prayer! Recite the offering prayer! for the sake of non-repetition (*ajāmitā*). For he would commit repetition if he were to say, "Recite the offering prayer for Tanūnapāt! Recite the offering prayer for Iḍa! Therefore, he says only, "Recite the offering prayer! Recite the offering prayer! for the subsequent ones.
He offers the *samidh* oblations.

The spring is indeed the *samidh*; it was by means of the spring that the gods won [the sacrifice], and by means of the spring they drove their rivals away. This sacrificer now wins by means of the spring, and by means of the spring he drives his rivals away; therefore, he offers the *samidh* oblations.
Then he offers to Tanūnapāt.

Tanūnapāt is indeed the summer, for in summer the body of these creatures is scorched; it was the summer that the gods chose then, they excluded their rivals from the summer, and so this sacrificer now chooses the summer and excludes his rivals from the summer. That is why he offers to Tanūnapāt.

He offers the *iḍā*. For the *iḍā* is indeed the rain; thus it is the rain that is the *iḍā*. Whatever small crawling creature there is that is driven out by the summer and winter, it moves about in the rainy season as if seeking food that has been offered as *iḍā*. Therefore, the *iḍā* is the rain. By means of this, the gods appropriated the rain; their rivals fled from the rains. Verily, he (the sacrificer) now appropriates the rain for himself, and his rivals flee from the rains. That is why he offers the *iḍā*.

Then he offers the *barhis* (sacrificial grass). For the *barhis* is indeed the autumn (*śarad*), since it is said, "The autumn is the *barhis*. Those plants which have been withered by the summer and winter grow during the rainy season; in the autumn they lie spread out in the form of sacrificial grass. Therefore, the autumn is the *barhis*.

By this, the gods appropriated the autumn for themselves as a means of excluding their rivals from the autumn. In the same way, this sacrificer now appropriates the autumn for himself and excludes his rivals from the autumn. That is why he offers the *barhis*.
Then he offers with "Svāhā! Svāhā!

The utterance "Svāhā" is indeed the end of the sacrifice, and winter is the end of the seasons, for it follows after spring. By means of the end, the gods thus appropriated the end; by the end they drove their rivals away from the end. In the same way, this sacrificer now appropriates the end by means of the end; by the end he drives his rivals away from the end. Therefore, he offers with "Svāhā!"
This, indeed, is that very spring from which one returns again after winter; for from this very source he is born again. And he who knows this thus, verily, is born again in this world.
He offers with the words, "May they partake! May he partake! This is for the sake of avoiding sameness;

for he would commit a repetition if he were to offer with either "may they partake, may they partake" or "may he partake, may he partake. "May they partake" is feminine, and "may he partake" is masculine; thus a productive union is brought about. Therefore, he offers with "may they partake! may he partake!"
Then, at the fourth fore-offering, he pours together [the butter] upon the *barhis* grass.

The *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the clarified butter is seed; thus, that seed is poured into the offspring. By means of that poured seed, these offspring are born again and again. Therefore, at the fourth fore-offering, he pours together [the butter] upon the *barhis*.

Indeed, a battle is set in motion for him who sacrifices with the fore-offerings (*prayāja*). Of two combatants engaged in battle, he who comes as a friend to the other wins; in this case, the ladle (*juhū*) comes as a friend to the *upabhṛt*. By that, he conquers. Therefore, at the fourth fore-offering, he pours [the butter] together upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū*; he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt*. Thus, for the sacrificer, he makes his hateful rival pay tribute. The eater indeed follows the *juhū*, and that which is to be eaten follows the *upabhṛt*; thus, for the eater, he makes that which is to be eaten pay tribute. Therefore, he pours [the butter] together at the fourth *prayāja*.
He pours it together without touching it.

For if he were to touch it, he would cause the sacrificer to be touched by his hateful rival; he would cause the giver to be touched by the consumer. Therefore, he pours it together without touching it.
Then he places the *juhū* ladle upon the *upabhṛt*.
He thus places it upon the sacrificer, upon his rival; he places it upon the eater, upon the firstborn. Therefore, he places the *juhū* upon the *upabhṛt*.
The gods indeed said, "Come, let us complete the entire sacrifice right where it has been won; if the Asuras and Rakṣases should attack us, our sacrifice will already be completed."

At the final fore-offering, by means of the *svāhā* call alone, they completed the entire sacrifice. With "Svāhā to Agni," they completed the butter-portion for Agni; with "Svāhā to Soma," they completed the butter-portion for Soma; and with "Svāhā to Agni," they completed that cake-offering which belongs to Agni and is never omitted at either [sacrifice].
Then, according to the respective deities.

"Obeisance! O gods who drink the clarified butter!"—with these words they completed the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. For the gods who drink the clarified butter are indeed the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. "May Agni, graciously accepting the clarified butter, partake of it"—with this they completed the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering, for Agni is indeed the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. Thus, even now, the sacrifice is completed in the very same manner as the gods completed it. Therefore, at the final *prayāja*, he offers with "Svāhā! Svāhā! as many times as there are oblations. He thereby completes the entire sacrifice following its victory. Therefore, if anything contrary to the rule should be done in the sacrifice after that point, one should not heed it; let him know, "My sacrifice is complete. This very sacrifice was exhausted, just like that which has been offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the *svāhā*-call, and the *hutam* (offered).
Those gods desired:
"How indeed might we cause this sacrifice to swell again? How might we make it free from weariness? With that which is free from weariness, let us proceed."
That ghee which remained in the juhū-ladle, he [took].

With that same [ladle] with which they had completed the sacrifice, they poured the oblations over as before; thus they made them swell again and rendered them free from weariness, for ghee is indeed free from weariness. Therefore, having performed the last fore-offering (prayāja), he pours ghee over the oblations as before; he thereby makes them swell again and renders them free from weariness, for ghee is indeed free from weariness. Therefore, whenever he cuts off a portion of any oblation, he pours ghee over it again; he thereby makes it swell again and renders it free from weariness, for ghee is indeed free from weariness. But when he cuts off a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt, he does not pour ghee over it again, for he has no further oblation of that [remaining] portion to offer into the fire.

He offers the *samidh* oblations. The *samidhs* are indeed the vital breaths; he thus kindles the vital breaths, for by the vital breaths this person is kindled. Therefore, one should say, "Touch him," if he should be afflicted with illness. If he is warm, one should hope for him, for he is then kindled; but if he is cold, one should not hope for him. Thus he places the vital breaths within him; that is why he offers the *samidh* oblations.
Then he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt.
Tanūnapāt is indeed semen; it is semen that he thus pours forth. Therefore, he sacrifices to Tanūnapāt.
He offers the *iḍā*.

For offspring indeed are the *iḍā*. When seed has been shed and offspring is produced, then it moves about as if desiring food, seeking what is offered (*iḍita*). He thus causes that very thing to be born; therefore he offers the *iḍā*.
Then he offers to the sacrificial grass (barhis).
The sacrificial grass is indeed abundance; it is abundance that he thus causes to be produced. That is why he offers to the sacrificial grass.

Then he sacrifices with "Svāhā! Svāhā! Winter, indeed, is the *svāhā*-utterance among the seasons; for winter brings these creatures under its own control. Therefore, in winter, the plants wither, the leaves of the trees fall off, birds become as if exhausted, and birds fly as if unable to hold themselves up; a wicked man becomes as if his hair has fallen out. For winter brings these creatures under its own control. He who knows this makes that half [of the year] truly a *svāhā*-utterance for the sake of prosperity and the eating of food, on whichever side he may be.

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. They did not conquer by means of staffs or bows. Being unsuccessful in their conquest, they said: "Come, let us seek victory through speech alone, the Brahman. Whoever among us does not follow along with the utterance of our speech in its paired form, he shall suffer total defeat; then the others shall win everything. "So be it," the gods replied. Then the gods said to Indra: "Utter [the word]!"
Indra said, "One for me! Then the others said, "One for us! Thus they found that very couple, for one male and one female constitute a couple.
"Two are mine," said Indra; "then two are ours," said the others. Thus they found that very pair, for two and two indeed constitute a pair.
"Three are mine," said Indra; "then three are ours," said the others. Thus they found that very pair, for three and three indeed constitute a pair.
"Four are mine," said Indra;
"then four are ours," said the others. Thus they found that very pair, for four and four indeed constitute a pair.
"Five are mine," said Indra.

Then the others could find no pair, for there is no pair beyond five; thus these two [sets] become "five, five. Thereupon the Asuras were utterly defeated; the gods conquered the Asuras in everything and excluded the Asuras, their rivals, from everything.
Therefore, when the first fore-offering has been performed, he should say:
"One for me," and "One for him whom I hate"—if he does not hate anyone, he should say, "For him who hates us and whom we hate."
At the second fore-offering, he says: "Two for me," and "Two for him who hates us and whom we hate."
At the third fore-offering, he says: "Three are mine;
three are his who hates us and whom we hate."
At the fourth fore-offering, he says: "Four are mine";
"Four are his who hates us and whom we hate."
At the fifth fore-offering, he says, "Five for me!

[and adds], "Nothing whatsoever belongs to him who hates us or whom we hate. He who knows this, being himself fivefold, overcomes his enemy; thus he gathers everything to himself and excludes his rivals from everything.
The seasons indeed sought a share in the sacrifice among the gods, saying, "Give us a share in the sacrifice;
do not exclude us from the sacrifice; let there be a share for us as well in the sacrifice."
The gods did not perceive that.
While the gods remained unaware, the seasons turned toward the Asuras—the enemies of the gods, those who hated them, their rivals.

They indeed made for themselves that intelligence which they now possess, following which they hear these [words]. For in former times, some went about plowing and sowing, while others went reaping and threshing; yet for them, plants ripened perpetually even without being tilled.
That indeed became an offense against the gods.
Thinking, "He hates us more than he used to; he acts with hostility toward us," they considered: "How can we contrive it so that this shall be otherwise than it is now?"
They said, "Let us address the seasons themselves. [The others asked,] "By what means? [They replied,] "Let us worship them first in the sacrifice."
Then that Agni said:

"Now, since you used to sacrifice to me first of all in the past, where shall I be? We shall not cause you to fall from your abode. Because they, while summoning the seasons, did not cause Agni to fall from his abode, therefore Agni is unshakable. Indeed, he does not fall from his abode in whatever abode he resides, who thus knows this Agni as unshakable.

Those gods said to Agni, "Go, you yourself must consecrate them. Agni went and said, "O Ṛtus, I have indeed found a share for you among the gods at the sacrifice. "How have you found us? they asked. "They will worship you first at the sacrifice," he replied.

The seasons said to Agni, "Let us share you among ourselves, for you have not obtained a portion of the sacrifice among us gods. Thus this Agni was shared among the seasons with the formulas: "O Agni, kindling-sticks; O Agni, Tanūnapāt; O Agni, libations; O Agni, sacrificial grass; O Agni, Svāhā! Indeed, he who performs that meritorious rite while reciting these [formulas] becomes one who has truly been shared in it. And because the seasons, which possess Agni, cook all these herbs for him, he for whom Agni is intended prospers. This is so for one who thus knows this Agni as being shared among the seasons.
Regarding this they say:

"Since they invoke the *prayāja* offerings last, why then do they sacrifice them first? For they assigned these to the end of the sacrifice, saying, "We shall sacrifice you first"; therefore, they invoke them last but sacrifice them first.

By the fourth fore-offering (prayāja), the gods obtained the sacrifice; by the fifth, they completed it. Then, that part of the sacrifice which remained uncompleted beyond that, by means of it, they attained the heavenly world.

As they were going to the heavenly world, they were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases; they placed Agni in front, a slayer of Rakṣases, a repeller of Rakṣases; they placed Agni in the middle, a slayer of Rakṣases, a repeller of Rakṣases; they placed Agni behind, a slayer of Rakṣases, a repeller of Rakṣases.

If the Asuras and Rakshasas had hemmed them in from the front, Agni himself—slayer of Rakshasas, the repeller of Rakshasas—would have driven them away; if they had hemmed them in from the middle, Agni himself—slayer of Rakshasas, the repeller of Rakshasas—would have driven them away; if they had hemmed them in from behind, Agni himself—slayer of Rakshasas, the repeller of Rakshasas—would have driven them away. Thus, protected on all sides by Agnis, they attained the heavenly world.

In the same way, he thus obtains the sacrifice by the fourth fore-offering (prayāja) alone; he brings it to completion with the fifth. Then, whatever part of the sacrifice remains uncompleted beyond that, by means of that he attains the heavenly world.

When he offers the butter-portion (ājyabhāga) to Agni, he thereby places Agni in front as a slayer of the Rakṣases, a repeller of the Rakṣases. And when there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni, he thereby places Agni in the middle as a slayer of the Rakṣases, a repeller of the Rakṣases. And when he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, he thereby places Agni behind as a slayer of the Rakṣases, a repeller of the Rakṣases.
