If the Asuras and Rakṣases should attack him from the front, Agni himself—slayer of Rakṣases, the repeller of Rakṣases—drives them away; if they should attack from the middle, Agni himself—slayer of Rakṣases, the repeller of Rakṣases—drives them away; if they should attack from behind, Agni himself—slayer of Rakṣases, the repeller of Rakṣases—drives them away. Thus protected on all sides by fires, he attains the heavenly world.

If he should recite this [formula] for him at the beginning of the sacrifice, he should say to him in return: "You will meet with a primary affliction; you will become either blind or deaf. These indeed are the primary afflictions, and so it shall surely come to pass.

If he should recite [the invitatory verse] from the middle of the sacrifice, one should say to him: "You shall be without offspring and without cattle. For offspring and cattle are indeed the middle; thus it will surely come to pass.
If someone should challenge [the ritual] at the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should say to him:
"Unestablished and poor, you shall quickly go to that world. And so it would indeed be. Therefore, one should not be a challenger; for even one who knows thus becomes superior.
One indeed conquers by means of the fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) for the duration of a year;

he truly conquers him who knows its doors. For what could one do with those houses if one were not to distinguish them from within? As they belong to him, so [he understands]: spring is its door, winter is its door. Verily, he thus enters that year, which is the heavenly world. The year is indeed everything, and everything is imperishable. By this, his merit becomes imperishable and his world becomes imperishable.

Regarding this they say: "To which deity do the Ājya-lauds belong? One should reply: "They belong to Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is undefined, and the Ājya-lauds are undefined; thus these indeed have the sacrificer as their deity, for the sacrificer is Prajāpati in his own sacrifice. For by him the officiating priests are commissioned, and they weave [the sacrifice] and bring him forth.

Having spread a layer of clarified butter (ājya) beneath, he takes two portions from the sacrificial oblation (havis) and then pours clarified butter over them; thus this oblation is offered mixed with clarified butter. Indeed, it is offered by the sacrificer himself as mixed with clarified butter, whether he performs the sacrifice far away or nearby; for just as if one were to sacrifice while being present at the end [of the rite], so indeed does the sacrifice of one who knows this become accomplished. And even if he should do much evil, he does not indeed go outside the sacrifice, provided he knows this.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. Because they obstructed it with that, it is called the *yūpa*. This, indeed, was heard by the seers (*ṛṣis*) in tradition.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. They then set about searching for it.
They wandered about, wearying themselves;

for by means of weariness, indeed, the gods and the seers used to win that which was to be won by them. The gods either inspired them with zeal or they themselves resolved: "Come, let us go to where the gods attained the heavenly world. They wandered about, asking, "What inspires you? What inspires you? Then they saw the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) crawling about as a tortoise; they all agreed upon it, saying, "This is indeed the sacrifice."

They said, "Stand for the Aśvins! Stand for Sarasvatī! Stand for Indra! But he simply crawled away. Then [they said], "Stand for Agni! Thereupon he stood still. Thinking, "He has indeed stood for Agni," they took him up within the fire and offered him as a complete oblation; for the oblation is the food of the gods. Then the sacrifice became pleasing to them; they emitted it and performed it. This same sacrifice, from the higher to the lower, is recited, just as a father [recites it] to his son who is a religious student.
He indeed offered that cake first for those [deities] who had made the sacrifice attractive to them;
therefore it is called *puroḍāśa*. For "puroḍāśa" is indeed the same as "purodāśa. This very cake, belonging to Agni, consisting of eight potsherds, is never omitted at either [sacrifice].

He does not offer the full-moon oblation, nor the new-moon oblation; for the full-moon oblation is indeed the Agni-Soma offering, and the new-moon oblation is the Sāṃnāyya. This sacrifice is already established for both occasions, so that he may not depart from the sacrifice. It is for this reason, surely, that it is performed beforehand of the full moon, and likewise of the new moon; and that is why it is performed here.

If someone should approach him, saying, "Sacrifice for me with an *iṣṭi*," he should sacrifice for him with this very [offering]. Whatever desire the seers sacrificed for when they offered it, that desire was fulfilled for them. Whatever desire one sacrifices for with this sacrifice, that desire is fulfilled for him. For whatever deity the oblation is taken, it is indeed offered in Agni; and if he were about to offer in Agni, what other deity could he designate? Therefore, [it is] for Agni alone.
Agni, indeed, is all the deities;
for in Agni they offer oblations to all the deities. Just as if one were to run to all the deities individually, so it is with that; therefore, [the offering] is for Agni alone.
Agni is indeed the most manifest among the gods;
one should therefore run to him whom one considers the most manifest, and thus [run] to Agni alone.
Agni, indeed, is the most soft-hearted among the gods;
one should have recourse to him whom one considers the most soft-hearted—therefore, [one should seek refuge] with Agni alone.
Agni is indeed the nearest of the gods;
one should run to him whom one considers the nearest among those to be approached; therefore, [one should run] to Agni alone.

If he should perform an *iṣṭi*, he should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deity in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), for that is the characteristic form of an *iṣṭi*. The *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* should be verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhanvatī*); the two *ājyabhāga* offerings should be *vārtraghna* verses; and the two *saṃyājyā* verses should be *virāj* verses.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed had a son who was three-headed and six-eyed; he had three mouths, and because he was of such a form, he was named Viśvarūpa (the All-formed).
Of him, there was one head for drinking Soma, one for drinking Surā, and one for eating food; Indra hated him and cut off those heads of his.
From that which was his drinking of Soma, the Kapiñjala bird came into being; therefore it is as if tawny, for King Soma is indeed tawny.
Now, from that which was the drinking of *surā* liquor, the *kalaviṅka* bird came into being; therefore it cries out as if intoxicated, for one speaks as if intoxicated after drinking *surā*.

Then, from that which was left over from his hunger, the partridge (tittiri) came into being; therefore it is, as it were, most multiform, for from it there are indeed drops of ghee, drops of fat, and drops of honey as if dripping upon its feathers—such was the form of food that he consumed by means of it.
Tvaṣṭṛ became enraged, thinking, "Has he indeed slain my son? He then procured Soma that was devoid of Indra; just as this Soma had been pressed, so too was it devoid of Indra.
Indra indeed reflected: "They are surely excluding me from the Soma.

Just as a stronger man might act toward one who is weaker, he, without being invited, drank the bright (śukra) Soma that was in the wooden trough (droṇakalaśa). It injured him; it rushed out from all his vital breaths (prāṇas), but it did not rush out from his mouth. Then it rushed out from all his other vital breaths. That is why there is this Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice; in it, that [incident] is explained, how the gods healed him.

Tvaṣṭṛ became enraged, thinking, "Alas! He has consumed the Soma without inviting me. He himself then wrought a destruction of the sacrifice. Whatever bright [Soma] remained in the Droṇakalaśa vessel, he caused it to flow forth with the words, "O enemy of Indra, grow! Having reached Agni, it came into being; some say it came into being within Agni itself. It came into being as both Agni and Soma—possessing all knowledge, all glory, all food, and all prosperity.

Because he came into being while rolling (*vartamāna*), therefore he is Vṛtra; and because he came into being while crawling on his belly (*apāt*), therefore he is Ahi. Danu and Danāyū embraced him like a mother and a father; therefore they call him Dānava.
Now, as for what he said, "O enemy of Indra, grow strong!"—therefore Indra himself slew him. For had he ever said, "O enemy of Indra, grow strong," he would surely have destroyed Indra forever.

Then, as to why he said, "Grow!"—therefore, indeed, it grew sideways only by the measure of an arrow, and forward by the measure of an arrow; it flowed down to the western ocean and down to the eastern one. As long as it was, so long did it remain a consumer of food.
To him, indeed, the gods used to bring food in the forenoon, humans at midday, and the ancestors in the afternoon.

Indra, thus driven away and wandering, called out to Agni and Soma: "O Agni and Soma, you two indeed belong to me, and I belong to you; yet this [demon] belongs to neither of you. Why do you allow this Dasyu to grow? Turn back toward me!"

The two of them said, "What would happen to us from that? For them, he offered this cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma; therefore, there is a cake on eleven potsherds dedicated to Agni and Soma.
Those two turned back toward him;

after them followed all the gods, all knowledge, all glory, all food, and all prosperity. Having sacrificed with this, Indra became that which is now Indra. This, indeed, is the significance of the Full Moon sacrifice. Whoever, knowing thus, performs the Full Moon sacrifice, attains that very prosperity, becomes possessed of such glory, and becomes an eater of such food.
When Vṛtra was indeed slain, he lay there collapsed like a squeezed-out leather bag, or like a bellows from which the flour has been shaken out; Indra rushed toward him, intending to kill him.
He said:

"Do not strike me! You are indeed that very thing which I am now; do not destroy me, lest I become otherwise. "Then let food be mine," he said. "So be it," he replied. He split him in two. That which was his gentle essence, he made into the moon. And that which was his demonic (asurya) part, with that he pierced these creatures through the belly. Therefore they say, "Vṛtra was the eater of food then, and Vṛtra is the eater of food now. For when that [moon] waxes full, it swells from this very world. And when these creatures desire food, they bring tribute to that very Vṛtra, the belly. Whoever thus knows this Vṛtra as the eater of food, he indeed becomes an eater of food.
Then those deities who had followed Agni and Soma said: "O Agni and Soma, you two indeed receive the largest share among us; therefore, let us have a share along with you."

The two of them said, "What would accrue to us from that? [Agni and Soma replied,] "Whatever oblation one may offer to whichever deity, they shall sacrifice to you two first with clarified butter. Therefore, to whichever deity they offer an oblation, they sacrifice to Agni and Soma first with portions of clarified butter; but this does not apply at the Soma-sacrifice nor at the animal sacrifice, for they had said, "To whichever deity one may offer an oblation [there alone]."
That Agni said: "Let them offer to you all in me alone; I shall share that among you within myself. Therefore, they offer to all the gods in Agni; therefore they say, "Agni is all the deities."

Then Soma said: "Let them offer me alone for all of you; I shall share that [offering] with you within myself. Therefore, they offer Soma for all the gods; therefore, they say, "Soma is all the deities."

Now, because all the gods were established in Indra, therefore they say, "Indra is all the deities; Indra is the best of the gods. Indeed, in this way the gods became threefold, each belonging to a single deity. And he who knows this thus becomes the sole preeminent one among his own people.

This world is indeed twofold; there is no third: the moist and the dry. That which is dry belongs to Agni, and that which is moist belongs to Soma. Now, since this [world] is composed of these two alone, why is so much performed? Because the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) belong to Agni and Soma, the low-voiced sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja) belongs to Agni and Soma, and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to Agni and Soma. Since one obtains all this by means of just one of them, why is so much performed? For such is the power and the procreative capacity of Agni and Soma.

The sun is indeed of the nature of Agni; the moon is of the nature of Soma. Day is of the nature of Agni; night is of the nature of Soma. That half-month which waxes is of the nature of Agni; that which wanes is of the nature of Soma.

"By the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) alone one obtains the sun and the moon; by the silent sacrifice (upāṃśuyāja) alone one obtains day and night; and by the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) alone one obtains the half-months—so say some."

Regarding this, Āsuri said: "By means of the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), he obtains whichever two [days] he desires; by means of the low-voiced offering (upāṃśuyāja), he obtains day and night; and by means of the cake-offering (puroḍāśa), he obtains the half-months. 'May everything be obtained by me! May everything be conquered! With everything may I slay Vṛtra! With everything may I slay my hateful rival!'—it is for this reason that this much is performed."
Regarding this, they say:

"What is this kinship (jāmi) that is being performed? Since there is the butter for Agni and Soma, and the cake for Agni and Soma, that which is not separated [from the other] is kinship. But by this very means there is no kinship: one part belongs to the butter and the other to the cake; thus one becomes as it were different from the other, and the other as it were different from the other. Having recited a Ṛc verse, he offers with the word 'juṣāṇa' (enjoying); having recited a Ṛc verse, he offers with a Ṛc verse; thus one becomes as it were different from the other, and the other as it were different from the other. By this very means there is no kinship: he offers the butter in a low voice (upāṃśu), and the cake loudly (uccais). That which is in a low voice is the form belonging to Prajāpati; therefore, for that [butter], he recites an invitatory verse (anuvākyā) in the Anuṣṭubh metre, for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and Prajāpati is speech."

By means of this Upāṃśuyāja, the gods, having approached whichever of the Asuras they desired, struck them with the thunderbolt at the Vaṣaṭ-call. In the same way, this sacrificer, by means of this Upāṃśuyāja, having approached his evil, hateful rival, strikes him with the thunderbolt at the Vaṣaṭ-call. Therefore, he performs the Upāṃśuyāja.

Verily, having recited a *ṛc*, he offers with the word "juṣāṇa" (enjoying); accordingly, these creatures with teeth on only one side are produced, for the *ṛc* is bone and the tooth is bone; thus he makes this bone on only one side.
Then, having recited a Ṛc, he offers with a Ṛc.

Accordingly, these creatures with teeth on both sides are born; for the Ṛc is bone, and the tooth is bone, and thus he makes this bone on both sides. These indeed are the two kinds of creatures: those with teeth on one side and those with teeth on both sides. He who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice of the procreation of Agni and Soma, truly becomes abundant in offspring and cattle.

When he is about to fast for the full-moon sacrifice, he should not eat too much, as it were; for by that [moderation], he swallows this belly belonging to the Asuras with his oblations, while in the morning he belongs to the gods—this indeed is the proper procedure for the full-moon sacrifice.
He should indeed fast at the very moment [of the sacrifice], thinking:
"Right now I shall slay Vṛtra; right now I shall slay my hateful rival."
He should indeed fast on the later day alone.

For he who fasts on the current [day] moves as it were against his own kin; for when two [days] have met, it is uncertain which one will overcome the other, or which one will overcome the other. Now, he who fasts on the later day is like one who would grind down an opponent who has turned away and is not returning; he would simply be a slayer of another. Such is the case for him who fasts on the later day.
He should indeed fast on that very day.

For just as one might grind what has already been killed by another, so it is when he fasts on the later day; he becomes a mere imitator of another's deed and a follower of another's fast. Therefore, he should fast on that very day.

When Prajāpati was creating living beings, his joints gave way. Now, Prajāpati is indeed the year; these are its joints: the junctions of day and night, the full moon, the new moon, and the beginnings of the seasons.

With his joints dislocated, he was unable to join them together. The gods healed him with these oblation-sacrifices: by means of the Agnihotra, they healed and joined together his joint at the junctions of day and night; by means of the Full-moon and New-moon sacrifices, they healed and joined together his joint at the Full-moon and New-moon days; and by means of the Seasonal sacrifices, they healed and joined together his joints at the beginnings of the seasons.

With its joints joined together, it rose up toward this food—the very food of Prajāpati that exists here. He who, knowing this, fasts at the proper time, truly heals the joints of Prajāpati; Prajāpati protects him, and he becomes a consumer of food in exactly that way who, knowing this, fasts at the proper time. Therefore, one should indeed fast at the proper time.
The two butter-portions (ājyabhāgau) are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice;
therefore he offers them in front, for these eyes are in front. Thus he places the eyes in front, and that is why these eyes are in front.

Some offer the Āgneya Ājyabhāga in the eastern half of the northern half, and the Saumya Ājyabhāga in the eastern half of the southern half, saying, "Thus we place the two eyes in front. But that is somewhat uncertain; for the oblations are indeed the self of the sacrifice. Whatever he offers before the other oblations, by that he places the two eyes in front. He should offer the oblations at the very point where he considers the fire to be most brightly kindled, for oblations are successful only through an offering made into a well-kindled fire.
He indeed recites a *ṛc* and then offers with the formula "juṣāṇena.
Therefore, these two eyes, though boneless, are joined to the bony [head]. Now, if he were to recite a *ṛc* and then offer with a *ṛc*, he would surely make it bone, not an eye.
These, indeed, are they.

The form of Agni and Soma is inherent in this very [eye]: that which is white belongs to Agni, and that which is black belongs to Soma; or alternatively, that which is black belongs to Agni, and that which is white belongs to Soma. That which one looks with is the form of Agni, for when one looks, the eyes become as if dry, and what is dry belongs to Agni. That which one sleeps with is the form of Soma, for when one has slept, the eyes become as if moist, and Soma is indeed moist. He who knows these two Ājyabhāga portions of the eye becomes possessed of sight in this world until old age, and he becomes possessed of sight in the other world as well.

When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, he, considering himself weak and fearing "I have not slain him," went into hiding; he went to the furthest distances. The gods indeed knew: "Vṛtra has been slain, but Indra is lying hidden."
They set out to search for him.

Agni was the deity among the gods, Hiraṇyastūpa among the seers, and Bṛhatī among the meters. Agni found him; he came to this night together with him. He is indeed the Vasu of the gods, for he is their hero.

Those gods said, "Truly, today Vasu dwells with us—he who has blown upon us. For those two, they prepared this common oblation, just as one might cook a common mess of rice or a goat for two kinsmen or two friends who have arrived together; in that same way, they offered this common oblation to those two, a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni.
Indra said:
"When I hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, I was terrified; I am as it were emaciated. This does not satisfy me. Make for me that which will satisfy me. "So be it," the gods replied.

Those gods said, "Nothing other than Soma would satisfy him; let us collect Soma for him. They collected Soma for him. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, which is the moon. When this [moon] is not seen either in the east or in the west on that night, it comes to this world; it enters right here into the waters and the plants. It is indeed the *vasu* (wealth) of the gods, for it is their food. Because he dwells here as their *amā* (at home) on that night, therefore it is called *Amāvāsyā*.

Having caused it to settle with cow-products, they collected it: what he had eaten from the plants, that from the plants; what he had drunk from the waters, that from the waters. Having thus collected it, having pressed it, and having made it strong, they gave it to him.
He said, "It indeed nourishes me, but it does not settle within me; devise a way so that it may settle within me. They settled it within him by means of boiled milk.

This very thing, being indeed the same—being milk, being Indra’s own essence—is nevertheless called by different names. Because he said, "It impels me," therefore it is called *dadhi* (curd); and because they prepared him with boiled milk (*śṛta*), therefore it is called *śr̥ta* (boiled).

Just as a stalk swells, so does he swell; he drives away evil and jaundice. This indeed is the significance of the New Moon sacrifice. He who, knowing this, performs the *saṃnayya* offering, truly swells with offspring and cattle and drives away evil. Therefore, one should indeed perform the *saṃnayya* offering.
Regarding this they say:

"One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not offer the *saṃnāya* (curdled milk mixture); for this is indeed a Soma oblation, and it is not secured for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice; therefore, one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not offer the *saṃnāya*."
Therefore, one should lead it forward in the same way.

For we have heard that in this connection he said: "Surely, do not perform the Soma sacrifice for me; rather, you shall prepare for me this means of strengthening. He replied, "This does not satisfy me; provide me with that which will satisfy me. Therefore, they prepared that means of strengthening for him. Consequently, even one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice should lead it forward in the same way.

The full-moon sacrifice is indeed the slayer of Vṛtra, for by it Indra slew Vṛtra; and this new-moon sacrifice is likewise the slaying of Vṛtra, for they provided nourishment to him after he had slain Vṛtra.

This very Full-moon sacrifice is indeed the slayer of Vṛtra; and this moon is Vṛtra. When, on that night, he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then by means of this [sacrifice] he destroys him entirely and leaves nothing remaining of him. Verily, he who knows this destroys all evil and leaves nothing remaining of evil.

Regarding this, some indeed fast after seeing [the moon], thinking, "Tomorrow it will not rise; thus the food of the gods remains undiminished, and we shall offer it to them from here. That is indeed successful when, while the previous food is still undiminished, another food arrives; he becomes truly possessed of abundant food. But for one who does not sacrifice with Soma, yet sacrifices with milk—that King Soma indeed remains there.

Then, just as before, they eat only the plants and drink only the waters; those [cows] yield only milk. Now, this King Soma is the food of the gods, which is the moon. When he is not seen either in the east or in the west during that night, he comes to this world; he enters here into the waters and the plants. Having gathered him from the waters and the plants, they generate him from the oblations. Having been born from the oblations, he is seen in the west.

This very food of the gods indeed circulates without ever being exhausted; and for him who knows this thus, food becomes inexhaustible in this world and his merit becomes imperishable in the other world.

On that very night, food for the gods falls away from them and comes to this world. Those gods desired, "How can this come back to us? How can it not simply perish and go away forever? They placed their hope in those who perform the *saṃnaya* sacrifice, thinking, "These very ones, having gathered it together, will give it back to us. Indeed, both one's own kin and strangers place their hope in him who knows this; for people place their hope in whoever attains the highest state.

Now, this very one who shines yonder is indeed Indra; and that which is the moon is Vṛtra. He is his rival, as it were; therefore, even though he has risen far away in the past, on this night he sinks down right near him, and he enters his open mouth.
Having swallowed it, he rises;
he is seen neither in front nor behind. Indeed, he swallows his hateful rival; "He truly exists as this alone, and he has no rivals," so they say of one who knows this thus.
Having cleared it out, he discards it.

Once cleared, it is seen from behind; it swells up again. It swells up again for the sake of this very food-eating. Indeed, if an enemy or rival of his prospers through trade or by some other means, he prospers again for the sake of this very food-eating, provided that he knows this thus.

Regarding this, some perform the offering saying, "To Mahendra," arguing that he was Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra, but having slain Vṛtra, he became Mahendra just as a great king becomes [Mahārāja] after conquering; therefore they say "To Mahendra. However, one should rather offer it saying, "To Indra," for he was indeed Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra, and it was Indra who slew Vṛtra; therefore, one should offer it saying, "To Indra."

He drives away the calves with a branch of the *parṇa* tree. Now, as to why he drives away the calves with a *parṇa* branch: when Gāyatrī flew toward Soma, her foot was cut off as she was bringing it. As she stretched out [to seize him], she lopped off a leaf (*parṇa*). That [leaf] fell, either from Gāyatrī or from King Soma, and having fallen, it became a *parṇa* tree; therefore it is called *parṇa*. He thinks, "Whatever of Soma is deposited there, let that also be here"; for this reason, he drives away the calves with a *parṇa* branch.
He gathers it together with the formula, "For food thee!
For strength thee! When he says "for food thee," he says it for the sake of rain; when he says "for strength thee," he says it for that vigorous sap which is produced from rain.
Then they drive the calves away from their mothers.

He touches the calf with a branch, saying, "Ye are winds! For he who blows here is indeed Vāyu; he causes all this to swell—whatever he rains down here, he is the sweller of these [cows]. Therefore he says, "Ye are winds. Some say, "Ye are approaching winds," for the second one comes toward it; but one should not speak thus.

Then he touches one of the mothers with a branch, having separated her from her calf, saying: "May the divine Savitṛ impel you. For Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; [thinking] "Impelled by Savitṛ, may she prepare the sacrifice," he therefore says, "May the divine Savitṛ impel you."
"For the most excellent rite":
sacrifice is indeed the most excellent rite; therefore, he says, "for the most excellent rite."
"Swell up, O inviolable ones, as a portion for Indra!"—
just as one points out the oblation for a deity when taking it up, even so does he point it out for the deity when he says, "Swell up, O inviolable ones, as a portion for Indra."
"May they be prolific, free from disease, and free from consumption"—in this there is nothing hidden.

"May no thief master you, may no evil-speaker [master you]"—by this he means to say, "may no destructive demons (nāṣṭrā) master you. "May you be many and firm with this cattle-lord"—by this he means to say, "may you be many and not depart from this sacrificer."

Then, either to the east of the Āhavanīya shed or the Gārhapatya shed, he hides a branch, saying, "Protect the cattle of the sacrificer! By this means, through the Brahman, he entrusts the sacrificer's cattle to it for their protection.
Over that [strainer] he makes it pure with the formula, "Thou art the purifier of wealth. The sacrifice, indeed, is wealth; therefore he says, "Thou art the purifier of wealth."
Then, on that night, he offers the Agnihotra with barley-gruel (yavāgū).

For this milk has already been designated as the oblation for a specific deity; if he were to offer it with milk, it would be as if one were offering to one deity an oblation that had already been taken out for another. Therefore, on that night, he offers the Agnihotra with barley-gruel. While the Agnihotra is being offered, the Ukha pot is prepared; then he says, "Announce when she has been let loose," and when he announces, "She has been let loose."

Then he takes up the pan with the words, "Thou art heaven; thou art earth. By saying this, he indeed praises it and thereby strengthens it when he says, "Thou art heaven; thou art earth. With the words, "Thou art Mātariśvan’s cauldron," he thus prepares the sacrifice; he heats it just as one would heat a cauldron (gharma). With the words, "Thou art all-sustaining; by the highest support, stand firm, do not waver! he makes it firm and renders it unshakable. By saying, "May thy lord of the sacrifice not waver,"—for the lord of the sacrifice is the sacrificer—he thereby invokes freedom from wavering for the sacrificer.
Then they set down the strainer.

He should indeed set it down facing east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or he may set it down facing north, for the north is the direction of men. This strainer is indeed he who blows here; he blows across these worlds. Therefore, he should set it down facing north.

Just as they purify King Soma with a filter, even so does he purify this; for that filter with which they purify King Soma has its fringes directed toward the north; therefore, he should place it facing north.

He places it down with the formula, "Thou art the purifier of wealth. The sacrifice, indeed, is wealth; therefore he says, "Thou art the purifier of wealth. With the words, "Hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed," he thus praises it and magnifies it when he says, "Hundred-streamed, thousand-streamed."
Then he remains silent until three [cows] have been milked; for the sacrifice is speech, and thus he extends the sacrifice without disturbance.

He consecrates it as it is being brought: "May the god Savitṛ purify thee with the filter of Vasu, with a hundred streams, well-purifying. Just as they purify King Soma with a filter there, even so does he purify this here.

Then he asks, "From whom did you milk?"—"From that one," she replies. "She is Viśvāyu. Then he asks the second: "From whom did you milk?"—"From that one," she replies. "She is Viśvakarman. Then he asks the third: "From whom did you milk?"—"From that one," she replies. "She is Viśvadhāyā. In that he asks, he thereby bestows heroic powers upon them. He milks three; for these worlds are three; he thus gathers this from these very worlds. Then he speaks his desire.

Then, having caused the best cow to be milked, he pours a small amount from the vessel with which she was milked into that [milk], stirs it, and pours it back, thinking, "Whatever of the milk has been lost here, let that also be here," for the sake of the completeness of the essence; for when it rains, plants are born, and by eating the plants and drinking the water, this essence comes into being; therefore, it is for the sake of the completeness of the essence. Having poured it out, he seasons it; he thus makes it strong, and that is why, having poured it out, he seasons it.

He sprinkles it, saying, "I sprinkle thee, the portion of Indra, with Soma. Just as when he takes the oblation for a deity he specifies it, so now he specifies it for the deity when he says, "thee, the portion of Indra. By saying, "with Soma I sprinkle thee," he makes it palatable for the gods.

Then he covers it with a vessel full of water turned face upwards, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits and demons (rakṣas) touch this from above. For water is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, by means of that thunderbolt, he drives away the destructive spirits and demons from here. Therefore, he covers it with a vessel full of water turned face upwards.

He covers it, saying, "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation. Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he entrusts this oblation to the sacrifice for its protection. Therefore he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation."
Verily, he who exists is born with a debt;
as soon as he is born, [he owes it] to the gods, the seers, the ancestors, and to men.
Whenever he performs a sacrifice, by that very act he incurs a debt to the gods; for it is this which he does for them—namely, that he sacrifices to them and offers oblations to them.

Now, when he recites [the Veda], by that he incurs a debt to the seers (ṛṣis); for he performs this service for them, as they say of one who has studied the Veda: "He is a treasure-keeper for the seers."
Now, when one desires offspring, by that very fact a debt is incurred toward the ancestors; for he performs this service for them in that his offspring becomes continuous and uninterrupted.

Now, in that he provides clothing, by that he incurs a debt to human beings; for when he clothes them and gives them food, he performs this service for them. He who performs all these [duties] is one who has fulfilled his task; for him everything is attained, everything is conquered.

That debt which he incurs toward the gods at birth—he discharges it when he sacrifices; and when he offers oblations in the fire, he discharges it by that. Therefore, whatever one offers in the fire is called an *avadāna* (a sacrificial portion).
That indeed becomes a fourfold portioning.

This, namely, is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), then the offering verse (yājyā), then the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and then that deity for whom the oblation is intended as the fourth. For thus are the deities dependent upon the portions, or rather, the portions are dependent upon the deities. That which would be a fifth portioning is redundant; for to whom indeed would he offer it? Therefore, it becomes a fourfold portioning.
Moreover, it consists of five portions.

The sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; such is the perfection of the fivefold portion. He indeed becomes rich in offspring and cattle for whom the fivefold portion is prepared by one who knows this. Now, that which is the fourfold portion is well-known among the Kuru-Pañcālas; therefore, it is made fourfold.

He should indeed cut off only as much as is necessary; for if he were to cut off too much, he would make it human, and that which is human is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice," he should therefore cut off only as much as is necessary.

Having spread a layer of clarified butter (ājya), he takes two portions of the sacrificial food (havis) and then pours clarified butter over them from above. For there are indeed two offerings: one is the Soma-offering, and the other is the clarified-butter offering. Of these, the Soma-offering is unique; whereas this clarified-butter offering—which consists of the oblation-sacrifice (haviryajña) and the animal sacrifice (paśu)—he thereby makes into clarified butter itself. Therefore, there is clarified butter on both sides. Indeed, clarified butter is what is dear to the gods; thus he makes it dear to the gods. Therefore, there is clarified butter on both sides.
That [earth] is indeed the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), and this [heaven] is the offering verse (*yājyā*).

Both of these are females; their union is the *vaṣaṭ*-call itself. Now, that which is this *vaṣaṭ*-call is he who shines yonder. Rising, he indeed hastens toward that [heaven], and setting, he hastens toward this [earth]. Through this, they two procreate this progeny of theirs, which is their offspring.

Having recited the invitatory verse (anuvākyā) and having run through the offering verse (yājyā), he utters the vaṣaṭ-call from behind. For a male approaches a female from behind; thus, having placed both [verses] in front, he causes them to be approached by the male vaṣaṭ-call. Therefore, one should either offer together with the vaṣaṭ-call or after the vaṣaṭ has been uttered.
The *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed the vessel of the gods.

Just as one would take up [food] from a vessel and offer it, so it is with that; for if one were to offer before the *vaṣaṭ*-call, it would be as if that [offering] were smeared on the ground below—such would it be. Therefore, one should either offer together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or once the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.
It is just as if one were to pour semen into the womb;

so it is with that. Now, if one were to offer the oblation before the *vaṣaṭ*-call, it would be as if the semen poured into the womb were to belong to another woman. Therefore, one should either offer the oblation together with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, or once the *vaṣaṭ*-call has been uttered.
That [heaven] indeed is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), and this [earth] is the offering verse (yājyā).

That [heaven] is the Gāyatrī, and this [earth] is the Triṣṭubh. He recites the Gāyatrī; in doing so, while reciting that [heaven], he recites this [earth], for that [heaven] is the invitatory verse and this [earth] is the Gāyatrī.

Then he sacrifices with a Triṣṭubh verse. He sacrifices with this one because it is the *yājyā* (offering verse) for that [other verse]; over that [other verse] he utters the *vaṣaṭ* call, for that [other verse] is indeed a Triṣṭubh. Thus he makes these two a pair; therefore these two enjoy together. Following the enjoyment of these two, all these creatures enjoy together.
He should indeed recite the invitatory verse as if counting it.

For that [heaven] is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), for it is great; indeed, that form belongs to the Bṛhat-sāman. With the offering verse (yājyā), they hasten quickly; for this [earth] is the offering verse, for it is the Rathantara; indeed, that form belongs to the Rathantara. One summons with the invitatory verse and bestows with the offering verse. Therefore, the form of the invitatory verse is: "I call, we call; may he come and sit upon this sacred grass (barhis). For with that [verse] one summons; and the form of the offering verse is: "Eat the oblation, enjoy the oblation; O bull, sprinkle it, taste it, drink! For with that [verse] one bestows.

That which has its mark in the east shall be the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*), for that [eastern direction] is indeed the invitatory verse; below that [mark] of yonder [direction] are the moon, the stars, and the sun.
Now, that which has its mark above should be the *yājyā* verse; for this is the *yājyā*, and its mark above consists of the plants, the trees, the waters, the fire, and these creatures.

That indeed is a successful invitatory formula (anuvākyā) from whose first word one pronounces the name of the deity; that is a successful offering formula (yājyā) from whose last word one utters the *vaṣaṭ* over the deity. For the deity is indeed vigor (*vīrya*), and the verse is vigor; thus, having encompassed it on both sides with vigor, he presents the oblation to whichever deity it belongs.

He indeed utters "vaug. The *vaṣaṭ*-call is speech; he thus pours forth seed through speech. He says "ṣaṭ"; the seasons are six; he thus pours forth that seed in the seasons, and the seasons, having received the poured seed, produce these creatures. Therefore, he utters the *vaṣaṭ* in this manner.

Now, both the gods and the asuras, being the offspring of Prajāpati, came to their father Prajāpati’s inheritance. Of these two half-months, that which waxes the gods took possession of, and that which wanes the asuras took possession of.
Those gods desired:

"How might we also win over this [world] which belongs to the Asuras? They went about praising and toiling, and they beheld this sacrifice of oblations, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*). They sacrificed with them; having sacrificed with them, they won over this [world] as well.

That which belonged to the Asuras—when these two [the sun and moon] revolve together, then a month comes into being; by months, the year; and the year is indeed everything. Thus, the gods appropriated everything belonging to the Asuras and excluded the rival Asuras from everything. He who knows this appropriates everything belonging to his rivals and excludes his rivals from everything.
That which belonged to the gods was *yava*, for by it the gods joined together (*ayuvata*); that which belonged to the Asuras was *ayava*, for by it the Asuras did not join together.

Moreover, they say otherwise: that which belonged to the gods was *ayava* (non-barley), for the Asuras did not appropriate it; that which belonged to the Asuras was *yava* (barley), for the gods appropriated it. *Sabdamah* is the day, *sagara* is the night, the *māsas* are *yavyā*, and *sumeka* is the year. Indeed, "sumeka" is its name because it is well-measured (*su-mita*). Since there are both *yavas* and *ayavas*, and because one measures (*yav*) as it were, and because he becomes their Hotṛ, therefore they call it the *Yāvihotra*.

By means of sacrifice, indeed, the gods ascended to heaven; then that god who rules over cattle was left behind here. Therefore they say he is "Vāstavya" (the Dweller), for he remained behind at the dwelling-place.
By the very same path by which the gods ascended to heaven, they continued to move along, chanting and exerting themselves; but that god who rules over cattle remained behind here.
He reflected:
"Alas, they will exclude me from the sacrifice. He stepped out after them and, moving forward, rose up from the north; that is the time for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

Those gods said, "Do not let it fall apart! He replied, "In that case, do not exclude me from the sacrifices; provide for me a share within the oblation. They said, "So be it. He drew it together; he did not cast it away, nor did he harm anyone.
Those gods said,
"Consider how we may offer an oblation to him with all the sacrificial offerings that have been taken for us."
They said to the Adhvaryu:
"Pour clarified butter over the sacrificial oblations as before, cause them to swell again for the sake of a single portion so that they may not be stale, and then cut off the portions one by one."

The Adhvaryu then poured clarified butter over the oblations as before; he caused each single portion to swell again and made them free from weariness (ayātayāman), and then he cut off one portion from each. Therefore they say, "It belongs to Vāstu," for that which remains when the oblations have been offered is indeed the *vāstu* (site/remainder) of the sacrifice. Consequently, for whichever deity the oblation is taken, the Sviṣṭakṛt is everywhere partaken of along with it, for the gods everywhere partook of him.

Now, it is performed with the words, "To Agni. For he is indeed that god; these are his names: "Śarva," as they call him in the East; "Bhava," as the Bāhīkas call him; "Paśūnām Pati" (Lord of Beasts), "Rudra," and "Agni. Of these, his other names are not peaceful at all, but "Agni" is the most peaceful; therefore, it is performed with the words, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" (the well-offering-maker).

They said, "Whatever we have sacrificed here in you over there, make that well-sacrificed for us. He made it well-sacrificed for them; therefore, he is called Sviṣṭakṛt (the maker of the well-sacrificed).
Having recited the invitatory verse (anuvākyā), he looks on:

"Agni Sviṣṭakṛt has sacrificed; Agni has sacrificed to the dear abodes of Agni"—thereby he mentions the butter-portion belonging to Agni. "He has sacrificed to the dear abodes of Soma"—thereby he mentions the butter-portion belonging to Soma. "He has sacrificed to the dear abodes of Agni"—thereby he mentions that cake which belongs to Agni and is not displaced from either [offering].
Then, according to the respective deities:

"He has sacrificed to the dear abodes of the gods who drink the clarified butter"—by this he refers to the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings, for the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings are indeed the gods who drink the clarified butter. "May he sacrifice to the dear abodes of Agni, the Hotṛ"—by this he refers to Agni as the Hotṛ. Having thus prepared this offering for him, the gods then made peace with him through it; they invited him back to his dear abode. Therefore, he contemplates in this manner.

Regarding this, some perform the invocation of the deity first, before the *ayāṭ* formula, saying, "He has sacrificed to Agni," "He has sacrificed to Soma. But one should not do it thus; for those who perform the invocation of the deity first, before the *ayāṭ* formula, they act in a contrary manner toward the sacrifice. For when he speaks for the first time, he speaks the *ayāṭ* formula itself. Therefore, one should perform the *ayāṭ* formula first.
"May he worship his own greatness.

For when he invokes those deities there, he also invokes his own greatness. Therefore, before this, nothing whatsoever is done for the sake of his own greatness; it is here that he gratifies him. Thus, this [deity] of his becomes invoked not in vain. That is why he says, "May he worship his own greatness."
"Come, O you who are worthy of sacrifice, for food!
Food, indeed, is progeny; thus he makes this progeny inclined toward sacrifice, and so these progeny move about, sacrificing, praising, and toiling.

"May Jātavedas accept the oblations at the sacrifice"—by this he prays for the success of the sacrifice; for when the gods accept the oblation, by that they indeed achieve great victory. Therefore he says, "May they accept the oblation."

Now, as for these two, the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā*, which are most appropriately assigned here: the third pressing belongs to the *Sviṣṭakṛt*, and the third pressing belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). "Piprīhi devān uśato yaviṣṭha" (Satisfy the desiring gods, O youngest one)—this is the *vaiśvadeva* character of the *anuvākyā*. "Agne yad adya viśo adhvarasya hotaḥ" (O Agni, whatever today of the people's sacrifice, O Hotṛ)—this is the *vaiśvadeva* character of the *yājyā*. Since these two possess such forms, they thus have the form of the third pressing; therefore, indeed, these two are the most appropriately assigned *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* in this context.
These two verses are indeed in the Triṣṭubh metre.

Now, that which belongs to the Sviṣṭakṛt is the site of the sacrifice, and the site is devoid of power; whereas the Triṣṭubh is power and vigor. Thus, he places power and vigor into the site, into the Sviṣṭakṛt; therefore, these two verses are in the Triṣṭubh metre.
Moreover, they are indeed in the *anuṣṭubh* metre;

for the *anuṣṭubh* is a dwelling-place (*vāstu*), and the *Sviṣṭakṛt* is a dwelling-place: he thus places a dwelling-place in a dwelling-place. A dwelling-place is indeed slippery; he whose [offerings] are in the *anuṣṭubh* metre while he knows this slips away from offspring and cattle.

Now Bhāllaveya made the *anuṣṭubh* the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) and the *triṣṭubh* the offering verse (*yājyā*), thinking, "I am grasping both together. He fell from his chariot; having fallen, he even broke his arm. He reflected, "What have I done that I have come to this distress? He thought it was because he had performed something contrary (*viloma*) in the sacrifice. Therefore, one should not do anything contrary; both verses should be of the same metre—either both *anuṣṭubhs* or both *triṣṭubhs*.
He indeed cuts from the northern half;

he offers in the northern half, for this is the quarter of this deity. Therefore, he cuts from the northern half and offers in the northern half. For it was from that very quarter that he arose; they appeased him from that very place. Therefore, he cuts from the northern half and offers in the northern half.
He offers that [oblation] as if apart from the other oblations.

The other oblations are followed by the birth of cattle; the Sviṣṭakṛt belongs to Rudra, and if he were to conjoin it with the other oblations, he would subject the cattle to Rudra. His household cattle would then go away, being utterly destroyed. Therefore, he offers it as if apart from the other oblations.

This indeed is that sacrifice by which the gods ascended to heaven; this is the Āhavanīya fire, and that which was left behind here is the Gārhapatya fire; therefore, they draw it forth from the Gārhapatya towards the east.
Or rather, he should place it at eight steps;
for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and by means of the Gāyatrī, he thus ascends to heaven.
One should study it in eleven sections;
for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and by means of the Triṣṭubh, he thus ascends to heaven.
He should lay it down on twelve potsherds.

The Jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables; by means of the Jagatī, he thus ascends to heaven. There is no fixed measure here; wherever he himself may think in his mind, there he should lay it down. And even if he draws out [the fire] only a little toward the east, by that very act he ascends to heaven.

Regarding this they say: "One should cook the sacrificial offerings on the Āhavanīya fire. For from there the gods ascended to heaven; thenceforth, praising and toiling, they moved about, thinking, "On this fire let us cook the offerings; on this let us extend the sacrifice. If one were to cook the offerings on the Gārhapatya fire, it would be as if one were stumbling away from the offerings. The Āhavanīya is the sacrifice; [therefore one should think], "On the sacrifice itself we shall extend the sacrifice."

Moreover, they cook on the *gārhapatya* fire itself; for this [āhavanīya] is indeed the *āhavanīya*, yet it is not truly so for that purpose for which they would cook what is uncooked in it, nor for that purpose for which they would offer what is cooked in it. Therefore, he may do as he desires in either case.

That very sacrifice said: "I am indeed afraid of nakedness. "What is your protection against nakedness? "Let them strew grass all around me. Therefore, they strew grass all around the fire. "I am indeed afraid of thirst. "What is your satisfaction? "May I be satisfied after the satisfaction of a Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, when the sacrifice is completed, one should say, "Let the Brāhmaṇa be gratified"; thus he satisfies the sacrifice itself.
Thinking, "May I be united with her as a pair, whether by day or at dawn," he united with her.
That indeed became an offense against the gods:
"He who thus makes his own daughter our sister!"

Those gods said, "This god who rules over animals acts with excessive overreaching, he who thus makes his own daughter our sister; pierce him! Rudra, advancing toward him, pierced him; his semen was discharged prematurely, and from that indeed it came into being.
Therefore, this was declared by the Seer:

"When the father, having united with his own daughter, poured forth his seed upon the earth. This refers to the *Agnimāruta* hymn; therein it is explained how the gods generated that seed. When the wrath of those gods departed, they healed Prajāpati and cut out that splinter from him. Indeed, Prajāpati is the sacrifice itself.
They said,
"Devise a way so that this [offering] shall not go away, and so that it may be less than the oblation."

They said, "Carry this to Bhaga as he sits to the south; Bhaga will eat it, and thus it will become as if it were offered as a libation. So they carried it to Bhaga as he sat to the south, and Bhaga looked at it; his eyes burst out. Truly, that was how it was; therefore they say, "Bhaga is blind."

They said, "Surely it has not subsided here; let us offer this to Pūṣan. So they offered it to Pūṣan, and Pūṣan ate it; he knocked out his own teeth. Thus, indeed, it was then; therefore they say, "Pūṣan is toothless. Therefore, when they prepare a pap for Pūṣan, they make it of flour that has been ground, just as if for one who is toothless.

They said, "Surely we have no hope here; let them carry this away to Bṛhaspati. So they carried it away to Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati then had recourse to Savitṛ for instigation, saying, "Savitṛ is indeed the instigator of the gods; let him instigate this for me. Thereupon Savitṛ, as the instigator, instigated it for him; and so, being instigated by Savitṛ, it did not injure him. From that time onwards it has been appeased. This is the underlying reason why there is the *prāśitra* (the portion to be consumed).

When he cuts off the *prāśitra* (the portion for the Brahman), he thereby fashions out of that very thing whatever in the sacrifice is pierced and whatever belongs to Rudra. Then he touches water; water is a means of pacification, so he pacifies it with water. Then he cuts off the *iḍā* portions from the victims.

He should indeed cut off only as much as is necessary; in that way the splinter is removed. Therefore, he should cut off only as much as is necessary. He should provide clarified butter on one side—either below or above—so that it becomes like a hollow channel; in that way it flows out. Therefore, he should provide clarified butter on one side—either below or above.
Having spread a layer of clarified butter, he cuts two portions from the sacrificial food and then pours clarified butter over them; this is exactly like the cutting of portions in a sacrifice.

Therefore, one should not carry it around by the front. Some indeed carry it around by the front, [thinking] that cattle approach the sacrificer from the front toward the west; however, he would subject the cattle to the power of Rudra if he were to carry it around by the front. His cattle and household would go away as if being struck down. Therefore, he should simply step across transversely. Thus he does not subject the cattle to the power of Rudra; he fashions him (the sacrificer) outwards transversely.
He accepts it with the formula:
"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I accept thee."
Just as in the past Bṛhaspati ran to Savitṛ for impulsion, thinking, "Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods;

let him impel this for me," and so Savitṛ, the impeller, impelled it for him, and thus, being impelled by Savitṛ, he was not harmed—so too does this [sacrificer] now run to Savitṛ for impulsion. For Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thinking, "Let him impel this for me," Savitṛ, the impeller, impels it for him, and thus, being impelled by Savitṛ, he is not harmed.
He eats it with the formula, "I eat thee with the mouth of Agni. For nothing whatsoever harms Agni, and thus this does not harm him either.
Therefore, one should not chew with the teeth, lest this power of Rudra injure his teeth; therefore, one should not chew with the teeth.
Then he sips water; water is peace, so with that water he pacifies by means of peace; then, having rinsed the vessel.

Then they bring him the Brahman’s portion. For the Brahman sits to the south of the sacrifice as its protector; knowing this to be his share, he remains there. They brought him the *prāśitra* (the fore-portion), and he ate it. Now, that which they bring to him as the Brahman’s portion, by that he becomes a sharer. Whatever part of the sacrifice remains uncompleted from that point onward, he protects it. Therefore, indeed, they bring him the Brahman’s portion.
He should indeed remain strictly silent.

For they tear asunder and destroy the sacrifice who perform the *iḍā* offering of the cooked sacrifice (*pākayajña*) in the middle of the [Soma] sacrifice. Among the officiating priests, the Brahman is the best physician; it is he who heals the sacrifice. He would not heal it if he were to speak while seated there; therefore, he should remain strictly silent.

If he should utter human speech before that time, he should then mutter a verse or a sacrificial formula belonging to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he takes up the sacrifice again—this is indeed the expiation for that.

When he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth," then the Brahman mutters: "This sacrifice, O Savitṛ, the gods have proclaimed to thee. Thereby he has recourse to Savitṛ for instigation, for he is the instigator of the gods. "To Bṛhaspati, the Brahman"—for Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman of the gods; thus he announces it to him who is the Brahman of the gods. Therefore he says, "To Bṛhaspati, the Brahman. "By him protect the sacrifice, by him the lord of the sacrifice, by him protect me"—in this there is nothing obscure.
"May the speed of the mind enjoy the clarified butter"—for by the mind indeed all this is attained;

thus, by the mind alone he attains all this. "May Bṛhaspati extend this sacrifice; may he make this sacrifice unimpaired"—he thereby joins together what has been torn asunder. "May all the gods rejoice here"—for all the gods are indeed the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ); thus, by means of the All, he joins it together. If he should so desire, he should say, "Establishment!"; but if he should not so desire, he need not heed it.
In the morning, they brought water for Manu to wash his hands, just as people bring it with both hands for washing today; while he was washing himself, a fish entered his hands.

He spoke these words to him: "Sustain me; I will carry you across. "How will you carry me across? he asked. "The flood will sweep away all these creatures; then I will carry you across," he replied. "What is your sustenance? he asked.

He said: "As long as we remain small, our danger from predators is indeed great; even one fish swallows another. First, keep me in a jar; when I have grown beyond that, then dig a pit and keep me in it; when I have grown beyond that, then cast me into the ocean. Only then will I be free from danger."
"Kaṣa has always been here.

For he increases his seniority; therefore, in such-and-such a year, a flood will come. Prepare a boat for me and wait. When that flood has risen, you shall board the boat, and then I will carry you across."

Having made him thus, he cast him into the ocean. When that year had arrived, he prepared a boat and waited for it. When the flood rose, he boarded the boat. A fish swam up to him; he fastened the boat’s rope to the fish’s horn, and by means of it, he was carried over that northern mountain.

He said: "I have indeed saved you. Tie a boat to a tree; however, let not the water reach you while you are on the mountain. As far as the water rises, so far must you descend. He descended exactly that far. This is why there is the descent of Manu from the northern mountain. The flood swept away all those creatures, and here Manu alone remained.
Desiring offspring, he wandered about performing austerities.

There, too, he sacrificed with the *pākayajña* (cooked sacrifice); he offered clarified butter, curds, whey, and clotted curds into the waters. Then, after a year, a woman came into being; she rose up dripping with moisture, and clarified butter would remain standing in her footprint. Mitra and Varuṇa united with her.

They said to her, "Who are you? She replied, "Say that I am the daughter of Manu. "No," they said, "we belong to him who begot us. She said, "I belong to him alone who begot me. They both desired her; she either perceived it or did not perceive it, and so she went away. She came to Manu.

Manu said to her, "Who are you? She replied, "I am your daughter. He asked, "How so, O Blessed One? How can I have a daughter? She said, "Those offerings of ghee, curds, whey, and clotted milk which you poured into the waters—you produced me from them; I am that blessing (āśis). Make me fit for the sacrifice. For if you make me fit for the sacrifice, you will become rich in offspring and cattle; whatever blessing you shall invoke with me, all that shall be fulfilled for you. So they made her fit for the sacrifice in the middle of it, for this is the middle of the sacrifice, namely that which lies between the fore-sacrifices (prayāja) and the after-sacrifices (anuyāja).
Exerting himself with those two, he practiced austerities, desiring offspring.
Through them, he brought forth this progeny which is the progeny of Manu; and whatever blessing he invoked by means of them, all that was fulfilled for him.
This very Iḍā is the source.
He who, knowing this, proceeds with the Iḍā, is born with that same progeny with which Manu was born; and whatever blessing he invokes with her, all that is fulfilled for him.
It indeed consists of five cuttings;
for the *iḍā* is cattle, and cattle are fivefold; therefore it consists of five cuttings.

Having divided the *iḍā*, he breaks off the eastern half of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and places it to the east of the *dhruvā* ladle; having handed it to the *hotṛ*, he goes toward the south.
He anoints the Hotṛ here;
he anoints the lips of the Hotṛ [with the formula]: "With the lord of the mind, I eat of what has been offered by thee, for the sake of desire and for the sake of the out-breath."
Then he smears it here on the Hotṛ; he smears it on the Hotṛ’s lips with the formula: "I eat of what has been offered by thee, O Lord of Speech, for the sake of strength and the upward breath."

Manu, indeed, was afraid of this: "This is the most vulnerable point of my sacrifice, namely this Iḍā belonging to the domestic sacrifice; what if the Rakṣases should destroy my sacrifice here? He caused her to reach that place before the Rakṣases, thinking, "Before the Rakṣases! Before the Rakṣases! In the same way, he now causes her to reach that place before the Rakṣases, thinking, "Before the Rakṣases! Before the Rakṣases! And as to why he does not eat it visibly, it is so that he may not eat it without having invoked it; thus he causes her to reach him when he smears it upon his lips.
Then he portions out [the sacrificial portion] into the hand of the Hotṛ.

Although it is already a collected portion, he thereby places her visibly upon the Hotṛ; through that which has entered his own self, the Hotṛ invokes a blessing for the sacrificer. Therefore, he portions it out into the hand of the Hotṛ.

Then he calls out in a low voice. For Manu indeed was afraid of this, thinking: "This most essential part of my sacrifice is this Iḍā, who belongs to the domestic sacrifice; what if the Rakṣases should destroy my sacrifice here? He called her out in a low voice, saying, "Before the Rakṣases! Before the Rakṣases! And so does this sacrificer now call her out in a low voice, saying, "Before the Rakṣases! Before the Rakṣases!"

He invokes: "The Rathantara has been invoked together with the earth; may the Rathantara invoke me together with the earth! The Vāmadevya has been invoked together with the intermediate space; may the Vāmadevya invoke me together with the intermediate space! The Bṛhat has been invoked together with the sky; may the Bṛhat invoke me together with the sky! Thus, while invoking this [earth], he invokes these worlds and these Sāmans.
"The cows have been invoked together with the bull"—the *iḍā* is indeed cattle;
thus he invokes her cryptically. By saying "together with the bull," he invokes her as being accompanied by a mate.
"Invoked by the seven hotṛs!"—
thereby he invokes her with the seven hotṛs and with the Soma sacrifice.
"Upahūtā iḍā taturiḥ!"—thus he invokes her directly; "taturiḥ," he says, because she indeed overcomes all evil; therefore he says, "taturiḥ."
"The friend has been invited;

let there be a draught"—the friend and the draught are indeed the vital breaths; thus he invites the vital breath. "He has been invited—Heg!"—thus he invites the body; thus he invites it in its entirety.

Then he performs the invocation: "Iḍā, invoked! Invoked Iḍā! May Iḍā invoke us; O invoked Iḍā! By this, he invokes her directly while she is already invoked. For she who was there was indeed a cow; and since a cow has four feet, he therefore invokes her four times.

He indeed calls upon her four times; yet he calls upon her as it were variously, to avoid sameness—for he would commit a repetition if he were to call "Iḍā invoked! Iḍā invoked!"—but rather he should call, "Invoked is Iḍā! or "O Iḍā, invoked! Thus he calls her hitherward; and by saying "Invoked is Iḍā," he calls her thitherward. By saying "May Iḍā call us hither," he does not exclude himself from this, and it becomes as it were otherwise. By saying "Iḍā invoked," he again calls her hitherward; thus he calls her both hitherward and thitherward.

"Manu’s daughter, Ghṛtapadī. For Manu indeed begot her first; therefore he says, "Manu’s daughter. [He says] "Ghṛtapadī" because ghee (ghṛta) stood in her footprint (pade); therefore he says, "Ghṛtapadī."

And as for "belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa": that which he united with Mitra and Varuṇa is indeed the Maitrāvaruṇa animal victim. With the words, "The Brahman, invited by the gods," he invokes the Brahman, for he is their Brahman. With "Invited, invited are the divine Adhvaryus; invited are the human ones," he thus invites both the divine Adhvaryus and those who are human. The divine Adhvaryus are the calves, while the others are the human ones.
"Those who protect this sacrifice and those who shall increase the lord of the sacrifice.

For it is these Brahmins—those who have heard the sacred lore and are learned in the Vedas—who indeed protect the sacrifice; for they extend it and they generate it. Thus he makes amends to them. And calves indeed increase the lord of the sacrifice; for he whose calves are most numerous, he truly increases as the lord of the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "and those who shall increase the lord of the sacrifice."

"Invoked are Heaven and Earth, the first-born, the observers of Truth, the goddesses, the daughters of the gods"—with these words he invokes these two, Heaven and Earth, within which all this universe is contained. "Invoked is this sacrificer"—with this he invokes the sacrificer. Now, as to why he does not here utter his name: it is because the sacrifice has already been offered; for were he to utter the name during the *iḍā*, he would make it human. And that which is human is indeed a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice," he therefore does not utter the name.

"In the subsequent sacrifice to the gods, I am invited"—by this he cryptically expresses for him a hope for life itself; for having sacrificed previously while living, one then sacrifices again later.
Thus, he cryptically invokes for him offspring itself;
for he who has offspring goes to that world with his own self, and then his offspring performs sacrifice in this world. Therefore, offspring is superior to the sacrifice to the gods.
Thus, he cryptically prays for cattle for him; for he who possesses cattle, having sacrificed first, sacrifices again later.
"At the offering of more abundant oblation, you are invited.
By this, he cryptically invokes life for him; for having first sacrificed while living, he subsequently offers ever more abundant oblations.

Thus, he cryptically prays for offspring for him; for he who has offspring exists as one in his own person, and then, moreover, through his offspring, he is made into tenfold oblation. Therefore, offspring is the greater part of the sacrificial offering.
Thus, he indirectly prays for cattle for him;
for he who possesses cattle, having sacrificed once, performs the oblation again and again.

This indeed is the prayer: "May I live; may I have offspring; may I attain prosperity. Now, when he prays for cattle, he prays for prosperity, for cattle are indeed prosperity. Thus, by means of these two prayers, everything is obtained; therefore, these two prayers are performed here.

"May the gods enjoy this offering of mine!"—when he says, "Invited upon it," he thereby invokes the success of the sacrifice; for when the gods enjoy the offering, by that they indeed achieve great victory. Therefore he says, "May they enjoy it."
They indeed consume it;
they do not offer it into the fire. For the *iḍā* is cattle, [thinking] "Lest we should consume the cattle in the fire," therefore they do not offer it into the fire.

It is offered in the vital breaths itself: partly in the Hotṛ, partly in the Sacrificer, and partly in the Adhvaryu. Now, when he has broken off the eastern half of the sacrificial cake and places it in front of the Dhruvā-spoon—the Dhruvā being indeed the Sacrificer—that becomes the portion consumed by the Sacrificer. And as for the fact that he does not eat it visibly before him, thinking, "Lest I should eat while the sacrifice is not yet completed," that very act constitutes his consumption. All eat it, thinking, "May there be offerings made for me in all [the priests]. Five eat it; the Iḍā is indeed cattle, and cattle are fivefold; therefore, five eat it.
Then, where he proceeds:

having divided that sacrificial cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass (barhis). This is the portion for the ancestors; for the intermediate directions are four, and the ancestors are indeed the intermediate directions. Therefore, having divided the sacrificial cake into four parts, he places it upon the sacrificial grass.

Then, at the point where he says, "The Heaven and Earth are invoked," he places [the portion] for the Āgnīdhra; the Āgnīdhra eats it with the formula: "The Earth, the mother, is invoked; may the Earth, the mother, invoke me; from the Āgnīdhra-fire, svāhā! The Sky, the father, is invoked; may the Sky, the father, invoke me; from the Āgnīdhra-fire, svāhā! For this Āgnīdhra-fire is indeed Heaven and Earth; therefore he eats in this manner.
Then, at the point where he invokes a blessing, he mutters:

"May Indra bestow this power upon me; may the generous lords attend us with wealth; may our blessings be fulfilled; may our blessings be true. This is indeed the acceptance of blessings; for whatever blessings the officiating priests invoke here for the sacrificer, those very blessings he accepts and makes his own.
Then they cleanse themselves with the two strainers.

For they have performed this rite with the *iḍā* of the domestic sacrifice; now, purified by the strainers, they think, "We shall extend that part of the sacrifice which remains from here onwards. Therefore, they cleanse themselves with the two strainers.
Then he mixes those two strainers with the prastara-bunch.

The prastara is indeed the sacrificer, and the two strainers are the out-breath and the in-breath; thus he places the out-breath and in-breath in the sacrificer. That is why he mixes those two strainers with the prastara-bunch.
They indeed carry forward these two firebrands for the sake of the after-offerings (anuyāja).

For this fire becomes exhausted after having carried the sacrifice to the gods; thinking, "Let us perform the after-offerings with a fire that is not exhausted," they therefore carry forward these two firebrands.
They touch them again;

they thus nourish this fire once more and make it fresh. Thinking, "In that which is fresh, we shall extend that part of the sacrifice which remains uncompleted beyond this point," they therefore touch them again.

Then he places a kindling-stick upon the fire. He thereby kindles it; for when it is kindled, he thinks, "Whatever part of the sacrifice remains uncompleted from this point upward, may we extend that. That is why he places a kindling-stick upon the fire.
The Hotṛ consecrates it with the formula:

"This is thy fuel, O Agni; through it grow and swell; may we also grow and swell. Just as he recites over the fire when it is being kindled, so does he recite here. This is the duty of the Hotṛ; however, if he should think that the Hotṛ does not know [the ritual], the sacrificer himself may also consecrate it.

Then he cleanses it. He thereby yokes it; for that which remains of the sacrifice from this point upward, being thus yoked, shall carry it. That is why he cleanses it. He cleanses it once each time. For in the beginning, they used to cleanse it thrice for the gods, thinking, "Let us not do as we did for the gods. Therefore, he cleanses it once each time to avoid repetition; for he would commit a repetition if he were to cleanse it thrice first and thrice afterwards. Therefore, he cleanses it once each time.
He cleanses it with the formula:

"O Agni, winner of the prize, I cleanse thee, the winner of the prize, who hast run for the prize. At first he says "who will run," for at that time he is as if about to run; but here he says "who hast run," for here he has indeed run; therefore he says, "who hast run."
Then he performs the after-offerings (anuyājas).

Whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, they all indeed become worshipped thereby. Since he now offers these as if to cattle after all those [deities] have been worshipped, they are therefore called *anuyājas*.
Now, as for why he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*):

the after-offerings are indeed the *chandas* (metres), and the *chandas* are the cattle of the gods. Just as here on earth cattle, when harnessed, carry [burdens] for men, even so the *chandas*, when harnessed, carry the sacrifice for the gods. When the *chandas* had satisfied the gods, then the gods satisfied the *chandas*. That is what occurred previously: that the *chandas*, being harnessed, carried the sacrifice to the gods, and that they fully satisfied them.
Now, as to why he performs the after-offerings (*anuyāja*):

the after-offerings are indeed the metres; it is the metres he thus gratifies, which is why he performs the after-offerings. Therefore, if one were to drive a horse with a carriage, having unyoked it, one should say, "Let it drink; make it well-fed. This, indeed, is the way to show gratitude for the use of the carriage.

He indeed offers the *barhis* first. Now, that is the smallest metre; yet the Gāyatrī is joined as the first of the metres. It was by its very power that [the eagle], having become a falcon, fetched the Soma from heaven. Some consider this to be improper, because the Gāyatrī, being the smallest metre, is joined as the first of the metres. But here, the gods arranged the metres in their proper order during the *anuyāja* offerings, so that there might not be a state of "evil-reversal" (*pāpavasyasa*).
He indeed offers the *barhis* first.

This world is the *barhis*, and the plants are the *barhis*; he thus places the plants in this very world. These plants are established in this world; everything that moves (*jagat*) rests upon it, and for that reason this earth is the *jagatī*. Thus they made the *jagatī* the first.
Then he sacrifices to Narāśaṃsa as the second.

Narāśaṃsa is indeed the intermediate space, and men are indeed offspring; these offspring move about in the intermediate space, crying out. For when one speaks, they say, "He recites" (śaṃsati); therefore Narāśaṃsa is the intermediate space. The Triṣṭubh is indeed the intermediate space; thus they made the Triṣṭubh the second.
Then Agni was the last;
Agni is indeed the Gāyatrī, so they made the Gāyatrī the last. Thus, by means of this well-ordered arrangement, the meters became firmly established; therefore, this [world] is free from disorder.

"Offer to the gods," thus says the Adhvaryu; "to each god," [he says] for all of them, the Hotṛ. For the gods of the gods are indeed the meters, since cattle are their [the gods'] [source], and cattle are the house; for the house is a firm foundation. And the Anuyājas are the meters; therefore, the Adhvaryu says, "Offer to the gods," and the Hotṛ says, "to each god," for all of them.

Regarding the formula "In the winning of wealth, of the bestowal of wealth," the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered for the deity and the offering is made to the deity; yet here, among the *anuyāja* offerings, there is no deity, as in the case of the verse "The divine *barhis*. For there, there is neither Agni, nor Indra, nor Soma, nor the god Narāśaṃsa. According to the truth, there is not even one [deity] here. Or rather, the Agni who is here is the Gāyatrī, by way of their common origin.
Now, as to why he offers with the words, "For the winning of wealth, for the bestowing of wealth":

Agni is indeed the winner of wealth, and Indra is the bestower of wealth. There is indeed a deity among the meters; it is to Indra and Agni that the *vaṣaṭ* is thus uttered, and it is to the deity that the offering is made.
Then, having performed the final after-offering (anuyāja), he brings together [the portions] and offers them.

These indeed are the fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings; just as in the case of the fore-offerings he causes the enemy who hates the sacrificer to pay tribute there, so here he causes him to pay tribute in the after-offerings. Thus, in this very way, he causes tribute to be paid in the after-offerings.

He indeed separates the two offering-spoons. With the *juhū* held in his right hand, he moves it eastward, saying: "May I win following the victory of Agni and Soma; I push forward with the impulse of strength. With the *upabhṛt* held in his left hand, he moves it westward, saying: "May Agni and Soma drive away him who hates us and whom we hate; I push him away with the impulse of strength"—if the sacrificer performs the rite himself.

If, however, it is the Adhvaryu, he should say: "May this sacrificer follow the victory of Agni and Soma; by the impulse of strength (vāja), I push him forward; may Agni and Soma drive away him whom this sacrificer hates and whoever hates him; by the impulse of strength, I push him away. This is for the full moon sacrifice, for the oblation of the full moon belongs to Agni and Soma.
Then, on the new moon day:

"May I conquer following the victory of Indra and Agni; by the impulse of strength (*vāja*), I push him forward. May Indra and Agni drive away him who hates us and whom we hate; by the impulse of strength, I cast him out"—if the sacrificer performs this himself.

If, however, it is the Adhvaryu, he says: "May this sacrificer follow Indra and Agni’s victory with his own victory; by the impulse of strength (*vāja*), I project him forward; may Indra and Agni drive away him whom this sacrificer hates and whoever hates him; by the impulse of strength, I cast him out.
