This is at the new moon sacrifice, for the oblation of the new moon belongs to Indra and Agni; thus he rearranges [the verses] according to the respective deities. This is why he rearranges them in this manner.
The sacrificer indeed follows the *juhū* ladle;

he who acts with hostility toward him follows the *upabhṛt* ladle. He thus raises the sacrificer forward and pushes away backward him who acts with hostility toward him. The eater indeed follows the *juhū* ladle; food follows the *upabhṛt* ladle. He thus raises the eater forward and pushes away backward the food that is to be eaten.
This, indeed, is so:

it is from the same person that both the eater and the one eaten are produced; therefore, they say, "In the fourth generation, or in the third, we come together. Thus, even while gambling, those of noble birth sit [thinking], "It is because of this. Therefore, that is so.
Then he anoints the enclosing-sticks with the *juhū* ladle.

With that very ladle by which he has offered to the gods and by which he has completed the sacrifice, he thus gratifies the enclosing-sticks; therefore he anoints the enclosing-sticks with the *juhū*.

He anoints it with the formula, "For the Vasus thee! For the Rudras thee! For the Ādityas thee! These indeed are the three classes of gods—the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas; thus he says, "For these thee."
Then, having reached the enclosing-sticks, he causes the announcement to be made.

For it is to the enclosing-sticks that he makes this announcement; the announcement is indeed the sacrifice, and by means of the sacrifice he thus directly gratifies the enclosing-sticks. Therefore, having reached the enclosing-stick, he causes the announcement to be made.
Having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled.

For these enclosing sticks are indeed the divine Hotṛs, since they are fires; thus, when he says, "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled," he means this. He says, "for auspicious speech," because the gods themselves become yoked to him so that he may speak what is right and do what is right; therefore he says, "for auspicious speech. [He says], "the human one has been sent forth for the *sūktavāka*"; by this he impels this human Hotṛ for the *sūktavāka*.
Then he takes up the prastara-bunch.

The prastara is indeed the sacrificer; thus, he now sends the sacrificer safely back to that very place where his sacrifice went—either to the world of the gods, for his sacrifice has gone to the world of the gods, and so he leads the sacrificer back to the world of the gods.
If he should desire rain, [he should perform this rite].

With this very formula he should take it up: "May Heaven and Earth agree! For when Heaven and Earth agree, then it rains; therefore he says, "May Heaven and Earth agree. "May Mitra and Varuna favor thee with rain"—by this he means, "May he who rules over the rain favor thee with rain. Now, he who rules over the rain is this wind that blows here; for though it blows as one, it enters into man as the forward and backward breaths—these being the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna). And Mitra and Varuna are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath. Thus he means, "May he who rules over the rain favor thee with rain. He should take it up with this very formula, for whenever it rains, it anoints him all over; he thereby makes it an oblation, thinking, "Having become an oblation, may it go to the world of the gods."
He anoints the tip of the *juhū* ladle, the middle part of the *upabhṛt*, and the base of the *dhruvā*. For the *juhū* is like the tip, the *upabhṛt* like the middle, and the *dhruvā* like the base.
He anoints it with the words, "May the birds go forth, licking what has been anointed.

He thus causes him, having become a bird, to fly up from this world of men toward the world of the gods. He carries it low; for there are two reasons why he should carry it low: the *prastara* is indeed the sacrificer, so he does not strike it away from this very foundation, but rather brings down the rain right here.

He carries it away. When he says, "Go to the spotted mares of the Maruts," he thereby says, "Go to the world of the gods. When he says, "Go to the spotted mares of the Maruts," [he means]: "Having become a speckled cow (vaśā), go to heaven; from there, bring rain for us. This earth is indeed the speckled cow (pṛśni-vaśā), for whatever food—whether rooted or rootless—is established upon her, by that she is the speckled cow. Thus he says, "Having become this [earth], go to heaven; from there, bring rain for us. For from rain, vigorous sap and well-being are produced; therefore he says, "From there, bring rain for us."
Then he pulls out a single blade of grass.

The sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) is indeed the sacrificer; if he were to throw the entire grass-bundle into the fire, the sacrificer would quickly go to yonder world. Thus, the sacrificer lives long here as long as his human lifespan lasts; it is for that very reason that he pulls out this one blade.
Having held it for that moment, he throws it back into the fire;

thereby he causes that very part of his self which had gone elsewhere to return to him. Now, if he were not to throw it back, he would indeed exclude the sacrificer from the world; thus, he does not exclude the sacrificer from the world.

He piles it up facing east, for the east is the direction of the gods; or he piles it up facing north, for the north is the direction of men. They should pile it up with their fingers alone, not with wooden sticks or other timber. [They do this thinking: "Let us not treat this like the other corpse. Therefore, they should pile it up with their fingers alone, not with wooden sticks. This is when the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*.
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw it after!

By this he means, "Make that very part of his self which has gone elsewhere go back to him. Having thrown it silently, he touches himself with the formula, "O Agni, you are the protector of sight; protect my sight. Thereby he does not exclude his own self from being consumed by the fire.

Then he says, "Converse!"—by this he means, "Make him converse with the gods. [The Adhvaryu says,] "Has he come, O Agnidh?"—by this he means, "Has he indeed come? The other replies, "He has come"—by this he means, "He has been made known," or "He has been awakened. [The Adhvaryu says,] "Make him heard!"—by this he means, "Make him known to the gods," or "Awaken him. [The Agnidh says,] "Śrauṣaṭ!"—by this he means, "They know him," or "They have awakened him. In this way, both the Adhvaryu and the Agnidh lead the sacrificer to the world of the gods.

Then he says, "Go safely to the divine Hotṛs. For these enclosing-sticks are indeed the divine Hotṛs, since they are fires; it is to them that he thus bids a safe journey. Therefore he says, "Go safely to the divine Hotṛs. When he says, "Welfare to the human ones," he thereby prays for safety for this human Hotṛ.

Then he throws the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) into the fire; he throws the middle enclosing-stick first: "O Agni, that enclosing-stick which you, a god, were encircled by when hidden by the Paṇis—that very one I bring back to you according to your pleasure, lest this one should cause you to lose consciousness. With the words, "The beloved path of Agni has been reached," he combines the other two.
Then he lifts up both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*.
He makes this very act an oblation, thinking, "May it go to the world of the gods after having become an oblation. Therefore, he lifts up both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*.
He indeed takes it up for all the gods.

For whatever oblation is taken that has not been specifically assigned to a deity, all the deities consider themselves entitled to a share in it; yet, when taking the clarified butter as an oblation, he does not assign it to any specific deity. Therefore, he takes it up for all the gods; this is the Vaiśvadeva oblation in the sacrifice.

He takes them up together with the formula, "May those standing on the grass-bunch be large, for they are full of sap. For indeed, the grass-bunch alone remains as the residue. With the words, "The gods who stand on the grass-bunch and the enclosing-sticks," he refers to the fact that both the grass-bunch and the enclosing-sticks have been thrown into the fire. With the words, "All of you, chanting this speech toward us," he makes it belong to the All-gods (Vaiśvadeva). With "Sitting upon this sacred grass, rejoice! Svāhā! Vāṭ!"—this becomes for him like an oblation offered with the Vaṣaṭ-call.

If they take the sacrificial oblation from a cart, they unyoke it at the pole of that very cart, saying, "From where we yoke, from there let us unyoke," for from where they indeed yoke, from there they unyoke. And if [the oblation] is in a vessel or on a wooden sword (sphya), they unyoke it saying, "From where we yoke, from there let us unyoke," for from where they thus yoke, from there they unyoke.
Indeed, these two offering-spoons are the two yoke-poles of the sacrifice.

He yokes these two when he proceeds with the sacrifice; having set them down, he cuts off the portions—just as one would unyoke a draft animal, so it is with them. He brings them to this "liberation" at the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; he sets them down there and unyokes them. He yokes them again at the *anuyāja* offerings; having performed the *anuyājas*, he comes to this liberation; he sets them down there and unyokes them. He yokes them again when he takes hold of them together; having reached that goal toward which he yoked them, he finally unyokes them. Indeed, offspring follow the sacrifice; therefore, this person yokes and then unyokes, and then yokes again; having reached that goal toward which he yoked them, he finally unyokes them at the end. He sets them down [with the words]: "Ye two are full of ghee, ye two are the leaders; guard us! Ye two are in bliss, place me in bliss!"—by this he means to say, "Ye two are successful, place me in success."

When he says, "The divine Hotṛ-priests have been sent forth for the auspicious utterance; the human one has been sent forth for the Sūktavāka," whatever the Hotṛ recites thereafter, he recites it as if it were a hymn (sūkta). He thereby invokes a blessing for the sacrificer. Now, this is the blessing he invokes at the conclusion of the sacrifice. It is a twofold matter why he invokes the blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
He who sacrifices generates the sacrifice;

for by this [formula] the officiating priests are enjoined, and they extend it, and thus generate it. Then he pronounces the benediction; the sacrifice inclines that benediction toward him, thinking, "May the benediction which I have pronounced go to him who generated me. Therefore, he pronounces the benediction at the conclusion of the sacrifice.

He who sacrifices with this sacrifice indeed gratifies the gods—partly by means of the Ṛg-verses, partly by means of the Yajus-formulas, and partly by means of the oblations. Having gratified the gods, he becomes one who has entered into their fellowship; having entered into their fellowship, he then invokes a blessing. The gods incline toward him that very blessing which he invokes, thinking, "He has sent it to us. Therefore, he invokes the blessing at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Then he undertakes [the practice].

"This has become auspicious for Heaven and Earth," he says, for it has indeed become auspicious for him who has reached the conclusion of the sacrifice. "We have succeeded in the Sūktavāka and the Namovāka," he says; for both the Sūktavāka and the Namovāka belong to the sacrifice itself. "We have prospered in the sacrifice, we have found the sacrifice," this is what he thereby says. "O Agni, you are the speaker of the hymn (Sūktavāk), listening to Heaven and Earth," he says; he thereby says to Agni, "You are the speaker of the hymn, listening to these two, Heaven and Earth. "May Heaven and Earth be full of protection for you, O sacrificer, at this sacrifice," he says; that is to say, "May Heaven and Earth be full of food for you, O sacrificer, at this sacrifice."

"May they be horned and life-giving"—by this he means, "May they be horned for you and life-giving. "Without a wound, without a blemish"—by this he means, "Do not be afraid of anything; let no one find out this prosperity of yours."

"With wide pastures, makers of fearlessness"—by this he means, "May your two pastures be wide and free from fear. "With rain-giving heavens, with water-giving [heavens]"—by this he means, "May your two heavens be rich in rain."

"May they be auspicious and refreshing," he says; by this he means, "May they be auspicious for you and refreshing. "Full of vigor and full of milk," he says; by this he means, "May they be full of essence and fit for your livelihood."
"And easy to approach, and easy to ascend. By this he means:

"May that [world] of yours be easy to approach, which you approach from below; may this [world] of yours be easy to ascend, which you ascend from above. "Of those two, for the sake of distinction"—by this he means: "of those two, not being in discord."

"Agni has enjoyed this oblation; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more glorious"—thus he speaks of the butter-portion belonging to Agni. "Soma has enjoyed this oblation; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more glorious"—thus he speaks of the butter-portion belonging to Soma. "Agni has enjoyed this oblation; he has grown strong; he has made it greater and more glorious"—thus he speaks of that cake which belongs to Agni and is unchanging in both cases.
Then, according to the respective deities.

"The gods who drink the clarified butter have enjoyed the clarified butter; they have increased; they have made it greater and more glorious"—thus he speaks of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. For the gods who drink the clarified butter are indeed the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings. "Agni, by means of his office as Hotṛ, has enjoyed this oblation; he has increased; he has made it greater and more glorious"—thus he speaks of Agni by means of his office as Hotṛ. In this way, he takes notice of whichever deities have been sacrificed to, thinking, "This one has enjoyed the oblation; that one has enjoyed the oblation. He thus invokes the prosperity of the sacrifice itself; for when the gods enjoy the oblation, by that they achieve great victory. Therefore he says, "He has enjoyed it"; and "he has increased," for whenever the gods enjoy the oblation, they even make it as large as a mountain. Therefore he says, "He has increased."
"Great, they have made it greater," he says.
The sacrifice is indeed the "greatness" (maha) of the gods, for they make it as it were greater; therefore he says, "Great, they have made it greater."

"In this divine-reaching invocation may he prosper"—by saying "In this divine-reaching invocation may he succeed," he says this very thing; when he says, "This sacrificer, so-and-so, desires," he pronounces his name and thereby directly bestows upon him the blessing.
"He prays for long life":
that which is the superior sacrifice to the gods in the world beyond is here manifest as long life.

"He prays for 'good offspring' (suprajāstva)," it is said. Now, that which is there [in the other world] is the preparation of further oblations; here, however, one who would perform this [rite] should pray for the visible blessing of good offspring. But he should rather say, "He prays for the subsequent sacrifice to the gods"; for that alone is life, that is offspring, and that is cattle.

"He further prays for the performance of the oblation; he thus prays for the *sajātavanasyā*. The *sajātās* (kinsmen) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), for one is born together with the vital breaths; thus he prays for the vital breaths."
"He prays for a divine abode.

Indeed, he who sacrifices sacrifices with the thought, "May there be a place for me even in the world of the gods. He thus makes him one who has attained that very world of the gods. "Whatever he prays for with this oblation, may he obtain it; may he prosper in it"—by saying this, he means: "May everything that he prays for with this oblation be fully accomplished for him."

Now, these indeed are the five blessings he pronounces; three at the *iḍā*—these make eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is vigor; thus he brings these blessings to completion as vigor.
One should not make more than this;
for he would make it excessive if he were to make more than this. Whatever is excessive in the sacrifice, that is left over for his hateful enemy. Therefore, one should not make more than this.

"May the seven younger ones also grant this to him"—by this he means, "may the gods grant their approval to this for him. "May the god Agni win this from the gods, and we, O Agni, from man"—by this he means, "may the god Agni win this from the gods, and may we win this for him from Agni."
"Both what is sacrificed for and what is acquired.

For they sought after this sacrifice as it were, and they found it; therefore he says, "both what is sacrificed for and what is acquired. "And may both Heaven and Earth protect him from distress"—by this he means, "may both Heaven and Earth guard him from misfortune."

Regarding this, some say: "Both for me," thinking, "In this way the Hotṛ does not exclude himself from the blessings. But one should not speak thus; for the blessing belongs to the sacrificer. What part of it belongs to the officiating priests? Whatever blessing the officiating priests invoke during the sacrifice, that belongs to the sacrificer alone. He who says, "Both for me," does not establish that blessing anywhere. Therefore, he should simply say, "And both for him."
"Here is the resort of beauty," he says.
Whatever is good in the sacrifice, that he thereby places in him; therefore he says, "Here is the resort of beauty."
And as for this "Homage to the gods," it is that having reached the conclusion of the sacrifice, he pays homage to the gods; therefore he says, "And homage to the gods."
Then he spoke concerning Śamyu.
For Śamyu Bārhaspatya indeed directly perceived the completion of the sacrifice; he departed for the world of the gods, and thus that [knowledge] became as if hidden from human beings.

Or rather, this was heard by the seers: Śamyu Bārhaspatya indeed directly knew the completion of the sacrifice, thinking, "I shall go to the world of the gods. They adopted that very completion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya had known. They said to Śamyu, "Adopt that very completion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya knew. He now adopts that very completion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya knew; therefore, he says, "O Śamyu! And because he says "O Śamyu!", for that reason he says, "O Śamyu!"
He proceeds with the formula, "We choose that truth of these two. By this he means: "We choose that conclusion of the sacrifice which Śamyu Bārhaspatya discovered."

"Success for the sacrifice, success for the lord of the sacrifice!"—for he indeed seeks success for the sacrifice and success for the lord of the sacrifice who completes the sacrifice. "May there be divine well-being for us, may there be well-being for men"—by this he says, "May there be well-being for us among the gods, and well-being among men. "May the healing power rise upward"—by this he says, "May this sacrifice of ours ascend upward to the world of the gods."

"May it be well with our bipeds, may it be well with our quadrupeds. This entire world consists of nothing more than the biped and the quadruped; thus, having reached the conclusion of the sacrifice, he brings welfare to them. Therefore he says: "May it be well with our bipeds, may it be well with our quadrupeds."
Then he touches [the earth] with the words, "With this.

For when one has entered upon the office of a priest (*ārtvijya*), he becomes, as it were, non-human; this earth, indeed, is the foundation. Thus he establishes himself upon this very foundation. Thereupon he becomes human once again; therefore he touches [the earth] with the words, "With this."
When they are about to perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, they turn back toward the west;
the Adhvaryu takes up the *juhū* and the *sruva*, the Hotṛ takes up the *veda*, and the Agnīdh takes up the butter-melting spoon.
Now, some say that the Adhvaryu should go around the front of the Āhavanīya fire; however, one should not do it thus, for if he were to go there, he would be outside the sacrifice.
Some say that the Adhvaryu goes behind the wife;

but one should not do so. For the Adhvaryu is the eastern half of the sacrifice, and the wife is the western half. It would be as if one were to place a head upon the buttocks; indeed, he would be excluded from the sacrifice by doing so.

Some say that the Adhvaryu goes between the wife [and the fire]; but one should not do so, for he would thereby exclude the wife from the sacrifice. Since he should go, therefore he goes along the front of the Gārhapatya and between it and the Āhavanīya. Thus he does not remain outside the sacrifice; and just as he moves between them while performing the ritual, that indeed becomes his path of movement.

Then they perform the joint offerings for the wives. From the sacrifice indeed offspring are born; being born from the sacrifice, they are born from a productive union; being born from a productive union, they are born at the end of the sacrifice. Thus he causes these offspring to be born at the end of the sacrifice from that productive union; therefore, from that productive union at the end of the sacrifice, these offspring are born. That is why they perform the joint offerings for the wives.
He sacrifices to four deities.
Four indeed constitute a pair; a pair is indeed a couple, for two by two they truly exist as a couple. Thus, this act of procreation is performed; therefore, he sacrifices to four deities.
They indeed have clarified butter as their oblation;
clarified butter is seed, and it is seed that he thus pours out; therefore they have clarified butter as their oblation.
Therefore they proceed in a whisper; for one proceeds as it were in secret with a mate, and that which is whispered is as it were in secret; therefore they proceed in a whisper.
Then he sacrifices to Soma; Soma is indeed seed, so it is seed that he thus pours out; therefore he sacrifices to Soma.
Then he sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed; therefore, he sacrifices to Tvaṣṭṛ.
Then he sacrifices to the wives of the gods.

For seed is established in the womb, and from that it is born; thus he establishes the seed, once poured, in the wives themselves as the womb, and from that it is born. Therefore, he sacrifices to the wives of the gods.
When he sacrifices to the wives of the gods, he places a screen before them.

Indeed, the deities remain seated as long as the *sam-iṣṭayajus* oblation has not been offered, thinking, "Let him now offer this for us. He thus places a screen between himself and them. Therefore, these human women desire men from behind a screen; as Yājñavalkya used to say, "They are like those [divine wives], though they appear to be such."
Then he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati.
This Agni is indeed this world; it is this world that he thus causes these creatures to procreate toward. These creatures are born toward this world; therefore, he sacrifices to Agni Gṛhapati.
It ends with the *iḍā*;

for here there are no enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) and no grass-bundle (*prastara*). Or rather, since there he makes the sacrificer go to his own place by means of the *prastara*—for the wife follows her husband—so too is his wife made to go to her own place. One might think that he should perform whatever constitutes the form of the *prastara*, and therefore it should indeed end with the *iḍā*; yet, for this reason, the form of the *prastara* is nevertheless performed.
If he were to assume the form of the *prastara* (grass-bundle),
then just as he previously caused the sacrificer to go safely by means of the *prastara*, so now he causes the wife to go safely by this very means.
If he should take the form of the *prastara* [bunch of grass],
he plucks a single blade from the *veda*, anoints its tip with the *juhū* ladle, its middle with the *sruva* spoon, and its base in the vessel.
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw [the ladle] after!
Having thrown it after silently, he touches himself with the formula, "O Agni, you are the protector of the eye; protect my eye. Thus, he does not exclude himself from the subsequent throwing.

Then he says, "Converse [with the Agnīdh]. [The Agnīdh responds: "He has come, O Agnīdh; make me hear! [The Adhvaryu says: "Auṣaṭ! Well-being to the divine Hotṛs; prosperity to the human ones; pronounce the *śaṃyuvāka*."
Then he takes up both the *juhū* and the *sruva* ladles together.
He does this so that he may make an oblation right there; thinking, "Having become an oblation, let it go to the world of the gods," he therefore takes up both the *juhū* and the *sruva* together.
He indeed takes it up for Agni.

"O Agni of unimpaired life, come unhurt!"—for Agni is indeed immortal; therefore he says, "of unimpaired life. "Come unhurt"—for Agni is indeed most excellent; therefore he says, "come unhurt. "Protect me from the lightning-flash, protect me from bondage, protect me from ill-sacrificed offerings, protect me from bad food"—this he says, "guard me from all calamities. "Make our food free from poison"—food is indeed "pitu"; thus he says, "make this food of ours free from disease and sinless. "In a well-seated womb"—this he says regarding himself. "Svāhā! Vāṭ!"—thus it becomes for him as if it were offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call.
Then the wife unties the *veda*.
The altar (*vedi*) is indeed female and the *veda* is male; the *veda* is prepared for the sake of union. Now, when he takes hold of it at the sacrifice, thereby a productive union is brought about.
Now, as for why the wife unties the Veda: the wife is indeed female and the Veda is male; thus a productive union is brought about. Therefore, the wife unties the Veda.
She loosens it [with the formula]:

"Thou art the Veda; by that [means] through which thou, O divine one, becamest the Veda for the gods, by that mayest thou become the Veda for me. If she should wish to perform it with a Yajus formula, she should do so with this very one.
He spreads the Veda-grass over the altar.

The altar is indeed a female, and the Veda-grass is a male; for from behind, the male approaches the female. Having thus approached her from behind with the male Veda-grass, he causes her to be impregnated. Therefore, he spreads it over the altar.
Then he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*.

[He does so thinking,] "May my sacrifice be completed while facing forward. Now, if he were to perform the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings after having offered the *samiṣṭayajus*, his sacrifice would indeed be completed while facing backward. Therefore, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* at this point, [thinking,] "May my sacrifice be completed while facing forward."
Now, as to why it is called the *samiṣṭayajus*:

whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, all of them indeed become "sacrificed-to together" (*samiṣṭāḥ*) at that time; and because he offers this [oblation] when they have all been sacrificed-to together, therefore it is called the *samiṣṭayajus*.

Now, as to why he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*: whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, they indeed sit waiting, thinking, "Let him now offer this to us. It is these very deities that he thus dismisses each to their proper place, wherever their course lies. Furthermore, he has generated this sacrifice when he performed it; having generated it, he establishes it where its foundation lies. That is why he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*.

He offers with the words, "O gods, knowers of the way. For the gods are indeed knowers of the way; by saying "having known the way," he means "having known the sacrifice. By saying "go ye on the way," he thereby dismisses them each to their proper place. With the words, "O Lord of the Mind, O God, this sacrifice—Svāhā!—place it in the wind," he means this: the sacrifice is indeed this wind that blows here. Having thus gathered together this sacrifice, he establishes it in this very sacrifice; he unites sacrifice with sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Svāhā! Place it in the wind."
Then he offers the *barhis*.
The *barhis* is indeed this world, and the *barhis* consists of plants; thus they place plants in this very world. These plants are established in this world; therefore he offers the *barhis*.
Or rather, he offers that as something redundant;

for the *samiṣṭayajus* is indeed the end of the sacrifice. Whatever comes after the *samiṣṭayajus* is redundant. When he offers the *samiṣṭayajus*, then he offers these [plants]; therefore these plants are born redundant and measureless.
He offers:

"May the sacrificial grass be anointed with the oblation and with clarified butter; may it be anointed with the Ādityas, with the Vasus, with the Maruts, and with Indra and the Viśvedevas. May that which is offered with 'svāhā' go to the celestial sky."
Then, having gone around to the south, he pours out the *praṇītā* water.

For when he extends this sacrifice, he indeed yokes it; if he were not to pour it out, the sacrifice, being unreleased and turned away, would surely consume the sacrificer. Thus, the sacrifice does not consume the sacrificer; therefore, having gone around to the south, he pours out the *praṇītā* water.

He pours it out: "Who releases you? He releases you. For whom does he release you? For him he releases you—for nourishment. Thus he declares the highest prosperity for the sacrificer. With the same [ladle] with which he brings it forward, he pours it out; for with that by which they yoke a draft-animal, they unyoke it; for with a thong they yoke a draft-animal, and with a thong they unyoke it. Then, with the husks, he throws down the black antelope skin underneath on each side, saying: "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases."

The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice while their father Prajāpati, the year, was still present, each thinking, "This shall be ours; this shall be ours."
Then the gods.

Having gathered together the entire sacrifice, they then excluded those who were the most wicked portion of the sacrifice; with the animal's refuse and the chaff of the grain-offering, they deprived them of their share, thinking, "May they be thoroughly excluded from the sacrifice. Indeed, he whom they exclude while he is entitled to a share is truly well-excluded; but as for him whom they exclude while he is not entitled to a share, he remains there crying out, "I have obtained my wish—what have you given me? The gods assigned that very share to them which they had originally prepared; therefore, this sacrificer now makes that same share for them. Now, when he throws the black antelope skin down lower and lower, he causes them to enter blind darkness where there is no fire. Likewise, by saying, "The blood of the animal is your portion, O Rakṣases," he causes it to enter blind darkness where there is no fire. Therefore, they do not prepare the *tadanī* (the blood-vessel) of the animal, for that is the portion of the Rakṣases.
When the sacrifice has been completed, having gone around by the south, he pours out the full vessel;

for it is thus that it becomes turned toward the north—therefore, having gone around by the south, he pours out the full vessel. "May there be a place for me in the world of the gods," with this thought indeed one sacrifices who sacrifices; this sacrifice of his goes forth toward the world of the gods, and following after it is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) which he gives. Following after the sacrificial gift, the sacrificer takes hold of it.

This is either the path of the gods or the path of the fathers. On both sides of it stand two flaming points of fire, burning intensely. They burn against him who is to be burned; they let pass him who is to be let pass. Water is peace; thus he pacifies this very path.

He pours it out full; for the full is indeed everything, and thus he pacifies him with everything. He pours it out continuously and without interruption; by means of that which is continuous and uninterrupted, he pacifies him.
Furthermore, as to why he pours out the full vessel:

whatever in the sacrifice is performed incorrectly, that they tear apart and wound; water is a means of pacification, so he pacifies it with water, that which is the means of pacification, and he heals it with water.
He pours it out full;
for the full is everything—thus he unites it with everything. He pours it out continuously and without interruption; thus he unites it with that which is continuous and uninterrupted.
Then he receives it with his joined palms, reciting:

"We have united with splendor, with nourishment, with our bodies, and with a gracious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the giver of good gifts, bestow wealth upon us; may he smooth over for us whatever has been injured. Thus he joins together whatever has been torn asunder.
Then he touches his face.

There is a twofold reason why he touches his face: water is indeed immortality; thus he touches himself with immortality, and he also makes this rite part of his own self. Therefore, he touches his face.
Then he strides the Viṣṇu-strides.

He who sacrifices with this sacrifice indeed gratifies the gods—sometimes as it were with Ṛg-verses, sometimes as it were with Yajus-formulas, and sometimes as it were with oblations. Having gratified the gods, he becomes one who has entered into them; having become one who has entered into them, he strides toward them.

Furthermore, as to why he strides the Viṣṇu-strides: Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride for the gods, which is this very stride of theirs. With his first step he touched this [earth], with the second this intermediate space, and with the last the sky. Truly, Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, strides this stride for him; therefore he strides the Viṣṇu-strides. Now, they mostly stride from here onwards toward the future.
Then Viṣṇu strode across that earth.

"By the Gāyatrī metre, he is excluded from that [world] who hates us and whom we hate; Viṣṇu strode through the intermediate space with the Triṣṭubh metre, and by that he is excluded from it—[he] who hates us and whom we hate; Viṣṇu strode through heaven with the Jagatī metre, and by that he is excluded from it—[he] who hates us and whom we hate. Having thus ascended these worlds, this is the goal, this is the firm foundation: he who shines yonder. His rays are the doers of good deeds. Now, that which is the supreme light—that is Prajāpati, or the heavenly world. Thus, having ascended these worlds, he goes to that goal, to that firm foundation. But one who desires to give instruction from here should step downwards from above; for that is why he steps downwards from above.

First [they conquered] the sky, then this atmosphere, and from there they drove away their rivals by not retreating; in the same way, this sacrificer now conquers by first conquering with a retreat—first the sky, then this atmosphere, and from there he drives away his rivals by not retreating. This earth, indeed, is the foundation; thus he establishes himself upon this very foundation.
Then Viṣṇu strode across that in heaven.

"By the Jāgata metre, he is excluded from that [world] who hates us and whom we hate; Viṣṇu strode out in the intermediate space by the Triṣṭubh metre—by that he is excluded, he who hates us and whom we hate; on earth Viṣṇu strode out by the Gāyatra metre—by that he is excluded, he who hates us and whom we hate—from this food, from this foundation. For on this [earth] all this food is founded; therefore he says, "from this food, from this foundation."
Then he looks toward the east; for the east is the direction of the gods, therefore he looks toward the east.
He looks out:

"We have gone to the light," for the gods are indeed the light; thus he says, "We have gone to the gods. "We have become united with the light," for he thereby says, "We have become united with the gods."
Then he gazes at the sun.
This is the goal, this is the support; thus he goes to that goal, to that support. Therefore, he gazes at the sun.

He gazes upward [and says]: "Thou art self-existent, the best ray. For the sun is indeed the best ray; therefore he says, "Thou art self-existent, the best ray. "Thou art the giver of luster; give me luster"—this is what I say, Yājñavalkya used to say; for this is what a Brahmin should desire: that he may possess the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). Moreover, Aupoditeya used to say: "This one will surely give me cattle; thou art the giver of cattle, give me cattle. Whatever desire he desires, that desire of his is fulfilled.
Then he turns around, saying, "I turn around following the turning of the sun. Having gone to that course and that foundation, he turns around following the turning of that very [sun].

Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire. There is a twofold reason why he worships the Gārhapatya: the Gārhapatya is indeed the house, and the house is the foundation; thus he establishes himself upon that very foundation which is the house. Furthermore, he worships it for as long as his human lifespan remains here; for that reason, he worships the Gārhapatya.

He approaches [the fire] with the formula: "O Agni, lord of the house, may I be a good lord of the house through thee, O Agni, as lord of the house; mayest thou be a good lord of the house through me, O Agni, as lord of the house. There is nothing here that is obscure. "May our household duties not be single," he says; by this he means, "may our household duties not be afflicted. "A hundred winters," he says; by this he means, "may I live for a hundred years. One need not pay much heed even when saying this, for a man lives even longer than a hundred years; therefore, one need not pay much heed even when saying this.
Then he turns around, saying, "I turn around following the turning of the sun. Having thus attained this course and this support, he turns around following the turning of that very [sun].
Then he utters his son's name, thinking, "May this son of mine continue my vigor. If there were no son, he would utter his own name instead.

Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "May my sacrifice be completed from the front," and he worships it silently. Then he releases the vow, saying, "Here I am, who I truly am. For when he enters upon the vow, he becomes, as it were, non-human; it would not be appropriate for him to say, "Here I pass from truth to untruth. But indeed, he becomes human again; therefore, he should release the vow with the words, "Here I am, who I truly am. Now, as for the fact that he brings together [the materials] from here and there:

The reason why these are called "preparations" (sambhāra) is that from wherever the fire's components are taken, from each of those places he gathers them; thus, as it were by glory, by divinity, by cattle, and by a pair, he thereby completes him while gathering [the materials].
Then he scrapes [the ground].
Whatever of this earth has been stepped upon or trampled by him, that very thing he thereby digs out; then he establishes it on the very sacrificial earth. That is why he scrapes.
Then he sprinkles with water.

This indeed is the gathering of water, that he sprinkles with water; and as to why he gathers water—water is food, for water is indeed food; therefore, when water comes to this world, then food is produced here. Thus, by means of food, he thereby causes him to prosper.

The waters are indeed female, and fire is male; he thus endows him with this productive union. For by the waters all this [world] is pervaded; having pervaded him with the waters, he establishes him. Therefore, he brings together the waters.

Then he collects gold. For Agni indeed set his heart upon the waters, thinking, "May I be united with them. He united with them and poured his seed into them; that became gold. Therefore it has the appearance of fire, for it is the seed of Agni; therefore they find it in the waters, for he poured it into the waters. Therefore one does not wash it, nor does one do anything [to it], for it is glory, being the seed of the gods. By means of this glory he makes him prosper; he thus establishes the entire Agni together with its seed. That is why he collects gold.

Then he gathers saline soil. For yonder sky indeed gave these cattle to this earth; therefore they say that saline soil (*ūṣara*) is favorable for cattle, for these are truly cattle. Thus he directly provides him with cattle. Having come from yonder, they are established on this earth; they consider them to be the essence of these two, heaven and earth. He thus provides him with the essence of these two, heaven and earth. That is why he gathers saline soil.

Then he gathers mole-dust. For the moles know the essence of this earth; therefore, moving deeper and deeper into this earth, they are fattest, for they know its essence. Wherever they know the essence of this earth, from there they throw it up. Thus he endows him with the very essence of this earth. That is why he gathers mole-dust. They call one who attains prosperity "purīṣya"; for *purīṣa* and *karīṣa* are the same thing. It is for the attainment of that very thing that he gathers mole-dust.

Then he gathers gravel. The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. This earth was quivering like a lotus leaf; the wind used to blow it about like that. It went toward the gods and toward the Asuras. Wherever it went toward the gods...
Then they said: "Come, let us consolidate this foundation; upon it, being firm and unshakable, let us establish the two fires. From that, we shall exclude our rivals from her."

Just as one might stretch a hide with stakes, so did they strengthen this foundation; this foundation was firm and not loose. Upon that firm and not loose foundation, they established the fires, and then they deprived their rivals of it.

In the same way, he now strengthens this foundation with pebbles; upon that firm and unshakable foundation he establishes the two fires. Thereby he excludes his rivals from it. That is why he gathers the pebbles.
He indeed gathers these five materials; for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year.

Regarding this they say: "There are only six seasons of the year. [If one were to offer only five], then procreation would be performed in a deficient manner; for from a deficiency these creatures are born, and that which is more excellent is the subsequent one. Therefore, there are five. But if it be said that there are indeed six seasons of the year, then Agni himself is the sixth of them; thus, in this way, it becomes non-deficient.

Regarding this they say: "One should not gather even a single requisite. For all these requisites exist upon this earth; when he establishes the fires upon this earth, he thereby obtains all the requisites. Therefore, they say one should not gather even a single requisite. However, one should indeed gather them. For when he establishes the fires upon this earth, he thereby obtains all the requisites; and that which is accomplished by means of the gathered requisites is truly accomplished. Therefore, one should indeed gather them.
One should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās.

For the Kṛttikās are indeed the lunar mansion of Agni; thus, he who establishes the fires under the lunar mansion of Agni acts in accordance with what is proper (saloma). Therefore, one should establish the fires under the Kṛttikās.

"One, two, three, or four"—thus [one might speak of] other constellations; but these Kṛttikās are the most numerous. He thus attains abundance; therefore, one should establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās.
These, indeed, do not deviate from the eastern quarter;

for all other constellations deviate from the eastern quarter. Thus, these two [fires] of his are established in that very eastern quarter; therefore, one should establish the fires under the Kṛttikās.
Now, as to why one should not establish the sacred fires under the Kṛttikās:

in the beginning, these were the wives of the stars; for they used to call the Seven Rishis "the stars" (ṛkṣāḥ). They became separated from their mates, for the Seven Rishis rise in the north while these [Kṛttikās] are in the east. Now, he who is separated from his mate is indeed incomplete. Thinking, "Lest I be separated from my mate," one should therefore not establish the fires under the Kṛttikās.
Therefore, one should indeed place them.
Agni is the mate of these bricks; by means of Agni as their mate, they are made successful. Therefore, one should indeed place them.
One should establish the sacred fires under Rohiṇī.

Indeed, it was under Rohiṇī that Prajāpati, desiring offspring, established the fires and created progeny. Those progeny of his, once created, stood firm and uniform, like so many Rohiṇīs; that is why Rohiṇī is called "Rohiṇī. He who, knowing this, establishes the fires under Rohiṇī, truly becomes multiplied with offspring and cattle.

In Rohiṇī, indeed, the cattle took up the fires with the thought, "May we ascend to the desire of men. They thus ascended to the desire of men; and that very desire which the cattle ascended to among men, that same desire he attains among cattle who, knowing this, establishes the fires under Rohiṇī.
One should establish the sacred fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa.

This Mṛgaśīrṣa is indeed the head of Prajāpati; the head is prosperity, for the head is indeed prosperity. Therefore, of a region, whoever is the most excellent, people say of him, "He is the head of that region. Prosperity indeed comes to him who, knowing this, establishes the fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa.

Now, as to why one should not establish the sacred fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa: this is indeed the body of Prajāpati; for it was there that they pierced him with a three-jointed arrow, as they say. He abandoned this body, for the body is a mere site, unfit for sacrifice and devoid of power. Therefore, one should not establish the fires under Mṛgaśīrṣa.
One should indeed establish it on that very day.

For there is no site belonging to this god, nor anything unfit for sacrifice, nor any body that does not belong to Prajāpati; therefore, one should establish it on that very day. One should perform the re-establishment of the fires under the Punarvasū constellation.
One should establish the sacred fires under the Phalgunī stars.

These Phalgunīs are indeed Indra’s lunar mansion; they are also his namesakes, for Indra’s secret name is Arjuna, and these stars are called Arjunīs. They call them "Phalgunīs" cryptically, for who would dare to utter his secret name? The sacrificer is indeed Indra; thus he establishes the two fires under his own lunar mansion. Indra is the deity of the sacrifice; by this means, his establishment of the fires becomes possessed of Indra. He should establish them under the former (Pūrva-phalgunīs); then creative power (*kratu*) is placed before him. Or he may establish them under the latter (Uttara-phalgunīs); then prosperity that increases day by day (*śvaḥ-śreyasa*) comes to him as one characterized by upward progress.
One who desires, "May it be given to me," should place the fires in his hand; for that which is given with the hand is indeed given directly, and thus it is surely given to him.
One should establish the two fires under the constellation Citrā.

Both the gods and the Asuras, being offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another; both of them desired to ascend to yonder world, the very sky. Then the Asuras piled up the Rauhiṇa fire-altar, thinking, "By this we shall ascend to yonder world."
Indra indeed reflected:
"If they build this [altar], they will surely overcome us. Thereupon, he went forth as one calling himself a Brāhmaṇa, having tied a single brick to himself.
He said, "Come, let me set this one down as well. "So be it," he replied, and he set it down. Consequently, their fire-altar was piled up with very little effort.

Then he said, "I shall give back that one which is mine. Having seized it, he pulled it out; when it was pulled out, Agni collapsed, and following Agni's collapse, the Asuras collapsed. He made those very bricks into thunderbolts and cut off their necks.

The gods, having come together, said: "Truly we have become *citra* (variegated/shining), since we have slain so many rivals. That is indeed the reason for the *citrā* constellation's name being *citrā*. He who, knowing this, establishes his fires under the *citrā* constellation becomes truly *citra*; he slays his rivals, he slays his hateful enemy. Therefore, a Kṣatriya alone should strive for this lunar mansion, for he is as if desirous of slaying his rivals and as if desirous of conquering them.
In the beginning, indeed, these were various separate sovereignties (kṣatra).
Just as that sun is [now], so did he, upon rising, take away their vigor and sovereignty; therefore he is named Āditya, because he took away (ādatta) their vigor and sovereignty.

Those gods said, "Verily, those were not constellations (kṣatrāṇi); verily, those were not constellations. That is indeed the reason for the "constellation-ness" (nakṣatratva) of the constellations. Therefore, one should have the sun as his constellation; for he took away their heroic power and their sovereignty (kṣatra). If, however, one should desire a constellation, this sun is indeed the unfailing constellation. By means of this very auspicious day, he may undertake whatever among these constellations he desires. Therefore, one should indeed have the sun as his constellation.

Spring, summer, and the rainy season—these seasons are the gods; autumn, winter, and the cool season—these are the fathers. That half-month which waxes is the gods; that which wanes is the fathers. Day indeed is the gods, night is the fathers. Furthermore, the forenoon of the day is the gods, the afternoon is the fathers.

These very seasons are the gods and the fathers. He who, knowing this, invokes them as "the gods, the fathers,"—to him the gods come to the invocation of the gods, and the fathers come to the invocation of the fathers; the gods favor him at the invocation of the gods, and the fathers favor him at the invocation of the fathers, he who, knowing this, invokes them as "the gods, the fathers."
Wherever it turns northward, it is then among the gods; it protects the gods at that time. And wherever it turns southward, it is then among the fathers; it protects the fathers at that time.

When it turns northward, one should establish the fires at that time; the gods have their evil struck away, and he strikes away his evil. The gods are immortal, and for him there is no hope for immortality; he attains a full lifespan—he who establishes the fires then. But when it turns southward, he who establishes the fires then has his evil not struck away; the ancestors have their evil not struck away. The ancestors are mortal; he dies before his full lifespan—he who establishes the fires then.
The spring is indeed the Brahman;

the summer is the Kṣatra; the rainy season is the Viś. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should establish his sacred fires in spring, for the spring is the Brahman; therefore, a Kṣatriya should establish his fires in summer, for the summer is the Kṣatra; therefore, a Vaiśya should establish his fires in the rainy season, for the rainy season is the Viś.
He who should desire, "May I be endowed with spiritual luster," should establish his fires in spring; for spring is indeed the Brahman, and he truly becomes endowed with spiritual luster.

Now, if one should desire, "May I be the ruling power through prosperity and glory," he should establish the fires in summer; for summer is indeed the ruling power, and he truly becomes the ruling power through prosperity and glory.

Now, he who should desire, "May I become abundant in offspring and cattle," should establish the fires during the rainy season. For the rainy season is indeed the common people (viś), and the common people are food. He who, knowing this, establishes the fires during the rainy season, truly becomes abundant in offspring and cattle.

Now these seasons are indeed twofold, both having their evil struck away; the sun alone is the striker-away of their evil. As it rises, it strikes away the evil of both these [classes of seasons]. Therefore, whenever the sacrifice may come upon him, he should then establish the two fires; he should not wait for tomorrow, for who knows what tomorrow will bring for a mortal?
On the day before his fire-laying (agnyādheya) is to take place, he should eat only during the day.
For the gods indeed perceive the mind of a human being; they know that his fire-laying is to be on the morrow, and all the gods come to his house. They fast in his house; that is the Upavasatha.

Indeed, it would be improper for anyone to eat before others among men who do not eat; how much more so for one to eat before the gods who do not eat? Therefore, one should eat only during the day; however, one may indeed eat at night if one wishes, for there is no observance of vows for one who has not established the sacred fires, since he remains merely a human being as long as he has not established the fires. Therefore, one may indeed eat at night if one wishes.

Now, some indeed bind a goat [to the sacrificial post], saying, "The goat belongs to Agni; [this is done] for the sake of Agni's completeness. But one should not do so. If he should have a goat, he should give it to the Āgnīdhra priest in the morning; by that very act, he obtains that desired object. Therefore, one should not pay heed to that.

Then they cook rice for four eaters, thinking, "By this we shall gratify the meters. They say, "Just as one would have a vehicle well-fed before setting out on a journey, so is this," but one should not do it that way. Whatever Brahmins dwell in his family, whether they be officiating priests or non-officiating priests, by means of them he attains that desire; therefore, he should not pay heed to that.

Having poured clarified butter upon it, and having poured clarified butter [onto three Aśvattha twigs], they place three fuel-sticks of Aśvattha wood on the fire, anointed with ghee, reciting verses containing the words "fuel" and "ghee," saying, "We wish to obtain this very essence of the *śamī* tree. Now, if one were to place them on the fire for a full year beforehand, he would indeed attain that desire; therefore, one should not pay heed to that.
Regarding this, Bhāllaveya said:

Just as one who intends to do one thing might do another, or intend to say one thing might say another, or intend to go by one path might set out by another—so it is with this: if one were to cook that rice for the four priests, it would indeed be a failure; for it is not fitting that in that fire one should place a fuel-stick or offer an oblation with a Ṛg-verse, a Sāman-chant, or a Yajus-formula. And when they either take it away as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) or cause it to be followed [by the fire], they do so thinking, "It will become the Anvāhāryapacana fire," for they indeed take it away as a sacrificial fee, or they cause it to be followed.
Now, the gods are awake;

thus he turns toward the gods themselves. Being more possessed of the gods, more wearied, and more ascetic, he establishes the two fires. Even so, he may sleep at his pleasure, for there is no performance of vows for one who has not yet established the fires, since as long as he has not established the fires, he remains merely a human being. Therefore, he may indeed sleep at his pleasure.

Now, some, having churned [the fire] before sunrise, lift it up facing east after sunrise, saying, "We thus encompass both day and night for the attainment of out-breathing and in-breathing, and of mind and speech. One should not do it in that way; for in that case, both of his fires remain unestablished until sunrise, since they churn it before sunrise and lift it up facing east after sunrise. He who should churn the Āhavanīya fire after sunrise—he indeed would attain that [attainment].

The gods are indeed the day; the fathers have not had their evil struck away. He does not strike away his evil who churns before the sun has risen—the fathers are mortal, for he dies before his full span of life. The gods have had their evil struck away; he strikes away his evil. The gods are immortal; there is no hope for immortality for him [who churns at night], yet he reaches a full lifespan. The gods are prosperity; he goes to prosperity. The gods are glory; he indeed becomes glorious—he who, knowing this, churns after the sun has risen.
Regarding this they say:

"Since Agni is not established with the Ṛg, nor with the Sāman, nor with the Yajus, then by what is he established? He is indeed established by the Brahman through the Brahman. Speech is the Brahman; of that speech, truth alone is the Brahman. These very Vyahṛtis are indeed truth. Thus, he is established for him by means of truth alone.

"Bhūḥ," indeed, Prajāpati generated this earth; "Bhuvaḥ," the intermediate space; "Svaḥ," the sky. As great as all this is—namely, these worlds—by means of all that is it [the fire-altar] established.

"Bhūḥ," indeed, Prajāpati generated the Brahman; "Bhuvaḥ," the Kṣatra; and "Svaḥ," the Viś. All this that exists is as much as the Brahman, the Kṣatra, and the Viś; thus, by means of all this, he is consecrated.

"bhūḥ," indeed, Prajāpati generated for himself; "bhuvaḥ," [he generated] offspring; "svaḥ," [he generated] cattle. As much as this whole world is—namely, self, offspring, and cattle—with all that he is established.

He indeed lays down the Gārhapatya fire with only "bhūrbhuvaḥ. For if he were to lay it down with all [the vyāhṛtis], with what would he lay down the Āhavanīya? He leaves two syllables remaining; thereby these [syllables] become fresh and not exhausted. With all five of them—namely "bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ"—he lays down the Āhavanīya. These amount to eight syllables. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is Agni's metre; thus he establishes him by means of his own metre.

Now, when the gods were about to establish the two fires, the Asuras and Rakṣases guarded them, saying, "No fire shall be born; you shall not establish the two fires. Because they guarded (rakṣan) them, therefore they are called *rakṣāṃsi*.

Then the gods beheld this thunderbolt: when they raised that horse in front [of the fire], Agni was born in its safety, security, and shelter from the wind. Therefore, wherever one is about to churn the fire, one should say, "Bring the horse hither! It stands facing the east; thus one raises the thunderbolt, and in its safety, security, and shelter from the wind, Agni is born.
It should indeed face the east;
for it increases immeasurable vigor. If he cannot find one that faces the east, it may be any horse whatsoever; if he cannot find a horse, it should even be an ox, for such is the nature of the ox.
Where they carry him facing eastward, they lead the horse in front; thus, striking away the destructive spirits and demons from the front, they carry him forward in safety and freedom from harm.
They should indeed carry him away in such a way that he turns toward him;

for this Agni is the sacrifice, and thus the sacrifice enters him from the front. The sacrifice quickly approaches him, whereas from whomsoever it turns away, from him the sacrifice likewise turns away. If anyone were to say of him in that case, "The sacrifice has turned away from him," it would likely be so.

This, indeed, is the vital breath (prāṇa). They should carry it back in such a way that this [breath] would treat him favorably; for the vital breath enters him from the front, but because he turns away, the vital breath turns away from him. If someone were to say of him in that situation, "The vital breath has turned away from him," it is possible that it would indeed be so.
This sacrifice is indeed he who blows here.

They should carry him in such a way that he would attend to it facing it; for thus the sacrifice enters him facing him, and so the sacrifice quickly approaches him. But as for why he turns away: the sacrifice turns away from him. If someone were to say of him at that time, "The sacrifice has turned away from him," it is possible that it would indeed be so.

This, indeed, is the vital breath (prāṇa). They should certainly carry him away in such a way that the vital breath would attend him from behind; for the vital breath enters him from behind, and because he turns his back [on life], the vital breath turns its back on him. If someone were to say of him in that situation, "The vital breath has turned its back on him," it might well come to pass exactly so; therefore, they should carry him away in that very manner.

Then he makes the horse step upon [the fire]. Having made it step upon it, he leads it eastward; he turns it back again; he releases it toward the north. The horse is indeed vigor; he turns it back so that this vigor of his shall not be turned away from him. Therefore, he turns it back again.
He places it on the footprint of a horse;
the horse is indeed vigor; verily, he thus bestows vigor upon him; therefore, he places it on the footprint of a horse.
He first touches water silently;
then he lifts it up and touches it again; with the third [formula], "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he places it on the fire. For these worlds are three; thus he obtains these very worlds. This is one way.
Now this is the second [offering].

He touches the tip [of the fire] silently, then he lifts it up; with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he places it down with the second [verse]. For if one who is not established on this [earth] lifts a burden, he is unable to lift it and it indeed crushes him.

When he touches [the water] silently, it is upon this foundation that they become established; thus, being established upon this foundation, he lays the fires, and so he does not waver. Now, Āsuri Pāñci Mādhuki held this view: "Everything else is, as it were, unsettled; therefore, one should raise the fire with the first [verse] alone and lay it down with 'Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ'—that indeed is the settled. Therefore, one may do as one desires.
Then, having circumambulated from the east.

Having taken hold of the front half of the fire-sticks, he recites: "As the sky by its abundance, as the earth by its breadth. When he says, "as the sky by its abundance," he means, "May I become as manifold as that sky is with its stars. When he says, "as the earth by its breadth," he means, "May I become as vast as this earth is wide. "On thy back, O Earth, place of divine worship"—for he places him on her very back. "Thee, Agni, the eater of food, for the sake of eating food"—Agni is indeed an eater of food; thus he means, "May I become an eater of food. This is a prayer for a blessing; if he so desires, he may mutter this, but if he does not desire it, he need not pay attention to it.

Then he worships with the verses of the Queen of Serpents: "This spotted bull has stepped forth; he has settled before his mother, and as he goes toward heaven, he approaches his father. Moving between the two bright realms, he breathes out from his breath. The Great One has looked out upon the sky; he shines through thirty domains. Speech is bestowed upon the Bird of Heaven, day after day, throughout the days. Thus, whatever part of this [sacrifice] remains unobtained here—whether by means of the ritual materials, the constellations, the seasons, or the placing of the fire—that very thing becomes obtained for him by this [worship]. Therefore, he worships with the verses of the Queen of Serpents.
Regarding this they say:

"One should not worship with the verses of the Serpent Queen (Sarparājñī). This earth, indeed, is the Serpent Queen; whatever one establishes upon her, thereby one obtains all desires. Therefore, they say: "One should not worship with the verses of the Serpent Queen."
Having drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, he offers the Full Oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Now, as to why he offers the Full Oblation: this Agni is indeed produced from himself as a consumer of food; he thus provides him with this food, just as one would provide a newborn child or a calf with the breast. In this same way, he provides him with this food.

He is appeased by this food and desists from the subsequent oblations being cooked. For he would surely burn either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer, since those two move closest to him if one were not to offer this oblation into him; therefore, one offers this oblation.
He offers that [oblation] when it is full;

for the full is indeed everything, and thus he satisfies him with everything. He offers with the utterance "svāhā"; for the utterance "svāhā" is undefined, and the undefined is indeed everything; thus he satisfies him with everything.

That which Prajāpati offered as the first oblation, he offered it with "Svāhā! Indeed, this [oblation] is its primary cause; therefore, one offers with "Svāhā! At that [offering], he grants a boon; for a boon is everything, and thus he satisfies him with everything.
Regarding this they say:
"Having offered this very oblation, one need not attend to the subsequent sacrificial offerings; for by this alone one obtains that desire for which one offers the subsequent sacrificial offerings."
He offers it to Agni Pavamāna.
Pavamāna is indeed the vital breath; he thus bestows the vital breath upon him. He bestows it upon him by means of the *vetu* formula, for the vital breath is food, and this oblation is food.
Then he offers to Agni Pāvaka.
Food indeed is purifying (pāvaka); thus he bestows food upon him. He bestows it by means of this very [offering], for this oblation is food manifest.
Then he offers to Agni Śuci.

For the bright (śuci) is indeed vigor; that which shines forth from him is his bright vigor. He thus bestows vigor upon him by means of this very [offering]. Indeed, when he offers this oblation to him, then his bright vigor shines forth.
Therefore they say:

"Having offered this very oblation, one need not pay further heed to the subsequent sacrificial offerings; by this alone one obtains that desire for which he offers the subsequent sacrificial offerings. Nevertheless, one should indeed offer the subsequent sacrificial offerings, for that which is "yonder" (adaḥ) is, as it were, invisible, whereas this (idaṃ) is, as it were, visible.

When he offers to Agni Pavamāna, [it is because] the vital breaths (prāṇas) indeed are Pavamāna. For when one is born, then there is the vital breath; and as long as one is not yet born, one breathes along with the vital breath of the mother. Or rather, it is just as when [the child] is born, that he thereby bestows the vital breath upon him.
Now, as to why he offers to Agni Pāvaka:
food is indeed purifying (pāvaka); thus, as soon as he is born, he bestows this food upon him.

Now, as to why he offers to Agni Śuci: purity is indeed vigor; for when one grows through food, then vigor arises. Having thus strengthened him with food, he places this pure vigor within him; therefore [the offering] is made to Agni Śuci.
That very thing is indeed as if inverted.
For when Agni turned away from the gods toward men, he reflected: "Let me not turn toward men with my entire self."
He deposited these three bodies of his in these worlds:

that form of his which was *pavamāna*, he deposited on this earth; then that which was *pāvaka*, in the intermediate space; and then that which was *śuci*, in the sky. The seers who existed at that time perceived this: "Agni has indeed turned away from us with his entire self. Therefore, they offered these oblations for him.

When he offers to Agni Pavamāna, he thereby obtains whatever form of his is on this earth; and when he offers to Agni Pāvaka, he thereby obtains whatever form of his is in the intermediate space; and when he offers to Agni Śuci, he thereby obtains whatever form of his is in heaven. Thus he establishes the entire Agni without omission. Therefore, one should indeed offer the subsequent oblations.

The first oblation has separate sacrificial grass (barhis); the two following have the same sacrificial grass. This world is indeed the first oblation, then this atmosphere is the second, and the sky is the third. For this earth is broad, the atmosphere is swaying, and yonder sky is swaying; "May both of them be opposing it," he thinks; therefore, the two following have the same sacrificial grass.
All the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) consist of eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla).

The Gāyatrī indeed has eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is Agni’s metre; he thus establishes him by means of his own metre. All these together amount to twenty-four potsherds. The Gāyatrī indeed has twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is Agni’s metre; he thus establishes him by means of his own metre.
Then he offers a pap (caru) to Aditi.
For he who offers these oblations indeed departs from this world; for he goes as one ascending these worlds.
As to why he offers a pap to Aditi:
this earth is indeed Aditi; she is the foundation. Thus, he establishes himself upon this very foundation. Therefore, he offers a pap to Aditi.

"Its two *saṃyājyā* verses should be in the *virāj* metre," they say; "for this [earth] is indeed *virāj*. Or they may be in the *triṣṭubh* metre, for this [earth] is indeed *triṣṭubh*; or they may be in the *jagatī* metre, for this [earth] is indeed *jagatī*. However, they should be in the *virāj* metre.

A cow is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). For this earth, like a cow, milks out all desires for human beings; a cow is a mother, and like a mother, this earth supports human beings. Therefore, a cow is the sacrificial fee. This is one way of proceeding.

Now follows this second [offering]: he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni alone. For that which is for Agni Pavamāna, Agni Pāvaka, and Agni Śuci is, as it were, indirect; whereas by this [offering], he establishes him directly and manifestly. Therefore [he offers] to Agni. Then he offers a pap (caru) to Aditi; whatever is the significance of the pap, that is its significance.
They indeed slay this sacrifice when they perform it.

When they press the King [Soma], they slay him; when they quiet and dissect the victim animal, they slay it; and with the mortar and pestle, and with the lower and upper grinding stones, they slay the Haviryajña.
This very sacrifice, being struck down, was not capable of functioning.

The gods made it capable by means of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās); because they made it capable (adakṣayan) by means of sacrificial gifts, therefore they are called dakṣiṇās. Whatever part of this sacrifice, once struck down, falters, that very part he now makes capable by means of these sacrificial gifts; thus the sacrifice becomes successful. Therefore, one gives sacrificial gifts.
He should indeed give six;
for there are six seasons in the year, and the year is the sacrifice, Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, with so many [cows] he bestows prosperity.
He should give twelve.
There are indeed twelve months in a year; the year is the sacrifice, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—with so many [gifts] he bestows power.

He should give twenty-four [cows]. There are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year; the year is the sacrifice, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—with so many he bestows prosperity. This is the measure of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā). However, he should indeed give more according to his faith; that is what it means when one gives sacrificial gifts.

There are indeed two kinds of gods: the gods who are [the celestial] gods, and those Brahmins who have studied and are learned in the Vedas—they are the human gods. For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: oblations belong to the [celestial] gods, and sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the human gods, the Brahmins who have studied and are learned in the Vedas. With oblations one gratifies the [celestial] gods, and with sacrificial fees the human gods, the Brahmins who have studied and are learned in the Vedas. Both these kinds of gods, being gratified, place him in the world of bliss.

Just as one would place seed in a womb, even so do the officiating priests place the sacrificer in this world. That he gives this to them is because they have brought him to this state; such is the nature of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Both were indeed without a self (anātman), for they were mortal; and being mortal, they were without a self. Among those mortals, Agni alone was immortal. Both sides lived upon that immortality; and whenever they killed anyone among them, he would indeed become that [immortal] again.

Then the gods remained as it were the very least in number; they moved about praising and toiling, thinking, "May we overcome our enemies, the Asuras, and mortals. They beheld this immortal establishment of the sacred fires (Agnnyādheya).

They said, "Come, let us place this immortality within ourselves; having placed this immortality within ourselves, having become immortal and invincible, we shall overcome our mortal enemies who are subject to death."
They said, "This Agni belongs to both of us; let us nevertheless announce it to the Asuras."
They said, "We shall indeed establish the two fires; then what will you do?"
They said, "Then we shall indeed set him down here; burn grass here, burn wood here, cook rice here, cook meat here. That which the Asuras set down is what humans eat today.

Then the gods placed it within their own inner selves. Having placed this immortality within their own inner selves, they became immortal; having become invincible, they overcame their mortal enemies who were vulnerable. In the same way, this sacrificer now places that immortality within his own inner self. He has no hope for immortality [in the sense of eternal life], yet he attains a full lifespan. He indeed becomes invincible; even an enemy seeking to strike him down cannot strike him. Therefore, when one who has established the sacred fires and one who has not established them compete, the one who has established the fires prevails, for at that time he is indeed invincible and immortal.
Now, when they churn him here, he breathes out as soon as he is born;

for Agni is breath—thus, while he is already born, he causes him to be born. He then breathes in again; thus he places him within his own self. This Agni of his is thereby established within his own self.

Having kindled it, he fans it into flame with the thought, "Here I shall sacrifice; here I shall perform good deeds. In this way, he fans into flame that fire which has been placed within his inner self.
"He has passed between; he has turned away.

Indeed, no one whatsoever passes between this [person] while he lives, for that fire which has been established within his inner self does not pass between him. Therefore, one should not heed it if it should go out, for that fire which has been established within his inner self does not go out as long as he lives.
These fires are indeed the vital breaths:
the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya are the Prāṇa and Udāna, and the Anvāhāryapacana is the Vyāna.

Now, for this very establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), truth alone is the ritual service (*upacāra*). He who speaks the truth—just as if one were to sprinkle a kindled fire with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), so does he cause it to blaze up; his splendor becomes greater and greater, and day by day he becomes better. But he who speaks untruth—just as if one were to sprinkle a kindled fire with water, so does he cause it to go out; his splendor becomes less and less, and day by day he becomes worse. Therefore, one should speak only the truth.

Now, his kinsmen said to Aruṇa Aupaveśi, "You are indeed old; lay the fires for us. He replied, "Do not say that to me. Remain restrained in speech. One who has established the sacred fires must never speak untruth; while speaking, he should never utter an untruth. Such is the practice of truthfulness alone."

Varuṇa, desiring sovereignty, established this [fire]; he attained sovereignty. Therefore, whether one says it or not, they say, "Varuṇa is king. Soma, desiring glory, became glorious. Therefore, whether one obtains it at a Soma sacrifice or not, both come to possess glory; they come to see this very glory. He who, knowing thus, establishes [the fire] becomes glorious and attains sovereignty.

In the fire, indeed, the gods deposited all forms—both those that are domestic and those that are wild—either when they were about to set out for victory, or for the sake of moving at will, thinking: "May this one, our most excellent protector, guard us."

Agni desired to hide those [seasons]. Having gathered them together, he entered the seasons, thinking, "Let me go back. When Agni had thus become invisible to the gods, they were distressed, saying, "What is to be done here? What wisdom is there here?"
Then Tvaṣṭṛ perceived this re-establishment of the fires;

he established them, and thereby he attained the beloved abode of Agni. He emitted for him both kinds of forms—those that are domestic and those that are wild. Therefore they say, "Forms indeed belong to Tvaṣṭṛ," for every form belongs to Tvaṣṭṛ. And other creatures, as far as they go, remain as if they were he himself.
For him, moreover, one should perform the re-establishment of the fire (*punarādheya*).

In this very way, he approaches the beloved abode of Agni; he releases both kinds of forms for him—those that are domestic and those that are wild—and these two kinds of forms are seen in it. That is indeed the highest state; they long for him, and thus he prospers; it is also truly conducive to the world.
This sacrifice belongs to Agni;

Agni is light, the burner of evil. He burns away his evil, and he becomes light itself here through prosperity and fame. Thereafter, he becomes light in the world beyond through the attainment of the world of merit. This, then, is why one should establish the fires.

One should indeed install it during the rainy season. The rainy season is all the seasons, for the rainy season is truly all the seasons. Thus, people look back upon the years, saying, "In those days we had rain; in those days we had rain. The rainy season is indeed the form of all the seasons; for that which they say, "Today it is as if summer," occurs in the rainy season, and that which they say, "Today it is as if winter," also occurs in the rainy season. The rainy season is the beginning of the rainy season.

Now, this very thing is its indirect form: that which blows from the east is the form of spring; that which thunders is the form of summer; that which rains is the form of the rainy season; that which lightens is the form of autumn; and that which lifts up [the rain] after it has rained is the form of winter. The rainy season is all the seasons. He entered the seasons; verily, he produces him from the seasons.
