The sun indeed is all the seasons: when it rises, that is spring; when it is the time for milking (saṃgava), then summer; when it is midday, then the rainy season; when it is afternoon, then autumn; and when it sets, then winter. Therefore, one should establish the fires at midday alone; for then it is nearest to this world, and thus he produces it from its very midst, from that which is nearest.
Or rather, this person is as if pursued by evil;

thus, that [evil] becomes his lowest part, as if it were cast beneath his feet. It is precisely this that he crushes down as the lowest evil. Therefore, one should indeed establish the fire at midday.

He indeed draws it out with *darbha* grasses. Previously, he used pieces of wood to draw it out; if he were to use wood first and then wood again, he would commit a repetition and cause a conflict. *Darbha* grasses are water, and rain is water; having entered the seasons, he now fashions it from water by means of water. Therefore, he draws it out with *darbha* grasses.
Having made a cake of rice with *arka* and *palāśa* wood, he places it where he is about to establish the *gārhapatya* fire; he then establishes that *gārhapatya* fire upon it.

Having made a cake of barley with *arka* and *palāśa* wood, he places it where he is about to establish the Āhavanīya fire; he then establishes the Āhavanīya, saying, "We thus interpose these two fires between those two [previous] fires. But one should not do it in that way, for they are already separated by the nights.
He offers a sacrificial cake on five potsherds to Agni;
for it, there are five-footed *paṅkti* verses as the invitatory and offering formulas. For the seasons are five; he entered the seasons, and thus he now brings him forth from the seasons.
It is entirely dedicated to Agni;
for in this way Tvaṣṭṛ approached the beloved abode of Agni, therefore it is entirely dedicated to Agni.
Therefore they proceed in a low voice.

For when one wishes to perform a rite exclusive to a kinsman or a friend, he becomes as it were concealed by that act; whereas other sacrifices belong to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva), this one belongs exclusively to Agni (niṣkevalya). And since that which is as it were concealed is performed in a low voice, therefore they proceed in a low voice.
He performs the final *anuyāja* offering loudly;
for at that time he is as one who has completed his task, since everyone indeed recognizes what has been accomplished.

Having called for the Śrauṣaṭ, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the fuel-sticks (samidhaḥ). This is an indirect form pertaining to Agni; however, he should rather say, "Recite the offering prayer for the fires (agnīn)," for that is the direct form pertaining to Agni.
He sacrifices:

"O Agni, may you partake of the clarified butter! Vauṣaṭ! May Agni partake of the clarified butter! Vauṣaṭ! May [the gods] through Agni partake of the clarified butter! Vauṣaṭ! May Agni partake of the clarified butter! Vauṣaṭ!"
Then he says, "Svāhā to Agni! [and offers] the butter-portion for Agni.

If they are intent upon Pavamāna, he says, "Svāhā to Agni Pavamāna! If they are intent upon Agni Indumat, he says, "Svāhā to Agni Indumat! He performs the sacrifice with: "Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to the butter-drinking Agnis! May Agni, being pleased, accept the butter!"
Then he says, "Recite for Agni! He recites the butter-portion for Agni:

"Awaken Agni with a hymn, as he is being kindled, the immortal one; may he place our offerings among the gods. For when he has been removed from the fire, he is, as it were, asleep; he thus awakens him and rouses him. He performs the sacrifice with the formula: "May Agni, enjoying it, partake of the butter."

Now, if they should be intended for Agni Pavamāna, he should say, "Recite for Agni Pavamāna! He recites: "O Agni, you purify our lives; speed forth strength and food for us; drive far away the malicious one. Thus it becomes addressed to Agni. Soma indeed is Pavamāna; therefore, they lead him away from the Soma-related butter-portions. He offers with the formula: "May Agni Pavamāna, being pleased, enjoy the butter."

Now, if the fires should remain for Agni Indumat, he should say, "Recite for Agni Indumat! He then recites: "Come, O Agni, let me speak these other songs to you; grow strong by these drops. Thus it becomes entirely pertaining to Agni. For *indu* is indeed Soma; therefore, they lead [the offering] away from the butter-portion belonging to Soma. He offers with the formula, "May Agni, accompanied by *indu*, graciously accept the butter. In this way, he makes everything pertain to Agni.
Then he says, "Recite for Agni" regarding the oblation;
"Sacrifice to Agni"; "Recite for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"; "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Now, when he says, "Sacrifice to the gods," he thereby means, "Sacrifice to the fires."
He performs the sacrifice:

"May Agni for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure, accept it—Vauṣaṭ! May Agni indeed for the winning of wealth, for the granting of treasure, accept it—Vauṣaṭ! May the divine Agni Sviṣṭakṛt... Thus he himself performs the after-offerings (anuyājas) dedicated to Agni.
Now, these are the six case-endings he offers: four in the *prayāja*s and two in the *anuyāja*s. There are six seasons; he entered the seasons, and thus he now fashions him from the seasons.

There are either twelve or thirteen syllables; for there are either twelve or thirteen months in the year. He entered the seasons from the year; thus he fashions him out from the seasons and from the year. Not even two [syllables] together, to avoid sameness; for it would be a repetition if two were together. "May they enjoy," "let him enjoy"—this is the form of the *prayāja* offerings. "For the winning of wealth, for the bestowing of wealth"—this is the form of the *anuyāja* offerings.

Gold is its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This sacrifice belongs to Agni; gold is the seed of Agni, therefore gold is the sacrificial fee. Or it is an ox, for it is connected with Agni by virtue of its carrying power; for its carrying power is as if burnt by fire, since "Agni is the carrier of the oblation for the gods. It indeed carries [the offering] for men; therefore the ox is the sacrificial fee.
In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe.

He thought, "How indeed may I procreate? He exerted himself and practiced austerity; he generated Agni from his mouth. Because he generated him from his mouth, Agni is a consumer of food. Whoever knows this Agni as a consumer of food becomes, indeed, a consumer of food.
He indeed generated him first among the gods; therefore he is Agni.

For "Agni" is truly his name, since he is called Agni. As soon as he was born, he went forward (*peyāya*); for whoever goes first (*pūrva*) goes at the beginning (*agra*). Thus they say of him: "He goes at the beginning. This is his nature as Agni.

Prajāpati reflected: "I have indeed produced this Agni from myself as an eater of food; yet there is no other food here besides me whom he might eat. At that time, the earth was indeed barren, for neither herbs nor trees existed; that alone was in his mind.

Then Agni turned toward him with his mouth wide open. As he was terrified, his own greatness departed from him; for speech is indeed his own greatness, and it was speech that departed from him. He sought an oblation within himself; he wiped [his hands]. Because he wiped them, these two [lips] became hairless. There he perceived an oblation of ghee or an oblation of milk; yet in truth, both of those are simply milk.
She did not find favor with him.

As if mixed with *keśa* grass, he sprinkled her, saying, "Drink the night! From that, plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*) came into being; therefore they are called *oṣadhayaḥ*. He wiped his hand a second time; there he found another oblation—either an oblation of clarified butter or an oblation of milk, for both of these are indeed milk.

She gratified him. He hesitated, thinking, "Should I offer the oblation? Or should I not? His own greatness (Svaḥ) spoke to him, saying, "Offer it! Prajāpati understood, "My own greatness has spoken to me. He offered with "Svāhā! Therefore, the oblation is offered with "Svāhā! Then he who shines yonder rose up; from that, he who blows here came into being; and from that, Agni turned away.
Having offered that oblation, Prajāpati was propagated;

he saved himself from Agni, from death, which was about to devour him. Verily, he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, is propagated with that same propagation with which Prajāpati was propagated; and thus indeed does he save himself from Agni, from death, which would otherwise consume him.

Wherever he dies, wherever they place him upon the fire, there he is born from that very fire; then the fire burns his body alone. Just as one might be born from a father or a mother, even so is he born from the fire. Indeed, he who does not offer the Agnihotra is never truly reborn; therefore, the Agnihotra must be offered.

This, indeed, was the birth from doubt: that Prajāpati doubted; while doubting, he held fast to what was better, and he brought himself to safety from Agni, from death, as he was being born. He who knows this birth from doubt—whatever he doubts—he indeed holds fast to what is better.
Having offered it, he wiped his hands; from that, the vikaṅkata tree arose.

Therefore, this is the tree fit for sacrifice and fit for sacrificial vessels. From that, these heroes of the gods were born: Agni, he who blows here (Vāyu), and Sūrya. Indeed, he who thus knows these heroes of the gods, a hero is born to him.

They said, "We indeed belong to our father Prajāpati; come, let us create that which shall belong to us. Having enclosed themselves, they praised with the Gāyatra [Sāman], omitting the *hiṃkāra*. That which they enclosed became the ocean, and this very earth is its *stotra*.

Having praised her, they stepped forward facing east, thinking, "Let us go back. The cows had gathered together; she, looking up at them, uttered the sound "hiṃ. The gods understood: "This is the *hiṃ* of the Sāman. Before that time, the Sāman was indeed without the *hiṃ*. This is the *hiṃ* of the Sāman in the cow; therefore, this [cow] is a source of livelihood. Indeed, he becomes a source of livelihood for others who knows this *hiṃ* of the Sāman in the cow.

They said, "Truly, we have brought forth something auspicious, for we have brought forth a cow; for this [cow] is indeed the sacrifice, since without a cow no sacrifice is performed; for she is indeed food, for whatever food there is, that is the cow."

This indeed is their name, and this is the name of the sacrifice; therefore, one should recite it as "sādhu puṇyam" (well-being, merit). For many indeed become these [names] for him, and the sacrifice becomes inclined toward him who, knowing this, recites it as "sādhu puṇyam."
Agni set his mind upon her, thinking, "May I have union with her.

He united with her and poured his seed into her; it became milk. Therefore, when this cow is pregnant, the milk is boiled [hot], for it is Agni’s seed. Consequently, whether she is black or red, the milk remains white, for it is like Agni, being Agni’s seed. Therefore, the first-milked milk is warm, for it is Agni’s seed.

They said, "Come, let us offer this! To whom shall we offer this first? Agni said, "To me! "To me! said he who blows here (Vāyu). "To me! said Sūrya. They could not reach an agreement; having failed to agree, they said, "Let us go to our father Prajāpati; to whichever of us he says this should be offered first, to him we shall offer it first. They went to their father Prajāpati and said, "To whom among us shall this be offered first?"

He said: "To Agni [belongs] the fire; by means of the *anuṣṭhā* (the following day), he shall procreate his own seed, and thus you shall procreate. And for you [is this]: to Sūrya. And as to that which the fire consumes when being offered, that belongs to him who blows here (Vāyu). Therefore, even now they offer in this very same way: to Agni in the evening and to Sūrya in the morning; and as to that which the fire consumes when being offered, that belongs to him who blows here."

Having become gods, they procreated this progeny which is their progeny; they won this victory which is their victory. Agni won this very world, Vāyu the intermediate space, and Sūrya the sky. He who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra, procreates that same progeny which these [gods] then procreated, and wins that same victory which these then won. And he indeed becomes a sharer of the same world as them who, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra. Therefore, the Agnihotra must indeed be offered.
The Agnihotra is indeed the sun;
because it rose from this oblation at the beginning, therefore the sun is the Agnihotra.

When he offers in the evening after the sun has set, thinking, "May I offer this while he is here," and when he offers in the morning before the sun has risen, thinking, "May I offer this while he is here"— therefore they say that the sun is the Agnihotra.

Now, when it sets, it enters Agni as its very womb, becoming an embryo; and all these creatures become embryos following that embryo, for they lie down together, being in harmony. And as for the night, he makes it concealed, for embryos are, as it were, concealed.

When he offers in the evening after the sun has set, he offers to that which is already an embryo; he acts upon that which is already an embryo. Because he offers to that which is already an embryo, therefore these embryos live without eating.

Now, as to why he offers at dawn before the sun has risen: he thereby causes him (the sun) to be born; thus, having become brilliance, he rises shining forth. Indeed, he would never rise if he were not to offer this oblation into him; therefore, he offers this oblation.

Just as a snake might cast off its skin, so does he free himself from evil during the night; and just as a snake might cast off its skin, so does he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, free himself from all evil. Following the procreation of this very [Agni], all these creatures are born after him; for they are released according to their purpose.

He who takes out the Āhavanīya fire before the setting of the sun—these rays are indeed the Viśve Devās; and that which is the highest light is Prajāpati, or it is Indra. Now, the Viśve Devās come to the house of one who offers the Agnihotra; from him whose fire has not been taken out when they arrive, the gods depart. That which causes the gods to depart fails him; and both he who knows it and he who does not know it alike say, "The sun has set upon his fire while it was still unremoved. Thus it is said.

Now, as for him who takes out the Āhavanīya fire before sunset: just as one would wait upon a superior person who is about to arrive with a prepared dwelling, so it is in this case. When [the fires] come to that [fire] which has been taken out, they enter the Āhavanīya; they settle down in the Āhavanīya.

When he offers in the evening after the sun has set, he offers to them while they have entered into Agni; and when he offers in the morning before the sun has risen, he offers to them while they have not yet departed. Therefore, we consider the Agnihotra of those who offer after sunrise to be interrupted, as Āsuri used to say: "It is just as if one were to bring food into an empty dwelling."
This life indeed consists of two things:

that which has roots and that which is rootless. Both of these gods and men subsist upon; the animals are the rootless and the plants are the rooted. Having eaten the plants, which are the rooted, and having drunk water, from that this essence comes into being.

When he offers in the evening after the sun has set, he thinks, "I shall offer this sap of life to the gods, so that we may live upon what belongs to them. When he eats thereafter during the night, he eats only the remains of the offering, having set aside his portion; for one who performs the Agnihotra eats only the remains of what has been offered.
Now, when he offers in the morning before the sun has risen, he thinks:

"I shall offer to the gods from this sap, this life-force, which they possess and upon which we depend. Therefore, whatever he eats during that day, he eats only the remains of the offering, having set aside his portion like a sacrificial oblation; for one who performs the Agnihotra is indeed an eater of the remains of the offering.

Regarding this they say: "All other sacrifices come to an end; only the Agnihotra does not come to an end, even after twelve years, for it has a definite conclusion. Yet this very [Agnihotra] is endless: having offered in the evening, one knows, 'I shall offer in the morning'; and having offered in the morning, one knows, 'I shall offer again in the evening. Thus, this Agnihotra is never-ending. Following its non-termination, these creatures are born. Indeed, he who knows this Agnihotra as never-ending is himself born with prosperity and offspring through its non-termination."

Having milked it, he places it on the fire. Regarding this, they say: "When it has been boiled, one should then offer it. However, one should not let it boil over; for if one were to let it boil over, one would surely burn it. Indeed, seed that is burnt is sterile; therefore, one should not let it boil over.
Having placed it on the fire, he should indeed offer it.

For this [milk] is the seed of Agni; it is already cooked by that very fact, and because they place it on the fire, it is thereby indeed cooked. Therefore, having placed it on the fire, he should offer it.

He illumines it with that [fire], thinking, "Now it is cooked. Then he pours water back into it for the sake of appeasement and for the completeness of the essence. For when it rains here, then plants are born; having eaten the plants and drunk the water, from that this essence arises. Therefore, it is for the sake of the completeness of the essence. Thus, if there should be only milk available for drinking, he should tell him to pour a little of it back in for the sake of appeasement and for the completeness of the essence.
Then he draws up four times.

This milk has been prepared in four ways; then, taking fuel-sticks, he hastens forward for the offering with kindled fire. Without having set down the first oblation, he offers it. For if he were to set it down, it would be as if one were to place food between oneself and someone to whom one intends to bring it to eat; such would that be. But because he does not set it down, it is as if one were to bring food to someone and, having brought it, place it right before them—such is this. Having set down the second [oblation], he offers it; he thus makes these two of different powers. For these two oblations are indeed Mind and Speech; he thereby separates Mind and Speech. Therefore, although Mind and Speech are the same, they are yet distinct.

He indeed offers twice into the fire, wipes [the ladle] twice, eats twice, and draws up [the ghee] four times; that makes ten. For the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the Virāj; thus he brings this sacrifice into correspondence with the Virāj.

When he offers in the fire, he offers among the gods; therefore the gods exist. Then, when he wipes [the ladle], he offers among the ancestors and the plants; therefore the ancestors and the plants exist. Then, when having offered he eats, he offers among human beings; therefore human beings exist.
Indeed, those offspring who are not included in the sacrifice perish;
in this very way, he now causes these surviving offspring to participate at the opening of the sacrifice. Thus, cattle are made to share in it, since cattle follow after men.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "One should certainly not think of it as being like a [sacrificial] rite; rather, it is like a *pākayajña* (cooked-offering sacrifice). For whatever one cuts off with the offering-spoon (*sruc*) in another sacrifice, all that one offers into the fire; but here, having offered into the fire, one steps aside, sips water, and licks the residue—this is its character as a *pākayajña*. This is its form pertaining to cattle, for the *pākayajña* pertains to cattle."
This very one was indeed the first oblation;

that same one which Prajāpati offered in the beginning. Then, as these [beings]—namely Agni, he who blows here (Vāyu), and Sūrya—became established like animals, therefore this second oblation is offered.

That which is the first libation is the deity of the Agnihotra; therefore, he offers to her. Now, that which is the second is the portion for Sviṣṭakṛt; therefore, he offers it in the northern half, for this is the direction of Sviṣṭakṛt. This second libation is offered for the sake of pairing, for a pair is a productive couple.
These two oblations are precisely that pair:
the past and the future, the born and the yet to be born, the arrived and the hope, today and tomorrow; they follow after that very pair.
The self alone is what has come to be;

for what has come to be is indeed certain (addhā), and the self is indeed certain. The progeny alone is what will be; for what will be is indeed uncertain (anaddhā), and the progeny is indeed uncertain.
The self alone is what has been born, for that which is born is indeed certain (addhā), and the self is indeed certain.
Progeny alone is what is yet to be born, for that which is yet to be born is uncertain (anaddhā), and progeny is indeed uncertain.
The self alone is what has come;
for truly, that which has come is the real, and the self is the real. Progeny alone is hope; for truly, hope is the real, and progeny is the real.
The self alone is today;
for that which is today is indeed certain (addhā), and the self is certain. Offspring are tomorrow; for that which is tomorrow is uncertain (anaddhā), and offspring are uncertain.
That which is the first oblation is offered for oneself;

he offers it with a mantra, for that which is a mantra is manifest (addhā), and that which is the self is manifest. Then, that which is the subsequent oblation is offered for offspring; he offers it silently, for that which is silent is unmanifest (anaddhā), and that which is offspring is unmanifest.

He offers with the formula: "Agni is light, light is Agni, svāhā! Then in the morning, he offers: "Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā! Thus it is offered by means of truth itself; for when the sun sets, then Agni is the light, and when the sun rises, then Sūrya is the light. Indeed, that which is offered by means of truth goes to the gods.

Now, it was indeed this that a carpenter told to Āruṇi, who desired spiritual luster: "Agni is luster, light is luster; Sūrya is luster, light is luster. He who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, truly becomes possessed of spiritual luster.
That very thing is indeed the form of procreation itself.

"Agni is light, light is Agni, Svāhā!"—by this, he encloses the seed on both sides with light by means of the deity; for seed that is enclosed on both sides is procreated. Thus, having enclosed it on both sides, he causes it to be procreated.
Then in the morning:

"Sūrya is light, light is Sūrya, svāhā!"—thus he encloses the seed on both sides with light by means of the deity; for seed, when enclosed on both sides, comes forth. Having thus enclosed it on both sides, he causes it to be born; that is the form of procreation.
Regarding this, Jīvala Cailaki said:
"Āruṇi performs only the act of impregnation; he does not bring about birth. One should therefore offer this oblation in the evening.

Then, in the morning, he offers with: "Light is Sūrya; Sūrya is light, svāhā! He thus places the light outside by means of the deity; for seed that has been produced remains outside, and so he causes this [seed] to be born.

Regarding this they say: "In the evening one offers the sun into the fire, and in the morning one offers the fire into the sun. But that is indeed the practice of those who offer after sunrise; for when the sun sets, then fire is the light, and when the sun rises, then the sun is the light. This [other view] is not a true distinction; the true distinction is that the offering is made to that deity which is the actual deity of the Agnihotra—namely, with the formula, "Agni is the light, light is Agni, Svāhā!"—and there one does not say, "To Agni, Svāhā! Then, in the morning, with the formula, "The sun is the light, light is the sun, Svāhā!"—and there one does not say, "To the Sun, Svāhā!"
With this very [formula] he should offer:

"In harmony with the god Savitṛ"—this is for the sake of impulsion by Savitṛ; "in harmony with Night, possessing Indra"—thereby he effects a union with Night and makes it possessed of Indra, for Indra is the deity of the sacrifice; "may Agni, being pleased, accept [the offering], Svāhā!"—thereby he offers directly to Agni.

Then, in the morning: "In unison with the god Savitṛ"—this contains the word *savitṛ* for the sake of impulsion; "in unison with Uṣas, accompanied by Indra"—this refers either to the day or to the dawns; he thus creates a union between the days and the dawns. He says "accompanied by Indra," for Indra is the deity of the sacrifice. "May Sūrya, being pleased, accept it, Svāhā!"—thus he offers directly to Sūrya. Therefore, one should offer in this very manner.

They said, "Who shall offer this for us? "A Brāhmaṇa alone," they replied. "Brāhmaṇa, offer this for us. "What will be mine from that? "The remains of the Agnihotra itself. Now, what he leaves remaining in the offering-spoon (sruk) is the remains of the Agnihotra; but as for what is in the pot (sthālī), it is as if one were pouring out a full vessel. Therefore, whoever might drink that, a non-Brāhmaṇa should certainly not drink it, for they place it over the fire; therefore, a non-Brāhmaṇa should not drink it.
Indeed, these deities dwell in whoever exists: Indra, King Yama, Naḍa Naiṣidha, Anaśnan Sāṅgamana, and Asan Pāṃsava.
Now, this Āhavanīya fire is indeed Indra;

and this Gārhapatya fire is King Yama; and this Anvāhāryapacana fire is Naḍa Naiṣidha. Because they bring this [Anvāhāryapacana] every day from the south, therefore they say: "Day by day, Naḍa Naiṣidha leads King Yama from the south."

Now, that fire which is in the assembly hall is indeed the one who eats not, for it is the gathering place of those who do not eat. Because they approach it even without having eaten, therefore this one does not eat. And when they remove the ashes and cast them away, these are the very dust of the seat. He who knows this thus—that "these deities dwell within me"—conquers all these worlds and wanders through all the worlds.
Their attendance is as follows:

whatever attendance one performs by standing near and sitting near the Āhavanīya fire in the evening and in the morning, that indeed is its attendance. Then, whatever one does upon returning and either sits or lies down near the Gārhapatya fire, that indeed is its attendance. Furthermore, whenever, while walking along, one remembers the Anvāhāryapacana fire, one should attend to it mentally; that indeed is its attendance.

Then, in the morning, having remained for a moment in the assembly hall without eating, he may wander about at will; that itself is his attendance upon [the fires]. Or, wherever he approaches the place where the ashes have been removed, that itself is his attendance upon them. In this way, indeed, these deities become attended by him.

The Gārhapatya fire indeed has the sacrificer as its deity; now, this Anvāhāryapacana fire has the rival as its deity. Therefore, one should not carry it forward day by day. For those who, knowing this, do not carry it forward day by day, no rivals exist. Indeed, this [Anvāhāryapacana] is the Anvāhāryapacana fire itself.
They should bring it on the very day of preparation (upavasatha). Wherever they intend to sacrifice for him, in that way this [fire] becomes brought for him not in vain.
When it has newly set, they should bring it;

they should cook it in that [fire], and the Brāhmaṇas should eat it. If, however, they do not find that, he should say, "Let even the milk of a cow be placed on the fire," and he should say, "Let the Brāhmaṇas be made to drink it. For those of his enemies become more wretched who act in this way toward one who knows thus. Therefore, he should indeed desire to do exactly so.

Now, when this [fire] has first been kindled, it then becomes as if smoking; that is Rudra. If one should desire, "May I eat food just as Rudra pursues these creatures—with distrust, with violence, or as if with a blow—so may I eat food," then he should offer at that time. He who, knowing thus, offers at that time, indeed obtains that food.

Now, when it becomes especially bright, then he indeed becomes Varuṇa. He who should desire, "May I eat food in such a way that Varuṇa, as it were, seizes these creatures, as it were, overpowers them, and as it were, strikes them down, so that they attend upon me"—he should then offer the oblation. Indeed, he who, knowing this, offers at that time, obtains that very food.

Now, when it becomes thus kindled, and the smoke rises high while it crackles with supreme vigor, then indeed it becomes Indra. He who should desire, "May I be like Indra in prosperity and fame," should then offer an oblation; for he who, knowing this, offers at that time, attains that very food.

Now, when the flame of one who is dying becomes as it were turned back or sideways and subsides, then he indeed becomes Mitra. If someone should desire, "May I eat this food with the friendliness of Mitra," regarding whom they say, "This Brahmin is the friend of all, for he does not harm anyone," then he should offer the oblation at that time. He who, knowing this, offers the oblation at that time, surely obtains that food.

Now, when these embers appear as if shining, then this indeed becomes the Brahman. He who should desire, "May I be endowed with the splendor of Brahman," should then offer his oblation. He who, knowing thus, offers at that time, surely obtains that food.
One should strive for one of these for a year.

If he offers the oblations himself, or if another offers for him, yet he offers in various ways, it is as if one were digging for water or some other food and were to turn back prematurely; such is that case. But he who offers them together, it is as if one were digging for water or some other food and were to strike through to it quickly; such is that case.
These oblations are indeed the spades for obtaining food;
he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, digs up that very food.
That which is the first oblation is the gods; then that which is the second is human beings; and what he leaves remaining in the ladle is the cattle.
He indeed offers the first oblation as it were less, and the latter as it were more; he leaves as it were more remaining in the ladle.

In that he offers the first oblation in a smaller measure, it is because the gods are fewer than men; and in that he offers the second oblation in a larger measure, it is because men are more numerous than the gods; and in that he leaves a remainder in the ladle in a larger measure, it is because cattle are more numerous than men. Indeed, for one who, knowing this, performs the Agnihotra, his dependents become fewer while his cattle become more numerous. That is truly successful for whom the dependents are few and the cattle are many.

When Prajāpati created living beings, he created Agni; as soon as he was born, he set his mind on burning everything here, making it all a single mass of flame. Then those creatures that existed at that time resolved to crush him. Unable to endure this, he approached a human being.

He said: "I cannot endure this; come, let me enter you. Having brought me forth, sustain me. Just as you will sustain me after having brought me forth in this world, so shall I sustain you after having brought you forth in the other world. "So be it," he replied. Having brought him forth, he sustained him.
When he establishes the two fires, he thereby generates him;

having generated him, he maintains him. Just as this [father] here in this world, having generated him, maintains him, so indeed does this [Agni] there in yonder world, having generated him, maintain him.
Therefore, one should not extinguish it prematurely;

for he becomes exhausted prematurely, and just as he becomes exhausted prematurely for him in this world, so indeed does he become exhausted prematurely for him in that world. Therefore, one should not extinguish it prematurely.
Wherever he dies, wherever they place him upon the fire, there he is born again from the fire; being thus a son, he becomes a father.
Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer:

"A hundred autumns are before us, O Gods, within which you have brought about the aging of our bodies, wherein sons become fathers; do not harm us in the midst of our journeying life. For he, being a son, becomes a father again; this is why one should establish the two fires.
This, indeed, is that very Death; he is this one who shines there.

Because he is that very Death, therefore those creatures which are on this side of him die; but those which are beyond him are the gods, and therefore they are immortal. All these creatures are bound to his rays by their vital breaths (prāṇas); therefore, the rays extend down toward the vital breaths.

Whomever he desires, taking away that person's vital breath, he rises up; that person dies. Indeed, whoever goes to that world without having escaped this Death, just as in this world one does not heed a prisoner who is securely bound, but kills him whenever one wishes, even so in that world he causes him to die again and again.

When he offers two oblations in the evening after the sun has set, he thereby establishes himself upon these two front feet of this Death. Then, when he offers two oblations in the morning before the sun has risen, he thereby establishes himself upon these two hind feet of this Death. Rising up, this [Sun] rises having taken him with it; thus he is released from this Death. This is the release from Death in the Agnihotra. Indeed, one who knows this release from Death in the Agnihotra is released from repeated death.

Just as the point of an arrow [is its foremost part], so is the Agnihotra among sacrifices; for by that by which the point of an arrow goes, the entire arrow goes. By this, all his sacrificial rites have passed beyond death.

For day and night, as they revolve in yonder world, wear away a person's merit; however, because day and night are directed hitherward from that [world], thus indeed day and night do not wear away his merit.

Just as one standing on the seat of a chariot might look down upon the two wheels of the chariot revolving above him, even so does he, though situated below, look down upon day and night from beyond them. Indeed, day and night do not diminish the merit of one who thus knows this transcendence of day and night.
Having gone around the Āhavanīya fire from the east, he passes between the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya.

Indeed, the gods do not know a human being; they know him as he passes between these two, thinking, "This one is indeed offering this for us. Agni is the repeller of evil. As he passes between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya, those two repel his evil. Thus, with his evil repelled, he becomes light itself through prosperity and glory.
Or rather, the door of the Agnihotra is to the north;
just as one would enter through a door, so it is with that. But he who comes and sits to the south does so as if he were moving outside.

This Agnihotra is indeed a boat for attaining heaven. Of this very boat that leads to heaven, the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires are the two sides of the ship's hull; and the one who offers the milk is the steersman.

When he drives her up facing the east, he thus drives her toward the eastern direction, toward the heavenly world; through her, he attains the heavenly world. Her ascent is from the north; she thus brings him to completion in the heavenly world. Now, as to him who comes and sits on the south side: just as one might arrive at a ford that has already been crossed and be left behind, or be excluded from it, so it is in that case.

Now, this fuel-stick which he places on the fire is a brick; the mantra with which he offers is that *yajus* with which he lays down this brick. Indeed, whenever a brick is laid down, then an oblation is offered. Thus, these very *agnihotra* oblations are offered upon those bricks of his once they have been laid down.
Agni is indeed Prajāpati;

Prajāpati is the year. Year after year, the Agnihotra of one who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra, is completed by means of the piled fire-altar (citya), and year after year he attains the piled fire-altar. This Agnihotra of his is thus completed by means of the piled fire-altar, and he attains the piled fire-altar.
There are seven hundred and twenty verses; and when he offers the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning, those two oblations become his oblations throughout the year.
Seven hundred and twenty [oblations].

Indeed, year after year, his Agnihotra becomes equal to the Great Litany (mahad uktha); year after year he attains the Great Litany, he who, knowing this, offers the Agnihotra. Thus, indeed, his Agnihotra becomes equal to the Great Litany; he attains the Great Litany.

In the fire, indeed, the gods deposited all animals— both those that are domestic and those that are wild— either when they were about to set out for victory, or for the sake of acting according to their will, or thinking, "May this one, the best protector, protect us."

Agni desired to hide from them; having seized them, he entered the night, thinking, "I will come back again. When Agni had thus disappeared, the gods became aware of it, saying, "He has indeed entered here; he has entered the night. As the night was returning, they waited upon him in the evening, saying, "Give us our cattle; give us our cattle back! To them, Agni gave the cattle back again.
Therefore, one should worship the two fires for that purpose.

The two fires are indeed the givers; it is to them that he thus makes his request. He should worship them in the evening, for in the evening the gods worshipped them. To him who, knowing this, worships them in this manner, these two grant cattle.
Now, as for why one should not perform the *upasthāna* (reverential attendance):

In the beginning, both gods and men existed here together. Whatever was not possessed by men, they would ask of the gods, saying, "This indeed we do not have; let this be ours. Out of resentment toward that very begging, the gods disappeared, thinking, "Lest I should cause harm; lest I should become an object of hatred. Therefore, one should not perform the *upasthāna*.
Now, as to why he should indeed stand near [the fire]:

the sacrifice belongs to the gods, while the blessing belongs to the sacrificer; but this oblation is indeed the sacrifice for him, and the blessing is the sacrificer's. Therefore, by standing near it, he secures whatever belongs to him in that regard. For this reason, he should indeed stand near it.

Now, as for why one should not perform worship: if a man follows a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya while praising them, thinking, "This one will give to me; this one will build a house for me," then whoever seeks to please him with wealth or with work, to him he thinks that [gift] should be given. But he who says, "What are you to me, you who do not give to me?"—he is liable to hate him, and he is liable to fall into despair. Therefore, one should not perform worship. Indeed, when he kindles the fire and offers oblations, it is precisely this that he begs for; therefore, one should not perform worship.
Now, as for why one should indeed perform the *upasthāna* (homage):

whether one obtains a giver through begging or not, a husband does not always take notice of his wife. But when she says, "I am your wife; support me," then he knows her and regards her as his wife. Therefore, one should indeed perform the *upasthāna*; this is the complete reason why one should perform the *upasthāna*.

Having become Prajāpati himself, he pours his seed—that which is the Agnihotra—into as much as he rules over and as much as follows him; thus, by approaching [the fire], he transforms this entire world and procreates this entire world.
He begins with the *upavatī* verse.

This earth is indeed "near" (*upa*) because it is near to two things: for whatever is born here, that is born near to her; and whatever perishes, that is buried near to her. Thus, by means of day and night, it becomes more and more inexhaustible; he therefore begins with this inexhaustible abundance.

He said: "Approaching the sacrifice" (*upaprayanto adhvaram*)—the sacrifice (*adhvara*) is indeed the *yajña*; thus he says, "approaching the sacrifice. "'Let us speak the mantra unto Agni'" (*mantraṃ vocemāgnaye*)—for he is about to speak this mantra unto him. "'And may he hear us from afar'" (*āre asme ca śṛṇvata*)—even if he is far away from us, he will surely hear this; thus he says, "think of us even in this way."

"Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of the earth; he quickens the seeds of the waters"—thus he runs after [the sacrifice]. Just as a suitor might say something auspicious, "You are indeed the descendant of such-and-such a lineage; you are truly fit for this," so is this [verse].

Then [he worships] Indra and Agni with the verse: "Both Indra and Agni, I invoke you both; may you both rejoice together in the gift. Both are givers of food and riches; I invoke you both for the winning of booty. This one who shines yonder is indeed Indra; when he sets, he enters the Āhavanīya fire. Thus he worships them both while they are together, thinking, "May they both, being together, grant me [boons]. Therefore, [the offering belongs] to Indra and Agni.

"This is your seasonal womb, from which, once born, you shone forth; knowing that, O Agni, ascend it, and then increase our wealth"—for "wealth" (rayi) is indeed prosperity; thus he says, "Make this prosperity of ours ever greater and greater."
This is the first [verse]:

"He has been established by the establishers as the Hotṛ-priest, the most worthy of sacrifice, to be praised at the rites—him whom Apnavāna and the Bhr̥gus caused to shine forth, the wonderful, all-pervading one, for every house. He runs after him just as one might run after someone saying, "Run after him! This verse follows him closely. Just as a suitor might speak auspiciously, saying, "You are indeed the descendant of such-and-such a lineage; you are truly capable for this task," so too does this verse say of him exactly what he is. When it says, "the wonderful, all-pervading one, for every house," it is because he is indeed all-pervading (*vibhū*) for every house.

"Following its ancient splendor, the bold ones have milked the bright milk from the seer who wins a thousand"—this is indeed the highest of all gains, namely the gain of a thousand; it is for the attainment of that very thing that he says, "the milk from the seer who wins a thousand."
This is the *samāhārya* [section] consisting of six verses.

Of these, the first verse contains the word "upava" and the last contains the word "pratna. We have already explained why it is called *upavatī*; as for "pratna," that which was in the beginning is indeed "pratna" (the ancient), for as many gods as there were in the beginning, so many gods are there now; therefore, that is "pratna. Between these two [verses], all desires are contained. These two, being in agreement, bestow all desires upon him.

He mutters the first verse three times and the last verse three times; for sacrifices have a threefold beginning and a threefold conclusion. Therefore, he mutters the first verse three times and the last verse three times.

For whatever one performs incorrectly here while offering the Agnihotra— whether by word or by deed— that one cuts away from oneself, whether it be from one's life-span, from one's luster, or from one's progeny.
Truly, O Agni, you are the protector of the body;
protect my body. O Agni, you are the giver of life; give me life. O Agni, you are the giver of splendor; give me splendor. O Agni, whatever is deficient in my body, that do you fulfill for me.

Whatever one does wrongly here while offering the Agnihotra—whether by word or by deed—one cuts away from oneself [a portion] of life-span, or of luster, or of offspring; "May that be replenished for me again," he says thereby, and thus it is replenished for him again.
Kindling thee...

"A hundred winters we would kindle thee, the radiant one"—by this he means, "May we live for a hundred years. "So great as thou art, we would kindle thee"—when he says, "the radiant one," he means this. "Full of vigor, O bestower of vigor; full of power, O bestower of power"—by this he means, "May we be full of vigor, and mayest thou be a bestower of vigor; may we be full of power, and mayest thou be a bestower of power. "O Agni, the subduer of rivals, we who are undeceivable [kindle] thee, the undeceivable one"—by this he means, "Through thee, may we make our rivals more wretched."

"O Citrāvasu, may you attain well-being to the further shore"—this he mutters three times. Citrāvasu is indeed the night, for she dwells as it were having gathered up the various (citrāṇi) things; therefore, nothing variegated is seen from that [dark] night.

By this means, indeed, the seers of old reached the safe end of the night; by this means, the destructive spirits and Rakshasas did not find them during that night. By this very same means, he now reaches the safe end of the night, and the destructive spirits and Rakshasas do not find him during the night. Standing, he mutters as much as this.
Then he sat down.

"May you, O Agni, unite with the splendor of the Sun"—this he says because when the sun sets, it enters the Āhavanīya fire. "With the praise of the Ṛṣis"—this he says because he stands worshipping (upasthāna). "With the beloved abode"—the oblations are indeed his beloved abode; thus he says this by means of the oblations. "May I unite with long life, with splendor, with offspring, and with abundance of wealth"—just as you have united with these, so may I [unite] with long life, splendor, offspring, and abundance of wealth. By saying "with abundance" (bhūmnā), he means "may I thus unite with these."

Then he approaches the cows, saying: "Ye are food; may I partake of your food! Ye are greatness; may I partake of your greatness!"—by this he means to say, "Whatever powers are yours, whatever majesties are yours, may I partake of those! "Ye are strength; may I partake of your strength!"—by this he means to say, "Ye are sap; may I partake of your sap! "Ye are the increase of wealth; may I partake of your increase of wealth!"—by this he means to say, "Ye are abundance; may I partake of your abundance!"
"O Revatīs, rejoice!"—for cattle are indeed rich (revat), therefore he says, "O Revatīs, rejoice! In this womb, in this stall, in this world, in this dwelling;
stay right here, do not depart! By this he means for himself alone: "Do not depart from me!"

Then he touches the cow, saying: "Thou art united, possessing all forms. For cattle are indeed possessed of all forms; therefore he says, "possessing all forms. When he says, "Enter me with vigor," he means "with sap"; when he says, "with the state of being a lord of cattle," he means "with abundance. Thus he speaks.
Then he approaches the Gārhapatya fire.

He pays homage to the Gārhapatya with the verse: "O Agni, to thee day by day, O dispeller of darkness, we come with devotion, bringing homage. By this, he offers homage to him so that he may not harm him.
"He who shines over the sacrifices, the guardian of the cosmic order (ṛta), the radiant one, increasing in his own abode"—by saying "in his own abode," he means:
"This which is mine is indeed yours; therefore, make it greater and greater for us. This is what he says.

"O Agni, be easy of access to us like a father to his son; stay with us for our well-being. Just as a father who is easy of access to his son does not harm him in any way, so do thou be easy of access to us, and may we not harm thee in any way—this is what he thereby says.
Now follow the two-footed verses:

"O Agni, be our closest friend, our protector, and our auspicious guardian. As the Vasu, Agni, with wealth-renowned fame, come hither and grant us most brilliant riches. O most radiant one, O shining lord, we now entreat you for the welfare of our friends. Be mindful of us; hear our call; deliver us from every malicious person."

Or rather, when he stands by the Āhavanīya fire, he begs for cattle; therefore he stands by it with various meters, for cattle are indeed of various kinds. And when [he stands by] the Gārhapatya, he begs for men; therefore he first uses a triplet in the Gāyatrī meter, for the Gāyatrī is the meter of Agni; thus he approaches him with his own meter.
Now as for the two-footed verses:

the two-footed verses have man as their meter, for this man is indeed two-footed; it is men that he thereby entreats, for he entreats men. Therefore there are two-footed verses. He who, knowing thus, pays worship becomes possessed of cattle and possessed of men.
Then he approaches the cow with the words, "O Iḍā, come!

O Aditi, come! For the cow is indeed Iḍā, and the cow is indeed Aditi. He touches her with the words, "Come, you who are desirable," for desires have entered into these [cows] for men; therefore he says, "Come, you who are desirable. With the words, "May the fulfillment of your desires be in me," he means to say, "May I be dear to you."

Then, standing between the Āhavanīya and Gārhapatya fires and looking toward the fire while facing east, he mutters: "O Brahmaṇaspati, make me a winner of Soma, like Kakṣīvat who was the son of Uśij; he who is wealthy, the dispeller of disease, the finder of riches, and the increaser of prosperity—may he attend us! May he who is swift attend us! Let not the curse of the stingy man, nor the malice of a mortal, reach us; protect us, O Brahmaṇaspati!"

Or rather, when he worships the Āhavanīya fire, he worships heaven; and when he worships the Gārhapatya fire, he worships the earth; and this [third] is the intermediate space, for this is the quarter of Bṛhaspati, since he worships this very quarter; therefore, he mutters the Bārhaspatya formula.

"May the protection of the three be great—the heavenly protection of Mitra and Aryaman, the unassailable protection of Varuṇa—for over them, neither at home nor on difficult paths, does the evil-speaking enemy have power. For they, the sons of Aditi, bestow eternal light upon the mortal for the sake of life. In this [verse] it says, "nor on difficult paths"; for these paths that lie between heaven and earth are indeed "difficult paths," since one stands upon them; therefore he says, "nor on difficult paths."
Then follows the verse addressed to Indra. Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice;

thus he performs this worship of Agni as one accompanied by Indra. "Never art thou barren, O Indra, nor dost thou fail the donor"—the donor is indeed the sacrificer; thus he says, "Thou dost not harm the sacrificer. "Yea, Maghavan, evermore thy gift, the gift of the god, increases"—he thereby says, "Make this prosperity of ours increase more and more."

Now follows the Sāvitrī: Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, all these desires of his are fulfilled for him when they are impelled by Savitṛ. It is: "We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the god Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts."

Then follows the verse addressed to Agni: "Thus he finally entrusts himself to Agni for protection: 'May thy unassailable chariot reach us from every side, wherewith thou protectest the donors. The donors are indeed the sacrificers; for with that chariot of his which is most invincible, he protects the sacrificers. 'With that chariot of thine which is most invincible, wherewith thou protectest the sacrificers—with that, guard us on all sides!'—this is what he says. He mutters this three times."
Then he utters his son's name, thinking, "May this son of mine continue my heroic lineage. If there were no son, he would utter his own name.
Then, when the Agnihotra has been offered, he stands in worship:

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. By saying "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," he thereby perfects his speech through truth itself. Through that perfection, he invokes a blessing: "May I be well-nourished with nourishments!"—thereby he invokes prosperity.
Or rather, this long-standing worship of the fires is indeed a prayer for blessings;

this [present rite] is also a prayer for blessings, and by this much alone one obtains all of that. Therefore, one should worship with this alone. "Indeed, it is with this very [rite] that we perform our service," so said Āsuri.
Now, when about to depart on a journey,
he first pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire, and then to the Āhavanīya fire.
He pays homage to the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "O manly one, protect my offspring. For he (the fire) rules over offspring; thus he entrusts his offspring to it for protection.
Then he worships the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "O Praised One, protect my cattle! For this [fire] is the lord of cattle; thus he entrusts the cattle to it for their protection.
Then he either sets out on foot or causes [the cart] to be driven.

When he thinks it is time, having gone as far as that, he releases his speech. Then, having been away on a journey and looking back, when he thinks it is time, he restrains his speech. Even if a king should be encountered on the way, he must certainly not approach him.
He first pays reverence to the Āhavanīya fire, and then to the Gārhapatya.
The Gārhapatya is indeed the house; the house is indeed the foundation. Thus, he establishes himself upon that foundation, in the house.

He stands by the Āhavanīya fire, [reciting]: "We have come to the all-knowing one, the best finder of wealth for us; O Agni, sovereign ruler, bestow upon us splendor and power! Then, having sat down, he pulls out blades of grass.
Then he worships the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra:

"This Agni is the lord of the house, the Gārhapatya, the best winner of wealth for his progeny; O Agni, lord of the house, attain glory, attain power! Then, having sat down, he plucks away blades of grass. Indeed, by means of this recitation, most people perform this worship.

He should indeed remain silent. For when a superior person—whether a Brāhmaṇa or a king—dwells with someone, it is not fitting for that person to say to him, "Protect this for me; I shall depart. And since these superiors dwell here—the gods and the fires—who indeed would dare to say to them, "Protect this for me; I shall depart"?
The gods indeed know the mind of a human being.
The Gārhapatya fire knows: "He has come to me for protection. He then silently stands by the Āhavanīya fire; that Āhavanīya fire knows: "He has come to me for protection."

Then he either sets out on his journey or causes [the carriage] to drive forward. When he thinks it is the right time, having reached that point, he releases his speech. Then, having been away on a journey and looking back, when he thinks it is the right time, he restrains his speech. Even if a king should be encountered on the way, he must not approach him at all.

He first worships the Āhavanīya fire; then he worships the Gārhapatya. He worships the Āhavanīya silently, and having sat down silently, he plucks away the grass-blades; he worships the Gārhapatya silently, and having sat down silently, he plucks away the grass-blades.
Now, therefore, follows the ritual treatment of the house itself.

Now, when a householder has returned from being away, his house-hold indeed becomes as if terrified of him, thinking, "What will he say here? What will he do? Those houses tremble before anyone who speaks or does anything there; they are liable to throw the family into disorder. But those houses take refuge with one who neither speaks nor does anything there, thinking, "He did not speak here, nor did he do anything. Even if he should be quite angry here, he should nevertheless do only that which he would have intended to say or do; this is the proper conduct toward the household.

The beings indeed approached Prajāpati, saying, "Beings are indeed creatures; ordain for us that we may live. Then the gods, having put on the sacrificial thread and bent their right knees, approached him. He said to them, "Sacrifice is your food, immortality is yours, vigor is yours, and the sun is your light."

Then the ancestors, wearing their sacred threads over the right shoulder and bending their left knees, sat down before him; he said to them, "Your food is month by month; your svadhā is speed of thought; the moon is your light."

Then human beings sat down around him, having made a lap for themselves while remaining covered; he said to them: "Your food is in the evening and in the morning; your offspring are death; fire is your light."

Then the animals drew near to him; he made for them a favorable arrangement, saying, "Whenever you obtain [food], whether at the proper time or at an improper time, then eat. Therefore, whenever these [animals] obtain [food], whether at the proper time or at an improper time, they then eat.
Now, they say that the Asuras also constantly approached him;

he gave them darkness and illusion, thinking, "The Asura-illusion indeed exists. Yet those creatures were utterly defeated; and these very creatures live in exactly the same way as Prajāpati ordained for them.
The gods do not transgress it at all.

Neither the ancestors, nor animals, nor even some humans transgress [this law]. Therefore, he who becomes fat among men becomes fat in an unwholesome way; for he falls away, for he does not even have the strength to move about, since he becomes fat by having committed falsehood. Therefore, one should indeed eat only in the evening and in the morning. He who, knowing this, eats only in the evening and in the morning, reaches the full span of life; whatever he utters with his speech, that indeed comes to pass, for he protects this divine truth. This is the Brāhmaṇa called "Splendor" (Tejas), for he is able to observe its vow.

This, indeed, is for those who give to the ancestors month by month: when this [moon] is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he gives to them. For that which is the moon is King Soma, the food of the gods; on this night it wanes. When it has waned, he gives; thus he brings about concord among them. Now, if he were to give while it has not waned, he would indeed cause discord between the gods and the ancestors. Therefore, when this is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he gives to them.
He gives it in the afternoon;
for the forenoon belongs to the gods, the midday to humans, and the afternoon to the ancestors; therefore, he gives it in the afternoon.

Behind the Gārhapatya fire, having placed the sacrificial cord over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and sitting facing south, he takes this [grain]. Rising from that very spot and standing to the north of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, facing south, he threshes it; he husks it only once, for the fathers have departed once and for all; therefore, he husks it only once.
He cooks it.

When it has been placed on the fire, he pours clarified butter over it; for they offer to the gods while [the food] is in the fire, they take it out for men, and this is likewise for the ancestors; therefore, when it has been placed on the fire, he pours clarified butter over it.
Having taken it out, he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods.

Indeed, he who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices turns toward the gods; yet, by performing this Pitṛyajña, he has acted as if toward the fathers. Therefore, he now makes amends to the gods. Impelled by the gods, he then gives this to the fathers. That is why, having taken it out, he offers two oblations into the fire for the gods.
He offers to both Agni and Soma.
When he offers to Agni, it is because Agni is shared in all [sacrifices]; and when he offers to Soma, it is because Soma has the ancestors as his deity; therefore, he offers to both Agni and Soma.

He offers: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svāhā! To Soma Pitṛmat, Svāhā! He places the stirring-spoon into the fire; that is the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering. Then, to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he draws a line once; that is the portion for the altar. For the fathers have departed once and for all; therefore, he draws the line only once.
Then he places a firebrand behind [the food].

For if he were to give this to the fathers without having placed a firebrand, the Asuras and Rakṣasas would surely scatter it; but thus the Asuras and Rakṣasas do not scatter it for the fathers. Therefore, he places a firebrand behind.
He deposits it with the words:

"Those who, assuming forms, being Asuras, move about by their own power—those who carry off strongholds and weakholds—may Agni drive them away from this world. For Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; therefore he deposits it in this manner.
Then, taking a water vessel, he causes them to wash their hands, saying, "N.N., wash yourself!

for the sacrificer's father; "N.N., wash yourself! for the grandfather; and "N.N., wash yourself! for the great-grandfather. This is just as one would sprinkle someone who is about to receive a blessing.
Now, the cuttings are made once, near the roots.

For the gods are like the top, men are like the middle, and the ancestors are like the root; therefore the cuttings are made near the roots. They are cut once, for the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore they are cut once.
He spreads them out with the right hand; there he gives.

Indeed, one offers to the gods saying "sa vā" (he indeed), as it were; for they offer to the gods [saying] "sa vā," while they take up [the portion] for men. But for the ancestors it is thus; therefore, he gives [saying] "iti."

He gives [the gift], saying, "This, O so-and-so, is for your father. Regarding this, some say, "And for those who follow you"; however, one should not speak thus. For he belongs together with those who are his own; therefore, he should simply say, "This, O so-and-so, is for your father," "This, O so-and-so, is for your grandfather," and "This, O so-and-so, is for your great-grandfather. Thus, when he gives from here toward the further side, it is because the ancestors have indeed once for all departed away.
There he mutters:
"O Fathers, rejoice here; satisfy yourselves according to your respective portions. By this, he means to say, "Eat according to your respective portions."
Then he turns around so as to face away;

for the ancestors are, as it were, hidden from men, and thus this becomes hidden. "He should remain until the sun sets," they say, "for so long indeed is the duration of a day. Having sat there for just a moment, he—
Then, having made them rise, he mutters:
"The fathers have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their portion. By this he means: "They have eaten according to their portion."

Then, taking a water-pot, he causes them to wash their hands, saying, "N.N., wash yourself! for the sacrificer's father; "N.N., wash yourself! for the grandfather; and "N.N., wash yourself! for the great-grandfather. This is just as if one were to sprinkle water upon someone who has already eaten.

Then, having loosened the knot of his garment, he pays homage. The knot of the garment is indeed sacred to the Fathers; therefore, having loosened the knot, he pays homage. Homage is indeed the sacrifice; he thus makes them worthy of sacrifice. He pays homage six times, for there are six seasons, and the Fathers are the seasons; therefore he pays homage six times. "O Fathers, give us houses," he says, for the Fathers are the masters of houses; this is the prayer for blessing at this rite. Then, having set down the balls of food, he smells them. That which is the sacrificer's portion, he places pieces cut from the balls into the fire once, and he throws back the firebrand.

Regarding this, Kahoḍa Kauṣītaki said: "This [Soma] is indeed the essence of these two, heaven and earth; having offered this essence to the gods, we shall then consume it. Therefore, one should perform the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice.
Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said:

"The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the Asuras smeared both kinds of plants—those upon which humans subsist and those upon which cattle subsist—with a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) and with poison, thinking, 'In this way we shall surely overcome the gods. Consequently, neither humans nor cattle ate them; and these creatures perished from starvation."

The gods heard of this: "Verily, these creatures are perishing through fasting. They said, "Come, let us drive this away from them. "By what means? "By the sacrifice alone. By the sacrifice indeed, the gods then brought about that which was their proper order, as did the seers.

They said, "To whom shall this belong? They could not reach an agreement, each saying, "It shall be mine, it shall be mine. Having failed to reach an agreement, they said, "Let us run a race for this; whoever among us wins, this shall belong to him. "So be it," they said, and they ran a race for it.
Indra and Agni conquered them;
therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni, for Indra and Agni conquered their share. Wherever Indra and Agni stood after having conquered, there the All-Gods followed.

Indra and Agni are indeed the nobility (kṣatra), and the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ) are the common people (viś). Wherever the nobility conquers, the common people are indeed included therein; so he included all the gods. Therefore, this oblation of cooked rice (caru) for the Viśve Devāḥ is offered.

Regarding this, they say that one should offer it with old grains. "Indra and Agni are indeed the nobility (kṣatra); let me not cause the nobility to ascend [to a higher status]," so they think. However, both of them should consist of new grains; for since one is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and the other is a cooked mess (caru), by that very fact the nobility is not made to ascend. Therefore, both should consist of new grains.

Then all the gods said, "This is indeed the essence of these two, Heaven and Earth; come, let us share in it. They assigned this portion to them: this cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. Therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth. This earth itself is its potsherd, for this [earth] is indeed one; therefore, it is offered on one potsherd.
This is the reason for the reproach:

for whatever deity the oblation is taken, the Sviṣṭakṛt is everywhere entitled to a share; yet here he offers it all entirely and does not cut off a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt—that is the reproach—and so, once offered, it turns back.

Regarding this they say: "This cake on one potsherd has overturned; it will bewilder the kingdom. This is not a reason for concern, for the Āhavanīya fire is the foundation of oblations. Even if it were to turn back ten times after reaching the Āhavanīya, one should pay no heed to that. However, others say: "Who would enter into such a compact? Therefore, one should sacrifice only with clarified butter (ājya). Indeed, clarified butter is the manifest essence of these two, heaven and earth. Thus, he directly gratifies them with their own manifest essence, their own sacrificial food. Therefore, one should sacrifice only with clarified butter.

By means of this very sacrifice, the gods, having sacrificed, drove away the *kṛtyā* (witchcraft) and the poison from both kinds of plants—those upon which humans subsist and those upon which cattle subsist. Thereafter, humans ate [the plants] and cattle grazed [them].

Now, as to why he performs this sacrifice: "Surely no one at all does this for him in such a way," [thinking] "He is merely smearing him with some kind of magic spell or poison," so say the gods; yet it is precisely this that he does. And whatever portion the gods assigned to themselves, that very portion he now makes for them. Furthermore, he makes both kinds of plants—those upon which humans subsist and those upon which cattle subsist—free from disease and free from blemish. These creatures subsist upon those plants of his, which are thus free from disease and free from blemish. For this reason, indeed, he performs this sacrifice.

The sacrificial fee for this is a cow born of its first calf; for this [offering] is, as it were, the foremost. If he has already performed sacrifices, let him sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices and then perform this [offering]; but if he has not yet performed sacrifices, they should cook this four-fold portion of boiled rice on the Anvāhāryapacana fire, and the Brāhmaṇas should eat it.

There are indeed two kinds of gods: the gods who are the gods themselves, and those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in them—they are the human gods. As is an oblation offered with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, so does this [gift] become for him. In that regard, he should give whatever he is able; for they say, "A sacrificial offering (*havis*) should not be without a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He should not offer it in the *agnihotra*; for he would cause a conflict if he were to offer it in the *agnihotra*. One thing is the *āgrayaṇa*, and another is the *agnihotra*; therefore, he should not offer it in the *agnihotra*.
Prajāpati, indeed, performed this sacrifice first, desiring offspring, [thinking]:
"May I become abundant with progeny and cattle; may I attain prosperity; may I possess glory; may I be an eater of food."

He was indeed named Dakṣa. Because he performed this sacrifice first, it is called the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice; some, however, call it the Vasiṣṭha sacrifice, for Vasiṣṭha is indeed this very [sacrifice], and they name it after him. He sacrificed with this sacrifice, and having sacrificed with this sacrifice, he became that which is this progeny of Prajāpati and that which is prosperity. Verily, he who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, procreates such progeny and attains such prosperity; therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice.
Therefore, Pratīdarśa Śvekna performed that sacrifice.

For those who opposed him, it was as if there were a dispute; indeed, for one who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, it becomes as if there were a dispute. Therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice.
He came to him.

Suplā Sārñjaya studied the sacred lore; therefore, he studied this sacrifice and another as well. Having studied them, he went back to the Sṛñjayas. The Sṛñjayas recognized him, saying, "He has come to us after studying our sacrifice. They said, "He has indeed come to us together with the gods, since he has come after studying our sacrifice. Thus, Suplā Sārñjaya was truly Sahadeva (he who comes with the gods). There is even a traditional saying to that effect: "Or rather, he gave another name to his enemy, Suplā. He performed that sacrifice. Having performed that sacrifice, whatever progeny and whatever prosperity belonged to the Sṛñjayas, that became theirs. Whosoever, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, he procreates that same progeny and attains that same prosperity. Therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice.

Devabhāga Śrautarṣa was the domestic priest (purohita) of both the Kurus and the Sṛñjayas; indeed, that is the highest position. Truly, it is a high position for one to be the priest of a single kingdom, but how much more so for one who is the priest of two? He who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, attains a state of supreme eminence. Therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice.

Therefore, Dakṣa Pārvati performed that sacrifice; even now these Dākṣāyaṇas have attained sovereignty. Indeed, he who, knowing this, sacrifices with this [offering] attains sovereignty here. For that reason, one should sacrifice with this. Each cake (*puroḍāśa*) is offered on successive days. By this, his prosperity becomes free from rivals and unassailable. He sacrifices at two full-moon festivals and two new-moon festivals. Two indeed constitute a pair; thus a productive pair is created.

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the previous day at the full moon: those are two deities, and two indeed constitute a pair; thus a productive pair is created.
Then, in the morning, there is a cake for Agni and the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra; these are two deities, and two indeed constitute a pair. Thus, this very procreative union is brought about.

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Indra and Agni on the previous day, at the new moon—those are two deities, and two indeed constitute a pair; thus a productive pair is thereby created.

Then, in the morning, there is a cake for Agni and a dish of curds for Mitra and Varuna. The cake for Agni is indeed [offered] so that he may not depart from the sacrifice; but these two, Mitra and Varuna, are two deities, and two indeed constitute a pair. Thus, this procreative union is brought about. This is his form by which he becomes manifold and by which he procreates.

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the day before the full moon: that very same animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma which he performs on the fast-day is indeed his [sacrifice] at this time.
Then, in the morning:

there is a cake (puroḍāśa) for Agni and the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra. Of this [sacrifice], the cake for Agni is the morning pressing, for the morning pressing belongs to Agni; and the Sāṃnāyya for Indra is his midday pressing, for the midday pressing belongs to Indra.

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Indra and Agni on the previous day, on the new moon night—that constitutes his third pressing; for the third pressing belongs to the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ), and Indra and Agni are indeed the All-gods.

Then, in the morning, there is a cake for Agni and a curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa. The cake for Agni is indeed [offered] so that he may not depart from the sacrifice. Now, as for that barren cow which he immolates as the Anūbandhyā for Mitra and Varuṇa—that itself constitutes his curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa. Having performed both the Full-moon and the New-moon sacrifices, he conquers as much as he would conquer by performing the Soma-sacrifice; thus, indeed, it becomes a "Great Sacrifice" (Mahāyajña).
Now, as for that which [is performed] on the previous day:

He sacrifices with the Agniṣomīya offering on the full moon day. By this very [offering], Indra slew Vṛtra; by this very [offering] he conquered that victory which is his. In the same way, this sacrificer slays evil, the hateful rival, by means of this [offering], and in the same way he conquers. Now, as for why he prepares the *sāṃnāyya*: the *sāṃnāyya* belongs to the new moon (*amāvāsya*), and "new moon" is far away; rather, it is milk. With this essence they gratified him who had slain Vṛtra. Indeed, he who, knowing this, prepares the *sāṃnāyya* on the full moon day, quickly casts off evil. King Soma, the moon, is indeed the food of the gods. On the previous day they press it, intending to consume it in the morning; they consume it when it wanes.

Now, as for the fact that he sacrifices with the offering to Agni and Soma on the day before the full moon: he thereby presses it out; into that which has been pressed, he places this essence; by means of this essence, he makes it strong and sweetens it. Indeed, the oblation becomes sweet for the gods, and his oblation becomes sweet for the gods, for him who, knowing this, prepares the *saṃnayya* offering on the full moon day.

Now, as for the fact that on the previous day he sacrifices with the offering to Indra and Agni at the new moon: the two deities of the New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed Indra and Agni; it is to these very ones that he thus sacrifices directly and perceptibly. Indeed, the New and Full Moon sacrifices have been truly performed by him who knows this.

Then, in the morning, there is a cake for Agni and a dish of curds for Mitra and Varuṇa. The cake for Agni is indeed [offered] so that he may not depart from the sacrifice; moreover, these two half-months are Mitra and Varuṇa: that which waxes is Varuṇa, and that which wanes is Mitra. On this night, both of them come together; thus he gratifies them both while they are together. Verily, everything becomes gratified for him and everything is attained by him who knows this.

On that very night, Mitra pours his seed into Varuṇa; it is through that seed that he is reproduced when [the moon] becomes full. Therefore, on this occasion, the curdled milk (payasyā) dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is most appropriately prepared.
The new moon (Amāvāsyā) is indeed the occasion for the *sāṃnāyya* offering;

therefore, that same [offering] is performed on the full moon (Paurṇamāsī). If he were to perform the *saṃnayana* even then, he would commit a redundancy and cause strife. Thus, having gathered him from the waters and the plants, he causes him to be born from the oblations (*āhuti*). Having been born from the oblations, he is seen afterwards.
He thus causes him to be born from a productive union:

the *payasyā* is the female and the *vājina* is the seed; and indeed, what is born from a productive union is born directly from that union. He thus causes him to be born from this productive union; therefore, the *payasyā* is used here.
Then he offers the whey to the Vājins.

The Vājins are indeed the seasons, and the whey is seed; thus, in due order, this seed is infused. The seasons then bring forth these creatures from the seed that has been infused. Therefore, he offers the whey to the Vājins.
He offers as it were from behind the sacrifice;

for a bull, having approached from behind, runs upon a female and pours his seed into her. He indeed offers first in front [of the fire], saying, "O Agni, accept! and he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*; that is the portion for the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. He indeed offers first in front.
Then he sprinkles the quarters with ghee, saying:

"To the quarters, to the intermediate quarters, to the directed quarters, to the separated quarters, to the upward quarters—svāhā to the quarters! There are five quarters and five seasons; thus, by means of the seasons, he brings about union with the quarters.

Indeed, only five consume it: the Hotṛ, the Adhvaryu, the Brahman, the Āgnīdhra, and the sacrificer. For there are five seasons; thus the form of the seasons is thereby produced. He thereby establishes that seed, once poured, within the seasons. The sacrificer consumes first, thinking, "May I first take hold of the seed"; and also, "May the seed be established in me, the last," he thinks. With the words, "Invited! Invite! they make this [the Soma] itself.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He reflected, "How indeed may I procreate? He exerted himself and practiced austerity; he created offspring. Once created, those offspring of his perished; they became these very birds. Man is indeed closest to Prajāpati; for man is two-footed, and therefore birds are two-footed.

Prajāpati reflected: "Just as indeed I was formerly alone, even so am I now alone. He created a second [race], but they vanished from him; they are these small crawling creatures other than snakes.
