"He created a third," they say; they also vanished from him; they are these snakes. Regarding these two classes, Yājñavalkya said, "But according to the Ṛgveda, there are three."
While performing the *ṛc* chants, Prajāpati grew weary and reflected:

"How is it that my created offspring perish? He perceived this very thing: "It is indeed through lack of food that my offspring perish. He caused milk to swell within his own breasts first of all; he created the offspring, and those offspring of his, having been created, reached for his breasts and from that they came into being. These, therefore, are the ones who have not perished.

Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "Three generations have passed away. This refers to those that perished; thus he has declared this. "Others have settled around the *arka* (glory). The *arka* is indeed Agni; thus, those progeny which did not perish have settled around Agni; of them he has declared this.

"Great in power, he stood within the worlds"—this was indeed said in reference to Prajāpati. "The purifying one has entered the golden ones"—the golden ones are indeed the quarters; this purifying wind has entered them, and it is these very quarters that this ṛc refers to. These creatures are born in the same manner as Prajāpati created creatures. For whenever the breasts of a woman swell, or the udder of cattle, then what is born is born; and having reached those breasts, they come into being.

That milk, indeed, is food; for it was this that Prajāpati first produced as food. And offspring are truly food, for they come into being from food. For those [cows] for whom there is milk, they come into being from that [milk] by resorting to the two teats; and those for whom there is no milk, they cause them to eat as soon as they are born. Thus, even they come into being from food alone; therefore, offspring are indeed food.
He who desires offspring,
by sacrificing with this oblation, ordains for himself the sacrifice as Prajāpati come into being.
Now, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni.
Agni indeed is the mouth of the deities and the progenitor; he is Prajāpati. Therefore, it is dedicated to Agni.
Then there is a *saumya* rice-porridge.
Soma, indeed, is seed; thus he pours the seed, Soma, into Agni, the progenitor. This constitutes a productive union at the beginning.
Now follows the offering to Savitṛ:
there is a sacrificial cake on twelve or eight potsherds; for Savitṛ is the impeller of the gods, and Prajāpati is the progenitor from the middle [of the universe]; therefore, it belongs to Savitṛ.
Then there is a pap for Sarasvatī and a pap for Pūṣan.

Sarasvatī is indeed a female and Pūṣan is a male; that is a productive pair. From this very productive pair on both sides, Prajāpati created offspring—both those upward from here and those downward from there. In the same way, he (the sacrificer) now creates offspring from this very productive pair on both sides—both those upward from here and those downward from there. Therefore, these five oblations come into being.
Now, therefore, follows the locus of the *payasyā* offering.

There is a cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the clans, the clans of the gods. They moved about here as if unrestrained. They approached Prajāpati, who was performing the sacrifice, and said: "We shall surely churn apart these creatures whom you are about to create with this oblation."

Prajāpati reflected: "My former creatures have perished; if these [present ones] also destroy themselves, nothing at all will remain. He assigned this portion to them: this cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts. This is that cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts. As to why it is on seven potsherds—it is because the host of the Maruts consists of sevens. Therefore, there is this cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
One should indeed perform it with the verse "To them who are self-strong" (*taṃ vai svatavobhya*).

For they themselves made this their portion; therefore, those who do not find the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses for the self-strong ones, that [offering] should indeed be for the Maruts. This is performed for the sake of the non-injury of creatures; therefore, it is dedicated to the Maruts.
Now, therefore, regarding the curd-mixture (payasyā) itself:

from milk indeed creatures come into being, and by milk they are produced. Thus, he provides for them that very thing from which they were produced and from which they originate. Those creatures whom he creates by means of the preceding oblations, they are produced from this milk, from this curd-mixture.
In that [offering] there is a pair:

the woman is the curd (payasyā) and the seed is the whey (vājina). From that pair, the entire immeasurable universe was produced. Because the entire immeasurable universe was produced from this pair, it belongs to the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadevī).
Now there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

By means of these oblations, Prajāpati, having created living beings, enclosed them within Heaven and Earth; thus these creatures are enclosed by Heaven and Earth. In the same way, he who creates living beings by means of these oblations encloses them within Heaven and Earth. Therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth.

Now, therefore, follows the procedure. They do not prepare the high altar (uttaravedi), thinking, "Let it be unrestrained; let everything be unrestrained; let it be for the Viśvedevas. The sacrificial grass (barhis) is tied together in three parts, and that is again made into one, for this is the form of procreation. For this is procreation: the father, the mother, and that which is born is the third; therefore, though being threefold, it becomes one again. Branches (prasva) are tied to it, and he takes them as the prastara-bunch; for this is procreation, and the prasva is indeed procreation; therefore, from the prasva, he takes the prastara.
Having set down the oblations, they churn the fire.

For indeed, after Agni was born, the creatures of Prajāpati were born; and so likewise, after this [sacrificer's] Agni is born, his own offspring are born. Therefore, having set down the oblations, they churn the fire.

There are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings. The Virāj consists of ten syllables; thus, he makes this Virāj deficient on both sides for the sake of procreation. From this very procreative source, which is deficient on both sides, Prajāpati created offspring—both those above here and those below here. In the same way, he (the sacrificer) creates offspring from this very procreative source, which is deficient on both sides—both those above here and those below here. Therefore, there are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings.

There are three *samiṣṭayajus* offerings; for this oblation-sacrifice is, as it were, greater than other *haviḥ-yajñas*, in that it has nine *prayājas* and nine *anuyājas*. Moreover, there may be only one; for it is indeed a *haviḥ-yajña*, and its sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a first-born cow.
By means of this very sacrifice, Prajāpati sacrificed.

That progeny which belongs to Prajāpati and that prosperity which is Prajāpati’s—this very progeny he produced and this very prosperity he attained. Whoever, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, produces that same progeny and attains that same prosperity; therefore, one should indeed perform this sacrifice.

By means of the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, Prajāpati indeed created offspring. Once these offspring of his were created, they ate Varuṇa’s barley; for barley was originally Varuṇa’s. Because they ate Varuṇa’s barley, they are called Varuṇapraghāsas.
Varuṇa seized them;

seized by Varuṇa, they became distended and lay down, breathing out and breathing in, and lying down and sitting up. Indeed, the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna) did not depart from them, but all the other deities departed. Because of those two alone, his creatures did not perish.
With this oblation Prajāpati healed himself;
both his offspring that were already born and those that were yet unborn he released from Varuṇa’s noose, and thus his offspring were born free from disease and free from blemish.

Now, as to why he performs these sacrifices in the fourth month: it is not, indeed, that Varuna seizes his offspring in that manner; rather, the gods did so, and he now does the same. Both those offspring of his that have been born and those that are yet unborn, he releases from Varuna’s noose. Thus his offspring are born free from disease and free from blemish. For this reason, he performs these sacrifices in the fourth month.
There are indeed two altars and two fires.

As to why there are two altars and two fires: it is so that he releases the creatures from Varuna’s noose on both sides—from here upwards and from there downwards; therefore there are two altars and two fires.
He scatters the *uttaravedi* (high altar) only on the northern altar, not on the southern one.

Varuṇa is the nobility (*kṣatra*) and the Maruts are the common people (*viś*). He thus places the nobility above the common people; therefore, these subjects wait upon the Kṣatriya seated above them. For this reason, he scatters the *uttaravedi* only on the northern altar, not on the southern one.
Now, there are these same five oblations.

By means of these oblations, Prajāpati created offspring; by means of them, he released the offspring from Varuṇa’s noose on both sides—from above here and from below here. Therefore, there are these five oblations.

Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. Indra and Agni are indeed the out-breathing and the in-breathing; just as one would do a good deed for one who has done a good deed, so it is with this. For it was because of these two that his offspring did not perish. Thus, by means of the out-breathing and in-breathing, he heals the offspring and bestows the out-breathing and in-breathing upon them. Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni.
In both cases there are curd-offerings (*payasyā*).

Indeed, creatures originate from milk and are produced from milk. Therefore, from that very source from which they were produced and from which they originate, he thereby releases creatures from Varuna’s noose on both sides—from above here and from below here. That is why there are curd-offerings in both cases.

The northern one belongs to Varuṇa. For Varuṇa indeed seized his offspring; thus he visibly releases the offspring from the noose of Varuṇa. The southern one belongs to the Maruts. It is for the sake of avoiding sameness that it belongs to the Maruts; for he would create a state of sameness if both were dedicated to Varuṇa. Moreover, the Maruts sought to destroy his offspring from the south; he appeased them with this share, and therefore the southern one belongs to the Maruts.
He scatters *karīra* fruits for both of them.
Indeed, Prajāpati created comfort for his creatures by means of the *karīra* fruits; verily, this sacrificer now creates comfort for his creatures.
Of both of them he strews *śamī* leaves and *palāśa* leaves.
Prajāpati indeed made peace for his creatures with *śamī* leaves and *palāśa* leaves; verily, he now makes peace for these creatures.
Now, there is a cake on one potsherd for Kāya.

Prajāpati indeed bestowed comfort upon his creatures by means of this cake on one potsherd for Kāya; verily, this sacrificer now bestows comfort upon the creatures by means of this cake on one potsherd for Kāya. Therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for Kāya.
Then, on the preceding day,
having made barley grains huskless on the Anvāhāryapacana fire and having warmed them slightly, they prepare for them as many Karambha-pots as there are members of the household, plus one in excess.
There too, they fashion a ram and a ewe.
If one should find wool from non-sheep on that ram and that ewe, one should wash it and attach it; but if one should not find wool from non-sheep, then even wool from *kuśa* grass may be used.
Now, as for the fact that there is both a ram and a ewe:

the ram is indeed Varuṇa’s victim in visible form; thus he visibly releases offspring from Varuṇa’s noose. They are made of barley, for Varuṇa seized those who had eaten barley. They are a pair, and thus he releases offspring from Varuṇa’s noose by means of a pair.
He places the ewe upon the northern milk-mixture and the ram upon the southern; for thus is a pair properly constituted, since the woman lies on the left side of the man.
The Adhvaryu places all the sacrificial oblations upon the northern altar,
while the Pratiprasthātṛ places this very curd-mixture upon the southern altar.
Having brought the oblations near, he churns the fire; having churned the fire and cast it into the hearth, he makes an offering over it.

Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite for the fire being kindled! Both of them place fuel on the fire; both leave two kindling-sticks remaining; both pour the two prior libations. Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "O Agnīdh, sweep around the fire! Even though the command has been given, the sweeping has not yet been performed.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ returns. When he is about to lead the wife forward, he asks her, "With whom do you consort? For a woman commits an offense against Varuṇa when she consorts with one man while belonging to another; furthermore, he asks it so that she might not offer the oblation with a hidden thorn in her heart. Therefore he asks. Indeed, a sin becomes less manifest when it is spoken of, for it then becomes truth; therefore he asks. If she does not confess, that would be harmful to her kinsmen.
He causes her to recite:
"We invoke the devouring Maruts, the destroyers of enemies, who are well-pleased with the groats. Just as there is a puronuvākyā, so too does he, by means of this verse, call them from these vessels.
These indeed correspond to each person;

as many as there may be householders, so many they are, with one in excess. By this, for each person individually, he releases those offspring of his that have already been born from Varuna’s noose. There is one in excess; by that, he releases those offspring of his that are yet unborn from Varuna’s noose. Therefore, there is one in excess.

The vessels are made of wood, for food is eaten from wooden vessels; they are made of barley, for Varuna seized the creatures when they had eaten barley. He offers with a winnowing basket, for food is prepared with a winnowing basket; the wife offers, and thus he releases the offspring from Varuna’s noose by means of a pair.
He offers before the sacrifice, before the oblations.

The people (viś) are indeed eaters of unoffered food, and the Maruts are the people. When Prajāpati’s creatures were seized by Varuṇa, torn asunder, and lay gasping, breathing, lying down, and sitting up, the Maruts then crushed out the evil from them. In the same way, the Maruts crush out the evil from his creatures; therefore he offers before the sacrifice, before the oblations.

He offers in the southern fire with the verse, "Whatever sin we have committed in the village or in the forest... For whether in the village or in the forest, sin is indeed committed; "whatever in the assembly or through the senses"—by saying "in the assembly," he means that which is human; by saying "through the senses," he means that which pertains to the gods; "whatever sin we have committed, this we expiate with Svāhā!"—by this he means: "Whatever sin we have committed, from all of that may we be released."
Then he mutters the verse addressed to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
For when the Maruts struck away the evil from Prajāpati’s creatures, he reflected: "May these [Maruts] not strike away my creatures."
He recited this verse addressed to Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
Indra is indeed the nobility and the Maruts are the common people; [he did so thinking], "May the nobility be established and the common people be settled. Therefore, it is addressed to Indra.

O Indra, protect us here in these battles along with the gods; for indeed, O impetuous one, there is your great assistance. The song of the Maruts, who possess the oblation, praises the bountiful one whose youthful power is mighty.
Then he makes her recite:

"The doers of the rite have performed the rite"—for the doers of the rite have indeed performed the rite—"together with speech, bringing bliss"—for they have performed it together with speech—"having performed the rite for the gods"—for having indeed performed the rite for the gods—"go ye to the setting, being together"—for those who have been married from elsewhere are indeed together; therefore he says, "being together. "Go to the setting," he says; for the wife is the hind part of the sacrifice; he has thus seated her facing eastward toward the sacrifice. The home is the setting, the home is the foundation; he thus establishes her in the home, in the foundation.

The Pratiprasthātṛ comes out having carried back [the oblation]. They sweep the fire; once the fire has been swept, both of them pour the two northern Āghāra-libations. Then the Adhvaryu alone, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, chooses the Hotṛ. The chosen Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat at the northern altar. Having sat down, he gives the impulse. Both of them, being thus impelled, take up the offering-spoons and step across. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite the offering-verse for the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*). Saying "Recite! Recite! at each of the fourth *prayāja* offerings, the two of them, pouring together [the butter], perform nine *prayāja* offerings.
Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite for Agni.

Both of them, having taken four portions of clarified butter for the Āgneya Ājyabhāga, step across; having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and both of them offer the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then the Adhvaryu alone says, "Recite for Soma.

Both of them, having taken four portions of clarified butter each for the Soma-portion of the clarified butter, step across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Offer the sacrifice to Soma," and both of them offer it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Whatever is to be performed with speech, the Adhvaryu alone performs it, not the Pratiprasthātṛ; thus, the Adhvaryu alone calls for the *śrauṣaṭ* here, where the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
The Pratiprasthātṛ merely imitates what has been done.

Varuṇa is indeed the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś); thus he makes the common people imitate and follow the nobility. For were the Pratiprasthātṛ also to call for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he would make the common people rebellious against the nobility; therefore, the Pratiprasthātṛ does not call for the *śrauṣaṭ*.

The Pratiprasthātṛ, having taken up the two offering-spoons (srucau), stands by; then the Adhvaryu alone proceeds with these oblations: with a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on twelve or eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Sarasvatī, a pap for Pūṣan, and a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni.
Now, when they are about to proceed with these two milk-dishes, they exchange them.

That ram which is for the Maruts he places in the dish for Varuṇa; that ewe which is for Varuṇa he places in the dish for the Maruts. As to why they thus exchange them: Varuṇa is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), and the male is vigor; they thus bestow vigor upon the nobility. The female, however, is without vigor, and the Maruts are the common people (viś); they thus make the common people without vigor. Therefore, they exchange them in this manner.
Then the Adhvaryu himself says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Varuṇa.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [in the offering ladle], then cuts two portions from this curd-mixture dedicated to Varuṇa. Along with one of those two portions, he places the ram. Then he pours clarified butter over it from above, anoints the two cut portions, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Varuṇa," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

The Adhvaryu, holding the two *sruva*-ladles in his left hand and grasping the Pratiprasthātṛ from behind with his right hand, says: "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts! The Pratiprasthātṛ spreads a base of clarified butter (*ājya*) [in the *upabhṛt*], then makes two cuttings from this *mārutyā payasyā*. Along with one of these two cuttings, he places the ewe; then he pours clarified butter over it from above, anoints the two cuttings, and steps across. Then the Adhvaryu himself, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, says: "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.

Then the Adhvaryu alone proceeds with the cake on one potsherd for Kāya. Having proceeded with the cake on one potsherd for Kāya, the Adhvaryu himself says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. The Adhvaryu cuts off portions from all the oblations once each; then the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off a portion from this very curd-mixture once. Then they both pour clarified butter over them twice from above. Both step across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, they both make the offering.
Then the Adhvaryu himself cuts off the Prāśitra portion;

having taken a portion of the Iḍā, he hands it over to the Pratiprasthātṛ. Thereupon, the Pratiprasthātṛ also cuts off twice from the curd-mixture for the Maruts, and then sprinkles it twice with clarified butter from above. Having invoked the blessing, they perform the purification.
Then the Adhvaryu himself says: "O Brahman, I shall proceed."

Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, [the Agnīdh] says, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fires! Thereupon the Adhvaryu pours the clotted butter (pṛṣadājya) into the two offering-spoons. Now, if there is clotted butter for the Pratiprasthātṛ, he pours that out in two parts; but if there is no clotted butter there, he pours whatever butter is in the upabhṛt-spoon in two parts. Both of them step across [the altar]; having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, the Adhvaryu alone says, "Sacrifice to the gods! and "Sacrifice, sacrifice! At every fourth after-offering (*anuyāja*), they both pour together; thus they perform with nine after-offerings. In that there are nine fore-offerings (*prayāja*) and nine after-offerings, he thereby releases creatures from Varuṇa’s noose on both sides—from here upwards and from there downwards. Therefore, there are nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings.
Having set down both [the spoons], they separate the *sruca* ladles;

having separated the *sruca* ladles and anointed the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), and having reached toward the enclosing-stick and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu alone says: "The divine Hotṛ-priests have been impelled for the auspicious utterance; the human one has been sent forth for the *sūktavāka*. Then the Hotṛ begins the *sūktavāka*. Now both of them together pluck up the two *prastara* bundles, both throw them into the fire, and both, having grasped blades of grass, sit waiting until the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*.
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw them into the fire!
Both of them throw them into the fire, and both touch themselves.

Then he says, "Converse! [The Agnīdh replies: "He has come, O Agnīdh; make him hear! Śrauṣaṭ! Well-gone to the divine Hotṛs; well-being to the human ones; speak for peace and prosperity! It is the Adhvaryu who speaks this. Then both of them throw the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) into the fire; both, having taken up the offering-spoons (sruc), set them down on the wooden sword (sphya).

Then the Adhvaryu himself, having returned, performs the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives; the Pratiprasthātṛ remains waiting, and having performed the *saṃyāja* offerings for the wives, the Adhvaryu comes out.

He offers three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. The Pratiprasthātṛ silently takes up the offering-spoon. Now, those two garments which were worn by the two sacrificers at the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice should be used here as well. Then, taking the scrapings mixed with the dregs of this Varuṇa-mixture of curdled milk (*payasyā*), they go to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). For this is related to Varuṇa; it is for the sake of release from Varuṇa. No Sāman is sung there, for nothing whatsoever is done with a Sāman in this case; rather, silently, having descended into the water, he immerses himself.

"O Avabhṛtha, O Nicumpuṇa! You are the one who descends, O Nicumpuṇa. Through the gods, I have washed away the sin committed against the gods; through mortals, I have washed away the sin committed against mortals. O God, protect me from harm in the loud-voiced [battle]! He may give these two garments to whomever he desires; for they do not belong to the consecrated. Just as a snake would cast off its skin, so does he cast off all evil.

Then, having shaved his hair and beard and having consigned the two fires into himself, he moves away from the sacrificial ground; for it is with this [rite] that he sacrifices, and it would not be appropriate to offer the Agnihotra on the high altar. Therefore, he moves away. Having gone home and churned out the fires, he performs the Full-moon sacrifice. These Cāturmāsya offerings are, as it were, a discontinued sacrifice, whereas the Full-moon sacrifice is a settled and established sacrifice. Thus, by means of that settled sacrifice, he finally finds firm support. That is why he moves away.

By means of the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings, Prajāpati indeed released his creatures from the noose of Varuṇa; thus his creatures were born free from disease and free from blemish. Now, by these Sākamedha offerings, the gods slew Vṛtra; by means of these very offerings they conquered that victory which is theirs. In the same way, this sacrificer slays evil, his hateful rival, and likewise conquers. Therefore, he performs these sacrifices in the fourth month. He performs them on two successive days.

On the preceding day, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Anīkavat. For indeed, the gods, having made Agni their vanguard, advanced against Vṛtra, intending to slay him; and Agni, being brilliance, was not shaken. In the same way, this sacrificer, intending to slay his wicked, hateful rival, advances after making Agni his vanguard; and Agni, being brilliance, is not shaken. Therefore, [the offering is] for Agni Anīkavat.

Then, at midday, he offers a pap to the Sāṃtapana Maruts. For it was the Sāṃtapana Maruts who scorched Vṛtra at midday; scorched, he lay there panting as if breathless and torn asunder. In the same way, the Sāṃtapana Maruts scorch the evil, the hating rival of this sacrificer; therefore [the offering is] to the Sāṃtapana Maruts.

Then, for the Maruts, the householders: having driven away the calves with a branch and having milked the cows into a vessel containing a strainer, he cooks that sacrificial pap (caru). For it is indeed a pap; wherever they throw in rice grains, that becomes the sacrificial essence (medhas). The gods took that sacrificial essence in the morning, intending to slay Vṛtra; and so does this sacrificer now, intending to slay his evil, hateful rival, take that sacrificial essence. As to why it is rice cooked in milk: milk is indeed sacrificial essence, and rice grains are sacrificial essence; thus he places both kinds of sacrificial essence within himself. Therefore, it is rice cooked in milk.

Its covering is that very same [grass] which was spread for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas; on that very spread-out altar, they place the enclosing sticks and the wood chips. Having thus caused the milk to be collected, he cooks the sacrificial porridge (caru); having cooked it, he sprinkles it with clarified butter and removes it from the fire.
Then he washes two flat dishes or two bowls.

They lift this [ladle] up from those two in two ways; having made a vessel for pouring ghee between them, he pours ghee into it, and he cleans the *sruva* and the *sruk*. Then, taking these two portions of cooked rice, he goes up; taking the *sruva* and the *sruk*, he goes up. Having touched this very altar that has been strewn with grass, and having laid the enclosing sticks around, he places as many wood-shavings as he desires upon the fire. Then he sets down these two portions of cooked rice, and he sets down the *sruva* and the *sruk*. The Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat, and taking the *sruva* and the *sruk*, he speaks.
"Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter from the ghee-pouring on the southern rice-offering for the Āgneya-ājyabhāga, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter from the ghee-pouring on the northern rice-mess for the Soma-portion of the clarified butter, he steps across. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Soma," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the Maruts, the householders.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter from the ghee-pouring over the southern mess of boiled rice; he takes two cuttings from it, then pours clarified butter over the top, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Maruts, the householders! and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!

He makes an under-layering of ghee from the northern portion of the cooked rice; from that he cuts off two portions, then pours ghee over them, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* he offers it. Then he cuts off the *iḍā* portion itself, but not the *prāśitra*; having invited [the priests], they perform the purification. This is one way of proceeding.
Now, this is the second [section].

That very [altar] which has been strewn for the Maruts Sāṃtapanas becomes the sacrificial altar (vedi). Upon that very strewn altar, they set down the enclosing sticks (paridhis) and the wood-shavings (śakalas). Having thus milked [the cows], he cooks the sacrificial porridge (caru). He does not place the clarified butter (ājya) nearby; having cooked it, poured the ghee over it, and removed it from the fire, he anoints it. He removes the ghee into a pot and cleanses both the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladle (sruk). Then, taking that very porridge together with its vessel, he goes out; taking the ghee in the pot, he goes out; and taking the dipping-spoon and the ladle, he goes out. Having touched this very strewn altar and laid the enclosing sticks around, he places as many wood-shavings as he desires upon the fire. Then he sets down that very porridge together with its vessel, sets down the ghee in the pot, and sets down the dipping-spoon and the ladle. The Hotṛ priest sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat, and taking the dipping-spoon and the ladle, he speaks.
"Recite the invitatory verse for Agni.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter from the pot for the Āgneya Ājyabhāga offering, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter from the vessel itself for the Soma-portion of the clarified butter, he steps across; having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Soma," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Maruts, the householders.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [in the ladle], then cuts two portions from this sacrificial cake, then pours clarified butter over them, anoints the places from which the portions were cut, steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for the Maruts, the householders! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [in the ladle], then takes a single portion from this sacrificial pap, then pours clarified butter over it twice from above. He does not smear back the portion that was taken; he steps across, and having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

Now, he cuts off only the iḍā-portion and not the prāśitra. Having invoked the deities, they consume [the iḍā]; as many members of the household as there may be who are entitled to eat the remains of the sacrificial food (haviruciṣṭāśa), so many should consume it; moreover, the officiating priests (ṛtvij) may also consume it, and furthermore, other Brāhmaṇas may also consume it, provided there is plenty of cooked rice. Then, having covered this pot (kumbhī) which has not been consumed, they set it aside for the sake of the "Full-Spoon" (pūrṇadarva) offering. They let the calves join their mothers; thereby the cattle take the essence (megha) into themselves. That night he performs the Agnihotra with barley-gruel (yavāgū); in the morning, they milk the cow that is to be given away (nivānyā) for the Pitṛyajña.

Then, either when the morning oblation has been offered or when it has not yet been offered—whichever he may desire—he scoops from that unbaked pot with a ladle, saying: "Full, O ladle, fly away; full, return again! Like goods, let us barter for food and strength, O Śatakratu! Just as there is a *puro'nuvākya* verse, so by this [verse] he calls him to this portion.

Then he should say, "Call the bull. If it bellow, some say that this is the *vaṣaṭ*-call; one should offer the oblation at that *vaṣaṭ*-call. Moreover, he thereby calls Indra by his own form for the slaying of Vṛtra; for the bull is indeed the form of Indra. Thus, by its own form, he calls him for the slaying of Vṛtra. If it bellows, he should know: "Indra has come to my sacrifice; my sacrifice is accompanied by Indra. But if it does not bellow, the Brāhmaṇa sitting to the south should say, "Offer!"—for that is the speech of Indra.
He offers [the oblation], saying:
"Give to me; I give to thee. Bestow upon me; I bestow upon thee. Thou bringest a gift for me; may I bring a gift for thee. Svāhā!"

Then he offers a cake on seven potsherds to the Maruts, the sportive ones. For indeed, when Indra had come to slay Vṛtra, the Maruts, the sportive ones, gathered around him and sported about him, magnifying him; even so do they now gather around and sport about this sacrificer as he is about to slay his evil, hateful rival, magnifying him. That is why it is for the Maruts, the sportive ones. Now follows the Mahāhavis; its ritual procedure is the same as that of the Mahāhavis.

By means of the Mahāhavis, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra; by it they won that very victory which is theirs. In the same way, this sacrificer slays evil, his hateful rival, and likewise wins the victory; therefore, he performs this sacrifice with it.
This is its procedure:

they strew the high altar (uttaravedi), they take the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), they churn the fire, there are nine fore-offerings (prayāja) and nine after-offerings (anuyāja), there are three *samiṣṭayajus* oblations; then there are these very five sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*).
As for the fact that there is a cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni:
it was indeed by means of Agni’s brilliance that they struck him down; yet Agni, being brilliance itself, was not shaken. Therefore, it is dedicated to Agni.
Now, as for the fact that there is a pap of cooked rice for Soma:
it was indeed by means of King Soma that they slew him; therefore, since he has Soma as his king, there is a pap of cooked rice for Soma.
Now, as for the cake for Savitṛ:
it is either on twelve potsherds or on eight potsherds. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; it was only when impelled by Savitṛ that they slew him. Therefore, there is this offering to Savitṛ.
Now, as for the fact that there is a pap offering to Sarasvatī:
Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; and it was Speech itself that cheered him on, saying, "Strike! Slay! Therefore, there is a pap offering to Sarasvatī.
Now, as to why there is a pap for Pūṣan:
this earth, indeed, is Pūṣan; she delivered him over to his slayer, and by her he was delivered over and slain. Therefore, there is a pap for Pūṣan.

Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni. By means of this they indeed slew him. Agni is brilliance and Indra is power and vigor; with these two powers they slew him. Agni is the priesthood (brahman) and Indra is the nobility (kṣatra); having joined together both the priesthood and the nobility and made them allies, with those two powers they slew him. Therefore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Indra and Agni.

Now there is a sacrificial pap for Mahendra. Indeed, he was Indra before the slaying of Vṛtra; but having slain Vṛtra, he became Mahendra, just as a great king becomes [known] after having conquered. Therefore there is a sacrificial pap for Mahendra. And he thus makes him truly great for the slaying of Vṛtra; for that reason also there is a sacrificial pap for Mahendra.
Then there is a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.

For all this work was indeed performed by the gods when they had sacrificed with the Sākamedha offerings and were victorious; and all this work is performed and everything is conquered by him who has sacrificed with the Sākamedha offerings and is victorious. Therefore, there is a cake on one potsherd for Viśvakarman.

By means of this very sacrifice, the gods, having sacrificed, became that progeny of the gods and that prosperity which they now possess. Verily, he who, knowing this, sacrifices with this sacrifice, procreates that same progeny and attains that same prosperity; therefore, one should indeed sacrifice with this.
By means of the Mahāhavis, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra;
by it they won that very victory which is theirs. And those whom they had slain in that battle, they restored by means of the Pitṛyajña; for they were the Pitṛs—therefore it is called the Pitṛyajña.
Spring, summer, and the rainy season—these are those which they conquered; autumn, winter, and the cool season—those are the ones which they restored again.

Now, as to why he performs this sacrifice: it is not as if anyone were killing him; rather, he does this just as the gods did. He provides for them that very share which the gods assigned to them, and he protects those whom the gods set in motion. He leads his own ancestors to a better world. And whatever of his own self is here destroyed or diminished by his failure to act, that he restores again by this [sacrifice]. That is why he performs this sacrifice.

He offers a cake on six potsherds to the Soma-possessing Fathers, or to Soma accompanied by the Fathers; for there are six seasons, and the Fathers are the seasons—therefore it consists of six potsherds.

Then, for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs, they prepare parched grains on the Anvāhāryapacana fire; then they grind half of them, while the other half remains as parched grains unground—those are the parched grains for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs.
Then for the Agniṣvātta fathers:

from the milk of a cow that has recently calved, stirred once with a single splinter, there is a mash; for the fathers have departed once and for all, therefore it is stirred once. These are the oblations.

Now, those who have sacrificed with Soma are the Pitṛs called Somavant; then, those who conquer the world by means of cooked food given as a gift are the Pitṛs called Barhiṣad; and then, those who are neither of these two, whom Agni himself consumes while eating them, are the Pitṛs called Agniṣvātta—these indeed are the Pitṛs.

Behind the Gārhapatya fire, having placed the sacrificial cord over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and sitting facing south, he takes this cake on six potsherds. Rising from that very spot and standing to the north of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, facing south, he threshes it; he cleans the grain once only, for the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore, he cleans it only once.
He places the two millstones on the south side;

he places the six potsherds in the southern half of the Gārhapatya fire-altar. As to why they resort to this southern quarter—it is because this quarter belongs to the Fathers; therefore, they resort to this southern quarter.

Then, to the south of the Anvāhāryapacana fire, he prepares a four-cornered altar; he makes the corners correspond to the intermediate directions. For there are four intermediate directions, and the ancestors are indeed the intermediate directions; therefore, he makes the corners correspond to the intermediate directions.
In the middle of that he establishes the fire.

For the gods, facing westward, turned toward men from the east; therefore, one offers to them while standing facing the east. The Pitṛs are on all sides; the Pitṛs are indeed the intermediate quarters, for these intermediate quarters are, as it were, on all sides. Therefore, he establishes the fire in the middle.

From that very spot he first takes up the *stambayajus*. Having offered the *stambayajus*, he first encloses [the altar] with the formula "Now," then "Now," then "Now. Having enclosed it with the first enclosure, he draws lines and carries away whatever is to be carried away. In the same manner, he encloses it with the second enclosure; having enclosed it with the second enclosure and smoothed it down, he says, "Set down the sprinkling waters. They set down the sprinkling waters, they place the fuel and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) nearby, and he cleanses the offering-spoons (*sruk*). He goes out with the clarified butter (*ājya*), and having placed the sacred thread over his left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), he takes portions of the clarified butter.
Regarding this they say:

"One should take twice in the *upabhṛt* ladle, for there are two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) here. But one should rather take eight times in the *upabhṛt*, lest one should depart from the proper form of the sacrifice; therefore, one should take exactly eight times in the *upabhṛt*. Having taken the clarified butter, he again becomes one who wears the sacred cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*).
The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters.

He first sprinkles the fuel, then the altar, and then they hand him the sacrificial grass (barhis); he places it down with its knot toward the east. Having sprinkled it and poured water over it, he loosens the knot but does not take a prastara-bunch, for the fathers have once and for all turned away; therefore, he does not take a prastara.
Then, having loosened his girdle, he goes around thrice counter-clockwise while strewing [the grass].

Having thus strewn it thrice counter-clockwise, he leaves a remnant as far as the place for the prastara-bunch. Then he goes around again thrice clockwise. As to why he goes around again thrice clockwise: those three ancestors whom he has followed down to, from them he now withdraws back toward this, his own world; that is why he goes around again thrice clockwise.
He lays down the enclosing-sticks with the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) alone;

he spreads the prastara-bunch with the dakṣiṇā and does not place the two separating-blades (vidhṛtī) between them. For the fathers have departed once and for all; therefore, he does not place the two separating-blades between.
There he places the *juhū* ladle;

then the *upabhṛt* to the east; then the *dhruvā*; then the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); then the parched grains (*dhānā*); and having placed the stirred drink (*mantha*), he touches all the oblations together.
All of them, having become invested with the sacrificial cord (yajñopavītin), [proceeded];
thus the sacrificer and the Brahman priest were surrounded from behind, while the Agnīdh was in front.
Therefore they proceed in a whisper;
for the ancestors are, as it were, hidden, and that which is whispered is, as it were, hidden; therefore they proceed in a whisper.
They move about in an enclosed space.
The ancestors, indeed, are as if hidden; this enclosed space is, as it were, hidden; therefore they move about in an enclosed space.

Then, while placing the fuel on the fire, he says, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled! The Hotṛ recites that single *sāmidhenī* verse three times; for the fathers have departed once and for all, and therefore the Hotṛ recites that one *sāmidhenī* verse three times.

He recites: "Desiring thee, we lay thee down; desiring thee, we kindle thee. Desiring, bring hither the desiring fathers to eat the oblation. Then he says: "Bring Agni hither! Bring Soma hither! Bring the Soma-drinking fathers hither! Bring the Barhis-sitting fathers hither! Bring the Agni-consumed fathers hither! Bring the butter-drinking gods hither! Bring Agni for the office of Hotṛ! Bring thy own greatness hither! Having thus invoked them, he sits down.
Then, having called for the announcement, he does not choose the Hotṛ priest.

This is indeed a sacrifice to the Fathers; "lest I place the Hotṛ among the Fathers," he thinks, and therefore he does not choose a Hotṛ. He simply says, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! and the Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat. Having sat down, he gives the impulse. Being impelled, the Adhvaryu takes the two offering-spoons and steps across to the west. Having stepped across and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to the kindling-sticks (*samidhaḥ*). He performs four fore-offerings (*prayāja*) excluding the one for the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). "The sacrificial grass is offspring; lest I place offspring among the Fathers," he thinks, and therefore he performs four fore-offerings excluding the one for the sacrificial grass. Then they proceed with the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*). Having proceeded with the two butter-portions...

All of them, having placed the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītinaḥ), thinking, "We shall proceed with these oblations," the sacrificer and the Brahman walk around in front, while the Āgnīdhra walks behind; then they cause the announcement to be made: "Oṃ svadhā!"—the response is "Astu svadhā!"—and the Vaṣaṭ-call is "Svadhā namaḥ!"
Regarding this, Āsuri said:

"They should indeed cause the announcement to be made, they should cause the response to be made, and they should utter the *vaṣaṭ* call; let us not deviate from the established rule of the sacrifice."

Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Soma-possessing Fathers," or "for Soma accompanied by the Fathers. He recites two invitatory verses; for by one [verse] they cause the gods to move forward, and by two [verses] the Fathers, since the Fathers have indeed turned away once and for all. Therefore, he recites two invitatory verses.

He spreads clarified butter [as a base]. Then he cuts off portions from this sacrificial cake; together with that, he takes portions of the parched grains, and together with that, portions of the stirred drink. He places them all at once upon the fire. Then he pours clarified butter over them twice from above. He anoints the places from which the portions were cut. Without stepping across the altar, he stands up right there, calls for the *śrauṣaṭ*, and says, "Sacrifice to the Soma-possessing Fathers! At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ* call, he makes the offering.

Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs. He spreads a layer of clarified butter [in the ladle], then takes a portion from these parched grains; together with that, he takes a portion of the stirred drink (mantha), and together with that, a portion of the cake. He places them all at once into the fire, then pours clarified butter over them twice from above. He anoints the portions [of the offering] and does not step across [the altar]. Rising from his place toward the east, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering verse for the Barhiṣad Pitṛs," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the oblation.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the Agniṣvātta fathers.

He spreads a layer of clarified butter [on the ladle], then takes a cutting from this stirred offering (mantha). Together with that, he takes a cutting from the cake; together with that, from the parched grains. He places them all at once [into the fire], then pours clarified butter over them twice from above. He anoints the cuttings back [with butter] and does not step across [the altar]. Rising right there, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the Agniṣvātta fathers! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Then he says, "Recite for Agni Kavyavāhana.
This is for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering; for Havyavāhana belongs to the gods and Kavyavāhana to the ancestors. Therefore, he says, "Recite for Agni Kavyavāhana."

He spreads clarified butter [as a base]. Then he cuts portions from this sacrificial cake; together with that, he takes portions of the parched grains, and together with that, portions of the stirred drink. He places them all at once into the offering ladle. Then, from above, he pours twice more clarified butter over them. He does not re-anoint the cut portions, nor does he step across [the altar]. Rising from right there, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni Kavyavāhana," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.

As for the fact that he does not step beyond [the altar], but rather, having risen from right here, he offers: for the fathers have indeed once and for all departed; and as for the fact that he cuts off portions for all at once: for the fathers have indeed once and for all departed. And as for the fact that he cuts off the portions crosswise: the fathers are indeed the seasons; it is thus that he interlinks the seasons and joins the seasons together. Therefore, he cuts off the portions crosswise.

Now, some indeed place this very mash for the Hotṛ; the Hotṛ, having invited him, merely smells it and hands it to the Brahman; the Brahman merely smells it and hands it to the Āgnīdhra; the Āgnīdhra merely smells it—and they do this, however, just as they cut off portions of the *iḍā* and the *prāśitra* at another sacrifice, so too should they cut off portions from this one. Having invited him, they merely smell it; they do not eat it. "But we think it should indeed be eaten," said Āsuri, "for whoever offers in the fire."

Then, whichever of the two is about to give—the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer—he takes a vessel of water and goes around three times, sprinkling towards the left. He causes the sacrificer’s father to wash his hands, saying, "O so-and-so, wash! "O so-and-so, wash! for the grandfather; and "O so-and-so, wash! for the great-grandfather. Just as one would pour water over someone who is being consecrated, so it is in this case.

Then, having taken a portion of this sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), he places it in his left hand; having taken a portion of the parched grains (dhānā), he places them in his left hand; having taken a portion of the stirred drink (mantha), he places it in his left hand.
He extended this intermediate direction along the corner.

In that [corner], he gives to the sacrificer’s father, saying, "N.N., this is for you! Then, in the corner along this intermediate direction, he gives to the sacrificer’s grandfather, saying, "N.N., this is for you! Then, in the corner along this intermediate direction, he gives to the sacrificer’s great-grandfather, saying, "N.N., this is for you! Then, in the corner along this intermediate direction, he wipes [the vessel] with the words, "O fathers, rejoice here; satisfy yourselves according to your respective portions! By this he means, "Eat according to your respective portions! In that he thus gives to the fathers, he thereby does not exclude his own fathers from this sacrifice.

Having all put on their sacrificial threads (*yajñopavīta*) and gone out toward the north, they stand worshipping the *Āhavanīya* fire. For he who has established the sacred fires and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices approaches the gods; yet, since they have just performed the sacrifice to the ancestors, they now make amends to the gods.

They worship the Āhavanīya fire with two verses addressed to Indra, for the Āhavanīya is indeed Indra. [The verses are: "They have eaten and rejoiced; they have shaken off their dear [impurities]. The self-luminous sages have praised thee with a most recent hymn. Now yoke thy two bay horses, O Indra! We would pay homage to thee, O Maghavan, who art fair to behold. Now, O chariot whose seat is full, being praised, thou goest according to our will. Now yoke thy two bay horses, O Indra! Thus they say.

Then, having returned, they stand by the Gārhapatya fire, reciting: "We call back the mind with the Nārāśaṃsa hymn and with the prayers of the Fathers; may our mind come back to us for wisdom, for skill, for life, and that we may long behold the sun! May the divine folk, O Fathers, give back our mind to us; may we be united with the company of the living! For they have indeed performed this rite as if it were a sacrifice to the Fathers, and thus they now join themselves once more to the living; therefore he says, "May we be united with the company of the living."

Then, whichever one gives, he, having again placed the sacred thread over his right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and approached, mutters: "The fathers have rejoiced; they have partaken according to their portions. By this, he means to say: "They have eaten according to their portions."

Then, taking a water-pot, he goes around three times, sprinkling from left to right; he causes the sacrificer’s father to wash his hands, saying, "O so-and-so, wash! "O so-and-so, wash! [he says for] the grandfather, and "O so-and-so, wash! for the great-grandfather. This is just as one would sprinkle water upon someone who has eaten. As for why he again goes around three times, sprinkling from left to right: it is so that this rite may be completed from left to right; therefore, he again goes around three times, sprinkling from left to right.
Then, having lifted up the fringe of his garment, he pays homage.

For the fringe belongs to the Fathers; therefore, having lifted up the fringe, he pays homage. Homage is indeed the sacrifice; thus he makes them worthy of sacrifice. He pays homage six times, for there are six seasons, and the Fathers are the seasons; thus he establishes the sacrifice in the seasons. Therefore, he pays homage six times. "O Fathers, give us houses," he says; for the Fathers are the lords of houses. This is the prayer for blessing at this rite.
Having all put on their sacrificial threads (yajñopavītin),
intending to proceed with the two after-offerings (anuyāja), the sacrificer and the Brahman priest go around behind, while the Āgnīdhra sits down in front and the Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat.

Then he says, "O Brahman, I shall set forth. Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, [the Adhvaryu] says, "O Agnīdh, cleanse the fire! Taking up the two offering-spoons, he steps across toward the west. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Sacrifice to the gods! He performs two after-offerings (*anuyāja*) excluding the *barhis*. [The reason is: "The *barhis* is offspring; let me not place offspring among the Fathers. Therefore, he performs two after-offerings excluding the *barhis*.
Then, having set down the two offering-spoons, he separates them;

having separated the two spoons and anointed the enclosing-sticks, and having reached toward an enclosing-stick and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says: "The divine Hotṛs have been impelled for the utterance of auspicious speech; the human [Hotṛ] has been sent forth for the *sūktavāka*. Thereupon the Hotṛ begins the *sūktavāka*, while the Adhvaryu does not pluck the *prastara* (grass-bundle) but remains waiting in this manner until the Hotṛ recites the *sūktavāka*.
Then the Āgnīdhra says, "Throw [the wooden sword] into the fire! He does not throw anything at all into the fire; he merely touches himself in silence.

Then he says, "Converse [with the Hotṛ]. [The Hotṛ responds: "The Agnīdh has come; make me hear, O Śrauṣaṭ! To the divine Hotṛs, 'svagā'; to the human ones, 'well-being'; pronounce 'śaṃ-yoḥ'! He merely touches the enclosing-sticks (paridhis) but does not throw them into the fire; then he collects this sacrificial grass (barhis) together with the enclosing-sticks.

Now, some collect the remains of the oblation together; but one should not do so, for these are indeed the remains of what has been offered. [Thinking,] "We shall offer into the fire that which is the remains of what has been offered," they should therefore either throw them into water or consume them.
By means of the Mahāhavis, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra;

by it they won that very victory which is theirs. Furthermore, those arrows which struck them in that battle, they extracted as splinters by these very [oblations] when they sacrificed with the Tryambaka offerings, and they pulled them out.

Now, as to why he sacrifices with these: "Surely no arrow of his ever misses its mark," so the gods thought; and it is for this reason that he performs this sacrifice. Both his offspring that have been born and those that are yet unborn he releases from Rudra's power; thus his offspring are born free from disease and free from blemish. For this reason, indeed, he sacrifices with these.
They indeed belong to Rudra, for they are the arrow of Rudra;
therefore they belong to Rudra. They consist of a single cake (ekakapāla), because [the sacrificer] thinks, "May they be for a single deity"; therefore they consist of a single cake.

These [sacrificial cakes] indeed correspond to each person; as many householders as there may be, they are one more than that. Thus, for each person, he releases those offspring of his who have already been born from the power of Rudra by means of each one [cake]. They are one more than that; thus he releases those offspring of his who are yet unborn from the power of Rudra. Therefore, they are one more than that.

Behind the Gārhapatya fire, having placed the sacrificial cord over his left shoulder (yajñopavītī) and sitting facing north, he takes these [grains]. Rising from that very spot and standing facing north, he threshes them; he places the lower and upper millstones facing north, and he arranges the potsherds on the northern half of the Gārhapatya hearth. As for why they resort to that northern quarter—it is because this is the region of this deity; therefore, they resort to that northern quarter.
They may indeed be anointed;
for an oblation is anointed. Or rather, they should be left unanointed; for Rudra would be likely to strike down the cattle if one were to anoint them. Therefore, they should remain unanointed.

Having placed them together in a vessel, he takes a firebrand from the Anvāhāryapacana fire, goes northward, and offers the oblation; for this is the direction of that god. He offers on the path, for that god moves along the path. He offers at a crossroads; for the crossroads is indeed his well-known and familiar place of rest. Therefore, he offers at a crossroads.
He offers with the middle leaf of the Palāśa tree.
The leaf of the Palāśa is indeed Brahman; thus he offers with Brahman itself. He cuts portions from all [the cakes], but he does not cut a portion from one which remains as a surplus.

He offers the oblation, saying: "This is thy portion, O Rudra; together with thy sister Ambikā, accept it, Svāhā! For Ambikā is indeed the name of his sister; with her this is his portion. Because this is his portion together with a woman, they are called Tryambakas. Thus he releases from the power of Rudra those offspring of his that have been born.
Now, that one which remains over, he scatters upon a mole-hill with the words:

"This, O Rudra, is thy portion; the mole is thy animal. Thus he assigns the mole specifically among the animals for him, and thereby he does not harm the other animals. As for why he scatters it: embryos are indeed hidden away, and what is scattered is as if hidden away; therefore he scatters it. And thus he releases from the power of Rudra those offspring of his that have not yet been born.
Then, having returned, they mutter:

"We have appeased Rudra, we have appeased the three-eyed god, so that he may make us more prosperous, so that he may make us better, so that he may inspire us. You are a remedy, a remedy for the cow, for the horse, for man; you are a remedy, a blessing for the ram and the ewe. This is indeed the prayer for success of this ritual act.

Then they walk around three times counter-clockwise, striking their left thighs, [saying]: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity; may he release me from death as a cucumber from its stem—[may he not release me] from immortality! This is indeed the blessing of this rite; it is this very blessing that they invoke. For it is truly auspicious for one who is released from death not to be released from immortality; therefore he says, "May he release me from death, [not] from immortality."

Therefore, even young maidens go around [the fire] saying, "Let us share in Bhaga's fortune. For she who is Rudra’s sister, named Ambikā, she indeed rules over Bhaga; therefore, even young maidens go around [the fire] saying, "Let us share in Bhaga's fortune."

For these women there is this mantra: "We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the bestower of husbands; may I be released from here like a cucumber from its stalk—neither from here nor from there. When she says "from here," she means "from her kinsmen"; when she says "nor from there," she means "nor from her husbands. For husbands indeed are the support for a woman; therefore she says, "nor from there."
Then they again go around three times in a sunwise direction, striking their right thighs, with this same mantra.

As to why they again go around three times in a sunwise direction: "May this rite be completed in a sunwise manner for us," they think; therefore they again go around three times in a sunwise direction.

Then the sacrificer, having placed these [remnants] in his joined palms, throws them upwards so that a cow cannot reach them; thus he fashions for himself a small portion [of the sacrifice]. While seeking to lick them, they touch them; they thereby provide a remedy for themselves; therefore, while seeking to lick them, they touch them.
Having tied those two bags together.

Having tied it either to a bamboo staff or to a post at both ends, he goes toward the east; and if he should find a tree, or a stump, or a bamboo, or an anthill, he fastens it there with the formula: "This is thy garment, O Rudra; with it, go beyond the Mūjavat mountains. For they travel along a path by means of a garment; thus he directs him toward that very garment. Wherever his course lies, there indeed is his course beyond the Mūjavat mountains; therefore he says, "Go beyond the Mūjavat mountains. With the words, "With thy bow unstrung, O wielder of the Pināka," he means to say, "Pass by us, being auspicious and non-injurious. With the words, "Clad in a skin," he truly puts him to sleep; for while sleeping, he injures no one; therefore he says, "Clad in a skin."
Then they turn back toward the south.

Looking back, they return; having returned, they touch water. For they have indeed moved along with that which belongs to Rudra; water is a means of pacification, so they pacify themselves with water as a means of pacification.

Then, having shaved his hair and beard and having consigned the fires into himself, he moves away from the sacrificial ground; for it is with this [rite] that he sacrifices, as it is not appropriate that he should offer the Agnihotra on the high altar (uttaravedi). Therefore he moves away. Having gone home and churned out the fires, he performs the Full-moon sacrifice. These Cāturmāsya offerings are, as it were, a neglected sacrifice, whereas the Full-moon sacrifice is a well-ordered and established sacrifice. Thus, by means of that well-ordered sacrifice, he finally establishes himself. That is why he moves away.

The merit of one who performs the Cāturmāsya sacrifices indeed becomes inexhaustible. For he conquers the year; therefore his merit becomes inexhaustible. He performs the sacrifice by dividing it threefold; he conquers by dividing it threefold. The year is indeed everything, and the inexhaustible is indeed everything. By this, his merit becomes truly inexhaustible. Having become the season itself, he thus goes unto the gods. The gods' merit is indeed inexhaustible; by this, his own merit becomes truly inexhaustible. This is why one sacrifices with the Cāturmāsyas.

Now, as to why one should sacrifice with the *Cunāsīrya*: whatever prosperity belonged to the gods when they had performed the *Sākamedha* sacrifices and were victorious, that was *cuna*; and whatever essence belonged to the year after it had been won, that was *sīra*. Thus, by taking hold of both that prosperity which belonged to the gods when they had performed the *Sākamedha* sacrifices and were victorious, and that essence which belonged to the year after it had been won, he makes them his own; therefore, he sacrifices with the *Cunāsīrya*.
This is its modification:

they do not throw up the high altar (uttaravedi), they do not take the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), and they do not churn the fire; there are five fore-offerings (prayāja), three after-offerings (anuyāja), and one *samiṣṭayajus*.

Now, there are these same five oblations. By means of these oblations, Prajāpati created offspring; by means of these he released the offspring from Varuṇa’s noose on both sides. By means of these the gods slew Vṛtra, and by means of these they conquered—that victory which is theirs. In the same way, this sacrificer, by means of these, takes possession of both that prosperity which belonged to the gods when they had sacrificed with the Sākamedhas and were victorious, and that essence of the year which had been won; having grasped both of these, he makes them his own. Therefore, there are these five oblations.
Then there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Śuna and Sīra; its significance is the same as that which we have previously explained regarding the Śunāsīrya sacrifice.
Now, there is milk for Vāyu.

For milk, indeed, creatures recognize when they have been born; [he offers it] thinking, "May the creatures recognize me as a conqueror, for the sake of prosperity, glory, and the eating of food. Therefore, there is milk.

Now, as for why it belongs to Vāyu: this wind that blows here is indeed Vāyu; he causes all this to swell, whatever it is that rains here. When it has rained, plants are born; having eaten the plants and drunk the water, from that [water] this milk arises from the waters. For he (Vāyu) indeed produces this; therefore it belongs to Vāyu.

Then there is a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya. He who shines yonder is indeed Sūrya; he guards all this, both by what is good and by what is not good. He ordains all this, both in what is good and in what is not good. "May he, being pleased with me as I have conquered, guard me by what is good and ordain me in what is good"—thinking thus, there is therefore a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya.

Its sacrificial fee is a white horse; thus, the form of him who shines yonder is produced. If he should not find a white horse, even a white ox may serve; thus, the form of him who shines yonder is produced.

Whenever he performs the Sākamedha sacrifices, he should perform them with the Cunāsīrya; for in that he sacrifices three times in the year, by that very act he attains the year. Therefore, he should sacrifice with this at whatever time.

Regarding this, some desire to extend the performance over nights; if he should desire to extend it over nights, he should sacrifice with the Cunāsīrya on that [full moon] which was observed previously in the month of Phālguna.

Now, if one should undergo initiation, the full moon of Phālguna should not pass by again while he has not yet sacrificed; for it would be as if one were to undertake a journey again before having completed the previous one. Therefore, the full moon of Phālguna should not pass by again while he has not yet sacrificed—this applies to one who is relinquishing [the vow].
Now, however, for one who performs the sacrifice again:

on the previous day he should sacrifice with the Śunāsīrya for the full moon of Phālguna; then in the morning with the Vaiśvadeva; then with the Full Moon sacrifice—this is for one performing it again.
Now, therefore, concerning the turning around:
this sun is indeed facing in all directions; it sucks up everything here—whatever exists—that dries up. Therefore, it faces in all directions, and for that reason, it is an eater of food.
This fire has faces on all sides;
for from whatever side they place fuel into the fire, it burns from that very side. Therefore, it has faces on all sides, and therefore it is a consumer of food.
Now, this person has faces on one side only;
he becomes facing in all directions when he turns [the fire]. He thus becomes an eater of food just as these two [fires] are; therefore, whoever knows this should turn [the fire].

Regarding this, Āsuri said: "What indeed does it matter about the face, even if one were to shave all the hair from it? Since he sacrifices three times a year, by that very act he becomes one whose face is turned in every direction and thus an eater of food; therefore, he need not concern himself with turning [the fire]."
Regarding this, they say:

"By means of the Sākamedha offerings, the gods indeed slew Vṛtra; by them they won that victory which is theirs. But truly, the gods slew Vṛtra by all the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; by all of them they won that victory which is theirs.

They said, "With what king, with what army shall we fight? Agni replied, "With me as king, with me as army. With Agni as king and Agni as army, they conquered for four months; they encompassed them with the Brahman and with the threefold knowledge (the Veda).

They said, "With whom as king, with whom as leader shall we fight? Varuṇa replied, "With me as king, with me as leader. With Varuṇa as king and Varuṇa as leader, they conquered the other four months; and they encompassed them with the Brahman and with the threefold knowledge (the Vedas).

They said, "With whom as king, with whom as leader shall we fight? Indra said to them, "With me as king, with me as leader. With Indra as king and Indra as leader, they conquered the other four months; and they encompassed them with the Brahman and with the threefold knowledge (trayi vidyā).

When he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, it is by means of Agni as king, by means of Agni as the vanguard, that he conquers the four months; there is a three-striped porcupine quill and a copper razor. That which is the three-striped porcupine quill is the form of the triple science (the Vedas); the copper razor is the form of Brahman, for Agni is Brahman, and Agni is indeed red; therefore, the razor is of copper. With that he shaves [the hair]. Thus, he encompasses him both by means of Brahman and by means of the triple science.
Now, as to why he sacrifices with the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings:

it is by means of Varuṇa himself, the king, and by means of Varuṇa as his vanguard, that he conquers the next four months. There is a three-striped porcupine quill and a copper razor; with these he shaves [the hair]. Thus, he encompasses him both by means of the Brahman and by means of the triple knowledge (trayī vidyā).
Now, as to why he sacrifices with the Sākamedhas:

it is by means of Indra himself as king, and by means of Indra as his vanguard, that he conquers the other four months. There is a three-striped porcupine quill and a copper razor; therewith he shaves [the head]. Thus, he encompasses him both with the Brahman (the sacred word) and with the triple knowledge (the three Vedas).

When he sacrifices with the Vaiśvadeva, he then becomes Agni himself; he wins union with Agni and residence in the same world as Agni. Then, when he sacrifices with the Sākamedha offerings, he becomes Indra himself; he wins union with Indra and residence in the same world as Indra.

In whichever season he goes to that world, that season hands him over to the next season, and the next season hands him over to the one after that; he goes to the highest station, the supreme goal—thus it is for the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. Regarding this they say: "They do not find fault with the performer of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, for he indeed goes to the highest station, the supreme goal. Thus they choose a place for the sacrifice to the gods.

They should choose that which is the highest; for whatever else lies beyond the earth, from that indeed the gods ascended to heaven. He who undergoes consecration (dīkṣate) ascends after the gods; he sacrifices on a sacrificial ground (devayajana) that possesses the gods. If he were to lie down upon anything other than the earth, it would be as if he were lower or more wretched; therefore, they should choose that which is the highest.

That altar-ground should be even; being even, it should be level; being level, it should not be sloping; being level, it should slope toward the east, for the east is the direction of the gods. Or it may slope toward the north, for the north is the direction of men. On the south side, however, it should be somewhat elevated; for this is the direction of the ancestors. If it were sloping toward the south, the sacrificer would quickly go to yonder world; therefore, the sacrificer lives long. Thus, on the south side, it should be somewhat elevated.
It should not extend beyond the measure of the sacrificial ground (devayajana) in front;

for he would thereby cause his hateful rival to exceed him. It may, however, extend as much as one desires to the south or likewise to the north. But that sacrificial ground is truly successful where a space equal to the sacrificial ground remains behind; for quickly indeed does the subsequent performance of sacrifice come to him. Thus far concerning the sacrificial ground.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "We went to Vārṣṇya to choose a site for a sacrifice to the gods. Sātyayajña said to him: 'This entire earth is indeed a sacrificial ground for the gods; wherever on it one performs the sacrifice after having demarcated the area with a Yajus formula, that is suitable.'"
The officiating priests are indeed the sacrificial ground for the gods.
Those Brahmins who have heard the scriptures, who are learned in the Vedas, and who are wise—when they perform the sacrifice, that is truly unshakable; we consider it as if it were closest to us.
They erect either a hall or a pavilion with its ridge-pole facing east;
for the east is the direction of the gods. Since the gods turned westward toward men from the east, therefore one offers to them while standing facing the east.

Therefore, one should not sleep with one's head toward the west, lest one sleep having stretched out toward the gods. That direction which is south belongs to the ancestors; that which is west belongs to the serpents, for it is from there that the gods departed; that which is north is deficient (ahīnā). The northern direction belongs to humans; therefore, for human beings, they construct a hall or a shed with its beams facing north, for the north is the direction of men. However, for one who is consecrated (dīkṣita), the beams face east, not for one who is not consecrated.
They enclose this very altar so that it may not be rained upon;

for indeed, he who undergoes consecration approaches the gods and becomes one of the deities. The gods are, as it were, hidden from men, and this enclosure is, as it were, a place of concealment; therefore they enclose it.
Therefore, not everyone should undertake it; rather, only a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya should do so, for they alone are worthy of sacrifice.
He indeed should not converse with everyone.

For he who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*) approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities. Now, the gods do not converse with everyone—only with a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, for they alone are worthy of sacrifice. Therefore, if he should find himself in conversation with a Śūdra, he should say to one of these [three]: "Look at this one! Look at this one! This is the proper conduct for one who has been consecrated.
Then, taking the fire-drills in his hand, he enters the hall.

Approaching the central pillar on the eastern side, he recites this sacrificial formula: "We have come to this place of sacrifice upon the earth where all the gods took delight. By this, it becomes pleasing to him through all the gods; and as for those Brahmins here who are learned and well-versed in the Vedas—when those learned Brahmins look at him with their eyes, by that it becomes pleasing to him through them.

As it is said: "Wherein all the gods have rejoiced"—thereby this becomes acceptable to him through all the gods. "Crossing over with Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus"—for by means of Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus they reach the conclusion of the sacrifice; thus he says, "May I reach the conclusion of the sacrifice. "May we rejoice together with the increase of wealth and with food"—the increase of wealth is abundance, and abundance is prosperity; thus he invokes this very blessing. "May we rejoice together with food"—they say of one who attains prosperity and reaches the highest state that "he rejoices in food"; therefore he says, "May we rejoice together with food."
He should undergo initiation in the afternoon.

Before the shaving of his hair and beard, he may eat whatever he desires or whatever is available, for from that point on his eating consists only of the sacrificial food (vrata). However, if he has no desire to eat, he may certainly refrain from eating.

Then they enclose the hall on the north side. There he places a water-pot; the barber stands there, and he has his hair and beard shaved and his nails clipped. Indeed, there is an impurity in man where the waters do not reach him; for it is in his hair, beard, and nails that the waters do not reach him. Therefore, when he has his hair and beard shaved and his nails clipped, it is so that he may become pure for the consecration (*dīkṣā*).

Now, some shave their whole heads, saying, "Having all become pure, we shall undergo consecration. But one should not do so; for when one shaves his hair and beard and trims his nails, he thereby becomes pure. Therefore, one should indeed shave his hair and beard and trim his nails.
He indeed trims his nails first;

first those of the right hand, or first those of the left—this is in the manner of men, whereas among the gods it is otherwise; first those of the thumbs, or first those of the little fingers—this is in the manner of men, whereas among the gods it is otherwise.
He first causes the gift of a cow to be extended on the right;
or, in the case of humans, first on the left, for such is the way among the gods.
