He first moistens the hair on the right side with the formula: "May these divine waters be propitious to me.

When he says, "May these divine waters be propitious to me," it is because water is indeed a thunderbolt, for water is a thunderbolt; therefore, wherever these waters flow, they make a hollow, and where they stand still, they burn it up. Thus, by this act, he pacifies that very thunderbolt; so, being pacified, this thunderbolt does not harm him. Therefore he says: "May these divine waters be propitious to me."

Then he places a young blade of darbha grass in between, saying, "O herb, protect him! For the razor is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the razor, does not injure him. Then he applies the razor, saying, "O axe, do not harm him! For the razor is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the razor, does not injure him.
Having cut [the hair], he throws it into the water-vessel.

He silently moistens the hair at the back of the head; silently he places a young blade of darbha grass between [the head and the razor]; silently, having applied the razor, he cuts [the hair] and throws it into the water-vessel.
Then he hands the razor to the barber; he shaves the hair and beard. When he shaves the hair and beard—

Then he bathes. Man is indeed impure in that he speaks untruth; by that he is foul within. Water, however, is pure. "Having become pure, I shall undergo consecration," he thinks. Water is a means of purification; "Purified by the purifier, I shall undergo consecration," he thinks. For this reason, he bathes.

He bathes, [reciting]: "May the Waters, our mothers, cleanse us; may those who purify with ghee purify us with ghee. That indeed is truly purified which they have purified with ghee; therefore he says, "May those who purify with ghee purify us with ghee. "For they, the goddesses, carry away every defilement"—for "every" means "all," and "defilement" refers to that which is impure; for they carry away from him all that is impure. Therefore he says, "For they, the goddesses, carry away every defilement."
Then he steps out toward the northeast, saying:
"Pure and purified, I go upward from these [waters]. Indeed, pure and purified, he goes upward from these [waters].
Then he puts on the garment for the sake of completeness; he thus bestows his own skin upon him, for this skin which belongs to the cow was originally the skin of man.

Those gods said, "The cow indeed supports all this. Come, let us place this skin which is on the man onto the cow; by means of it, she shall endure the rain, by means of it the cold, and by means of it the heat."
Having stripped it from the man, they placed that skin upon the cow; with it, he endures rain, with it the snow, and with it the scorching heat.

For man was indeed cut up; therefore, wherever a blade of grass or something else cuts him, from that very spot blood flows out. Upon him they placed this skin—namely, a garment. Therefore, no one other than a man wears a garment, for they placed this skin upon him. For this reason, one should desire to be well-clad, thinking, "May I be endowed with my own skin. Consequently, people even wish to see one who is ill-clad if he is wearing fine clothes, for he is truly endowed with his own skin.
If one were naked at the end [of the rite], he would become a cow;
for the cow knows, "I wear his skin," and being afraid, she trembles, thinking, "He will take my skin away. Therefore, cows draw near to one who is well-clad.

Of this very garment, Agni is the border; Vāyu is the inner lining; the Pitṛs are the girdle; the Sarpas are the fringe; the Viśve Devas are the warp-threads; and the Nakṣatras are the weft-threads. For indeed, all these gods are dependent upon it; therefore, it becomes the garment of the consecrated.
Or it may be new (unwashed) cloth, for the sake of its being unworn-out.

He should tell someone to beat it, thinking, "Whatever unclean part of this has been cut or woven, let that become clean for him. If, however, it is new, he should sprinkle it with water, thinking, "Let it be clean. Moreover, one may also undergo consecration using that which is kept as a garment for one who has bathed, provided it has not been washed by beating.

He puts it on with the formula: "Thou art the body of consecration and austerity. For previously this was the body of one who was not yet consecrated, but now it is that of consecration and austerity; therefore he says, "Thou art the body of consecration and austerity. With "Thee, the auspicious and helpful, I put on," he means to say, "Thee, the auspicious and excellent, I put on. With "Nourishing a fair complexion," he says this because previously he nourished an evil complexion as one who was uninitiated, whereas here it is a fair one; therefore he says, "Nourishing a fair complexion."
Then he causes him to enter the hall.

One should not eat the meat of a cow or a bull; for these two—the cow and the bull—support this entire world. The gods said, "The cow and the bull support this entire world; come, let us place whatever strength belongs to other animals into the cow and the bull. So they placed whatever strength belonged to other animals into the cow and the bull. Therefore, the cow and the bull eat most abundantly. Now, he who eats the meat of a cow or a bull eats as if eating everything; it is like reaching the very end [of his life]. A portent arises for him: "He has struck down a fetus in his wife," or "He has caused a miscarriage"—such is the evil reputation that follows. Therefore, one should not eat the meat of a cow or a bull. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "I do indeed eat it, provided it is well-fleshed."

Having led forward the waters, he offers a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu. Indeed, Agni is all the deities, for it is into Agni that one makes offerings to all the deities; and Agni is the lower limit of the sacrifice while Viṣṇu is the upper limit. Thus, having encompassed all these deities and having encompassed the entire sacrifice, [he performs] the consecration (dīkṣā). Therefore, there is a cake on eleven potsherds for Agni and Viṣṇu.

Regarding this, some offer a caru-oblation to the Ādityas; for there is a verse concerning this: "Eight sons of Aditi were born from her own body; with seven she went forth to the gods, but Mārtāṇḍa she cast away."

There were indeed eight sons of Aditi, whom the gods call the Ādityas; however, there were only seven of them unaltered, for she brought forth the eighth, Mārtaṇḍa, as a mere embryo. He was indeed a mass of uncertainty; some say he was as tall as a man, both upright and across.

Then those gods, the Ādityas, said: "Since they have followed us in birth, let that [birth] be just like that [other one]. Come, let us transform him. They transformed him, just as this person here is transformed. Having cut up his flesh and distributed it, from that the elephant came into being. Therefore they say, "One should not accept an elephant as a gift, for the elephant is born from man. He whom they thus transformed was Vivasvat Āditya; these creatures are his offspring.
He said:

"He shall prosper among his offspring who offers this oblation of cooked rice (caru) to the Ādityas. Indeed, he prospers who offers this oblation of cooked rice to the Ādityas; however, this one for Agni and Viṣṇu is well-known.
For this sacrifice there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses;

he offers to the deities in a whisper; there are five *prayāja* offerings and three *anuyāja* offerings; they perform the *saṃyājas* for the wives [of the gods] for the sake of completeness; however, he does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus*, thinking, "Lest, having put on this garment of the consecrated, I should reach the end before the completion of the sacrifice," for the *samiṣṭayajus* is indeed the end of the sacrifice.

Then, standing in front of the hall, he anoints himself. Man is indeed a wound when unclothed; by anointing himself, he becomes one who is no longer wounded. For man’s skin belongs to the cow, and this fresh butter comes from the cow; thus he provides him with his own skin. That is why he anoints himself.

That indeed becomes fresh butter. Ghee belongs to the gods, while the melted liquid (phāṇṭa) belongs to men; but this [fresh butter] is neither ghee nor is it the melted liquid—it is indeed ghee, yet it is the melted liquid for the sake of freshness. Thus, by means of that which is not stale, he makes him who is not stale.

He anoints him from the head downwards to the feet in the direction of the hair, saying: "Thou art the milk of the great ones. "Great" (mahī) is indeed one name for cows; this is their milk, therefore he says, "Thou art the milk of the great ones. "Thou art the giver of splendor; give me splendor"—in this there is nothing obscure.
Then he anoints his eyes.

"The eye of man is indeed a wound; 'May it be healed for me,' so Yājñavalkya used to say. For his eye was as if diseased, and the film on it was indeed pus. By anointing his eyes, he thus makes them free from wounds."

Wherever the gods slew the Asura-Rakṣasas, there Śuṣṇa the Dānava, falling backward, entered the eyes of men. He is this very pupil which shines like a little boy; therefore, when about to undertake this sacrifice, he encloses it on all sides with a stone-fortress, for collyrium is indeed stone.
It is from Mount Trikakuda.

For when Indra slew Vṛtra, that which was his eye became that mountain Trikakuda; therefore, because it is from Trikakuda, he thereby bestows sight upon the eye. That is why it is from Trikakuda. If he should not find [ointment] from Trikakuda, let it even be from another mountain, for the kinship of ointment is indeed the same.
He anoints it with a reed-shaft.

The reed-shaft is indeed a thunderbolt, for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases. It has tufts; for this Rakṣas, which is rootless and cut off on both sides, wanders through the intermediate space, just as this man, being rootless and cut off on both sides, wanders through the intermediate space. Thus, in that it has tufts, it is for the sake of driving away the Rakṣases.
He first anoints the right [hand], for in human practice it is the left that comes first; but in the manner of the gods, it is thus.
He anoints it with the formula, "Thou art the eyeball of Vṛtra," for this is indeed the eyeball of Vṛtra; "Thou art the giver of sight, give me sight"—in this there is nothing obscure.
He anoints the right [side] once with a Yajus formula, once silently;
then the left he anoints once with a Yajus formula and twice silently. Thus he makes that which is on the left superior.

Now, as to why he anoints five times: the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he thus obtains it by means of five [anointments]. Therefore, he anoints five times.
Then he purifies him with a strainer of *darbha* grass.

Man is indeed impure in that he speaks untruth; by that he is putrid within. *Darbha* grass is pure; [the thought is], "Having become pure, let me undergo consecration (*dīkṣā*). *Darbha* grass is indeed a means of purification; [the thought is], "Purified by the means of purification, let me undergo consecration. Therefore, he purifies him with a strainer of *darbha* grass.
Or rather, it should be one;
for this [wind] blows as one alone. It is by means of the very form of that [one wind] that it exists; therefore, it should be one.
Moreover, there may also be three;

for this one indeed blows as a single entity, yet having entered within the person, it is divided threefold as prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna. Therefore, they should be three, according to the measure of that very [breath].
Moreover, there may also be seven;
for these vital breaths in the head are indeed seven, therefore there should be seven. Or rather, there should be thrice-seven, which is twenty-one; this is the perfect number.
He purifies it with seven [verses] each.

"May the Lord of Thought purify me"—the Lord of Thought is indeed Prajāpati; thus he says, "May Prajāpati purify me. "May the Lord of Speech purify me"—the Lord of Speech is indeed Prajāpati; thus he says, "May Prajāpati purify me. "May the divine Savitṛ purify me"—he who is purified by the divine Savitṛ is indeed well-purified; therefore he says, "May the divine Savitṛ purify me. "With a flawless strainer"—that which blows here is indeed the flawless strainer; thus he says this. "By the rays of Sūrya"—the rays of Sūrya are indeed the purifiers; therefore he says, "by the rays of Sūrya."
"Of thee, O lord of the strainers," he says; for he indeed becomes the lord of the strainers.

"Of thee, purified by the strainers," he says; for he indeed becomes purified by the strainers. "Whatever desire I may purify, that I may accomplish," he says; this means, "May I reach the completion of the sacrifice."
Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite the commencement of the blessings:
"O gods, we seek from you what is desirable as the sacrifice proceeds; O worshipful gods, we invoke your blessings. Thereupon, the officiating priests, being his own, pronounce blessings for him.

Then he lowers his fingers. He recites: "Svāhā! The sacrifice from the mind," twice; "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere," twice; "Svāhā! To heaven and earth," twice; "Svāhā! I take hold from the wind," with which he closes his fists. For the sacrifice is not to be taken hold of as if it were manifest, like this staff or this garment; the gods are indeed beyond the eye, and the sacrifice is beyond the eye.

When he says, "Svāhā! I take hold of the sacrifice with the mind," he thereby takes hold of it with the mind. When he says, "Svāhā! From the wide atmosphere," he thereby takes hold of it from the atmosphere. When he says, "Svāhā! From heaven and earth," he thereby takes hold of it from these two, heaven and earth, upon which all this rests. When he says, "Svāhā! I take hold from the wind," since the wind is indeed the sacrifice, he thereby takes hold of the sacrifice directly.

Now, as to why he says "svāhā, svāhā": the utterance "svāhā" is indeed the sacrifice; thus he places the sacrifice within himself. At this very point he restrains his speech; for speech is the sacrifice, and thus he places the sacrifice within himself.

Then he leads him into the hall. He goes behind the Āhavanīya fire and in front of the Gārhapatya; this is his path of movement until the Soma-pressing. As for why this is his path of movement until the Soma-pressing: the fire is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and the consecrated one is the embryo. Between the womb and the embryo, the embryo moves about. Since it moves here and there, and turns hither and thither, therefore these embryos move about and turn hither and thither. Therefore, this is his path of movement until the Soma-pressing.

All the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) of the consecration (*dīkṣā*) are indeed "uplifting" (*audgrabhaṇa*). For he who undergoes consecration lifts himself up from this world toward the world of the gods; it is by means of these very sacrificial formulas that he thus uplifts himself. Therefore they say: "All the sacrificial formulas of the consecration are uplifting. Now, they call these intermediate ones "the uplifting ones," for they are oblations; and the sacrifice is an oblation. While the muttering of the sacrificial formula is the sacrifice in its transcendent form, the oblation is the sacrifice in its manifest form. Thus, by means of this sacrifice, he uplifts himself from this world toward the world of the gods.

Then, those three oblations which he offers with the *sruva* ladle are called the "learned formulas" (*ādhītayajūṃṣi*), offered for the sake of completeness; the fourth is offered for the sake of desire. Now, that which he offers fifth with the *sruc* ladle is the actual *audgrabhaṇa* offering; for he offers it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is indeed the sacrifice.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unattainable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. And because they obstructed it with that, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
Or rather, this was heard by the seers.
They gathered the sacrifice; just as that sacrifice was gathered, so indeed does he gather the sacrifice when he offers these oblations.
He offers those five oblations;
for the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he thus obtains it by means of five, and therefore he offers five.
Now, therefore, regarding the oblation itself:
"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!"—for at first he intends, "May I perform sacrifice. Thus, whatever part of the sacrifice is here [in these formulas], that he gathers together and makes his own.

"To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for by means of wisdom and the mind one thinks, "May I sacrifice. Thus, whatever part of the sacrifice is here, that he thereby gathers together and makes his own.
"To initiation, to austerity, to Agni, svāhā!"—this is merely spoken;
it is not actually offered as an oblation.
"To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, Svāhā!

Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and the sacrifice is speech; Pūṣan is indeed cattle, for Pūṣan is nourishment, and nourishment is cattle; and cattle are the sacrifice. Thus, whatever part of the sacrifice is here, that he now gathers together and makes his own.
Regarding this they say:
"These oblations are offered as if they were unreal, unstable, and godless; for therein is neither Indra, nor Soma, nor Agni."

"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, Svāhā!"—for Agni is indeed truly established; whatever one offers in the fire, by that very act these [oblations] become truly offered and thereby established. Therefore, in all cases one offers with "To Agni, Svāhā! From that, these are called the *ādhītayajūṃṣi* (the formulas studied for recitation).

"To Ākūti, to Prayuj, to Agni, svāhā!"—for indeed, at the very beginning, one forms the intention (ākūti) in oneself, "May I sacrifice," and he then applies that to himself when he performs the rite; thus these two deities, Ākūti and Prayuj, become established within his own self.

"To Medhā, to Manas, to Agni, svāhā!"—for it is indeed by means of wisdom (medhā) and the mind (manas) that one intends, "May I sacrifice. Thus these two deities, wisdom and the mind, become established within his self.

"To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agni, Svāhā! Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and the sacrifice is speech; thus this deity of his is established within his own self as speech. Pūṣan is cattle, for Pūṣan is nourishment, and nourishment is cattle; cattle are the sacrifice, so these cattle of his are established within his own self as cattle. Because these deities are established within his own self, they are called the Ādhītayaḥ-yajūṃṣi (the "Established Formulas").

Then he offers the fourth oblation with: "O divine waters, vast, bringing welfare to all; O Heaven and Earth, and wide Atmosphere—we shall serve Bṛhaspati with our oblation, Svāhā! This [verse] is indeed closer to the sacrifice, for it mentions the waters, and the sacrifice is indeed the waters. It mentions the worlds, saying, "O Heaven and Earth, and wide Atmosphere. And it says, "We shall serve Bṛhaspati with our oblation, Svāhā"; for Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, and the sacrifice is the Brahman. Thus, this [verse] is indeed closer to the sacrifice.

Now, as for that which he offers with the offering-spoon as the fifth oblation—that indeed is the sacrifice manifestly; for he offers it with an *anuṣṭubh* verse, and the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is the sacrifice.

Then, whatever clarified butter remains in the *dhruvā* vessel, he pours that into the *juhū*. Three times he takes [butter] from the *ājyasthālī* into the *juhū* with the *sruva*; the third time he takes it, he fills the *sruva* completely.
He offers, saying:
"May every mortal choose the friendship of the god who leads; everyone strives for wealth; may he choose glory so that he may prosper—svāhā!"
This very [verse] becomes a *pañkti* by means of the deities:

"Of every god" (*viśvo devasya*) refers to the Vaiśvadeva; "of the leader" (*netuḥ*) refers to the Sāvitra; "may the mortal choose" (*marto vurīta*) refers to the Maitra; "may he choose glory" (*dyumnaṃ vṛṇīta*) refers to the Bārhaspatya—for Bṛhaspati is indeed glory; "may he prosper" (*puṣyata*) refers to the Pauṣṇa.

This very [offering] becomes a pentad by means of the deities; the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year. By this [offering], he attains that which is a pentad by means of the deities.
Or he offers it with an Anuṣṭubh verse;
for the Anuṣṭubh is speech and the sacrifice is speech: thus he directly attains the sacrifice.
Regarding this they say:

"One should offer this one alone for whatever desire [one seeks], for by this very [offering] one attains that desire, even though the others are offered. Now, if he were to offer it as a single [oblation], he should offer it full; for the full is indeed everything, and thus by this he attains everything. Furthermore, when he fills the dipping-spoon (sruva), he thereby fills the offering-ladle (sruk); he offers it full, and thus it is said that all [the offerings] are indeed offered.

Or he offers it with an Anuṣṭubh verse. This very Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-one syllables: ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, ten vital breaths, and the self as the thirty-first, in which these vital breaths are established. For man is of such extent; the sacrifice is man, for the sacrifice is commensurate with man. As great as the sacrifice is, as much as its measure is, so much does he obtain by this when he offers with the thirty-one-syllabled Anuṣṭubh.
To the south of the Āhavanīya fire, he spreads two black antelope skins with their necks pointing eastward;
upon these two he consecrates him. If there are two, that is the form of these two worlds; thus he consecrates him upon these two worlds.
The two ends become connected;
for these two worlds, the lower and the upper, are as if connected at their ends. Having subsequently joined these two worlds together as a pair, he consecrates him upon them.

When it becomes one, that is the form of these worlds; he thus consecrates him upon these worlds. Those which are white are the form of heaven, those which are black are the form of this earth; or alternatively, those which are black are the form of heaven and those which are white are the form of this earth; and those which are brownish-yellow are the form of the intermediate space. Thus he consecrates him upon these worlds.
Then he would cast it back later toward the end;
therefore, having paired these very worlds together, he consecrates him upon them.

Then, behind the black antelope skin, he sits down with his knees bent and facing eastward. At the very point where the white and black hairs meet, he touches it and mutters: "Ye two are the artistic forms of the Ṛcs and Sāmans. For that which is a counterpart is an "artistic form" (śilpa); thus he says, "Ye two are the counterparts of the Ṛcs and the Sāmans."
"Let us undertake this for you two.
Indeed, he who undergoes initiation becomes an embryo; he enters into the meters, and therefore his fingers become bent inward, for embryos have their fingers bent inward.

When he says, "I take hold of you two," he thereby means, "I enter into you two. When he says, "Protect me until the conclusion of this sacrifice," he thereby means, "Guard me until the completion of this sacrifice."

Then he mounts with his right knee, saying: "Thou art a refuge; grant me refuge. This is indeed the skin of the black antelope; that is its human refuge, but among the gods it is a refuge; therefore he says, "Thou art a refuge; grant me refuge. He says, "Homage be to thee; do not harm me. For he who mounts the sacrifice mounts upon something superior, since the sacrifice is the black antelope skin. Thus he makes amends to that sacrifice, and so the sacrifice does not injure him; therefore he says, "Homage be to thee; do not harm me."
He should sit first as if at the rear part [of the cart].

For if he were to sit down in the middle first, should anyone then pull him along from behind, he would either spill or fall; it would surely happen just so. Therefore, he should sit down first as if at the rear part.
Then he puts on the girdle.

The Aṅgirases, it is said, found weakness among those who were consecrated; they did not allow themselves any food other than their vow. They saw this strength, this completion; they placed that strength in the middle of their own bodies, and by means of it they attained completion. In the same way, this sacrificer now places that strength in the middle of his own body, and by means of it he attains completion.

It is indeed made of hemp; for hemp is soft. When Prajāpati was born as an embryo from this sacrifice, that which was his innermost membrane (*ulba*) became the hemp; therefore, hemp emits a pungent smell. And that which was his outer caul (*jarāyu*) became the garment of the consecrated; for the membrane is inside the caul, and therefore this garment is worn between [the body and] the other cloth. Just as Prajāpati was born from there as an embryo from this sacrifice, even so is he now born from here as an embryo from this sacrifice.
It indeed consists of three parts;
for food is threefold, and cattle are food. The father is one part, the mother is the second, and that which is born is the third; therefore, it consists of three parts.

It is bound with a cord of muñja grass. The reed is indeed a thunderbolt; [this is] for the sake of warding off evil spirits. It is let loose by letting go of the tufts of hair. If it were let loose in a forward direction (prasalavi), it would be like other human ropes. If it were let loose in a backward direction (apasalavi), it would belong to the Pitṛs as its deity. Therefore, it is let loose by letting go of the tufts of hair.

He removes it with the formula, "Thou art strength, belonging to Aṅgiras," for the Aṅgirases indeed perceived this strength; [he continues,] "Soft as wool, bestow strength upon me"—in this there is nothing obscure.
Then he hides the fringe of his garment with the words, "Thou art the fringe of Soma.
For previously this was the fringe of one who was not consecrated, but now it is that of the consecrated; it belongs to Soma, therefore he says, "Thou art the fringe of Soma."
Then he covers himself.
He who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣā*) becomes, as it were, an embryo; for an embryo is indeed covered by the amnion and the placenta; therefore, he covers himself.

He covers himself [with the skin], saying: "Thou art Viṣṇu’s protection; protection for the sacrificer. For he who undergoes consecration becomes both of these here: Viṣṇu and the sacrificer. When he undergoes consecration, he becomes Viṣṇu; when he performs the sacrifice, he becomes the sacrificer. Therefore he says: "Thou art Viṣṇu’s protection; protection for the sacrificer."
Then he ties a black antelope horn to his girdle.

Both the gods and the Asuras, being the offspring of Prajāpati, came to the inheritance of their father Prajāpati. The gods took possession of Mind, while the Asuras took possession of Speech; thus the gods took possession of the sacrifice, while the Asuras took possession of Speech. The gods took possession of that [higher] world, while the Asuras took possession of this [lower] world.

Those gods said to the sacrifice, "This speech is indeed a woman; address her, and she will surely call you. Or rather, he himself considered, "This speech is indeed a woman; let me address her, and she will surely call me. He addressed her, but she at first showed him aversion from afar; therefore, when a woman is addressed by a man, she at first shows aversion from afar. He said, "She has indeed shown me aversion from afar."

They said, "O venerable one, please address her; she will surely call out to you. He addressed her, and she spoke to him as if with leafless lips. Therefore, when a woman is addressed by a man, she speaks as if with leafless lips. He said, "She has indeed spoken to me as if with leafless lips."

They said, "O venerable sir, please address her; she will surely call you. He addressed her, and she called him. Therefore, even today, a woman calls a man by his name. He said, "She has indeed called me."

Those gods reflected: "This speech is indeed a woman; therefore, tell her, 'Come to me while I am standing right here,' and when she has come, report back to us. She then went to him while he was standing there. Therefore, a woman goes to a man while he is standing after he has performed his toilet. When she had come to them, he reported back to them: "She has indeed come."
The gods withheld that [speech] from the Asuras;

having taken it for themselves and enclosed it within Agni, they offered it as a complete oblation, for the oblation is the food of the gods. That very Anuṣṭubh which they offered, that indeed the gods then made their own. Those Asuras, deprived of speech, saying "O alas! O alas! were utterly defeated.

In this regard, they also uttered this saying: "That barbarian (mlecha) is to be shunned; therefore, a Brahmin should not speak like a barbarian. For that speech belongs to the Asuras, or rather, it is not [divine] at all. He who knows this seizes the speech of his hateful rivals; those [rivals], being deprived of their speech, perish."
This very sacrifice meditated upon Speech: "May I be united with her in sexual union. He copulated with her.
Indra indeed reflected:
"A great monster will surely be born from this union of the sacrifice and speech; let it not overcome me. So Indra himself, having become an embryo, entered into that union.
When he was born after a year, he reflected:
"Truly mighty is this womb which has borne me; surely some great and formidable being might be born after me, and it might overcome me."
Having wound it around her, he covered her with it;

he placed it upon the head of the sacrifice, for the sacrifice is Kṛṣṇa (the Black One). That which is the sacrifice is this black antelope skin, and that which is the womb is this black antelope horn. And because Indra wound it around her and covered her, it is called *āveṣṭita* (wound around). Just as Indra was born from there, having become an embryo from this union, even so is he born from there, having become an embryo from this union.

Or rather, he binds it as if it were turned upward; for the womb indeed bears the embryo while turned upward. Then he touches the forehead, over and above the right eyebrow, saying, "Thou art Indra’s womb. For this is indeed Indra’s womb; for from here he enters when entering, and from here he is born when being born. Therefore he says, "Thou art Indra’s womb."

Then he draws lines [on the altar], saying, "Make the crops well-grown. He thereby generates the sacrifice. For when there is a good harvest, then one is fit for sacrifice; when there is a bad harvest, then one is not even fit for oneself. Thus, he generates the sacrifice.

Now, if he is not initiated, he may scratch himself with a piece of wood or with his fingernail; for he who is initiated becomes an embryo. If one were to scratch an embryo with a piece of wood or a fingernail, it would be cast out and die; therefore, the initiated man would become scabby. Or else, following the semen of the initiated man, the seeds would be produced as scabby. But one's own womb does not harm the seed; this black antelope horn indeed becomes his own womb, and thus it does not harm him. Therefore, the initiated man should scratch himself only with a black antelope horn, and with nothing other than a black antelope horn.
Then he hands him a staff;
the staff is indeed a thunderbolt, for the sake of warding off evil spirits.
It is made of Udumbara wood;
the Udumbara is indeed food and vigor. It is for the attainment of vigor and the eating of food that it is made of Udumbara wood.
It is equal to the mouth;
for such indeed is its vigor as is the vigor that exists—namely, that which is equal to the mouth.
He raises it with the verse:

"Be raised up, O Lord of the Forest; standing erect, protect me from distress until the completion of this sacrifice. By saying "standing erect, protect me," he means "protect me until the conclusion of this sacrifice."
Regarding this, some say:

"One should clench one's fingers and restrain one's speech, for from that point on one will not recite anything at all. But one should not do so; for just as if one were to try to overtake someone running away with his back turned and fail to catch him, even so he fails to overtake the sacrifice. Therefore, one should clench one's fingers only there [at the end], and restrain one's speech only there.

Now, when one who has been consecrated utters a Ṛc, a Yajus, or a Sāman, he thereby begins the sacrifice with firmness, indeed with firmness; therefore, he should fold his fingers there and restrain his speech there.

Now, as to why he restrains his speech: the sacrifice is indeed speech; it is thus that he places the sacrifice within himself. And when he, being restrained in speech, utters a word, the sacrifice, having been released, turns away from him. In that case, he should mutter either a verse or a sacrificial formula addressed to Viṣṇu; for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and thus he takes hold of the sacrifice again. This is the expiation for that.

Then one proclaims: "This Brāhmaṇa is consecrated, this Brāhmaṇa is consecrated. By this, he announces to the gods that he has indeed been announced; he says, "He who has attained the sacrifice is of great heroism; he has become one of you—protect him! He says this three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.

Now, as to why he says "a Brāhmaṇa": previously, his birth was indeed as if non-existent, for it is said that the *rakṣases* follow after a woman. Thus, they deposit the seed as mere *rakṣases*. But here, one is truly born—he who is born from the *brahman*, who is born from the sacrifice. Therefore, even if he be a *rājanya* or a *vaiśya*, one should call him a "Brāhmaṇa," for he is born from the *brahman*, he is born from the sacrifice. Therefore they say: "One should not kill a performer of a *savana*; for a performer of a *savana* is indeed a sinner."
He restrains his speech;
he remains with his speech restrained until sunset, because he restrains his speech.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs today. They said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unattainable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. And because they obstructed it with that, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
Or rather, this was heard by the seers;
they gathered together the sacrifice, just as this sacrifice was gathered, so indeed does he who undergoes consecration gather the sacrifice; for speech is the sacrifice.
At sunset, he releases that speech.

Prajāpati is indeed the year, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; the year consists of day and night, for these two, revolving around it, bring it about. Having been consecrated during the day, he reached the night; having thus obtained the entire sacrifice, in its full measure, he releases his speech.

Regarding this, some release their speech upon seeing a star, saying, "At this point, it has set by nightfall. One should not do so; for what would happen if there were clouds? Therefore, one should release speech at the very moment one considers it to have set by nightfall.

For this reason, some release their speech, saying, "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! We cause the sacrifice to swell; we join the sacrifice together. But one should not do so; for he who releases his speech in this manner neither causes the sacrifice to swell nor does he join it together.

With this very [formula] he should release his speech: "Observe the vow! Observe the vow! Agni is the Brahman, Agni is the sacrifice, the tree is worthy of sacrifice. For this indeed becomes his sacrifice here; it is the oblation just as the *agnihotra* was before. Thus, having gathered the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice, he establishes the sacrifice in the sacrifice; he extends the sacrifice by means of the sacrifice, for his vow thus becomes continuous until the Soma-pressing. He says it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.
Then, having turned toward the fire, he releases his speech.
He who releases his speech by means other than this neither nourishes the sacrifice nor makes it whole. When he utters speech for the first time, he utters the truth of speech.

"Agni is Brahman"—for Agni indeed is Brahman; "Agni is the sacrifice"—for Agni indeed is the sacrifice; "the tree is worthy of sacrifice"—for trees indeed are worthy of sacrifice, for if there were no trees, humans would not be able to sacrifice; therefore he says, "the tree is worthy of sacrifice."

Then they cook the sacrificial food for him. Indeed, he who undergoes consecration approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities. The oblation of the gods must be cooked, not uncooked; therefore they cook it. He himself consumes that as his fast-food (vrata), and does not offer it in the fire. As to why he himself consumes it as his fast-food and does not offer it in the fire: [it is because] he has become one of the deities.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and vanished. And because they obstructed it with that, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.

Or rather, it was heard by the seers. They gathered together the sacrifice, just as this sacrifice here has been gathered. Indeed, he who undergoes initiation (*dīkṣate*) is the sacrifice here; for he extends it, he brings it forth. Whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away here, whatever has been milked out, that very thing he now causes to swell again: when he himself consumes the fast-food (*vrata*), and does not offer it in the fire. For were he to offer it in the fire, he would not cause it to swell; indeed, whether one offers or does not offer, one should think [of it as] offering.

These indeed are the vital breaths: born of the mind, yoked by the mind, possessing skill and will. Speech is Agni; out-breath and in-breath are Mitra and Varuṇa; sight is Āditya; and hearing is the Viśve Devas. It is into these very deities that his offering becomes thus sacrificed.
Now, regarding this, some say:

At the first fast-milk, they sow both rice and barley, saying, "By means of both juices, let us replenish here whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away or milked out. However, if the cow that yields the fast-milk does not yield, he may take the fast-milk from whichever animal he desires, for in this way both rice and barley are held by him in connection with it. But one should not do it thus; he who sows both rice and barley neither replenishes nor restores the sacrifice. Therefore, let him sow only one or the other. For these two, rice and barley, are his oblation; when they are his oblation, then they are held by him in connection with it. And if the cow that yields the fast-milk does not yield, he may take the fast-milk from whichever animal he desires.

Now, some people, at the first vow, throw in all kinds of herbs and all kinds of fragrant substances, thinking: "If affliction should befall the consecrated one, he shall treat it with whatever he desires from that point on, as if treating it with the vow. But one should not do so; for they perform what is human in the sacrifice, and that which is human is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice," if affliction should befall the consecrated one, he should treat it with whatever he desires from that point on, for completion itself is auspicious.
Then he hands over the vow to him.

Having passed the human time—the evening milk during the latter part of the night and the morning milk during the afternoon—he distinguishes it; for by this very act, he distinguishes between the divine and the human.

Then, when he is about to give him the vow-food, he makes him touch water with the verse: "We meditate upon the divine thought, the very gracious, for our aid; may it bestow splendor, carry the sacrifice, and provide us with easy paths. For previously, a human being cleanses himself before eating; but here, it is for the sake of the divine thought that he does so. Therefore he says: "We meditate upon the divine thought, the very gracious, for our aid; may it bestow splendor, carry the sacrifice, and provide us with easy paths. Whenever he is about to undertake any portion of the vow, let him touch water with this very formula.
Then he performs the vow-offering with the formula:

"O gods born of the mind, yoked by the mind, possessing skill and wisdom—may they favor us; may they protect us; to them, svāhā! Thus, this becomes for him like an oblation offered with the vaṣaṭ-call.
Then, having performed the vow, he touches his navel.

"O waters, become refreshing when drunk; be very gracious within our bellies. May those divine, immortal, and truth-increasing waters, free from disease, free from sickness, and sinless, be sweet for us. Verily, he who undergoes initiation approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities. Now, the oblation of the gods must not be poured over, yet the one who bestows the vow (the *vrata-prada*) acts falsely by pouring water over the vow, thereby violating the vow. This [formula] is the expiation for that; thus it does not become a false act for him, nor does he violate the vow. Therefore he says: "O waters, become refreshing when drunk; be very gracious within our bellies. May those divine, immortal, and truth-increasing waters, free from disease, free from sickness, and sinless, be sweet for us. Whatever portion of the vow he has consumed and then touches his navel, let him touch it with this very formula. Who knows whether the one who bestows the vow might have poured water over the vow?
Then, when he is about to eat, he says:

With that black antelope horn, he strikes a clod of earth or something else with the formula: "This is thy sacrificial body. This earth, indeed, is the divine place of sacrifice; she must not be defiled by the consecrated one. Having thus lifted up her sacrificial body, he voids his own non-sacrificial body upon her with the words: "I release the waters, not offspring. Both of these indeed come from here: water and seed. He thus releases only the water, not the offspring. With the words, "The sin-releasing ones, consecrated with Svāhā," for they release him from sin—that which was pent up within the belly—therefore he says, "the sin-releasing ones. With the words, "Enter the earth, consecrated with Svāhā," he means to say: "Having become oblations, enter the earth in a state of peace."

Then he places a clod of earth [on the footprint]. [He says: "Be united with the earth! This earth is indeed a goddess, the place for sacrificing to the gods; she must not be defiled by one who is consecrated. By this act, having lifted from her that sacrificial body, he has smeared upon it an unsacrificial body. Now, he places that very sacrificial body back into her. Therefore he says, "Be united with the earth."
Then, having entrusted himself to Agni, he sleeps.

He who undergoes consecration (*dīkṣate*) approaches the gods; he becomes one of the deities. Now, the gods do not sleep, yet for him sleep remains unattained. Agni is the Lord of Vows (*Vratapati*) among the gods; having entrusted himself to him, he sleeps. "O Agni, do thou keep watch well; may we rejoice well," he says; this means, "O Agni, do thou be awake; we shall sleep. "Protect us, being vigilant," he says; this means, "Guard us, being heedless of none. "Make us wakeful again," he says; this means, "Act so that, having slept, we may wake safely from here."
Now, where one has slept.

He makes him recite: "May mind return to me; may life return to me; may breath return to me; may the self return to me; may sight return to me; may hearing return to me. For indeed, all these depart from one who sleeps, yet the breath alone does not; having slept, he unites again with them. Therefore he says: "May mind return to me; may life return to me; may breath return to me; may the self return to me; may sight return to me; may hearing return to me. And: "May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable, the protector of the body, Agni, protect us from misfortune and from blame. This he says so that Agni may guard us from whatever wrong deed has been committed here through sleep or otherwise. Therefore he says: "May Vaiśvānara, the undeceivable, the protector of the body, Agni, protect us from misfortune and from blame."

Now, when one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) speaks what is unrighteous or becomes angry, he makes his vow false and violates his vow; for non-anger indeed belongs to the consecrated. Agni is the lord of vows among the gods; it is to him that he now resorts, saying: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, O god, among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices. This is the expiation for that; thus, his act does not become falsely done, nor does he violate his vow. Therefore he says: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows, O god, among mortals; you are to be praised at the sacrifices."

Now, when they bring [gifts] to the consecrated one, he makes him recite over them: "O Soma, grant this much; bring more! For that which they bring to the consecrated one, Soma indeed bestows upon him. When he says, "O Soma, grant this much," he means "Grant us this much, O Soma. When he says, "Bring more," he means "Bring us more. And when he says, "May the divine Savitṛ, the giver of wealth, give us wealth," it is so that this [gift] becomes impelled by Savitṛ for the purpose of giving to him.

Before sunset he says, "O initiated one, restrain your speech," and at sunset he releases that speech; before sunrise he says, "O initiated one, restrain your speech," and at sunrise he releases that speech. This is for the sake of continuity: he thus connects the day with the night, and the night with the day.
One should not approach him when he is moving about elsewhere for the sake of study.

The sun should not rise while he is sleeping. For if it were to set while he is away from home, it would leave him behind during the night; and if it were to rise while he is sleeping, it would leave him behind during the day. In this case, there is no expiation; one must simply guard against it. He should not descend into water before the final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), nor should rain fall upon him; for it is improper that he should descend into water or that rain should fall upon him before the avabhṛtha. Furthermore, he speaks his speech in a faltering manner, not in the ordinary human way; in that he speaks his speech in a faltering manner, not in the ordinary human way.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [world] of ours be made unattainable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers might suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (yūpa), and vanished. Because they obstructed it with that, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
Or rather, this was heard by the seers. They gathered the sacrifice;

just as this sacrifice was gathered, so indeed does he who undergoes initiation gather the sacrifice. Speech is the sacrifice. Whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away here, whatever has been milked out, that he now replenishes when he speaks his speech in a low, faltering tone—not human and not flowing forth. For if he were to speak human speech flowing forth, he would not replenish it. Therefore, he speaks his speech in a low, faltering tone, not human and not flowing forth.

He indeed consecrates himself by means of speech; for he consecrates himself for the sake of the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is indeed speech. This which is called "the consecrated" (dīkṣita) is truly one who has been consecrated by speech.
He offers the introductory oblation of cooked rice to Āditya.

Indeed, while the gods were performing the sacrifice on this earth, they excluded her from the sacrifice; she then caused them to be bewildered regarding the sacrifice, thinking, "How is it that while they are performing the sacrifice upon me, they exclude me from the sacrifice? Thus, they did not recognize that sacrifice.
They said,
"Since we have indeed forgotten the sacrificial procedure for this very [offering], how is it that our greatness has not diminished, and how is it that we do not know it?"
They said, "While performing the sacrifice upon this very [earth], we have excluded her from the sacrifice; it is she who has confounded our sacrifice. Let us resort to her alone."
They said, "Since we have indeed fixed our minds on the sacrifice upon you alone, why has it been obscured for us? Why do we not understand it?"
She said:

"While weaving the sacrifice within me, you have excluded me from the sacrifice. Therefore, it was I who caused your sacrifice to fail. Now, provide a portion for me; then you shall see the sacrifice, and then you shall understand it."
"So be it," said the gods.

"The Prāyaṇīya shall be yours alone, and the Udayanīya shall be yours alone. Therefore, this very Āditya becomes the Prāyaṇīya, and Āditya becomes the Udayanīya; for this earth is indeed Aditi. Then they beheld the sacrifice and performed it.
When he offers the *caru* for Aditi as the introductory oblation, it is for the very sake of beholding the sacrifice;

thinking, "Having beheld the sacrifice, I shall purchase [the Soma] and extend it," he therefore offers the *caru* for Aditi as the introductory oblation. Now, that oblation had already been set aside, but the deity had not yet been sacrificed to.
Then Pathyā Svasti became pleasing to them;
they sacrificed to her. Pathyā Svasti is indeed speech, and the sacrifice is speech; thus they saw the sacrifice and performed it.
Then Agni consented to them; they sacrificed to him.
They saw that which belonged to Agni in the sacrifice: whatever was dry in the sacrifice, that belongs to Agni. Having seen that, they performed it.
Then Soma became pleasing to them; they sacrificed it.
They saw that which was the *saumya* (Soma-related) portion of the sacrifice; for whatever is moist in the sacrifice is *saumya*, and that they saw and performed.
Then Savitṛ became pleasing to them; they sacrificed to him.
Savitṛ is indeed cattle, and the sacrifice is cattle; thus they beheld the sacrifice and performed it. Then they sacrificed to whichever deity the oblation had been set aside for.
Now, these are the five deities whom he sacrifices to. That sacrifice which was indeed bewildered was fivefold; they recognized it through these five deities.
The seasons were bewildered;
they recognized them by means of these very five deities.
The five directions were bewildered;
they became aware of them through these very five deities.

They discerned the northern direction by means of the Pathyā Svasti; therefore, in this region, speech speaks from the north among the Kurus and Pañcālas, for this is speech in its primary essence. By means of it they discerned the northern direction, and the northern direction belongs to it.
[They recognized] the eastern direction alone.

By means of Agni they recognized it; therefore, having taken up Agni from behind toward the east, they worship him, for by means of him they recognized the eastern direction, and the eastern direction is his own.

They discerned the southern direction by means of Soma; therefore, they carry the purchased Soma toward the south. Therefore they say, "Soma has the Pitṛs as its deity," for by means of him they discerned the southern direction, and the south is indeed his quarter.

They discerned the western direction by means of Savitṛ. He who shines yonder is indeed Savitṛ; therefore he moves westward, for by him they discerned the western direction, and the western direction belongs to him.

They recognized the upward direction by means of Aditi; for Aditi is this earth, and therefore upon her the plants grow upward and the trees grow upward, because they recognized the upward direction by means of her, and because that direction is indeed upward.

The guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, while the introductory (prāyaṇīya) and concluding (udayanīya) offerings are the two arms. Since the arms are on both sides of the head, therefore these two oblations—the introductory and the concluding—occur on both sides of the guest-offering.

Regarding this they say: "Whatever is done at the Prāyaṇīya, that should be done at the Udayanīya; whatever sacrificial grass belongs to the Prāyaṇīya, that becomes the sacrificial grass for the Udayanīya. Having set that aside, he puts it down; having wiped that pot—along with its scrapings and the stirring-stick—he sets them aside. Those who are the officiating priests of the Prāyaṇīya become the officiating priests of the Udayanīya. Thus, because this same thing is performed in the sacrifice, the two arms are similar and of the same form.

One should not do it in that way. One may indeed throw this sacrificial grass (barhis) into the fire; likewise, having cleansed the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa), one should set down the pot. Those who are the officiating priests (ṛtvij) of the introductory sacrifice (prāyaṇīya) are the officiating priests of the concluding sacrifice (udayanīya). Even if they have departed, others may take their place. Since he sacrifices to the same deities and the oblations (havīṃṣi) are the same, by that very fact his two arms become similar and of the same form.
He indeed sacrifices to five deities at the introductory offering (prāyaṇīya) and to five at the concluding offering (udayanīya);

therefore there are five fingers on this side and five on that side. It concludes with the *śamyu*-formula, and they do not perform the joint sacrifice for the wives. For the arms are the forepart of one's own body; thus he prepares the forepart of the sacrifice. Therefore it concludes with the *śamyu*-formula, and they do not perform the joint sacrifice for the wives.
Soma was indeed in heaven, but here on earth were the gods.

Those gods desired, "May Soma come to us; with him, once he has arrived, let us sacrifice. They created these two magical beings, Suparṇī and Kadrū; this is explained in the Brāhmaṇa concerning the *dhiṣṇya* hearths, regarding how that story of Suparṇī and Kadrū unfolded.

The Gāyatrī flew toward them for the sake of the Soma. As she was bringing it back, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu stole it from her. The gods realized, "The Soma has indeed been carried away to the other side; it does not come to us because the Gandharvas have stolen it."

They said, "The Gandharvas are indeed lustful for women; let us send Speech to them, and she will come back to us together with Soma. They sent Speech to them, and she came back to them together with Soma.

Those Gandharvas followed them and said, "Soma is yours, but Speech is ours. The gods replied, "So be it; but if she has come here, do not carry her off by force; let us call her back. So they called her back.
The Gandharvas said to her, "We know the Vedas indeed; we know them, we know them!"

Then the gods, having created the lute itself, sat down playing it and singing: "Thus indeed we shall sing; thus we shall delight you. She turned toward the gods. Truly, she turned toward them in vain—she who turned away from those who were praising and reciting, for dancing and singing. Therefore even now, women are associated with what is vain, for speech turned away in this manner; and other women follow her, which is why these [women] cling most closely to him who dances or who sings.
Now, both of these were among the gods:

Soma and Speech. When one purchases Soma, it is for the sake of arrival; "I shall sacrifice with what has arrived," he thinks. For he who sacrifices with unpurchased [Soma] indeed sacrifices with Soma that has not arrived.

Then, whatever clarified butter remains in the *dhruvā* vessel, he divides that four times into the *juhū* ladle; having tied a piece of gold with a blade of sacrificial grass and placed it therein, he offers it, thinking, "May I offer with the entirety of the milk. For milk and gold are of common origin, for both are the seed of Agni.
He places gold [in the pan], saying:

"This is thy pure body, this is thy splendor. For gold is indeed splendor; thus he says, "Be united with that, go to radiance. When he says, "Be united with that," he means "be joined with that"; when he says, "Go to radiance," Soma is indeed radiance, so he means "go to Soma."

Just as the gods then sent her forth to buy Soma, even so does he now send her forth to buy Soma. For the cow used for buying Soma is, in its essential nature, Speech; he gratifies her with this oblation so that, being gratified, she may purchase the Soma.
He offers with the formula, "Thou art swift" (*jūrasi*).

For "thou art swift" is indeed one of her names. With the words, "held by the mind" (*dhṛtā manasā*), for this speech is held by the mind; indeed, the mind precedes speech. [One says,] "Speak thus; do not speak that. For if there were no mind, speech would speak incoherently. Therefore he says, "held by the mind."

"Accepted for Viṣṇu"—by this he means "accepted for Soma. "'Whom we shall impel'—'at the impulse of thee, whose impulse is true'"; by this he means "be thou of true impulse for us; impel Soma for us. "'May I attain the restraint of the body, Svāhā!'—he indeed attains the restraint of the body who reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice; 'may I reach the conclusion of the sacrifice,' this is what he thereby says.
Then he takes out the gold;
he thereby establishes gold among men. If he were to offer it together with the gold, he would indeed cast that gold away from men, and gold would not be found among men.

He draws it out with the formula: "Thou art bright; thou art the moon; thou art nectar; thou belongest to the All-gods. Having offered the entire milk, he says "thou art bright" because this [milk] is indeed bright; "thou art the moon" because this is indeed the moon; "thou art nectar" because this is indeed nectar; "thou belongest to the All-gods" because this belongs indeed to the All-gods. Having released [the vessel], he throws a blade of grass onto the sacrificial grass (barhis) and ties a piece of gold to the cord.

Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter, he says, "Hold on, O Sacrificer! They uncover the southern door of the hall; the Soma-purchase cow stands there. He has indeed sent her forth while she was already dispatched; for the Soma-purchase cow is Speech by its very nature. By means of this oblation, he has sent her forth, thinking, "With her, being well-pleased, I shall purchase the Soma."
Then, having gone outside, he consecrates [it] with a mantra.

"Thou art thought (cit), thou art mind (manas)"—for this speech follows after the mind or the thought. "Thou art intelligence (dhī), thou art the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)"—for by means of this intelligence, men desire to live on through what has been recited, as it were, through what has been spoken at will, as it were, and through songs; therefore he says, "Thou art intelligence, thou art the sacrificial fee," for she is indeed the sacrificial fee. "Thou art a Kṣatriya, thou art worthy of sacrifice"—for she is indeed a Kṣatriya, and she is indeed worthy of sacrifice. "Thou art Aditi, double-headed"—because when one speaks with her in a contrary way, doing what is later first and what is earlier later, she is thereby double-headed; therefore he says, "Thou art Aditi, double-headed."
"Be thou for us well-forward and well-returning," he says;

by this he means, "Be thou well-forward for us, go thou toward the Soma for us. "Be thou well-returning for us, come thou back again with the Soma for us," by this he means; therefore he says, "Be thou for us well-forward and well-returning."
"May Mitra bind you by the foot," he says.

For this rope belongs to Varuṇa; if it were bound with a rope, it would belong to Varuṇa, and if it were not bound at all, it would be as if it were lost. That which belongs to Mitra is free from Varuṇa's power. Thus, when he says, "May Mitra bind you by the foot," it becomes for her as if she were bound with a rope, yet not [bound] by Varuṇa.
"May Pūṣan protect the paths," he says.
Pūṣan is indeed this earth; for him whose protector on the path is this [earth], no stumbling occurs at all. Therefore he says, "May Pūṣan protect the paths."
"To Indra, the overseer."

When he says, "To Indra, the overseer," he thereby says, "With a good overseer. When he says, "May the mother approve, may the father approve, may the brother born of the same womb approve, may the friend of the same herd approve," he thereby says, "By that birth of yours which is approved by them, come hither for the Soma. When he says, "O Goddess, go to the God," she is indeed a goddess who goes to a god, namely to the Soma; therefore he says, "O Goddess, go to the God. "Soma for Indra"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "Soma for Indra. "May Rudra turn you back"—he says this so that there may be no loss, for cattle do not pass beyond Rudra. "Come back again in safety, O friend of Soma"—he thereby says, "Come back to us in safety together with Soma."
Just as the gods then sent her forth for Soma and she came back to them together with Soma, even so does he now send her forth for Soma, and she comes back to him together with Soma.

Just as of old the gods called her away from the Gandharvas and she returned to the gods, even so does the sacrificer now call her away and she returns to the sacrificer. They drive her out toward the north, for the north is the direction of men; it is the same for the sacrificer, therefore they drive her out toward the north.
He steps after her seven steps;

he thus wins her, and that is why he steps after her seven steps. For where the meters born of Speech exist, the Śakvarī consists of seven feet and is the most excellent among them; it is this very meter that he thereby wins from beyond toward himself. That is why he steps after her seven steps.
He indeed follows along by means of the very form of Speech:

"Thou art wealthy; thou art Aditi; thou art Ādityā; thou art Rudrā; thou art Candrā. For she is indeed wealthy, she is indeed Aditi, she is indeed Ādityā, she is indeed Rudrā, she is indeed Candrā. "May Bṛhaspati cause thee to rest in happiness"—Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman; thus he says, "May Bṛhaspati turn thee toward prosperity. "Rudra, together with the Vasus, has looked upon thee"—he says this for the sake of non-destruction, for cattle do not pass beyond Rudra.

Then they sit around the seventh footprint. He places gold in the footprint and offers an oblation; for no oblation is offered except in fire, and gold is indeed the seed of Agni; thus this oblation of his becomes offered as one accompanied by fire. Clarified butter (ājya) is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra); he wins her by means of that thunderbolt, the clarified butter, and having won her, he makes her his own.

He offers with the formula: "Aditi has heated thee on her head. Aditi is indeed this earth, for he offers on her head. "On the earth's place of sacrifice"—for he offers on the earth's place of sacrifice. "Thou art the station of Iḍā, rich in ghee, svāhā!"—Iḍā is indeed the cow, for he offers at the station of the cow. "Rich in ghee, svāhā!"—for this offering becomes rich in ghee when poured over.

Then, taking up the wooden sword (sphyá), he traces around [the altar]. The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt; it is with the thunderbolt that he thus traces around. He traces around three times; by means of this threefold thunderbolt, he encloses it on all sides so that it may not be overstepped.

He draws around it, saying, "Rejoice in us!"—by this he says, "Rejoice in the sacrificer. Then, having scraped up the soil, he pours it into the pot, saying, "In us is thy kinship"—by this he says, "In the sacrificer is thy kinship."
Then he pours water upon it.

For wherever they wound or strike it while digging, water is a means of pacification; thus, with water as a means of pacification, he pacifies it, and with water he heals it. Therefore, he pours water upon it.

Then he hands over the footprint to the sacrificer with the words, "In thee be wealth. Wealth, indeed, is cattle; thus he says, "In thee be cattle. The sacrificer accepts it with the words, "Mine be wealth. Wealth, indeed, is cattle; thus he says, "May cattle be in me."
Then the Adhvaryu touches himself, saying, "May we not be separated from the abundance of wealth. Thus, the Adhvaryu does not exclude himself from the cattle.
Then they carry the footprint back to the wife.
The house is indeed the support for the wife; thus he establishes her in that very support, the house. Therefore, they carry the footprint back to the wife.

The Neṣṭṛ makes her recite, "Thence riches... Then he causes her to look at the Soma-purchase cow; for Soma is indeed a male and the wife is a female, and here that which is the Soma-purchase cow becomes Soma; thus a productive union is brought about. Therefore, he causes her to look at the Soma-purchase cow.

He counts: "I have counted with the goddess's insight, together with the far-seeing Dakṣiṇā. Do not steal away my life, nor may I, O hero, lose yours. O Goddess, may I find a hero in your sight. He thus invokes this very blessing; for a hero is indeed a son. "May I find a son in your sight"—this is what he says.

That one which is brown with reddish-brown eyes is the Soma-purchasing cow. For when Indra and Viṣṇu divided a thousand [cows] into three parts, one remained over; they produced her by dividing her into three parts. Therefore, even now, if anyone were to divide a thousand [cows] into three parts, one would remain over.

She who is brown with reddish-brown eyes is the one for purchasing Soma; she who is red is the "Vr̥tra-slaying" one, whom the king here brings forth after winning a battle. And she who is red with white eyes belongs to the Pitṛs; it is her whom they slaughter here for the ancestors.

That which is brown with reddish-brown eyes should be the Soma-purchasing cow; if he does not find one that is brown with reddish-brown eyes, it should be ruddy; if he does not find one that is ruddy, it should be red and a slayer of Vṛtra; having found a red one, he should not even entertain the hope for one that is white-eyed.

She should be unimpregnated. For this cow for purchasing Soma has speech as its source; and this speech is not exhausted, and she who is unimpregnated is speech that is not exhausted. Therefore, she should be unimpregnated. She should be one that is not mutilated, not hornless, not one-eyed, not earless, not marked with a brand, and not seven-hoofed; for she is of a single form, and speech indeed is of a single form.
Having poured out the water, he washes his hands.
As to why he washes his hands: ghee is a thunderbolt and Soma is seed; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I should injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, the ghee. Therefore, he washes his hands.
Then he ties gold to this [sacrificial post].

For there are these two things, and no third: truth and untruth. The gods are truth, and human beings are untruth. Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; [he thinks], "By means of truth may I touch the shoots; by means of truth may I drive away Soma. Therefore, he ties gold to this [post].

Then he gives the directions: "Bring the Soma-wrapper! Bring the Soma-binding-cloth! Bring the turban! That which is most beautiful should be the Soma-wrapper; for this becomes his garment, and his garment is indeed beautiful. For he who serves him with what is beautiful prospers. But as for him who says, "Whatever it may be," whatever it happens to be, that is what it becomes. Therefore, let that which is beautiful be the Soma-wrapper, and whatever it may be, the Soma-binding-cloth.
If he should find a turban, let it be the turban;

if he should not find a turban, let him cut off a piece two or three finger-breadths wide from the Soma-cloth itself to serve as the turban. Either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer takes up the Soma-wrapping cloth, and whoever [takes] the Soma-cloth.
Then they search for the king in front;
there a water-pot has been placed, and a Brahmin sits beside it; toward that, they proceed facing eastward.
When they have arrived, he causes them to recite.

"Say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Gāyatra portion'; say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Triṣṭubh portion'; say this for me to Soma: 'This is your Jagatī portion'; say this for me to Soma: 'Go to the sovereignty over the names of the metres'—for when he is being purchased, he is indeed purchased for one purpose alone: for the kingship of the metres, for the sovereignty of the metres. For they indeed slay him when they press him; therefore he says this to him: 'I purchase you for the kingship of the metres, for the sovereignty of the metres, not for slaughter. Then, having gone forward, he sits down facing the east."

He touches it, saying, "Thou art ours," for this [cup] becomes as if his own once he has arrived; therefore he says, "Thou art ours. "The bright one is to be drawn from thee," for he is about to draw the bright cup from it. "Let them sort thee out," he says this for the sake of completeness.

In this regard, some, having found either a blade of grass or a piece of wood, throw it away; but one should not do so. Soma is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), while other plants are the common people (viś); the common people are the food of the nobleman. It would be as if, having swallowed something, one were to spit it out after picking it up and discarding it—such is that act. Therefore, he should simply touch it with the words, "May they discern thee, O Discerner! Thus, those who are his discerners discern him.

Then the cloth: he spreads out a double or a quadruple fold, with its fringe toward the east or toward the north; upon it he measures out the King (Soma). Because he measures out the King, therefore there is a measure among men, and whatever other measure there may be.
He measures it with the Sāvitrī verse.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, this [Soma] becomes available for purchase for him.
He measures with an *aticandā* verse.
This *aticandā* indeed contains all the meters; thus, for him, this [sacrifice] becomes measured by all the meters. Therefore, he measures with an *aticandā* verse.
He measures it out.
I praise with song that god Savitṛ between the two worlds, the one of seer-like wisdom, whose impulse is true, who bestows jewels—the beloved, the sage of inspired thought.
He whose lofty intelligence has shone forth at the impulse of the impeller—Hiraṇyapāṇi, the one of good will, has measured out the light with his form.
With this [verse] he pours it out together with all [the verses];

with this [he pours it out] with four; with this with three; with this with two; with this with one; with this very same one again; with this with three; with this with four; and with this with all [the verses], he pours it out together by means of his joined palms.
He measures out both upwards and downwards.

In that he measures out upwards and downwards, he thereby makes these fingers distinct from one another; therefore these [fingers] are born separately. But if he were to measure with all [the fingers] together, they would indeed be born as if clung together; therefore he measures out both upwards and downwards.

Or rather, when he measures out both the forward and the backward steps, he thereby makes these [directions] possessed of diverse powers; therefore these possess diverse powers, and for this reason he measures out both the forward and the backward steps.
Moreover, as to why he measures out both the forward and the backward [steps]:

it is the Virāj he thus yokes, both turned hitherward and turned away. Turned away, she carries the sacrifice to the gods; turned hitherward, she protects men. Therefore, indeed, he measures out both the forward and the backward [steps].
Now, as to why he measures ten times:
the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Soma is of the nature of the Virāj; therefore, he measures ten times.

Then, having gathered together the ends of the Soma-cloth, he ties them with the turban, saying, "For the creatures thee! For it is for the sake of the creatures that he buys this [Soma]; thus he makes this very head and shoulders of his appear as if covered within.

Then he makes a space with his finger in the middle, saying, "May the subjects breathe after you! For by bringing it together as it were, he makes it, as it were, breathless; thus he releases the breath right there in the middle for it. As it breathes from there, the subjects breathe after it; therefore he says, "May the subjects breathe after you! He hands it over to the Soma-seller; now, therefore, follows the bargaining itself.

He indeed stakes the King; because he stakes the King, therefore all this is staked at once. He says, "O Soma-seller, is your King Soma for sale? "For sale," says the Soma-seller. "Then I shall buy him from you. "Buy him," says the Soma-seller. "I shall buy him from you for a sixteenth part (kalā). "King Soma is surely worth more than that," says the Soma-seller. "King Soma is indeed worth more than that, but the greatness of the cow is great," says the Adhvaryu.

From the cow comes fresh milk; from that, boiled milk; from that, curdled milk; from that, whey; from that, the thickening agent; from that, butter; from that, clarified butter; from that, curdled cheese; from that, the whey-essence.
"I will buy [Soma] from you for a hoof," he says.

"King Soma is worth more than that," says the Soma-seller. "King Soma is indeed worth more than that; great, however, is the greatness of the cow," says the Adhvaryu. Having enumerated these very ten powers, he says, "I buy [Soma] from you for a foot, for half [of a cow], for a cow. "King Soma has been bought," says the Soma-seller. "Declare the birds! he says.

He said: "The moon is yours, your garment, your goat, your cow, your pair of cattle, and three others are yours. Because they bargain at a lower price but settle for a higher one, therefore all this merchandise is bargained at a lower price but settled for a higher one. Now, as for the fact that the Adhvaryu alone proclaims the virtues of the cow and not those of the Soma—the Soma-vendor does so because Soma is exalted; for Soma is a god. Therefore, the Adhvaryu magnifies the cow, thinking, "Beholding its virtues, let me buy it. That is why the Adhvaryu alone proclaims the virtues of the cow and not those of the Soma, the Soma-vendor.
Now, as to why he stakes five times:
the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he attains it by means of these five. Therefore, he stakes five times.
Then he makes him recite over the gold:

"The bright I buy from thee with the bright," for he buys this bright [Soma] with the bright, namely the Soma with the gold; "the radiant with the radiant," for he buys this radiant [Soma] with the radiant, namely the Soma with the gold; "the immortal with the immortal," for he buys this immortal [Soma] with the immortal, namely the Soma with the gold.
Then he causes the Soma-seller to tremble with the words, "In thy possession is the cow";

by this he means, "In thy possession is the cow for the sacrificer. Having brought it toward the sacrificer, he sets it down with the words, "In us be thy bright ones"; thus he bestows vigor upon himself, while the Soma-seller merely takes away the body; that [vigor] the Soma-seller then receives from him.
Then he makes her recite over a she-goat whose face is turned toward him:

"Thou art the body of austerity. For this she-goat was indeed produced from the austerity of Prajāpati; therefore he says, "Thou art the body of austerity. "The color of Prajāpati," he says, because she brings forth three times in a year, she is thus the color of Prajāpati. "Thou art purchased with the highest animal," he says, because she brings forth three times in a year, she is thus the highest animal. "May I thrive with a thousandfold prosperity"—this he utters as a prayer for blessing; for a thousand is abundance, and thus he says, "May I attain abundance."

He gives the goat with this [formula] and takes up the king [Soma] with this. For this goat is indeed called "Ājā" (the Impeller); for by means of her he impels him (Soma) from the end. They call her "Ajā" (the Goat) cryptically.

Then he takes up the King (Soma) with the words, "As a friend, come to us, O bestower of good friends. By this he means, "Come to us as one who is auspicious and peaceful. Having pushed back the garment on the sacrificer's right thigh, he places him there with the words, "Enter Indra's right thigh. For the sacrificer here indeed becomes Indra; therefore he says, "Enter Indra's right thigh. With the words, "Desiring him who desires," he means "the beloved entering the beloved. With the words, "Gentle, into the gentle," he means "the auspicious entering the auspicious."
Then he points out the Soma-purchasers:

"O Svāna, Bhrāja, Aṅghāri, Bambhāri, Hasta, Suhasta, Kṛśānu—these are your Soma-purchasers; guard them, let no one deceive you! These are indeed the portions of the Dhiṣṇya hearths; these are the names of the Dhiṣṇyas, and it is these very names that he has thus assigned to them.

Then he uncovers himself here. He who is consecrated becomes an embryo; embryos are indeed covered, as if by the inner membrane and the outer membrane. Him [the sacrificer] has now brought forth here; therefore he uncovers himself. For he becomes an embryo here; therefore he is covered, for embryos are, as it were, covered by the inner membrane and the outer membrane.

Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; do not abandon me to good conduct. While he is seated, this [Agni] approaches him; when he has arrived, he rises up, which makes his action improper and causes him to violate his vow. This [recitation] is the expiation for that; thus his action does not become improper, nor does he violate his vow. Therefore he says: "O Agni, protect me from evil conduct; do not abandon me to good conduct."
Then, taking the King (Soma), he rises with the formula:

"With long life, with good life, we have risen after the immortals. For he who rises after the purchased Soma indeed rises after the immortal; therefore he says, "With long life, with good life, we have risen after the immortals."
Then, taking the king, he approaches the ascent with the verse:
"We have set out upon the path that leads to well-being and is free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth."
The gods, indeed, while performing the sacrifice, [were struck with doubt].
