They were terrified by the attachment of those Asuras and Rakshasas; they saw this Yajus as a means of well-being (svastyayana). By means of this Yajus, having struck away the destructive spirits and Rakshasas, they attained well-being in the safety, freedom from destruction, and shelter of this Yajus. In the same way, this sacrificer, having struck away the destructive spirits and Rakshasas by means of this Yajus, attains well-being in the safety, freedom from destruction, and shelter of this Yajus. Therefore he says: "We have entered upon the path that leads to well-being and is free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth."
They carry it away, saying "That indeed";
they transport it by means of a cart, for they are thus magnifying it; therefore they carry the seed on the head and transport it by means of a cart.

Now, as to why he buys [the Soma] at the edge of the waters: the waters are indeed sap; thus he buys it together with its sap. And as to why there is gold: he buys it together with its brilliance (*śukra*). And as to why there is a garment: he buys it together with its skin (*tvacas*). And as to why there is a she-goat: he buys it together with its heat (*tapas*). And as to why there is a milch-cow: he buys it together with its milk-mixture (*āśir*). And as to why there are two of a pair: he buys it together with its mate. He should buy it with exactly ten [objects], not with fewer than ten; for the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and Soma is of the nature of the *virāj*; therefore he should buy it with exactly ten, not with fewer than ten.

He spreads a black antelope skin in the nest with the formula, "Thou art the skin of Aditi"; the significance of this is the same as before. Then he places him [the Soma] upon it with, "Sit on the seat of Aditi. Aditi is indeed this earth, and she is the foundation; thus he establishes him upon this very foundation. Therefore he says, "Sit on the seat of Aditi."
Then, having approached it in this manner, he causes [the sacrificer] to recite:

"The bull propped up the sky, the atmosphere. Indeed, when the gods were performing the sacrifice, they were afraid of an attack from the Asura-Rakshasas; they made him (Agni) a greater obstacle for them by saying, "The bull propped up the sky, the atmosphere."

"He measured out the breadth of the earth"—by this he wins over these worlds; for there is neither slayer nor killer of him by whom these worlds have been won. Therefore he says, "He measured out the breadth of the earth."

"He has sat down as sovereign over all beings"—by this he makes all this world secure; for there is neither slayer nor destroyer of him by whom all this has been made secure. Therefore he says, "He has sat down as sovereign over all beings."

"All these are the ordinances of Varuṇa"—by this he makes all this, whatever exists here, follow after him as his path, so that there is no one at all who rises up against him; therefore he says, "All these are the ordinances of Varuṇa."

Then he wraps it with the Soma-wrapper, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (nāṣṭrā) and Rakṣasas touch it. For this [Soma] becomes an embryo; embryos are, as it were, hidden, and that which is wrapped is, as it were, hidden. The gods are, as it were, hidden from men, and that which is wrapped is, as it were, hidden; therefore, indeed, he wraps it.
He puts on the saddle.

"He has stretched the atmosphere over the forests"—for this atmosphere is indeed stretched over the forests, over the tops of the trees. "Speed in the horses, milk in the cows"—speed is indeed vigor; the stallions are males; thus he bestows vigor upon males. "Milk in the cows"—for this milk is indeed placed within the cows. "Varuṇa [placed] wisdom in hearts, Agni among the people"—for this wisdom, swift as thought, has entered into the hearts; "Agni among the people"—for this Agni is indeed among the people, among the creatures. "He placed the sun in heaven, Soma on the mountain"—for yonder sun is indeed placed in heaven; "Soma on the mountain"—for Soma is indeed on the mountains; therefore he says, "He placed the sun in heaven, Soma on the mountain."

Now, if there are two black antelope skins, he fastens one of them as a support for the binding-cord; but if there is only one, having cut off the neck of the black antelope skin itself, he fastens it as a support for the binding-cord with the verse: "Mount the eye of Sūrya, the pupil of Agni's eye, where thou goest with thy dappled steeds, shining, O wise one. By this, he indeed places Sūrya in front; thus Sūrya goes in front, striking away the destructive spirits and demons, and so they carry [the fire] around in safety and freedom from destruction.
The two boards are raised and elevated;
standing between them, the Subrahmaṇya priest urges on the horse. For he becomes superior through this ascent—indeed, who is worthy to ascend him? Therefore, standing between them, he urges him on.
He drives [the cart] forward with a Palāśa branch.

For when Gāyatrī flew toward Soma, as she was bringing him back, her foot slipped; reaching out, she cut off a leaf (parṇa). That [leaf], having fallen, became a Palāśa tree; therefore it is called "Palāśa. [He does this] thinking, "Whatever of Soma is here deposited, let that also be here. Therefore he drives [the cart] forward with a Palāśa branch.
Then two oxen are driven forward.
If they should both be black, or if one of them is black, one should know in that case: "Parjanya will rain this year; there will be abundant rain. This is the sign of knowledge.

Then he yokes them with: "O two ruddy ones, you who bear the yoke! For they are indeed ruddy, and they are indeed yoke-bearers. "May you be yoked without shedding tears! For they are indeed yoked without shedding tears. "Unharmed!"—that means "not slaying heroes. "Impellers of prayer!"—for they are indeed impellers of prayer. "Go in safety to the house of the sacrificer!"—he says this so that the destructive spirits and demons may not harm them on the way.
Then, having walked around from behind and reached the place where there is no support, he says, "Recite for the purchased Soma," or "For the Soma being carried around," whichever way he may desire.
Then he causes [the disciple] to recite:

"Thou art auspicious for me; descend, O Lord of the World! For he indeed becomes auspicious for him, and therefore he pays no heed to another. Even kings come to him as his guests; he greets the king first, for he is indeed auspicious. Therefore he says, "Thou art auspicious for me. "Descend, O Lord of the World"—for he is the lord of the worlds—"towards all abodes. The limbs are indeed all the abodes; it is thus towards the limbs that he speaks. "Let not those who lie in wait find thee! Let not those who waylay find thee! Let not the malevolent wolves find thee! He says this so that the destructive spirits and Rakṣases may not find him on the way.

"Having become a hawk, fly away!"—he thus causes him to fly away having become a bird; for the Rakshas, the destroyers, do not follow after that which is fierce. Of birds, the hawk is indeed the most powerful and strongest; it is as one who has become that very [bird] that he causes him to fly away when he says, "Having become a hawk, fly away."
Then they carry the very body away, saying, "Go to the house of the sacrificer; there it shall be prepared for us. There is nothing here that is obscure.

Then he calls the Subrahmaṇyā. Just as one might say to those for whom he intends to cook on a certain day, "On such-and-such a day I shall cook for you," even so does he announce the sacrifice to the gods with the words, "Subrahmaṇyo! Subrahmaṇyo! For the Subrahmaṇyā indeed causes the Brahman to move toward the gods. He says it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.

"O Indra, come!"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "O Indra, come. "O Lord of the Bay Horses, come! O Ram of Medhātithi! O Menes of Vṛṣaṇaśva! O Gaura-avaskandin, thou who didst cry out to Ahalyā!"—by these very exploits of his, he thereby seeks to delight him.

"O Kauśika, you call him a Brāhmaṇa Gautama! This was indeed always known by Āruṇi; that he is called "Gautama" was discovered only now. If he so desires, he may say this; but if he does not desire it, he need not pay heed to it. "On such-and-such a day there will be the Soma-pressing"—thus he says until the day of the pressing arrives.
"O gods and Brahmins, come!
Thus he addressed both the gods and the Brahmins, for there is need here of both—both of the gods and of the Brahmins.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ stands before the hall with the animal victim for Agni and Soma. "Agni and Soma indeed place him between their jaws who undergoes consecration; for that initiatory offering belongs to Agni and Viṣṇu. He who is Viṣṇu is Soma, and he who undergoes consecration becomes the sacrificial food. Thus they place him between their jaws; therefore, he ransoms himself by means of the animal victim."

Now, some indeed bring a firebrand from the Āhavanīya fire, saying, "This is Agni, this is Soma; we shall depart together with these two present. But one should not do so; for wherever these two are, they are always together.
It indeed has two forms, for it belongs to two deities.
Regarding the two deities, they say it should be a black-spotted antelope, for that is its most perfect form; if one should not find a black-spotted one, then it may also be a red-spotted one.
While he recites over it:

"Homage to the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa; pay reverence to that great god, the Truth! To the far-seeing, god-born banner, to Sūrya, the son of Heaven—proclaim it! By this, he indeed offers homage to him and thereby establishes a bond of friendship with him.
Then the Adhvaryu releases the mounting-block;

he props it up with the support-pole, saying, "Thou art Varuna's prop," and he draws out the two pins, saying, "Ye two are Varuna's pin-releasers. As for why he says, "Ye two are Varuna's pin-releasers," it is because this Soma, once purchased, now belongs to Varuna.
Then four men take up the king's throne-seat;
two men take it up for him as a human king, and then four for him who rules over all at once.
It is made of udumbara wood;
for the udumbara is indeed food and vigor. It is made of udumbara wood for the attainment of vigor and the eating of food. Therefore, it is made of udumbara wood.
It is not navel-deep;

for food is established here, and Soma is food—therefore it is not navel-deep. It is indeed at this very place that the receptacle of semen is located, and semen is Soma—therefore it is at this depth.

He touches it with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa's Truth. Then he spreads the black antelope skin with the formula: "Thou art the seat of Varuṇa's Truth. Then he places him [the Soma] upon it with the formula: "Sit thou on the seat of Varuṇa's Truth. As to why he says, "Sit thou on the seat of Varuṇa's Truth," it is because at this moment he becomes related to Varuṇa.
Then he causes him to enter the hall.
While causing him to enter, he makes him recite: "Those abodes of thine which they worship with oblation—may all those encompass this sacrifice.

O Soma, increasing our wealth, furthering us, rich in heroes, not slaying our heroes, enter the dwellings. By "duryān" (dwellings), he indeed means houses; thus he says, "O auspicious one, peaceful, and doer of no evil, enter our houses."

In this connection, some indeed pour out a vessel of water, saying, "Just as one brings water for a king who has arrived, so is this. But one should not do so; for they perform what is human at the sacrifice, and that which is human is a failure of the sacrifice. Thinking, "Lest I should cause a failure in the sacrifice," he should therefore not pour it out.
The guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, while the introductory (prāyaṇīya) and concluding (udayanīya) offerings are the two arms.
Since the arms are on both sides of the head, therefore these two oblations—the introductory and the concluding—occur on both sides of the guest-offering.
Now, as to why it is called *ātithya* (hospitality):

this purchased Soma indeed comes as a guest; for him he prepares this hospitality, just as one might cook a large bull or a large goat for a king or a Brahmin—that being a human oblation, he thus prepares this divine hospitality for him.
Regarding this they say:
"One should take [the portion] after passing over the first. For where they do not show honor to an Arhat who has arrived, he indeed becomes angry there; thus he is truly honored.
Furthermore, one of them might be liberated while the other is unliberated;
if he were to take [the horse], because one was liberated he would have come [as a guest], and because the other was unliberated he would have been honored [as a host].

One should not do it in that way; rather, having unyoked him and led him forward, one should take [the milk]. For as is the conduct of the gods, so indeed is the conduct of men. Therefore, as long as he has not been unyoked in human practice, they do not bring water for him nor do they pay him honor, for he is not yet arrived. But when he is unyoked, then they bring water for him and then they pay him honor, for then he has truly arrived. Therefore, having unyoked him and led him forward, one should take [the milk].
He should take it up as if in great haste; thus he becomes honored. His wife takes hold of him from behind.

Indeed, while being carried around, the sacrificer takes hold of him from behind, and here the wife likewise; thus they both take hold of him from both sides as a couple. For when a worthy person arrives, everyone in the household indeed exerts themselves; thus he becomes honored.

He should indeed take it with another sacrificial formula than that used for other oblations. For when he is being purchased, he is purchased as one portion alone, for the sovereignty of the meters, for the supreme dominion of the meters; and the meters are his attendants on both sides. Just as there are non-royal royal functionaries—charioteers and village headmen—attending upon a king, even so are the meters his attendants on both sides.
That is certainly not appropriate:

that one should take [the Soma] for the metres alone. For wherever they cook for a worthy man, those who are around him share in the portion—such as non-kings who serve the king, the charioteers, and the village headmen. Therefore, wherever one takes [the Soma] for this [deity], at that very place one should cause the metres to share in the portion.
He takes it up with the formula, "Thou art the body of Agni; for Viṣṇu, thee! For the Gāyatrī is indeed Agni; thus he causes the Gāyatrī to partake in it.
"You are the body of Soma; for Viṣṇu, you!
Soma is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), and the Triṣṭubh is the nobility; thus he causes the Triṣṭubh to share in it.
"Thou art the guest-offering for the guest; for Viṣṇu, thee!
This is his special share, just as there is a special share for the most excellent; even so is this his, apart from the meters.

"For thee, the eagle, the bearer of Soma; for Viṣṇu, thee!"—thereby he causes the Gāyatrī to share in it. Since that Gāyatrī, having become an eagle, brought the Soma from heaven, she is therefore the eagle, the bearer of Soma; by that very power he thus causes her to share in this second part.
"To Agni for thee, the giver of the increase of wealth; to Viṣṇu for thee.
The increase of wealth is indeed cattle, and the Jagatī meter is cattle; thus he causes the Jagatī to participate in it.

Now, as to why he draws [the Soma] five times: the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he thus obtains it by means of those five. Therefore, he draws it five times. And as to why he draws it saying, "For Viṣṇu thee! For Viṣṇu thee!", it is because he draws it for Viṣṇu—he who draws it for the sacrifice [draws it] for Viṣṇu.

There is a cake on nine potsherds. The guest-offering is indeed the head of the sacrifice. The Gāyatrī consists of nine syllables: there are eight which he recites, and the *praṇava* is the ninth. The Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [offering] belongs to the fore-part of the sacrifice. Therefore, there is a cake on nine potsherds.
The enclosing-sticks (paridhi) are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.

The gods indeed perceived this *kārṣmarya* tree among the lords of the forest as a slayer of Rakṣases. Since the Guest-offering (*ātithya*) is the head of the sacrifice, they thought, "Lest the destructive Rakṣases injure the head of the sacrifice. Therefore, the enclosing-sticks are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.

The *prastara* bundle is made of *āśvavāla* grass. Once, the Sacrifice fled from the gods; it became a horse and turned away. The gods, pursuing it, seized its tail-hairs and plucked them out. Having plucked them out, they cast them together, and from that these plants arose—the *āśvavāla* grasses. The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the Sacrifice, while the tail-hairs are its hind part. In that the *prastara* is made of *āśvavāla* grass, he thus encompasses the Sacrifice on both sides.

The two separating blades are made of *ikṣu* grass, so that the sacrificial grass and the *prastara* bundle may not become entangled. Then, having purified the clarified butter, he takes all the portions of clarified butter in four ladlings each; for there are no after-offerings (*anuyāja*) here.

Having set down the oblations, he churns the fire. The guest-offering (ātithya) is indeed the head of the sacrifice; they truly produce him when they churn him, for one who is being born is born first from the head; thus he produces the sacrifice first from the head. Agni is all the deities, for into Agni they offer to all the deities; the guest-offering is the head of the sacrifice; thus he endows the sacrifice with all the deities from the very head. Therefore, he churns the fire.
He takes up a piece of wood for friction, saying, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni. For it is here that Agni is born; therefore he says, "Thou art the birthplace of Agni."
"You two are testicles," he says; for these two which are born together from a woman, these very ones they are.

Then he places the lower churning-stick (adharāraṇi) with the words, "Thou art Urvaśī. Then he touches the upper churning-stick (uttarāraṇi), which serves to melt the clarified butter, with the words, "Thou art Āyu," and he places it upon the lower one with the words, "Thou art Purūravas. For Urvaśī was a celestial nymph (apsaras) and Purūravas was her husband; and that which was born from that union was Āyu. In this very same way, he generates the sacrifice from this union. Then he says, "Recite for Agni while being churned!"

He churns [the fire], saying: "With the Gāyatrī metre I churn thee; with the Triṣṭubh metre I churn thee; with the Jagatī metre I churn thee. Thus he churns him indeed with the metres. He recites the metres after the one being churned; thereby he causes the metres to follow the sacrifice. When he is born, he says, "Recite for the one born! as for that sun, the rays [follow]. While throwing [the fire] into the hearth, he says, "Recite for the one being thrown! when it is being thrown.

He follows it with the formula: "Be of one mind for us, of one heart, and free from blemish; do not harm the sacrifice, nor the lord of the sacrifice, O Jātavedas; be auspicious to us today. He speaks this to them for the sake of peace, so that they may not harm each other.
Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle, he makes an offering over the fire with the formula:

"The fire moves, entered into the fire; the son of the seers, the protector against curses. May he, being gracious, sacrifice for us here with a good sacrifice, never failing, as an oblation for the gods—*svāhā*! For they have generated this [fire] by means of the oblation; they sent it forth with this oblation; therefore he makes the offering in this manner.
It concludes with the *iḍā*; they do not perform the after-offerings (*anuyāja*).

The guest-offering (*ātithya*) is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and the head is the forepart; thus he prepares the forepart of the sacrifice. If he were to perform the after-offerings, it would be as if one were to take away the feet from the head and place them back on it; therefore, it concludes with the *iḍā*, and they do not perform the after-offerings.
When the gods had performed the guest-offering (ātithya), discord (saṃmad) overcame them;

they scattered in four directions, each unable to endure the other's splendor: Agni with the Vasus, Soma with the Rudras, Varuṇa with the Ādityas, and Indra with the Maruts—though some say Bṛhaspati with the Viśvedevas. Now, those who scattered in four directions were indeed the Viśvedevas; as they were thus scattered, the Asuras and Rākṣasas followed and separated them.
They realized: "We have indeed become worse;

the Asuras and Rakṣases have followed after us, and we are falling into the power of our enemies. Come, let us agree and stand for the glory of one. They stood for the glory of Indra; therefore they say, "Indra is all the deities; Indra is the best among the gods."
Therefore, they should not quarrel among themselves.

Whoever among them becomes as it were more distant, he separates himself from them; they do what is pleasing to their enemies and fall into the power of their enemies. Therefore, they should not quarrel. He who, knowing this, does not quarrel, does what is displeasing to his enemies and does not fall into the power of his enemies. Therefore, one should not quarrel.
They said,
"Come, let us act in such a way that this [sacrifice] shall remain imperishable for us from time immemorial."

Those gods gathered together their beloved bodies and dear abodes. They said, "By this [means] let him be separated from us, by this let him be scattered—whoever among us should transgress this. "Of whom shall he be the witness? they asked. "Of Tanūnapāt Śākvara," they replied. Now, this very Tanūnapāt Śākvara has entered here as the witness of creatures; these are the two, Prāṇa and Udāna.

Therefore they say: "The gods do not know the mind of a human being. One forms a volition with the mind; that reaches the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the vital breath [reaches] the wind (*vāta*); the wind reports it to the gods according to the mind of the person.
Therefore, this has been declared by the Seer:
"One intends with the mind; that [intention] goes to the wind; the wind announces it to the gods, saying, 'O Puruṣa, such is your mind.'"

Those gods gathered together their beloved bodies and dear abodes. They said, "By this [vow] let him be separated from us, by this let him go astray—whoever among us should transgress this. Even now, the gods do not transgress that; for what would they be if they were to transgress? For they would be speaking untruth. The gods indeed observe one vow alone: truth itself. Therefore, their victory is invincible and their glory is such. Thus indeed does his victory become invincible and his glory [become great], for he who, knowing thus, speaks the truth. This, then, is the *tānūnaptra* (the covenant of the body) according to its origin.

Those gods cast together their beloved bodies and dear abodes; then these [priests], taking up the clarified butter, cast together their beloved bodies and dear abodes. Therefore, one should not enter into a close association with everyone, thinking, "Lest I should enter into a close association with my beloved bodies and dear abodes. For he with whom one does enter into such association, one should not deceive; for it is said: "One must not deceive a *tanūnaptr̥* (one who shares the same body)."
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"I draw thee for Āpati, for Paripati. For he who blows here, he indeed both flies hither (ā-patati) and flies around (pari-patati); it is for him that he draws [the cup]. Therefore he says, "I draw thee for Āpati, for Paripati."
"To Tanūnapāt, the Śākvara"—for he who blows here is indeed Tanūnapāt, the Śākvara; it is for him that he draws [the libation], therefore he says, "To Tanūnapāt, the Śākvara."

"For the most powerful one, for the most vigorous one"—this [Agni] is indeed the most powerful and the most vigorous; it is for him that he draws [the libation], therefore he says, "for the most powerful one, for the most vigorous one."
Then they indeed touch one another.

For the gods, having come together more closely, said: "In this way he shall be among us hereafter, lest he should overstep this [bond] of ours. And in the same way these [priests] now come together, thinking: "In this way he shall be among us hereafter, lest he should overstep this [bond] of ours."
They reflect upon this.

"Unassailable, unassailable, the vigor of the gods"—for the gods were indeed unassailable and unassailable when they were together, speaking with one voice and holding fast to one purpose; "the vigor of the gods"—these are indeed the bodies dear to the gods, their beloved abodes; "beyond reproach, protectors against reproach, not to be reproached"—for the gods have crossed over all reproach; "may I straightway go to truth"—by this he means, "May I speak the truth, may I not transgress it"; "place me in well-being"—for the gods placed themselves in well-being when they spoke the truth and performed what was true; therefore he says, "Place me in well-being."
Now, as for those who are "the gods" (taddevāḥ):

They deposited together their cherished bodies and dear abodes; they placed them all together in Indra. Now, he who shines yonder is indeed Indra; for in the beginning he did not shine, but was just as dark as this other [earth] is now. It is by that very power (vīrya) that he now shines. Therefore, if many should undergo consecration (dīkṣā), they should hand over the fast-food (vrata) to the householder alone after pouring it out, for he among them becomes the vessel of Indra. But if one should undergo consecration accompanied by sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), they should hand over the fast-food to the sacrificer himself after pouring it out, for they say, "The sacrificer is Indra."

Now, those beloved bodies and dear abodes which the gods had gathered together—that they struck together became the *sāman*. Therefore, they say: "The *sāman* is truth; the *sāman* is born of the gods."
When the gods had performed the guest-offering (ātithyeṣṭi), discord (samada) overcame them;

they settled that discord by means of the Tanūnaptra rites. They sought an atonement for this: because they had spoken evil of one another, they did not arrange a second consecration (dīkṣā) before the final bath (avabhṛtha). They then perceived this intermediate consecration.
They stripped off their skin by means of fire itself;

for fire is austerity and initiation is austerity—they thus underwent an intermediate initiation. Because they underwent this intermediate initiation, it is called the *avāntaradīkṣā*. They drew their fingers closer together and drew their girdle closer; though it was already wound around them, they wound it around once more. And so does this person now perform an expiation for whatever he has done contrary to his vow or spoken contrary to his vow prior to this point.

He has his skin singed by fire itself; for fire is austerity, and initiation is austerity; thus he undergoes an intermediate initiation. He makes his fingers closer together and his girdle tighter; though it was already fastened, he now fastens it again. By this, the gods indeed obtained offspring.
They turned their skin inside out by means of fire alone;

for fire is indeed the maker and progenitor of the couple. Thus they obtained offspring; they drew their fingers closer together and drew their girdle closer together, thereby placing offspring within themselves. And so does this sacrificer now obtain offspring.
He is enveloped by fire itself;
for fire is the maker and progenitor of the couple, and thus he attains offspring. He makes his fingers closer together and his girdle tighter; thereby he brings offspring into himself.

When the gods were consecrated, whoever among them neglected the kindling of the fires or the private recitation of the Vedas, the Asuras and Rakṣases sought to slay him, substituting one for another in form and another for another. They would approach him saying evil things: "Is this not what you wished to do to me? "Did you not seek to slay me? Only Agni spoke thus to another, and no other spoke thus to Agni.
They said, "O Agni, did they speak thus to you? He replied, "I spoke neither to another, nor did another speak to me."
They understood: "This one is indeed our best protector against the Rākṣasas;

let us assume his very form, for by that we shall escape the Rākṣasas and by that we shall attain the heavenly world. They became the very form of Agni; by that they escaped the Rākṣasas and by that they attained the heavenly world. In the same way, this sacrificer now becomes the very form of Agni; by that he escapes the Rākṣasas and by that he attains the heavenly world. Indeed, by placing the fuel-stick upon the fire, he enters the intermediate consecration (avāntaradīkṣā).

He places a fuel-stick on the fire with the formula: "O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee [is] the guardian of vows. For Agni is the lord of vows among the gods; therefore he says, "O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee [is] the guardian of vows. "That body of thine which is this one, let it be in me; that body of mine which is this one, let it be in thee; O Lord of Vows, let our vows be together"—with these words, he exchanges his skin with Agni. "May the Lord of Consecration approve my consecration; may the Lord of Penance approve my penance"—with these words, he enters the intermediate consecration. He draws his fingers closer together and draws his girdle tighter; thus, that which was already wrapped around him is now wrapped even more tightly.
Then they attend upon him with the boiling waters;
for Agni is heat and the boiling waters are heat; therefore they attend upon him with the boiling waters.
Then, having touched the *madantī* waters, they cause the King (Soma) to swell.

Now, as to why they cause the King to swell after touching the *madantī* waters: ghee is indeed a thunderbolt and Soma is seed; "Lest we injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, the ghee"—for this reason they cause the King to swell after touching the *madantī* waters.

Regarding this they say: "Since this nourishment, the guest-offering for Soma, is being performed, they should first nourish him, then the intermediate consecration, and then the *tānūnaptra* formulas. But one should not do it in that way; for such is the procedure of the sacrifice. Here, indeed, they found a conflict among them; they first entered into an agreement, then [performed] the intermediate consecration, and then the nourishment.

Now, when they cause it to swell: Soma is indeed the god; for Soma was in heaven. Soma was indeed Vṛtra, and these mountains and stones are his body; from that, this plant called *uśānā* is born—so said Śvetaketu Auddālaki. Having brought that [plant] here, they press it; by means of the consecration (*dīkṣā*), the *upasad*s, the *tānūnaptra* rites, and the swelling, they make it into Soma. And in the same way, he now makes this [earth] into Soma by means of the consecration, the *upasad*s, the *tānūnaptra* rites, and the swelling.
They say, "It is honey made by bees.

The sacrifice, indeed, is honey made by bees, and these officiating priests are the honey-making bees. Just as honey-makers would cause the honey to swell, even so do they cause this sacrifice to swell.

By means of the sacrifice, indeed, the gods won this victory which is now theirs. They said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unassailable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, obstructed it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and disappeared. And because they obstructed it with that, therefore it is called the *yūpa*.
Or rather, this was heard by the seers.

They brought together the sacrifice; just as this sacrifice was brought together, so indeed does he who undergoes initiation bring together the sacrifice. Speech is the sacrifice; thus, whatever of the sacrifice has been drained away here, whatever has been milked out, that very thing he now causes to swell again.
Having become six, they indeed cause it to swell;
for there are six seasons, and having become the seasons themselves, they cause it to swell.
They cause them to swell.

"O divine Soma, may ray after ray of thine swell," he says; thus he causes each individual ray of his to swell. "For Indra, the winner of the single prize"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "for Indra. "Winner of the single prize"—formerly, for every single one of the gods, one hundred rays used to swell as the single prize. Or rather, ten by ten they swell for thee. "May Indra swell for thee, and mayest thou swell for Indra"—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; thus he causes that very deity of the sacrifice to swell. "Mayest thou swell for Indra"—he thereby bestows this swelling upon him. "Swell us, thy friends, with gain and wisdom"—when he gains anything, that is what he means by "gain"; and when he recites [the verses], that is what he means by "wisdom. "May I attain thy true blessing, O divine Soma"—there is indeed one blessing for these, both for the priests and for the sacrificer: "May we reach the conclusion of the sacrifice. By this he means, "May I reach the conclusion of the sacrifice."

Then they make amends on the *prastara* grass-bundle. The sacrifice indeed proceeds from the north; yet here, having gone along toward the south, they cause it to swell. The sacrifice is Agni; thus they place the sacrifice behind them, and that they do wrongly. They are cut off from the gods, for the *prastara* is the sacrifice; therefore they take hold of the sacrifice again. This is the expiation for that: thus this act of theirs does not become wrongly done, nor are they cut off from the gods. Therefore, they make amends on the *prastara*.
Regarding this they say:

"Should they conceal [the fire] when it has been anointed, or when it has not been anointed? One should indeed conceal it when it has not been anointed, for the non-throwing back (anupraharaṇa) belongs specifically to that which has been anointed.
They make amends, saying:

"Wishes for wealth, sent forth for Bhaga, for the Ṛta for those who speak Ṛta"—by this he means "truth for those who speak truth. "Homage to Heaven and Earth!"—thereby they make amends to these two, Heaven and Earth, upon whom all this rests.

Then, having plucked up the *prastara* (grass-bundle), he says, "O Agnidh, come with the Madantī waters! The Agnidh replies, "With the Madantīs. He carries it over the fire again and again. As for why he does not throw it into the fire: from this point onward, he will be performing the rites with it; therefore, by carrying it over the fire again and again, that very act serves as its substitute for being thrown into the fire. He hands it to the Agnidh, and the Agnidh places it down.
The Upasads are indeed the neck of the sacrifice, and the Pravargya is its head.
Therefore, if there is a Pravargya, they perform the Pravargya first and then proceed with the Upasads; thus they restore the neck.

Those which are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) in the forenoon become the offering verses (*yājyā*) in the afternoon; those which are the offering verses become the invitatory verses. He thus interlinks them; therefore these joints of the neck are interlinked, and so are these bones.

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the Asuras built forts in these worlds: one of iron in this world, one of silver in the intermediate space, and one of gold in the sky.

The gods indeed desired to win that [fortress]. They sat near it with these Upasads; because they sat near it (upāsīdan), they are called Upasads. They shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds; therefore they say, "One conquers a fortress by means of the Upasads. And insofar as they perform the Upasads here, they thereby conquer this human fortress.

By means of these Upasad rites, indeed, the gods shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds. In the same way, this [sacrificer] likewise does not have anyone else build fortresses for him in this world; he shatters these very worlds and conquers these worlds. Therefore, he performs the sacrifice with the Upasads.
Now, these indeed have clarified butter as their oblation.

Clarified butter is a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, the clarified butter, the gods shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds. In the same way, he now shatters these worlds and conquers these worlds by means of this thunderbolt, the clarified butter. Therefore, they have clarified butter as their oblation.
He takes eight times with the *juhū* ladle and four times with the *upabhṛt*; however, they say otherwise: "One should take four times with the *juhū* and eight times with the *upabhṛt*."

He indeed takes eight times with the *juhū* ladle and four times with the *upabhṛt*; thus he makes that thunderbolt heavy, and with that heavy thunderbolt he cleaves these worlds and conquers these worlds.
Agni and Soma are indeed the yoke-fellows among the gods;

he draws [the oblation] together with them. For Viṣṇu alone, however, he offers only one of the two libations—that which he performs with the dipping-spoon (sruva). Having offered the second libation, he strides forward, thinking, "May I conquer for victory. Therefore, he offers only one of the two libations, that which is performed with the sruva.
Then, having called for the announcement, he does not formally choose the Hotṛ.
He simply says, "Sit down, O Hotṛ! The Hotṛ sits down on the Hotṛ’s seat; having sat down, he gives the impulse. Being impelled, the Adhvaryu takes up the two offering-spoons.
Having stepped across, he says, "Recite for Agni.
Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Agni," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Soma. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Offer the oblation to Soma," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

Now, when there is clarified butter in the *upabhṛt* ladle, while pouring it together, he says, "Recite for Viṣṇu"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice to Viṣṇu," and offers the oblation when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

When he offers while standing in one place, it is not as when one moves about during the performance; rather, he does so for the sake of conquest, thinking, "May I conquer. Now, when he sacrifices to these deities, he thereby prepares a thunderbolt: Agni is its point, Soma its barb, and Viṣṇu its socket.
The year is indeed the thunderbolt.
Agni is the day, Soma is the night; and that which is between them is Viṣṇu. Thus he makes the revolving year.
The year is the thunderbolt.

By means of this year as a thunderbolt, the gods indeed shattered the fortresses and conquered these worlds. In the same way, he now shatters these worlds by means of this year as a thunderbolt and conquers these worlds; therefore, he sacrifices to these deities.

He should indeed perform three *upasads*. For there are three seasons in a year; thus the form of the year is created, and it is the year that he thereby consecrates. He proceeds twice with one [offering] and twice with the other.
These amount to six;
for there are six seasons in the year—it is the form of the year that is thus produced, and it is the year that he thereby consecrates.

If, however, he should perform twelve *upasads*, there are indeed twelve months in a year; thus the form of the year itself is created, and it is the year that he thereby consecrates. He proceeds twice with one [kind of wood] and twice with the other.
These amount to twenty-four;
for there are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year. Thus, the form of the year is produced, and it is the year itself that he thereby consecrates.
When he performs [the rites] in the evening and in the morning, it is thus that he attains perfection.

When he performs them in the forenoon, he conquers; and when he performs them in the afternoon, it is as if he has won well. And when he offers the oblation—this is indeed a fortress they attack; having conquered it, they enter their own [home], which is now secure.
When he moves about, he fights; when he stands still, he conquers; and when he offers the oblation, he enters that very [deity] which is already present.

He offers with the verse with which he is about to perform twice on a single day: "O Agni, that iron-seated body of thine, most excellent, dwelling in the abyss—may it drive away the fierce word, may it drive away the dazzling word, svāhā! For such indeed was that [body]: it was made of iron.

Then he offers with the verse with which he was about to proceed twice on one day: "O Agni, that body of thine which lies in the dust, most excellent, dwelling in the depths—may it drive away the fierce word, may it drive away the dazzling word, svāhā! For such indeed was its form; for it was silver.

Then he offers with the verse with which he was about to proceed for the first day: "O Agni, that golden form of thine, most excellent, which has warded off harsh speech, which has warded off dazzling speech—Svāhā! For such indeed was its form; it was golden. And if he should perform twelve *upasad*s, he should proceed with one [verse] for four days and with another for four days.
Now, therefore, regarding the Upasads themselves:

some Upasads are "longer" (paraurvī) and others are "shorter" (paro'hrī). Those for which he milks one cow on the first day, then two, then three—those are the longer ones. And those for which he milks three cows on the first day, then two, then one—those are the shorter ones. Indeed, those that are shorter are the longer ones, and those that are longer are the shorter ones.
By austerity, indeed, they conquer the world.

For him, this austerity becomes ever higher and more excellent; he conquers a world that is ever higher and better, and he indeed becomes wealthier in this world—he who, knowing thus, undergoes the Upasad rites for more than three days. Therefore, one should undergo the Upasad rites for more than three days. But if he should undergo twelve Upasads, he should have [the cow] milked for three days during the four-day period, for two days during the next four-day period, and for one day during the final four-day period.
Now, from that which is the easternmost, tallest, and principal pillar, he strides three steps forward to the east and drives in a peg; that is the *antaḥpāta* (inner limit).
Therefore, from the middle gnomon, she strides fifteen steps to the south and drives in a gnomon there; that is the southern hip.
Therefore, from the middle gnomon, he strides fifteen steps to the north and drives in a gnomon; that is the northern hip.
Therefore, from the middle peg, he strides thirty-six steps toward the east and drives in a peg; that constitutes the eastern half.
Therefore, from the central peg, he strides twelve steps to the south and drives in a peg; that is the southern shoulder.
Therefore, from the middle peg, he strides twelve steps toward the north and drives in a peg; that is the northern shoulder. This is the measurement of the altar.
Now, as for why it is thirty steps behind:

the Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and by means of the Virāj the gods established themselves in this world; in the same way, this sacrificer now establishes himself in this world by means of the Virāj.
Moreover, there may be thirty-three;
for the Virāj consists of thirty-three syllables, and by means of the Virāj, he becomes firmly established in this world.
Now, as to why the eastern side is thirty-six steps long:

the Bṛhatī indeed consists of thirty-six syllables; by means of the Bṛhatī, the gods attained the heavenly world. In the same way, this sacrificer now attains the heavenly world by means of the Bṛhatī itself; thus, that becomes his divine Āhavanīya fire-altar.
Now, as to why it is twenty-four steps wide in front:

the Gāyatrī indeed consists of twenty-four syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [altar] is at the fore-part of the sacrifice, therefore it is twenty-four steps wide in front—this is the measure of the altar.
Now, as to why it is wider behind:

they praise a woman by saying she is "wider behind" and "broad-hipped. Furthermore, in that it is wider behind, he thereby makes the organ of generation wider behind; therefore, from this wider organ of generation behind, these creatures are produced.
The high altar (uttaravedi) is indeed the nose of the sacrifice;
and because they scatter it upon the northern part of the altar, it is called the "high altar."
In the beginning, there were indeed two kinds of progeny here:

the Ādityas and the Aṅgirases. Of these, the Aṅgirases first prepared the sacrifice; having prepared the sacrifice, they said, "O Agni, announce this Soma-pressing of ours to the Ādityas tomorrow, and cause them to sacrifice for us with this sacrifice."
Those Ādityas said:
"Devise a plan so that the Aṅgirases shall officiate as priests for us alone, and we shall not [officiate] for the Aṅgirases."

They said, "Indeed, there is no departure from the sacrifice other than through the Soma-pressing; let us remain right here until the pressing. They gathered the sacrifice together, and having prepared the sacrifice, they said, "O Agni, you have announced to us that the pressing is tomorrow; therefore, we announce to you that the pressing is this very day, for the Aṅgirases as well. You shall be our Hotṛ."
They sent another [messenger] back;
and those Aṅgirasas, having returned to Agni, were as if incensed, saying, "How is it that you, acting as our messenger, did not attend to us?"

He said: "They chose me while I was blameless; having been chosen by the blameworthy, I was unable to withdraw. Therefore, one who has been chosen by a blameless person should not withdraw. With this [rite], the Aṅgirasas caused the Ādityas to perform the Sadyaḥkrī sacrifice; that is the Sadyaḥkrī.
They brought speech as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for them;
they did not accept it, saying, "We shall lose [the sacrifice] if we accept it. Thus, that part of the sacrificial work which belonged to the sacrificial fee was not released from the sacrifice.

Then they brought the sun as the sacrificial fee for them. They accepted it; therefore, indeed, the Aṅgirases used to say, "We are truly the officiating priests; we are worthy of the sacrificial fee. Or rather, this one who shines yonder has been accepted by us. Therefore, a horse that is white and ready for immediate use is the sacrificial fee.

A gold plate is placed before it; thus the form of him who shines yonder is made. If he should not find a white horse, even a white ox may serve; a gold plate is placed before it, and thus the form of him who shines yonder is made.
Speech became angry with them, saying:

"By what kinship, by what excellence is he superior, that he has accepted him and not me? Thereupon she departed from them; having become a lioness, she went about between the two sides—between the gods and the Asuras as they were arrayed for battle—seizing [the prey]. The gods called upon her, and the Asuras called upon her. Agni was the messenger of the gods, and Saharakṣas was the messenger of the Asuras, being an Asura-Rākṣasa.

She was about to return to the gods, and they said to her, "If you should return to us, what would be ours from that? She replied, "The first oblation to Agni shall reach you. Then she said to the gods, "Whatever blessing you shall invoke through me, all of that shall be fulfilled for you. Thus she returned to the gods.
Now, as for why he sprinkles the *uttaravedi* while the fire is being maintained:

it is because the gods then said of her, "The oblation shall reach you before the fire"; thus, this oblation now reaches her before the fire. For she is Speech by her very nature. And as for why he scatters [the earth] upon the *uttaravedi*: it is for the sake of the completeness of the sacrifice; for the sacrifice is Speech, and she is indeed Speech.
He measures it with a yoke and a pin;

for where they lead [the oxen] with the yoke and from where they lead them with the pin, by means of the yoke and the pin they yoke the draft-animal. Since she (the earth) formerly moved about as a lioness, being unappeased, he now yokes her at this sacrifice by that very means.

Therefore, one should not accept a sacrificial gift that has been turned back; for it becomes a lioness and destroys him, yet one should not fail to give it away, for it becomes a lioness and destroys him. One should not give it to anyone other than oneself, for one would thereby perform the sacrifice elsewhere than in one's own person. Therefore, if there should be someone who, though a kinsman, is as if wicked, to him one should give this gift. In that he gives it, it does not become a lioness and destroy him; and in that he gives it to a kinsman, he does not perform it elsewhere than in his own person. This is the proper support for a sacrificial gift that has been turned back.

Then he takes up the wooden pin (śamyā) and the wooden sword (sphya). He steps westward three strides from that stake which is situated in the eastern half and the northern half; there he traces around the pit (cātvāla). This is the measure of the pit, though there is no fixed measure here: wherever he himself thinks fit in his mind, he should trace the pit in front of the rubbish-heap (utkara).
From the edge of the altar, he places a yoke-pin pointing northward; he then traces around it, saying, "Thou art my path for heat. By this, he says this very thing: "Upon her, one goes forth heated."

Then, in front of it, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) pointing northward; he draws a line around it, saying, "May there be a path for me to find. By this, he says this very thing: "For on this [earth] one goes having found [the goal]."

Then, while it is being measured out, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) towards the east; he draws a line around it with the words, "Protect me from distress," by which he means this: "Wherever there is distress, protect me from that."

Then, on the north side, he places a wooden pin (śamyā) pointing eastward; he then draws a line around it with the words, "Protect me from being shaken. By this, he means this very thing: "Where there is shaking, protect me from that."
Then he carries [the fires]. Wherever he carries them, there he sits down beside the Āgnīdhra fire-altar.

Indeed, he carries them while uttering the very names of the fires. For those same fires which the gods chose at the beginning for the office of Hotṛ fled away; they crawled into these very earths—two of them right here on this earth, and two beyond it. It is by that very correspondence that he carries them.

He strikes, saying, "O Agni Vaidheya, O Agni Angiras, come with the name Āyu! By that which he has run forward, he bestows life-span; by that, he impels him. Having taken [the earth] with the words, "Thou who art on this earth," he lays it down with, "With that name of thine which is inviolable and worthy of sacrifice, with that I lay thee down. By this he means: "With that name of thine which is inviolable by Rakṣases and worthy of sacrifice, with that I lay thee down. He carries it for the fourth time with, "Thee for the enjoyment of the gods"; by this he means: "I carry thee, acceptable to the gods. He carries it from the four-cornered Cātvāla pit; for there are four quarters, and thus he carries it from all these quarters.
Then he arranges it [with the formula]:

"Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; be fit for the gods! When she, having become a lioness, used to roam about there in a non-peaceful manner, it is for that very reason he says to her, "Thou art a lioness. By saying "overcoming rivals," he means, "May we, through thee, make our rivals more wretched. By saying "be fit for the gods," he prepares the high altar—which is indeed a woman—for the gods.

He makes it a yoke's length on all sides, or ten steps for the sacrificer in each direction; for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, the Virāj is speech, and the sacrifice is speech. He makes it like a navel in the middle so that he may sprinkle [the butter] while sitting in one place.
He sprinkles it with water.

Since she, having become a lioness there, moved about unappeased, and water is appeasement, he appeases her with water. The high altar (uttaravedi) is indeed a woman; he thus sends her forth for the gods, and therefore he sprinkles it with water.

He sprinkles it with water, saying, "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; be pure for the gods! Then he strews sand over it. Sand is indeed an ornament, for sand shines as it were. Sand is the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara; since he is about to place the fire upon this [altar], the fire does not injure it in that way. Therefore he strews sand over it. He strews it, saying, "Thou art a lioness, overcoming rivals; be beautiful for the gods! Then he covers it, and she dwells upon it during that night.
They place fuel on the fire;

they prepare the supporting ladles, set the clarified butter over the heat, and cleanse the dipping-spoon (sruva) and the offering-ladle (sruk). Then, having purified the clarified butter, he takes five portions of it when the fuel has become well-kindled.

Then, while they lift up the fuel, they bring forward the supporting-sticks. Then [the Adhvaryu] says, "Recite for the fire being carried forth! Follow along with the single wooden sword! The Pratiprasthātṛ follows along with the single wooden sword from that middle step which is at the rear part of the altar; thus he thereby connects what has been cut off between the Gārhapatya fire and the altar by means of this intermediate passage.

Now, some indeed step out following the northern altar; but one should not do so. Rather, he should step out following the middle enclosing-stake (maṇḍala). They then come back and go to the northern altar.
The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters.

Standing facing the north, he first sprinkles from the front, saying: "May Indra’s shout protect thee from the front with the Vasus. By this he means: "May Indra’s shout guard thee from the front with the Vasus."
Then he sprinkles from behind with:
"May Pracetas protect you from behind with the Rudras. By this he means: "May Pracetas guard you from behind with the Rudras."
Then he sprinkles on the south side with the formula:
"May Manojavā protect thee from the south along with the Pitṛs. By this he means to say: "May Manojavā guard thee from the south along with the Pitṛs."
Then he sprinkles from the north:
"May Viśvakarman protect thee from the north with the Ādityas. By this he means: "May Viśvakarman guard thee from the north with the Ādityas."
Now, as for the sprinkling waters that remain:

of those two front corners [of the altar], he pours out the southern one along its edge outside the altar with the formula, "Here I cast forth this heated water from outside the sacrifice. Whatever fierce heat she (the earth) displayed when she became a lioness and moved about unappeased, that very heat he now casts forth from her, from outside the sacrifice. If he does not intend to practice sorcery, he does so; but if he intends to practice sorcery, he should point it out, saying, "Here I cast forth this heated water against so-and-so. He pierces him with that heat, and he, suffering from that heat, goes to yonder world.

When the fire is being held [over it], he sprinkles the high altar (uttaravedi) with ghee. For when the gods said of her at that time, "The first oblation to Agni shall reach you," it is for that very reason that the first oblation to Agni now reaches her. And because she said to the gods, "Whatever blessing you shall invoke through me, all that shall be fulfilled for you," therefore the officiating priests now invoke a blessing for the sacrificer by means of this [altar], and it is fulfilled for him in its entirety.
Indeed, by performing this one act, he performs two:
namely, when he sprinkles the *uttaravedi*, and also that which is like a navel in their midst—the southern of the two front corners.

Upon that [ladle] he pours the libation: "Thou art a lioness, Svāhā! Then, on the northern of the two rear [spoons], [he says]: "Thou art a lioness, winning the Ādityas, Svāhā! Then, on the southern of the two rear [spoons], [he says]: "Thou art a lioness, winning the Brahman, winning the Kṣatra, Svāhā! For in the Yajus formulas, the blessing is manifold; thus he prays for both the Brahman and the Kṣatra, both powers.
Then, on the northern side of the two preceding ones, he says:

"Thou art a lioness, bringing good offspring, bringing abundance of wealth, Svāhā! By saying "bringing good offspring," he prays for progeny; by saying "bringing abundance of wealth"—for abundance of wealth is indeed plenitude—he prays for that plenitude.

Then he pours the libation in the middle, saying, "O Siṃhyā, bring the gods for the sacrificer, svāhā! Thus he brings the gods for the sacrificer; then he raises the ladle, saying, "For the beings, thee! Beings indeed are offspring; thus he says, "For offspring, thee!"

Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). With the formula, "Thou art firm; steady the earth," he lays down the middle one; with "Thou art dwelling in the firm; steady the atmosphere," the southern one; and with "Thou art dwelling in the unshakable; steady the sky," the northern one. He scatters the filling-materials (*sambhāra*) with the formula, "Thou art Agni’s soil. As to why there are these filling-materials, it is for the sake of Agni’s completeness.
The body, indeed, is of *pītudāru* wood. Therefore, when the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) are made of *pītudāru*, he thereby provides this [Agni] with a body; he makes him complete.
Guggulu is indeed his flesh;
thus, when there is guggulu, he thereby provides him with flesh and makes him complete.
Fragrance, indeed, is its *sugandhitejana* (fragrant-smoke).
Therefore, as to why there is *sugandhitejana*, it is by means of fragrance that he thus provides for him and makes him complete.

Now, as for the fact that there is a tuft of hair from a bull: Agni indeed stayed for one night between the two horns of a bull; therefore, whatever part of Agni was left behind there, that he thinks, "Let that also be here," and so there is a tuft of hair from a bull. Therefore, one should pluck and bring a tuft from the part of the head nearest to it; but if he cannot find such, he may bring any at all. Now, as for the enclosing-sticks (paridhis): they serve for protection, for the other enclosing-sticks come quite close to him.
The sacrifice is indeed man;
therefore the sacrifice is man, because man extends it. While it is being extended, it is ordained to be as large as man himself; therefore the sacrifice is man.
His head indeed is the Havirdhāna;
it belongs to Viṣṇu by deity. And because Soma is contained within it—Soma being the oblation (*havis*) of the gods—it is therefore called the Havirdhāna.
His mouth indeed is the Āhavanīya fire;
when he offers an oblation into the Āhavanīya, it is just as if he were pouring it into his own mouth.
The stūpa itself is its sacrificial post;
his two arms are the Āgnīdhrīya and Mārjālīya sheds.
His belly indeed is the *sadas*;

therefore they consume [the sacrificial food] in the *sadas*, for whatever one eats here, all that is established in the belly. And because all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) sat down (*asīdan*) in it, it is called the *sadas*; and these Brahmins of various lineages sit down in it for that very reason.
Now, these two fires which are behind [the altar] are his two feet; for as he is being measured out, he is fashioned to be exactly as large as a man. Therefore, the sacrifice is a man.

The *havirdhāna* shed has doors on both sides, and the *sadas* has doors on both sides; therefore, this person, having been completely covered, gazes out from within. He stands near the two *havirdhāna* sheds when they have been sprinkled.
They turn them together:
the southern one with the southern [pole] and the northern one with the northern; whichever is larger should be the southern one.

When those two have come together, they lay the roof-covering (cadiḥ) upon them; if they should not find a roof-covering, they fasten a wall of the same measure as the roof-covering against the front beam (rarāṭyā). They enclose it with uprights, and they lay the roof-covering behind it, or else a wall of the same measure as the roof-covering.

Then, having entered again and taken four portions of clarified butter, he offers the oblation to Savitṛ for impulsion. For Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thinking, "Impelled by Savitṛ, we shall extend the sacrifice," he therefore offers the oblation to Savitṛ.

He offers with the verse: "They harness the mind, and they harness the thoughts. For it is by means of both mind and speech that people perform the sacrifice. When he says, "They harness the mind," he thereby harnesses the mind; and when he says, "and they harness the thoughts," he thereby harnesses speech. For by means of this speech, people strive through every thought—as if with recited verses, as if with spontaneous utterances, and as if with songs. With these two thus harnessed, they perform the sacrifice.

"O sages of the great sage, the wise one"—those Brahmins who have heard [the Vedas] and are learned in sacred lore are indeed the "sages"; it is to them that he refers by saying "of the great sage, the wise one. "The great, wise one"—the sacrifice is indeed the great, wise one; it is the sacrifice that he thereby refers to. "He alone, knowing the ways, has ordained the priestly offices"—for they indeed ordain the priestly offices while extending the sacrifice. "Great is the praise of the god Savitṛ, Svāhā!"—this is the oblation to Savitṛ, which he offers for the sake of impulsion.
Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter, [he proceeds].

He goes out by the southern door; they lead the wife out. Having placed gold upon the southern track of the southern *havirdhāna* cart, he offers with the formula: "Viṣṇu strode through this; he has placed his foot in three places; it is gathered in his dust, Svāhā! He pours the residue into the hand of the wife; she anoints the corner of her eye. With the formula, "O you two who hear the gods, proclaim this among the gods," he hands over the ladle and the butter-melting spoon to the *pratiprasthātṛ*. They lead the wife around behind both fires.

Having taken four portions of clarified butter, the Pratiprasthātṛ places a piece of gold on the southern track of the northern *havirdhāna* cart and offers the oblation with the formula: "O Viṣṇu, you two have become rich in cattle, rich in milch-cows, and rich in good pasture for the sake of man’s service; you two have propped apart the two worlds, O Viṣṇu; you have supported the earth on all sides with your rays, Svāhā! He then pours the residue from the *saṃsrava* ladle into the hand of the wife and anoints her eye with it, saying: "O you two who are heard by the gods, proclaim this among the gods! This is why he offers in this manner.

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases. The clarified butter (ājya) is indeed a thunderbolt; with this thunderbolt of clarified butter they struck down the destructive Rakṣases from the south, so that they could not follow their path. In the same way, this sacrificer now strikes down the destructive Rakṣases from the south with this thunderbolt of clarified butter, so that they cannot follow his path. As for why he offers with two verses addressed to Viṣṇu, it is because the Soma-cart (havirdhāna) belongs to Viṣṇu.
Now, as for the fact that he anoints the axle of the wife’s cart with heat:

this is indeed an act of procreation. For when both the woman and the man are heated, then the seed is emitted, and from that offspring is born. He anoints it from behind, for the seed is emitted from behind. Then he says, "Recite for the two oblation-holders as they are being moved forward!"

Then he causes [the two poles] to be recited over: "Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice. The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus he says, "Go forward, fashioning the sacrifice. "Lead the sacrifice upward; do not falter"—by this he means, "Lead this sacrifice upward to the world of the gods; do not falter. By saying "do not falter," he thereby invokes freedom from stumbling for him. They should set them in motion as if lifting them up together so that they do not creak. For this speech of the axle is demonic; he does so thinking, "Lest the demonic speech speak here. (This applies) if they should creak.
He should recite this:
"O Goddess, do not speak ill of our own cattle-pen; do not speak ill of our life; do not speak ill of our progeny. This is indeed the expiation for that.
Regarding this they say:

"One should step three strides westward from the *uttaravedi* and there establish the two *havirdhāna* sheds; that is the measure for the two *havirdhānas*. But there is no fixed measure here; wherever one thinks best in one's mind—neither too close nor too far—that is where one should establish them.
He addresses them:

"May you two take delight here on the summit of the earth. For this indeed becomes the summit of the earth; for his Āhavanīya fire is in heaven. He places them in the nave, for that is the form of security.
Then, having gone around by the north, the Adhvaryu supports the southern *havirdhāna* cart with the verse:

"Now I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly regions, who propped up the highest dwelling place, striding out in three steps, the wide-strider; for Viṣṇu, thee! Thereupon, he drives in a wedge on the other side, just as is done in human practice.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ props up the northern *havirdhāna* cart with the formula:

"O Viṣṇu, from the sky or from the earth, or from the great, wide mid-region, O Viṣṇu, fill both your hands with wealth; bestow it from the right and from the left! With the formula "For Viṣṇu, thee," he drives in the wedge on the other side. And as for why they perform this with formulas dedicated to Viṣṇu even in a human rite—it is because the *havirdhāna* belongs to Viṣṇu.
Then, having touched the middle roof-plate, he makes [the sacrificer] recite:

"Viṣṇu is praised for that heroic deed, like a dread beast, prowling, dwelling in the mountains; in whose three wide strides all beings abide. This indeed is his upper skull-plate, for upon it, as it were, the other skull-plates abide; therefore he says, "they abide upon it."
Then, having touched the forehead-strap, he makes him recite:

"Thou art the forehead of Viṣṇu"; for this indeed is his forehead. Then, having touched the two side-posts, he makes him recite: "Ye are the nostrils of Viṣṇu"; for these indeed are his nostrils. And as for this roof-covering which is behind, this indeed is his skull-bone, that which is behind.
Then he sews it with a cord made of *laspona* grass, saying, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s seam.

Then he makes a knot, saying, "Thou art Viṣṇu’s firm one," so that it may not fall apart. He adjusts it during the performance of the ritual; thus, no seizing spirit finds either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer. When it is completed, he touches it, saying, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava," for the Soma-cart is indeed sacred to Viṣṇu.
Or rather, two under-hollows are dug out.

The oblation-holder (havirdhāna) is indeed the head of the sacrifice; those four hollows which are here in the head—these two here and those two there—it is these very ones that he thus makes. Therefore, he digs out the under-hollows.

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the Asuras buried spells and secret charms (*valaga*) in these worlds, thinking, "In this way we shall surely overcome the gods."

The gods indeed desired to win that back. With these [verses], they dug out the *kṛtyā* and the *valagas*. For when one digs up a *kṛtyā*, it becomes powerless and futile; in the same way, if any hateful rival here digs *kṛtyās* and *valagas* into this place, he digs them up again by this act. Therefore, he digs the *uparavas*. He digs beneath the front part (*prauga*) of the southern *havirdhāna* cart.
He takes up the spade with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. The significance of this sacrificial formula is the same [as before]. For this spade is indeed a woman; therefore he says, "Thou art a woman."
He traces around those [spots] with a spade one span in length, saying:
"Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases. For the spade is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rakṣases.
Now, regarding these two [altars] in front:
one should first trace around the southern one of those two, then the northern one of the two behind, then the southern one of the two behind, and finally the northern one of the two in front.
Now they say otherwise:

one should first trace around the northern of the two western [altars], then the southern of the two eastern ones, then the southern of the two western ones, and then the northern of the two eastern ones; or alternatively, one may trace them all together in order. However, one should trace around this very one last of all, which is the northern of the two eastern ones.
He digs them just as they were previously marked out and just as before.

With the words, "Thou art great, of great wealth," he thus praises and magnifies them. When he says, "Thou art great, of great wealth," he means, "Speak a great word for Indra. Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice, and the Soma-cart (havirdhāna) belongs to Viṣṇu; thus he makes it belong to Indra. Therefore he says, "Speak a great word for Indra."

"With 'The Rakṣas-slayer, the Valaga-destroyer'— for these are dug for the destruction of the Rakṣases and the Valagas— and 'Belonging to Viṣṇu'— for speech belongs to Viṣṇu in the two Havirdhāna sheds."
He throws them out exactly as they were dug up, saying:

"I cast out this worm (valaga) which an outsider or a courtier has buried for me. Whether it be an outsider or a courtier who buries a magical spell (kṛtyā) as a worm, he thus casts those very things out.
"Here I dig up that charm which an equal or an unequal has buried for me"— whether an equal or an unequal buries a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) as charms, he digs those very things up with this [formula].
"Here I dig up that charm which my kinsman or my non-kinsman has buried for me"— whether it be a kinsman or a non-kinsman who buries the *kṛtyā* and the charms, he thereby digs them all up.

"Here I cast out that charm which a kinsman or a stranger has buried for me"—whether it be a kinsman or a stranger who buries the *kṛtyā* and the charms, he thereby casts them out; saying "I cast out the *kṛtyā*," he finally throws it away, and thus he casts out the *kṛtyā*.
He should dig them to the depth of an arm's length;

for this is the interior, and by means of the interior he thus confounds the witchcraft. He joins them together crosswise; if he cannot do so crosswise, he may join them even straightwise; therefore these vital breaths are joined together at the further end.
He touches them exactly as they were dug: "Thou art self-ruling, the slayer of rivals;

thou art all-ruling, the slayer of the arrogant; thou art people-ruling, the slayer of demons; thou art universal-ruling, the slayer of enemies. This is indeed a blessing for this ritual act; he thereby invokes a blessing.
Then the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer touch [the two poles].

The Adhvaryu stands at the southern one of the front pair, and the sacrificer at the northern one of the rear pair. The Adhvaryu asks, "O Sacrificer, what is here? He replies, "Auspiciousness. The Adhvaryu says in a low voice, "May that be ours together."
Now, the Adhvaryu stands to the south of the two rear [stones], and the sacrificer to the north of the two front ones.

The sacrificer asks, "Adhvaryu, what is here? and he replies, "A blessing. The sacrificer says, "May that be mine. When they thus touch one another, they thereby make their vital breaths (prāṇas) companions; therefore these vital breaths are in close union with one another. Now, as to why he replies "A blessing" when asked: he speaks only what is auspicious in human speech; therefore, when asked, he replies, "A blessing. Then he sprinkles [the stones]; for there is indeed one purpose for sprinkling: he thereby makes them pure (medhya).
He sprinkles them with the formula:

"You are the slayers of Rakṣases, the slayers of secret spells. For they are indeed slayers of Rakṣases and slayers of secret spells; he sprinkles them saying, "I sprinkle you, who belong to Viṣṇu," for they indeed belong to Viṣṇu.

Then, those sprinkling waters which remain, he pours them into the pits; thus he places those very waters that are in the vital breaths (prāṇas) therein, and therefore these waters are in these vital breaths.

He pours it out with the formula, "I pour you out, the Rakshas-killers, the charm-killers, belonging to Vishnu. Then he spreads the sacrificial grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward; thereby he places those very hairs which are in the vital breaths, and for that reason these hairs are on these vital breaths.

He spreads [the grass] with the formula: "I spread you, the slayers of Rakṣases, the destroyers of spells, belonging to Viṣṇu. Then he covers the sacrificial grass over [the altar] as if it were his own body; for these [blades] are indeed his hair.
Then he places the two pressing-boards;

"I place you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu," for these are indeed his two jaws. Then he heaps earth around them; "I heap around you two, the Rakṣas-slayers, the Valaga-slayers, belonging to Viṣṇu"—he thus makes them firm and not loose.
Now, the pressing-skin is cut out;

it is entirely red, for this is indeed its tongue. As to why it is entirely red, it is because this tongue is, as it were, red. He places it down with the formula, "Thou art Vaiṣṇava," for it belongs to Viṣṇu.
Then he brings down the pressing-stones.

The stones are indeed his teeth; thus, when they press with the stones, it is just as if one were chewing with one's teeth. He sets them down with the words, "Ye belong to Viṣṇu," for these belong to Viṣṇu; this is the head of the sacrifice that has been restored.
His belly indeed is the *sadas*;

therefore they consume [the sacrificial food] in the *sadas*, for whatever one eats here, all that is established in the belly. And because all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) sat down (*asīdan*) in it, it is called the *sadas*. These very Brahmins of various lineages sit in it, being of the nature of Indra by their deity.
In the middle of that [sadas] he erects a post of Udumbara wood.
The Udumbara is indeed food and vigor; the sadas is his belly. By placing it in the middle, he bestows upon him food from all sides. Therefore, he erects the Udumbara post in the middle.
Now, from that middle stake which is at the rear half of the altar, he strides six steps eastward; he strides a seventh step to the south for the sake of perfection. There he traces around a pit.
He takes up the spade with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. The significance of this sacrificial formula (yajuḥ) is the same [as that of the preceding one]. For this spade is indeed a woman; therefore he says, "Thou art a woman."
Then he traces around the pit with the formula:
"Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases. The spade is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rakṣases.
Then he digs.

He throws up the mound of earth toward the east. Having measured it out together with the sacrificer, he trims the Audumbara post; he places it in front, facing eastward, and he lays sacrificial grass of this same length upon it from above.

Now, the sprinkling waters consist of barley-grains. Water, indeed, is the essence of plants; therefore, plants that are eaten alone do not satisfy. Plants, moreover, are the essence of water; therefore, water that is drunk alone does not satisfy. But when both are mixed together, then they do satisfy, for at that time they possess essence. "One should sprinkle with waters that possess essence"—thus it is said.
The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then all the plants went over to the gods; only the barley did not go over to them.
The gods indeed desired to win that back; with these [grains], they gathered all the plants of their rivals. Because they gathered (ayuvata) them, therefore they are called *yava*.

They said, "Come, let us place that which is the essence of all plants into the barley. They placed that which was the essence of all plants into the barley; therefore, where other plants wither, these (barley) grow on even more, for they had thus placed the essence into them. And in like manner, this sacrificer now excludes all the plants of his rivals by means of these (barley grains); therefore, the sprinkling waters consist of barley.

He scatters barley-grains [with the formula]: "Thou art barley; keep away from us hatred, keep away enmities. There is nothing here that is obscure. Then he sprinkles [the grains]; for the significance of sprinkling is one: he thereby makes them pure.
He sprinkles it, saying, "For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For earth thee! By this, he causes these very worlds to partake of strength and sap; he bestows strength and sap upon these worlds.

Then, those sprinkling waters which remain, he pours them into the pit with the words, "May the worlds, the seats of the fathers, be purified. For a dug-out pit is indeed sacred to the Fathers; he thus makes it pure for sacrifice.

Then he spreads the sacrificial grass, both with the tips pointing eastward and with the tips pointing northward, saying, "Thou art the seat of the fathers. For that part of it which is dug in belongs to the Pitṛs as its deity; thus, just as it would be fixed among plants when dug in, so indeed does it become fixed among these plants.
He raises it with the words:
"Prop up the sky, fill the atmosphere, be firm on the earth! By this, he causes these very worlds to partake in vigor and sap; he bestows vigor and sap upon these worlds.

Then he measures it out: "May Dyutāna Māruta measure thee! He who blows here is indeed Dyutāna Māruta; thus he measures it with him. "Mitra and Varuṇa by their firm law! Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath; thus he measures it with the out-breath and the in-breath.
Then he piles it up with the formula:

"I pile thee up, winning Brahman, winning Kṣatra, winning the increase of wealth. For in the *yajus* formulas, there is indeed much benediction; thus he prays for both Brahman and Kṣatra, both powers. "Winning the increase of wealth"—the increase of wealth is indeed abundance; thus he prays for abundance.
Then he sweeps around it, saying:
