"Strengthen the Brahman, strengthen the Kṣatra, strengthen life, strengthen progeny! This is indeed the blessing for this ritual act; he thereby invokes that very blessing. He performs the sweeping so as to be level with the ground; for either it is above the ground of the pit, or thus it is toward the gods, and in that way the pit does not remain filled with earth.
Then he pours water upon it.

For wherever they cause injury or strike [the earth] while digging it, water is a means of pacification; thus he pacifies it with that pacifying water and unites it with that water. Therefore, he pours water upon it.
Then, having approached it in this manner, he makes [the sacrificer] recite:
"Thou art firm; may this sacrificer be firm in this abode through offspring," or "through cattle. Whatever desire he desires, that desire of his is fulfilled.
Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle, he offers it over the summit, saying:

"O Heaven and Earth, may you be filled with ghee! Thus he causes these two, Heaven and Earth, to partake of strength and sap; he bestows strength and sap upon them. These two, being full of sap and providing sustenance, are what these creatures subsist upon.

Then he lays down the roof-coverings with the formula, "Thou art Indra’s roof-covering," for the sitting-hall belongs to Indra; and with "for all people," for Brāhmaṇas of all lineages sit therein. He places two roof-coverings on both sides, three to the north and three beyond them; these amount to nine. The sacrifice is indeed threefold, and the threefold consists of nine; therefore there are nine.

The *sadas* has its rafters pointing northward, while the *havirdhāna* has its rafters pointing eastward. Indeed, the *havirdhāna* belongs exclusively to the gods; therefore, they do not eat nor do they consume anything there, for this is the exclusive domain of the gods. Should anyone eat or consume anything there, his head would surely fall off. Now, these two—the *āgnīdhra* and the *sadas*—are shared; therefore, they eat and consume there, for these two are shared. Furthermore, the northern direction belongs to men; therefore, the *sadas* has its rafters pointing northward.
"O lover of songs, may these songs encompass you on every side;

may they, increasing after the one who increases, be dear to you as dear things. Indra, indeed, is the lover of songs, and the songs are the people (*viś*); thus he makes this ruling power (*kṣatra*) grow on all sides by means of the people. Therefore, this ruling power is encompassed on both sides by the people.

Then he sews it with the *laspūjanī* needle, saying, "Thou art Indra’s seamstress. Then he makes a knot, saying, "Thou art Indra’s firm [knot]," so that it may not fall apart; thus he seeks out the established ritual action, and in this way, no seizure finds either the Adhvaryu or the sacrificer. He touches it when it is completed, saying, "Thou art Indra’s," for the Sadas is indeed Indra’s.

Then, regarding the two *havirdhāna* sheds: having looked toward the rear half [of the shed], he erects it to the north of the *āgnīdhra*. Half of it should be within the altar (*antarvedi*) and half outside the altar (*bahirvedi*); or even more than half may be within the altar and less than half outside; or indeed the whole of it may be within the altar. Once it is completed, he touches it with the formula, "Thou art Vaiśvadeva. This is indeed Vaiśvadeva, because on the previous day all the gods dwell in it during the *vasatīvarī* waters; therefore, it is Vaiśvadeva.

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asura-Rakṣases. The Asura-Rakṣases assailed them from the south and conquered them at the Sadas. They caused these hearths of theirs to go out—those which are within the Sadas.

In former times, indeed, all these [fires] were burning—just as this Āhavanīya, just as the Gārhapatya, and just as the Āgnīdhrīya. But because they caused them to go down (udavāpayan), from that time on they no longer burn. They hemmed them in toward the Āgnīdhra; they even won half of the Āgnīdhra. Thereupon the Viśve Devās conquered immortality; therefore it belongs to the Viśve Devās.

The gods rekindled them so that they might settle down; therefore, at each pressing (savana), they rekindle them. Therefore, he who is successful should act as the Āgnīdhra priest; for he who is well-known and learned in the sacred texts is successful. Therefore, they lead the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) first to the Āgnīdhra. For from there, all the gods won immortality; therefore, if one should find weakness among those consecrated, he should say, "Lead him to the Āgnīdhra's station," for then he will not be afflicted and will not come to harm. And because all the gods won immortality from there, it belongs to the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadeva).
His Dhiṣṇya hearths are indeed his brothers-in-law;
for those who are brothers-in-law are "the same-ankled" (samaṅka), and these [hearths] are his very own self.
Soma was indeed in heaven, while the gods were here on earth.

Those gods desired, "May Soma come to us; with him, once he has arrived, let us sacrifice. They created these two illusions, Suparṇī and Kadrū—Speech indeed was Suparṇī, and this [earth] was Kadrū. They caused a conflict between those two.
As they were being carried away, the two said, "Whichever of us sees herself further in the distance shall win from the other. "So be it," she replied. Then Kadrū said, "Look ahead!"
Suparṇī said:

"On the far shore of this ocean, a white horse grazes at a post; that I see. "Do you see that very same one? "Yes, I do," she replied. Then Kadrū said: "A hair of his is caught there, and the wind shakes it; that I see."

As for what Suparṇī said—"On the far shore of this ocean"—the ocean is indeed the altar; she thus spoke of the altar itself. When she said, "The white horse grazes at the stump," the white horse is Agni and the stump is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*). And as for what Kadrū said—"Its tail has become entangled; the wind shakes that [tail] over there, and that is what I see"—that was indeed the rope (*raśanā*).
Suparṇī said, "Come, let us fly there to find out which of us two wins. Kadrū replied, "You fly yourself; you shall indeed tell us which of us two wins."
Suparṇī flew away.
It happened exactly as Kadrū had said. When she had returned, he addressed her, saying, "Have you won, or have I? She replied, "I have. This is the explanation of the Suparṇī-Kadrū legend.
Kadrū said: "I have indeed defeated you;
that Soma is in heaven. Bring it from there for the gods, and with it, ransom yourself from the gods. "So be it," she replied. She created the meters, and Gāyatrī brought the Soma from heaven.
He was indeed placed between two golden Kushas.

They, with razor-sharp edges, struck him at every twinkling of the eye; they were indeed consecration and austerity. These Gandharvas, the guardians of Soma, protected him—these are the Dhiṣṇya fires, these are the Hotṛ-offices.
He cut off one of the two ears of Kuśī and gave it to the gods; that became the consecration (dīkṣā), and by means of it the gods were consecrated.
Then he cut off the second rib;
he gave it to the gods. By means of that, the gods undertook austerity; the Upasads are austerity, for the Upasads are indeed austerity.
With a *khadira* tree he indeed tore at Soma;

therefore it is called *khadira*. Because he tore (*akhidat*) with it, the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *khadira*, as is the wooden sword (*sphya*). He took it away from Acāvāka while he was guarding it; thus Acāvāka was deprived of it.
Indra and Agni extended him along;
for the procreation of offspring, therefore the Acāvāka priest belongs to Indra and Agni.

Therefore, those who have been initiated guard the king, thinking, "Lest they carry him off. For this reason, one should ensure he is well-guarded there; for if they carry him off while he is being guarded, he is indeed lost.

Therefore, students of sacred knowledge protect their teacher, thinking, "May he not carry off our houses, cattle, or food. Therefore, one should desire to guard him well there; for if they carry him away from his protection, he is indeed deprived by that act. By this means, Suparṇī ransomed himself from the gods; therefore they say, "The sacrificer is one who possesses a world of merit."

Indeed, a man, at the very moment of birth, is born with a debt to death by his very self. When he sacrifices, just as Suparṇī ransomed herself from the gods, even so does he now ransom himself from death.
With that [soma], the gods performed the sacrifice.

These Gandharvas, the guardians of the Soma, followed after them; having arrived, they said, "Give us a share in the sacrifice; do not exclude us from the sacrifice; let there also be a portion for us in the sacrifice."
They said, "What will come of that for us? [The other replied,] "Just as we were its guardians there in the next world, so shall we be its guardians here."

"So be it," the gods said. "They are indeed the Soma-purchasers. He thus designates these as the Soma-purchasers for them. Then he said to them: "At the third pressing, an oblation of ghee shall reach you, but not one of Soma; for the drinking of Soma has been taken away from you, and therefore you do not deserve a Soma-oblation. Thus, at the third pressing alone, this oblation of ghee reaches them, but not one of Soma, when he sprinkles the hearths with splinters.
Now, as for what they will offer in the fire:

"It shall pierce you," he said; "when they offer into the fire for you, that shall pierce you. And when they walk back and forth over you while carrying the Soma, "that shall pierce you. When they walk back and forth over them while carrying the Soma, that indeed protects them. Therefore, the Adhvaryu should not pass between the hearths (dhiṣṇyas), for the Adhvaryu carries the Soma; these [hearths] wait for him with gaping mouths. He would fall into their gaping mouths; either Agni would burn him up, or that god who rules over cattle would take offense at him. Therefore, if there should be business for the Adhvaryu in the hall, he should pass only to the north of the Āgnīdhrīya fire.
These very fires are piled up for the protection of Soma alone: the Āhavanīya in the east, the Mārjālīya in the south, the Āgnīdhrīya in the north, and those which are in the Sadas are in the west.

Or they scatter half of them and designate the other half; for they indeed resolved upon this: "Let us scatter half of the food and designate the other half, so that we may recognize that world from which we have come—namely, the world of heaven—and so that we shall not go astray."
By that which they scatter, they become manifest in this world; and by that which they dedicate, they become manifest in yonder world.

They indeed have two names; for they adopted these [names] thinking, "We have not succeeded with these names by which they have carried away our Soma; let us make second names for ourselves. They made second names, and by them they succeeded with those from whom their Soma-drinking had been taken away; then they caused them to participate in the sacrifice. Therefore they have two names. For this reason, a Brahmin, when his efforts are unsuccessful, should take a second name; he who, knowing thus, takes a second name, certainly succeeds.

When he offers in the fire, he offers among the gods; therefore the gods exist. And when they consume [the portions] in the Sadas, he offers among men; therefore men exist. And when the Nārāśaṃsa cups sit in the two Havirdhāna sheds, he offers among the fathers; therefore the fathers exist.
Those creatures indeed that were not included in the sacrifice perished;

in this very same way, he now causes these creatures that have not perished to share in the sacrifice: after men come the domestic animals, after the gods come the birds, the plants, and the trees—whatever exists here, all that is thus made to share in the sacrifice. Both these, the gods and men, together with the ancestors, used to drink together; this is that "drinking together" (sampā). Formerly they drank together while still visible, but nowadays they do so while invisible.
Verily, he who undergoes consecration undergoes it for the sake of the whole;

for he undergoes it for the sake of the sacrifice, and this whole world follows after that sacrifice. Having gathered together that sacrifice for which he undergoes consecration, he releases this whole world.
As for why he offers the Vaiśarjina oblations:

because he thereby releases everything here, they are called Vaiśarjina; therefore, whoever has completed his vow should take hold [of the sacrificer], but if he should go elsewhere, he need not pay heed to it. For when he offers these oblations, he thereby releases this entire world.

Furthermore, as to why he offers the Vaiśarjina oblations: Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he strode this stride for the gods, which is this very stride of theirs—he planted this earth with his first step, this intermediate space with the second, and the sky with the last. It is this same stride that Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, strides out for him when he makes these offerings; therefore, he offers the Vaiśarjina oblations.

In the afternoon, having strewn the altar (vedi) and having given half of the fast-food (ardhavratam), they enter [the sacrificial hall]; they place the fuel-wood (idhma) upon the fire, prepare the supporting ladles (upayamanī), set the clarified butter (ājya) over the heat, and cleanse the offering-spoons (sruk). The sacrificer places the King Soma in his lap. Then he scatters the earth from the footprint of the Soma-purchase cow behind the Gārhapatya fire; for one stands firm by means of a footprint, and it is for the sake of stability.

Now, some divide it into four parts: one part they place on those kindling-sticks (upayamanī) upon which they take out the Āhavanīya fire; with one part they anoint the axle; one part they place on these kindling-sticks; and one part he scatters behind the Gārhapatya fire.

One should not do it in that way. One should rather scatter [the grass] all at once behind the Gārhapatya fire. Then, having purified the clarified butter, he takes four portions into the Juhū ladle and five portions of speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) into the Upabhṛt ladle, saying: "Thou art light, of all forms; for speckled butter belongs to the Viśvedevas. They hold the ladles while the fuel-wood is blazing.
Then he offers:

"O Soma, you are the one who grants wide protection from bodily hatreds and those caused by others; svāhā! By this very [verse], he establishes himself upon this earth as his foundation; by this, he wins this world.
Then he offers a second oblation to the *aptu* (the one who has reached his goal), saying:

"May the swift one, enjoying the clarified butter, partake of it, Svāhā! For it was indeed with reference to this that he said: "I am afraid of the Rakṣas; may he carry me across so that the destructive Rakṣas do not injure me on the way, making me smaller than my foe, even as a mere drop—for a drop is indeed swift. They then carried him across, making him smaller than his foe, even as a mere drop, for a drop is indeed swift. Out of fear of the Rakṣas, therefore, he offers a second oblation to the *aptu*.

They lift the fuel; they bring forward the supporting ladles. Then he says, "Recite for the fire as it is being carried forth," or "Recite for Soma as he is being led forward"; however, one should simply say, "Recite for the fire as it is being carried forth."

They take up the pressing-stones, the *droṇakalaśa* vessel, the cups for Vāyu, the fuel, the enclosing-sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood, the *prastara* bunch of *aśvavāla* grass, the two separating-blades of *ikṣu* grass—that sacrificial grass is already tied together—and the two omentum-spits, the two cords, the two fire-drills, the churning-stick, and the two *vṛṣaṇa* pieces. Having taken all this, they go forward; thus this sacrifice goes upward.
When they come back, he makes them recite:

"O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knowest all ways; keep away from us the crooked sin; we shall offer to thee the most abundant word of homage. By this he places Agni in front; Agni goes in front, striking away the destructive spirits and demons; thus they carry [the fire] forward in safety and free from destruction. They return and arrive at the Āgnīdhra shed; he deposits it in the Āgnīdhra.
When it has been set down, he offers with the formula:

"May this Agni make room for us; may he go before us, shattering the adversaries; may he win prizes in the winning of prizes; may he, exulting, conquer the enemies, Svāhā! Thus, by this very means, he establishes himself upon that firm foundation in the intermediate space, and by this he wins over this world.
They set down those very pressing-stones and the *droṇakalaśa* and the *vāyavya* cups; then, taking the other [vessels], they come and place them to the north of the *āhavanīya* fire.

The Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters. He first sprinkles the fuel, then the altar, and then they hand him the sacrificial grass (barhis); he places it down with its knot toward the east. Having sprinkled it and poured water over it, he unties the knot. A prastara-bunch of *aśvavāla* grass is tied together; he takes it up. Having taken up the prastara, he spreads the sacrificial grass in a single layer. Having spread the grass, he lays around the enclosing sticks made of *kārṣmarya* wood. Having laid the enclosing sticks, he places two pieces of fuel on the fire. Having placed the two pieces of fuel...

Then he offers: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely; make wide room for our dwelling! Drink the ghee, O thou whose source is ghee; further and further extend the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! By this very [verse], when he offers with it, he establishes himself upon that heaven as his firm foundation, and by this he secures this world, in that he offers with this [verse].
Furthermore, as to why he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu:

having made him (Agni) smaller than his bonds, they have led him across; for a drop is indeed a small thing, and having reached that safety, he makes him what he truly is—the sacrifice itself, for Viṣṇu is the sacrifice. Therefore, he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.

Then, having set down the offering-spoons and touched water, he causes the King (Soma) to enter. Now, as to why he sets down the spoons, touches water, and then causes the King to enter: ghee is a thunderbolt and Soma is seed; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I should injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, the ghee. Therefore, having set down the spoons and touched water, he causes the King to enter.
He spreads a black antelope skin in the interior of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;
upon it he places the Soma, saying, "O God Savitṛ, this is thy Soma; guard it, let them not harm thee! Thus he entrusts it to the god Savitṛ for protection.
Then, having released [the offering], he stands in attendance.

"O divine Soma, as a god you have approached the gods; here do I [approach] men with increase of wealth"—for Agni and Soma place him between their jaws who undergoes consecration, since that offering of initiation belongs to Agni and Viṣṇu. He who is Viṣṇu is Soma; indeed, he who undergoes consecration becomes the sacrificial food of the gods. Thus they place him between their jaws. He is visibly released from the food of Soma when he says, "O divine Soma, as a god you have approached the gods; here do I [approach] men with increase of wealth. "Increase of wealth" (rāyaspoṣa) is indeed abundance; thus he says, "with abundance."

Then he steps out, saying: "Svāhā! May I be released from Varuṇa’s noose. For he who belongs to another is indeed within Varuṇa’s noose; thus, when he says, "Svāhā! May I be released from Varuṇa’s noose," he visibly frees himself from Varuṇa’s noose.
Then, saying "atha," he places a fuel-stick upon the Āhavanīya fire.

"O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee is the guardian of vows"—for Agni is indeed the lord of vows among the gods; therefore he says, "O Agni, guardian of vows, in thee is the guardian of vows. "That body of thine which was in me, let that be in thee; that body of mine which was in thee, let that be in me. As is fitting for us two, O Lord of Vows, let our vows be fulfilled; may the Lord of Consecration favor my consecration; may the Lord of Penance favor my penance. Thus he is visibly released from Agni; he sacrifices with his own true self. Therefore they eat of him at this point, for he has become human; therefore they take his name at this point, for he has become human. Now, as to why they do not eat before this: just as one would not eat of a sacrificial offering once it has been offered, so it is in this case. Therefore, one should not eat of the consecrated person until this point. Then, at this moment, he releases his fingers.
When about to cut the sacrificial post, he offers an oblation with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu; for the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu, therefore he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, as to why he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu:
Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; it is by means of the sacrifice that he thus approaches the sacrificial post. Therefore, he offers with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu.

If he offers with the *sruk* ladle, he offers after taking four spoonfuls of clarified butter; but if with the *sruva* spoon, he offers after dipping with the *sruva* itself, saying: "O Viṣṇu, stride out widely! Make wide room for our dwelling! O you whose source is ghee, drink the ghee! Further on and on the lord of the sacrifice! Svāhā!"
When there is clarified butter remaining, he takes that;
when there is a carpenter’s tool, the carpenter takes that; they come together and choose the sacrificial post (yūpa) which they have approved.
Having touched it thus, he mutters;

or else, standing behind it facing east, he addresses it: "I have gone beyond others, I have not approached others. For indeed, he goes beyond others and does not approach others; therefore he says, "I have gone beyond others, I have not approached others."
"I have found thee nearer than the farther, and farther than the nearer"—he cuts him down nearer than those who are beyond him, namely those who are further away from this one;

"and farther than the nearer"—for he indeed cuts him down farther than those who are below him, namely those who are closer to this one. Therefore he says, "I have found thee nearer than the farther, and farther than the nearer."
"We choose thee for that, O divine Vanaspati, for the sacrifice to the gods.

Just as one might choose someone from among many for a good deed, so that he would be well-disposed toward that task, even so does he choose him from among many for this good deed; thus he becomes well-disposed toward the felling.

"May the gods enjoy you for the sacrifice to the gods"—this is indeed successful, for that which the gods enjoy for a good deed is successful; therefore he says, "May the gods enjoy you for the sacrifice to the gods."
Then he touches it with the *sruva* spoon, saying, "For Viṣṇu, thee!
For the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, for it is for the sake of the sacrifice that he fells it; therefore he says, "For Viṣṇu, thee!"

Then he places a young blade of *darbha* grass between [the axe and the tree], saying, "O herb, protect him! For the axe is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the axe, does not harm him. Then he strikes with the axe, saying, "O hatchet, do not harm him! For the axe is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt, the axe, does not harm him.
The first chip that he cuts off, he takes up;
or he should cut it so that it does not strike against the axle, for they indeed carry it by means of the mind; thus the chariot is not obstructed.

He should cause it to fall facing eastward, for the east is the direction of the gods; or facing northward, for the north is the direction of men; or he may wish to obstruct it from the southern direction, for that is indeed the direction of the ancestors; therefore, he should wish to obstruct it from the southern direction.
As it is being felled, he addresses it with the mantra:

"Do not scratch the sky; do not injure the mid-region; be united with the earth. For that which they cut for the sacrificial post becomes a thunderbolt (*vajra*); therefore, when this thunderbolt is being felled, these worlds tremble. He thus pacifies it for these very worlds, so that, being pacified, it does not injure these worlds.

When he says, "Do not scratch the sky," he means "Do not injure the sky"; "do not injure the atmosphere"—in this there is nothing hidden; "be born from the earth" means "be in harmony with the earth. And when he says, "For this sharp axe has led you forth for great good fortune," it is indeed this sharp axe that leads him forth.

Then he makes an offering upon the stump. [He does this] thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits and demons rise up after this. Ghee is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, by means of the thunderbolt, he drives away the destructive spirits and demons, so that the destructive spirits and demons do not rise up after this. Furthermore, ghee is seed; he thus places seed in the trees, and from that seed, the trees are produced.
He offers the oblation with the mantra:
"From this, O divine Vanaspati, sprout forth with a hundred shoots; may we sprout forth with a thousand shoots. In this, there is nothing that is obscure.
He causes it to be worn;
it should be as long as he originally caused it to be worn.
One should shave [the hair] to the extent of five cubits;
for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; therefore, one should shave [the hair] to the extent of five cubits.
One should shave [the hair] around it to the extent of six cubits.
There are six seasons in a year; the year is the thunderbolt, and the sacrificial post is the thunderbolt. Therefore, one should shave [the hair] around it to the extent of six cubits.
One should have it trimmed to eight cubits.

The Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [fore-part] of the sacrifice is the fore-part. Therefore, one should have it trimmed to eight cubits.
One should have it trimmed to nine cubits;
for the sacrifice is threefold, and the threefold is indeed nine; therefore, one should have it trimmed to nine cubits.
One should cut it to eleven aratnis in length;

for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; since the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt and the post is a thunderbolt, therefore one should cut it to eleven aratnis.
One should cut it to twelve aratnis in length.
There are indeed twelve months in a year; the year is a thunderbolt, and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt. Therefore, one should cut it to twelve aratnis in length.
One should cut it to thirteen cubits in length.
There are indeed thirteen months in a year; the year is the thunderbolt, and the sacrificial post is the thunderbolt. Therefore, one should cut it to thirteen cubits in length.
One should cut it to fifteen cubits.
The thunderbolt is indeed fifteenfold; the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; therefore, one should cut it to fifteen cubits.
The sacrificial post for the Vājapeya consists of seventeen cubits.

Or rather, it should be of unlimited measure; for by means of this very unlimited thunderbolt, the gods conquered the unlimited. In the same way, he now conquers the unlimited by means of this very unlimited thunderbolt. Therefore, it should indeed be of unlimited measure.
It indeed has eight corners.
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [stone] is at the fore-part of the sacrifice, therefore it has eight corners.
He takes up the spade with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. The significance of this Yajus is the same [as before]. For this spade is indeed a woman; therefore he says, "Thou art a woman."
Then he traces around the pit with the formula:
"Here I cut off the necks of the Rakṣases. For the spade is indeed a thunderbolt; with the thunderbolt he thus cuts off the necks of the destructive Rakṣases.

Then he digs. He throws up the mound of earth toward the east; having leveled it with the upper part [of the post-hole], he digs the pit. He places the sacrificial stake (yūpa) in front of that, pointing eastward. He places sacrificial grass (barhis) of this same measure on top of it. Upon that, he places a chip of the stake. He places the top-ring (caṣāla) in front and on the side. Now, the sprinkling waters contain barley grains; the significance of this is the same as before.

He sows barley with the formula: "Thou art barley; bar from us hatred, bar away enemies. There is nothing here that is obscure. Then he sprinkles it; for the significance of sprinkling is one: he thereby makes it pure.

He sprinkles it, saying: "For heaven thee! For the atmosphere thee! For earth thee! The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus says, "I sprinkle thee for the protection of these worlds. It is for the protection of these worlds that he sprinkles it.

Then, those sprinkling waters which remain, he pours them into the pit with the words, "May the worlds, the seats of the Fathers, be purified. For a dug-out pit is indeed sacred to the Fathers; he thus makes it pure for sacrifice.

Then he spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis), both with the tips pointing eastward and with the tips pointing northward, saying, "Thou art the seat of the Pitṛs. For that which is dug in belongs to the Pitṛs as its deity; just as it would be firmly fixed among plants when dug in, so does it become firmly fixed among these plants.

Then he throws in a chip of the sacrificial post. Indeed, that which is the outer chip of trees is their vital energy (*tejas*); therefore, when they plane off the outer chip, the trees then wither, for that is their vital energy. When he throws in the chip of the post, he does so thinking, "May I set it up endowed with vital energy. And why it is this very chip and no other is because this one alone is consecrated by the *yajus*-formula and is fit for sacrifice; therefore he throws in the chip of the post.

He throws it forward with the formula, "Thou art the leader, easy of access for the Unnetṛs. For this [cup] is indeed cut off from the front; therefore he says, "Thou art the leader, easy of access for the Unnetṛs. "Know this one, he shall stand upon thee," he says; for he indeed stands upon it; therefore he says, "Know this one, he shall stand upon thee."

Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle, he makes an offering over the pit, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) and demons (*rakṣas*) should rise up from below. For clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt; thus, by means of the thunderbolt, he drives away the destructive spirits and demons, so that the destructive spirits and demons do not rise up from below. Then, having gone around to the front and sitting facing north, he anoints the sacrificial post. He says, "Recite for the post being anointed!"

He anoints it with the formula: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; and this sacrificial post is, in its essence, the sacrificer. And all this that exists here is honey; thus he brings him into contact with this entire universe. Therefore, as Savitṛ the impeller impels him, he says: "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey."

Then, having fastened the top-ring on both sides, he attaches it with the formula, "For the plants that bear good fruit. This [ring] which is gathered together in the middle is indeed its fruit; for this fruit is attached to the tree crosswise. Thus, he makes it so that it is like a binding that is pressed inward in the middle; therefore, it is gathered together as it were in the middle.
He anoints the Agniṣṭhā pillar to the very end.

The Agniṣṭhā is indeed the sacrificer, and the clarified butter is the essence; thus he anoints the sacrificer with the essence itself. Therefore, he anoints the Agniṣṭhā to the very end. Then he touches the girding around on all sides, and then he says, "Recite for the one being girt!"

It is recited: "With its top you have touched the sky; with its middle you have filled the atmosphere; with its base you have made firm the earth. The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt for the conquest of these worlds. By means of that thunderbolt, he secures these worlds and excludes his rivals from these worlds.
Then he measures [the post] with the verse:

"Those abodes of yours which we desire to reach, where the many-horned, unwearied cows are—there indeed is that highest, far-striding footstep of Viṣṇu, revealed as manifold. With this Triṣṭubh verse he measures it; for the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt and the sacrificial post is a thunderbolt; therefore he measures it with a Triṣṭubh.
Now he fixes the post at the corner facing the fire.

The sacrificer is indeed the post facing the fire, and the fire is the sacrifice; if he were to move the post facing the fire from its place, the sacrificer would move away from the sacrifice. Therefore, he fixes the post at the corner facing the fire right now. Then he sprinkles it all around, then he rubs it all around, and then he pours water upon it.
Then, having approached it in this manner, he makes [the sacrificer] recite:

"Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, from which he has made his vows manifest; Indra’s companion in battle. He who has raised up the sacrificial post has indeed hurled the thunderbolt. When he says, "Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu, from which he has made his vows manifest; Indra’s companion in battle," he thereby says, "Behold the victory of Viṣṇu. Indra is the deity of the sacrifice, and the sacrificial post belongs to Viṣṇu; he thus makes it possessed of Indra. Therefore he says, "Indra’s companion in battle."
Then he gazes at the top-ring (caṣāla):

"The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky. He who has raised up the sacrificial post has indeed hurled a thunderbolt; when he says, "The wise ever behold that highest step of Viṣṇu, like an eye extended in the sky," he thereby says, "Behold the victory of Viṣṇu."
Then he girds it.

He girds it indeed for the sake of non-nakedness; therefore he girds it right here, for it is here that this garment comes to be. He thereby bestows food upon him, for it is here that this food finds its support; therefore he girds it right here.
He encircles it with a triple cord;
for food is threefold, and cattle are food. The father, the mother, and that which is born is the third; therefore he encircles it with a triple cord.
He girds it with the formula:

"Thou art girt; may the divine subjects gird thee around; may wealth of men gird this sacrificer around. By saying, "may wealth of men gird this sacrificer around," he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer.

Then he hides a splinter of the sacrificial post (yūpa) with the formula, "Thou art the son of heaven. For this [splinter] is indeed his offspring; therefore, if there should be a set of eleven posts, he should hide each one in its own place without confusion. For him whose offspring is born thus, the offspring is born attentive and obedient. But for him who hides them confusedly, not each in its own place, his offspring is born bewildered and disobedient. Therefore, he should hide each one in its own place without confusion.
This is indeed made as a means of ascent to the heavenly world:
if there is a splinter from the sacrificial post, this is for the girdle; the splinter from the girdle is for the top-ring; and from the top-ring, he attains the heavenly world.
Now, as to why it is called *svaru*:
because it is cut off from this very [sacrificial post], its own wound (*aru*) becomes its own [healing] substance (*sva*); therefore it is called *svaru*.

That part of it which is dug in—by that he conquers the world of the fathers; then, that which is above the dug-in part up to the girdle—by that he conquers the world of men; then, that which is above the girdle up to the top-ring (caṣāla)—by that he conquers the world of the gods; then, that which is above the top-ring by two or three finger-breadths—the Sādhyas are the gods—by that he conquers their world. He who knows this indeed becomes a sharer of the same world as the Sādhyas, the gods.
He fixes it in the front half.

The sacrificial post is indeed a thunderbolt, and the staff is a thunderbolt; for one strikes after seizing the front half of the staff. This [front half] is the front half of the sacrifice; therefore, he fixes it in the front half.

By means of the sacrifice, the gods indeed won this victory which is theirs; they said, "How can this [victory] of ours be made unattainable by men? Having sucked out the essence of the sacrifice—just as honey-makers would suck out the honey—they drained the sacrifice, blocked it with the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and disappeared. Because they blocked it with that, it is called the *yūpa*. Since wisdom is in front and the speed of thought is in front, he fixes it in the eastern part.
It indeed has eight corners.
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the fore-part of the sacrifice; this [stone] belongs to the fore-part of the sacrifice, therefore it has eight corners.
The gods used to throw that [fire] after [the victim], just as some even now throw it after, thinking, "The gods did so"; then the Rakṣases drank up the sacrifice along with it.
Those gods said to the Adhvaryu:

"Offer the very splinter of the sacrificial post; then this [post] will be made 'well-said' (svagākṛta), and thus the Rakṣases will not spring up after the sacrifice, for this is indeed the raised thunderbolt."

Thus the Adhvaryu offered the very splinter of the sacrificial post; at that time, it was as if this [post] had been consecrated with the *svagā* call, and so the Rakṣases did not drink after the sacrifice, thinking, "This is indeed the raised thunderbolt."

In the same way, he now offers this very splinter of the sacrificial post (*yūpa-śakala*). Thus, it becomes consecrated with the *svagā* call; and so the Rakṣases do not follow after and drink up the sacrifice. For this [sacrifice] is indeed the raised thunderbolt. He offers it, saying: "May your smoke go to heaven, may your light go to the sky; fill the earth with ashes, svāhā!"

As great as the altar is, so great is the earth. The sacrificial stakes are indeed thunderbolts; thus, by means of these thunderbolts, he secures this very earth and excludes his rivals from it. Therefore, there is a set of eleven stakes, and there is a twelfth, the *upaśaya* (the lying-by stake), which is fashioned smooth; he places it to the south. As to why there is a twelfth *upaśaya*: [it is for the sake of completeness].

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases. Now, those [stakes] which are set up are like an arrow that has been shot; with such an arrow, one either strikes down [the enemy] or one does not strike him down. Or they are like a staff that has been struck; with such a staff, one either strikes him down or one does not strike him down. But this twelfth stake which lies ready is like an arrow drawn back but not yet released; it is like a raised weapon that has not yet been hurled. This is the thunderbolt (vajra) raised on the right side for the purpose of driving away the destructive spirits and Rakṣases. Therefore, there is a twelfth stake lying ready.

He deposits it with the formula: "This is thy place on earth; thy animal is one from the forest. For both the animal and the sacrificial post belong to the forest; thus he assigns to him specifically an animal from the forest, and thereby this [post] becomes possessed of an animal. Regarding this, they say that the setting up of the eleven posts is for the sake of the morrow's Soma-pressing; however, some indeed set them up already today, saying, "They set up the post for the sake of the morrow's pressing, so that it may be ready for the morrow's pressing. And so it is said.

One should not do it in that way. He should erect the post right at the Agniṣṭha pillar; for having erected this post, the Adhvaryu does not pass by it until the encircling with the cord. Indeed, they remain that night without being encircled. That is a matter of reproach. For they erect the post for the sake of cattle, and they immolate the cattle in the morning; therefore, he should erect it only in the morning.

Whichever [post] should be to the north of the *agniṣṭha*, that one he should erect first, then the southern one, then the northern one, and finally the one on the southern side; in this way, it becomes oriented toward the north.
Moreover, they say otherwise:
one should first erect the southern post from the Agniṣṭha, then the northern, then the southern, and finally the northernmost; thus his ritual action is completed towards the north.
That which is the longest should be on the southern side;
then the one shorter than that, and then the one shorter still on the northern side; thus it becomes wider toward the north.

Then they erect the wife’s sacrificial post for the wives. Indeed, it is for the sake of completeness that the wife’s post is erected; he then immolates an animal for Tvaṣṭṛ. For Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed, and thus he (the sacrificer) now transforms that emitted seed. It has testicles, for he who has testicles is a procreator; therefore it has testicles. He should not complete the sacrifice; he should release it after the fire has been carried around it. If he were to complete it, he would bring about the end of his offspring; thus he releases his offspring. Therefore he should not complete it; he should release it after the fire has been carried around it.
The sacrificial animal and the sacrificial post are indeed one.

For they never immolate an animal without the sacrificial post. Now, as to why it was so: at first, the animals did not submit to this [post] when they were about to become food, just as they have now become food; for just as this two-footed human stands upright, even so did those two-footed ones move about, standing upright.
Then the gods saw this thunderbolt:

that sacrificial post (yūpa) which they had raised up; out of fear of it, they cowered, and thereby they became four-footed, and thereby food came into being—just as this food exists for living beings. For indeed, these [beasts] stood still for him; therefore, they immolate the victim at the sacrificial post alone, and never without the sacrificial post.

Then, having brought forward the victim and churned the fire, he binds it. As to why it is done in this way: in the beginning, the animals were not at all willing to become the sacrificial offering for him; however, now that they have become the offering, they are offered into the fire. The gods hemmed them in, and being thus hemmed in, they did not submit.

They said, "These people do not know the course of this [fire] when they offer oblations into it, nor do they know this foundation. Let us obstruct them from this very foundation, churn out fire, and offer fire into the fire; then they will understand: 'This indeed is the course of the oblation, this is the foundation; one offers the oblation into fire. Then they will come down [to us], and then they will be well-disposed toward the sacrifice."

Having hemmed them in and churned out fire, they offered fire into fire; they understood: "This indeed is the course of the oblation, this is its foundation; it is truly into fire that one offers the oblation. Then they descended [into the water], and thereafter they became well-disposed toward the sacrifice.

In the same way, having restrained the victim and churned the fire, he offers fire into the fire; for he knows: "This indeed is the course of the oblation, this is its foundation; they say that the oblation is offered into the fire. Thereupon he descends [to the victim], and thereupon he becomes well-disposed toward the sacrifice. Therefore, having brought the victim near and churned the fire, he binds it.

Regarding this they say: "One should not perform the preparatory rite (upākaraṇa), nor should one churn the fire; rather, having taken the rope, one should go straight up to the horse, address it, and yoke it. But one should not do it in that way; for if one were to act thus, it would be as if one intended to perform something contrary to the sacred law (adharma). Therefore, one should proceed in this very manner.
Then, taking a blade of grass, he performs the introductory rite with the formula,
"Possessing a second, may he restrain [the enemy]," for one who has a second is indeed powerful.

He takes up a blade of grass. "Thou art the assistant," he says, for a second person indeed assists; therefore he says, "Thou art the assistant. "The divine subjects have approached the gods," he says; for these cattle are indeed the divine subjects. When he says, "The divine subjects have approached the gods," he thereby means, "They have stood still for the gods."
"The most excellent carriers, the Uśijas"—for the gods are indeed wise; therefore he says, "the most excellent carriers, the Uśijas."
"O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, rest in the wealth!

Tvaṣṭṛ indeed rules over cattle, and cattle are wealth; when the gods said to Tvaṣṭṛ—who was not standing still—'Come near and join us,' that is what he means when he says, "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, rest in the wealth!"
"May the oblations be sweet for thee! he says;
for when they submitted themselves to him, thinking, "We shall become the sacrificial offering," therefore he says, "May the oblations be sweet for thee!"

"O Revatīs, rejoice! For cattle are indeed wealthy; therefore he says, "O Revatīs, rejoice. "O Bṛhaspati, hold fast the riches! Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and the riches are the cattle. When these [cattle] were not standing still, the gods enclosed them on the far side by means of the Brahman alone; thus they did not escape. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encloses them on the far side by means of the Brahman alone; thus they do not escape. Therefore he says, "O Bṛhaspati, hold fast the riches. Having made a noose, he fastens it; now follows the ritual for the tethering itself.
Having made a noose, he binds it [to the sacrificial post] with the formula:
"O divine oblation, I bind thee with the noose of Ṛta. For this rope belongs to Varuṇa; thus he binds him with the very noose of Ṛta. In this way, this rope belonging to Varuṇa does not harm him.
"Be bold, O man! he says.
Indeed, no man was able to be bold toward him at first; but when he fastens this divine oblation with the noose of *ṛta*, then the man becomes bold toward it. Therefore he says, "Be bold, O man!"
Then he fastens [the victim]:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I fasten thee, acceptable to Agni and Soma. Just as when taking the oblation for a deity one specifies it for that deity, even so does he here specify it for these two deities. Then he sprinkles it; for the significance of sprinkling is one and the same: he thereby makes it pure.

He sprinkles it with the formula, "From the waters, from the plants! He thereby makes it sacrificially pure from that very source from which it originates; for when it rains here, then the plants are born, and by eating the plants and drinking the water, this sap originates; from sap comes semen, and from semen come animals. Thus, he makes it sacrificially pure from that very source from which it originates and from which it is born.
"May your mother permit you, may your father permit you"—for he is born from both his mother and his father;

thus, from the very source from which he is born, he thereby makes him pure for sacrifice. "May your brother born of the same womb permit you, may your friend of the same herd permit you"—by this he says, "I take hold of you with the permission of that which is your birth. "I sprinkle you, acceptable to Agni and Soma"—thereby he makes him pure for sacrifice for those two deities for whose sake he takes hold of him.

Then he takes hold of it with the formula, "Thou art the drinker of water," whereby he makes it pure within; then he sprinkles it from below with, "May the divine waters make it palatable; may the oblation for the gods be well-tasted," whereby he makes it pure on all sides.

Then he says, "Recite for Agni as he is being kindled. Having poured the northern libation and having gone around so as not to let the two ladles touch, he anoints the victim with the *juhū* ladle. The northern libation is indeed the head of the sacrifice, and here the victim is the sacrifice; thus he restores the head to the sacrifice itself. Therefore, he anoints the victim with the *juhū*.

He anoints it on the forehead with the words, "May thy breath unite with the wind"; on the shoulders with, "May thy limbs [unite] with those worthy of sacrifice"; and on the hips with, "May the lord of the sacrifice [unite] with his blessings. By this, he says: "Obtain that desire for which they immolate the animal."

This indeed belongs to the victim being immolated. "The breath has entered the wind; obtain that which your breath shall enter the wind"—this is what he says. "With limbs worthy of sacrifice"—for they sacrifice with his limbs; "obtain that which they shall sacrifice with your limbs"—this is what he says. "He, the lord of the sacrifice, [obtains] the blessing"—for by this he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer; "obtain that which they shall invoke a blessing for the sacrificer through you"—this is what he says. He sets down the two offering-spoons, and then he causes the announcement for the *pravara* (the choosing of the Hotṛ); the significance of that is the same as before.
Then he causes the second announcement to be made.

For there are two Hotṛ-priests here; he causes the announcement for the Maitrāvaruṇa, but he chooses the Sacrificer himself, saying, "Agni is the leader of the divine clans," for Agni is the mouth of the deities; therefore he says, "Agni is the leader of the divine clans. "And this Sacrificer [is the leader] of men," for he is subordinate to that one on whose side he sacrifices; therefore he says, "And this Sacrificer [is the leader] of men. "May their household-fire shine undisturbed, may they both live through two winters!"—by this he means: "May their household-fires be free from affliction for a hundred years."
"May you two unite in riches, but not in bodies," he says. He means this: "Unite only in riches, but not even in bodies.

For if they were to unite even in bodies, Agni would burn up the sacrificer. When he offers in the fire, he thereby gives that [offering] to Agni. Then, whatever blessing the officiating priests invoke for the sacrificer here, Agni fulfills all of that for him. Thus, they unite only in riches, but not in bodies; therefore he says, "May you two unite in riches, but not in bodies."
Now, when the Hotṛ has proceeded and sits down upon the Hotṛ’s seat, having sat down, he gives the impulse; being impelled, the Adhvaryu takes up the two offering-spoons.
Then they proceed with the Āprī verses. Now, as to why they proceed with the Āprīs:

he who is consecrated (dīkṣita) gathers the sacrifice together with his whole mind and his whole self, and he desires to carry it forth; his self becomes, as it were, emptied. They replenish him with these Āprī verses. Because they replenish him, they are called Āprīs; therefore they proceed with the Āprīs.
These, indeed, are the eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*).

There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, and the self (*ātman*) is the eleventh, in which these vital breaths are established. A person is indeed of this extent; thus they cause his entire self to swell. Therefore, there are eleven fore-offerings.

Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt for the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*)," and "Prompt, prompt! at every fourth fore-offering (*prayāja*), pouring together [the butter] as he proceeds with ten fore-offerings. Having performed the ten fore-offerings, he says, "Bring the *śāsa*"; indeed, they call the knife the *śāsa*.
Then he takes a splinter from the sacrificial post (*yūpa*).

Having first anointed it with the *juhū* ladle, he touches the forehead of the victim with it, saying, "Anointed with ghee, may you two protect the cattle. For the splinter of the post is indeed a thunderbolt, the *śāsa* (the wooden knife) is a thunderbolt, and the clarified butter is a thunderbolt; having thus gathered this entire thunderbolt together, he makes it his protector, thinking, "Lest the destructive spirits (*nāṣṭrā*) and demons (*rakṣas*) should harm him. He then buries the splinter again, saying, "May this be your recognized corner," as he hands over the *śāsa*. He sets down the two ladles.
Then he says, "Recite for the fire being carried around!

Taking up a firebrand, the Āgnīdhra carries the fire around it. Now, as to why he carries the fire around: he thus encloses it with fire so that no destructive spirits or demons may touch it; for Agni is the repeller of the demons, therefore he carries the fire around it. He carries it around it at the very spot where they roast it.
Regarding this they say:

"One should again take up that same firebrand, or else, having churned out another fire right there, they should cook it on that; for this [fire] is indeed the Āhavanīya, yet it is not truly so, because if they were to cook what is uncooked upon it, it would be for that purpose, or if they were to offer what is cooked upon it, it would be for that purpose."
One should not do it in that way;

for what he does when he carries fire around it (paryagni) is as if it were already swallowed. It would be just as if one were to take back what has been swallowed, pick it out, and hand it over to someone else—that is how it would be. Therefore, they should crush the embers from this very firebrand (ulmuka), and upon them they should cook this [offering].
Then, taking a firebrand, the Āgnīdhra goes forward in front;

he thus places Agni in front so that Agni, driving away the destructive spirits and demons, goes before them, and they lead the animal through a place free from danger and destruction. The Pratiprasthātṛ takes hold of it with the two omentum-spits, the Adhvaryu takes hold of the Pratiprasthātṛ, and the sacrificer takes hold of the Adhvaryu.

Regarding this they say: "The sacrificer should not touch him, for they lead him away to death; therefore he should not touch him. However, one should indeed touch him; for they do not lead him away to death whom they lead away for the sake of the sacrifice; therefore he should indeed touch him. If he were not to touch him, he would exclude himself from the sacrifice; therefore he should indeed touch him. Thus it becomes touched indirectly: the Pratiprasthātṛ [touches] by means of the two omentum-spits, the Adhvaryu [touches] the Pratiprasthātṛ, and the sacrificer [touches] the Adhvaryu; in this way it becomes touched indirectly.

Then, from the strewn altar, the Adhvaryu takes two blades of grass; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "O Hotṛ, give the precept for the oblations to the gods"—this is the formula for the Vaiśvadeva portion in the animal sacrifice.

Then he causes [the sacrificer] to recite: "O wealthy one (Revati), prosper the sacrificer! Vāc is indeed Revati; because she speaks much, by that speech Vāc is "wealthy. When he says, "Enter into what is dear," he means, "Enter into safety. When he says, "From the wide mid-air, in harmony with the divine Vāta," the Rakṣas roams through the mid-air, rootless and cut off on both sides, just as this man, rootless and cut off on both sides, roams through the mid-air. By saying, "In harmony with the divine Vāta, from the wide mid-air," he means, "Being in agreement with Vāta, protect him from the mid-air. Thus he speaks when he says, "From the wide mid-air, in harmony with the divine Vāta."

"Sacrifice with the self of this oblation," he says; he thereby says to Speech, "Sacrifice with the self of this uninjured oblation. "Be united with his body," he says; he thereby says to Speech, "Be united with the body of this uninjured oblation."

Now, when they cut him up there, he throws down a blade of grass in front [of the victim] with the words, "O wide one, place the lord of the sacrifice on the wider [sacrifice]. He thereby strews sacrificial grass for him so that the oblation may not be spilled. Whatever of him is spilt here while being cut up, that settles upon this [grass]; thus it does not come to naught.

Then they return and sit facing the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "Lest we be witnesses while this one is being slaughtered. They do not strike it with a blow from above, for that would be human; rather, they turn its head toward the west, for that belongs to the Pitṛs. Having covered its mouth, they either lay it down on its side or hang it up. He does not say, "Kill! Slay! for that would be human; he says, "Slaughter it! It has gone to the gods," for it is indeed among the gods that it goes; therefore he says, "It has gone."

When they pierce him [the sacrificial animal], he offers before the immolation with the words, "Svāhā to the gods! Then, when he says, "The victim is immolated," he offers again with, "To the gods, Svāhā! Some gods have their *svāhā*-utterances first, while others have their *svāhā*-utterances later; it is these very gods whom he thus gratifies. Both classes of gods, being gratified, carry him to the heavenly world. These two oblations are for the sake of the victim; if he so desires, he may offer them, but if he so desires, he may also disregard them.
When he has declared, "The animal has been consecrated," then the Adhvaryu says, "O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife! and the Neṣṭṛ leads up the wife, carrying the water for washing the feet.

He makes her recite: "Homage to thee, O Ātāna! For the Ātāna is indeed the sacrifice, since they stretch out the sacrifice; therefore, the sacrifice is the Ātāna. Now, she who is the wife is the hind part of the sacrifice; he is about to propitiate the sacrifice by making her face eastward. Thus he makes amends to that very sacrifice, and so the sacrifice does not harm her. Therefore he says, "Homage to thee, O Ātāna!"

"Go forward, unassailable!"—by this he means, "Go forward, free from rivals. "Along the streams of ghee, along the paths of Truth"—by this he means, "Go straight forward. "O divine waters, carry us pure; well-served among the gods, may we be well-served as those who serve"—by this he purifies the waters themselves.

Then the wife touches the breaths of the victim with water. As to why she touches the breaths with water: the oblation of the gods is indeed living, and that of the immortals is immortal; yet when they quiet it and when they dissect it, they kill the victim. Water, however, is the breaths; thus she places those breaths into it. In this way, the oblation of the gods becomes truly living, and that of the immortals becomes immortal.
Now, as for why the wife touches [the fire]:
the wife is indeed a woman, and from a woman these creatures are born; he thus causes him (Agni) to be born from this woman. Therefore the wife touches [it].

He touches [the various parts of his body]: "I purify thy speech," he says to the mouth; "I purify thy breath," to the nostrils; "I purify thy sight," to the eyes; "I purify thy hearing," to the ears; "I purify thy navel," to that undefined breath; "I purify thy penis," or "I purify thy anus," to that breath which is behind. Thus he bestows the vital breaths and sets them in motion. Then, having gathered [his feet] together, he says, "I purify thy footsteps and thy movements. For one stands firm by means of the feet; it is for the sake of stability that he thus establishes him.

Then, with whatever water remains—whether half of it or however much there may be—the sacrificer and [the two priests] first sprinkle him from the head; they thereby place the vital breaths within him and cause him to move forward from that point.
In that they make [it] harsh and establish it, water is peace; therefore, with water, as peace, you two appease it, and with water, you two join it together.

They sprinkle him with: "May your mind swell; may your speech swell; may your breath swell; may your eye swell; may your ear swell. Thus they restore his vital breaths, thus they enliven them. [They sprinkle] with: "Whatever in you is harsh, whatever is solid—may that swell; may it grow firm."
Now, as for that which they make cruel and that which they establish—the waters are peace;

therefore, with those waters, you two appease it by means of peace; with those waters, you two join it together; "may that be purified for you," thus saying, you two make it pure; "for the sake of days and nights," thus saying, they pour out [the water] behind the animal.
Now, as for why they make it harsh and why they establish it— thinking, "Lest these days and nights be unappeased"— therefore, they pour water behind the animal with the words, "To the waters."
Then they turn the animal over onto its back.

He places a blade of grass between [the animal and the sword], saying, "O plant, protect it! For the sword is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt-sword does not harm him. Then he applies the sword, saying, "O axe, do not harm it! For the sword is indeed a thunderbolt; thus this thunderbolt-sword does not harm him.
That which is the known support, with that he places [the stone];
for it is consecrated by the Yajus and is thus fit for sacrifice. Of the blade of grass, he holds the tip in his left hand at the vital breaths, and he takes the base with his right hand.
When it swells,
he anoints both sides from where this blood emerges with the formula, "Thou art the portion of the Rakṣases," for this blood is indeed the portion of the Rakṣases.

He stands over it, saying: "I stand over this Rakṣas; I strike down this Rakṣas; I lead this Rakṣas into the lowest darkness. Thus, by means of the sacrifice itself, he strikes down the destructive Rakṣases. As for the fact that it is rootless and cut off on both sides: rootless indeed and cut off on both sides is this Rakṣas as it roams about in the intermediate space, just as this man, being rootless and cut off on both sides, roams about in the intermediate space. Therefore, it is rootless and cut off on both sides.
Then they pull out the omentum.

With it he covers the two omentum-roasting spits, saying, "O Heaven and Earth, may you be covered with ghee! Thus he causes these two, Heaven and Earth, to partake of strength and sap; he bestows strength and sap upon them. Endowed with sap and fit for sustenance, these creatures subsist upon them.
The two omentum-spits are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.

For when the gods first immolated a victim, as it was being dragged toward the north, its marrow fell downward; from that this tree was born. Because it fell downward as it was being dragged, it is called *kārṣmarya*. By means of that very essence, he thus completes him and makes him whole; therefore the two omentum-spits are made of *kārṣmarya* wood.
He lets it soak;

he heats it over the animal-cooking fire, and thus it becomes cooked here as well. The Āgnīdhra takes up a firebrand, and they go along behind the Cātvāla pit. They come and arrive at the Āhavanīya fire. The Adhvaryu throws this blade of grass into the Āhavanīya with the words, "O Vāyu, for the drops!"—for this is the kindling-stick for the drops.
Then, standing on the north side, he heats the omentum.

For he is about to pass beyond the fire; having gone around to the south, he intends to cook it. He thus propitiates the fire for him. Thus, this fire does not harm him as he passes by. Therefore, standing on the north side, he heats the omentum.

They carry it between the sacrificial post and the fire. As for why they do not carry it across [the middle]: "Lest we should join the sacrifice with something uncooked by carrying it along the same path as other oblations"; and as for why they do not carry it outside: "Lest they should place it outside the sacrifice by carrying it past the front of the post. Therefore, they carry it between the post and the fire; having gone around to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ cooks it.

Then, having taken up clarified butter with the *sruva*-ladle, the Adhvaryu makes an offering over the omentum, saying, "May Agni accept the clarified butter, Svāhā! Thus these drops of his, being cooked and made into oblations accompanied by the cry of *Svāhā*, reach Agni.

Then he says, "Recite for the drops. He recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops. As to why he recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops: rain indeed has its starting point here [on earth], for from here Agni wins the rain; by means of these drops he wins those drops, and thus these drops rain down. Therefore, he recites verses addressed to Agni for the drops when the oblation is cooked.

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "It is cooked; proceed. Taking up the two ladles, the Adhvaryu steps across, calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, and says, "Prompt for the oblations consecrated with *svāhā*! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering.
Having offered the omentum, he first bastes it with clarified butter, and then with the speckled butter.

Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus indeed baste the speckled butter first, saying, "The speckled butter is the vital breath. Regarding this, a Caraka-Adhvaryu once reproached Yājñavalkya for doing so, saying: "This Adhvaryu has surely excluded the vital breath; the vital breath will abandon him."
He used to look at his arms and say:

"These two arms have turned grey; where indeed has the word of the Brāhmaṇa gone?"—one should not heed such [a thought]. For this is the final fore-offering (prayāja). In the case of a Haviryajña, at the final fore-offering, one first bastes the *dhruvā* ladle, for he is about to offer the first two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*) from it. Or rather, here he is about to offer the omentum (*vapā*) first; therefore, he should first baste the omentum, then the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*). As for why he does not baste the animal itself, it is so that he shall not baste what is uncooked. In that he bastes the omentum, by that very act his entire animal becomes basted. Therefore, he should first baste the omentum, then the clotted butter.
Then he spreads a layer of clarified butter;

then he places a fragment of gold; then, while cutting off the omentum, he says, "Recite for the omentum and the fat of the goat for Agni and Soma"; then he places a fragment of gold; then he pours clarified butter over it twice from above.

Now, as to why there are two pieces of gold on both sides: they indeed strike the victim when they offer it into the fire; gold is immortal life, so he establishes himself in immortal life, and thus he rises from there and thus he lives. Therefore, there are two pieces of gold on both sides. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the omentum and the fat of the goat for Agni and Soma," but he does not say "it has been set forth"; rather, he says "it has been set forth" once the *prasava* (impulse) has occurred, and he makes the offering when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered.

Having offered the omentum, he makes the two omentum-roasting spits meet and throws them after [the offering], saying: "Svāhā! Go to the Maruts of the upward sky! He does this so that these two [spits] do not remain here as those by which they have roasted the omentum.
As to why they proceed with the omentum:

for whichever deity they immolate the animal, it is that very deity whom they gratify with this sacrificial essence (medha). When that deity has been gratified by this sacrificial essence and has become pacified, she desists from the subsequent oblations while they are being cooked; therefore, they proceed with the omentum.
Then they sprinkle themselves at the *cātvāla* pit.

For they do something cruel when they quiet the victim and when they dissect it; water is a means of pacification, so they appease it with water as a means of pacification, and they heal it with water. That is why they sprinkle themselves at the *cātvāla*.

He offers a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belonging to the same deity as the animal victim. As to why he offers the sacrificial cake: rice and barley are indeed the essence (medha) of all animals; with that very essence he thus provides for it and makes it complete. Therefore, he offers the sacrificial cake.

Now, as for why, after performing with the omentum, he performs with this cake: they extract this omentum from the middle; verily, from the middle he thus supplies him with this essence, making him complete. Therefore, having performed with the omentum, he performs with this cake. This indeed is its bond of connection, wherever this animal cake is offered subsequently.
Then he instructs the slaughterer:
"Make it move three times; of that which has moved three times, make the heart the last part," for the sacrifice is threefold.

Then he instructs the slaughterer: "If they ask you, 'O slaughterer, is the oblation cooked?', say simply, 'It is cooked. If they say, 'Sir, it is not cooked; it is not cooked,' [then respond accordingly]."

Then, having dipped the *juhū* ladle into the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), the Adhvaryu goes out and asks, "O slaughterer, is the oblation cooked? "It is cooked," he replies. "That belongs to the gods," the Adhvaryu says in a low voice.
As for why he asks this:
the oblation of the gods must indeed be cooked, not uncooked; for the slaughterer knows whether it has been cooked or remains uncooked.

Now, as to why he asks, "Shall I proceed with the boiled [milk]?"—if it has not been boiled, it becomes boiled as an oblation for the gods; it becomes boiled for the sacrificer, and thus the Adhvaryu remains blameless, while the sin falls upon the slaughterer. He asks three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. And as to why he says, "That belongs to the gods": that which is boiled belongs to the gods; therefore he says, "That belongs to the gods."
He sprinkles the heart first.

The heart is indeed the self, the mind; the speckled butter is the vital breath. Thus he places the vital breath in the self, in the mind. In this way, it becomes the very life of the gods as their oblation—the immortal among the immortals.
He pours the clarified butter over it, saying:
"May your mind unite with the mind; may your breath unite with the breath. He does not utter "svāhā," for this is not an oblation; they then remove the animal from the fire.
They carry it behind the *cātvāla* pit, between the sacrificial post and the fire.

Now, as to why they do not carry it along the middle—by which they would carry the other oblations—it is because [the victim] is already cooked; "lest we should approach the sacrifice with what is mangled and mutilated limb by limb. And as to why they do not carry it outside along the front of the sacrificial post—they would thereby place it outside the sacrifice. Therefore, they carry it between the sacrificial post and the fire. Having set it down to the south, the Pratiprasthātṛ cuts off the portions. The Plakṣa branches serve as the northern covering; he cuts off the portions upon them. Now, as to why the Plakṣa branches serve as the northern covering...

In the beginning, when the gods first immolated a victim, Tvaṣṭṛ vomited it out from its head, thinking, "They shall not immolate it thus. For animals belong to Tvaṣṭṛ; this very thing is the brain in the head and the marrow in the spine. Therefore, that [part] is as if vomited, for Tvaṣṭṛ vomited it out; therefore one should not eat it, for it is what has been vomited by Tvaṣṭṛ.
His sacrificial essence (medhas) fell downward; it became this lord of the forest (vanaspati).

The gods beheld it, and therefore it is called "Prakhya"; for "Prakhya" is indeed the name of the Plakṣa tree. By means of that very sacrificial essence, he thus completes him and makes him whole. Therefore, branches of the Plakṣa tree serve as the northern covering (uttarabarhis).

Then he spreads a layer of clarified butter (ājya) in both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt* ladles, as well as in the *vasāhomahavanī* vessel and the *samavattadhānī* vessel; then he places two pieces of gold (*hiraṇyaśakala*) into both the *juhū* and the *upabhṛt*.

Then he recites the invitatory formula for the Manotā deity over the oblation. Now, as to why he recites the invitatory formula for the Manotā over the oblation: all the deities indeed gather around the animal being immolated, thinking, "He will mention my name! He will mention my name! For the animal is the oblation for all the deities; the minds of all those deities are woven into the animal. It is these very [minds] that he thus gratifies. In this way, the minds of the deities, having gathered together, become not in vain. Therefore, he recites the invitatory formula for the Manotā over the oblation.
He first cuts a portion from the heart itself.

Now, although it is in the middle [of the body], he first cuts from the heart; for the heart is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), since it is from there that this vital breath moves upward. The animal is indeed the vital breath; as long as one breathes with the vital breath, so long is one an animal. But when the vital breath departs from him, then, having become mere wood, he lies there useless.
The heart, indeed, is the victim.

He cuts from that [victim] first from its own self; therefore, even if some other portion of the victim should be omitted, one should not heed it, for he has already cut from that entire victim when he cuts from the heart first. Therefore, although it is situated in the middle, he cuts from the heart first, and then according to the preceding order.
Then [he cuts] from the tongue;
for it stands out from the fore-part. Then from the breast, for that is from there. Then from the single-moving foreleg, then from the two sides, then from the thin part, then from the two kidneys.
He divides the rectum into three parts: he cuts off the thick part for the Upayaḍs;
having divided the middle part into two, he places it in the Juhū ladle; and the thin part goes to the Tryaṅgas. Then, from the single-portioned buttock, he cuts off this much into the Juhū.
Then, regarding the *upabhṛt* ladle:

having cut the rectum from the three-part foreleg and having divided it into two parts, he makes the offering; then, from the three-part hindquarter; then he places two pieces of gold upon it, and finally he pours clarified butter over it.

Then he takes the fat-oblation. He says, "Thou art gliding," for the fat indeed glides; therefore he says, "Thou art gliding. "May Agni cook thee," he says, for Agni indeed cooks this; therefore he says, "May Agni cook thee. "May the waters blend with thee," he says, for the waters indeed bring together this essence from the limbs; therefore he says, "May the waters blend with thee."

"By the rush of the wind, thee!"—for he who blows here blows along the intermediate space; it is indeed for the intermediate space that he draws [the butter]. Therefore he says, "By the rush of the wind, thee!"
"With the speed of Pūṣan. This, indeed, is the speed of Pūṣan, for he draws [the cup] for him; therefore he says, "with the speed of Pūṣan."
"Lest it be distressed by the heat," he says;
for this indeed is the heat, and from it he draws [the juice]; therefore he says, "Lest it be distressed by the heat. Then, subsequently, he twice pours clarified butter over it.
Then he stirs it with his side or with the *vāsī* knife, saying, "May the two be separated. By this, he drives away the destructive *rakṣas* demons from here.

Now, if there is any broth remaining, he pours it into the *samavattadhānī* (the vessel for the cut-off portions); he throws into it the heart, the tongue, the breast, the ribs, the kidneys, and the rectum; then, from above, he twice pours clarified butter over them.
Now, as to why there are two pieces of gold on both sides:

they indeed strike down this animal when they offer it into the fire; gold is immortal life. Thus he becomes established in immortal life; thus he rises up from there, and thus he comes to live. Therefore, there are two pieces of gold on both sides.

Now, as to why he cuts obliquely from the left foreleg and the right hindleg, and from the right foreleg and the left hindleg: therefore this animal moves its feet obliquely; for if he were to cut straight across, this animal would move its feet straight on. Therefore he cuts obliquely. Furthermore, as to why he does not cut from the head, nor from the shoulders, nor from the backbone, nor from the two hind-thighs.

In the beginning, the Asuras indeed immolated an animal sacrifice. The gods, out of fear, did not venture near it. This Earth then said to them, "Do not be so bold as to seize this; I shall be the supervisor over this for you, so that they will proceed with it exactly as they ought."
She said:

They offered up one portion of the oblation and left the other remaining. That which they left remaining were these very portions (the *avaddānāni*). Then the gods allotted three limbs for the Sviṣṭakṛt; therefore there are three limbs. Now the Asuras cut off from the head, the two shoulders, the spine, and the two hind thighs; therefore one should not cut from those. And because Tvaṣṭṛ struck at the spine (*anūka*), therefore one should not cut from the spine. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for the oblation of the goat to Agni and Soma"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the oblation of the goat to Agni and Soma. He does not say "it has been set forth" (*prasthitam*); when the Soma has been pressed, he says, "It has been set forth."
Between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*, he offers the *vasāhoma* (fat-oblation).

From here indeed this sacrificial essence has risen upwards; from it, these creatures subsist upon this sap of the earth. The *vasāhoma* is the sap of heaven, and the sacrificial essence is the sap. By means of sap, he thus intensifies the sap; therefore, this sap, even while being consumed, is not exhausted.

Now, as for why he offers the fat-oblation between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*: this earth is one half-verse and yonder sky is the other half-verse; between heaven and earth is the intermediate space. It is indeed for the intermediate space that he offers; therefore, he offers the fat-oblation between the two half-verses of the *yājyā*.

He offers with the formula: "O drinkers of ghee, drink the ghee! O drinkers of fat, drink the fat! You are the oblation of the atmosphere; Svāhā! With this sacrificial formula addressed to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva), he offers; for the atmosphere belongs to the All-gods. Since by means of it these creatures move about in the atmosphere, both breathing out and breathing in, it therefore belongs to the All-gods. He offers at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* with whatever portions have been cut into the *juhū* ladle.

Then, dipping the *juhū* ladle into the clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*), he says, "Recite for Vanaspati"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt for Vanaspati," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.
