Now, as to why he offers to Vanaspati: he thereby makes this very sacrificial post (*yūpa*), which is a thunderbolt (*vajra*), a sharer in the sacrifice. Vanaspati is indeed Soma; he thus makes the animal itself into Soma. And as to why he offers between the two oblations: he thereby pervades both of them; therefore he offers between the two oblations.

Then, as he brings together the portions that are in the *upabhṛt* ladle, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt [the Hotṛ] for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.

Now, with what remains of the fat-oblation, he sprinkles the quarters, saying: "To the quarters, the fore-quarters, the intermediate quarters, the sub-quarters, the upper quarters—from the quarters, svāhā! The fat-oblation is indeed essence; thus he bestows essence upon all these quarters. Therefore, this essence is found in every direction.

Then he touches the victim. This is now the time for touching; as for why he touches it earlier, it is because he fears that those who wait upon him might seize the victim. However, if he does not fear seizure, he may touch it right then.
"The breath belongs to Indra; may it settle in every limb; the out-breath belonging to Indra is deposited in every limb.

Thus, when he is cut limb by limb, he joins him together with the in-breath and the out-breath. "O divine Tvaṣṭṛ, let much of thine come together, that which is of one mark, even though it has become of various forms"—by this he makes him whole again. "May thy mother and father rejoice after thee as thou goest to the gods for help, O friend"—thus, at the very place where they have offered for him, having made him whole, he unites him; so his self becomes whole in yonder world.
There are indeed three sets of eleven in the sacrificial animal:

eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*), eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*), and eleven concluding offerings (*upayaja*). There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, and ten vital breaths—namely, the out-breath (*prāṇa*), the up-breath (*udāna*), and the through-breath (*vyāna*). Such is the person who is the highest among animals, after whom all other animals follow.
Regarding this they say:
"What is performed in the sacrifice by which the vital breath becomes auspicious for all the limbs?"
When he divides the rectum into three parts—
the rectum is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa)— this very breath, stretched out forward, moves along it.
When he divides the rectum into three parts—
one third for the *upayaj* offerings, one third in the *juhū* ladle, and one third in the *upabhṛt* ladle— by that means the vital breath becomes auspicious for all the limbs.

But indeed, one should sacrifice an animal that brings him prosperity, if it should be lean. Whatever remains of the omentum of the belly, he should thrust that into the anus. The anus is indeed the vital breath; this breath extends forward, and along it this breath moves. The animal is indeed the vital breath; for as long as one breathes with the breath, so long is one an animal. But when the breath departs from him, then, having become mere wood, he lies useless.
The cow is indeed the animal;

the fat is indeed the sacrificial essence (medhas). Thus he brings it into contact with the sacrificial essence. And if it is fleshy, then it has already attained the sacrificial essence of its own accord.
Then he takes the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya). For this consists of two things: clarified butter and curd. A pair, indeed, is a productive union; thus, this productive union is brought about.

Therefore he proceeds with the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). The after-offerings are indeed cattle, and the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) is milk; thus he places this milk into the cattle. This milk is deposited within the cattle, for the speckled butter is breath, and the speckled butter is food, and breath is indeed food.
Therefore, he performs the after-offerings (anuyāja) in front;

he thereby places that vital breath which is here in front. He offers the supplementary offerings (upayaj) behind; he thereby places that vital breath which is here behind. Thus these two vital breaths are established on both sides: that which is above and that which is below.
Now, one of these two offers the *vaṣaṭ* call for both:

for the Adhvaryu and for him who performs the after-offerings (*upayaj*). And because he performs the after-offerings while [the main sacrifice] is being performed, they are called "after-offerings" (*upayaja*). Furthermore, when he performs the after-offerings, he thereby causes procreation; for he performs them from behind, and from behind offspring are produced from a woman.
He offers the supplementary oblations:
"Go to the ocean, svāhā! The ocean is indeed water, and water is seed; he thus pours forth seed.
"Go to the intermediate space, svāhā!
Indeed, offspring are born after the intermediate space; thus he causes them to be born after the intermediate space.
"Go to the god Savitṛ, svāhā!"—Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he brings this [offspring] forth.
"Go to Mitra and Varuna, Svaha!
Mitra and Varuna are indeed the out-breath and the in-breath; he thus places the out-breath and the in-breath within his offspring.
"To day and night, hail!
For it is after day and night that creatures are born; thus he causes them to be born after day and night.
"Go to the meters, svāhā!
There are indeed seven meters, seven domestic animals, and seven wild animals; he thus causes both of these to be produced.
"Go to heaven and earth, svāhā!

Prajāpati, having created the creatures, enclosed them within heaven and earth; thus these creatures are enclosed by heaven and earth. In the same way, this sacrificer, having created the creatures, now encloses them within heaven and earth.

Then he performs the supplementary offerings (*atyupayaja*). If he were not to perform these supplementary offerings, there would be only as many creatures as were created at the beginning, and they would not procreate; but because he performs the supplementary offerings, he causes them to be born. Therefore, these creatures are born again and again in succession.
He performs the *atyupayaj* offering with the formula, "Go to the sacrifice, svāhā! The sacrifice is indeed water, and water is seed; thus he pours out seed.
"Go to Soma, svāhā! Soma is indeed seed; he thus pours out seed.
"Go to the divine sky, svāhā!
The divine sky is indeed the waters; the waters are seed; thus he pours forth this very seed.
"To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!"—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed this earth, for she is the foundation; thus he causes him to be born toward this very foundation.
Then, when he wipes his face, he says, "May my mind enter my heart. In this way, the sacrificer does not exclude himself from the sacrifice.
Then they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tail.
The tail is indeed the hind part; from the hind part of a female, offspring are born. Thus, when they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tail, he causes that very offspring to be born.
He cuts from the interior for the wives of the gods;
for from the interior offspring are born to a woman. He cuts from above for Agni Gṛhapati; for from above the male mounts the female.
Then they go to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) with the heart-spit.

For when the victim is being immolated, its heart becomes dry; from the heart comes the heart-spit. Now, that part which they cut from the cooked flesh is fit for enjoyment; therefore, one should roast it on the spit only after cutting it off. When the victim has been moved three times, he plucks out the heart and places it as the final portion upon the spit.
Then he offers the heart-spike.

He should not throw it away on the earth, nor into the waters. For if he were to throw it away on the earth, it would pierce the plants and the trees with its sharp point; and if he were to throw it away into the waters, it would pierce the waters with its sharp point. Therefore, he should neither throw it on the earth nor into the waters.

Having descended into the water, he should hide [the sacrificial post] where there is a junction between the dry and the wet; but if he should be weary of descending, he should pour out a vessel of water in front of the sacrificial post and hide it where there is a junction between the dry and the wet, saying, "Do not harm the waters nor the plants. Thus he does not harm the waters nor the plants. He says, "O King Varuna, from every bond, from that release us! When they say 'O inviolable one,' when we swear by 'O Varuna,' from that release us! Thereby he releases him from every bond of Varuna, from everything belonging to Varuna.
Then he consecrates it with mantras.

"May the waters and plants be friendly to us; may they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. For when they proceed with this [rite], the waters and plants indeed withdraw from him and stand apart; however, by this he makes a covenant with them, and so they enter him again. This is the expiation performed in that case. He does not perform it for the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, nor for the one dedicated to Agni; rather, he performs it for the barren cow (*vaśā*) which is the *anūbandhyā*. For the entire sacrifice concludes with her. Thus, when they proceed with the barren cow, the rite of the heart-spit for both the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma and the one dedicated to Agni is thereby accomplished.
Prajāpati, having created offspring, felt as if he were emptied out.
Therefore his offspring turned away; his offspring did not remain for his prosperity or for the eating of food.
He reflected: "I am the intermediate space;

I have been emitted for this desire of mine, yet that desire of mine has not been fulfilled. My offspring have turned away from me; my offspring have not remained for the sake of prosperity and the eating of food."
That Prajāpati reflected:
"How indeed might I replenish myself, so that my creatures might return to me and remain for my glory and for the sake of food?"
Desiring offspring, he performed worship, exerted himself, and practiced austerities.

He beheld this set of eleven offerings; having sacrificed with these eleven, Prajāpati replenished his own self again, and offspring returned to him and remained with him for the sake of prosperity and the eating of food. Having sacrificed, he became truly more prosperous.
For this purpose, one should sacrifice with the set of eleven victims.

Thus, indeed, he prospers with offspring and cattle; offspring turn toward him and remain for his glory and for the eating of food. Having sacrificed, he becomes more prosperous; it is for this purpose that one sacrifices with the set of eleven victims.
He first immolates an animal for Agni.
For Agni is the mouth of the deities, the progenitor; he is Prajāpati, and he is indeed the sacrificer. Therefore, it is dedicated to Agni.

Then follows the offering to Sarasvatī. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech Prajāpati then replenished himself; speech returned to him; he made speech subject to his own will. In this same way, this sacrificer now replenishes himself by means of speech; speech returns to him; he makes speech subject to his own will.
Then [he offers] to Soma.

Soma is indeed food; by means of food, Prajāpati then replenished himself, food turned back toward him, and he made food subordinate to himself. Verily, by this very act, he now replenishes himself with food, food turns back toward him, and he makes food subordinate to himself.
Now, as to why it follows that of Sarasvatī:
Sarasvatī is indeed speech, and Soma is food; therefore, he who is consecrated by means of speech becomes truly an eater of food.
Then follows the offering to Pūṣan. Pūṣan is indeed cattle;

by means of cattle, Prajāpati then replenished himself again. Cattle turned back toward him; he made cattle subject to his own self. Verily, by means of cattle, this sacrificer now replenishes himself; cattle turn back toward him; he makes cattle subject to his own self.
Now follows the offering to Bṛhaspati.

Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; by means of the Brahman, Prajāpati thereby replenished himself again, the Brahman turned back toward him, and he made the Brahman favorable to himself. Verily, by this [offering], he now replenishes himself through the Brahman, the Brahman turns back toward him, and he makes the Brahman favorable to himself.
Now, as to why there is [an offering] following that to Pūṣan:

Pūṣan is indeed cattle, and Bṛhaspati is the Brahman. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the most bold toward cattle, for they have been placed within him, deposited in his mouth; therefore, having given away all that, he wanders about clothed in skins.

Now follows the Vaiśvadeva offering. All indeed are the Viśve Devāḥ; with everything, Prajāpati thereby replenished himself again; everything turned back toward him; he made everything subject to himself. Verily, by this [offering], he now replenishes himself with everything; everything turns back toward him; he makes everything subject to himself.

Now, as to why it follows that which belongs to Bṛhaspati: Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman, and the All-Gods are this entire universe; he thus makes the Brahman the mouth of this entire universe. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa is the mouth of this entire universe.

Then [he offers] to Indra. Indra is indeed power and vigor; by means of that very power and vigor, Prajāpati nourished himself again. Power and vigor returned to him; he made power and vigor conform to his own self. By means of that very power and vigor, this [sacrificer] now nourishes himself; power and vigor return to him; he makes power and vigor conform to his own self.
In that the Vaiśvadeva offering follows it, Indra is indeed the nobility (kṣatra) and the Viśvedevas are the common people (viś); he thus places food before him.

Then [he offers] for the Maruts. The Maruts are indeed the people (*viś*), and the people are the abundance (*bhūman*). By means of that abundance, Prajāpati then replenished himself; abundance turned toward him, and he made abundance subject to himself. Verily, by this act, he now replenishes himself with abundance; abundance turns toward him, and he makes abundance subject to himself.
Now, as for the fact that it follows the one dedicated to Indra:

Indra is the nobility (kṣatra) and the All-gods are the common people (viś); the Maruts are indeed the common people. Thus, by means of the common people, he makes this nobility prosper on both sides; so this nobility is made prosperous on both sides by the common people.

Then there is the offering to Indra and Agni. Agni is indeed brilliance, and Indra is sensory power and vigor; by means of both these powers Prajāpati nourished himself again, and both powers returned to him. He made both powers his own limbs. By means of both these powers this sacrificer now nourishes himself, and both powers return to him; he makes both powers his own limbs.
Now follows the Sāvitra [offering].
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, all these desires of his are fulfilled as they are impelled by Savitṛ.
Then he immolates the animal dedicated to Varuṇa at the end;
thereby he releases him from every bond of Varuṇa and from everything pertaining to Varuṇa.
Therefore, if there should be a set of eleven sacrificial posts (*yūpaikādaśinī*),
one should bind the animal dedicated to Agni to the post standing nearest the fire, and then lead up the others in the prescribed order.
If there should be a set of eleven animals,
they should immolate the one dedicated to Agni at the sacrificial post, and the others according to their respective order.
They lead them northward from here;
they lead the one dedicated to Agni first, then the others in their proper order.
They fix them here.
They first fix the one dedicated to Agni on the southern side; then, having led the others further north, they fix them in the same order as before.
Regarding them, where they proceed with the omenta,
they proceed first with the omentum of the one dedicated to Agni, and then with those of the others in their respective order.
Where they proceed with those [oblations],
they proceed first with the one dedicated to Agni, and then with the others in their regular order.
When the head of the sacrifice was indeed cut off, its essence flowed away and entered the waters; by that very essence the waters flow, and it is that flowing essence which they perceive as such.
When he goes for the Vasatīvarī waters, he thereby brings that very essence and places it in the sacrifice; he makes the sacrifice full of essence. Therefore, he goes for the Vasatīvarī waters.
He indeed distributes them at all the pressings;
thus he bestows essence upon all the pressings and makes all the pressings full of essence. Therefore, he distributes them at all of them.
One should indeed draw [the soma] from those that are flowing;
for that is the essence of the sacrifice, therefore one should draw it from those that are flowing.
These [cups] are drawn for protection;
for everything else here that exists, whatever it may be—even this wind that blows—melts away, yet these alone do not melt away. Therefore, one should draw them from flowing waters.

One should take [the draught] by day, thinking, "May I take the essence of the sacrifice while seeing it. Therefore, one should take it by day; for he takes it for him who shines yonder (the Sun). Indeed, he takes it for all the gods, for his rays are all the gods. Therefore, one should take it by day; for he is truly in heaven, and therefore indeed one should take it by day.

Indeed, all the gods come to the house of the sacrificer. He who takes the Vasatīvarī waters before the setting of the sun does so just as one would wait upon a superior person with a prepared dwelling when he is about to arrive; in that same way, they enter this oblation and fast upon these Vasatīvarī waters—this is the Upavasatha.
If the sun should set upon him while the [Soma] has not yet been taken, an expiation is performed there:

if he has previously sacrificed, he should take it from the *nināhya* (the stored Soma); for his [Soma] has already been taken during the day. But if he has not previously sacrificed—if someone who has sacrificed and is either staying near him or has departed—should be present, one should take it from that person’s *nināhya*; for his [Soma] has already been taken during the day.

If he should not find either of these two, he should go forth taking a firebrand; holding it above him, he should take [the water], or he should take it while holding gold above him. Thus, the form of that which shines yonder is produced.
Now, therefore, he takes [the water]:

"These waters are rich in oblation," for the essence of the sacrifice has entered into them; therefore he says, "These waters are rich in oblation. "May the one rich in oblation come hither," for the sacrificer, being rich in oblation, causes him to come hither; therefore he says, "May the one rich in oblation come hither."
"The god is possessed of oblation, the sacrifice.
The sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus, he makes that sacrifice for which he draws [the butter] possessed of oblation. Therefore he says, "The god is possessed of oblation, the sacrifice."
"May Sūrya be possessed of the oblation," he says.
He indeed draws [the cup] for him who shines yonder; for he draws it for all the gods, since all the gods are his rays. Therefore he says, "May Sūrya be possessed of the oblation."

Having brought them, he places them behind the Gārhapatya fire with the formula, "I place you in the seat of Agni whose house is secure," by which he means, "I place you in the seat of Agni whose house is uninjured. Then, when the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma is completed, he carries them around; saying, "Step aside," the sacrificer sits down in front of the two Havirdhāna carts, and he takes up those [spoons].

He goes out by the southern door. He places them on the southern hip [of the altar], saying, "Ye are the portion of Indra and Agni," for he takes them from all the gods, and Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods. Having brought them back again, he places them in front of the wife; then, having gone around behind the wife, he takes them up.
He takes it out by the north;

he places those [bricks] on the northern hip with the formula, "You are the portion of Mitra and Varuṇa. He should not place them thus, for that would be redundant and the ritual symmetry (sampad) would not be achieved. He should rather say, "You are the portion of Indra and Agni"; thus it is not redundant and the ritual symmetry is achieved.

These waters are carried around for protection. Agni is in front, and then these are carried all around; they strike away the destructive spirits and the Rākṣasas. He deposits them in the Āgnīdhra fire-hall with the words, "Thou art the portion of the Viśve Devas"; thereby he causes the Viśve Devas to lie down within them. These indeed are the best of dwellings; therefore they are called *vasatīvarī*. Truly, he who knows this becomes the best of those who dwell.
These indeed are seven sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).

With four he draws [the milk], with one he places it behind the Gārhapatya fire, with one he carries it around, and with one at the Āgnīdhra; thus they are seven. For when the meters born of speech are sevenfold, the *śakvarī* is their ultimate limit. It is for the sake of this perfection that there are seven sacrificial formulas.
They awaken them;

having touched water, they go together to the Āgnīdhra shed; they take the portions of clarified butter (ājya), and having taken the portions of clarified butter, they come and set down the clarified butter.
Then he brings down the King (Soma).
This earth is indeed the foundation, the birthplace of these creatures; it is toward this very foundation that he thus brings him down. He extends him over her; he causes him to be born from her.

He brings it down between [the pressing stones]. The sacrifice is indeed breath; thus he does not place the sacrifice outside of the body. He places it upon the pressing stones facing each other. Soma is the nobility (kṣatra) and the pressing stones are the common people (viś); he thus places the nobility over the common people. As to why they face each other: he thereby makes the common people face the nobleman and speak in his favor. Therefore, they face each other.
He brings it down with the formula, "For the heart thee!

For the mind thee! He says this for the sake of the sacrificer's desire; for by means of his heart and mind, the sacrificer desires that very desire for which he performs the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "For the heart thee! For the mind thee!"

"To the sky thee! To Sūrya thee!"—by saying "To the sky thee! To Sūrya thee," he says, "To the world of the gods thee! And when he says, "To the gods thee! May this sacrifice go upward to the gods among the gods as an oblation," since the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*, he thereby says, "Place this sacrifice upward in the sky among the gods."
"O King Soma, descend upon all these creatures!"—
thereby he brings him down for the sovereignty and kingship over these creatures.
Then, having released [the offering], he stands in attendance.

"May all subjects descend unto thee"—in saying "thou, descend unto all subjects," he acts as if out of order. Soma is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), so he makes the superior and inferior confused; and accordingly, this world is made confused. But here he acts in the proper order, as it was before, when he says, "May all subjects descend unto thee"; thus he causes him to descend with these very subjects. Therefore, when a Kṣatriya approaches, these subjects, the common people (viś), descend to meet him; they wait upon him from below. Having descended, the Hotṛ priest becomes one who is about to recite the morning litany (prātaranuvāka).
Then, while placing the fuel-stick on the fire, he says:

"Recite for the gods who come in the morning! The gods who come in the morning are indeed the meters, and the after-offerings (anuyājas) are the meters. They proceed with the after-offerings, saying, "Prompt for the gods! Sacrifice to the gods!"

Regarding this, some say, "Recite for the gods. But one should not say that; for the gods who come in the morning are the meters, and the after-offerings (anuyājas) are the meters. They proceed with the after-offerings saying, "Prompt for the gods! Sacrifice to the gods! Therefore, one should simply say, "Recite for the gods who come in the morning."
Now, when he places the kindling-stick on the fire, he thereby kindles the metres.

And when the Hotṛ recites the Morning Litany (Prātaranuvāka), he thereby causes the metres to swell again and makes them fresh; for the metres were indeed exhausted by the gods—the gods attained the heavenly world by means of the metres. For here they neither chant nor recite; thus he causes the metres to swell again and makes them fresh. With those metres, being now fresh, they perform the sacrifice. Therefore, the Hotṛ recites the Morning Litany.

Regarding this they say: "Who is the respondent (*pratigara*) for the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*)? The Adhvaryu should remain awake and wait; when he blinks his eyes, that indeed is his response. However, one should not do it that way; even if he feels sleepy, he may sleep as much as he wishes. When the Hotṛ concludes the morning litany, there is a *pracaraṇī* ladle present; having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter into it, he offers an oblation.

When the head of the sacrifice was indeed cut off, its sap flowed away and entered the waters. On the previous day, he brings that [sap] back with the *vasatīvarī* waters; thus, he now reaches whatever sap of the sacrifice remains there.

When he offers this oblation, he spreads out this very essence of the sacrifice and secures it; and those deities for whom he offers this oblation, he thereby gratifies them. Being satisfied and gratified, they bend this essence of the sacrifice toward him.
He offers the oblation.

"May Agni hear my call with the fuel," he says; by this he means, "May Agni hear this of mine; may he recognize it as mine. "May the Waters and the divine Dhiṣaṇās hear," he says; by this he means, "May the Waters hear this of mine; may they recognize it as mine. "May the pressing-stones hear, like those who know the sacrifice," he says; by this he means, "May the pressing-stones hear this of mine; may they recognize it as mine. For the pressing-stones are indeed wise, when he says, "like those who know the sacrifice. "May the god Savitṛ hear my call, Svāhā! he says; by this he means, "May the god Savitṛ hear this of mine; may he recognize it as mine. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he partakes of the essence of the sacrifice.

Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter and moving northward, he says, "O Hotṛ, seek the waters! By saying "O Hotṛ, seek the waters," he means this very thing. Now, when the Hotṛ recites from that point onward, he thereby spreads out this very sap of the sacrifice and secures it; and he also follows after these [waters], thinking, "Lest the destructive, flesh-eating demons (nāṣṭrā rakṣāṃsi) should harm them in the interval."
Then he issues the command:

"O Camasādhvaryu of Maitrāvaruṇa, come hither! O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wives! O Ekadhanins, you [should come]! O Agnīdh, you should attend to the Vasatīvarī waters at the Cātvāla pit with the Hotṛ’s cup!"—this indeed is the formal command.

They go out toward the north, behind the *cātvāla* pit and in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed. They proceed in whichever direction there is water; they indeed go together with their wives, and as to why they go together with their wives: [it is for this reason].
When the head of the sacrifice was indeed cut off, its essence flowed away and entered the waters; the Gandharvas, who were the guardians of Soma, protected it.
Those gods said:
"These Gandharvas here are indeed a source of destruction; how can we bring this essence of the sacrifice here into a place that is free from fear and free from destruction?"

They said, "The Gandharvas are indeed fond of women; let us go with our wives, for the Gandharvas will surely be attached to our wives. Then we shall bring back this essence of the sacrifice to a place free from fear and harm."
They went together with their wives;
the Gandharvas lusted after those very wives, and then they carried away this essence of the sacrifice to a place free from fear and destruction.

In the same way, this [sacrificer] goes forth with his wives; the Gandharvas cling to those very wives, and then he brings back this essence of the sacrifice to a place free from fear and destruction.
He offers water as an oblation.
When this oblation has been offered, this essence of the sacrifice approaches it; he rises up toward it and, having made it manifest, he seizes it.
And, again, as to why he offers this oblation:

he thereby spreads out that very essence of the sacrifice and secures it; he asks for it from the waters, and he gratifies those very deities to whom he offers this oblation; they, being satisfied and pleased, yield up this essence of the sacrifice to him.
He offers the oblation.

"O divine waters, O child of the waters"—for the waters are indeed divine, therefore he says, "O divine waters, O child of the waters. "Whichever wave of yours is fit for the oblation"—by this he means, "whichever wave of yours is worthy of sacrifice. "Powerful, most intoxicating"—when he says "powerful," he means "possessing vigor"; when he says "most intoxicating," he means "most sweet. "Give that to the gods among the gods"—by saying this, he has entreated them; when he says "give that to the gods among the gods," [it is for] "those who drink the pure," for the pure is indeed truth; thus he means "to those who drink the truth. "Of whomsoever you are the portion, Svāhā!"—for this is indeed their portion.
Then he pours this oblation over with the cup of Mitrāvaruṇa, saying, "Thou art a furrower.

Just as a coal might be consumed by fire, even so this oblation becomes consumed by this deity. He is about to pour these waters upon the King (Soma); and since the ghee in the cup of Mitrāvaruṇa is a thunderbolt and Soma is seed, he pours it over [the Soma] lest he should injure the seed, Soma, with the thunderbolt, the ghee. Therefore, he pours it over.

Then he draws [the water], saying, "I draw thee for the imperishability of the ocean. The ocean is indeed the waters; thus he bestows imperishability upon the waters. Therefore, even when such an amount of enjoyment is being consumed, the waters are not exhausted. Following that, they draw the ekadhanas; following those, the pānnejanas.
Now, as to why he draws [the cup] with the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup:

when the sacrifice departed from the gods, the gods then made it go forward by means of the *praiṣas* (directions), caused it to shine forth by means of the *puroruks*, and announced it by means of the *nivit*s; therefore, he draws [the cup] with the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup.
They come forward;

the Agnīdh stands at the pit with the Vasatīvarī waters and the Hotṛ’s cup. He makes them touch one another over the pit—the Vasatīvarī waters and the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup—with the formula: "The waters have united with the waters, the plants with the plants. He thus unites both that essence of the sacrifice which was brought on the previous day and that which is brought today.
Now, regarding this, some indeed say:

When they pour the *vasatīvarī* waters into the Maitrāvaruṇa’s cup, they do so saying, "We thus mix together both that essence of the sacrifice which was brought on the previous day and that which is brought today. But one should not do it in that way; for when he pours them into the *ādhavanīya* jar, it is there that both essences of the sacrifice are mixed. Then he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters into the Hotṛ’s cup from the *nigrābhya* waters. As to why he makes them touch over the *cātvāla* pit: from there, indeed, the gods ascended to heaven; he thus causes the sacrificer to follow along that path leading to the heavenly world.
They come;

the Hotṛ asks him, "O Adhvaryu, hast thou found the waters?"—by this he means to say, "Hast thou found them? He replies to him, "Yea, I have found them; they have bowed down to me"—by this he means to say, "I have found them, and moreover, they have inclined toward me."

If it should be an Agniṣṭoma sacrifice: if there should remain a residue in the *pracaraṇī* ladle sufficient for an oblation, he should offer that; but if it should not be sufficient for an oblation, he takes another fourfold portion of clarified butter and offers it with the verse addressed to Agni: "O Agni, the mortal whom you protect in battles and whom you urge on in the contests for booty—he shall be the master of eternal refreshments, Svāhā! Thus he offers with a verse to Agni. For the Agniṣṭoma is indeed Agni; he thereby establishes the Agniṣṭoma in Agni. He uses a verse containing the word "mortal" (*marta*), for the Agniṣṭoma is commensurate with man. Thus he should offer if it should be an Agniṣṭoma.

If it should be an Ukthya sacrifice, he should touch the middle enclosing-stick; for there are three enclosing-sticks and three Ukthas, and by these the sacrifice is established at that time. But if it should be an Atirātra or a Ṣoḍaśin, he should neither offer an oblation nor touch the middle enclosing-stick; rather, having risen and gone silently, he should enter. Thus he distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order.
The odd and the even become single-units (*ekadhana*).

There are three or five, five or seven, nine or eleven, eleven or thirteen, thirteen or fifteen. This is a pair, a couple, a productive union. Now, that one which remains over exceeds the prosperity of the sacrificer; he indeed is their "single-unit" (*sadhana*) who exceeds the prosperity of the sacrificer. Because he is their "single-unit," they are called *ekadhana*.

Then they sit down around the two pressing-boards. Then he ties a piece of gold to this [pressing-stone]. For this world is twofold, indeed there is no third: truth and untruth; the gods are truth, and men are untruth. Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; [he thinks], "By means of truth may I touch the Soma-stalks; by means of truth may I drive away the Soma. Therefore, indeed, he ties a piece of gold to this [stone].

Then he takes up the pressing-stone. These pressing-stones are indeed made of stone; for Soma is divine, and Soma is in heaven. Indeed, Soma was Vṛtra; those mountains and those stones are his body. By means of that very body he thus completes him, making him whole. Therefore they are made of stone. For they indeed slay him when they press him; they slay him with this [stone], and thus he rises from there, and thus he comes to life. Therefore the pressing-stones are made of stone.

He takes it up with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a giver. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he takes it up. "With the arms of the Aśvins"—the Aśvins are the two Adhvaryu priests; thus he takes it with their very arms, not with his own. "With the hands of Pūṣan"—Pūṣan is the distributor of portions; thus he takes it with his very hands, not with his own. For this [sacrificial post] is a thunderbolt, and no human being is its bearer; therefore, he takes it up by means of these deities.
"He gives (rāvāsi)":

when they press him with this [Soma], he becomes an oblation; when one offers an oblation, then one gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). For he bestows these two things—the oblations and the sacrificial fees—therefore he says, "Thou art a giver."

"Make this sacrifice profound"—for *adhvara* is indeed sacrifice; thus he says, "Make this great sacrifice. "'Most excellently pressed for Indra'—Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says 'for Indra. 'Most excellently pressed'—this means 'most well-pressed. 'With the highest purifier'—the Soma is indeed the highest purifier; therefore he says 'with the highest purifier. 'Full of vigor, full of sweetness, full of milk'—when he says 'full of vigor, full of sweetness, full of milk,' he thereby means 'full of sap.'"
Then he restrains his speech.

For when the gods were performing the sacrifice, they were afraid of an attack from the Asura-Rakṣasas; they said, "Let us sacrifice in a whisper; let us restrain our speech. So they sacrificed in a whisper and restrained their speech.
Then he brings the *nigrābhyā* waters.

He makes him recite over them: "Ye are the Nigrābhya waters, heard by the gods; satisfy me! Satisfy my mind! Satisfy my speech! Satisfy my breath! Satisfy my eye! Satisfy my ear! Satisfy my self! Satisfy my offspring! Satisfy my cattle! Satisfy my troops! May my troops not thirst! For water is indeed sap; it is over these that he invokes this blessing: "Satisfy me in my whole self! Satisfy my offspring! Satisfy my cattle! Satisfy my troops! May my troops not thirst! That which is this Upāṃśusavana stone is Vivasvat Āditya by origin; it is his Vyāna breath.
He measures it out.

For they indeed strike him down when they press [the Soma]; they strike him with this [measure], and thus he rises from there and thus he comes to life. And as to why he measures it out: therefore there is measure among men, and whatever other measure there may be.

He measures it out, saying: "For Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras. Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "For Indra, thee. By saying "accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras," he thereby gives a share to the Vasus and the Rudras following after Indra. By saying "for Indra, thee, accompanied by the Ādityas," he thereby gives a share to the Ādityas following after Indra. By saying "for Indra, thee, the slayer of the adversary," the adversary is indeed the rival; thus he says, "for Indra, thee, the slayer of rivals. This is his special portion (*uddhāra*); just as there is a special portion for the chief, so is this his, apart from the other gods.
"For thee, O Soma-bearer, for the falcon"—with these words he measures out for the Gāyatrī;

"for Agni, thee, the bestower of increase of wealth"—Agni indeed is the Gāyatrī, so he measures out for the Gāyatrī. Since the Gāyatrī, having become a falcon, brought the Soma from heaven, she is therefore the Soma-bearing falcon; by that very power of hers, he measures out this second portion.
Now, as to why he measures five times:
the sacrifice is commensurate with the year, and there are five seasons in the year; he thus obtains it by means of five [measures]. Therefore, he measures five times.
He touches it with the formula:

"O Soma, with that light of yours which is in heaven, which is on earth, and which is in the wide mid-region—with that, make wide room for this sacrificer’s wealth; speak in favor of the giver. For when he first became the sacrificial offering for the gods, he reflected: "May I not become the offering for the gods with my entire self. He then deposited these three bodies of his in these three worlds.
The gods indeed desired to win that [Agni].

By means of this very [rite], they obtained these bodies of his, and he became the complete sacrificial offering for the gods. In the same way, by means of this very [rite], he obtains these bodies of his, and he becomes the complete sacrificial offering for the gods; therefore, he touches him thus.
Then he pours in the *nigrābhya* waters.

The waters indeed slew Vṛtra; by that very power the waters flow. Therefore, nothing whatsoever can stop them as they flow. They went according to their own will, thinking, "For what purpose should we stand still, we by whom Vṛtra was slain? Indeed, all this that exists—whatever there is here, even he who blows here (the wind)—was standing still for Indra.

Indra said, "All this world that stands here belongs to me; therefore, you must stand for me. They asked, "What shall be ours from that? He replied, "The first draught of King Soma shall be yours. "So be it," they said, and they stood for him. As they stood there, he held them down upon his breast. Because he held them down upon his breast (*urasi nyagṛhṇīta*), they are called *nigrābhyās*. In the same way, the sacrificer now holds them down upon his breast. This is their first draught of King Soma, namely when he pours them in together with the *nigrābhyās*.

He pours it out with the words, "Ye are refreshing, ye are Vṛtra-conquering. For the waters are auspicious; therefore he says, "Ye are refreshing. He says, "Vṛtra-conquering," for these [waters] slew Vṛtra. With the words, "The well-wishers of bounty, the wives of immortality," for the waters are indeed immortal. With the words, "O goddesses, lead this sacrifice to the gods," there is nothing here that is obscure. With the words, "Invited, drink of the Soma," they, being invited, partake of the first portion of King Soma.

Now, when about to strike, he should meditate in his mind upon whomsoever he hates, thinking, "I strike this one, not you. For they indeed censure him who kills even a human Brāhmaṇa; how much more so him who kills this divine one? For Soma is indeed divine. They kill him when they press him; they kill him with this [act]. Thus he rises up from there, thus he comes to life, and thus he becomes free from sin. Even if he does not hate anyone, he should at least meditate upon a blade of grass in his mind; thus he becomes free from sin.
He strikes.

"Do not fear, do not tremble"—by this he says, "Do not be afraid, do not tremble; I strike at that one, not at you. "Bestow strength"—by this he says, "Bestow sap. "O two bowls, being firm, be firm; bestow strength"—by this he refers to these two pressing-boards, so some say. But why [should he say this]? For even if one were to break these two boards, these two, heaven and earth, would surely tremble before this uplifted thunderbolt; thus he pacifies it by means of these two, heaven and earth, and so, being pacified, it does not injure him. "Bestow strength"—by this he says, "Bestow sap. "The evil has been struck, not Soma"—by this he strikes away all his evil.
He indeed presses three times;
he gathers three times; he undergoes four suppressions. That makes ten. The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Soma is of the nature of the Virāj; therefore, he completes it ten times.
Now, as to why he goes to the *nigrābha* (the water-drawing):

when this [Soma] first became the sacrificial offering for the gods, it then looked toward these quarters, thinking, "May I be touched by these quarters, by a mate, by my own dear abode. The gods, therefore, touched it with these quarters, by a mate, by its own dear abode, when they went to the *nigrābha*; and in like manner, this sacrificer now touches it with these quarters, by a mate, by its own dear abode, when he goes to the *nigrābha*.

He approaches [the fire] with the words: "From the east, from the west, from the north, from the south—let the quarters run toward thee! Thereby he causes him to come into contact with these quarters, with their union, with their dear abode. With the words, "O Mother, come forth; let us find our kin,"—"Mother" (ambā) indeed means a woman, and the quarters are women; therefore he says, "O Mother, come forth. "Let us find our kin" (samarīrvidāma)—"kin" (arīḥ) means offspring; thus he says, "Let us recognize our offspring. Therefore, even those offspring who are as if far apart recognize one another; that is why he says, "let us find our kin."
Now, as to why he is named Soma:

when he first became the sacrificial offering for the gods, he reflected, "May I not become the offering for the gods with my entire self. He then hid away that body of his which was most dear to him. The gods missed it and said, "Pull it out again; let us have the offering together with this very body! He pulled it out from afar, saying, "This is indeed mine!"—therefore he is named Soma.

Now, as to why it is called *yajña*: they indeed slay it when they press it; then, when they bring it forth, it is born while being extended. Because it is born (*jāyate*), it is therefore *yañja*; for *yañja* is indeed the same as *yajña*. Thus, what is called *yajña* is [derived from] this very word *yañja*.
There he also spoke these words:

"O most powerful god, you indeed shall praise the mortal; O Maghavan, there is no comforter other than you. O Indra, I speak this word to you. Being a mortal, he indeed said this: "You alone shall be our progenitor, and none other than you."

Then they draw the cups from the *nigrābhya* waters. The waters indeed slew Vṛtra; by that very power the waters flow. From those flowing waters he takes the *vasatīvarī* waters; from the *vasatīvarī* waters come the *nigrābhya* waters; from the *nigrābhya* waters they draw the cups. By that very power they draw the cups. From the *hotṛ*-cup [they take them], for the *ṛc* is female and the *hotṛ* is male; from a female indeed these creatures are born. Thus he causes him to be born from this female, the *ṛc*, the *hotṛ*. Therefore, from the *hotṛ*-cup [the cup is taken]; for the *upāṃśu* is his vital breath.
The Vyāna is the Upāṃśusavana stone, and the Udāna is indeed the Antaryāma cup.
Now, as to why it is called *upāṃśu*: the cup named *Aṃśu* is indeed Prajāpati; this [cup] is his breath. Because it is his breath, therefore it is called *upāṃśu*.
He takes it from the *bahis-pavitra* (the outer strainer).

He thereby places the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in him directed outwards; thus this vital breath of his flows outwards. He purifies it with the *aṃśu* stalks, thinking, "May it be purified. He purifies it with six [stalks]; for there are six seasons; he thus purifies it by means of the seasons.
Regarding this they say: "When he purifies with the *aṃśu* cups silently, all the Soma juices are purified by the filter; but by what means then are his *aṃśu* stalks purified?"
He pours them down with the formula:

"O Soma, that which is thy inviolable, watchful name—for that, O Soma, to thee, to Soma, svāhā! Thus, by means of the *svāhā* call itself, his stalks become purified. For this cup is indeed everything, for it is the form of all the pressings.

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack by the Asuras and Rakṣasas. They said, "Let us complete the sacrifice; if the Asuras and Rakṣasas should attack us, our sacrifice shall remain completed."

They completed the entire sacrifice at the morning pressing itself: by means of this very cup (graha) they completed it from the perspective of the Yajus; by the first Stotra, from the perspective of the Sāman; and by the first Śastra, from the perspective of the Ṛc. With that sacrifice thus completed, they proceeded further with the ritual. Even now, this sacrifice is completed in exactly the same way: by this very cup it is completed from the perspective of the Yajus; by the first Stotra, from the perspective of the Sāman; and by the first Śastra, from the perspective of the Ṛc. With that sacrifice thus completed, he proceeds further with the ritual.
He presses it eight times;
for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī—thus, the morning pressing is indeed performed.

He draws it with the formula, "Flow pure for Vācaspati! Vācaspati is indeed the breath; this cup is the breath, therefore he says, "Flow pure for Vācaspati! With the words, "By the shoots of the bull, purified by the hands," he purifies it by means of the shoots of Soma; therefore he says, "By the shoots of the bull. "Purified by the hands"—the hands are indeed the *gabhasti*s; for he purifies it with his two hands.
Then he presses eleven times;
for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh; thus, this midday pressing is performed.

He takes it up with the words, "O God, purify yourself for the gods," for he, being a god, purifies himself for the gods; and with the words, "Thou art the portion of those [gods]," for he is indeed their portion.
Then he presses twelve times;
for the Jagatī consists of twelve syllables, and the third pressing belongs to the Jagatī; thus, the third pressing is thereby performed.

He takes it up [with the words], "Make our nourishments honey-sweet"; he thereby places essence in him and makes him palatable for the gods; therefore, though this [victim] has been slain, it does not rot. Then, when he offers it, he thereby brings it to completion.

"Eight times eight," they say, "one should press [the Soma] for one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is Brahman; thus he indeed becomes possessed of spiritual luster."
That [Soma] has been pressed twenty-four times;

for there are twenty-four half-months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—just so much does he thereby establish.

"Five times five [stotras] he should press for one who desires cattle," they say; for cattle are fivefold, and thus he indeed wins cattle. Or, there are five seasons in the year; Prajāpati is the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. As great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is, so much does he thereby complete. This is the deliberation; however, it is performed in the other way.

Having taken it, he wipes it, thinking, "Lest it drip. He does not set it down, for this is its breath; therefore, this breath moves about while not being set down. If, however, he should perform an act of exorcism, then he should set it down, saying, "I set thee down as the breath of so-and-so! In that way, indeed, there is no longer anything remaining in it. Because he does not release it [from the altar], both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer live long.

Moreover, he may even place it [on the fire] with the formula: "I shut off the breath of so-and-so. Thus, there is nothing in that which he does not set down; by this, he does not disturb the vital breaths.
While still within [the ladle], he utters "svāhā.

For the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Asuras and Rakṣases should strike down this cup of ours before its offering"; so, while it was still within, they offered it with the utterance of "svāhā," and while it was already offered, they offered it into the fire. In the same way, this sacrificer now offers it with the utterance of "svāhā" while it is still within, and while it is already offered, he offers it into the fire.

Then he goes out, saying, "I follow the wide atmosphere. Indeed, the Rakṣas roams through the atmosphere, rootless and severed on both sides, just as this man here is rootless and severed on both sides as he roams through the atmosphere. This Yajus is the Brahman that slays the Rakṣas; by means of this Brahman, he makes the atmosphere free from fear and free from destruction.
Then he chooses a boon.
For the gods indeed strongly desire the offering of this cup; they grant him this boon, thinking, "May he offer this cup quickly. Therefore, he chooses a boon.

He offers it with the formula, "Thou art self-made. This cup is indeed his vital breath; it is made by himself and born from himself, therefore he says, "Thou art self-made. "For all powers, celestial and terrestrial"—for he is indeed born of himself for the sake of all these creatures. "May Tvaṣṭṛ [fashion] thy mind"—the mind is Prajāpati; thus he says, "May Prajāpati fashion thee. "Svāhā! To thee, O auspicious one, to Sūrya!"—thereby he performs the *svāhā*-utterance first and then addresses the supreme deity.
He has indeed offered this to yonder sun that shines there.

This sun is everything; thus he makes him the most excellent of all. Now, if he were to make the deity inferior and place the *svāhā*-utterance above it, it would indeed be superior to yonder sun; therefore, he makes the *svāhā*-utterance inferior and the deity superior.
Then, having offered, he wipes the ladle upwards;

he thus bestows the vital breath upon him directed away from himself. Then, with his hand turned upwards, he wipes towards the east on the middle enclosing-stick; he thus bestows the vital breath upon him directed away from himself, saying, "For the gods who drink the rays of light, thee!"
Indeed, he has offered this oblation in that very orb which shines yonder;
those who are its rays are the gods who drink the light-particles (marīcipas), and it is them he thus gratifies. These gods, being gratified, carry him up to the heavenly world.
Now, of this very cup.

There is neither an invitatory verse (anuvākyā) nor an offering verse (yājyā); he offers it with this mantra alone, and by this it becomes for him possessed of an invitatory verse and possessed of an offering verse. Now, if he should practice sorcery, let him offer that shoot which is clinging to his arm, or his chest, or his garment, saying: "O divine shoot! For whomsoever I curse thee—that is the truth! By the crushing blow, he is struck down—phaṭ! Just as one who is being beaten might run away, so does this [shoot] spill from those being pressed; thus, for him against whom he performs this rite, nothing remains, whether running or not running away. He deposits it with, "Thee for out-breathing (prāṇa)!", for this is indeed his out-breathing.

Some, indeed, place it on the southern half, saying, "For he moves along this direction"; but one should not do so; rather, one should place it on the northern half, for there is no other [direction] beyond this oblation. He places it with the words, "Thee for out-breathing (prāṇa)," for this is his out-breathing.
Then he takes up the Upāṃśusavana stone;

he does not touch it with the fringes of the cloth nor with the filter, for it is as if already cleansed by water. If a stalk of wool should adhere to it, he should brush it away with his hand and set it down facing northward with the words, "For the through-breathing (vyāna) thee!"—for this indeed is its through-breathing.
The out-breath (prāṇa) is indeed his Upāṃśu cup;
the diffused breath (vyāna) is the Upāṃśusavana stone; and the upward breath (udāna) is the Antaryāma cup.

Now, as to why it is called the Antaryāma: that which is the Prāṇa is the Udāna, and that is the Vyāna. When he draws the Upāṃśu cup, he thereby places that outward-turned Prāṇa within him; when he draws the Antaryāma cup, he thereby places that inward-turned Udāna within him. This Udāna of his is thus within the self (antarātman); and because it is within the self, and because by means of it these creatures are held together, therefore it is called the Antaryāma.
He draws it from within the strainer;

he thus places the out-breath (udāna) within him in a backward direction. This out-breath of his is established within the self. By this, even the Upāṃśu cup becomes drawn for him from within the strainer, for these two—the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma—are the same, being the out-breath and the in-breath (prāṇa). By this, moreover, this [cup] of his does not fail among the other cups.
Now, as to why he purifies the Soma with the filter:

when Soma indeed oppressed his own domestic priest, Bṛhaspati, he gave it back to him; through that, he was appeased. Therein, however, there remained a surplus of sin because he had surely directed his mind toward the oppression of the Brahman.
The gods purified him with a strainer;

he, being fit for sacrifice and purified, became the oblation for the gods. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now purifies him with a strainer; he, being fit for sacrifice and purified, becomes the oblation for the gods.
Now, as to why the cups are drawn by means of the *upayāma* (support):

this earth is indeed Aditi; for her is that introductory oblation (*prāyaṇīya-havis*), and that is the *caru* for Āditya. That [oblation] is, as it were, prior to the Soma-pressing. She, this Aditi, desired a share among the gods at the pressing, saying, "Let there be a portion for me even when the pressing has been completed."

Those gods said, "This sacrifice has been assigned to the deities by you; let the cups be drawn for the deities, and let the oblations be offered to the deities. "So be it," he replied. This, then, is his portion at this pressing.
Now, as to why the cups are drawn with a support (upayāma):
this earth is indeed the support; she supports this food for animals, humans, and trees. From here upwards are the gods, for the gods are in heaven.

In that the cups are drawn with the *upayāma* formula, they are thus drawn by means of this very [earth]; and in that he deposits them in the womb, this earth is indeed the womb of all this, for from her these creatures have been born.
The officiating priests indeed carry that Soma, having become seed; for when seed is poured into what is not a womb, it perishes; but when he places it in the womb, he places it in this very [earth].
These two, Prāṇa and Udāna, are indeed his two cups.

Of these two, he offers one after sunrise and the other before sunrise, for the sake of distinguishing Prāṇa and Udāna; thus he distinguishes Prāṇa and Udāna. Therefore, although these two are exactly the same, they are called by different names: "Prāṇa" and "Udāna."
These two cups, indeed, belong to day and night.
Of these two, he offers one after sunrise and the other before sunrise; thus, for the sake of distinguishing day and night, he distinguishes day and night themselves.
The Upāṃśu cup, which is [essentially] day, he offers at night; thus he places the day into the night. Therefore, even when it is mixed with pressed Soma, something of the day is still discernible.
He offers it at night during the middle watch;
he offers it when the sun has risen. He thus places this day within the night; therefore, as that sun rises, it does not burn up these creatures, and by this means these creatures are protected.

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]. "Thou art taken with a support," he says; the significance of "with a support" has already been explained. "Within, O Maghavan, drink the Soma!"—Maghavan is indeed Indra, and Indra is the leader of the sacrifice; therefore he says "O Maghavan. "Drink the Soma!"—this means "Protect the Soma! He says "uruṣya rāya eṣo yajasva" (Save our wealth, O Lord, perform the sacrifice!); "wealth" (rāyas) refers to cattle, so this means "Protect the cattle! "Perform the sacrifice!"—the "desires" (iṣas) are indeed offspring; thus he makes these offspring eager for sacrifice. These offspring, performing sacrifices, move about praising and toiling.

"I place you between heaven and earth; I place the wide atmosphere between; in harmony with the lower and higher gods"—by saying this, he makes it belong to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*). Since by means of this [cup] these creatures move about in the atmosphere, both those that breathe upward and those that breathe downward, it therefore belongs to the All-gods. "O Maghavan, rejoice in the Antaryāma!"—Maghavan is indeed Indra, and Indra is the leader of the sacrifice; therefore he says "O Maghavan. And as to why he draws it "within, within" (*antara-antara*), he thereby says, "I place thee within myself."
Having taken it, he wipes it, thinking, "Lest it drip.

He does not set it down, for this is its out-breath (udāna); therefore, this out-breath moves about without being set down. However, if he should practice sorcery, then he should set it down, saying, "I set down the out-breath of so-and-so!"

If he should set down the *upāṃśu* cup, then he should set this one down; if he does not set down the *upāṃśu*, he should not set this one down. If he should cover the *upāṃśu*, then he should cover this one; if he does not cover the *upāṃśu*, he should not cover this one. As is the ritual procedure for the *upāṃśu*, so it is for this one, for these two—the *upāṃśu* and the *antaryāma*—are identical, being indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the up-breath (*udāna*).

Now, the Carakas indeed offer those two with two separate mantras, saying, "These two, prāṇa and udāna, have distinct powers; we shall thus make his prāṇa and udāna distinct. One should not do it in that way, for they confuse the prāṇa and udāna of the sacrificer; rather, one should offer them silently.

In that he offers with a mantra while whispering, by that very act this [offering] of his also becomes offered with a mantra; why then should he offer silently? For these two, the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma, are the same, being indeed the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna).
With the very same mantra with which he offers the Upāṃśu cup, he offers this one as well:
"Thou art self-made for all powers, celestial and terrestrial; may the mind attend thee, Svāhā! O auspicious one, [be] unto Sūrya!"—the connection of the Yajus has been stated.
Then, having offered the oblation, he wipes the cup downwards;
for whereas one wipes upwards after offering the Upāṃśu cup, here he wipes downwards—he thereby places the out-breathing (udāna) within him directed towards himself.
Then, with the hand turned downwards, he wipes along the middle enclosing-stick from west to east;

or, having offered the Upāṃśu cup, with the hand turned upwards he wipes along the middle enclosing-stick from east to west, and then here, with the hand turned downwards, he wipes along the middle enclosing-stick from west to east. He thereby places the out-breathing (udāna) in him directed towards the west; [with the words] "For the gods who drink the rays of light, thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.
Having stepped back toward it, he deposits it with the formula, "For the upward breath (udāna) thee!

for this [cup] is indeed his upward breath. He deposits them so that they touch one another; thus he brings the out-breath (prāṇa) and the upward breath into contact and joins the out-breath and the upward breath together.
Or those [stones] lie motionless until the third pressing;

therefore these humans sleep. At the third pressing, they are put back into use; therefore these humans, having slept, wake up. These [stones] move about unceasingly, following the very form of the sacrifice; for the sacrifice is fashioned like a bird. Of that [sacrifice], the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups are the two wings, and the Upāṃśusavana stone is the body.

Or else they lie there motionless until the third pressing; for that which is extended is indeed the sacrifice, and therefore these birds fly with their wings spread out and not drawing them in; yet at the third pressing they are employed again, and therefore these birds fly with their wings drawn in close together—this is according to the form of the sacrifice.

This Upāṃśu cup is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa), for the Upāṃśu is the out-breath; for while breathing out here on earth, one breathes out toward this very [cup]. That Antaryāma cup is indeed the upward-breath (udāna), for the Antaryāma is the upward-breath; for while breathing up toward yonder world, one breathes up toward that very [cup]. The Upāṃśusavana stone is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa), for the Upāṃśusavana is the through-breath (vyāna); for while breathing through the intermediate space, one breathes through it.
Or rather, his Aindravāyava cup is indeed speech.

This is with respect to the self (adhyātma). When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, he, thinking himself weak and fearing "I have not struck him," went into hiding; and the gods likewise hid themselves away from there.
Those gods said, "We do not know whether Vṛtra is slain or whether he is alive; come, let one of us find out whether Vṛtra is slain or if he lives."

They said to Vāyu: "This indeed is Vāyu who blows here; O Vāyu, find out this: whether Vṛtra is slain or whether he lives. You are the swiftest among us; if he shall live, you alone will return most quickly."

He said, "What would be mine from that? [Indra replied,] "The first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma shall be yours. "So be it," [said Vāyu]. Vāyu went to where Vṛtra was lying struck down. He said, "Vṛtra is slain; do whatever one would do when he is slain."

Those gods set forth, just as those about to obtain a portion [of a sacrifice]. That which one obtained became dedicated to a single deity; that which two obtained became dedicated to two deities; that which many obtained became dedicated to many deities. Because they seized it with vessels (*pātra*), therefore they are called *grahas* (libations).
It became putrid for them;
being thus fetid and foul-smelling, it blew upon them; it was not fit for an oblation, nor fit for food.

Those gods said to Vāyu, "O Vāyu, blow upon this for us; make this palatable for us. He said, "What shall be mine from that? [They replied,] "They shall call these vessels by your name alone. He said, "So be it; but you must blow along with me."

The gods struck off as much of its fragrance as they could; they placed that among the animals. This is that very stench of a corpse found in animals; therefore, one should not inhale the smell of a corpse, for it is the fragrance of King Soma.
One should not spit upon it.

Therefore, even if one should think oneself as if attached [to disease], one should walk around it with the wind blowing toward oneself. For Soma is prosperity, and consumption (*yakṣma*) is evil. Just as when a superior person approaches, an inferior person steps back, even so does consumption step back from him.
Then Vāyu blew through the other;

he made it palatable, and thus it was sufficient for the oblation and sufficient for food. Therefore, although these belong to various deities, they are called "Vāyavya" (belonging to Vāyu). This is his first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma, and these are what they call his vessels.
Indra indeed reflected:
"Vāyu has received the largest share of this sacrifice of ours, as well as the first *vaṣaṭ*-call of King Soma; they even call these his vessels. Well then, let me seek a share in this."

He said, "Vāyu, grant me a share in this cup. [Vāyu asked], "What would come of that? [Bṛhaspati replied], "Speech shall speak only what is articulated. [Vāyu said], "If speech speaks only what is articulated, then I will grant you a share. Thereupon, this cup for Indra and Vāyu came into being; previously, it belonged to Vāyu alone.

Vāyu replied, "Only a fourth is yours. Indra said
The two of them went back to Prajāpati for further questioning.

Prajāpati divided the draught into two parts; he said, "This indeed belongs to Vāyu. Then he again divided half of it into two parts; he said, "This indeed belongs to Vāyu," and "This is yours," thus assigning the fourth part to Indra. Since that which is fourth is a *turīya*, therefore this draught became the Aindraturīya draught.

Of this very cup, there are two *puroruc* verses: the first is addressed to Vāyu, the second to Indra and Vāyu; two *anuvākyā* verses: the first is addressed to Vāyu, the second to Indra and Vāyu; two *praiṣa* calls: the first is addressed to Vāyu, the second to Indra and Vāyu; and two *yājyā* verses: the first is addressed to Vāyu, the second to Indra and Vāyu. In this way, he caused him to share in a fourth part after each fourth part.

He said: "If they have divided me into fourths and fourths, then speech shall speak only its fourth part as articulated. That which humans speak is this fourth part of speech as articulated; that which animals speak is this fourth part of speech as unarticulated; that which birds speak is this fourth part of speech as unarticulated; and that which this small crawling vermin speaks is this fourth part of speech as unarticulated.
Therefore, this has been declared by the seers:
"Speech is measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech is what humans speak."

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]: "O Vāyu, drinker of the pure, come to us; a thousand are your teams, O possessor of all boons. I offer to you the intoxicating juice, O God, of which you have held the first draught. For Vāyu, thee! Thus he says.
Then, having set it aside, he brings it back: "O Indra and Vāyu, these [Somas] are pressed;

come hither with refreshments, for the drops of Soma long for you both. "Thou art taken with a support; for Vāyu, for Indra and Vāyu, thee! With this, he deposits it. As to why he says, "for the two who are well-pleased (sajoṣas)," that which is Vāyu is indeed Indra, and that which is Indra is Vāyu; therefore he says, "This is thy womb; for the two who are well-pleased, thee!"

Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed his *kratu* (will) and *dakṣa* (skill). This is with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). When he desires in his mind, "May this be mine; may I do this," that is his *kratu*; and when that [desire] of his comes to fruition, that is his *dakṣa*. Mitra is indeed *kratu*, and Varuṇa is *dakṣa*. Mitra is the sacred power (*brahman*), and Varuṇa is the ruling power (*kṣatra*). The sacred power is the one who conceives the plan, and the Kṣatriya is the executor.
In the beginning, these two—brahman and kṣatra—dwelt apart. Then the brahman was indeed able to stand without the kṣatra, namely Mitra, apart from Varuṇa.
Varuṇa is not a kṣatriya apart from the Brahman;
for whatever deed Varuṇa performed that was not impelled by Mitra the Brahman, it did not succeed for him at all.

Varuṇa was the Kṣatra and Mitra was the Brahman. Varuṇa addressed Mitra, saying, "Come to me; let us unite. I shall place you in front; impelled by you, I shall perform my work. "So be it," he replied. They united, and from that, this Maitrāvaruṇa cup (graha) came into being.
He is indeed the domestic priest (purodhā).

Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should not desire the office of domestic priest for every Kṣatriya, for these two together produce both good and evil deeds; nor indeed should a Kṣatriya appoint every Brāhmaṇa as his domestic priest, for these two together produce both ill-done and evil deeds. When Varuṇa performed that ritual act, impelled by Mitra the Brāhmaṇa, it indeed succeeded for him.

That is indeed appropriate: if a non-Kṣatriya were a Brāhmaṇa, and he were to obtain a king, that would be successful for him. But this is truly inappropriate—that a Kṣatriya becomes a non-Brāhmaṇa; whatever action he performs, even if it is impelled by the Brāhmaṇa Mitra, it does not succeed for him. Therefore, a Kṣatriya who is about to perform an action must certainly approach a Brāhmaṇa; then that action, impelled by the Brāhmaṇa, succeeds for him.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Mitra and Varuna, you who increase the Truth, this Soma has been pressed for you; hear my call here! You are taken with a support; I take you for Mitra and Varuna."
He mixes it with milk.

Now, as to why he mixes it with milk: Soma was indeed Vṛtra. When the gods slew him, they said to Mitra, "Do you also slay him! But he did not wish to do so, saying, "I am the friend of all; being a friend, I shall not become a non-friend. They said, "Then we shall exclude you from the sacrifice! He replied, "I too will slay him. Thereupon the cattle departed from him, thinking, "Being a friend, he has become a non-friend. He was deprived of his cattle. The gods then restored him to his cattle by mixing (the Soma) with milk; and so does this sacrificer now restore him to his cattle when he mixes it with milk.
Regarding this they say:
"He never indeed desired to kill him. Therefore, what milk there is here belongs to Mitra, while the Soma itself belongs to Varuṇa; for that reason, he mixes it with milk.

He mixes it. "May we, having won wealth, rejoice with riches; may the gods [rejoice] with the oblation, as cows with pasture. "O Mitra and Varuṇa, bestow upon us that cow for all time, one that does not kick away. "This is your womb; for Ṛta and Āyu, you!"—with these words he sets it down. As to why he says, "for Ṛta and Āyu, you!": *Ṛta* is indeed the Brahman, for Mitra is the Brahman and *Ṛta* is the Brahman; *Āyu* is Varuṇa, for Varuṇa is the year and the year is *Āyu*. Therefore he says, "This is your womb; for Ṛta and Āyu, you!"
The ear, indeed, belongs to the Aśvins;

therefore, he consumes [the soma] while turning it all around, for with this ear he hears from every direction. Now, when the Bhṛgus or the Aṅgirases attained the heavenly world, Cyavana the Bhārgava—or Cyavana the Āṅgirasa—remained behind there, having become decrepit and assuming the form of a magical creature (kṛtyā).

Śaryāta Mānava was once traveling with his village folk when he settled down as a neighbor right there. While his sons were playing, they took this decrepit creature—who had the appearance of a *kṛtyā*—and, thinking him worthless, pounded him with clods of earth.
He became enraged with the Śāryātas;
he laid a curse upon them, for a father fought with his son and a brother with his brother.
Śaryāta indeed reflected: "Because of whatever I have done, I have fallen into this calamity. He then called together the cowherds and the shepherds and said to them:

He said, "Who among you saw anything today? They replied, "This very man, worn out and like a malevolent spirit, lies there; thinking him worthless, the boys pelted him with clods of earth. He understood: "That must indeed be Cyavana."
Having yoked the chariot and taken Sukanyā Śāryātī with him, he set out and arrived at the place where the seer was.

He said: "O Seer, homage to you! Because I did not know [you], I have harmed you. Here is Sukanyā; with her I make amends to you. May my village be at peace. From that very moment his village became peaceful; from that very moment Śaryāta Mānava ceased his pursuit, thinking, "Lest I harm him further."
The Aśvins, indeed, were wandering about here performing medical cures. They approached Sukanyā; they desired a pair [of children] from her, but she did not conceive.

The two of them said, "Sukanyā, why do you lie beside this decrepit man who looks like a magical apparition? Come away with us! She replied, "He for whom my father gave me—I shall not leave him while he lives. Then that seer understood her intention.

He said, "Sukanyā, what did those two say to you? She explained it to him. Having been thus informed, he said, "If they say this to you again, you must say to them: 'You two are certainly not both complete, nor are you both prosperous; moreover, you are censuring my husband. If they then ask you, 'In what way are we incomplete, and in what way are we unprosperous? you must say to them: 'Make my husband young again, and then I will tell you. They approached her again and said exactly this to her.

She said, "You two are certainly not as complete as you were before, nor are you as prosperous; yet you both criticize my husband. They asked, "In what way are we incomplete, and in what way are we unprosperous? She said, "Make my husband young again, and then I will tell you."
The two of them said, "Enter this lake; with whatever age he desires, with that he shall emerge. He entered that lake, and with whatever age he desired, with that he emerged.

The two said, "Sukanyā, why are we incomplete? Why are we unsuccessful? Harṣi replied to them, "In Kurukṣetra these gods are performing a sacrifice; they exclude you two from the sacrifice. That is why you are incomplete and that is why you are unsuccessful. Thereupon the Aśvins departed from that very place; they arrived while the gods were performing the sacrifice, at the time when the Bahiṣpavamāna had been chanted.
The two of them said, "Invite us! The gods replied, "We will not invite you; you have wandered among men too much, mingling with them as physicians."

The two said, "Verily, you are sacrificing with a headless sacrifice. "How, with a headless one? they asked. "Invite us, and then we will tell you," they replied. "So be it," they said, and invited them. For them, they drew this cup for the Aśvins; those two became the Adhvaryu priests of the sacrifice, and they restored that head of the sacrifice. This is explained in the Brāhmaṇa of the Divākīrtyas, how they restored the head of the sacrifice. Therefore, this cup is drawn when the Bahiṣpavamāna has been chanted, for they arrived when the Bahiṣpavamāna had been chanted.

The two of them said, "We two are indeed the principal ones of the sacrifice, we who are the Adhvaryus here; let him bring this cup for us first, before the cups for the dual deities. For them, they brought that cup first, before the cups for the dual deities; therefore, this tenth cup is drawn, yet the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered only at the third. Now, as for [the mention of] the Aśvins—it is these two, Heaven and Earth, that are manifestly the Aśvins, for these two have pervaded (āśnuvātām) all this. They are "garlanded with lotuses" (*puṣkarasrajau*): Agni is the lotus of this [earth], and Āditya is that of yonder [heaven].

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]. "O Aśvins, with that whip of yours which is honey-sweet and full of truth, sprinkle the sacrifice. "Thou art taken with a support; for the Aśvins thee! With this formula he draws it. "This is thy womb; for the two honey-loving ones (mādhvī) thee! With this he deposits it. He draws it with a verse containing the word "honey" (madhumatī), and he deposits it with "for the two honey-loving ones thee. As to why he draws it with a verse containing "honey" and deposits it with "for the two honey-loving ones thee," [it is because...]

Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed told them the Brāhmaṇa named Madhu; that is their beloved abode, and by means of this he approaches that very [abode] for them. Therefore, he draws [the cup] with a verse containing the word "honey" (madhumatī), and he deposits it with the formula, "Thee for the two honey-loving ones."

Now, these cups are smooth. The cup for Indra and Vāyu has a rim; that is its second form, and therefore it belongs to two deities. The cup for Mitra and Varuṇa has a goat’s lip; that is its second form, and therefore it belongs to two deities. The cup for the Aśvins has a camel’s lip; that is its second form, and therefore it belongs to two deities. Now, as for the phrase "the two Aśvins," the Aśvins are indeed the two chief ones, and this mouth is like a camel’s lip; therefore the cup for the Aśvins has a camel’s lip.
The two eyes, indeed, are his Śukra and Manthin offerings.
That which shines yonder is the Śukra; because it shines there, it is the Śukra. The Moon, indeed, is the Manthin.
He mixes it with groats;

he thus makes it into a stirred drink (*mantha*). Therefore, this [sun] is the *manthin* cup. Indeed, these two are the eyes of these creatures; for if these two were not to rise, people here would not even be able to discern their own hands.
Of these two, one is the eater; the first is the other, the eater. The *śukra* cup is the first, and the *manthin* cup is the eater.
Of those two, one follows the *Ādya* cup;

the *Ādya* follows the other, the *Śukra*. The *Manthin* follows the *Ādya*. They are drawn for one [set of deities] and offered to another: they are drawn for Śaṇḍa and Marka—the Asuras and Rakṣases—and offered to the deities. This is why it is so.
Wherever the gods struck down the Asuras and Rakṣases, they were unable to strike down these two; for whatever rite the gods performed, those two would bewilder them and quickly flee away again.

Those gods said, "Consider how we may drive these two away. They said, "Let us draw cups for them; they will come down to us, and having taken possession of them, we shall drive them away.
