They drew cups for the two of them, and the two came down; having taken possession of them, they drove them away. Therefore, the cups are drawn for Caṇḍa and Marka, and they are offered to the deities.
Yājñavalkya also said:
"Should I not rather draw [the cups] for the deities themselves? For this [world] is, as it were, of the nature of conquest. Thus he indeed deliberated upon that matter, but he did not act upon it.
Some indeed make this the *puroruc* for the *śukra* cup:
"This Vena impels those whose womb is the speckled one, the light-enveloped, the measurer of the mid-world. This they do as a form of him who shines yonder, when he says, "the light-enveloped."
But he should indeed use this as the *puroruc* for the *śukra* cup.

"As of old, as before, as always, as now, [I praise] the most excellent one, seated on the sacrificial grass, the finder of light"—for he is indeed the eater, and he follows after the eater; for he is the eldest, therefore he says, "the most excellent one, seated on the sacrificial grass, the finder of light. "The facing enclosure, the roaring, the swift, the victorious, in whom you grow great"—"You are taken with a support; for Śaṇḍa, you! This is your womb; protect heroism!"—thus he settles it. For he is indeed the eater, and he follows after the eater; for he is a hero, therefore he says, "This is your womb; protect heroism! He places it in the southern half, for he moves along this very direction.
Then he draws the Manthin cup:

"This Vena, whose womb is the speckled one, whose covering is light, impels [the waters] in the measuring of the mid-air; at the meeting of the waters and the sun, the sages lick him with their thoughts like a child—thou art taken with a base; for Marka, thee!"

He mixes it with groats. As to why he mixes it with groats: Varuna, indeed, once crushed the eye of King Soma; it swelled, and from that the horse (aśva) came into being. Because it came into being through swelling (aśvayat), therefore it is called "horse" (aśva). A tear of his fell down, and from that the barley (yava) came into being; therefore they say, "Barley belongs to Varuna. Thus, whatever part of his eye was lost there, by that very means he now makes him whole and complete. That is why he mixes it with groats.
He mixes it.

"In whose offerings you two, like the mind, accept the sharp inspired hymns with power, rushing forward—he who, possessing great manly strength, has mixed the quarters with the arrows in his hand. He settles it with, "This is thy womb; protect the offspring! For these people are to be eaten by him, and these subjects are indeed to be eaten; therefore he says, "This is thy womb; protect the offspring!"

There are two sprinkled splinters of the sacrificial post and two unsprinkled ones. The Adhvaryu takes up one sprinkled and one unsprinkled; likewise, the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up one sprinkled and one unsprinkled. The Adhvaryu takes up the *śukra* cup, and the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the *manthin* cup.

The Adhvaryu wipes [the vessel] with an unbesprinkled chip of the sacrificial post, saying, "Wiped away is Śaṇḍa!"; in the same way, the Pratiprasthātṛ wipes [his], saying, "Wiped away is Marka! As they take up [the vessels], they drive away the Asuras and Rakṣases. The Adhvaryu goes out, saying, "May the gods who drink the Śukra lead you forth!"; the Pratiprasthātṛ [goes out], saying, "May the gods who drink the Manthin lead you forth! Thus, these two lead them forth for the sake of the deities alone.
With their elbows joined behind the Āhavanīya fire, they place them on the high altar (uttaravedi).

The Adhvaryu places one on the southern hip, and the Pratiprasthātṛ on the northern; not letting go of them, they say, "Thou art unassailable," whereby they make the high altar unassailable by the Rakṣases. For these two are about to pass around the fire, or rather, they are about to cross over it; thus they appease it, and so the fire does not harm them as they pass around.

The Adhvaryu goes around [the fire], saying, "Rich in heroes, go around, procreating heroes! For he (Agni) is indeed an eater, and the hero follows the eater; therefore he says, "Rich in heroes, go around, procreating heroes. He says, "With abundance of wealth, [favor] the sacrificer! In saying this, he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer when he says, "With abundance of wealth, [favor] the sacrificer!"

Then the Pratiprasthātṛ goes around [the fire], saying, "Generating offspring, go around with good offspring," for these subjects are indeed eaters; therefore he says, "Generating offspring, go around with good offspring. He says, "Toward the sacrificer with the increase of wealth"; by this, he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer when he says, "Toward the sacrificer with the increase of wealth."
Having covered them, they go out;

they thus make these two invisible, which is why no one sees these two, the sun and the moon, as they move forward. Having gone around to the front, they uncover them and offer while standing in front; they thus make these two visible, which is why everyone sees these two, the sun and the moon, as they move backward. Therefore, no one sees the semen being poured forward, but everyone sees it when it is produced behind.

The two join their elbows behind the sacrificial post; if Agni does not press against them, they join them; but if Agni should press against them, they should join their elbows even in front of the post. The Adhvaryu says, "Uniting with heaven and earth, the bright one with bright luster," and the Pratiprasthātṛ says, "Uniting with heaven and earth, the churning one with churning luster. They thus provide a resting place for the eyes and join the eyes together; therefore these eyes are joined on both sides by the bones.

The Adhvaryu throws away an unbesprinkled chip of the sacrificial post with the formula, "Śaṇḍa is cast out," and in the same way the Pratiprasthātṛ [throws one] with, "Marka is cast out. Thus, before the oblations, the Asuras and Rakṣases are driven away.

Then the Adhvaryu throws a sprinkled chip of the sacrificial post into the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Thou art the support of the Śukra cup"; in the same way, the Pratiprasthātṛ does so with the words, "Thou art the support of the Manthin cup. These two are indeed fuel-sticks for the eyes; he thus kindles the two eyes, and therefore these two eyes are kindled.
There he mutters:
"O divine Soma, may we be givers of undecaying, heroic wealth and abundance. This is indeed the blessing of this ritual; thus he invokes this very blessing.
Then, having called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says:

"Prompt [the Hotṛ] for the Soma-pressings of the morning libation, which are bright, dripping with honey; for Indra, the Somas are set forth! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu makes the offering; following him, the Pratiprasthātṛ; and following him, the Chamasādhvaryus.
Standing in front, those two indeed offer the oblations. These two are the eyes; thus they place the eyes in front, and therefore these eyes are in the front.
Standing on both sides of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), they offer oblations.
Just as there are two nostrils, so is the sacrificial post; therefore, these two eyes are on either side of the nose.
When these two have been consecrated with the *vaṣaṭ*-call, they are offered with a mantra.

By this, indeed, these two partake of that which is offered throughout the entire pressing. And because they are offered throughout the entire pressing—since these two are most manifestly Prajāpati, for they are his eyes, and the eye is truth, and Prajāpati is truth—therefore they are offered throughout the entire pressing.
He offers:
"He is the first consecration, the possessor of all boons; he is the first Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni; he is the first Bṛhaspati, the wise one. To that Indra, offer the pressed [juice] with 'Svāhā'!"

When he offers [the oblation], saying, "She is the first, he is the first," it is because, indeed, of the emitted seed, the two eyes are the very first things to come into being; therefore he offers, saying, "She is the first."
Then he issues the command.

"Let the Hotṛ’s cup go forward; let the Brahman’s, the Udgātṛs’, and the Sacrificer’s go forward; let those of the Sadasyas go forward! O Camasādhvaryus of the Hotṛs, turn back and pour more of the Śukra-grain!"—this is the formal command. Having gone around, the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue from the Adhvaryu’s vessel into his own; he thereby causes the first offering to be taken as a tribute. The Adhvaryu pours that into the Hotṛ’s cup for consumption, for the consumption belongs to the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ* call. The *vaṣaṭ* call is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That vital breath had turned away from him while he was uttering the *vaṣaṭ*; since consumption is the vital breath, he thus places the vital breath back into himself.
Now, as for why they do not carry these two cups westward, nor carry away other draughts—these two are indeed the eyes; he pours their residue into the Hotṛ’s cup.

Then they fill up the cups of the Hotṛs. These remnants are indeed the remains of what has been offered; they are not sufficient for a further oblation. It is these very remnants that they now cause to swell again, so that they become sufficient for an oblation. Therefore, they fill up the cups of the Hotṛs.
Then they cause the Hotṛ-priests to perform the joint offerings.

For the Hotṛ-priests, when harnessed, carry the sacrifice to the gods; it is them that they thus satisfy, thinking, "Being satisfied and gratified, may they carry the sacrifice to the gods. Therefore, they cause the Hotṛ-priests to perform the joint offerings.

He recites the consecration formula either when the first *hotrā* has been offered, or when the last one has been offered: "May the *hotrās* be satisfied with the honeyed [oblation]—those which have been well-sacrificed, well-pleased, and well-poured, with the cry 'svāhā'! This is indeed the satisfaction of the *hotrās*. Then, having gone back, he sits down facing westward, saying, "The *agnīdh* has sacrificed. For here the *agnīdh* is the last of those who sacrifice; therefore he says, "The *agnīdh* has sacrificed."
The Āgrayaṇa cup is indeed his self.

It belongs to him entirely, for this self is everything; therefore he draws it with this [earth]. For this [earth] is a vessel (sthālī), and he draws it with a vessel; for this [earth] is everything, and this cup is everything—therefore he draws it with this.
He draws it full.
Truly, the full is everything; this cup is everything; therefore he draws it full.
He draws [the cup] for the Viśve Devas.
The Viśve Devas are indeed everything; this cup is everything; therefore he draws it for the Viśve Devas.
He draws it at all the pressings;
for all the pressings are indeed everything, and this cup is everything—therefore he draws it at all the pressings.
If it should fail for want of a king, they should extend it from that very point and expand it from there;

for the Āgrayaṇa is the self, and from the self all these limbs proceed. Therefore, at the end, he draws the Hāriyojana cup; thus, in the self, in this very foundation, the sacrifice finally finds its firm support.
Now, as to why it is called Āgrayaṇa:
when one, taking up that pressing-stone, restrains his speech, it is at this point that she spoke first; because she spoke there first (*agre*), therefore it is called Āgrayaṇa.
It was indeed out of fear of the Rākṣasas that they uttered this speech.
From here he draws six cups toward the east; now this is the seventh. There are six seasons in the year, and the year is indeed everything.

The gods spoke this speech first here when all was conquered, free from fear, and free from destruction; and in the same way, this sacrificer speaks this speech first here when all is conquered, free from fear, and free from destruction.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"O gods who are eleven in heaven, who are eleven upon earth, who dwell in the waters by your greatness as eleven—O gods, enjoy this sacrifice! You are taken with a support; you are the Āgrayaṇa, the good Āgrayaṇa. By this, he makes his speech free from redundancy (ayātayāman). Therefore, although it is the same, he speaks it in reverse order to avoid repetition (ajāmitā); for he would commit a repetition if he were to draw it saying, "You are the Āgrayaṇa, you are the Āgrayaṇa. Therefore he says, "You are the Āgrayaṇa, the good Āgrayaṇa."
"Protect the sacrifice; protect the lord of the sacrifice."

He thus addresses Speech, which has been released: "Guard the sacrifice! and "Protect the lord of the sacrifice!"—he thus addresses Speech, which has been released: "Guard the sacrificer! for the sacrificer is indeed the lord of the sacrifice. "May Viṣṇu protect you with his power; do you protect Viṣṇu!"—he thus addresses Speech, which has been released: "Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; may the sacrifice guard you with its vigor. "Do you protect Viṣṇu!"—he thus addresses Speech, which has been released: "Do you guard the sacrifice! and "Protect the pressings!"—thereby he addresses this cup, for it corresponds to all the pressings.
Then, having grasped the fringe of the woollen filter, he utters the sound *hiṃ*.

This very speech, being exhausted, became weary; when that speech was weary, the gods restored breath to it by means of the *hiṅkāra* alone. The *hiṅkāra* is indeed breath; for the *hiṅkāra* is truly breath, therefore one cannot utter the *hiṅkāra* while holding his nostrils closed. By means of that breath, she (speech) recovered her strength; for when one who is weary regains his breath, then he recovers his strength. In the same way, when this speech is weary, he restores breath to it by means of the *hiṅkāra* alone, and by means of that breath, it recovers its strength. He utters the *hiṅkāra* three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.
Then he says, "Soma purifies himself.

That very thing which they did not announce out of fear of the Asuras and Rakshasas, that he now announces here when everything has been conquered and there is no fear or harm; he makes it manifest. Therefore he says, "Soma purifies himself."
"For this priesthood, for this nobility"—thus he speaks for both the priesthood and the nobility. "For this sacrificer who presses the juice, it flows clear"—thus he speaks for the sacrificer.

Regarding this they say: "Having said only this much, he should set it down; for all this that exists is just this much—namely, the priesthood (brahman), the nobility (kṣatra), and the peasantry (viś). Indra and Agni are indeed all this; therefore, having said only this much, he should set it down."

He should indeed say it yet again: "For sap, for strength, he purifies. By saying "for sap," he says this for the sake of rain; by saying "for strength," he says this for that vigorous essence which is produced from rain. "For the waters, for the plants, he purifies"—by this he says it for both the waters and the plants. "For heaven and earth, he purifies"—by this he says it for these two, heaven and earth, upon whom all this rests. "For well-being, he purifies"—by this he says, "for what is good."

Regarding this, some say, "It purifies for the sake of spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*)," but one should not speak thus. When he says, "For this *brahman*," that itself is what he says for the sake of spiritual luster. He sets it down with, "Thee for all the gods; this is thy womb; thee for all the gods. For he draws it for all the gods. He sets it down in the middle, for this is its self (*ātman*), and this self is, as it were, in the middle. To the south is the *ukthya* vessel, and to the north is the *āditya* vessel.
This Ukthya is indeed his undefined self;

for this vital breath (prāṇa) is his very self, and it is undefined. It is his life-span itself; therefore, he draws it with this [spoon]. For this [spoon] is a bowl (sthālī), and he draws it with a bowl. For this [bowl] is undecaying and immortal; and life is undecaying and immortal. Therefore, he draws it with this.
He draws it full;
for that which is full is everything, and that which is life is everything; therefore he draws it full.
His very life-span is that *dhruva* cup;
by it his self is joined together, and his joints are made continuous. Therefore, even though it has not yet been drawn, this last cup remains for the *acāvāka*.
Then he brings down the King (Soma).

He pours out a third of the *vasatīvarī* waters; thus the joint meets. He makes the first part of the later pressing the last part of the earlier one, and what belongs to the later pressing he makes first, and what belongs to the earlier one he makes last. Thus he interlocks them; therefore these joints are interlocked—this one overlapping thus, and this one overlapping thus.

In the same way, at the midday pressing, the last cup belongs to this Acchāvāka even before it has been drawn. Then he pours out the third portion of the Vasatīvarī waters; thus the joint meets together. He makes the first part of the subsequent pressing the last part of the preceding one; what belongs to the subsequent he makes first, and what belongs to the preceding he makes last. Thus he interlinks them; therefore these joints are interlinked—this one thus overlapping that one, and that one thus overlapping this one. Since his body is joined by this, therefore this is his life-span.
This very [cup] is the wish-fulfilling cow, the special portion for Indra.

He draws it out from three Ukthas at the morning pressing, and from three at the midday pressing; that makes six times. For there are six seasons, and the seasons ripen all these desires; thus indeed this is the wish-fulfilling cow, the special portion for Indra.
He draws that cup without a *puroruk* formula;

for the *uktha* is a *puroruk*, the *ṛc* is a *puroruk*, the *sāman* is the cup, and whatever else he mutters, that is the *yajus*. These [Vedic texts] were originally divided: half belonged to the *ṛcs*, half to the *yajus*, and half to the *sāmans*.

Those gods said, "Come, let us place these [syllables] within the Yajus formulas; thus this knowledge will become much more abundant. They placed them within the Yajus formulas, and from that, this knowledge became much more abundant.
As to why he draws it without a *puroruk*:

for the *uktha* is indeed the *puroruk*, and the *ṛc* is the *puroruk*; since he draws it apart from the *ukthas*, by that very act it becomes possessed of a *puroruk* for him; therefore, he draws it without a *puroruk*.
Now, therefore, he indeed takes [the draught].

"You are taken with a support; for Indra, the mighty, the vigorous"—Indra indeed is the deity of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "for Indra, for thee. "The mighty, the vigorous"—by saying "the mighty, the vigorous," he means "the powerful. "I take thee, the one to be praised"—for he takes him for the sake of the hymns (uktha). "O Indra, that which is thy might"—by this he means "that which is thy power. "For him, for thee, for Viṣṇu"—for he takes him for the life-span of the sacrifice; therefore he says, "for him, for thee, for Viṣṇu. "This is thy womb; for the hymns, thee!"—thus he settles him, for he takes him for the sake of the hymns.
He divides it with the formula:

"I take thee, the one who aids the gods, for the gods, for the life of the sacrifice. One might perform this as an instruction if he so wished; however, he should rather divide it according to the respective deities.

"For Mitra and Varuna, thee, the one who promotes the gods, I take for the life of the sacrifice"—thus [he says] for the Maitrāvaruṇa; for they chant the praise for him in verses addressed to Mitra and Varuna, he recites the *anūśaṃsa* in verses addressed to Mitra and Varuna, and he performs the offering with a verse addressed to Mitra and Varuna.

"For Indra thee! I take thee, the one who aids the gods, for the life of the sacrifice"—thus [he says] for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin; for they praise him with verses addressed to Indra, he recites after them with verses addressed to Indra, and he sacrifices with a verse addressed to Indra.

"For Indra and Agni, thee—the one who promotes the gods—for the life of the sacrifice, I take thee," [he says] for the Acchāvāka; for they praise him with verses addressed to Indra and Agni, he recites the *anuśaṃsana* for Indra and Agni, and he offers the oblation with a verse to Indra and Agni. "For Indra, thee! [he says] at the midday pressing, for the midday pressing belongs to Indra.
Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus draw it out separately:

"Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, the god-pleasing, for the gods, the hymn-pleasing, for the hymns, as one dear to Mitra and Varuṇa. This is thy womb; for Mitra and Varuṇa, thee! Thus he deposits it. With "Thou art a renewed oblation," he touches the vessel.
"You are taken with a support;

I take you, who are dear to the gods, for the gods; who are dear to the hymns, for the hymns; who are pleasing to Indra. This is your resting place; for Indra, you! With these words he deposits it. "You are a repeated oblation," with this he touches the vessel.

"You are taken with a support; I take you, who are dear to the gods, for the gods; you, who are dear to the hymns, for the hymns; you, who are pleasing to Indra and Agni. "This is your womb; for Indra and Agni, you!"—with these words he deposits it. Here he does not touch the vessel with the formula "You are the oblation again. At the midday pressing, he touches the vessel with "For Indra, you! For Indra, you!", for the midday pressing belongs to Indra. Twice he touches the vessel with "You are the oblation again," and silently he sets down the third [portion].
One should not take it with the *upayāma* formula;

nor should one place it in the womb-vessel (*yoni*), for it has already been taken with the *upayāma* formula at the beginning, and it has already been placed in the womb-vessel at the beginning, to avoid repetition (*jāmitā*). Indeed, one would commit a repetition if one were to take it here also with the *upayāma* formula, or if one were to place it in the womb-vessel. Now, as for why he touches the vessel with the words "Thou art the oblation again" (*punarhavir asi*), it is because he is about to take a draught from it once more; however, he should pay no heed to that [formula], and should simply set it down silently.

This, indeed, is his vital breath (*prāṇa*): that which is in front is Vaiśvānara, and that which is behind is Dhruva. Formerly, they used to draw these two cups first, namely the Dhruva and the Vaiśvānara. Even now, only one of these two is drawn, namely the Dhruva. If he should learn of it from the Carakas or from anyone else, he should pour it into the cup of the sacrificer; but this [other cup] is poured into the Hotṛ’s cup.
Or rather, that which is below his navel is this very self of his;

this [cup] is his life itself. Therefore, he draws it with this [ladle]. For this [ladle] is a vessel (sthālī), and he draws it with a vessel; for this [ladle] is ageless, and life is ageless and immortal; therefore, he draws it with this.
He draws it full;
for that which is full is everything, and that which is life is everything; therefore he draws it full.
He draws [the cup] for Vaiśvānara.
Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; the year is life-span; therefore he draws [the cup] for Vaiśvānara.
It is drawn at the morning pressing;
it remains lying there from that time until the end, and thus he carries it through all the pressings.
He should not let it down while the hymn is being chanted;
for if he were to let it down while the hymn is being chanted, the sacrificer would not live out the year.

While that [laud] is being chanted, he pours it down; thus he leads this [sacrifice] beyond the twelfth laud. In this way, he attains a life-span that passes from one to another; thus the sacrificer lives for a long time. Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa should sit through the Agniṣṭoma; he should not move away from its oblations, nor should he urinate. In this way, he attains a full life-span, for this [Agniṣṭoma] is his life-span; thus he reaches a full life-span.
Or rather, that part of his which is below the navel is this [part] of his self.

If, before this offering, he were to urinate or discharge semen, he would surely urinate it away; thinking, "Lest I should urinate it away," for this reason the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is performed. And that indeed belongs to the sacrificer himself, for this is that part of the sacrificer's own self.
That [sacrifice] indeed becomes an Agniṣṭoma.

Soma is indeed glory; therefore, both he who obtains [something] at the Soma sacrifice and he who does not both come [to it], for they come desiring to behold that very glory. Now, when the Brāhmaṇas, having spread out together, consume [the remains], they place that glory within themselves. He who, knowing this, consumes [it], truly becomes glory itself.

Now, these very [singers] creep along while performing the Agniṣṭoma-sitting; having placed this glory nearby, they creep away, and thus they become turned away from glory. Therefore, having grasped it, he places that glory back within himself. He who, knowing this, becomes an Agniṣṭoma-sitter, goes forth having become the most glorious among them.

The gods and the asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this sacrifice while their father Prajāpati, the year, was still to come, each thinking, "This shall be ours; this shall be ours."

Then the gods, praising and toiling, went about; they saw this Agniṣṭomasadya. By means of this Agniṣṭomasadya, they appropriated the entire sacrifice and excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice. In the same way, this sacrificer, by means of this Agniṣṭomasadya, appropriates the entire sacrifice and excludes his rivals from the sacrifice. Therefore, it is called the Agniṣṭomasadya.

Having taken it, he places it in the northern *havirdhāna* cart, thinking, "The cups (*graha*) are indeed the vital breaths; let me not confuse the vital breaths. He places the other cups on strewn grass, but this one he places after clearing away [the grass], without placing even a blade of grass between.

Or rather, that which is above his navel—this part of his self is indeed, as it were, above; and since what is strewn [around] is above the navel, he places [the cup] upon that which is strewn. Then, having cleared this [spot], he places it there without putting even a blade of grass between.

Or rather, that which is below his navel is this part of his self; for that which is below the navel is, as it were, lower, and this [part] is indeed lower. Therefore, having pushed this [fire-pan] aside, he sets it down without even a blade of grass intervening.

This indeed is Prajāpati, this sacrifice which is performed; from it these creatures were born, and even now they are born after it. Because he sets them down on what has been strewn, therefore those creatures that are born after them establish themselves on this earth by means of something other than their own bodies—those, namely, that stand on hooves, for they establish themselves on this earth by means of something other than their own bodies. But because he sets down this [Soma] after spreading it out without placing even a blade of grass between, therefore those creatures that are born after it establish themselves on this earth by means of their own bodies: both humans and wild beasts.

This, indeed, he makes another part superior to this very earth when he strews [the sand]; for those offspring which are born after [the earth] has been strewn, they establish themselves upon it by means of their hooves, which are distinct from their own bodies.

Now, this is what they offer in the Āhavanīya fire: the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), parched grains (dhānā), groats (karambha), curds (dadhi), and clotted curds (āmikṣā). It is just as if one were pouring [food] into the mouth; that is how it is. Yet this [fire] remains uniform in form, like water alone. Therefore, whatever food of various forms he eats with that mouth, he causes it all to flow out through this breath (prāṇa) as something of a single form, just like water. And as for why it is named "the Steadfast" (dhruva): [it is because it remains constant].

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakṣases. The Asuras and Rakṣases assailed them from the south and struck down these southern cups; they even struck down this southern *havirdhāna* cart, but they were unable to strike down this [northern one]. That northern *havirdhāna* cart supported the southern *havirdhāna* cart. Because they were unable to strike it down, it is called *dhruva* (the firm).

They indeed guard it. This [Agni] is the head of this Gāyatrī; the Gāyatrī is the sacrifice. There are twelve Stotras and twelve Śastras, which makes twenty-four; for the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables. Of that [Gāyatrī], this is the head. The head is prosperity (*śrī*), for the head is indeed prosperity; therefore, they say of one who is the best in a region, "He is the head of that region. For the best would suffer distress if this [Agni] were to suffer distress. The best is the sacrificer; thinking, "Lest the sacrificer suffer distress," they therefore guard it.

This [Agni] is indeed a calf. The Gāyatrī is this sacrifice; there are twelve Stotras and twelve Śastras, which makes twenty-four. The Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables; he is its calf. When they guard him, they guard these calves for milking, just as one guards these calves so that this milk may be milked. In this way, this Gāyatrī shall milk all desires for the sacrificer; therefore, they guard him.

Now, as for why the Adhvaryu and the Pratiprasthātṛ both step out and step forward: just as one would tend to a cow with a tethered calf, so do they tend to this cup; he pours it out, for he thereby causes the Gāyatrī to flow forth, thinking, "May this Gāyatrī, being offered, milk all desires for the sacrificer. That is why he pours it out.

He pours it down, saying, "With a firm mind and with firm speech, I pour down Soma; I take it up. Or [he says], "So that Indra may make these people of ours free from rivals and of one mind. By this he means: "So that Indra may make these subjects, these people of ours, free from rivals and of one mind for the sake of prosperity, glory, and the eating of food."
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"The gods have generated Agni Vaiśvānara— the head of heaven, the messenger of earth, born in the cosmic order (ṛta)—
the seer, the sovereign, the guest of men— as a vessel for their mouths."

"You are taken with a support; you are Dhruva (the Steadfast), the steadfast dwelling, the most steadfast of the steadfast, the most immovable of the immovable. This is your womb: for Vaiśvānara, you! With these words he deposits it, having pushed aside [the grass] without placing even a blade of grass in between, for he draws this [cup] for Vaiśvānara.
Having taken the portions for the planets and having gone out, he performs the offering of the droplets.

As to why he performs the offering of the droplets: whatever droplets of his might spill here, those he thereby makes to go safely (*svagā*) into the Āhavanīya fire; for the Āhavanīya is the resting place of oblations. Therefore, he performs the offering of the droplets.

He offers with the formula: "That drop of thine which falls, that stalk of thine... For that which indeed falls as a small drop is the *drapsa*; thus he says "that drop of thine. By "that stalk of thine," he means the stalk. "Shaken by the pressing-stones from the lap of the two bowls"—for it is shaken by the pressing-stones and falls from the two *adhiṣavaṇa* vessels; or "from the Adhvaryu, or from the filter"—for it falls either from the hands of the Adhvaryu or from the filter. "That I offer for thee, mentally consecrated by *vaṣaṭ*, Svāhā! Thus, this becomes for him like an offering consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ*-call.

Then, from the strewn altar, the Adhvaryu takes two blades of grass; these two Adhvaryus enter first as the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*udāna*) of the sacrifice. Then the Prastotṛ is indeed the speech (*vāk*) of the sacrifice; then the Udgātṛ is the self (*ātman*), Prajāpati, of the sacrifice; then the Pratihartṛ is either the physician or the diffused breath (*vyāna*).

The sacrificer indeed takes hold of these five officiating priests; for as great as this entire sacrifice is, so great are these five officiating priests. The sacrifice is fivefold; thus the sacrificer takes hold of the sacrifice itself.

Then he throws a blade of grass toward the *cātvāla* pit with the formula, "Thou art the stepping-off place of the gods. For when the gods attained the heavenly world by means of the sacrifice, they ascended from this very *cātvāla* upward to the heavenly world; thus, he causes the sacrificer to follow that path leading to heaven.

Then he silently throws a blade of grass in front of the Udgātṛs. For these Udgātṛs are indeed the Stoma, Prajāpati; they unite with this universe, and this universe arises from them. It is for them that he places this blade of grass as a cover, so that it does not unite with the Adhvaryu, nor does it arise from him. Then, when they mutter, the Udgātṛs indeed mutter at this point.
Then he introduces the chant with the words, "Soma purifies himself.

He indeed introduces the chant facing away, and they chant facing away. For these chants, the *pavamāna* lauds, are turned toward the gods; for by means of them, the gods attained the heavenly world facing away. Therefore, he introduces the chant facing away, and they chant facing away.

"Turn hither!"—thus they say regarding other chants; but they chant with the *dhurs* facing toward [the center]. These creatures indeed turned back toward these chants; therefore, these creatures are born again, turning back toward [their origins].
Now, as to why they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* here: there, at the beginning, yonder sun was;

the seasons, having enclosed him on all sides, ascended from here upwards toward the heavenly world. That very sun shines, established in the seasons. In the same way, the officiating priests, having enclosed the sacrificer on all sides, ascend from here upwards toward the heavenly world. Therefore, they chant the *bahiṣpavamāna* here.
This Bahiṣpavamāna is indeed a ship for reaching heaven;

the officiating priests are its oars and rudders that carry one across to the heavenly world. There is only one who can sink it: he who is blameworthy. Just as one might sink a ship after having boarded it when it was full, so does he sink it. Thus, the entire sacrifice is a ship for reaching heaven; therefore, one should strive to exclude anyone who is blameworthy from every sacrifice.

Then, having been praised, he utters this speech: "O Agnīdh, distribute the fires; strew the sacrificial grass; prepare the sacrificial cakes; bring the animal! He distributes the fires—the Agnīdh kindles them for him; he strews the sacrificial grass—he kindles them over the strewn grass, thinking, "I shall offer to the gods. "Prepare the sacrificial cakes"—for he is about to proceed with the cakes; "bring the animal"—for he is about to dedicate the animal.

Then, having entered again, he draws the Āśvina cup; having drawn the Āśvina cup and gone out, he winds the cord around the sacrificial post; having wound the cord around the post, he dedicates the animal victim. Thus, he bestows essence upon it.

Once it has been seized at the morning pressing, it remains lying there until the third pressing while being prepared; thus he places essence into this entire sacrifice and permeates the whole sacrifice with essence.

Therefore, at the Agniṣṭoma, he immolates an animal for Agni; for it is consistent that he should immolate one for Agni at the Agniṣṭoma. If it were an Ukthya sacrifice, he should immolate a second one for Indra and Agni, for the Ukthas belong to Indra and Agni. If it were a Ṣoḍaśin sacrifice, he should immolate a third one for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra. If it were an Atirātra sacrifice, he should immolate a fourth one for Sarasvatī; for Sarasvatī is Speech, and Speech is female, and Night is female. Thus, he distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order.
Then he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) belonging to the Soma-pressings.

Soma is indeed divine, for Soma was in heaven. "Soma was indeed Vṛtra; his body is what the mountains and stones are; from that this herb called uśānā is born," so said Śvetaketu Auddālaki. "Having brought that [herb] here, they press it," he said.

When he immolates the victim, he thereby bestows essence upon it; and when he proceeds with the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) of the Soma-pressing, he thereby bestows the vital sap (medha) upon it; thus this [victim] of his becomes truly Soma.
All [the offerings] belong to Indra.
Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; therefore, all [the offerings] belong to Indra.
Now, as for the fact that there are the sacrificial cake, parched grains, groats, curds, and clotted curds—it is so that those deities of the sacrifice may be well-pleased.

Or, having eaten this cake, he desires: "May I eat parched grains; may I eat groats; may I eat curds; may I eat clotted curds"—all these are his desires. Those who are the deities of the sacrifice, may they be well-pleased. Now, as for why this curdled milk for Mitra and Varuṇa (payasyā) is provided only at the morning pressing and not at the other two pressings.
The Gāyatrī indeed carries the morning pressing;

the Triṣṭubh, the midday pressing; and the Jagatī, the third pressing. Now, the Triṣṭubh carries the midday pressing not alone, but together with the Gāyatrī and the Bṛhatī; and the Jagatī carries the third pressing not alone, but with the Gāyatrī, the Uṣṇih, the Kakubh, and the Anuṣṭubh.
The Gāyatrī alone carries the morning pressing;

it does so by means of these two fivefold sets: the fivefold set of the Stotra and the fivefold set of the oblations. There are four Ājya-stotras and the Bahiṣpavamāna is the fifth; this is a five-part Pankti. By means of this fivefold Stotra-set, the Gāyatrī, no longer alone, carries the morning pressing.

There is a cake for Indra, parched grains for the two Haris (Aśvins), groats for Pūṣan, curdled milk for Sarasvatī, and whey for Mitra and Varuṇa; this is the five-footed Paṅkti. By means of this fivefold oblation, the Gāyatrī, though not alone, carries the morning pressing. For the sake of the perfection of this very Paṅkti, this whey for Mitra and Varuṇa is prescribed specifically at the morning pressing, and not at the other two pressings.
Having eaten [the portion], saying "We have been invited," he rises;

taking a piece of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), at the point where the *acāvāk* priest, having sat down, recites, he places that piece of the sacrificial cake into his hand and says, "O *acāvāk*, speak what is to be spoken by you. For the *acāvāk* had indeed fallen away.
Indra and Agni extended him along;

for the procreation of offspring, therefore the Acāvāka belongs to Indra and Agni. He partakes fully through this oblation—both by placing that fragment of the sacrificial cake in his hand for him, and by reciting this ancestral lineage (ārṣeya); thus he attains fulfillment.

When the Acāvāka has sat down, he proceeds with the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha). Now, as to why he proceeds with the seasonal cups once the Acāvāka has sat down: the Acāvāka is indeed a pair; for the Acāvāka belongs to Indra and Agni, and Indra and Agni are two—a pair, for a pair is productive. From this productive pair, he brings forth the seasons and the year.
Moreover, when the Acāvāka has sat down, he proceeds with the seasonal cups (ṛtugraha).
The seasons are indeed the year, and the year is everything; thus he causes everything to be born. Therefore, when the Acāvāka has sat down, he proceeds with the seasonal cups.
One should indeed draw twelve of them;

for there are twelve months in a year, therefore one should draw twelve. Or rather, one may also draw thirteen, on the grounds that there is a thirteenth month; however, one should draw only twelve, for this is the perfect number.
He takes [the Soma] from the Droṇakalaśa.
The Droṇakalaśa is indeed Prajāpati; he thus causes the seasons and the year to be born from this Prajāpati.

He takes [the libation] with two vessels that have openings on both sides. Why? Because those two have openings on both sides, therefore this year revolves around its ends. Having taken it, he does not set it down; therefore this year is unsettled.
He does not recite an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*);

for by means of the invitatory verse he summons [the season], and this season is already present, whether it be by day or by night. He does not utter the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-call (*anuvaṣaṭkāra*), lest he should exclude the seasons. They both take up the first two cups together, and the last two together; thus they encompass all this by means of the year, and so all this is encompassed by the year.

One of them goes out first, while the other enters; therefore these months proceed in succession. For if both were to go out together or both were to enter together, these months would surely pass separately; therefore one goes out first and the other enters.

With "By the seasons," those two perform six [pressings]; thereby the gods created the day. With "By the seasons," they performed four; thereby they created the night. If it had been only this much, there would have been only night, and it would not have passed away.
Those two indeed move twice above with the words "by the season";
the gods placed the day before that, therefore this is today's day, then the night, then tomorrow's day will be.

With "by the season," the gods created humans; with "by the seasons," they created cattle. Because they created cattle in the middle with that [formula], therefore these cattle are held on both sides and have come under the control of humans.

Having performed six [oblations] with "By the seasons," they transpose the two vessels; having performed four [oblations] with "By the seasons," they transpose the two vessels in the other way. Thus, on one side the gods created the day and on the other side the night; on one side the gods created humans and on the other side the cattle.

Now, therefore, he draws [the cups]. "Thou art taken with a support; for Madhu thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Mādhava thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ draws [the cup]. These two indeed belong to spring. Because in spring the plants are born and the trees bear fruit, therefore these two are Madhu and Mādhava.
"Thou art taken with a support;

for Śukra thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Śuci thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two indeed are the cups of the summer season. Because it burns most intensely during these two months, therefore they are called Śukra and Śuci.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Nabhas thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Nabhasya thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two indeed belong to the rainy season (vārṣika); from yonder sky it rains, and therefore these two are Nabhas and Nabhasya.

"Thou art taken with a support; for sap thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the juice]; "Thou art taken with a support; for strength thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two [juices] belong to the autumn. Because in autumn the plants ripen as sap and strength, therefore these two are indeed sap and strength.

"Thou art taken with a support; for strength thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for the month Sahasya thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two indeed belong to the winter season. Because in winter he (the cold) brings these creatures under his own control, as it were by force, therefore these two months are called Saha and Sahasya.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Tapaḥ (Heat), thee!"—with these words the Adhvaryu draws [the cup]; "Thou art taken with a support; for Tapasya (Cold), thee!"—with these words the Pratiprasthātṛ [draws]. These two indeed are the two Śaiśira (Winter) months. Because it freezes most intensely during these two, therefore these two are Tapaḥ and Tapasya.
"You are taken with a support;

for Aṃhasaspati you!"—with these words he draws the thirteenth cup, if he should draw a thirteenth. Then the Pratiprasthātṛ pours the residue into the Adhvaryu’s cup, or the Adhvaryu pours the residue into the Pratiprasthātṛ’s cup, and he brings it for consumption.
Then the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the draught for Indra and Agni with a cup that has not been consumed.

As to why he draws the draught for Indra and Agni with a cup that has not been consumed: one does not offer the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call after the seasonal draughts; however, since he is about to draw the draught for Indra and Agni for those [seasonal draughts], they thus become accompanied by the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call through this very draught for Indra and Agni.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the draught for Indra and Agni:

he has indeed generated this entire universe when he drew the seasonal draughts; he now generates this entire universe and establishes it upon out-breathing and in-breathing. Thus, this entire universe is established upon out-breathing and in-breathing, for Indra and Agni are out-breathing and in-breathing, and these two, heaven and earth, are out-breathing and in-breathing; for upon these two, this entire universe is established.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the draught for Indra and Agni:

he has indeed procreated all this when he drew the seasonal draughts; having procreated all this, he now places out-breathing and in-breathing within this very universe. These two, out-breathing and in-breathing, are thus established within this entire world.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Indra and Agni, come to the pressed juice with our songs, to the desirable cloud;
drink of this, impelled by our prayer."
"You are taken with a support; for Indra and Agni you are. "This is your womb; for Indra and Agni you!"—with these words he deposits it, for he draws it for Indra and Agni.
Then he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup.

Indeed, he has procreated all this when he has drawn the seasonal cups; for if it were only as much as that, then there would be only as many creatures as were created in the beginning, and they would not have multiplied.
Now, as for the fact that he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:

it is this entire universe, these very creatures, that he thus causes to go forth each according to its kind; therefore these creatures are born again and again. He draws it with the Śukra vessel; for that which shines yonder is indeed the Śukra, and its rays are the All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ); therefore he draws it with the Śukra vessel.
Then he draws [the cup]:

"O Viśve Devas, you who protect the people, come hither; you who give to the giver, to the pressed juice! You are taken with a support; for all the gods, you! This is your womb; for all the gods, you! Thus he deposits it, for he draws it for all the gods.
The Hotṛ indeed sings this when he recites;
the Adhvaryu responds to him as he sings this, and therefore it is called "Pratigara" (the response).
He calls out to him as he is seated facing east;
for all others besides the Udgātṛ perform their priestly duties facing east, and thus his priestly duty is indeed performed from the very beginning.
Prajāpati, indeed, is the Udgātṛ; the Ṛc is the Hotṛ.

This Prajāpati, the Udgātṛ, pours seed into the Ṛc, which is the Hotṛ, who is a woman. That which is poured when there is chanting, the Hotṛ brings forth by means of the Śastra (recitation). He sharpens it, just as this person is sharpened; and because he sharpens it, therefore it is called Śastra.
Having thus assisted him, he responds with the *pratigara*.

This is indeed like pressing down upon the seed once it has been cast; for if he were to respond while standing with his face turned away, that seed, having been cast, would surely perish and no offspring would be produced. But by both of them facing each other, they cause that cast seed to be generated.

The meters indeed belong to the gods; for by means of the meters the gods attained the heavenly world. The response (*pratigara*) is indeed exhilaration (*mada*); whatever exhilaration is in the *ṛc*, that is the essence (*rasa*) in the *sāman*. Thus he places that essence into the meters and makes them free from weariness. With those meters, being free from weariness, they extend the sacrifice.

Therefore, if he should recite by half-verses, he should respond at every half-verse; if he should recite by quarters, he should respond at every quarter. For when one who is reciting draws breath, the Asuras and Rakṣases descend upon the sacrifice; he joins it together with the response so that the destructive Rakṣases do not descend upon it, and he thus cuts off the world of his rival for the sacrificer.
In the beginning, indeed, the metres consisted of four syllables each.

Then the Jagatī flew toward Soma; she departed after leaving behind three syllables. Then the Triṣṭubh flew toward Soma; she departed after leaving behind one syllable. Then the Gāyatrī flew toward Soma; she returned bringing those syllables as well as Soma. Thus the Gāyatrī became eight-syllabled; therefore they say, "The Gāyatrī is eight-syllabled."

With her they performed the morning pressing; therefore the morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī. With that same [metre] they performed the midday pressing. Triṣṭubh said to her: "I will come to you with three syllables; invite me; do not exclude me from the sacrifice. "So be it," she replied. She invited her. Thereupon the Triṣṭubh became eleven-syllabled; therefore they say, "The midday pressing belongs to the Triṣṭubh."
With that very [syllable], they performed the third pressing.

The Jagatī said to her, "I will come to you with one syllable; invite me, lest I be excluded from the sacrifice. "So be it," she replied, and she invited her. Thereupon the Jagatī became twelve-syllabled; therefore they say, "The third pressing belongs to the Jagatī."
Regarding this they say:

"All the pressings are indeed Gāyatrī-like, for it was by means of the Gāyatrī that she (Sarasvatī) approached. Therefore, one should respond at the morning pressing when [the verse] is complete, for the Gāyatrī arrived complete. At the midday pressing, one should respond with a verse containing the word "mada" (intoxication), for she arrived having left behind one syllable; by that very means he completes her and makes her whole.
Where the Triṣṭubhs are recited, it is "threefold" at the third pressing;
for indeed, having left behind three syllables, she arrived. By means of those very [syllables], he thus completes her and makes her whole.

Wherein the *dyāvāpṛthivya* [laud] is recited—these two, heaven and earth, indeed, these creatures subsist upon; thus he places this essence into these very two, heaven and earth. Upon them, being full of essence and fit for subsistence, these creatures subsist. He should respond with "Om" alone; for that is truth, and the gods know that.

Now, some indeed respond with "Othāmodaiva vāk" (Othāmoda, speech!), saying, "The response is speech; thus we obtain speech. But one should not do so. For in whatever way one responds, speech is already obtained by him, since he responds by means of speech. Therefore, one should respond simply with "Om"; for that is the truth, and the gods know that.
He presses with "ihā ihā";
he thereby causes Indra himself to come hither. With "bṛhad bṛhat," he thereby causes Indra himself to come hither.
He draws the Śukra and the Manthin cups first;
for this pressing is characterized by the Śukra. Then he draws the Āgrayaṇa, for it is drawn at all the pressings. Then the Marutvatīya, and then the Ukthya, for the Ukthas are present here as well.
Now, some indeed, having drawn the Ukthya cup, then draw the Marutvatīya; but one should not do it in that way; rather, having drawn the Marutvatīya, one should then draw the Ukthya.

He draws these five cups; for this midday Pavamāna is indeed the thunderbolt, therefore it consists of fifteen verses and has five Sāmans, for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold. With these five cups he strikes, for there are five fingers here, and with the fingers one strikes.
Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra.

Having slain Vṛtra—the evil—he led the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) away into a conquered, fearless, and secure place. Therefore even now, whenever they chant with this Mādhyandina Pavamāna, then the sacrificial gifts are led away into a conquered, fearless, and secure place. In the same way, he now hurls the thunderbolt at his evil, hateful rival by means of these five cups; having slain Vṛtra—the evil—he leads the sacrificial gifts away into a conquered, fearless, and secure place. For this reason, he draws these five cups.

In that he draws the Marutvatīya cups: this midday pressing is indeed Indra’s exclusive libation; with it he sought to slay Vṛtra, and with it he desired to conquer. The Maruts, however, having departed, stood by an Aśvattha tree. Indra is the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś); for by means of the common people, a ruler becomes powerful. Therefore, the two seasonal vessels should be made of Aśvattha wood; yet they are actually made of Kārṣmarya wood.
Indra addressed them, saying, "Come over to me; with your strength I shall slay Vṛtra. They said, "What will accrue to us from that? For them, he drew these two Marutvatīya cups.

They said, "Let us approach him with power after having hidden it away. So they approached him with power after having hidden it away. Indra perceived this, thinking, "They have indeed approached me with power after having hidden it away."

He said, "Return together with your power (ojas)! [Indra said,] "Then indeed, take for us a third draught from them. He took that third draught for them with the formula: "Thou art taken with a support; thee for the Maruts' power! They returned to him together with their power. With them he conquered; with them he struck down Vṛtra. Indra is the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś). By means of the common people, the nobleman becomes powerful. Thus he bestows power upon the nobility. Therefore, he draws the Marutvatīya cups.
He should indeed draw [the cup] for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and not for the Maruts themselves.

For if he were to draw it for the Maruts, he would make the people (viś) rebellious against the nobility (kṣatra). But here, he causes the Maruts to share in Indra; thus he makes the people submissive to the nobility, following its will and obedient to it. Therefore, he should draw it for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, and not for the Maruts themselves.

He was indeed afraid they might depart from him—that they might go away from him or be supported elsewhere. He thus made them non-departing; therefore, one should draw [the cup] for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, but not for the Maruts themselves.

He draws [the cups] with two Ṛtu-vessels. The year is indeed the seasons; it is the sacrifice. Those [seasons] are directly manifested at this morning pressing when he draws the Ṛtu-cups. Now, they are manifested indirectly at the midday pressing when he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu-vessels. The Maruts are indeed the people (viś), and the people are food. The seasons cook all this food; therefore, he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two Ṛtu-vessels.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
"O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, drink the Soma here, just as you drank of the pressed juice at Śāryāta’s.
Under your guidance and in your protection, O Hero, the sages who perform excellent sacrifices desire to win [favor]."
You are taken with a support; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, you! This is your birthplace; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, you!
"The bull accompanied by the Maruts, increasing, the one whose enemy is not a child, the divine ruler Indra, the all-conquering, the fierce giver of victory—him we invoke here for new protection.

"Thou art taken with a support; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, thee! This is thy womb; for Indra accompanied by the Maruts, thee! "Thou art taken with a support; [I take] thee with the vigor of the Maruts"—with these words he draws the third cup.
Then he draws the Mahendra cup.

Indra had indeed become mingled with evil when he was with the Viś and the Maruts; just as one might eat from a common vessel with the Viś for the sake of victory, so it was when they drew this cup for him in common with the Maruts.

Just as the gods, when all was conquered, free from fear and free from destruction, pulled out the reed from its sheath, so did they pull him out from all evil when they drew the Māhendra cup; and even so does this sacrificer, by drawing the Māhendra cup, become released from all evil, just as a reed would be freed from its sheath.

Furthermore, as to why he draws the Māhendra cup: before the slaying of Vṛtra, this one was indeed Indra; but having slain Vṛtra, he became Mahendra, just as a great king becomes [Mahārāja] after conquering. Therefore he draws the Māhendra cup; and he thereby truly makes him great for the slaying of Vṛtra. For this reason also he draws the Māhendra cup. He draws it with the Śukra vessel; for that which burns yonder is indeed the Śukra (the Bright), and he is also the Great One (Mahān). Therefore he draws it with the Śukra vessel.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"Great is Indra, man-like, filling the people, and doubly vast, undecaying in his powers; for our sake he has grown strong in heroic deeds; broad, wide, well-fashioned by the makers. "Thou art taken with a support; for Mahendra thee! With "This is thy womb; for Mahendra thee," he deposits it, for he draws it for Mahendra.
Then, having brought it near, he utters this speech:

"Pressers, press! Unload the mortars! Agnīdh, mix the *āśira*! Take heed of the Soma-offering!"—thus indeed they press for the third pressing, they unload the mortars for the third pressing, the Agnīdh mixes the *āśira* for the third pressing, and he cooks the *saumya* pap for the third pressing. For these two pressings, the morning pressing and the midday pressing, are indeed full of bright juice and full of essence; but this third pressing has its bright juice drained away. It is from this very midday pressing that he thus reproduces it; and so his third pressing becomes full of bright juice and full of essence. Therefore, he speaks this speech here.
They indeed slay this sacrifice when they extend it;

when they press the King (Soma), they slay him; when they quiet and dissect the victim animal, they slay it; and with the mortar and pestle, and with the lower and upper grinding stones, they slay the Haviryajña.
This very sacrifice, being struck down, was not capable of functioning.

The gods made it capable by means of sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās); because they made it capable (adakṣayan) by means of sacrificial gifts, therefore they are called dakṣiṇās. Whatever part of this sacrifice, having been struck down, falters, that very part he now makes capable by means of these sacrificial gifts; thus the sacrifice becomes successful. Therefore, one gives sacrificial gifts.

In the Havis-sacrifice, they indeed give six or twelve; however, the Soma-sacrifice should never have less than a hundred as its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Prajāpati is manifestly the sacrifice, and man is nearest to Prajāpati. He has a life-span of a hundred years, a hundredfold luster, and a hundredfold vigor; therefore, one satisfies him with exactly a hundred, not with less than a hundred. For this reason, the Soma-sacrifice should not have less than a hundred as its fee. Otherwise, the officiating priests would not consider themselves worthy of the sacrificer, thinking, "He is no longer a support for us; they will kill him but will not satisfy him."

There are indeed two kinds of gods: the gods who are the gods themselves, and those who are the human gods—namely, the Brahmins who have heard the sacred texts and are learned in them. For them, the sacrifice is divided into two parts: oblations belong to the gods, while sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belong to the human gods—the Brahmins who have heard the sacred texts and are learned in them. With oblations one gratifies the gods, and with sacrificial fees one gratifies the human gods, the Brahmins who have heard the sacred texts and are learned in them. Both these classes of gods, being gratified, carry him to the heavenly world.

Now, these very sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) belong to the officiating priests alone. For they prepare for him another self—this sacrifice consisting of the Ṛg, the Yajus, the Sāman, and the oblation—and that becomes his self in yonder world. Therefore, because "they have generated me," one should give the sacrificial fees only to the officiating priests, and not to those who are not officiating priests.

Then, having returned to the Gārhapatya fire, he offers the Dakṣiṇā oblations. Having tied a piece of gold in a cloth used for the ten-day sacrifice and placed it [on the ladle], he offers them. He who sacrifices indeed sacrifices with the thought, "May there be a place for me in the world of the gods. His sacrifice goes forth toward the world of the gods; following after that, he gives a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). The sacrificer follows, holding onto the sacrificial fee.

There are indeed four sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā): gold, a cow, a garment, and a horse. It is not appropriate that one should place the foot of a horse [into the fire], nor that a cow should place its foot [therein]. Therefore, having tied gold to a garment used for the ten-night rite and placed it [in the fire], he offers the oblation.
He offers with two verses addressed to Sūrya.
For that world [the sky] is hidden by darkness; having dispelled the darkness by means of this light, he ascends to the heavenly world. Therefore, he offers with two verses addressed to Sūrya.
He offers with this verse:

"The rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that everyone may behold him, Svāhā! This is done with a Gāyatrī verse; for this earth is a Gāyatrī, and she is the foundation. Thus, he establishes himself upon this very foundation.
Then he offers the second oblation with this Triṣṭubh verse: "The brilliant face of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni;
Sūrya has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space—he, the soul of all that moves and stands, Svāhā! By means of this verse, he indeed approaches the world.

Then, at the Āgnīdhra fire-altar, he offers two oblations, or one. Now, as to why he offers two or one at the Āgnīdhra fire: Agni indeed rules over cattle, and they settle around him on every side; he gratifies him with this oblation, and being gratified, he gives his consent to him; thus, with his consent, he bestows [the cattle].
He offers the oblation:
"O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God, you who know all ways. Drive away from us the crooked sin;

we shall offer to you the most abundant word of homage, Svāhā! Then, if he intends to give a horse, whether already harnessed or unharnessed, he should offer a second oblation; but if not, he need not pay heed to it.

He offers the oblation with: "May this Agni create wide space for us; may he go before us, shattering the adversaries; may he win prizes in the contest for booty; may he, exulting, conquer the enemies, Svāhā! For the horse is indeed a winner of booty.
Then, taking gold, he approaches the sacrificial hall.

To the south of the altar, the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) stand; standing in front of the hall, he addresses them with the mantra: "By means of your form, I have approached your form. Indeed, in the beginning, the cattle were not willing to be given away; they concealed their own forms and presented themselves only with their bodies. Then the gods approached them from the middle of the sacrifice by means of their own forms; recognizing their own forms, they came down [to the gods], and being well-disposed, they became fit for giving. In the same way, this sacrificer now approaches them from the middle of the sacrifice by means of their own forms; recognizing their own forms, they come down [to him], and being well-disposed, they become fit for giving.
"Thus let Tutha, the all-knowing, distribute them to you.

Tutha is indeed the Brahman; thus he distributes them by means of the Brahman. For the Brahman knows both those who are worthy of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇīya*) and those who are not worthy of sacrificial gifts; thus these gifts of his come to be given only to one who is worthy of sacrificial gifts, and not to one who is not worthy of sacrificial gifts.
"Go by the path of Ṛta," he says;
for whoever goes by the path of the gods goes by the path of Ṛta. "The moon is the sacrificial fee"—thus they go by means of this light.
Then he approaches the Sadas, saying, "Behold the heaven! Behold the atmosphere! By this he means: "May I behold the world through you, the sacrificial gift."
Then he looks toward the assembly hall, saying, "Exert yourself with the members of the assembly"; by this he means, "May the members of the assembly not overlook you."

Then, taking gold, he approaches the Āgnīdhra fire, saying: "May I today find a Brāhmaṇa who has a father and a grandfather. For he who is well-known and of a well-known lineage is one who has a father and a grandfather; and when one gives even a few sacrificial gifts to a person who is well-known, one wins great merit through them. "A seer and of seers' descent"—for he who is well-known and learned in the Vedas is a seer and of seers' descent; "with a gift of well-placed wealth"—for such a person indeed possesses well-placed wealth as his sacrificial fee.
Then, having approached in this manner.

He gives gold to the Āgnīdhra with the words, "Given by us, go among the gods. For whatever sacrificial gift one gives with a generous mind and without hesitation, by that he wins great things. With the words, "Go among the gods," he sacrifices thinking, "May there be a place for me in the world of the gods" for whoever sacrifices; thus he makes him a sharer in the world of the gods. With the words, "Enter the giver," he says, in effect, "Enter me. Thus these [gifts] do not perish from him as they turn away. Now, as to why he gives the sacrificial gift first to the Āgnīdhra: from him indeed all the gods won immortality; therefore he gives the sacrificial gift first to the Āgnīdhra.
Then, having approached in this very manner:

He gives gold to the descendant of Atri. For when they recite that morning litany (prātaranuvāka), they used to praise this very thing in former times: "Atri was indeed the Hotṛ-priest among the seers; then this seat (sadas) was flooded with the darkness of the Asuras. Those seers said to Atri: 'Come here! Drive away this darkness! He drove away that darkness, saying: 'This is indeed light—he who has struck down this darkness. To him they brought this light, gold, as a sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā); for gold is light. By means of that brilliance and power, the seer struck down the darkness; and now this sacrificer likewise strikes down the darkness by means of that same light. Therefore, he gives gold to the descendant of Atri."

Then [he gives] to the Brahman; for the Brahman protects the sacrifice from the south. Then to the Udgātṛ, then to the Hotṛ, then to the two Adhvaryus seated at the Havirdhāna shed. Then, having returned, to the Prastotṛ, then to the Maitrāvaruṇa, then to the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin, then to the Potṛ, then to the Neṣṭṛ, then to the Acchāvāka, then to the Unnetṛ, then to the Grāvastut, then to the Subrahmaṇyā, and finally he gives to the Pratihartṛ as the last. For this one is indeed the Pratihartṛ; thus he hands these over to him at the very end. In this way, these [gifts] do not perish by turning away from him.

Then he says, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts. At the very beginning, when Prajāpati gave [the Soma], Indra reflected: "He will give away all this; nothing at all will remain for us. He raised that thunderbolt, saying, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts" so that he would not give; then he did not give. Even now, that same thunderbolt is raised while saying, "Recite for Indra accompanied by the Maruts," so that he may not give; then he does not give.
There are indeed four sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).

Gold: by this he protects his own life-span, for gold is life; he gave that to the Āgnīdhra as he was performing the duties of the Āgnīdhra. Therefore even now a gift of gold is given to the Āgnīdhra.
Then the cow: by this he protects the breath of his own self, for the cow is breath; the cow is food, for the cow is food; and food is breath. He gave her to Rudra as the Hotṛ priest.
Then the garment: by this he protects the skin of his own self, for a garment is indeed the skin; that [garment] he gave to Bṛhaspati as he sang the Udgītha.

Now as for the horse: the horse is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus places the thunderbolt at the head [of the sacrifice]. "May I also have a share in the world of Yama," so thinks he who sacrifices when he sacrifices; he thus makes him a sharer in that very world of Yama. He gave it to Yama, the Brahman.
He receives the gold with the formula:
"May Varuna give thee to me for Agni. For indeed, Varuna gave this to Agni; [he says], "May I attain immortality; be thou a giver of life to the giver, and a source of bliss to me, the receiver."
Then he approaches the cow with the formula:
"May Varuna give thee to me for Rudra. For Varuna indeed gave her to Rudra. [He continues: "May I attain immortality; be thou breath to the giver and vigor to me, the receiver."
Then he takes back the garment with the formula:
"May Varuna give thee to me for Brihaspati. For Varuna indeed gave this to Brihaspati. [He continues: "May I attain immortality; be thou a skin to the giver, and joy to me, the receiver."
Then he approaches the horse with the formula:
"May Varuṇa give thee to me for Yama. For Varuṇa indeed gave this [horse] to Yama. [He continues: "May I attain immortality; O horse, be a gift for the giver and vigor for me, the receiver."

Now, as for whatever else he gives, he gives that out of desire alone, thinking, "May this also be mine in the other world. He acknowledges it thus: "Who gave? To whom did he give? Desire gave; to Desire did he give. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. O Desire, this [is yours]. Thus he assigns it to the deity.

Regarding this they say: "One should not transfer [the merit] to the deity; for whichever deity one kindles, that deity, being kindled, becomes better and better day by day. And whichever fire one places fuel upon, that fire, being kindled, becomes better and better day by day. He who, knowing this, accepts [a gift], truly becomes better and better day by day. Just as one would offer an oblation into a kindled fire, so does he offer this [gift] which he studies and gives. Therefore, while studying, one should not transfer [the merit]."
There are indeed three classes of gods:

the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas. Their Soma-pressings are divided accordingly: the morning pressing belongs to the Vasus, the midday pressing to the Rudras, and the third pressing to the Ādityas. Now, the morning pressing of the Vasus is unmixed, the midday pressing of the Rudras is unmixed, but the third pressing of the Ādityas is mixed.

Those Ādityas said, "Just as this morning libation of the Vasus is unmixed and the midday libation of the Rudras is unmixed, so do not offer this cup of ours before it is mixed. "So be it," the gods replied. They offered this cup after the midday libation had concluded, but before the third libation. Even now, that same cup is offered in exactly the same way: after the midday libation has concluded, but before the third libation.
Those Ādityas said:
"We are neither in this libation nor in the other; [we wish that] the Rākṣasas might not harm us."
They said to the deities of the dual-divinities:
"We are indeed afraid of the Rākṣasas; come, let us enter into you."
The Dvidevatyas said, "What will come of that for us? The Ādityas replied, "You shall have the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* performed after us. Saying, "So be it," they entered the Dvidevatyas.

When he proceeds with the cups for the dual deities at the morning pressing, then the Pratiprasthātṛ should draw [the remnant] from the Droṇakalaśa into the Āditya cup with the formula, "Thou art taken with a support"—only so much [is said]. The Adhvaryu alone causes the announcement; the Pratiprasthātṛ offers after the Adhvaryu's offering, pouring out the remnant with "For the Ādityas, thee! In this same manner it is done for all [the cups].

Now, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ draws [the cup] back again: the Ādityas said, "You have entered among those belonging to two deities; you shall be offered the *anuvashat* by us. Indeed, that second oblation which one offers belongs to the Sviṣṭakṛt; these [cups] are offered the *anuvashat* for the sake of the Sviṣṭakṛt. Thus, these of his become offered with the *anuvashat* and have their Sviṣṭakṛt performed. He offers on the northern half, for this is the quarter of this deity; therefore he offers on the northern half.

Furthermore, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ takes it back: they entered into the cups belonging to two deities; he thus releases them from those very ones into which they had entered. Then he covers it, for they were afraid of the Rakṣases, saying: "O Viṣṇu of wide stride, this is thy Soma; guard it, let them not harm thee! Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; he thus entrusts it to the sacrifice for protection. Then he says: "The midday pressing being completed, before the third pressing, come hither, O sacrificer!"

The Adhvaryu, the Sacrificer, the Āgnīdhra, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Unnetṛ, and whoever else is an attendant, all enter together; they close both doors, for they were afraid of the Rākṣasas. Then the Adhvaryu takes the Āditya-vessel and the Āditya-cup; he draws [the Soma] from above the Pūtabhṛt, lest it should drip out.
Then he takes [the water] with the mantra:
"Never art thou barren, O Indra; never dost thou fail the donor. More and more, O Maghavan, does thy divine gift increase. For the Ādityas, thee!"

One should not take it with a prefixing formula (upayāma), for it has already been taken with a prefixing formula at the very beginning; this is to avoid repetition (ajāmitā). For he would indeed commit a repetition if he were to take it here as well with a prefixing formula.
Then, having drawn it out, he pours it back in:
"Never art thou negligent; thou guardest both births. O Āditya, the fourth libation is thy power; thou hast attained immortality in heaven. For the Ādityas, thee!"
Then he takes the curds.

The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas, and cattle follow after the Ādityas; thus he places this milk among the cattle. "This milk is placed within the cattle," they say; "he should take it from the middle, for this milk of the cattle is, as it were, in the middle. But rather, he should take it from the hind part, for this milk of the cattle is, as it were, at the hind part.

Furthermore, as to why he takes curds: these remnants of the oblations have been offered and are no longer sufficient for a further offering; he thus causes them to swell again so that they become fit for an offering. Therefore, he takes curds.
He takes it up with the formula:
"The sacrifice approaches the favor of the gods; O Ādityas, be gracious! May your benevolence turn hitherward toward us, which is the best finder of room even out of distress. For the Ādityas, thee!"
He mixes it with the Upāṃśusavana stone.
For this Upāṃśusavana stone is, by its very nature, Vivasvat Āditya; or rather, this [cup] belongs to Āditya. Thus he gratifies him in his own portion.

He does not touch it with the fringe nor with the filter; for these two libations, the morning pressing and the midday pressing, are indeed bright and full of essence, whereas this third pressing has its essence squeezed out. In that he does not touch it with the fringe nor with the filter, thereby his third pressing becomes bright and full of essence. Therefore, he does not touch it with the fringe nor with the filter.

He looks at it, saying, "O Vivasvat Āditya, this is your draught of Soma; intoxicate yourself with it! Then he hands the *upāṃśusavana* stone to the *unnetṛ*. Then he says to the *unnetṛ*, "Release the pressing-stones! He releases them either into the *ādhavanīya* jar or into the cup.
Having raised up the King (Soma), [he proceeds];
for the third pressing belongs to the Ādityas, and the pressing-stones follow the Ādityas; thus he gratifies them in their own portion. They throw open the two doors.

Then, having covered [the vessel], he goes out; for they were afraid of the Rākṣasas. Then he says, "Recite for the Ādityas. At this point, if he should desire it, he may look at [the offering]; but rather, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he should look at it. He says, "Prompt for the Ādityas—the beloved ones, whose abodes are beloved, whose vows are beloved, the lords of the great dwelling, the overseers of the wide mid-region! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the offering; he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call, lest he should cast the cattle into the fire. He hands over the two residues to the Pratiprasthātṛ.

Then, having approached again, he takes up the Āgrayaṇa vessel; they spread out the filter with its fringes pointing northward; the Adhvaryu causes [the Soma] to flow down; the Pratiprasthātṛ receives it from the Āgrayaṇa; and the Unnetṛ brings the residues either with a cup or with a dipping-vessel.
He draws the Āgrayaṇa from four streams.
The third pressing belongs to the Ādityas, and cows indeed follow the Ādityas; therefore, this milk of cows is divided into four parts. That is why he draws the Āgrayaṇa from four streams.
Now, when the Pratiprasthātṛ takes up the two remnants, this becomes the Āditya cup;

for one does not utter the *anuvaṣaṭ* call for the Āditya cup. Indeed, it is from this [cup] that he is about to draw the Sāvitra cup; thus, by means of the Sāvitra cup itself, his [Āditya cup] becomes accompanied by the *anuvaṣaṭ* call.
Furthermore, as for why the Pratiprasthātṛ collects the two residues:

formerly they offered these libations mixed with those [residues] before the third pressing; this libation is indeed drawn for the sake of the third pressing, so that the Ādityas enter into the third pressing and thus do not remain outside the sacrifice. Therefore, the Pratiprasthātṛ collects the two residues.

The mind, indeed, is his Savitṛ; therefore he draws the Sāvitra cup. The breath, indeed, is his Savitṛ; thus he places that very breath in him in front when he draws the Upāṃśu cup. He places that very breath in him behind when he draws the Sāvitra cup. These two breaths are placed on both sides of him: that which is above and that which is below.

The seasons are indeed the year, which is the sacrifice.
