Those [seasons] are explicitly provided for there at the morning pressing when he draws the seasonal cups (*ṛtugraha*); but here at the midday pressing, they are provided for implicitly when he draws the Marutvatīya cups with the two seasonal vessels (*ṛtupātra*). Indeed, in this case, they do not draw any cup specifically for the seasons, nor is any cup drawn using the two seasonal vessels.
This Savitṛ is indeed he who shines yonder; he is also all the seasons. Thus the seasons and the year are clearly established at the third libation; therefore, he draws the cup for Savitṛ.
He draws it either with the Upāṃśu cup or with the Antaryāma cup.

For Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the Upāṃśu is his breath; therefore he draws it with the Upāṃśu cup, or with the Antaryāma cup, for these two are the same, since the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma are the out-breath (prāṇa) and the in-breath (udāna).
He draws [the cup] from the Āgrayaṇa.
Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the Āgrayaṇa is his self; thus he places the mind in the self. Savitṛ is indeed his breath, and the Āgrayaṇa is his self; thus he places the breath in the self.

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]: "O Savitṛ, grant us what is desirable today, what is desirable tomorrow, and what is desirable day by day; for, O God, through this prayer, may we be sharers in the desirable abundance of your vast domain. "You are taken with a support; you belong to Savitṛ; you are the bestower of delight; you are the bestower of delight; bestow delight upon me; quicken the sacrifice; quicken the lord of the sacrifice; [grant] fortune! Thus he says.

Having taken it, he does not set it down; for Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and therefore this mind is not set down. Savitṛ is indeed his breath, and therefore this breath moves about while not set down. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the god Savitṛ"; having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt the offering for the god Savitṛ. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he offers, but he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ*. For Savitṛ is indeed his mind, [thinking] "Lest I should consume the mind in the fire"; and Savitṛ is indeed his breath, [thinking] "Lest I should consume the breath in the fire."
Now, with the cup not yet consumed, he draws the Vaiśvadeva draught.

As to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva draught with the cup not yet consumed: he does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭ* call for the Sāvitra draught; it is from this [Sāvitra] that he is about to draw the Vaiśvadeva draught. Thus, by means of the Vaiśvadeva itself, his [Vaiśvadeva] becomes one for which the *anuvaṣaṭ* call has been made.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:

Savitṛ is indeed his mind, and the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ) are all this [universe]. Thus, he makes all this follow after and conform to the mind; therefore, all this follows after and conforms to the mind.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:

Savitṛ is indeed his breath, and the All-gods (Viśve Devāḥ) are this entire universe; he thus places both out-breathing and in-breathing within this whole universe, for these two are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing within this whole universe.
Furthermore, as to why he draws the Vaiśvadeva cup:

the third pressing belongs to the All-gods (Vaiśvadeva), and it is so called from the perspective of the Sāman; and because the third pressing is called Vaiśvadeva from the perspective of the Ṛc, therefore this very [cup] is drawn from the perspective of the Yajus and from the perspective of the preparatory rite when he draws this Mahāvaiśvadeva cup.
He draws that from the *pūtabhṛt* vessel;

for the *pūtabhṛt* belongs to the All-gods (*vaiśvadeva*), since from it they draw out [the soma] for the gods, from it for men, and from it for the ancestors; therefore the *pūtabhṛt* belongs to the All-gods.
He draws that cup without a *puroruk* formula.

For he draws it for all the gods; and all the gods are everything—whatever Ṛg-verses, whatever Yajus-formulas, and whatever Sāman-chants there are. Since he draws it for all the gods, by that very fact this cup of his becomes possessed of a *puroruk*; therefore, he draws it without a *puroruk*.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]: "Thou art taken with a support;

thou art a good refuge, a good foundation. Breath indeed is the good refuge and the good foundation. "Homage to Bṛhadukṣa! Prajāpati indeed is Bṛhadukṣa; thus he says, "Homage to Prajāpati! "Thee for the All-gods! This is thy womb: thee for the All-gods! With these words he deposits it, for he draws it for the All-gods. Then, having gone forward, he sits down facing the east.

When the Hotṛ recites this verse: "With one and with ten, O self-existent one; with two for the sacrifice and with twenty; with three and with thirty, O Vāyu, unyoke those teams here"—then at this verse addressed to Vāyu, the vessels are unyoked. For animals have Vāyu as their leader; Vāyu is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), and by means of the vital breath, animals move about.
He indeed departed from the gods with the sacrificial animals.
The gods addressed him at the morning pressing, but he did not return; they addressed him at the midday pressing, but he still did not return; they addressed him at the third pressing.

As he was about to turn back, he said: "If I were to turn back, what would be mine from that? [The other replied: "These vessels shall be yoked by you alone, and they shall be unyoked by you. Therefore, these vessels are yoked when he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu at the morning pressing; and these vessels are unyoked when he says, "O Vāyu, unyoke those teams here," for the *niyuts* are indeed cattle; thus, it is by means of cattle that these vessels are unyoked.

If he had returned at the morning pressing—the morning pressing belonging to the Gāyatrī, and the Gāyatrī being the Brahman—then cattle would have belonged only to the Brāhmaṇas. If he had returned at the midday pressing—the midday pressing belonging to Indra, and Indra being the Kṣatra—then cattle would have belonged only to the Kṣatriyas. But since he returned at the third pressing—the third pressing belonging to the Viśvedevas, and the Viśvedevas being all this [universe]—therefore, these cattle are found everywhere.

He proceeds with the *caru* offering for Soma. Soma is indeed the sacrificial food (*havis*) of the gods; thus, this very oblation is prepared for Soma himself, so that Soma remains uninterrupted. It is a *caru*; for the *caru* is the food of the gods, since the *caru* is boiled rice (*odana*), and boiled rice is manifest food. Therefore, it is a *caru*.
Therefore, he does not proceed with it at the morning pressing, nor at the midday pressing;
for these two pressings, the morning pressing and the midday pressing, belong exclusively to the gods, whereas Soma belongs to the Pitṛs as his deity.

If he were to proceed at the morning pressing or at the midday pressing, he would indeed cause discord between the gods and the ancestors; therefore, he proceeds at the third pressing. For the third pressing belongs to the All-gods (Vaiśvadeva), and thus he avoids discord. He does not recite an invitatory verse (anuvākyā), for the ancestors have departed once and for all; therefore, he does not recite an invitatory verse.

Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter and called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice the clarified butter! and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered. Thus, he interposes this between those offerings which have been made prior to that; in this way, he brings about concord.
Having spread a base of clarified butter,

he takes two portions from the caru, then pours clarified butter over them, calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*, says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Soma-oblation," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Sacrifice the clarified butter! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he offers it. He thereby interposes this between those oblations which he is about to offer hereafter; thus he creates a lack of conflict. If he should so desire, he may sacrifice on both sides; or if he should so desire, he may sacrifice on only one side.
Now, there is a sacrificial ladle called the *pracaraṇī*.

Having taken four ladlings of clarified butter in that [spoon], the Adhvaryu sprinkles the hearths (dhiṣṇiyas) with fire-sticks. As to why he sprinkles the hearths with fire-sticks: it is because the gods said to them, "At the third pressing, an offering of clarified butter shall reach you, but not one of Soma; for your share of the Soma-drinking has been taken away from you. Therefore, this offering of Soma does not reach them at the third pressing, nor does an offering of Soma; rather, it is an offering of clarified butter that reaches them at the third pressing alone. When he sprinkles the hearths with fire-sticks, he sprinkles them with these very sacrificial formulas (yajus), according to where they were strewn and in their original order, ending finally at the Mārjālīya hearth.

Now, some indeed perform the *punarāghāra* libation on the Āgnīdhrīya fire, thinking, "In this way the ritual will be completed toward the north. But one should not do so; rather, the final libation should be performed on the Mārjālīya fire itself.

When the Adhvaryu sprinkles the hearths with the fire-sticks, then the Pratiprasthātṛ draws the Pātnīvata cup. From the sacrifice offspring are produced; being produced from the sacrifice, they are produced from a union; being produced from a union, they are produced at the end of the sacrifice. Thus he produces them at the end of the sacrifice from a productive union. Therefore, these offspring are produced from a productive union at the end of the sacrifice; that is why he draws the Pātnīvata cup.
He draws that [Soma] with the Upāṃśu cup.

If he should draw the Sāvitra [cup] with the Upāṃśu cup, he should draw this one with the Antaryāma cup; if he should draw the Sāvitra with the Antaryāma cup, he should draw this one with the Upāṃśu cup. For these two are the same, namely the Upāṃśu and the Antaryāma; for the breath is the Upāṃśu and the breath is the Antaryāma. The breath is indeed the male, and the wife is the female; thus a productive union is brought about.
He draws that cup without a *puroruk* verse;
for the *puroruk* is indeed vigor, and he does so thinking, "Lest I place vigor in women"; therefore, he draws it without a *puroruk*.

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]: "Thou art taken with a support; O divine Soma, of thee who art pressed by Bṛhaspati... Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus he says, "of thee who art impelled by the Brahman, O divine Soma. When he says, "of Indu, the possessor of power," he means "of the one possessed of vigor. By saying, "may I succeed in drawing the cups for the wives," he does not actually draw them for the wives at this moment, lest he should place vigor in women; therefore, he does not draw them for the wives at this time.

Now, whatever remains as residue in the *pracaraṇī* ladle, with that he mixes it; he thus enriches it, whereas by mixing the other cups he impoverishes this one. Ghee is indeed a thunderbolt (*vajra*); with this thunderbolt of ghee, the gods, while striking, struck down the wives and deprived them of their power. Struck down and deprived, they could no longer exercise power over themselves nor over their inheritance. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now, with this thunderbolt of ghee, strikes down the wives and deprives them of their power. Struck down and deprived, they can no longer exercise power over themselves nor over their inheritance.

He mixes it [with milk], saying: "I am above, I am below; that which is the intermediate space, that has become my father; I have seen the sun on both sides; I [know] that which is the supreme secret of the gods. In that he mixes it with the words "I, I," he thereby bestows virility upon males.
Then he says, "O Āgnīdh, recite the offering prayer for the Pātnīvata!

The Āgnīdh is indeed a male and the wife is a female; thus a productive union is brought about. He offers with the words, "O Agni, accompanied by the wives! For Agni is a male and the wife is a female; thus a productive union is brought about.
"In harmony with the god Tvaṣṭṛ."

Tvaṣṭṛ indeed transforms the emitted seed; therefore, he (the Adhvaryu) now transforms this emitted seed. He offers [the oblation] on the northern half [of the fire] with the words, "Drink the Soma, Svāhā! Those other oblations are the gods, while these are the wives; for thus is the union of a couple arranged, since the woman lies upon the man from the north. The Adhvaryu brings a portion for the Agnīdh; the latter says, "Adhvaryu, invite me! One should not invite him in return, for what invitation can there be for one who is slain and cast out? Yet, one should indeed invite him in return. They offer into his fire and utter the *vaṣaṭ* call; therefore, one should indeed invite him in return.
Then he issues the command:

"O Agnīdh, sit in the lap of the Neṣṭṛ; O Neṣṭṛ, lead up the wife and have her look at the Udgātṛ; O Unnetṛ, pour out [the Soma] following the Hotṛ’s cup, so that the Soma does not remain over," provided it be an Agniṣṭoma.

If it should be an Ukthya sacrifice, he should say, "Make the Soma swell. Holding that very vessel, he sits down on the lap of the Neṣṭṛ. For the Āgnīdhra is Agni by nature, and the Neṣṭṛ is a woman; the Āgnīdhra is the male and the Neṣṭṛ is the female—thus a productive union is brought about. The Neṣṭṛ leads up the wife and makes her look at the Udgātṛ with the words, "Prajāpati, you are the male, the placer of seed; place seed in me! For the Udgātṛ is Prajāpati and the wife is the female—thus a productive union is brought about.
The meters are indeed the cattle of the gods.

Just as here on earth cattle, when yoked, carry burdens for men, so do the meters, when yoked, carry the sacrifice for the gods. When the meters satisfied the gods, then the gods satisfied the meters; from that time forth it came to pass that the meters, being yoked, carried the sacrifice to the gods and fully gratified them.
Then he draws the Hāriyojana cup.
The Hāriyojana is indeed the metres; it is thus the metres that he satisfies. Therefore he draws the Hāriyojana cup.
Or rather, he draws it as an excess.

For when he has drawn the Śamyu-formula, he then draws this [cup]; for the gods are this [earth], then the meters are an excess, then humans are an excess, and then cattle are an excess; therefore, he draws it as an excess.

He draws [the draught] into the Droṇakalaśa. Soma was indeed Vṛtra; when the gods slew him, his head rolled away and became the Droṇakalaśa. Whatever essence flowed together into it, that was indeed excessive. This cup is excessive; thus he places that which is excessive into that which is excessive. Therefore, he draws [the draught] into the Droṇakalaśa.
He draws that cup without a *puroruk* verse;
for he draws it for the metres. Since he draws it for the metres, by that very fact it becomes possessed of a *puroruk* for him; therefore he draws it without a *puroruk*.
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:

"Thou art taken with a support; thou art the bay horse, the yoker of bays; for thee, with the two bays! The two bays are indeed the Ṛc and the Sāman, for it is with the Ṛc and the Sāman that he draws this [cup].

Then he pours in the parched grains with the formula, "Ye are the parched grains for the two bay steeds, together with Soma, for Indra. Thus, whatever here is both measured and unmeasured, that entire thing he consumes.
The Unnetṛ calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call "Oṃ śrāvaya").

Or rather, the Unnetṛ is the one who is redundant; for he does not call for the *āśrāvaṇa* of anyone else, since this cup is redundant. Thus, being redundant himself, he places that which is redundant into it. Therefore, the Unnetṛ calls for the *āśrāvaṇa*.

Having placed [the cup] upon the head, he causes it to be heard; for this [cup] is its head. Then he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for the parched grains and Soma," and having caused it to be heard, he says, "Prompt the offering of the parched grains and Soma that have been set forth. At the *vaṣaṭ* call he offers, and at the subsequent *vaṣaṭ* call [he offers again]. Then they seek to lick the parched grains for consumption.

Now, some carry the *droṇakalaśa* over to the *hotṛ*, saying, "It is the portion for the one who utters the *vaṣaṭ*. But one should not do so; for while the other portions are according to the cups (*camasa*), this one is an additional portion. Therefore, the portion of all belongs to this [vessel], and thus they desire to obtain the parched grains (*dhānā*) for the sake of consuming them.

They should not chew them with their teeth, thinking, "These are indeed cattle; let us not cause injury to the cattle. They consume them by means of the vital breaths (prāṇas) alone, saying, "That which is thy food, winning horses, that which is thy food, winning cows. For these are indeed cattle; therefore he says, "That which is thy food, winning horses, that which is thy food, winning cows. "Of thee, whose sacrificial formulas have been offered, whose hymns have been chanted"—for the sacrificial formulas have indeed been offered and the hymns have been chanted—"of thee, whose praises have been recited"—for the praises have indeed been recited—"of thee, who art invited, I eat as one invited"—for being invited, he eats this as one who is invited.

They should not scatter them into the fire, lest they should offer what is impure (ucchiṣṭa) into the fire; rather, they pour them down upon the high altar (uttaravedī), so that they do not remain outside the sacrifice.

Then they touch the full vessels together. Regarding those which some call "the Soma-draughts in the waters": just as one who is yoked might pull [a load], so do these who perform the office of the officiating priests; and indeed, when one is yoked, he may stumble or be injured. Water is a pacifier and a remedy. Therefore, whatever in this case they stumble over or injure themselves, water—as a pacifier—pacifies that; with water they heal that. That is why they touch the full vessels together.
They touch themselves together, saying:

"We have united with splendor, with milk, with our bodies, and with a gracious mind. May Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow wealth upon us and smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured. By this, they heal whatever has been torn asunder.
Then they touch their faces.

There is a twofold reason why they touch their faces: water is indeed nectar; thus they touch themselves with nectar, and they also place this very rite within themselves; therefore they touch their faces.

Now, he offers these nine *samiṣṭayajus* oblations. As to why he offers nine *samiṣṭayajus*: there are nine *stotriya* verses in the *bahiṣpavamāna* chant; thus this *virāj* is deficient on both sides for the sake of procreation. From this very procreative source which is deficient on both sides, Prajāpati created offspring—both those moving upward from here and those moving downward from there. In the same way, he (the sacrificer) creates offspring from this very procreative source which is deficient on both sides—both those moving upward from here and those moving downward from there.
The *hiṅkāra* is the tenth of the *stotriya* verses;
the *svāhākāra* is [the tenth] of these. Thus, this deficient *virāj* of his becomes one consisting of ten-by-ten.

Now, as to why they are called *samiṣṭayajūṃṣi*: whatever deities he invites by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, all those deities indeed become "sacrificed-to together" (*samiṣṭāḥ*). Because he offers these oblations after all those [deities] have been sacrificed-to together, therefore they are called *samiṣṭayajūṃṣi*.

Now, as to why he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations: the self of one who has sacrificed becomes, as it were, emptied; for whatever he possesses, that he gives away. Therefore, with these three [oblations], he replenishes that very self once again.
Now, as for the three subsequent oblations which he offers:

whatever deities he invokes by means of this sacrifice, and for whomsoever this sacrifice is performed, they remain waiting, thinking, "Let him offer these *samistayajus* oblations for us. He now dismisses them each to their proper place, according to where their course lies.
Now, as for those three final oblations which he offers:
when they have extended this sacrifice—that is, when they have generated it—he establishes it where its foundation lies; therefore, he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations.

He offers: "O Indra, lead us together with mind and with cattle. By saying "with mind," he causes that which was depleted of mind to swell; by saying "with cattle," he causes that which was depleted of cattle to swell. "Together with patrons, O Maghavan, together with well-being, together with the *brahman* that is made by the gods"—by saying "with the *brahman*," he causes that which was depleted of the *brahman* to swell. "In the favor of the gods worthy of sacrifice, Svāhā!"

"May we be united with splendor, with milk, and with our bodies"—by saying "with splendor," he causes him who has been depleted of splendor to swell; by saying "with milk," since milk is indeed essence, he causes him who has been depleted of essence to swell. "We have gone forth with a gracious mind; may Tvaṣṭṛ, the giver of good gifts, bestow wealth upon us, and may he smooth over whatever in our bodies is injured"—thereby he joins together what was torn asunder.

"May Savitṛ enjoy this; may Prajāpati, the god who guards the treasure, Agni, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Viṣṇu, being in harmony with offspring, bestow wealth upon the sacrificer—Svāhā! By saying, "bestow wealth upon the sacrificer—Svāhā," he thereby replenishes again that which had been emptied.

"O gods, we have made easy paths for you to sit, you who have come here, enjoying this libation"—thus he says, "O gods, we have made easy paths and seats for you to sit, you who have come here, enjoying this libation. "Bearing and bringing the oblations"—by this he dismisses the deities; "let those who are without vehicles go bearing [the offerings], and let those who have vehicles go bringing them"—this is what he means by saying, "bearing and bringing the oblations, O Vasus, bestow riches upon us, Svāhā!"
Whom you brought hither.

"O God Agni, impel those willing gods to their own abode"—thus he says to Agni: "Bring hither those gods! Bring hither those gods! He thereby says to him: "Send forth those gods whom you have brought hither, wherever their course lies. "Having eaten and having drunk, all"—for they have indeed eaten the sacrificial animal and the cake (*puroḍāśa*); "having drunk"—for they have indeed drunk King Soma; therefore he says, "Having eaten and having drunk, all, do ye ascend to the breath, the heat, and the light, Svāhā! Thus he truly dismisses the deities.

"For we have chosen you here, O Agni, as the Hotṛ-priest at this proceeding sacrifice. Successfully have we sacrificed; successfully have you performed the service. Knowing the way, come to the sacrifice, O wise one—Svāhā! With this [verse], he releases Agni; he lets Agni go forth.

"O gods, you who know the way!"—for the gods indeed know the way; "having found the way," he thereby says, "having found the sacrifice. "Having gone the way," by this he releases [the sacrifice] according to its proper course. "O Lord of the Mind, O God, place this sacrifice in the wind, Svāhā!"—this wind is indeed the sacrifice. Having gathered this sacrifice together, he establishes it in that sacrifice; he unites sacrifice with sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Svāhā, place it in the wind!"

"O sacrifice, go to the sacrifice; go to the lord of the sacrifice; go to your own womb, Svāhā!"—by this he establishes the sacrifice, which is already complete, in its own womb. "This is your sacrifice, O lord of the sacrifice, accompanied by the Sūktavāka and possessing all heroes; enjoy it, Svāhā!"—by this he finally establishes the sacrifice, which is already complete, accompanied by the Sūktavāka and possessing all heroes, within the sacrificer.

He indeed goes down to the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha). As to why he goes down to the purificatory bath: whatever essence had come into him from the oblations, that they have produced; now this body contains no essence, so it must not be cast away. They carry it down into the water; for water is essence—thus he places that essence into it, and unites him with that essence; thus he produces him from there, and once he is born, he brings him forth. Because they carry it down into the water, it is therefore called the *avabhṛtha*.
Then he offers the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations;

for the *samiṣṭayajus* are indeed the end of the sacrifice. Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus*, they go together toward the *cātvāla* pit with whatever is around this [altar]. He throws the black antelope horn and the girdle into the *cātvāla*.

"May I not become a *mahiṣ* (water-snake), may I not become a *pṛdāku* (adder)! This indeed is the *svagā*-formula for the *ṛjīṣa*: when they throw it into the water, then this very formula serves as its *svagā*. For snakes are like ropes, and the abodes of snakes are like wells. There is indeed a mutual rivalry between humans and snakes; he says this so that it may not come into contact with them. Therefore he says, "May I not become a *mahiṣ*, may I not become a *pṛdāku*."

Then he makes [the sacrificer] recite: "For King Varuṇa has made wide for Sūrya a path to follow. By this he means: "Just as this wide, secure, and uninjured path is for Sūrya, so may this wide, secure, and uninjured path be for me."

"He has made feet for him where there were no feet to step upon. For even if one becomes footless, this [verse] is indeed sufficient for his recovery. "And he is the expeller, piercing even the heart"—thereby he releases him from every sin and evil originating in the heart.
Then he says, "Sing the Sāman!

Or he may say, "Recite the Sāman," but he should rather say, "Sing it," for they sing the Sāman. Now, as to why he sings the Sāman: it is so that this body of the sacrifice shall not be harmed by the destructive Rākṣasa-demons outside; for the Sāman is the repeller of the destructive Rākṣasas.
He sings in the south-eastern quarter;
for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases. He sings in the *aticandas* metre; this *aticandas* indeed comprises all the metres; therefore he sings in the *aticandas*.
He sings:
"Agni burns, he strikes down; ahāva! ahāva!"—it is thus that he drives away the destructive spirits and the Rakṣasas from here.
They go out toward the north, behind the *cātvāla* pit and in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed; they proceed in whichever direction there is water.
If there should be a stagnant pool among flowing waters, he should descend into those waters;

for those waters which do not flow among the flowing ones are seized by Varuṇa, and the *avabhṛtha* bath is related to Varuṇa; thus it is for the sake of freedom from Varuṇa. But if he should not find such, he may descend into whatever waters he can find.
While leading him away from the darkness, he makes him recite:
"Homage to Varuṇa! Varuṇa’s noose is stepped over. Thereby he releases him from every noose of Varuṇa and from everything pertaining to Varuṇa.

Then, having taken four portions of clarified butter and having cast a fuel-stick into the fire, he makes an offering with the verse: "The face of Agni has entered the waters; the Son of the Waters, the Lord, protecting the divine power, in every house shall sacrifice a fuel-stick, O Agni. May thy tongue rise up toward the clarified butter, Svāhā!"

For the gods, indeed, caused Agni to enter into the waters to whatever extent they wished, thinking, "Lest from here the destructive spirits and Rakṣases should rise up," for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases. He kindles him with this fuel-stick and with this oblation, thinking, "When he is kindled, I shall offer to the gods."

Then, having taken another fourfold portion of clarified butter and having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the *samidhs*. He performs four fore-offerings (*prayāja*s) excluding the one for the *barhis*. The *barhis* is indeed offspring, and the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) belongs to Varuṇa; [he does this] so that Varuṇa may not seize the offspring. Therefore, he performs four fore-offerings excluding the one for the *barhis*.
Now, there is a cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa.

Whatever sap of his had gone forth with the oblations, that he has now produced; but this body contains no sap, for the cake is indeed sap. He thus places that sap into it; he unites him with that sap and produces him from it. As soon as he is born, he in turn produces him. That is why there is a cake on one potsherd for Varuṇa.

Having spread a layer of clarified butter, while cutting off a portion of the sacrificial cake, he says, "Recite for Varuṇa! At this point, some indeed cut off two portions from the *ṛjīṣa* (the soma-residue), but one should not do so; for that [residue] becomes a mere carcass and is not fit for an oblation. He cuts off two portions, pours clarified butter over them once, and anoints the place of cutting. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering-verse for Varuṇa," and when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering.

Then, having spread a layer of clarified butter and placing a portion of the sacrificial cake upon it, he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer for Agni and Varuṇa! This is for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; as for why he does not say "for Agni," it is so that Varuṇa may not seize Agni. If he were to take two portions from the *soma*-dregs later on, then he takes one portion here; or if he should not care for that, he then pours clarified butter over it twice from above. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for Agni and Varuṇa! and at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, he makes the oblation.
Now, these indeed are six oblations; for there are six seasons in the year, and Varuṇa is the year; therefore there are six oblations.

This is the way of the Ādityas. "These sacrificial formulas (yajus) belong to the Ādityas," they say. As long as his will may be, he should desire to perform it in this very manner; but if the sacrificer should tell him to perform it otherwise, then he should do so otherwise: he should offer these same four fore-offerings (prayāja) without the barhis-grass, two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), [an offering to] Varuṇa, [and one to] Agnī-Varuṇa, and two after-offerings (anuyāja) without the barhis-grass. That makes ten; for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the Virāj; thus he brings the sacrifice into correspondence with the Virāj.
This is the way of the Aṅgirases.

Having performed one of these two rites, he causes that jar in which there is the *ṛjīṣa* to float away with the formula, "Into the ocean is thy heart; into the waters. The ocean is indeed the waters, and the waters are sap; thus he places this sap into it and unites him with this sap; thereby he generates him from this [sap]. Once generated, he himself brings him forth with the words, "May the plants and the waters enter thee. Thus he places both kinds of sap into him: that which is in the plants and that which is in the waters. With the words, "O Lord of the Sacrifice, at the recitation of the hymns and the utterance of homage, we shall serve thee with the cry of 'svāhā'," he places whatever is good in the sacrifice into him.
Then, having released [the Soma], he worships with the formula:

"O divine waters, this is your embryo. For this is indeed the embryo of the waters; "bear him well-pleased and well-nourished"—thereby he entrusts him to the waters for protection. "O divine Soma, this is your place"—for the waters are indeed his place—"in that place, rain down and sprinkle around"—"in that, be auspicious for us and protect us from all afflictions"—this is what he thereby says.
Then he causes him to bathe with the formula: "O bath, O Nicumpuṇa! Thou art a gliding one, O Nicumpuṇa!

Through the gods, I have washed away the sin committed against the gods; through mortals, the sin committed against mortals. For by this he has indeed washed away the sin committed against the gods through the gods, with Soma as king; and by this he has washed away the sin committed against mortals through mortals, with the animal victim and the cake. "O God, protect me from the injury of the far-reaching one!"—by this he says, "Protect me from all calamities."

Then, having come down and bathed, they run after one another's backs; putting on other two garments, they go up. Just as a snake would free itself from its skin, so does he free himself from all evil. No sin whatsoever remains in him as long as he does not yet eat as a child. By the same way they went out, they return again. Having returned, he places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "Thou art the kindler of the gods. By this he kindles the sacrificer himself; for following the kindling of the gods, the sacrificer is kindled.
He proceeds with the *caru* offering to Āditya for the concluding ceremony (*udayanīya*).

As to why there is this *caru* for Āditya: when the gods said of her at that time, "Thine alone shall be the introductory offering (*prāyaṇīya*), thine alone the concluding offering (*udayanīya*)," he thereby makes her share in both of these.

When he performs the sacrifice here while intending to go there to buy the King (Soma), for that reason it is called the *Prāyaṇīya* (the introductory offering); and when he performs the sacrifice here after emerging from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), for that reason this is called the *Udayanīya* (the concluding offering). Indeed, these two are one and the same oblation: the *Prāyaṇīya* belongs to Aditi, and the *Udayanīya* belongs to Aditi; for this earth is indeed Aditi.
He indeed first sacrifices to Pathyā Svasti.

Regarding this, the gods resorted to Speech itself when things were not clearly discerned, for by means of Speech even that which is bewildered is discerned; then, once it is discerned, he performs the rite as before.

He sacrifices first to Agni, then to Soma, then to Savitṛ, then to Pathyā Svasti, and then to Aditi. Pathyā Svasti is indeed speech, and Aditi is this earth; thus the gods established speech upon this very earth, and so this speech speaks, being firmly established upon her.
Then he immolates the barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa as the Anūbandhyā sacrifice.
This is indeed another sacrifice that is performed; it is simply a Paśubandha, for the Samiṣṭayajus offerings constitute the very end of the sacrifice.
In this regard, as for the fact that there is a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa:
whatever of the sacrificer has been well-sacrificed, Mitra takes that of his; and whatever of his has been ill-sacrificed, Varuṇa takes that of his.

Regarding this they say: "Where was the sacrifice when it was lost? Now, whatever of his Mitra takes as well-sacrificed (sviṣṭa), that very thing he, being pleased by this [offering], restores to him; and whatever of his Varuṇa takes as ill-sacrificed (duriṣṭa), that too he, being pleased by this, makes well-sacrificed for him and restores it to him. Thus, this becomes his own sacrifice, his own good deed.
Now, as for the fact that there is a barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa:

when the gods brought forth the seed that had been shed, that was the *āgnimāruta* hymn; in it that [event] is explained—how the gods brought forth that seed, from which the embers (*aṅgāra*) came into being, from the embers the Aṅgirases, and after that the other animals.
Then, when only the dust of these [waters] remained.

From that, the donkey came into being; therefore, wherever there is dust, people say, "It is surely a place for donkeys. Then, when no essence whatsoever remained, from that this barren cow (vaśā) belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa came into being. Therefore, she does not bring forth offspring, for seed originates from essence, and from seed come animals. Because she came into being at the very end, she follows after the end of the sacrifice. For this reason, this barren cow dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa is most appropriately prepared here. If one should not find a barren cow, even a barren cow that has been a bull may serve as a substitute.
Then the Viśvedevas desired immortality;
from that, the [offering] to the Viśvedevas arose, and then that to Bṛhaspati; that is the end, for Bṛhaspati is indeed the end.

He who would give a thousand or more should sacrifice all these; for everything is indeed obtained and everything is conquered by him who gives a thousand or more. All these [cows] are exactly as before: first the one for Mitra and Varuṇa, then the one for the Viśve Devas, and then the one for Bṛhaspati.

Moreover, those who sit for a long sacrificial session—for a year or more—should sacrifice all of these; for everything has been obtained by them and everything conquered by those who sit for a long sacrificial session for a year or more. All these [animals] are exactly as before.

Then he performs the Udavasānīyā sacrifice. He offers a cake on five potsherds to Agni; for this [sacrifice], there are five-footed *paṅkti* verses as the invitatory and offering prayers (*yājyā-anuvākyā*). Now, the sacrifice of one who has already sacrificed becomes, as it were, exhausted; it turns away from him. But Agni is indeed all sacrifices, for in Agni they perform all sacrifices—both those that are domestic offerings (*pākayajña*) and those that are otherwise. Thus he takes hold of the sacrifice once again; in this way his sacrifice becomes unexhausted, and in this way it does not turn away from him.
Now, as to why there is a cake on five potsherds:

the invitatory and offering verses consist of five-footed *paṅkti* meters; the sacrifice is indeed fivefold (*pāṅkta*). Thus he takes hold of the sacrifice once again; in this way his sacrifice becomes fresh and not exhausted, and thus it does not turn away from him.

Gold is its sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). This sacrifice indeed belongs to Agni; gold is the seed of Agni, therefore gold is the sacrificial fee. Or it may be a draft-ox, for that too belongs to Agni by virtue of its carrying power; indeed, its carrying power is as if scorched by fire.

Then, having taken clarified butter in four ladlings, he offers it with a verse addressed to Viṣṇu: "Stride out widely, O Viṣṇu; make wide room for our dwelling. Drink the ghee, O thou whose source is ghee; further on and on the lord of the sacrifice, Svāhā! Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he takes hold of the sacrifice once again. In this way his sacrifice becomes free from weariness, and likewise it does not turn away from him. At that point, he should give whatever he can afford, for they say, "An oblation should not be without a sacrificial fee. Now, when this Udavasānīyā sacrifice is completed, he then offers the evening oblation; at the proper time, he offers the morning oblation.

He seizes a barren cow. Having seized it, they quiet it; having quieted it, he says, "Extract the omentum. Having extracted the omentum, he should say, "Search for the embryo," touching it as he speaks. If they do not find one, why should they care? But if they do find one, an expiation is performed there.
That is certainly not appropriate:

that they, thinking it to be one, should proceed with only one; or that, thinking them to be two, they should proceed as if with two. He should instruct that they prepare both a cooking-pot and a turban.
Then they proceed with the omentum.

Just as the performance of that [animal sacrifice] is done—with the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer returning after having proceeded with the omentum—the Adhvaryu says, "Draw out this embryo. He should not, however, draw it out from the belly; for they draw it out from the belly only when it is diseased or dead. When the embryo is fully developed, it then moves backward through the birth canal. Having even torn open the hips, he should tell him to draw it out backward.
He consecrates it as it is being brought down with the formula:

"Let the ten-month-old embryo come forth together with the afterbirth. When he says, "let it come forth," he thereby bestows vital breath upon it; and when he says, "ten-month-old," for it is when the embryo is fully developed that it becomes ten-month-old—even though it may not actually be ten months old, he makes it ten-month-old by means of this Brahman, the Yajus formula.
"With the placenta" means:

just as a ten-month-old fetus would come forth with the placenta, so he says this; "as this wind moves, as the ocean moves"—he thereby bestows vital breath upon him. "So this ten-month-old one has been born with the placenta" means: just as a ten-month-old fetus would be released along with the placenta, so he says this.

Regarding this they say: "How should one prepare this embryo? They say that one should cut portions from each of its limbs, just as the cutting of portions is done for other sacrificial offerings. But one should not do it in that way; for indeed, this [embryo] has its limbs unformed. One should cut off the necks from below and let this sacrificial essence (medha) drip into this pot; for this sacrificial essence drips from all of its limbs, and thus a portion is taken from all of its limbs. They cut the portions of the barren cow (vaśā), just as the cutting of portions is performed for them.
They cook those [limbs] on the animal-cooking fire.

Having wrapped this very sacrificial essence (medha) in a turban, they place the embryo at the side of the animal-cooking fire. When it is cooked, he then offers oblations over the portions as they are taken up; they do not remove this sacrificial essence from the animal, but rather they remove that very sacrificial essence.
They carry it behind the *cātvāla* pit, between the sacrificial post and the fire.

Having set it down to the south, the *pratiprasthātṛ* performs the cutting; then he spreads an underlayer of ghee in the two offering-spoons. Then he calls for the recitation for the *manotā*. They cut the portions from the victim, the cow, in the same manner as the cutting of those [other] portions.
Now, there is a *pracaraṇī* ladle;

into it the Pratiprasthātṛ spreads an underlayer of ghee for the fat portion, cuts off two portions, pours ghee over them once, and anoints the places from which the portions were cut. Then, having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt! At the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu offers the oblation, and the Pratiprasthātṛ makes his offering following the Adhvaryu's offering.
"Whose sacrificial embryo you are."

Unfit for sacrifice indeed are embryos; by means of this very Brahman-formula he thus makes it fit for sacrifice. "Whose womb is golden"—for they indeed cut open her womb when they draw it out from there; gold is immortal life. He thus makes that womb of hers immortal. "Him whose limbs are uninjured, him I have united with his measure, Svāhā!"—if it be a male; "Her whose limbs are uninjured, her I have united with her measure, Svāhā!"—if it be a female. And if the embryo is undistinguished as to sex, he should offer with the formula for a male, for embryos are indeed males: "Him whose limbs are uninjured, him I have united with his measure, Svāhā! For they indeed make it go apart from its measure when they draw it out from there; having thus made it complete by means of this Brahman-formula, he unites it again with its measure in the middle of the sacrifice.
Then the Adhvaryu proceeds with the Vanaspati offering.

Having proceeded with the Vanaspati, while bringing together the portions that are in the Upabhṛt-ladle, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. The Pratiprasthātṛ steps across; he takes all this very essence (medha). Then he sprinkles it twice from above with clarified butter. Having called for the *āśrāvaṇa*, he says, "Prompt! At the utterance of the *vaṣaṭ*, the Adhvaryu offers the oblation, and the Pratiprasthātṛ offers his oblation following the Adhvaryu's.

"Purudasmo viṣurūpa induḥ"—"Purudasma" means "one who gives much," for that is what he says when he says "purudasma"; "viṣurūpa" (multiform), for embryos are indeed multiform; "indurantarmahimānamānañja dhīraḥ"—for this wise one is indeed anointed within the mother; "ekapadīṃ dvipadīṃ tripadīṃ catuṣpadīmaṣṭāpadīm bhuvanānu prathantāṃ svāhā"—by saying this, he causes her to expand. Having sacrificed with the eight-footed [verse], he conquers even more than before, provided that he has indeed sacrificed with the eight-footed one.

Regarding this they say: "Where should one place this embryo? They should hang it upon a tree; for embryos have the intermediate space as their abode, and the tree is like the intermediate space; thus he establishes it in its own proper abode. However, they also say: "If someone were to speak ill of him there, saying, 'They will hang this dead man on a tree,' so indeed it would come to pass."
They should carry him down into water;

for water is the foundation of this entire universe, and thus he establishes him in water itself. Regarding this, they say: "If someone were to speak ill of him there, saying, 'He will die in the water,' it would surely happen so."
They should scatter it upon a mole-hill.

This earth, indeed, is the foundation of all this; thus he establishes him upon this very foundation. Regarding this, they say: "If someone were to utter a curse against him there, saying, 'Soon they will make a burial mound for this dead man,' it would surely come to pass exactly so."
One should offer it to the Maruts on the very fire for cooking the animal victim.

For the Maruts are the gods who do not eat oblations; this uncooked embryo is, as it were, like an offering that has not been made. Moreover, this [embryo] has already been brought from the Āhavanīya fire to the fire for cooking the animal victim; thus, it does not remain outside the sacrifice, nor is it as if offered directly into the Āhavanīya. The Maruts are indeed the gods; therefore, he establishes it within the Maruts themselves.

Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, while the embers are still hot, he takes up that embryo together with its turban. Standing facing the east, he offers it with a verse addressed to the Maruts: "O Maruts, mighty ones of heaven, you who drink in whose dwelling—he is the best protector of people. He does not utter *svāhā*; for the Maruts are the eaters of the non-offered among the gods, and what is offered without *svāhā* is as if unoffered. Since the Maruts are indeed the gods, he thereby establishes him among the Maruts themselves.
Then he stirs it with coals, saying:
"May Heaven and Earth, the great and the broad, sprinkle this sacrifice; may they nourish us with their sustenances."
Indra, indeed, is the Ṣoḍaśī. Once, the beings surpassed that Indra; for the beings are indeed the creatures (prajāḥ), and they became as if equal to him through this [sacrifice].

Indra indeed reflected: "How might I stand over all this? How might all this be on my lower side? He saw this cup; he drew it. He stood over all this, and all this became on his lower side. Verily, he who knows thus and for whom they draw this cup stands over all this, and all this becomes on his lower side.
Therefore, this was declared by the Seer:

"The sky did not even reach your greatness, when you stood upon the earth with one hip. Indeed, that sky did not even reach one of his hips; thus he surpassed all this, and all this became inferior to him. Verily, for one who knows this and for whom they draw this cup, he surpasses all this, and all this becomes inferior to him.
He draws it with a verse containing the word "hari";

they chant praises in verses containing "hari," and he recites the after-chant in verses containing "hari. For *hara* (seizing power) is indeed vigor; Indra seized the *hara*, the vigor, of his enemies, the Asuras. In the same way, this sacrificer now seizes the *hara*, the vigor, of his rivals. Therefore, he draws it with a verse containing "hari"; they chant praises in verses containing "hari," and he recites the after-chant in verses containing "hari."
Or rather, he draws it with an Anuṣṭubh verse.

The morning pressing belongs to the Gāyatrī, the midday pressing to the Triṣṭubh, and the third pressing to the Jagatī; but the Anuṣṭubh is redundant, and so he thereby causes this [cup] to be redundant. Therefore, he draws it with an Anuṣṭubh verse.
He draws it with a four-cornered vessel.
There are indeed these three worlds; thus he reaches these very worlds by means of the three corners, and with the fourth corner he overflows it. Therefore, he draws it with a four-cornered vessel.
One should indeed draw it at the morning pressing;
having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, that which was drawn at the morning pressing remains until this time, and thus one causes it to exceed all the pressings.
One might take it at the midday pressing;

having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, this is indeed the deliberation: one should rather take it at the morning pressing itself, having drawn the Āgrayaṇa. Having been taken at the morning pressing, it remains lying there from that time until now.

Then he draws [the cup]: "Mount the chariot, O slayer of Vṛtra; your two bay horses have been yoked by prayer. May the pressing-stone turn your mind hitherward with its sound. You are taken with a base; for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin, you! This is your womb; for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin, you!"
Or with this [verse]:

"Harness the two long-maned, vigorous bay steeds that fill the girth-bands; then, O Indra, drinker of Soma, come to listen to our songs. You are taken with a base; for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin, you! This is your womb; for Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin, you!"
Then, having approached, he introduces the chant with the words, "Soma has flowed over;

come hither!"—he thus causes him (Soma) to flow over. He introduces it before sunset and recites the after-verse after sunset; thereby he joins day and night together. Therefore, he introduces it before sunset and recites the after-verse after sunset.

In the beginning, all the gods were indeed alike; they were all meritorious. Among all those who were alike and all those who were meritorious, three desired: "May we be preeminent"—namely Agni, Indra, and [Viṣṇu].
Worshipping and toiling, they went about.

They saw these *atigrāhya* cups; they drew them. Because they drew them beyond (the others), they are called *atigrāhya*. They became surpassing; even as these [cups] now stand out, so indeed does he become who, knowing this, has these cups drawn for him.
Verily, in the beginning there was no luster in Agni.
That luster which is now in him, he desired: "May this luster be in me. He saw this cup; he drew it, and then that luster came to be in him.

In the beginning, indeed, there was no such strength as this strength that is now in him. He desired, "May this strength be in me. He saw this cup; he drew it, and then this strength came to be in him.
In the beginning, indeed, there was no radiance in the sun;

that which is this radiance here [in the sun] was in him. He desired, "May this radiance be in me. He saw this cup and drew it. Then this radiance came to be in him. Truly, those who draw these cups for one who knows thus bestow upon himself these splendors and these powers.
One should indeed draw those [cups] at the morning pressing.
Having drawn the Āgrayaṇa, [one knows that] the Āgrayaṇa is the self; for this [body] has many parts that are redundant to the self, such as the liver, the heart, and so forth.

One should draw them at the midday pressing, or having drawn the Ukthya cup, when about to begin the ritual. For this Ukthya is indeed its undefined self; thus, this is merely a deliberation. One should rather draw them at the morning pressing itself, after having drawn the Āgrayaṇa cup.
These are offered following the oblation of the Māhendra cup alone.

For this Māhendra cup is indeed Indra’s exclusive draught; his exclusive chant (stotra) is this very one, and his exclusive recitation (śastra) is this very one. The sacrificer is indeed Indra, and these [cups] are drawn for the sake of the sacrificer’s desire; therefore, they are offered following the oblation of the Māhendra cup alone.

Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]: "O Agni, purify yourself, O skillful one; bestowing upon us splendor and heroic vigor, grant me wealth and prosperity. You are taken with a support; for Agni, for splendor, you are taken. This is your womb; for Agni, for splendor, you are taken."

Rising with vigor, having drunk together, you shook your jaws, O Indra, after drinking the Soma pressed in the vessel. You are taken with a support; for Indra of vigor, you! This is your womb; for Indra of vigor, you!
His banners have become visible;
his rays extend across the people, shining like fires. You are taken with a support; for Sūrya, for splendor, you! This is your womb; for Sūrya, for splendor, you!
Their consumption [is as follows]:

"O Agni, full of splendor, may I be full of splendor among men, for you are full of splendor among the gods; O Indra, most powerful, may I be most powerful among men, for you are most powerful among the gods; O Sūrya, most radiant, may I be most radiant among men, for you are most radiant among the gods. Indeed, he who knows this and for whom these cups are drawn bestows these splendors and these powers upon himself.
One should indeed draw those [cups] during the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha.
During the first three days, one should draw the cup for Agni on the first day, that for Indra on the second, and that for Sūrya on the third; in this very manner, day by day.
Some indeed take them during the latter three days;

but one should not do so. One should take them during the former three days. If one intends to take them during the latter three days, one should first take them during the former three days and then take them during the latter three days. In this very way, according to the proper sequence, they are taken only on the Viśvajit, the one-day sacrifice (ekāha) consisting of all the Pṛṣṭhas.
This indeed is Prajāpati—
the sacrifice which is being performed, from which these creatures were born, and even now they are born after it.
The goats are born after the Upāṃśu vessel;
that very [vessel] is employed again in the sacrifice, and therefore these creatures are born again and again upon returning.
The offspring are born following the Antaryāma vessel;
that very [vessel] is employed again in the sacrifice, and therefore these offspring are born again and again upon returning.

Now, because he offers the *upāṃśu* oblation first while both of these [the goat and the sheep] are together, therefore, when both goats and sheep are together, the goats go first and the sheep follow behind.
Now, because he wipes upwards after having offered the *upāṃśu* oblation,
therefore these goats go as if stepping upon the other [cows].

Now, because he wipes downwards after offering the Antaryāma cup, therefore these sheep go about as if digging with their heads turned downwards. These goats and sheep are indeed most manifestly [the offspring] of Prajāpati; therefore, being born three times a year, they produce two or three [young] at each birth.
Following the cup of semen indeed, human beings are procreated.

That very thing is employed again in the sacrifice; therefore these creatures are procreated again and again. This indeed is the bright [Soma] who shines yonder; he is also Indra. Man is indeed the one among animals who belongs to Indra; therefore he rules over animals.
The one-hoofed animal is born after the *ṛtupātra* cup;

indeed, that [cup] is used again in the sacrifice, and therefore these creatures are born again and again. Thus, as it were, the *ṛtupātra* is the head of the one-hoofed animal. Following the *āgrayaṇa*, the *ukthya*, and the *āditya* cups, cattle are born; these [cups] are indeed used again in the sacrifice, and therefore these creatures are born again and again.
Now, as for the goats:
they are born after the smallest vessels; therefore, though they give birth three times a year, they produce only two or three, being thus the smallest, for they are born after the smallest vessels.
Now, as for the cows:

since they are born after the largest number of vessels, therefore these, being born once a year, produce only one calf at a time, yet they are the most numerous, for they are born after the largest number of vessels.

Then, from the *droṇakalaśa*, he finally draws the *hāriyojana* cup. The *droṇakalaśa* is indeed Prajāpati; he turns toward these creatures, protects them, and smells them. This indeed happens to him when he procreates them.

There are indeed these five cups, after which these creatures are produced: the cup for the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma [libations], the Śukra cup, the Ṛtu cup, the Āgrayaṇa cup, and the Ukthya cup. There are five seasons in the year; Prajāpati is the year; Prajāpati is the sacrifice. And if there are six seasons in the year, then the Āditya cup is the sixth among them.
But there is indeed one cup:
that by which these creatures are procreated, namely the Upāṃśu cup; for the Upāṃśu is breath, and Prajāpati is breath, for everything here follows after Prajāpati.

This indeed is Prajāpati, who is this sacrifice that is being performed; from him these creatures were born, and even now they are born after him. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he causes the Avakāśas to be recited.
He causes the first [verse] to be recited in a whisper.

"For my out-breathing, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus [he addresses] the Upāṃśu-sacrifice; "For my through-breathing, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus the Antaryāma; "For my up-breathing, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus the Aindravāyava; "For my speech, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus the Maitrāvaruṇa; "For my will and skill, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus the Āśvina; "For my hearing, O giver of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus the Śukra and Manthin; "For my two eyes, O givers of luster, flow pure for luster"—thus [he addresses] the Śukra and Manthin cups.

Then the Āgrayaṇa: "For myself, O giver of splendor, flow pure for splendor! Then the Ukthya: "For my vigor, O giver of splendor, flow pure for splendor! Then the Dhruva: "For my life-span, O giver of splendor, flow pure for splendor! Then the two Ambhṛṇas: "For all my offspring, O givers of splendor, flow pure for splendor! For the two Ambhṛṇas belong to the All-gods (vaiśvadeva); from there they draw for the gods, from there for men, and from there for the ancestors; therefore the two Ambhṛṇas belong to the All-gods.

Then [he addresses] the Droṇakalaśa: "Who art thou? Which one art thou? Prajāpati is indeed "Ka. "Whose art thou? What is thy name? Prajāpati is indeed "Ka" by name. "We have meditated upon thy name"—for he indeed meditates upon his name. "Thee whom we have satiated with Soma"—for he indeed satisfies him with Soma. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he invokes a blessing for each limb: "May I be rich in offspring through my offspring"—thereby he invokes offspring; "rich in heroes through my heroes"—thereby he invokes heroes; "rich in nourishment through my nourishments"—thereby he invokes prosperity.
One should certainly not allow them all to enter at once.

Rather, one should allow in someone who is well-known, or someone who is dear to him, or someone who is learned in the Vedas (*anūcāna*) and can reach them through his learning. Having drawn the Āśvina cup, he generates the entire sacrifice; having generated that entire sacrifice, he places it within himself and makes it his own.

Now, these indeed are the thirty-four *vyāhṛtis*, which are called expiations (*prāyaścittis*). This sacrifice that is being performed is Prajāpati; from him these creatures were born, and even now they are born after him.

There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, these two, Heaven and Earth, as the thirty-third, and Prajāpati as the thirty-fourth; thus he makes him into Prajāpati. This indeed exists, for that which is immortal exists; and that which is mortal is this very thing. He is this Prajāpati, for Prajāpati is everything; thus he makes him into Prajāpati. Therefore, there are these thirty-four utterances (vyāhṛtis) called expiations (prāyaścittis).
Some call these the "limbs of the sacrifice," but they are indeed the joints of the sacrifice; thus, this sacrifice, while being extended, proceeds becoming these very deities.

If the cow that yields the *gharma* milk should stray, they should go to another; at the very same time as they used to cause her to swell [with milk] previously, they should station her facing north, or facing east in front of the hall.
Now, regarding those two tufts of hair on either side of the tail-bulb which grow upwards:

in that one which is on the right, he offers these thirty-four oblations of clarified butter. For as great as this entire sacrifice is, so great are these thirty-four sacrificial utterances (*vyāhṛti*). Thus, he places the whole of this entire sacrifice within her; for it is from her that she causes the *gharma* to swell. This is the expiation performed in that case.

Now, if something should fail in the sacrifice, having observed that, he should offer an oblation: in the *Dīkṣā* and *Upasad* rites into the Āhavanīya fire, and when the Soma has been pressed into the Āgnīdhra fire. For whenever there is a failure in the sacrifice, a joint of the sacrifice becomes disjointed; whichever deity is present there at that time, with her he heals it, and with her he joins it together.
Now, if it should spill over:

He should pour water over it, for by water all this is pervaded; it is for the attainment of everything. With a verse addressed to Viṣṇu and Varuṇa—since whatever one praises here belongs to Varuṇa—he causes all this to be attained. "By whose might the regions were propped up, who are most heroic and most powerful in their deeds, who rule as irresistible through their strength, O Viṣṇu and Varuṇa, come to the first invocation! Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; thus he praises him. Varuṇa is the one who causes attainment. Thus, for whichever deity he praises and whichever deity causes attainment, he heals by means of both of them and unites them by means of both.

Then he should touch it, saying: "The sacrifice has gone to the gods in heaven; may wealth come to me from that. The sacrifice has gone to men in the intermediate space; may wealth come to me from that. The sacrifice has gone to the fathers in the earth; may wealth come to me from that. To whatever world the sacrifice has gone, from that may prosperity have come to me"—this is what he thereby says.
Regarding this, Āruṇi indeed said:

"Who would sacrifice, thinking that he would become worse through the failure of the sacrifice? Or rather, [who would think] 'I shall become better through the failure of the sacrifice'? He said that very thing when he approached these blessings.

Now, when he gives a thousand at this three-night sacrifice, it is thereby made "thousandfold. On the first day, he leads forward three hundred and thirty-three; likewise on the second day, he leads forward three hundred and thirty-three; and likewise on the third day, he leads forward three hundred and thirty-three. Then this "thousandfold" [offering] remains in excess.
"It should indeed be three-colored," they say, "for this is its most characteristic form.
However, it should rather be a reddish-brown cow with black spots, for that indeed is its most characteristic form.
It should be unimpregnated.
For this thousand-verse *Ayātayāmnī* is speech by its very nature; and this speech is *Ayātayāmnī* (unexhausted) when it is unimpregnated. Therefore, it should be unimpregnated.

One should lead it forth on the first day. This thousand-fold [cow] is, by its very nature, Speech; this thousand is the offspring born of that Speech. She goes first, and her offspring follows after her. Or rather, one should lead it forth on the last day; then her offspring goes first, and she follows after it. This is indeed a point for deliberation: one should lead it forth on the last day, so that her offspring goes first and she follows after it.

To the north of the two Havirdhāna carts and to the south of the Āgnīdhra shed, he causes her to smell the Droṇakalaśa; for the Droṇakalaśa is indeed the sacrifice—he thus shows her the sacrifice itself.
"Smell the jar;

let the drops enter thee abundantly"—for he who gives a thousand becomes, as it were, emptied; thus, by saying "Smell the jar; let the drops enter thee abundantly," he causes him who was emptied to swell again.
"Return with strength again," he says;
thereby he causes that which was emptied to swell up again when he says, "Return with strength again."
"May she milk for us a thousandfold"—
by saying "may she milk for us a thousandfold," he causes that which was emptied by the thousandfold [sacrifice] to swell up again.
"May wealth, broad-streamed and full of milk, enter me again"—
by saying "may wealth enter me again," he causes that which was emptied to swell up once more.
Then he whispers into her right ear:

"O Ida, Ranti, Havya, Kāmyā, Candrā, Jyoti, Aditi, Sarasvatī, Mahī, Viśrutī—these, O inviolable one, are thy names; announce me as a doer of good deeds to the gods. Or he may say, "Speak thus! For these indeed are her names among the gods. By saying this, he means: "By those names of thine among the gods, announce me as a doer of good deeds to the gods."

They direct it [the fire] toward that [spot]. If it should move forward when not yet stepped upon by a man, one should know: "This sacrificer has succeeded; he has won the auspicious world. If it should move northward, one should know: "The sacrificer will become more excellent in this world. If it should move westward, one should know: "He will be like a *tilvila* of beans, a *tilvila* of grain. If it should move southward, one should know: "The sacrificer will depart quickly from this world. These are the signs of knowledge.

Now, those thirty-three [verses] which are added to these three sets of thirty—into these they incorporate this [Virāj]. For they indeed tear asunder this Virāj when they dissect it; torn apart is that Virāj which has been disintegrated. The Virāj consists of ten syllables; thus he restores the Virāj in its entirety. He should give it to the Hotṛ, for the Hotṛ is possessed of a thousand (sahasra); therefore, he should give it to the Hotṛ.
He should appoint two *unnetṛ*s.

To whichever of the two does not cause the announcement (*āśrāvayet*), to him he should give this [virāj]. For that *unnetṛ* who, being an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), does not cause the announcement, is unsuccessful; and this *virāj* which is deficient is unsuccessful. Thus, he bestows what is unsuccessful upon one who is unsuccessful.
Regarding this they say:

"One should not give anything in addition to a thousand, for by means of a thousand alone one obtains all desires. But Āsuri said on this matter: "One may indeed give according to one's desire; for by means of a thousand one obtains all desires, and by desire everything else has already been given by him."

Or, if he intends to give a chariot that is already yoked, or if he should give it when the omentum of a barren cow has been offered, or at the Udavasānīyā sacrifice
When leading the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās), he should lead them in groups of ten without deficiency.

If he intends to give one [cow] to someone, he should assign her to ten [of those ten]; if he intends to give two to someone, he should assign them to five [of those ten]; if he intends to give three to someone, he should assign them to three [of those ten]; if he intends to give five to someone, he should assign them to two [of those ten]. In this way, up to a hundred, his Virāj becomes non-deficient and thus becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadughā) in yonder world.

Now, when he performs this sacrifice with the twelve-day rite arranged by meters (*vyūḍhacandas*), he arranges the cups (*graha*) and the Udgātṛ and the Hotṛ arrange the meters. This first three-day period (*tryaha*) is well-known as having its meters arranged in order (*samūḍhacandas*); at that time, he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu (*aindravāyavāgra*).
Then, on the fourth day, he arranges the ritual order;

they transpose the cups and the meters. He draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa. This fourth day belongs to Prajāpati; the Āgrayaṇa is indeed the self, and Prajāpati is the self. Therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.

Having taken it, he does not set it down, thinking, "The cups (grahas) are indeed the vital breaths; let me not confuse the vital breaths. For were he to set it down, he would confuse the vital breaths. They wait upon it while holding it fast. Then he draws the cups. Now, when he draws the cups, at whatever time that [cup] is due, having uttered the *hiṃ* call, he sets it down. Then this fifth day becomes well-known. On that day, he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.

Then, on the sixth day, he arranges the ritual order; they arrange the cups and the meters. He draws the cups beginning with the Śukra cup; for this sixth day belongs to Indra. Now, that which shines yonder is indeed the Śukra, and he is also Indra; therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Śukra.

Having taken it up, he does not set it down, thinking, "The cups are indeed the vital breaths; let me not confuse the vital breaths. For were he to set it down, he would indeed confuse the vital breaths. They wait upon it while holding it, and then he draws the cups. And when he draws the cups, then, at the very time for this [cup], he sets it down.
Then, on the seventh day, they arrange the formations;

they arrange the cups and the meters. He draws the cups beginning with the Śukra cup, for this seventh day belongs to the Bṛhatī meter. That which shines yonder is indeed the Śukra, and he is also the Bṛhat; therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Śukra.

Having taken it, he does not set it down, thinking, "The cups are indeed the vital breaths; let me not confuse the vital breaths. For were he to set it down, he would indeed confuse the vital breaths. They wait upon it while holding it, and then he draws the cups. Now, when he draws the cups, at whatever time that [specific cup] is due, at that very time he sets it down. Then this eighth day becomes well-known; on that day, he draws the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu.
Then, on the ninth day, they arrange the ritual order;

they arrange the cups and the meters. He draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa. For this ninth day belongs to the Jagatī meter, and the Āgrayaṇa is the self; indeed, all this world is the self, the Jagatī. Therefore, he draws the cups beginning with the Āgrayaṇa.

Having taken it up, he does not set it down. For the cups (grahas) are indeed the vital breaths; [he thinks], "Lest I should confuse the vital breaths. For if he were to set it down, he would indeed confuse the vital breaths. They wait upon it while holding it up. Then he draws the cups. And when he draws the cups, then, at the very time for this [cup], having uttered the *hiṃ* call, he sets it down.
Regarding this they say:

"One should not transpose the cups (grahas), for the cups are indeed the vital breaths (prāṇas); one should not confuse the vital breaths. For if he were to transpose them, he would confuse the vital breaths; therefore, he should not transpose them.
Therefore, he should indeed transpose them.
For the cups are the limbs; these limbs one lies down upon in various transpositions at will; therefore, he should indeed transpose them.
Therefore, one should not transpose them at all.

For the cups (grahas) are indeed the vital breaths; [one should think], "Lest I confuse the vital breaths. Indeed, he would confuse the vital breaths were he to transpose them; therefore, he should not transpose them.

What then does the Adhvaryu do there, when both the Udgātṛ and the Hotṛ transpose the meters? Indeed, it is the Adhvaryu who transposes them: in that he draws the cups at the morning pressing with the Aindravāyava first, at the midday pressing with the Śukra first, and at the third pressing with the Āgrayaṇa first.
If they should steal the Soma, one should say, "It runs away. If they find it, why should they care? But if they do not find it, then an expiation is performed.
There are indeed two kinds of *phālguna* flowers:

those with red blossoms and those with reddish-brown blossoms. One should press those *phālguna* flowers that have reddish-brown blossoms; for these reddish-brown *phālguna* flowers are a limb of Soma. Therefore, one should press those with reddish-brown blossoms.

If they should not find red flowers, one should press the "hawk-brought" [Soma]. For when Gāyatrī flew toward Soma, as she was bringing it back, a shoot of Soma fell; that became the hawk-brought [Soma]. Therefore, one should press the hawk-brought [Soma].

If they should not find the *śyena*-seized [Soma], they should press *ādāra* plants; for when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, the sap that spurted out from it became the *ādāra* plants; therefore, one should press *ādāra* plants.
If they should not find any *ādāra* plants, one should press *aruṇa-dūrvā* grass; for this *aruṇa-dūrvā* is indeed a substitute for Soma. Therefore, one should press *aruṇa-dūrvā*.

If they cannot find aruṇa-dūrvā grass, they may press whatever green kuśa grass is available; in that case also, one should give only a single cow as a gift. Then, having emerged from the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), one should undergo initiation again, for in that instance the expiation is indeed a renewed sacrifice. This applies to those whose Soma has been stolen.
Now, the ritual for the water-pot and so forth.

If the *kalaśa* should break, he should say, "Do you wish to obtain [the Soma]? If they should obtain it, they should pour back as much as a handful or a cupful from the other *ekadhanas* and proceed according to their capacity. But if they should not obtain it, they should pour from the *āgrayaṇa* itself, add the other *ekadhanas*, and proceed according to their capacity. If the *kalaśa* should break after the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇās*) have been led away, there too he should give only one cow. Then, having emerged from the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), he should be consecrated again; for in that case, a new sacrifice is indeed the expiation. Thus ends the section on the breaking of the *kalaśa*.

Now, regarding the surplus Soma: if the Agniṣṭoma should be exceeded, one should draw the Ukthya from the Pūtabhṛt vessel; if the Ukthya should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Ṣoḍaśin; if the Ṣoḍaśin should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Night (Rātri-stotra); if the Night should be exceeded, they should proceed to the Day (Ahargaṇa). But indeed, there is no such thing as a true surplus.
This Aṃśu cup is indeed Prajāpati;

it is his very self, for this Prajāpati is the self. Thus, they fashion this self of his when they draw this cup. Into that [self], he places these vital breaths (prāṇas), according as these cups are explained as the vital breaths. Verily, the sacrificer becomes possessed of his entire body in yonder world.
It is like having a support for its commencement: where they take this [cup], it has a support; but where they do not take it, it is as if without support. Therefore, he indeed takes the Aṃśu cup.
Or he draws it with a vessel made of Udumbara wood;
for this [Soma] is Prajāpati, and the Udumbara is related to Prajāpati; therefore he draws it with a vessel made of Udumbara wood.

He draws it with a four-cornered vessel. There are indeed these three worlds; thus he obtains these very worlds by means of the three [verses]. Prajāpati, however, is the fourth beyond these worlds; thus he obtains Prajāpati by means of the fourth. Therefore, he draws it with a four-cornered vessel.
He indeed takes up the pressing-stone silently;
he pours out the stalks silently; he pours water upon them silently; having lifted it up silently, he presses once; he offers this silently without drawing breath; thus he makes it Prajāpati.
Now, gold is tied to this [cow];
he smells it. Whatever he scratches here or whatever he licks off, that gold is immortal life; thus he places that immortal life within himself.
Regarding this, Rāma Aupatasvini said:
"One may breathe at will and drink at will; indeed, when one offers silently, it is precisely thereby that he makes [the offering] Prajāpati."
Now, gold is bound to this [bowstring];
he smells it. Whatever he cuts or scrapes off there, gold is immortal life; thus he places that immortal life within himself.
Regarding this, Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi said:

"One should lift it up and take it, but one should not press it; for they do press [the Soma] for other deities, and thus he would act differently from how he acts for other deities. But when he lifts it up, that itself constitutes its being pressed."

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "One should indeed press [the Soma]; for the unpressed Soma did not exhilarate Indra, nor do the pressed juices [exhilarate] Maghavan when there is no prayer (brahman). This was declared by the Seer. Indeed, one does not press [Soma] for any other deity even once; therefore, he acts otherwise than that, just as he does for other deities. For this reason, one should indeed press [it].
Twelve first-born heifers are the sacrificial fee;
for there are twelve months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year; the sunbeam is Prajāpati; thus he makes him into Prajāpati.
They have twelve embryos;
they are twenty-four, for there are twenty-four half-months in a year. Prajāpati is the year, and the sun (Aṃśu) is Prajāpati; thus he makes him into Prajāpati.
Now Kaukūṣṭha gave as sacrificial fees these twenty-four first-calf heifers that had calved for the first time, and a bull as the twenty-fifth, and gold; this indeed was what he gave.
Indeed, this [Soma] should not be taken from just anyone;
for it is his very self that must be taken from one who knows it, or from one who is dear to him, or from one who is learned in the Vedas and might attain it through his recitation.

It is to be drawn at the *sahasra* [sacrifice]; for the *sahasra* is everything, and this [cup] is everything. It is to be drawn at the *sarvavedas* [sacrifice]; for the *sarvavedas* is everything, and this is everything. It is to be drawn at the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭhas*; for the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭhas* is everything, and this is everything. It is to be drawn at the *vājapeya* and the *rājasūya*; for that is everything. It is to be drawn at the *sattra*; for the *sattra* is everything, and this is everything. These are the [proper] drawings.
Verily, they go to him who shines there;

for those who sit for a year-long session, it is said that in six months they reach him who shines there. This is declared according to the Sāman: in that his form is fashioned, it is declared according to the Ṛc; and this very thing is declared according to the Yajus, by way of preliminary performance, when they draw him—that is, they go to him by means of this very [rite].
Now, therefore, he draws [the cup]:
