"The rays bear aloft that god Jātavedas, Sūrya, so that all may see him. You are taken with a support; for Sūrya, for splendor, you! This is your womb; for Sūrya, for splendor, you! Thus he says.

Now, therefore, regarding the Paśvayana sacrifice itself: one should proceed by means of the eleven animal victims. He immolates the first victim for Agni, then one for Varuṇa, and then again one for Agni; in this very manner one should proceed with this set of eleven victims.
Moreover, one should sacrifice an animal every day specifically to Indra and Agni.

Agni is indeed all the deities, for into Agni they offer oblations to all the deities; Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice. Thus, he does not offend any of these deities, nor does he offend that which is the deity of the sacrifice.
Now, therefore, follows the procedure for the Stomāyana sacrifice.

At the Agniṣṭoma, one should sacrifice an animal dedicated to Agni; for it is consistent that an animal dedicated to Agni should be sacrificed at the Agniṣṭoma. If it is an Ukthya, one should sacrifice a second animal dedicated to Indra and Agni, for the Ukthas belong to Indra and Agni. If it is a Ṣoḍaśin, one should sacrifice a third animal dedicated to Indra, for the Ṣoḍaśin belongs to Indra. If it is an Atirātra, one should sacrifice a fourth animal dedicated to Sarasvatī, for Sarasvatī is speech; speech is female, and the night is female. Thus, he distinguishes the sacrificial rites according to their proper order. These are three courses of the year; whichever of these he may desire, by that he should proceed. There are two additional animals to be sacrificed: on the Vaiṣuvata day, he sacrifices a solar animal, and on the Mahāvrata day, an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Now, therefore, regarding the Mahāvratīya [cup] itself:

When Prajāpati was creating the creatures, his joints gave way. With his joints dislocated, he was unable to hold himself together. Then the gods went about praising and toiling; they saw this Mahāvratīya [cup], they drew it for him, and with it they set his joints together again.

With his joints joined together, he rose up toward this food—that which is the food of Prajāpati. Now, what is the eating of men is the *vrata* (vow/observance) of the gods. "Great indeed has become this *vrata* by which he has grown great," they said; therefore it is called the Mahāvrata.

Thus indeed do these become who sit for a year-long session. Just as Prajāpati sat when he was creating creatures, and just as Prajāpati rose up toward food at the end of the year, even so do those who, knowing this, draw this cup, rise up toward food at the end of the year.
Or rather, one should draw it for Indra Vimṛdh (the Subduer of Enemies).

For all their enemies (*mṛdh*) are indeed slain and everything is conquered by those who sit for the year-long rite. Therefore [it is drawn] for Vimṛdh: "O Indra, drive away our enemies; cast down those who attack us! Whoever seeks to harm us, send him down into the lowest darkness!"
"You are taken with a support; for Indra, the dispeller of foes, you! This is your womb; for Indra, the dispeller of foes, you!"

And also for Viśvakarman. For those who sit through the year, every deed of theirs is accomplished and everything is conquered; therefore [it is offered] to Viśvakarman. "We invoke today for our protection Viśvakarman, the Lord of Speech, swift as thought in the contest; may he enjoy all our invocations, he who is the source of all well-being, the doer of good deeds, for our aid. "Thou art taken with a support; for Indra, for Viśvakarman, thee! This is thy womb; for Indra, for Viśvakarman, thee! Thus [he says].

If, however, one should know [the verse] addressed to Indra and Viśvakarman, one should draw [the cup] in that very manner: "O Viśvakarman, by means of this strengthening oblation, you made Indra a protector who cannot be slain;
to him the many tribes bowed down, so that he might be the fierce one, worthy of invocation."
"You are taken with a support; for Indra Viśvakarman you! This is your womb; for Indra Viśvakarman you!"
This indeed is the *graha* (seizer): he who shines yonder, by whom all these creatures are seized. Therefore they say, "We seize the *grahas," for they move about as those possessed by the *grahas*.
Speech indeed is the grasper;
for by speech all this is grasped—how much more so that which is the grasper that is speech?
The name itself is the grasper;
for by means of the name all this is grasped. How much more so that which is the name? Although we know the names of many, yet by that [name] they are not grasped by us.
Food itself is the grasper;
for by food all this is grasped. Therefore, as many as eat our food, they are all grasped by us; such is the established order.

This Soma-cup is indeed food. Whatever deity for whom he draws this cup, that deity, being grasped by him through this cup, fulfills for him whatever desire he draws it with. He stands in adoration either of the rising or the setting sun, saying: "O Cup, seize so-and-so with such-and-such a misfortune; let so-and-so not attain this!"—or if he hates someone, he says: "Let this desire not be fulfilled for him! But for the one for whom he thus stands in adoration, that desire is never fulfilled.

The gods, while performing the sacrifice, were afraid of an attack from the Asuras and Rakshasas. They said, "Who will sit to our south? Then we shall perform the sacrifice to the north in a place free from fear and danger."
They said, "He among us who is the most powerful shall sit on the south; then, in a place free from fear and harm, we will attend to the sacrifice from the north."
They said, "Indra is indeed the most heroic among us; let Indra sit on the south side, and then we shall perform the sacrifice from the north in a place free from fear and harm."
They said to Indra:
"You indeed are the most powerful among us; sit you on the south side, and then we shall perform the sacrifice from the north, in a place free from fear and free from destructive spirits."
He said.

"What would happen to me from that? [Indra asked. "The Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin shall chant the *brahmasāman* for you," they said. Therefore, one should choose the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin. Indra was the Brahman priest; for this office belongs to Indra. That Indra sat on the south side, and then they performed the sacrifice on the north side, in a place free from fear and harm. Therefore, whoever is the most vigorous should sit on the south side, and then they should perform the sacrifice on the north side, in a place free from fear and harm. Indeed, he who is the most learned among the Brāhmaṇas is the most vigorous of them. Now, as for the fact that whoever becomes the Brahman priest sits in silence, it is for this reason that whoever is the most vigorous should sit on the south side, and then they should perform the sacrifice on the north side, in a place free from fear and harm. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇas sit on the south side, and then they perform the sacrifice on the north side, in a place free from fear and harm.

When he says, "O Brahman, we shall chant the Stotra; O Praśāstṛ," then the Brahman mutters: "O God Savitṛ, they have announced this sacrifice of thine to Bṛhaspati the Brahman; protect the sacrifice with that, protect the lord of the sacrifice with that, protect me with that; chant at the impulsion of Savitṛ. Its significance is exactly the same as before; indeed, it is with this that most people perform the service.

But he should perform the service with this very [formula]: "O God Savitṛ, O Bṛhaspati, impel! He approaches Savitṛ for instigation, for he is the instigator of the gods. "O Bṛhaspati, impel!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman of the gods; thus he says this to him who is the Brahman of the gods. Therefore he says, "O Bṛhaspati, impel!"

Then the Maitrāvaruṇa priest mutters: "Impelled by the god Savitṛ, accepted by Mitra and Varuṇa. By this he approaches Savitṛ for impulsion, for he is the impeller of the gods. "Accepted by Mitra and Varuṇa"—Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed the deities of the Maitrāvaruṇa; thus he addresses those very deities of the Maitrāvaruṇa. Therefore he says, "accepted by Mitra and Varuṇa."

The triple knowledge is indeed the threefold Veda: the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants. The Ṛg-verses are this very earth, for upon her one praises; he who praises is speech itself, for it is by speech that he praises. The Yajus-formulas are the intermediate region, and the Sāman-chants are the sky. This triple knowledge is employed at the Soma sacrifice.
By means of the Ṛg-veda one conquers this very world;

by means of the Yajur-veda, the intermediate space; and by means of the Sāma-veda, heaven itself. Therefore, even if only one branch of knowledge has been recited for someone, he should desire to explain the construction of the other two as well: by means of the Ṛg-veda he conquers this very world, by means of the Yajur-veda the intermediate space, and by means of the Sāma-veda heaven itself.
This, indeed, is that:

the thousandfold progeny of speech consists of two parts for Indra and a third for Viṣṇu; the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants belong to Indra, and the Yajus-formulas belong to Viṣṇu. Therefore, they perform the duties in the Sadas with the Ṛc and the Sāman, for the Sadas belongs to Indra.
Then, with these sacrificial formulas (yajus), they carry this Viṣṇu, the sacrifice, as if in front; therefore it is called *puraścaraṇa*.
Speech indeed is the *ṛc*s and the *sāmans*;

the mind is the *yajus* formulas. Wherever this speech was present, there everything was performed and everything was understood. But wherever the mind was present, nothing at all was performed there and nothing was understood; for no one understands anything for one who is merely meditating with the mind.

Those gods said to Speech, "Go forward and prepare this! She replied, "What shall be mine from that? They said, "Whatever is offered in the sacrifice with the *svāhā* call, without the *vaṣaṭ* call—that shall be yours. Therefore, whatever is offered in the sacrifice with the *svāhā* call, without the *vaṣaṭ* call, belongs to Speech. She went forward and prepared this: "Do this! Do this! she said.
Therefore, they indeed perform [the rites] with ṛg-verses in the Havirdhāna shed:
he recites the Prātaranuvāka, he recites the Sāmidhenīs, and he praises the pressing-stones; for in this way the two became yoked together.
Therefore, they indeed perform these acts in the Sadas:
they raise the Udumbara post for the Yajus, they construct the Sadas, and they strew the Dhiṣṇya hearths; for in this way, the two became united.

They enclose this very *sadas* for the sake of this union, thinking, "Let this union be performed as if in secret. That union is indeed frustrated which another beholds; therefore, even if one sees husband and wife performing their union, they both run away and perform an expiation (*āgas*). Therefore, one should say to anyone looking into the *sadas* through a place other than the door, "Do not look! For it would be as if one were looking at a union being performed; however, one may look through the door at will, for that is a door made by the gods.

In this very way they enclose the *havirdhāna* shed. [They do so thinking: "Lest this couple should perform their union as it were openly. For that union is indeed unsuccessful which another person beholds. Therefore, even if one sees husband and wife performing their union, they run away from it and bring about only sin (*āgas*). Therefore, one should say to anyone looking at the *havirdhāna* through a non-door: "Do not look! For if one were to see a couple performing their union, that would be so; however, one may look through the door at will, for the door is made by the gods.

This Sāman is indeed a bull, and it approaches the Ṛc, which is a woman, in the assembly-hall. From that union Indra was born. Indeed, from the brilliance of both the Ṛc and the Sāman, this brilliance was born; for they call him "Indra" who shines yonder.

Now, this Soma is the male and the waters are the female; he approaches them in the oblation-holder (havirdhāna). From that union the moon was born. That food which is produced from the waters and from Soma is indeed the moon, for the moon is the food of him who shines yonder. Thus, he both procreates the sacrificer and produces for him food; he procreates the sacrificer from the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants, and he produces for him food from the waters and from Soma.

By means of the Yajus, indeed, the gods first performed the sacrifice, then by the Ṛc, and then by the Sāman; even now, people likewise perform the sacrifice first by the Yajus, then by the Ṛc, and then by the Sāman. That which is called "Yajus" is indeed [the essence of] the sacrifice.

Wherein indeed the gods milked these sciences for their desires, therein the science of the Yajus milked the most desires; yet it was as if most worn out, and it did not equal the other sciences, nor did the world of the atmosphere equal the other two worlds.
Those gods desired:
"How indeed might this [earthly] knowledge be a counterpart to the other two knowledges? How might the intermediate world be a counterpart to the other two worlds?"

They said, "Let us perform the rites with the Yajus formulas in a whisper; then this knowledge will counterbalance the other knowledge, and then the world of the intermediate space will counterbalance the other two worlds."

They moved about in whispers; they were thereby causing these [Yajus] to swell. Then this science (the Yajurveda) stood opposite the other sciences, and from that, the intermediate world stood opposite the other two worlds. Therefore, the Yajus formulas, though being defined, are also undefined; therefore, this intermediate world, though being defined, is also undefined.

He who performs with the Yajus formulas in a low voice truly causes them to swell; they, being swollen, cause him to swell. But he who performs loudly indeed dries them up; they, being dried up, dry him up.

Speech indeed is the *ṛcs* and the *sāmans*; the mind is the *yajus*. Those who perform [the rites] with both the *ṛc* and the *sāman* become speech; and those who perform them with the *yajus* become the mind. Therefore, nothing whatsoever is done by the *adhvaryu* that is not directed by him. When the *adhvaryu* says, "Recite! or "Sacrifice!", then they do what is performed with the *ṛc*. And when the *adhvaryu* says, "The Soma is being purified; come hither!", then they do what is performed with the *sāman*. For speech does not speak without having been reached by the mind.
This very mind is the Adhvaryu priest;
he moves as if in front, and therefore it is called *puraścaraṇa*. Indeed, he who knows this becomes, as it were, pre-eminent in prosperity and fame.

This, indeed, is the very preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*). He who shines yonder—following his procedure—one should perform the rite; having drawn the cup, one should turn back according to his procedure; having responded to the recitation, one should turn back according to his procedure; having offered the cup, one should turn back according to his procedure. He is indeed the sustainer. Whoever, knowing this, is able to act according to his procedure, is indeed able to sustain those dependent upon him.

That which is the consecration (dīkṣā) is indeed the sitting (niṣad); that is the sacrificial session (sattra). Therefore they say of them, "They sit. And when they thereafter extend the sacrifice, they go forth; he who is the leader leads them. Therefore they say of them, "They go forth."

That which is the consecration (dīkṣā) is the sitting (niṣad); that is the session (sattram), that is the journey (ayanam), that is the sacrificial session-journey (sattrāyaṇam). And when, having reached the conclusion of the sacrifice from there, they rise up, that is the rising (utthānam); therefore they say, "They rose up from these [days]. This, then, is the preliminary discourse.
Now, those who are about to undergo initiation settle together.

If they are intending to pile the fire-altar, they mount the fires onto the two kindling woods and come together to the place where they are about to sacrifice with the animal victim for Prajāpati; having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this animal victim for Prajāpati.
They place his head [on the lap].
If their consecration (dīkṣā) does not coincide on that day, they consign the fires into the kindling woods (araṇis), return each to his own place, and offer the oblations.

Now, on the day when their initiation comes together, they mount the fires onto the kindling woods (*araṇis*) and proceed to the place where they are to be initiated; the householder himself churns first at the middle of the hall. Then half of the others sit to the south and half to the north. Having churned and added fuel, they proceed together, each taking a single firebrand. They establish the *gārhapatya* fire from the householder’s own *gārhapatya*, and having drawn out the *āhavanīya* from that very *gārhapatya*, they undergo initiation. For them, the *āhavanīya* is common, but the *gārhapatyas* are separate during the *dīkṣā* and *upasads*.
Now, on the day their purchase takes place, on that day he lays down the Gārhapatya altar;

then, on the Upavasatha day, he lays down the Dhiṣṇya altars for the others. At the time of the Vaisarjina offerings, the wives come forward from the east; they abandon these other fires once the Vaisarjina has been offered.
He leads the king forward.

This fire on the Āgnīdhra hearth is already held ready; then, each taking a single firebrand, they go out to their respective Dhiṣṇya hearths. "With those very firebrands of theirs, they strike [the king]," so said Yājñavalkya, "those who do so in that manner. This, indeed, is one way of proceeding.

Then this is the second [case]: having consigned the fires into the kindling woods themselves, they proceed to where they are about to sacrifice with an animal for Prajāpati; having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this animal for Prajāpati.
They place his head [on the fire].
If their consecration (dīkṣā) does not coincide on that day, they cause the fires to ascend into the kindling woods (araṇis), return each to his own place, and offer the oblations.

Now, on the day their initiation comes together, they mount the fires onto the kindling-woods (araṇis) and go to where they are about to be initiated; the householder himself churns first, and then the others, sitting around him, churn. As each fire is produced, they cast it into the Gārhapatya fire of the householder. Having drawn out the Āhavanīya from the householder’s very Gārhapatya, they undergo initiation. For them, the Āhavanīya is common and the Gārhapatya is common during the initiations and the Upasad days.
Then, on the day when their purchase takes place, on that day he piles the Gārhapatya altar;

then, on the Upavasatha day, he piles the Dhiṣṇya hearths for the others. At the time of the Vaisarjina offerings, the wives come forward from the east; they abandon this other fire once the Vaisarjina has been offered.
He leads the king forward.

This fire of the Āgnīdhra is already prepared; then, each taking a single firebrand, they go out to their respective hearths (dhiṣṇya). They indeed create a conflict among themselves, and through that conflict he finds them; they become subject to his will, and he finds that half in which they sacrifice—those who act in this manner.
Now this is the third [place]:
they converse over the two kindling woods belonging to the householder himself; those who depart from here—this is the second course.
Now, this is the third.

The two fires of the householder alone converse: "That fire which shall be produced from here—let that be common to us. What we shall win by this sacrifice, what we shall win by this animal offering—that let it be common to us. Let our good deeds be common; but whatever evil one may do, let that belong to him alone. Having spoken thus, the householder first causes the fires to mount [into the kindling woods], then he causes them to mount for the others, or they themselves cause them to mount. They go to where they are about to sacrifice with the animal dedicated to Prajāpati; having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they sacrifice with this animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
They place his head [on the lap].
If their consecration (dīkṣā) does not coincide on that day, they should consign the fires into the kindling woods (araṇis), return each to his own place, and offer the oblations.
Now, on the day when their consecration comes together—

The two forest-fires of the householder alone converse: "That fire which shall be produced from this [wood] shall be ours in common. What we shall win by this sacrifice, what we shall achieve by this sacrificial session—that shall be ours in common. Our good deeds shall be in common; but whatever evil one may do, that shall belong to him alone. Having spoken thus, the householder first causes the fires to ascend [into the kindling woods], and then he causes them to ascend for the others; or they themselves cause them to ascend. They come to where they are to be consecrated. Having churned the fire, added fuel, and drawn out the Āhavanīya fire, they undergo consecration. For them, the Āhavanīya remains the same, and the Gārhapatya remains the same during the consecrations and the Upasad days.
Now, on the day their purchase takes place, on that day he piles the Gārhapatya layer;

then, on the Upavasatha day, he piles the Dhiṣṇya hearths for the others. At the time of the Vaisarjina offerings, the wives come forward from the east; they abandon this other fire once the Vaisarjina has been offered.

He leads the King (Soma) forward. This fire in the Āgnīdhra shed is already prepared; then, taking a single fire-brand each, they go apart to their respective hearths. That which is done there is not left undone. As for why they have separate hearths: it is so that there may be more ample space for the performance of the rites. And as for why they have separate sacrificial cakes: it is so that there may be more of the oblation remaining for the sake of completion.

Now, by that very sacrifice with which the gods quickly struck away evil and won this victory—this is their victory—it was for this reason that they were prepared. Indeed, the gods had a single householder, a single sacrificial cake, and a single hearth-altar (dhiṣṇya), and thus they quickly struck away evil and were quickly procreated. In the same way, these [sacrificers] who have a single householder, a single sacrificial cake, and a single hearth-altar quickly strike away evil and are quickly procreated.
Now, as for this: in the former case, there is a hall with its rafters pointing northward; that is human.

There the Āhavanīya fire is common [to all], but the Gārhapatyas are separate; that is a distinct arrangement. Only at the Gārhapatya of the householder do they perform the *saṃyājana* of the wives with the tail of the victim (*jāghanī*); the others remain seated, performing their offerings with clarified butter (*ājya*). That is a distinct arrangement.
Now, in this case, there is a hall with its ridge-pole facing east.

Thus, among the gods, the Āhavanīya fire is the same, the Gārhapatya is the same, and the Āgnīdhrīya is the same; this sacrificial session is as successful as a one-day sacrifice (ekāha) is successful. For it, there is no failure; its procedure is entirely the same, except for that which pertains to the hearths (dhishṇyas).

The gods indeed performed a sacrificial session, thinking, "May we attain prosperity, may we have glory, may we be eaters of food. This food that they had conquered slipped away from them; for food is cattle, and it was the cattle themselves that wished to slip away from them, thinking, "If these [gods] are exhausted, they will not harm us; how indeed will they be able to manage us?"

They offered these two oblations in the Gārhapatya fire. The Gārhapatya is indeed the house, and the house is the foundation; thus they settled them right within the house, and so that food which had been won by them did not depart from them.

In the same way, those who sit for a sacrificial session (sattra) sit thinking, "May we attain prosperity, may we have glory, may we be eaters of food. For them, this conquered food—namely cattle, for cattle are indeed food—seeks to depart from them. [The gods thought: "If these men, being exhausted, do not harm us, how indeed will they be able to overcome us?"

They offer these two oblations in the Gārhapatya fire. The Gārhapatya is indeed the house, and the house is indeed the foundation; thus they settle them right in the house, so that this food which has been won by them does not depart from them.
In the same way, from this [person], this food that has been brought forth desires to depart, thinking: "How indeed might he not harm me? How might he overcome me?"

After that, he eats of it first only sparingly; thus he coaxes it, thinking, "It has not been as I thought; it has surely not harmed me. Thus he draws near to it. He who, knowing this, is able to observe its vow, truly becomes a lover of food and an eater of food.

Now, on this tenth day, the rising from the sacrificial session (sattrasthāna) is performed. Among them, one by one remains restrained in speech, swelling his voice; with that voice, thus swollen and free from weariness, they extend the subsequent day. Then the others are released for either carrying firewood or Vedic study; there they also eat.

In the afternoon, having approached and touched water, they enter the wife’s hall (*patnīśālā*). While they are holding on to one another, he offers these two oblations: "Here is delight; here do ye rejoice; here is steadfastness; here is self-steadfastness, Svāhā! This, indeed, he says regarding the cattle; it is the cattle that they thus secure for themselves.

Then he offers the second oblation with the words, "Pouring forth the supporter for his mother. By this, he says, "pouring forth Agni from the earth"; "the supporter, sucking his mother"—by this, he says, "Agni sucking the earth"; "may he bestow upon us increase of wealth, svāhā! Increase of wealth is indeed cattle; thus they secure cattle for themselves.
They go out toward the east;

they enter the two *havirdhāna* sheds from the west facing east, whereas when about to perform the sacrifice they would have been from the east facing west; such is the case at the conclusion of the *sattra*.

They chant the Sāman upon the rear pole of the northern Havirdhāna cart, saying, "The prosperity of the sacrificial session. By this, they indeed attain success. Or rather, they do so on the northern hip of the Uttaravedi; however, that is more commonly practiced.

[They chant] on the rear pole of the northern *havirdhāna* cart: "We have gone to the light; we have become immortal. For those who perform a sacrificial session (*sattra*) indeed become light and become immortal. "We have ascended from the earth to heaven"—for those who perform a sacrificial session indeed ascend from the earth to heaven. "We have found the gods"—for they indeed find the gods. "The heavenly light"—they conclude with a threefold finale, for they are indeed the heavenly light and they are indeed light. Thus, whatever is the form of this *sāman*, that very thing becomes those who perform a sacrificial session.
They crawl beneath the axle of the southern *havirdhāna* cart;

just as a snake might slough off its skin, so do they free themselves from all evil. They crawl with an *aticandas* verse; for the *aticandas* is indeed all the meters. Thus, evil does not overtake them. Therefore, they crawl with an *aticandas* verse.
They glide away.
O Indra and Parvata, you who fight in the van, strike down each one who would attack us; strike him down with the thunderbolt, strike each one down.
Let him fall into a far-distant place, or into a thicket, if he should seek to reach it.
"O Hero, may you, the destroyer, crush our enemies on every side—crush them from all sides!"
They go out toward the east;
they enter the Sadas from the front facing westward, for while they were about to sit, they were behind facing eastward, but it is thus at the conclusion of the Sattra.
They sit down according to their respective seats.

The essence of Speech, once won by the gods, desired to depart from them. It sought to slip away beyond this earth; for this earth is Speech, and its essence is the plants and the trees. They reached it with this Sāman, and being reached, it turned back toward them. Therefore, upon this earth, plants grow upwards and trees grow upwards. In the same way, the essence of Speech, once won by these [singers], now desires to depart from them. It seeks to slip away beyond this earth; for this earth is Speech, and its essence is the plants and the trees. They reach it with this Sāman, and being reached, it turns back toward them. Therefore, upon this earth, plants grow upwards and trees grow upwards.

They praise with the verses of the Queen of Serpents (*sarparājñī*). This earth, indeed, is the Queen of Serpents; thus, by means of her, they obtain all this. It is performed by oneself as the *prastāva* and not sung after by another, so that no one else might overhear it. For if another were to perform the *prastāva*, he would cause an excess; if another were to sing after it, he would cause an excess; if another were to overhear it, he would cause an excess. Therefore, it is performed by oneself as the *prastāva* and not sung after by another.

The Hotṛ recites the Caturhotṛ formulas; he thus recites in praise that which has already been praised. If the Hotṛ does not know them, the Gṛhapati should recite them; however, the recitation belongs to the Hotṛ alone.
Now follows the response of the Adhvaryu:
"These sacrificers have succeeded; it has turned out well for them. By this he utters something auspicious in human speech.
Then they engage in a theological discussion (*brahmodya*) regarding the dialogues (*vākovākya*).

For all that belongs to those who perform a sacrificial session (*sattra*) is indeed obtained and all is won by them. They have moved about with the *yajus* formulas; thus they obtained those and secured them. They have recited the *ṛc* verses; thus they obtained those and secured them. They have chanted with the *sāman* chants; thus they obtained those and secured them. Now, that which among these remains unobtained and unsecured is this very Brāhmaṇa consisting of dialogues; that they obtain and secure by means of this [discussion].
Having approached the Audumbarī post, they restrain their speech.

For those who perform the sacrifice with speech indeed exhaust the sacrifice and drain it dry; for the sacrifice is speech. Therefore, before this [day], each one of them sits restraining his speech, swelling up that speech; with that speech, thus swollen and not exhausted, they perform the subsequent day. Now, on this [day], all speech is obtained and released; therefore, everyone restrains their speech and swells up that speech; with that speech, thus swollen and not exhausted, they perform the Atirātra.
They sit holding onto an Audumbarī post;
for the Udumbara is strength and food; thus, by means of strength, they cause speech to swell.

When the sun has set, they go out toward the east. They sit behind the Āhavanīya fire and in front of the two Havirdhāna carts; while they remain restrained in speech, the Pratiprasthātṛ, himself restrained in speech, carries the Vasatīvarī waters around them. They may release their speech with whatever desire they have been sitting for, for the ancient seers used to perform a sacrificial session (sattra) according to their specific desires, thinking, "This is our desire; may it be fulfilled for us. If, however, they have many desires—whether a desire for the world, for offspring, or for cattle—they may release their speech accordingly.
With this very [formula] they should release their speech:

"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ. By means of truth they thus make their speech successful; with that success they pray for blessings: "May we be well-progeny through our offspring"—thereby they pray for offspring; "May we be rich in heroes through our heroes"—thereby they pray for heroes; "May we be well-nourished through our nourishment"—thereby they pray for prosperity.
Then the householder invokes the Subrahmaṇyā.

Or rather, whomsoever the householder may designate, some indeed invoke the Subrahmaṇyā separately; however, the householder himself should invoke the Subrahmaṇyā, or whomsoever the householder may designate. Having sought permission from him, they place the fuel-sticks upon the fire. "In the beginning, this world was non-existent."

Regarding this they say: "What was that non-existent (asat) which existed in the beginning? The *ṛṣis* indeed were that existent in the beginning. Regarding this they ask: "Who are those *ṛṣis*? The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are the *ṛṣis*. Because, prior to all this [creation], they moved about (*ariṣan*) seeking this [world] through toil and austerity (*tapas*), therefore they are called *ṛṣis*. He kindled it with his faculty of perception; because he kindled (*ainddha*) it, therefore he is called *Indha*; and he is indeed *Indha*.

That which is the breath in the middle—this indeed is Indra; they call these vital breaths "the Indras" cryptically (*parokṣam*), for the gods love the cryptic. These, being kindled, created seven men of various kinds.

They said, "Indeed, being thus, we shall not be able to procreate; let us make these seven persons into one person. They made those seven persons into one person. That which was above the navel, they compressed into two; that which was below the navel became two wings, one person, and the foundation was one person.

Now, that which was the glory (*śrī*) and the essence (*rasa*) of these seven persons, they drew it upward; that became his head. Because they drew up the glory, it is called "head" (*śiras*). Upon this very head, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) took refuge; therefore, the vital breaths are called "glories" (*śriyaḥ*). And because they took refuge in the whole, it is called "body" (*śarīra*).
That very person became Prajāpati;
he who was that person, Prajāpati, is this very Agni who is being built up.

He indeed becomes a sevenfold person (*saptapuruṣa*). For this person is sevenfold: four are his self and three are the wings and tail. Indeed, of that person, four are the self and three are the wings and tail; and because he increases the self by one person, by that vigor this self raises up the wings and tail.
Now, as for the fire which is placed upon the altar-site:

whatever prosperity and whatever essence belongs to these seven persons, that they now carry upward; that is his head. All the gods are supported in it, for in it one offers oblations to all the gods; therefore, indeed, it is the head.

This very Puruṣa, Prajāpati, desired, "May I become more, may I procreate. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he first created Brahman alone—that is, the triple Vidyā. That became his foundation; therefore they say, "Brahman is the foundation of all this. Therefore, having studied [the Veda], one finds a firm footing, for Brahman is that foundation. Established upon that foundation, he practiced austerity.
He created the waters.

From the world of speech itself, speech was created as his [portion]; it pervaded all this, whatever there is here. Because it pervaded (*āp*) everything, therefore they are called *āpaḥ* (waters); because it chose (*vṛ*) it, therefore they are called *vāḥ*.

He desired: "May I be born from these waters. He entered the waters together with this threefold knowledge (the Veda). From that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "Let there be! Let there be more! That is what he said. Then Brahman itself was first created—the threefold knowledge itself. Therefore they say, "Brahman is the first-born of all this," for indeed, from that Person, Brahman alone was first created. That [Brahman] was created as his very mouth. Therefore they call one who has studied the Vedas "one who is like Agni," for Brahman is indeed the mouth of Agni.

Now, that embryo which was within became Agni. Because he was created as the beginning (*agra*) of all this, therefore he is Agni; for "Agni" is indeed his secret name (*parokṣa*), since the gods love what is secret. And that tear which had flowed out became the horse (*aśru*); for "horse" (*aśva*) is indeed its secret name, since the gods love what is secret. And that which was like foam became the donkey. And that essence which was smeared upon the potsherd became the goat. And that which was the potsherd became the earth.

He desired: "May I produce from these [waters] this [earth], which is food. He compressed it and cast it into the waters. That essence of it which flowed away became the tortoise; and that which was splashed upwards—this is that which is born here above the waters. This [earth] followed after all those very waters; thus, this world appeared as a single form, namely water alone.

He desired: "May I become more, may I procreate. He exerted himself; he practiced austerity. Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he emitted foam. He perceived: "This form is indeed different; it becomes more when one exerts oneself. Having exerted himself and practiced austerity, he emitted clay, dry soil, mud, sand, gravel, stone, iron, gold, herbs, and trees. With these, he overspread this earth.
Now, these are indeed the nine creations.
This [earth] was created; therefore they say, "Agni is threefold," for this earth is Agni, since the entire Agni is built upon her.

"Has this been established? he asked. That became the earth; he spread it out, and it became the Pṛthivī (the Earth). Thinking herself whole and complete, she sang; because she sang (*agāyat*), she is called Gāyatrī. Moreover, they say that Agni himself, thinking himself whole and complete upon her back, sang; because he sang, Agni is called Gāyatra. Therefore, indeed, whoever thinks himself whole and complete either sings, or delights in singing, or delights in what has been sung.

Prajāpati desired: "May I become more, may I procreate. He entered into union with the earth by means of Agni; from that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "May it ripen! By which he meant, "May it ripen; may there be more."

That embryo which was within became Vāyu; then that tear which had been shed became birds; then the essence that was smeared upon the skull-bone became the rays of light; and that which was the skull-bone became the intermediate space.

He desired, "May I become more, may I procreate. He entered into union with the atmosphere by means of the wind; from that, an egg was formed. He touched it, saying, "Bear glory! Thereupon, yonder sun was emitted. This [sun] is indeed glory. Now, as for the tear that had flowed out, it became the dappled stone; they call it the "tear-stone" (aśma) cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. Then, whatever moisture was smeared upon the shell-bowl became the rays; and what the shell-bowl itself was, that became the sky.

He desired: "May I become more, may I procreate. He entered into union with the sun as his female counterpart; from that, an egg evolved. He touched it, saying, "Bear this seed! From that, the moon was created. This indeed is the seed. Now, those tears which had flowed forth became the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Then, the fluid that was smeared upon the shell became the intermediate quarters. And that which was the shell itself became the quarters.
Having created these worlds, he desired:
"May I create those offspring who would belong to me in these worlds."
He entered into union with speech through the mind;
he became pregnant with eight drops, and those eight Vasus were emitted; he placed them upon this earth.
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with speech; he became eleven drops within his womb, and from them the eleven Rudras were created; he placed them in the intermediate space.
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with Speech; she became pregnant with twelve drops, and from them the twelve Ādityas were created; he placed them in the sky.
By means of the mind alone, he entered into union with Speech; he became pregnant and created all the gods; he placed them within the quarters.

Moreover, they say: "When Agni had been created, the Vasus followed after him and he placed them upon this earth; the Rudras [followed] Vāyu and he placed them in the intermediate space; the Ādityas [followed] Āditya and he placed them in the sky; the Viśve Devās [followed] Candramas and he placed them in the quarters."

Now they say: Prajāpati, having created these worlds, established himself upon the earth; for him these plants ripened as food, and he ate that. He became pregnant; from his upward vital breaths (prāṇas) he created the gods, and from those downward vital breaths he created mortal offspring. Therefore, whatever he created at any time, he created it in that manner. Yet Prajāpati alone created all this, whatever exists here.

Having created offspring and having run the entire race, he collapsed. Therefore, indeed, whoever runs the entire race collapses. From him, having collapsed, the vital breath (prāṇa) departed from the middle; when it had departed, the gods abandoned him.

He said to Agni, "Unite me. [Agni asked], "What will come of that for me? [Prajāpati replied], "They shall call me by your name. For it is by whichever of one's sons one prospers that they call the father, the grandfather, the son, and the grandson by that [son's] name; they shall call me by your name. Therefore, unite me. "So be it," [said Agni]. Agni united him. Therefore, although he is Prajāpati, they call him Agni. And indeed, those who know this call their father, grandfather, son, and grandson by his name.

He said to him: "Upon what shall I place you? "Upon the beneficial (hita)," he replied. "The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the beneficial; for the vital breath is beneficial to all beings. Because he placed it upon the beneficial, therefore one says: 'I shall place,' 'I am placing.'"

Regarding this they say: "What is the beneficial (hita), and what is the placed-upon (upahita)? The vital breath (prāṇa) alone is the beneficial; speech is the placed-upon, for this speech is indeed placed upon the vital breath like something set down. The vital breath alone is the beneficial; the limbs are the placed-upon, for these limbs are indeed placed upon the vital breath like something set down.
Thus, this [altar] was his *citya*;

for it was to be piled (*cetavya*) by him, and therefore it is called *citya*. This altar of the sacrificer likewise becomes a *citya*, for it is to be piled by him; and for that very reason, it is called *citya*.

These, indeed, are those five bodies of his which fell apart: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; these are those very same five layers. In that he piles five layers, he piles him with those very bodies. Because he piles them, they are called "layers" (citayaḥ).
He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is the year;

and those five bodies of his which fell apart are the seasons—for there are five seasons—and these five layers (citayaḥ) are the seasons. Thus, when he piles up five layers, he piles him up by means of the seasons; and because he piles them up (cinoti), they are called layers (citayaḥ).

That Prajāpati, the year, who fell apart—he is this very wind that blows here; and those five bodies of his which fell apart were the seasons. There are indeed five directions, and these five layers (of the altar) are the directions. In that he piles up five layers, he piles it up with the directions; and because he piles them up, they are called "layers" (citayaḥ).
Now, that fire which is deposited upon the piled altar is yonder sun; he is indeed this very fire that has been piled. This much, then, was that for which Agni restored him.
Now they say:

Prajāpati, having been shattered, said to the gods, "Restore me! Those gods said to Agni, "In you we shall heal this father Prajāpati. He replied, "I will indeed enter into all of this. They said, "So be it. Therefore, although he is Prajāpati, they call him Agni.
The gods healed him with oblations in the fire.

Whatever oblation they offered, that became a baked brick and entered into him. Since they were produced from what was sacrificed (*iṣṭa*), therefore they are called *iṣṭakā*s; therefore they bake the bricks with fire; they thus make them into oblations.
He said, "In proportion as you offer oblations, in that same measure there is pleasure for me. Because pleasure (kam) arose for him when he sacrificed (iṣṭe), therefore they are called *iṣṭakā*.
Regarding this, Aṅktākṣya said:
"Only he who knows the bricks that possess sacrificial formulas (yajuṣmatī) and those that do not should pile the fire-altar; for in that way, he heals his father Prajāpati even more."
Now, Tāṇḍya used to say:

"The bricks accompanied by sacrificial formulas (*yajuṣmatya*) are indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the space-filling bricks (*lokapṛṇā*) are the common people (*viś*). The nobleman is the eater, and the common people are the food. Where there is more food for the eater, that kingdom becomes prosperous and thrives. Therefore, one should lay down more space-filling bricks. This is what those two said; however, the established practice is otherwise than this.

He is both father and son. In that he created Agni, he is the father of Agni; in that Agni restored him, Agni is his father. In that he created the gods, he is the father of the gods; in that the gods restored him, the gods are his fathers.
Both of these indeed come to be: father and son; Prajāpati and Agni; Agni and Prajāpati; Prajāpati and the gods; and he who knows this becomes Prajāpati himself.

He lays it down with the formula: "With that deity. That deity is indeed Speech. "In the manner of Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed Breath. "Sit thou firm!"—that is, "sit thou steady," and also, "sit thou established. Thus he builds him up by means of both Speech and Breath; for Agni is Speech and Indra is Breath, and Agni belongs to Indra and Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by so much he thus builds him up. Indra and Agni are all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by so much he thus builds him up.

Regarding this they say: "Why is the fire-altar built upon this [earth]? Indeed, when that deity fell apart, she flowed along this very earth with her essence. When the gods restored her, they gathered him (the fire) from out of this very [earth]. This is one and the same brick—this very earth—for this earth is indeed Agni; for upon this [earth] the entire fire-altar is built. And this [earth] has four corners, for the quarters are its corners; therefore the bricks have four corners, for all the bricks follow after this [earth].
Regarding this, they say:

Since it thus consists of one brick, how then does it consist of five bricks? This earth itself is the first brick made of clay; whatever else made of clay he places here, that is all one single brick. Then, when he places the heads of the animals, that is the animal brick. When he places the gold plate and the golden man, and when he sprinkles with chips of gold, that is the gold brick. When he places the two offering-spoons, the mortar and pestle, and the fuel-sticks which he lays down, that is the wooden brick. When he places the lotus leaf, the tortoise, the curds, honey, ghee, and whatever food he places here, that is the fifth brick, namely food. Thus it consists of five bricks.

Regarding this they say: "Which part is the head of the brick? Some say, "That part which one touches while reciting the Yajus formula. He should, therefore, recite the Yajus formula after touching the upper half of the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; for thus all these bricks become turned toward that *svayamātṛṇṇā*. But he should not do so. These bricks are indeed his limbs and joints. Just as one would make a head on every limb and at every joint, so it would be. Rather, that very place where the piled fire is finally deposited—that is the head of all these bricks.
Regarding this they say: "How many animals are laid down in the fire-altar? One should indeed say, "Five," for he lays down these five animals.
Then one should say, "One.
For this earth is indeed "Avis" (the Protectress), since she protects all these creatures; and this earth is also Agni, for upon her the entire fire-altar is built. Therefore, one should say, "One."

Then he should say, "Two. "The two" refers to this [earth] and that [sky]; for these two indeed sustain all these creatures. Since this earth is clay and that sky is water, and bricks consist of both clay and water, therefore he should say, "Two."
Moreover, he should say, "A cow.
For these worlds are indeed the cow; whatever goes (gacati) into these worlds, that is why they are the cow. And this piled fire-altar is these worlds. Therefore, he should say, "A cow."

Regarding this they say: "For what desire is the fire-altar built? "Having become a *suparṇa* (eagle), it shall carry me to heaven," so says one; but one should not know it thus. For having assumed this form, the vital breaths became Prajāpati; having assumed this form, Prajāpati created the gods; having assumed this form, the gods became immortal. Whatever the vital breaths became by means of this, whatever Prajāpati [became], and whatever the gods [became], that very thing one becomes by means of this.
In the beginning, this universe was indeed Prajāpati alone.

He desired, "May I exist; may I be reproduced. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. From him, thus exerted and heated by austerity, the waters were emitted. Therefore, from a person who has been heated, water is produced.
The waters said, "Where shall we be? He said to them, "Perform austerity! They performed austerity; they emitted foam. Therefore, foam is produced from heated water.

The froth said, "Where am I? Where are you? He said, "Perform austerity. It performed austerity; it created clay. Indeed, this is what the froth performs austerity when it floats, enveloped in water; when it is struck down, it becomes clay itself.

The clay said, "Where am I? Who are you? "Perform penance," he said. She performed penance and produced sand. This is why clay is heated when they plow it; therefore, even if they plow very smooth ground, it becomes as if sandy. That is the extent of what she meant by "Where am I? Who are you? and "Where am I? Who are you? respectively.

From the sand he created gravel; therefore, sand ends in gravel. From the gravel, stone; therefore, gravel ends in stone. From the stone, iron; therefore, they smelt iron from stone. From iron, gold; therefore, iron that has been smelted much becomes as if it were the color of gold.
That which was emitted flowed; because it flowed (*akṣarat*), it is therefore called the "syllable" (*akṣara*). Because it flowed eight times, that became the eight-syllabled *gāyatrī*.
"Has this been established? he asked.

That became the foundation (*bhūmi*); he spread it out, and it became the earth (*pṛthivī*). Upon this foundation, the beings and the lord of beings consecrated themselves for the year-long rite; the lord of beings was the *gṛhapati*, and Dawn was the wife.

Now, those beings were the seasons, and he who was the lord of beings was the year. And those two wives, the dawns, were the goddess Uṣas. These beings and the lord of beings, the year, poured their seed into Uṣas; after a year, a boy was born, and he wept.

Prajāpati said to him: "O boy, why do you weep, since you have been born from the toil of austerity? He replied: "I am indeed not freed from evil; I have no assigned name. Give me a name. Therefore, one should give a name to a son who has been born; for by that, one drives away his evil. One may even give a second and a third name; in each case, one thereby successively drives away his evil.
Rudra said to him, "You are Rudra.
Now, because he gave him that name, Agni became his form; for Rudra is indeed Agni. Because he wept (arodat), therefore he is Rudra. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me another name."
He said to him, "Thou art Sarva.
Now, because he gave him that name, water became his form; for water indeed is Sarva, since from water all this is born. He said, "I am indeed greater than that; give me yet another name."

Paśupati said to him, "Thou art Asī. Now, because he gave him that name, plants became his form; for Paśupati is indeed the plants. Therefore, when cattle obtain plants, they become masters [of them]. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me yet another name!"
He said to him, "Thou art Ugra.

Now, because he gave him that name, Vāyu became his form; for Vāyu is indeed Ugra, therefore when it blows with great force, they say, "Vāyu blows as Ugra. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me yet another name."
He said to him, "You are the thunderbolt (aśani).

Now, because he gave him that name, his form became lightning; for the thunderbolt is indeed lightning. Therefore, when lightning strikes someone, people say, "The thunderbolt has killed him. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me yet another name!"
Bhava said to him, "Thou art Bhava.

Now, because he gave him that name, Parjanya became his form; for Parjanya is indeed Bhava, since from Parjanya all this comes into being. He said, "I am indeed greater than that; give me yet another name!"
The Great God said to him, "Thou art Mahān.
Now, because he gave him that name, he became the Moon; for Prajāpati is the Moon, and Prajāpati is indeed the Great God. He said, "I am indeed greater than this; give me yet another name."
He said to him, "Thou art Īśāna.

Because he gave him that name, he became the form of Āditya; for Āditya is indeed Īśāna, since Āditya rules over all this. He said, "I am indeed as much as this; do not give me a name greater than this."
These are the eight forms of Agni;
the youth is the ninth—he is indeed Agni, the threefold.
Furthermore, there are eight forms of Agni;

the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; therefore they say, "Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. This very boy entered into those forms; for people do not see Agni as a boy, but rather they see these very forms of his, since he entered into these forms.
One should pile this very altar during the year itself.

"One should recite [the invitatory verses] after a year," so some say; "for they shed that seed after a year, and after a year the boy was born; therefore one should pile [the altar] after two years and recite after two years. But rather, one should pile it after a year and recite after a year; for whatever seed is shed, that very thing is born, and having been born, it lies there changing and growing. Therefore, one should pile it after a year and recite after a year. He gives a name to that which has been piled; thereby he strikes away its evil. He gives it a bright name, saying, "Thou art bright (citras)," for Agni is all that is bright.

Prajāpati meditated upon the forms of Agni. He sought after that boy who had entered into the forms; and Agni perceived him, thinking: "My father Prajāpati is indeed seeking me. Come now, let me become that form which he does not know."
He saw these five animals:
the man, the horse, the cow, the sheep, and the goat; because he saw them, they are called *paśus*.
He entered into these five animals;
he became these five animals, and Prajāpati indeed searched for him.
He saw these five animals; because he saw them, they are called "animals" (paśu); and because he saw him within them, they are indeed "animals."

He reflected: "These indeed are fires; let me construct these very ones as my own self. Just as fire, when kindled, blazes forth, so does their eye blaze; just as smoke rises from fire, so does their warmth rise; just as fire burns what is placed upon it, so do they eat; just as the ashes of fire settle down, so does their refuse settle. These indeed are fires; let me construct these very ones as my own self. He intended to offer them to various deities: a man to Viśvakarman, a horse to Varuṇa, a bull to Indra, a ram to Tvaṣṭṛ, and a goat to Agni.

He reflected: "I have indeed intended these [animals] for various deities; I desire the forms of Agni; well then, let me offer them to the Agnis according to my desire. So he offered them to the Agnis according to his desire. Now, as to why it is said "to the Agnis," it is because he meditated upon many forms of Agni; and as to why it is said "according to desire," it is because he offered them out of desire. Having led those animals, which had been gratified and encircled by fire, toward the north, he slaughtered them.

He reflected: "Those glories which I have bestowed, they are now in my heads; come, let me place the very heads [as bricks]. He cut off his own heads and placed them down, and then he cast the other trunks into the waters. He completed the sacrifice with a goat, thinking, "Let not my sacrifice be torn asunder," and "The sacrifice is indeed the self; let not this self of mine be torn asunder. Having sacrificed with that animal, Prajāpati saw that he had not reached the end of this fire-altar.

He reflected: "I shall search for that very Self which floated away into the waters. He searched for it; and what remained of those waters after they had been cast away, he gathered together—that water, and the clay that was in it. Having brought both together, the clay and the water, he made them into bricks. Therefore, a brick consists of these two things: clay and water.

He reflected: "If I were to prepare this very being as food for myself," he cooked it with fire; he thereby made it immortal. This oblation is indeed immortal. [He thought: "I shall become mortal, a corpse, not having shaken off evil. "Ah! Let this which they cook with fire become immortal. Therefore, they cook the bricks with fire; they thus make them immortal.
He saw them by means of a victim after having sacrificed with it; therefore they are called *iṣṭakā*s.

For this reason, one should make the bricks only after sacrificing with a victim; for those which one makes before the victim, they are indeed not true *iṣṭakā*s; moreover, that [which is done before] is quite another thing altogether.

Those which were those splendors (śrī) are these heads of the animals; and those which were those trunks (kusindha) are these five layers (citī). Now, when he piles up the layers after having placed the heads of the animals, he thereby joins those trunks together by means of these very heads.

All these animals are Agni; therefore, animals delight in Agni, for it is in him that Agni is established, since Agni is indeed the animals. Thus, by means of the animals, the animals themselves delight in him. Therefore, he who possesses animals becomes possessed of Agni through them all. Prajāpati intended to sacrifice here with all these; that is the ultimate limit of Agni.

Regarding this, some say: "One should sacrifice with all these animals right here; for if one were to sacrifice with all of them here, one would go to the very end of Agni. One should not do so, for he would then overstep the gods, or he would stray from the path, or what would he then collect? These layers (citis) are indeed the very materials (kusindhāni) he collects; therefore, one should not do so.
Furthermore, as to why he immolates these animals:

he thereby provides a dwelling-place for Agni, for no one delights in what is not a dwelling-place. The dwelling-place is indeed food; he thus places it before him, and Agni, beholding it, turns toward him.
The man, the horse, the ox, the sheep, and the goat—these indeed are all the animals;
animals are food. Thus, as much as there is food, that he places here in front; seeing this, Agni turns toward him.
There are five;
for these five layers are indeed five fires, and it is into these that he places these five abodes; thus Agni, beholding him, turns toward him.
As for the words "to the fires":
these altars are indeed many fires; and as for "for what desire": it is so that the sacrificer may obtain whatever desire he performs this rite with.

He seizes the man first; for the man is the first of animals. Then the horse, for the horse follows after the man; then the cow, for the cow follows after the horse; then the sheep, for the sheep follows after the cow; then the goat, for the goat follows after the sheep. Thus he seizes them in order of precedence, according to their excellence.

Their cords should be of uneven lengths: for the man, the longest; then shorter; then shortest. Thus he makes the cords of the animals according to their respective forms, so as to avoid confusion between superior and inferior. However, they may all indeed be equal—equal and similar in every way—for all these are equal and all are similar; for they are called fires, and they are called food; therefore they are equal, and therefore they are similar.
Regarding this, they say:

"How does this five-brick Agni of his come to be entirely undertaken in the animal sacrifice? In the potsherds for the sacrificial cake, indeed, this first brick made of clay is obtained; then, in that he immolates the animal, thereby the animal-brick is obtained; then, in that there are two pieces of gold on both sides of the omentum, thereby the gold-brick is obtained; then, in that there are the fuel, the sacrificial post, and the enclosing sticks, thereby the wooden-brick is obtained; then, in that there are the clarified butter, the sprinkling waters, and the sacrificial cake, thereby food—the fifth brick—is obtained. Thus, indeed, this five-brick Agni of his comes to be entirely undertaken in the animal sacrifice."
Their *sāmidhenī* verses are twenty-four;
for the year consists of twenty-four half-months, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much does he thus kindle him.
Or again, as to why there are twenty-four:
the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatrī nature; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by so much he thus kindles him.

Or again, as to why there are twenty-four: man indeed consists of twenty-four parts—ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and four limbs. Man is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much does he thus kindle him.
He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs.

The Gāyatrī is the breath, and the Triṣṭubh is the self; with the Gāyatrīs he kindles his breath, and with the Triṣṭubhs his self. The Triṣṭubhs are in the middle and the Gāyatrīs on both sides, for this self is in the middle and the breaths are on both sides. He recites more Gāyatrīs before and fewer after, for these breaths are more numerous in front and fewer behind.
He recites:

"May the months, O Agni, and the seasons strengthen thee. When Agni restored Prajāpati after he had become disjointed, he said to him: "With those kindling verses (sāmidhenī) that are commensurate with me, do thou enkindle me."
He saw these [verses]:

"O Agni, may the seasons and the years increase thee"—that is, "may both the seasons and the years increase thee"; "the years, the seers, and the truths"—that is, "may the years, the seers, and the truths increase thee"; "shine forth with the divine light of heaven"—for yonder sun is the divine light of heaven; "thereby shine thou forth," that is what he means; "illumine all the four quarters"—that is, "illumine all the four quarters."

These [verses] have a single explanation. They refer to this very [Agni]; insofar as one should prepare him, join him together, and generate him, they are addressed to Agni. They are addressed to Prajāpati because when Agni saw them, they were addressed to Agni; and because he kindled Prajāpati with them, they are addressed to Prajāpati.
There are twelve Āprī verses;
twelve months are a year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gratifies him.

Or again, why there are twelve: the Jagatī consists of twelve syllables; this earth is indeed the Jagatī, for upon it all this world moves. This earth, moreover, is Agni, for upon it the entire Agni is built up. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus gratifies him.
Or again, why there are twelve:

the Jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables; the Jagatī is all the metres, and all the metres are Prajāpati; Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much he thus gratifies him.
"These are his upright fuel-sticks," it is said;
when they restored the relaxed Prajāpati with fire, he said to him, "With those Āprī verses that are equal to me, with them do thou gratify me."
He saw these [verses]:

"His fuel-sticks stand upright"—for indeed, the fuel-sticks of this kindled fire stand upright; "the bright flames of Agni stand upright"—for indeed, its bright flames and rays stand upright; "most radiant"—that is, "most powerful"; "of the fair-faced one"—for Agni is fair-faced on every side; "of the son"—because he generates him, he is his son.

These [verses] have a single explanation. They refer to this very [Agni] alone, just as one would prepare him, join him together, and generate him. They belong to Agni and to Prajāpati: because Agni saw them, they belong to Agni; because he gratified Prajāpati with them, they belong to Prajāpati.
They are uneven, having uneven feet;
they have uneven syllables, for the meters are indeed uneven. Moreover, those limbs of his which are uneven, he gratifies them with these [verses].
The animal cake is for Vaiśvānara;
for all the fires are indeed Vaiśvānara, and it is for the attainment of all the fires.

Moreover, as for Vaiśvānara: these layers (citayas) are indeed the seasons, or rather, the fires are the seasons; the seasons are the year, and Vaiśvānara is the year. If it were said, "the fires," that would be redundant. It is offered on twelve potsherds—the year has twelve months, and Vaiśvānara is the year. The invitatory and offering verses (yājyā-anuvākyā) belong to Agni, for the sake of obtaining the forms of Agni; they contain the word "desire" (kāma), for the sake of obtaining desires.

Now, some, having found these animal heads, lay them down [with the formula] "Thus indeed"; they think, "In both ways these are animals. But those who do so become mortal corpses, for those [heads] have not been propitiated. Indeed, they once laid them down in this manner for Āṣāḍhi Sauśromateya, and he died very quickly thereafter.
Some, however, make them out of gold, saying, "They are immortal bricks. But those are indeed not immortal bricks, for they are not the heads of animals.
Some, indeed, make them out of clay.

"These animals have indeed perished; whatever has perished, this earth is the support of it all. Therefore, we shall collect them from wherever these animals have gone. One should not do so. For those who do not know their ritual procedure (*āvṛt*) and their Brāhmaṇa explanation, these [animals] would remain lost to them. He should instead sacrifice these five animals as many times as he desires. Prajāpati was the first to sacrifice these; Śyāparṇa Sāyakāyana was the last. Now, in the interval between them, they used to sacrifice these very same ones. But nowadays, only these two are sacrificed: the one for Prajāpati and the one for Vāyu. Their Brāhmaṇa explanation is set forth hereafter.
The Carakas sacrifice an animal dedicated to Prajāpati.
Having piled the fire-altar, Prajāpati became Agni; therefore, when he sacrifices this animal, he reaches the very end of Agni.
He becomes dark-spotted;
for the hair of one who is dark-spotted is of two kinds, white and black—a pair, a productive union—and that is his form belonging to Prajāpati. He becomes hornless, for Prajāpati is indeed hornless.
There are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses for him.

There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first; this is Prajāpati, and Agni is Prajāpati. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus kindles him.
Or again, as to why there are twenty-one:

man indeed consists of twenty-one parts—ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first. Man is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much does he thus kindle him.

He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs; their significance has been explained. Indeed, the significance of the verse-recitation has been explained. He pours the libation with a verse containing the word "Hiraṇyagarbha. Hiraṇyagarbha is Prajāpati, and Agni is Prajāpati. There are twelve Āprī verses; their significance has been explained. Indeed, the significance of the verse-recitation has been explained. The animal-cake belongs to Prajāpati; whatever is the significance of the animal sacrifice is the significance of the cake-offering. It is on twelve potsherds; there are twelve months in a year, and the year is Prajāpati. The invitatory and offering verses contain the word "ka"; for Prajāpati is indeed "Ka."

Then he offers this [sacrifice] to Vāyu Niyutvat: he offers a white, hornless goat. Prajāpati, having created living beings, looked upon them; from his excessive joy, his seed fell away, and it became a white, hornless goat with testicles. Seed is indeed sap; as great as the sap is, so great is the self. In that he offers this [goat], he thus reaches the end of Agni. It is white, for seed is white; it is hornless, for seed is hornless. It belongs to Vāyu; Vāyu is indeed the out-breath (prāṇa). It belongs to Niyutvat; the Niyuts are the up-breath (udāna). He thereby places both the out-breath and the up-breath into him.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this white, hornless goat to Vāyu Niyutvat: when the gods restored Prajāpati after he had become disjointed, they placed that vital breath (prāṇa) which had departed from his center into him by means of this animal; in the same way, this sacrificer now places it into him. It belongs to Vāyu, for Vāyu is indeed the vital breath; it belongs to Niyutvat, for the *niyuts* are indeed the out-breath (*udāna*); thus he places both the in-breath and the out-breath into him. It is white, for Vāyu is white; it is hornless, for Vāyu is hornless.

For this [fire-altar], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses. The year is indeed seventeenfold: twelve months and five seasons; the year is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus kindles him.
Or rather, as to why there are seventeen:

man indeed consists of seventeen parts—ten vital breaths, four limbs, the trunk as the fifteenth, the neck as the sixteenth, and the head as the seventeenth. Prajāpati is man, and Prajāpati is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much he thus kindles him.

He recites both Gāyatrīs and Triṣṭubhs; their significance has been explained. The *anuvāka* for the *āprī*-verses consists of twelve verses; their significance has been explained. The animal-cake offering belongs to Prajāpati; regarding this, Māhitthi used to say, "The desire which the Carakas claim is attained in the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati is indeed attained here."

Moreover, as to why the victim is dedicated to Vāyu and the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is dedicated to Prajāpati: half of Prajāpati is Vāyu and half is Prajāpati. If both were dedicated to Vāyu, or both were dedicated to Prajāpati, only half of him would have been prepared and not the other half. But since the victim is dedicated to Vāyu and the animal-cake is dedicated to Prajāpati, by this he indeed prepares that entire, complete Prajāpati.

Furthermore, as to why there is an animal sacrifice for Vāyu and a cake-offering (paśupuroḍāśa) for Prajāpati: when the gods restored Prajāpati after he had become disjointed, they placed that vital breath (prāṇa) which had departed from his center back into him by means of this animal sacrifice; then, by means of this cake-offering, they restored his body. As to why it belongs to Prajāpati: Prajāpati is indeed the self (ātman). It is offered on twelve potsherds; the year has twelve months, and Prajāpati is the year. The invitatory and offering verses contain the word "ka" (who), for Prajāpati is "Ka."
Now, as to why he offers the omentum first: he thereby places that vital breath which is here in front into him.

And as to why they proceed with this [offering] from the middle: for this self is in the middle. And as to why they proceed with the oblation afterwards: he thereby places that vital breath which is here above into him. The invitatory and offering verses should contain the word "white" (śukla), for the sake of obtaining white forms; and they should contain the word "niyut," for the sake of obtaining whatever form is associated with the *niyuts*.

Regarding this, they say: "The two [verses] for the omentum should indeed be those containing the word 'white' (śuklavatī). For whatever is white in the animal is the omentum; and the two verses for the oblation should contain the word 'niyut' (niyutvatī), for the sake of obtaining that form of the oblation which contains the word 'niyut'."
And as to why he immolates this animal victim.

In this victim, indeed, is the form of all victims. That it is hornless and bearded—that is the form of man, for man is hornless and bearded. That it is hornless and maned—that is the form of the horse, for the horse is hornless and maned. That it has eight hooves—that is the form of the cow, for the cow has eight hooves. And as to the fact that its hooves are like those of a sheep—that is the form of the sheep; and that it is a goat—that is the form of the goat. Thus, when he immolates this one, by that very act all these victims become immolated for him. Therefore, whichever of these rites may be prepared for him—these are indeed the five victims, or this one belonging to Prajāpati, or this one belonging to the *niyut* (the team of horses).
"One should sacrifice it on the full moon day;
one should sacrifice it on the new moon day," so say some. "For that moon is Prajāpati; he dwells here on this night. Thus, it is as if one were to sacrifice while [the deity] is standing nearby."
That [sacrifice] indeed takes place on the full moon day.

That moon is indeed the animal; the gods sacrifice it on the full moon day. Thinking, "Where the gods sacrifice this, there let me also sacrifice it," he therefore sacrifices on the full moon day. Furthermore, as to why it is on the full moon day: the full moon night was indeed the first to dawn; for that reason also, he sacrifices on the full moon day.
That indeed takes place on the Phālgunī day itself.
For this Phālgunī full moon is the first night of the year, while the later one is the last; thus, by means of the earlier one, he begins the year at its very beginning.

Having indeed performed the Full-moon sacrifice, he should then immolate the victim. For by means of the Full-moon sacrifice, Indra, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—and being freed from evil, undertook this rite; in the same way, this sacrificer, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—by means of the Full-moon sacrifice itself and being freed from evil, undertakes this rite.
That [sacrifice] is indeed performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
For by means of these animals, Prajāpati strove to perform this rite; it was as if held together, as if not yet fully articulated. Therefore, it is performed in a low voice.
Moreover, as for why it is performed in a whisper:
this rite belongs to Prajāpati, for one undertakes this rite with Prajāpati; and Prajāpati is indeed undefined.
And as to why it is whispered:
seed is indeed here in the sacrifice; seed is poured out in a whisper. The omentum, the animal cake, and the oblation—this much constitutes the animal.

On the eighth day he prepares the fire-pan (ukhā). This day belongs to Prajāpati; this work, the fire-pan, belongs to Prajāpati. Thus, on a day belonging to Prajāpati, he performs a rite belonging to Prajāpati.
Or rather, as for the Aṣṭakā:
that which is the Aṣṭakā is a joint of the year, and that which is the fire-pan (ukhā) is a joint of Agni; thus he joins joint with joint.
Or rather, it is on the Aṣṭakā day.

For the Aṣṭakā is indeed the fire-pan (ukhā), the storehouse (nidhi); the two [side] bricks are the two ends, the transverse one is the girdle-band (rāsnā). Thus there are four [layers], and four more directed upwards; that makes eight. On the Aṣṭakā day he thus makes it the Aṣṭakā.
He undergoes initiation on the new moon day;
for it is from the new moon that the sacrifice is extended. Thinking, "From where the sacrifice is extended, from there I shall cause the sacrifice to be born," he initiates himself.
Or rather, on the new moon day:

when he undergoes consecration, he pours his own self—which has become seed—into the fire-pan as a womb. For him, he prepares this space beforehand; he is born toward that prepared space when he becomes consecrated. Therefore they say: "A man is born toward a prepared space."
If he were to be consecrated for less than a year, he would place bricks that are not worlds, and the bricks would exceed the worlds;

and if, having made more worlds, he were not to place bricks accordingly, the worlds would exceed the bricks. But when he is consecrated on the new moon day and purchases [the Soma] on the new moon day, then as many worlds as he makes, so many bricks he places; thus his entire fire-altar is built during the waxing fortnight.
Regarding this, they say:

If there were as many bricks for this fire-altar as there are days and nights in the period of purchase, then those days which are after the purchase—how would those worlds of his be provided with bricks? Well, when one has been initiated on the new moon day and purchases [the Soma] on the new moon day, he lays down as many bricks as the extent of the world he makes; and those days which are after the purchase, in that space the Adhvaryu builds the fire-altar. For where could he build it, if that space did not exist? As many as are the days and nights of the year, so many are the bricks of this fire-altar. And there is also a thirteenth month; for these days which are after the purchase constitute a thirteenth month. Thus, by those bricks of the thirteenth month, those worlds of his become provided with bricks. In this way, the worlds and the bricks become equal.

On that very first full moon, he immolates the victim; on that which is the first Aṣṭakā, he collects the materials for the fire-pan (ukhā); on that which is the first new moon, he undergoes initiation. Indeed, it is those very days of the year which are the first that he here begins, and those he thereby attains. Now, therefore, as to the ritual correspondence.

Regarding this they say: "How does his ritual action reach Agni for a year? How is he made to correspond with Agni through the year? Now, of these five animals, there are twenty-four *sāmidhenī* verses and twelve *āprī* verses; that makes thirty-six. There are eleven *anuyāja* offerings and eleven *upayaj* offerings; that makes fifty-eight.
Then there are forty-eight.
