The Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables; this earth is indeed the Jagatī, for upon it all this world moves. This earth is also Agni, for upon it the entire Agni is built up. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.

Or, as to why there are forty-eight: the Jagatī consists of forty-eight syllables; the Jagatī is all the metres, and all the metres are Prajāpati; Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become.

Now, as for those which are ten: that is the Virāj consisting of ten syllables; Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions; the directions are Agni; there are ten vital breaths; the vital breaths are Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become.
The omentum and the animal cake—these make sixty;

there are sixty days and nights in a month. He thus attains the month; the month attained, he attains the season; the season, the year. Thereby he attains Agni, who is the year, as well as the desires that are in the year. And whatever else besides this there is—the food that is in the year, all that he attains.

Now, regarding this sacrifice to Prajāpati: there are twenty-one *sāmidhenī* verses and twelve *āprī* verses; that makes thirty-three. There are eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*) and eleven by-offerings (*upayaj*); that makes fifty-five. The omentum, the animal cake, and the oblation—that makes fifty-eight. Whatever desire there is in relation to fifty-eight, one attains it right here. There are two libations of ghee (*āghāra*); that makes sixty. Whatever desire there is in relation to sixty, one attains it right here. And whatever else there is beyond this—whatever food there is in the year, all that is contained therein.
Now, regarding this [offering] accompanied by the *niyut* [horses]:

There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses and twelve *āprī* verses; that makes twenty-nine, and with one more, thirty. There are eleven after-offerings (*anuyāja*) and eleven by-offerings (*upayāja*); that makes fifty-one. The omentum, the animal cake, and the oblation—that makes fifty-four. The two libations of clarified butter (*āghāra*) and the two *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings—that makes fifty-eight. Whatever desire there is in fifty-eight, he obtains it right here. The offering to the Lord of the Forest (*vanaspati*) and the fat-oblation (*vasāhoma*)—that makes sixty. Whatever desire there is in sixty, he obtains it right here. And whatever else besides this there is—the food in the year, that very thing he obtains. Thus indeed does this rite of his reach Agni the Year-long; thus it is perfected through the Year and through Agni.
Regarding this, they say:

One should not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations for this animal sacrifice, nor should one descend into the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the heart-spit. For this animal is the commencement of Agni, while the *samiṣṭayajus* are the dismissal of the deities and the *avabhṛtha* is the conclusion. [He does this] thinking, "Lest I should dismiss the deities at the very commencement, lest I should bring the sacrifice to a final close. However, he should indeed conclude it. Having sacrificed with this animal, Prajāpati saw that he did not reach the end of this Agni; therefore, one should conclude it. Furthermore, as to why he concludes it: this animal is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). If one were to leave a gap in it, one would leave a gap in the vital breath; and if one were to leave a gap in the vital breath, one would die from that very cause. Therefore, one should indeed conclude it. Now, concerning the vows (*vrata*).
Regarding this, they say:

Having sacrificed with this animal victim, he should not sleep on high, nor eat meat, nor engage in sexual intercourse. For this animal victim is indeed the preliminary consecration (*dīkṣā*); it is improper for one who is consecrated to sleep on high, to eat meat, or to engage in sexual intercourse. But this is not really a consecration, for there is neither a girdle nor a black antelope skin. He makes this [animal] his very brick; therefore, he may indeed sleep on high at will. Whatever food there is here, that is cattle; thus all that is obtained and commenced by him here. Of whatever foods there are except honey, he may eat of them all as he pleases, provided he obtains them. But he should not engage in sexual intercourse before the curd-offering to Mitra and Varuṇa; the significance of that has been explained above.

Regarding this they say: "One should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at this sacrifice, lest this sacrifice of mine be without a fee. [They say: "One should give the fee prescribed for the Brahman priest; for the Brahman is indeed the whole sacrifice, so his entire sacrifice becomes successful. One should not do so, for he thereby makes this [Brahman] a brick. Just as one would give [a fee] for each individual brick, such is that act. On that very day, he should give whatever may be available to him.

The gods indeed said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek ye a layer. While they were reflecting, Prajāpati perceived this first naturally-perforated layer; therefore, one lays it down with Prajāpati.

Agni said to him, "I will come to you. "By what means? "By means of cattle. "So be it. He spoke thus regarding the cattle-brick; for this Dūrvā-brick is indeed the cattle-brick. Therefore, the Dūrvā-brick is laid down immediately after the first naturally-perforated brick (svayamātṛṇā). Consequently, plants are not separated from her, cattle are not separated, and Agni is not separated, for he approached by means of this very brick.

They said, "Reflect ye indeed!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)!", that is, "Seek one from here upwards. While they were reflecting, Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman perceived the atmosphere as the second naturally-perforated layer; therefore, he places it with Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman.

Vāyu said to them, "I will come to you. "By what means? they asked. "By the quarters," he replied. "So be it. He then spoke by means of the quarter-bricks (*diśyā*). Therefore, the *diśyā* bricks are laid down immediately adjacent to the second *svayamātṛṇṇā*. Thus the quarters are not separated from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), for Vāyu is not separated [from them]; indeed, he approached by means of these very bricks.

They said, "Reflect ye indeed! By which they meant, "Seek ye a layer (citi)!"—that is, "Seek ye one from here upwards! While they were thus reflecting, Parameṣṭhin perceived the third layer, the naturally-perforated one, as belonging to the sky; therefore, he places it with Parameṣṭhin.

Tama said to Āditya, "I will come to you. "By what means? he asked. "By the *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler)," he replied. "So be it," [said Āditya]. This, indeed, is the *lokampṛṇā*; by means of its own self, he spoke thus. Therefore, the third *svayamātṛṇā* (self-perforated brick) is laid down immediately adjacent to the *lokampṛṇā*. Consequently, this Āditya is not separated from the sky; for he is not separated from it, since he approached by means of this [brick].
These six deities indeed became this entire universe—whatever exists here.

Those gods and seers said, "These six deities have indeed become this entire universe; find out how we too may be present here. They said, "Let us reflect (cetayadhvam). By this they meant, "Seek a layer (citim icata). "Seek it so that we too may be present here," they said. While they were thus reflecting, the gods perceived the second layer and the seers perceived the fourth.

They said, "Let us approach. "By what means? "By that which approaches within these worlds. "So be it. Thus, by that which is above the earth and below the atmosphere, the gods approached; this is the second layer. Then, by that which is above the atmosphere and below the sky, the seers (ṛṣis) approached; this is the fourth layer.
When they said, "Meditate! (cetayadhvam), they were indeed saying, "Seek a layer" (citim icata). And because they saw [the layers] while meditating, they are therefore called "layers" (citayaḥ).

Prajāpati saw the first layer; Prajāpati himself is its seerhood (ārṣeya). The gods saw the second layer; the gods themselves are its seerhood. Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman saw the third layer; they themselves are its seerhood. The Ṛṣis saw the fourth layer; the Ṛṣis themselves are its seerhood. Parameṣṭhin saw the fifth layer; Parameṣṭhin himself is its seerhood. He who thus knows this seerhood of the layers—his layers become possessed of seers and possessed of kinship.

The gods indeed said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi). While they were reflecting, Savitṛ saw these Sāvitra formulas; because Savitṛ saw them, they are called Sāvitra. He offered this eightfold-drawn oblation; having offered it, he saw this [layer] as established in eight ways, the Aṣāḍhā, which had already been created before.

When they said, "Reflect ye," they indeed meant, "Seek ye a layer. And because they saw [the fire-altar] while reflecting, it is therefore called a "layer" (citi). The oblation is indeed the sacrifice; and because they saw it after performing the sacrifice, it is therefore called a "brick" (iṣṭakā).
This very [offering], though being one, he offers with eight *yajuṣ* formulas consisting of eight portions; therefore, this [earth], though being one, is divided into eight parts.
He offers it while holding it upwards;
he thus holds this [earth] upwards with forms, and therefore this [earth] is held upwards with forms.
He offers that [oblation] continuously.

For the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should follow after us here. They saw this continuous oblation for the purpose of preventing the Rakṣases and destroyers from following after; therefore, he offers it continuously.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this oblation: this Agni is Savitṛ; he gratifies him beforehand with this oblation. Having sacrificed to and gratified him, he then gathers him together. Because he gratifies Savitṛ with this [verse], they are called Sāvitra formulas; for that reason, indeed, he offers this oblation.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this oblation: Savitṛ is this Agni; with this oblation he pours him out in front as seed. For whatever kind of seed is poured into the womb, such a one is born. Since he pours Savitṛ out as seed with this [oblation], they are called Sāvitra formulas; for that reason, indeed, he offers this oblation.
And here both the *sruva* and the *sruk* ladles are employed.
The *sruk* is indeed speech and the *sruva* is breath; for by means of speech and breath, the gods first performed this ritual work. Therefore, there is both the *sruva* and the *sruk*.
Furthermore, as for the *sruva* and the *sruk*: he who was Prajāpati is this *sruva*;

the *sruva* is indeed breath (*prāṇa*), and Prajāpati is breath. And she who was Speech (*vāc*) is this *sruk*; Speech is indeed female (*yoṣā*), and the *sruk* is female. And those waters which went forth from the world of Speech—those are these very oblations which one offers.
He offers that [oblation] continuously;
for those waters flowed continuously. Now, he who was Prajāpati entered the waters together with the threefold knowledge—that very one is he who now offers with these sacrificial formulas.

Those which are the first three are these worlds; then that which is the fourth *yajus* is the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), it is the *jagatī* [meter], for the *jagatī* is all the meters, and all the meters are the triple knowledge. Then those which are the four last are the quarters; these worlds and the quarters are Prajāpati, and this is the triple knowledge.

He offers with the verse, "Yoking the mind first. Prajāpati is indeed the one who yokes; he yoked the mind for this rite. Because he yoked the mind for this rite, therefore Prajāpati is called "the Yoker" (yuñjāna).
"For Savitṛ, having perceived the light of Agni, has brought it from the earth for truth and for thought.

Savitṛ is indeed the mind, and thoughts are the vital breaths; "having perceived the light of Agni" means "having seen the light of Agni"; "he has brought it from the earth" means that he indeed brings it from the earth.
"With a concentrated mind," he says;

he thus yokes the mind itself for this rite, for with an unconcentrated mind one is not able to do anything at all. "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he says; this means "impelled by the god Savitṛ. "For the sake of heaven, through power," he says; this means "so that by this rite one may go to the heavenly world"; he says "through power" because it is indeed through power that one goes to the heavenly world.

"Having yoked the gods, Savitṛ"—Savitṛ is indeed the mind, and the gods are the vital breaths; "going to heaven with prayer"—for he has yoked them with prayer for this world, for the sake of this rite; "he who will create the great light"—the great light is yonder sun, and that very one is this Agni, whom they are about to prepare; "may Savitṛ impel them"—that is to say, "impelled by Savitṛ, may they perform this work."
"They harness the mind and they harness the thoughts."

"Both mind and these vital breaths he yokes for this work"—the wise one (vipra) is Prajāpati, and the wise ones (viprāḥ) are the gods; "of the great, the wise one"—Prajāpati indeed is the great, the wise one; "he ordains the priestly offices (hotrāḥ)"—for when he is built up, then he ordains the priestly offices, since the priestly offices are ordained over him once he is built up; "the finder of the way"—for he indeed found this way; "the one alone"—for he alone found all this way; "great is the praise of the god Savitṛ"—that is to say, great is the praise of the god Savitṛ.
"I yoke for you both the ancient prayer with prostrations."

Breath is indeed the ancient Brahman; food is its name, and that very thing is this oblation. By means of this very oblation, he says, "May it reach the wise one," so that the sacrificer may have fame and renown among both gods and men through his food. He yokes the vital breaths for this rite with food, saying, "May the song of praise go forth like a path for us. Thus he says, "May all the sons of immortality hear! Prajāpati is indeed immortality, and all the gods are his sons. "Those who abide in the celestial abodes"—the celestial abodes are these worlds; thus he refers to those gods who are in these worlds.

"Whose departure others indeed followed"—Prajāpati indeed performed this rite first, and thereafter the gods performed it; "the gods [sang] the greatness of the god with vigor"—the sacrifice is indeed the greatness; thus, "the gods [sang] the sacrifice, the heroism, of the god with vigor. "He who measured out the earthly realms, he is Etaśa"—whatever there is on this earth, that is the earthly; all that he measures out, for with his rays he stretches across it; "the god Savitṛ, by his greatness, [measured] the regions"—these worlds are indeed the regions, and yonder sun is the god Savitṛ; him he measures out by means of his greatness.

"O God Savitṛ, impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for the sake of fortune!"—for that Sun is indeed the god Savitṛ, and the sacrifice is fortune; thus he says this: "Impel the sacrifice; impel the lord of the sacrifice for the sake of fortune. "May the celestial Gandharva, the purifier of intentions, purify our intention"—for that Sun is indeed the celestial Gandharva, and intention is food; thus he means: "The purifier of food, may he purify our food. "May the Lord of Speech make our speech sweet"—for this ritual action is speech, and the Lord of Speech is the vital breath; thus he means: "May the vital breath make this ritual action of ours sweet."
"O God Savitṛ, lead this sacrifice of ours forward."

Yonder sun is indeed the divine Savitṛ. Whatever sacrificial work he leads forward, that reaches its goal safely and without failure. "Devāvyam" means "he who has praised the gods. "Sakhividam satrājitam dhanajitam svarjitam" means "one who finds all this. "Ṛcā stomam samardhaya" means "with the Ṛc, perfect the Stoma. "Gāyatreṇa rathantaram bṛhadgāyatravartanī" refers to the Sāmans. "Svāhā" refers to the Yajus formulas. This threefold knowledge (the Trayī Vidya) is born first; just as it was born there [in the beginning], so is it now. And that fire which was created then is this very fire which is built hereafter.
These eight are the Sāvitra formulas.

The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much he thus pours him forth when he has become seed. These [syllables] become nine—the Svāhā-call being the ninth; for there are nine quarters, and Agni is the quarters; there are nine vital airs, and Agni is the vital airs. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much he thus pours him forth when he has become seed. These become ten—the oblation being the tenth; for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten quarters, and Agni is the quarters; there are ten vital airs, and Agni is the vital airs. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become.
When this oblation had been offered, Agni went away from the gods.

The gods said, "Agni is indeed cattle; let us seek him by means of cattle; he will manifest himself in his own form. They sought him with cattle, and he manifested himself in his own form. Therefore, indeed, cattle manifest themselves in their own form. Ga.

They said, "If we search for [the victim] with all [of us], they will become exhausted, unfit for consumption, or useless—whether it be a cow for a horse, or a man for a horse, or a horse for a man, or a man for a man; but if we search for the whole with a non-whole, then we shall find the whole. So they perceived this one animal in place of two animals: the donkey, representing both the cow and the sheep. Because they perceived this one animal in place of two animals, therefore this one [animal] has a double seed.
[He took] a man from among men.
He who does not protect the gods, nor the ancestors, nor men—he is indeed a useless man. Therefore, we sought him with all our cattle; they were not exhausted, yet they became unfit for subsistence.

He seeks it with three [verses]. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus seeks him. There are five in total: the fire-altar consists of five layers, there are five seasons in the year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.

They are bound with cords made of Muñja grass. Agni departed from the gods and entered into the Muñja; therefore it is hollow, and for that very reason it is as if smoky-red within. This Muñja grass is the womb of Agni; Agni is these cattle. Indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury. For one who is being born is born from a womb; [he binds them] so that he may be born from a womb as he is being born.

They are threefold; for Agni is threefold. They are made with horse-hair thongs; for the horse-hair thong lies all around the mouth, and the womb lies all around the embryo; thus this form of the womb is produced.

They stand facing east: first the horse, then the ass, then the goat; for thus they are in their proper order. That which was the tear that flowed then is this horse; that which was the foam as it were is this ass; and that which was the moisture smeared on the potsherd is this goat. And that which was the potsherd is this clay, which they are about to fetch. Indeed, he was created in the beginning from these very forms; it is from those very forms that he now causes him to be born.
They stand on the south side.

For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike our sacrifice from the south. They saw this thunderbolt, namely yonder sun; for yonder sun is this horse. Having driven away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the south by means of this thunderbolt, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer now, having driven away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the south by means of this thunderbolt, performs this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.
The Āhavanīya fire is to the south;

this spade lies to the north. The Āhavanīya is indeed a male, and the spade is a female; for a male lies to the south of a female. It is at the distance of a cubit, for a male lies at the distance of a cubit from a female.
It should be made of bamboo.

Agni departed from the gods and entered the bamboo; therefore it is hollow. He fashioned these joints all around as armor for the sake of non-confusion; wherever he was scorched, those places became speckled.

That [reed] should be speckled; for it belongs to Agni. If he cannot find a speckled one, it may even be unspeckled, but it must be hollow; for that which is hollow belongs to Agni. This bamboo is the womb of Agni, and this clay is Agni. Indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury. For one who is being born is born from a womb; "May he be born from a womb," [he thinks].

It should be a span in measure; for this speech here speaks at the distance of a span. However, it is indeed an elbow in measure; for the elbow is the arm, and by the arm strength is performed. Thus, it becomes commensurate with strength.
It would be sharp on one side;

for this speech is indeed sharp on one side, yet it becomes sharp on both sides, for this speech is sharp on both sides: in that by means of it one speaks both what pertains to the gods and what pertains to men, and also both the truth and the untruth; therefore, it is sharp on both sides.
And as to why it is sharp on both sides:
from this very [edge] of the flint comes its vigor; thus, he bestows vigor upon her from both sides.

Moreover, because it is sharp on both sides—the gods, having discovered him, dug him out from these worlds; and in the same way, this [sacrificer], having discovered him, digs him out from these worlds.

When he digs "yad" (that), he digs him out from this world; then, when it rises upwards, he digs him out from yonder world; and when it moves between, he digs him out from the intermediate world; thus he digs him out from all these worlds.
He takes it up.

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins"—impelled by these deities, he thus takes it up with them. "With the Gāyatrī metre, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee, like Aṅgiras, with the Gāyatrī metre"—thus he says; this is by means of the metre, and he thereby places the Gāyatrī metre in her. "From the seat of the earth, bring Agni Purīṣya, like Aṅgiras"—for *purīṣa* (filling soil) is indeed cattle; thus he means, "from the lap of the earth, bring Agni who is beneficial to cattle, like Agni. "Like Aṅgiras, with the Triṣṭubh metre"—he thus takes her up with the Triṣṭubh metre, and he thereby places the Triṣṭubh metre in her.

"Thou art a spade," he says; for this is indeed a spade, and thus he takes hold of it with truth. "Thou art a woman," he says; for the spade is a thunderbolt and the woman is a female, and a female does not injure anyone; he thus appeases her for the sake of non-injury. "With thee may we be able to dig out Agni in this place," he says; "this place" means this very spot, so he says, "with thee may we be able to dig out Agni in this place. "With the Jagatī metre, like Aṅgiras," he says; thus he takes hold of her with the Jagatī metre, and moreover, he places the Jagatī metre within her.
He takes it up with three verses; Agni is threefold:

as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus takes it up. Having taken it up with three, he then consecrates it with the fourth. For indeed, the gods, having taken it up with three, then bestowed vigor upon it with the fourth; in the same way, this sacrificer, having taken it up with three, bestows vigor upon it with the fourth.

"Having placed it in his hand, Savitṛ..."—for she is indeed placed in his hand; "bearing the spade (abhri)," for he bears her; "golden," for she is made of gold, being composed of the metres; "having perceived the light of Agni"—that is, having seen the light of Agni; "he brought [her] from the earth," for he brings her from the earth; "with the Anuṣṭubh metre, like Aṅgiras"—thereby he takes her up with the Anuṣṭubh metre, and thus he bestows the Anuṣṭubh metre upon her. These very metres are this spade; it is made of bamboo for the sake of support.

Some indeed make it golden, saying, "For it is described as being made of gold. One should not do so; rather, since this [sacrificial ladle] is the meters, it is therefore gold—the immortal is gold, for the meters are immortal.

He takes it up with four [formulas]. For all speech consists of four syllables: "vāk" (speech) is one syllable, and "akṣaram" (syllable) is three syllables. Now, that which is the single syllable "vāk" is this very same *anuṣṭubh* which is the last; and as for the three syllables "akṣaram," these are those preceding sacrificial formulas (*yajus*). Thus, he digs the fire-altar with the whole of speech, and he gathers the materials with the whole of speech; therefore, he does so with four.
Or rather, as to why he does so with four: there are indeed four quarters;

it is thus in the four quarters that he bestows speech. Therefore, speech speaks in the four quarters. He takes it up with both metres and sacrificial formulas; that makes eight—four quarters and four intermediate quarters. It is thus in all the quarters that he bestows speech. Therefore, speech speaks in all the quarters.
This hand becomes the spade; then he consecrates the animals with a mantra.
For it was here that the gods, seeking them out, placed vigor in them beforehand; in the same way, this [sacrificer], seeking them out, now places vigor in them beforehand.
He consecrates the horse with the mantra: "O steed, run forth!

For that which is swift is "tūrta," and that which is swifter than swift is "pratūrta. "Along the widest expanse"—this earth is indeed the widest expanse; thus he means, "along this expanse. "In heaven is thy highest birth, in the atmosphere thy navel, upon the earth thy womb"—thereby he makes him these deities: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya; he thereby bestows vigor upon the horse.
Then, regarding the donkey:

"Yoke ye two the donkey," with these words he addresses both the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer; "in this course, O ye of raining wealth"—that is, "in this ritual act, O ye of raining wealth"; "bearing Agni, well-disposed toward us"—that is, "bearing Agni sent forth by us. Thus he bestows vigor upon the donkey.
Then [he offers] the goat with [the verse], "In every need, O most powerful one;

in every contest, we invoke thee. "Vāja" is indeed food; thus, "in every rite, the most powerful one; in food after food, we invoke thee. "O friends, Indra for our protection"—that is, "the possessor of power for our protection. He thereby bestows vigor upon the goat.
He consecrates them with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows vigor upon these [bricks].
Then he makes them step forward toward the east;
thus he seeks him with these animals. He does not touch them, thinking, "Lest this Agni should injure me," for these animals are indeed Agni.

He makes the horse step forward with the formula: "Speeding forward, come hither; trampling down the malevolent. Malevolence is indeed evil; thus, "Come hither, speeding, trampling down evil"—this is what he says. "To Rudra's domain of the Gaṇas, come as a bringer of bliss"—for cattle belong to Rudra; thus, "To that deity of yours which is the domain of the Gaṇas, come as a bringer of bliss"—this is what he says. He thereby searches for him (the sacrificer) by means of the horse.
Then [he addresses] the donkey:

"Traverse the wide atmosphere, creating safe pastures and security. As the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. "With Pūṣan as his companion"—Pūṣan is indeed this earth; thus, "with her as his companion," he says. It is with the donkey that he thus searches for him.
Then [he says]:

"From the lap of the earth, bring Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras"—that is to say, "from the lap of the earth, bring Agni who is beneficial to cattle, like Agni. Thus he searches for him by means of the goat.

He seeks him with three [verses]. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus seeks him. With three [verses] he addresses [the fire-pan] from the front; that makes six. Six are the seasons, and the year is the seasons; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.
These fires become kindled; now, they gather the clay.

These worlds are indeed these fires; when they are kindled, then these worlds are kindled. Formerly, the gods sought after the sacrificial work from these worlds. Therefore, when he brings the clay having passed beyond these fires, he thereby seeks after it from these worlds.
They go eastward;
for the eastern quarter belongs to Agni. Thus he searches for him in his own quarter, and he finds him in his own quarter.
They proceed with the words, "We would kindle Agni Purīṣya in the manner of Aṅgiras"; this means, "We would kindle the Agni who is favorable to cattle, in the manner of Agni."

Then he looks at the Anaddhāpuruṣa (the man bound with cords) with the words, "We shall bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras. This means, "We shall bear the fire-favoring Agni like Agni. Thus, he searches for him by means of the Anaddhāpuruṣa.
Now, an ant-hill with a hollow interior is placed midway.

He gazes at it, thinking: "This is indeed an ant-hill; these worlds are indeed this [ant-hill]. For the gods sought to seize him limb by limb within these worlds; in the same way, this sacrificer now seeks to seize him limb by limb within these worlds."
"Agni has looked along the forefront of the dawns"—thereby they sought him in the dawns;

"day after day, the first Jātavedas"—thereby they sought him in the days; "along the wide rays of the sun"—thereby they sought him in the rays of the sun; "you have stretched across heaven and earth"—thereby they sought him in heaven and earth; they found him. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now finds him. When he sees him from afar, then he puts on that garment and they go to the clay.
Then he consecrates the horse with a mantra:

"The gods indeed said, 'Let us strike away the evil from this one. Evil is indeed weariness; [they thought], 'Let us strike away weariness, the evil, from this one. They struck away its weariness, its evil; in the same way, this [priest] now strikes away its weariness, its evil."
"Having come, he shakes off all adversaries on his path"—for his path has indeed been reached;

"all adversaries," that is, all evils, he shakes off. Therefore, when a horse has run its course, it shakes itself. "He desires to behold Agni with his eye in the great gathering-place"—this earth is indeed the great gathering-place; thus, "in this great gathering-place, he desires to see Agni with his eye."
Then he makes him step upon it.
For this [horse], having discovered this [earth] for the gods, announced it to them just as one would say, "It is right here."
And as to why he makes him step forward:

the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakshasas, the destroyers, should smite this [Agni] of ours here"; therefore they made yonder sun as a protector over him from above. Now, that horse is indeed yonder sun; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now makes that thunderbolt as a protector over him from above.

"Having stepped upon the earth and Agni with thy radiance, O steed"—for radiance is indeed sight; thus he means, "Having stepped upon the earth and Agni with thy sight, O steed. "Having encompassed it with the earth, tell us where we may dig it out"—that is to say, "having probed the earth, tell us where we may dig this [horse] out."

Then he strokes him. For the gods, when he had spoken thus, endowed him with vigor; in the same way, this [priest] now endows him with vigor who has spoken thus: "The sky is your back, the earth your seat, the atmosphere your self, the ocean your womb. By saying "thus you are, thus you are," he means this. "Having looked around with your eye, trample upon those who attack," by which he means, "having looked around with your eye, trample upon all evils. He does not touch [the horse], for the horse is a thunderbolt; he does so thinking, "Lest this thunderbolt injure me."
Then he causes him to step out.

The gods indeed said, "What shall we step upon for him?"—"Great good fortune! they said; they made him step upon great good fortune. In the same way, this one now makes him step upon great good fortune with the words, "Step forth for great good fortune!"—that is, "Step forth for your own great good fortune! Therefore, among animals, the horse is the most fortunate. "From this place"—that is, "from where you stand"—"O giver of wealth," for he gives wealth to these [beings]; "O vigorous one," for he is indeed vigorous; "may we be in the favor of the earth, digging Agni in her lap"—that is, "may we be in the favor of this earth, digging Agni in her lap."
Then he addresses him as he departs.

The gods indeed praised and magnified him when he had spoken thus, just as one would praise and magnify a donor; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now praises and magnifies him. "He has stepped forth"—for he has indeed stepped forth—"the giver of wealth" (*draviṇodā*), for he gives wealth to these [beings]; "the vigorous steed" (*vājy arvā*), for he is both a vigorous steed and a racer. "He has made a fair world, a well-made one on earth"—that is, "he has made a fair world, a well-made one on earth. "Thence let us dig out Agni of the fair countenance"—that is, "thence let us dig him out. He is indeed of fair countenance on all sides. "Ascending to the highest firmament"—the firmament (*nāka*) is indeed the heavenly world; thus, "ascending to the heavenly world, to the highest firmament. He leads it toward the south, where the other two animals are; they stand facing eastward to the south. Whatever significance there was for the place being to the south in that [other] case, that is the significance here as well.

Then, having sat down, he offers an oblation upon the clay. Regarding this, the gods said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! While meditating, they saw this oblation; they offered it, and having offered it, they saw these worlds as the fire-pan (ukhā).

They said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! While reflecting, they saw this second libation; having offered it, they saw these "All-Lights" (viśvajyotis), namely these deities: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, for these deities indeed are the All-Light. In the same way, the sacrificer, having offered these two libations, sees both these worlds as the fire-pan (ukhā) and these deities as the All-Lights. He offers with two interlinked [formulas]; thereby he interlinks both these worlds and these deities.
Moreover, when he offers these two oblations, he gratifies both the clay and the water;
having sacrificed and gratified them, he then gathers them together. He offers with two interlinked verses; thereby he interlinks the clay and the water.

He offers with clarified butter. Clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt; he thus makes this thunderbolt his protector. Moreover, clarified butter is seed; he thus pours forth seed. He offers with the *sruva* ladle; the *sruva* is indeed a male, and the male pours forth seed. He offers with the utterance *svāhā*; the *svāhā* is indeed a male, and the male pours forth seed.

"I sprinkle thee with mind and ghee"—that is to say, "I offer thee with mind and ghee. "Dwelling facing all beings"—for he indeed dwells facing all beings. "Broad, vast with transverse vigor"—for he is broad and vast with transverse vapor (smoke). "Most extensive, impetuous in food, visible"—that is to say, "possessing space, devouring food with foods, shining."

"I sprinkle him who faces every direction"—that is, "I offer oblation to him who faces from all sides. "May he enjoy that with a mind free of demons"—that is, "may he take pleasure in that with a mind that is not ill-disposed. "Agni, the glory of men, of desirable appearance"—for this Agni is indeed the glory of men and of desirable appearance. "He is not to be touched while flickering with his body"—for he is not to be touched while flickering with his body as he blazes.

He offers two oblations. The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he pours him forth as seed. With two verses addressed to Agni, he pours Agni himself forth as seed. In that they are addressed to Agni, by that it is Agni; and in that they are Triṣṭubhs, by that it is Indra—for Agni is of the nature of Indra and Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he pours him forth as seed. Indeed, Indra and Agni are all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he pours him forth as seed.
He offers in the footprint of the horse;
for this horse is Agni, and thus these two oblations of his become offered in Agni itself.
Then he draws a line around it; he thereby establishes its measure for him, just as one might say, "You are exactly this much."

Furthermore, as to why he traces it around: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this one here"; they therefore enclosed him within this fortress. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encloses him within this fortress. The spade is a thunderbolt; verily, he thus makes the thunderbolt his protector. He traces it around on all sides; verily, he thus makes the thunderbolt his protector on every side. He traces it around three times; verily, he thus makes for him that threefold thunderbolt as his protector.
The sage, lord of booty, goes around.

"O Agni, we [place] thee around as a fort," and "Thou, O Agni, by days..."—by thus praising Agni with these verses containing the word *pari* ("around"), he makes for him a protective armor (*varman*). For forts are surrounded; by means of verses addressed to Agni, he thus makes for him a fort of fire. This very fort of fire stands blazing. With three verses, he makes for him a triple fort; therefore, the triple fort is the supreme form of forts. He makes each successive line wider by means of each successively larger metre; therefore, the successive lines of forts become wider. For the lines are indeed the forts.
Then he digs it in this [ground].

The gods were indeed afraid of this, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this [Agni] of ours. Therefore, they made this very earth his body for protection, thinking, "The body shall protect the body. It should be level with the surface; thus this earth becomes his body. And as to why it is level with the surface: this earth is the womb and this [clay] is the seed. For that which exceeds the womb of the seed becomes abortive, and that which is less than it is deficient. That which is level with the surface is indeed the perfect form of the seed. It is four-cornered; for there are four quarters, and he thus digs him out from all the quarters.
Then he digs for him from here.

For the gods, having discovered him, dug for him; in the same way, this sacrificer, having discovered him, now digs for him with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, from the lap of the earth, I dig thee, Agni Purīṣya, in the manner of Aṅgiras. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs for him from the lap of the earth with these deities, digging for Agni, the source of cattle, in the manner of Agni.
"O Agni, thee, the luminous, the fair-faced..."—for this Agni is indeed luminous and fair-faced.

"Shining with undecaying luster"—that is to say, blazing with undecaying flame. "The auspicious one, who does not harm creatures, Agni Purīṣya from the seat of the earth, let us dig up like Aṅgiras"—that is to say, the auspicious one, who does not harm creatures, Agni who is beneficial to cattle, let us dig up from the lap of the earth like Agni himself.
He digs with two [hands].

The sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus digs him. Moreover, this form consists of two things: clay and water.
He digs, saying, "I dig, we dig.
Prajāpati dug, saying, "I dig," and the gods dug, saying, "We dig"; therefore one says, "I dig, we dig."

While digging with the spade, he says, "I dig; we dig. For the spade is speech; this bamboo spade is made for the sake of a beginning. By means of this spade, which is speech, the gods dug him out; in the same way, he now digs him out by means of this spade, which is speech.
Then he collects it on a black antelope skin.

The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; he thus collects it on the sacrifice itself. It is with the hair-side up; the hairs are the metres; he thus collects it on the metres. He spreads it out silently; the black antelope skin is the sacrifice, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati, for Prajāpati is undefined. To the north of it is the significance [of its position]; it has the neck toward the east, for that is the way of the gods.

Then he collects it on a lotus leaf. The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; he thus pours that seed into the womb. For whatever seed is poured into the womb becomes capable of procreation. He spreads it out with a mantra; for the mantra is speech, and the lotus leaf is speech.

"You are the back of the waters, the womb of Agni," he says; for this is indeed the back of the waters and the womb of Agni. "Swelling on all sides around the ocean," he says; for it indeed swells on all sides around the ocean. "Growing great upon the lotus," he says; that is, "growing, become greater, O lotus! "Spread yourself out according to the measure and breadth of heaven," he says, and as he strokes it along, he means: "This Agni is indeed yonder sun; no one other than heaven is able to encompass its breadth. By becoming heaven itself, grant us this space"—this is what he thereby says.
After that, he spreads out a black antelope skin.

The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; this [earth] is the black antelope skin, for this earth is the sacrifice, since upon it the sacrifice is performed. The sky is the lotus leaf; the sky is indeed the waters, and the lotus leaf is the waters. Moreover, that [sky] is above this [earth].

Then he touches them; he thereby bestows consciousness upon these two [stones] with the words, "Ye are a refuge and ye are a shield. For they are indeed his refuge and his shield. "Both of you, unbroken and abundant"—for these two are indeed unbroken and both are abundant. "Dwell together, spacious"—that is to say, "dwell together, providing room. "Bear Agni Purīṣya"—that is to say, "bear Agni who is beneficial to cattle."

"Dwell together, ye finders of light; united by breast and by soul"—that is, "Dwell together with this one, ye finders of light, united by breast and by soul. "Bearing within you Agni, the luminous and eternal"—for yonder sun is indeed this Agni; he is luminous and eternal, and these two bear him between them. Therefore he says, "the luminous and eternal."
He touches them with two [verses].

The sacrificer has two feet, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just that much he thus establishes a mutual recognition between these two. Moreover, this form is indeed twofold: the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf.

Then he touches the lump of clay with the words, "Thou art of the soil," which means "thou art favorable to cattle"; "the all-supporter," for he indeed supports all this; "Atharvan was the first to churn thee forth, O Agni"—Atharvan is indeed the vital breath, and the vital breath churned him forth in the beginning; "that which was created as fire in the beginning, that thou art"—he says this so as to make him that very thing.

Then he encloses it with a spade on the south side and with his hand on the north side; [he does so] with the verse, "Thee, O Agni, Atharvan churned forth from the lotus. The lotus is indeed the waters, and Atharvan is the breath; for the breath indeed churned him forth from the waters in the beginning. "From the head of the whole worshipper"—this means "from the head of this entire universe."

"Thee, Dadhyañc, the Ṛṣi, the son of Atharvan, kindled"—Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa is indeed Speech; he kindled him from there. "The slayer of Vṛtra, the breaker of forts"—Vṛtra is indeed evil; thus it means "the slayer of evil, the breaker of forts."

"The Pāthya bull kindled thee, the greatest slayer of Dasyus"—the Pāthya bull is indeed the mind; he (the mind) kindled him from there. "The winner of wealth in every battle"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

With *gāyatrī* verses. The *gāyatrī* is breath; he thus bestows breath upon him. There are nine feet of those [verses]; there are indeed nine vital airs (*prāṇas*). With seventy [syllables], for there are three vital airs: out-breath (*prāṇa*), up-breath (*udāna*), and through-breath (*vyāna*); he thus places these very ones in his head. Furthermore, there are two downward-facing ones; he thus places these very ones in him.

Now these two subsequent verses are in the Triṣṭubh metre. The Triṣṭubh is indeed the self; by means of these two, he thus prepares his very self. "Sit down, O Hotṛ, in your own place, being wise"—the Hotṛ is indeed Agni, and his own place is the black antelope skin; "being wise" means "being knowing. "Settle the sacrifice in the womb of good action"—the black antelope skin is indeed the womb of good action. "God-pleasing, worship the gods with the oblation"—that is, "being a god yourself, as one who carries the gods, worship the gods with the oblation. "O Agni, bestow great vigor upon the sacrificer"—thus he invokes a blessing for the sacrificer.

"He is the Hotṛ, knowing his place on the Hotṛ’s seat"—Agni indeed is the Hotṛ, and the black antelope skin is the Hotṛ’s seat; "knowing" means "the wise one. "The brilliant, shining, very skillful one has sat down"—"brilliant" means "shining," and "very skillful" means "possessing great power. "He whose care is for unimpaired vows, the most excellent"—for he is indeed the most excellent one whose care is for unimpaired vows. "Agni, the bringer of thousands, the pure-tongued"—a thousand is everything; thus, "Agni, the bringer of everything, the pure-tongued. With two Triṣṭubh verses addressed to Agni [he does this]; their significance has already been explained.
Now, this last verse is a Bṛhatī; for this [Agni], when built up, becomes a Bṛhatī.
Just as the seed is cast into the womb, so is it born; and because he makes this [last verse] a Bṛhatī here, therefore this [Agni], when built up, becomes a Bṛhatī.

"Settle down, for you are great"—it is this very seed that he thus causes to settle once it has been poured; therefore, the seed settles when poured into the womb. "Shine forth, O best invoker of the gods"—that is to say, "blaze up, O best invoker of the gods. "Send forth your ruddy smoke, O Agni, worthy of sacrifice, O praised one, beautiful to behold"—for when he is kindled, he indeed sends forth his ruddy smoke; "beautiful to behold," for he is, as it were, visible.

These amount to six. Six seasons are a year; Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. And in that it corresponds to the year, it corresponds to the Bṛhatī, for the year is the Bṛhatī: there are twelve full moons, twelve Aṣṭakās, and twelve new moons—that makes thirty-six, and the Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables. He brings it from the south towards the north; for seed is poured from the south into the womb from the north, and this is now its womb. He brings it without interruption, for the non-interruption of the seed.
Then he pours water upon it;
for whatever of this [earth] is injured or torn apart, that is joined together by water. By means of water alone, he thus extends and joins together what of it is injured and torn apart.

"Release the divine waters, honey-sweet, for the health of offspring"—honey is indeed sap; thus he means "sapful, for the health of offspring. "From their standing place, let the plants rise up with goodly fruit"—for from the standing place of the waters, the plants do indeed rise up with goodly fruit.
Then he joins it together with air.
Whatever of this [body] is injured or mangled, that is indeed joined by air; by means of air alone he thus extends and joins together what was injured and mangled in her.

"May Vāyu Mātariśvan place [the embryo] within you"—for this wind that blows here is indeed Vāyu Mātariśvan; "the heart of her who lies extended, which has been opened"—for her heart is indeed opened as she lies extended; "who moves among the gods with their breath"—for he moves among all the gods with their breath; "to whom, O god, let there be the *vaṣaṭ* for thee!"—Prajāpati is indeed *ka*; it is to him that he thus offers this *vaṣaṭ*. There is no other oblation so great as this.

Then he joins her with the quarters. For whatever of hers is injured or mangled, that is joined by the quarters; by the quarters alone he thus heals and joins together what was injured and mangled in her. He joins this quarter and that quarter; therefore these two quarters are joined together. Then this one and that one; therefore these two also are joined together. "Thus," "thus," "thus," "thus"—that is from right to left, for that is the way of the gods. By this very means medicine is prepared; by this very means he heals her.
Then he takes up both the black antelope skin and the lotus leaf.

The lotus leaf is indeed the womb; thus he takes up that seed which has been poured with the womb. Therefore, the seed poured with the womb is taken up. "Well-born, together with light, he has sat down in the shelter, the protection, the heaven"—for he is indeed well-born, and he sits down in this shelter, this protection, and the heaven, together with the light.
Then he girds him.

He thus joins that seed in the womb; therefore the seed joined in the womb does not fall away. With a cord—for with a cord they yoke what is to be yoked—he uses one made of muñja grass, triple-stranded; the significance of this has been explained.

He wraps it around with the verse, "O Agni, put on this multiform garment, O radiant one. For the rope used in the sacrifice belongs to Varuṇa; having thus made it non-Vāruṇa, he causes it to be wrapped around just as one would cause a garment to be put on.

Then, taking it up, he rises. This Agni is indeed yonder sun; he thus causes yonder sun to rise. With the words, "Arise, O thou of good rites,"—for the *adhvara* is indeed the sacrifice—he means, "Arise, O thou worthy of fair sacrifice. With "Protect us with divine wisdom," he means, "With that wisdom of thine which is divine, protect us. With "And for seeing, with great light, O thou of fair splendor," he means, "For the sake of sight, with great light, O thou of fair splendor. With "O Agni, come hither with fair praises,"—for those who carry [the oblation] are the "fair praises"—he means, "O Agni, come hither with those who carry [the oblation]."
Then he holds him up from here toward the east.

Yonder sun, indeed, is this Agni; he thus places that sun here above, facing eastward. Therefore, yonder sun is placed here above, facing eastward. With the words, "Stand up for our protection, like the god Savitṛ," the meaning is just as the sacrificial formula (yajus) expresses. With "Standing upright, a winner of booty," he means that standing upright, he wins booty, which is food. With "When we call upon him with ointments and with singers," the "ointments" are his rays and the "singers" are the priests; he says this regarding them. He holds it over his arm, for he is beyond the reach of the arm from here. Then he lowers it; having lowered it, he holds it above the navel. The significance of this is explained above.
This is his hand; then he consecrates the animals.
For when the gods were about to collect these [animals], they first placed vigor within them; in the same way, this sacrificer, being about to collect them, first places vigor within them.
He consecrates the horse with the mantra: "Thou art born as a germ of the two worlds.

These two worlds, heaven and earth, are indeed the *rodasī*; he is born as their germ. "O Agni, thou art beautiful, distributed among the plants"—for he is indeed beautiful, distributed among all plants. "The bright infant has passed beyond the darkness and the nights"—for this bright infant indeed shines forth beyond the darkness and the nights. "He goes forth from his mothers, bellowing loudly"—the plants are indeed his mothers; from them he goes forth bellowing loudly. Thus he bestows vigor upon the horse.
Then [the verse] for the donkey:

"Be firm, O thou of strong-limbed body; be swift, O steed, O racer"—that is to say, "be firm and of strong-limbed body, and be swift and a racer, O steed. "Be broad, be easy to sit upon, thou who carriest Agni's soil"—that is to say, "be broad and well-seated, thou who carriest Agni's cattle. He thereby bestows vigor upon the donkey.

Then [he addresses] the goat: "Be a crest for human offspring, O Aṅgiras! For Agni is indeed Aṅgiras, and the goat belongs to Agni; he thus pacifies him for the sake of non-injury. "Do not burn heaven and earth, nor the atmosphere, nor the trees"—this means "do not harm all this"; he thereby bestows vigor upon the goat.
He consecrates it with three [verses].
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows vigor upon these [bricks].
Then he holds it up above these animals;

thus he gathers it together with these animals, yet he does not touch them. For animals are a thunderbolt and this [clay] is seed; [he does so] thinking, "Lest I injure this seed with the thunderbolt," and also, "This is Agni and these are the animals; lest this Agni injure these animals."

He holds [the fire] over the horse with the verse, "Let the prize-winning steed go forth, neighing loudly. "Let the prize-winning steed go forth, neighing loudly" means "let the prize-winning steed go forth, neighing repeatedly. "The braying donkey flies along"—in this sacrificial formula for the horse, he mentions the donkey; thereby he places sorrow upon the donkey. "Bearing Agni Purīṣya, may he not fall before his full span of life"—"bearing Agni, who is beneficial to cattle, may he not fall from this ritual action before its completion," so it means. Thus he prepares him (Agni) by means of the horse.
Now, regarding the donkey: "Bearing Agni, the bull, the bull.

For Agni is a bull and the donkey is a bull; thus that bull bears the bull. "The offspring of the waters, belonging to the ocean"—for he is indeed the offspring of the waters and belongs to the ocean; thus he collects him by means of the donkey.
Then he takes it away with the words, "O Agni, come for the feast!"—that is, "come for the enjoyment. Thus, by means of the Brahman, the Yajus formula, he takes it away from this Sūdra caste.

Now as for the goat: "Rita, Satya; Rita, Satya. This fire, indeed, is *ṛta*, and yonder sun is *satya*; or rather, yonder [sun] is *ṛta* and this [fire] is *satya*. But this fire is both of these; therefore he says, "Rita, Satya; Rita, Satya. He thus equips him with the goat.
He gathers it with three verses;

Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gathers him. He consecrates it with three verses from the front; that makes six, the significance of which has been explained.

Then they turn these animals back. Of them, the goat goes first, then the donkey, then the horse; then from here, the horse goes first, then the donkey, then the goat. The horse follows the Kṣatriya; the donkey follows the Vaiśya and the Śūdra; the goat follows the Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, for those who go from here.

The horse goes first; therefore, when the Kṣatriya goes first, the other three castes follow behind him. And because the goat goes first when they are coming from there, therefore, when the Brāhmaṇa goes first, the other three castes follow behind him. But because the donkey goes first neither when they are going from here nor from there, therefore a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya never follow behind a Vaiśya and a Śūdra; thus they go in this way to avoid confusion. Moreover, by means of the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya, he thus encompasses these two castes on both sides and makes them subject to himself.

Then he looks at the Anaddhāpuruṣa (the man of straw) with the words, "We bear Agni Purīṣya like Aṅgiras. This means, "We bear the fire that is favorable to cattle, like Agni himself. Thus he gathers him together with the Anaddhāpuruṣa.
Holding it above the goat, he goes forward.
The goat indeed belongs to Agni; thus he gathers it by means of its own self, its own deity. Moreover, the goat is the Brahman; thus he gathers it by means of the Brahman.

Then he brings him down with the words: "O plants, welcome this auspicious Agni as he approaches you. For the plants are afraid of him as he approaches, thinking, "May he not harm us. He thus puts him at ease among them, saying, "Welcome him; he approaches you as one who is auspicious; he will not harm you. "Driving away all misfortunes and diseases, sit down; drive away from us evil intent"—that is to say, "driving away all misfortunes and diseases, sit down; drive away from us every evil."
"O plants, receive him!

You who possess flowers and bear good fruit"—this is their perfect form, for they are indeed perfect when they possess flowers and bear good fruit; "receive him in his perfection," this is what he means. "This germ of yours, born of the seasons, has taken its seat in the ancient dwelling-place"—this germ of yours, belonging to the seasons, has taken its seat in the eternal dwelling-place.
He brings it down with two verses; the sacrificer has two feet, and the sacrificer is Agni:

as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he thus brings him down. He brings it down from the south toward the north; the significance of that has been explained. It is dug up and sprinkled where he brings it down; for they place the fire on ground that is both dug up and sprinkled. Sand is scattered there; the significance of that is as stated above.

It is enclosed on all sides. For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this [sacrifice] of ours here"; therefore, they enclosed it with this fortress. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now encloses it with this fortress. Moreover, this [enclosure] is indeed the womb, and this [altar] is the seed; for the seed is poured as it were secretly into the womb. Thus, this form of the womb is produced. Therefore, even with his own wife, he desires to move about as if secretly.
Then he unties it. Whatever impurity there was in him while he was thus bound, that he now places outside of him; and furthermore, he causes him to be born from this very womb.

"Flaming with broad radiance"—that is, "shining with broad radiance. "Drive away the haters, the demons, and diseases"—that is, "drive away all evils. "May I be in the protection of the great, well-protecting Agni, under the guidance of the one who dwells with us"—with these words he invokes a blessing.

Then, having gathered the goat's hair, he lets the animals loose toward the north-east. For this direction, the north-east, belongs to both gods and men; he thus places the animals in that direction, and therefore both gods and men subsist upon animals.
These waters are boiled with a decoction of *parṇa* leaves.

This is indeed for the sake of stability; and as to why it is with a *parṇa* decoction: the *parṇa* is Soma, and Soma is the moon; this is one form of Agni, and it is for the attainment of that very form of Agni.
He pours them out with the verse, "O Waters, you indeed are sources of bliss.

For whatever deity a Ṛg-verse is recited in accordance with, and whatever deity a Yajus-formula [expresses], that indeed is the deity, that is the Ṛk, and that is the deity of the Yajus. These waters are indeed this triplet of verses; and those waters which appeared as a single form, those very ones he now makes into this form.

Then, having produced foam, he adds it [to the clay]. That which was produced as the second form, namely foam—that very form he now makes. And that clay which he mixes there is indeed the clay; that which was produced as the third form—verily from these forms he produces him in the beginning. From these very forms he now generates him.

Then he mixes it with goat-hair. This is indeed for the sake of stability. And as to why it is with goat-hair: the gods gathered this [sacrificial food] from the animals, and in the same way this one now gathers it from the animals. As to why it is specifically with goat-hair—it is because the form of all animals is present in the goat; and as to why it is hair, it is because hair is form.

"Mitra, having united the earth and the ground with light"—Mitra is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the vital breath performed this rite at the beginning. "The well-born Jātavedas; I unite thee for health for the sake of offspring"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance (*bandhu*).

Now, these three things—sugar, stone, and iron filings—are ground; he mixes them [with the clay] for the sake of stability. And as to why he does so with these: this earth was created in such a measure at the beginning; thus, he makes it exactly as large as it was when it was created in the beginning.

"The Rudras, having mixed the earth, kindled the great light"—for yonder sun is this very Agni; thus indeed the Rudras, having mixed the earth, kindled the great light. "Their unceasing radiance, bright, shines among the gods"—for this very radiance of theirs is unceasing and bright, shining among the gods.
He mixes it with two [verses].
The sacrificer has two feet, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he thus mixes him.

Then he kneads it with the formula: "United with the Vasus, with the Rudras. For this clay is indeed united with both the Vasus and the Rudras—that which is with Mitra is with the Vasus, and that which is with the Rudras is with the Rudras. "The clay fit for the work by the wise," for they are indeed wise; "this clay, made soft by the two hands—may Sinīvālī fashion it," for Sinīvālī is speech; thus he means, "May she, having made it soft with her two hands, fashion it."

"Sinīvālī with beautiful braided hair, with a beautiful head-dress, with beautiful ornaments"—Sinīvālī is indeed a woman; this is the perfect form of a woman, namely that she has beautiful braided hair, a beautiful head-dress, and beautiful ornaments; he thus endows her with this very perfection. "May she, O Aditi, place the fire-pan into my hands for you"—Aditi is indeed this earth; it is to her that he says this.

"Let Aditi fashion the fire-pan with power, with her arms, and with wisdom"—for she indeed fashions it with power, with her arms, and with wisdom. "As a mother bears her son in her lap, so let her bear Agni in her womb"—that is to say, as a mother would bear her son in her lap, even so let her bear Agni in her womb.
He mixes it three times.

Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus mixes him. He mixes him with two verses; that makes five. Five-layered is the fire-altar; five are the seasons; the year is the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. With three verses he pours water upon it; that makes eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. Moreover, this earth was created in the beginning as consisting of eight syllables; thus, as great as this earth was created in the beginning, so great he now makes her.

Then he takes a lump of clay, as much as is sufficient for the foundation, with the formula: "Thou art the head of Makha. Makha, indeed, is the sacrifice; this [lump] is its head. The Āhavanīya fire is the head of the sacrifice, and it is for the Āhavanīya that he is about to build this [altar]; therefore he says, "Thou art the head of Makha."
And as to why he says, "Thou art the head of Makha":
this [Agni] is being born when he is built up; for one who is born is born from the head and from the mouth; [he does so] thinking, "May he be born from the head and from the mouth."
He proclaims it.

"May the Vasus fashion thee with the Gāyatrī metre, after the manner of Aṅgiras!"—for this world is indeed that treasure, and it was this the Vasus fashioned with the Gāyatrī metre; in like manner does he now fashion it with the Gāyatrī metre. "After the manner of Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed the breath—"Thou art firm"—that is, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Thou art the earth"—for this treasure is indeed the earth—"Sustain for me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic vigor, and kinsmen for the sacrificer!"—the Vasus, having fashioned this world, invoked this blessing upon it; in like manner does the sacrificer, having fashioned this world, invoke this blessing upon it. Having made it a span in measure, he then raises its rim on all sides.
Then he places the eastern peg.

"May the Rudras fashion thee with the Triṣṭubh metre, like Aṅgiras"—for this is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa), and it was that which the Rudras fashioned with the Triṣṭubh metre; in the same way, he now fashions it with the Triṣṭubh metre. "Like Aṅgiras"—for Aṅgiras is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). "Thou art firm"—that is, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Thou art the intermediate space"—for this is indeed the intermediate space, the excavation. "With thy stream bestow upon me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic strength, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—for the Rudras, having fashioned the intermediate space, invoked this blessing therein; in the same way, the sacrificer, having fashioned the intermediate space, invokes this blessing therein. Having smeared it and smoothed it, he proceeds.
Then he places the northern elevation.

"May the Ādityas fashion thee with the Jagatī metre, like Aṅgiras!"—for this (brick) is indeed the sky; the Ādityas fashioned it with the Jagatī metre, and so does he now fashion it with the Jagatī metre. "Like Aṅgiras"—for Aṅgiras is indeed the breath—"Thou art firm"—that is, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Thou art the sky"—for this (brick) is indeed the sky. "With a stream bestow upon me offspring, abundance of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic strength, and kinsmen for the sacrificer"—for the Ādityas, having made the sky, invoked this blessing upon it; and in the same way, the sacrificer, having made the sky, invokes this blessing upon it.
Then he performs with this fourth sacrificial formula.

"May all the gods, the Vaiśvānaras, fashion thee with the Anuṣṭubh metre, after the manner of Aṅgiras!"—this sacrificial formula refers to the quarters. For it was the All-gods, the Vaiśvānaras, who by means of this fourth sacrificial formula placed the quarters within these worlds, within the fire-pan (ukhā). In like manner, the sacrificer now places the quarters within these worlds, within the fire-pan, by means of this fourth sacrificial formula. "After the manner of Aṅgiras"—Aṅgiras is indeed the breath; "thou art firm"—that is, "thou art steady," and also "thou art established. "Thou art the quarters"—for this sacrificial formula is indeed the quarters. "Bestow upon me, for the sacrificer, offspring, increase of wealth, lordship over cattle, heroic strength, and kinsmen"—the All-gods, the Vaiśvānaras, having fashioned the quarters, invoked this blessing upon them. In like manner, the sacrificer, having fashioned the quarters, invokes this blessing upon them.
Therefore, he makes these worlds both from within and from without;
thus, by this [brick], he makes the quarters of these worlds both from within and from without, for the quarters are indeed unlimited.
He makes it exactly a span high and a span wide;
for Viṣṇu, as an embryo, is a span long, and this is his womb; thus he makes the womb commensurate with the embryo.
If it should be larger than a span, one should make it smaller with this *yajus*;
if it should be smaller, one should make it larger with this.

If there should be only one animal, he should make it one span wide; but if there should be five animals, he should make it five spans wide, or else the measure of an arrow; for the arrow is vigor, and thus it becomes commensurate with vigor. However, in former times, the arrow was indeed five spans long.
Then he lays down the crosswise girdle (rāsnā).

This indeed is the quarters; for the gods, having made these worlds into the fire-pan (ukhā), made them firm with the quarters and enclosed them with the quarters. In the same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into the fire-pan, makes them firm with the quarters and encloses them with the quarters.
He lays it down on the third part from the top;
for there the ends of these worlds meet, and thus he unites them.
"Thou art the girdle of Aditi," he says;
for the rope in the sacrifice belongs to Varuṇa; having thus made it a girdle belonging not to Varuṇa, he spreads it around.
Then he makes four [bricks] facing upwards;

he does so silently, for these are indeed the quarters. For the gods, having made these worlds into a fire-pan (ukhā), made them firm on all sides by means of the quarters; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into a fire-pan, makes them firm on all sides by means of the quarters.
These same bricks belong to this (altar).

For these indeed supported it at that time, and in the same way they support it now. That part which is above is made firm by this one (the *tiraścī*) running across; and that part which is below is made firm by these (other bricks).
They raise up the breasts at the front of these [cups].

For the gods, having made these worlds into a *ukhā* (fire-pan), milked all desires by means of these breasts; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having made these worlds into a *ukhā*, milks all desires by means of these breasts.

This very [fire-pan] is indeed a cow. These worlds are the fire-pan; these worlds are the cow. That which is this transverse girdle is her udder; it is placed at one-third [of its height], for the udder of a cow is at one-third [from the bottom].
He raises her teats;
he raises those teats from the udder, and she becomes four-teated, for a cow is indeed four-teated.

Some indeed make it two-teated, or even eight-teated; one should not do so. For those animals that have fewer teats than a cow, and those that have more teats, are less fit for subsistence; thus they make this [cow] less fit for subsistence, and moreover, they do not actually make it a cow at all, but rather a bitch, a ewe, or a mare. Therefore, one should not do so.
Then he approaches its opening with the words, "May Aditi grasp thy opening.

Aditi is indeed speech; for having fashioned her thus, the gods caused her to stand firm by means of speech, and Aditi is speech. In the same way, this sacrificer, having fashioned her thus, causes her to stand firm by means of speech.

Having taken it up, he sets it down with the words, "Having made the great fire-pan," which means "having made the large fire-pan"; "the womb of clay for Agni," for this womb of Agni is indeed made of clay; "Aditi gave it to her sons so that they might cook," for Aditi, having made it, gave it to the gods, her sons, for cooking; and in the same way, this sacrificer, having made it, now gives it to the gods for cooking.
Some, however, perform three [of these].

"These three worlds are these very worlds; the fire-pan (ukhā) is these worlds," so they say. "Furthermore, for the sake of mutual expiation: 'If the other one should break, we shall carry [the fire] in the other; if the other, then in the other,'" they argue. One should not do it in that way. For this first treasure is this world; that which is the former enclosure is the intermediate space (antarikṣa); that which is the upper one is the sky (dyu). And as for this fourth sacrificial formula, that is indeed the quarters (diśas). Now, all this that exists is only as much as these worlds and the quarters. If he were to bring [the fire] here from elsewhere, he would cause an excess. Whatever is done in excess in the sacrifice is left over for the sacrificer's hateful enemy. As for the expiation for a broken [pan], that is explained in the subsequent section.
Of this very [altar], he makes the Aṣāḍhā brick first.

This earth, indeed, is the Aṣāḍhā; for of these worlds, this one was created first. He makes it from this very clay, for of these worlds, this one is the queen (mahiṣī). She is the queen because she is the first to be found. She is the queen.
It becomes a foot in measure;
for the foot is indeed a foundation, and this earth is the foundation. It is drawn with three lines, for this earth is threefold.

Then he makes the fire-pan (*ukhā*); thereby he creates these worlds. Then he makes the Viśvajyotis bricks; these are the deities Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, for these deities indeed are the "all-light" (*viśvaṃ jyotiḥ*). He makes them from that very same clay; thus the sacrificer fashions these deities out of these worlds. He makes them; they have three lines drawn on them, for these deities are threefold. Thus with regard to the deities.

Now with reference to the self. The self itself is the fire-pan (ukhā), and speech is the Aṣāḍhā brick; he places that one in front, for speech is placed in front of the self. He makes it from this very same clay, for this speech is indeed part of the self. He makes it into a buffalo-cow, for speech is a buffalo-cow. It is engraved, for speech is divided threefold: Ṛc-verses, Yajus-formulas, and Sāman-chants; moreover, these are the three forms of speech: the low-voiced, the intermediate, and the loud.
Then he makes the fire-pan (ukhā).

He then makes himself; he then makes the Viśvajyotis bricks. Offspring indeed is the Viśvajyotis, for offspring is the light of all; thus he effects procreation. He makes them from this very same clay; thereby the sacrificer fashions offspring from his own self. The sacrificer makes them; thereby the sacrificer creates offspring from his own self. He makes them without any interval; thereby he creates offspring from his own self without any interval. He makes them one above the other; thereby he creates offspring from his own self one after another. They are marked with three lines, for procreation is threefold: father, mother, and son; moreover, the embryo, the amnion, and the chorion.

He prepares these with the sacrificial formula (yajus), while the others are prepared without the formula; these are expressed, while the others are unexpressed; these are limited, while the others are unlimited.

This Agni is Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is both the defined and the undefined, the limited and the unlimited. Thus, when he performs what is done with a sacrificial formula (*yajuṣkṛta*), he thereby perfects that form of his which is defined and limited; and when he performs what is not done with a sacrificial formula (*ayajuṣkṛta*), he thereby perfects that form of his which is undefined and unlimited. He who, knowing this, performs it in this manner, truly perfects this entire and complete Prajāpati. Now, he leaves over a lump for the *upaśaya* brick for the sake of expiations.

Then he fumigates it. This is both for its stability and to ensure the continuity of the ritual action. Furthermore, as to why he fumigates it: the fire-pan is the head of the sacrifice, and the smoke is the breath; thus he places breath into the head.
He fumigates with horse-hair.

The horse belongs to Prajāpati, and Agni is Prajāpati; one's own self does not injure its own self, so it is for the sake of non-injury. He fumigates with hair, for that which has been chewed is exhausted; thus he does not injure the horse, nor the other animals.

"May the Vasus fumigate thee with the Gāyatrī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras; may the Rudras fumigate thee with the Triṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras; may the Ādityas fumigate thee with the Jagatī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras; may all the gods belonging to Viśvānara fumigate thee with the Anuṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras; may Indra fumigate thee, may Varuṇa fumigate thee, may Viṣṇu fumigate thee. With these very deities he thus fumigates it.

There are seven horse-powers; there are seven sacrificial formulas; these deities are sevenfold; there are seven vital breaths in the head. And even though [the formulas] are recited many times as "seven by seven," it is indeed seven; thus he places the seven vital breaths in the head itself.
Then he digs him into this earth.

For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this one here"; therefore, they made this earth his very self for protection, thinking, "The self will protect the self."
He digs it with an Aditi verse;
for Aditi is this earth, and one does not injure one's own self by oneself. If he were to dig with another deity, he would indeed injure him.

"May Aditi, the goddess, accompanied by the Viśvedevas, dig thee out in the lap of the earth like Aṅgiras, O pit!"—for this pit is indeed for the gods. Here the reed-spoon settles down; this well has four corners, for there are four quarters, and thus he digs it from all the quarters. Then, having placed the supporting layer, he lays down the *aṣāḍhā* brick silently, for he makes that one first.
Then he places the fire-pan (ukhā) [on the hearth], saying:

"May the divine wives of the gods, who are accompanied by all the gods, place thee, O pan, in the lap of the earth, in the manner of Aṅgiras. For of old, the divine wives of the gods, who are accompanied by all the gods, placed it in the lap of the earth in the manner of Aṅgiras; with those very wives he thus places it. And they are indeed the plants; for the wives of the gods are the plants, since everything here is supported by the plants; with the plants he thus places it. Then he places the Viśvajyotis bricks silently. Then, having placed the cooking-vessel, he kindles it.

"May the goddesses Dhiṣaṇās, accompanied by all the gods, kindle thee on the seat of the earth like Aṅgiras," he says; for in the beginning, those goddesses Dhiṣaṇās, accompanied by all the gods, kindled her on the seat of the earth like Aṅgiras; it is with them that he now kindles her. She is indeed Speech; for Dhiṣaṇā is Speech, and by Speech all this is kindled; it is by means of Speech that he thus kindles her. Then, while looking at these three sacrificial formulas, he mutters them.

"O divine Varūtris, accompanied by all the gods, do you bake this fire-pan on the seat of the earth, as the Aṅgirases did!
