For of old, the divine Varūtris, accompanied by all the gods, baked it on the seat of the earth as the Aṅgirases did; with them he now bakes it. And these are indeed the days and nights; for the Varūtris are the days and nights, since by means of the days and nights all this is encompassed; with the days and nights he thus bakes it.

"May the divine Gnas, accompanied by all the gods, cook thee in the lap of the earth like Angiras," he says. For of old, the divine Gnas, accompanied by all the gods, cooked her in the lap of the earth like Angiras; with them he now cooks her. These are indeed the metres; for the Gnas are the metres, since by means of the metres they go to the heavenly world. It is by means of the metres that he thus cooks her.

"May the divine Mothers, with uncut wings, accompanied by all the gods, bake thee on the seat of the earth like Aṅgiras, O pot! For in the beginning, those divine Mothers, with uncut wings and accompanied by all the gods, baked her on the seat of the earth like Aṅgiras; it is with them that he now bakes her. And they are indeed the stars; for the stars are the Mothers, since those people who are doers of merit go to the heavenly world, and these are their lights. It is with the stars that he thus bakes her.

He digs with one [verse], he places [the earth] with one, he kindles [the fire] with one; he cooks with one, he bakes with two; therefore, twice a year does food ripen. These amount to six; the year has six seasons, and Agni is the year: as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become.
Then, with the words, "Now for Mitra, the supporter of the people," he proceeds with the Maitra formula as far as it extends.
For Mitra harms no one, nor does anyone harm Mitra; likewise, he does not harm her, nor does she harm him. He should sow it at daybreak and harvest it at daybreak, for the day belongs to Agni.
He digs it up with a Yajus formula addressed to Savitṛ.
Savitṛ is indeed the impeller; thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he digs it up. "May the god Savitṛ dig thee up—well-handed, well-fingered, well-armed, and with power! For all this is indeed Savitṛ.
Then he turns it over with the words:
"Unwavering on the earth, fill the regions and the quarters. This means: "Unwavering, do thou fill the regions and the quarters on the earth with thy essence."
Then he raises it up with the formula:
"Rising, become great," for these worlds, having risen, are indeed great; "Stand up, thou art firm," that is to say, "Stand up, thou art stable and well-established."
Having taken hold of it, he sets it down with the formula:

"O Mitra, I entrust this fire-pan to you, so that it may not break; let it not shatter. Vāyu, who blows here, is indeed Mitra; it is to him that he thus entrusts it for protection. These worlds are protected by Mitra; therefore, nothing whatsoever among these worlds is destroyed.

Then he mixes it; this is for the sake of stability and also to ensure the continuity of the ritual action. Furthermore, as to why he mixes it: the fire-pan (ukhā) is the head of the sacrifice, and the milk is the vital breath (prāṇa); thus he places the vital breath into the head. Moreover, the fire-pan is indeed a woman; he thus places the milk into a woman, and therefore milk is found in a woman.
He moistens it with the milk of a she-goat.

From the grief of Prajāpati the she-goat was born, and Prajāpati is Agni; one does not injure oneself by oneself, so it is for the sake of non-injury. And as for why it is with a she-goat: the she-goat eats all plants; thus he moistens it with the essence of all those plants.
May the Vasus moisten you.

"By the Gāyatrī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the Rudras anoint thee; by the Triṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the Ādityas anoint thee; by the Jagatī metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras, may the All-gods, belonging to all men, anoint thee; by the Anuṣṭubh metre, in the manner of Aṅgiras. It is with these very deities that he thus anoints it. Indeed, with whichever deities one performs the making, with those same ones one fumigates and with those same ones one anoints; for whoever performs a ritual act knows its proper procedure. Therefore, with whichever deities one performs the making, with those same ones one fumigates and with those same ones one anoints.
There are many oblations.

Whether it be in the building of the fire-altar (agnicityā) or not in the building of the fire-altar, there are indeed rites that surpass others—those which surpass other rites are called "surpassing" (atīni). Among them, the building of the fire-altar, the Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, and the Aśvamedha are such; because they surpass those other rites, therefore they are called "surpassing."

There is an offering on eleven potsherds to Agni and Viṣṇu; that is the initiatory rite of the sacrifice. There is an offering on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara and a pap to Āditya; these belong to Agni.

If he were to offer only the oblation to Agni and Viṣṇu, and not the other two oblations, the initiation would belong only to the Soma-sacrifice (adhvara) and not to the fire-altar; and if he were to offer only the other two oblations, and not the one to Agni and Viṣṇu, the initiation would belong only to the fire-altar and not to the Soma-sacrifice.
He offers both:
for this rite belongs to both the Adhvara and the Agni; it is both an Adhvara rite and an Agni rite. The Adhvara comes first, and then the Agni; for the Agni rite is subsidiary to this rite.

As for this offering to Agni and Viṣṇu, its Brāhmaṇa explanation is the same as that for the preliminary rite. There is a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara; for all fires are Vaiśvānara, and it serves to obtain all the fires. It is on twelve potsherds because there are twelve months in a year, and Vaiśvānara is the year.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this Vaiśvānara oblation: he is about to generate this Agni Vaiśvānara; he pours him out here beforehand, at the initiation offering, as seed. For whatever kind of seed is poured into the womb, such a one is born. Since he pours this Vaiśvānara out here as seed, therefore he is born there as Vaiśvānara.
Furthermore, as to why he offers these two oblations:

Vaiśvānara is indeed the nobility (kṣatra), and this rice-pap for the Ādityas is the common people (viś). He thereby establishes both the nobility and the common people; he offers the Vaiśvānara first, and having thus established the nobility, he provides for the common people.
This one [oblation] belongs to a single deity;

it establishes that kṣatra in a single place and establishes prosperity in a single place. The other is a *caru* (porridge) for many deities; this *caru* is indeed a multiplicity of rice grains, and the Ādityas are a multiplicity among the gods; thus he bestows multiplicity upon the clan (*viś*). This is with respect to the deities.
Now with reference to the self:
the head is indeed Vaiśvānara, and this Āditya-caru is the self; thus he makes both the head and the self. He offers the Vaiśvānara first; having thereby made the head, he then makes the self.
This one becomes single;

for the head is indeed one, while the other, the sacrificial pap (caru), belongs to many deities. This pap is the abundance of rice grains, and this self is the abundance of the limbs; thus, he bestows abundance upon the limbs within the self.
This [oblation] consists of ghee;

for the Ādityas have ghee as their vessel. Thus he gratifies them with their own portion, with their own essence. These oblations are offered in a whisper; for seed is here in the sacrifice, and seed is indeed poured out in a whisper.
Then he offers the Audgrabhaṇa oblations.

By means of the Audgrabhaṇas, the gods indeed lifted themselves up from this world to the heavenly world; because they lifted themselves up (udagṛhṇata), they are called Audgrabhaṇas. In the same way, the sacrificer now, by means of the Audgrabhaṇas, lifts himself up from this world to the heavenly world.

These indeed become more numerous, whether in the building of the fire-altar (agnicityā) or in that which is not the building of the fire-altar; their significance has been explained. They are of both kinds; their significance has been explained. First come those of the sacrifice (adhvara), then those of the fire-altar; their significance has likewise been explained.

He offers five oblations behind the altar; for the sacrifice is fivefold, and as great as the sacrifice is, as great as its measure is—with just that much he thus pours this [seed] into it once it has become seed. There are seven [oblations] for Agni, for Agni consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons in the year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus pours this [seed] into it once it has become seed. These two sets together amount to twelve; there are twelve months in the year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—that much does it become.
He offers:
"To Ākūti, to Agni Prayuj, Svāhā! For from Ākūti this rite first came into being; thus he now yokes that very thing for this rite.
"To the mind, to Meghā, to Agni Prayuja, svāhā!"—for it was from the mind that this rite first came into being; thus he now applies that very [mind] to this rite.
"Mind, having known Agni, being employed—Svāhā!
For from mind, indeed, this rite first came into being; he now employs that very same thing for this rite.
"Of speech, the support; to Agni, the impeller, Svāhā!"—for at the beginning, this ritual action of speech came into being; he now yokes that very speech for this ritual action.
"To Prajāpati Manu, svāhā!
Prajāpati indeed is Manu, for he has thought over all this; Prajāpati performed this rite in the beginning, and thus he now employs him for this very rite.
"To Agni Vaiśvānara, svāhā!"—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; for the year performed this rite first, and he now employs it for this very rite.

Then he offers the Sāvitrī oblation. Savitṛ indeed performed this rite first; thus he now employs him for this very rite: "May every mortal choose the friendship of the god, the leader; everyone seeks wealth, let him choose glory that he may prosper—Svāhā! He who chooses the friendship of the god Savitṛ chooses both glory and prosperity; he who performs this rite chooses his friendship.
Now, some indeed [do this] with those [verses].

They offer these Audgrabhaṇa oblations into the fire-pan (ukhā) itself; for these are offered for the sake of desires, and the fire-pan is the very self of the sacrificer. [Thinking,] "We shall establish all the desires of the sacrificer within his own self," they do so. But one should not do it in that way. For when this sacrifice has been completed, whatever essence there was in those oblations, that now blazes forth as this flame. Therefore, when the sacrifice is completed and the Audgrabhaṇa oblations have been offered, he heats the fire-pan over the fire; thus this sacrifice mounts upon it, and it sustains that sacrifice. Therefore, only when the sacrifice is completed and the Audgrabhaṇa oblations have been offered should he heat the fire-pan.

It is strewn with a mat of *muñja* grass. [The purpose] is indeed that it may be set ablaze; and furthermore, as to why it is with a mat of *muñja* grass: this *muñja* is the womb of Agni. Indeed, the womb does not harm the embryo—for the sake of non-injury—and one who is being born is born from a womb; [he does this] so that he may be born from a womb as one being born.
There is an inner layer of hemp; let him light it up. Now, as for the layer of hemp:

from whatever womb Prajāpati was emitted, its caul was *umā* and its afterbirth was hemp. Therefore, these [fibers] are foul-smelling, for they are indeed the afterbirth. The afterbirth does not harm the embryo; it is for the sake of non-injury. One is born with an afterbirth; "May he be born with an afterbirth," [he thinks]. Thus he is born with an afterbirth.
Standing, he joins it; for these worlds are the fire-pan, and these worlds are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is indeed most powerful.
Standing facing north-east;
for standing facing north-east, Prajāpati created the creatures.
Moreover, as for his standing facing north-east:
this direction, which is both north and east, belongs to both gods and men.
Moreover, as to why he stands facing northeast:

in that direction lies the door to the heavenly world; therefore, standing facing northeast, he offers the oblations. Standing facing northeast, he leads the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās); thus, by means of the very door to the heavenly world, he causes the wealth to enter.

"Do not be afraid, do not be harmed"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu). "O Mother, be bold and act as a hero!"—the fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed a woman, and "O Mother" is a form of address for a woman. "Act as a hero like yourself"—for Agni and [the pan] are about to perform this work together; thus they both become performers of this task.

"Strengthen yourself, O Goddess Earth, for well-being!"—as the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its significance. "Thou art the Asura-magic (*māyā*) made by *svadhā*"; *asu* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and this is its magic made by *svadhā*. "May this oblation be pleasing to the gods"—he thereby speaks of those very oblations he is about to offer into this fire. And furthermore, "Unharmed, do thou rise up in this sacrifice"—just as one who is unharmed and uninjured might rise up in this sacrifice, so does he say this.
He joins it with two [verses].

The sacrificer has two feet; the sacrificer is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus consecrates her. With a Gāyatrī and a Triṣṭubh verse: the Gāyatrī is breath, the Triṣṭubh is the self (ātman). So great indeed is an animal as its breath and its self are. Thus, with as much as an animal is, with just that much he consecrates her. Moreover, the Gāyatrī is Agni, and the Triṣṭubh is Indra; and Agni belongs to Indra and Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus consecrates her. Indra and Agni are all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus consecrates her. There are seven steps for those two verses; the fire-altar consists of seven layers, and there are seven seasons in the year. The year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—so great does that become.
When Agni heats it, then the flame mounts upon it; for the fire-pan is indeed a woman and Agni is a man. Therefore, when the man heats the woman, he then places seed within her.

Now, some say that if the flame rises slowly, they throw down coals, thinking, "This fire is both ways. One should not do so; for an animal is born with bones, yet they do not thrust it down as if it already had bones at the very beginning. They place it as if it were seed; and this flame is indeed boneless seed. Therefore, one should let the flame rise alone.
When he ascends that flame, he then places a fuel-stick upon this fire; for this fire has now entered into her as seed, and he thus places this generation within that seed.

That [wood] should be of the *karmuka* tree. Both the gods and the Asuras were descendants of Prajāpati and they contended with one another. The gods, having made Agni their vanguard, marched against the Asuras; the Asuras cut off the tip of his raised flame, and it settled upon this earth. It became the *kṛmuka* tree; therefore it is sweet in taste, for it is that very essence; therefore it is red, for it is flame. This *kṛmuka* is indeed Agni; he thus bestows upon him (the sacrificer) the origin of Agni.
It is a span in measure;
for Viṣṇu, as an embryo, is indeed a span in measure. Thus, he bestows upon it a growth commensurate with its own self.

It is placed in ghee. For whatever womb Agni was emitted from, ghee was its amnion; therefore it blazes up toward it, for this is its very self. Therefore it has no ash, for the self enters the self. Indeed, the amnion does not harm the embryo; [it is done] for the sake of non-injury. "May he be born from the amnion, may he be born being born from the amnion"—thus [he thinks].
He places that [kindling-stick] on the fire with the verse:

"O thou whose food is wood, whose drink is ghee!"—this means "O thou whose food is trees, whose nourishment is ghee. "The ancient, desirable Hotṛ"—this means "the eternal, desirable Hotṛ. "The wonderful son of strength"—strength indeed is *sahas*, so this means "the wonderful son of strength. Standing, he places it with the utterance of *svāhā*; the significance of this has been explained above.
Verily, the fire-pan is the self; the muñja grass and the hemp are the womb, the membrane is the caul, the clarified butter is the embryo, and the fuel is the fetus.

The outer layer is of *ukhā* grass; inside are *muñja* reeds, for the self is outside and the womb is inside. The outer layer is of *muñja* grass; inside are *śaṇa* fibers, for the womb is outside and the afterbirth (*jarāyu*) is inside. The outer layer is of *śaṇa* fibers; inside is clarified butter, for the afterbirth is outside and the membrane (*ulba*) is inside. The outer layer is of clarified butter; inside is the fuel-stick (*samidh*), for the membrane is outside and the embryo is inside. From these, indeed, one being born is born; it is from these very things that he thus causes him to be born.
Then he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood.

That which Prajāpati offered as the first oblation, having offered it, where he wiped his hands, from that the *vaikaṅkata* tree came into being. This *vaikaṅkata* is that very first oblation; he offers it into him now, and thereby he gratifies him with it. "From the further region, come hither toward the nearer ones, to where I am, come to me"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
Then he places a branch of the Udumbara tree.

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. All the trees of the forest went over to the Asuras, but the Udumbara alone did not desert the gods. Having conquered the Asuras, those gods seized the trees of the Asuras.

They said, "Come now! Whatever vital energy and sap there is in these trees, let us place it in the Udumbara tree; if they should depart, they will depart exhausted, like a milked-out cow or an ox that has finished its load. Thus, whatever vital energy and sap was in those trees, they placed it in the Udumbara. Therefore, by means of that vital energy, it ripens in rivalry with all other trees; for this reason, it is always moist and always milky. The Udumbara is indeed all food and all trees; he thus gratifies him with all food and kindles him with all trees.

"From the furthest distance"—this means "from that which is the furthest distance. "O you with ruddy horses, come here"—for the ruddy horse is indeed the horse of Agni. "Fertile, much-beloved"—this means "beneficial to cattle and dear to many. "O Agni, do thou overcome the adversaries"—this means "O Agni, do thou overcome all evils."

Then he places on [the fire] what has been cut by an axe. This one is born when he is built up; he is born for all kinds of food. Now, that which is cut by an axe is one kind of food; with that he gratifies him. With the verse, "O Agni, whatever logs we place upon thee, let all that be ghee for thee; enjoy that, O youngest one,"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance. Thus, whatever has been cut by an axe, he makes palatable for him; having made it food, he presents it to him.

Then he places the lower layer (adhaḥśaya). As he is being built up, he is born; he is born for all kinds of food. Now, this lower layer is one kind of food; with it he gratifies him. "What the upajihvikā eats, what the ant (vamra) creeps over"—for either the upajihvikā eats that, or the ant creeps over it—"may all that be ghee for thee; enjoy that, O youngest one! As the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. Whatever there is of the lower layer, that he makes palatable for him; having made it food for him, he sets it down.
Now these subsequent sticks are made of *palāśa* wood.

The *palāśa* is indeed the Brahman; he thus kindles him with the Brahman. And as to why they are of *palāśa* wood: the *palāśa* is indeed Soma, and the oblation of Soma is the highest oblation; he thus offers that to him and thereby gratifies him.
"Bringing [offerings] day by day without fail"—this means bringing [them] day by day without becoming intoxicated.

"As fodder for the horse that stands [there]"—this means as fodder for the horse that stands [in its stall]. "Rejoicing with wealth, prosperity, and nourishment"—this means rejoicing with wealth (*rāya*), prosperity (*poṣa*), and nourishment (*iṣ*). "O Agni, may we, your neighbors, not come to harm"—he says this so that his neighbor may not suffer harm, just as he himself does not suffer harm.

"At the navel of the earth, while the fire is being kindled"—for this is indeed the navel of the earth where this [fire] is here being kindled; "for the increase of great wealth," that is, "we invoke for both wealth and great prosperity"; "gladdening with juice," for he is indeed intoxicated with juice; "of great praise," for he is indeed one of great praise; "the worshipful," that is, "the worthy of sacrifice"; "the conqueror, Agni, who overcomes in battles," for Agni is indeed a conqueror and one who overcomes in battles.
"Those armies that are rushing forward,
those burglars with their tusks among the people, whoever acts as an enemy toward us, and whatever person hates us, who reviles us and seeks to harm us— reduce all of them to ashes!"

The gods, having made him food for whomever hated them and whomsoever they themselves hated, placed it within him; thus they gratified him, and food became his. He burned away the evil of the gods. In the same way, the sacrificer, having made him food for whomever hates him and whomsoever he himself hates, places it within him; thus he gratifies him, and food becomes his. He burns away the evil of the sacrificer.
He offers these eleven [oblations].
This applies for one who is not a Kṣatriya or who has no domestic priest (purohita); for that which is elevenfold is incomplete, and he who is not a Kṣatriya or has no purohita is incomplete.
There are twelve [cups] for either a Kṣatriya or a Purohita;
indeed, all that which is twelve is the whole, and all that which is the Kṣatriya or the Purohita is the whole.

He places [the fire] for the domestic priest with the formula: "Sharpened is my sacred word, sharpened is my vigor and strength; sharpened is the victorious dominion of him whose domestic priest I am. Thereby he sharpens both his sacred word and his dominion.

Now, for the Kṣatriya: "I have raised up their arms, I have raised up their splendor and their strength; with my *brahman* I destroy the enemies, I exalt my own people"—thus he speaks so as to destroy the enemies and exalt his own people. However, one should rather place both of these [formulas] together. For this Agni is both the *brahman* and the *kṣatra*; he thus kindles this very Agni with both of these, with the *brahman* and with the *kṣatra*.
These amount to thirteen;
there are thirteen months in a year, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food he thus gratifies him.
They are the size of a span.

Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed a span in measure; this food is commensurate with his own self. With food that is commensurate with one's own self, he thus gratifies him. For that food which is commensurate with one's own self protects and does not injure; that which is more than that injures, and that which is less than that does not protect. He places the fuel-sticks while standing; the significance of this will be explained later. With the utterance of "Svāhā," this seed has been poured out; this Agni is that [seed]. If he were to place pieces of wood into it without the utterance of "Svāhā," he would injure him. Those [sticks] are not oblations because they are merely fuel-sticks; but in that he uses the utterance "Svāhā," they become food, for "Svāhā" is indeed food. Thus, he does not injure him.
Then, having stepped the Viṣṇu-strides.

Having worshipped with the Vātsapra hymn, when the sun has set, he first throws out the ashes. For by this food and these fuel-sticks he gratifies him (Agni). Of that food which has been eaten, this impurity settles down as ashes; he thus separates him from it. When his impurity has been struck away, he releases his speech; having released his speech, he places a fuel-stick on the fire. By this food he gratifies him for the night. With the words, "Bringing [the fuel] day after day without failing," its significance has already been explained. He thereby invokes safety and well-being for the night. And whatever else he adds during the night, he adds it to him as an act of oblation.
Then, when the sun had risen in the morning.

First he throws out the ashes; for by this food and by this fuel-stick he gratifies him (Agni). And whatever evil has settled in that food which he consumed during the night, he now drives it away from him by means of those ashes. Into him, from whom that evil has been driven out, he releases speech. Having released speech, he puts on a fuel-stick; thus he gratifies him with food day by day. "Bringing [fuel] daily without fail"—the significance of this has been explained. He thereby invokes for himself this safety and well-being for the day. And whatever else he puts on during that day, he puts it on as an act of offering for him.
As day and night revolve, they encompass the year; and the year indeed comprises all this. Therefore, he invokes for himself this security and well-being by means of the day.

Now, when they hand over the fast-food (vrata) to him, he then dips a fuel-stick (samidh) into the fast-food and places it on the fire. Regarding this, some say: "He should not dip [the stick] into the fast-food; rather, he should offer it as a libation (āhuti). But [others say]: "That which an initiated person (dīkṣita) might offer as a libation is indeed improper."
He should indeed anoint it.

For that [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self. If he were not to anoint it, he would not satisfy that divine self; but since he does anoint it, he thereby satisfies that divine self. As for the fact that it is an oblation by means of a fuel-stick, yet it is anointed during the vow—thereby it is food, for the vow is indeed food.
Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he then observes the vow.

For that [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; and indeed, the gods come first, and then human beings. Therefore, having placed a fuel-stick on the fire, he then observes the vow.

"O Lord of food, give us food! means "O Lord of nourishment, give us nourishment. "Free from disease, full of vigor," means "free from hunger, full of vigor. "Further the giver,"—the giver is indeed the sacrificer; thus, "further the sacrificer. "Bestow strength upon our two-footed and four-footed creatures"—this is the invocation of a blessing. As for the expiation he mentions for a broken [ladle], that is explained in the subsequent section.

If this fire-pan (ukhā) should break, one should pour it into another new pot that has a wide opening; for this pan that breaks indeed suffers affliction, while this deity is unafflicted, [thinking], "In one who is unafflicted, may I support him who is unafflicted. Thereupon, he throws a potsherd from the original pan into the front; thus, indeed, he does not fall away from its womb.

Then, having brought clay and having ground both the fire-pan (*ukhā*) and the reserve lump (*upaśayā*), he mixes them and fashions the fire-pan according to this same procedure. He brings the materials forward silently, without a sacrificial formula, and having baked it, he pours [the mixture] around it; the ritual act itself is the expiation in that case. Then, having placed that potsherd back into the fire-pan and having again ground both the fire-pan and the reserve lump, he mixes them and sets them aside for the sake of further expiations.

Now, if this fire in the *ukhā* should go out, it indeed goes back to the *gārhapatya*, for it was brought from the *gārhapatya*. Having taken it up again from the *gārhapatya* itself toward the east and having kindled it, he should place the *ukhā* on it according to that same procedure; he should bring it near silently, without a sacrificial formula, as soon as the fire mounts it.

Then he performs the two expiations. For he establishes this fire for the sake of all his desires; therefore, whatever of his desires is cut off when the fire goes out, that he now extends and joins together. He performs both expiations—the expiation for the sacrifice and the expiation for the fire. The former is for the sacrifice, and then for the fire; the significance of that has already been explained.
Having taken a portion of the clarified butter with the fuel-stick while sitting, he offers an oblation, saying:

"To Viśvakarman, Svāhā! Then, rising up, he places a fuel-stick on the fire, saying: "May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus kindle thee again; may the Brahmins, O leader of wealth, kindle thee again with sacrifices. This means: "May these deities kindle thee again. "With ghee, do thou increase thy body; may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled"—by this he says: "Do thou increase [thyself] with ghee; may all those desires for which the sacrificer placed thee [on the fire] become true for him."

Now, if the Gārhapatya fire should go out, it has indeed gone into the two kindling woods (araṇīs), for from the two kindling woods it was brought forth; therefore, having churned it out from the two kindling woods and rekindled it, he performs the expiation.

Now, if the Āhavanīya fire should go out while the Soma-pressing has begun, it goes back to the Gārhapatya, for it was brought from the Gārhapatya; therefore, having carried it eastward from the Gārhapatya by means of a visible flame and having rekindled it, he performs the expiation. Whatever sacrifice may be in progress at that time, he should perform the expiation for that sacrifice; the expiation for the fires is the same.
Now, if the Āgnīdhrīya fire should go out, it goes back to the Gārhapatya, for it was brought from the Gārhapatya;

having carried it from the Gārhapatya eastward along the north of the Sadas and enkindled it, he performs the expiation. And if the Gārhapatya should go out, its significance has already been explained.
Having fastened on a golden plate, he carries it;
for this golden plate is indeed truth, and truth alone is able to sustain him. By means of truth the gods carried him, and by means of truth he now carries him.

Now, that which is the Truth is yonder sun; it is made of gold, for gold is indeed light and this [sun] is light; gold is immortality and this [sun] is immortality. It is circular, for he is circular; it has twenty-one knobs, for he is the twenty-first; it bears the knob on the outside, for his rays are the knobs, and his rays are indeed on the outside.
And again, as to why he carries it after having fastened on the gold plate:
yonder sun is this gold plate; for no mere human being is able to go toward this Agni in human form; rather, by means of this very form, he carries that [divine] form.
Furthermore, as to why he carries the gold plate after fastening it on:
this seed that has been poured out is indeed Agni; the gold plate is brilliance and vigor. He thus places brilliance and vigor into that seed.
As for the fact that he wears the gold plate after fastening it on:

the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay this one of ours here"; therefore they made yonder sun his protector from close at hand. For yonder sun is indeed this gold plate; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now makes him his protector from close at hand.

It is sewn upon a black antelope skin. The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; the sacrifice is indeed capable of supporting him. By means of the sacrifice the gods carried him; by means of the sacrifice he now carries him. It is with the hair-side up; for the hairs are the meters, and the meters are indeed capable of supporting him. By means of the meters the gods carried him; by means of the meters he now carries him.

It is woven through both the white and the black hairs; for these two are the forms of *ṛk* and *sāman*, and it is fitting that he should be restrained by *ṛk* and *sāman*. By means of *ṛk* and *sāman*, the gods carried him; with *ṛk* and *sāman* he now carries him. The linen cord for the gold disk (*rukma*) is threefold; its significance has already been explained.
He wears it above the navel;
for yonder sun is this gold plate, and he is indeed above the navel.
Or rather, it should be above the navel;

for semen, progeny, brilliance, and vigor are below the navel, while the gold plate (rukma) is brilliance, vigor, and power—[he places it above] lest the gold plate consume his semen, progeny, brilliance, and vigor.
Or rather, it is above the navel;

for that part of the victim which is above the navel is indeed more pure, while that which is below the navel is more closely connected with refuse. Thus, he carries him by means of that part of the victim which is most pure.
Or rather, it is above the navel.

For that which is the immortal part of the vital breath (prāṇa) rises upward from the navel by means of the upward-moving vital breaths; whereas that which is mortal passes beyond the navel in the opposite direction. Thus, he brings this [victim] into correspondence with that very immortal part of the vital breath, and thereby he sustains it.
Then he carries him on a throne-seat.
This earth, indeed, is the throne-seat, for upon it all this is seated; this earth is indeed capable of supporting him. On her the gods carried him, and with her he now carries him.

It is made of Udumbara wood. The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; he thus supports him with strength and sap. Moreover, the Udumbara is all these trees; all these trees are worthy to carry him. With all these trees the gods carried him; with all these trees he thus carries him.

It is a span high; for Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed a span, and this is his womb; thus he makes the womb commensurate with the embryo. It is a cubit wide; for a cubit is the arm, and by the arm manly power is exerted; thus it becomes commensurate with manly power. For manly power alone is able to sustain him; by means of manly power the gods carried him, and by means of manly power he carries him now.
The feet have four corners; the verses to be recited over them have four corners.

There are indeed four quarters, and it is the quarters that are capable of carrying him. By means of the quarters the gods carried him; by means of the quarters he now carries him. It is woven with cords of Muñja grass, triple-stranded; the significance of this has been explained. It is smeared with clay; the significance of this has also been explained, and furthermore, it is for the sake of preventing burning.

Then he carries him by means of a sling. These worlds are indeed this Agni, and the quarters are the sling; for by the quarters these worlds are able to stand firm, and because they are able (śaknuvanti), it is called a sling (śikya). He carries him by means of the quarters. It has six strands, for there are six directions. It is made of Muñja grass and is threefold; its significance has already been explained. It is smeared with clay; its significance has also been explained, and furthermore, it is to prevent burning.

Water is its foundation; for these worlds are founded upon water. The sun is the attachment; for these worlds are attached to the sun by means of the quarters. He who knows this thus, by this very form, supports that form.
And as to why he carries him by means of a sling:

this Agni is the year, and the sling is the seasons; for by means of the seasons the year is able to stand firm, and because it is able [to stand], therefore it is called a "sling" (śikya). He carries him by means of the seasons; it has six cross-beams, for there are six seasons.
Day and night are its foundation;

for this year is established upon day and night, and the moon is its attachment, for this year is attached to the moon by means of the seasons. He who knows this thus, bears this form by means of that very form. Verily, he who knows this becomes one who has maintained the year; but for him who does not know this, it remains merely something attended upon for a year. This is with respect to the deities.

Now with reference to the self: the self itself is the fire; the breaths are the sling, for by means of the breaths this self is able to stand, and because it is able [to stand], therefore it is a sling. By means of the breaths he thus supports it. It has six cross-beams, for there are six breaths.
His very mind is his foundation;

for this Self is established in the mind, being attached to food, since this Self is attached to the vital breaths through food. He who knows this thus, by means of that very form, sustains this form.
Then he carries him with the fire-pan (ukhā).
These worlds, indeed, are the fire-pan; these worlds are indeed capable of carrying him. By means of these worlds the gods carried him; by means of these very worlds he now carries him.
As for why it is called an *ukhā*:

by means of this rite and this procedure, the gods dug these worlds out; because they dug them out (*udakhanaṃs*), it is called *utkhī*. They call it *ukhā* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic.

Now, "tad vā u" consists of two syllables; the sacrificer is two-footed, and Agni is the sacrificer. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus supports him. That is the pot (kumbhī), that is the cooking-vessel (sthālī). That makes six; there are six seasons in the year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—so great does that become.
Then he encloses it with two wooden rims (iṇḍva).
Yonder sun is indeed this Agni; day and night are the two wooden rims. He thus encloses yonder sun with day and night; therefore, it is enclosed by day and night.
Furthermore, as to why he encloses it with two clods of earth:

this Agni is indeed yonder sun, and these two worlds are the two clods; he thus encloses yonder sun by means of these two worlds. Therefore, he is enclosed by these two worlds. They are circular, for these two worlds are circular. They are made of Muñja grass and are threefold; the significance of that has been explained. They are smeared with clay; the significance of that has also been explained, and furthermore, it is to prevent them from burning through.

Now, therefore, follows the correspondence. The stool, the pan, the sling, the cord for the gold plate, the fire, and the gold plate—these are six. There are six seasons; the year consists of the seasons, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become. These [with the two feet] are eight; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become.
Now follows the attainment of all prosperity:

there are four feet, four verses to be recited, the sling, and the loop for the gold plate; and whatever else consists of rope, that is the sling; the fire-pan and the gold plate are the two [additional] items—thus there are thirteen. Thirteen months make a year, and Agni is the year; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does this become.
Standing, he puts it on.
For yonder sun is this gold disk; indeed, yonder sun stands, as it were. Moreover, standing one is more powerful. Standing facing north-east, its significance has been explained.

"Visible, the golden disk has shone far and wide"—for this golden disk, being visible, indeed shines far and wide; "shining for the sake of glory with life that is hard to surpass"—for his life is indeed difficult to die, and he shines for the sake of glory; "Agni became immortal by means of vital powers"—for by all vital powers he indeed became immortal; "When Dyaus begat him"—for Dyaus indeed begat him; "she of good seed"—for she is indeed of good seed, whose seed he is.
Then he grasps it with two fingers.

"Night and Dawn, of one mind, though of different forms"—Night and Dawn are indeed day and night; "of one mind, though of different forms, they suckle the one infant together. Whatever there is of day and night, they suckle this very one together. "The sun shines between heaven and earth"—while carrying (the fire), he mutters this sacrificial formula; for these two are indeed heaven and earth, and that which shines between them is this very one; therefore, while carrying it, he mutters this formula. "The gods sustained Agni, the giver of wealth"—having taken hold of it, he sets it down. The gods who give wealth are indeed the vital breaths; they sustained him thus at the beginning, and by means of them, he sustains him now.

Then he fastens the sling-rope with the verse: "The Seer puts on all forms. The Seer is indeed yonder sun, and he has sent forth the sling-rope of all forms. "Auspicious for the two-footed and the four-footed"—rising, he indeed sends forth what is auspicious for both the two-footed and the four-footed. "Savitar, the Excellent One, has looked upon the vault of heaven"—the vault of heaven is indeed the world of heaven; rising, he looks down upon it. "He shines following the departure of the Dawn"—the Dawn indeed dawns first, and shining after her dawning, he rises up.
Then he fashions it from this [clay] with the *vikṛti* formula;
he thereby fashions that very semen once it has been emitted, and therefore the semen emitted in the womb is fashioned.
"You are Suparṇa, the Garuḍa."

Vigour indeed is Suparṇa Garutman; he thus endows him with vigour. "The Trivṛt is thy head"—he makes the Trivṛt Stoma his head. "The Gāyatra is thine eye"—he makes the Gāyatra his eye. "The Bṛhat and Rathantara are thy wings"—he makes the Bṛhat and Rathantara his wings. "The Stoma is the self"—he makes the Stoma his self. "The Pañcaviṃśa and the metres are the limbs"—the metres indeed are his limbs. "The Yajus-formulas are the name"—that which they call "Agni" is his name consisting of the Yajus-formulas. "The Vāmadevya Sāman is thy body"—the body is the self; thus he says, "The Vāmadevya is thy body, the self. "The Yajñāyajñiya is the tail"—he makes the Yajñāyajñiya the tail. "The Dhiṣṇya hearths are the hoofs"—for by means of the Dhiṣṇyas he is established in this world. "Thou art Suparṇa Garutman; go to heaven, fly to the light!"—having thus made him Suparṇa Garutman, he says, "Go to the gods, fly to the heavenly world!"

Now, he fashions this very one here with wings and a tail; for in whatever way the seed is fashioned in the womb, in that same way it is born. Since he fashions this one here with wings and a tail, therefore this one is born there with wings and a tail.

Regarding this, some consecrate it with this modified formula and then pile another altar—either a *droṇaciti*, or a *rathacakraciti*, or a *kaṅkaciti*, or a *praugaciti*, or one with *praugas* on both sides, or one with leveled earth (*samuhyapurīṣa*). One should not do so; for that would be as if one were to cut off the embryo while it still has wings and a tail. Therefore, one should pile it only as a *suparṇaciti*.

With this modification, he holds it from here upwards toward the east. For that Agni is yonder sun; he thus places yonder sun from here upwards toward the east, and therefore yonder sun is placed from here upwards toward the east. He holds it beyond the reach of his arms, for he (the sun) is indeed beyond the reach of one's arms from here. Then he lowers it; having lowered it, he holds it above the navel—the significance of this has already been explained.

Then he strides the Viṣṇu-strides. For the gods, having become Viṣṇu, strode across these worlds; because they strode while being Viṣṇu, they are called "Viṣṇu-strides. In the same way, the sacrificer, having become Viṣṇu, strides across these worlds.
That which is Viṣṇu is the sacrifice;

that which is the sacrifice is this very one, namely this fire here in the fire-pan. Having made this very self their own, the gods stepped forth into these worlds; in the same way, the sacrificer, having made this very self his own, steps forth into these worlds.

Standing facing north-east—indeed, it was standing facing north-east that Prajāpati created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides; in the very same way, the sacrificer now creates offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides while standing facing north-east.

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu," he says; for having become Viṣṇu, he strides. "Conquering the rivals," he says; for here he indeed slays his rivals. "Mounting the Gāyatrī metre," he says; for he mounts the Gāyatrī metre. "Stride along the earth," he says; for he strides along the earth. He strikes forward; he steps with his foot and lifts Agni upward, for he ascends upward.

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu"—for having become Viṣṇu, he strides; "slayer of the adversary"—here he slays the adversaries; "the Triṣṭubh metre thou dost ascend"—he ascends the Triṣṭubh metre; "stride along the intermediate space"—he strides along the intermediate space. He strikes down one foot as he strides; he lifts up the fire, for he ascends upwards.

"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu. For having become Viṣṇu, he strides; "slaying those who act as enemies," for here he slays those who act as enemies. "Mount the Jāgata metre," for he mounts the Jāgata metre. "Stride along after heaven," for he strides along after heaven. He strikes out, he steps forward, and he lifts up the fire upwards, for he ascends upwards.
"Thou art the stride of Viṣṇu.

For having become Viṣṇu, he strides, thinking, "May I slay those who act as enemies"; thus here he slays those who act as enemies. "Ascend the Anuṣṭubh metre," he says; he ascends the Anuṣṭubh metre. "Stride along the quarters," he says; he gazes along all the quarters. He does not set down his foot, lest these worlds perish. He raises the fire upwards only, for he ascends it.
Then he takes it up with the words, "Now him.
For the gods indeed desired, "May we become Parjanya in form"; by means of this self, they became Parjanya in form. In the same way, the sacrificer, by means of this self, becomes Parjanya in form.

"Agni has cried out like the thundering sky," for Parjanya, as it were, cries out while thundering over the earth; "licking the ground, he anoints the plants," for Parjanya, licking the earth, indeed anoints the plants; "as soon as born, being kindled, he looked abroad," for as soon as he is born, he makes all this world visible; "he shines between the two worlds with his light," for the two worlds are heaven and earth, and he shines between them with his light; he raises [his arms] beyond the reach of his arms, for Parjanya is beyond the reach of arms.
Then he brings it down.

For whatever essence there is in this world, whatever constitutes subsistence—by means of that, he ascends these worlds upwards. Agni, indeed, is the essence in this world, and Agni is the subsistence. If it were only thus (without being brought down), there would be neither essence nor subsistence in this world. But in that he brings it down, he places essence and subsistence right here in this world.
Moreover, as to why he descends again:

when he ascends from here upwards to these worlds, that ascent is, as it were, directed away. But this earth is indeed the foundation; if it were only so (without descending), the sacrificer would fall away from this world. Now, when he descends again, he thereby returns toward this very foundation and establishes himself firmly upon this foundation.
When he thus descends, it is because he has won these worlds from here upwards.

That victory which is merely directed away is, as it were, a partial victory; for others indeed take possession of what he has won. But for him who wins in both ways, there is freedom of movement therein. Thus, when he descends, he wins these very worlds both from here upwards and from there downwards.

"O Agni, thou who turnest back! Turn back toward me, O Agni Aṅgiras! With vigor, with wealth—return to me with all this! With these words he descends four times; for four times he ascends upright. As many times as he ascends upright, so many times does he descend. Having brought him down, he holds him above the navel; the significance of that has been explained.

Then he addresses it with the mantra: "Agni is life; verily, he thus bestows life upon himself. "I have brought thee hither"—for they indeed bring him hither—"thou hast entered within"—verily, he thus bestows life within himself—"stand firm, unshakable"—verily, he thus bestows life firmly within himself—"may all the people desire thee"—the people are indeed food; thus, "may all food desire thee"—"may thy kingdom not fall away from thee"—the kingdom is prosperity; thus, "may prosperity not fall away from thee."

Then he unties the sling-loop and the gold-plate loop. The sling is indeed Varuṇa’s; thus he is released from Varuṇa’s noose. With a verse addressed to Varuṇa, he is released from Varuṇa’s noose by means of his own self, by his own deity. [The verse is: "O Varuṇa, loosen the highest bond from us, unloosen the lowest, and unloosen the middle one. As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu). Then [he says]: "And may we, O Āditya, be sinless in your service for the sake of Aditi. Aditi is indeed this earth; thus he means, "May we be sinless toward you and toward her."
Then he holds him up with the words, "Thus him.

For having fashioned him there [in the fire], he now holds him up from there toward the east. He holds him up with the words, "Him thence. If it were only that much, he would indeed have come to a stop right there; but because he holds him up with the words, "Thus him," therefore he, having gone thus, returns again.
"Great and upright, he has stood at the forefront of the dawns."

For he stands tall at the forefront of the dawns; having emerged from the darkness, he has come with light. Indeed, having emerged from the darkness of the night, he comes with the light of the day. "Agni, fair-limbed, with his radiant glow"—for Agni is indeed fair-limbed with his radiant glow. "As soon as born, he has filled all dwellings"—these worlds are indeed all the dwellings, and as soon as he is born, he fills them. He holds it out beyond the reach of his arms, for he is indeed beyond the reach of arms from here. Then he brings it down; he thus returns toward this very foundation and establishes himself upon this very foundation. He does so with a Jagatī verse, for these worlds are of the nature of the Jagatī; from there, he extends downward over these worlds.
"The swan dwelling in purity," and so forth.

"That sun, indeed, is the swan dwelling in the light; the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere"—Vāyu, indeed, is the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere. "The Hotṛ dwelling on the altar"—Agni, indeed, is the Hotṛ dwelling on the altar. "The guest"—for he is the guest of all beings. "Dwelling in the house"—this means dwelling in the uneven places. "Dwelling among men"—the breath is indeed "dwelling among men," for men are *nara*; thus he speaks of that which is this breath, Agni, among men. "Dwelling in the best"—for he dwells in all the best things. "Dwelling in the truth"—this means dwelling in reality. "Dwelling in the sky"—for he dwells in all the skies. "Born of water, born of cow"—for he is born of water and born of cow. "Born of truth"—this means born of reality. "Born of rock"—for he is born of rock. "Truth"—this means reality. "Great"—he places him down, for he is great. Having thus made him into what he is, he places him down.
With two syllables;
the sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he thus establishes him.
Then he worships him with this [verse]:
"For indeed, it is as if he were lightening his burden when he strides through these worlds, both together and separately; he offers this to him for the sake of non-injury."
Moreover, as to why he pays reverence:

the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest this one should harm these worlds of ours from close by. They thereby appeased him for these very worlds; in the same way, this sacrificer now appeases him for these worlds.

"Sit down, O Agni, in the lap of this mother; having become auspicious through your own luster, sit for me, O Agni, indeed as one who is auspicious. By saying "auspicious, auspicious," he thus pacifies him for the sake of non-violence; and so he does not harm these worlds with his heat.
He worships with three [verses].

These worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he makes amends for him; moreover, with just that much he pacifies him for these worlds.
Then he worships with the Vātsapra hymn.

For Prajāpati, having created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, bestowed long life upon them by means of the Vātsapra; in the same way, this sacrificer, having created offspring by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, bestows long life upon them by means of the Vātsapra.
This very thing is the "Dākṣāyaṇahasta" (the hand of Dakṣa's daughter), namely the Vātsapra hymn.

Therefore, if one should desire of a newborn child, "May he attain a full lifespan," one should touch him with the Vātsapra; thus one bestows longevity upon him as he is born, and so he indeed attains a full lifespan. Now, if one should desire of a child, "May he be vigorous," one should address him from the front with the Vikṛti hymn; thus he indeed becomes vigorous.

"Agni was first born from heaven"—the breath, indeed, is heaven; from the breath, he was first born. "From us, the second time, Jātavedas"—when they then generated him a second time in human form. "The third time in the waters"—when they then generated him a third time from the waters. "Nṛmaṇas, the unceasing"—Prajāpati is Nṛmaṇas, and Agni is the unceasing. "Kindling him, the well-disposed one praises him"—for whoever kindles him, he generates him as a well-disposed one.
"I know, O Agni, your three forms in three ways."

"Agni, Vāyu, Āditya—these indeed are those three triads of his; 'knowing them, thy stations are distributed in many places'—this refers to how they are distributed in many ways. 'Knowing thy supreme name that is in secret'—*yaviṣṭha* (the youngest) is indeed his supreme name in secret. 'Knowing that fountain from which thou hast come'—the waters are the fountain, for he first came from the waters. 'Thee, O manly-minded one, in the ocean within the waters'—Prajāpati is indeed the manly-minded one; thus it means 'thee, Prajāpati, in the waters. 'Thee, O Agni, the man-beholding, in the udder of heaven'—Prajāpati is indeed the man-beholding one, and the waters are the udder of heaven. 'Thee, standing in the third realm'—the sky is indeed the third realm. 'The mighty ones increased thee in the lap of the waters'—the vital breaths are the mighty ones; thus it means 'the vital breaths increased thee in the sky.'"

These [verses] have a single explanation. They are addressed to Agni and are in the Triṣṭubh metre. In that they are addressed to Agni, he is thereby Agni; and in that they are Triṣṭubhs and eleven in number, he is thereby Indra. For Agni is of the nature of Indra-Agni; he worships him with as much as his measure is. Indeed, Indra and Agni are all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities; he worships him with as much as his measure is.
Furthermore, as for why the Viṣṇukrama and Vātsapra rites are performed.

By the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created offspring; by that much he thus approaches him. By the Vātsapra, Prajāpati created this world; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Agni; by the Vātsapra, the atmosphere; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Vāyu; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the sky; by the Vātsapra, Āditya; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the quarters; by the Vātsapra, the moon; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created what has been; by the Vātsapra, what will be; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created wealth; by the Vātsapra, hope; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the day; by the Vātsapra, the night; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the bright fortnights; by the Vātsapra, the dark fortnights; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the half-months; by the Vātsapra, the months; by the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati created the seasons; by the Vātsapra, the year. Thus, in that there are both the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra, by means of these he creates all this.
Furthermore, as to why there are the Viṣṇu-strides and the Vātsapra:

by means of the Viṣṇu-strides, Prajāpati set out toward the heavenly world; he saw this resting place, the Vātsapra, and with it he rested for the sake of avoiding burning. For when that which is yoked is not unyoked, it is liable to burn; in the same way, the sacrificer now sets out toward the heavenly world by means of the Viṣṇu-strides and rests with the Vātsapra.

Having indeed stepped the Viṣṇu-steps, he then immediately worships with the Vātsapra hymn; it is just as if one were to set out on a journey and then immediately unyoke [the team]. For men follow the ordinance of the gods; therefore, even here among men, when a village sets out on a journey, they settle down immediately.

Or rather, the Viṣṇu-strides pertain to day and night; the Vātsapra pertains to day and night; thus he goes by means of day and night and becomes secure in day and night. Therefore, even here on earth, a human village, having gone by means of day and night, becomes secure in day and night.

He indeed strides the Viṣṇu-steps for exactly half of the year, and worships with the Vātsapra for the other half; for the heavenly world is in the middle of the year. If he were to stride for less than half, he would not reach this heavenly world; and if he were to stride for more than half, he would pass beyond and lose sight of this heavenly world. But since he strides for half and worships for half, having thus reached the heavenly world at the right time, he releases his hold upon it.
Through these two, he indeed undergoes a reversal;

it is such that he may attain liberation over a long journey. He combines both the Viṣṇukrama and the Vātsapra at the beginning and at the end. The Viṣṇukramas are the day, and the Vātsapra is the night. Prajāpati, when about to procreate this universe and having procreated it, encompasses it on both sides with day and night.
Regarding this they say:

"Since the Vishnu-strides are performed during the day and the Vatsapra during the night, both then belong to the day and not to the night; how then do they both come to be performed for him on the night as well? To this they reply: When he is being consecrated, he combines both of these in the afternoon on the preceding day—for that which is the afternoon is indeed the night—and then, when he is about to perform the Samnivapa, he combines both of these in the forenoon on the following day—for that which is the forenoon is indeed the day. Thus, indeed, both of them come to be performed by him on the day, and both on the night.

On the day when he is about to pour out [the ashes], on that morning after the sun has risen, he first throws out the ashes. Having thrown out the ashes, he releases his speech; having released his speech, he places a fuel-stick on the fire. Having placed the fuel-stick, he carries the ashes down into the water. Just as there is a specific manner for carrying them down, so having taken up some of the ashes, he returns, pours them into the pan (ukhā), and stands by it worshipping; then he performs the expiations.

If it be the day of the Viṣṇu-strides, having performed the Viṣṇu-strides, he should worship with the Vātsapra hymn; but if it be the day of the Vātsapra, having worshipped with the Vātsapra, he should perform the Viṣṇu-strides and conclude with the Vātsapra, for he should not conclude with the Viṣṇu-strides. It would be as if, having set out on a journey, one did not return; whereas in that he concludes with the Vātsapra—the Vātsapra being a firm foundation—it is as if he were to establish himself and bring [the sacrifice] to rest. Therefore, he should indeed conclude with the Vātsapra.
"One should carry the fire while bearing it on a wagon," so they say.

Both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another. The gods moved about with a wagon, while the Asuras were without wagons. Moving about with a wagon, the gods perceived this ritual act; for indeed, moving about with a wagon, the gods perceived this ritual act. Therefore, the sacrificial formulas (*yajūṃṣi*) for the cake-offerings belong to the wagon, and those for the fire belong to the wagon.

He who is carried about as a bridegroom goes to the gods by his action; indeed, a divine action is performed by him. But he who is not carried about as a bridegroom goes to the Asuras by his action; indeed, an Asuric action is performed by him.

Regarding this, some say: "He has indeed been led away by himself; he goes forth with the Viṣṇu-steps and comes to rest with the Vātsapra. One should not understand it thus. For his going forth is divine, namely the Viṣṇu-steps, and his coming to rest is divine, namely the Vātsapra. But this which he goes forth is his human going forth, and that in which he comes to rest is his human coming to rest.

This Agni is Prajāpati. Indeed, Prajāpati is both that which is the gods and that which is human beings. In that there are the Viṣṇu-steps and the Vātsapra, he thereby prepares for him that form of his which is divine; and in that he is driven about (vanīvāhyate), he thereby prepares for him that form of his which is human. Verily, he who knows this and has him driven about prepares this entire, complete Prajāpati. Therefore, one should certainly have him driven about.

On the day he is about to set out, he should have a fire placed to the north of the [sacrificial] fire, facing east; then he places a kindling-stick upon it. For when the gods were about to go forth, they gratified him from the front with food by means of this kindling-stick; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now gratifies him, as he is about to go forth, from the front with food by means of this kindling-stick.

"Serve Agni with fuel"—that is, "Honor Agni with fuel. "Awaken the guest with clarified butter; offer the oblations in him"—that is, "Awaken the guest with clarified butter; offer the oblations in him. He says "awakened," for he indeed awakens him by this.
Then he lifts it up.

"May all the gods bear you up with their thoughts, O Agni"—for indeed, in the beginning, all the gods bore him up with their thoughts, for that was their thought at that time; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now bears him up with his thoughts, for this is his thought at that time. "Be thou auspicious to us, fair-faced, full of light"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. He places it to the south, facing north; the significance of that is as follows: having poured the Gārhapatya fire into a pot, he places another [fire] upon it. If he should so desire, he may mount upon it or walk beside it.
Then he yokes the two oxen:

first the right one, then the left; for thus it is among the gods, otherwise among men. In whichever direction he intends to go, he should first set out toward the east; for the east is Agni's quarter, and so he proceeds toward his own quarter.

"Go forth, O Agni, full of light, with thy auspicious flames"—this means, "O Agni, go forth, thou who art full of light, with thy auspicious, blazing flames. "Shining with great beams, do not harm our offspring with thy body"—this means, "shining with great flames, do not harm our offspring through thyself."
Whenever the axle creaks, he should then mutter this sacrificial formula: "This speech of the axle is indeed asurya; he thereby appeases it and makes it belong to the gods."

Moreover, as to why he mutters this sacrificial formula (*yajus*): whenever one lets out a cry while something is being placed upon an axle, that cry belongs to that very thing; and when one lets out a cry while something is being placed upon the fire, that cry belongs to Agni alone. Thus, the gods praised and magnified Agni; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now praises and magnifies him with the words, "Agni has roared, like the thundering sky. The significance of this has already been explained.

If he should release [the fire] before the time for dwelling, the fire would be as if on a cart; therefore, when he releases it for the sake of dwelling, having placed the cart in front, he digs up the ground to the north and sprinkles it. Wherever he brings it down, he brings it down from the south toward the north; the significance of this has been explained.
Then he places a kindling-stick upon it.

For when he had gone away, the gods gratified him from above with food by means of this kindling-stick; in the same way, this sacrificer now gratifies him, who has gone away, from above with food by means of this kindling-stick.

"Forward this Agni of Bharata shall be heard"—Bharata is indeed Prajāpati, for he sustains (*bibharti*) all this. "When he shines forth with great light like the sun"—that is, "when he shines forth with great light like the sun. "He who has stood against Pūru in battles"—Pūru was indeed a name of an Asura-Rakṣasa; against him Agni stood in battles. "The divine guest has shone, auspicious to us"—that is, "the divine guest, shining, [has become] auspicious to us. By means of a verse containing the word "stood" (*sthitavatī*), he establishes him for his dwelling, for he is already present there.
Now, therefore, follows the correspondence.

He places a kindling-stick (samidh) with the first [verse], he lifts it up with one, he proceeds with one, and he consecrates the axle with one; with the fifth, he places the kindling-stick itself. That makes five. The fire-altar consists of five layers; there are five seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—so great does this become.

Now, therefore, regarding the consumption of ashes. In the beginning, the gods scattered these ashes; they said, "If we were to prepare ourselves with this while it remains exactly as it is, we shall become mortal corpses, not freed from evil. But if we scatter them away, we shall place that which belongs to Agni outside of Agni. Consider how we may do this. They said, "Meditate! By which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek how we may do this."

While reflecting, they perceived this: "Let us carry it into the waters; for the waters are the foundation of all this. Having established it there where the foundation of all this is, we shall generate from the waters that which belongs to Agni here. So they carried it into the waters, and in the same way, this sacrificer now carries it into the waters.

"O divine Waters, receive this ash; make for it a pleasant and fragrant place! For that which has been consumed becomes exhausted; thus he says this: "Make for it a most fragrant place. "Let the women bow down to him"—the waters are indeed the women, for from the waters all this is born. "With good husbands"—for the waters have Agni as their good husband. "Bear him in your lap like a mother her son"—that is to say, "bear him just as a mother would bear her son in her lap."
"In the waters, O Agni, is your seat"—this means "in the waters, O Agni, is your womb.

"You follow after the plants"—for he indeed follows after the plants while being an embryo. "You are born again"—for he is indeed born again as an embryo. "You are the embryo of these plants, the embryo of the trees, the embryo of every living being, O Agni, you are the embryo of the waters"—thus he makes him the embryo of this entire universe.

He consumes it with three [verses]. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus consumes it. First with one, then with two; or first with two, then with one. He consumes it twice; thus, by means of those animals that are two-footed, he thereby consumes it.

Then he takes [the ashes] away. Now, that which here belongs to Agni, he generates from the waters by means of this [verse]: "With this [water], indeed, medicine is prepared; with this very [water] he thus collects him. "Having settled with the ash in his womb, the waters and the earth, O Agni"—for he has indeed settled with the ash in his womb, the waters, and the earth. "Having united with thy mothers, thou, full of light, hast sat down again"—this means "having joined with thy mothers, thou, full of light, hast sat down again. "Having sat down again in thy seat, again with vigor and wealth"—this means "return to me with all this."

He takes it up with four [verses]. Thus, by means of those animals that have four feet, he thereby equips him; and since cattle are indeed food, he thereby equips him with food. He pours it down with three [verses]; that makes seven. The fire-altar consists of seven layers, there are seven seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—so great does this become.

Having taken some of the ashes and returned, he scatters them into the fire-pan and stands worshipping it. For when one carries the fire down into the water, he does what is improper; he thus makes amends to it for the sake of non-injury. With two verses addressed to Agni containing the word "awake" (budh), he makes amends to Agni himself, so that Agni may take heed of this speech of his.
"O youngest one, grant me the understanding of this speech."

"O youngest one, understand this word of mine"—this refers to [the offering] being presented. "Of the most bountiful, O self-dependent one"—this means of that which is presented in the greatest measure, O self-dependent one. "One reviles, another praises"—one person reviles while another praises. "I, as thy worshipper, praise thy body, O Agni"—this means "I, as thy worshipper, praise thy body, O Agni. "Be thou a liberal patron, O lord of wealth, giver of wealth; drive away from us our enemies"—he says this so that he may indeed drive away our enemies from him. He worships with two verses, a Gāyatrī and a Triṣṭubh; the significance of that has been explained.
These become nine:
the nine directions, the directions are Agni; the nine vital breaths, the vital breaths are Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become.
Then he performs the two expiations (*prāyaścitti*).

For he establishes this fire for the sake of all his desires; whatever of his desires is here cut off when water is poured into the fire, that he thereby reconnects and joins together. He performs both expiations: the significance of those [fires] which have gone out in the fire-altar has already been explained.

These amount to ten; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the *virāj*; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, so great does that become. When he is about to pile the Gārhapatya fire, he sweeps it away with a Palāśa branch. For he settles [the earth] when he piles the Gārhapatya; and whosoever have piled the fire-altars, they are all settled upon this very [earth]. Thus, when he sweeps it away, he sweeps away those who are already settled, thinking, "Lest I should settle those who are already settled."

"Go away, depart, and creep away from here"—he says this so that they may indeed go away, depart, and creep away from here. "Those who creep about in the belly"—this he says of those [snakes]; "those who are here, ancient ones, and those who are new"—this means those who are here as eternal ones and those who are of the present time.
"Yama gave the resting place of the earth. For Yama indeed rules over this resting place; he himself grants him a resting place upon this earth.
"O Fathers, ye have made this world for us.

Yama is indeed the nobility (kṣatra) and the fathers are the common people (viś). For when a nobleman, being in agreement with the common people, grants him a dwelling on this earth, that is a well-granted gift. And so, Yama, being in agreement with the common people—the fathers—grants him a dwelling on this earth.

He sweeps away with a *palāśa* branch. The *palāśa* is indeed Brahman; thus he sweeps away those who have settled there by means of Brahman. He does so with a mantra; the mantra is indeed Brahman; thus he sweeps away those who have settled there by means of Brahman. He throws it toward the north.
Then he scatters saline soil.
The Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and saline soil is cattle; he thus places cattle in this world, and therefore these cattle are here in this world.

Furthermore, as to why he scatters the *ūṣa* (salt-earth): Prajāpati created offspring; he created them with different amnions (*ulba*), and they did not agree with one another. He desired, "May they agree," so he made them have a common amnion. He made the *ūṣa* their common amnion, and they agreed. Therefore even now, those who share a common amnion agree with one another. Indeed, he who sacrifices sacrifices with the thought, "May I be of the same amnion with the gods. Thus, when he scatters the *ūṣa*, he becomes of the same amnion with the gods.

"Thou art consciousness," he says; for by this they indeed became conscious of the sustaining of desire. The saline earth (ūṣāḥ) is cattle, and the sustaining of desire is cattle; "May thy sustaining of desire be in me," he says, which means, "May cattle be in me. With these he covers the entire Gārhapatya fire-altar. The Gārhapatya layer is indeed the womb, and the saline earth is the caul; thus he covers the entire womb with the caul.
Then he scatters sand.
Sand is indeed the ash of Agni Vaiśvānara; he is about to pile this very Agni Vaiśvānara, and fire does not burn its own ash excessively. This is for the sake of non-excessive burning.
Moreover, as to why he scatters sand:

sand is indeed the seed of Agni Vaiśvānara; for he is about to pile this very Agni Vaiśvānara, and nothing indeed is produced from that which is seedless—[he scatters it] so that [the fire] may be produced from this seed.
"Thou art the ash of Agni; thou art the soil of Agni.

For the ash of Agni is exhausted, whereas the sand is unexhausted; he thus makes it unexhausted. With that [sand] he covers the entire Gārhapatya hearth. The Gārhapatya altar is indeed the womb, and the sand is the seed; he thus places the seed in the entire womb.

Then he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (pariśrit). The enclosing-stones are indeed the womb; thus he encloses this emitted seed within the womb. Therefore, the emitted seed is enclosed by the womb.

Furthermore, as to why he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (pariśrit): the Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and the enclosing-stones are the waters; he thus surrounds this world with water. He surrounds it on all sides with the ocean; therefore the ocean flows around this world on every side. It is turned towards the right; therefore the ocean flows around this world towards the right. It is by means of a dug-out trench; therefore the ocean flows around this world by means of a dug-out trench.

"O piling, thou art piled!"—for he piles them up; "O piling around, thou art piled around!"—for he piles them around; "Be ye piled upwards!"—saying this, he lays them down upright; therefore the ocean swells upwards. Now, if he were to lay them down sideways, the ocean would surely wash away all this [world] at once. He does not settle them, for the waters are unsettled; nor does he pronounce the *sūdadohas* verse over them.
The enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*) are indeed the bones;

the *sūdadohas* verse is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). There is no vital breath in the bones. With a single sacrificial formula (*yajus*), he lays down many bricks, for water is a single form. And as to why there are many enclosing-stones, it is because the waters are many.
That [altar] is indeed the womb;

the enclosing stones are the outer membrane, the saline earth (ūṣā) is the seed. The enclosing stones are outside and the saline earth is inside, for the womb is outside and the membrane is inside; the saline earth is outside and the sand is inside, for the membrane is outside and the seed is inside. From these, indeed, one being born is born; it is from these very things that he thus causes him to be born.
Then he piles this [fire-altar] from there; he thereby transforms this very seed that has been cast, for it is for this reason that the seed cast into the womb is transformed.
He lays down four bricks facing eastward: two behind, transverse, and two in front.

Those four which he lays down facing eastward constitute the body; as to why there are four, it is because this body is fourfold. Now, those two which are behind are the thighs, and those two which are in front are the arms; and where the body is, there indeed is the head.

Verily, he fashions him here with wings and a tail; for in whatever way the seed is fashioned in the womb, in that same way it is born. Since he fashions him here with wings and a tail, therefore he is born there with wings and a tail.

Although it indeed possesses wings and a tail, they do not see it as having wings and a tail; therefore, they do not see the embryo in the womb according to its true form. But when they see it there with wings and a tail, then they see the born embryo according to its true form.
He lays down four of them first.

For when one comes into being, it is indeed the self that comes into being first. Sitting to the south facing north, he lays down the first brick on the northern end; thus this fire-altar of his becomes built directed toward his own self.

"This is that Agni in whom Indra placed the pressed Soma"—the Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and the pressed Soma is the waters; thus, in this world, Indra placed the waters in his belly while crying out. "In his thousandfold belly like a swift steed"—the thousandfold prize is indeed the waters. "Having won, O Jātavedas, thou art praised"—this means, "O Jātavedas, having been built up, thou art being built up."

"O Agni, that splendor of yours which is in heaven"—the sun, indeed, is his splendor in heaven; "on earth," this [terrestrial] fire is on earth; "and that which is in the plants and in the waters, O worshipful one"—he thereby refers to that fire which is in the plants and in the waters; "wherewith thou hast spread out the wide mid-region"—that is Vāyu; "he who is brilliant, he who is radiant, the surging one, beholding men"—this means "he who is great, the radiant, the surging one, beholding men."

"O Agni, you go toward the flood of heaven"—the waters indeed are that flood of heaven, and it is them he approaches with his smoke. "And you have spoken to the gods who are the wise ones"—the breaths are indeed the gods who are the wise ones, for they send forth all thoughts.
