"Those which are beyond the luminous realm of the sun, and those which stand below"—the luminous realm is indeed this world where the sun shines; thus he speaks of both the waters that are beyond it and those that are below it.
"Purīṣyas agnayaḥ" means "the fires that are favorable to cattle.

"Prāvaṇebhiḥ sajoṣasaḥ" is a form belonging to the beginning (prāyaṇa), for the Gārhapatya fire is indeed the beginning of Agni. "Juṣantāṃ yajñamadruho 'namīvā iṣo mahīḥ" means "May they, free from malice and free from disease, enjoy the sacrifice and the great refreshments"; that is to say, "may they, free from malice and free from hunger, enjoy the sacrifice and the great refreshments."
He lays them down separately;

he thereby bestows upon the self those various desires that exist within it. He settles them all at once; he thereby makes the self one. He pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them; for the *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); by means of the vital breath he thus connects and unites this [self].

Then, having gone around by the rear, sitting to the north and facing south, he places the southern one of the two rear bricks with the formula: "O Agni, the *iḍā*, the many-wondrous gain of cattle. For the *iḍā* is indeed cattle; thus he invokes this blessing for him regarding cattle. "To him who calls most constantly, he grants success"—the sacrificer is indeed the one who calls. "May there be for us a son, a descendant, a progenitor"—the son is indeed offspring. "O Agni, may that benevolence of thine be with us"—thus he invokes a blessing.
Then the northern one:

"This is thy seasonal womb from which, being born, thou didst shine"—this means, "This is thy eternal seasonal womb from which, being born, thou didst blaze. "Knowing that, O Agni, ascend; then increase our wealth"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
These two are his thighs.

He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these two thighs are separate. There are two of them, for there are indeed two thighs. He lays them down behind, for these two thighs are behind. They touch each other at the tips, for these two thighs touch each other at the tips.

Then, having gone around again by that same way, sitting to the south facing north, he places the northern of the two front [bricks] first with the formula: "Thou art a layer (cit); by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm. Then the southern one with: "Thou art a layer-around (paricit); by that deity, in the manner of Aṅgiras, sit thou firm."

These two are his arms. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these two arms are separate. There are two of them, for there are these two arms. He lays them down in the front part, for these two arms are in the front. They touch each other at their tips, for thus these two arms touch each other at their tips. Now, he lays them down thinking, "these," and "these," and "these"; that is from left to right (*dakṣiṇāvṛt*), for that is the way among the gods.

He lays down eight bricks. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. Five times he settles them; five-layered is the fire-altar, five seasons are a year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. Eight bricks he settles five times—that makes thirteen; thirteen months are a year, and there are thirteen layers of loose soil for the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.

Then he lays down the Lokampṛṇā brick. Its significance is as follows: there are three preceding ones; Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. There are ten subsequent ones; their significance is as follows: first two, then ten, then one—for thus they build up the layer. These amount to thirteen; their significance has already been explained.
These two groups together amount to twenty-one.
There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; he thus establishes yonder sun upon this fire.

There are indeed twenty-one enclosing stones. There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and this Agni here; that makes twenty-one. He thereby establishes this Agni upon yonder sun. Now, when he lays them down in this manner, he establishes these two in each other; thus these two are established in each other. Indeed, he brings these two together here as two sets of twenty-one, for it is here that both of them—namely the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya—become so.
Then he throws down the loose soil. Its significance is as follows:

he brings it from the edge of the *cātvāla* pit; since the *cātvāla* is Agni, this [soil] thus becomes truly related to Agni for him. It should be level with the surface; its significance has already been explained.
It is one fathom in measure;

for man is indeed one fathom high, and man is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is Agni. Thus he makes a womb commensurate with his own self. It is circular, for the womb is circular; moreover, this Gārhapatya fire is this world, and this world is indeed circular.
Then he pours those two together;

he thereby effects a mutual agreement between them [with the words]: "Be ye in harmony, may your thoughts be united, may your vows be united; O Agni, thou art the one who dwells in the soil; be ye two of one mind for us. He thus pacifies them both so that there may be no injury, lest they should harm one another.
He pours it out with four [verses].

Thus, by means of those animals that have four feet, he thereby establishes a connection between these two; moreover, since cattle are indeed food, he thereby establishes a connection between these two by means of food.
One should not look at it when it is empty; thinking "lest I look at it when it is empty," for if one were to look at it when empty, it would swallow him up.

Then he pours sand upon it. Sand is indeed the seed of Agni Vaiśvānara; he thus pours that seed, which has become Agni Vaiśvānara, into this [altar]. It should be level with the surface; the significance of that has already been explained.
Then he unyokes her, so that she shall not be burned;

for if that which is yoked is not unyoked, it is consumed by fire. Indeed, when she was yoked, she brought forth seed; she has now given birth to this Agni here, and now she takes up another [seed]. The fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed a woman; therefore, when a woman has first brought forth seed, she then takes up another.

"Like a mother her son, the earth [bears] the one who is full of soil"—that is, "like a mother her son, the earth [bears] the one who is rich in cattle. "She has laid Agni in his own womb"—that is, "she has indeed laid Agni in his own womb. "May Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, release her"—for the seasons are indeed all the gods; thus Prajāpati Viśvakarman, in harmony with all the gods and the seasons, releases her. He places her to the north of the fire at the distance of a cubit; the significance of this has been explained.
Then he pours milk into it.

For he thus bestows seed, and then he bestows milk; for the fire-pan (ukhā) is indeed a woman, and therefore when a woman bestows seed, she then bestows milk. The sand is below and the milk is above, for seed is below and milk is above. He pours it into the middle so that he may subsequently place the human head upon it.

Prajāpati created offspring. Having created offspring and having exhausted himself in every contest for supremacy, he became relaxed. From him, thus relaxed, the vital breath (prāṇa) departed from the middle; then strength departed from him. When that had departed, he fell down. From him, having fallen, food flowed out. Whatever of his eye remained settled, from that his food flowed out. Indeed, there was then no support whatsoever here.
Those gods said, "There is indeed no other support than this; let us prepare this very father Prajāpati, for he shall be our support."
They said to Agni:
"There is indeed no other support than you; let us prepare this father Prajāpati upon you, and that shall be our support. He replied: "What will accrue to me from that?"

They said, "Prajāpati is indeed food; let us eat this food with you as our mouth; may this food belong to us who have you as our mouth. "So be it," he replied. Therefore, the gods eat food with Agni as their mouth; for to whichever deity they offer an oblation, they offer it in Agni alone, since the gods made Agni their mouth for that food.
That breath which issued from his middle is this very wind that blows; and that vigor which issued from him is yonder sun; and that food which flowed from him is whatever food exists in the year.

The gods enclosed it in the fire-altar. When it had been thus enclosed, Agni ascended it; that very vital breath which had departed from its middle entered it again, and they placed it within him. Then, whatever vigor had departed from it, they placed that within it; then, whatever food had flowed away from it, they placed that within it. Having restored it entirely and in its completeness, they raised it upwards. Those whom they raised upwards are these worlds.

This very world is his foundation. Now, the fire that is in this world is his downward vital breath (*avāṅ prāṇa*); the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is his self (*ātman*); and the wind that is in the intermediate space is that which is the vital breath in the self. The sky is his head; the sun and moon are his two eyes. That which rested upon the eye is the moon; therefore it is more closed up [than the sun], for from it food flowed forth.
This, indeed, is that foundation which the gods then established; even today it remains that very foundation, and from this point on, it shall continue to be so.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up. As for this pan (ukhā) lying empty before the pouring [of the fire], it is just as Prajāpati lay empty when his vital breath had departed, his vigor had departed, and his food had flowed away; such is its form.
He places it on the fire.

Just as the gods then placed it on the fire for him, so now Agni mounts it when it has been placed; that very vital breath which had gone out from his center, that same one enters it, and he places it within him. Then, when he wears the gold plate after fastening it on, he thereby places in him that vigor which had gone out from him. And when he lays on the fuel-sticks, he thereby places in him that food which had flowed away from him.
He indeed establishes them in the evening and in the morning.

For food flowed from both that day and that night; these [bricks] should be placed in the entire year, for that Prajāpati from whom they departed was the year. Thus, he places all this in him, in that entire whole. If one were not to do this for him, he would not place all this in him. "One must not even look at [the fire-altar] before it has been carried for a year," Vāmakakṣāyaṇa used to say, "lest I see this father Prajāpati being cut asunder. Having prepared it entirely and completely in a year, he raises it upwards, just as the gods raised it up there.
Of this [altar], this world is the *gārhapatya* fire-chamber.

Now, that fire which is in the *gārhapatya* is the fire that is in this world; it belongs to him. And that which is between the *āhavanīya* and the *gārhapatya* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Now, that fire which is in the *āgnīdhrīya* is the wind that is in the intermediate space; it belongs to him. The *āhavanīya* itself is the sky. And that fire which is in the *āhavanīya*—those two are the sun and the moon; it is his very self (*ātman*).

His head indeed is the Āhavanīya fire. Now, that fire which is in the Āhavanīya is this very vital breath (prāṇa) in the head. As to why it has wings and a tail—it is because this vital breath in the head has wings and a tail. The eye is the head; the right ear is the right wing; the left ear is the left wing; the vital breath is the middle body; and speech is the tail, the foundation. Since the vital breaths, having consumed food by means of speech, find their support therein, therefore speech is the tail, the foundation.

Now, that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is the self (ātman). Then, the fire on the Āgnīdhrīya altar is his vital breath (prāṇa) within the inner self; it is his foundation (pratiṣṭhā), while the Gārhapatya is his downward breath (avāṅ prāṇa). And the fire that is in the Gārhapatya is his downward breath.

Some indeed pile it as three layers, saying, "For these downward breaths are three. One should not do so; they thus cause it to be redundant. For those who do so [destroy] the perfection of the twenty-one-fold Stoma, the perfection of the Anuṣṭubh, and the perfection of the Bṛhatī. For this is indeed one single form: the womb itself, the procreation itself—namely, these downward breaths. For when one voids urine or excrement, that very thing is produced.
Now, therefore, follows the correspondence.

There are twenty-one bricks and nine sacrificial formulas; that makes thirty. Together with the settling and the *sūdadohas* verses, that makes thirty-two. The *anuṣṭubh* consists of thirty-two syllables; thus, this is indeed an *anuṣṭubh*.
There are twenty-one enclosing formulas;

the formula for the removal [of the earth] is the twenty-second. There is a formula for the saline soil (ūṣa), a formula for the sand, a formula for the loose earth (purīṣa), and a formula for the pouring together [of the materials] with four [formulas]; he releases [the horse] with the fifth. Then there are three [more]; this makes thirty-two syllables, which is the Anuṣṭubh—this is that Anuṣṭubh.
Now, these two Yajus formulas are indeed the Anuṣṭubh, for the Anuṣṭubh is speech. And that which is this twofold form of speech—the divine and the human, the loud and the soft—that is these two.

Now, these three *anuṣṭubh* verses are indeed this Gārhapatya altar. When they here bring together these three *anuṣṭubhs*, it is because at that time all these worlds become present here. Then, from those, they take one thirty-two-syllable *anuṣṭubh* to the Āhavanīya; that is the Āhavanīya, that is the sky, and that is the head. Now, the other remains here; that is the Gārhapatya, that is the foundation, and that is this world.
Now, as for these two *yajus* formulas:

that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and that is the body (*ātman*). Since there are two of them, therefore that which is between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya is narrower; and therefore, among these worlds, the intermediate world is the narrowest.

This very speech, divided threefold, is the *anṛṣṭubh*. This Agni follows it, having become the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That fire which is in the *āhavanīya* altar is the *prāṇa*; that is yonder sun. Now, that fire which is in the *āgnīdhrīya* altar is the diffused breath (*vyāna*); that is this wind which blows here. And that fire which is in the *gārhapatya* altar is the upward breath (*udāna*); that is this fire which is in this world. One who knows thus indeed prepares the whole of speech, the whole of breath, and the whole of the self.

This very [altar] is indeed the Bṛhatī. Those two sets of thirty-two syllables make thirty-two; then these two Yajus-formulas make thirty-four; Agni himself is the thirty-fifth. The metre does not depart from one syllable, nor from two; that [remaining] part consists of two syllables, which makes thirty-six. The Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables; for this [Agni], when built up, attains the form of the Bṛhatī. Just as the seed is poured into the womb, so is it born; and because he thus makes this Bṛhatī here, therefore this [Agni], when built up, attains the form of the Bṛhatī.
Regarding this, they say:

This world here is the Gārhapatya fire; the atmosphere is the Dhiṣṇya fires; and the sky is the Āhavanīya fire. Now, since the atmospheric world is not separated from this world, why does he build the Āhavanīya after building the Gārhapatya, and then the Dhiṣṇyas? Originally, these two worlds existed together. When they were being separated, that space which was between them became the atmosphere; its name was "Īkṣam" (the Seen). Before that, it was said, "this Īkṣam has come between," and therefore it is called "Antarikṣa" (the Intermediate Space). As for the fact that he builds the Āhavanīya after building the Gārhapatya: these two worlds were indeed first emitted. Then, having returned, he throws up the Dhiṣṇyas to ensure there is no gap in the ritual work; furthermore, while the two ends are being perfected, the middle is also perfected.

Now, therefore, they carry away the Nairṛta bricks. For the gods, having built the Gārhapatya altar, ascended it; the Gārhapatya is indeed this world, so they ascended this very world after having prepared it. They beheld only that darkness which was invisible.

They said, "Consider how we may drive away this darkness, this evil. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer (citi)"; "Seek a layer" means, "Construct it so that we may drive away this darkness, this evil."

As they were reflecting, they saw these bricks belonging to Nirṛti; they laid them down, and by means of them they struck away that darkness, that evil. For Nirṛti is indeed evil; and because they struck away evil, Nirṛti, by means of these, therefore these bricks belong to Nirṛti (nairṛtyaḥ).

This very thing is now performed which the gods performed; that evil was indeed driven away by the gods themselves. But when he performs this [rite], it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did"; furthermore, whatever evil there is, whatever destruction (nirṛti), that he drives away by means of these [verses].
Because he drives away evil and destruction by means of these, therefore they are called *nairṛtya* (pertaining to Nirṛti).
Furthermore, as for why they carry these Nairṛti bricks:

when the gods restored Prajāpati after he had fallen apart, they poured him, who had become seed, into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb—for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, they prepared this year as a foundation; this world is indeed the Gārhapatya fire, and in it they procreated him. Whatever evil, whatever mucus, whatever membrane, and whatever afterbirth there was of him, that they removed from him by means of these bricks. Because they thereby removed his evil and Nirṛti (Destruction), therefore these bricks are called Nairṛti.

In the same way, the sacrificer pours himself as seed into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb; for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, she prepares this foundation after a year—this very world; for this world is the Gārhapatya fire. In it he procreates him. Whatever evil, whatever phlegm, whatever inner membrane, and whatever outer membrane belongs to him, that he removes from him by means of these [bricks]. Because he thus removes his evil and destruction (nirṛti) by means of these, therefore they are called Nairṛtī bricks.

They are a foot high; he thus places that evil, Nirṛti, beneath his feet. They are without marks; for what does not exist is unmarked—he thus makes that non-existent evil into Nirṛti. They are baked with husks; for husks belong to Nirṛti; by means of those belonging to Nirṛti, he performs this rite belonging to Nirṛti. They are black, for that darkness was black, and moreover, Nirṛti is indeed black.

With those [bricks], they go in this direction. This is indeed the quarter of Nirṛti; thus he places Nirṛti in that very quarter of Nirṛti. Where there may be a self-made pit, a cleft, or a chasm, there he should lay them down; or where the earth of this [site] is rent asunder, or where plants do not grow—there he seizes Nirṛti for her. Thus he places Nirṛti in that very part of the earth belonging to Nirṛti. Having made them "world-sharers" by laying them down facing away from him, he lays them down.
"He seeks him who does not press [the Soma] and does not sacrifice.

Indeed, Nirṛti seeks out him who neither presses nor sacrifices; "follow the track of the thief, follow the track of the robber"—this means "follow the track of the thief and follow the track of the robber," and also, "as a thief or a robber goes into hiding, so go into hiding"; "seek another than us"—this means "seek one who does not possess such knowledge"; "O Goddess Nirṛti, let there be homage to you"—by this act of homage he drives her away.

"Homage be to thee, O Nirṛti of sharp splendor"—for Nirṛti indeed has sharp splendor; he thus pays homage to her with these words. "Loosen this iron bond"—for with an iron bond indeed does Nirṛti bind him whom she binds. "In agreement with Yama and Yamī"—Yama is Agni and Yamī is this earth (the altar), for by these two everything here is held together; "in agreement with these two"—this is what it means. "Raise him up to the highest firmament"—the firmament is indeed the heavenly world; "raise the sacrificer up to the heavenly world"—this is what it means.
"I offer that which was in your terrible mouth."

Terrible indeed is Nirṛti; he offers this upon her seat when he performs that rite dedicated to her deity. "For the release from these bonds," he says, referring to those bonds by which one is bound. "Thee whom the people hail as 'Earth' (bhūmi)," he says; for this earth is indeed "Bhūmi," and he who exists becomes part of her. "I know thee thoroughly, O Nirṛti," he says; that is to say, "I know thee completely as Nirṛti. For this earth is indeed Nirṛti, and she causes him to perish who perishes. Just as if one were to say, "You are so-and-so, the son of such-and-such; I know you, do not harm me," even so does he speak this; for one who is known and addressed does not cause harm.

He does not touch it, thinking, "Nirṛti is indeed evil; let me not be touched by evil. He does not set it down, thinking, "Setting down is a firm foundation; let me not establish evil as a foundation. He does not recite the *sūdadohas* verse over it, for the *sūdadohas* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); he thinks, "Let me not connect or join evil with the vital breath."

Some place them facing downward on the far side, thinking, "Nirṛti is indeed evil; let us not follow after evil Nirṛti. One should not do so; one should place them facing away. Thus, one drives away evil Nirṛti in a direction away from oneself.
He lays down three bricks.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he repels evil and destruction.
Then [he places] a stool and a sling.

He places the *ruk*, the noose, and the *iṇḍva* in that second half; for the noose belongs to Nirṛti, and thus he is released from the noose of Nirṛti with the words: "The noose which the goddess Nirṛti bound upon thy neck, so that it could not be untied"—for by one who does not know this, it would indeed be un-tieable. "That I loosen for thee, not from the middle of thy life"—life, indeed, is Agni; and that which is the built Gārhapatya is its middle, while the Āhavanīya is unbuilt; therefore, whether a young man builds the fire-altar or an old man, he says, "not from the middle of thy life. Then: "Eat this food, being impelled"—food is indeed *pitṛ*; thus, "eat this food, being set free. These verses are in the *triṣṭubh* metre; the *triṣṭubh* is a thunderbolt, and by means of the thunderbolt he thus repels evil, Nirṛti.

There are three bricks: the throne-seat, the sling, and the loop for the gold plate; then there are two *iṇḍva* stones—that makes eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he strikes away evil and destruction.

Then, between [the two fires], he pours out water from the *udacamas* vessel. Water is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of the thunderbolt, he thus interposes a barrier against evil and destruction (*nirṛti*). "Homage to Prosperity (*bhūti*), who has done this here," they say as they rise up. For it was for the sake of prosperity that the gods first performed this rite; they offered this homage to her. And so does this sacrificer now perform this rite for the sake of prosperity; he offers this homage to her. They go forward without looking back; thus they leave behind evil and destruction without looking back.
Having returned, he stands in worship before the fire.
For he acts improperly when he goes in that direction while the fire is only half-piled; he thus makes amends to it for the sake of non-injury.
Furthermore, as to why he worships [the Gārhapatya fire]:

the Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and the Gārhapatya is a foundation; for this earth is the foundation. Now, when he goes toward that direction, he goes, as it were, along a pathless way; therefore, when he worships, he returns to this very foundation and establishes himself upon this very foundation.

"He is the dwelling-place, the gatherer of riches"—for this world is indeed a dwelling-place and a gatherer of riches. "'He beholds all forms with his powers'"—this means he beholds all forms with his powers. "'Like the god Savitṛ, whose law is true, like Indra, he has taken his stand at the meeting of the paths'"—the significance of this is exactly as the sacrificial formula itself states.
Then he pours out the *prāyaṇīya* oblation.

At its call to the preparer of the oblation (*haviṣkṛt*), he releases his speech. Having released his speech, he performs the *stambayajus* rite; having performed the *stambayajus*, and having enclosed the site with the first enclosure and having drawn lines, he says, "Bring it thrice! and the Āgnīdhra brings it three times.
Having returned, he proceeds with the Prāyaṇīya offering.

Having proceeded with the Prāyaṇīya, he yokes the plough. For when the gods were about to consecrate him (Agni), they first gratified him with food; in like manner, this sacrificer, being about to consecrate him, first gratifies him with food. It is a plough (sīra); for "plough" (sīra) is indeed "flow" (sera); he thus bestows nourishment (irā) upon him.
It is made of Udumbara wood;
the Udumbara is indeed strength and sap, so he thus endows it with strength and sap. Having woven a fringe of Muñja grass, it is threefold; the significance of this has already been explained.

Standing behind the southern hip of the fire-altar and facing the northern shoulder as it is being joined, he addresses it with the mantra: "The seers yoke the ploughs; they stretch out the yokes separately. Those who possess knowledge are the seers; they indeed yoke the plough and stretch out the yokes separately. "The wise ones among the gods for the sake of bliss"—bliss is indeed the sacrifice; thus, "the wise ones among the gods stretching out the sacrifice."

"Yoke the ploughs, stretch out the yokes! For they indeed yoke the ploughs and stretch out the yokes. "Sow the seed here in the prepared womb"—for that which is the furrow is made into a womb for the seed; for were one to pour seed into what is not a womb, it would be just so [fruitless] when he sows in unploughed ground. "May the song and the quick hearing be full of bounty"—the song is speech and the quick hearing is food. "May the sickle come nearer to the ripened crop"—for when the food is ripe, then they approach it with the sickle. He yokes with two verses, a Gāyatrī and a Triṣṭubh; the significance of this has been explained.
He yokes the right ox first, then the left;
thus it is among the gods, for otherwise it is among men. It consists of six oxen, or twelve oxen, or twenty-four oxen, which is a correspondence to the year itself.
Then he ploughs it.

Ploughing is indeed food; for when the gods were about to prepare him (Agni), they first placed food within him. In the same way, this one, being about to prepare him, now places food within him from the front.
He indeed draws out only the body;

he does not place that food into the wings and the tail, but rather into the body. That food which is placed in the body protects the body and the wings and the tail; but that which is in the wings and the tail protects neither the body nor the wings and the tail.

He ploughs the first furrow from the southern half of the fire-altar, between the enclosing stones, towards the east, with the mantra: "May the ploughshares furrow the earth happily; may the ploughmen follow happily with the oxen. By saying "happily, happily," he indeed makes it successful, for that which is successful is "happily"; thus he makes this very [earth] successful.
Then, with the rear half [of the furrow], he ploughs towards the north, [with the mantra]:

"May the furrow be anointed with ghee and honey"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu). "Permitted by all the gods and the Maruts"—for both the All-gods and the Maruts are masters of the rain. "Full of vigor, swelling with milk"—milk is indeed sap; thus, "full of vigor, swelling with the sap of food," is what it means. "O furrow, turn towards us with milk"—that is to say, "O furrow, turn towards us with sap."
Then, with the second half-verse:

"The plough, well-pointed"—this means "the plough, rich in wealth"; "auspicious, seeking Soma"—Soma is indeed food, and that he digs up; "a cow, a fat ewe, and a plump one"—and "a wagon for a chariot," for all this he digs up as he ploughs.
Then, with the first half-verse, he ploughs the southern furrow:

"O yielder of desires, milk forth desire for Mitra and Varuṇa, for Indra, for the two Aśvins, for Pūṣan, for progeny, and for the plants. Agriculture indeed belongs to all the gods; thus he says, "Milk forth all desires for these deities. He ploughs first with "iti," then with "atha," then with "iti," then with "atha"—that is the rightward turn, for that is the way among the gods.
He ploughs four furrows with a Yajus formula.
Thus, whatever food there is in the four quarters, that he places in him by means of this Yajus; for the Yajus is indeed truth (addhā), and these quarters are indeed truth.

Then he ploughs the body itself. Whatever food there is in the year, that he now places in it. He does so silently; for what is silent is undefined, and the undefined is everything. Thus, by means of everything, he places this food in it. He ploughs first [the head], then [the right side], then [the left side], then [the tail]; for that is the way of the gods (dakṣiṇāvṛt).
He ploughs three furrows each time;
Agni is threefold—whatever the extent of Agni, whatever his measure, by that much he bestows this food upon him.
He plows twelve furrows silently;
twelve months are a year, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much he bestows this food upon him.
These two groups together amount to sixteen;

Prajāpati consists of sixteen parts, and Agni is Prajāpati. Thus, he places in him food that is commensurate with his own self. Indeed, food that is commensurate with the self protects it and does not harm it; that which is more harms it, and that which is less does not protect it.
And again, as to why he ploughs it:

when the gods were about to prepare this [altar] for him, they first placed the vital breaths (prāṇas) in it; in the same way, this one, being about to prepare it, first places the vital breaths in it. There are furrows, for these vital breaths are indeed in the furrows.
He ploughs four furrows with a Yajus formula.

Thus he places those four manifest vital breaths (prāṇa) which are in the head into him. It is indeed by means of a Yajus; for the Yajus is truly the real (addhā), and these vital breaths in the head are indeed the real.
Furthermore, as for why he draws out the self:
he thereby places those vital breaths (prāṇas) which are within the self into this [altar]; he does so silently, for who indeed knows how many these vital breaths within the self are?

Then he unyokes them: "Having attained that desire for which you were yoked, be unyoked, O inviolable ones! For these are indeed inviolable among the gods; "O paths leading to the gods," for with these he performs a divine rite; "We have gone to the further shore of this darkness"—darkness is indeed hunger—thus, "we have gone to the further shore of this hunger"; "we have reached the light," for he who reaches the gods and the sacrifice reaches the light. Then he lets them loose toward the north-east; the significance of that has been explained. He gives them to the Adhvaryu, for he is the one who performs the work with them; however, he should assign them at the time of the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
Then he places a bunch of darbha grass.
For the gods then placed plants there; in the same way, the sacrificer now places plants there.

And as to why he lays down a bunch of *darbha* grass: when this [Agni] is built up, he is born; he is born for all kinds of food. Now, these *darbhas* are both kinds of food, for they are both water and plants. Indeed, those waters which, loathing Vṛtra, bubbled up on the dry land became *darbhas*. Because they bubbled up (*dṛbh*), they are called *darbhas*. These *darbhas* are pure and sacrificially fit waters that have flowed forth from Vṛtra. Since they are *darbhas*, they are plants; thus he gratifies him with both kinds of food.

Regarding the *sītāsamara*: speech indeed is the *sītāsamara*, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are the furrows (*sītā*); this meeting belongs to them. For food is placed within speech by means of the vital breaths; from the very middle he thus places food within him. He does so silently; for that which is silent is undefined, and the undefined is everything. By means of everything, he thus places food within him.
Then he makes an offering over it.

When this [Agni] is built up, he is born; he is born for the sake of all food. This ghee is the essence of all this, for it is the essence of both the waters and the plants. He thus gratifies him with the essence of all this. As great as the essence is, so great is the self; he thus gratifies him with the essence of all this by means of his own self. As great as the essence is, so great is the self; he thus gratifies him with everything by means of his own self. With fivefold-drawn [ghee], for the fire-altar has five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food does he thus gratify him.
And as to why he makes an offering over it:

when the Rishis, the vital breaths, first prepared this Agni, they assigned this share to him beforehand; therefore they are called "those who have a prior share. When he makes the offering, he thereby gratifies those very Rishis, the vital breaths, who previously assigned that share to him, with fivefold-drawn clarified butter; the significance of this has been explained.
And as to why he makes an offering over it:

whatever forms he is about to place upon this fire, whatever *stomas*, whatever *pṛṣṭhas*, and whatever *chandas* there are—for them he makes this a fore-share. It is these very things that he thus gratifies with the fivefold-drawn clarified butter; the significance of that has already been explained.

And as to why he offers over it: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "This work is long; surely the Rakṣases, the destroyers, might not slay this [Agni] here. They saw this completion before the conclusion of that work; they completed it entirely right there and built it up right there. In the same way, this sacrificer now completes it entirely right there and builds it up right there.
"In union with the year" is the layer (*citi*); "with the days" is the loose soil (*purīṣa*).

"In union with the Dawn" is the layer; "with the ruddy ones" is the loose soil. "In union with the Aśvins" is the layer; "with their wondrous deeds" is the loose soil. "In union with Sūrya" is the layer; "with Etaśa" is the loose soil. "In union with Vaiśvānara" is the layer; "with Iḍā" is the loose soil. "With ghee" is the layer; "Sva" is the loose soil; "Ha" is the layer.

These are thirteen utterances (vyāhṛtis). There are thirteen months in a year, and there are thirteen layers of earth (purīṣa) for the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. He offers with clarified butter; for this clarified butter is Agni—he thus builds up Agni himself. With fivefold-drawn butter he offers, for the fire-altar consists of five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great he thus builds him up. Holding it upwards, he offers; he thus builds Agni upwards by means of the layers.
Then he pours out the water-cups.

For the gods indeed said, "Meditate!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! While meditating, they saw rain as the layer; they placed it in this [fire-altar], and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it in this [altar].

There are water-scoops. Water, indeed, is rain; he thus bestows rain upon this [sacrificer]. With a cup made of Udumbara wood—its significance has already been explained—he uses one with four corners. There are indeed four quarters; he thus bestows rain upon him from all the quarters.
He pours out three cups of water each time;
Agni is threefold—whatever the extent of Agni is, whatever his measure is, by that much he bestows rain upon him.
He pours out twelve water-cups on the ploughed ground.
There are twelve months in a year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he bestows rain upon this [earth].

He pours it out on the ploughed land; therefore it rains upon the ploughed land. If he were to pour it out only on the ploughed land and not on the unploughed, it would rain only on the ploughed land and not on the unploughed. And if he were to pour it out only on the unploughed land and not on the ploughed, it would rain only on the unploughed land and not on the ploughed. He pours it out both on the ploughed and on the unploughed; therefore it rains both on the ploughed and on the unploughed.
He pours it out three times, both on the ploughed and the unploughed ground.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he bestows rain upon him.
Or rather, as to why he pours out the water-cups:
when the gods were about to consecrate him, they first placed water within him; in the same way, this one, being about to consecrate him, first places water within him.
He pours out three cups of water each time;
Agni is threefold—whatever the extent of Agni is, whatever his measure is, by that much he thus bestows water upon him.
He pours out twelve water-cups on the ploughed ground.
There are twelve months in a year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus bestows water upon him.

He pours it out on the ploughed land; he thus places water in the vital breaths. For if he were to pour it out only on the ploughed land and not on the unploughed, there would be water only in the vital breaths and not in the other part of the self. And if he were to pour it out only on the unploughed land and not on the ploughed, there would be water only in the self and not in the vital breaths. He pours it out both on the ploughed and the unploughed; therefore these waters are present in both places, in the vital breaths and in the self.
He pours them out on both the ploughed and the unploughed ground;
Agni is threefold, as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus bestows water upon him.
He pours out fifteen water-cups;
for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold; by means of this very fifteenfold thunderbolt, he strikes away all evil from him.
Then he sows all kinds of herbs.

The gods indeed said, "Meditate ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citim icata)! While meditating, they perceived food as the layer; they placed it in this [fire-altar], and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it in this [altar].

It becomes all-herbal medicine; for that food which is all-herbal is indeed all food, and thus he places all food in him. He should set aside one of those foods and not eat it for as long as he lives. With a cup made of Udumbara wood—its significance has already been explained—he sows with a four-cornered [cup]; for there are four quarters, and thus he bestows food upon him from all the quarters. He sows with Anuṣṭubh verses; for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and by means of speech food is eaten.
He sows with three verses each;
Agni is threefold—whatever the extent of Agni, whatever his measure, by that much he bestows this food upon him.
He sows on the ploughed ground with twelve verses.
There are twelve months in a year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows this food upon him.

He sows on ploughed ground; therefore food ripens on ploughed ground. For if he were to sow only on ploughed ground and not on unploughed, then food would ripen only on ploughed ground and not on unploughed; and if he were to sow only on unploughed ground and not on ploughed, then food would ripen only on unploughed ground and not on ploughed. But since he sows both on ploughed and on unploughed ground, therefore food ripens both on ploughed and on unploughed ground.
With three [verses] he sows on both the ploughed and the unploughed ground.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he bestows this food upon him.
And as to why he sows all kinds of herbs:
when the gods were about to prepare him (Agni), they first healed him with every medicine; in the same way, this one, being about to prepare him, now first heals him with every medicine.
It becomes a universal medicine;
for everything that is a universal medicine is a remedy for all this, and thus he heals him with every kind of remedy.
He sows with three ṛg-verses at a time;
Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he heals him.
He sows on the ploughed ground with twelve ṛg-verses.
Twelve months are a year, and Agni is the year; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he heals him.

He sows on the ploughed ground; he thereby heals the vital breaths. For if he were to sow only on the ploughed ground and not on the unploughed, he would heal only the vital breaths and not the other part of the self. And if he were to sow only on the unploughed ground and not on the ploughed, he would heal only the self and not the vital breaths. He sows both on the ploughed and on the unploughed; thus he heals both the vital breaths and the self.
With three [verses] he sows both on the ploughed and the unploughed ground.
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus heals him.

He pours out fifteen water-cups and sows with fifteen verses; that makes thirty. The Virāj consists of thirty syllables, and the Virāj is indeed all food. Thus, he bestows all this entire food upon him.

"The herbs that were born first, three ages before the gods"—the gods are indeed the seasons; thus these [herbs] are born three times before them: in spring, in the rainy season, and in autumn. "Of the brown ones, I..."—the brown one is indeed Soma, and the herbs belong to Soma. "The herbs have a hundred abodes"—this refers to the fact that this person has a hundred-year lifespan, a hundred-fold value, and a hundredfold strength; these are his hundred abodes. "And seven"—he thereby refers to these seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in the head.

"A hundred, O Mother, are your abodes, and a thousand are your shoots"—this refers to how you have grown forth in a hundred ways and a thousand ways. "And you, who possess a hundred powers, make this man of mine free from disease"—this means "whomsoever I am healing."
These [verses] have a single explanation;

they are directed toward this very [Agni], just as one would heal him and bring him across. They are Anuṣṭubhs; for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and speech is the universal remedy. Thus, by means of this universal remedy, he heals him.
Now, therefore, regarding those [rites] that are both defined and undefined:

with a *yajus* formula he yokes two oxen, silently the others; with a *yajus* he plows four furrows, silently the others; silently he places a bunch of *darbha* grass, with a *yajus* he makes an offering over it, silently he pours out the water-jars, and with a *yajus* he sows the seed.
This Agni is Prajāpati.

Both of these belong to Prajāpati: the defined and the undefined, the limited and the unlimited. Thus, when he performs with a Yajus formula, he thereby perfects that form of his which is defined and limited; and when he acts silently, he thereby perfects that form of his which is undefined and unlimited. Verily, he who, knowing this, performs it in this manner, restores Prajāpati in his entirety and completeness. The external forms are defined, while the internal ones are undefined; for this Agni is an animal, and therefore the external forms of an animal are defined, while the internal ones are undefined.

The Gārhapatya fire-altar is built up, while the Āhavanīya is not yet built up; then he purchases the King (Soma). This world is indeed the Gārhapatya, and the sky is the Āhavanīya; and that wind which blows here is this Soma. He thus places him between these two worlds, and therefore this wind blows between these two worlds.

Moreover, when the Gārhapatya fire-altar has been built but the Āhavanīya has not yet been built, he then purchases the King (Soma). Agni is the self and Soma is the breath; thus, he places that breath in the middle of the self. Therefore, this breath is in the middle of the self.

Furthermore, when the Gārhapatya fire-altar has been built but the Āhavanīya has not yet been built, he then purchases the King (Soma). The two fires are indeed the self, and Soma is the essence; he thus unites the self with its essence. Therefore, this very self is permeated through and through by its essence.

Having purchased and carried around the King (Soma), he then prepares for him the guest-offering (ātithya-havis). At the call to the preparer of the oblation (haviṣkṛt), he releases his speech; then he intertwines this sacrificial work of the Adhvara with the work of the fire-altar (agni-karma) for the sake of the uniformity of the ritual, so that "this ritual may be one and the same."

Moreover, as to why he interlinks them: the fire-altar is the self and the sacrifice is the vital breath; he thus places the vital breath in the middle of the self. Therefore, this vital breath is in the middle of the self.
Moreover, as to why he interlinks them:

the two fires are indeed the self, and the sacrifice is the essence; he thus attaches the self to the essence. Therefore, this very self is attached to its extremity by means of the essence. Then he goes halfway toward the Āhavanīya fire.

Now, some indeed sweep away with a Palāśa branch on both occasions, saying, "For on both occasions he piles [the fire]. One should not do so; for by means of the Gārhapatya he settles down, and by means of the Āhavanīya he rises upward. Therefore, one should not do so.
Then he pours saline soil (ūṣa) only on the Gārhapatya fire, not on the Āhavanīya.
The Gārhapatya is indeed this world, and saline soil is cattle; thus he places cattle in this world, and therefore these cattle are here in this world.
Then he places a lotus leaf on the Āhavanīya fire-altar, not on the Gārhapatya;

for the lotus leaf is water and the Āhavanīya is the sky: he thus places water in the sky. On both altars he scatters sand; for sand is seed, and it is everywhere that seed is transformed; therefore, [he does this] so that there may be transformation from that seed.

He pours them out with two different mantras. The Gārhapatya is indeed the world of men, and the Āhavanīya is the world of the gods; these two are distinct, namely the divine and the human. He pours them out over the Āhavanīya with a longer mantra and over the Gārhapatya with a shorter one, for the lifespan of the gods is longer and the lifespan of men is shorter. Before the enclosing stones, he pours sand over the Gārhapatya; sand is indeed seed, [thinking] "From this seed may these creatures be produced."
Regarding this they say:

"If the enclosing stones are the womb and the sand is the seed, then since he first pours the sand on the Gārhapatya fire before the enclosing stones, how is it that his seed becomes enclosed without being spilled? The saline soil (ūṣāḥ) is indeed the amnion; thus, when he first pours down the saline soil, by means of this amnion his seed becomes enclosed without being spilled. Then he consecrates the enclosing stones at the Āhavanīya fire; the significance of that has already been explained. Then he pours down the sand; the sand is indeed seed. Thus, by means of this womb, his seed becomes enclosed without being spilled.
Then he touches [the oblation] at the Āhavanīya fire with the two verses containing the word "āpyāna" (swelling), but not at the Gārhapatya.

For the Gārhapatya is this world, and the Āhavanīya is the heavenly world. Now, the sacrificer has indeed been born in this world; he is to be caused to be born in the heavenly world. Therefore, when he touches it at the Āhavanīya with the two verses containing "āpyāna," and not at the Gārhapatya, he thereby causes him to be born in the heavenly world.
Then he lays down the *logeṣṭakā* bricks.
These worlds are indeed this fire-altar; the quarters are the *logeṣṭakā* bricks. He thus places the quarters within these worlds; therefore, these quarters are situated within these worlds.
He brings fire from outside;
for those quarters which are within these worlds belong to him, and those quarters which are beyond these worlds—he now places them in this [fire].
This altar outside the sacrificial ground is indeed the altar;
those quarters which are within it have already been obtained by him, and now he places in this [altar] those quarters which are beyond it.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the space-bricks (*lokeṣṭakā*):

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital essence flowed away in all directions; when the gods restored him, they placed that essence in him by means of these space-bricks; in the same way, this sacrificer now places it in him.
He brings fire from outside;
for that essence of his which was in these worlds has been obtained, and he now places within this [fire-altar] that essence which had flowed away beyond these worlds.
This altar outside the sacrificial ground is indeed the altar.
That essence of it which has reached this [altar] is already obtained; now, that essence of it which flowed away beyond this, he places that very thing into this [altar].
He brings it with the wooden sword.
The wooden sword is indeed a thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is vigor; this [earth] is indeed found through vigor. One finds what is to be found through vigor.
He brings it from the front.

"May he not harm me, he who is the progenitor of the earth"—Prajāpati indeed is the progenitor of the earth; thus, "may Prajāpati not harm me. "He who, of true law, pervaded the sky"—that is, "he who created the sky of true law. "And he who first begat the shining waters"—the waters are indeed men; thus, "he who first created men. "To which god shall we do worship with oblation?"—Prajāpati is indeed Ka; thus, "to him let us do worship with oblation. Having brought that [brick], he places it within the enclosing stones upon his own self. Whatever essence flowed away in the eastern direction, that he now bestows upon this [altar]; moreover, he thereby bestows the eastern direction upon it.

Then on the south side: "Turn hither, O Earth, with sacrifice and with milk!"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. "The fire, impelled, has ascended thy omentum"—whatever indeed is upon her, that is her omentum; that the fire, being impelled, having been kindled, ascends. Having taken it, he places it upon himself between the two joints of the wings. Whatever sap flowed away in the southern direction, that he now bestows upon this altar; and thus he bestows the southern quarter itself upon it.

Then afterwards [he says]: "O Agni, that which is thy bright, that which is thy radiant, that which is thy pure, and that which is thy worthy of sacrifice"—Agni is indeed this earth; he thus speaks of her. "That we bring for the gods"—that is to say, "we bring that for this divine work. Having brought it, he places it within the junction of the tail and the body. Whatever essence flowed away in the western direction, that he now puts into this [earth]; moreover, he thereby bestows the western quarter upon it. He should not fetch it directly from behind, lest he should fetch the essence away from the path of the sacrifice; rather, he fetches it as if from a distance.
Then, from the north.

"I have taken from here sap and strength"—that is, "I have taken from here sap and strength. "'The womb of Ṛta'—Ṛta is indeed truth; thus, 'the womb of truth. "'The stream of the buffalo'—the buffalo is indeed Agni, for since he was born great, he has pervaded everything. "'May it enter me in the cattle and in my bodies'—the body is indeed the self; thus, 'may it enter me both in the cattle and in my self. "'I cast away exhaustion, hunger, and disease'—he thus scatters the sand. Whatever exhaustion, hunger, or disease there is, that he places in this direction; therefore, in this direction creatures are hungry. Having brought it back, he lays it down upon himself between the two joints of the wings. Thus, whatever essence flowed away in the northern direction, that he now places in him; moreover, he thereby bestows the northern direction upon him.

These are the quarters. He lays them down on every side; thus he establishes the quarters on every side. Therefore the quarters are on every side. On every side he lays them facing together; thus he establishes the quarters facing together on every side. Therefore the quarters face together on every side. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for the quarters are separate. Standing, he lays them down, for the quarters are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is indeed more powerful.
These are the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas (yajuṣmatya iṣṭakāḥ).
He places them only in the body (ātman), not in the wings or the tail; for it is in the body that the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas are placed, not in the wings or the tail.
Regarding this they say:

"How do these become cooked, boiled, and offered? Indeed, these are the essence, for the essence is self-boiled; moreover, whatever comes into contact with this Agni Vaiśvānara, that very thing becomes cooked, boiled, and offered.

Then he throws up the high altar (uttaravedi). This earth is indeed the altar; the sky is the high altar, and the quarters are the space-filling bricks (logeṣṭakā). Therefore, when he places the space-filling bricks between the altar and the high altar, he thereby places the quarters between these two worlds. For that reason, the quarters are between these two worlds. He makes it a yoke’s length on all sides, or forty paces, whichever way he may desire. Then he scatters sand; the significance of this has been explained.
He scatters them on the high altar (uttaravedi).

The high altar is indeed the womb; he thus pours that seed into the womb. For whatever seed is poured into the womb becomes capable of procreation. With these [bricks], he covers his entire self; he thereby places seed in his whole self. Therefore, seed originates from his entire self.

"O Agni, yours is glory and vigor"—smoke, indeed, is his glory and vigor, for it makes him famous in yonder world. "Greatly shine forth your rays, O radiant one"—greatly shine forth your rays, O possessor of abundant wealth. "O you of great luster, through your power, grant us food worthy of praise"—power is indeed strength; "O you of great luster, through your strength, grant us food worthy of praise"—this is what it means. "You bestow upon the donor, O wise one"—the donor is indeed the sacrificer; "you bestow upon the sacrificer, O wise one"—this is what it means.

"Purifying in luster, bright in luster"—for he is indeed purifying in luster and bright in luster; "with undiminished luster you rise up with your light"—that is, "with undiminished luster you shine forth with your light"; "the son, moving between the two mothers, attends them"—for he, as a son, moving between the two mothers, does indeed attend them; "you fill both worlds"—the two worlds are indeed heaven and earth, and he fills both of them: the upper one with smoke and this one with rain.

"O Jātavedas, Son of Strength, with excellent praises"—this means "O Jātavedas, Son of Strength, with beautiful hymns. "Rejoice, well-disposed toward our thoughts"—this means "shine forth, well-disposed toward our thoughts. "In thee they have placed abundant food, O thou of many forms"—this means "in thee they have placed food that has many forms. "Wondrous aids, born of beauty"—the significance of this is exactly as the sacrificial formula itself.
"O Agni, ruling, spread yourself with creatures"—creatures, indeed, are human beings;

thus it means, "O Agni, shining, spread yourself with human beings. "To us, riches, O immortal"—this means, "Bestowing wealth upon us, O immortal. "Of beautiful form, you shine forth"—for he indeed shines forth from that beautiful form. "You bestow winning power"—this means, "You bestow eternal power."

"The wise ordainer of the sacrifice" (iṣkartāram adhvarasya pracetasam)—the sacrifice is indeed the *adhvara*; thus it means "the wise ordainer of the sacrifice. "Dwelling in great bounty" (kṣayantam rādhaso mahaḥ)—this means "dwelling in great wealth. "The gift of lovely fortune, great nourishment" (rātim vāmasya subhagām mahīm iṣam)—this means "the gift of lovely fortune, great nourishment. "Thou bestowest winning wealth" (dadhāsi sānasim rayim)—this means "thou bestowest eternal wealth."

"Ṛtāvānam" means "the possessor of truth. "Mahiṣam" refers to Agni, for Agni is indeed the buffalo (mahiṣa). "Viśvadarśatam" means "visible to all," for this Agni is visible to all. "Agnim sumnāya dadhire puro janāḥ" means that people place him in front for the sake of bliss; "bliss" (sumna) is indeed the sacrifice, so they place him in front for the sake of the sacrifice. "Śrutkarṇaṃ saprathastamaṃ tvā girā daivyaṃ mānuṣā yuge" means "O divine one, we humans invoke you at every age with our song—you who have ears that hear and are most far-reaching"; that is to say, we invoke you, the god, with our song, you who are most far-reaching.

This very Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed this [altar]. These sand-grains are scattered for the sake of commencing; he thus pours into him the seed that is Agni Vaiśvānara. By means of a six-verse hymn, for there are six seasons, and the year is the sixfold; and the year is Vaiśvānara.
Regarding this they say:
"Since sand is called semen, what is the form of their semen? One should reply: "White," for semen is white; and also "speckled," for semen is, as it were, speckled.
Regarding this they say:

"When he scatters dry sand over moist seed, how do these [sands] become moist and take on the form of seed? The meters are indeed sap, and sap is moist; thus, when he scatters them with the meters, in this way they become moist for him and take on the form of seed.

Regarding this they say: "How is it that these [sand-grains] of his are placed by means of day and night? Indeed, day and night are two—the bright and the dark; and the two sand-grains are the white and the black. Thus indeed are these [grains] of his placed by means of day and night.

Regarding this they say: "How is it that these [bricks] are laid down by him as corresponding to the days and nights—neither deficient nor redundant? The days and nights are indeed infinite, and the sand-grains are infinite; thus, these [bricks] are laid down by him as corresponding to the days and nights—neither deficient nor redundant. And why is the *candas* (meter) "of the ocean" (*samudriya*)? The ocean is indeed infinite, and the sand-grains are infinite; therefore, the *candas* is "of the ocean."
Regarding this they say:

"How is it that these [sand layers] come to be laid down separately and diversely by means of the *yajus* formulas? The *yajus* is indeed the mind; thus this mind, which is the *yajus*, pervades all the sand. In this way, indeed, these [layers] of his come to be laid down separately and diversely by means of the *yajus* formulas.
Regarding this they say:

"How do these [bricks] of his come to be laid down with all the meters? Because he scatters them with this six-verse hymn; for as many syllables as there are in the seven meters, so many syllables are there in this six-verse hymn. Thus indeed, these [bricks] of his come to be laid down with all the meters.

Furthermore, as to why he scatters sand: this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the whole Brahman; and that which is the sand is the part of the Brahman that has been lost (utsanna), while that which is not lost is this very Agni who is being built up. Thus, when he scatters the sand, he restores to him that part of the Brahman which was lost. He scatters them uncounted and unlimited, for who indeed knows how much of the Brahman was lost? Verily, he who, knowing this, scatters the sand, constructs this Prajāpati in his entirety and completeness.

Regarding this they say: "What is the number of these countless [grains]? One should say, "Two," for there are two kinds of sand, white and black; or one should say, "One hundred and twenty-seven," for so many are the days and nights of the year; or one should say, "Two hundred and fifty-two," for so many are the syllables of this six-verse hymn; or one should say, "Twenty-five," for semen is twenty-fivefold.
These are the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas (yajuṣmatya).

He lays them down only on the body (ātman), not on the wings or tail; for it is on the body that the bricks possessed of sacrificial formulas are laid down, not on the wings or tail. He does not settle them, thinking, "Lest I should cause the seed and procreation to become stationary."
Then he touches them with two verses containing the word "swelling.

He thereby causes this seed that has been shed to swell; therefore, the seed that is shed swells within the womb. With two verses addressed to Soma—Soma being breath—he places breath into the seed; therefore, the seed that is shed comes into existence through breath. For were it to come into existence without breath, it would indeed putrefy. This *sūdadohas* verse here is indeed breath, for Soma is breath and the *sūdadohas* is breath.
Swell up; let [the waters] gather unto you.

"O Soma, [bestow] manly vigor from all sides"—manly vigor, indeed, is seed; "swell up, let [it] come together unto thee from every side, O Soma"—this means "let the seed [come together unto thee] from every side"; "be thou at the gathering of strength"—strength, indeed, is food; this means "be thou at the gathering of food"; "thy milks and thy strengths come together"—milk, indeed, is sap, and strengths are in food; this means "let thy saps and foods come together"; "manly vigor, overcoming the assailants"—this means "seeds, overcoming evil"; "swelling for immortality, O Soma"—he thereby bestows immortality upon procreation, and therefore procreation is immortal; "place in heaven the highest glories"—the moon, indeed, is his highest glory in heaven, for it makes him famous in yonder world. He causes [Soma] to swell with two verses, a Gāyatrī and a Triṣṭubh; the significance of that has been explained.

Now, therefore, regarding the correspondence of numbers: he lays down four earth-bricks; he scatters [the sand] with a verse of six lines; he causes it to swell with two verses. That makes twelve. Twelve months are a year, and Agni is the year. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does this become.

Having touched [the altar] with the two "filling" verses, he returns and proceeds with the guest-offering (ātithyeṣṭi). Having performed the guest-offering, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites. Having performed the Pravargya and Upasad rites, they then settle this layer (citi) upon the hide. As for why it is on a hide: the hide is indeed form; it is for the attainment of forms. It is on the hairy side; the hair is indeed form; it is for the attainment of forms. It is on a red one, for all forms are indeed red; it is for the attainment of all forms. It is on the hide of an ox; the ox is Agni; it is for the attainment of the forms of Agni. It is with the neck toward the east, for that is the way among the gods.

With the tip of that [sacrificial grass], he spreads it before the Gārhapatya fire, within the altar, with the hair-side upwards and the point directed eastward; they then settle this layer (citi) together, and then he sprinkles it. As to why he sprinkles it: he thereby makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. He does so with clarified butter (ājya), for that is pure and fit for sacrifice. Moreover, it is to prevent [the sacrificer] from ascending again; for no other oblation whatsoever do they sprinkle with clarified butter. He sprinkles silently; for what is silent is undefined, and everything is indeed undefined. By means of the undefined, he thus makes it pure and fit for sacrifice. Moreover, it is to prevent him from ascending again; for no other oblation whatsoever do they sprinkle silently.
And as to why he sprinkles it: this is indeed the sacrificial food (havis), and he thus pours clarified butter over it.

For that sacrificial food which is anointed and which is poured over with butter is acceptable and pure. It is with clarified butter, for they pour clarified butter over the sacrificial food; silently, for they pour clarified butter over the sacrificial food silently. He does so with *darbha* grass, for they are pure and fit for sacrifice; with the tips, for the tip belongs to the gods.
Regarding this they say:

"Since he sprinkles only the first layer, how does this entire Agni become sprinkled? How is it led forward upon the hide? How is it led forward by the horse? In that he sprinkles the bricks of all the layers here, thus indeed this entire Agni of his becomes sprinkled; thus it is led forward upon the hide, and thus it is led forward by the horse; they then lift up this layer.
Then he says, "Recite for the fires as they are being hurled forth.

Indeed, when the gods were about to advance toward this sacrifice and were spreading it out, the Rakshasas, the destroyers, sought to strike them, saying, "You shall not sacrifice; you shall not spread the sacrifice! Having made these fires and these bricks into razor-edged thunderbolts, they hurled them at them; with these they struck them down. Having struck them down, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.

This very thing is done now which the gods did then; for those Rakṣases were already struck down by the gods. But when he performs this rite, he thinks, "I shall do what the gods did. Moreover, having made these fires and these bricks into thunderbolts with razor-sharp edges, he hurls them at whatever Rakṣas and whatever evil there may be; with these he strews them down. Having strewn them down, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and free from destructive powers.
As for the words "to the fires":
these altars are indeed many fires; and as for the words "to those being carried forth," he indeed carries them forth.
Regarding this, some recite:

"The fires belonging to the soil, in harmony with the downward-flowing streams. This has the form of a departure; one should not do so. Instead, one should recite Gāyatrī verses addressed to Agni that contain [words of] desire: "May Vatsa direct his mind toward thee," "To thee, O best of Angirases," and "Agni in his dear abodes."
He recites the verses addressed to Agni.

By means of verses concerning Agni, he obtains the forms of Agni; by means of verses concerning desires, he obtains desires. They are in the Gāyatrī metre, for Agni is of Gāyatrī nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he pours him forth as seed. There are three of them, for Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he pours him forth as seed. These amount to seven, together with the two repeated three times; seven-layered is the fire-altar, seven are the seasons, and the year is the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become. He recites them in a low voice; for seed here in the sacrifice is indeed in a low voice, and seed is poured out in secret. Reciting from behind, he follows along, guarding the sacrifice from behind by means of the metres.
Then they lead a white horse in front.

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay us here. They saw this thunderbolt—namely, yonder sun; for that horse is indeed yonder sun. Having struck away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the front with this thunderbolt, they attained well-being in a place free from danger and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer, having struck away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the front with this thunderbolt, attains well-being in a place free from danger and destruction. They approach the fire; they place the layer of the tail on the south side, and they make the horse step upon it from the north side.
With the verse beginning "That [Agni] from the northern quarter," they lead him eastward between the enclosing stones;

thereby he drives away evil from the eastern quarter. He leads him southward; thereby he drives away evil from the southern quarter. He leads him westward; thereby he drives away evil from the western quarter. He leads him northward; thereby he drives away evil from the northern quarter. Having thus driven away the Rakṣases and the destroyers from all quarters, he then releases him northward and eastward; the significance of this has already been explained.

He causes the horse to smell this layer as it goes westward. Yonder sun is indeed this horse, and all these creatures are these bricks. In that he makes it smell them, yonder sun thus smells these creatures. Therefore, indeed, everyone thinks, "I am this [whole world]," by virtue of Prajāpati’s creative power. And as to why he makes it smell it while going westward—it is because, as it goes westward, it smells all these creatures from behind.
Moreover, as to why he makes [the horse] smell [the earth]:

Yonder sun is this horse, and these worlds are these *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks. Thus, when he makes it smell, yonder sun thereby weaves these worlds together upon a thread; and the significance of that thread is what is above it.

Furthermore, as to why he causes [the horse] to smell [the water]: Agni went away from the gods and entered the waters. The gods said to Prajāpati, "Search for him; he will reveal himself to you, his own father. He, becoming a white horse, searched for him. He found him emerging from the waters upon a lotus leaf. He (Agni) looked at him, and he (the horse) scorched him. Therefore he scorched him; therefore the white horse has a face as if scorched, and is prone to having sore eyes. But he (Prajāpati), thinking only of the right moment or of doing him harm, said to him, "I grant you a boon."
He said:
"Whoever should seek you by means of this form, he indeed finds you. Thus, whoever seeks him by means of this form, he finds him; having found him, he indeed builds him up.

It should be white; for that which shines yonder has that as its form. If he should not find a white one, it may even be non-white; but it should be a horse. If he should not find a horse, it may even be an ox; for the ox belongs to Agni, and Agni is the remover of all evils.
Now, therefore, concerning the mounting itself.

Some indeed mount it from the front facing westward, or from behind facing eastward; one should not do so. This Agni is an animal; for when one mounts an animal from the front facing westward, he strikes it with its two horns; and when one [mounts] from behind facing eastward, he strikes it with its feet. One should mount it by means of the self alone; for that animal which one mounts by means of the self carries him across and does not injure him. They mount whatever animal they mount from the north side alone. Having mounted and performed the work pertaining to the high altar (uttaravedi) upon the fire, he should take the fire into himself. Having taken the fire into himself, he sings the Satya-Sāman and lays down a lotus leaf; from this [proceeds] its [further ritual].
Then, when evening has come, they lead this horse around.

For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakshasas, the destroyers, should slay this [horse] of ours here"; therefore, they made yonder sun its protector. Yonder sun is indeed this horse; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now makes that thunderbolt his protector.

Or he leads it around until the sun has set; for this [sun] becomes his manifest guardian by day, while the Rakṣases are indeed the companions of the night; thus he makes this thunderbolt his guardian throughout the night. He leads it around on all sides; verily, he makes this thunderbolt his guardian on every side. He leads it around three times; verily, he makes this triple-layered thunderbolt his guardian. Then he releases it toward the north-east; the significance of that has been explained. Then it turns back again; the significance of that is as stated above.
When about to build the fire-altar, he takes the fire into himself.

For he generates this very one from his own self; and as one is born from what [one is], such indeed one becomes. If he were to pile the fire-altar without having taken the fire into himself, he would generate a mortal from a mortal, a man from a man, one whose evil has not been struck away from one whose evil has not been struck away. But when he piles it after having taken the fire into himself, he generates fire from fire, an immortal from an immortal, one whose evil has been struck away from one whose evil has been struck away.

He takes it up, saying, "I take Agni first within myself"; thus he first takes Agni within himself. With the words, "For increase of wealth, for good offspring, for heroic strength," he thereby takes all blessings within himself. With the words, "May the deities attend upon me," he thereby takes all the gods within himself. Whatever he is about to produce from himself, all that he takes within himself. Having taken Agni within himself while standing, he then sits down and builds [the altar]. For this Agni is an animal; therefore, an animal, having conceived the embryo while standing, gives birth after sitting down.
Then he sings the *sāman* of truth.
Regarding this, the gods said: "Let us make truth his mouth; we shall become true; truth will follow after us; that desire of ours which we intend to accomplish with this [rite] shall become true."
They sang this true *sāman* in front;
they thereby made it his mouth, and they became truth. Truth followed after them, and that desire of theirs which they had when they performed this became truth for them.
In the same way, this sacrificer:
when he sings the *satya-sāman* in front, he makes truth his mouth; he becomes truth, truth follows him, and that desire of his which he performs with this [rite] becomes true.
Now, as for that which is Truth:

it is indeed the waters, for the waters are Truth. Therefore, they say that whatever the waters flow over is the form of Truth. The waters made themselves the beginning of all this; therefore, whenever the waters flow, then all this—that which exists here—is born.
Then he lays down a lotus leaf. The lotus leaf is indeed a womb; it is thus a womb that he lays down.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down a lotus-leaf: the lotus is indeed the waters, and this [earth] is their leaf; for just as this lotus-leaf here is placed upon the waters, so is this [earth] placed upon the waters. This is the womb of Agni, for this is Agni, since the whole of Agni is built up upon her. It is this very [earth] that he thus lays down. He lays it down immediately after the Truth; he thereby establishes this [earth] upon the Truth. Therefore, she is established upon the Truth; therefore, she alone is the Truth, for she is the most manifest of these worlds.
"You are the back of the waters, the womb of Agni."

"For this is the back of the waters; this is the womb of Agni; swelling on all sides around the ocean"—for the ocean indeed swells on all sides around him as he grows; "growing great upon the lotus"—that is, "grow great upon the lotus"; "spread out with the measure and width of heaven"—he thus strokes it along. For this Agni is yonder sun, and no one other than heaven is able to encompass his width; "having become heaven itself, sustain him"—this is what he thereby says. He lays it down with the *svarāj* formula, for self-sovereignty belongs to the waters. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; the significance of that has been explained.

Then he lays down the gold plate (*rukma*). Yonder sun, indeed, is this gold plate; for he outshines all these creatures. They call him "the shining one" (*rocaḥ*) cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. It is yonder sun that he thus lays down. It is made of gold, circular, and has twenty-one knobs; its significance has been explained. He lays down a knob below; for the knobs are its rays, and its rays are indeed below it.
He places it upon a lotus leaf;
the lotus leaf is indeed the womb, and thus he establishes it in the womb.
And again, as to why he places it on a lotus leaf: the lotus leaf is indeed a foundation;

this earth is the lotus leaf, and this earth is the foundation. For whoever is not established upon this [earth], even though he be far away, he remains unestablished. But this [sun] is established upon this [earth] by means of its rays; thus he establishes it upon this very foundation.
And as to why he lays down a lotus leaf.

Indra, having slain Vṛtra, thinking "I have not finished," entered the waters. He said, "I am indeed afraid; build me a fortress. They gathered together that essence of the waters which was there and raised it upwards; they made that for him into a fortress. Because they made a fortress (puram) for him, therefore it is called *pūṣkara*; they call it *puṣkara* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. In that he places it on a lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*), he establishes him upon that very essence of the waters which they gathered together and upon that fortress which they made for him.
"Brahman was born first in the east."

Yonder sun, indeed, is the Brahman; day after day he is born in the east. "From the boundary, Vena has opened the bright realms" (VS 13.3). The "boundary" is the middle; these worlds are the "bright realms," and yonder sun is Vena. Because, when about to be born, he looked out (avenat), therefore he is called Vena.
