He rises, raining down upon those very boundaries from the middle. "His lowest stations are near" (VS 13.4); the quarters, indeed, are his lowest stations, for upon them he stands. "The womb of the existent and the non-existent he opens" (VS 13.5). These worlds are indeed the womb of the existent and the non-existent, for that which exists and that which does not exist are born from these very worlds. He lays it down with a Triṣṭubh verse, for he is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Having settled it, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over it; its significance has already been explained.

Then he places the man. He is Prajāpati; he is Agni; he is the sacrificer. He is made of gold; for gold is light, and Agni is light; gold is immortality, and Agni is immortality. He is a man, for Prajāpati is indeed a man.
And furthermore, as to why he lays down the Puruṣa.

From Prajāpati, when he was relaxed, the beautiful body departed from his middle. When that [body] had departed, the gods abandoned him. Where the gods restored him, there they placed this beautiful body in his middle. In it the gods took delight; because the gods took delight (aramanta) in this beautiful body of his, therefore it is called "hiranya," for hiranya is what is truly delightful. The gods love the cryptic; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places this beautiful body in his middle. In it the gods take delight. That beautiful body of his is indeed the breath; he thus places the breath in his middle.
He places that gold plate (rukba) thereon.
This gold plate is indeed yonder sun; and that person who is in this orb—that very one he thus places thereon.

He lays it down face upwards. For the gods said, "If we were to lay these two facing downwards, they would burn up this entire world; if they were facing away, they would burn away from us; but if they were facing each other, this light would be between them, and moreover, they would injure one another. They laid one of them facing downwards and the other facing away. This gold plate (rukma) shines towards us with its rays, while this man (puruṣa) stands upright with his vital breaths (prāṇas). He lays him down facing forward, for this fire-altar is built facing forward.

"Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning"—for this Hiraṇyagarbha indeed arose in the beginning. "Born, he was the sole lord of all that exists"—for he, having been born, was the sole lord of all this that exists. "He supported the earth and this heaven"—for he indeed supported both heaven and earth. "To which god shall we offer worship with our oblation?"—Prajāpati is indeed Ka; thus, "to him let us offer worship with our oblation."

"The drop has fallen upon the earth and across the sky"—the drop is indeed that Āditya; he falls upon both the sky and the earth, meaning "upon yonder one" and "upon this one. "Upon this womb and upon that which was before"—this means "upon this world and upon yonder one," and also "that which is being piled here now and that which was piled there before. "Moving along the common womb"—for he indeed moves along this common womb. "I offer the drop according to the seven Hotṛ-offices"—the drop is indeed that Āditya, and the seven Hotṛ-offices are the quarters; he thus establishes that Āditya in the quarters.
He lays down two with two verses; the sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni:

as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus lays him down. He does so with two Triṣṭubh verses, for he (Agni) is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Having settled them, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over them; the significance of that has already been explained.
Then he sings the Sāman.
Indeed, the gods, having laid down this Person, saw him exactly as they see this dry plank.
They said, "Find out how we may place vigor in this person. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer; seek how we may place vigor in this person."

While they were reflecting, they saw this *sāman* and sang it; they placed that vigor (*vīrya*) into it. In the same way, he now places that [vigor] into him. He sings over the man; he thus places vigor into the man. He sings over the variegated one (*citram*), for Agni contains all variegated things. Having laid him down, he should not go around to the east of him, lest this Agni should injure him.

Then he worships with the names of the serpents. These worlds, indeed, are the serpents; they glide along by means of this entire [world]—whatever there is here. This Agni, indeed, is the self (ātman) of all these gods. Those gods, having laid down this self, were afraid, thinking: "Lest these worlds glide away from us by means of this self."
They saw these names of the serpents;

with them they worshipped, and with them they established these worlds for him and made them bend down. Because they made them bend down (*anamayan*), therefore they are called the "names of the serpents" (*sarpa-nāman*). In the same way, when the sacrificer worships with the names of the serpents, he establishes these very worlds for him and makes these worlds bend down; thus, by this means, they do not glide over his self.
Furthermore, as to why he worships with the names of serpents:

these worlds are indeed the serpents, for whatever creeps (sarpati) exists within these very worlds; thus, when he worships with the names of serpents, he pacifies everything that is destructive, whatever is harmful, and whatever is baleful within these worlds.

"Adoration be to the serpents, whichever ones are upon the earth; those in the intermediate space, those in heaven—to those serpents, adoration! By saying this, he pays homage to all the serpents that exist in these three worlds.

"Those arrows of the Yātudhānas"—some say these are those sent by the Yātudhānas who bite; or rather, those that dwell in the trees or those that lie in holes. "Homage to those serpents!"—he thus pays homage to those serpents that are in the trees and those that lie in holes.

"To those who are in the bright realm of heaven, or who are in the rays of the sun, or whose seat has been established in the waters—to those serpents, homage! Wherever these [serpents] may be, it is to them that he thus pays homage. "Homage, homage"—homage is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, he thus pays homage to them with this salutation. Therefore, one should not say to anyone who is unworthy of sacrifice, "Homage to you!"; for that would be as if one were to say to him, "Sacrifice to you! It is just so.
He worships with three [verses].

These worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he establishes these worlds for him. Moreover, by that much he pacifies all this. He worships while standing; for these worlds are, as it were, standing, and moreover, one who stands is indeed more powerful.

Then, having sat down beside it, he makes an offering upon it with clarified butter taken five times; the significance of this has been explained. Moving around it on all sides, he thus gratifies it with food from all directions.
And as to why he makes an offering over it.

Having laid down this self, the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should slay us here. They saw these Rakṣas-slaying *pratisaras* (protective amulets) with the verse, "Make thy strength wide-spreading like a net. For these *pratisaras* are indeed Rakṣas-slayers; by means of these *pratisaras*, having driven away the Rakṣases and destroyers from all directions, they prepared this self in a place free from fear and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer, by means of these *pratisaras*, having driven away the Rakṣases and destroyers from all directions, prepares this self in a place free from fear and destruction.
He offers with clarified butter.

The clarified butter is indeed a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, he thus repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers. With fivefold-drawn butter, for the fire-altar consists of five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers. With verses addressed to Agni—for Agni is light, the slayer of Rakṣases—he thus repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers by means of Agni himself. With Triṣṭubh verses—for the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt—he thus repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers by means of the thunderbolt. Moving around on all sides, he thus repels the Rakṣases and the destroyers from every direction.

Then, sitting to the east of the fire facing west; then from the north, facing south; then from the front, facing east; then, having gone around by the rear, sitting to the south facing north—that is a movement to the right, for that is the way among the gods. Then, having gone around again, sitting behind facing east—thus indeed his work becomes performed in the forward direction.
Then he lays down two offering-spoons (*sruc*).

The two spoons are indeed the arms; thus he restores the arms to him. As to why they are two spoons: the arms are indeed two spoons. This [spoon] is the shoulder-blade and this is the handle; there are two of them, for these two arms are two. He lays them down at the sides, for these two arms are at the sides.
He places one made of *kārṣmarya* wood to the south.

The gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike our sacrifice from the south. They saw this Rakṣas-slaying tree, the Kārṣmarya; having driven away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the south by means of this tree, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer now, having driven away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the south by means of this tree, performs this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. It is filled with clarified butter; for clarified butter is a thunderbolt—by the thunderbolt itself he thus drives away the Rakṣases, the destroyers, from the south.
Then he places an Udumbara branch to the north.
The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; verily, he thus bestows strength and sap upon it. It is filled with curds; curds are indeed sap; verily, he thus bestows sap upon it.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down two offering-spoons (sruc):

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, Agni took his fiery luster (tejas) and drew it away toward the south; he ate his belly there after drawing it out, and because he ate his belly after drawing it out, therefore the kārṣmarya tree exists. Then Indra, taking his vital force (ojas), stepped away toward the north, and he became the udumbara tree.
He said to them:

"Come here and give back to me that by which you have departed from me. He said, "Give us all food. They said, "Then enter me as my two arms. "So be it," they replied. He gave them all food; they entered him as his two arms. Therefore, food is prepared with the two arms and eaten with the two arms, for he gave all food with the two arms.

He places one made of Kārṣmarya wood on the south with the formula, "By Agni's brilliance, I settle thee. Whatever brilliance of his that Agni had taken away and drawn toward the south, he now restores that to him. With the verse, "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit,"—for that Agni is indeed this very one—he places it with a Gāyatrī verse; for Agni is of Gāyatra nature: as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much does he place it. It is filled with ghee; for ghee belongs to Agni; thus he gratifies him with his own portion, with his own delight.
Then he places a block of udumbara wood to the north.

With the words, "By Indra's power I settle thee," he places that very power of his—Indra’s power—which Indra took and went away toward the north, back into him; with the words, "Thou art the leader of the sacrifice and of the region," for he indeed is that Indra. As for its being addressed to Agni, it is because it is a rite for Agni; and as for its being a Triṣṭubh, it is because Indra is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Since Agni is of the nature of Indra and Agni, he thus lays it down with as much as Agni is, with as much as is his measure. Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods, and Agni belongs to all the deities; he thus lays it down with as much as Agni is, with as much as is his measure. It is filled with curds; for curds belong to Indra—he thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence.

Indra and Agni are indeed his two arms; they approach him together with splendor and vigor. Having made a man appear on his chest at that very moment, wherever he reaches it, he draws them there and lays them down; for this is the world of these two.

Some lay these down crosswise, saying, "For these two arms are indeed transverse. One should not do so; one should lay them down facing eastward, for this Agni is built facing the east. Moreover, in this way the two arms are more powerful. He lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these two arms are separate.

Regarding this they say: "One should not make arms for this man, for these two spoons are his arms; let me not make an excess. However, one should indeed make them, for these two spoons follow after these two arms of his; moreover, they are his two wings; furthermore, whatever forms he is about to place upon this fire-altar, whatever *stomas*, whatever *pṛṣṭhas*, and whatever *chandas* there are—these constitute the formation and the growth of those two. Therefore, one should indeed make the two arms of this man.

He lays down the *svayamātṛṇā* brick. This earth, indeed, is the *svayamātṛṇā*; it is this very earth that he thus lays down. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the man; for the *svayamātṛṇā* is food, and this earth is the *svayamātṛṇā*, and this earth is food, since all food is cooked upon her. Thus he places food for him so that it is not separated from him; he places that food higher and higher for him.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *svayamātṛṇā* brick: the *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed breath, for it is by its own self that it pierces through; thus it is breath that he lays down. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the man. The *svayamātṛṇā* is breath, and this earth is the *svayamātṛṇā*; and this earth is indeed breath, for whatever is possessed of breath, all that it supports. Thus he places breath within him without separation; he places breath higher and higher within him.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick:
when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him and departed; as they were departing, he sat down, having reached a firm foundation.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and that which was his foundation is this first *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. Therefore, when he lays this down here, he restores to him that very part of his own self which belonged to her; for that reason, he lays this one down here.

He lays it down with the Prajāpati-formula; for Prajāpati himself laid this down from his own self. "Thou art firm" (dhruvā asi) means "thou art steady" (sthirā asi), and also "thou art established" (pratiṣṭhitā asi). "A support" (dharuṇā)—the support is indeed a foundation. "Spread by Viśvakarman"—Prajāpati is indeed Viśvakarman; thus, "by him thou art spread. "May the ocean not overwhelm thee, nor the eagle"—the ocean is indeed the gold plate (rukma), and the eagle is the person (puruṣa); thus, "may those two not overwhelm thee. "Unwavering, do thou make the earth firm"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu).

"May Prajāpati settle thee!"—for Prajāpati saw this first layer. "On the back of the waters, on the seat of the ocean"—for this is indeed the back of the waters and the seat of the ocean. "Widely extending, broad"—for it is indeed widely extending and broad. "Spread out! Thou art the earth"—that is to say, "Spread out! And thou art the earth."

"Bhūr asi" (Thou art Bhūḥ). "Bhūḥ" means this earth; "thou art the earth" means this very earth. "Thou art Aditi" means this [earth] is indeed Aditi, for she gives all this. "The all-sustainer" (viśvadhāyāḥ) means everything here is placed within her. "The supporter of the whole world" (dhartrī viśvasya bhuvanasya) means the supporter of the entire world. "Firm the earth, make firm the earth, do not harm the earth"—this means: "Firm thyself, make firm thyself, do not harm thyself."

"For all out-breathing and in-breathing, for diffused breathing and upward breathing"—the naturally perforated brick (*svayamātṛṇā*) is indeed the vital breath; "for all this," he says, "for support and for movement. These worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks, and these worlds are the support and the movement. "May Agni protect thee"—that is, "may Agni guard thee"; "with great well-being"—that is, "with great prosperity"; "with most peaceful shelter"—that is, "with that shelter which is most peaceful. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; its significance has already been explained. Then he sings a *Sāman*; its significance follows later.
Regarding this they say:

"How is it that this person is not laid down upon the *svayamātṛṇā* (self-perforated brick)? Food indeed is the *svayamātṛṇā*, and breath is the *svayamātṛṇā*; thus, a person is indeed not laid down [separately] from food and breath.

Then he lays down the Dūrvā-brick. The Dūrvā-brick is indeed cattle; it is cattle that he thus lays down. Those very cattle with which Agni here approached without interval—those he now lays down. He lays it down immediately adjacent to the Svayamātṛṇā brick. The Svayamātṛṇā is indeed this earth; he thus places cattle close to her. He lays each one higher than the last; he thus bestows cattle upon her in ascending order.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down a *dūrveṣṭakā* brick:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, those hairs of his that fell away became these plants; then, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departed from the middle of him, and when it had departed, he fell down.
He said, "Verily, this one has not injured me," because he said, "Do not injure me" (*mā adhūrvīt*), therefore it is *dhūrvā*;

they call it *dūrvā* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. This is the ruling power (*kṣatra*), for this is breath; the other plants are its sap. By laying down this brick, he lays down all plants.

Where the gods restored him, they placed this vital breath (*prāṇa*), this essence, in his center; in the same way, he now places it in him. He lays that [brick] immediately upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. For the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed this earth; thus he places plants upon her. He places each subsequent one higher than the last; thus he places plants upon her. It should have both roots and a top for the sake of completeness. He should lay it so that, once placed upon the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, it reaches the ground; for these [plants] are born from this very earth and grow along it.

"Growing forth from joint to joint, from knot to knot," for she indeed grows forth from joint to joint, from knot to knot. "So may you spread out for us with a thousand and a hundred"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

"Thou who extendest with a hundred, thou who growest forth with a thousand"—for she indeed extends with a hundred and grows forth with a thousand; "to thee, O divine brick, we shall pay worship with an oblation"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu). With two [verses] he lays it down; its significance has been explained. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; its significance has been explained.
Then he lays down the Dviyajuṣ brick.

Indra and Agni desired, "May we go to the heavenly world. They saw this brick, the Dviyajuṣ; they laid it down, and having laid it down, they went to the heavenly world from this foundation. In the same way, when the sacrificer lays down the Dviyajuṣ, he does so thinking, "By that same form and by performing that same rite through which Indra and Agni went to the heavenly world, may I go to the heavenly world. As for its name 'Dviyajuṣ', it is because those two deities saw it; and furthermore, as to why he lays down the Dviyajuṣ, the Dviyajuṣ is indeed the sacrificer.
Regarding this they say:

"He who is that very sacrificer is that golden person; now, what is his form? That [golden person] is his divine self, while this [sacrificer] is his human [self]. In that he is made of gold, that is his immortal form, for gold is the immortal form of a god; and in that this [altar] is made of clay, that is his human form.

If he were to lay down only that [brick] and were not to leave this one remaining, the sacrificer would quickly depart from this world. But since he leaves this one remaining, he thereby leaves behind that which is his human form; thus, by means of this self, he attains a full lifespan.

If he were not to place it alongside [the other bricks], he would not recognize this divine self; but because he places it alongside, he thus recognizes this divine self. He places it immediately adjacent to the *dūrvā*-brick; for the *dūrvā*-brick is cattle, and he thereby establishes the sacrificer in cattle.

Regarding this they say: "How do these two bodies of his become continuous and unbroken by means of the vital breath (prāṇa)? The *svayamātṛṇā* brick is indeed the vital breath, and the *dūrveṣṭakā* brick is the vital breath; the sacrificer is the *dviyajuḥ* brick. When he lays down the *dūrveṣṭakā* brick immediately after the *svayamātṛṇā*, he thereby makes the vital breath continuous with the vital breath and joins them together. And when he lays down the *dviyajuḥ* brick immediately after the *dūrveṣṭakā*—for the *dūrveṣṭakā* is the vital breath and the *dviyajuḥ* is the sacrificer—in this way, indeed, these two bodies of his become continuous and unbroken by means of the vital breath.

"Those lights of thine, O Agni, which are in the sun; those lights of yours, O gods, which are in the sun"—with these [verses] he lays down the *ruc* (light) one by one. Light, indeed, is immortality; verily, he thus bestows immortality upon him. He lays them down with two verses; the significance of this has been explained. Moreover, this form is twofold: clay and water. Having settled them, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them; the significance of this has been explained.
Then he lays down the two *retaḥsic* bricks.

These two worlds are indeed the *retaḥsic*, for these two worlds pour forth seed (*retaḥ*). From here, this [world] pours forth seed upwards as smoke; there it becomes rain. From there, they pour that rain back down; between these two, creatures are born. Therefore, these two worlds are the *retaḥsic*.

"Virāj has supported the light"—this world is indeed Virāj, and it supports this Agni as the light. "Svarāj has supported the light"—yonder world is indeed Svarāj, and it supports yonder sun as the light. Both these worlds are Virāj and Svarāj; he lays them down separately, for separate are these two worlds. He settles them once, thereby making them common; therefore, the ends of these two worlds meet together.

And as to why he lays down two Retahsic bricks: the two testicles are indeed the Retahsic; for he who has testicles is the one who pours forth seed. With the words, "The Virāj held the light; the Svarāj held the light,"—for these two testicles are indeed the Virāj and the Svarāj, and they both hold this light, namely the seed, and Prajāpati himself. He lays them down separately, for separate are these two testicles; he settles them once, thereby making them common; therefore they are connected by a common bond. He lays them down immediately after the Dviyajuṣ brick; the Dviyajuṣ is the Sacrificer, and thus he places the testicles immediately adjacent to the Sacrificer.
Then he lays down the Viśvajyotis (all-light) brick.

Agni indeed is the first Viśvajyotis, for Agni is indeed the all-light in this world; it is Agni that he thus lays down. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the two Retahsic bricks. The two Retahsic bricks are these two worlds; he thus places Agni in close proximity to these two worlds. He lays it down between them, for Agni is indeed between these two worlds.
And as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis (all-light) brick:

offspring indeed is the Viśvajyotis, for offspring is indeed all light; he thus lays down that which is procreation. He lays it down so as not to be separated from the two Retahsic bricks; for the two Retahsic are the testicles, and he thereby places procreation within the testicles. He lays it down between them, for within the testicles offspring is produced.

"May Prajāpati settle thee!"—for Prajāpati saw this first layer on the back of the earth as the luminous one; "on the back of the earth, the luminous one"—for this Agni is indeed luminous on the back of the earth.

"For all out-breathing, for in-breathing, for diffused breathing"—the Viśvajyotis is indeed the breath; he thus bestows breath upon this whole universe when he says, "bestow all light," which means "bestow every light. "Agni is your overlord"—he thereby makes Agni the overlord of this [brick]. Having set it down, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over it; its significance has already been explained.
Then he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*).

These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons that he lays down. "Madhu and Mādhava, the two spring seasons"—these are their names; it is by means of these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once; he thereby makes it one season.

Now, as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds. Of that [year], this world is the first layer; of this world, the spring season is the first layer. Therefore, when he lays these down here, he thereby restores to him whatever of his own self these two constitute; that is why he lays them down here.
And as to why he lays these two down here.

This Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; his foundation is indeed the first layer, for spring is his foundation. When he lays these two down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this body of his; therefore he lays these two down here. He lays them down immediately adjacent to the Viśvajyotis bricks. The Viśvajyotis are offspring; thus he places offspring immediately adjacent to the seasons. Therefore offspring are born following after the seasons; for by means of the seasons they perceive him while still in the womb, and by means of the seasons once he is born.
Then he lays down the Aṣāḍhā brick.
This earth, indeed, is the Aṣāḍhā; it is this very earth that he thus lays down. He lays it down in the eastern half, for this earth was created first.

She is named Aṣāḍhā. Both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, were contending with one another. Those gods saw this brick, this very Aṣāḍhā; they laid it down. Having laid it down, they overcame their rivals, their enemies, the Asuras, from all this [world]. Because they overcame (asahanta), therefore it is called Aṣāḍhā. In the same way, the sacrificer, having laid this down, overcomes his hateful rival from all this [world].

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Aṣāḍhā brick: the Aṣāḍhā is speech; by means of speech, the gods then overcame the Asuras—their rivals and enemies—from out of this entire universe. In the same way, the sacrificer now overcomes his hateful rival from out of this entire universe by means of speech. The gods thus laid down speech; in the same way, the sacrificer now lays down speech.
This earth is the bearer of the desirable (vāmabhṛt).

The desirable is indeed the vital breaths (prāṇa), for whatever is possessed of breath, she supports it all; therefore she is the bearer of the desirable. But speech, indeed, is also the bearer of the desirable. The desirable is the vital breaths, and food is placed within speech by means of the vital breaths; therefore speech is the bearer of the desirable.
All these vital breaths are this Aṣāḍhā brick.

He lays it down in the eastern half; he thus places the vital breaths in front. Therefore, these vital breaths are in front. He should not place any other brick possessed of a sacrificial formula (yajus) in front of it in this layer, lest he should cover over the vital breaths.

As for why he places five Vayasyā bricks in front: the waters are indeed food, and the vital breaths are not covered over by food. He places them immediately adjacent to the two Ṛtavyā bricks; thus he establishes speech within the seasons. This speech, established in the seasons, speaks.
Regarding this they say:

"Since the *viśvajyotis* and the *aṣāḍhā* are the offspring and speech, why does he place the two seasonal bricks between them? The two seasonal bricks are indeed the year; thus, by means of the year, he interposes speech for the offspring. Therefore, it is at the time of a full year that offspring utter speech.

"Aṣāḍhā art thou, the overcoming. For by her the gods indeed overcame the Asuras; "overcome the enemies, overcome those who attack," for as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance. "Thou art of thousandfold strength; do thou quicken me"—a thousand is indeed everything; thus, "thou art of all-strength; do thou quicken me," is what he says. Having settled her, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over her; its significance has already been explained.
Regarding this they say:

"Why are the other bricks laid down facing downwards, while these are laid down facing eastward? He should reply: "There are indeed two wombs; one is the womb of the gods, and the other is the womb of men. The gods have their procreation facing eastward, while men have their procreation facing westward. Therefore, when he lays these down facing eastward, he causes the sacrificer to be born from the very womb of the gods."

He lays down a tortoise. The tortoise is indeed essence; it is essence that he thus lays down. That essence of these worlds which, when they were cast into the waters, flowed away, is this very tortoise; it is him that he thus lays down. As great as the essence is, so great is the self; and this self is indeed these very worlds.

That which is its lower bowl is this world; it is as if established, for this world is indeed established. And that which is the upper bowl is the sky; it is as if its ends are drawn apart, for the sky has its ends drawn apart. And what is between them is the intermediate space. This [fire-altar] is these very worlds; he thus lays down these very worlds.

He anoints it with curds, honey, and ghee. Curds are indeed the form of this world, ghee that of the intermediate space, and honey that of yonder world; he thus endows it with its own forms. Moreover, curds are indeed the essence of this world, ghee that of the intermediate space, and honey that of yonder world; he thus endows it with its own essences.
"Sweet are the winds for him who observes the Law"—whatever deity a *ṛc* verse refers to, and whatever deity a *yajus* formula refers to, that indeed is the deity;

this triplet is that very deity, and this *yajus* is that very deity. And this triplet is indeed honey. Honey is essence; he thus bestows essence upon him. It consists of three *gāyatrī* verses; the significance of that has already been explained.

As for his being named Kūrma: having assumed this very form, Prajāpati created the creatures. Because he created (asṛjata), he fashioned (akarot); because he fashioned, therefore he is called Kūrma. Kaśyapa is indeed Kūrma; therefore they say that all creatures are descendants of Kaśyapa (Kāśyapī).

That tortoise is yonder sun; it is yonder sun that he thus lays down. He lays it down facing westward from the east; he thereby places yonder sun facing westward from the east, and therefore yonder sun is placed facing westward from the east. To the south of the Aṣāḍhā brick: the tortoise is a male and the Aṣāḍhā is a female; for a male lies to the south of a female. At the distance of a cubit: for a male lies at the distance of a cubit from a female. This Aṣāḍhā is the queen of all the bricks; being to the south of her, he comes to be to the south of all the bricks.

Moreover, as to why he lays down the tortoise: the tortoise is indeed breath, for breath makes all these creatures; it is breath that he thus lays down. He lays it down in front, facing westward; he thereby places breath in front, facing westward. Therefore, breath is placed in front, facing westward. He places it turned toward the man (the sacrificer); he thereby places breath in the sacrificer. It is to the south of the Aṣāḍhā brick; the tortoise is breath and the Aṣāḍhā is speech. Breath is indeed the male of speech; breath is the couple.
"He crosses over the depth of the waters.

For this is indeed the deepest part of the waters where he (the sun) now shines. "May the Sun not scorch thee; may Agni Vaiśvānara [not scorch thee]"—this means, "May the Sun not injure thee, nor may Agni Vaiśvānara. "Behold the offspring with unwithered wings"—for all these bricks which are here are indeed all these offspring; thus he says, "Behold them uninjured and unharmed. "May the celestial rain attend thee"—he says this so that the celestial rain may indeed attend him.
Then he makes it move: "He has glided along the three seas, the heavenly worlds.

These indeed are the three seas, the heavenly worlds; having become a tortoise, he has glided along them. "The lord of the waters, the bull of the bricks"—for he is indeed the lord of the waters, the bull of the bricks. "Clothed in soil, in the world of the well-done"—for soil is cattle; thus, "clothed in cattle, in the world of the well-done. "Go there where the ancients have passed away"—that is, go there where the ancients went by means of this rite.

"May the great heaven and earth for us"—that is, "may the great heaven and earth [be] for us. "May they sprinkle this sacrifice"—that is, "may they protect this sacrifice. "May they sustain us with nourishments"—that is, "may they support us with nourishments. With the last [verse], he lays down two relating to heaven and earth, for the tortoise is heaven and earth.

He lays down three [bricks]; these worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus lays him down. He anoints them with three [verses]; that makes six; the significance of that has been explained. There are Avakā plants below and Avakā plants above; the Avakās are indeed the waters; he thus places him in the midst of the waters. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over it; the significance of that has been explained.

Then he lays down the mortar and pestle. Viṣṇu desired, "May I be an eater of food. He saw these two bricks, the mortar and pestle; he laid them down, and having laid them down, he became an eater of food. In the same way, when the sacrificer now lays down the mortar and pestle, he does so with the thought: "By that form and by performing that act through which Viṣṇu became an eater of food, may I become an eater of food. These two, the mortar and pestle, are all food; for by means of the mortar and pestle food is prepared, and by means of the mortar and pestle it is eaten.
He places them on the line of the two Retahsic bricks.

The two Retahsic bricks are the ribs, and the ribs are in the middle; thus he places this food for him in the very middle. He places them on the northern side; he thereby places this food higher for him. It is at the distance of a cubit (aratni); for food is eaten from the distance of a cubit.
They become a span in size.

For Viṣṇu, the embryo, is indeed a span in size; this food is commensurate with his own self, and thus he places this food within him. Now, that food which is commensurate with one's self protects it and does not injure it; that which is more than that injures it, and that which is less than that does not protect it.

They are made of Udumbara wood. The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; he thus bestows strength and sap upon him. Moreover, since the Udumbara is all these trees, by placing these two, he places all trees. They are at the level of the two Retahsic bricks; for these two are the Retahsic, and it is in these two that he places the trees. Therefore, there are trees on these two [sides]. It is four-cornered; for there are four quarters, and thus he places the trees in all the quarters. Therefore, there are trees in all the quarters. In the middle it is contracted, for the sake of the form of a mortar.

Furthermore, as to why he places the mortar and pestle: when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital breath (prāṇa) sought to depart from the middle; he held it fast with food. Therefore, the vital breath is held by food; for whoever eats food, he breathes.
When the vital breath was seized, food sought to depart from him; he grasped it with the vital breath. Therefore, food is grasped by the vital breath; for whoever breathes, he eats food.
When both of these had been taken, Vitality (ūrj) desired to depart from him;
he seized it with both of these. Therefore, Vitality is taken by means of both of these. For whoever eats food, breathes, and is thereby strengthened—[it is by means of these two that this occurs].

When *ūrj* (vital energy) was seized, these two desired to depart from him; he seized them with *ūrj*. Therefore, both of these proceed by means of *ūrj*; for whoever gains *ūrj*, he breathes and eats food.

These [elements], having been grasped by one another, entered into the self by being grasped by one another; and as this food was entering, all the gods entered after it, for everything here lives by means of food.
Regarding this, the following verse has been uttered:

"He indeed became that breath"—for he indeed became that breath. "Having become great, Prajāpati"—for he indeed became great when these gods entered him. "'Enjoying, enjoying, having found (vittvā)'—the breaths are the enjoyers and food is what is enjoyed; thus, 'having found all this' is what it means. Because he caused the breaths to breathe within the body (*pūri*), and the self (*ātman*) is indeed what is filled (*pūryat*), and because he caused the breaths to breathe, therefore the breaths are the gods. And because Prajāpati caused them to breathe, therefore Prajāpati is the breath. That which is the breath is this Gāyatrī; and that which is the food is the deity Viṣṇu; and that which is the *arg* is this Udumbara tree.

He said: "Verily, this one has lifted me up from all evil. Because he said, "It has lifted me up (udabhārṣīt)," therefore it is called *udumbhara*. Indeed, they call it *udumbara* cryptically (*parokṣa*), for the gods love the cryptic. [Because he said,] "May it make wide room for me," therefore it is called *urukara*. Indeed, they call it *ulūkhalam* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. This mortar (*ulūkhalam*) is the womb of all vital breaths; the head, indeed, is the womb of the vital breaths.
It becomes the measure of a span;

for the head is, as it were, the measure of a span, being four-cornered; for the head is, as it were, four-cornered, being gathered together in the middle; for the head is, as it were, gathered together in the middle.
Where the gods restored him, they placed all this within him:

breath, food, and vigor. In the same way, he now places this within him. At the level of the two Retahsic bricks; for the two Retahsic are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle; thus he places all this within him in the very middle.

"Behold the deeds of Viṣṇu!"—the deed is indeed the power of Viṣṇu; thus he says, "Behold the powers of Viṣṇu. "From whom he has observed the vows"—the vow is indeed food; thus he means, "from whom he has made food manifest. "The fitting friend of Indra"—for he is indeed the fitting friend of Indra. He lays them down with a verse addressed to two deities, for the mortar and pestle belong to two deities. He settles them once; he makes them uniform, for this food is uniform. Having settled them, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them; the significance of that has been explained.

Then he lays down the fire-pan (ukhā). The pan is indeed a womb; it is thus the womb that he lays down. He lays it down upon the mortar (ulūkhalam); the mortar is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa). Whatever is above this [earth] is indeed the intermediate space. The intermediate space is the middle; he thus places the womb in the middle. Therefore, the womb of all beings is in the middle, even among the trees.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the fire-pan (ukhā):

Prajāpati, when he fell apart, was indeed this very pan; these worlds are the pan, and these worlds are Prajāpati. He places it upon the mortar; thus he establishes him in this entire universe—in breath, in food, and in strength—and moreover, he places him so that he is not separated from this entire universe.
Then, having ground the *upaśaya* and made it into a face-shaped vessel, he pours it in front of the fire-pan (*ukhā*); for this indeed is its place, and thus it remains unseparated from it.

Regarding this they say: "How does this become cooked, boiled, and prepared for him? It becomes so because it is consecrated with a sacrificial formula (yajuṣ); moreover, whatever one approaches this Agni Vaiśvānara with, by that very act it becomes cooked, boiled, and prepared.
"Thou art firm, a supporter,"—the significance of this has been explained.

"From here he was born first from these wombs, Jātavedas"—for indeed, from these wombs Jātavedas was first born. "May he, knowing, carry the oblation to the gods by means of the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Anuṣṭubh"—for it is by means of these metres that he, knowing, carries the oblation to the gods.

"Delight in food, in wealth; in power, in luster, in vigor, in offspring"—this means "delight in all this. "Thou art a sovereign ruler (samrāj), thou art a self-ruler (svarāj)"—for he is indeed both a sovereign ruler and a self-ruler. "May the two Sarasvatī springs flow toward thee"—Sarasvat is the mind and Sarasvatī is speech; these are the two Sarasvatī springs, and the meaning is "may those two flow toward thee. He lays it down with two verses; the significance of that has been explained. Moreover, this form consists of two things: clay and cattle. Having settled it, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over it; the significance of that has been explained.
Then he offers an oblation upon it.

For previously, this seed was indeed poured into her—namely, the sand—and now he covers that; therefore, the seed poured into the womb is covered. He offers with clarified butter, using a dipping-spoon (sruva), with the utterance "svāhā," and with two Gāyatrī verses addressed to Agni; the significance of this has been explained.

"O Agni, yoke those which are yours; yoke those who best invoke the gods"—with these two verses containing the word "yoke," he thus joins the seed in the womb; therefore, the seed joined in the womb does not come forth.

If it has been carried for a year, then he should offer oblations over it; for that which has been carried for a year is the whole, and what he offers over it is the whole. But if it has not been carried for a year, he should merely stand by it; for that which has not been carried for a year is incomplete, and what he stands by is incomplete. Nevertheless, he should indeed offer oblations over it.

This Agni is an animal; he is here entirely and completely prepared. His downward breath is the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; his hips are the *dviyajus*; the two *retaḥsic* bricks are his ribs; the *viśvajyotis* is his hump; the two *ṛtavyā* bricks are his neck; the *aṣāḍhā* is his head; and the tortoise—those vital breaths which are in the tortoise and those vital breaths which are in the head, they are those very breaths of his.

Now, he builds this very [altar] facing eastwards from here upwards; for this Agni is yonder sun, and thus he places yonder sun facing eastwards from here upwards. Therefore, yonder sun is placed facing eastwards from here upwards.
Then he turns him around from left to right;
he thus turns that sun around from left to right, and therefore that sun moves around these worlds from left to right.

The womb is the mortar; the upper hearth (ukhā) becomes the upper [part] and the lower mortar the lower [part], for the belly is above and the womb is below. The male organ is the pestle; it is as if rounded, for the male organ is as if rounded. He places it on the right side, for the male lies on the right side of the female. That which is the food of the prepared animal is the dūrvā-brick. Now, its northern half is more elevated; for this Agni is an animal, and therefore the left side of a well-fed animal is more prominent.

He lays down the heads of animals. The heads of animals are indeed cattle; it is cattle that he thus lays down. He lays them down in the fire-pan (ukhā). The fire-pan is these worlds, and the heads of animals are cattle; he thus places cattle in these worlds. Therefore, cattle exist in these worlds.
Furthermore, as for the fire-pan (ukhā):

the fire-pan is indeed the womb, and the animal heads are the cattle; he thus establishes the cattle in the womb. Therefore, although cattle are being eaten and cooked, they are not exhausted, for he establishes them in the womb.

Moreover, as to why he lays down the heads of the sacrificial animals: those glories (śrī) are indeed these heads of the animals; and those trunks (kusindha) are these five layers (citayaḥ). Now, those five layers are these worlds; and that which is this fire-pan (ukhā) is these very worlds. Thus, when he lays down the heads of the animals in the fire-pan, he thereby joins those trunks together with these very heads.
He places them in front, facing westward.

For when Prajāpati desired to seize these animals, they, being about to be seized, sought to flee away; he grasped them by their vital breaths, and having grasped them by their vital breaths, he placed them within himself from the front toward the back.
This very thing is done:

what the gods did, that he does now, thinking, "Lest these cattle of ours wish to stray away; rather, I shall do what the gods did. Moreover, having thus gathered them together within his vital breaths, he places them in himself from the front backward.
And again, as to why he lays down the heads of the animals.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He desired, "May I create food; may I procreate. From the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) he fashioned out the animals: from the mind (*manas*) the human, from the eye the horse, from the breath the cow, from the ear the sheep, and from speech the goat. Because he fashioned them out from the vital breaths, therefore they say, "Animals are the vital breaths. The mind is indeed the first of the vital breaths; because he fashioned the human out from the mind, therefore they say, "The human is the foremost of animals, the most powerful. The mind is indeed all the vital breaths, for in the mind all the vital breaths are established; because he fashioned the human out from the mind, therefore they say, "The human is all animals," for all these belong to the human.

Having created this food, he placed it within himself from the front toward the back; therefore, whoever creates food places it within himself from the front toward the back. That [food] is indeed in the fire-pan (ukhā); for the fire-pan is the belly, and thus he places that food in the belly.
Then he throws pieces of gold into them.

Gold, indeed, is breath; now, when these animals are being slaughtered, their vital breaths depart from them. Therefore, in that he throws pieces of gold into them, he thereby bestows the vital breaths upon them.

He throws [the chips] seven times. There are indeed seven vital breaths in the head; he thus places them in this [altar]. Now, if there should be five animals, he should throw them seven times each fivefold. For he lays down these five animals; and since there are seven vital breaths in each individual animal, he thereby places the vital breaths in all of them.

Now, some do it even when there is only one animal: they throw [the chips] seven times each five times over; for he lays down these five animals, and there are seven vital breaths in each single animal, thinking, "Thus we place the vital breaths in all of them. But one should not do so; for in this one animal is the form of all animals. Thus, what he throws into this one, that indeed places the vital breaths in all of them.
He first pours [the ghee] into the mouth [of the ladle], with the words:

"The streams flow together like milch-cows. Food, indeed, is the "milch-cows"; thus he says this so that food may flow together toward the mouth. "Purified within by the heart and the mind"—for food is purified by the heart and the mind when they exist within. "I behold the streams of that clarified butter of him who is upright"—by this he refers to those very oblations which he is about to offer into this fire. "The golden reed in the midst of the fire"—by this he refers to this very golden person.

With "To the Ṛc thee!"—the Ṛc is indeed breath, for by means of breath one praises; with "To the Ruk thee!"—the Ruk is indeed breath, for by means of breath one shines, and moreover, everything here shines for the sake of breath; with "To the Bhās thee!"—with "To the Jyotis thee!"—for these two eyes are indeed radiant and luminous; with "This has become the vigor of the whole world, of Agni Vaiśvānara"—here [is] Agni, luminous with light; with "The gold plate is resplendent with splendor"—here [he uses] two verses containing the word "all," for hearing is indeed all-encompassing.
Then he takes up the human head;
he thereby magnifies it, saying, "Thou art a giver of a thousand; for a thousand thee! A thousand is indeed everything; thus he means, "Thou art the giver of everything; for everything thee!"
Then he lays them down.

He places the man first; having reached him by means of his own vigor, he thus establishes him in the middle, with the other animals on both sides. He thereby places the man as the eater in the midst of the animals; therefore, the man alone is the eater in the midst of the animals.
The horse and the sheep he places to the north;
he thus places these two animals in that direction, and therefore these two animals are most numerous in that direction.
He places the cow and the goat on the south;
he thus places these two animals in that direction, and therefore these two animals are most numerous in that direction.
He places a man upon the milk.

Milk is indeed cattle; he thus establishes the sacrificer in cattle. "Anoint the solar embryo with milk"—the solar embryo is indeed this person (puruṣa); thus he means, "anoint him with milk. "The image of a thousand, multiform"—man is indeed the image of a thousand, for man is equal to a thousand. "Guard him with thy heat; do not disregard him"—this means, "protect him with thy flame; do not injure him. "Make him live a hundred years while being built up"—he thereby makes man among cattle one who lives a hundred years; therefore, man alone among cattle lives a hundred years.

Then, on the north side, he places the horse with the verse, "The speed of Vāta. For the horse is indeed the speed of Vāta; and with "the navel of Varuṇa," for the horse belongs to Varuṇa. With "the horse born in the midst of the flood," the flood (*sarira*) is indeed the waters, and the horse is born of the waters. With "the tawny child of the rivers, whose foundation is the rock," the rock (*adri*) is indeed the mountain, and the waters have the mountains as their foundation. With "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven," these worlds are indeed the highest heaven; thus, "do not harm him in these worlds"—this is what he means.

Then, on the south side, [he places] the cow with the verse, "The unceasing, ruddy drop" (*ajasram indum aruṣam*). The "drop" (*indu*) is indeed Soma; and this cow is that very Soma which is unceasing. "The supporter" (*bhuraṇyu*) means "the sustainer. With "I praise Agni, the first-thinker, with prostrations" (*agnim īḷe pūrvacittiṃ namobhiḥ*), [it is said]; for the cow belongs to Agni. "The first-thinker" (*pūrvacitti*); for they carry forth Agni toward the east, and they attend upon him facing the east. "He who is being fashioned according to the joints and the seasons" (*sa parvabhir ṛtuśaḥ kalpamānaḥ*); for when he (Agni) is piled up, then he is fashioned according to his joints and the seasons. "Do not harm the cow, the Aditi, the Virāj" (*gām mā hiṃsīr aditim virājam*); for the cow is indeed the Virāj, and the Virāj is food, and the cow is food.

Then, on the north side, [he places] a ewe with the verse, "The ewe, the protectress, the navel of Tvaṣṭṛ and Varuṇa. For this ewe belongs both to Varuṇa and to Tvaṣṭṛ; and with the words, "Born from the highest realm," the highest realm is indeed the ear, for the quarters are the highest realm, and the quarters are the ear. With the words, "The great, thousandfold magic of the Asura," he means "the great, thousandfold magic of the Asura. And with the words, "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven," the highest heaven is these worlds; thus he means, "Do not harm him in these worlds."
Then, on the south side, [he places] the goat with [the verse],

"The fire which was born from Agni"— for this fire was indeed born from Agni— "from the heat of the earth or from the sky"— for what was born from the heat of Prajāpati was born from the heat of both the sky and the earth— "by whom Viśvakarman generated offspring"— the goat is indeed speech, and from speech Viśvakarman generated offspring— "O Agni, may thy wrath spare him"— as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
These are the animals;
he lays them down separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for these animals are separate.
Then he makes an offering over the human head.
The sacrifice is indeed an oblation; thus he makes the man among the animals worthy of sacrifice. Therefore, it is the man alone who sacrifices among the animals.

Moreover, when he offers this upon it, he places vigor in the head. He offers with clarified butter; for clarified butter is a thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is vigor—he thus places vigor in him. With the utterance "svāhā"; for the "svāhā" is a bull, and the bull is vigor—he thus places vigor in him. With a Triṣṭubh verse; for the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is vigor, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor—he thus bestows vigor upon him by means of vigor.
Having recited a half-verse, he utters "svāhā.
For the Ṛc is indeed bone; having separated this skull-bone, he places therein that vigor which is within the head.
Then, having recited the latter half-verse, he utters "svāhā.
Joining together this skull-bowl, he places in it that vigor which is above the head.
"The brilliant array of the gods has risen"—this person there is indeed the sun;

thus, this brilliant array of the gods rises. "The eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni"—for he is the eye of both these, the gods and the humans. "He has filled heaven, earth, and the intermediate space"—for rising, he fills these worlds. "Sūrya, the soul of all that moves and stands"—for he is the soul of all this, both that which moves and that which stands.
Then he worships with the *utsarga* formulas.

For when Prajāpati desired to obtain these animals, they, being about to be obtained, became distressed; by means of these *utsargas*, they drove away their distress and evil. In the same way, this sacrificer now drives away their distress and evil by means of these *utsargas*.

Now, some indeed, when they set down whichever animal, release its impurity, thinking, "Lest we set down the impurity, the evil, upon [the next one]. But they actually do set down the impurity, the evil, upon it; for the impurity which they release from the preceding one, they set down together with the succeeding one.

Some, however, perform the worship while moving about, thinking, "We cast upward the heat. They indeed cast off the heat, which is evil, for by this rite one goes upward; thus they cast upward the heat.

He should cast out the fire externally. For this fire is these worlds; he thus places the impurity outside of those worlds. Outside the altar—this altar is indeed this earth—he thus places the impurity outside of her. Standing facing north, for in that direction are these cattle; he thus places the impurity upon those very cattle where these cattle are.
He first releases it for the person.

For he lays that one down first with the words: "Do not harm this two-footed animal. This two-footed animal is indeed man; thus, "do not harm him. "Thousand-eyed, being piled for the sacrifice"—he is thousand-eyed by means of the gold chips; "for the sacrifice" means "for food. "The Mayu animal, O Agni, accept as the victim"—the Mayu is indeed a Kimpuruṣa; thus, "O Agni, accept the Kimpuruṣa. "Building up thy bodies therewith, settle down"—the body is the self; thus, "building up therewith, perfect thyself. "Let thy heat reach the Mayu, let thy heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both upon the Mayu and upon him whom he hates.

Then for the horse: "Do not harm this one-hoofed animal"—for this horse is indeed a one-hoofed animal; thus he means, "do not harm him. "The loudly neighing steed among the prize-winners"—for he is indeed a loudly neighing steed among the prize-winners. "I assign to thee the wild Gaura"—thus he assigns the wild Gaura to it. "Building up thy bodies therewith, mayest thou sit down"—that is, "building up, perfect thyself with that. "May the heat afflict the Gaura, may the heat afflict him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both upon the Gaura and upon him whom he hates.
Now, concerning the cow.

"This thousand-streamed, excellent spring"—this cow, being milked, is indeed that thousand-streamed, excellent spring. "In the midst of the flood,"—the flood is these worlds; "being milked in these worlds," he means this. "Milking Aditi for ghee for the people"—Aditi indeed milks ghee for the people. "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven"—the highest heaven is these worlds; "do not harm him in these worlds," he means this. "The wild gavaya I assign to thee"—he thus assigns the wild gavaya to him. "Building up thy bodies therewith, settle down"—"building up therewith, perfect thyself," he means this. "Let thy heat reach the gavaya; let thy heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both upon the gavaya and upon him whom he hates.
Now, regarding the sheep.

"This woolly one"—that is, "the wool-bearing one. "The navel of Varuna," for the sheep belongs to Varuna. "The skin of animals, both two-footed and four-footed," for it is indeed the skin of both kinds of animals, the two-footed and the four-footed. "Tvashtar’s first-born among offspring"—for Tvashtar indeed fashioned this first form. "O Agni, do not harm him in the highest heaven!"—the highest heaven is these worlds; thus he means, "Do not harm him in these worlds. "I assign to thee the wild camel"—he thereby assigns the wild camel to him. "Building up thy bodies therewith, mayest thou sit down"—that is, "Building up therewith, perfect thyself. "May thy heat reach the camel, and may thy heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat upon the camel and upon him whom he hates.
Now, regarding Ajya:

"Unborn indeed was he born from Agni’s heat"—for what was born from Prajāpati’s heat was indeed born from Agni’s heat. "He beheld his progenitor in the beginning"—Prajāpati is indeed the progenitor; thus, "he beheld Prajāpati in the beginning. "By him the gods attained godhead in the beginning"—the goat is indeed speech, for by speech the gods attained godhead in the beginning. "By him the worthy ones ascended the ascent"—the heavenly world is the ascent; thus, "by him the worthy ones ascended the heavenly world. "I assign to thee the wild śarabha"—thereby he assigns the wild śarabha to him. "Building up thy bodies therewith, settle down"—that is, "building up therewith, perfect thyself. "May thy heat reach the śarabha, may thy heat reach him whom we hate"—thereby he places the heat both upon the śarabha and upon him whom he hates.
Regarding this they say:

"That pain and evil which Prajāpati drove away from these animals became these five animals; they have departed from the essence of sacrifice, they are impure and unfit for sacrifice. A Brāhmaṇa should not eat of them. He places them in this direction; therefore, in this direction Parjanya does not rain where these [animals] are."

Having returned, he stands worshipping the fire-altar. For he does what is improper when he goes outside the sacrificial ground while the fire-altar is only half-built; he now makes amends to that very fire for the sake of non-injury. With a verse addressed to Agni, he makes amends to Agni himself. With a Gāyatrī verse, for Agni is of Gāyatrī nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he makes amends to him. With an undefined verse—for the undefined is everything—with everything he thus makes amends to him. With one containing the word "yaviṣṭha," for "yaviṣṭha" (the youngest) is his dear abode. Indeed, because as soon as he was born he overcame all this, therefore he is called yaviṣṭha.

"O youngest one, [protect] the giver"—the giver is indeed the sacrificer; "protect the men"—men are indeed human beings; "hear our songs"—this means "hear this praise of ours"; "and protect our offspring and yourself"—offspring is indeed progeny; thus, "protect both the progeny and yourself."
Having ascended the fire-altar and gone around behind the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick, he lays down the *āpyā* bricks.

These *āpyā* bricks are indeed water; for water has departed from these animals. In that he lays down the *āpyā* bricks, he thereby places water into these very animals. He lays them down so as not to be separated from the animals; thus he places water within the animals without separation. He lays them down five by five, for there are these five animals. He lays them down on all sides; thus he places water into them on every side.

Now, those fifteen [verses] that come first are the *apasyās*; the waters are indeed the thunderbolt (*vajra*), and the thunderbolt is fifteenfold. Therefore, wherever the waters flow, they strike away evil right there; for the thunderbolt strikes away the evil of that region. Therefore, when it rains, one should walk about uncovered, thinking: "May this thunderbolt of mine strike away my evil."

Now, as for those five additional ones: they are the *candas* (metres). The metres are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; and meat is the food of cattle. Furthermore, it is from these cattle that meats have departed. In that he lays down the *candas*, he thereby places the meats back into these very cattle. He lays them down so as not to be separated from the cattle; thus he places the meats so as not to be separated from the cattle. The *apasyās* are inside and the *candas* are outside, for the waters are inside and the meats are outside.

Regarding this they say: "If these are the waters and these are the meats, then where is the skin and where are the hairs? Food, indeed, is the skin of the animal, and food is the hair. Now, when he lays down the *candasyā* bricks, that is the skin of the animal, and that is its hair. Furthermore, those hairless pieces which are in the fire-pan (*ukhā*) are the hairs. The fire-pan is on the outside and the animal heads are on the inside; for the hairs are on the outside and the body is on the inside. "Whether by one way or by another," Śāṇḍilya used to say, "we prepare all the animals in their entirety."
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Apasyā bricks:

from Prajāpati, when he had become relaxed, the waters flowed away; when they had flowed away, he entered into them, and because he entered into them, there are twenty of them. They flowed forth from his fingers; the fingers are indeed the extremities, and from the very extremities those waters flowed away from him.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those waters which flowed away from him are these very Apasyā bricks. Thus, when he lays down these bricks, he restores to him those very waters which flowed away from him; therefore, he lays them down here.
"With 'I settle thee in the wave of the waters,'" [he says].
Vāyu, indeed, is the wave of the waters; for when he blows hither and thither, then the waters flow. He settles it in Vāyu.
"With 'I set thee down in the surge of the waters,'" he says;
for the surge of the waters is indeed the plants, since wherever the waters moisten and stand still, there the plants are born; thus he places it among the plants.
"With 'I set thee down in the ashes of the waters,'" he says;
for the cloud is indeed the ash of the waters, and he sets it down in the cloud.
"I set thee in the light of the waters.
Now, lightning is indeed the light of the waters; he thus sets it in lightning.

"With 'I set thee down in the course of the waters,'" he says; for this earth is indeed the course of the waters, since the waters go toward it; upon this earth he sets it down. Thus, those waters which flowed away from these forms of his, he now restores to him; moreover, he thereby bestows these very forms upon him.
"In the ocean, I settle thee in thy seat"—the ocean is indeed the vital breath; he thus settles it in the vital breath.

"With 'I set thee down in the ocean as thy seat'—the ocean is indeed the mind; from the ocean that is the mind, the gods dug out the threefold knowledge with speech as their shovel. Regarding this, this verse is recited: 'The gods who dug out from the ocean with sharp shovels—may the fortunate man today know that place where they deposited the offering. The ocean is the mind, the sharp shovel is speech, the threefold knowledge is the offering; this verse is recited, and he thus deposits it in the mind."
"With 'I seat you on the body in the seat,' he seats it;
for the body is speech, and thus he seats it in speech."
"I settle thee in the abode of the waters.
The eye, indeed, is the abode of the waters, for therein the waters always abide; he thus settles it in the eye.

"With 'I settle thee in the seat of the waters,'" he says; for the seat of the waters is indeed the ear; he thus settles it in the ear. Whatever waters flowed away from these forms of his, those he now restores to him; moreover, he thereby bestows these very forms upon him.
"I settle you in the seat of the waters," he says.
The sky, indeed, is the seat of the waters, for the waters are settled in the sky; thus he settles them in the sky.
"With 'I set thee in the abode of the waters,' he sets it in the atmosphere; for the atmosphere is indeed the abode of the waters; thus he sets it in the atmosphere."
"I set thee in the womb of the waters," he says;
for the ocean is indeed the womb of the waters; he thus sets it in the ocean.
"I set thee in the soil of the waters," he says;
for sand is indeed the soil of the waters; he thus sets it upon the sand.

"With 'I set thee in the domain of the waters,' he sets it in food, for the domain of the waters is indeed food; thus he restores to him those waters which flowed away from these forms of his, and moreover, he bestows these very forms upon him."
"With the Gāyatrī metre I settle thee;

with the Triṣṭubh metre I settle thee; with the Jagatī metre I settle thee; with the Anuṣṭubh metre I settle thee; with the Paṅkti metre I settle thee. Thus, those waters of his which flowed forth from these metres, he now restores to him; moreover, he thereby places these very metres within him.

These are the fingers. He places them on all sides, for these fingers are on all sides; he places them at the ends, for these fingers are at the ends. He places them in four parts, for these fingers are in four parts; he places them five by five, for these fingers are five by five; he places them separately, for these fingers are separate. He settles them each once; he thus makes them uniform, and therefore the vital-airs (prāṇabhṛt) are connected with one another. He places them.

The vital breaths are indeed the "breath-supporters"; it is thus the vital breaths that he lays down. He lays them down in the first layer; for this first layer is the forepart of this fire-altar, and so he places the vital breaths in front. Therefore, these vital breaths are in the front.

He lays them down ten by ten; for there are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Even though he lays them down many times ten by ten, it is still ten each time. Five times he lays them down ten by ten; for he lays down these five animals, and in each single animal there are ten vital breaths. Thus he places the vital breaths in all of them. He lays them down so as not to be separated from the animals; he thus places the vital breaths in the animals without separating them from them. He lays them down on every side; he thus places the vital breaths in them on every side.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks:

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital breaths (prāṇas) departed, having become deities. He said to them, "Come to me; restore to me that by which you have departed from me. They replied, "In that case, create that food for us so that we may fast while looking upon it. "Then let us both create it," they said. "So be it. Then those vital breaths and Prajāpati created this food, namely these Prāṇabhṛt bricks.

He places it in front with the words, "This one was in front. Agni, indeed, is in front; as to why he says "in front," it is because they carry the fire forward and attend to it facing forward. And as to why he says "was" (*bhuva*), Agni is indeed "become" (*bhū*); for from Agni all this comes into being. Agni, having become breath, stood in front; it is that very form he thus lays down.
His vital breath is the son of the earth.

From that form, Agni, he fashioned forth the vital breath (prāṇa); [thinking] "Spring is the abode of the vital breath," he fashioned forth the spring season from the vital breath; [thinking] "The Gāyatrī belongs to spring," he fashioned forth the Gāyatrī metre from the spring season; [thinking] "The Gāyatra belongs to the Gāyatrī," he fashioned forth the Gāyatra Sāman from the Gāyatrī metre; [thinking] "The Upāṃśu cup belongs to the Gāyatra," he fashioned forth the Upāṃśu draught from the Gāyatra Sāman; [thinking] "The Trivṛt belongs to the Upāṃśu," he fashioned forth the Trivṛt Stoma from the Upāṃśu draught; [thinking] "The Rathantara belongs to the Trivṛt," he fashioned forth the Rathantara Pṛṣṭha from the Trivṛt Stoma.
The seer Vasiṣṭha.

The *ṛṣi* Vasiṣṭha is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Because he is the best (*śreṣṭha*), he is Vasiṣṭha; and because he dwells most extensively (*vastṛtama*), for that reason also he is Vasiṣṭha. "By thee, taken by Prajāpati"—that is, "by thee, created by Prajāpati. "I take the vital breath for the offspring"—thus he places the vital breath in front. He lays them down separately; he thereby places those various desires in the vital breath. He settles them once; he thus makes the vital breath one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cut the vital breath asunder. This brick consists of three parts: the *yajus*-formula, the settling, and the *sūdadohas* verse. That is threefold. Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—having made it so, he lays it down.

Then on the south: "This one on the south is Viśvakarman. This wind that blows here is indeed Viśvakarman, for he makes all this; and as to why he calls him "the southern" (dakṣiṇa), it is because he blows most predominantly toward the south. Vāyu, having become the mind, stood on the south; he now lays down that very form.
"His mind is indeed Vaiśvakarman."

From that form, Mind fashioned Wind; from Mind he fashioned the summer season, saying, "The summer is mental"; from the summer season he fashioned the Triṣṭubh metre, saying, "The Triṣṭubh belongs to summer"; from the Triṣṭubh metre he fashioned the Svara-sāman, saying, "The Svara-sāman belongs to the Triṣṭubh"; from the Svara-sāman he fashioned the Antaryāma cup, saying, "The Antaryāma belongs to the Svara-sāman"; from the Antaryāma cup he fashioned the Pañcadaśa-stoma, saying, "The Pañcadaśa belongs to the Antaryāma"; from the Pañcadaśa-stoma he fashioned the Bṛhat-pṛṣṭha, saying, "The Bṛhat belongs to the Pañcadaśa."

"Bharadvāja the Seer. Mind, indeed, is Bharadvāja the Seer; "vāja" (strength) is food. He who supports the mind supports food and strength; therefore, mind is Bharadvāja the Seer. "With thee, taken by Prajāpati"—that is, "with thee, created by Prajāpati"—"I take the mind for my offspring. Thus he places the mind on the south. He lays them down separately; those various desires that are in the mind, those he thereby bestows. He settles them once; he thus makes the mind one. Now, if he were to settle them separately, he would surely cut the mind asunder. This brick is threefold (*trivṛt*); its significance has been explained.

Then, afterwards: "This one behind is all-encompassing. Now, that which is all-encompassing is yonder sun; for as soon as he rises, this whole world becomes an open space. As to why he says "behind," it is because they see him only when he is moving westward. For the eye, having become the sun, stood behind; it is that very form he now lays down.
"His eye is indeed all-pervading."

From that, he fashioned the eye from the form [of the year] and the Āditya; "The rains are the offspring of the eye," thus he fashioned the rainy season from the eye; "The Jagatī is the offspring of the rains," thus he fashioned the Jagatī metre from the rainy season; "From the Jagatī, the Ṛkṣama," thus he fashioned the Ṛkṣama Sāman from the Jagatī metre; "From the Ṛkṣama, the Śukra," thus he fashioned the Śukra cup from the Ṛkṣama Sāman; "From the Śukra, the Saptadaśa," thus he fashioned the Saptadaśa Stoma from the Śukra cup; "From the Saptadaśa, the Vairūpa," thus he fashioned the Vairūpa Pṛṣṭha from the Saptadaśa Stoma.

"Jamadagni is the Ṛṣi. The eye, indeed, is the Ṛṣi Jamadagni; because by means of it one sees the world and also thinks, therefore the eye is the Ṛṣi Jamadagni. "With thee, taken by Prajāpati"—that is, "with thee, created by Prajāpati. "I take the eye for the subjects"—thus he placed the eye in the west. He lays them down separately; those various desires that are in the eye, those he thereby bestows. He settles them once; he thus makes that eye one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely split the eye asunder. This brick is threefold (*trivṛt*); its significance has been explained.

Then on the north: "This [brick] from the north, the light. The quarters are indeed the north; as to why he says "from the north," it is because the quarters are higher than this entire world. And as to why he says "the light," the quarters are indeed the heavenly world. The quarters, having become the ear, stood on the north; it is that very form he now lays down.

"His ear is the *sauva* [Soma-vessel]. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*); from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant.
