From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup; from the *manthin* cup, the twenty-one-fold hymn-form; from the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra. From the *vairāja* Pṛṣṭha-stotra, he fashioned the *vairāja* chant. From that form, the quarters, he fashioned the ear; from the ear, the autumn season; from the autumn season, the *anuṣṭubh* metre; from the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the *aiḍa* Sāman; from the *aiḍa* Sāman, the *manthin* cup
"The seer is Viśvāmitra."

The ear is indeed the seer Viśvāmitra; because one hears with it on all sides, and because everything becomes a friend (*mitra*) to him on every side, therefore the ear is the seer Viśvāmitra. With the words, "By thee, taken by Prajāpati," which means "by thee, created by Prajāpati," he says, "I take the ear for offspring. He thus causes the ear to reach the north. He lays them down separately; he thereby bestows upon the ear those various desires that exist in the ear. He settles them once, for he makes the ear one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cut the ear asunder. This brick is threefold (*trivṛt*); its significance has been explained.

Then, in the middle: "This one above is intelligence. The moon is indeed "above"; as for why he says "above," the moon is indeed above. And as for why he says "intelligence" (mati), speech is indeed intelligence, for by means of speech one thinks (manute) all this; and speech, having become the moon, stood above. He thus lays down that very form.
Speech does not transcend her.

From that form, the moon, he fashioned speech; "Winter is [the season] of speech," thus he fashioned the winter season from speech. "The Paṅkti is [the metre] of winter," thus he fashioned the Paṅkti metre from the winter season. "For the Paṅkti, the Nidhanavat," thus from the Paṅkti metre he fashioned the Nidhanavat Sāman. "For the Nidhanavat, the Āgrayaṇa," thus from the Nidhanavat Sāman he fashioned the Āgrayaṇa cup. "From the Āgrayaṇa, the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa," thus from the Āgrayaṇa cup he fashioned the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas. "From the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa, the Śākvara and Raivata," thus from the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas he fashioned the Śākvara and Raivata Pṛṣṭhas.

"Viśvakarman is the seer"—for Viśvakarman is indeed speech; by speech all this was made, therefore speech is Viśvakarman the seer. "By thee, taken by Prajāpati"—that is, "by thee, created by Prajāpati. "I take speech for the subjects"—with these words he causes speech to descend from above. He lays them down separately; those various desires that are in speech, those he thereby bestows upon it. He settles them once; he thus makes speech one. Now, were he to settle them separately, he would surely cut speech asunder. This brick is threefold (trivṛt); its significance has been explained.
This indeed is that food which the vital breaths and Prajāpati created; for the entire sacrifice is of this extent, and the sacrifice is the food of the gods.

He lays them down ten by ten; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is indeed all food: he thus bestows all this complete food upon him. He lays them down on every side; he thus bestows all this complete food upon him from every side. These very Virāj bricks sustain these vital breaths; because they sustain the vital breaths, they are called "Prāṇabhṛt" (breath-sustainers).

Regarding this they say: "What are the vital breaths? What are the sustainers of the vital breaths? The vital breaths themselves are the vital breaths; the limbs are the sustainers of the vital breaths, for the limbs sustain the vital breaths. But the vital breaths themselves are the vital breaths; food is the sustainer of the vital breaths, for food sustains the vital breaths.
Regarding this they say:
"How do all these [verses] of his become addressed to Prajāpati? Because he says in all of them, "With thee, taken by Prajāpati," in this way indeed all these of his become addressed to Prajāpati.

Regarding this they say: "Since one praises after the cup has been drawn and recites the Śastra, why then does he place the Ṛks and Sāmans before the cups? One must indeed look to the completion of the ritual action. For with an Ṛk as the introductory verse (pratipad), the cup is drawn; upon the Ṛk, the Sāman is sung. Therefore, when he places the Ṛks and Sāmans before the cups, that is his [preparation]. And when the Stotra and Śastra come after the cups, that is his [completion]; and when he places the Stomas and Pṛṣṭhas after the cups, that is likewise his [completion].
Regarding this they say:

"Since these three—namely the cup (graha), the chant (stotra), and the recitation (śastra)—are performed together, and here one sets down both the cup and the chant, how is it that the recitation is also set down for him here? Whatever is the chant, that indeed is the recitation; for those very verses upon which they chant, those same ones he recites after. In this way, indeed, the recitation is also set down for him here."

Regarding this they say: "Just as [one passes] from father to son, so do they speak of the first three [stages]; but why does he pass from the *ṛc* to the *sāman*? The *sāman* is indeed the husband of the *ṛc*. If one were to speak there also as [one does] from father to son, it would be as if one were to call a son his husband; therefore, he passes from the *ṛc* to the *sāman*. And why does he continue the sequence three times? He continues that sequence for the father, the son, and the grandson; therefore, he gives [the inheritance] to them one after another.

Those which he places in front are the Prāṇabhṛts; those which are behind are the Cakṣurbhṛts, and they are the Apānabhṛts; those which are on the south are the Manobhṛts, and they are the Vyānabhṛts; those which are on the north are the Śrotrabhṛts, and they are the Udānabhṛts; and those which are in the middle are the Vāgbhṛts, and they are the Samānabhṛts.

Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus lay down other bricks called the Apānabhṛts, Vyānabhṛts, Udānabhṛts, Samānabhṛts, Cakṣurbhṛts, Manobhṛts, Śrotrabhṛts, and Vāgbhṛts; one should not do so, for they shine forth excessively there. Indeed, all these forms are already laid down right here.
Having first laid down [bricks] in front, he lays them down behind.

For the out-breathing (apāna), having become the in-breathing (prāṇa), moves along as far as the tips of the fingers; and the in-breathing, having become the out-breathing, moves along as far as the tips of the fingers. Thus, by laying them down in front and then behind, he makes these two breaths continuous and joins them together. Therefore, these two breaths are continuous and joined.
Then, having laid them down on the south, he lays them down on the north.

For the out-breathing (vyāna), having become the up-breathing (udāna), circulates as far as the tips of the fingers; and the up-breathing, having become the out-breathing, circulates as far as the tips of the fingers. Thus, when he has laid them down on the south, he lays them down on the north; he thereby makes these two breaths continuous and joins them together. Therefore, these two breaths are continuous and joined.
Now, as for those which he places in the middle:

He places that vital air (prāṇa) within the range of the two Retahsic bricks. For the two Retahsic bricks are the ribs, and the ribs are in the middle; thus he places the vital air in the very middle of him. He places them on all sides; thus he places the vital air in him on every side. Moreover, this rectum is indeed the vital air; it is encircled all around the navel. He places them both lengthwise and crosswise; therefore these vital airs in the body run both lengthwise and crosswise. He places them so that they touch one another; he thereby extends and connects the vital airs. Therefore these vital airs are continuous and interconnected.
Some, having placed a man [on top], set it down.

This indeed is the vital breath (prāṇa), and these bricks sustain it; because they sustain the vital breath, they are called "breath-sustainers" (prāṇabhṛt). One should not do it in that way, for this golden person is indeed the vital breath itself, and this fire-altar which is laid out here is his body. If these bricks were not to reach its limbs, then the vital breath would not reach those limbs of his. And whatever limb the vital breath does not reach, that either withers or decays. Therefore, one should place them so as to be set right upon the enclosing stones (pariśrit). And those which he places in the middle—with them this body of his is filled; and they are indeed not separated from him.

Regarding this they say: "Since he says, 'This one in front is Bhuvas; this one on the south is Viśvakarman; this one behind is Viśvavyacas; this one on the north is Svar; this one above is Mati,' the quarters are thus recited in their proper order. But why does he lay them down in diagonal positions? The Prāṇabhṛts are indeed the vital breaths. If he were to lay them down according to the directions [in their proper order], this vital breath would indeed circulate only forward and backward. But because he lays them down in diagonal positions, even though they have been recited in that manner, therefore this vital breath, while moving forward and backward, circulates diagonally through all the limbs and the entire body.

This Agni is that very animal; he is here prepared whole and complete. Those bricks which he lays down in front are his two fore-limbs; those which he lays down behind are his two thighs; and those which he lays down in the middle are the body. He lays them down on the range of the two Retahsic bricks; for the two Retahsic are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle, for this body is in the middle. He lays them down on every side, for this body extends on every side.
Regarding this they say:

"Since in the preceding groups one lays down each single *stoma* and each single *pṛṣṭha*, why does he here lay down two *stomas* and two *pṛṣṭhas*? [The answer is: This is his very self; he thereby makes this self the eldest, the best, and the most powerful among the limbs. Therefore, this self is the eldest, the best, and the most powerful among the limbs.
Regarding this they say:

"How is it that this entire Agni becomes completely prepared in every single brick? The marrow is the Yajus-formula, the bone is the brick, the flesh is the placing (sādana), the skin is the *kṣudadohas* verse, the hair is the Yajus-formula for the loose earth (purīṣa), and the food is the loose earth itself. In this way, indeed, this entire Agni becomes completely prepared in every single brick.
This is that Agni who is the whole of life.
Whoever knows this Agni as the whole of life, he indeed reaches a full span of life.
Now, therefore, regarding the bending and stretching:

some touch the piled altar with the formula for bending and stretching, saying, "This Agni is an animal; when an animal bends its limbs and stretches them out, it then performs its strength by means of them."

"You are the *saṃvatsara*, you are the *parivatsara*, you are the *idāvatsara*, you are the *idvatsara*, you are the *vatsara*. May your dawns be in order; may your days and nights be in order; may your half-months be in order; may your months be in order; may your seasons be in order; may your year be in order. Go forth to return, come together and spread out! You are the well-winged eagle; by that divinity, like Aṅgiras, sit firm! Thus [he says].
Moreover, Śāṭyāyani used to say:
"One indeed heard the sound of two wings snapping together as they were being stroked with this [formula]; therefore, one should stroke it with this very [formula]."
Now, it is said that Svarhinnāgnajit spoke thus:

Either Nagnajit Gāndhāra said this, or it was Prāṇa. For breathing-in and breathing-out (sam-añcana-prasāraṇa) is indeed Prāṇa; for whichever limb possesses Prāṇa, that it bends together and extends. One should apply [the mortar] from the outside to that which has already been gathered; thus he bestows upon it the Prāṇa of bending and extending, so that it bends together and extends. That is indeed the bending and extending; as for what he said, "Like a kinsman of a Rājanya," he spoke thus because even if they were to apply [the mortar] from the outside a hundred or a thousand times, they would not truly bestow Prāṇa upon it. For that which is the Prāṇa in the self is the very same Prāṇa. Now, when he lays down the Prāṇabhṛts, he thereby bestows upon it the Prāṇa of bending and extending, so that it bends together and extends. Then he lays down two Lokampṛṇās in that corner; the significance of those is explained above. He scatters loose earth (purīṣa); the significance of that is explained above.
He lays down the second layer.
For when the gods had built the first layer, they ascended it; this world is indeed the first layer, and having prepared this very world, they ascended it.

They said, "Reflect!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer; seek it from here upwards. While reflecting, they saw this second layer: that which is above the earth and below the atmosphere. To them, this world seemed as if unstable and as if not firmly established in their minds.

They said to the two Aśvins, "You two are indeed the Brahmins and physicians; lay down this second layer for us. They asked, "What will come of that for us? [The others replied,] "You two alone shall be the Adhvaryus for our building of this fire-altar. "So be it," they said. Then the two Aśvins laid down this second layer for them. Therefore they say, "The two Aśvins are the Adhvaryus of the gods."
He lays it down.

"Seated on the firm, born from the firm, seated firmly"—for that which is steady and established is "firm. Now, this world of theirs seemed to them in their minds as if unsteady and unestablished; having made it steady and firm, they set it down with the words, "Seat thyself well upon the firm foundation"—that is to say, "Seat thyself well upon the firm foundation. "Rejoicing in the first banner of the Ukhyāgni"—the fire in the pan is indeed the Ukhyāgni, and its first banner is this first layer; "rejoicing in that," he says. "May the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, settle thee here"—for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryus who placed it there.

"Kulāyinī, Ghṛtavatī, Puraṃdhi"—for the second layer is indeed like a nest (*kulāya*). "Sit on the pleasant seat of the earth"—the first layer is indeed the earth; thus he means, "sit on her auspicious, pleasant seat. "May the Rudras and Vasus sing to thee"—this means, "may these deities sing to thee. "Swell these prayers for the sake of prosperity"—this means, "favour these prayers for the sake of prosperity. "O Aśvins, Adhvaryus, settle here"—for the two Aśvins were the Adhvaryus who laid [the bricks] down.

"By your own skill, O son of Dakṣa, sit here"—this means "by your own power, sit here. "For the great joy of the gods' assembly"—this means "for the great favor and the great joy of the gods. "Be like a father to his son, very gracious"—just as a father is pleasant and very gracious to his son, so be very gracious. "With a body that is easy of access, settle down"—the body is indeed the self; thus it means "settle down with a self that is easy of access. "May the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, seat you here"—for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryus who placed [the bricks] here.

"Thou art the soil of the earth. The first layer is indeed the earth; this second layer is like its soil. "Apsas by name"—that is, "Rasa (sap) by name. "May all the gods welcome thee"—that is, "may all the gods welcome thee. "With the Stomas as thy back, rich in ghee, mayest thou sit here"—those Stomas which he will spread upon her, with those she becomes "Stoma-backed. "Bestow upon us wealth with offspring"—that is, "bestow upon us wealth with offspring. "May the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, settle thee here"—for the Aśvins were the two Adhvaryus who placed [the layers].

These are the quarters. He places them within the range of the two Retahsic bricks; for these two are indeed the Retahsic, and thus he places the quarters within these two. Therefore, he places the quarters within these two. He places them on all sides; thus he places the quarters on all sides. Therefore, the quarters are on all sides. He places them facing each other on all sides; thus he places the quarters facing each other on all sides. Therefore, the quarters face each other on all sides. He places them separately, settles them separately, and pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over them separately, for the quarters are separate.

Then he lays down [the brick] in the fifth direction. That direction which is upwards is indeed the *dikṣā*; that upward direction is yonder sun; it is yonder sun that he thus lays down. He lays it down between the southern direction and that [brick]; he thereby places yonder sun between the southern direction and that [brick]. Therefore, this [sun] moves between the southern direction and that [brick].

"On the back of Aditi I set thee down"—Aditi is indeed this earth; he thus establishes him upon this very foundation. "The supporter of the atmosphere, the prop of the quarters, the mistress of the worlds"—for he is indeed the supporter of the atmosphere, the prop of the quarters, and the lord of the worlds. "Thou art the wave, the drop of the waters"—the wave is indeed sap. "Viśvakarman is thy seer"—Viśvakarman is Prajāpati; thus he means, "Thou art created by Prajāpati. "May the Aśvins, the two Adhvaryus, settle thee here"—for the Aśvins were indeed the two Adhvaryus who deposited [the bricks].
Furthermore, as to why he lays down these Ashvini bricks:

when Prajapati had become relaxed, the deities took him and departed. Of him, that which was above his foundation and below his middle, the Ashvins took that and stood apart after having stepped away.
He said to them: "Come near; restore to me that by which you two have stepped out from me.

They asked, "What will become of us from that? He replied, "This very thing shall become part of my own self, having you two as its deities. "So be it," they said. Then the Aśvins restored that to him.

Now, these five Ashvini bricks are that part of this self of his; in that he lays them down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this self of his. That is why he lays these down here.

"Of firm foundation, of firm origin, thou art firm. For that which is stable and firmly established is "firm" (*dhruva*). Now, this [altar] of his was, as it were, unstable and unfirm for himself; therefore, having made it stable and firm, they set it down.
"The nest-maker, the butter-rich, the wise one"—for this is indeed like a nest for his own self;

"with your own powers, O power-bestower, sit here"—this is for the sake of making his own self inexhaustible. "Thou art the soil of the earth"—for this is indeed connected with soil for his own self. [He places it] at the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the two *retaḥsic* are the ribs, and this is for the sake of connecting his own self with the ribs. He places it on all sides, for the Aśvins restored this for him on all sides.
Then he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*).

These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons that he lays down. "The bright and the pure, the two summer seasons"—these are their names; it is by means of these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once; he thereby makes it one season.
Now, as to why he lays these down here:

this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds. That part of it which is above the earth and below the atmosphere is its second layer; that is its summer season. It is for that reason that he lays these down here.

Moreover, as to why he lays these two bricks here: this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year. That part of him which is above the foundation and below the middle is his second layer; that is his summer season. In that he lays these two bricks here, he thereby restores to him that very part of his body which these two represent; therefore he lays these two bricks here.
Then he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks.
This indeed is that second layer which the Aśvins then laid down for these [worlds]; having laid it down, they came to possess all this, whatever exists here.

Those gods said, "The Aśvins have indeed become all this; find out how we may also obtain a share here. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! Seek how we may also obtain a share here. While meditating, they saw these Vaiśvadeva bricks.

They said, "The Aśvins indeed became this universe; let us lay down the layer of the Aśvins in accordance with the Aśvins. So they laid down the layer of the Aśvins in accordance with the Aśvins. Therefore, they call this the Aśvinī layer. Thus, as was the conclusion of the previous layers, so is the conclusion of these; for they laid down the layer of the Aśvins in accordance with the Aśvins.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks: those Viśve Devas who saw this second layer and who approached it with this essence—those very ones he now lays down. These are all creatures; he lays them down in the region of the two Retahsic bricks. For these two, the Retahsic, are these two worlds; thus he places creatures within these two worlds. Therefore, creatures are within these two. He lays them down on every side; thus he places creatures on every side, and therefore creatures are on every side. He lays them down following the regional (diśyā) bricks; thus he places creatures in the quarters, and therefore there are creatures in all the quarters.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks:
from Prajāpati, when he had become relaxed, all creatures went forth from the middle of this womb; they entered him once this part of his body had been restored.

He who was that Prajāpati who fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up. And those offspring which went out from his middle are these Vaiśvadeva bricks. Thus, when he lays these down, he causes those very offspring which went out from his middle to enter into him again. He lays them down on the level of the two Retahsic bricks; for the two Retahsic are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle: thus he causes these offspring to enter into him from the middle. He lays them down on all sides; thus he causes these offspring to enter into him from every side.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Vaiśvadevī bricks: when this part of his own self had been restored, Prajāpati desired, "May I create offspring; may I propagate. Having become united with the seasons, the waters, the vital breaths, the year, and the Aśvins, he produced these offspring. In the same way, the sacrificer, having become united with these deities, produces these offspring. Therefore, the word "in unison" (sajūḥ) recurs in all of them.
"In harmony with the seasons."

He generated the seasons; having indeed become united with the seasons, he generated them. "In harmony with the ordinances (vidhā),"—the ordinances are indeed the waters, for by the waters all this is ordained; having indeed become united with the waters, he generated them. "In harmony with the gods,"—he thereby generated the gods, those whom they call "gods. "In harmony with the gods who are the sustainers of life (vayonādh),"—the gods who are the sustainers of life are indeed the vital breaths, for by the vital breaths all this is bound together as life; moreover, the gods who are the sustainers of life are the meters, for by the meters all this is bound together as life. Having indeed become united with the vital breaths, he generated them. "For Agni Vaiśvānara, thee!"—Agni Vaiśvānara is indeed the year; having indeed become united with the year, he generated him. "O Aśvins, Adhvaryus, settle him here!"—having indeed become united with the Aśvins, he generated him.

With "In unison with the Vasus," he offers on the south; thereby he generated the Vasus. With "In unison with the Rudras," he offers on the west; thereby he generated the Rudras. With "In unison with the Ādityas," he offers on the north; thereby he generated the Ādityas. With "In unison with the All-gods," he offers above; thereby he generated the All-gods. These [verses] have the same beginning and the same end, but differ in the middle. Because they have the same beginning and the same end, he, having become united with the same deities both in front and behind, generated [the gods]; and because they differ in the middle, he generated various different offspring in the middle.
Then he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks.
For the gods said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer! While reflecting, they saw Vāyu as the layer; they placed it in him, and in like manner does this one now place it in him.

He lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks. Vāyu is indeed breath; he thus places breath in this [altar]. On the level of the two Retahsic bricks—heaven and earth are indeed the two Retahsic; it is in these two that he places Vāyu. Therefore, Vāyu is in these two. He lays them down on all sides; he thus places Vāyu on all sides. Therefore, Vāyu is on all sides. He lays them down facing each other from all sides; he thus places Vāyu facing in every direction. Therefore, having become oriented in every direction, he blows from all quarters. He lays them down following the Diśyā bricks; he thus places Vāyu in the quarters. Therefore, Vāyu is in all the quarters.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Prāṇabhṛt bricks: it is in these very offspring that he thereby places the vital breaths. He lays them down immediately after the Vaiśvadevī bricks; thus he places the vital breaths in the offspring without interruption. With the formulas, "Guard my out-breathing! Guard my in-breathing! Guard my diffused breathing! Make my eye shine far and wide! Make my ear famous!"—it is these well-ordered vital breaths that he thereby places in them.
Then he lays down the Apasyā bricks.

For the gods said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)! While reflecting, they saw rain as the layer; they placed it in this [fire-altar], and in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it in this [altar].

He lays down the Apasyā bricks. The waters are indeed rain; he thus bestows rain upon this [sacrificer]. He lays them down on the range of the two Retahsic bricks; these two are the Retahsic, and it is in these two that he bestows rain. Therefore, it rains in these two. He lays them down on all sides; he thus bestows rain on all sides. Therefore, it rains from all sides. He lays them down facing each other on all sides; he thus bestows rain facing each other on all sides. Therefore, having come together from all sides, it rains from all directions. He lays them down following those dedicated to Vāyu; he thus bestows rain in the wind. Therefore, to whichever direction the wind goes, rain follows that direction.

Moreover, as to why he lays down the Apasyā bricks: it is in these very vital breaths that he thereby places water. He lays them down separated from the Prāṇabhṛt bricks; thus he places water in the vital breaths without interruption. Furthermore, water is indeed food; he thus places food in the vital breaths without interruption. With the formula, "Swell the waters, quicken the plants; protect the two-footed and the four-footed; send rain from heaven," he thereby places this well-ordered water in these very [breaths].
Then he lays down the Chandasyā bricks.

For the gods said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer! While reflecting, they saw the cattle as the layer; they placed them in this [Agni]. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now places them in him.
He lays down the *candas* (metres).

The metres are indeed cattle; he thus bestows cattle upon him. He lays them down on all sides; he thereby bestows cattle on every side, and therefore cattle are found everywhere. He lays them down following the *apasyās*; he thereby establishes cattle in the waters, and therefore when it rains, then cattle find their firm support.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the metres:

when Prajāpati had become relaxed, the animals departed from him, having become the metres. Gāyatrī, having become the metre, reached them with vital power; because Gāyatrī reached them, for she is the swiftest of metres. Having become that, Prajāpati reached these animals with vital power.
"The head is vigor"—Prajāpati is indeed the head; he became vigor. "Prajāpati is the metre"—Prajāpati himself became the metre.
"Kṣatra is our strength.
Prajāpati is indeed the kṣatra; he became the strength (vayas). "Mayaṃda is the metre. That which is undefined is mayaṃda, and Prajāpati is indeed undefined; thus Prajāpati himself became the metre.
"Support, vigor"—Prajāpati is indeed the support;
he became vigor. "Overlord, meter"—Prajāpati is indeed the overlord; Prajāpati himself became the meter.
"Viśvakarman is the bird," he says.

Prajāpati indeed is Viśvakarman; he became the bird. "Parameṣṭhin is the metre," he says. Prajāpati is indeed Parameṣṭhin, for they (the waters) abide in the highest place; thus Prajāpati himself became Parameṣṭhin the metre.
And these, indeed, are they.

There are four ages and four meters; that makes eight, for the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables. This indeed is that Gāyatrī, which, having become that, Prajāpati reached these animals by means of age. Therefore they say of an old animal, "It has been reached by age. And therefore, in all cases, the word "age" (vayas) recurs as "age" (vaya). Now, those animals which went away from him are these fifteen [bricks] placed above; for cattle are a thunderbolt, and the thunderbolt is fifteenfold. Therefore, he who possesses cattle truly strikes away evil; the thunderbolt indeed strikes away his evil. Therefore, whichever direction one brings a beast, one follows that very direction which is established by the thunderbolt.
With "The goat by vigor," he obtained the goat through vigor; with "The triple-footed metre," the one-footed metre is indeed the triple-footed; having become one-footed, the goats went forth.
"Vṛṣṇi, vaya!"—with "vṛṣṇi," he attained vigor; "viśālaṃ candaḥ"—the *viśāla* meter is indeed the two-footed meter, and having become two-footed, the vital breaths (*vayaḥ*) departed upward.
"Puruṣa, vaya!"—he attained Puruṣa by means of *vaya*. "Tandra, chandas!"—*tandra* is indeed the *chandas* Paṅkti; for having become the Paṅkti, the Puruṣas departed.
"A tiger by age"—he attained a tiger by age.
"The invincible meter"—the invincible meter is indeed the *virāj*; the *virāj* is food, and food is invincible. Having become the *virāj*, the tigers stepped forth.

"The lion is the age," he says; by this he attains the lion through its age. "The Cadi is the metre," he says; for the Cadi is indeed the Atichandas, since it covers all the metres; having become the Atichandas, the lions stepped forth. Thereupon, he lays down the defined animals and the defined metres.
"A two-year-old ox in age"—he obtained a two-year-old ox as his age; "the Bṛhatī metre"—having become the Bṛhatī, they indeed went forth as two-year-old oxen.
"The bull, the strength"—with these words, they reached the bull with strength. "The *kakubh* meter"—having become the *kakubh*, the bulls stepped forth.
"Ṛṣabha is our age.
They attained the bull by means of their age; "Satobṛhatī is the metre"—having become Satobṛhatīs, they indeed went forth as bulls.
"Anaḍvānvaya" means "the ox obtained through age. [It refers to] the *paṅkti* metre; for having become the *paṅkti*, the oxen indeed went forth.
‘The cow with age’:
by means of age he obtained the cow; ‘the Jagatī metre’—having become the Jagatī, the cows indeed went forth.
"Tryavi as age"—he attains the three-year-old as age; "Triṣṭubh as meter"—having become the Triṣṭubh, they went forth as three-year-olds.
"Divyavāḍvaya" means that they attained the age of a *dityavāh* (a two-year-old horse); "Virāṭ chandaḥ" means that having become the *virāj*, the *dityavāh*s departed.
"Five-footed, fivefold. By means of his age he attained the five-footed; "the Gāyatrī metre"—for having become the Gāyatrī, they indeed stepped forth as five-footed.
"Trivatsa as vigor"—by means of vigor they attained the trivatsa; "Uṣṇih as meter"—having become the uṣṇih meter, the trivatsas indeed went forth.
Regarding the phrase "turyavāḍvaya":
having reached the age of a four-year-old draught-ox, they became the *anuṣṭubh* metre; and having become the *anuṣṭubh*, they ascended as four-year-old draught-oxen.

These indeed are those animals which Prajāpati obtained by means of the *vayas*. He took an animal first, then a *vaya*, then a *candas*; for by enclosing them with both the *vayas* and the *candas*, he placed them within himself and made them his own. In the same way, this sacrificer now, having enclosed them with both the *vayas* and the *candas*, places them within himself and makes them his own.

This Agni is indeed that animal; he is here prepared whole and complete. Those bricks which he places in front are its head; those which he places to the south and to the north are its body; and those which he places behind are its tail.
He places it first in the east;

for of one being born, the head is born first. Then, having placed it on the south, he places it on the north, thinking, "May this body be born together with [the head]. Then [he places it] in the west; for of one being born, the tail is born last.

Those metres which are the longest and those animals which are the largest, he places in the middle; he thereby makes the animal the most excellent at its middle, and therefore the animal is most excellent at its middle. Then those animals which are the strongest, he places on the south side; he thereby makes the right half of the animal stronger, and therefore the right half of the animal is stronger.
He makes the two smallest [fingers] the fore-part and the hind-part.

Because those four were the smallest there, they are therefore the smallest here; and because he places the smallest animals here, for that reason these are the smallest. He thus makes the two smallest parts of the animal its fore-part and its hind-part; therefore the fore-part and the hind-part of the animal are the smallest, and therefore the animal stands up with the fore-part and sits down with the hind-part. Then he lays down two space-filling bricks (*lokampṛṇā*) in this corner; the significance of those two is explained above. He scatters loose earth (*purīṣa*); the significance of that is explained above.
He lays down the third layer.
For when the gods, having built the second layer, ascended, they ascended after having prepared that very space which is above the earth and below the atmosphere.

They said, "Reflect!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer; seek upwards from here. While reflecting, they perceived the atmosphere itself as the third layer, the Bṛhatī. That world became pleasing to them.

They said to Indra and Agni, "Do you two lay down this third layer for us. They asked, "What will come of that for us? [The reply was: "You two shall be the most excellent among us. "So be it," they said. Indra and Agni then laid down this third layer for them. Therefore they say, "Indra and Agni alone are the most excellent of the gods."
He lays them down for Indra and Agni;
he settles them with Viśvakarman. For Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman—they indeed saw this third layer; therefore, he lays them down for Indra and Agni and settles them with Viśvakarman.

Furthermore, as to why he lays them down for Indra and Agni and settles them with Viśvakarman: when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him and departed; of him, Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman took the middle part and stood apart.
He said to them:

"Come to me and restore to me that by which you have departed from me. They asked, "What will become of us from that? He replied, "This part of my own self shall belong to you as your own deity. They said, "So be it. Then Indra, Agni, and Viśvakarman restored that to him.

Now, that which is this middle *svayamātṛṇṇā* is that very self of his; and when he lays this one down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to this self of his. Therefore, he lays this one down here.

"O Indra and Agni, do you two make firm the unshaking brick"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance. "With your back you push apart heaven, earth, and the intermediate space"—for with her back she indeed pushes apart heaven, earth, and the intermediate space.

"May Viśvakarman settle thee!"—for Viśvakarman indeed saw this third layer; "on the back of the atmosphere, wide-extending, spreading out"—for this is the back of the atmosphere, wide-extending and spreading out; "support the atmosphere, make firm the atmosphere, do not injure the atmosphere"—this means: support yourself, make yourself firm, do not injure yourself.

"For all out-breathing and in-breathing, for diffused breathing and upward breathing"—the naturally perforated brick is indeed the breath; "for the support of all this" means for the support of all this; "for movement"—these worlds are indeed the naturally perforated bricks, and these worlds are the support and the movement. "May Vāyu protect thee"—that is, "may Vāyu guard thee"; "with great well-being"—that is, "with great prosperity"; "with most peaceful shelter"—that is, "with that shelter which is most peaceful. Having settled it, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has been explained. Then he sings a Sāman; its significance follows later.
Then he lays down the Diśyā bricks.

The regional bricks (diśyā) are indeed the quarters; it is the quarters he thus lays down. Those very quarters by which Vāyu approached from there without interruption—those he now lays down. And those same ones he lays down in front of the bunch of Darbha grass and the clod-bricks. Yonder sun is these [bricks]; he thus places yonder sun upon the quarters and piles him within the quarters. If they were to remain only there, they would be outside; for that part of the fire-altar which is prior to the lotus-leaf is outside the womb. When he brings them here and lays them down, he establishes them in their proper womb, the lotus-leaf. Thus they do not become external. He lays them down immediately adjacent to the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick. The middle *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); he thus places the quarters immediately adjacent to the intermediate space. He places them one above the other; thus he places the quarters one above the other relative to the intermediate space. On the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks—he is these two *retaḥsic*s; he thus places the quarters within these two. Therefore, the quarters are within these two. He lays them down on all sides; he thus places the quarters on all sides. Therefore, the quarters are on all sides. He lays them down facing each other on all sides; he thus places the quarters facing each other on all sides. Therefore, the quarters face each other on all sides.

And as to why he lays down the Diśyā bricks: the quarters are indeed the metres. The eastern quarter is the Gāyatrī, the southern the Triṣṭubh, the western the Jagatī, the northern the Anuṣṭubh, and the upward direction the Paṅkti. The metres are cattle, and the middle layer is the intermediate space; he thus places cattle in the intermediate space. Therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode.
And again, as to why he lays down the Diśyā bricks.

The quarters are indeed the *candāṃsi* (metres), and cattle are the *candāṃsi*; cattle are food, and the middle is the centre. He thus places that food in the middle. He lays them down immediately adjacent to the *svayamātṛṇā* brick; for the *svayamātṛṇā* is breath—he thereby places food immediately adjacent to breath. They are higher, for he thereby places food higher than breath. He places them on the level of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the two *retaḥsic* are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle—he thus places that food in him right in the middle. He lays them down on all sides; he thereby places that food in him on every side.

"Thou art the sovereign, the eastern quarter; thou art the far-shining, the southern quarter; thou art the self-ruling, the western quarter; thou art the all-ruling, the northern quarter; thou art the overlord, the great quarter"—these are their names; it is by mentioning their names that he thus lays them down. He lays them down separately, he settles them separately, and he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse over them separately, for the quarters are separate.
Then he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick.

Vāyu indeed is the central Viśvajyotis, for Vāyu is the universal light in the world of the atmosphere; it is Vāyu whom he thus lays down. He lays it down immediately adjacent to the bricks of the quarters; he thereby places Vāyu within the quarters, and therefore Vāyu is present in all the quarters.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis (all-light) brick:

offspring, indeed, are the Viśvajyotis, for offspring are the light of all; he thus lays down that which is procreation. He lays it down immediately adjacent to the two regional bricks; he thereby places offspring in the quarters, and therefore offspring exist in all the quarters.

"May Viśvakarman settle thee"—for Viśvakarman indeed beheld this third layer on the back of the intermediate space as luminous; "on the back of the intermediate space, the luminous one"—for on the back of the intermediate space is this luminous Vāyu.
"For all out-breathing and in-breathing;

for diffused breathing"—for the Viśvajyotis is indeed breath, and breath serves all this. "Bestow all light," he says; that is, "bestow every light. "Vāyu is your overlord," he says; he thus makes Vāyu its overlord. Having settled it, he pronounces the Sūdadohas verse over it; the significance of that has already been explained.

Then he lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). These seasonal bricks are indeed the seasons; it is thus the seasons he lays down. "Nabhas and Nabhasya, the two rainy seasons"—these are their names; it is by these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once, thereby making it one season. He lays them down on *avakā* plants and covers them with *avakā* plants; the *avakā* plants are indeed water. Thus he places water in this season; therefore, it rains most abundantly in this season.

Then, as for the northern ones: *iṣ* (food) and *ūrj* (strength) are the names of the two autumn seasons; it is by these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once, thereby making the season one. He places them on *avakā* plants; the *avakā* plants are indeed water, so he thus places water at the beginning of this season. Therefore, it rains at the beginning of this season, but not from above. He does not cover them over from above; therefore, it does not rain in that same way from above.

Now, as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds. Of that [year], the middle layer is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa); the rainy season and the autumn are its intermediate space. Therefore, when he lays these down here, he restores to him that which belongs to his own self; that is why he lays these down here.
And as to why he lays these down here:

this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; the middle layer is his very middle, and the rainy and autumn seasons are the middle of the year. Thus, when he lays these down here, he restores to him that which belongs to his own self; therefore he lays these down here.

Now, these four seasonal bricks he places in the middle layer; two each in the other layers. Cattle are indeed four-footed, and the middle layer is the intermediate space (antarikṣa). He thus places cattle in the intermediate space; therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode.
Or rather, there are four [verses] because cattle are four-footed; cattle are food, and the middle layer is the middle; thus he places that food in the middle.
Or again, why there are four:
the intermediate region consists of four syllables, while the other layers consist of two syllables each; thus, having made it as large as the intermediate region, he lays them down.
Or rather, as to why there are four:
this Agni is an animal; he thus makes the animal widest at its middle, and therefore an animal is widest at its middle.

Now, these are the four seasonal bricks; the Viśvajyotis is the fifth, and there are five regional bricks—that makes ten. The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food. The middle layer is the middle; thus he places that food in the middle. He lays them down immediately adjacent to the Svayamātṛṇṇā brick. The Svayamātṛṇṇā is indeed the vital breath; he thus places food immediately adjacent to the vital breath. Those [other bricks] are higher; he thus places food higher than the vital breath.
Then he lays down the Prāṇabhṛts (vitality-supporting bricks).

The Prāṇabhṛts are indeed the vital breaths; it is thus the vital breaths that he lays down. There are ten of them, for there are ten vital breaths. He lays them down in the front part, for these vital breaths are in the front. With the words, "Protect my life-span! Bestow light upon me!"—light is indeed the vital breath—he thereby says, "Bestow the vital breath upon me! He lays them down immediately adjacent to the Ṛtavyās; the vital breath is indeed Vāyu (the wind), and since Vāyu is in the seasons, he thus establishes Vāyu in the seasons.
Then he lays down the *candas* (metres).
The metres are indeed cattle; the middle layer is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). He thus places cattle in the intermediate space; therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode.
And as to why he lays down the *candas* (metres):
the metres are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; the middle layer is the middle [of the body]; thus he places that food in the middle.
He lays down twelve each time.

The Jagatī indeed consists of twelve syllables; the Jagatī is cattle, and the middle layer is the intermediate space. Thus he places cattle in the intermediate space; therefore, cattle have the intermediate space as their abode.

Or rather, why twelve by twelve? The Jagatī metre consists of twelve syllables; the Jagatī is cattle, and cattle are food. The middle layer is the middle part [of the body]; thus he places food in the middle. He places them immediately after the Prāṇabhṛts; he thereby places food immediately adjacent to the vital breaths. Those [bricks] are placed higher; he thereby places food higher than the vital breaths.

"Māyaṃ chandas": this world is indeed *māyaṃ*, for this world is as if measured (*mita*); "pramā chandas": the intermediate region is indeed *pramā*, for the intermediate region is as if measured from this world; "pratimā chandas": yonder world is indeed *pratimā*, for it is as if reflected (*pratimita*) in the intermediate region; "asrīvayaś chandas": food is *asrīvayaḥ*; whatever food is in these worlds, that is *asrīvayaḥ*, and also whatever food flows forth from these worlds, that is *asrīvayaḥ*. Now, therefore, he lays down the *chandas* bricks with their specific etymologies.

The Paṅkti metre, the Uṣṇih metre, the Bṛhatī metre, the Anuṣṭubh metre, the Virāj metre, the Gāyatrī metre, the Triṣṭubh metre, and the Jagatī metre—these are the eight metres, with the Virāj as the eighth, which he lays down in their explicit forms. By saying "the Earth is a metre, the Atmosphere is a metre," he lays down those metres which have these as their deities; by saying "Agni is a deity, Vāta is a deity," he lays down those very metres which are indeed the deities.
He lays down both those that are defined and those that are undefined.

If he were to lay down all of them as defined, food would become limited and it would be exhausted; and if he were to lay down all of them as undefined, food would be beyond perception and no one would even see it. Therefore, he lays down both the defined and the undefined; thus, defined food, while being eaten, is not exhausted.

Now, these three sets of twelve he lays down; that makes thirty-six. The Bṛhatī consists of thirty-six syllables. This indeed is that Bṛhatī which the gods saw as the third layer, the intermediate space (antarikṣa); of this very Bṛhatī, the gods were the highest.
Moreover, as for why he lays down these bricks:
when Prajāpati had become relaxed, all beings and all the quarters departed from him.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those beings who departed from him are these bricks. Thus, when he lays down these bricks, he restores to him those very beings who had departed from him.
Now, those ten which he lays down first are that moon;

they become ten, for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is food, and the moon is food. Then those thirty-six which follow are the half-months and the months: twenty-four half-months and twelve months. The moon, indeed, is the year and all beings.

Where the gods fashioned him, there they placed all these beings within him; in the same way, this [sacrificer] now places them within him. He lays those [bricks] down immediately after the seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā); he thus establishes all beings within the seasons.

Then he lays down the Vālakhilyās. The Vālakhilyās are indeed the vital breaths; it is the vital breaths that he thus lays down. As to why they are called "Vālakhilyās": when there is a piece of land that is not joined to two cultivated fields (*urvarā*), they call that a "waste" (*khila*); and these vital breaths are separated by only the width of a hair (*vāla*). Because they are separated by only the width of a hair, they are therefore called "Vālakhilyās."
He lays down seven in front and seven behind. As for those seven which he lays down in front: these are the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) that are here in front; it is these he thus places in him.

Now, as for the seven [verses] behind, he thereby makes these vital breaths of theirs face backward; therefore, whatever food one eats with these [limbs], that one passes through by means of these [breaths].
And as to why he lays down seven in front:

there are indeed these seven vital breaths (prāṇas) in front—namely, the four limbs of the arms and hands, the head, the neck, and that which is above the navel is the seventh; for the vital breath is in every limb. These, then, are the seven vital breaths in front; it is these he thus places in him.

Now, as for those seven [bricks] behind: there are indeed these seven vital breaths (prāṇas) behind—namely, the four thighs and knees, the two feet, and that which is below the navel as the seventh; for the vital breath is in every limb. These, then, are the seven vital breaths behind, and it is these he places in him.
"Thou art the head, the sovereign;
thou art firm, the supporter, the upholder, the sustainer; the ruler, the controller, the restrainer; thou art firm, the bearer. By these [formulas], he thus fixes the firm vital breaths within him.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Vālakhilyās:

by means of the Vālakhilyās, the gods indeed traversed these worlds—both upwards from here and downwards from there. In the same way, the sacrificer now traverses these worlds by means of the Vālakhilyās—both upwards from here and downwards from there.
With "Thou art the head, the ruler," he ascended this world;

with "Thou art firm, the supporter," the intermediate world; with "Thou art the upholder, the sustainer," that world; and with "For life thee! For luster thee! For agriculture thee! For security thee!"—these four [formulas] refer to four-footed cattle, and cattle are food. By means of these four-footed cattle and by means of this food, they established themselves in yonder world; and in the same way, the sacrificer now establishes himself in yonder world by means of these four-footed cattle and by means of this food.
That [altar] is indeed like a tree growing on the further side;
this earth is the foundation. The gods returned to this foundation, and in the same way, the sacrificer now returns to this foundation.
With "Thou art a restrainer, O King," he ascended this world;

with "Thou art a restrainer, a restrainer," the intermediate world; with "Thou art firm, a supporter," this world. With "Thee for food, thee for strength, thee for wealth, thee for prosperity"—these four [formulas] refer to four-footed cattle, and cattle are food. By means of these four four-footed cattle, by means of this food, they established themselves in this world. In the same way, the sacrificer now establishes himself in this world by means of these four four-footed cattle, by means of this food.
Now, therefore, follows the consecration itself.

Those eleven bricks which he lays down—this first section (anuvāka) is the intermediate region; that is the self (ātman). As to why there are eleven of them: the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the intermediate region is of the nature of the Triṣṭubh. Now, those sixty bricks which follow are Vāyu, they are Prajāpati, they are Agni, and they are the sacrificer.
Now, those which he places in front are his head;
they are ten in number, for there are ten vital breaths, and the vital breaths indeed are the head. He places them on the eastern side, for this head is in the front.

Now, those [bricks] which are on the south side—those which are above the middle and below the head, they are his [limbs] there; and those which are behind—those which are above the foundation and below the middle, they are his [limbs] there; the foundation itself is on the north side.
Now, as for those seven Vālakhilyā bricks which he lays down in front:

these are the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) that are here in front; it is these he thus places in him. He lays them down so as not to be separated from these ten; he thereby places the vital breaths so as not to be separated from the head.

Now, as for those seven [bricks] behind: these are the seven vital breaths (prāṇas) that are here behind; he thus places them in him. He places them so as not to be separated from these twelve; he thereby places the vital breaths so as not to be separated from his own self. This Vāyu Prajāpati is indeed completely encompassed on all sides within this Traiṣṭubha intermediate space (antarikṣa). Thus, when he lays down the third layer, having prepared both Vāyu and the intermediate space, he lays them down. Then he lays down two Lokampṛṇā bricks in that corner; the significance of those is explained above. He scatters loose soil (purīṣa); the significance of that is explained above.
He lays down the fourth layer.
For the gods, having built the third layer, ascended; the third layer is indeed the intermediate space; thus, having perfected the intermediate space, they ascended.

They said, "Reflect!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citim icata)"; "Seek it from here upwards. While reflecting, they perceived this fourth layer: that which is above the intermediate space (antarikṣa) and below the sky. To them, this world seemed as if unstable and as if without support, causing them mental distress.

They said to Brahman, "Let us place you here. He replied, "What will be mine from that? [They said,] "You shall be the most excellent among us. "So be it," he said. They then placed Brahman there. Therefore they say, "Brahman indeed is the most excellent of the gods. By this fourth layer, these two, heaven and earth, are supported. The fourth layer is indeed Brahman; therefore they say, "By Brahman heaven and earth are supported. He lays down the Stomas; the Stomas are the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are indeed Brahman; thus he lays down Brahman itself.
And again, as to why he lays down the Stomas.

The gods indeed said this to Prajāpati: "Let us place you here. He replied, "So be it. But he did not say, "What will become of me from that? Whatever Prajāpati desired from the gods, they said, "What will become of us from that? Therefore, when a father desires something from his sons, they say, "What will become of us from that?"; and when the sons [desire something] from the father, he says, "So be it," for thus did Prajāpati and the gods speak together in the beginning. He lays down the Stomas; the Stomas are indeed the vital breaths, and Prajāpati is indeed the vital breaths; it is Prajāpati himself whom he thus lays down.
And as to why he lays down the Stomas:

those very Rishis who saw this fourth layer were sustained by this essence; it is them that he now lays down. He lays down the Stomas; for the Stomas are the vital breaths, and the Rishis are indeed the vital breaths—it is the Rishis that he thus lays down.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Stomas:

when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took [his parts] and departed. Of him, that which was above the middle and below the head, Vāyu took and stood apart, having become both the deities and the years.

He said to him: "Come to me; give back to me that by which you have departed from me. He asked, "What will I have from that? [The other replied,] "This part of my self shall belong to you as having you for its deity. "So be it," he said. Then Vāyu restored this to him.

Now, as for these eighteen first ones: that which these are is that part of his own self; and when he places them here, he thereby restores to him that very part of his self which these constitute. That is why he places them here. He places the Stomas; the Stomas are indeed the vital breaths, and Vāyu is indeed the vital breaths; it is Vāyu himself whom he thus places here.

He places it in front with the words, "The Swift, the Trivṛt. He thus places that which is the Trivṛt Stoma; as to why he calls it "the Swift," it is because this is the swiftest of the Stomas. Moreover, Vāyu is indeed "the Swift, the Trivṛt," for he moves through these three worlds. As to why he calls him "the Swift," it is because he is the swiftest of all beings; having become Vāyu, he stood in the east. It is that very form he now places there.

"Shining, fifteen. He thus lays down that which is the fifteenfold *stoma*. As to why he says "shining": the shining one is indeed the thunderbolt, and the fifteenfold is the thunderbolt; moreover, the shining one is the moon, and it is fifteenfold, for it waxes for fifteen days and wanes for fifteen days. As to why he says "shining": the moon indeed shines. Having become the moon, he stood on the south side; it is that very form which he now lays down.

"Vyomā is seventeenfold. He thus lays down that very seventeenfold *stoma*. As to why he calls it "Vyomā": Vyomā is indeed Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is seventeenfold; moreover, Vyomā is the year, which is seventeenfold—twelve months and five seasons. As to why he calls it "Vyomā": the year is indeed Vyomā. Having become the year, it stood on the north side; it is that very form he now lays down.
"The twenty-first is the support."

That which is the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (stoma), that he now lays down. As to why he calls it "the supporter" (dharuṇa): the supporter is indeed a foundation, and the twenty-one-fold is a foundation. Moreover, yonder sun is the twenty-one-fold supporter; for him there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun himself is the twenty-one-fold supporter. As to why he calls it "the supporter": when this [sun] sets, then everything here is supported; having become the sun, he stands behind [all things]. Thus he lays down that form. Now he lays down the forms of the year.

"The *pratūrti* is eighteenfold. He thus lays down that which is the eighteenfold *stoma*. Moreover, the *pratūrti* is indeed the year; it consists of eighteen parts: twelve months and five seasons—the year itself being the *pratūrti* consisting of eighteen. As to why he calls it *pratūrti*: for the year propels (*pratirati*) all beings; it is that very form he thus lays down.

"The penance is the nineteenfold," he says. He thus lays down that very nineteenfold Stoma. Moreover, the year is the penance that is nineteenfold: its twelve months, six seasons, and the year itself as the nineteenth; it is penance because they call it "penance" (tapas), for the year heats (tapat) all beings. It is that very form he thus lays down.

"The Abhīvarta with twenty" — he thus lays down that very Stoma which has twenty. Moreover, the Abhīvarta with twenty is the year; it consists of twelve months and seven seasons, and the year itself is the Abhīvarta with twenty. As for why it is called "Abhīvarta," it is because the year overcomes (abhivartate) all beings; it is that very form he now lays down.

"The radiance, the twenty-two-fold"—he thereby lays down that very twenty-two-fold Stoma. Moreover, the twenty-two-fold radiance is indeed the year: its twelve months, seven seasons, two—the day and night—and the year itself is the twenty-two-fold radiance. As to why he calls it "radiance" (varcas), it is because the year is the most radiant of all beings; thus he lays down that very form.

"The twenty-third is the *sambharaṇa* (the gathering). He thus lays down that which is the twenty-threefold hymn-form (*stoma*). Moreover, the year is indeed the twenty-threefold *sambharaṇa*: it consists of thirteen months, seven seasons, two—the day and night—and the year itself is the twenty-threefold *sambharaṇa*. As to why he calls it *sambharaṇa*, it is because the year has gathered together all beings; thus he lays down that very form.
"The womb is twenty-fourfold.

He places that which is the twenty-fourfold hymn-form (stoma) there; moreover, the twenty-fourfold womb is indeed the year, for it has twenty-four half-months. As to why he calls it the "womb": the year is indeed the womb of all beings. Thus, he places that very form there.

"The embryos are the twenty-fivefold [stoma]. He thus lays down that very twenty-fivefold stoma. Moreover, the twenty-fivefold embryos are indeed the year; its twenty-four half-months are the embryos, and the year itself is the twenty-fifth embryo. As to why he calls them "embryos": the thirteenth month, having become an embryo, enters the seasons; it is that very form which he thus lays down.

"Ojas-triṇava. He thus lays down that which is the Triṇava Stoma. As to why he calls it "Ojas" (strength): the thunderbolt is indeed strength, and the Triṇava is the thunderbolt; moreover, the year is Ojas-triṇava. For it consists of twenty-four half-months and two days and nights—the year itself is Ojas-triṇava. As to why he calls it "Ojas": the year is indeed the strongest of all beings; it is that very form he thus lays down.

"The thirty-onefold creative power (kratu). He thus lays down that very thirty-onefold hymn-form (stoma). Moreover, the thirty-onefold creative power is indeed the year: its twenty-four parts are the half-months, and six are the seasons; the year itself is the thirty-onefold creative power. As to why he calls it "creative power" (kratu): for the year makes (karoti) all beings; it is that very form which he thus lays down.

"The Trayastrimsha is the foundation. He thus lays down that which is the Trayastrimsha Stoma; as to why he calls it "the foundation," it is because the Trayastrimsha is indeed a foundation. Moreover, the year is the foundation, and the Trayastrimsha is the year: its twenty-four half-months, the six seasons, and the two, day and night—the year itself is the foundation, the Trayastrimsha. As to why he calls it "the foundation," the year is indeed the foundation of all beings; he thus lays down that very form.

"The thirty-fourfold is the summit of the radiant one (bradhna). He thus lays down that which is this thirty-fourfold Stoma. Moreover, the thirty-fourfold is indeed the summit of the radiant one, the year; for it consists of twenty-four half-months, seven seasons, and two, the day and night—the year itself being the thirty-fourfold summit of the radiant one. As to why he calls it "the summit of the radiant one": the summit of the radiant one is indeed self-sovereignty (svārājya), and the thirty-fourfold is self-sovereignty; he thus lays down that very form.

"The vault (nāka) is thirty-sixfold. He thus lays down that very thirty-sixfold Stoma; moreover, the vault is indeed the year, which consists of thirty-six parts: twenty-four half-months and twelve months. As to why he calls it the "vault" (nāka): for no one who has gone there meets with distress (nāka); moreover, the vault is indeed the year, and the year is the heavenly world; it is that very form he thus lays down.

"The turning-around (vivarta) is the forty-eightfold [stoma]. He lays down that which is indeed the forty-eightfold stoma. Moreover, the year itself is the forty-eightfold turning-around: twenty-six half-months, thirteen months, seven seasons, and two days and nights. As for why he calls it "turning-around," it is because from the year all beings turn around; thus he lays down that very form.
"The fourfold hymn-form (catuṣṭoma) is the supporter."

That which is the Catuṣṭoma Stoma, that he now lays down. As to why he calls it "Dhartra": Dhartra is indeed a support, and the Catuṣṭoma is a support; moreover, Vāyu is indeed the Catuṣṭoma Dhartra. He is praised with these four quarters; as to why he calls it "Dhartra": Dhartra is indeed a support, and Vāyu is the support of all beings. Thus he lays down that very form. He lays down Vāyu first and Vāyu last; by means of Vāyu, he thus encloses all these beings on both sides.
Now, he lays down these eighteen bricks; they are two sets of threefold ones. The threefold is indeed the breath, and the breath is Vāyu; this layer is Vāyu.
Or rather, there are eighteen;

for the year is eighteenfold—twelve months and five seasons—and Prajāpati is the year, and Prajāpati is eighteenfold. Agni is Prajāpati; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much having been made, he lays them down.
Then he lays down the *spṛt* bricks.
For when that [body] of his was restored, Prajāpati became pregnant with all beings; while they were still within him as an embryo, evil—death—seized them.
He spoke to the gods.

"By you together with these, may I deliver all these beings from evil, from death!"—"What will be ours from that?"—"Choose! he said. Some said, "Let there be a share for us"; others said, "Let there be lordship for us. Having made a share for some and lordship for others, he delivered all beings from evil, from death. Because he delivered (aspṛṇot) them, therefore it is called *spṛt*. In the same way, the sacrificer, having made a share for some and lordship for others, delivers all beings from evil, from death. Therefore, in all [the formulas], the word *spṛtam* follows after each one.
"Agni is your portion;

the lordship belongs to Dīkṣā"—for Dīkṣā is indeed speech; having made Agni the portion, he established speech in the position of lordship. "The Brahman is protected by the Trivṛt-stoma"—by means of the Trivṛt-stoma, he rescued the Brahman of creatures from evil, from death.
"Thou art Indra's portion;

Viṣṇu's overlordship. Having thus made it Indra's portion, he established Viṣṇu as the overlord. "The Kṣatra has been won; the Pañcadaśa Stoma!"—by means of the Pañcadaśa Stoma, he rescued the Kṣatra of the subjects from evil and death.
"You are the portion of those who watch over men;

the sovereignty of Dhātṛ. The gods are indeed those who watch over men; having made a portion for the gods, he established the sovereignty for Dhātṛ. "The birthplace is won; the seventeenfold hymn-form. The birthplace is indeed the people; by means of the seventeenfold hymn-form, he delivered the people among the progeny from evil, from death.

"You are the portion of Mitra; you are the sovereignty of Varuṇa. Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*), and Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*). Having made the out-breath his portion, he established sovereignty for the in-breath. "The rain of heaven, the wind is delivered; the twenty-one-fold hymn-form (*stoma*). By means of the twenty-one-fold hymn-form, he delivered both the rain and the wind for living beings from evil, from death.

"You are the portion of the Vasus; you are the sovereignty of the Rudras. Mitra is indeed the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and Varuṇa is the in-breath (*apāna*); having made the portion for the out-breath, he established sovereignty for the in-breath. "The rain of heaven, the wind is released; the twenty-onefold hymn-form (*stoma*). By means of the twenty-onefold hymn-form, he delivered both the rain and the wind for living beings from evil, from death.
"You are the portion of the Ādityas;

the overlordship of the Maruts"—having thus made a portion for the Ādityas, he established overlordship for the Maruts. "The embryos are saved; the twenty-fivefold Stoma"—by means of the twenty-fivefold Stoma, he delivered the embryos of creatures from evil, from death.
"Thou art the portion for Aditi;

the overlordship for Pūṣan"—Aditi is indeed this [earth]; having made her a portion, he established the overlordship for Pūṣan. "Vigor is won; the Triṇava Stoma"—by means of the Triṇava Stoma, he freed the vigor of creatures from evil, from death.
"Thou art the portion of the god Savitṛ;

Bṛhaspati’s overlordship. Having thus made a portion for the god Savitṛ, he established overlordship for Bṛhaspati. "The convergent quarters are delivered; the Catuṣṭoma Stoma!"—by means of the Catuṣṭoma Stoma, he delivered all the quarters of living beings from evil, from death.

"Thou art the portion of the *yavas*; the overlordship of the *ayavas*. The *yavas* are indeed the bright fortnights (*pūrvapakṣas*), and the *ayavas* are the dark fortnights (*aparapakṣas*); for all this world both unites (*yuvate*) and does not unite (*ayuvate*). Having made the bright fortnights his portion, he established the dark fortnights as his overlordship. "The creatures have been rescued by the forty-fourfold hymn-form (*stoma*). By means of the forty-fourfold *stoma*, he rescued all creatures from evil, from death.
"Thou art the portion of the Ṛbhus;

the overlordship of the Viśve Devas"—having thus made the portion for the Ṛbhus, he established the overlordship for the Viśve Devas. "The existent has been won; the thirty-threefold Stoma"—by means of the thirty-threefold Stoma, he freed all beings from evil, from death. In the same way, the sacrificer now frees all beings from evil, from death, by means of the thirty-threefold Stoma.
He lays down these ten bricks.

The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just that much he rescues all these beings from evil, from death.
Then he lays down the two seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*).

These two seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is the seasons themselves that he thus lays down. "Saha and Sahasya, the two winter seasons"—these are their names; it is by means of these very names that he lays them down. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months. He settles them once, thereby making it one season.

Now, as to why he lays these down here: this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds. That part of it which is above the intermediate region and below the sky is his fourth layer; that is his winter season. Thus, when he lays these down here, he restores to him that very part of his body which these two [bricks] represent; therefore, he lays these down here.

Moreover, as to why he lays these two bricks here: this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year. That part of him which is above the middle and below the head is his fourth layer; that is his winter season. When he lays these two bricks here, he thereby restores to him that very part of his body which these two represent; therefore he lays these two here.
Then he lays down the Sṛṣṭi bricks.
Prajāpati, having indeed freed all beings from evil and death, then desired: "May I create offspring; may I propagate."

He said to the vital breaths (prāṇas): "With you together, let me procreate these creatures. They asked, "By what means shall we praise? He replied, "By me and by yourselves. Saying, "So be it," they praised with both the vital breaths and Prajāpati. Whatever the gods do, they do by means of a Stoma; for the Stoma is indeed the sacrifice, and thus they do it by means of the sacrifice. Therefore, in all cases, the expression "they praised, they praised" continues to apply.

"With one they sang praises"—Speech, indeed, is the one; with speech they then sang praises. "Creatures were sustained"—creatures were here sustained. "Prajāpati was the overlord"—Prajāpati was here the overlord.

"With three they sang praises"—the vital breaths are indeed three: the out-breath (prāṇa), the up-breath (udāna), and the through-breath (vyāna); with these they then sang praises. "The Brahman was created"—the Brahman was created here. "Brahmaṇaspati was the overlord"—Brahmaṇaspati was the overlord here.

"With five they sang praises"—it was with these very vital breaths (prāṇas), of which the mind is the fifth, that they sang praises. "Beings were created"—beings were indeed created here. "The Lord of Beings was the overlord"—the Lord of Beings was indeed the overlord here.

"With seven they sang praises" means that with those very seven vital breaths in the head they sang praises. "The seven seers were created" means that the seven seers were created here. "Dhātṛ was the overlord" means that Dhātṛ was the overlord here.

"With nine they sang praises. There are indeed nine vital breaths: seven in the head and two downward ones; with those very [breaths] they then sang praises. "The ancestors were created," at this point the ancestors were created. "Aditi was the sovereign lady," at this point Aditi was the sovereign lady.

"With eleven they sang praises"—the ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and the self as the eleventh; with that very thing they sang praises. "The seasons were created"—the seasons were indeed created here. "The seasonal deities were the overlords"—the seasonal deities were indeed the overlords here.

"With thirteen they sang praises. There are ten vital breaths, two foundations, and the self is the thirteenth; with that very thing they sang praises. "The months were created," the months were indeed created here. "The year was the overlord," the year was indeed the overlord here.
"With fifteen they praised.

There are ten fingers on the hands, four arms, and that which is above the navel is the fifteenth; with that very thing they praised. "The Kṣatra was created"—the Kṣatra was indeed created here. "Indra was the overlord"—Indra was indeed the overlord here.
"With seventeen they praised.

There are ten toes, four thighs and knees, two feet, and that which is below the navel is the seventeenth; with that very thing they praised. "Domestic animals were created," for domestic animals were created here. "Bṛhaspati was the overlord," for Bṛhaspati was the overlord here.

"With nine and ten they praised," for there are ten fingers on the hand and nine vital breaths; with these very [limbs] they then praised. "Let the Śūdra and the Ārya be released," and so the Śūdra and the Ārya were released here. "Let Day and Night be the two sovereign mistresses," and so Day and Night were the two sovereign mistresses here.
"With twenty-one they praised.

There are ten fingers on the hands and ten on the feet, and the self is the twenty-first; with that very thing they then praised. "One-hoofed animals were created," meaning one-hoofed animals were created here. "Varuṇa was the overlord," meaning Varuṇa was the overlord here.
"With twenty-three they praised.

There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, two feet as supports, and the self as the twenty-third; with that very thing they then praised. "Small cattle were created," for small cattle were indeed created there. "Pūṣan was the overlord," for Pūṣan was indeed the overlord.

"With twenty-five they praised. There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, four limbs, and the self as the twenty-fifth; with that very thing they praised. "Wild animals were created," meaning wild animals were created here; "Vāyu was the overlord," meaning Vāyu was the overlord here.
"With twenty-seven they praised," he said.

There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, four limbs, two feet, and the self as the twenty-seventh; with that very thing they then praised. "Heaven and earth went apart," he said; heaven and earth indeed went apart here. "The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas followed after," he said; the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas indeed followed after here. "They were the overlords," he said; they indeed were the overlords here.
"With twenty-nine they praised," he said.

There are ten fingers on the hands, ten toes on the feet, and nine vital breaths; with these very [limbs] they then praised. "The trees were created," he said; the trees were created here. "Soma was the overlord," he said; Soma was the overlord here.
"With thirty-one they praised.

There are ten fingers on the hands, ten on the feet, ten vital breaths, and the self is the thirty-first; with that very [self] they then praised. "Creatures were created," they say; here creatures were indeed created. "The Yavas and Ayavas were the overlords"; here the bright and dark fortnights were indeed the overlords.
"With thirty-three they praised.

There are ten fingers, ten toes, ten vital breaths, two feet, and the self as the thirty-third; with that very thing they praised. "The beings were pacified": all beings here were pacified. "Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin was the overlord": Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin was the overlord here.
Now, these indeed are those [same ones].

He lays down seventeen bricks. The year, Prajāpati, is seventeenfold; he is the progenitor. By means of this seventeenfold Prajāpati, the year, as a progenitor, he caused these creatures to be born. That which he caused to be born, he created; and because he created them, they are called "creations" (sṛṣṭi). Having created them, he established them within himself. In the same way, the sacrificer, by means of this seventeenfold Prajāpati, the year, as a progenitor, causes these creatures to be born; having created them, he establishes them within himself. He places them on the level of the two Retahsic bricks. The two Retahsic are the ribs, and the ribs are the middle; thus he establishes these creatures in the very middle of him. He places them on every side; thus he establishes these creatures on every side of him.

Now, therefore, follows the turning along. One lays down a brick containing the *trivṛt* on the east, one containing the *ekaviṃśa* on the west, one containing the *pañcadaśa* on the south, and one containing the *saptadaśa* on the north.

This indeed belongs to Prajāpati. When a brick possessed of the Trivṛt-stoma had been laid down, and one possessed of the Pañcadaśa-stoma was about to be laid, Death sat down [thinking], "He will lay this down here; I shall seize him there. He saw him; having perceived him and moved around him, he laid down a brick possessed of the Ekaviṃśa-stoma.
