Death came upon the one possessed of the Ekaviṃśa-stoma; he laid down a brick possessed of the Pañcadaśa-stoma. Death came upon the one possessed of the Pañcadaśa-stoma; he laid down a brick possessed of the Saptadaśa-stoma. There, indeed, he cast down Death; there he bewildered him. In the very same way, the sacrificer now casts down all evils here and bewilders them here.

Then the northern ones: on a [brick] containing the *trivṛt*[-stoma], he places one containing the *trivṛt*; on one containing the *ekaviṃśa*, one containing the *ekaviṃśa*; on one containing the *pañcadaśa*, one containing the *saptadaśa*; and on one containing the *saptadaśa*, one containing the *pañcadaśa*. Because he thus places them crosswise, they are called the *akṣṇayāstomīyā*s. Moreover, because these *stoma*s are otherwise than in their regular order, for that reason also they are called the *akṣṇayāstomīyā*s. Furthermore, the gods placed them in this manner, whereas the Asuras did otherwise; consequently, the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated.

This Agni is indeed that animal; he is here prepared whole and complete. His two heads are the two *trivṛt* bricks. As to why they are *trivṛt*, the head is threefold. There are two of them, for the head consists of two skull-bones (*kapāla*). He places them in the front part, for this head is in the front.
The two [bricks] are the *pratiṣṭhā* (foundation) and the *ekaviṃśavatī* (possessing the twenty-onefold).
As to why they are *ekaviṃśavatī*: the twenty-onefold is indeed the foundation; there are two of them because the foundation is a pair. He lays them down behind, for this foundation is behind.

The two arms are possessed of the fifteenfold [stoma]. As to why they are possessed of the fifteenfold, it is because the arms are fifteenfold. There are two of them, for these two arms are indeed two. He places them on the sides, for these two arms are on the sides.

The two bricks containing the word "seventeen" are food. As to why they contain the word "seventeen," it is because food consists of seventeen parts; there are two of them, for food has two syllables. He places them immediately adjacent to the two bricks containing the word "fifteen"; thus he places food immediately adjacent to the two arms. The two bricks containing the word "fifteen" are on the outside, and the two containing the word "seventeen" are on the inside; thus he encloses the food on both sides with the two arms.

Now, those which he places in the middle are the body. He places them on the level of the two *retahsic* bricks; for the two *retahsic* are the ribs, and the ribs are in the middle, for this body is in the middle. He places them on all sides, for this body is on all sides. Now, that which is other than this is redundant. Whatever among the gods is redundant, that consists of the *chandas* (metres). Those *chandas* are cattle; those cattle are auspicious marks (*lakṣmī*). Those auspicious marks are yonder sun; he is to their south.
Now, some place them immediately after the two bricks consisting of threefold formulas, saying, "These are the jaws and the tongue.

They say that the fourteen are the jaws and the six are the tongue. One should not do so; they leave a deficiency behind, as if one were to place the lower jaws after the upper jaws, or as if one were to place a second tongue after the first tongue. That which is the head is indeed the jaws and the tongue.

Now, some place these bricks in the intermediate direction, saying, "Yonder sun is indeed these; we thus place yonder sun in this direction. One should not do so; for those are indeed other rites by which one places him here.

Some, indeed, place them on the right side, saying, "Thus we place this auspicious mark on the right side. Therefore, they call one who has a mark on the right side "one possessing an auspicious mark. On the left side [they place them] for a woman, for the woman's abode is on the left; that is what is done there. But he should rather place them in front; for where the head is, there are the jaws and the tongue. Thus he places this auspicious mark in the mouth. Therefore, they call one who has a mark on the mouth "one possessing an auspicious mark."
This indeed is the piling of Brahman.

Because they placed Brahman down, it is the Brahman-layer; because they placed Prajāpati down, it is the Prajāpati-layer; because they placed the Ṛṣis down, it is the Ṛṣi-layer; because they placed Vāyu down, it is the Vāyu-layer; because they placed the Stomas down, it is the Stoma-layer; because they placed the vital breaths down, it is the Prāṇa-layer. Whatever [deity] one may know [to have been placed], by that very fact this layer of his becomes possessed of its lineage and its kinship. Then he places two Lokampṛṇā bricks in that corner; their significance is above that. He scatters loose soil; its significance is above that.
He lays down the fifth layer.
Indeed, having built the fourth layer, the gods ascended; having prepared that which is above the atmosphere and below the sky, they ascended it.

They said, "Reflect!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)!"—"Seek it from here upwards! While reflecting, they perceived the sky itself as the Virāj, the fifth layer; that world shone forth for them.
They desired:

"Let us make this world free from rivals and free from affliction. They said: "Consider how we may make this world free from rivals and free from affliction. They said: "Meditate! By which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)"; they meant, "Seek it so that we may make this world free from rivals and free from affliction."

As they were reflecting, they saw these *asapatna* bricks; they laid them down, and by means of them, they made this world free from rivals and unassailable. Because they made this world free from rivals and unassailable by means of these, therefore these are called *asapatna*. In the same way, when the sacrificer now lays these down, he makes this very world free from rivals and unassailable. He lays them down on all sides; thus, on every side, he makes this world free from rivals and unassailable. He lays them down in the furthest part; thus, he makes this entire world free from rivals and unassailable.
Then he lays down the Virāj bricks.

This indeed is that Virāj which the gods saw as the fifth layer, the Virāj; he lays them down ten by ten, for the Virāj consists of ten syllables and this layer is the Virāj. He lays them down on all sides; for he who reigns in only one direction does not truly reign, but he who reigns in all directions—he alone truly reigns.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down these *asapatnā* bricks:

when this part of Prajāpati’s self had been restored, evil assailed him from every side. He saw these *asapatnā* bricks and laid them down; by means of them, he struck away that evil. For an enemy (*sapatna*) is indeed evil; and because he struck away the evil enemy by means of these, therefore they are called *asapatnā*.

This very thing is done: what the gods did, that he now does; that evil does not approach him, yet when he performs this, it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did. Moreover, whatever evil there is, whatever rival there is—that he repels by means of these bricks. Because he repels evil and the rival by means of these, they are called *asapatnāḥ* (the "rival-less"). He places them on all sides; thus he repels evil and the rival from every side. He places them in the furthest part; thus he repels evil and the rival from his entire self.

He places it in front with the words, "O Agni, drive away our born enemies," for as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu). Then he places it behind with the words, "By force, drive away our born enemies," for as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

That which was in front was Agni; that which was behind was Agni. By means of Agni they thus drove away evil from the front, and by means of Agni from behind. In the same way, the sacrificer now drives away evil from the front by means of Agni, and from behind by means of Agni.

Then on the south side: "The Ṣoḍaśī-stoma, vigor, wealth"—this is the Triṣṭubh, for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables. The intermediate space belongs to the Triṣṭubh, and there are four quarters; this very thing is the fifteenfold thunderbolt. That sun yonder is the sixteenth part, the bearer of the thunderbolt. With this fifteenfold thunderbolt and with this Triṣṭubh, he (the Sun) struck away evil from the south. In the same way, the sacrificer now strikes away evil from the south with this fifteenfold thunderbolt and with this Triṣṭubh.
Then on the north side:

"The forty-fourfold Stoma, splendor, wealth"—for the Triṣṭubh consists of forty-four syllables, and the thunderbolt is of Triṣṭubh nature. With this forty-fourfold thunderbolt, with this Triṣṭubh, he struck away evil from the north. In the same way, the sacrificer now strikes away evil from the north with this forty-fourfold thunderbolt, with this Triṣṭubh.
Then, in the middle:

"Thou art the filling of Agni. The fourth layer is indeed the Brahman, and Agni is the Brahman; this fifth layer is, as it were, its filling. The significance of the phrase "the waters by name" has already been explained.
He lays that one down transversely toward the east.

For by this brick Prajāpati cut off the root of evil; in the same way, he now cuts off the root of evil with this one. He places it on the right side, for the thunderbolt is extended from right to left; by placing it between the two southern bricks, he makes room for its extension.

That which was in front is the out-breath (prāṇa), and that which was behind is the in-breath (apāna). By means of the out-breath he struck away evil from the front, and by means of the in-breath from behind; in the same way, the sacrificer now strikes away evil from the front by means of the out-breath, and from behind by means of the in-breath.

Then those two which were on both sides are his two arms; whatever evil was on both sides of him, he struck that away with his two arms. In the same way, whatever evil belongs to the sacrificer on both sides, he strikes that away with his two arms alone.
The food is like dung.
Whatever evil was above him, he drove that away by means of food; in the same way, whatever evil is now above this sacrificer, he drives that away by means of food.

Whenever one who knows this breathes out, he thereby strikes away whatever evil is before him; and when he breathes in, he thereby strikes away whatever is behind him; and when he performs work with his arms, he thereby strikes away whatever is on all sides; and when he eats food, he thereby strikes away whatever is above him. Indeed, one who knows this strikes away evil at all times, even while sleeping. Therefore, one should not speak ill of one who possesses such knowledge, lest one should incur his evil.

Then he lays down the *candasyā* bricks. Prajāpati, having freed himself from evil, death, desired food; therefore, even now, one who is ill, having become better, desires food. They hope for him: "He desires food, he will live. To him the gods gave this food—these *candasyā* bricks. The metres (*chandāṃsi*) are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; they gratified him with them. Because they gratified him with them, they are called "metres" (*chandāṃsi*).
He lays them down ten by ten;
for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is all food: he thus bestows all this food upon him. He lays them down on every side; he thus bestows all this food upon him from every side.

"Evāc-candaḥ"—this world is indeed *evāc-candaḥ*; "varivāc-candaḥ"—the intermediate space is indeed *varivāc-candaḥ*; "śambhūc-candaḥ"—the sky is indeed *śambhūc-candaḥ*; "paribhūc-candaḥ"—the quarters are indeed *paribhūc-candaḥ*; "āc-candaḥ"—food is indeed *āc-candaḥ*; "manaścandaḥ"—Prajāpati is indeed *manaścandaḥ*; "vyacaścandaḥ"—yonder sun is indeed *vyacaścandaḥ*.
"Sindhuścanda" (the impetuous Sindhu).

The *sindhu* metre is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the *samudra* metre is the mind (*manas*). The *sarira* metre is speech (*vāc*); the *kakubh* metre is the vital breath; the *trikakubh* metre is the upward-breath (*udāna*). The *kāvyam* metre is the triple science (*trayī vidyā*); the *aṅkupam* metre is the waters. The *akṣarapaṅkti* metre is yonder world; the *padapaṅkti* metre is this world. The *viṣṭārapaṅkti* metre is the quarters. The *kṣuro bhrajaḥ* metre is yonder sun. The *ācat* metre is food; the *pracat* metre is food.
"Saṃyaccanda" means "one who restrains desire."

The night, indeed, is the *saṃyac-candas* (the binding metre), and the day is the *viyac-candas* (the spreading metre); the day, indeed, is the *viyac-candas*. The *bṛhat-candas* (the great metre) is yonder world; the *rathantara-candas* (the chariot-metre) is this world. The *nikāya-candas* (the gathering metre) is the wind; the *vivadha-candas* (the carrying metre) is the intermediate space. The *gira-candas* (the song-metre) is food; the *bhrajas-candas* (the blazing metre) is Agni. The *saṃstuc-candas* (the praising metre) and the *anuṣṭubh-candas* (the eight-syllabled metre) are speech itself—the *saṃstuc-candas* is speech, and the *anuṣṭubh-candas* is speech. The *evas-candas* (the going metre) and the *varivas-candas* (the wide metre)—their significance has already been explained.

"Vayaścandas"—food indeed is the *vayaścandas*; "vayaskṛccandas"—Agni indeed is the *vayaskṛccandas*; "viṣpardhāścandas"—that world (the sky) indeed is the *viṣpardhāścandas*; "viśālaṃ candas"—this world (the earth) indeed is the *viśālaṃ candas*; "cadiścandas"—the intermediate space indeed is the *cadiścandas*; "dūrohaṇaṃ candas"—that sun indeed is the *dūrohaṇaṃ candas*; "tandraṃ candas"—the *paṅkti* meter indeed is the *tandraṃ candas*; "aṅkāṅkaṃ candas"—the waters indeed are the *aṅkāṅkaṃ candas*.
Now, those which he places in front:

of these, the first is the out-breathing (prāṇa), the second the through-breathing (vyāna), the third the up-breathing (udāna), the fourth the up-breathing, the fifth the through-breathing, the sixth the out-breathing, the seventh the out-breathing, the eighth the through-breathing, the ninth the up-breathing; the tenth here is the sacrificer himself. This very sacrificer is thus supported and established upon this Virāj, which consists of breaths; he places them both directed hitherward and directed awayward, and therefore these vital breaths move both hitherward and awayward.
Now, as for those on the south:

Agni is the first of them, Vāyu the second, Āditya the third, Āditya the fourth, Vāyu the fifth, Agni the sixth, Agni the seventh, Vāyu the eighth, Āditya the ninth, and the Sacrificer himself is the tenth here. This very Sacrificer, having been carried upward and established upon this Virāj consisting of the deities, lays down the bricks facing both hitherward and thitherward; therefore these gods face both hitherward and thitherward.
Now, as for those which are behind:

this world is their first, the intermediate space the second, the sky the third, the sky again the fourth, the intermediate space the fifth, this world the sixth, this world again the seventh, the intermediate space the eighth, the sky the ninth, and the sacrificer himself is the tenth here. This very sacrificer, resting upon and established in this Virāj, lays down these bricks—those directed hitherward and those directed thitherward; therefore these worlds are both directed hitherward and directed thitherward.
Now, as for those [bricks] on the north side:

summer is their first, the rainy season the second, winter the third, winter the fourth, the rainy season the fifth, summer the sixth, summer the seventh, the rainy season the eighth, and winter the ninth; the sacrificer himself is the tenth here. This very sacrificer is supported and established upon this Virāj consisting of the seasons; he lays them down facing both hitherward and thitherward, and therefore these seasons move both hitherward and thitherward.
Then again:
those which he places in front are the vital breaths; they are ten in number, for there are indeed ten vital breaths. He places them in the eastern half, for these vital breaths are in the front.
Now, those which are on the south are these deities: Agni and the Earth, Vāyu and the Intermediate Space, Āditya and the Sky, the Moon and the Stars, as well as Food and Water.
Now, as for those that are behind,
they are the four quarters, the four intermediate quarters, the zenith, and this [earth].
Now, those that are on the north are the months: two of spring, two of summer, two of the rainy season, two of autumn, and two of winter.
Then again:

that which is the first decade is this world, the second is the intermediate space, and the third is the sky. By means of the first decade they ascended to this very world, by the second to the intermediate space, and by the third to the sky; in the same way, the sacrificer now ascends to this very world by the first decade, to the intermediate space by the second, and to the sky by the third.
That [set of ten] is like a branch growing upward;

this earth, indeed, is the foundation. The gods returned to this foundation, and in the same way the sacrificer now returns to this foundation. Now, that which is the last set of ten is this world; therefore, just as there is a beginning for the first set of ten, so too is there one for the last, for these two sets of ten are the same—this very world.

Now, these indeed are forty bricks and forty sacrificial formulas; that makes eighty. Food is eighty. Whatever he says here, having made that food into eighty, he bestows it upon him; thereby he gratifies him.

Then he lays down the Stomabhāgā bricks. This, indeed, was Prajāpati’s food; Indra set his mind upon it, and he desired to depart from him. He said to him, "Why do you depart? Why do you leave me? He replied, "Give me the essence of this food; enter into me together with that. "So be it," he said. He gave him the essence of that food, and he entered into him along with it.

He who was that Prajāpati is this very Agni who is now being built up; and that which was food is these Chandasyās; and that which was the essence of the food is these Stomabhāgas. And he who was Indra is yonder Āditya; he is indeed the Stoma, for whatever they praise with, they praise him alone; he gave this portion to that Stoma, and because he gave this portion to that Stoma, therefore they are called Stomabhāgas.
"By means of the ray, quicken truth for the sake of truth."

This ray is indeed food; the ray is food. Having joined together this [food] and its essence, he causes it to enter into himself, saying, "With the forward-moving law, quicken the law. This forward-moving one is indeed food; the forward-moving one is food. Having joined together this [food] and its essence, he causes it to enter into himself. With the following one, "quicken heaven by heaven. This following one is indeed food; the following one is food. Having joined together this [food] and its essence, he causes it to enter into himself. Whatever he says here, having joined together that [food] and its essence, he causes it to enter into himself. "With yonder eater, quicken the eater; thou art the eater; for yonder overlord, quicken vigor with vigor. These are established in three ways, for food is established in three ways.

Moreover, as to why he lays down the Stomabhāgās: the gods, having built the Virāj layer, ascended it; they said, "Reflect ye!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer! While reflecting, they saw the firmament, the heavenly world, and they laid it down. That which is the firmament, the heavenly world, these are those Stomabhāgās. Thus, when he lays them down, he lays down the firmament, the heavenly world.

Of those, the first three are this world; the second is the intermediate space; the third is the sky. Those that are the fourth are the eastern direction; those that are the fifth are the southern direction; those that are the sixth are the western direction; those that are the seventh are the northern direction.

Now, these bricks are twenty-one in number; these worlds and the quarters are twenty-one, for these worlds and the quarters are the foundation, and these worlds and the quarters are the twenty-first. Therefore, they say, "The twenty-first is the foundation."
Now, as for those eight bricks that remain over:

the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman. That which is the Brahman is this very thing which shines as the sun-disk. It shines established upon that twenty-first foundation; therefore, it does not fall away.
Now, regarding this, some indeed say:

They lay down the thirtieth brick with the formula: "The glory of appearance for the Kṣatriya; may it quicken the Kṣatriya power. [They say: "The Virāj consists of thirty syllables; this layer is the Virāj. One should not do so, for they cause the twenty-one-fold totality to be exceeded, as well as the Gāyatrī totality. This is indeed Indra’s world. For those who use a Virāj that is deficient, they make their hateful rival rise up against them in Indra’s world, and they drive Indra out from his own world. The sacrificer is indeed Indra in his own sacrifice; for those [who do so], they make the hateful rival rise up against the sacrificer in the sacrificer’s world, and they drive the sacrificer out from his own world. This very fire which they bring here is the sacrificer by his very nature; and he is indeed the thirtieth brick in this context.
He lays them down at the limit of the Aṣāḍhā brick.
The Aṣāḍhā is speech, and this [mixture] is essence; he thus places the essence in speech. Therefore, among all the limbs, it is by means of speech alone that one perceives the essence of food.
Furthermore, as for the Aṣāḍhā brick:
this earth is indeed the Aṣāḍhā, and yonder sun is the Stomabhāgas; he thus establishes yonder sun upon this earth as its foundation.

Furthermore, regarding the Aṣāḍhā brick: this earth, indeed, is the Aṣāḍhā, and the Stomabhāgās are the heart. He thus places the mind in that heart; therefore, one perceives with the mind by means of the heart upon this earth. He lays them down on all sides; he thus places the mind in the heart from every side, and therefore one perceives with the mind by means of the heart on this earth from every side. Moreover, these are auspicious marks (lakṣmīs); he thus bestows them upon himself from every side. Therefore, they say of him who has auspicious marks on every side that he is "one possessed of auspicious marks."
Then he covers them with loose soil.
The loose soil is indeed food, and this is its essence; he thus makes it concealed, and therefore the essence of food is, as it were, hidden.
And as to why it is with loose soil (*purīṣa*):
the loose soil is indeed food, and this [layer] is sap; thus he connects and joins together both the food and the sap.
Moreover, as for the fact that it is with loose soil (purīṣa):
the Stomabhāgas are indeed the heart, and the loose soil is the pericardium; he thus covers the heart with the pericardium.

Moreover, as to why it is with soil (purīṣa): this Agni is the year; he thus separates him from that [year] by means of the layers and the soil-fillings. Those which are the first four layers are the four seasons; then, having laid down the Stomabhāga bricks, he scatters the soil—that is the fifth layer, that is the fifth season.

Regarding this they say: "Since the other layers end with the *lokampṛṇā* bricks, why does he not place a *lokampṛṇā* here? What is the *lokampṛṇā* here? Indeed, yonder sun is the *lokampṛṇā*, and this layer is that very [sun]. This layer is itself the *lokampṛṇā*. Now, that which is above this up to the loose earth (*purīṣa*) is the sixth layer; it is the sixth season.
Then he pours down loose soil;
there he places the Vikarṇī brick, sprinkles it with chips of gold, and places the fire upon it—this is the seventh layer, this is the seventh season.
But those are indeed only six;
for the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā belong to that sixth layer.
There are indeed five of them;

with a sacrificial formula he pours loose soil on the others, but here he does so silently, and for that reason this is not a layer. Furthermore, the other layers end with *lokampṛṇā* bricks, but here he does not place a *lokampṛṇā*; for that reason also this is not a layer.
But indeed, they are only three:

this world is the first layer, and the sky is the last; and those which are these three [intermediate layers] are the atmosphere. Now, this atmosphere is, as it were, one; yet they are thus three, thus five, thus six, thus seven.

He lays down the Nākasad bricks. The gods, indeed, are the Nākasads; here this entire Agni has been prepared, and he is here the firmament (nāka), the heavenly world. In that world the gods sat down; because the gods sat down in that firmament, the heavenly world, they are therefore called the Nākasads. In the same way, when the sacrificer lays these down, he sits down in that very firmament, the heavenly world.

And as to why he lays down the Nākasad bricks: the gods, it is said, saw this vault, this heavenly world; they were these Stomabhāga bricks. They said, "Find out how we may sit upon this vault, in this heavenly world. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer! Seek how we may sit upon this vault, in this heavenly world."

While reflecting, they saw these bricks; they laid them down as the *nākasads*, and by means of them they sat down (*asīdan*) upon that firmament, in the heavenly world. Because they sat down upon that firmament, in the heavenly world, by means of them, therefore these are called *nākasads*. In exactly the same way, when the sacrificer lays them down, he thereby sits down upon that very firmament, in the heavenly world.

He lays them down in the quarters. The quarters are indeed that firmament, the heavenly world; he thus settles them in that very world, the heaven. At the boundary of the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*); for the seasonal bricks are the year, and the year is the heavenly world; he thus settles them in that very world, the heaven. Within the *stomabhāga* formula; for this is indeed that firmament, the heavenly world; he thus establishes them therein.
He places it in front.

"The eastern quarter is the queen"—for this eastern quarter is indeed named the queen; "the Vasus are the gods, the overlords"—for the Vasus are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Agni is the repeller of missiles"—for Agni is indeed here the repeller of missiles; "may the Trivṛt Stoma support thee on earth"—for by means of the Trivṛt Stoma she is supported on earth; "may the Ājya Uktha steady thee for steadiness"—for by means of the Ājya Uktha she is steadied on earth for steadiness; "the Rathantara Sāman for stability in the atmosphere"—for by means of the Rathantara Sāman she is established in the atmosphere; "may the Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [support thee]"—the Ṛṣis are indeed the vital breaths, for that Brahman is the first-born; "may they expand thee with the measure and width of heaven"—that is to say, "may they expand thee with as much width as there is in heaven"; "and this Sustainer and Overlord"—these two are Speech and Mind, for these two sustain all this; "may they all, being in agreement, seat thee and the sacrificer on the back of the firmament, in the world of heaven"—as the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance.
Then, on the south side.

"Thou art Virāj, the southern quarter," for this southern quarter is indeed named Virāj; "the Rudras are the gods, the overlords," for the Rudras are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter; "Indra is the repeller of missiles," for Indra indeed is here the repeller of missiles; "may the Pañcadaśa-stoma support thee on earth," for by the Pañcadaśa-stoma this [quarter] is supported on earth; "may the Praüga-uktha prop thee for steadiness," for by the Praüga-uktha this is propped on earth for steadiness; "the Bṛhat-sāman for stability in the atmosphere," for by the Bṛhat-sāman this is established in the atmosphere; "the Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [support thee]"—the significance of this has been explained.
Then afterwards.

"Thou art the sovereign (*samrāj*), the western quarter," he says; for this western quarter is indeed named the sovereign. "The Ādityas are thy gods, the overlords," he says; for the Ādityas are indeed the gods who are the overlords of this quarter. "Varuṇa is the warder-off of missiles," he says; for Varuṇa is indeed here the warder-off of missiles. "May the seventeenfold hymn-form (*stoma*) support thee on earth," he says; for by the seventeenfold hymn-form this [quarter] is supported on earth. "May the Marutvatīya hymn (recitation) steady thee for steadiness," he says; for by the Marutvatīya hymn this is steadied on earth for steadiness. "May the Vairūpa Sāman establish thee in the atmosphere for stability," he says; for by the Vairūpa Sāman this is established in the atmosphere for stability. "May the Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [support thee]," he says; the significance of that has been explained.

Then on the north: "The self-ruling is this northern quarter"—for this northern quarter is indeed called the self-ruling; "the Maruts are the presiding deities"—for the Maruts are indeed the presiding deities of this quarter; "Soma is the warder-off of missiles"—for Soma indeed is here the warder-off of missiles; "may the twenty-one-fold hymn support thee on earth"—for by the twenty-one-fold hymn it is indeed supported on earth; "may the Niṣkevalya hymn prop it for steadiness"—for by the Niṣkevalya hymn it is indeed propped on earth for steadiness; "the Vairāja Sāman for stability in the atmosphere, O King"—for by the Vairāja Sāman it is indeed established in the atmosphere; "the Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [support thee]"—the significance of this has been explained.
Now, in the middle.

"Thou art the sovereign lady, the Great Quarter," for this quarter is indeed named the Sovereign Lady, the Great. "The All-Gods are thy overlords," for the All-Gods are indeed the overlords of this quarter. "Bṛhaspati is the warder-off of missiles," for Bṛhaspati is indeed here the warder-off of missiles. "May the Triṇava and Trayastriṃśa Stomas support thee on earth," for by means of these two Stomas, the Triṇava and the Trayastriṃśa, she is supported on earth. "May the Vaiśvadeva and Āgnimāruta Ukthas steady thee for steadiness," for by means of these two Ukthas, the Vaiśvadeva and the Āgnimāruta, she is steadied on earth for steadiness. "The Śākvara and Raivata Sāmans for stability in the atmosphere," for by means of these two Sāmans, the Śākvara and the Raivata, she is established in the atmosphere. "The Ṛṣis, the first-born among the gods, [support thee]"—the significance of this has been explained.
The whole sacrifice is indeed this much;

and the sacrifice is the self of the gods. Having thus made the sacrifice their own self, the gods seated themselves upon this firmament, in the heavenly world. In the same way, the sacrificer, having made the sacrifice his own self, seats himself upon this firmament, in the heavenly world.
Then he lays down the five-crested bricks.

The Nākasads are indeed the sacrifice, and the five-crested bricks are also the sacrifice. Now, those four officiating priests with the householder as the fifth are the Nākasads; the Hotrās are the five-crested bricks. That which is the Hotrās is indeed redundant; and that which is redundant is a crest (cūḍa). Since there are five redundancies, they are therefore called the five-crested bricks.
And as to why he lays down the *nākasad* and *pañcacūḍā* bricks:

the *nākasads* are indeed the self, and the *pañcacūḍās* are the mate; for the mate is half of this self. When one is together with a mate, then one is whole, then complete; it is for the sake of completeness.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *nākasad* and the *pañcacūḍā* bricks:

the *nākasads* are indeed the self, and the *pañcacūḍās* are offspring. That which is offspring is indeed an excess of the self; and that which is an excess is a crest (*cūḍā*). Since there are five of them in excess, they are called the *pañcacūḍās*.

And again, as to why he lays down the Nākasads and the Pañcacūḍās: the Nākasads are indeed the quarters, and the Pañcacūḍās are also the quarters. Those five quarters which are directed hitherward from yonder sun are the Nākasads; those which are directed away from it are the Pañcacūḍās. Those quarters which are directed away from yonder sun are indeed redundant; and that which is redundant is the crest (cūḍa). Since there are five redundant ones, they are therefore called Pañcacūḍās.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the five *cūḍā* bricks:

the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* and destroyers should strike these worlds from above. They therefore made these—the *hetis* and *prahetis*—the guardians of these worlds from above. In the same way, the sacrificer now makes these the guardians of these worlds from above.
May those who cast these missiles and counter-missiles be restrained.
He places it in front.

"This one before us, the golden-haired"—Agni, indeed, is "before" (puraḥ), for they lift up Agni facing forward and attend upon him facing forward. Now, as to why he says "golden-haired" (harikeśa): Agni is like gold (hari) because his rays are like those of the sun. "And Rathagṛtsa and Rathaujas, the army-leader and the village-chief"—these are the two spring seasons. "Puñjikasthalā and Kratusthalā, the two Apsarases"—Māhitthi used to say, "These are the intermediate direction and the sub-direction. But [the text] says: "The army and the assembly; the biting beasts are the weapon, and human slaughter is the missile. For when people suffer in the army and in the assembly, the biting beasts are the weapon and human slaughter is the missile; that which they kill one another is human slaughter, the missile. "To them let there be homage!"—thus he pays homage to them. "May they be gracious to us!"—thus they are gracious to him. "Whom we hate and whoever hates us, him we place within their jaws!"—whomsoever he hates and whoever hates him, him he places within their jaws. He should say, "I place so-and-so in their jaws," regarding whom he hates; then indeed there is no turning back from him. Yet one need not pay heed to this, for he whom one who knows this hates is already self-condemned.
Then, on the south side.

"This one is Dakṣiṇā Viśvakarman. This Vāyu who blows here is indeed Viśvakarman, for he makes all this; and as to why he calls him "Dakṣiṇā," it is because he blows most predominantly toward the south. His Rathasvana and Rathecitra are the Senānī and Grāmaṇī; these two are the summer seasons. Menakā and Sahajanyā are the Apsarases; as for "the direction and the intermediate direction," Māhitthi used to say, "But those two are heaven and earth. "The Yātudhānas are the missile, the Rakṣases are the counter-missile"—the Yātudhānas are indeed the missile here, and the Rakṣases are the counter-missile. "To them let there be homage!"—the significance of this has been explained.
Then afterwards.

"This one behind is Viśvavyacas"—for yonder sun, indeed, is Viśvavyacas; for as soon as he rises, this whole world becomes spacious (*vyacas*). As to why he says "behind" (*paścāt*), therefore they see him only when he is moving westward. "Rathaprota and Asamaratha are his *senānī* and *grāmaṇī*"—these are the two rainy seasons. "Pramlocantī and Anumlocantī are the two Apsarases"—these, Māhitthi used to say, are the intermediate direction and the quarter; but they are rather day and night, for those two set forth (*pra-mlocataḥ*) and set down (*anu-mlocataḥ*). "Tigers are the missile, snakes are the hurled missile"—the tigers, indeed, are the missile here, and the snakes are the hurled missile. "To them let there be homage!"—the significance of this has been explained.
Then, from the north.

"This one from the north, the gatherer of wealth"—the sacrifice, indeed, is from the north; and as to why he says "from the north," it is because the sacrifice approaches from the north. And as to why he says "the gatherer of wealth," they gather the sacrifice together, saying, "This is wealth. "Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi are his army-leader and village-chief"—these two are the autumnal seasons. "Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī are the Apsarases"—Māhitthi said, "The quarters and the intermediate quarters"; but Veda said, "The altar and the offering-spoon; the altar is Viśvācī and the offering-spoon is Ghṛtācī. "The waters are the missile, the wind the projectile"—the waters, indeed, are the missile here and the wind the projectile, for from there the wind blows warm and from there it blows cold. "To them let there be homage!"—the significance of this has been explained.
Now, in the middle.

"This one above, with wealth below"—Parjanya, indeed, is above; as to why he says "above," it is because Parjanya is above. And when he says "with wealth below," it is because from here below, wealth—namely rain and food—is bestowed upon creatures. Senajit and Suṣeṇa are his two army-leaders and village-chiefs; they are the two winter seasons. Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti are his two Apsarases; so said Māhitthi, [adding] "the quarters and the intermediate quarters. Āhuti and Dakṣiṇā are his two wives; "the thunderbolt is his weapon, lightning his missile"—for here the thunderbolt is indeed the weapon and lightning is the missile; "to them let there be homage"—the significance of this has been explained.
These indeed are their missiles and counter-missiles;

those which the gods made as guardians above these worlds, and those who were the creatures—these are the army-leaders and village-headmen; and that pair which was there—these are the Apsarases. Thus all those gods, having become complete and whole together with their offspring and their mate, settled in this vault, in the heavenly world. In the same way, the sacrificer, having become complete and whole together with his offspring and his mate, settles in this vault, in the heavenly world.

Now, he lays down these ten bricks. The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and this layer is the Virāj; thus, these are indeed five [sets], for he lays them down two by two. These are the blessings of Agni; he lays them down in the last layer, for the last layer is the end of Agni, and so he utters the blessings of Agni at the very end. There are five of them, for there are five blessings in the sacrifice. Then he scatters loose soil between them; for these two bricks are indeed two fires, and he does this lest these two fires should burn each other up. Moreover, loose soil is food; thus he brings about harmony between the two by means of food.

Now, therefore, follows the turning around. Having first laid down [the bricks] in the east, he lays them down in the south, then in the west, then in the north, and finally in the middle. Then, having first laid down the subsequent ones in the east, he lays them down in the south, then in the north, then in the middle, and finally in the west. For the heavenly world is entered from below. Indeed, the gods, having completely enclosed these worlds on all sides, entered the heavenly world from below. In the same way, the sacrificer, having completely enclosed these worlds on all sides, enters the heavenly world from below.

He lays down the *candasyā* bricks. At this point, this entire Agni has been prepared; he (Agni) then desired glory (*śrī*). Previously, indeed, he was not capable of sustaining that glory; therefore, even now people say, "This one is not capable of sustaining glory, nor kingship, nor the leadership of a village. To him, the gods bestowed this glory—namely, these *candasyā* bricks. The metres are cattle, and cattle are food; and food is glory.

He lays down three *tricā* bricks. The animal is indeed threefold: father, mother, and son; and also the embryo, the amnion, and the chorion. Moreover, food is threefold: cultivation, rain, and seed. There is only one *aticandā* brick, for she alone surpasses all the meters. She who is that prosperity (*śrī*) is the Great Hymn (*mahad-uktha*). That which is the Great Hymn is these very *candasyā* bricks.

Its head consists of Gāyatrīs; its trunk, Triṣṭubhs; its spine, Jagatīs; its wings, Paṅktis. Then, taking four syllables from each of these Kakubs, he lays them down as Atichandas verses; thus each one becomes an Atichandas, while the others become Gāyatrīs. That which consists of Bṛhatīs amounts to eighty Gāyatrīs; that which consists of Uṣṇihs amounts to [eighty] Uṣṇihs. Now, whatever is the Vaśa verse, whatever the two half-verses, whatever the Aindrāgna verse, and whatever the Āvapana—these are the Atichandas. Furthermore, whatever is the Nada, whatever the Sūdadohas, whatever the word-appendages (padanuṣaṅgas), and whatever else here is performed with Anuṣṭubhs—all that belongs to the Anuṣṭubhs.
The two-footed are the foundation.

This much indeed is the Great Hymn (mahaduktha); the Great Hymn is prosperity. The gods bestowed this entire prosperity upon him; in the same way, this [sacrificer] bestows all this prosperity upon him.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Chandasyā bricks:

the gods, it is said, saw this vault, this heavenly world; they entered it by means of these Stomabhāgā bricks. As they were entering, Prajāpati entered last. That which is Prajāpati is these very Chandasyā bricks.

The Gāyatrīs are its head. As to why they are Gāyatrīs: the head is indeed Gāyatra; there are three of them, for the head is threefold; he places them in the front part, for this head is in the front.
The *triṣṭubh* verses belong to the chest.
He places them within the range of the two *retaḥsic* bricks; for the *pṛṣṭhas* are the two *retaḥsic*s, and the chest is the counterpart of the *pṛṣṭhas*.
The *jagatī* verses are the hips.

As far as he places the *triṣṭubh* verses behind the *svayamātṛṇā* brick in front, so far behind it are the *jagatī*s. For this *svayamātṛṇā* is that vital breath which is here in the middle; and as far from this vital breath as the chest is in front, so far behind are the hips.
The *anuṣṭubh*s are the two thighs; he places them immediately after the *jagatī*s, for he thus places the thighs in immediate proximity to the hips.

The ribs are *bṛhatī*s; the breast-bones are *kakubh*s. Therefore, he places the *bṛhatī*s between the *triṣṭubh*s and the *kakubh*s; hence these ribs are fastened on both sides, to the breast-bones and to the collar-bones.
The necks are *uṣṇih* verses. He places them immediately adjacent to the *gāyatrī* verses; he thus places the necks so that they are not separated from the head.

The wings are *paṅkti* verses. As to why they are *paṅkti*s: the wings are fivefold; he places them on the sides, for these two wings are on the sides. He places that metre which is larger on the south side; he thereby makes the right half of the animal more vigorous, and therefore the right half of the animal is more vigorous.

The *Aticchandas* verses are the belly. The meters (*chandāṃsi*) are indeed cattle, and cattle are food; the belly eats food, for the belly indeed eats food. Therefore, when food reaches the belly, it becomes consumed and loses its original form. Since these [verses] eat cattle—the meters—they are called *Attichandas*. They are called *Attichandas* because they eat the meters; this is an indirect designation (*parokṣa*), for the gods love the indirect.

The womb is filled with excrement. He lays these two down touching each other, for the belly and the womb are indeed in contact; they are joined together by excrement, for excrement is indeed flesh, and by flesh the belly and the womb are joined. The former brick is an *aticandā*, the latter is filled with excrement; for the belly is higher and the womb is lower.
He lays them down facing east;

for this fire-altar is built facing the east, and moreover, the belly is directed forward and the womb is directed forward. Outside the Stomabhāgas is the heart; for the Stomabhāgas are the heart, and the heart is indeed highest, then the belly, and then the womb.

He places them to the south of the *svayamātṛṇā* brick. Then, in the first layer, he places the *udara* (belly) and the *yoni* (womb) to the north of the *svayamātṛṇā*. That which is this breath (*prāṇa*) in the middle—this *svayamātṛṇā* is that; thus he places both the belly and the womb on both sides of that breath. Therefore, on both sides of this breath, there are both the belly and the womb.
The *pratiṣṭhās* consist of two-footed verses.

As to why they are two-footed: a pair is indeed a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). There are three of them, for a triad is a firm foundation. He lays them down behind; for what is behind is a firm foundation.
This is his well-made self.

Therefore, for whomsoever they thus fashion this well-made self, he indeed comes into being with that well-made self; but for whomsoever they fashion it otherwise than this, they fashion a badly made self for him, and he indeed comes into being with that badly made self.
Therefore, these two Sāman-concluding formulas (nidhanas) are recited: "The Arka of the gods in the highest heaven; the gods of the Arka in the highest heaven.

For when the gods were entering [the body], Prajāpati entered last; therefore he says, "The Arka of the gods in the highest heaven. And as for why he says, "The gods of the Arka in the highest heaven": this Agni is indeed the Arka, and all the gods have entered into him in his highest layer (citī); therefore he says, "The gods of the Arka in the highest heaven."

He lays down the Gārhapatya fire-altar. Having obtained this, the gods indeed thought themselves successful; they said, "By what means have we succeeded in this? They replied, "By the Gārhapatya itself. "Having built the Gārhapatya and ascended it, we perceived the first layer; from the first, the second; from the second, the third; from the third, the fourth; from the fourth, the fifth; and from the fifth, this [world]," they said.

They said, "Find out how this success may belong to us alone. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)," for they were saying, "Seek that by which this success may belong to us alone."

As they were reflecting, they perceived this: "Let us bring this here and place it down. Having brought it here, they placed it down. Regarding it, they disputed: the Vasus from the east, the Rudras from the south, the Ādityas from the west, the Maruts from the north, and the Viśve Devas from above, each saying, "Let us place it here! Let us place it here!"

They said, "Let us place it right in the middle; being placed in the middle, it shall belong to all of us. So they placed it in the middle. They thereby placed that success within themselves; from the very center, from the very center, they placed that success within themselves. In the same way, when the sacrificer places the Gārhapatya fire-altar, he places that very success within himself; from the very center, from the very center, he places that success within himself.
And as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya hearth:
the Gārhapatya is indeed food, and this piled Agni is the eater; he thus places that food within the eater. He places it in the middle; verily, he thus bestows food upon him in the very center.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya:

the sacrificial altar (vedi) is indeed the world of the gods, and yet this [fire] is built outside the altar; when he brings it here and lays it down, he thereby establishes it upon the altar, in the world of the gods.

Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Gārhapatya fire-altar: the lotus leaf is indeed a womb, and this (fire-altar) has been built outside the womb; for that work of the fire-altar which is done prior to the lotus leaf is outside the womb. When he brings it here and lays it down, he thereby establishes it in the womb, upon the lotus leaf; thus it is not outside. He lays down eight bricks; the significance of that has been explained. He builds it with these very same formulas and in this same manner; for that which was yonder is this very one, and having brought that very one here, he lays it down.
Then he lays down the *citi* again.

For when the gods had piled the Gārhapatya altar, they did not perceive success (*rāddhi*) in it; for the piling of the Gārhapatya is a womb, and the success of a womb is indeed seed and procreation. In that womb, they did not perceive seed and procreation.
They said, "Consider how we may place seed and procreation in this womb. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer; seek how we may place seed and procreation in this womb."

While they were reflecting, they saw this Punashchiti (re-building layer) and laid it down; thus they placed generative seed in this womb, in the very middle. In the very middle they thus placed generative seed in this womb. In the same way, when the sacrificer lays down the Punashchiti, he places generative seed in this very womb; in the very middle he thus places generative seed in this womb.

Some indeed place it on the hind-part [of the altar], saying, "From the hind-part, seed is poured; at the junction with the tail, from the tail, seed is poured. One should not do so; for those who do so place the seed and procreation outside the womb. He should place it in the middle; thus he places the seed and procreation directly within the womb.
He lays down eight bricks.

The Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he pours him forth when he has become seed. He settles it five times; the fire-altar consists of five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he pours him forth when he has become seed. There are eight bricks, and he settles them five times—that makes thirteen; the year has thirteen months, and there are thirteen layers of earth (purīṣa) for the fire-altar; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the *punar-citi* (re-piling):

he indeed does what is improper when he piles the *gārhapatya* altar higher than the *āhavanīya*. Therefore, when he lays down the *punar-citi*, he brings back that very same fire which was already piled and piles it again upon it. Because he piles it again after it has already been piled, it is called the *punar-citi*.

Now, some place the Gārhapatya fire-altar in the rear half and the Punashchiti and Āhavanīya in the front half, saying, "These two are indeed the Gārhapatya and the Āhavanīya; thus these two fires are [properly] arranged. One should not do so; for the Gārhapatya is this world and the Āhavanīya is the sky, and that (the sky) is above this (earth). Therefore, one should place it (the Punashchiti) only above it.

Moreover, as to why he lays down both the Gārhapatya and the Punar-citi: these two are the altar (vedi) and the high-altar (uttaravedi) of Agni; whereas those two which he previously pours out belong to the Adhvara sacrifice, these two belong to Agni. Thus, when he has laid down these two and then sets down the Agni, he establishes him upon both the altar and the high-altar.

And as to why he further places a layer (citi): this is indeed a renewed sacrifice, and this is a higher worship of the gods; thus he places a renewed sacrifice and a higher worship of the gods, and the renewed sacrifice inclines toward him.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Punashcitī (the re-piling):

that very Agni whom the Rishis, the vital breaths, constructed in the beginning—him he now piles up again. And because he piles him again when he has already been piled, it is therefore called the Punashcitī.

"With that austerity by which the seers entered the sacrificial session"—this he says of those very seers. "Kindling Agni, bringing forth the light"—this means kindling Agni, they brought forth the heavenly world. "In that vault of heaven I have placed Agni"—the heavenly world is indeed the vault of heaven. "Whom they call Manu with the strewn sacrificial grass"—those who are wise are the Manus; he is always one for whom the sacrificial grass is strewn.

"May we follow him with our wives, O gods, with our sons, our brothers, and our gold"—by this he means, "may we all follow him with everything. "Seizing the firmament (nāka) in the world of the well-done"—the firmament is indeed the heavenly world; thus, "seizing the heavenly world in the world of the well-done. "Upon the third ridge in the luminous realm of heaven"—this third ridge is indeed the luminous realm of heaven where that [sun] shines.

"He has mounted the middle of speech, the active one"—this is indeed the middle of speech where this [altar] is built; "the active one" means the sustainer; "this Agni, the lord of the good, the wise one"—this means this Agni is the protector of the virtuous, being conscious; "placed on the back of the earth, shining brightly"—this means placed on the back of the earth, blazing; "let him place beneath his feet those who attack us"—this means let him cast all evils beneath his feet.

"This Agni is most heroic, bestowing vigor"—this means "this Agni is most powerful, bestowing vigor. "May he shine forth a thousandfold, unwearied"—this means "may he blaze a thousandfold, being vigilant. "Radiantly shining in the midst of the flood"—the flood is indeed these worlds; thus, "shining in these worlds. "Approach the celestial abodes"—this means "proceed toward the heavenly world."
"Fall down together; come together to him"—this he says to those seers:

"Fall down toward him and come together unto him. "O Agni, prepare the paths that lead to the gods"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. "Making the parents young again"—the parents are indeed speech and mind, for speech and mind are these two youthful parents. "Thou hast followed after them, weaving this thread upon thee"—this he says regarding that very thread which was woven by the seers.

"Wake up, O Agni; do thou watch over us"—by this he says to this Agni, "Wake up loudly and watch over him. "May you two unite the sacrificial offering and the pious work, and this [Agni]"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. "In this abode, in the higher one"—the sky, indeed, is the higher abode. "May the All-gods and the sacrificer sit down"—thereby he causes the sacrificer to sit down together with the All-gods.

"With that whereby thou carriest a thousand, O Agni, whereby [thou carriest] all wealth"—this is his most firmly established abode, whereby he carries a thousand and whereby he carries all wealth; "with that lead this sacrifice of ours to heaven, to go among the gods"—that is to say, "with that lead this sacrifice of ours to the heavenly world, to go among the gods. "This is thy seasonal womb"—the significance of this has already been explained. He lays down eight bricks; the significance of that has also already been explained.

He lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*). These seasonal bricks are the seasons; it is thus the seasons he lays down. Now, these seasonal bricks are everything; for the seasonal bricks are the year, and the year is all this; it is thus all this that he lays down. Moreover, this is procreation: the seasonal bricks are the year, and the year is procreation; it is thus procreation that he lays down.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*):

the seasonal bricks are the nobility (*kṣatra*), and these other bricks are the common people (*viś*). He thus places the nobility as an eater among the common people. He lays them down in all the layers; he thereby places the nobility as an eater among the entire common people.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*):

this Agni is the year, and he is joined together by means of the seasonal bricks; thus he extends and connects the year with the seasons. These bricks have different beginnings but the same endings; for the seasons were created, and once created, they were indeed distinct from one another.

They said, "In this state, we shall certainly not be able to procreate; let us unite with forms. They united with forms during each individual season; therefore, in each single season, the form of all the seasons is present. As for the fact that they have various beginnings—it was because they were created separately—and as for the fact that they have a common conclusion—it was because they united through their forms.
He lays them down with the formula:

"Tapa and Tapasya, the two dewy seasons"—these are their names; it is by means of these very names that he thus lays them down. Yonder sun, indeed, is Tapa; therefore these two seasons are not separated from him. And because these two seasons are not separated from him, they are called Tapa and Tapasya.
"Thou art the inner bond of Agni."

This Agni is the year; he is joined together by the seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā). Thus he extends and unites the year with the seasons. With the words, "May heaven and earth be in order! May the waters and plants be in order!"—he thus brings all this into order by means of the seasons. With the words, "May the fires be in order separately, for my pre-eminence, being of one vow"—for these bricks are indeed separate fires; he says this so that they may be in order for the pre-eminence of these two seasons. With the words, "The fires which are of one mind between these two, heaven and earth"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance. With the words, "May the two winter seasons, being well-adjusted, enter together as the gods entered Indra"—just as the gods entered Indra, so may these two seasons enter for the sake of pre-eminence. There are two bricks, for a season consists of two months; he settles them once, and thus he makes the season one.
Now, as to why he lays these down here:

this Agni is the year, and the year is these worlds; of that [year], the fifth layer is indeed the sky, and the summer season is its sky. Therefore, when he lays these down here, he thereby restores to him whatever of his own self these two constitute; that is why he lays them down here.
Furthermore, as to why he lays these two down here:

this Agni is Prajāpati, and Prajāpati is the year; the fifth layer is his head, and the cool season (Śiśira) is his head. Therefore, when he lays these two down here, he thereby restores to him that which belongs to his own self; that is why he lays these two down here.
He places the two seasonal bricks in front of both the *svayamātṛṇā* and the *viśvajyotis*.

The highest *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed the sky, and the highest *viśvajyotis* is the sun; thus he places the seasons between the sky and the sun. Therefore, the seasons are indeed here below from this point. Moreover, this is procreation: he thereby establishes procreation here below between the sky and the sun. Therefore, it is from here below that offspring are born. For what is beyond this point is indeed stationary; for as many gods as there were in the beginning, so many gods there are.
Then he places the two seasonal bricks above the first naturally-perforated brick and above the first Viśvajyotis brick.

This earth is indeed the first naturally-perforated brick, and Agni is the first Viśvajyotis; thus he places the seasons above that. Therefore, from here upwards the seasons proceed. Moreover, this is procreation; he thereby places procreation upwards from here, and therefore offspring are born only upwards from here.

One should not transpose them, thinking, "Lest I transpose the seasons. For indeed, when one dies, the seasons are transposed for him; therefore, at whatever place one lays down the first two, there he should lay down all of them.

Now, these seasonal bricks (ṛtavyā) are indeed these worlds; he thus builds up these worlds upwards by means of the layers (citis). Moreover, the seasonal bricks are the nobility (kṣatra); he thus builds up the nobility upwards by means of the layers. Furthermore, the seasonal bricks are the year; he thus builds up the year upwards by means of the layers. He should not place any other brick possessed of a sacrificial formula (yajuṣmatī) upon them from above, lest he should place the common people (viś) over the nobility.
These indeed are the *saṃyānī* bricks.

For by means of the seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, the gods went together through these worlds—from here upwards and from there downwards; in the same way, the sacrificer now goes together through these worlds by means of the seasonal bricks—from here upwards and from there downwards.
Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus lay down other bricks as the *saṃyānīs*, but one should not do so; for they would thereby cause an excess, and these very [bricks] are indeed the *saṃyānīs*.
Then he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick.
The sun, indeed, is the highest Viśvajyotis, for the sun is the all-light in yonder world; it is the sun that he thus lays down.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick:
offspring indeed are the Viśvajyotis, for offspring are the light of all; it is thus the power of procreation that he lays down.
He places the Viśvajyotis brick in front of the Svayamātṛṇṇā.

The highest Svayamātṛṇṇā is indeed the sky, and the highest Viśvajyotis is the sun; he thus places the sun on this side of the sky, and therefore the sun shines only towards this side from there. Moreover, this is procreation; he thus places the procreative power of the sky on this side, and therefore procreation occurs only towards this side from there.

Then, upon the first naturally-perforated brick, he lays down the Viśvajyotis brick on top. This first naturally-perforated brick is indeed this earth; the Viśvajyotis is Agni. Thus he places Agni upwards from here; therefore Agni blazes upwards from here. Moreover, this is procreation; thus he places procreation upwards from here; therefore offspring is produced upwards from here alone.

Then, upon the middle *svayamātṛṇā* brick, he lays down the *viśvajyotis* brick from above. The middle *svayamātṛṇā* is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and the middle *viśvajyotis* is Vāyu. Thus, he places Vāyu in the intermediate space; therefore, this Vāyu is in the intermediate space.

These are indeed the luminaries. When he lays these down in this manner, he thereby establishes these luminaries in their proper alignment. Therefore, from here upwards Agni blazes; yonder Sun shines downwards; and this Vāyu blows crosswise in the intermediate space.
"May Parameṣṭhin settle thee!"—for Parameṣṭhin saw this fifth layer; "the luminous one on the back of heaven"—for yonder luminous Āditya is indeed on the back of heaven.

"For all out-breathing, for in-breathing, for diffused breathing"—for the Viśvajyotis is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa), and the vital breath serves all this; "granting all light," that is, "granting every light. "Sūrya is your overlord"—he thus makes Sūrya its overlord. Having set it down, he pronounces the *sūdadohas* verse; its significance has already been explained.
These indeed are the "unifying" (saṃyānī) bricks.

For by means of these Viśvajyotis bricks, the gods united these worlds—from here upwards and from there downwards; in the same way, the sacrificer unites these worlds by means of the Viśvajyotis bricks—from here upwards and from there downwards.
Now, the Caraka-Adhvaryus lay down other bricks as the *saṃyānīs*, but one should not do so; for they would thereby cause an excess, and these very [bricks] are indeed the *saṃyānīs*.
Then he lays down the Lokampṛṇā brick.

Yonder sun, indeed, is the Lokampṛṇā, for he fills these worlds; it is yonder sun that he thus lays down. He lays it down in all the layers; these layers are indeed these worlds, so he places yonder sun in these worlds. Therefore, he (the sun) shines for all these worlds.
Moreover, as to why he lays down the Lokampṛṇā brick:

the Lokampṛṇā is the nobility (kṣatra), and these other bricks are the common people (viś). He thus places the eater among the people; he lays it down in every layer, and thereby places the eater among the entire people.

This [first] one alone becomes [the Kṣatriya]; he makes that power (kṣatra) abide in one place and the prosperity (śrī) abide in one place. Now, as for the second [set], that is a pair; for a pair is indeed half of this self. When one is together with a mate, then one is whole, then complete. For the sake of completeness, with a single sacrificial formula (yajus), he lays down many bricks; thereby he endows the power with vigor, making the power more vigorous than the people (viś). Then he lays down the others separately with various formulas; thereby he makes the people less vigorous than the power, speaking separately and having diverse thoughts.
He places it first on this corner;

he thereby places yonder sun in that direction. Then from here he goes around it from there, then from here he goes around it from there, then from here he goes around it from there, then from here he goes around it from there.
If he were to place it right there where he first placed it, then he would place it subsequently at the very top;

thus that sun, having traversed these worlds once, would not move further beyond them. Instead, having moved it forward, he places it subsequently at the topmost layer; thereby he causes that sun to move beyond these worlds. Therefore, that sun, never coming to rest, moves around these worlds again and again, turning toward the south.

"Fill the world, fill the aperture"—that is, "fill the space and fill the opening. And then, "sit thou firm"—that is, "sit thou steady and well-established. "Indra and Agni and Bṛhaspati have seated thee in this womb"—that is, "Indra, Agni, and Bṛhaspati have established thee in this womb. He does so with an Anuṣṭubh verse; for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and Indra is speech, and Indra is the Lokampṛṇā. He does not settle it (the brick), for it is already settled. He pronounces the Sūdadohas verse; for the Sūdadohas is breath: by means of breath he thus connects and joins it together.
Regarding this they say: "How does this Lokampṛṇā become unexhausted? Yonder sun, indeed, is the Lokampṛṇā, and he is unexhausted; moreover, speech is the Lokampṛṇā, and speech is indeed unexhausted.

Having laid down the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, he covers them with the *lokampṛṇā* brick. The *yajuṣmatī* bricks are indeed food, and the *lokampṛṇā* is the self; he thus encloses the food within the self. Therefore, food enclosed within the self becomes the self itself.
He indeed lays down the *yajuṣmatī* bricks only in the body, not in the wings or the tail;

thus he places that food in the body. For when food is placed in the body, it protects the body as well as the wings and the tail; but when it is placed in the wings and the tail, it protects neither the body nor the wings and the tail.

He lays down both the *yajuṣmatī* bricks and the *lokampṛṇā* bricks upon the body; therefore this body is double-layered and, as it were, more solid. He lays down the *lokampṛṇā*s alone in the wings and tail; therefore the wings and tail are, as it were, thinner. He lays them down on the body both lengthwise and crosswise; for the bricks are indeed bones, and therefore these bones in the body run both lengthwise and crosswise. But in the wings and tail they are laid down only lengthwise, for there is no bone at all in the wings and tail that runs crosswise. This, then, is the distinction between the built altar and the unbuilt: thus is the one built, and otherwise the other.

He indeed covers the *svayamātṛṇā* brick with the *lokampṛṇā*. The *svayamātṛṇā* is breath, and the *lokampṛṇā* is the sun; he thus kindles the breath by means of the sun. Therefore, this breath is warm. With that [brick], he covers his entire self; he thus kindles his entire self by means of the sun. Therefore, this entire self is warm. This, indeed, is the sign for one who will live and one who will die: one who will live is warm, while one who will die is cold.

In whichever corner he lays down the first two [bricks], from there he proceeds, covering them by tens, as far as the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; turning to the right, he proceeds along the rear of the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, covering it, and reaches the *anūkyā*; then, returning again, he covers that boundary.
He covers himself first;

for of one being born, it is indeed the self that is born first, then the right wing, then the tail, then the left wing; that is done moving to the right, for so it is among the gods; and thus yonder sun moves around these worlds from left to right.
This very vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed that *lokapṛṇā* brick.

With it, he covers his entire self; he thus places the vital breath within his whole self. For if any limb of his were not to be reached by this [brick], the vital breath would not reach that limb of his. And whatever limb the vital breath does not reach either dries up or withers away. Therefore, he should cover him entirely with this [brick].
He indeed builds up the wings and the tail from out of himself;

for it is from out of oneself that the limbs grow forth. Now, were he to lay down those bricks facing downward in front, it would be as if one were to take a limb from elsewhere and attach it to it—that is what it would be like.

One should not place a brick that is cracked or black. For that which is cracked is indeed afflicted (*ārta*), and that which is black is an afflicted form; [he does this] thinking, "Lest I construct for myself something afflicted. Nor should he cast away one that is uncracked, thinking, "Lest I make for myself something unafflicted external to my self. Having counted them according to the hearths (*dhiṣṇya*), those which exceed the *virāj* meter should not be placed on the northern altar. Indeed, they are afflicted. He should break them and throw them onto the rubbish-heap (*utkara*); for the rubbish-heap is the resting-place of what is excessive. Thus, he establishes them in that very place which is the resting-place of the excessive.

Now, therefore, regarding the measures of the bricks: one should place bricks measuring a foot (pāda) in the first and the last layers; for the foot is a foundation, and what is the foot is also the hand. The tallest bricks should be the size of the thigh, for there is no bone larger than the thigh. Three of the layers should have three lines drawn across them, for these worlds are threefold; two layers may have an unlimited number of lines, for these two layers are the essence, and the essence is indeed unlimited. However, all the layers should indeed have three lines drawn across them, for all these worlds are threefold.

Now, therefore, concerning the insertion of the bricks. Whatever brick one knows to be "possessing a sacrificial formula" (yajuṣmatī), that one should place in the middle layer. The middle layer is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa); and the intermediate space is the receptacle for all beings. Moreover, the bricks possessing formulas are food, and the middle layer is the belly; thus he places that food in the belly.
Regarding this they say:

"One should not place them down, lest one should exceed. Yet, he should indeed place them down; for these bricks are placed down for the sake of desires, and there is nothing that exceeds desires. However, he should not place them down at all; for the gods did only this much.
Then he scatters loose soil.
Now, loose soil is indeed flesh; he thus covers it with flesh. Having laid down the bricks, there are bones in this [altar]; he thus covers those bones with flesh.
He indeed scatters [the earth] upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick.

The *svayamātṛṇā* is breath, and the loose soil is food; he thus places food in the breath. Thereby he covers his entire self. Therefore, whatever food is placed in the breath protects the entire self and pervades the entire self.

"One should not sow seed upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick," some say, "for the *svayamātṛṇā* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); one must not cover the vital breaths. However, he should indeed sow there; for the vital breaths are supported by food. Indeed, the vital breaths of one who does not eat food wither away. For him for whom they act in this manner, he comes into being in the other world like a dry, hollow metal image. Therefore, he should sow seed upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick itself.

Having sown [the seeds] upon the *svayamātṛṇā* brick, he goes along covering it with the spine; then, turning to the right, he goes along covering it from the enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) behind the *svayamātṛṇā*, and again up to the spine.
He covers himself first;
for of one being born, it is the self that is born first, then the right wing, then the tail, then the left wing; that is done moving to the right, for such is the way among the gods.

This very purīṣa is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). With it, he covers his entire self; he thus places the vital breath within his whole body. For if this [purīṣa] were not to reach a certain limb of his, the vital breath would not reach that limb of his. And whatever limb the vital breath does not reach, that either withers or decays. Therefore, he should cover his entire body with this.

"All have magnified Indra"—for all beings indeed magnify Indra. "With songs, him who is as wide as the sea"—this he says of his greatness. "The best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors"—for he is indeed the best of chariot-warriors among chariot-warriors. "The lord of strengths, the master"—strengths (*vāja*) are indeed food; thus he means "the lord of foods, the master. With an Anuṣṭubh verse addressed to Indra he scatters [the earth], for the loose soil (*purīṣa*) belongs to Indra. Now, this loose soil is one half of Agni, and the brick is the other half.
Regarding this they say:

"Since he lays down the bricks with all the meters and for all the deities, yet here he sows [the seeds] with one [verse] dedicated to a single deity, how is this half of Agni? Indra, indeed, is all the gods; therefore, in that he sows with a verse addressed to Indra, by that it is half of Agni. And in that it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter—since the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and speech is all the meters—by that also it is half.
Then he lays down the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā.

The Vikarṇī is indeed Vāyu, and the highest Svayamātṛṇā is the Sky; he thus lays down Vāyu and the Sky. He lays them down on the topmost [layers], for Vāyu and the Sky are at the topmost. He lays them down touching each other, for Vāyu and the Sky are in contact. He lays down the Vikarṇī first; he thereby places Vāyu within the Sky. Therefore this wind blows only towards us.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Vikarṇī brick:

when they cause the horse to smell the layer there, then yonder sun strings these worlds together on a thread; that thread is Vāyu, and that which is Vāyu is this Vikarṇī. Thus, when he lays down this brick, yonder sun strings these worlds together on a thread.
Moreover, as to why he lays down both the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā:

the Vikarṇī is indeed life-span (āyus) and the Svayamātṛṇā is breath (prāṇa); thus he lays down both life-span and breath. He lays them down on the topmost layer, for life-span and breath are at the topmost [of the body]. They are in contact, for life-span and breath are in contact. He lays down the Vikarṇī first and then the northern one; by means of life-span he thus encompasses breath on both sides.

"Like a courser in the pasture, when he has emerged from the great enclosure, then the wind blows after his flame; and then, indeed, thy path becomes black"—for when the wind blows after his flame, then his path becomes black. He lays it down with a *triṣṭubh* verse, for Vāyu is of the *triṣṭubh* nature; with a verse addressed to Agni, for this is a rite of Agni; with an undefined verse, for Vāyu is undefined. Now, as to why he says "the wind": Vāyu is indeed the wind.
Then he lays down the Svayamātṛṇā brick with the formula:

"In the seat of Āyu I settle thee. Āyu indeed is this [brick]; this is its seat. "Protecting," for he protects all this; "in the refuge," for all this is in his refuge. "Of the ocean," for this is the heart of the ocean; "the radiant, the shining," for the sky is radiant and shining. "By whom thou shinest upon the sky, upon the earth, and upon the wide atmosphere," for thus does he shine upon these worlds.
"May Parameṣṭhin settle thee!"—
for Parameṣṭhin indeed beheld this fifth layer.
Furthermore, as to why he lays down the Parameṣṭhin brick:
when Prajāpati had become disjointed, the deities took him and departed; Parameṣṭhin, having taken his head, stepped aside and stood apart.

He said to him: "Come to me; give this back to me by which you have departed from me. He asked, "What will be mine from that? [Parameṣṭhin replied: "This part of my own self shall belong to you as having you as its deity. "So be it," he said. Then Parameṣṭhin restored that to him.
Now, that which is the highest naturally-perforated brick is this very self of his;
and when he lays it down here, he thereby restores to him that part of his self which belongs to it. That is why he lays it down at this point.

"On the back of the sky, wide and broad"—for this back of the sky is indeed wide and broad; "support the sky, make firm the sky, do not injure the sky"—this means "support yourself, make firm yourself, do not injure yourself."

"For all out-breathing, in-breathing, diffused breathing, and up-breathing"—the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is indeed the breath; for all this, the breath is the foundation and the means of movement. "For the foundation, for movement"—these worlds are indeed the *svayamātṛṇṇās*, and these worlds are the foundation and the means of movement. "May Sūrya protect thee"—that is, "may Sūrya guard thee. "With great well-being"—that is, "with great prosperity. "With most peaceful protection"—that is, "with that protection which is most peaceful."

He lays them down separately, for wind and sky are separate; he settles them once, thereby making them common, for life-breath and out-breath are common. Both of these are indeed pebbles, both are self-perforated, for life-breath and out-breath are indeed common. Then he pronounces the *sūdadohas* over them; the *sūdadohas* is indeed the life-breath; by means of the life-breath he thus connects and joins them together.
"Those [waters] of his, yielding milk," so it is said.

The waters, indeed, are the *sūda*; food is the milking. "They mix Soma with the dappled ones"—food, indeed, is the dappled one. "In the birth of the gods"—the year, indeed, is the birth of the gods. "The clans"—the sacrifice, indeed, is the clan, for in the sacrifice all beings are contained. "In the three luminous realms of heaven"—the three pressings are the luminous realms; by this he refers to the pressings. With an *anuṣṭubh* verse he does so, for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and speech is all the vital breaths; thus he connects and joins them by means of both speech and vital breath. This *sūdadohas* verse, though being one, extends over all the bricks. The *sūdadohas* is indeed the vital breath; therefore, this vital breath, though being one, extends over all the limbs and the entire body.
Then he sings the Sāmans over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.
