These worlds, indeed, are the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; these are those pebbles. Having laid them down, the gods saw them as being just like this—just as these dry pebbles are now.

They said, "Consider how we may place sap, a means of subsistence, into these worlds. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)"; that is, "Seek it so that we may place sap, a means of subsistence, into these worlds."

While reflecting, they saw these Sāmans and sang them; by means of them, they placed within these worlds the essence that provides sustenance. In the same way, when the sacrificer sings these Sāmans, he thereby places within these very worlds the essence that provides sustenance.
He sings over the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks.
These worlds are indeed the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; he thus places within these very worlds sap and sustenance.

He sings over these sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis), namely "bhūr," "bhuvaḥ," and "svar. "Bhūḥ" is indeed this world; "bhuvaḥ" is the intermediate space; and "svar" is yonder world. Thus, he places within these very worlds essence and sustenance.

These [sāmans] indeed have different beginnings (prastāva) but the same endings (nidhana). As to why they have different beginnings: they saw them as diverse. And as to why they have the same endings: there is indeed only one foundation for the sacrifice, and the ending is one—the heavenly world itself. Therefore, they have "light" (jyotis) as their ending, which is the heavenly world.
Then he sprinkles it with chips of gold.
At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; therein the gods placed this supreme immortal form, and in the very same way, this sacrificer now places this supreme immortal form in him.
And again, as to why he sprinkles it with chips of gold:
he thereby places that lovely form of his—the *rukma* and the man—in the middle from the front; and then he covers this whole thing from above with a lovely form.

By two hundred each; for the sacrificer consists of two parts, and Agni is the sacrificer: as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much he bestows this highest immortal form upon him. Five times [he offers], for the fire-altar has five layers, five seasons are a year, and the year is Agni: as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much he bestows this highest immortal form upon him. With a thousand [he offers], for a thousand is everything; by everything indeed he bestows this highest immortal form upon him.

Standing behind [the altar], he faces east; then, having moved to the north, he faces south; then, from the front, he faces west; then, having gone around by the rear, standing to the south, he faces north—this is the clockwise movement (dakṣiṇāvṛt), for that is the way among the gods. Then, having gone around again, standing behind, he faces east; thus his work is indeed performed facing forward.

"You are the measure of a thousand; you are the counterpart of a thousand; you are the counter-measure of a thousand; you are a thousandfold; for a thousand, you!"—this means "You are indeed all, for all are you. For a thousand is everything; thus it means "Everything are you, for everything are you."
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the layers (citi) and the fillings (purīṣa).
This very world is the first layer; the cattle are the filling. In that he covers the first layer with the filling, he thereby covers this world with cattle.
The intermediate space itself is the second layer;
the birds are the loose soil. In that he covers the second layer with loose soil, he thereby covers the intermediate space with birds.
The third layer is indeed the sky;
the loose soil is the stars. In that he covers the third layer with loose soil, he thereby covers the sky with the stars.

The sacrifice itself is the fourth layer; the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) are the loose soil. In that he covers the fourth layer with loose soil, he thereby covers the sacrifice with the sacrificial gifts.
The sacrificer himself is the fifth layer;
the loose soil is offspring. In that he covers the fifth layer with loose soil, he thereby covers the sacrificer with offspring.
The world of heaven itself is the sixth layer;
the gods are the loose soil (purīṣa). In that he covers the sixth layer with loose soil, he thereby covers that world of heaven with the gods.

The seventh layer is indeed immortality; he places that as the highest. He thus bestows immortality upon this whole [universe] as its highest. Therefore, immortality is the highest of this whole [universe]; therefore the gods are not separated from it, and therefore they are called "immortal. This is with regard to the deities.

Now as to the internal [correspondence]. That which is this foundation and that downward breath—this is the first layer. The earth-fill (purīṣa) is flesh. When he covers the first layer with earth-fill, he thereby covers those parts of his own self with flesh. Having laid down the bricks, the bones are the bricks; bone is that [earth-fill]; he thus covers those [bones] with flesh. He does not cover [the bones] from below; therefore these vital airs are not covered from below. But he covers them from above; he thereby covers those parts of his own self with flesh from above. Therefore, those parts of his own self are covered with flesh from above and leave no space.

That which is above the foundation and below the middle—that is the second layer. Flesh is the loose soil; when he covers the second layer with loose soil, he thereby covers that part of his own self with flesh. Having laid down bricks, the bricks are bones; thus he covers those bones with flesh. He lays down loose soil and covers it with loose soil; he thereby covers both sides of that part of his own self with flesh. Therefore, this part of his self is covered on both sides with flesh and leaves no space.

The middle [part] itself is the third layer. That which is above the middle and below the neck is the fourth layer; the neck itself is the fifth layer; the head itself is the sixth layer; the vital breaths themselves are the seventh layer. He places that as the highest; he thus places the vital breaths of this entire [body] as the highest, and therefore the vital breaths of this entire [body] are the highest. He places earth-fillings (*purīṣa*) upon it; the earth-filling is indeed flesh; with flesh he establishes the vital breaths. He does not cover them over from above; therefore these vital breaths are not covered over from above. Now, therefore, he offers the Śatarudriya oblation.

Herein this entire fire has been consecrated; he is Rudra here as the deity. Into him the gods placed this immortal, supreme form. He stood there shining, desiring food. Therefore the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest he should injure us."

They said, "Let us prepare food for him; with that we shall appease him. For him they prepared this food, the Śāntadevatya; with it they appeased him. Because they appeased this god with it, therefore it is called the Śāntadevatya; indeed, they call this *Cāturmāsya* sacrifice the *Śatarudriya* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. In the same way, he now bestows upon him this highest immortal form. He stands there shining, desiring food; for him he prepares this food, the Śāntadevatya, and with it he appeases him.

He offers with *jartila* seeds. He who is being built up is born; he is born for all kinds of food. Now, these *jartila* seeds are both kinds of food: that which is domestic and that which is wild. Insofar as they are sesame seeds, they are domestic; insofar as they ripen on unploughed ground, they are wild. With both kinds of food, therefore, he gratifies him—both with the domestic and with the wild.
He offers with an Arka leaf;
the Arka is food, and thus he gratifies him with food.
He offers in the enclosing-stones;
for these enclosing-stones are Agni, and thus his oblations become offered as if they were in Agni himself.
And as to why he offers this Cāturudriya oblation:

When Prajāpati had become relaxed, the deities departed from him; however, one god alone did not abandon him: it was Wrath (Manyu). He stood there, spread out across the interior. He wept; those tears which fell from him settled upon this Wrath. He became Rudra, with a hundred heads, a thousand eyes, and a quiver containing a hundred arrows. As for the other drops that fell, they became countless thousands and entered these worlds. Because he wept (rudita), they are called Rudras. This very Rudra—with a hundred heads, a thousand eyes, and a quiver of a hundred arrows—stood there with his bow strung, ready to strike, terrifying [all] and seeking food. Therefore, the gods were afraid of him.
They said to Prajāpati:

"We are indeed afraid of him, lest he should injure us," they said. He replied, "Prepare food for him; with that, appease him. For him they prepared this food, the *Caturudriya*; with it they appeased him. Because they appeased Rudra, who has a hundred heads, with this, therefore it is called the *Caturudriya*. "Because they appeased the hundred-headed Rudra with this" (*yad etaṃ śataśīrṣāṇāṃ rudram etenāśamayan*), therefore it is [also] called the *Śataśīrṣa-rudra-śamanīya*. Indeed, they call it the *Caturudriya* cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. In the same way, this one prepares this food for him, the *Śatarudriya*, and with it he appeases him.
He offers oblations of Gavedhuka-grain groats.
For wherever that deity lay shattered, from there the Gavedhukas came into being; thus he gratifies him with his own portion and his own essence.
He offers with an Arka leaf.
For it was through the desire of this very god that the Arka tree came into being; thus he gratifies him with his own portion and his own sap.

He offers in the enclosing-stones. The enclosing-stones are indeed the hair; there is no poison in hair, nor does anything injure it. Standing to the north of the fire, he offers on the northern half of it. For in this direction lie the abodes of this god; thus he gratifies him in his own quarter and sacrifices to him in his own quarter.
He first makes the *svāhā* offering at knee-deep [water].
That which is knee-deep is, as it were, below; and this world is, as it were, below. Thus he gratifies those Rudras who entered this world.
Then [he offers] at the height of the navel.

That which is at the height of the navel is, as it were, the middle; and the intermediate region (antarikṣaloka) is, as it were, the middle. Thus he gratifies those Rudras who entered the intermediate region.
Now, [the layer] reaching up to the mouth:

that which reaches up to the mouth is, as it were, above; and that world yonder is, as it were, above. Thus he gratifies those Rudras who entered that world by means of the *svāhā*-utterance. The *svāhā*-utterance is indeed food; verily, he gratifies them with food.
"Salutation to thee, O Rudra, for thy wrath," he says.

That wrath which was extended within him, to that he thus pays homage. And also, "And salutation to thy arrow, and salutation to thy two arms"—for he stood there terrifying [the world] both with his arrow and with his two arms.
This very one is the divine Kṣatra;

he who became possessed of a hundred heads is the Kṣatra, while these others who arose from the drops are the Viś (the people). For this Kṣatra, these Viś offered up this first fore-share (*uddhāra*). By means of this first Anuvāka, they gratified him; in the same way, this [priest] now offers up this fore-share for him, and thereby gratifies him. Therefore, this [Anuvāka] belongs to a single deity; it belongs to Rudra, for by means of it he gratifies him.

These sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) are fourteen in number. There are thirteen months in a year; Prajāpati is the fourteenth, and Prajāpati is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food he thus gratifies him. "Homage, homage!"—homage is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice, by means of this salutation, he pays him homage. Therefore, one should not say "homage to you" to anyone who is not worthy of sacrifice; for that would be just as if one were to say to him, "Sacrifice to you. Such is that.

Then he offers to the pairs, saying, "Homage to such-and-such and to such-and-such. This is just as if one were to say, "May you two and this one not harm me"; in this way he speaks. For indeed, one who is known and addressed does not cause harm.

"Adoration to Hiraṇyabāhu! Adoration to the Leader of the Army and to the Lord of the Quarters!"—this very one is indeed Hiraṇyabāhu, this one is the Leader of the Army, and this one is the Lord of the Quarters. Therefore, whatever here has a single deity, by that he gratifies him alone; he thus makes the nobility (kṣatra) a sharer with the people (viś). Therefore, whatever belongs to the people, the nobleman is a sharer therein. Now, those thousands that were innumerable and entered these worlds—those are the deities to whom he offers this oblation.
Then he offers to those who have been born.

For these Rudras entered into these beings that have been born; wherever they are, it is there that he thus gratifies them. Moreover, these are the lineages of the Rudras among the gods, and men follow the pattern of the gods; therefore, these are the lineages of men. Thus, he gratifies them according to their respective births.

Some of them pay homage on both sides, while others pay homage on only one side. Those who pay homage on both sides are indeed more terrible and less peaceful; therefore, he pacifies them by means of this sacrifice and homage on both sides.
He indeed offers with "svāhā" at every eighty [verses]:

at the first section, then at eighty, then again at eighty; and as for the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) that follow the *āvatāna* sections, these are the "eighties" which are food; by means of food, he thus gratifies them.
Then he mutters these sacrificial formulas:

"Homage to you, the Kirikas! This is indeed his most familiar abode, just as a beloved son or one's own heart; therefore, whenever he has any doubt regarding this deity, he should offer oblations with these sacred utterances (*vyāhṛtis*). Thus he approaches the beloved abode of that deity, and so this deity does not harm him.

"Adoration to you, the Kirikas!"—for these indeed perform all this; "to the hearts of the gods"—these are Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, for they are the hearts of the gods; "adoration to the Vicinvatkas!"—for these indeed gather up all this; "adoration to the Vikṣiṇatkas!"—for these indeed consume him whom they wish to consume; "adoration to the Anirhatakas!"—for these are not driven away from these worlds.
Then he mutters the subsequent verses. "O Drāpi, Lord of the food!"—this one is indeed Drāpi;

he makes him run away (drāpayati) whom he wishes to cause to run away. "Lord of the food"—that is, "Lord of Soma. "O Daridra, O Blue-and-Red"—these are his names and these are his forms; by mentioning his name, he thus gratifies him. "Do not fear for these offspring, for these cattle; do not harm us, nor let anything afflict us"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
This very one is the divine Kṣatra.

For this Kṣatra, these subjects drew out that first portion (uddhāra) from the front, which is this first Anuvāka; then they drew out for it this [second] portion from above, and thereby they gratified it. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now draws out for it this portion from above, and thereby he gratifies it. Therefore, although this [section] belongs to a single deity, it is indeed dedicated to Rudra, for it is by this alone that he gratifies him.
There are these seven sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).

The fire-altar consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons; the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just so much food he thus gratifies it. These two sets together amount to twenty-one. There are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. This is the correspondence.
Then he offers the *avatāna* (unstringing) oblations.

For the gods, having gratified them with this food, then unstrung their bows with these *avatāna* offerings; in the same way, this sacrificer, having gratified them with this food, now unstrings their bows with these *avatāna* offerings, for with an unstrung bow one does not injure anyone.
"That indeed [stretches] for a thousand yojanas.
Now, that which is a thousand yojanas is indeed the furthest distance; and that which is the furthest distance, that very thing he stretches as these bows.
And as to why he says, "a thousand leagues":
this Agni extends for a thousand leagues, for there is nothing else beyond him; thus, when one offers in the fire, one thereby unstrings their bows at a distance of a thousand leagues.
"Innumerable thousands [of them] are in this great ocean"— wherever they are, he thus unstrings their bows.

He offers these ten arrows; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much does he thus unstring their bows.
Then he offers the descending oblations.

For indeed, having ascended from here upwards to these worlds, that ascent was, as it were, away from this world; and this [earth] is the foundation. Those gods returned toward this foundation, and in the same way, the sacrificer now returns toward this foundation.
Moreover, as to why he descends again:
it is thus that, while gratifying them, he follows after them; from there he withdraws himself for the sake of life. Thus, with this self, he reaches a full span of life.
And as to why he descends again:
it is indeed these Rudras whom he gratifies here from above, and them again from there towards this side.

"Let there be homage to the Rudras who are in heaven"—he thereby pays homage to those Rudras who are in yonder world. "Whose arrows are the rain"—the rain, indeed, is their arrows; for with the rain they strike down whomever they wish to harm.

"Adoration be to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space"—by this he pays homage to those Rudras who are in the world of the intermediate space. "Whose arrows are the wind"—the wind, indeed, is their arrows; by means of the wind they strike him whom they intend to harm.

"Adoration be to the Rudras who are on earth"—by this he pays homage to those Rudras who are in this world. "Whose food is the arrow"—food indeed is their arrows; for by means of food they strike down whomever they intend to harm.

From them, ten lines go eastward, ten southward, ten westward, ten northward, and ten upward. The Virāj consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the Virāj; there are ten directions, and Agni is the directions; there are ten vital breaths, and Agni is the vital breaths. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food does he thus gratify them.
And as to why he says "ten, ten":

Or there are ten fingers on the two hands; he thus offers this salutation with joined palms (añjali) to them in every direction. Therefore, being afraid of them, he offers this salutation, saying, "Let there be homage to them!"—thus he pays homage to them. "May they be gracious to us!"—thus they indeed become gracious to him. "Whom we hate and whoever hates us, him we place within their jaws"—whomsoever he hates and whoever hates him, him he places within their jaws. If he should hate someone, he might say, "I place so-and-so in their jaws"; but then there is no turning back from that. Yet one should not pay heed to this [particular naming], for he whom one who knows this hates is already effectively pointed out by himself.

He descends three times. Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies them. The utterance "svāhā" is indeed food; with food he thus gratifies them. Three times he ascends upright; that makes six, the significance of which has been explained.
Moreover, as to why he descends three times:
for he ascends upwards three times; as many times as he ascends upwards, so many times does he descend.

Then he throws that Arka leaf into the Cātvāla pit. For by means of this [leaf], he performs this Raudra rite; it is unappeased, and he thus conceals it so that no one may stand upon this unappeased thing, lest it should injure him. Therefore it is thrown into the Cātvāla. And as for why it is in the Cātvāla: the Cātvāla is indeed Agni, and so this Agni completely consumes it. Now, therefore, follows the ritual correspondence.
Regarding this, they say:

"How does this Śatarudriya obtain Agni as the year? How does it become identical with Agni as the year? This Śatarudriya consists of three hundred and sixty [verses], then thirty, then thirty-five. Now, those which are three hundred and sixty are as many as the days of the year; thus he obtains the days of the year. Then, those which are thirty are the thirty nights of a month; thus he obtains the nights of a month. Thus he obtains both the days and nights of the year. Then, those which are thirty-five: that is the thirteenth month; that is the self (ātman). Thirty are the self, two are the foundation (pratiṣṭhā), two are the vital breaths (prāṇa), and two are the head—thus making thirty-five. So great indeed is the year. In this way, his Śatarudriya obtains Agni as the year; in this way, it becomes identical with Agni as the year. Furthermore, so many indeed are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks that are laid down in the middle of the Śāṇḍila fire-altar. These bricks are indeed separate fires; thus these fires of his, being separate, become offered with the Śatarudriya.
Regarding this, they say:

"How does this *Caturudriya* obtain the Great Litany (*mahaduktha*), and how is it completed by means of the Great Litany? Those twenty-five sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) which are on both sides of the eighty [verses] constitute the twenty-five-fold self; where there is the self, that indeed is the head, and those are the wings and the tail. Now, as for those eighty [verses], that is the attainment of the eighties, for the Great Litany is designated by means of the eighty [verses]. And what is above the eighty [verses], that is precisely what is above the eighty verses of the Great Litany mentioned before. Thus, indeed, this *Caturudriya* obtains the Great Litany, and thus it is completed by means of the Great Litany.
Then he sprinkles him from this side.
For the gods, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya, then appeased him further; in the same way, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya, he now appeases him further.
He sprinkles it all around with water.

Water is indeed peace; he thus pacifies it. He sprinkles it all around on every side; he thus pacifies it on every side. He sprinkles three times; Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he pacifies him.
Moreover, as to why he sprinkles it around:

this Agni is indeed these worlds; he thus encircles these worlds with water. He encircles them with the ocean on every side; therefore the ocean flows all around these worlds. It turns to the right; therefore the ocean flows around these worlds turning to the right.

The Āgnīdhra sprinkles water around [the fire]. This Āgnīdhra is indeed Agni; for one does not harm oneself. It is for the sake of non-injury. From stone [he sprinkles], for from stone water originates; from the armpit [he sprinkles], for from the armpit water originates; from the right armpit [he sprinkles], for from the right armpit water originates.
"In the stone, in the mountain, is the strength that has taken its rest."

"Or rather, this sap is rested in the stone, in the mountains; from the waters, from the plants, from the trees—this milk has been gathered together. For from all this indeed has this milk been gathered together. "Bestow upon us that food and strength, O Maruts, being well-pleased! The Maruts indeed rule over the rain. "Hunger for the stone! he says as he sets it down; thus he places hunger in the stone, and therefore the stone is not eaten. Moreover, the stone is firm, and hunger is firm; thus he places the firm in the firm. "In me be thy strength," he says as he takes it up; thus he bestows strength upon himself. In the same way a second time, and in the same way a third time.
Having set it down, he turns it over three times.
For this [fire] seems to press lightly upon him as it goes around him on all sides; therefore, he makes amends to it for the sake of non-injury.
Moreover, as for why he turns away:
this [breath] indeed follows after him; therefore, he withdraws his self from it so that it may live. Thus, by means of this self, he attains a full lifespan.
It turns back three times;
for it goes around three times, and as many times as it goes around, so many times does it turn back.
Then, having placed that stone in a carrying-basket, they carry it off in this direction; for this is the quarter of Nirṛti, and thus he places the impurity in the very quarter belonging to Nirṛti.

The gods, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, then removed his heat and evil by means of this [offering]. In the same way, this [sacrificer], having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, now removes his heat and evil by means of this [offering].
He carries the fire outside.
This fire is indeed these worlds; thus he places the affliction outside of those worlds. Outside the altar: this altar is indeed this earth; thus he places the affliction outside of it.

He stands facing east on the southern hip of the altar and throws away the earth with the words, "May its heat reach him whom we hate! He thus causes the heat to reach the one he hates. He should say, "May its heat reach so-and-so," naming the one he hates; for then it does not return to him again. Yet one should not pay heed to this, for he whom one who knows this hates is already pointed out by himself. If the clod does not break, he should tell him to break it; for when it breaks, then the heat reaches the one he hates. They return without looking back, and thus they leave behind that heat and evil without looking back.
Having returned, he makes the bricks into milch-cows.

For the gods, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, and having struck away his pain and evil, returned and made the bricks into milch-cows; in the same way, this sacrificer, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, and having struck away his pain and evil, returns and makes the bricks into milch-cows.

"One should perform it while sitting," so say some, for "one milks a cow while sitting. However, one should indeed perform it while standing; for this Agni is these worlds, and these worlds are, as it were, standing; moreover, one who stands is more vigorous.
Standing facing north and east—this cow stands before the sacrificer facing west; for they approach the cow from the south while it stands facing west.
Wherever he reaches [the end], there...

Having touched it, he mutters this sacrificial formula: "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be milch-cows. For Agni indeed has power over the making of these into milch-cows; therefore, among all these deities, he addresses Agni alone. "One and ten, and the end and the beyond-the-end"—for that which consists of one and ten is the lower limit of abundance, while that which consists of the end and the beyond-the-end is the highest limit of abundance. Having thus enclosed them from the lower limit and from the highest limit, the gods made them into milch-cows. In the same way, this sacrificer now, having enclosed them from the lower limit and from the highest limit, makes them into milch-cows. Therefore, one need not even care to make many of them; for in the other world, he makes them many by means of the sacred word (brahman) and the sacrificial formula (yajus). And as to why he connects them together, he thereby connects his desires.
Furthermore, as to why he makes the bricks into milch-cows.

This Agni is indeed speech, for he is built up by speech. When he says, "One and ten, and the end and the beyond-end," one is speech, ten is speech, the end is speech, and the beyond-end is speech; thus the gods made speech itself into a cow. In the same way, the sacrificer now makes speech itself into a cow. And when he connects them together, he thereby connects speech itself. "O Agni, may these bricks of mine be cows for me there in yonder world"—verily, he makes them into cows in this world, and then he makes them into cows in yonder world. Thus these bricks nourish him in both worlds, both in this one and in that one.

"Ye are the seasons," he says; for these bricks are indeed the seasons. "The increasers of truth," he says, which means "the increasers of reality. "Ye are in the seasons, O increasers of truth," he says; for the bricks are the days and nights, and the days and nights abide within the seasons. "Dropping ghee, dropping honey," he says; thereby he makes them drop ghee and drop honey.

"Regarding the name 'Virāj': the gods indeed called these bricks by their names; as they addressed them in this way, those [bricks] turned toward them. But the Lokampṛṇās stood facing away, not having been given names, and were sinking down. They gave them the name 'Virāj', and they turned toward them. Therefore, after laying ten bricks each, he consecrates them with the Lokampṛṇā formula; thus he makes them Virājs, for the Virāj consists of ten syllables. [With the words] 'The wish-fulfilling, inexhaustible,' he thereby makes them wish-fulfilling and inexhaustible."

Then he drags it about with a frog, an *avakā* plant, and a branch of cane. For the gods, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, and having struck away his heat and his evil, then further appeased him; in the same way, this sacrificer, having appeased him with the Śatarudriya and with water, and having struck away his heat and his evil, now further appeases him. He drags it about on all sides; verily, he thus appeases him on every side.
Furthermore, as to why he draws it across:
when the Rishis, the vital breaths, first prepared this Agni, they sprinkled him with water; those waters spilled over and became frogs.

They said to Prajāpati, "That which was our pleasure has indeed gone downwards. He said, "Let this tree of yours know [it]; let him know it thoroughly. That is what they cryptically call the *vetasa* (cane), for the gods love the cryptic; for they said, "Our pleasure has gone downwards," therefore they became the *avākās*. They cryptically call them *avakās*, for the gods love the cryptic. These are the three kinds of water: the frog, the *avakā*, and the cane-branch. With these very three waters he thus appeases him.
Moreover, as to why he draws it along:

this Agni is born when he is built up; he is born for the sake of all food. And all this is food—namely, the frog, the avakā-plant, and the cane-shoots—for these are cattle, water, and trees. Thus, with every kind of food, he gratifies him.

With the frog, [he consecrates] the animals; therefore the frog is the least fit for the subsistence of animals, for it is exhausted. With the *avakā* plant, [he consecrates] the waters; therefore the *avakā* is the least fit for the subsistence of the waters, for they are exhausted. With the reed (*vetasa*), [he consecrates] the trees; therefore the reed is the least fit for the subsistence of the trees, for it is exhausted.

Having tied them to a bamboo pole, he drags them eastward between the enclosing stones on the southern side of the fire with the formula: "With the foam of the ocean, O Agni, we envelop thee; be thou purifying and auspicious unto us. This means: "We pacify thee with the waters belonging to the ocean."
Then he moistens [the grass] with the back part of his hand, saying:

"O Agni, we envelop thee with the afterbirth of the snow; be purifying and auspicious unto us. That which is the extreme cold of the cold is indeed the afterbirth of the snow; thus he means, "We appease thee with the extreme cold of the cold."
Then, with the second half [of the verse], he goes first: "Approach the earth, approach the reed;

descend into the rivers, O Agni, for you are the bile of the waters. Come hither with them, O female frog! And make this sacrifice of ours auspicious, O you of purifying color. As the sacrificial formula is, so is its explanation.
Then, with the first half [of the verse], he draws it toward the south:

"This is the gathering-place of the waters, the dwelling of the ocean; may your missiles burn others than us; O Purifier, be auspicious unto us. As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its application (bandhu). First he draws it forward, then thus, then thus, then thus; for that is the way of the gods (devatrā).
It draws itself forward first;

for of that which is coming into being, it is the self alone that comes into being first, then the right wing, then the tail, then the left wing; this is a movement from right to left, for such is the way among the gods.
He draws the wings and tail toward himself; he thus bestows peace inwardly.

First toward the front and then backward, he thus bestows peace directed hitherward. With the words, "O Agni, the Purifier, with thy light," he [lays down] the right wing; with "O Purifier, shining for us," the tail; and with "By the purifying, observant, and gracious form," the left wing. Because that which is auspicious and peaceful is indeed "purifying" (pāvaka), he thereby truly pacifies him.
He draws it with seven [strands].

The fire-altar consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons; the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just that much he thus draws it. He throws that bamboo-stick onto the rubbish-heap (utkara).

Then he chants around it with Sāman hymns. At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; therein the gods placed this supreme immortal form, and in the same way, he now places this supreme immortal form in him. They are Sāmans; for the Sāmans are the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are indeed immortality—he thus places that supreme immortal form in him. He chants all around; from every side he thus places that supreme immortal form in him.
Furthermore, as to why he sings around him with Sāmans:

the gods once desired, "Let us make this self of ours boneless and immortal. They said, "Find out how we may make this self boneless and immortal. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they surely meant, "Seek a layer (citi)"; they said, "Seek that [layer] so that we may make this self boneless and immortal."

They, being conscious and perceiving these commonalities, sang around him with them; by means of those Sāmans, they made this Self boneless and immortal. In the same way, when the sacrificer sings around him with the Sāmans, he thereby makes this very Self boneless and immortal. He sings around it on all sides; verily, on all sides he thus makes this Self boneless and immortal. He sings while standing; for these worlds stand, as it were; moreover, one who stands is indeed more powerful. Having uttered the *hiṅ* sound, he sings; for therein the Sāman becomes complete and whole.
He sings the Gāyatra first.
The Gāyatra is indeed Agni; he thus makes Agni his head. Moreover, he thereby makes his head boneless and immortal.

The Rathantara is on the right wing. This earth, indeed, is the Rathantara; for this earth is the most essential of these worlds, since all these essences are contained within it. That which is the most essential essence, they call "Rathantara" cryptically, for the gods love the cryptic. He thus makes this earth his right wing; moreover, he thereby makes that right wing of his boneless and immortal.
The *bṛhat* is on the left wing.
The *bṛhat* is indeed the sky, for the sky is the broadest; he thus makes the sky its left wing. Moreover, he thereby makes that left wing of his boneless and immortal.
The Vāmadevya is the self.
The Vāmadevya is indeed breath, and breath is wind; for wind is the self of all these gods. He thus makes this wind his own self; moreover, he thereby makes his own self boneless and immortal.

The *yajñāyajñiya* is the tail. The *yajñāyajñiya* is indeed the moon; for whatever sacrifice is completed, its essence goes to that very [moon]. Because every sacrifice goes to it, therefore the moon is the *yajñāyajñiya*. He thus makes the moon his tail; moreover, he thereby makes his tail boneless and immortal.
Then he sings the Heart of Prajāpati. Yonder sun, indeed, is the heart;

it is smooth, for the heart is smooth; it is circular, for the heart is circular. He sings it in himself, for the heart is in oneself; in the armpit, for the heart is in the armpit—specifically in the right armpit, for the heart is closer there. Thus he makes yonder sun his heart; moreover, he thereby makes his heart boneless and immortal.
He sings concerning both the creatures and the Lord of Creatures.
In that he sings concerning the creatures, he places the heart within the creatures; and in that he sings concerning the Lord of Creatures, he places the heart within Agni.
Moreover, as to why he sings among the creatures and in Prajāpati:
this Agni is indeed both the creatures and Prajāpati; thus, when he sings in the fire, he thereby places the heart within both the creatures and Prajāpati.

These indeed are the immortal bricks; he lays them down last. He thereby places immortality as the highest thing for this entire universe; therefore, immortality is the highest thing for this entire universe. No one other than the Adhvaryu should sing [the Sāman]; for these are bricks, and he would be disintegrated if anyone other than the Adhvaryu were to sing.

On the day of the Upavasatha, when the sun has risen in the morning, he releases his speech. Having released his speech, he takes five portions of clarified butter; therein he throws five chips of gold. Then these three—curds, honey, and clarified butter—are poured together into a vessel, a pot, or a large bowl; upon that, he places a handful of darbha grass.

Then he mounts the fire with the words: "Homage to thy heat, to thy flame; homage be to thy radiance! At this point, this entire fire has been consecrated; it is now capable of harming here, for it might harm that which one intends to harm, or rather, it harms whatever it harms by means of its heat, its flame, or its radiance. Thus, this [mantra] does not harm him through these [qualities]. With the words, "May thy missiles burn others than us; O Purifier, be auspicious unto us," as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
Having ascended the fire, he sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* stone with fivefold-drawn clarified butter; the significance of this has already been explained.
He sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick.
The *svayamātṛṇṇā* is breath; he thus places that food in the breath.
Moreover, as to why he sprinkles the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick:
this [brick] is indeed the high altar (*uttaravedi*) of Agni; whereas that which he previously sprinkled belongs to the *adhvara* sacrifice, this one he now sprinkles for Agni.
Looking at it there, he sprinkles gold;

for that which one sees is manifest, and manifest is the high altar (uttaravedi) here. Those [bricks] are already laid down; for that which is laid down is transcendent, and transcendent is this high altar.
He sprinkles it with the utterance *svāhā*.

For that which is the utterance *svāhā* is manifest, and manifest is this high altar (*uttaravedi*). He sprinkles it with the utterance *veṭ*; for that which is the utterance *veṭ* is unmanifest, and unmanifest is this high altar. He sprinkles it with clarified butter (*ājya*), for they sprinkle the high altar with clarified butter; with fivefold-drawn butter, for they sprinkle the high altar with fivefold-drawn butter; crosswise, for they sprinkle the high altar crosswise.

"To the one dwelling in men, Veḍ!"—the "dweller in men" is indeed the breath, for men are "nara"; thus he gratifies that fire which is this breath within men. "To the one dwelling in the waters, Veḍ!"—he thereby gratifies that fire which is in the waters. "To the one dwelling in the sacrificial grass, Veḍ!"—he thereby gratifies that fire which is in the plants. "To the one dwelling in the forest-trees, Veḍ!"—he thereby gratifies that fire which is in the trees. "To the one finding light, Veḍ!"—this fire is the finder of light; he thereby gratifies this very fire.
And as to why he says, "To the one sitting among men, veḍ!

To the one sitting in the waters, veḍ!"—these are indeed the names of this very Agni; he thus gratifies them and makes them deities by means of the oblation. For she alone is a deity for whom an oblation is taken, and not she for whom it is not taken; furthermore, he thereby assigns these very fires their names within this fire.
He offers these five oblations.
The fire-altar consists of five layers; there are five seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—by just so much food does he thus satisfy it.

Then he sprinkles it with curds, honey, and ghee. This Agni is born when he is built up; he is born for all food. Indeed, these—curds, honey, and ghee—are all food; thus he gratifies him with all food. He sprinkles from all sides; thus he gratifies him from all sides with all food.

Moreover, as to why he sprinkles him: here this entire Agni has been consecrated, and into him the gods placed this supreme form; in the very same way, this sacrificer now places that supreme form into him. Food, indeed, is form; and this is the highest food—namely, curds, honey, and ghee. Thus, whatever is the supreme form, that he places into him as the highest. He sprinkles him on all sides, even outside the enclosing stones; on every side he thus bestows this supreme form upon him. He does so with *darbha* grass, for they are pure and fit for sacrifice; he uses the tips, for the tip belongs to the gods.
And as to why he sprinkles him:

when the vital breaths, the seers, first prepared this Agni, they made for him that portion which is yonder sun in front, namely the *sajūr-abdīya* cup; and then, once he was piled up, they made for him this portion on top. Thus, when he sprinkles him, he gratifies those very vital breaths, the seers, who, having been piled up, made for him a portion on top—with curds, honey, and ghee; the significance of this has already been explained.

"Those gods who [are] among the gods, the most worthy of sacrifice among those worthy of sacrifice"—for these are indeed the gods among the gods, and they are the most worthy of sacrifice among those worthy of sacrifice; "they have waited for their year-long share"—for they indeed wait upon this year-long share; "eating the oblation, not eating [the offering], at this sacrifice"—for the vital breaths (prāṇas) do not eat the oblation; "let them themselves drink of the honey and the ghee"—that is to say, let them themselves drink of both the honey and the ghee.

"Those gods who attained godhead among the gods"—for these are indeed the gods who attained godhead among the gods; "those who are the precursors of this Brahman"—this Agni is Brahman, and they are his precursors; "without whom no abode whatsoever purifies itself"—for indeed, without the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), no abode whatsoever purifies itself; "neither from the ridge of heaven nor from that of earth"—not indeed on heaven nor on earth, but wherever there is a bearer of life, in that [they abide]. This is what it means.
He sprinkles him with two [verses].
The sacrificer has two feet, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus sprinkles him.

Then he descends, saying: "Giver of out-breathing, giver of in-breathing! For all these vital breaths are this built-up fire-altar; if he were not to utter here this self-consecration formula, then this [fire] would surely take away his vital breaths. But since he utters here this self-consecration formula, thus this [fire] does not take away his vital breaths. "Giver of out-breathing, giver of in-breathing, giver of diffused breathing, giver of luster, giver of wide space"—by saying "Thou art a giver to me," he says this very thing. "May thy missiles burn others than us; O Purifier, be auspicious unto us!"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
Having returned, he proceeds with the Pravargya and Upasad rites.

Having performed the Pravargya and Upasads, he then gives him either the vow-food (vrata) or the half-vow-food (vārḍhavrata). Then [he performs] the Pravargya and Upasads again, and then he puts away the Pravargya, having attained that desire for which he performed this Pravargya.
One should indeed set it down on a pool. For this [fire] becomes heated and glowing;

if he were to set it down on this earth, its heat would enter this earth; if he were to set it down in water, its heat would enter the water. But when he sets it down on a pool, he thus harms neither the waters nor this earth. In that he does not throw it into the waters, he does not harm the waters; and in that the waters flow around it on all sides—since water is a means of pacification—he thereby does not harm this earth. Therefore, one should set it down on a pool.
But rather, one should set it out on the fire-altar.
This fire-altar is indeed these worlds, and the enclosing stones are the waters; when he sets it out on the fire-altar, he thus sets it out upon the flowing waters.
Furthermore, as to why he deposits [the Pravargya] upon the fire:

this fire is indeed these worlds—Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—and these are the Pravargyas. If he were to deposit it elsewhere than on the fire, he would thereby place those gods outside of these worlds; but when he deposits it on the fire, he thus places those very gods within these worlds.
Moreover, as to why he sets it aside on the fire-altar:

the Pravargya is the head of the sacrifice, and this piled fire-altar is the body. If he were to set it aside elsewhere than on the fire-altar, he would place the head outside of the body; but since he sets it aside on the fire-altar, having thus prepared the body, he replaces the head upon it.
He sets aside the first Pravargya vessel when it has been touched by the *svayamātṛṇā* brick.

The *svayamātṛṇā* is the breath, the Pravargya is the head, and this piled fire-altar is the body; thus he connects and joins the head and the body with the breath. Having set aside the Pravargya, [he proceeds] according to its ritual setting aside.

When he is about to throw the fire back into the hearth, he offers oblations and lays on fuel-sticks; for the gods, when this one was about to go forth, gratified him beforehand with food—both with oblations and with fuel-sticks—and in the same way, this sacrificer now gratifies him beforehand with food—both with oblations and with fuel-sticks. He takes five portions of clarified butter; the significance of that has already been explained.

Then he takes sixteen ladlings. Prajāpati consists of sixteen parts; Agni is Prajāpati. He thus gratifies him with food proportionate to his own self. For that food which is proportionate to one's self sustains and does not injure; that which is more injures, and that which is less does not sustain. He takes them in the same offering-ladle, for he whom he gratifies is one and the same. He offers with two verses addressed to Viśvakarman; this Agni is Viśvakarman, and it is him he thus gratifies. He offers three oblations; Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food he thus gratifies him.
Then he places the fuel-sticks upon the fire.

Just as one would serve food after having satisfied [the guests], so it is with these Udumbara [branches]. The Udumbara is indeed strength and sap; verily, he thus gratifies him with strength and sap. They are moist; for that which is moist among trees is their uninjured, living part. Verily, by that which is the uninjured, living part of trees, he thus gratifies him. They are dipped in ghee; ghee belongs to Agni; verily, he thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own sap. They remain there for the whole night, for therein they become endowed with sap. He places three kindling-sticks on the fire; Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with so much food he thus gratifies him.
And as to why he offers these oblations:

when the gods were about to go forward, they prepared him in front with food by means of these oblations; in the same way, this sacrificer now prepares him who is about to go forward in front with food by means of these oblations.
He indeed takes up the fivefold-offering;

for this vital breath in the head is distributed fivefold—mind, speech, breath, eye, and ear—and it is this fivefold-distributed vital breath in the head that he thereby places in him. With the verse, "Agni with sharp flame," which contains the word "sharp," he sharpens his head with this [verse] for the sake of sharpness.
Then he takes sixteen portions.

There are eight vital breaths and eight limbs; he takes these in a common ladle to achieve this correspondence, for in the same self both the limbs and the vital breaths exist. He offers them separately, thereby providing a distinction between the limbs and the vital breaths. He offers with two verses addressed to Viśvakarman; this Agni is Viśvakarman, and it is him he thus consecrates. He offers three oblations, for Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food does he consecrate him. With seventeen verses, for Prajāpati is seventeenfold and Prajāpati is Agni: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much he consecrates him. With [the juice] drawn twenty-one times, for there are twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first—this is the correspondence he achieves.
And, again, as to why he lays on these kindling-sticks:

The gods, having prepared him completely and in his entirety, then gratified him with this food—namely, with these kindling-sticks. In the same way, this sacrificer, having prepared him completely and in his entirety, now gratifies him with this food—namely, with these kindling-sticks. They are made of Udumbara wood, fresh, and soaked in ghee; they remain there for the whole night. The significance of this has been explained. With the verses, "Lead him upward, lead him further on, O Indra, to whom we offer the oblation in our house," he offers them; as the sacrificial formula (Yajus) is, so is its significance. He places three kindling-sticks on the fire; Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food he thus gratifies him. He offers three oblations; that makes six; the significance of that has been explained.

Then he issues the directions: "Lift up the fuel; hold up the supporting grass-bunches; recite for the fire as it is being carried forward; O Āgnīdhra, follow with the single wooden sword; O Brahman, mutter the Apratiratha hymn."

Now, as the gods were about to enter upon this sacrifice and were spreading it out, the Asuras and the destructive Rākṣasas sought to strike them from the south, saying, "You shall not sacrifice; you shall not spread the sacrifice!"

Those gods said to Indra, "You indeed are the best, the strongest, and the most heroic among us; do you ward off these Rakṣases. He replied, "Let Brahman be my second. They said, "So be it. For him, they made Bṛhaspati his second; for Bṛhaspati is indeed Brahman. Having driven away the Asuras, the Rakṣases, and the destroyers from the south by means of both Indra and Bṛhaspati, they performed this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction.
This very thing is done now which the gods did then;

for those Rakṣases were already driven away by the gods. But when he performs this rite, it is with the thought, "I shall do what the gods did. Moreover, having driven away the Sūras, the Rakṣases, and the Nāṣṭrās from the south by means of both Indra and Bṛhaspati, he extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and free from the Nāṣṭrās.
He who is Indra is this Apratiratha hymn;

and he who is Bṛhaspati is this Brahman priest. Therefore, when the Brahman mutters the Apratiratha, it is by means of both Indra and Bṛhaspati that he drives away the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the destroyers from the south, and thus extends this sacrifice in a place free from danger and destruction. That is why the Brahman mutters the Apratiratha.

"Swift, sharpening his horns, terrible like a bull"—these twelve verses addressed to Indra are appropriate; there are twelve months in a year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by that much he strikes away the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the destroyers from the south. They are in Triṣṭubh meters; the Triṣṭubh is indeed the thunderbolt, and with the thunderbolt he thus strikes away the Asuras, the Rakṣasas, and the destroyers from the south. These amount to twenty-two Gāyatrīs; they are addressed to Agni, for this is a rite for Agni.
Then he lifts it up with the verse:
"May all the gods, O Agni, lift thee up with their thoughts"; the significance of this has already been explained.
Then they approach.

"May the divine goddesses protect the sacrifice in the five directions!"—both gods and Asuras were the offspring of Prajāpati, and they contended for the directions; the gods wrested the directions from the Asuras, and in the same way the sacrificer now wrests the directions from his hateful rival. "Divine"—he thus makes them divine. "May the goddesses protect the sacrifice"—that is, "may the goddesses protect this sacrifice. "Driving away lack of thought and evil thought"—lack of thought is indeed hunger; thus, "driving away hunger," he means. "Bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice prosperity of wealth"—that is, "bestowing upon the lord of the sacrifice both wealth and prosperity. "The sacrifice has stood upon the prosperity of wealth"—that is, "the sacrifice has stood upon both wealth and prosperity."

"In the kindled fire, he who magnifies," for the sacrificer is indeed "he who magnifies"; "winged with hymns," for the hymns are his wings; "worthy of praise," that is, "worthy of sacrifice"; "grasped," that is, "sustained"; "having taken up the heated *gharma*, they sacrificed," for having taken up this heated *gharma*, they did indeed sacrifice; "when the gods sacrificed the sacrifice with strength," for with strength the gods indeed sacrificed this sacrifice.

"To the divine supporter, the most pleasing one"—for he is indeed the divine supporter and the most pleasing; "the god-glory, the glorious-minded, the hundred-streamed"—for he is indeed the god-glory, the glorious-minded, the hundred-streamed; "having encompassed him, the gods went to the sacrifice"—for having encompassed him, the gods went to the sacrifice; "the gods stood performing the *adhvara* for the gods"—the *adhvara* is indeed the sacrifice; thus, "the gods stood performing the sacrifice for the gods."
"The oblation has been carried away; it has been prepared by the preparer for the sacrifice"—this means "it has been offered, well-offered.

"The fourth sacrifice, where the oblation goes," says the Adhvaryu while muttering the *yajuṣ* formulas in front; the Hotṛ recites the *ṛc* verses from behind; the Brahman mutters the *Apratiratha* hymn from the south—this indeed is the fourth sacrifice. "Then may our words and blessings be accepted"—this means "then may both our words and our blessings be accepted."

"Savitar, with sunbeams and golden hair, raises up his eternal light from the front. This Agni here is indeed that Āditya; he is this one with sunbeams and golden hair who, as Savitar, raises up this eternal light from the front. "At his impulse, Pūṣan goes forth, the knowing one. Pūṣan is indeed cattle; they move forth at his impulse. "Beholding all beings, the guardian. For he indeed beholds all this; he is truly the guardian of this entire world.

Now, those five regions which lie hitherward from yonder sun—those the gods wrested from the Asuras; and then they ascended them. In the same way, the sacrificer wrests them from his hateful rival and likewise ascends them. Moreover, by means of these [regions], the gods then attained that goal; and in the very same way, by means of these, this sacrificer now attains that goal.

Then he lays down a variegated stone. Yonder sun, indeed, is the variegated stone; it is yonder sun that he thus lays down. It is variegated, for the solar disc is variegated by its rays. He lays it down between the Āhavanīya and the Gārhapatya fires. The Gārhapatya is this world and the Āhavanīya is the sky; he thus places him between these two worlds. Therefore, he (the sun) shines between these two worlds.
At the place of the Āgnīdhra fire-altar;

for the Āgnīdhra is indeed the intermediate space (antarikṣa), so he thereby places him in the intermediate space. Therefore, his abode is the intermediate space; he is at the midpoint, for he has come from here to the midpoint.

This is that vital breath (prāṇa); he thus places the vital breath within himself. This is life-span (āyus); he thus places life-span within himself. This is food; for this life-span is indeed food, and food is indeed life-span. It becomes a stone (aśman), for a stone is firm; he thus makes that life-span firm. It becomes speckled (pṛśni), for food is, as it were, speckled.

He lays it down with the words: "This measurer sits in the midst of heaven," for he indeed sits as a measurer in the midst of heaven; "having filled the two worlds and the intermediate space," for rising, he fills these worlds; "he looks upon all the ghee-dripping ones," by which he means the offering-spoons and the altars; "between the former and the latter sign," that is, between this world and that world; and furthermore, "that which is being piled here now, and that which was piled there formerly."
"The bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged"—for he is indeed the bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged.

"He has entered the womb of the ancient father"—for he indeed enters this womb of the ancient father. "The dappled stone set in the midst of heaven"—for he is indeed set in the midst of heaven as the dappled stone. "He has strode across; he guards the two ends of the space"—for as he strides, he goes to the ends of these worlds.

He lays down two [bricks] with two [verses]. The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus lays him down. He does so with two Triṣṭubh verses, for he (Agni) is of the Triṣṭubh nature. He does not settle them, for he (Agni) is unsettled; nor does he pronounce the *sūdadohas* verse over them. The *sūdadohas* is indeed breath, and this (Agni) is breath; [he thinks], "Why should I place breath into breath? Having laid it down so that it may not be lost, he proceeds.

Then they approach with the verse, "Indra have all strengthened. Its significance has been explained. [With the words] "May the sacrifice that invokes the gods bring hither; may the sacrifice that invokes favor bring hither," it means that the sacrifice indeed invokes the gods and invokes favor. [With the words] "May the god Agni worship the gods and bring them hither," it means that the god Agni shall indeed worship the gods and bring them hither.
"May the impulse of strength seize me upward with an upward-seizing; then may Indra, by a downward-seizing, cast my rivals beneath me. As the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

"Both the uplifting and the lowering—O gods, you have increased the sacred power (brahman). Now, O Indra and Agni, scatter my rivals in all directions! As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its significance (bandhu).

Those four directions which are above yonder sun—those the gods wrested from the Asuras and then ascended them; and in like manner the sacrificer wrests them from his hateful rival and likewise ascends them. Moreover, by means of these the gods attained to that [world] from here, and in the same way this sacrificer now attains to that from here by means of them.
Then they mount the fire with the words, "Step forth with Agni to the vault.

The vault is indeed the heavenly world; thus he means, "Step forth with this Agni to that heavenly world. "Bearing the Ukhyā fire in their hands"—for they indeed bear this Ukhyā fire in their hands—"having gone to the back of heaven, the heavenly world, sit down mingled with the gods"—that is to say, "Having gone to the back of heaven, the heavenly world, sit down mingled with the gods."

"Go forward along the eastern quarter, O wise one!"—the eastern quarter indeed belongs to Agni; thus he says, "Go forward along your own quarter, O wise one. "O Agni, be an Agni before Agni for him"—that is, "Be an Agni before Agni for this man. "Shining forth, illumine all the quarters"—that is, "Shining forth, illuminate all the quarters. "Bestow strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds"—thus he invokes a blessing.
"From the earth I have ascended;

from the atmosphere I have ascended to heaven"—thus they go from the Gārhapatya fire to the Āgnīdhrīya fire, and from the Āgnīdhrīya fire to the Āhavanīya fire. "From the back of the firmament of heaven, I have gone to the light of heaven"—this means, "From the back of the firmament of heaven, I have gone to the world of heaven."
"Going to heaven, they have no need for support;

they ascend to the sky and the two worlds"—for indeed, those who go to the heavenly world have no need for support, they who, being well-knowing, have spread the sacrifice that flows in every direction. This very sacrifice is that which flows in every direction, and these alone are the well-knowing ones who spread it.

"O Agni, go forward as the first of those seeking the gods"—by this he says to this very Agni, "Go forward as the first of these who seek the gods. "The eye of the gods and of mortals"—for he is indeed the eye of both these, the gods and men. "Worshipping in harmony with the Bhrigus"—that is, "worshipping in harmony with the Bhrigus, the sacrificers. "May the sacrificers go to heaven in well-being"—that is, "may the sacrificers go to the heavenly world in well-being."

Those five directions which were in yonder world, those the gods wrested from the Asuras; and then they ascended them. In the same way, the sacrificer wrests them from his hateful rival and then ascends them. Moreover, by means of these [verses], the gods reached that goal from here; and in the very same way, this sacrificer reaches that goal from here by means of them.

Then he makes an offering over it. For when he had gone away, the gods gratified him from above with food by means of this oblation; in the same way, this sacrificer now gratifies him from above with food by means of this oblation. It is with the milk of a black cow that has a white calf: the black cow with a white calf is indeed the night, and yonder sun is her calf. He thus gratifies him with his own portion, with his own essence. While it is being held above, for he whom he gratifies here is above; for by milking, milk is given.

Moreover, as to why he offers over it: Agni is the head of the sacrifice, and the milk is the vital breath; he thus places the vital breath in the head. He should offer over it so that it flows toward the *svayamātṛṇṇā* brick; for the *svayamātṛṇṇā* is the vital breath and this [milk] is the sap—he thereby connects and joins the head and the vital breath with the sap. With the words, "Night and Dawn, of one mind, though diverse in form," the significance of this has already been explained.

"O Agni, thousand-eyed!"—for he is indeed thousand-eyed by means of the gold chips. "Hundred-headed"—for that Rudra was created there as hundred-headed. "A hundred are thy out-breathings, a thousand thy through-breathings"—for a hundred indeed are the out-breathings and a thousand the through-breathings of him who is hundred-headed. "Thou art lord of thousandfold wealth"—that is to say, "thou art lord of all riches. "To thee for that we pay homage, for strength, Svāhā!"—he is indeed strength; thus he gratifies him.
He offers with two verses.
The sacrificer is two-footed, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just that much he thus makes this offering.

Then he sets it down with the words, "Thou art a well-winged Garuḍa. For having fashioned him there as a well-winged Garuḍa, he fashions him as a well-winged Garuḍa; he piles him up as a well-winged Garuḍa, and having made him a well-winged Garuḍa, he finally sets him down with the words, "Sit upon the back of the earth; fill the atmosphere with thy luster; prop up the sky with thy light; spread out the quarters with thy splendor! For thus does he perform all this for him.

"Being invoked, fair-faced, in front"—that is, "being invoked, fair-faced, before us. "O Agni, sit down properly in thy womb"—this, indeed, is his own womb; "sit down properly in it," he means. "In this higher seat"—the sky, indeed, is the higher seat—"may all the gods and the sacrificer sit down"—thereby he causes the sacrificer to sit together with all the gods. With two verses he sets it down; the significance of that has been explained. With the *vaṣaṭ*-call [he offers]; its significance is as stated above.
Then he places fuel-sticks upon it.

For when he had gone forth, the gods gratified him from above with food, both by means of fuel-sticks and oblations; in the same way, this sacrificer now gratifies him, who has gone forth, from above with food, both by means of fuel-sticks and oblations.

He first places a kindling-stick of *śamī* wood. For when this oblation had been offered, he (Agni) blazed up and flared forth; therefore the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest he should destroy us. They saw this *śamī* tree and with it they appeased him. Because they appeased him with the *śamī*, it is called *śamī*; and in the same way, he now appeases him with the *śamī* for the sake of pacification alone, not for consumption.

"Of Savitṛ, the most excellent, I choose that wondrous, all-beneficent favor which Kaṇva milked forth—the swelling, thousand-streamed, great cow with her milk. Kaṇva indeed saw her; she, yielding a thousand streams, milked for him all desires. In the same way, she now yields a thousand streams and all desires for the sacrificer.

Then he places a fuel-stick of *vaikaṅkata* wood. Its symbolic significance has been explained. With the verse, "We would worship thee at thy highest birth, O Agni,"—the sky, indeed, is his highest birth; "we would worship with hymns in the lower abode"—the intermediate space, indeed, is the lower abode; "that womb from which thou hast arisen, that do I worship"—this, indeed, is his own womb; "worship that" is what he means to say. "To thee, when kindled, they have offered oblations"—for when this [fire] is kindled, then they offer oblations into it.
Then he places a fire-stick of udumbara wood.

The Udumbara tree is indeed sap and essence; verily, he gratifies him with sap and essence. It has ear-like protuberances (karṇaka); for the protuberances are cattle; verily, he gratifies him with cattle and with food. If he should not find one with protuberances, he should offer a drop of sour curds and place it thereon. In that he offers a drop of sour curds, that is the form of cattle. With the verse, "O Agni, shine forth, kindled before us," he places a Virāj verse; the Virāj is food; verily, he thus gratifies him with food. He places three fuel-sticks; Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with so much food he thus gratifies him.

Then he offers oblations. It is just as when one would serve food and then bring it near; so with the dipping-spoon (sruva) he offers the first, and with the offering-ladle (sruk) the latter. "O Agni, may we today fulfill for thee this purpose, touching the heart, like a horse with hymns, like a good rite—with our offerings," he says. "May I fulfill that hymn of thine which touches thy heart"—this is what he means. He offers with a Paṅkti verse; the Paṅkti has five feet, the fire-altar has five layers, the year has five seasons, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, with just so much food he thus gratifies him.

Then he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblation. This Agni is Viśvakarman; it is him he thus gratifies. "I offer thought with mind and ghee"—he means, "I offer their thought with both mind and ghee. "So that the gods may come hither"—he means, "so that the gods may come here. "The Hotrās, increasers of Truth"—he means, "the increasers of Truth. "To the lord of all existence I offer, to Viśvakarman"—he means, "to him who is the lord of all this that exists, to Viśvakarman, I offer. "Every day, food for eating"—he means, "food that is never exhausted, every day."
Then he offers the full-offering; for all this that is full, with all of that he thus gratifies him.

"Seven are thy kindling-sticks, O Agni"—the kindling-sticks are indeed the vital breaths, for the vital breaths enkindle him. "Seven tongues"—this he says regarding those seven men whom they made into one man. "Seven seers"—for there were indeed seven seers. "Seven dear abodes"—he thereby refers to the meters, for the meters are his seven dear abodes. "The seven priests worship thee in seven ways"—for these seven priests worship him in seven ways. "Seven wombs"—he thereby refers to the layers (of the altar). "Fill [them]! means "procreate! "With ghee"—ghee is indeed seed; thus he places seed in these worlds. "Svāhā!"—the utterance "Svāhā" is the sacrifice; he thereby makes all this once fit for sacrifice.

"Seven, seven," he says. The fire-altar consists of seven layers; there are seven seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just that much he thus gratifies it. He offers three oblations; the fire-altar is threefold. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just that much food he thus gratifies it. He lays on three kindling-sticks; that makes six. The significance of that has been explained.
He places the fuel-sticks while standing;

for the fuel-sticks are indeed bones, and bones, as it were, stand upright. He offers the oblations while sitting; for the oblations are indeed flesh, and flesh, as it were, sits down. The fuel-sticks are inside and the oblations are outside, for the bones are inside and the flesh is outside.

Now, therefore, follows the correspondence. He offers six oblations before and six after; they go for the speckled stone with six verses; he lays down the speckled stone with two verses; they go for the fire-altar with four verses; they ascend the fire-altar with five verses. Thus, there is one [verse] less than thirty; the thirtieth is indeed the oblation itself. He deposits the fire-altar with two verses; that makes thirty-two. The Anuṣṭubh consists of thirty-two syllables; this is that Anuṣṭubh.

Now, those three *anuṣṭubh* verses which they complete at the Gārhapatya fire—they bring one of them here. Since they bring this one here, that entire Agni has been consecrated here; yet he was not sufficient for this place to consume the food.
He said to Agni, "May you eat the food. "So be it," [Agni replied]. Therefore, as soon as they bring this [fire] here, it becomes sufficient for food and sufficient for oblations.
Moreover, they say:
"Prajāpati himself placed this dear son upon his breast. He who knows this thus indeed places his dear son upon his breast.

When they bring this [fire] here, those seven persons whom they formerly made into one person are indeed this very fire that is being built; and that which was their upward prosperity and essence which they gathered together is this very fire which they now bring here. Thus, when they bring it here, they gather together and elevate upwards that prosperity and essence which belonged to those seven persons. This is his head, and this fire is his body; having thus prepared his body, he restores the head to him.

Now, therefore, he offers to Vaiśvānara. At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is here the deity Vaiśvānara, and it is to him that he offers this oblation. He thus makes him a deity by means of the oblation. For whichever deity an oblation is taken, she is indeed a deity, but not she for whom no oblation is taken. It is on twelve potsherds; there are twelve months in a year, and Vaiśvānara is the year.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this Vaiśvānara oblation: he is about to generate this Agni Vaiśvānara; therefore, he pours him out there beforehand, during the initiation offering (*dīkṣaṇīyā*), as seed. For in whatever manner seed is poured into the womb, in that same manner it is born. Since he pours him out there as seed, therefore he is born here as Vaiśvānara. It is performed in a low voice (*upāṃśu*) there, for seed is indeed part of the sacrifice, and seed is poured out in a low voice. Here, however, it is spoken aloud (*nirukta*), for seed, once born, becomes manifest.
That Vaiśvānara is indeed these worlds:
this earth itself is Viśva-Agni-Nara; the intermediate space itself is Viśva-Vāyu-Nara; and the sky itself is Viśva-Āditya-Nara.
Those which are these worlds are his body;
this head is this very earth, and the plants are his beard. That which is this universe is speech, and Agni is speech. He is the man, and he is above it, for Agni is above this earth.

This very thing is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Therefore, this [part] is hairless, for the intermediate space is, as it were, hairless. This is the All; it is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the wind (*vāyu*), that man. It is situated in the middle of this [body], for the wind is in the middle of the intermediate space.

The sky is indeed the head; the stars are the hair. This sun is the eye of that Viśva, and he is the man. Thus, he (the altar) comes to have its head below, for the sun is below the sky. This Vaiśvānara is his head, and this built-up fire-altar is the body. Having thus prepared his body, he restores the head to it.
Then he offers to the Maruts.
The Maruts are indeed the vital breaths; it is the vital breaths he thus bestows upon him. Having offered to Vaiśvānara—the Vaiśvānara being the head—he thereby places the vital breaths in the head.

This one becomes one, for the head is indeed as it were one; the other seven are the seven potsherds. Or rather, even though they are made many times, seven by seven, they are still just seven; thus he places the seven vital breaths in the head itself.
This one has a defined form;

for the head, as it were, has a defined form, while the others are undefined, for the vital breaths (prāṇas), as it were, are undefined. Standing, he offers this [oblation], for the head, as it were, stands; sitting, he offers the others, for the vital breaths, as it were, sit.

Those two first *māruta* offerings which he makes—those are these two vital breaths; he offers them in the middle of the *vaiśvānara* cake, for these two vital breaths are indeed in the middle of the head.
Then as for the two second [oblations]:
he offers those two more closely together, for these two breaths are, as it were, closer together.

Now, as for those two which are third: he offers them more closely together, for these two vital breaths are, as it were, more closely joined. Speech indeed is the *araṇye'nūcya*; that *araṇye'nūcya* occurs in the forest, for by means of speech one encounters much that is terrible.
Furthermore, as to why he offers to Vaiśvānara and the Maruts:

Vaiśvānara is the nobility (kṣatra) and the Maruts are the common people (viś). Thus, he establishes both the nobility and the common people. He offers to Vaiśvānara first; having thus established the nobility, he then establishes the common people.
He becomes one;
he makes that kṣatra and that glory centered in one, while the others, being many, establish that abundance among the people (viś).
This is explicitly stated;

for the Kṣatriya power is, as it were, explicit, while the others are unexplicit—for the common people (viś) are, as it were, unexplicit. Standing, he offers this oblation; for the Kṣatriya power stands, as it were, while he offers the other oblations sitting; for the common people sit, as it were.

Indeed, that one [oblation] he offers with the ladle at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," accompanied by a *puro'nuvākyā* and a *yājyā*; the others he offers with his hand while seated with the utterance of "svāhā. He thereby makes the people (the *viś*) followers and subordinates who imitate the actions of the ruling power (the *kṣatra*).

Regarding this they say: "How do these [oblations] of his come to have an invitatory verse (*puro'nuvākyā*) and an offering verse (*yājyā*), and how are they offered with the ladle at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*? Well, of these seven-footed Marut-hymns, those which are the first three feet constitute the three-footed *gāyatrī* as the invitatory verse; then those which are the last four feet constitute the four-footed *triṣṭubh* as the offering verse. This very bowl is [the invitatory verse], this handle is [the offering verse], and the *svāhā*-utterance is the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance. In this way, indeed, these [oblations] of his come to have an invitatory verse and an offering verse, and are offered with the ladle at the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
Now, as for why he first offers the oblation to the Maruts on the south:
those seven rivers that flow eastward, they are that [cake] on seven potsherds; for there are indeed seven of those that flow eastward.
Now, that which he offers first on the north side is the Seasons; it consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven seasons.
Now, as for that second [oblation] which he offers to the south:
it consists of cakes on seven potsherds, for there are seven domestic animals; he offers it immediately after the former one, and thereby establishes the animals in the waters.
Now, as for that second [offering] which he offers on the northern [fire], it is for the Seven Seers;
it consists of seven potsherds, for there are indeed seven Seers. He offers it immediately after the first one; thus, he establishes the Seers within the seasons.
Now, as for that third oblation which he offers on the south:

it is for the vital breaths; it consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven vital breaths in the head. He offers it immediately after the preceding one; thus he places the vital breaths so that they are not separated from the head.
Now, as for that third [oblation] which he offers on the north: it is the meters;
it consists of seven potsherds, for there are seven meters, each increasing by four syllables. He offers it immediately after the previous one; thus he places the meters immediately after the Ṛṣis.

Now, as for those seven rivers that flow westward—that is what is recited in the forest; it consists of seven potsherds, for there are indeed those seven which flow westward. This is his downward vital breath of this Prajāpati; that is why it is recited in the forest. For the forest is, as it were, hidden away, and the downward vital breath is, as it were, hidden away. Therefore, those who drink from these rivers become more impure, more slanderous, and more prone to speaking evil. Whatever he says here—"O Maruts!"—he makes that food for him and presents it; thereby he gratifies him.
