That Vaiśvānara is indeed yonder Āditya;
and those Maruts which are the rays, they are those seven potsherds; for there are seven-by-seven groups of Maruts.
He offers oblations with the formulas:

"Śukrajyotis (Bright-light) and Citrajyotis (Variegated-light), Satyajyotis (Truth-light), and Jyotiṣmat (Radiant). These are their names; having thus prepared this very disk, he now assigns these rays to it by mentioning their names.
Now, therefore, he offers the Vasordhārā.

At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; he is here the Vasu. For him, the gods held forth this stream, and by it they gratified him. Because the Vasus held forth this stream for him, they call it the "Vasordhārā" (the Stream of Wealth). In the very same way, he now holds forth this stream for him, and by it he gratifies him.
And as to why he offers this "Stream of Wealth" (vasordhārā):

it is his consecration. For the gods, having prepared him entirely and completely, then consecrated him with these desires by means of this "Stream of Wealth. In the same way, this sacrificer, having prepared him entirely and completely, then consecrates him with these desires by means of this "Stream of Wealth"—with clarified butter taken five times, using a ladle made of Udumbara wood; the significance of that has already been explained.

Having offered to Vaiśvānara—the head, indeed, is Vaiśvānara, and it is through the head that food is eaten; moreover, he who is being consecrated is consecrated from the head. Having offered to the Maruts—the vital breaths, indeed, are the Maruts, and it is by means of the vital breaths that food is eaten; moreover, he who is being consecrated is consecrated within the vital breaths.

Now, that [offering] is indeed the *araṇye'nūcya*. For the *araṇye'nūcya* is speech; food is eaten by means of speech, and moreover, it is by means of speech that one being consecrated is consecrated. This is all wealth (*vasu*), for all these desires are wealth. This is a stream consisting of wealth (*vasumayī dhārā*), just as [a stream] of milk or ghee; even so, this oblation of clarified butter is offered for the sake of undertaking. Since this is a stream consisting of wealth, therefore they call it the "Bestower of Wealth" (*vasordhārā*).
He says:

"This for me and this for me—with this I gratify you and with this, and with this I consecrate you and with this; moreover, give this to me and this to me. As soon as that stream reaches the fire, then this sacrificial formula (yajus) should be recited.

The gods, having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having sprinkled him with this stream of wealth (vasordhārā), then asked him for these desires; and he, being sacrificed to, gratified, and consecrated, bestowed those desires upon them. In the same way, this [sacrificer], having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having sprinkled him with this stream of wealth, now asks him for these desires; and he, being sacrificed to, gratified, and consecrated, bestows those desires upon him. He joins the desires two by two so that there may be no separation, just as one would join two people who live apart, thinking, "May they be made fit through the sacrifice."

The gods indeed said, "By what means shall we receive these desires? They replied, "By our very self. The sacrifice is indeed the self of the gods, and the sacrifice is likewise the self of the sacrificer. Therefore, when he says, "May they prosper through the sacrifice," he means, "May they prosper through my very self."

He prepares it upon twelve; twelve months are a year, and the year is Agni: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies him, and with just so much food he thus consecrates him. He prepares it upon fourteen; he prepares it upon eight; he prepares it upon ten; he prepares it upon thirteen.
Then he offers the Ardhendrā oblations.
These Ardhendrā oblations are everything; verily with everything he thus gratifies him, and moreover, with everything he thus consecrates him.
Then he offers the cups (grahas).
The cups are indeed the sacrifice; by this food, which is the sacrifice, he gratifies him. Moreover, by this food, which is the sacrifice, he consecrates him.

Then he offers these oblations of the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) with the formulas, "Agni and my Gharma," and so forth; by means of these very sacrificial rites he thus gratifies him, and by means of these very sacrificial rites he thereby consecrates him.
Then he offers the uneven Stomas.

For by obtaining all desires through the uneven Stomas, the gods went to the heavenly world; in the same way, the sacrificer, having obtained all desires, goes to the heavenly world by means of the uneven Stomas.

"It is indeed from the thirty-threefold [stoma]," they say. The thirty-threefold is the end of the uneven stomas; it was from the very end that the gods went to the heavenly world. In the same way, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world from the very end.
Then he offers with the even-numbered [verses].

For the metres indeed said, "The uneven-numbered *stomas* are exhausted; let us go to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*. They went to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*; and in the same way, the sacrificer now goes to the heavenly world by means of the even-numbered *stomas*.
"Or rather, it is from the forty-eightfold [stoma]," he said.

"The forty-eightfold is indeed the end of the even stomas; thus the meters went to the heavenly world from the very end. In the same way, the sacrificer now goes to the heavenly world from the very end."

He says, "One for me, three for me, four for me, eight for me. Just as one climbing a tree would ascend by grasping each higher branch after the next, so it is when he offers the Stomas; for the Stomas are indeed food, and thus he consecrates him with food.
Then he offers the *vayaḥ* oblations.
The *vayas* are indeed cattle; verily, by means of cattle as food, he thus gratifies him; and furthermore, by means of cattle as food, he thus consecrates him.
Then he offers oblations while mentioning the names.

For the gods, having obtained all desires, then gratified him directly; in the same way, the sacrificer, having obtained all desires, now gratifies him directly with the words, "To Vāja, Svāhā! To Impulse, Svāhā! These are his names; it is by mentioning these names that he gratifies him.
These names are thirteen;

there are thirteen months in a year, and thirteen layers of earth (purīṣa) for the fire-altar. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just that much he thus gratifies him. And as to why he offers while mentioning the names by name: it is by mentioning the names by name that he thereby consecrates him.

Then he says: "This for thee, O friend; thou art a restrainer for Mitra, a restrainer; for strength thee, for rain thee, for the lordship over creatures thee! Food indeed is strength, and food is rain; by means of food, he thus gratifies him.

And as to why he says: "This is thy kingdom; thou art Mitra’s controller, O controller, for strength thee, for rain thee, for the lordship of creatures thee"—this means, "This is thy kingship; thou hast been consecrated. "Thou art the controller of Mitra, O controller," means "Thou art for our strength and for our rain, and thou art for the lordship of our creatures. He thus addresses him, saying, "Be this for all of us; we have consecrated thee for all this. Therefore, they address a consecrated human king in this very way.
Then he offers the *kalpa* oblations.

The *kalpas* are indeed the vital breaths; it is the vital breaths that he thus bestows upon him. With the words, "May life be perfected by the sacrifice! May breath be perfected by the sacrifice!"—it is these very vital breaths, thus made perfect, that he bestows upon him.

He offers twelve *kalpas*. Twelve months make a year, and the year is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he places these well-ordered vital breaths (*prāṇas*) in him. And as to why he offers *kalpas*: the *kalpas* are indeed the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are immortality; it is with immortality that he thus consecrates him.

Then he says: "The Stoma and the Yajus, the Ṛc and the Sāman, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara. This is indeed the threefold science (trayī vidyā). The threefold science is food; verily by means of food he thus gratifies him, and moreover, by means of food he thus consecrates him. "To heaven, O gods! We have become immortal," for he goes to heaven and indeed becomes immortal. "We have become the offspring of Prajāpati," for he indeed becomes the offspring of Prajāpati. "Vet! Svāhā!"—this "vet" is the Vaṣaṭ-call in its unmanifest form. Verily, food is offered to the gods either with the Vaṣaṭ-call or with the Svāhā-call; thus he gratifies him with both of these, with the Vaṣaṭ-call and with the Svāhā-call. Moreover, he consecrates him with both of these. At this point, he throws that offering-spoon into the fire, so that whatever part of it is smeared with clarified butter shall not remain outside the fire.
Of this very stream of wealth (vasordhārā), heaven indeed is the body, the clouds are the udder, lightning is the teat, and the stream itself is the flow; from heaven it comes down to the earth.
For her, the cow itself is the self;
the udder is the udder, the teat is the teat, and the flow is the flow; from the cow, she [the offering] supports the sacrificer.

Of that [offering], the sacrificer himself is the body; the raised arm is the ladle (*sruk*); the chest is the vessel; the stream [of milk] is indeed the stream [of the offering]. From the sacrificer [it goes] to the gods, from the gods to the cow, and from the cow back to the sacrificer. Thus this food of the gods, which is endless and inexhaustible, circulates. He who knows this thus—verily, for him this food becomes endless and inexhaustible. Now, therefore, regarding the correspondence (*sampad*).
Regarding this, they say:

"How does this stream of wealth (vasordhārā) reach Agni the Year? How does it correspond with Agni the Year? There are indeed three hundred and sixty [verses] in this stream of wealth, and then six, and then thirty-five. Now, as many days as there are in the year—three hundred and sixty—that many days of the year it reaches. And as for the six, the seasons are six; thus it reaches the nights of the seasons. Thus it reaches both the days and nights of the year. And as for the thirty-five: that is the thirteenth month; it is the self (ātman). Thirty are the self, two are the foundation (pratiṣṭhā), two are the vital breaths (prāṇa), and two are the head—that makes thirty-five. So great indeed is the year. In this way, his stream of wealth reaches Agni the Year; in this way, it corresponds with Agni the Year. So many indeed are the "bricks possessing formulas" (yajuṣmatya iṣṭakā) that are laid down in the middle of the Śāṇḍila fire-altar. These bricks are indeed separate fires; thus these fires of his become separately offered with the stream of wealth.
Regarding this, they say:

How does this stream of wealth (vasordhārā) attain the Great Litany (mahaduktha), and how is it completed by means of the Great Litany? Of this very stream of wealth, those nine first sacrificial formulas (yajus) are the Trivṛt-stoma head; then those forty-eight are the two twenty-four-fold wings; then those twenty-five are the twenty-five-fold body; then those twenty-one are the twenty-one-fold tail; then those thirty-three are the Vaśa-stotra; and then those eighty are the attainment of the eighties, for by means of the eighties the Great Litany is proclaimed. And what is above the eighties is that which is above the eighties of the Great Litany mentioned before; thus indeed does this stream of wealth of his attain the Great Litany, and thus is it completed by means of the Great Litany.
Then he offers the Vājaprasavīya oblation.
Vāja is indeed food; this is an offering for the production of food, and by means of it, he impels food for him.

For the gods, having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having [anointed] him with this stream of wealth (vasordhārā), then gratified him further; and in the same way, this sacrificer, having gratified him with this food, having consecrated him with these desires, and having [anointed] him with this stream of wealth, then gratifies him further.
And as to why he offers this Vājaprasavīya oblation: this is indeed his consecration.

For the gods, having gratified him with this food and having consecrated him with these desires and this stream of wealth (vasordhārā), then consecrated him yet further; and in the same way, this sacrificer, having gratified him with this food and having consecrated him with these desires and this stream of wealth, now consecrates him yet further.
It becomes all-herbal medicine;

for all this food is "all-herbal medicine," and thus he gratifies him with all this food, and moreover, he consecrates him with all this food. He should set aside one of those foods and not eat of it as long as he lives. With a cup made of Udumbara wood and a dipping-spoon (sruva) made of Udumbara wood—of these two, the significance has been explained—they should have four corners, for there are four quarters; thus he gratifies him with food from all the quarters, and moreover, he consecrates him with food from all the quarters.

Furthermore, as to why he offers this Vājaprasavīya oblation: these deities have been consecrated by this very consecration (sava) by which he is about to be consecrated; it is them he thus gratifies. They, being sacrificed to and gratified, grant their approval for this consecration to him; approved by them, he is consecrated. For indeed, he alone becomes a king whom other kings approve of for kingship, and not he whom they do not. Thus, when he offers into the fire, he consecrates Agni; and when he offers to those deities, he gratifies those gods who have authority over this consecration.
Or rather, he also offers these Pārtha oblations.

For the gods indeed desired this: "May we be consecrated right here by all the consecrations. They were consecrated right here by all the consecrations; in the same way, the sacrificer is now consecrated right here by all the consecrations.

Now, those which are the Pārtha oblations are the Vājaprasavīya of the Rājasūya; in that he offers them, he is consecrated by the Rājasūya. Then, as for the fourteen subsequent ones, of those the seven earlier are the Vājaprasavīya of the Vājapeya; in that he offers them, he is consecrated by the Vājapeya. And those which are the seven later are [the oblations] of Agni; in that he offers them, he is consecrated by the Agnisava.
He indeed performs the preliminary offerings of the Rājasūya, and then those of the Vājapeya.

For it is a king who becomes a performer of the Rājasūya, and an emperor (*samrāj*) who performs the Vājapeya. Kingship comes first, and then imperial sovereignty; therefore, having performed the Vājapeya, one should not perform the Rājasūya, for that would be a descent, just as if one who is already an emperor were to become a mere king—that is what it would be like.
He offers the final oblations to Agni.
For all these consecrations are the consecration of Agni; by means of the consecration of Agni, he becomes everything—both a king and a sovereign. Therefore, he offers the final oblations to Agni.

Then he consecrates him upon a black antelope skin. The black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice; it is thus upon the sacrifice that he consecrates him. It is with the hair-side up; for the hair are the meters; it is thus upon the meters that he consecrates him. It is on the north side, for that is its significance; it has the neck toward the east, for that is the way of the gods.

Some indeed sprinkle him from the south of the fire, thinking, "The service of food is from the south; thus we sprinkle him from the portion of food. One should not do so; for this is the direction of the ancestors, and he whom they sprinkle in that manner quickly goes to that direction.

Some indeed consecrate him at the Āhavanīya fire, thinking, "The Āhavanīya is the heavenly world; thus we shall consecrate him in the heavenly world. One should not do so. For that [Āhavanīya] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self. By means of this mortal self, they thereby attach that divine self of his to this human self—those who consecrate him in such a manner.
He should sprinkle him from the north alone.

For this northern-easterly direction belongs to both gods and men; he thus sprinkles him while he is dependent upon and established in his own quarter. Indeed, one who is established in his own abode does not come to harm.
One should consecrate a being who is seated; for a being who has already come into existence is, as it were, seated.

One should consecrate one who desires to become great while he is standing; for one who desires to become great is, as it were, standing. One should consecrate one who desires prosperity on a goat-skin; one who desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) on a black antelope skin; one who desires both on both skins. To the north of the tail, he spreads out the skin with the hair side up and the neck pointing eastward.
It touches the enclosing stones.

Now, because the black antelope skin touches the enclosing stones, his divine self becomes consecrated upon the black antelope skin; and because he sprinkles him while he stands touching the fire, he is not thereby severed from this divine consecration.
Having offered an oblation in the fire, he then sprinkles him with water.

This [fire] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods come first, and then humans. Therefore, having offered in the fire, he sprinkles him with what remains of that very [offering], and at this point he throws the dipping-spoon (sruva) after it.
Then, having turned around along his right arm, he sprinkles him with the formula:

"At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, with the sovereignty of Agni, I sprinkle thee. Sarasvatī is indeed speech; her entire restraint is this [formula]. Thus, impelled by Savitṛ, he sprinkles him with all this, with the restraint of Sarasvatī, the restrainer of speech, and with the sovereignty of Agni. At this point, he throws that cup into it so that what was smeared there shall not remain outside the fire.
He indeed consecrates him in the midst of the Pārthas;

for the Pārthas are the year, so he thus places him in the very middle of the year. He offers six oblations before and six after; for there are six seasons, and by means of the seasons he thus encompasses him on both sides as he is being consecrated. Bṛhaspati is the last of the former, and Indra is the first of the latter; Bṛhaspati is the priesthood (brahman) and Indra is the nobility (kṣatra). Thus, by means of both the priesthood and the nobility, he encompasses him on both sides as he is being consecrated.

Now, therefore, he offers the Rāṣṭrabhṛt oblations. The Rāṣṭrabhṛts are indeed kings, for they support kingdoms; these are the deities who have been consecrated by this very consecration (sava) by which he is about to be consecrated. He thus gratifies them; they, being sacrificed to and gratified, grant their approval to this consecration. Consecrated with their approval, he is consecrated. For he whom kings approve of as king becomes a king, and not he whom they do not. Now, in that kings support kingdoms, these gods are indeed kings; therefore, these are called the Rāṣṭrabhṛts.

Furthermore, as to why he offers these *rāṣṭrabhṛt* (sustainers of the kingdom) oblations: when Prajāpati had become relaxed, the pairs of opposites departed from him, having become Gandharvas and Apsarases. He became a chariot and went around them; having gone around them, he took them into himself and made them his own. In the same way, this sacrificer now goes around them, takes them into himself, and makes them his own.
He who was that Prajāpati when he became disjointed is this very Agni who is now being built up; and those pairs which went forth from him are these very deities to whom he now offers this oblation.
He offers to the Gandharvas and Apsarases;

for it was after becoming Gandharvas and Apsarases that they ascended. Moreover, the Gandharvas and Apsarases move about by means of fragrance and form; therefore, whoever approaches a woman desires both fragrance and form.

He offers pairs. For from a pair, indeed, procreation comes forth; he who is procreated becomes a ruler (*rāṣṭrin*), while he who is not procreated remains without a kingdom. Now, since these pairs sustain the kingdom, and these gods are themselves pairs, therefore these "kingdom-sustainers" (*rāṣṭrabhṛt*) are offered with clarified butter taken in twelve ladlings. There are exactly twelve oblations; the significance of this has already been explained.
He offers first to the male, and then to the females; thus he endows the male with superior vigor.

He offers to one male as it were, and to many females as it were; therefore even for one man there are many wives. He offers to the male with both the *vaṣaṭ* and the *svāhā* calls, but to the females with the *svāhā* call alone; thus he endows the male with superior vigor.

"Ṛtāṣāḍ ṛtadhāmā"—this means "the upholder of truth, whose abode is truth. "Agni is the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the plants"—for Agni, as the Gandharva, went forth together with the plants as his Apsarases, his mates. "Muda by name"—the plants are indeed *muda* (delights), for by means of the plants everything here rejoices. "May he protect this our priesthood and nobility; Svāhā to him! Vāṭ! Svāhā to them!"—the significance of this has already been explained.

Regarding the term "Saṃhita": yonder sun, indeed, is the Saṃhita, for he joins together day and night. Regarding "Viśvasāman": he is indeed the entire Sāman. "Sūrya the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the rays"—Sūrya, the Gandharva, went forth with his mates, the Apsarases, the rays. "Named Āyus"—for the rays float along as if they were long-lived. "May he protect this our priesthood and nobility"—the significance of this has already been explained.
"Suṣumṇa"—that means "one worthy of good sacrifice.

"Sūryaraśmi"—for the rays of the moon are indeed like the rays of the sun. "Candramas the Gandharva; his Apsarases are the constellations"—the moon is indeed the Gandharva, and he went forth together with the constellations as his Apsarases, his mates. "Bhekurayas by name"—these are indeed called Bhekurayas, for they produce light (*bhāṃ*) through the constellations. "May he protect this our priesthood and nobility"—the significance of this has already been explained.

‘The Swift’—that is ‘the quick. ‘All-pervading’—for he indeed makes all this space. ‘Vāta the Gandharva, his Apsarases are the Waters’—Vāta is indeed the Gandharva; together with the Waters as his Apsarases, his mates, he went forth. ‘He whose name is Strength’—the Waters are indeed strength, for from the Waters strength is born. ‘May he protect this our priesthood and nobility’—the significance of this has been explained.

"Bhujyu Suparṇa"—Bhujyu is indeed the sacrifice, for the sacrifice nourishes all beings; "the Gandharva Yajña, his Apsarases are the Dakṣiṇās"—the sacrifice is indeed the Gandharva, and it went forth together with its mate, the Apsarases, who are the Dakṣiṇās; "Stāvā by name"—the Dakṣiṇās are indeed Stāvā, for the sacrifice is praised by means of the Dakṣiṇās, and whoever gives a Dakṣiṇā is indeed praised. "May he protect this Brahman and Kṣatra"—the significance of this has already been explained.

"Prajāpati Viśvakarman"—Prajāpati indeed is Viśvakarman, for he made all this. "Mind the Gandharva, the Ṛks and Sāmans his Apsarases"—Mind indeed is the Gandharva; with the Ṛks and Sāmans as his Apsarases, he went forth in union. "The Iṣṭis by name"—the Ṛks and Sāmans are indeed the Iṣṭis, for by means of the Ṛks and Sāmans they pray, saying, "May it be thus for us! May it be so for us! "May he protect this our Brahman and Kṣatra"—the significance of that has already been explained.

Then he offers on the head of the chariot. This is indeed that consecration; this very thing is consecrated for him, which these deities authorize as his consecration—authorized by whom he is consecrated. For just as he becomes a king for whom kings authorize his kingship, and not he for whom they do not, so it is here: with clarified butter taken in five ladlings, those same five oblations are offered. The significance of this has already been explained.
From the head;

or rather, he is consecrated while being sprinkled from the head, for he holds him above while consecrating him; with the same mantra, for he consecrates him as one who is equal; with a complete circuit on all sides, he thus consecrates him from every side.
And again, as to why he offers on the head of the chariot.

Yonder sun, indeed, is this chariot. Having assumed that form, Prajāpati, having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own. In the same way, this [sacrificer], having encompassed them, places them within himself and makes them his own. While being held above, for he who, having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own, was held above. With the same mantra, for he who, having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own, was one and the same. With a circumambulation on all sides, for he who, having encompassed these pairs, placed them within himself and made them his own, did so on every side.
"O Lord of the world, O Prajāpati, grant us [protection]!

For he is indeed the lord of the world, the Prajāpati, "whose houses are above and whose [they are] here. For his houses are both above and here. "For this Brahman, for this Kṣatra"—for this Agni is indeed both the Brahman and the Kṣatra—"grant great protection, svāhā!"—that is to say, "grant great shelter, svāhā!"
Then he offers the Vātahomas.
This Agni is indeed these worlds, and the Vātahomas are Vāyu; he thus places Vāyu within these worlds, and therefore this Vāyu exists within these worlds.
He brings fire from outside;
for that wind which is within these worlds is indeed his own, and he now places that wind which is beyond these worlds into it.
This altar outside the sacrificial ground is indeed the altar.
That wind which is upon it has already reached him; now, he places that wind which is beyond this earth into him.
With joined palms.

For there is no such thing as reaching [the goal] by means of this [offering]; he offers with the utterance *svāhā*. Indeed, that chariot is yonder sun, and it is below the pole. He thus places the wind closer than the sun; therefore, this [wind] blows from here toward us.
"You are the ocean, the wind-bearer," he says.

That world above is indeed the ocean, the wind-bearer, "the giver of moisture," for it gives moisture; thus he places the wind that is in yonder world into this one. "Be auspicious, be propitious, blow upon me, Svāhā!"—that is to say, "be gracious and pleasant, blow upon me."
"Thou art Māruta, the host of the Maruts.

The world of the intermediate space is indeed Māruta, the host of the Maruts; he thus places therein that wind which is in the world of the intermediate space. "Be auspicious, be refreshing, blow toward me, Svāhā!"—that is to say, "be propitious and pleasant, blow toward me."

"Thou art the seeker of help, the worshipper," he says; for this world is indeed the seeker of help, the worshipper; thus he bestows upon this world that Vāyu which is in it. "The bringer of bliss, the bringer of joy, blow towards me, svāhā!"—that is to say, "Being auspicious and pleasant, blow towards me."
He offers with three [verses].
These worlds are three; moreover, Agni is threefold. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he places Vāyu within these [worlds].

And as to why he offers the Vātahomas: it is this very chariot that he thus yokes. For the gods yoked this chariot for the sake of all desires, thinking, "With it yoked, may we attain [our goals]"; and with it yoked, they attained all desires. In the same way, the sacrificer now yokes this chariot for the sake of all desires, thinking, "With it yoked, may I attain [my goals]"; and with it yoked, he attains all desires.

He yokes it with the Vāta-homas. The Vāta-homas are indeed the vital breaths; verily, he yokes it with the vital breaths. He yokes it with three; for there are three vital breaths—the out-breathing, the up-breathing, and the through-breathing—and with these he yokes it. Lower and lower than the pole; for they yoke the draft-animal lower and lower than the pole. With both hands; for they yoke the draft-animal with both hands. Moving around in turn; for they yoke the draft-animal moving around in turn.

He first yokes the right-hand pair, then the left-hand pair, and then the right-hand leader; for it is thus among the gods, whereas it is otherwise among men. He should not yoke that [horse] again, lest he yoke what has already been yoked; however, he should give it as a vehicle, thinking, "May I enjoy it when it is yoked. They carry it up over the Adhvaryu's dwelling, for it is above him; he gives it to the Adhvaryu, for he performs his work with it. But he should assign it at the time of the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās).
Then he offers the *ruṅnati* oblations.

At this point, this entire fire has been consecrated; it was here that it desired radiance (*ruc*), and the gods bestowed radiance upon it by means of these *ruṅnati* oblations. In the very same way, this sacrificer now bestows radiance upon it.

Moreover, as to why he offers the *ruṅnati* oblations: when Prajāpati had become relaxed, Ruṅ emerged from him; when the gods restored him, they bestowed radiance upon him by means of these *ruṅnati* oblations. In the same way, this sacrificer now bestows that radiance upon him.

"Those lights of thine, O Agni, which are in the sun; those lights of yours, O gods, which are in the sun—bestow light upon us among the Brāhmaṇas. By saying "light, light," he bestows immortality upon him, for light is indeed immortality. He offers three oblations; Agni is threefold: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he bestows light upon him.

Then he offers an oblation to Varuṇa. At this point, this entire Agni has been consecrated; he (Agni) is here the deity Varuṇa, and it is to him that he offers this oblation. He thus makes him a deity by means of the oblation. For she indeed is a deity for whom an oblation is taken, and not she for whom it is not taken. With a verse addressed to Varuṇa, he gratifies him by his own self, by his own deity.

Moreover, as to why he offers the oblation to Varuṇa: when Prajāpati had become relaxed, his vital power (vīrya) departed from him; when the gods restored him, they placed that vital power back into him by means of this [oblation]. In the same way, this [sacrificer] now places it into him. He does so with a verse addressed to Varuṇa; for Varuṇa is the ruling power (kṣatra), and the ruling power is indeed vital power. Thus, by means of the ruling power, he places vital power into him.

"Having performed penance, I go to you, praising with a prayer"—this means "I entreat you, praising with a prayer. "This the sacrificer desires through the oblations"—this means "this the sacrificer here desires through the oblations. "O Varuṇa, being unangered, be mindful of us here"—this means "O Varuṇa, not being angry, be mindful of us here. "O you of wide renown, do not steal away our life"—with this he pronounces a formal entrustment for himself.
Then he offers the continuous oblations for the *Arka* and the *Aśvamedha*.

This Agni, indeed, is the *Arka*, and yonder Āditya is the *Aśvamedha*; when these two were created, they were separate. The gods joined them together and made them whole by means of these oblations; in the same way, this sacrificer now joins them together and makes them whole by means of these oblations.
"Gold is the cauldron; Svāhā!
Indeed, that sun is the cauldron; he thus establishes yonder sun in this fire.
"Svarṇārkaḥ svāhā!"—
this Agni-Arka thereby establishes this Agni in yonder sun.
"Gold is the seed; svāhā!"—the sun, indeed, is the seed; he thus places him there in yonder world.
"Golden light, svāhā!"—this Agni is light; he places him back here.
"Gold is Sūrya; Svāhā!
Now, that sun yonder is indeed Sūrya; he thus places yonder sun as the highest over this entire universe, and therefore he is the highest of this entire universe.
He offers these five oblations.
The fire-altar consists of five layers; the year has five seasons; the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—by that much he thus extends and joins these two together.

And as to why he says, "Svarṇa Gharma, Svāhā! Svarṇa Arka, Svāhā!"—these are indeed the names of this very Agni; he thus gratifies them and makes them deities by means of the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is a deity, but not one for whom it is not taken. Moreover, he thereby establishes these very fires in this fire by mentioning their names.
He offers these five oblations.

The fire-altar consists of five layers; there are five seasons, and the year is the fire-altar. As great as the fire-altar is, as great as its measure is—with just so much food does he thus gratify it.
Now, therefore, regarding the sowing of oblations:

whatever oblation one may know to be accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa explanation, that he should offer at this time. For he yokes this chariot for the sake of desires; thus, whatever oblation he offers here, he offers it as something already attained.
Regarding this they say:

"One should not offer [the oblations], lest one should make them redundant. But he should indeed offer them; for these oblations are offered for the sake of desires, and there is nothing redundant among desires.
Then, having returned at the time for the hearths (dhiṣṇya), he pours out the earth for the hearths.

These hearths are indeed fires; it is these very fires that he thus builds up. These [hearths] are the common people (viś), and this built-up fire-altar is the nobility (kṣatra); he thereby establishes both the nobility and the common people. He builds that [central fire-altar] first, and then these [hearths]; having thus established the nobility, he establishes the common people.
He becomes one;
he makes that kṣatra and that prosperity abide in one place, while the others, being many, bestow confusion upon the people.

This [altar] consists of five layers; the others consist of a single layer. He thus bestows sovereign power (kṣatra) with its own strength; he makes the sovereign power more powerful than the common people (viś). He piles this one upwards; he thus piles the sovereign power upwards by means of the layers. The others he piles crosswise; he thereby makes the common people as those who sit beneath for the sake of the sovereign power.
With both—the *yajusmatī* and the *lokampṛṇā*—he piles this [altar].

By means of the *lokampṛṇā* alone, he bestows the ruling power (*kṣatra*) with its own vigor upon these [bricks]; he makes the ruling power more vigorous than the common people (*viś*), and the common people less vigorous than the ruling power.

In that he piles this [altar] with the *lokapṛṇā* bricks alone, the *lokapṛṇā* is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*); thus he places the nobility within the people (*viś*). He piles both: those of the sacrifice and those of the fire-altar; first those of the sacrifice, then those of the fire-altar. The significance of this has been explained. Whichever sacrificial hearth (*dhiṣṇya*) he pours out, that very one he piles. He piles the *āgnīdhrīya* first, for he pours it out first. Sitting to the south facing north, the significance of this has been explained.

Upon that [altar] he lays down eight bricks. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thus builds up. Of these, a speckled stone is the ninth. There are indeed nine vital breaths: seven in the head and two downward ones; it is these he thus places within him. That Agni who is deposited on the built [altar] is the tenth; there are indeed ten vital breaths. The Āgnīdhra fire-shed is in the middle; he thus places the vital breaths in the middle. For the vital breaths, being in the middle, move along the self, coming and going.
He lays down twenty-one bricks in the Hotṛ’s place;

there are indeed twenty-one enclosing-stones, and their significance has been explained. There are eleven Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin’s bricks; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, Indra is connected with the Triṣṭubh, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin is connected with Indra. There are eight each in the other places; their significance has been explained.

On the Mārjālīya mound there are six; for the seasons are six and the Pitṛs are six. The seasons, the Pitṛs, placed him on the south side; he is thus on their south side. He lays down these [bricks] here and those [bricks] there; he thereby makes the peasantry face toward the nobility.
Then he encloses them with the enclosing stones (pariśrit).

The enclosing stones are indeed water; with water he thus encloses them. He places them all around. Those waters which flow through a dug-out channel are the nobility (kṣatra), while these other waters which are here as ordinary water are the common people (viś). When he encloses that [altar] with a dug-out channel, he thereby bestows nobility upon the nobility; he encloses the nobility with nobility. And when he places these [stones] all around, he thereby bestows the common people upon the common people; he encloses the common people with the common people. As many Yajus-possessing bricks as there are for those [altars], so many are the enclosing stones; for as many Yajus-possessing bricks as there are for that [central altar], so many are the enclosing stones. Thus he makes the common people obedient followers and subordinates to the nobility.

Then he scatters loose soil upon these; its significance has been explained. He does so silently, for the people (the earth) are undefined. Then, following the cake-offering of the animal sacrifice to Agni and Soma, he offers the Aveṣṭi oblations to the quarters. This Agni is the quarters; it is to them that he offers these oblations. By means of the oblation, he thus makes them a deity; for she alone is a deity for whom an oblation is taken, and not she for whom no oblation is taken. There are five of them, for there are five quarters.

They gave [it]. One should offer this sacrifice consisting of ten oblations; it contains all the *stomas*, all the *pṛṣṭhas*, all the meters, all the quarters, and all the seasons—for this fire is indeed everything. Thus he makes him a deity by means of the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is truly a deity, but not that one for whom no oblation is taken. There are ten [oblations]; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables, and Agni is the *virāj*. There are ten quarters, and Agni is the quarters. There are ten vital breaths, and the vital breaths belong to Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food does he gratify him.

He should offer these oblations to the very deities themselves. These deities have been consecrated by this very consecration (sava) with which he is about to be consecrated; it is them he thus gratifies. When they have been worshipped and gratified, they grant their approval for this consecration to him. Approved by them, he is consecrated. For indeed, he becomes a king whom other kings approve of as king, and not he whom they do not. And because these deities have been consecrated by this very consecration, or rather, because these deities consecrate him for this very consecration, therefore these are called *devasvaḥ* (the gods' property).

They indeed have two names; for he who is pressed by means of a pressing-rite (sava) comes to have two names: that for which he is pressed and that by means of which he is pressed—this is his second name.
There are eight [verses].
The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just so much food does he thus gratify him.
Regarding this, they say:

"One should not offer these oblations, lest one should cause an excess," they say. However, one should indeed offer them; for these oblations are offered for the sake of desires, and there is no such thing as an excess of desires. Whatever oblation is offered following the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), that sacrificial essence (medhas) is placed right in the middle of the animal itself. He offers both sets: those of the Soma-sacrifice (adhvara) and those of Agni. First those of the Soma-sacrifice, then those of Agni; the significance of this has been explained. The animal-cake is offered loudly, while these [other] oblations are offered in a low voice (upāṃśu), for they are an iṣṭi. For the animal-cake he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer! Give the command! but for these [other] oblations he says, "Recite the invitatory prayer! Recite the offering prayer! For they are an iṣṭi. The Sviṣṭakṛt offering is common to both, as is the Iḍā; the deities have been sacrificed to, but the Sviṣṭakṛt is not yet brought together.
Then he touches him with the preliminary consecration:
"May Savitṛ impel you for all impulses; this Soma is your king; [he is] the king of us Brāhmaṇas. Thus he sets aside the Brāhmaṇas and makes them unfit to be eaten.

Then, in the morning, when about to commence the Prātaranuvāka, he yokes the fire with the words, "With what is yoked may we attain all. By means of that which is thus yoked, he attains all desires. He yokes it at the beginning of the entire ritual; therefore, whatever is performed hereafter, all that is accomplished when it is yoked.
He yokes them at the enclosing-sticks;
for these enclosing-sticks are fires—he thus yokes fire by means of fires.

Having touched the middle enclosing-stick, he mutters this sacrificial formula: "I yoke Agni with power and with ghee. Power indeed is strength; thus, "I yoke Agni with strength and with ghee" is what it means. "The celestial, fair-winged bird, great in vigor"—for he is indeed the celestial, fair-winged bird, great in vigor by means of his smoke. "By that may we go to the station of the Sun, ascending to the heavenly world, above the highest firmament"—this is what it signifies.
Then, regarding the southern [wing]:

"These two wings of yours, O Agni, are bird-like and ageless, with which you drive away the Rakṣasas; with those two may we fly to the world of the doers of good deeds, where the first-born, ancient seers have gone"—by this he refers to those aforementioned seers.
Then, on the northern side:

"The moon, Dakṣa, Śyena, the observer of Truth, the golden-winged bird, the swift one"—for gold is indeed immortality; thus he means "the immortal-winged bird, the sustainer. "Great, seated firmly in his place—homage be to you, do not harm me!"—with these words he pronounces a protection for himself.
Now, that which is the middle *yajus* is the body; and those two which are on either side are the wings. Therefore, they possess wings, for those two are indeed the wings.
With three [verses] he yokes him;
Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he thus yokes him.

Then, having pressed the King (Soma), he offers it into the fire. This is indeed that consecration; this is what is consecrated for him. Those deities by whom he is permitted to be consecrated—being permitted by them—he is consecrated. For he alone becomes a king for whom other kings permit his kingship, and not he for whom they do not. In that he offers into the fire, he thereby consecrates the fire; thus this divine self of his becomes consecrated with Soma, consecrated with immortality. Then he consumes [the Soma]; thereby he consecrates his own self; thus this personal self of his becomes consecrated with Soma, consecrated with immortality.
Having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.
This [offering] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods come first, and then humans. Therefore, having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.
Then he releases it:

having attained that desire for which he yokes it, when he is about to commence the Yajñāyajñīya stotra—the Yajñāyajñīya being indeed the heavenly world—he yokes it for the sake of reaching that; thus, having attained that desire for which he yoked it, he now releases it.
He indeed unyokes it before the stotra.

For if he were to unyoke it after the stotra, he would turn his back on that heavenly world and lose it; but since he unyokes it before the stotra, having reached the heavenly world at once, he then unyokes.
He unyokes it at the enclosing-sticks;
for he yokes it at the enclosing-sticks, and wherever they yoke a draft-animal, there indeed they unyoke it.

Having touched water at the two junctures (saṃdhyā), he mutters these two *yajus* formulas; thus the two *yajus* correspond to the three enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*). With the words "Thou art the head of heaven, the navel of the earth," he places [the stick] on the south; with "Thou standest upon the head of the universe, supported," he places it on the north—using two verses containing the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), for this [fire-altar] is indeed its head. He uses two verses containing the word "water" (*apsumatī*); for the *yajñāyajñiya* is the hymn of Agni Vaiśvānara, and water is peace; therefore, he uses two verses containing the word "water."

He unlooses it with two verses; for the sacrificer has two feet, and Agni is the sacrificer: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just so much he unlooses him. He yokes with three verses; that makes five. The fire-altar consists of five layers, the year has five seasons, and Agni is the year: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so great does that become.

Regarding this, some yoke [the horse] at the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra and unyoke it at the Udayanīya, saying, "The unyoking is indeed the form of the completion; why should we perform the form of completion before the actual completion? One should not do so. For day after day this sacrifice is extended, and day after day it is completed. Day after day he yokes it for the sake of going to the heavenly world, and day after day he goes to the heavenly world by means of it. Therefore, one should yoke it day after day and unyoke it day after day.

Moreover, it is just as at the Prāyaṇīya Atirātra: having recited the Sāmidhenī verses, one might say, "I shall recite them again at the Udayanīya. Such is that case; therefore, one should yoke [the fires] day after day and release them day after day.

Regarding this, Cāṇḍilya, having instructed the Kaṅkatīyas in the daily ritual, went forth as a wandering mendicant, saying: "Day by day indeed I shall yoke you; day by day I shall unyoke you. Therefore, one should yoke [the fires] day by day and unyoke them day by day.
Now, therefore, concerning the milk-vow:
one who is consecrated should subsist on milk; for indeed, the nectar departed from the gods.

They said, "Let us seek this through toil and austerity. So they sought it through toil and austerity. Having consecrated themselves, they became observers of the milk-vow; for this indeed is austerity: that one who, having consecrated himself, remains an observer of the milk-vow. They heard its sound.
They said, "It has indeed become closer; let us apply ourselves to even more austerity. They approached three udders, and there they beheld it.
They said, "It has indeed become closer; let us perform even more austerity. They performed two [more] breasts, but they saw that it had become even closer.
They said, "It has indeed become closer; let us apply ourselves to even more austerity. They approached a single breast, and they mastered it, yet they were not able to grasp it.

They said, "We are not able to overcome you; let us undergo all forms of austerity. On the day of preparation (upavasatha), they underwent fasting. Indeed, fasting is the totality of austerity; therefore, one should not eat on the day of preparation.

Having approached it in the morning and having pressed the Soma, they offered it into the fire; thus they placed immortality into the fire. For Agni is indeed the self of all the gods; so when they placed immortality into the fire, they placed immortality into their own selves. Thereupon, the gods became immortal.

That which is that immortal Soma—him the sacrificer even today seeks out through toil and austerity. Having been consecrated (*dīkṣita*), he becomes one whose vow is milk; for this indeed is austerity: that one who, having been consecrated, remains a milk-vow-keeper. He hears his sound [crying] "O day! O purchase! as it were.

He approaches three teats; he sees them from afar. He approaches two teats; he sees them more closely. He approaches one teat; he reaches it, yet he is not able to seize it. On the day of preparation (upavasatha), he undergoes fasting; for fasting is indeed all austerity. Therefore, one should not eat on the day of preparation.
Having approached that in the morning and having pressed it, he offers it in the fire;

thus he places immortality in the fire. Then he consumes it; thus he places immortality in himself. He becomes immortal. This indeed is the immortality of a human being: that he reaches the full span of life. And so, by means of this self, he reaches the full span of life.
Having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.
This [offering] is his divine self, while this [body] is his human self; for the gods come first, and then human beings. Therefore, having offered it into the fire, he then consumes it.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. Both the gods and the asuras, being the offspring of Prajāpati, came to the inheritance of their father Prajāpati: namely, speech, both truth and untruth—both truth and untruth. Both of them spoke truth, and both of them spoke untruth; speaking alike, they were indeed alike.
Those gods, having abandoned untruth, took hold of truth; the Asuras, however, having abandoned truth, took hold of untruth.
Then this Truth indeed reflected: "The gods have indeed cast aside untruth and seized upon truth among the Asuras; come now, I shall go to them. So it went to the gods.
Untruth indeed reflected upon this:
"When the Asuras abandoned truth among the gods and seized upon untruth, alas, I shall go to that! And so it went to the Asuras.

Those gods spoke only truth, while all those Asuras spoke untruth. Speaking the truth with persistence, those gods became, as it were, less heroic and less wealthy; therefore, indeed, he who speaks the truth with persistence becomes, as it were, less heroic and less wealthy. Yet in the end he truly prospers, for the gods indeed prospered in the end.

Then the Asuras, speaking untruth out of attachment, became like salt-encrusted earth; they were as if ruined. Therefore, indeed, he who speaks untruth out of attachment becomes like salt-encrusted earth and is as if ruined. But in the end, he surely perishes, for the Asuras ultimately perished.
Now, that which is truth is the triple science (trayī vidyā). Those gods said, "Having performed the sacrifice, let us extend this truth."

They performed the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering. The Asuras became aware of this, thinking, "Having prepared the sacrifice, the gods are now extending that truth; let us go there and seize what belongs to us. When they had arrived, the *samiṣṭayajus* of that [offering] had not yet been offered; therefore, they do not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* for that sacrifice. The gods, seeing the Asuras, snatched up the sacrifice and resolved to perform something else. Thinking, "They are doing something different," the Asuras went away again.

While those Pitṛs were [still] there, they offered the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice; the Asuras indeed perceived it even as it was being performed. Having reached the point where the call for the Śamyu-formula had been uttered, they arrived. Therefore, that sacrifice ends with the Śamyu. Those gods, having seen the Asuras and snatched away the sacrifice, resolved to perform something else entirely. Thinking, "They are doing something different," the Asuras went back again.

When those deceased ones had departed, they bought a king, led him away, and then offered him as the guest-offering (ātithya-havis) to them; but the Asuras became aware of this very act. When the *iḍā* had been invoked for that offering, they arrived. Therefore, that sacrifice ends with the *iḍā*. Seeing the Asuras, the gods snatched up the sacrifice and resolved to perform something else entirely. Thinking, "They are doing something different," the Asuras went away once more.

When those Pitṛs had departed, the Upasads performed; they recited only three *sāmidhenī* verses and sacrificed to the deities alone. They did not perform the *prayāja*s nor the *anuyāja*s, thereby setting aside both parts of the sacrifice; for they were most hurried there. Therefore, at the Upasads, having recited only three *sāmidhenī* verses, one sacrifices to the deities alone; one does not perform the *prayāja*s nor the *anuyāja*s, thus setting aside both parts of the sacrifice.

On the day of preparation (upavasatha), they immolated the animal sacrifice for Agni and Soma. But the Asuras became aware of this very act; while its *samiṣṭayajus* oblations were yet unoffered, they arrived. Therefore, one does not offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations for that animal sacrifice. Those gods then drove the Asuras away.

While those [Asuras] were departed, the gods performed the morning pressing day after day; the Asuras indeed became aware of that. They arrived just as the morning pressing was being completed; then those gods drove away the Asuras.

When those Pitṛs had departed, they performed the midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*). The Asuras became aware of this very act; they arrived just as that much of it had been completed, namely, up to the midday pressing. Then those gods drove away the Asuras.

While they were performing the ritual with the Savanīya animal among those *pretas*, the Asuras indeed perceived it; they had already accomplished as much of it as is done for this animal. Then those gods came upon the Asuras.

When those *pretas* had departed, they performed the third *savana*; they completed it. In that they completed it, they attained all truth. Thereupon the Asuras were scattered; thereupon the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prevails by his own self, and his hateful rival is defeated.

Those gods said, "These sacrifices of ours have come to a standstill; since we abandoned them, they have departed. Find out how we may bring them to completion. They said, "Meditate!"—by which they meant, "Seek a layer (citi)"; they said, "Seek that [way] by which we may bring these sacrifices to completion."

While they were reflecting, they saw these *samiṣṭayajus* offerings; they offered them, and by means of them they completed these sacrifices. Because they completed (*samasthāpayan*) them, they are called *saṃsthitayajūs*; and because they sacrificed together (*samayajan*), they are called *samiṣṭayajūs*.

Now, these are indeed nine sacrifices; these are the nine *samiṣṭayajus* offerings. When he offers them, he thereby brings these very sacrifices to completion. He offers both sets: those of the *adhvara* and those of the fire-altar (*agni*). First those of the *adhvara*, and then those of the fire-altar; the significance of that has already been explained.
He offers two oblations to Agni.

The sacrificer has two feet, and the sacrificer is Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, by just that much he thus brings the sacrifice to completion with the words: "The sacrifice has been offered by the Bhṛgus; may Agni, being offered, fulfill us."
These two groups together amount to eleven;
the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables and the Triṣṭubh is vigor; thus he brings this sacrifice into correspondence with vigor.
Or rather, there are eleven;

for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, Indra is of Triṣṭubh nature, Indra is the self of the sacrifice, and Indra is the deity. Thus, he establishes the sacrifice at the end in that which is both the self of the sacrifice and the deity.
Having offered the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, they proceed to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).

Having emerged from the purificatory bath and performed the concluding rite (*udayanīya*), he offers the oblations for the *devikās* following the animal-cake offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*) of the *anūbandhya* victim.

Having attained this, Prajāpati indeed considered himself successful; having established himself in the quarters, he stood firm, bestowing and arranging all this. Because he stood firm bestowing and arranging, he is therefore called Dhātṛ (the Ordainer). In the same way, the sacrificer, having established himself in the quarters, stands firm, bestowing and arranging all this.

Moreover, as to why he offers these oblations: this Agni is the quarters, and it is those very quarters that he places first—the bunch of darbha grass and the clod-bricks. Those are the breath-supporters (*prāṇabhṛt*): all [the bricks] in the first layer, all in the second, all in the third, and all in the fourth. Now, from the fifth layer upwards, there are the *asapatnā*, the *nākasad*, and the *pañcacūḍā* bricks; they went forth rising upwards. Prajāpati was afraid of them, thinking, "These, being turned away, will pass beyond this entire world. Becoming Dhātṛ, he went around them and established himself among them.
He who is that Ordainer (Dhātṛ) is this Āditya;
and that which is the furthest extent of the quarters is that upon which he stands while shining.
He who is that Dhātṛ is this very cake on twelve potsherds;

for the cake is on twelve potsherds, and there are twelve months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year, and Dhātṛ is Prajāpati. Now, as for that which is the furthest stride of the quarters—these are those former oblations: a pap for Anumati, a pap for Rākā, a pap for Sinīvālī, and a pap for Kuhū. When he offers these, he thereby establishes him (Agni) upon that which is the furthest stride of the quarters. He offers it all; this is for the sake of its completeness.

These indeed are the goddesses, for these quarters are the meters, and the meters are goddesses; and this Ka is Prajāpati. Because they are both the goddesses and Ka, they are called the Devikās. There are five of them, for there are five quarters.
Regarding this, they say:

"One should not offer these oblations, lest one should make them redundant," they say; however, one should indeed offer them, for these oblations are offered for the sake of desires, and there is nothing redundant regarding desires. Whatever oblation is offered following the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa), that sacrificial essence (medha) is placed right in the middle of the animal itself. He offers both: those of the Soma-sacrifice (adhvara) and those of the fire-altar (agni); first those of the Soma-sacrifice, then those of the fire-altar—the significance of this has been explained. The animal-cake is offered loudly, while these are offered in a low voice (upāṃśu), for these are an *iṣṭi*. For the animal-cake he says, "Recite the invitatory verse! Give the command! but for these, he says, "Recite the invitatory verse! Recite the offering verse! for these are an *iṣṭi*. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is the same, and the *iḍā* is the same.
Now, for this very animal sacrifice,
they offer the *samiṣṭayajus* oblations, they descend to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) with the heart-spike, for this animal sacrifice is completed by performing the rite with the heart-spike.
Having returned, he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations.

"All works"—this Agni is they; all these works have been performed by him here. He thus gratifies them and makes them a deity with the oblation. For that deity for whom an oblation is taken is indeed a deity, but not that one for whom it is not taken. Moreover, this Agni is Viśvakarman (the All-worker); it is him he thus gratifies.

Furthermore, as to why he offers the Vaiśvakarman oblations: the Sāvitra oblations are both the beginning and the rising of Agni, while the Vaiśvakarman oblations are the beginning and the rising. If he were to offer only the Sāvitra oblations and not the Vaiśvakarman ones, it would be as if he performed only the beginning and not the rising; that would be so. And if he were to offer only the Vaiśvakarman oblations and not the Sāvitra ones, it would be as if he performed only the rising and not the beginning; that would be so. He offers both; thus he effects both the beginning and the rising.

There are eight Vasus. Thus, just as their departure was, so does he make their emergence: the *svāhā*-utterance is the ninth of these; thus, just as their departure was, so does he make their emergence. The oblation is the tenth of these; thus, just as their departure was, so does he make their emergence. There he offers the oblation continuously; for the sacrifice there is indeed seed, [offered] for the non-interruption of the seed. Here, with the *sruva* ladle, he makes the *svāhā*-utterance, for the seed becomes manifest once it is born.

"From whatever intention, from the heart, or from the mind it was gathered, or from the eye—from all this, indeed, action first came into being. Follow after that to the world of the well-doers, where the seers who were first-born in ancient times have gone. By this, he refers to those very seers.

"This common dwelling, I entrust it to you"—the common dwelling is indeed the heavenly world; thus he entrusts it to him for the heavenly world. "The Lord of the Sacrifice, whom Jātavedas has brought hither as a guardian, shall follow you here; recognize him in the highest heaven"—as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.
"Know this!

O gods who dwell together in the highest heaven, perceive his form when he has come by the paths traveled by the gods, so that you may make manifest for us his sacrifices and pious works. As the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is, so is its explanation (*bandhu*). "Awake, O Agni, with [the power] wherewith thou carriest [the offerings]"—the explanation of these two [verses] is their meaning.

"With the sacrificial grass-bundle, with the enclosing-sticks, with the ladle, with the altar, and with the sacrificial strew— by means of this Ṛg-verse, lead this sacrifice of ours to heaven among the gods"— this means, "by means of these forms of our sacrifice, cause us to go to the heavenly world."

"What has been given, what has been received from others, what has been offered as a pūrtam, and whatever sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) there are—may Agni Vaiśvakarman place all that for us among the gods in heaven. This means: "Whatever we give now and whatever we shall give in the future, may this Agni Vaiśvakarman place all that for us in the heavenly world."
"Where the streams of honey and ghee do not fail—may Agni Vaiśvakarman place us in the heavenly world among the gods. As the sacrificial formula (yajus) is, so is its explanation (bandhu).
He offers eight oblations to Viśvakarman;
the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī: as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, with just so much food he thus gratifies him.
Having offered the Vaiśvakarman oblations, he gives him a name;
for when one is born entirely and completely, then they give him a name, and at this point he is indeed born entirely and completely.
Having thus performed the naming ceremony, he then worships him.

In every way, he builds this [altar] with his entire self. If he were not to utter this self-consecration formula here, then right here he would cut off his own self; but because he utters this self-consecration formula here, he does not cut off his own self. "Of those fires belonging to the five peoples that are upon this earth, thou art the highest; impel us toward life"—that is, "Of whatever fires there are consisting of five layers upon this earth, thou art the best among them; impel us forward for the sake of living. He does so with an Anuṣṭubh verse; for the Anuṣṭubh is speech, and speech is all the meters. Thus, by means of all the meters, he has driven it down for him. Having performed the worship and having caused the fire to ascend [into himself], he churns it out and performs the Udavasānīyā sacrifice.

Then he sacrifices with the curd-mixture dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa. He who performs this rite becomes divine among the gods; for this pair, Mitra and Varuṇa, is divine. If, without having sacrificed with this, he were to behave as a human being, that would be a descent, just as if one who is divine were to become human. But when he sacrifices with this curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa, he approaches that very divine pair. Having sacrificed with this, he may then act according to his desire and in accordance with what is fitting.

Furthermore, as to why he sacrifices with this curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa: when Prajāpati had become disjointed, his seed fell away; when the gods restored him, they placed that seed in him by means of this curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa. In the same way, this sacrificer now places it in him.

He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is this very Agni who is now being built up. And that seed which fell away from him is this curd-mixture for Mitra and Varuṇa (payasyā). Mitra and Varuṇa are indeed out-breathing and in-breathing, and it is out-breathing and in-breathing that transform the emitted seed. It is a curd-mixture because seed is milk; it is the sacrifice because the sacrifice is truly the seed of the sacrifice. It is performed in a whisper, for seed is emitted in a whisper; it is at the end, for seed is deposited at the end.
They proceed with the Vājina offering for that [altar].

He bestows the sacrificial fee upon it; "He should give a pair of hornless ones," so says Māhitthi, "for I consider this to be merely by way of a command. Indeed, this oblation offered on what is not a brick is a leaking oblation, a Soma-oblation [offered] where there is no brick."
He should lay down the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks themselves.
These worlds, indeed, are the *svayamātṛṇṇā*s; these worlds are this built-up fire-altar.
One should indeed lay down the seasonal bricks;
for the seasonal bricks are the year, and this piled fire-altar is the year.
One should indeed lay down the Viśvajyotis bricks;
for these deities are the Viśvajyotis, and these very deities are this piled Agni.

Furthermore, he should pile up the fire-altar again; for this is indeed a renewed sacrifice, and this is a higher worship of the gods. Thus he piles up a renewed sacrifice and a higher worship of the gods. Indeed, a renewed sacrifice approaches him. However, one should not do it in that way. For that very brick upon which the fire is placed when piled—that is what this entire fire-altar becomes. Therefore, whatever he offers in the fire, that becomes for him as if offerings had been made on the entire fire-altar when it is fully piled with wings and tail. In this way, these offerings of his become truly offered.

Indeed, all beings and all the gods become the embryo of him who maintains the fire. He who piles the fire-altar without having maintained it for a full year brings forth these same all-beings as his own embryo; and when one brings forth a human embryo, that indeed is what people look upon with disapproval. But what need is there to speak of this [fire-altar], for it is divine? "One must not be its officiating priest (ṛtvij) until it has been maintained for a year," Vātsya used to say, "lest I incur the guilt of bringing forth the seed of a god while it is being brought forth."

"One should pile [the altar] for at most six months," they say; "for embryos born after six months are living. If he should recite the Great Litany (*mahaduktha*) for one who has not carried the fire for a year, he should recite the *ṛca-aśītis*; for that which is not carried for a year is incomplete, and those *ṛca-aśītis* are incomplete. He would thereby further displace him from what is already displaced. Whether he has carried the fire for a year or not, he should recite the entire Great Litany.
Then Śāṇḍilyāyana went toward the East. Daivyampāti said to him, "Śāṇḍilyāyana, how is the fire-altar to be built? We are weary; we wish to build the fire-altar after it has been carried for a year."
He said:
"One may indeed build this [fire-altar] at will, provided that it has been carried for a year beforehand; for it is only when it has been so carried that one builds it."
Indeed, he may build this [altar] who intends to press Soma for a year; for it is this [altar] that directly sustains him with food through these oblations.
One may indeed build this [altar] at will;
for he who offers the Agnihotra for a year supports it, since he who offers the Agnihotra sustains it.

One may indeed build this altar for one who has been born for a full year. For Agni is breath; he thus sustains that breath. Now, when seed is emitted, the breath descends after it and finds it; because he finds (*vindate*) what is born (*jātam*), he is called Jātavedas. Therefore, one who knows this may also build it immediately upon being born. Whatever such a knower drinks or causes to be drunk, that becomes for him like oblations offered when the entire fire-altar, complete with wings and tail, has been built. Thus do these offerings of his become offered.

Indra saw this *sarpis-tvac* for the attainment of what was deficient, for the removal of what was redundant, and for the perfection of what was unsuccessful. Indeed, one who has piled the fire-altar is liable to encounter some misfortune or to stumble; but when Śyāparṇa Sāyakāyana heard this, he then undertook this ritual procedure.
This is the prosperity of the triad:
it is the prosperity of Agni; it is the prosperity of him who piles the fire-altar; it is the prosperity of him who causes the fire-altar to be piled.
Now, as to why he worships with this [verse]:

whatever of his he, whether knowing or unknowing, either leaves out or does not complete here, all that becomes attained for him by this [rite], as well as whatever of his was unattained. Furthermore, whatever desire there is in that Anuṣṭubh verse, that very desire he attains right here. Moreover, from this very rite he drives away the Rakṣases and the destroyers; they do not strike him down even if others utter curses against him. Therefore, one who knows this may, if he so desires, pile the fire-altar for another; for he is capable of becoming superior.
"For the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength;

O much-invoked one, [slay] Dānu who dwells there"—with these two first verses addressed to the slayer of Vṛtra he worships. For the gods, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—became free from evil and performed this rite; in the very same way, the sacrificer, having slain Vṛtra—the evil—becomes free from evil and performs this rite.

"O Indra, strike away our enemies! Like a fearsome wild beast that wanders and dwells in the mountains"—with these two verses addressed to the Dispeller of Enemies (Vaimṛdhī), which are the second ones, the gods, having struck away the enemies who are evil, performed this rite while being themselves freed from evil. In the very same way, the sacrificer, having struck away the enemies who are evil, performs this rite while being himself freed from evil.

"Vaiśvānara for our aid, Agni who is praised in heaven, praised on earth"—with these two verses addressed to Vaiśvānara as the third [part], the gods, having burnt away evil by means of Vaiśvānara and being freed from evil, performed this rite; in the same way, the sacrificer, having burnt away evil by means of Vaiśvānara and being freed from evil, performs this rite.

"May we attain our desire through your protection, O Agni"—with this one verse containing a wish, for the gods, having struck away evil with it, finally made all their desires one-pointedly their own by means of that single wish-containing verse; in the same way, the sacrificer, having struck away evil with the six-verse hymn, finally makes all his desires one-pointedly his own by means of that single wish-containing verse.

It consists of seven verses. The fire-altar has seven layers; there are seven seasons, seven directions, seven worlds of the gods, seven *stomas*, seven *pṛṣṭhas*, seven meters, seven domestic animals, seven wild animals, and seven vital breaths in the head. Whatever is sevenfold—whether relating to the deities or to the self—he thereby obtains all that. These verses resolve into the *anuṣṭubh*; for the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and by means of speech he thereby obtains whatever of his remains unobtained.

"One should worship with eight verses," so some say. With the second verse, "For we have granted your desire today," which contains the word 'desire' (kāma), there are seven preceding ones; thus they become eight. The Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, and Agni is of Gāyatra nature; as great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by that much one obtains for him whatever was not yet obtained. Moreover, in this way the two deities share equally. But one should not do it thus. These seven verses indeed become eight Anuṣṭubhs. Whatever desire there is in the eight-verse hymn, that one obtains right here.
He worships with verses addressed to Indra and Agni.

Agni belongs to Indra and Agni; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thereby obtains, whatever of him was not previously obtained. Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; Agni belongs to all the deities. As great as Agni is, as great as his measure is, so much of him he thereby obtains, whatever of him was not previously obtained.

Now, some indeed make this opening verse (pratipad) for every single ritual act, thinking, "Let us perform this rite which has its evil struck away. Others say that one should worship after having constructed a layer provided with loose soil (purīṣavatī citi), for there it becomes whole and complete. One may do as one desires; such is the rule regarding piling. Now, however, follows the rule regarding non-piling.
There are indeed three oceans:

Agni is the ocean of the *yajus* formulas, the *Mahāvrata* is the ocean of the *sāmans*, and the *Mahaduktha* is the ocean of the *ṛc* verses. He who performs these for another person dries up those very oceans; as they dry up, his meters dry up after them; as the meters dry up, the world dries up after them; as the world dries up, the self dries up after it; and as the self dries up, offspring and cattle dry up after it. Verily, he who performs these for another person becomes worse and worse day by day.

Now, if one should cause another to sacrifice with all other sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) without performing these [rites], his *candāṃsi* (metres) are replenished again from these very oceans; following the *candāṃsi* comes the world, following the world comes the self (*ātman*), and following the self come offspring and cattle. He who does not perform these for another becomes better day by day. Furthermore, this indeed is his divine, immortal self; he who performs these for another gives away that divine self to another, and only a withered stump remains.

Now, some, having performed [the rite], perform it again or have it performed again, saying, "This is the expiation. One should not do so; it would be as if one were to sprinkle water upon a dry stump—it would either rot or wither away. There is no expiation for this; thus one should know.

Now, Śāṇḍilya used to say: "Tura Kāvaṣeya built a fire-altar for the gods at Kārotyā. The gods asked him: 'O Sage, since they say that the piling of the fire-altar does not lead to the world of heaven, why then have you piled it?'"

He said: "What indeed is conducive to the world, and what is not? The sacrificer is indeed the self of the sacrifice, and the officiating priests are its limbs. Where the self is, there are the limbs; where the limbs are, there is the self. If the officiating priests are without a world, then the sacrificer is likewise without a world, for both share the same world. However, one should not bargain over the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); by bargaining, the officiating priests become worldless. This fire-altar is built in front, the year is above it, and the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*) is recited; from Prajāpati, when he was relaxed, the essence went upward."
He who was that Prajāpati when he fell apart is the year; and those joints of his which fell apart are the days and nights.

That Prajāpati, the year, who fell apart—he is this very Agni who is now being built up. And those joints of his, the days and nights, which fell apart—those are these very bricks. Thus, when he lays down these bricks, he restores to him those very days and nights, the joints, which had fallen apart; and so this sacrificial formula (yajus) is piled up right here and attained right here.

Now, that essence of his which went forth at the beginning became the Great Uktha; they follow that essence of his with the Ṛg and Sāman verses. As for the Yajus formula which goes before them there, it goes as a guide, just as one might think, "I will bring that one thing from over there for him. Such is its nature.

The Adhvaryu draws it with a *graha* (libation); because he draws it, it is called a *graha*. Before it goes the *yajus*; they reach it in the course of a year. The Udgātṛ bestows essence upon it by means of the Mahāvrata; for the Mahāvrata is all these *sāmans*, and thus he bestows essence upon it by means of all the *sāmans*. Upon it the Hotṛ bestows essence by means of the Great Recitation (*mahad uktham*); for the Great Recitation is all these *ṛcs*, and thus he bestows essence upon it by means of all the *ṛcs*.

When they chant the Stotra and when he recites the Śastra, then, at the utterance of the Vaṣaṭ-call, he offers this [oblation] into him; thus this essence enters into him. They do not perceive that "this Mahāvrata has been chanted and now lies still," nor do they perceive that "this is a great Uktha"; rather, they perceive it as Agni alone, for Agni is the self. Thus both of these—the Ṛc and the Sāman—having become essence, enter into him; and both the Ṛc and the Sāman enter into the Yajus.
This very Agni is a pair: the first layer and the second, the third and the fourth; then that Agni which is placed upon the fifth layer—that is the pair. Indeed, this self is a pair.

"The thumbs" are males; "the fingers" are females; "the ears" are males; "the eyebrows" are females; "the lips" are males; "the nostrils" are females; "the teeth" are males; "the tongue" is female. Thus, everything is a couple. By means of this self that is a couple, he enters into this fire which is a couple.

This is the union here as well: even though it is thus, there is indeed this union; for this Agni who is built up is Speech, since he is built up by means of speech.
