And that fire which is placed upon the built-up altar is Breath; Breath is indeed the male of Speech, and thus they form a union. This body is Speech, and the Breath within the body is the male; thus they form a union. By means of this self consisting of this union, he enters into this Agni, who is likewise a union.

This is the secret here: indeed, no doubt whatsoever remains regarding one's lack of offspring for him who thus knows these two as a couple—the Self and the Fire. Moreover, this Self truly desires food as his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), for it has been declared by the Seer: "He who is not our Self."

This food, once eaten, becomes twofold: that which is its immortal part rises upward from the navel through the upper vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and enters the air; then, that which is its mortal part passes beyond the navel and becomes twofold, entering this earth as both urine and feces. Now, that which enters this earth enters the fire-altar that has been built there; and that which enters the air enters the fire that is deposited upon the built altar—this indeed is the convergence here.

Prajāpati desired to obtain these worlds. He saw this self consisting of the three ages (*vayovidha*): Agni. He established it; by means of it, he obtained this world. He saw a second self consisting of the three ages: the Mahāvrata. He established it; by means of it, he obtained the intermediate region. He saw a third self consisting of the three ages: the Mahaduktha. He established it; by means of it, he obtained heaven.

This world, indeed, is this built fire-altar; the intermediate region is the Mahāvrata chant; and the sky is the Mahaduktha. Therefore, one should perform all these together: the fire-altar, the Mahāvrata, and the Mahaduktha; for these worlds were created together. As to why the fire-altar is built first: it is because this [earth] was the first of these worlds to be created. This is with respect to the deities.

Now, with reference to the self: the mind itself is the fire, the vital breath is the Great Vow (mahāvrata), and speech is the Great Hymn (mahaduktha). Therefore, one should undertake all these together, for the mind, the vital breath, and speech are together. And as to why the fire-altar is built first: it is because the mind is the first of the vital breaths.

The self alone is the fire; breath is the great vow; speech is the great hymn. Therefore, one should undertake all these together, for the self, breath, and speech are together. Since the fire is built first, it is because the self is the first to come into being when one comes into being.

The fire-altar is indeed the head; the Mahāvrata is the vital breath; the Mahaduktha is the self. Therefore, one should perform all these together, for the head, the vital breath, and the self are together. Now, since the fire-altar is built first, it is because the head is born first of one being born. Therefore, when all these are performed together, the Mahaduktha is manifested as the very essence of the self, for the Mahaduktha is the self.

Regarding this they say: "Since all these [sacrifices] are difficult to attain together, how is their attainment? [The answer is: "In the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma; one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma itself."

Now, of this very Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma, the Trivṛt Bahiṣpavamāna is its head; the Pañcadaśa and Saptadaśa are the two subsequent Pavamānas, which are its two wings; the Pañcadaśa Hotṛ-ājya, the Saptadaśa Pṛṣṭha, and the Ekaviṃśa Yajñāyajñīya are its tail.

Now, of these two—the fifteenfold and the seventeenfold—there are thirty-two stotriya verses. Of those, the twenty-five constitute the twenty-five-fold self; then, the seven that remain are the *parimādas*. These are indeed cattle, for the *parimādas* are cattle. This much indeed is the Mahāvrata; thus, he obtains the Mahāvrata right here.

Then the Hotṛ recites the seven metres, each increasing by four syllables, with the Virāj as the eighth; they contain three hundred and eighty-four syllables. Of these, that which consists of the eighties is the attainment of the "eighties," for it is by means of the eighties that the Mahaduktha is proclaimed. Then as for the forty-five: of those, the twenty-five is the twenty-five-fold body; where there is the body, there indeed are the head, the wings, and the tail. Then as for the twenty [remaining], that is the insertion. So much indeed is the Mahaduktha; thus he attains the Mahaduktha right here. All these [elements] are attained in the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma; therefore, one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma Agniṣṭoma alone.

Prajāpati created living beings. From the upward breaths alone he created the gods; from those downward breaths he created mortal creatures. Then, above the creatures, he created Death as their devourer.

Of that Prajāpati, one half was indeed mortal and one half was immortal. That which was his mortal part, he was afraid of it; being afraid, he entered this [earth], having become two-fold: clay and water.

Death said to the gods, "Where indeed has he gone who created us? They replied, "Fearing you, he has entered this earth. Death said, "Then let us search for him; let us gather him together; I will not harm him. The gods gathered him from her: whatever of him was in the waters, they gathered those waters; and whatever of him was in this earth, that was the clay. Having brought both together—the clay and the waters—they made them into bricks. Therefore, a brick consists of these two things: clay and water.
Thus, these indeed were his five mortal bodies: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; and these were his immortal [bodies]: mind, speech, breath, sight, and hearing.

He who was that Prajāpati is this very Agni who is being built up; and those five mortal bodies of his were these layers of loose earth (purīṣaciti), while those which were immortal were these layers of bricks (iṣṭakāciti).

Those gods said, "Let us make this [body] immortal. With those two immortal bodies, they enclosed this mortal body and made it immortal: by means of the two brick layers (iṣṭakā-citi), they [made] the loose-earth layer (purīṣa-citi); likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Then, having laid down the fifth layer, he scatters loose earth (purīṣa); there he lays down the Vakarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇṇā bricks, sprinkles them with chips of gold, and places the fire upon them. That is the seventh layer, which is immortal. Thus, by enclosing this mortal body of his between these two immortal bodies—the brick-layer and the loose-earth layer—they made it immortal. Thereby Prajāpati indeed became immortal; and in the same way, the sacrificer, having made this self of his immortal, becomes immortal.

Those gods did not know whether they had made him complete or not, whether they had excluded anything or not, nor whether they had reached the goal or not; they saw this verse: "May Agni, Indra, the god Bṛhaspati the Brahman, and all the Viśve Devas, being of one mind, protect our sacrifice for prosperity."

Of that [earth], there is indeed a portion belonging to Agni, one belonging to Indra, and one belonging to the Viśvedevas. Whatever of it belongs to Agni, they restored that part of this [Agni] by means of that [portion]; whatever belonged to Indra, they restored by means of that [portion]; and whatever belonged to the Viśvedevas, they restored by means of that [portion]. Thus, right there, they restored him in his entirety and completeness.

Now, when he worships with this [verse], whatever of his he—whether knowing or unknowing, or whether he overflows or does not complete—it all obtains through this for him; and since it becomes an Anuṣṭubh verse containing the word "home" (dhāmacat), and the Anuṣṭubh is speech and speech contains the "home," he thereby obtains for him whatever of his was unobtained. "One should worship after having made the layer provided with loose soil (purīṣavatī)," so say some, for there that [layer] becomes whole and complete.

Regarding this, they say: "One should worship with a verse containing the word 'yaviṣṭha' (the youngest), for that is his beloved abode, namely 'yaviṣṭha'. By means of that which is his beloved abode, he thereby obtains whatever of his has not yet been obtained. With a Gāyatrī verse addressed to Agni—since the fire-rite belongs to Agni, and Agni is of the Gāyatrī nature—he obtains it by as much as is Agni, by as much as is his measure; thus he obtains whatever of his has not been obtained. With an undefined verse, for everything is indeed undefined; by means of the whole, he thereby obtains whatever of his has not been obtained. [The verse begins: 'O thou, most youthful, of the donor... The significance of this has already been explained. Having constructed the layer provided with loose soil (purīṣavatī citiḥ), one should worship; for therein it becomes entirely complete."

In the beginning, Prajāpati was indeed both of these: the mortal and the immortal. His vital breaths were the immortal, and his body was the mortal. By means of this rite and by this procedure, he made himself at once undecaying and immortal. In the same way, the sacrificer becomes both of these: the mortal and the immortal. His vital breaths become the immortal, and his body is the mortal; by means of this rite and by this procedure, he makes himself at once undecaying and immortal.

He piles the first layer; that, indeed, is his very breath. And that is immortal, for the breath is immortal. That is the "Immortal Layer. Then he scatters loose soil; that, indeed, is his marrow. And that is mortal, for the marrow is mortal. He establishes it upon that immortal [breath], whereby this [marrow] of his becomes immortal.

He piles the second layer; that is indeed his out-breathing (apāna). That is immortal, for the out-breathing is immortal. This is the Immortal Layer. On both sides of this mortal [layer] he encloses it with the immortal; thereby this [mortal part] of his becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose earth; that is indeed his bone. That is mortal, for bone is mortal. He establishes it upon that immortal [layer]; thereby this [bone] of his becomes immortal.

He piles the third layer; that indeed is his vital air of diffusion (vyāna). That is immortal, for the vital air of diffusion is immortal. This is the "Immortal Layer. On both sides of this mortal [layer] he encloses it with the immortal; thereby this [mortal part] of his becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose soil; that is indeed his sinew. That is mortal, for the sinew is mortal. He establishes it upon that immortal [layer]; thereby this [sinew] of his becomes immortal.

He piles the fourth layer; that is indeed his out-breathing (udāna). That is immortal, for the out-breathing is immortal; it is the "Immortal Layer. He encloses this mortal [body] on both sides with the immortal; thereby this [body] of his becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose soil; that is indeed his flesh. That is mortal, for flesh is mortal; he establishes it upon that immortal [layer], and thereby this [flesh] of his becomes immortal.

He piles the fifth layer; that indeed is his Samāna, for the Samāna is immortal, and this layer is an immortal piling. This mortal [body] he encloses on both sides with the immortal; thereby this [body] of his becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose earth; that is indeed his fat, for fat is mortal. He establishes it upon that immortal [layer]; thereby this [fat] of his becomes immortal.

He piles the sixth layer; this, indeed, is his speech. For that is immortal, since speech is immortal; it is the immortal layer. This mortal [body] he encloses on both sides with the immortal; thereby this part of him becomes immortal. Then he scatters loose soil; that is his blood and his skin. That, indeed, is mortal, for blood is mortal and skin is mortal. He establishes this upon that immortal; thereby this part of him becomes immortal.

Now, these are six layers of bricks and six layers of loose soil; that makes twelve. Twelve months are a year, and the year is Agni. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much did Prajāpati then make himself whole, undecaying, and immortal. In the very same way, the sacrificer now makes himself whole, undecaying, and immortal.

Then, having laid down the Vikarṇī and the Svayamātṛṇā bricks, he sprinkles them with chips of gold and places the fire upon them. This is indeed the form that Prajāpati made for himself last of all; because it was at the end, this is the final form of his body. Therefore they say, "Prajāpati is golden. In the same way, the sacrificer makes for himself a golden form last of all; because it is at the end, this is the final form of his body. Therefore, whether people know this or not, they say, "The builder of the fire-altar becomes golden in yonder world."
Now, regarding this very point, Śāṇḍilya and Sāptarathavāhani were once disputing as teacher and pupil; Śāṇḍilya said, "This is his form," while Sāptarathavāhani said, "It is his hair."

Śāṇḍilya said: "Form indeed is that which has hair, and form is that which is hairless; this [altar] is indeed his form. That is truly so, just as Śāṇḍilya said: once the fire-altar has been built, the fire is led forward; after it has been led forward, the fuel-sticks and oblations are offered.

By means of the out-breath (prāṇa), indeed, the gods eat food; Agni is the out-breath of the gods, therefore they offer oblations before the gods, for by means of the out-breath the gods eat food. By means of the in-breath (apāna), humans eat food; therefore food is placed facing toward humans, for by means of the in-breath humans eat food.

Regarding this they say: "One who has built the fire-altar (Agnicit) should not eat fowl; for he who builds the fire-altar becomes the very form of fowl, and he is liable to meet with ruin. Therefore, one who has built the fire-altar should not eat fowl. But indeed, one who knows thus may eat it at will; for he who builds the fire-altar becomes the very form of Agni, and all this is the food of Agni. One who knows thus should know: "All this is my food."

Regarding this they say: "What is it that is performed in the fire by which the sacrificer overcomes repeated death? Indeed, he who piles the fire becomes the deity Agni; and Agni is immortality. The gods are prosperity; he attains prosperity. The gods are glory; he indeed becomes glorious—he who knows thus.

All these are indeed sacrifices: this piled fire-altar is the Agnyādheya; when he immolates the victim, that is the Agnyādheya; when he prepares the fire-pan (ukhā), those are the oblations of the Agnyādheya; when he undergoes initiation (dīkṣā), that is the Agnihotra; and when, having been initiated, he places two pieces of fuel on the fire, those are the two Agnihotra oblations.

Verily, he establishes [the fires] in the evening and in the morning, for they offer the Agnihotra oblations in the evening and in the morning; with the same mantra, for they offer the Agnihotra oblations with the same mantra. Now, the driving away of the cattle and the throwing down of the ashes—those two are the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa). Then, that which he piles up as the Gārhapatya fire—those are the Seasonal sacrifices (Cāturmāsya). Then, that which is from above the Gārhapatya up to the "All-herbs" (Sarvauṣadha) layer—those are the Ishtis. Then, that which is from above the Sarvauṣadha layer back to the layers (citibhyaḥ)—those are the Animal sacrifices (Paśubandha). Whatever Viṣṇu-strides (Viṣṇukrama) there are in these sacrifices, those are the Viṣṇu-strides; whatever muttering (japya) there is, that is the Vātsapra.

The peaceful *adhvara* is the first layer; the *rājasūya*, which precedes the *sava*s, is the second; the *vājapeya* is the third; the *aśvamedha* is the fourth; and the *agnisava* is the fifth. That with which he sings around the piled altar by means of the *sāman*s is the *mahāvrata*; and that which is the *udgātṛ*'s preliminary recitation there is the *catasrudriya*. The *vasordhārā* is the *mahaduktha*. Now, that which is after the *sāman*s and before the *vasordhārā*, and whatever there is as the *hotṛ*'s preliminary recitation therein—that is this [part]. And that which is after the *vasordhārā* is the *gṛhamedha*s. So many indeed are all the sacrifices; these he attains through the fire-altar.

Now, therefore, concerning the powers of sacrifice: indeed, in yonder world, the Agnihotra-offerer eats as much as he desires morning and evening; such is the vigor (ūrg) in that sacrifice. The performer of the New and Full Moon sacrifices eats for half a month at a time; the performer of the Seasonal sacrifices (Cāturmāsya) every four months; the performer of the Animal sacrifice every six months; and the Soma-sacrificer every year. But the builder of the Fire-altar (Agnicit) eats as he desires every hundred years. Now, this [immortality] is as much as a hundred years—indeed, it is immortal, infinite, and boundless. For him who knows this thus, this becomes truly immortal, infinite, and boundless; even if one were to strike him with a mere blade of grass, even that [act] of his becomes immortal, infinite, and boundless.

Prajāpati desired to go to the heavenly world. Prajāpati is indeed all animals—the man, the horse, the ox, the sheep, and the goat. He was not able [to fly] with these forms; he saw this self of his in the form of a bird, namely Agni. He composed him; having first gathered together [his wings] and then laid them on, he sought to fly up, but he was not able. Having gathered them together and laid them on, he flew up. Therefore even now, when birds gather their wings together and spread out their feathers, then they are able to fly up.

Or he measures it with his fingers; for man is indeed the sacrifice, and by him all this has been measured. His lowest measure is these fingers; thus he obtains that which is his lowest measure, and by means of that he measures him.

He measures it with twenty-four finger-breadths; for the Gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables, and Agni is of the nature of the Gāyatrī. As great as Agni is, as great as is his measure, by just so much does he measure him.

He scrapes four finger-breadths from both inner sides and removes four finger-breadths from both outer sides; as much as he scrapes, so much he removes. Thus he neither exceeds nor makes it deficient. It is the same for the tail and the same for the northern wing.

Then he makes the two joints of the wings; for there are two joints in the wings of a bird. At one-third [from the front], for at one-third from the front there are the two joints in the wings of a bird. In the middle third, for in the middle third there are the two joints in the wings of a bird. He raises it by four finger-breadths in front, and he draws it in by four finger-breadths behind. As much as he raises it, so much he draws it in; thus he neither exceeds nor makes it deficient.
At that junction, he lays down a single brick; thus he provides that single channel which lies alongside the junction of a bird's wings when it flies, and this [channel] here as well.

Then he makes the two wings curved, for the wings of a bird are indeed curved; he extends them four finger-breadths at the back and contracts them four finger-breadths at the front. As much as he extends them, so much does he contract them; thus he neither makes them excessive nor does he make them too small.

Then he makes it the highest form; for here this entire Agni has been consecrated, and into him the gods placed that highest form. In the same way, this sacrificer now places that highest form into him. He makes a thousand bricks marked with straight lines—those marked with a thousand [lines], and those marked with a thousand [lines].

Then, having laid down the fifth layer, he measures out the fire-altar in three parts; in the middle third, he lays down a thousand bricks marked with straight lines. This he does to provide those straight feathers of the bird which extend backward from the head to the tail.
Then he places the one marked "thousand" on the right; thereby he provides those curved feathers which are on the right side of this bird.

Then he places those drawn as "a thousand" on the north side; he thereby provides those curved feathers which are on the northern side of the bird. A thousand is everything, for the thousand is all; with everything he thus bestows this supreme form upon it. With three thousands—Agni is threefold; as great as Agni is, as great as his measure is—with just that much he bestows this supreme form upon him.

Those seven persons whom they made into one person became Prajāpati; he created offspring. Having created offspring, he rose upwards and went to that world where this sun now shines. At that time, there was no other worthy of sacrifice besides him. Therefore, the gods resolved to worship him by means of the sacrifice itself.

Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice. For by means of sacrifice the gods did indeed sacrifice to that sacrifice; "those were the first laws (dharmas)"—for those laws were indeed performed for the first time; "they, the majestic ones, attained the firmament (nāka)"—the firmament is indeed the heavenly world, and the gods are the majestic ones; thus, it means those gods who sacrificed to that sacrifice attained the heavenly world.

"In which the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide"—the Sādhyas, indeed, are the vital breaths; they first accomplished this very thing in this manner, desiring to become this [universe]; and even now they accomplish it. "Thereafter this other became worthy of sacrifice, the abundance of the immortal world"—thereafter, indeed, this other became worthy of sacrifice, whatever is immortal.
"The fair-winged, soaring one of Savitṛ was born first; he indeed follows his law. Prajāpati is the fair-winged, soaring one, and this Savitṛ is he; thus it means "Prajāpati follows his law."
He indeed becomes a sevenfold person, for this person is sevenfold: four are his self and three are the wings and tail; for of that person, four are the self and three are the wings and tail.

He measures it with a man with upstretched arms; for the sacrifice is indeed a man, and by him all this has been measured. This [measure] of his is the highest measure, namely when he has his arms upstretched; thus he obtains that which is his highest measure, and by means of that he measures it out. As for the fact that he is sprinkled with water at the tip of his foot, that he obtains by means of the *pariśrit* bricks. Therefore, one should dig outside the line for the sake of the *pariśrit* bricks.

Then he places two cubits (aratni) on the two wings; he thus bestows strength upon the wings. The wings are indeed the arms, and by means of the arms food is eaten; he thus makes room for food. As to why he places two cubits on the wings: it is because food is eaten from a distance of one cubit.

Then he places a span (vitasti) on the shoulder (puccha). He thereby bestows vigor upon the foundation; for the shoulder is indeed the foundation, and the span is the hand. By means of the hand, food is eaten; thus he provides that space for the sake of food. In that he places a span on the shoulder, he establishes him in food. And in that he places it there at a smaller distance, he thereby establishes him even closer to food. Moreover, this [space] is measured out as just this much; this is just this much. Thus, when he measures in this way, it is for the attainment of that very thing.

Or rather, this altar is the measure of the sevenfold altar. Having settled upon the place of sacrifice for the gods, having entered the hall of the wives by the eastern door, and having dug up the ground for the Gārhapatya fire, he sprinkles it with water. From the dug-up spot of the Gārhapatya, he strides seven steps eastward; from there, he measures out a fathom (vyāma) toward the east. In the middle of that, having dug up the ground for the Āhavanīya fire, he sprinkles it with water. From the eastern half of the fathom, he strides three steps eastward; that is the end of the altar (vedyanta).

These eleven steps, measured by a fathom’s span between the edge of the altar and the Gārhapatya fire, consist of the Triṣṭubh metre—of which there are eleven syllables; the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer repels the Rakṣases and the destructive spirits from the front of the sacrifice.

This is the womb of the altar; from this very womb the gods generated the altar. Now, that fathom which exists is the womb of the Gārhapatya fire; from this very womb the gods generated the Gārhapatya, and from the Gārhapatya, the Āhavanīya.

From the edge of the altar site, he measures out an altar thirty-six steps long toward the east, thirty steps across at the back, and twenty-four steps across at the front; that makes ninety. This is the ninety-step altar, and upon it he arranges the sevenfold fire-altar.

Regarding this they say: "How does this sevenfold [altar] correspond to this sacrificial altar? There are ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, four limbs, and the self (*ātman*) as the fifteenth. Thus for the second [altar], thus for the third; in six persons there are ninety. Then one person remains over. For a person is fivefold: hair, skin, flesh, bone, and marrow; the altar here is fivefold: the four quarters and the self as the fifth. In this way, this sevenfold [altar] corresponds to this sacrificial altar.

Now, some, intending to construct the northern altar, increase these steps and this fathom-measure, saying, "We are increasing the womb. One should not do so; for the womb does not increase along with the fetus once it is born. Only as long as the fetus remains within the womb does the womb grow; indeed, the growth of the fetus here is only to that extent.

Those who act in that way indeed cause this Father Prajāpati to fall from his perfection; having sacrificed thus, they become worse off, for they cause Father Prajāpati to fall from his perfection. As large as this altar of the sevenfold [sacrifice] is, so large he measures out the altar of the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice] fourteen times.
Then he measures a cord thirty-six paces long; he folds it into seven parts. Of this, he lays down three parts facing east and leaves out four.
Then he measures it at thirty steps; he folds it into seven parts; of these, he lays down three parts at the back and leaves out four.
Then he measures it at twenty-four steps; he contracts it into seven parts and lays down three of its parts in front, leaving four behind—this is the measurement of the altar.

Now, there are twenty-eight kinds of fires; twenty-eight men facing forward and twenty-eight lying crosswise—this is the body. Fourteen men are the right wing, fourteen the left, and fourteen the tail. One lays down fourteen cubits (*aratni*) on the right wing, fourteen on the left, and fourteen spans (*vitasti*) on the tail. Such is the measure of ninety-eight men, including the additional ones.
Then he measures out a cord of three puruṣas; he folds it into seven parts. Of this, he places four parts upon himself and three on the wings and tail.
Then he measures out a piece of ground one aratni long; he divides it into seven parts. Of this, he lays down three parts on the right wing, three likewise on the left, and leaves four remaining.

Then he measures out a span; he folds that into seven parts and lays down three of its parts at the tail, leaving four aside. In this way, this [altar] of one hundred and onefold measure is completed by means of this altar-ground.

Regarding this they say: "Since thirteen persons pass by, how is it that these do not fall away from their perfection? That which is the perfection of this seventh person is indeed the perfection of all of them.
Moreover, they say: Prajāpati himself, having fashioned his own self, filled whatever was deficient in it with these [sacrificial elements]; thus, indeed, it became complete.
Now, some indeed construct the first altar as having one kind of brick, and then each subsequent one with one more, up to an unlimited number of kinds; but one should not do so.

Or rather, in the beginning, Prajāpati was created sevenfold. Seeking to establish himself, he proceeded; he stood firm at the one-hundred-and-first-fold [sacrifice]. He who establishes a sacrifice less than the sevenfold cuts asunder this father Prajāpati; having sacrificed, he becomes worse off, for it is as if he has harmed one who is superior. But he who establishes more than the one-hundred-and-first-fold falls outside of this whole [universe], for Prajāpati is indeed this whole universe. Therefore, let him first establish the sevenfold, and then the ones increasing by one up to the one-hundred-and-first-fold; but let him not establish more than the one-hundred-and-first-fold. For thus he does not cut asunder this father Prajāpati, nor does he fall outside of this whole universe.

The year is indeed Prajāpati; Agni is all desires. This Prajāpati, the year, desired: "May I build up Agni, all desires, within myself. He divided himself into one hundred and one parts. Having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, he built up Agni, all desires, within himself. He became all desires; therefore, no desire remained outside him. Hence they say, "The year is all desires," for there is no desire whatsoever that exists outside the year.

In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, piles Agni—the entirety of all desires—into his own self; he becomes all desires, and therefore no desire remains outside of him.

That which is the year is yonder sun; he is this one who is of a hundred and onefold form. His rays are the hundred forms, and he who shines yonder is the one hundred and first; he is established upon all this. In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into a hundred and one parts, becomes established upon all this.

Or rather, that which is of one hundred and one kinds becomes sevenfold; for yonder sun is distributed in a hundred and one ways and established in the seven worlds of the gods. There are indeed seven worlds of the gods: the four quarters and these three worlds—these are the seven worlds of the gods, and in them he is established. In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into a hundred and one parts, becomes established in the seven worlds of the gods.

Or rather, as to why that which is of one hundred and one kinds attains to the sevenfold: for yonder sun is distributed in a hundred and one ways—he is established in the seven seasons, in the seven stomas, in the seven pṛṣṭhas, in the seven metres, in the seven vital breaths, and in the seven quarters; and in like manner the sacrificer, having divided himself into a hundred and one parts, becomes firmly established in all this.

Furthermore, as to why that which is of one hundred and one kinds becomes the sevenfold: yonder sun is indeed distributed in one hundred and one ways and is established upon the seven-syllabled Brahman. For Brahman consists of seven syllables: "Ṛk" is one syllable, "Yajuḥ" is two syllables, and "Sāma" is two syllables; and whatever else there is beyond that is Brahman itself. Brahman indeed consists of two syllables; thus all this is the seven-syllabled Brahman, and upon it he is established. In the same way, the sacrificer, having divided himself into one hundred and one parts, becomes established upon the seven-syllabled Brahman.
Therefore, they enclose it with seven by seven; thus, that which consists of one hundred and one parts becomes sevenfold, or rather, that which is sevenfold becomes one hundred and onefold.

Or rather, in the beginning, Prajāpati was created sevenfold; he beheld this self of his as divided into one hundred and one parts: fifty bricks among the breath-bearers and fifty sacrificial formulas—that makes one hundred; the settling and the *sūdadohas* verse make the one hundred and first. Having settled that which is common [to all], he consecrates it with the *sūdadohas*. By means of this self of one hundred and one parts, he won this victory and attained this distinction. In the same way, the sacrificer, by means of this self of one hundred and one parts, wins this victory and attains this distinction. Thus, the sevenfold becomes the one hundred and one-fold; that which is the one hundred and one-fold is the sevenfold, and that which is the sevenfold is the one hundred and one-fold. Such is the arrangement.

Now, therefore, regarding the piling itself: he piles [the altar] between the two Upasad days. For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakshas, the destroyers, should slay this [sacrifice] of ours here. They saw these fortresses—the Upasads; these worlds indeed are the fortresses. They entered them; having entered them, they prepared this body for themselves in a place free from danger and destruction. In the same way, the sacrificer, having entered these fortresses, prepares this body for himself in a place free from danger and destruction.

Furthermore, as to why he piles the two Upasads in between: the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should smite this [body] of ours here. They saw these thunderbolts—the Upasads are indeed thunderbolts—and they entered into them. Having entered them, they prepared this body of theirs in a place free from danger and destruction. In the very same way, the sacrificer now enters into these thunderbolts and prepares this body of his in a place free from danger and destruction.

This indeed is the austerity in the sacrifice that consists of the Upasads; for the Upasads are austerity. Because it is piled while in a state of austerity, it is therefore called the Tāpaścita (the Pile of Austerity). Now, as long as they perform the Upasads, so long do they perform the Pravargya. They perform the Upasads for a year, and the Pravargya for a year.
The Upasads are indeed the days and nights, and the Pravargya is the sun; he thus establishes yonder sun upon the days and nights, and therefore it is established upon the days and nights.

Now, if there are twenty-four [days], or if there are twenty-four half-months—the half-months being the *upasads* and the sun being the *pravargya*—he thereby establishes that sun upon the half-months; therefore, he is established upon the half-months.

Now, if there are twelve [days], for the months are twelve and the Upasads are the months while the Pravargya is the sun; he thus establishes that sun in the months, and therefore it is established in the months.
Now, if there are six or six Upasad days—the seasons being six and the Pravargya being the sun—he thereby establishes that sun in the seasons; therefore, this sun is established in the seasons.

Now, if there are three [Upasad days], these worlds are three; these worlds are the Upasads, and the Pravargya is Āditya. He thus establishes that Āditya in these worlds; therefore, he is established in these worlds.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of the layers (citi) and the fillings (purīṣa): one month is the first layer, one month is the filling; such is the desire in the spring season. Whatever desire there is in the spring season, all that he builds up for himself.
The second month is feces; such is the desire in the summer season. Whatever desire there is in the summer season, all that he collects for himself.

For one month [he eats] the third [part], for one month excrement; such is the desire during the rainy season. Whatever desire there is during the rainy season, all that he accumulates within himself.

For one month he eats only on the fourth meal-time, for one month he eats only excrement; such is the desire in the season. Whatever desire there is in the season, all that he accumulates within himself.

Then, on the fifth layer, he first lays down the *asapatnā* and *virāj* bricks on each successive day; the *stomabhāgā* bricks he lays down one by one every day and settles them all at once. He pronounces the *sūdadohas* formula over them once. For a month they carry the loose earth for the *stomabhāgā* bricks. Such is the desire fulfilled in the winter season. Whatever desire there is in the winter season, all that he thereby builds up within his own self.

For one month he eats the sixth meal, and for one month he eats only coarse food; such is the desire in the season of Āśvina. Whatever desire there is in the season of Āśvina, all that he collects for himself. Such indeed is the desire in twelve months and six seasons. Whatever desire there is in twelve months and six seasons, all that he collects for himself.

Now, three days pass by: the day on which he offers the Śatarudriya, the day of the Upavasatha, and the day of the Soma-pressing. In that they perform the Upasad rites during those days, these constitute the days and nights of that month. And as for the Pravargya rite, thereby he establishes Āditya in that season. Such indeed is the desire within thirteen months and seven seasons; thus, whatever desire there is in thirteen months and seven seasons, all that he builds up for himself.

He should press [the Soma] for a year; the year is indeed everything, and the one hundred and one-fold sacrifice is everything; thus, by means of everything, he obtains everything. If he is unable to do so for a year, he should sacrifice with the Viśvajit Atirātra, which has all the Pṛṣṭha-stotras; in that sacrifice, he should give away all his possessions (sarvavedasa). The Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas is indeed everything, and all his possessions are everything; the one hundred and one-fold sacrifice is everything; thus, by means of everything, he obtains everything.

Prajāpati is indeed the year, consisting of one hundred and one forms. His forms are the days and nights, the half-months, the months, and the seasons. There are sixty days and nights in a month; indeed, the days and nights of the year are completed within a month. There are twenty-four half-months, thirteen months, and three seasons; these constitute the hundred forms, and the year itself is the one hundred and first form.

It is sevenfold by means of the seasons: the six seasons and the year itself as the seventh division. Of this very year, that which shines yonder is the splendor; its rays are a hundred divisions, and the disk itself is the one hundred and first division.

It is sevenfold by way of the directions alone: those rays which are in the eastern direction constitute one variety; those in the southern, another; those in the western, another; those in the northern, another; those in the upward direction, another; those in the downward direction, another; and the orb itself is the seventh variety.
Before this [fire] is the world of Kāmapra; Kāmapra is indeed immortality, and that immortality is behind it. That which is that immortality is this very radiance which shines here.

This is indeed a manifold and wonderful gift; Savitṛ distributes it among these creatures—among the waters and among the plants and trees. Yet he gives more to some and less to others. Those to whom he gives more live longer; those to whom he gives less [live] shorter.

This very thing is expressed by the Ṛgvedic verse: "We invoke Savitṛ, the distributor of wonderful wealth and bounty, who beholds men. This is indeed all life; for that [life] is long and infinite. Thus, when they say, "May your life be long! May you live the full span of life here!", it means: "This world is yours; let this be yours. This is what it signifies.

The Speech that perceives speaks thus: "This very [immortality] is to be attained either by means of the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice], or by a hundred-year life; for he who ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold [sacrifice], or he who lives a hundred years—he indeed attains this immortality. Therefore, both those who know this and those who do not say, 'A hundred-year life is the way to the world. Consequently, one should not depart before the end of one's natural lifespan, for these worlds are indeed without light: namely, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and the year."

Now, those who die before twenty years have passed are joined with the worlds of days and nights; then those who die after twenty but before forty are joined with the half-months; then those who die after forty but before sixty are joined with the months; then those who die after sixty but before eighty are joined with the seasons; then those who die after eighty but before a hundred are joined with the year; and he who lives for exactly a hundred years, or even longer, indeed attains this immortality.

"By many sacrifices, indeed, one day and one night are measured. He who ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold [altar], or he who lives for a hundred years—he alone truly attains this most perfectly. Verily, he ordains the one-hundred-and-one-fold who maintains this [fire-altar] for a year; therefore, let him pile it only after it has been maintained for a year. Thus with reference to the deities.

Now, regarding the sacrifice: he measures out one hundred and one men with uplifted arms; that [altar] is of one hundred and one parts. It is of seven parts by means of the layers (*citi*); six layers contain the seasonal bricks (*ṛtavyā*), and Agni himself is the seventh part.

That [altar] indeed consists of one hundred and one forms: those fifty bricks which are the first and those which are the last make up one hundred forms; and those bricks which are laid down between them constitute the one hundred and first form.

That very same [sacrifice] is the splendor of the Yajus; the Yajus is one hundred and one-fold. Those which are the first fifty Yajus formulas and those which are the last ones constitute the hundred parts; and those Yajus formulas which are performed between them constitute the one hundred and first part. Thus, the sevenfold becomes the one hundred and one-fold. Whatever desire there is in the hundred-thousand-fold [sacrifice], that same [desire] exists in the one hundred and one-fold. By means of the sevenfold, one who knows this attains it.

In this very way, all sacrifices are of one hundred and one forms—consisting of the Āgnihotra, the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, words, syllables, ritual acts, and Sāman-chants. Whatever desire exists in the sacrifice of ten thousand years, whatever in the one hundred and one-fold, and whatever in the seven-fold, he who knows thus obtains that very thing through each and every sacrifice. Thus far with respect to the sacrifice.

Now, with reference to the self: these five fingers are fourfold each, as are the two wrists, the shoulder-blade, and the axle; that makes twenty-five. In this same way, these other limbs [are also fourfold]; they constitute one hundred parts, and the self itself is the one hundred and first part—thus it is said for the sake of establishing the sevenfold nature.

That very breath-energy (*prāṇatejas*), which is of one hundred and one forms, exists in every limb; for the breath is indeed in every single limb. Whatever desire there is in the hundred-thousandfold [sacrifice], whatever in the hundred-and-one-fold, whatever in the seven-fold, and whatever in all sacrifices—that very [desire] one who knows thus obtains through knowledge alone, for he knows himself as endowed with all sacrifices.

These three are fivefold: the year, Agni, and the person. Their fivefold forms are food, drink, prosperity, light, and immortality. That which is food in the year is [his] food; the waters are his drink; the night is indeed prosperity—for all beings dwell together in prosperity during the night; the day is the light; and the sun is immortality. This is with respect to the deities.

Now, with regard to the sacrifice: that food which is placed upon the fire is the food; the waters are the drink. The enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) are prosperity (*śrī*), for that is the form of the nights. The bricks with formulas (*yajuṣmatī*) are light (*jyotis*), for that is the form of the days. Agni is *ṛtam*, for that is the form of the sun. Thus indeed is it with regard to the sacrifice.

Now, with reference to the self: that which is food in man is indeed food; the waters are drink; the bones are beauty, for that is the form of the enclosing bricks; the marrow is light, for that is the form of the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; the vital breath is immortality, for that is the form of the fire-altar. "The vital breath is Agni; the vital breath is immortality," so they say.

From food, hunger is turned away; from drink, thirst; from prosperity, evil; from light, darkness; from the immortal, death. Indeed, all these turn away from him who knows this. He conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. Regarding this, one should worship it in the other world as "the immortal," and here on earth as "life. Some, however, worship it as "breath" (prāṇa), saying, "Breath is fire; breath is the immortal. One should not know it thus. For that which is breath is unstable. Indeed, it is also stated in a Yajus formula: "I loosen you from the midst of life. Therefore, one should worship it in the other world as "the immortal," and here on earth as "life. Thus, he attains a full lifespan.

The out-breath is the Gāyatrī, the eye is the Uṣṇih, speech is the Anuṣṭubh, the mind is the Bṛhatī, the ear is the Paṅkti; that which is this generative breath is the Triṣṭubh, and that which is this downward breath is the Jagatī. These, indeed, are the seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, which are performed upon the fire.

"The breath is the Gāyatrī. Now, whatever is the greatness and the power of the breath—that is this thousandfold [altar]. This power belongs to the breath alone; for if the breath were to depart from him while he is building it, then this fire-altar would not be built at all. By means of this very form of his, this [altar] becomes a thousand Gāyatrīs when it is completed.

"The eye is the Uṣṇih"—this refers to whatever greatness and whatever power belongs to the eye; this thousandfold [set] is indeed the power of the eye. For if the eye of him who is building were to depart, then this Agni would not be built up. By means of this very form of his, this [Agni] becomes built up as a thousand Uṣṇihs.

"Speech is the Anuṣṭubh"—this refers to whatever greatness and whatever power belongs to speech; this thousandfold [pile] is indeed the power of speech. For if speech were to depart from him while he is building, then this Agni would not be built up. By means of this very form of his, this [Agni] becomes built up as a thousand Anuṣṭubhs.

"The mind is the Bṛhatī"—this refers to that which is the greatness and the power of the mind; this thousandfold [altar] is indeed the power of the mind. For if the mind of one who is piling it were to depart, then this fire-altar would not be piled. By this very form of his, this [altar] becomes a thousand Bṛhatīs when completely piled.

The ear is the *paṅkti* (pentad). Whatever is the greatness, whatever is the power of the ear—that is this thousandfold [altar]. This power belongs to the ear alone; for if the ear were to depart from him while he is piling [the altar], then this fire-altar would not be piled. By means of this very form of his, this [altar] becomes piled as a thousand *paṅktis*.

"This very procreative breath is the Triṣṭubh. Thus, whatever greatness and whatever vigor belongs to this breath, that is this thousandfold; for it is the vigor of this very breath that, if it were to fail while he is building, then this fire-altar would not be built. By means of this very form of his, this [altar] becomes a thousandfold when built as a Triṣṭubh.

Now, as for this downward breath, it is the Jagatī. Whatever greatness and whatever vigor belongs to this breath, that is this thousandfold [altar]. For this is the vigor of this very breath: if this breath were to depart from him while he is building, then this Agni would not be built up. By means of this very form of his, this Jagatī becomes built up a thousandfold.

These seven meters, each increasing by four syllables, are established one upon another; likewise, these seven vital breaths in a person are established one upon another. Therefore, however much of the collection of meters a man who knows this recites—whether it be chanted, recited, praised, or placed as an oblation—it is indeed for him as if that very meter has been recited.
Regarding this they ask: "What is the metre, what is the deity of the head of Agni? The Gāyatrī is the metre, Agni is the deity; [this is] the head.
What is the meter? What is the deity? The necks: the uṣṇih is the meter, Savitṛ is the deity, the necks.
What is the metre? What is the deity of the *anūka*? The *bṛhatī* is the metre; Bṛhaspati is the deity of the *anūka*.
"What is the meter? What is the deity of the two wings? "The Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans] are the meter; Heaven and Earth are the deities of the two wings."
What is the meter? What is the deity of the middle? The Triṣṭubh is the meter; Indra is the deity of the middle.
What is the meter? What is the deity? "The hips" (śroṇī): the Jagatī is the meter, and Āditya is the deity of the hips.
What is the meter? What is the deity? Since from this vital breath semen is emitted, the meter is Atichandas and Prajāpati is the deity.
"What is the meter, and what is the deity, of this downward breath? "The *yajñāyajñīya* is the meter, and Vaiśvānara is the deity."

What is the meter? What is the deity? The meter is Paṅkti; the deity is the Maruts; [they are] the two ankle-bones.
"What is the meter? What is the deity of the two-footed [verse]? "The meter is Dvipadā; Viṣṇu is the deity of the two-footed [verse]."
What is the metre? What is the deity? The vital breaths (prāṇa). The metre is the vicchandā; the deity is Vāyu; the vital breaths are [the deities].

"What is the meter? What deity is there that is not redundant? "The meter has fewer syllables; water is the deity that is not redundant. This very knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā) consists of these [elements]; indeed, one becomes composed of these deities and this Self. For in this state, there is no other prayer for worldly prosperity.

The wise Śātaparṇeya approached Mahāśāla Jābāla. He said to him, "Knowing what have you come to me? "I know Agni," he replied. "Which Agni do you know? "Speech. "What does one become who knows that Agni? "He becomes eloquent," he said, "and speech does not desert him."

"Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what, have you come to me as a student? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The eye. "What becomes of him who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of sight," he replied; "the eye does not desert him."

"Do you know Agni? he said. "Knowing what have you come to me as a student? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The mind (manas). "What becomes of him who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of a mind," he said; "the mind does not desert him."

"Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what have you come to me as a student? "I know Agni. "Which Agni do you know? "The ear. "What becomes of him who knows that Agni? "He becomes possessed of hearing," he replied; "the ear does not desert him."

"Do you know Agni? he asked. "Knowing what have you come to me as a pupil? "I know Agni," he replied. "Which Agni do you know? "I know him who is all this; that is Agni. When this was said, [the teacher] descended from his seat and said, "Teach me that Agni, sir!"

He said: "That fire is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). When a person sleeps, then speech merges into the vital breath, the eye into the vital breath, the mind into the vital breath, and the ear into the vital breath. When he awakens, they are born again from the vital breath alone. This is with reference to the self (adhyātma)."

Now, with respect to the deities: that which is speech is indeed Agni; that which is sight is yonder sun; that which is mind is this moon; that which is hearing is the quarters; and that which is breath is this very wind that blows here.

When fire goes out, it blows along with the wind; therefore they say of it, "It has blown away," for it indeed blows along with the wind. When the sun sets, it enters the wind; so does the moon. In the wind the quarters are established; from the wind alone they are born again. When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters fire by his speech, the sun by his sight, the moon by his mind, the quarters by his hearing, and the wind by his breath. Having become composed of these very elements, he moves about having become whichever of these deities he desires.

Śvetaketu Āruṇeya was about to perform a sacrifice; his father said to him, "Which officiating priests have you chosen? He replied, "This Vaiśvāvasavya here shall be my Hotṛ. His father asked him, "Do you know, O Brāhmaṇa Vaiśvāvasavya—"

"Are there four great things? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four great things among the great? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four vows? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four vows among the vows? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *kyās*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *kyās* among the *kyās*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *arkas*? "I know them, sir," he replied. "Do you know the four *arkas* among the *arkas*? "I know them, sir," he replied.

"Do you know the *arka*?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arka* leaves?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arka* flowers?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arka* pods?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the two *arka* boxes?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the *arka* seeds?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the *arka* stone?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir. "Do you know the root of the *arka*?"—"Now, surely you will tell us, sir."

Now, as for what he said: "You know the four great ones; you know the four great among the great. Fire is great; of that great one, the great are the plants and the trees, for they are its food. Wind is great; of that great one, the great are the waters, for they are its food. The sun is great; of that great one, the great is the moon, for it is its food. Man is great; of that great one, the great are the domestic animals, for they are his food. These indeed are the four great ones; these are the four great among the great. These indeed are the four vows; these are the four vows among vows. These indeed are the four *kyās*; these are the four *kyās* among *kyās*. These indeed are the four *arkas*; these are the four *arkas* among *arkas*.

Now, as for what he said—"Do you know the Arka?"—he spoke indeed of the person (puruṣa). "Do you know the two Arka-leaves?"—he spoke indeed of the two ears. "Do you know the two Arka-flowers?"—he spoke indeed of the two eyes. "Do you know the two Arka-sheaths?"—he spoke indeed of the two nostrils. "Do you know the two Arka-caskets?"—he spoke indeed of the two lips. "Do you know the Arka-pods?"—he spoke indeed of the teeth. "Do you know the Arka-stone?"—he spoke indeed of the tongue. "Do you know the root of the Arka?"—he spoke indeed of food. This very person is the Arka-fire; he who meditates upon this person as the Arka-fire, thinking, "I am this Arka-fire," by that knowledge indeed has the Arka-fire built within his own self.
This very one who blows here is indeed the Yajus; for as he moves along, he generates all this, and following him as he moves, this world is born. Therefore, Vāyu alone is the Yajus.

This very space is *jūḥ*—namely, this intermediate region—for it is along this space that one hastens (*javate*). This *yajus* is both the wind and the intermediate region, because it is both *jūḥ* and *yajus*; therefore, this very [wind] is the *yajus*, for it goes (*eti*). This *yajus* is established upon the *ṛc* and the *sāman*; the *ṛc* and *sāman* carry it, and therefore the Adhvaryu performs his work with the same cups, while the *stotras* and *śastras* are different from one another. It is just as if, after making two horses gallop forward, one were to make two others run alongside them; such is that.

Agni indeed is the *puras* (the one in front), for these creatures worship having placed Agni in front. Āditya indeed is the *caraṇa* (the following); for when he rises, then all this moves. This is that *yajus* together with its *puraścaraṇa* with respect to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self: breath indeed is the Yajus, for breath, as it moves, generates all this; following breath as it moves, this world is born. Therefore, breath alone is the Yajus.

This very space is the *jūḥ*—this space that is within the self—for it is after this space that one hastens (*javate*). That is the *yajus*, both the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the space; and because it is both the *jūḥ* and the *yajus*, therefore it is the *yajus*. It is indeed the vital breath, for the vital breath goes forth (*eti*).

Food indeed is the Yajus, for by food one is born and by food one moves; this Yajus is established in food, and it carries food. Therefore, within the very same vital breath (prāṇa), various kinds of food are placed.

The mind alone is the *puras* (fortress), for the mind is indeed the first of the vital breaths; the eye is the *caraṇa* (footing), for by means of the eye this self moves. Thus, this *yajus* is established both with respect to the deities and with respect to the self, together with its *puraścaraṇa*. He who knows this *yajus* as being thus established both with respect to the deities and with respect to the self [attains the goal].
He who knows this becomes uninjured and unafflicted; he reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice in safety; he becomes the best among his own people, a leader, an eater of food, and a sovereign.

And whoever among his own people seeks to be a rival to one who knows this, he is not at all able to support his dependents; but he who follows him, or who indeed desires to support his dependents by following him—he alone is able to support his dependents.
This is the eldest Brahman, for there is nothing whatsoever superior to it; indeed, he who knows this becomes the eldest and the most excellent among his own people.

This very Brahman is without before and without after. He who knows this Brahman as being without before and without after—among his peers, no one whatsoever becomes superior to him; rather, those who are superior to him become even more superior. Therefore, he for whom someone might be superior should meditate upon the quarters as being prior to him; thus, indeed, [the quarters] do not harm him.

The secret doctrine (upaniṣad) of this very Yajus is its essence; therefore, by whatever measure of the Yajus the Adhvaryu draws the cup, it pervades both the Stotra and the Śastra, and it extends over both the Stotra and the Śastra. Just as the essence of food, by its very measure, sustains all food and extends over all food, so does it.

Satisfaction alone is his goal; therefore, when he is satisfied with food, he feels as if he has reached his destination. Bliss alone is his consciousness, and bliss is his self; indeed, all the gods have bliss as their self. This is the direct knowledge of the gods. He who knows this is no longer a mere human; he is truly one of the gods.

Knowing this, Priyavrata Rauhiṇāyana used to say of the wind as it blew, "Bliss is your self; whether you blow from here or from there. And so it would blow accordingly. Therefore, whatever blessing one desires among the gods, one should approach [the wind] with this very prayer: "Bliss is your self; may this desire of mine be fulfilled; may it be accomplished for me. Whatever desire he has, that desire is indeed accomplished for him. He who knows this attains this satisfaction, this goal, this bliss, and this Self.

This very *yajus* is whispered and undefined; for the *yajus* is breath, and breath has its abode in what is whispered. Therefore, if someone were to say to one who is reciting it clearly, "He has pronounced a deity that is not defined; breath shall depart from him," it would indeed happen so.

He who knows its expressed manifestation becomes manifest through fame and glory. With a low-voiced formula (*upāṃśu-yajus*), the Adhvaryu draws the cup; once drawn, it becomes manifest. With a low-voiced formula, he piles the fire-altar; once piled and fully built, it becomes manifest. With a low-voiced formula, he pours out the oblation; once cooked and prepared, it becomes manifest. Whatever he does with a low-voiced formula, once done and prepared, it becomes manifest. He who thus knows this expressed manifestation becomes manifest through fame, glory, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). Very quickly indeed he attains this knowledge; he truly becomes the Yajus itself, and they call him by the name "Yajus."

When the gods restored Prajāpati who had fallen apart, they poured him, who had become seed, into the fire-pan as a womb—for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. In that year, they prepared food for him; this very Agni who is now built up is that [food]. They enclosed it with their own self (ātman); being thus enclosed by the self, it became the self itself. Therefore, food enclosed by the self becomes the self itself.

In the same way, the sacrificer pours himself as seed into the fire-pan (ukhā) as a womb; for the fire-pan is indeed a womb. For him, he prepares this food during the year, which is this Agni who has been piled up. He encloses it within his own self; what is enclosed within his own self becomes his very self. Therefore, food that is enclosed within one's own self becomes one's very self.

He places it down with "vauṣaṭ," for "vau" is this [fire-altar] and "ṣaṭ" is these six layers; having thus made food consisting of six layers, he places it upon him as a covering. Food that is commensurate with one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more than that harms, and that which is less than that does not protect.

This very one is the *arka* (the hymn of praise), which they bring here as this fire; its food is the *kyam*, which is this piled fire—that is the *arkya* from the perspective of the Yajus. This very one is the *mahan* (the great); its food is the *vratam* (the vow)—that is the *mahāvrata* from the perspective of the Sāman. This very one is the *uktha*; its food is the *tham*—that is the *uktha* from the perspective of the Ṛc. Thus, though being one, it is designated in three ways.

Now, Indra and Agni were created—the priesthood and the nobility; Agni was the priesthood and Indra was the nobility. Once created, they remained separate. They said, "In this state, we shall not be able to produce offspring; let us both become one form. Thus, they both became one form.

Those two who are Indra and Agni, they are these two: the gold plate and the man. The gold plate is indeed Indra; the man is Agni. They are made of gold, for gold is light and Indra and Agni are light.
Gold is immortality, and Indra and Agni are immortality.

It is indeed Indra and Agni whom they build up; for whatever consists of bricks is Agni, and therefore they bake that with fire, because whatever is baked by fire is Agni. But what is the loose soil (purīṣa) is Indra; therefore they do not bake that with fire, lest it should be Agni alone and not Indra. Therefore, these two, Indra and Agni, are built up together.

Now, that fire which is deposited upon the altar is one form; both [the fire and the altar] become that. Therefore, by means of this very form, those two procreate these creatures. This is indeed a single brick, for the entire fire becomes that. That is the perfection of the brick. This is the single syllable "vaug"; the entire fire becomes that. That is the perfection of the syllable.

Seeing this, the seer proclaimed: "I praise what has been and what is to be—the Great Brahman, the one imperishable; the manifold Brahman, the one imperishable. For indeed, into this very syllable all the gods and all beings enter. This is both the priesthood (*brahman*) and the nobility (*kṣatra*): Agni is the priesthood, Indra is the nobility. Indra and Agni are the All-gods (*viśve devāḥ*); the All-gods are the common people (*viś*). Thus, this is the priesthood, the nobility, and the common people.

Indeed, Cyāparṇa Sāyakāyana, knowing this, said: "If indeed this ritual work of mine had been completed, my offspring alone would have become kings among the Salvas—my Brāhmaṇas, my Vaiśyas; but since this much of the ritual work was left incomplete, by that my progeny has surpassed them in both ways. This very [sacrifice] is prosperity, this is glory, this is the eater of food.
Indeed, having taught this to Vāmakakṣāyaṇa, Cāṇḍilya said: "You shall become prosperous, famous, and an eater of food. Verily, he who knows thus becomes prosperous, famous, and an eater of food.
This very Agni is Prajāpati himself; having prepared this Agni-Prajāpati, the gods then prepared for him this food within the year, which is this Mahāvratīya cup.

The Adhvaryu draws it with a cup; because he draws it, it is called a *graha*. Into it the Udgātṛ places essence by means of the Mahāvrata; for the Mahāvrata is all these Sāmans—thus, by means of all the Sāmans, he places essence in it. Into it the Hotṛ places essence by means of the Great Hymn (*mahad uktham*); for the Great Hymn is all these Ṛcs—thus, by means of all the Ṛcs, he places essence in it.

When they chant the stotra and when he recites the śastra, then, at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers this [oblation] into him. "Vauk" is indeed this [world], and "ṣaṭ" is this sixfold food; having made it so, he places it for him, proportionate to his own self. For that food which is proportionate to one's self protects and does not harm; that which is more harms, and that which is less does not protect.

This very one who has been built up as the fire-altar is indeed Arka; its food is the Ky, which is this Mahāvratīya cup—that is the Arkya from the perspective of the Yajus. This very one is Mahān (the Great); his food is the Vrata, which is the Mahāvrata [chant]—that is [the Arkya] from the perspective of the Sāman. And this very one is Uktha; his food is the Tha, which is the Uktha from the perspective of the Ṛc. Thus, being one, it is designated in three ways.

This very year is Agni Prajāpati. Of him, one half consists of the Sāvitra [bricks] and the other half of the Vaiśvakarman [bricks]. Eight indeed are his parts consisting of the Sāvitra bricks, and eight consist of the Vaiśvakarman bricks. Now, that rite which is performed between these two is Prajāpati himself, who is seventeenfold. That which is a part among humans is a syllable (*akṣara*) among the gods.

"Hair" consists of two syllables, "skin" of two, "blood" of two, "fat" of two, "flesh" of two, "sinew" of two, "bone" of two, and "marrow" of two; these are sixteen digits (*kalā*). Now, that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which moves within this interval is the seventeenth, Prajāpati himself.

Therefore, these sixteen digits bring food for this vital breath; when they are no longer able to bring it, he consumes them and departs. Therefore, for one who desires to eat, there is a sense of satisfaction, as he is being consumed by the vital breaths. Consequently, one who is afflicted becomes thin, for he has been consumed by the vital breaths.

Therefore, for this seventeenfold Prajāpati, they prepared this seventeenfold food, which is this Soma-sacrifice; and those sixteen parts of his are these sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij). Therefore, one should not appoint a seventeenth priest, lest one should make [the number] redundant. Now, whatever essence is here, whatever oblations are offered—that indeed is the seventeenfold food.

When they chant the praise and when he recites the after-shastra, then, at the utterance of "vaṣaṭ," he offers this [oblation] into him. "Vauk" is indeed this [world], and "ṣaṭ" is this sixfold food; having made it so, he places it for him, measured to his own self. For that food which is measured to one's own self protects and does not harm; that which is more harms, and that which is less does not protect.

This very one is the *arka* (the sun), which is this fire-altar (*agni*) that has been built; its food is the *kyam*, which is this Soma-sacrifice—that is the *arkya* with respect to the Yajus. This very one is the *mahān* (the great); its food is the *vratam*, which is the *Mahāvrata*—that is the *mahāvrata* with respect to the Sāman. This very one is the *ukta* (the spoken); its food is the *tham*, which is the *Uktha*—that is the *uktha* with respect to the Ṛc. Thus, being one, it is designated in three ways. With this food, he went upward together; he who went upward is that Āditya (the sun), and that by which he went upward with that food is this moon.

This very Arka is he who shines there; his food is the Kyi, which is this moon—this is the Arkya from the perspective of the Yajus. This very Mahān is he; his food is the Vrata, which is the Mahāvrata—this is [the Arkya] from the perspective of the Sāman. This very Uktha is he; his food is the Tha, which is the Uktha from the perspective of the Ṛc. Thus, being one, it is called threefold. This is with respect to the deities (adhidevatam).

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *arka*; its food is the *kya*, which is the *arkya* from the perspective of the *Yajus*. The breath itself is the *māha*; its food is the *vrata*, which is the *Mahāvrata* from the perspective of the *Sāman*. The breath itself is the *ukta*; its food is the *tha*, which is the *Uktha* from the perspective of the *Ṛc*. Thus, this one reality, being threefold, is so designated. This very same [reality] is that which pertains to the deities (*adhidevata*), and this is that which pertains to the self (*adhyātma*).
The year is indeed Prajāpati, Agni, King Soma, and the Moon. He himself declared his own nature to Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana: "As many lights as I have, so many bricks do I possess."

Of this very Saṃvatsara-Prajāpati, there are seven hundred and twenty days and nights as his lights; these are the *iṣṭakās*. There are three hundred and sixty *pariśrit* bricks, and three hundred and sixty *yajuṣmatī* bricks. This Saṃvatsara-Prajāpati created all beings—whatever is animate and whatever is inanimate, both gods and humans. Having created all beings, he felt as if he were emptied out; he was afraid of death.
He reflected: "How indeed might I cast all these beings back into myself, how might I place them back within myself; how indeed might I alone become the self of all these beings again?"
He divided himself into two parts; there were three hundred and sixty bricks for one part, and likewise for the other; yet he did not encompass it.
He made three selves; there were eighty-three bricks for each one, yet he did not reach [the goal].
He made himself fourfold; he did not encompass [the altar] with eight hundred bricks.
He made himself fivefold; there were one hundred and forty-four bricks for each [part], yet he did not reach [the goal].
He made himself sixfold, consisting of one hundred and twenty bricks; yet he did not pervade [the altar], nor did he become sevenfold.
He made eight for himself; he did not encompass the ninety bricks.
He made nine for himself; he did not encompass eighty bricks.
He made ten for himself and seventy-two bricks; he did not pervade [the body], nor did he become elevenfold.
He made himself twelvefold; he did not pervade the sixty bricks, nor did he divide into thirteen parts, nor into fourteen.
He made himself fifteenfold; he [then] laid forty-eight bricks, but he did not encompass them.
He made himself sixteenfold; he [then] consisted of forty-five bricks, yet he did not pervade them, nor did he become seventeenfold.
He made eighteen for himself; forty bricks remained, and he could neither complete [the altar] nor did it divide into twenty parts.
He made himself twentyfold; with thirty-six bricks he did not encompass them, nor did he become divided into twenty-one parts, nor twenty-two, nor twenty-three.

He made twenty-four for himself; he remained there with thirty bricks in the fifteenth arrangement. Because he remained in the fifteenth arrangement, therefore there are fifteen forms of the waxing moon and fifteen of the waning moon.

Now, because he made twenty-four of himself, therefore the year consists of twenty-four half-months. By means of these twenty-four self-forms consisting of thirty bricks each, he did not become distinct; he saw the forms of fifteen days as his own bodies, the *muhūrta*-bricks, which are space-filling (*lokampṛṇā*); and likewise fifteen of the night. Because they protect for a moment (*muhūrtam*), they are called *muhūrta*s; and because, though small, they fill these worlds, they are called *lokampṛṇā*s.

Verily, this [Agni] cooks all this—by means of days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and the year; and he cooks that which has been cooked by that [year]. "He is the cooker of the cooked," so said Bhāradvāja, for he cooks what has been cooked by that [year].
These amounted to ten thousand eight hundred in a year; he remained established therein for ten thousand and eight hundred [years].

Then he looked around at all beings; in the threefold knowledge alone he saw all beings, for here indeed is the self of all meters, of all hymns, of all vital breaths, and of all gods. This indeed exists, for that which is immortal exists; and that which is mortal is this very thing.
That Prajāpati reflected: "In the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā), indeed, all beings are contained; come now, let me fashion myself out of this very threefold knowledge."

He separated the Ṛg-verses into twelve thousand Bṛhatī verses; as many as these are the Ṛg-verses created by Prajāpati. They stood firm in the thirty-fold arrangement among the Paṅktis. Because they stood firm in the thirty-fold arrangement, therefore there are thirty nights in a month. And because they were in the Paṅktis, therefore Prajāpati is fivefold (pāṅkta). Those Paṅktis became eight hundred in number.

Then he separated the other two Vedas into twelve thousand Bṛhatī verses: eight of the Yajus and four of the Sāman. Of these two Vedas, that which was created by Prajāpati remained in the thirtieth arrangement among the Paṅktis. Because they remained in the thirtieth arrangement, there are thirty nights in a month; and because they were in the Paṅktis, Prajāpati is fivefold (pāṅkta). Those [verses] became exactly eight hundred and ten Paṅktis.
All those three Vedas became eighty thousand and eight hundred; in every single moment he attained eighty [verses], and in every single moment eighty [verses] were accomplished.

He, having become seed, poured himself—the self consisting of the *chandas*, consisting of the *stomas*, consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), and consisting of the deities—into the fire-pan as a womb within these three worlds. His first body was fashioned during the first half-month; further back, further back still; indeed, it was entirely and completely fashioned in the year itself.

In that he laid down the enclosing-stones (pariśrit), he laid down the night; after that, the fifteen muhūrtas; after each muhūrta, fifteen eighty-minutes (aśītis). And in that he laid down the Yajuṣmatī bricks, he laid down the day; after that, the fifteen muhūrtas; after each muhūrta, fifteen eighty-minutes. Thus he infused this threefold knowledge into his own self and made it his own self. He thus became the self of all beings here—consisting of the meters, consisting of the Stomas, consisting of the vital breaths (prāṇas), and consisting of the deities. Having become composed of these very things, he rose upward. He who rose upward is this very moon.
This is its foundation: that which yonder heats [the sun]. From this very one it was built up; upon this it was built up. Verily, he fashioned it from his own self; from his own self he generated it.

When he, being about to pile the fire-altar, undergoes initiation, it is just as Prajāpati then poured himself out as seed into these three worlds, into the womb that is the fire-pan (ukhā); even so does he now pour himself out as seed into the womb that is the fire-pan—consisting of the metres, consisting of the hymns (stomas), consisting of the vital breaths (prāṇas), and consisting of the deities. His first self is consecrated in the first half-month; further back than that, another; further back than that, another; in the year itself, the whole and complete [self] is consecrated.

In that he lays down a *pariśrit* (enclosing stone), he thereby lays down a night; following that, fifteen *muhūrtas*; and following each *muhūrta*, fifteen *aśītis*. And when he lays down a *yajusmatī* (brick with a formula), he thereby lays down a day; following that, fifteen *muhūrtas*; and following each *muhūrta*, fifteen *aśītis*. Thus, he implants this threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*) within himself and makes it his own. He thus becomes the self of all beings here—consisting of the *chandases*, consisting of the *stomas*, consisting of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and consisting of the deities. Having become composed of these very things, he ascends upwards.

This is its foundation: he who shines yonder (the sun). Indeed, it is built upon him; it is built upon him. He thus fashions it from his own self and procreates it from his own self. When one who knows this departs from this world, he then attains this very self—consisting of the meters, consisting of breath, and consisting of the deities. Having become composed of these, he ascends upwards, he who, knowing thus, performs this rite, or whoever knows this thus.

This year, indeed, is death; for it is this that diminishes the life of mortals by means of days and nights, and then they die. Therefore, this year is death itself. He who knows this year as death—death does not diminish his life by means of days and nights before old age, and he reaches his full span of life.

He indeed is the Ender (Antaka), for he reaches the end of the life of mortals by means of day and night; then they die. Therefore, he alone is the Ender. He who knows this Year as Death—Death the Ender—does not have his life's end reached by day and night before old age; he lives his full span of life.
Those gods were afraid of this Antaka, Death, Prajāpati, the Year, thinking: "Lest he should bring about the end of our life by means of day and night."

They performed these sacrificial rites: the Agnihotra, the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the Four-Monthly sacrifices, the Animal sacrifice, and the Soma sacrifice. Performing these sacrificial rites, they did not attain immortality.

They, too, piled the fire-altar; they laid down an unlimited number of enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*), an unlimited number of *yajuṣmatī* bricks, and an unlimited number of *lokampṛṇā* bricks, thinking, "As people here and now lay them down one by one, so did the gods do. But they did not attain immortality.

Worshipping and toiling, they went about seeking to win immortality. Prajāpati said to them: "Indeed, you do not lay down all my forms; you either leave something out or you do not complete it. Therefore, you do not become immortal."
They said, "Tell us that yourself, so that we may lay down all your forms."
