He said, "Lay down three hundred and sixty enclosing bricks; then lay down three hundred and sixty bricks with formulas; then thirty-six Lokampṛṇā bricks; then ten thousand and eight hundred; then you shall lay down all my forms, and then you will become immortal. The gods laid them down accordingly; thereafter the gods became immortal.

Death said to the gods, "In this very way all men shall become immortal; what, then, will be my share? They replied, "No one else besides him shall become immortal with the body. Only when you take away this share [of life] shall you become immortal apart from the body; then you shall become immortal through knowledge or through ritual action. Now, as for what they said—"through knowledge or through ritual action"—this fire is indeed that knowledge, and this fire is indeed that ritual action.

Those who know this thus, and those who perform this rite, after dying are born again; as they are being born, they attain immortality. But those who do not know this thus, and those who do not perform this rite, after dying are born again; they become the food of this very [sun] again and again.
When he piles the fire-altar, he thereby attains that very Agni, the end-maker, Death, the Year, Prajāpati—the one whom the gods attained; he lays it down just as the gods then laid it down.
By means of the *pariśrit* bricks he obtains his nights; by the *yajuṣmatī* bricks, the days, the half-months, the months, the seasons, the worlds, and the *ṛṇā* bricks, the muhūrtas.

Those enclosing stones which are the worlds of the nights serve as the acquisition of the nights themselves; they are the image of the nights. They amount to three hundred and sixty. For there are indeed three hundred and sixty nights in a year. Of these, he encloses twenty-one around the Gārhapatya fire, seventy-eight on the Dhiṣṇya hearths, and two hundred and sixty-one on the Āhavanīya fire.

Now follow those [bricks] accompanied by Yajus formulas: the bunch of Darbha grass, the clod-bricks, the lotus leaf, the gold plate and the golden man, the two offering-spoons, the naturally-perforated brick, the Dūrvā-brick, the two Retahsic bricks with two Yajus formulas, the Viśvajyotis, the two Ṛtavyā bricks, the Aṣāḍhā, the tortoise, the mortar and pestle, the fire-pan, the five heads of animals, fifteen Apasyā bricks, and five Chandasyā bricks.

Now, the second layer consists of five Aśvinī bricks, two Ṛtavyā bricks, five Vaiśvadevī bricks, five Prāṇabhṛt bricks, five Apasyā bricks, and nineteen Vayasyā bricks; these amount to forty-one, which is the second layer.

Now, the third layer consists of one *svayamātṛṇā* brick; five *diśyā* bricks; four *viśvajyotis* bricks; four *ṛtavyā* bricks; ten *prāṇabhṛt* bricks; thirty-six *candasyā* bricks; and fourteen *vālakhilyā* bricks—these make seventy-one bricks for the third layer.
Now, the fourth layer: eighteen first [bricks], then twelve, then seventeen; those make forty-seven bricks for the fourth layer.

Now follows the fifth layer: five *asapatnā* bricks, forty *virāj*s, thirty-nine *stomabhāgā*s, five *nākasad*s, five *pañcacūḍā*s, thirty-one *candasyā*s, eight *gārhapatya*s, one *citir* brick, eight *punaścitir* bricks, two *ṛtavyā*s, the *viśvajyotis*, the *vikarṇī*, the *svayamātṛṇā*, and the speckled stone (*aśmā pṛśni*); upon this layer the fire is deposited. These constitute one hundred and thirty-eight bricks; this is the fifth layer.

All those [bricks] amount to five hundred and forty. Of these, the three hundred and sixty which are the worlds of the days—their attainment is made through the days; they are the counterpart of the days, and they become three hundred and sixty. For there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year. Now, as for the thirty-six [remaining], the *purīṣa* (filling soil) is their thirty-seventh. Then, the twenty-four which are the worlds of the half-months—their attainment is made through the half-months; they are the counterpart of the half-months. And the twelve which are the worlds of the months—their attainment is made through the months; they are the counterpart of the months. Those two-by-two are the worlds of the seasons, for the non-emptiness of the seasons.

Now, those Lokampṛṇā bricks which are the "world-moments" (muhūrta-lokāḥ) constitute the attainment of the Muhūrtas; they are the measure of the Muhūrtas. There are ten thousand and eight hundred of them, for so many are the Muhūrtas in a year. Of these, he places twenty-one on the Gārhapatya hearth, seventy-eight on the Dhiṣṇya hearths, and the others on the Āhavanīya. Indeed, these are the forms of the year; thus, they are placed here as having been attained by him.

Now, some desire to bring this perfection to the Āhavanīya fire alone, saying, "These other fires have been piled elsewhere; why should we look for perfection here? But one should not do so. For he piles these ten fires: eight Dhiṣṇya hearths, the Āhavanīya, and the Gārhapatya. Therefore they say, "Agni is the Virāj," for the Virāj consists of ten syllables. Yet they designate all of them as "Agni" as if they were one, for these are all his forms. Just as the days and nights, half-months, months, and seasons are the forms of the year, even so these are all his forms.

Those who act in that manner indeed place these forms of his outside; moreover, they create a state of inverted order, making the common people (viś) an adversary and a counter-attacker against the ruling power (kṣatra). On the Āgnīdhra hearth, he places a speckled stone and then gazes upon it. Why should he gaze upon that one and not gaze upon the others? That by which he drives away Nirṛti and evil—that is the eleventh.
Regarding this they say: "Why does he not look upon them here? For he does not offer an oblation over them; indeed, it is by means of an oblation that a brick becomes complete and whole.

Regarding this they say: "How is it that these [bricks] are laid down so as not to exceed him? Indeed, these are his vigor; for vigor does not exceed a person. Verily, he who, knowing this, performs this rite—or whoever knows this—constructs this Prajāpati in his entirety and completeness.
While Prajāpati was creating offspring, evil death overcame him from all sides; he performed austerity for a thousand years, desiring to cast off evil.

As he was performing that austerity, lights rose upward from these hair-pits; those which were the lights are these very constellations (*nakṣatra*). As many as are these constellations, so many are the hair-pits; as many as are the hair-pits, so many are the moments (*muhūrta*) of a thousand-year period.

In the thousandth year, he completely purifies everything; that which he completely purified is this very wind that blows here. And as for that evil which he completely purified, it is this body. What man indeed could sustain [the sacrifice] for a thousand years? But one who knows thus sustains a thousand-year [sacrifice] through knowledge alone.

One should worship all these bricks as being thousandfold. With each thousand nights, one should worship each individual *pariśrit* brick as perfected; with each thousand days, each individual day-partaking brick; with each thousand half-months, each individual half-month-partaking brick; with each thousand months, each individual month-partaking brick; with each thousand seasons, each individual season-partaking brick; and with each thousand moments (*muhūrta*), each individual moment-partaking brick. With each thousand years, they who know this fire as perfected by the year know its thousandth part. But those who do not know it thus do not know even its thousandth part. Now, he who knows this, or who performs this rite, attains this entire, complete, Prajāpati-related fire which Prajāpati attained. Therefore, one who knows this should practice austerity. Whatever austerity one who knows this practices—even unto sexual union—all that of his becomes the heavenly world.

This very thing is expressed by the Rigvedic verse: "Not in vain is the toil which the gods protect. Indeed, for one who knows this, no toil whatsoever becomes in vain; and thus the gods protect all of this for him.

Now, as for the instructions of the Upanishads: the followers of Śākāyanya worship [Agni] as Vāyu; some say Agni is Āditya; and Śraumatya or Hāliṅgava used to say, "Agni is indeed Vāyu; therefore, whenever the Adhvaryu performs the final rite, he then passes into this very one."

Śāṭyāyani used to say: "The year itself is Agni. Of him, spring is the head, summer the right wing, the rainy season the left wing, the autumn season the middle body, and the winter and dewy seasons the tail and foundation. Speech is Agni, breath is Vāyu, the eye is Āditya, the mind is Candramas, the ear is the quarters, and the waters are the pair. Heat is the foundation; the months are the joints, the half-months are the veins, and the days and nights are the silver and golden wings. Thus he goes even unto the gods. One should indeed know, "Agni is the year"; one should know, moreover, "He becomes composed of that."

Celaka, the son of Śāṇḍilya, said: "These very three worlds are the layers provided with self-perforated bricks; the sacrificer is the fourth; and all desires are the fifth. One should know that by this [altar] they perfect these worlds, as well as the self and all desires."

Of this very Agni, speech is indeed the Upaniṣad; for by speech he is built up—with the Ṛg, the Yajus, and the Sāman. This refers to divine speech; and as for human speech, "Do this! Do that!"—by that [speech] he is likewise built up.

This very speech is threefold: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants. Therefore, Agni is threefold, for he is built up by means of this triad. Likewise, the year is threefold; and indeed, in this way also, it is threefold, since bricks that are threefold are laid upon him—those with masculine names, those with feminine names, and those with neuter names. And these limbs of man are likewise threefold: those with masculine names, those with feminine names, and those with neuter names.

This very Self is indeed threefold; by means of this threefold Self, he attains that threefold divine immortality. All those [bricks] are called "the bricks" (iṣṭakāḥ)—they are not called "the brick" (iṣṭakā), nor "the brick" (iṣṭakam)—in accordance with the form of speech. For all this, whether female, male, or neuter, is speech; by speech alone is all this attained. Therefore, he settles them all with the formula, "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras," and not with "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras" or "Sit thou firm like Aṅgiras. For it is speech that he thus consecrates.

That speech is yonder sun; he is death. Now, whatever is on this side of the sun, all that is seized by death. If anyone builds [the fire-altar] on this side of it, he builds it seized by death; he indeed delivers himself over to death. But he who builds it above this, by means of knowledge, he conquers death again; for by knowledge, this [altar] becomes built for him above this point.

This very speech is threefold: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāmans*. The *ṛc*s are the orb; the *sāmans* are the light; the *yajus* formulas are the person. Now, that which is this immortal light shining here is this lotus leaf. When one piles the fire after placing the lotus leaf, he thereby prepares for himself a self consisting of *ṛc*, *yajus*, and *sāman* within that very immortal [light], and he becomes immortal.
That which is this orb that shines is the Great Hymn (Mahaduktha);

it is the Rig-verses; it is the world of the Rig-verses. And that which is this radiance that blazes is the Great Vow (Mahāvrata); those are the Saman-chants; it is the world of the Saman-chants. And that person who is in this orb is Agni; those are the Yajus-formulas; it is the world of the Yajus-formulas.
This very threefold knowledge shines forth; even those who do not know this say, "This threefold knowledge indeed shines forth," for it is Speech that speaks while perceiving it.

This very person is in that orb; and this is the immortal, namely this light that shines. Therefore, death does not die there, for death is within the immortal; therefore it is not seen, for it is within the immortal.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "The immortal within death"—for this is indeed the immortal within death; "the immortal placed within death"—for within this person this orb shines, established therein. "Death clothes Vivasvat"—Vivasvat is yonder sun, for he clothes day and night; him death clothes, for he is encompassed on all sides by him. "The self of death is within Vivasvat"—for within this orb is the self of this person. Regarding this, there is this verse.

Of these two—of this radiance and of this person—this orb is the foundation. Therefore, one should not recite the Great Hymn (*mahaduktha*) for another, lest he cut away this foundation. For he who recites the Great Hymn for another cuts away this foundation for himself. Therefore, they greatly despise a reciter of the Hymn, saying, "He is a cutter-away of his foundation. This is with respect to the deities.

Now, with regard to the sacrifice: that orb which shines there is this very gold plate; and that radiance which blazes forth is this lotus leaf, for these waters are indeed the lotus leaf. And that person who is in this orb is this very golden person. Having thus prepared this triad, he places it here; following the completion of the sacrifice, he ascends upwards and enters into him who shines there. Therefore, one need not trouble oneself to extinguish the fire, for he becomes that [sun] over there at that time. Thus much with regard to the sacrifice.

Now, with regard to the self: that which shines as this orb, and that which is this golden disk (rukma), are this white part in the eye; and that which shines as this flame, and that which is this lotus leaf, are this black part in the eye. And that person who is in this orb, and that person who is made of gold—he is indeed this very person who is the person in the right eye.

This very Lokampṛṇā is that [brick]; this entire Agni attains to it. His mate is this person who is here in the left eye; for a mate is half of one's own self. Indeed, when one is together with a mate, then one is whole, then complete; for completeness. As to why there are two: a pair, indeed, is a productive couple. Therefore, two Lokampṛṇās are laid down each time; therefore, they lead forward the layer with two bricks.

This very one is Indra, who is the person in the right eye; and this [other] is Indrāṇī. For these two, the gods made this partition, the nose. Therefore, one should not eat at the end of a wife's meal, for a vigorous son is born from him; and she indeed gives birth to a vigorous son for whom he does not eat at the end of her meal.

This very Devavrata, the most excellent among men, the kinsmen of royalty protect; therefore, one who is heroic is born from them. It is the "Immortal-Speech" among birds; it produces the Kṣipraśyena.

Having returned to the space within the heart, those two become a couple; when they reach the end of their coupling, then this person sleeps. Just as, having reached the end of human coupling, one becomes as if unconscious, even so does he become as if unconscious at that time, for this is divine coupling, and it is the supreme bliss.

Therefore, one who knows this should sleep; for he thereby satisfies these two deities with their own beloved union. For this reason, one should not wake a sleeping person by shaking him, thinking, "Lest I harm these two deities while they are engaged in union. For this reason, the mouth of one who has slept appears as if smeared with phlegm; it is these two deities that pour forth seed, and from that seed all this comes into being, whatever exists here.

This very one is death: the person who is in this orb [of the sun] and the person who is here in the right eye. His two feet are fastened within his heart; having pulled them out, he departs. When he departs, then the person dies; therefore they say of one who has passed away, "He has been cut off."

This indeed is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for he leads forth all these creatures; these vital breaths are his own. When he sleeps, then these vital breaths enter into him as his own; therefore it is called "entering one's own" (*svāpyaya*). They cryptically call this sleep "sleep" (*svapna*); for the gods love the cryptic.

When he is asleep by means of these, he knows nothing of anyone; he does not form intentions with the mind, nor does he perceive the taste of food with speech, nor does he perceive smell with the breath, nor does he see with the eye, nor does he hear with the ear—for these are then merged into him. Being one, he has entered manifoldly into living beings; therefore, although she is one, the *Lokampṛṇā* (space-filler) pervades the entire fire-altar. And because he is indeed one, she is called "one" (*ekā*).

Regarding this they say: "Is death one, or are there many? One should reply: "It is both one and many. Insofar as it is that [death] over there, it is one; but insofar as it has entered here among living beings in manifold ways, it is many.

Regarding this they say: "Death is near; it is far away. One should say: "It is both near and far. It is near because of that which is here within oneself (*adhyātma*); it is far because of that which is there beyond.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "He shines, supported by food, in the flow of essences, the immortal. That which burns as this orb is the food; and that person who is in this orb is the eater. He shines, supported by that food—this is with respect to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self: this very body is the food, and that person who is in the right eye is the eater; he shines resting upon this food.

The Adhvaryu priests worship this very one as Agni, for he joins together all this; the Chandogas as Sāman, for in him all this is unified; the Bahvṛcas as Uktha, for he raises up all this; the Yātu-vids as Yātu, for by him all this is restrained; the serpents as Viṣa (poison), the serpent-knowers as Sarpa (serpent); the gods as Ūrj (strength), men as Rayi (wealth), the Asuras as Māyā (illusion), the ancestors as Svadhā, the knowers of divine beings as Devajana; the Gandharvas as Rūpa (form), the Apsarases as Gandha (fragrance). In whatever way they worship him, that indeed he becomes; becoming thus, he protects them. Therefore, one who knows this should worship him with all these names; for he becomes all this, and becoming all this, he protects him.

This very Agni consists of three bricks: one is a Ṛc, one is a Yajus, and one is a Sāman. Whatever Ṛc he lays down here, the gold plate (rukma) is its foundation; whatever [he lays down] with a Yajus, the person (puruṣa) is its foundation; and whatever [he lays down] with a Sāman, the lotus leaf (puṣkaraparṇa) is its foundation. Thus he is composed of three bricks.
Both of these—the gold plate and this lotus leaf—have merged into this Person; for both the Ṛc and the Sāman have merged into the Yajus, and thus he consists of a single brick.

This very one is death: the person who is in this orb and the person who is here in the right eye. He becomes the Self of one who knows thus. When one who knows thus departs from this world, he attains that very Self; he becomes immortal, for death becomes his Self.
In the beginning, this was neither non-existent nor existent; rather, in the beginning, this was as if it existed, yet it did not exist. That, indeed, was just the mind.
Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "Neither non-being nor being existed then"; for the mind is neither being nor non-being.

This mind, once created, desired to become manifest, more defined, and more substantial. It sought after its own self; it practiced austerity. It coalesced, and it beheld thirty-six thousand Arka-fires of its own self, consisting of mind, built of mind. They were studied by the mind alone, they were piled by the mind alone; by the mind the cups were drawn for them, by the mind they chanted, by the mind they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that was performed as consisting of mind, built of mind, in those fires which consist of mind. Whatever these beings here conceive with their minds—that is their doing; they pile those very fires, they construct them, they draw the cups for them, they chant over them, and they recite over them. Such indeed is the power of the mind, such is its creation, such is the extent of the mind: thirty-six thousand Arka-fires. Each one of them is as great as that former fire.

That mind created speech. This speech, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more embodied—and it sought after its own self. It performed austerity; it solidified, and it beheld thirty-six thousand fires of its own self, consisting of the *ṛk* verses, composed of speech, and built of speech. By speech alone were they studied; by speech were the cups drawn for them; by speech they chanted; by speech they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is—all that was performed within those fires composed of speech, built of speech, as something consisting of speech. Whatever these beings here speak by means of speech, that is their very creation; they build those fires, they pile them up; for them they draw the cups, for them they chant, for them they recite. Such indeed is the expansion of speech, such is its manifestation, such is speech: thirty-six thousand fires, the *ṛks*; each one of them is as great as that former fire.

That Speech created Breath. This Breath, once created, desired to become manifest, more defined, and more substantial. It sought after its own self; it practiced austerity; it coalesced; and it beheld thirty-six thousand Arka-fires of its own self, consisting of breath and built of breath. They were established by breath alone, they were piled up by breath alone, by breath the cups were drawn for them, by breath they chanted, and by breath they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is—all that was performed as consisting of breath within those fires which consist of breath and are built of breath. And whatever these beings here breathe with breath—that is their very work; it is them they establish, it is them they pile up; for them they draw the cups, in them they chant, and in them they recite. Such indeed is the manifestation of Breath, such is its creation, such is Breath: thirty-six thousand.

That Prāṇa created the Eye. This Eye, once created, desired to become manifest, more defined, and more substantial; it sought after its own self, it performed austerity, and it coalesced. It beheld thirty-six thousand Ātman-Agnes, Arka-fires consisting of the eye, piled with the eye. With the eye alone they were studied; with the eye they were built up; with the eye the cups were drawn for them; with the eye they chanted; with the eye they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed at the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that was performed as consisting of the eye, as piled with the eye, among those fires which consist of the eye and are piled with the eye. Therefore, whatever these beings here see with the eye—that is their very work; they build them up, they pile them, they draw the cups for them, they chant for them, and they recite for them. Such indeed is the manifestation of the eye, such is its creation, such is the extent of the eye: thirty-six thousand.

That [Mind] created the Eye and the Ear. This Ear, once created, desired to become manifest, more defined, and more substantial; it sought after its own self, performed austerity, and coagulated. It beheld thirty-six thousand Agnis of its own self—Aris (Suns) consisting of the Ear, built by the Ear. They were studied by the Ear alone, they were piled by the Ear alone, by the Ear the cups were drawn for them, by the Ear they chanted, and by the Ear they recited. Whatever ritual act is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is—it was all performed as consisting of the Ear, built by the Ear, within those Agnis which consist of the Ear and are built by the Ear. Whatever these beings here hear with the Ear, that is their very performance; it is them they establish, it is them they pile, for them they draw the cups, in them they chant, and in them they recite. Such indeed is the expansion of the Ear, such is its creation, so great is the Ear—thirty-sixfold.

He created the *tacrotra* rite; it coalesced into the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) as this compact mass, a compact mass of food. Indeed, the rite is incomplete without the vital breaths, and the vital breaths are indeed incomplete without the rite.

This very work (karman), once created, desired to become manifest, more defined, and more embodied. It sought after its own self; it practiced austerity. It coagulated and beheld thirty-six thousand Agnis—Arkas made of work, built of work. By work alone they were established; by work they were piled up; by work the cups were drawn for them; by work they chanted; by work they recited. Whatever work is performed at a sacrifice, whatever sacrificial rite there is—all that was performed as work upon those [Agnis] made of work, built of work. Therefore, whatever work these beings here perform, that is their very creation; they pile them up, they build them; for them they draw the cups, in them they chant, in them they recite. Such indeed is the expansion of work, such is its manifestation, such is work: thirty-six thousand.
He created the fire of action; for fire is more manifest than action, since they produce it by means of action and kindle it with action.

This Agni, once created, desired to become manifest—more defined, more substantial. He sought after his own self; he performed austerity. He grew great and beheld thirty-six thousand fires of his own self, which were suns made of fire, piled with fire. By fire alone they were studied; by fire they were piled; by fire the cups were drawn for them; by fire they praised; by fire they recited. Whatever rite is performed at the sacrifice, whatever sacrificial act there is—all that was performed by fire alone for those fires made of fire, for those who had piled the fire-altar, as something consisting of fire. And whatever of these beings kindles the fire—that is their doing; it is them they lay down, it is them they pile up; for them they draw the cups, for them they praise, for them they recite. Such indeed is the manifestation of Agni, such is his creation, such is Agni: thirty-six thousand fires, suns; and each one of them is as large as that former one.
These [fires] are indeed built of knowledge alone; all beings at all times build these for one who knows thus, even while he sleeps; for by knowledge alone they are built for one who knows thus.

This world, indeed, is this built-up fire-altar. Of it, the waters are the enclosing stones; men are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; the *sūdadohas* verses are the plants and trees; the loose soil is the oblations; the fuel-sticks are the fire; and the space-filler (*lokampṛṇā*) is the fire itself. All this, indeed, becomes the fire-altar; the entire fire-altar becomes the space-filler. He who knows this thus—having become the space-filler—becomes all this.

Indeed, this built-up fire-altar is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Of it, the junction of heaven and earth is the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*); for beyond the intermediate space, heaven and earth join together. Those enclosing-stones are the birds; the *yajuṣmatī* bricks are the rain; the *sūdadohas* verses are the rays; the loose soil is the oblations; the fuel-sticks are the wind; and the *lokampṛṇā* brick is the wind itself. Thus, all this indeed becomes the wind; that is the whole Agni.

This built-up fire-altar is indeed the sky. Its enclosing stones are the waters. Just as this chest here is closed up, so these worlds are within the waters. Those waters which are beyond these worlds are the enclosing stones; the gods are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; whatever food there is in this world is the *sūdadohas*; the stars are the *purīṣa*; the oblations are the fuel-sticks; and the sun is the *lokampṛṇā*. All this, indeed, becomes the sun alone; thus the whole Agni is the sun.

This built-up fire-altar is indeed the sun. Its enclosing-stones are the quarters; they are three hundred and sixty, for three hundred and sixty quarters surround the sun on all sides. The *yajus*-bricks are the rays; they are three hundred and sixty, for there are three hundred and sixty rays of the sun. When he places the *yajus*-bricks within the enclosing-stones, he thereby places the rays within the quarters. Now, that which is between the quarters and the rays is the *sūdadohas* verse. And that food which is in the quarters and in the rays is the *purīṣa*; those are the oblations, those are the fuel-sticks. And that which is designated as "quarters" and "rays" is the *lokampṛṇā* brick. Thus, all this—designated as "quarters" and "rays"—is the entire Agni.

This built-up fire-altar, indeed, consists of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). There are twenty-seven of these lunar mansions; for there are twenty-seven stars that attend upon each individual mansion. These amount to seven hundred and twenty, plus thirty-six. Of these, the seven hundred and twenty are the bricks: three hundred and sixty are the *pariśrit* bricks, and three hundred and sixty are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks. Then, as for the thirty-six that remain, that is the thirteenth month; it is the self (the body). Thirty are the self, two are the foundation, and two are the head. As to why there are two [for the head], it is because the word "head" (*śiras*) has two syllables. Now, what is between the mansions is the *sūdadohas*; what food is in the mansions is the *purīṣa*, those are the oblations, and those are the fuel-sticks. And what is called "the lunar mansions" is the *lokapṛṇā*. Thus, all this is indeed called "the lunar mansions," and that is the whole Agni.

Now, these indeed are twenty-one Bṛhatīs; the heavenly world is the twenty-one-fold, and the Bṛhatī is the heavenly world. Thus, he attains the heavenly world, as well as the twenty-one-fold Stoma and the Bṛhatī metre.

This built-up fire-altar is indeed the metres; these are the seven metres, each increasing by four syllables, which consist of triplets. Of these, there are seven hundred and twenty syllables, plus thirty-six. Now, those seven hundred and twenty are the bricks themselves: three hundred and sixty *pariśrit* bricks and three hundred and sixty *yajuṣmatī* bricks. Then, as for the thirty-six that remain, that is the thirteenth month; it is the body (*ātman*). Thirty make the body, two the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), two the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and two the head. As for why there are two [for the head], it is because the word for "head" (*śiras*) has two syllables.

Of this very Bṛhatī consisting of thirty-six syllables: those which are the first ten syllables are the ten-syllable *ekapadā*; then those which are twenty are the twenty-syllable *dvipadā*; then those which are thirty are the thirty-syllable *virāj*; then those which are thirty-three are the thirty-three-syllable [verse]; then those which are thirty-four are the thirty-four-syllable *svarāj*. And when this fire-altar is built with all the meters, that is the *aticandāḥ*. All these are indeed bricks; "brick" (*iṣṭakā*) has three syllables, and the *gāyatrī* has three feet; therefore this Agni is *gāyatra*. "Clay and water" (*mṛdāpaḥ*) has three syllables, and the *gāyatrī* has three feet; thus he is likewise *gāyatra*. Now, what is between the two meters is the *sūdadohas*. What food there is in the meters is the *purīṣa*; they are the oblations, they are the fuel-sticks. And what is called "the meters" (*chandāṃsi*) is the *lokampṛṇā*. Thus all this is called "the meters," and that is the whole Agni.

Now, these indeed are twenty-one Bṛhatīs; the heavenly world is the twenty-onefold, and the Bṛhatī is the heavenly world. Thus, he attains the heavenly world, as well as the twenty-onefold Stoma and the Bṛhatī metre.

This Agni, when built up, is indeed the year. Its enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) are the nights; they are three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty nights in the year. The days are the *yajuṣmatī* bricks; they also are three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in the year. Now, those thirty-six bricks which exceed [the total] are the thirteenth month—the self (the body)—consisting of half-months and months: twenty-four half-months and twelve months. What lies between day and night is the *sūdadohas*; what food is in the days and nights is the *purīṣa* (filling soil), those are the oblations, and those are the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). And that which is called "days and nights" is the *lokampṛṇā* (space-filler). Thus, all this is indeed called "days and nights"; that is the whole Agni.

Now, these indeed are twenty-one Bṛhatīs; the heavenly world is the twenty-one-fold, and the Bṛhatī is the heavenly world. Thus he attains the heavenly world, as well as the twenty-one-fold Stoma and the Bṛhatī metre.

This very self, indeed, is the piled fire-altar. Its enclosing stones (*pariśrit*) are his bones; they number three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty bones in a man. The *yajusmatī* bricks are his marrow; they also number three hundred and sixty, for there are indeed three hundred and sixty portions of marrow in a man. Now, as for those thirty-six bricks that remain over, that is the thirteenth month, the self, the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Of that [self], there are thirty parts in the body, two in the foundation, and two in the head. As to why there are two [in the head], it is because the head consists of two skull-bones (*kapāla*). Now, that by which these joints are held together is the *sūdadohas*. And this triad by which this self is covered—hair, skin, and flesh—that is the loose soil (*purīṣa*). What he drinks are the oblations (*āhuti*); what he eats are the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). And that which is called "the self" (*ātman*) is the space-filler (*lokaṃpṛṇā*). Thus, all this is called "the self," and thus the entire fire-altar is the self.
These, indeed, are those twenty-one Bṛhatī verses.

Indeed, all beings and all gods are this built-up fire-altar. All the gods and all beings are water; thus, these waters are this built-up fire-altar. Its enclosing-stones are the navigable rivers; they amount to three hundred and sixty. For indeed, three hundred and sixty navigable rivers encircle the sun on all sides. The navigable rivers themselves are the *yajushmati* bricks; they also amount to three hundred and sixty. For indeed, three hundred and sixty navigable rivers flow toward the sun. Now, that which lies between the navigable rivers is the *sūdadohas*. And as for those thirty-six bricks that remain over—this is the thirteenth month, the self (the body); he is this very golden person.

These two are its foundations: the gold plate and the lotus leaf; the waters and the solar disc are the two offering-ladles; the two arms are Indra and Agni; the two *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks are this earth and the intermediate space; the three *viśvajyotis* bricks are these deities—Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya—for these deities indeed are the "all-light" (*viśvaṃ jyotiḥ*). The twelve seasonal bricks are the year; that is the self (*ātman*). The five *pañcacūḍā* bricks are the sacrifice; those are the gods. Now, as for the *vikarṇī*, the *svayamātṛṇṇā*, the speckled stone, and the fire which is placed upon the altar—that is the thirty-fifth *lokampṛṇā*; the sacrificial formula (*yajus*) is the thirty-sixth. That is his very innermost self. He is in the midst of all the waters. He is endowed with all desires; for water is indeed all desires. He is desireless and possesses all desires, for no one has any desire for him.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "By means of knowledge they ascend to that place where desires have vanished; neither those who give sacrificial gifts nor those who practice austerity go there. Indeed, one who does not know thus does not attain that world through sacrificial gifts or through austerity; for that world belongs only to those who know thus.

The cloud is the dung; the moon is the oblations; the stars are the fuel-wood. When the moon dwells in a star, that is when the oblation dwells in the fuel-wood. This, indeed, is the food of the oblation, and this is its foundation; therefore the oblation is never exhausted, for this is its food and this is its foundation. Now, that which is called "the gods" (devāḥ) is the space-filler (lokampṛṇā); for all this is indeed called "the gods."

This is expressed by the Ṛgvedic verse: "O All-Gods, that Yajus of yours follows after. For here all beings and all gods indeed become the Yajus itself; thus the entire Agni attains the Lokampṛṇā brick. He who knows this thus—this whole world, having come into being, attains him through the Lokampṛṇā.

These, indeed, are twenty-one Bṛhatīs; the heavenly world is the twenty-one-fold, and the Bṛhatī is the heavenly world. Thus he attains the heavenly world, as well as the twenty-one-fold Stoma and the Bṛhatī metre.

Kuśri Vājaśravasa built a fire-altar. Suśravas Kauṣya said to him, "Gautama, when you built this fire-altar, did you build it facing forward? Did you build it facing backward? Did you build it facing downward? Did you build it facing upward?"
If you have caused him to recite facing eastward, it is just as if one were to bring food from behind to someone sitting with his face turned away; in that same way, he will not accept your oblation.
"But if you indeed approached him facing him, why then did you place his tail behind?"
Or, if you had piled it facing downwards, it would have been just as if one were to place food upon the back of someone lying face down; in that case, your oblation would not have accepted it.

"But if you have piled it face upwards, [know that] a bird, when flying face upwards, does not carry one to the heavenly world; it will not carry you to the heavenly world, and it will not lead you to heaven."
He said: "We have carried him eastward; we have carried him westward; we have carried him downward; we have carried him upward; we have carried him toward all the quarters."

In that he lays down the man facing eastward and the two offering-ladles facing eastward, it is built facing eastward; then, in that he lays down the tortoise facing westward and the heads of the animals facing westward, it is built facing westward; then, in that he lays down the tortoise turned downward and the heads of the animals turned downward, as well as the bricks turned downward, it is built turned downward; then, in that he lays down the man face upward, the two ladles face upward, the mortar face upward, and the fire-pan face upward, it is built face upward; then, in that he lays down bricks crawling all around the quarters, it is built on all sides.

Then, while they were driving the sacrificial animals, they drove up Agni with his head cut off. One of them said, "The head is indeed prosperity; they have cut off his prosperity; he will suffer total ruin. And so it indeed came to pass.
Then one said: "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed the head; he has torn out his vital breaths; he will quickly go to that world. And so it indeed came to pass.

Verily, this [altar] is built upright: namely, the bunch of darbha grass, the clod-bricks, the lotus leaf, the gold plate and the man, the two offering-spoons, the naturally-perforated brick, the dūrvā-brick, the two *dviyajus* bricks, the two *retaḥsic* bricks, the *viśvajyotis*, the two seasonal (*ṛtavyā*) bricks, the *aṣāḍhā*, and the tortoise. Now, that fire which is placed upon the completed altar is indeed its head most manifestly; therefore, one should not remove it.

Then these men came together: Aruṇa Aupaveśi, Satyayajña Pauluṣi, Mahāśāla Jābāla, Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, Indradyumna Bhāllaveya, and Jana Śārkarākṣya. They deliberated concerning Vaiśvānara, but they did not reach a consensus regarding Vaiśvānara.

They said, "This Aśvapati Kaikeya indeed knows Vaiśvānara at present; let us go to him. They came to Aśvapati Kaikeya, and he assigned them separate lodgings, separate honors, and separate Soma-sacrifices with a thousand [attendants] each. In the morning, still not having reached an agreement among themselves, they approached him with fuel in their hands, saying, "We come to you as pupils."

He said, "Venerable sirs, you who are learned in the Vedas and the sons of those learned in the Vedas—what is this? They replied, "The venerable one knows Vaiśvānara thoroughly; tell that to us. He said, "I indeed know Vaiśvānara thoroughly now; put on the fuel-sticks and approach me as my pupils."

He said to Āruṇi Aupaveśi, "Gautama, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? "As the earth alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is Vaiśvānara. For you know this Vaiśvānara as the foundation; therefore, you are firmly established with offspring and cattle. Verily, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as the foundation conquers recurrent death and reaches a full lifespan. But these two are the feet of Vaiśvānara; your feet would have withered away had you not come here. Or rather: "Your feet would have remained unknown to you had you not come here."

Then he said to Satyayajña Pauluṣi, "O Prācīnayogya, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? He replied, "As water alone, O King. [Prācīnayogya] said, "Yes," and continued, "This indeed is Rayi-Vaiśvānara (the Universal Fire of Wealth). Since you know this Rayi-Vaiśvānara, therefore you are wealthy and prosperous. Verily, he who knows this Rayi-Vaiśvānara conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. This, however, is only the bladder of Vaiśvānara; your bladder would have failed you had you not come here. Or rather, he said, "Your bladder would have remained unknown to you had you not come here."

Then he said to Mahāśāla Jābāla, "Aupamanyava, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? He replied, "O King, as space alone. [Śākalya] said, "Yes. "This indeed is the manifold Vaiśvānara; for you know this manifold Vaiśvānara, therefore you are rich in offspring and cattle. Verily, he who knows this manifold Vaiśvānara conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. This is the self of Vaiśvānara; your self would have perished had you not come here—your self would have remained unknown to you had you not come here," he said. Or rather, [the meaning is]: "Your self would have been unknown had you not come here."

Then he said to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi, "O Vaiyāghrapadya, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? He replied, "As Vāyu alone, O King. [Śākalya] said, "Yes. [Śākalya] said, "This is indeed Vaiśvānara as the manifold-pathed (pṛthagvartman). For you know this Vaiśvānara as the manifold-pathed; therefore, rows of chariots follow you in various directions. Verily, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as the manifold-pathed conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. This is the breath (prāṇa) of Vaiśvānara. Your breath would have failed you had you not come here; your breath would have remained unknown to you had you not come here," he said.

Then he said to Indradyumna Bhāllaveya: "O Vaiyāghrapadya, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? He replied, "As the sun alone, O King. [Śākalya] said, "Yes. "This, indeed, is Vaiśvānara of radiant splendor (*sutatejas*). Since you know this Vaiśvānara of radiant splendor, therefore this pressed Soma remains in your house today, being drunk, being cooked, yet not wasting away. Verily, he who knows this Vaiśvānara of radiant splendor conquers renewed death and attains a full lifespan. This, however, is only the eye of Vaiśvānara; your eye would have failed you had you not come here. Or rather, your eye would have remained unknown to you had you not come here."

Then he said to Jana Śārkarākṣya, "O Sāyavasa, as what do you know Vaiśvānara? "As heaven alone, O King," he replied. "Yes," he said, "this indeed is the Vaiśvānara who stands above all (Atiṣṭhā). Since you know this Vaiśvānara as the one standing above all, therefore you stand above your equals. Verily, he who knows this Vaiśvānara as the one standing above all conquers renewed death and attains a full lifespan. This is the head of Vaiśvānara; your head would have been struck off had you not come here. Or rather, [he said], "The head of Vaiśvānara would have remained unknown to you had you not come here."

He said to them: "Indeed, you have each known Vaiśvānara separately and have eaten food separately. The gods, however, when they had well understood him, attained him as one who is the measure of a span. But I shall explain him to you in such a way that I shall cause him to be attained as exactly the measure of a span."

He said, pointing to the head: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara as the Summit. Pointing to the eyes, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Brilliant Splendor. Pointing to the nostrils, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara of Diverse Paths. Pointing to the space within the mouth, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Abundant. Pointing to the principal waters (the saliva), he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Wealth. Pointing to the chin, he said: "This indeed is Vaiśvānara the Foundation. This very Agni Vaiśvānara is the person; he who knows this Agni Vaiśvānara thus—as having the form of a person and established within the person—conquers recurrent death, attains a full lifespan, and Vaiśvānara does not harm him even when he speaks.
This world consists of two things: the eater and the food. When these two come together, it is called only the eater, not the food.
He who is that eater is indeed Agni; whatever they place into him are his fuel-sticks (*āhitayaḥ*). These very things are called "oblations" (*āhutayaḥ*) cryptically; for the gods love the cryptic.
The Āditya is indeed the eater; the moon is his food-offerings, for the Āditya takes up the moon—thus with respect to the deities.
Now, with reference to the self: the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the eater; its fuel-sticks are food, for the breath takes up food—thus [it is] with respect to Agni.
Now, as for the *arka*: fire (*agni*) is indeed the *arka*; its oblations are the *kam*, for the oblations are indeed *kam* for Agni.
The sun, indeed, is the *arka*; its *kaṃ* is the moon, for the moon is *kaṃ* for the sun. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidevatam*).
Now, with reference to the self: the breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *arka*; its food is the *kam*, for food is indeed the *kam* (pleasure) for the breath. Such indeed is the nature of the *arka*.
Now, as for the *uktha*: Agni is indeed the *uk*, while the oblations are the *tham*; for it is by means of the oblations that Agni arises.
The Āditya is indeed the *uk*, and the Moon is the *thaṃ*; for by means of the Moon, the Āditya rises—this is with respect to the deities.

Now, with respect to the self: breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *uktha*, and food is its *tham*; for by means of food, breath arises. Thus, this man is of the nature of the *agni*, of the nature of the *arka*, and of the nature of the *uktha*. He who meditates upon this man as being of the nature of the *agni*, of the nature of the *arka*, and of the nature of the *uktha*—verily, the rival of such a knower withers away.

By means of breath, fire blazes; by fire, wind; by wind, the sun; by the sun, the moon; by the moon, the stars; and by the stars, lightning. Such indeed is the radiance in this world and in that world. He who knows this blazes with all this radiance in this world and in that world.

"One should meditate upon Brahman as Truth. Now, this person consists of volition; whatever his volition is when he departs from this world, with that same volition he passes into the next world and becomes [one with it]."

One should meditate upon that Self as consisting of mind, having breath for its body, whose form is light, whose nature is space, which assumes forms at will, swift as thought, whose resolve is true, whose steadfastness is true, which contains all fragrances and all tastes, which has pervaded all directions and this entire world, which is speechless and free from desire. Just as a grain of rice, or a grain of barley, or a grain of *śyāmāka* millet, or the kernel of a *śyāmāka* seed—so is this golden person within the inner self. Like a smokeless light, he is greater than heaven, greater than the ether, greater than this earth, and greater than all beings. He is the Self of breath; he is my Self. "After departing from here, I shall attain this Self"—he who possesses such certain knowledge has no doubt. Thus said Śāṇḍilya: "It is even so."

Dawn is indeed the head of the sacrificial horse; the sun is its eye, the wind its breath, and Vaiśvānara fire its open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse; the sky is its back, the atmosphere its belly, the earth its underbelly, the quarters its flanks, the intermediate quarters its ribs, the seasons its limbs, the months and half-months its joints, days and nights its feet, the stars its bones, and the clouds its flesh. The sand is its undigested food (uvadhya); the rivers are its intestines; the mountains are its liver and lungs; the herbs and trees are its hair. Rising is its forepart; setting is its hind part. When it yawns, it lightens; when it shakes itself, it thunders; when it urinates, it rains. Speech is its voice. By day, the Mahiman cup was born before the horse; its womb is the eastern sea. By night, the Mahiman cup was born after it; its womb is the western sea. These two Mahiman cups were produced on both sides of the horse. Having become a steed (*haya*), it carried the gods; as a stallion (*vājī*), the Gandharvas; as a racer (*arvan*), the Asuras; and as a horse (*aśva*), human beings. The ocean is its kin, the ocean is its womb.

In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here; this was covered by death alone, by hunger—for hunger is death. He created the mind with the thought, "May I have a self. He moved about worshipping, and from him, as he worshipped, the waters were produced. "While I was worshipping, water (ka) came into being for me," he thought; that is the essence of the *arkya* chant. Indeed, happiness (*kam*) comes to him who knows thus the essence of the *arkya*.

The waters, indeed, are the *arka*. That which was the foam of the waters solidified; it became the earth. Upon it he exerted himself. From him, thus exerted and heated, his essence emerged as heat and radiance: Agni.

He divided himself threefold: the sun as one third and the wind as one third. This very breath is thus distributed threefold. Of this [breath], the eastern quarter is the head; those two [solar regions] are the two arms. Then, its western quarter is the tail; those two [solar regions] are the two thighs. The south and the north are the two sides; the sky is the back, the atmosphere is the belly, and this earth is the chest. This [breath] is established in the waters; wherever it goes, there it finds support—so it is for one who knows this.

He desired, "May a second self be born from me. Through his mind, he entered into union with speech; he was Death in the form of hunger. That which was the seed became the year; for before that, there was no year. He bore him for as long as a year, and after that time, he brought him forth. When he was born, he opened his mouth to devour him; he made the sound "bhāṇ," and that became speech.

He thought, "If I should think of this [world] as food, I shall make it less food. With that speech and with that self, he created all this—whatever exists here: the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the meters, the sacrifices, progeny, and cattle. Whatever he created, he resolved to eat. Because he eats everything, that is the reason for Aditi’s name, Aditi. He who thus knows this nature of Aditi becomes the eater of all; everything becomes his food.

He desired, "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. From him, thus exhausted and heated by austerity, glory and vigor departed; for glory and vigor are indeed the vital breaths. When the vital breaths had departed, his body began to swell. His mind remained fixed upon that very body.

He desired: "May this [universe] be fit for sacrifice (medhya) for me; may I be endowed with a self through it. From that, the horse (aśva) came into being. Because it was fit for sacrifice (aśvat), therefore it became the sacrificial horse (aśvamedha). This indeed is the essence of the Aśvamedha for one who knows it thus. He truly knows the Aśvamedha who knows it in this way.

He did not consider it [the horse] to be confined; after a year had passed, he sacrificed it for himself and offered the other animals to the deities. They sacrificed that which was consecrated as belonging to all the deities and dedicated to Prajāpati. This indeed is the Aśvamedha: he who shines yonder (the sun). The year is his body, and this fire is the *arka* (flame); these worlds are its bodies. These two, the *arka* and the *medha*, become again a single deity—namely, Death. He conquers repeated death; death does not reach him; death becomes his own self. He attains a full lifespan and becomes one with these deities, whoever knows thus.

Now, the lineage: [it is] the same up to the son of Sāṃjīvī. The son of Sāṃjīvī [received it] from Māṇḍūkāyani; Māṇḍūkāyani from Māṇḍavya; Māṇḍavya from Kautsa; Kautsa from Māhitthi; Māhitthi from Vāmakakṣāyaṇa; Vāmakakṣāyaṇa from Vātsya; Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kuśri; Kuśri from Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana; Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana from Tura Kāvaṣeya; Tura Kāvaṣeya from Prajāpati; Prajāpati from Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent. Homage to Brahmā! The sacrifice is indeed the year, which is Prajāpati. Its door is this new moon day (amāvāsyā), and the moon itself is the bolt of the door.

He who establishes the two fires on the new moon day is like one who would enter a city through an open gate; he goes to the heavenly world from that very point—such is the case for him who establishes them on the new moon day.

Now, he who establishes the sacred fires under a lunar mansion is like one who would attempt to enter a city through a side-gate when the main gate is closed; he would be thwarted and remain outside the city. Even so it is with him who establishes the fires under a lunar mansion; therefore, one should not establish the fires under a lunar mansion.
On the day that he is seen neither in front nor behind, on that day one should fast; for on that day he comes to this world and dwells here in it.
All the gods dwell here, all beings, all deities, all seasons, all hymns, all *pṛṣṭha* chants, and all meters.

Indeed, for one who establishes the two fires on the new moon day, the two fires are established among all the gods, all beings, all deities, all seasons, all stomas, all prsthas, and all meters; therefore, one should establish the two fires only on the new moon day.

On that new moon of Vaiśākha, he should establish the fires; it coincides with Rohiṇī. Rohiṇī is indeed the self, progeny, and cattle; thus he establishes himself in the self, in progeny, and in cattle. The new moon is indeed the form of the establishment of the fires (agnyādheya); therefore, one should establish the two fires specifically on the new moon. One should perform the preliminary rite (anvārambha) on the full moon and undergo initiation (dīkṣā) on the new moon.

They indeed kill this sacrifice when they extend it; when they press the King (Soma), they kill him; when they quiet and dissect the animal, they kill it; and with the mortar and pestle, and the lower and upper grinding stones, they kill the Havis-sacrifice.

Having slain that sacrifice, he pours it as seed into Agni himself as its womb; for Agni is indeed the womb of the sacrifice, and from him it is born. He should thus bring those ten oblations to completion, for it is upon them that the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

This indeed is the sacrifice: he who blows here [the wind]. He blows as if he were one alone; yet he has entered within man and is distributed tenfold. Through these well-ordered vital breaths (*prāṇas*), he is born from the womb of Agni. This is the Virāj consisting of ten syllables; this is the perfection, this is the sacrifice.

Furthermore, there may be nine; he makes [the verses] less than that to form a Virāj for the sake of procreation, for from what is deficient these creatures are born. This is the perfection, this is the sacrifice.
Moreover, if there should be one extra [verse], it exceeds Prajāpati; this is the perfection, this is the sacrifice.
Moreover, there may even be two extra; for a pair is indeed a productive union, and thus this productive union is brought about. This is the perfection, this is the sacrifice.
Moreover, there may even be three extra [verses]; two by two they form a pair, a productive union, and that which is born is the third; this is the perfection, and this is the sacrifice.

Moreover, there may even be four extra [bricks]. For instance, as one is, so are four; or these worlds are three, and by means of three [bricks] he attains these very worlds. Prajāpati, indeed, is the fourth beyond these worlds; thus, by the fourth [brick], he attains Prajāpati himself. This is that perfection, this is the sacrifice.

If it is less than two, it is deficient and thus not a sacrifice; if it is more than five, it is redundant and thus not a sacrifice. This very [number] is for the sake of the perfection of ten; this [perfection] extends from twenty up to a thousand.

Those who sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices run a race. He should indeed sacrifice for fifteen years; in those fifteen years there are three hundred and sixty full moons and new moons. There are also three hundred and sixty nights in a year; thus he attains those nights.

Then he should sacrifice for another fifteen years; of those fifteen years there are three hundred and sixty full-moon and new-moon sacrifices, and there are indeed three hundred and sixty days in a year; thus he obtains those days, and thereby he obtains the year itself.

In the beginning, mortals indeed were the gods; as soon as they attained the year, they became immortal. The year is indeed everything, and everything is imperishable. By this, his merit becomes imperishable, and his world becomes imperishable.

He alone is the foremost among those who rush into battle who, knowing this, performs sacrifice for thirty years; therefore, one should indeed sacrifice for thirty years. However, if he should perform the Dākṣāyaṇayajña, then he may also sacrifice for fifteen years, for in that case the same perfection is attained; for he sacrifices at two full-moon festivals and two new-moon festivals, and thus indeed that perfection comes to be.

Having sacrificed with the Full Moon sacrifice, he subsequently prepares an offering for Indra Vimṛdh; he sacrifices with that in the same manner as the primary sacrifice. Having sacrificed with the New Moon sacrifice, he subsequently prepares a pap for Aditi; he sacrifices with that in the same manner as the primary sacrifice.

When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, he subsequently prepares an oblation for Indra Vimṛdh, [it is because] Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; yet, since the Full-moon oblation belongs to Agni and Soma, nothing there is done with the formula "To Indra thee! By this [subsequent offering], his oblation becomes possessed of Indra, and by this the sacrifice becomes possessed of Indra. And as to why it is for "Vimṛdh" (the Dispeller), it is because by means of the Full-moon sacrifice he slays all enemies and destroyers.

Now, as to why, after performing the New Moon sacrifice, he subsequently offers a pap to Aditi: King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, and he is the moon. When, on that night, the moon is not seen either in the east or in the west, then this oblation becomes, as it were, non-existent and lacks a firm foundation. This earth, however, is Aditi; she is manifest, and she is firmly established. By means of this [offering], his oblation thus becomes manifest and firmly established. This is the reason why he subsequently offers it; now, as to why one might not subsequently offer it.

When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, he subsequently prepares an oblation for Indra Vimṛdh, thinking, "May my sacrifice be possessed by Indra," then since the entire sacrifice belongs to Indra alone, by this means his sacrificial food becomes possessed by Indra, and by this means the sacrifice becomes possessed by Indra.

Now, as for the fact that after performing the New Moon sacrifice (*āmāvāsya*), one subsequently prepares a pap (*caru*) for Aditi: the subsequent offering (*anunirvāpya*) belongs to the New Moon. Or rather, it was on the Full Moon day that Indra slew Vṛtra; therefore, when he had slain Vṛtra, the gods prepared this oblation for him, which is the New Moon sacrifice. [The opponent asks: "Why should one prepare a subsequent offering in a subsequent offering? For that reason, one should not prepare a subsequent offering.

When, having sacrificed with the Full-moon offering, he subsequently offers another oblation, or having sacrificed with the New-moon offering, he subsequently offers another oblation, he rises up against his hateful rival. But for him who sacrifices at the Full moon with the Full-moon rite and at the New moon with the New-moon rite, his prosperity becomes free from rivals and unoppressed.

By means of the Full-moon sacrifice, the gods, sacrificing on the day of the full moon, and by means of the New-moon sacrifice, on the day of the new moon, quickly struck away evil and were quickly procreated. He who, knowing this, sacrifices on the full moon with the Full-moon sacrifice and on the new moon with the New-moon sacrifice, quickly strikes away evil and is quickly procreated. If he should perform the subsequent offering, he should give a sacrificial fee; for they say, "A sacrificial oblation must not be without a fee. Indeed, the *anvāhārya* rice is the fee for the Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices. This applies both to the subsequent offering and to the case of one for whom the moon has risen after the commencement.

Regarding this, some fast on seeing [the moon] thinking, "It will not rise tomorrow," either because of a cloud or because they have failed to recognize it; yet then it rises for them. If the oblation has not been taken when the moon rises, that is well known. The ritual practice is as follows: the milk and curd of the previous day serve as the thickening agent for the oblation; they release the calves and then drive them away again.

In the afternoon, he drives them away with a leafy branch. This is exactly like that well-known New Moon oblation. However, if he does not intend to observe the vow, or if the moon should rise when the oblation has already been taken out, then he should act otherwise: having thoroughly husked these very same rice grains, he bakes a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Dātṛ (the Giver) from those which are the smallest.

Now, that which was milked on the previous day and turned into curds is for Indra Pradātṛ; then, he cooks this rice-mash (caru) with the rice-grains just now milked for Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa, for it is indeed a caru wherever they pour in rice-grains.

Now, when this happens, it is indeed King Soma, the food of the gods, who is that moon; he has approached it and has reached it for him. Agni, the giver, gives it to him; Indra, the bestower, presents it to him. Indra and Agni give the sacrifice to him; with that sacrifice given by Indra and Agni, he performs the sacrifice. Now, as for the words "to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa": Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice. And as for "Śipiviṣṭa": that which he approached and reached is, as it were, a part of the sacrifice that has become "scattered" (śipta); therefore, [the address is] "to Śipiviṣṭa. In that regard, one should give whatever one is able to give, for they say, "A sacrificial oblation (havis) must not be without a dakṣiṇā. Then, when [the moon] does not rise, he should fast.

Thinking "Today is the new moon," he observes the fast; yet this [moon] is seen in the west. This is indeed the celestial dog; it looks upon the sacrificial animals of the sacrificer. That would be detrimental to the cattle if no expiation were performed. Therefore, out of fear of this very moon, they do this.
They approach him with this [formula]. By this they call it "the burning," and by this they call it "the dog-bitten."

The hare-marked one belongs to the moon; for Soma is indeed the moon, the food of the gods, and they press him on the full-moon day. During the dark fortnight, he enters the waters and the plants; for cattle eat the waters and the plants. Thus, on this night, he brings him together for the sake of the cattle.

Thinking, "Today is the new moon," he observes the fast; yet this [moon] is seen in the west, and thus the sacrificer departs from the path of the sacrifice. Regarding this they say: "What should he do? Should he sacrifice after departing from the path of the sacrifice, or should he not sacrifice? He should indeed sacrifice, for there is no other way out. Day after day it rises larger; having sacrificed according to the rite of the new moon, he then performs an additional offering on that very day or on the following day.

For this [sacrifice], there are three oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pathikṛt (the Maker of the Way), a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Vṛtrahan (the Slayer of Vṛtra), and a cake on twelve potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara.
When he offers to Agni Pathikṛt (the path-maker), since Agni is indeed the maker of paths, Agni provides this path for him by which the sacrificer has gone astray from the path of sacrifice.

Now, as for [the offering] to Indra Vṛtrahan: Vṛtra is indeed evil, he who stands obstructing prosperity from auspicious and righteous action; that very evil, Vṛtra, he now slays by means of Indra himself, the Vṛtrahan; therefore it is for Indra Vṛtrahan.

Now, as to why he offers a cake on twelve potsherds to Agni Vaiśvānara: when Indra slew Vṛtra, he burnt him up entirely with Agni Vaiśvānara; thus he burnt away all his evil. In the same way, this sacrificer, having slain the evil Vṛtra by means of Indra the slayer of Vṛtra, burns him up entirely with Agni Vaiśvānara; thus he burns away all his evil. Indeed, for one who, knowing this, performs this sacrifice, not even the slightest evil remains behind.

For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deities in a whisper; whichever [deities] he desires, those he makes into the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses; likewise for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and likewise for the two *saṃyājyā* verses.
He gives a bow with three arrows as the sacrificial fee; for with a bow they ward off a dog, and thus he wards this one off when he gives a bow with three arrows as the sacrificial fee.

He gives a staff as the sacrificial fee; for with a staff one drives away a dog, and so he thereby drives away this [dog]. This is indeed the prescribed sacrificial fee; however, he may also give something else in its place. Whatever other sacrificial fees there may be, let him give whatever is available among them. For this is a sacrifice pertaining to cattle; even if it has not been specifically prepared, he should certainly perform it.

In the beginning, this world was indeed only water, a mere ocean. It desired, "How might we be reproduced? They exerted themselves; they practiced austerity. While they were practicing austerity, a golden egg came into being. At that time, the year had not yet been produced. This golden egg floated about for as long as the duration of a year.

Then, after a year, a person came into being; he was Prajāpati. Therefore, it is only after a year that a woman, a cow, or a mare brings forth, for Prajāpati was born after a year. He burst open this golden egg; at that time, there was no foundation whatsoever. Supporting this very golden egg, he floated about for as long as the duration of a year.

He desired to expand after a year; he uttered "Bhūḥ," and this earth came into being; "Bhuvaḥ," and that intermediate space came into being; "Svaḥ," and yonder sky came into being. Therefore, even now a child desires to expand after a year, for it was after a year that Prajāpati uttered those words.
Indeed, when Prajāpati first spoke, he spoke only monosyllables and disyllables; therefore, a child, when speaking for the first time, speaks only monosyllables and disyllables.

Or rather, these five syllables he made into the five seasons; these are the five seasons. Thus, when these worlds had been born, Prajāpati arose within the year. Therefore, a child should rise up at the very time of the year, for Prajāpati arose at the time of the year.
He was born with a lifespan of a thousand years; just as one might see the far shore of a river, he beheld the far shore of his own life.

Worshipping and toiling, he wandered about, desiring offspring; he deposited his generative power within himself alone. With his mouth, indeed, he created the gods; those gods, having been created, reached the sky. That they were created reaching the sky—that is the godhead of the gods. For him who had created them, it was as if day had come; that it was as if day came for him who had created them—that is the godhead of the gods.
Then, with that downward breath, he created the Asuras; they were created by reaching down to this very earth. For him who had thus created them, it became as if darkness.

He thought, "I have indeed created evil for myself; for him to whom I have created it, darkness has come. He then pierced them with that very evil, and from that they perished. Therefore they say: "There is no such thing as a conflict between gods and Asuras, except what appears in narrative or in legend"; for it was from that very evil that Prajāpati pierced them, and from that they perished.

Therefore, this was declared by the seer: "You do not wish to fight on any day whatsoever; O Maghavan, you have no enemy at all. That which they call your battles is merely an illusion; today you do not wish to fight an enemy, nor indeed in the past."

When it was light for him after he had created the gods, he made that into the day; and when it was dark for him after he had created the Asuras, he made that into the night. These two became day and night.

Prajāpati reflected: "I have indeed crept (atsāriṣam) over everything, since I have created these deities. He became the year; for that which is called "saṃvatsara" is indeed "he who has crept over" (saṃ-tsara). Whoever knows thus this "year-ness" of the year—whichever evil creeps over him by means of illusion, it does not overcome him; and whoever he intends to harm, it surely comes upon him, provided he knows thus this "year-ness" of the year.

Prajāpati reflected: "I have indeed created this, the year, as an image of myself. Therefore they say, "Prajāpati is the year," for he created this as an image of himself. Moreover, the word *saṃvatsara* has four syllables, and *prajāpati* also has four syllables; thus, this is indeed his image.
Now, these deities were indeed created from Prajāpati: Agni, Indra, Soma, and Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati.
They were born with a lifespan of a thousand years; just as one might see the far shore of a river, so did they behold the far shore of their own lifespan.

They moved about, praising and toiling. Then Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati, beheld this sacrifice, namely the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa). He sacrificed with them; having sacrificed with them, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He became the waters. Indeed, the waters are all this. Because they abide in the highest place—for whoever digs here finds only water—and because it rains from that highest place, namely from the sky, therefore he is named Parameṣṭhin.

That Parameṣṭhin said to his father Prajāpati, "I have seen a sacrifice that fulfills all desires; with it, I shall cause you to sacrifice. "So be it," he replied. He caused him to sacrifice. Having sacrificed, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He became the vital breath (prāṇa). Verily, this whole world is the vital breath. This vital breath is indeed he who blows here; he is Prajāpati. His vision is this: "Whatever one knows, it blows thus. Whatever breathes, that is Prajāpati. Whoever knows this vision of Prajāpati thus, he truly becomes manifest.

That Prajāpati said to his son Indra, "Let me cause you to sacrifice with this wish-fulfilling sacrifice, with which Parameṣṭhin sacrificed for me here. "So be it," he replied. He caused him to sacrifice. Having sacrificed, he desired, "May I alone be all this. He became Speech; for Speech indeed is all this. Therefore they say, "Indra is Speech."

Indra said to his two brothers, Agni and Soma, "Let me perform for you both this sacrifice which fulfills all desires—the very same with which my father Prajāpati sacrificed for me. They replied, "So be it," and he performed the sacrifice for them. Having sacrificed, they both desired, "May we become this entire universe. Of the two, one became the eater of food and the other became the food; Agni became the eater of food and Soma became the food. Indeed, this entire world is both the eater of food and the food.

These same five deities sacrificed with this sacrifice that fulfills desires. Whatever desire they had when they sacrificed, that desire was fulfilled for them. Indeed, whatever desire one sacrifices with this sacrifice, that desire is fulfilled for him.

Having sacrificed, they beheld the eastern quarter; they made it the eastern one, and thus this quarter is indeed the east. Therefore these creatures creep along toward the east, for they made that [quarter] the east. "Let us make it come hither," they said; they made it into *ūrj* (nourishment), thinking, "May we behold this *ūrj*. That became yonder sky.

Then they looked toward the southern direction and made it the Dakṣiṇā (the sacrificial gift). That is why this direction is called the Dakṣiṇā; therefore, from the south alone the sacrificial gifts are presented, and from the south they drive [the victim] forward, for they made this the Dakṣiṇā. "Let us make another one from here," they said, and they made that world. "Let us see this world indeed," they said, and it became this intermediate space (antarikṣa). This is indeed that world. Just as this earth is a manifest support in this world, even so this intermediate space is a manifest support in that world. Because one who is here does not see that world, therefore they say, "That world is beyond the eye" (parokṣa).

Then they saw the western quarter; they made it their hope (*āśā*). Therefore, when one finds something after going eastward, he goes toward that very quarter, for they made it their hope, thinking, "Let us make this one [our] hope from here. They made it prosperity (*śrī*); they thought, "May we behold this prosperity. That became this earth. This earth is indeed prosperity; therefore, whoever obtains the most from her becomes the most excellent.

Then they looked toward the northern direction and made it water, thinking, "Let us make it favorable for us from here. They established that as *dharma*; for water is indeed *dharma*. Therefore, whenever water comes to this world, everything here becomes exactly according to *dharma*. Moreover, when there is drought, the stronger then seizes the weaker; for water is *dharma*.
Now, these indeed are the eleven deities: the five fore-offerings (prayāja), the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga), the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, and the three after-offerings (anuyāja).

These are the eleven oblations; by these oblations, indeed, the gods conquered these worlds and these quarters; and in the same way, this sacrificer conquers these worlds and these quarters by means of these oblations.

The intermediate quarters are those same four Patnīsaṃyāja offerings; for the gods won the intermediate quarters with the four Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, and so does he win the intermediate quarters by means of these.
By means of this Iḍā, the gods indeed conquered food; in the same way, he too conquers food by means of this. This, then, is the perfection regarding the deities in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
Now, with reference to the self: these five vital breaths in a person, excluding the two eyes, are themselves the five fore-offerings (prayāja); the two eyes are the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga).

This downward breath is indeed the Sviṣṭakṛt. Because he offers it as if it were inferior to the other oblations, therefore all the vital breaths recoil from this breath. And because he cuts portions for the Sviṣṭakṛt from all the sacrificial offerings, therefore whatever comes upon these vital breaths, all that converges into this very one.

There are three phalli, and they are those same three after-offerings (anuyāja). That which is the longest after-offering is like this longest phallus. Regarding it, they say: "One should sacrifice without drawing breath"; for thus does this [act] of his become unfailing.

He should indeed strike it once, for this has but one joint; and as for that which is jointless, it either stands with its stalk cut through or it hangs down. Therefore, this [tree] both stands high and falls; therefore he should strike it only once.

The two arms and the two thighs—those are four; the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings are the foundation. This breath here is the *iḍā*; because he does not offer it into the fire, and because it is as if not burnt, therefore this breath is unobstructed.

The invitatory and offering verses (*yājyā-anuvākyā*) are indeed the bones, and the oblation (*havis*) is the flesh; this is measured by the metre. Since the invitatory and offering verses are [of fixed length], therefore the bones remain the same in both the fat person and the lean person. But since he takes up the oblation both more and less, therefore the flesh of the fat person becomes fat, and the flesh of the lean person becomes lean. By means of this sacrifice, one worships whichever deity one desires, for whomsoever there is an oblation.

These, indeed, are the oblations that are not to be omitted. For if one were to omit any of these, it would be as if he were to crush a limb or extract the vital breath; thus, other oblations are indeed brought forward and taken away.
Now, these indeed are sixteen oblations; for man consists of sixteen parts, and the sacrifice is man; therefore there are sixteen oblations.

Regarding that, they establish this rule for the undertaking of the vow: "If he does not eat, he belongs to the ancestors; if he eats, he eats beyond the gods. Therefore, one should eat forest-food; thus they settle it.

If he eats cultivated plants, he eats the essence of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa); if he eats wild plants, he eats the essence of the sacrificial grass (barhis); if he eats anything from a tree, he eats the essence of the fuel-wood (idhma); if he drinks milk, he eats the essence of the Sāṃnāyya offering and the clarified butter (ājya); if he drinks water, he eats the essence of the consecrated waters (praṇītāḥ); if he does not eat at all, he becomes one whose deity is the ancestors (pitṛdevatya).

Regarding this they say: "What is its support?
