One should indeed perform the Agnihotra oneself during these nights; for when he eats after having offered, by that he becomes one whose deity is the Pitṛs. This [eating] is indeed an oblation; and because he offers this oblation within himself, he does not eat of those sacrificial portions.

Indeed, all nights converge in these [two] nights: all the nights of the waxing fortnight converge in the full-moon night, and all the nights of the waning fortnight converge in the new-moon night. He who, knowing this, himself offers the oblation on the fast-day—verily, for him it is as if he has always offered the oblation himself.

The gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another. Then the Asuras, through sheer arrogance, asked, "In whom indeed shall we offer oblations? and they proceeded offering oblations into their own mouths. Through that very arrogance, they were utterly defeated. Therefore, one should not be arrogant; for arrogance is the very gateway to defeat.
Then the gods went about offering oblations into one another; to them Prajāpati gave himself. Sacrifice was theirs, for sacrifice is indeed the food of the gods.
Having offered himself to the gods, he then created this image of himself, namely the sacrifice; therefore they say, "Prajāpati is the sacrifice," for he created this as an image of himself.

By means of this sacrifice, he ransomed himself from the gods. When he undertakes the vow, just as Prajāpati then delivered himself to the gods, even so does he now deliver himself to the gods. Therefore, he should conduct himself with self-restraint during that night, just as one would conduct oneself with the sacrificial oblation; for he becomes the oblation for the gods.

Now, when he performs the sacrifice, it is by means of the sacrifice itself that he ransoms himself from the gods, just as Prajāpati ransomed himself; and when he offers the oblation, it is by means of the oblation that he ransoms the sacrifice: the oblation by the invitatory verse, the invitatory verse by the portioning-off, the portioning-off by the offering-verse, the offering-verse by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, and the *vaṣaṭ*-call by the libation. Of this, the libation alone remains unransomed.

Just as a tree that has been broken off at the top, so does his sacrifice become; he redeems the oblation by means of the *anvāhārya* (the guest-offering). Because he brings back (*anvāharati*) what was deficient in the sacrifice, it is called *anvāhārya*. Thus, indeed, his entire sacrifice becomes redeemed. This sacrifice, indeed, becomes the self of the sacrificer in yonder world; and the sacrificer who, knowing this, performs the sacrifice with the redemption, is reborn in yonder world with his whole body intact.

Indeed, a man is born thrice. First, he is born from his mother and father; then, when the sacrifice comes to him and he performs it, he is born for the second time; and when he dies, and they place him upon the fire, and he arises therefrom, he is born for the third time. Therefore, they say that a man is born thrice.

He recites these eleven *sāmidhenī* verses; for there are ten vital breaths in man and the self is the eleventh, in which these breaths are established. Man is indeed of such a measure; thus he generates him in his entirety. Now, that which follows the *sāmidhenīs* is the foundation; having generated him, he thereby establishes him upon that foundation.

There are nine utterances for the new-born; there are nine vital breaths in man. Thus he causes him to be born a second time. The *āśrāvaṇa* and the *pratyāśrāvaṇa* are its foundation. Then, that which is declared as the birth at the creation, by that he causes him to be born a third time; the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings themselves are the foundation therein.

For a man is indeed born thrice; in this very way, he thus causes him to be born thrice from the sacrifice. Of those eleven [verses], he recites the first one three times and the last one three times.

These are the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; two *āghāra* libations; five *prayāja* offerings; the *iḍā*; three *anuyāja* offerings; the *sūktavāka*; and the *śamyorvāka*—these constitute thirteen oblations. Then there is that which one takes up together during the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings, and the *samiṣṭayajus*.

These are the fifteen oblations; for these fifteen oblations, these are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*); these fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses are the invitatory verses for these [oblations], and these are the offering verses (*yājyā*) for those invitatory verses. Whatever mantra there is here, whatever *nigada*, that is the form of the offering verse. By this, indeed, his oblations become possessed of invitatory verses; by means of these *sāmidhenīs* and these oblations, these invitatory verses become possessed of offering verses and possessed of oblations.
He recites the Gāyatrī as the invitatory verse (anuvākyā). The Gāyatrī indeed has three feet; these worlds are three. Thus, the gods established these very worlds.
Then he sacrifices with a Triṣṭubh verse; for the Triṣṭubh has four feet, and cattle have four feet: thus the gods established cattle in these worlds which were already firmly established.
The *vaṣaṭ*-call consists of two syllables; man, indeed, has two feet. Thus they established that two-footed man upon these four-footed animals as their firm foundation.

This very man is two-footed and established among the cattle; in this very way, he establishes these worlds. When the worlds are established, he establishes the cattle; when the cattle are established, he establishes himself. Thus, this man is established among the cattle—he who, knowing thus, performs the sacrifice.

Now, when he offers at the *vaṣaṭ*-call—this *vaṣaṭ*-call is indeed that which shines yonder; it is Death. Thus he prepares him beyond Death, and thereby he causes him to be born from that [Death]. He is thus released from that Death. For the sacrifice becomes his self; having become the sacrifice itself, he is thereby released from that Death. And by this, all his sacrificial rites are likewise released from that Death.

Now, this oblation which he offers—this indeed becomes his self in yonder world. When one who knows this departs from this world, then this oblation calls out to him from behind, saying, "Come! I am indeed your self here. Because it calls out (*āhvayati*), it is therefore called an *āhuti* (oblation).

In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman; it created the gods. Having created the gods, it caused them to ascend into these worlds: Agni into this very world, Vāyu into the intermediate space, and Sūrya into the sky.

Then, as for those worlds which are above this one, and those deities who are above these, he caused those deities to ascend into those worlds. Just as these worlds here are manifest and these deities are manifest, even so were those worlds manifest and those deities manifest in which he caused those deities to ascend.

Then Brahman itself went to the further shore. Having gone to that further shore, it looked about, thinking: "How indeed might I re-descend into these worlds? It re-descended by means of two things alone: by form and by name. Whatever has a name, that is "name"; and even that which has no name, whatever one knows by its form as "this is its form," that is "form. This world consists of just this much: namely, form and name.
These two indeed are the great powers of Brahman; he who knows these two great powers of Brahman truly becomes a great power himself.

These two are the great wonders of Brahman. He who knows these two great wonders of Brahman becomes indeed a great wonder himself. Of these two, form is the greater; for even that which is called "name" is truly form. He who knows the greater of these two becomes greater than he from whom he desires to be greater.

In the beginning, mortals indeed were the gods. When they attained the Brahman, then they became immortal. That which he pours out with the mind—mind is indeed form, for by the mind one knows, "This is form"; through that he obtains form. And that which he pours out with speech—speech is indeed name, for by speech one utters a name; through that he obtains name. Now, this whole world is as much as form and name; he obtains all that. All is indeed imperishable; by this, his well-done deed becomes imperishable, and his world becomes imperishable.

Now, this very thing is performed when the oblation is offered with a verse addressed to Agni: just as the sacrifice became pleasing to the Ṛṣis, so they performed it; while they were performing that sacrifice, the Gandharvas approached them and began to point out their mistakes, saying, "In this part you have exceeded," or "In this part you have made a deficiency. When their sacrifice was completed, they then showed them those points, saying, "In this part you have indeed exceeded," or "In this part you have made a deficiency."
Whatever they made excessive, that became like mountains; whatever they made deficient, that became like chasms and fissures.

When he pronounces the *śamyor* formula, he touches [the altar] with: "O Sacrifice, homage to thee! And do thou rest in the auspiciousness of the sacrifice; rest in my well-offered [sacrifice]. Whatever he makes redundant, he pacifies that by means of the word "homage" (*namaḥ*). And whatever he makes deficient, by the word "and" (*ca*) it becomes no longer deficient. With "rest in the auspiciousness of the sacrifice," he pacifies both those things, for whatever in the sacrifice is neither deficient nor redundant, that is auspicious (*śiva*). With "rest in my well-offered [sacrifice]," he pacifies both those things, for whatever in the sacrifice is neither deficient nor redundant, that is well-offered (*sviṣṭa*). Thus, for one who knows this and touches it in this way, his sacrifice becomes performed as neither deficient nor redundant. Therefore, one should touch it in this very manner. Now, those Gandharvas were Śūrpa, Yavamān, Kṛṣi, Udvalin, Dhāna, and Antarin.
This indeed is the Full Moon who shines yonder; for day after day he is indeed full. And this very one is the New Moon, namely the moon; for he is, as it were, visible (dṛś).

Moreover, they say otherwise: the moon itself is the full-moon day, for after its filling, people call it "Paurṇamāsī" (the Full-Moon Day); and this very sun that shines is the new-moon day, for he is, as it were, seen [only at the beginning of the dark fortnight].
This [earth] alone is the full moon, for she is indeed full; that [sky] alone is the new moon, for that sky is, as it were, visible.

The night indeed is the full moon, for this night is as if full; the day indeed is the new moon, for this day is as if seen [at the beginning]. This, then, is the investigation of the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices from the perspective of the gods.

Now, with reference to the self: the *udāna* breath is indeed the Full Moon (*pūrṇamās*), for by the *udāna* this person is, as it were, filled; the *prāṇa* breath is indeed the New Moon (*darśa*), for this *prāṇa* is, as it were, seen. Thus, these two—the consumer of food and the giver of food—are the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

The out-breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the eater of food, for by means of the out-breath this food is eaten; the up-breath (*udāna*) is indeed the giver of food, for by means of the up-breath this food is given. He who knows these two—the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices—as the eater of food and the giver of food, becomes truly an eater of food, and food is indeed bestowed upon him.

The mind alone is the Full Moon sacrifice (*pūrṇamāsa*), for this mind is, as it were, full; speech alone is the New Moon sacrifice (*darśa*), for this speech is, as it were, seen (*dadarśa*). Thus, these two—the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa—are directly perceived within the self (*adhyātma*). When, on the day of preparation (*upavasatha*), one eats the food that introduces the vow (*vratopāyanīya*), by that he gratifies these two directly perceived [sacrifices] within the self; and by means of the sacrifice, he gratifies the two divine [sacrifices] in the morning.

Regarding this they say: "Since no oblation is taken saying, 'For the Full Moon,' nor is an oblation taken saying, 'For the New Moon'; since one does not say, 'Recite for the Full Moon,' nor 'Recite for the New Moon'; and since one does not say, 'Sacrifice to the Full Moon,' nor 'Sacrifice to the New Moon'—then by what means do his Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices become performed? That which he pours as an Āghāra-libation with the mind—for the mind is the Full Moon—he thereby sacrifices to the Full Moon. And that which he pours as an Āghāra-libation with speech—for speech is the New Moon—he thereby sacrifices to the New Moon. By this, indeed, his Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices become performed.

Regarding this, some offer two *caru* oblations—one to Sarasvant on the full moon day and one to Sarasvatī on the new moon day—saying, "In this way, we perform the New and Full Moon sacrifices visibly. However, one should not do so; for Sarasvant is indeed Mind and Sarasvatī is Speech. When he pours these two libations (*āghāra*), it is precisely through that that his New and Full Moon sacrifices become performed. Therefore, he should not offer these two *caru* oblations.

Regarding this they say: "He who sacrifices with the New and Full Moon sacrifices becomes one who has made a formal vow (āgūrtin). For having sacrificed with the Full Moon sacrifice, he knows, 'I shall sacrifice with the New Moon sacrifice'; and having sacrificed with the New Moon sacrifice, he knows, 'I shall sacrifice again with the Full Moon sacrifice. Thus, by means of his vow alone, he goes to that world. When he goes to that world, how does he become one who has not made a vow? It is because when he pours the two libations (āghāra) on both occasions, thereby his New and Full Moon sacrifices are completed. Since he goes to that world only after the New and Full Moon sacrifices have been completed, in this way he becomes one who has not made a vow."

Even now they offer the horse-sacrifice to the gods; regarding this, they say, "The other [sacrifices] are merely the ordinary horse-sacrifice. But indeed, that which is the moon is truly this very horse-sacrifice.

Regarding this they say: "At every step one offers an oblation of the sacrificial horse. When he performs the Agnihotra in the evening and in the morning, he offers two oblations in the evening and two in the morning; these make four oblations. Now, the horse is four-footed; thus, at every single step of his, an oblation is offered for him.

Regarding this they say: "When the horse has turned back, one performs the sacrifice. This King Soma is indeed the food of the gods, namely the moon. When, on that night, he is seen neither in the east nor in the west, then he comes to this world; he turns back in this world.

When he sacrifices with the New-moon offering, he prepares this sacrifice for him as one that has already turned away; and when he sacrifices with the Full-moon offering, he thereby immolates the Ashvamedha and, having immolated it, offers it to the gods. For they immolate the other Ashvamedha after a year; but this month, revolving, makes up the year. Thus, for him, the Ashvamedha becomes immolated year after year.

Indeed, they sacrifice this very Aśvamedha month after month. For whoever, knowing thus, offers the Agnihotra and performs the New and Full Moon sacrifices, his Aśvamedha is indeed sacrificed month after month; for his Agnihotra and the New and Full Moon sacrifices thus culminate in the Aśvamedha.

The *praṇītā* waters are indeed the head of the sacrifice; when he brings forward the *praṇītā* waters, he thereby prepares the head of the sacrifice. He should know: "My head is being prepared here."
The vital breath alone is its fuel, for by the vital breath all this is kindled—whatever breathes, whatever blinks, and whatever moves. He should know: "I am indeed this fuel."

The *sāmidhenī* verses follow his sequence; therefore, he should say to them, "Recite for me as if continuously," for this sequence is indeed continuous. His mind and speech are the two *āghāra* libations—Sarasvant and Sarasvatī. He should know: "My mind and speech are the two *āghāra* libations—Sarasvant and Sarasvatī."

The five fore-offerings (prayāja) are these very five vital breaths in his head. His first fore-offering is the mouth; the second is the right nostril; the third is the left nostril; the fourth is the right ear; and the fifth is the left ear. Now, because he pours together [the butter] at the fourth fore-offering, therefore this hearing is covered within by a membrane. The two eyes are the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga). He should know: "These two are indeed my eyes."
Now, that cake for Agni is his right side; the low-voiced offering (upāṃśuyāja) is his heart, and because they perform it in a low voice, this heart is as if hidden.
Now, that cake for Agni and Soma is its northern half; or, if it is the Sāṃnāyya offering for Indra, that is its middle portion; the Sviṣṭakṛt is its poison, and the Prāśitra is its bile.

When he cuts off the *prāśitra* portion, it is just as they cut away what was pierced in Prajāpati; even so, they cut away from him that which is wrapped, that which is knotted, and that which belongs to Varuṇa. He should know: "Just as they cut away what was pierced in Prajāpati, even so do they now cut away from me this which is wrapped, this which is knotted, and this which belongs to Varuṇa."
The belly itself is his *iḍā*; just as they cut portions together into the *iḍā* here, even so this food of all forms is gathered together within the belly.

There are three after-offerings (*anuyāja*); these are his three downward breaths. His two arms are the *sūktavāka* and the *śamyorvāka*. There are four offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*); for there are four supports: the two thighs and the two knee-caps. His *samisṭayajus* is the two fore-feet.

Those are twenty-one oblations: two Āghāra-libations, five Prayāja-offerings, two Ājyabhāga-portions, and the cake for Agni—that makes ten; then the Upāṃśuyāja for Agni-Soma, the cake for Agni-Soma, Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the Iḍā, three Anuyāja-offerings, the Sūktavāka, and the Śamyorvāka; and then that which he takes up together during the Patnīsaṃyāja-offerings, as well as the Samiṣṭayajus.

These are twenty-one oblations. There are twelve months in a year, five seasons, and three worlds—that makes twenty; and this one who shines yonder is the twenty-first. This is the goal, this is the foundation; he thus goes to that goal, to that foundation.
Regarding this, Āruṇi indeed said: "Month by month, I become co-resident with that sun; I know that perfection of the New and Full Moon sacrifices."

Regarding this they say: "Is the self-sacrificer (ātmayājī) better, or the god-sacrificer (devayājī)? One should say, "The self-sacrificer. Now, he is indeed a self-sacrificer who knows: "By this [offering], this limb of mine is being refined; by this, this limb of mine is being established. Just as a snake might cast off its skin, even so is he released from this mortal body, from evil. Consisting of the *Ṛg*, consisting of the *Yajuṣ*, consisting of the *Sāman*, and consisting of oblations, he attains the heavenly world.

Now, he is indeed a worshiper of the gods who knows: "I am sacrificing here to the gods alone; I am serving the gods. He is like one who, being inferior, brings tribute to a superior, or like a Vaiśya bringing tribute to a king. He does not win as great a world as the other does.

The year is the sacrifice. Verily, for him who knows that "the year is the sacrifice," his sacrifice is performed within this very year; moreover, whatever is done during the year, all of that becomes attained, secured, and won by him.

The seasons are the officiating priests. He who knows that "the seasons are the officiating priests" indeed has his sacrifice performed by the seasons at its conclusion; moreover, whatever is performed during the seasons, all of that becomes attained, secured, and won for him.

"The months are the oblations. He who knows that "the months are the oblations" has his sacrifice performed within the months; moreover, whatever is done during the months, all of that becomes obtained, secured, and conquered for him.

The half-months are the vessels for the oblations. Verily, he who knows that "the half-months are the vessels for the oblations" has his offerings successfully completed within the half-months; moreover, whatever is performed during the half-months, all of that becomes attained, secured, and conquered by him.

Day and night are his attendants. Verily, he who knows that day and night are his attendants—within those very days and nights his sacrifice becomes established; moreover, whatever is performed during the day and night, all of that becomes attained, secured, and won by him.

This [earth] is the first *sāmidhenī*, Agni the second, Vāyu the third, the intermediate space the fourth, the sky the fifth, Āditya the sixth, the moon the seventh, the mind the eighth, speech the ninth, austerity the tenth, and the Brahman the eleventh. For these indeed kindle all this; by means of these all this is kindled. Therefore they are called *sāmidhenīs*.

He indeed recites the first verse three times. In that he recites it the first time, he thereby conquers the eastern quarter; in that he recites it the second time, he thereby conquers the southern quarter; and in that he recites it the third time, he thereby conquers the upward quarter.

He recites the last verse three times. In that he recites it for the first time, he thereby conquers the western quarter; in that he recites it for the second time, he thereby conquers the northern quarter; in that he recites it for the third time, he thereby conquers this very earth as his foundation. Thus indeed, by means of these [verses], he conquers these worlds and these quarters.
The first libation is indeed *ṛta*, and the latter is *satya*; verily, he wins both *ṛta* and *satya*. Moreover, whatever is to be won through *ṛta* and *satya*, all that he surely wins.
Radiance is the first fore-offering, honor the second, glory the third, spiritual luster the fourth, and food the fifth.

He should consecrate the first fore-offering with, "May I be full of brilliance"; the second with, "May I be full of honor"; the third with, "May I be glorious"; the fourth with, "May I be endowed with spiritual luster"; and the fifth with, "May I be an eater of food. Indeed, he who knows this thus becomes full of brilliance, full of honor, glorious, endowed with spiritual luster, and an eater of food.
Knowing this, Śvetaketu Āruṇeya indeed said: "Who, indeed, among future generations would desire to see a great serpent-like winding course, if they knew this glory of the Prayāja offerings?"

The first butter-portion (ājyabhāga) is indeed the past, and the latter is the future; verily, he wins both the past and the future. Moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the past and the future, all that he wins.

The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to Brahmā-Agni; he who knows that "the sacrificial cake belongs to Brahmā-Agni" indeed encompasses Brahmā, and whatever is to be won by means of Brahmā, all that he wins.

The *upāṃśuyāja* is the ruling power (*kṣatra*). Verily, he who knows that "the *upāṃśuyāja* is the ruling power" secures for himself the ruling power; moreover, whatever is to be won by the ruling power, all that he wins. Now, as to why some perform the *upāṃśuyāja* while others do not: therefore they announce it both loudly and in a whisper for the sake of the ruling power.

The cake for Agni is the superior one. Verily, he who knows that "the cake for Agni is the superior one" secures the people; moreover, whatever is to be won by the people, all that he indeed wins. Now, because the cake for Agni and the low-voiced offering (upāṃśuyāja) come first, therefore both the spiritual power (brahman) and the ruling power (kṣatra) are established upon the people.

The *sāṃnāyya* offering is the kingdom. He who knows that "the *sāṃnāyya* is the kingdom" indeed secures the kingdom for himself; moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the kingdom, all that he wins. Now, as to why some perform the *saṃnayana* (the mixing of the milk) while others do not: therefore the kingdom both unites and disperses.
Austerity is the Sviṣṭakṛt. He who knows that "austerity is the Sviṣṭakṛt" indeed secures austerity for himself; moreover, whatever is to be won by austerity, all that he wins.

The world is the *prāśitra*. He who knows that "the world is the *prāśitra*" indeed secures the world; moreover, whatever is to be won by means of the world, all that he wins. He does not suffer from the world because of a fragment (*lava*); for indeed, in yonder world, people suffer from the world because of a fragment. But he who knows thus does not suffer from the world even after having committed much evil.
"Śraddheḍā. He who knows that [name] as "Śraddheḍā" indeed gains faith; moreover, whatever is to be won through faith, all that he wins.
The first after-offering is the thunderbolt itself; the second is the hailstone; the third is the meteor.

He should consecrate the first after-sacrifice with, "O lightning, strike so-and-so! [naming] whomsoever he hates; the second with, "O hail-stone, strike so-and-so!"; and the third with, "O firebrand, strike so-and-so!"

Whosoever dies suddenly, him the Anuyāja called Aśani strikes; whosoever dies as if mixed with flowing blood, him the Anuyāja called Hrāduni strikes; and whosoever dies as if mixed with smoke, him the Anuyāja called Ulkuṣī strikes.

This is indeed the weapon of the sacrifice; by this very weapon the gods brought about the defeat of the Asuras. In the same way, a sacrificer who knows this brings about the defeat of his evil, hateful rival.

If that sacrifice were to end with the after-offerings (anuyāja), it would end with a thunderbolt, it would end with hailstones, or it would end with a portent; therefore, the sacrifice of the gods ends either with the *iḍā* or with the *śamyu*.

By means of the *prayāja* offerings, the gods went to the heavenly world; the Asuras pursued them, but they repelled them with the *anuyāja* offerings. Therefore, when the *anuyāja* offerings are performed, the sacrificer repels his hateful enemy and adversary.

The *prayāja* offerings are indeed the out-breaths (*prāṇa*), and the *anuyāja* offerings are the in-breaths (*apāna*). Therefore, the *prayāja*s are offered facing forward, for that is the form of the out-breath; the *anuyāja*s are offered facing backward, for that is the form of the in-breath. These *anuyāja*s are indeed the *upasads* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices; therefore, they are offered facing backward in the form of the *upasads*.

The *sūktavāka* is the completion (*saṃsthā*). Verily, he who knows that "the *sūktavāka* is the completion" secures the completion; moreover, whatever is to be won by the completion, all that indeed he wins, and he reaches the end of his life.

The *śamyorvāk* is the foundation. He who knows that "the *śamyorvāk* is the foundation" indeed secures the foundation; moreover, whatever is to be won by means of a foundation, all that he wins, and he goes to the foundation.

Those gods performed these Patnīsaṃyāja offerings behind them; they thus placed a pair above for the sake of procreation. In that the Patnīsaṃyājas are offered, he places a pair above for the sake of procreation. Verily, one is born after the procreation of the gods; he who knows this is born through pair after pair.
Food is the Samiṣṭayajus. He who knows that food is the Samiṣṭayajus indeed secures food for himself; moreover, whatever is to be won by means of food, all that he wins.

The year is the sacrificer; the seasons perform the sacrifice for him. Spring is the Āgnīdhra; therefore, forest fires rage in spring, for that is the form of Agni. Summer is the Adhvaryu; summer is indeed as if heated, and the Adhvaryu steps forth as if heated. The rainy season is the Udgātṛ; therefore, when it rains heavily, it is like the rhythmic beating of a Sāman. Autumn is the Brahman; therefore, when the grain ripens, people say, "The creatures possess the Brahman. Winter is the Hotṛ; therefore, in winter, animals sit still after the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered. These deities indeed perform the sacrifice for him. If those who are not skilled in the *iṣṭi* should perform the sacrifice for him, he should meditate mentally upon these very deities; these deities then perform the sacrifice for him.

Now, this very southern edge of the altar is the scale. Whatever one does that is good, that is within the altar; and whatever one does that is not good, that is outside the altar. Therefore, one should sit as if merely touching the southern edge of the altar. For they place [the burden] on the scale in yonder world, and it will follow whichever side it inclines toward—whether it be the good or the evil. But he who knows thus mounts the scale even in this world, and he is released from the weighing in yonder world. Indeed, his good deed carries him across, but his evil deed does not.

Speech, indeed, is the Agnihotra-cow of this Agnihotra, and the mind is the calf. Thus, this mind and speech, while being the same, are yet distinct; therefore, they tie both the calf and the mother with the same rope. Faith is its brilliance, and truth is its clarified butter.
Janaka Vaideha then asked Yājñavalkya: "Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya? "I know it, O Emperor," he replied. "What is it? "Milk alone."

"If there were no milk, with what would one offer? "With rice and barley. "If there were no rice and barley, with what would one offer? "With whatever other herbs there are. "If there were no other herbs, with what would one offer? "With whatever wild herbs there are. "If there were no forest herbs, with what would one offer? "With water. "If there were no water, with what would one offer?"

He said, "In that case, there was indeed nothing here at all; rather, this was merely being blown away as truth within faith. "Do you know the Agnihotra, Yājñavalkya? he asked. "I give you a hundred cows," he replied.

Regarding this, there are these verses: "How indeed does the learned Agnihotrin dwell away from his home? How is his poetic wisdom maintained? How is he continuously connected with the fires? How is it that he remains as one who has not gone abroad?"—this is precisely what [the text] expresses.

"He who is the swiftest among beings—he, the knowing one, finds it while wandering; such is his poetic power, such is his continuity through the fires"—this he says regarding the mind; for by means of the mind alone, his [sacrifice] remains as if not gone away.

"When he has gone far away and then becomes heedless there—into what does his offered oblation enter, which they offer in his house?"—by this he means: "When he has gone far away and then becomes heedless there, into what does that oblation of his become offered? //

"He who is awake among all beings, he who supported all that is born—in him is this oblation of his offered, which they offer in his house. By this, he speaks of the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, they say: "The vital breath itself is the Agnihotra."

Whosoever indeed knows the six pairs in the Agnihotra, he is procreated through pair after pair with all forms of progeny—both the sacrificer and his wife. That is one pair; therefore, his Agnihotra should have a wife, thinking, "May I obtain this pair. The calf and the Agnihotra-cow are one pair; therefore, his Agnihotra-cow should have a male calf, thinking, "May I obtain this pair. The pot and the embers are one pair; the offering-spoon and the dipping-spoon are one pair; the Āhavanīya fire and the fuel-stick are one pair; the oblation and the utterance *svāhā* are one pair. These, indeed, are the six pairs in the Agnihotra. He who knows them thus is procreated through pair after pair with all forms of progeny.

Brahman indeed delivered the creatures to Death; he did not, however, deliver the religious student (brahmacārin) to him. He [Death] said, "Let there be for me also a share in this. [Brahman replied], "On whichever night the student does not bring fuel, on that [night] he dwells having cut off a portion of his own life-span. Therefore, a religious student should bring fuel, lest he dwell having cut off a portion of his life-span."

He who enters upon the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) enters upon a long sacrificial session (dīrghasattra). The fuel-stick he places on the fire when entering is the introductory offering (prāyaṇīyā); that which he places when about to bathe is the concluding offering (udayanīyā); and those which are placed in between are his sacrificial sessions. Thus does a Brahmin enter upon the life of a religious student.
He enters the elements in four ways: with one foot into fire, with one foot into death, with one foot into the teacher; his fourth foot remains within himself alone.
When he brings a fuel-stick for Agni, he thereby ransoms that very foot of his which is in Agni; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he makes himself as it were poor and begs with shamelessness, he thereby ransoms that very foot of his which is in Death; having consecrated it, he places it within himself, and it enters him.

Now, when he carries out the word of the teacher and performs service for the teacher, he thereby purchases that very foot of his which is in the teacher; having consecrated it, he bestows it upon him, and it enters into him.

"One should certainly not beg after having bathed; for by begging after having bathed, one conquers water, and conquers the hunger of kinsmen and the hunger of ancestors. Regarding this, they say: 'He who knows thus should beg from whichever woman he considers most praiseworthy; that is conducive to the world. If he should not find another woman from whom to beg, he may even beg from his own teacher’s wife, or even from his own mother. Let no seventh night pass for him without having begged. All the Vedas enter him who knows thus and conducts himself in this manner. Just as a fire blazes when well-kindled, even so does he who knows thus and practices studentship (brahmacarya) shine forth after having bathed."

Uddālaka Āruṇi, having been chosen by the northerners, acted as their *dhāvaka* (runner). A gold coin (*niṣka*) had been placed upon him; for this was indeed the practice among the ancient *dhāvaka*s who were chosen: they would have a single prize (*ekadhana*) placed upon them out of fear of being challenged. Fear seized those Brahmins of the north.

"This Brahmin here, the son of a Brahmin, belongs to the Kuru-Pañcāla people; if he does not yield half [the kingdom] to us, come, let us challenge him to a theological debate (brahmodya). "With which hero? "With Svaidāyana. Now, Śaunaka was indeed Svaidāyana.

They said, "O Svaidāyana, let us fight this man with you as our hero. He replied, "Stay here for now; let me first find out who he is. He approached him, and as he had approached, he called out, "Svaidāyana! The other responded, "Yes, O son of Gautama! Thereupon, he resolved to question him right then and there.

"O son of Gautama, he alone should be chosen to drive the people who knows the eight ājyabhāga offerings of the New and Full Moon sacrifices: five in the middle as the havis-portions, six for Prajāpati, and eight above as the ājyabhāga offerings."

O son of Gautama, he alone is fit to drive the people [in the sacrificial procession] who knows this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why these offspring are born without teeth; why they are born [with teeth]; why their teeth fall out; why they stand firm again; why in the final stage of life all of them fall out once more; why the lower teeth are born first and then the upper; why the lower teeth are smaller and the upper are broader; why the canines are larger; and why the molars are equal in size.

O son of Gautama, he alone should be chosen to drive the people who knows this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices: why these offspring are born with hair; why their beards, armpits, and private parts grow again as it were; and why one first becomes grey on the head, and later, in the final stage of life, becomes grey all over.

O son of Gautama, he who knows this regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices may indeed drive away the people; for he knows why the seed of a boy, once emitted, does not come to fruition; why it comes to fruition in his middle age; and why it no longer comes to fruition in his final age.

"He who knows the golden Gāyatrī, whose wings are light, which carries the sacrificer to the heavenly world—to him he gave a gold coin, saying, 'You are a learned man, O Svaidāyana; indeed, one who knows the true gold gives gold. Having hidden it away, he went out. They asked him, 'What had become of this son of Gautama?'"

He said, "If anyone were to revile you, O Brahmin, son of a Brahmin, his head would surely fall off. Thereupon they departed from that very place. Then, carrying fuel in his hand, he returned to him and said, "I wish to come to you as a pupil. [The other asked], "What do you intend to study? [Śvetaketu replied], "Explain to me those very questions which you asked me. He said, "I shall explain these to you even though you have not yet been initiated."

Therefore, he said this to him: "There are two Āghāra-libations, five Prayāja-offerings, and the butter-portion for Agni as the eighth; these are the eight butter-portions at the beginning. The butter-portion for Soma is the first of the oblation-portions, for Soma is indeed an oblation. The cake for Agni, the low-voiced sacrifice (Upāṃśuyāja) for Agni-Soma, the cake for Agni-Soma, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt—these are the five oblation-portions in the middle."

The *prāśitra*, the *iḍā*, that which he places for the *āgnīdhra*, the portion for the *brahman*, the portion for the sacrificer, and the *anvāhārya*—these six belong to Prajāpati; the three *anuyājas*, the four *patnīsaṃyājas*, and the *samiṣṭayajus* as the eighth—these eight are the subsequent *ājyabhāgas*.

Now, because the fore-offerings (*prayāja*) are without invitatory formulas (*puro'nuvākyā*), therefore these creatures are born toothless; and because the oblations (*havis*) have invitatory formulas, therefore their teeth grow; and because the after-offerings (*anuyāja*) are without invitatory formulas, therefore their teeth fall out; and because the offerings to the wives (*patnīsaṃyāja*) have invitatory formulas, therefore their teeth remain fixed; and because the *samiṣṭayajus* formula is without an invitatory formula, therefore in their final stage of life all their teeth fall out once again.

Now, because one offers with the *yājyā* after having recited the *anuvākyā*, therefore the lower [teeth] grow first, and then the upper; and because one offers with a *triṣṭubh* after having recited a *gāyatrī*, therefore the lower teeth are smaller and the upper are broader. And because he pours the two libations forward, therefore the fangs are larger; and because the two *saṃyājyās* consist of the same metre, therefore the rows of teeth are equal.

Now, because he spreads the sacrificial grass (barhis), therefore these creatures are born with hair; and because he spreads the prastara-bunch as it were again, therefore their beards, armpit hair, and body hair grow back again. And because he throws the prastara-bunch into the fire first by itself, therefore one becomes grey first on the head; and because he throws the entire sacrificial grass into the fire afterwards, therefore in the final stage of life one becomes grey all over.

Now, because the fore-offerings (prayāja) have clarified butter as their oblation, therefore the seed that is shed in a child does not come to fruition; it is just like water, for clarified butter is like water. And because they sacrifice in the middle of the sacrifice with sour milk and the cake, therefore it comes to fruition in his middle age; it is just like a drop, for seed is like a drop. And because the after-offerings (anuyāja) likewise have clarified butter as their oblation, therefore it does not come to fruition again in his final age; it is just like water, for clarified butter is like water.

The altar itself is the Gāyatrī. Those eight butter-portions (ājyabhāga) which are in front are its right wing; those eight butter-portions which are above are its left wing. This very Gāyatrī, tawny-colored and having light for wings, carries the sacrificer who knows this thus to the heavenly world.

Now, therefore, regarding the taking up of the two offering-spoons: some skilled practitioners, considering themselves wise, take up the *juhū* with the right hand and the *upabhṛt* with the left; one should not do so. For if someone were to say of him in that case, "This Adhvaryu has surely made the sacrificer's hateful rival a counter-attacker, one who rises against him," it would indeed be likely to happen exactly so.

In this very manner he should act: having grasped the *juhū* with both hands, he should place it upon the *upabhṛt*; there is no deliberation regarding that [act], for it is beneficial to cattle and conducive to long life. He should take it up without clinking it together; if he were to let them clink together, lack of security and prosperity would befall the sacrificer; therefore, he should take it up without clinking them together.

Now, therefore, concerning the stepping across: one Adhvaryu indeed scatters the sacrificer’s cattle with the thunderbolt, while another gathers them together for him by means of the thunderbolt. That Adhvaryu scatters the sacrificer’s cattle with the thunderbolt who, intending to call for the *āśrāvaṇa*, steps across with his right foot and calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* with his left; whereas he gathers them together for him who, intending to call for the *āśrāvaṇa*, steps across with his left foot and calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* with his right—this latter one indeed gathers them together for him.

Now, therefore, regarding the holding [of the two spoons]. On this point, some who consider themselves experts hold up their arms and keep the two *sruva*-spoons aloft. One should not do so; for if someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has indeed made his arms into spears; he will become one with spear-like arms," it would likely come to pass exactly so. Rather, this is the central breath (*prāṇa*); therefore, one should hold them by lowering them toward that [breath].

Now, therefore, concerning the *āśrāvaṇa* (the call for the response): there are six ways of sounding the *āśrāvaṇa*—downward, horizontal, upward, wretched, outwardly resplendent, and inwardly resplendent.

This indeed is the downward way: he who, having lifted something up high, sets it down softly—he who desires that someone should become worse off should lift it up high for him and set it down softly; by that, he becomes worse off.

Now, this is the horizontal [method]: with exactly as much as he takes up, he deposits it. If he should desire that one be neither better nor worse, he should deposit it with exactly as much as he took up; by that, he becomes neither better nor worse.

Now, as for this "upward" [movement]: when one takes up [the fire] slowly and places it down loudly, if he should desire of someone, "May he become more excellent," he should take him up slowly and place him down loudly; by that, he becomes more excellent.

Now, this is indeed wretched when one makes the *aṇu*, *dīrgha*, and *asvara* tones audible; for if someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has surely made the sacrificer wretched, one who dwells near his hateful enemy," it would likely come to pass exactly so.

Now, this [offering] is devoid of splendor; for when one opens the lips wide and calls for the *āśrāvaṇa* loudly and without tone, the tone is indeed splendor—thus he places that splendor outside himself, and he becomes hungry.

Now, this is the one who possesses internal splendor: when he closes his lips and calls for the announcement in a loud voice, that loud voice is indeed splendor; thus he places splendor within himself and becomes an eater of food.

Having pushed it down upon his chest as if it were something pleasant, he should finally place the *ubhayatobārhatam* chant loudly; there is no further deliberation required for that, for it is conducive to cattle and promotes long life.

Now, therefore, regarding the oblation: some who consider themselves experts, having brought down the offering-spoon (sruk) facing eastward, having offered, and having carried it around, place it upon the secondary spoon (upabhṛt). One should not do so; for if someone were to say of him then, "This Adhvaryu has surely made the sacrificer submissive to his hateful rival who dwells near him," it would likely come to pass exactly so.

Some, having brought down the *sruk* from the side, having offered it, and having carried it around, place it upon the *upabhṛt*; one should not do so. For if someone were to say of him at that point, "This Adhvaryu has indeed launched the oblations through a non-pathway; he will either break or become worm-eaten," it would likely happen exactly so.

One should do exactly thus: having brought down the *sruc* towards the east, having offered, and having drawn [the butter] back by that same path, one should place it into the *upabhṛt*. There is no deliberation regarding this; it is conducive to cattle and conducive to long life.

One Adhvaryu indeed burns up the oblations, while another satisfies them. That Adhvaryu who, having offered the clarified butter (ājya), offers the portions (avadāna) is one who burns up the oblations; regarding him, an unseen voice spoke: "This Adhvaryu truly burns up the oblations. But he who, having offered the clarified butter, offers the portions, and then finally pours more clarified butter over them—he indeed satisfies them. When they are satisfied, the gods fill for him golden cups.

Regarding this, Yājñavalkya said: "In that one spreads an underlayer [of ghee], takes a portion, and pours ghee over it, by that very act he satisfies them; when they are satisfied, the gods fill their golden cups for them. Now, Śaulbāyana was the Adhvaryu priest for those whose householder was Ayasthūṇa.
He said, "This sacrificial session here has lean cattle and little clarified butter, yet this man considers himself the householder."

He said, "O Adhvaryu, you have indeed not been kind to us; these are those two offering-ladles which you were unable to take up for a year. If I had instructed you in their use, you would have multiplied with offspring and cattle and carried [the sacrificer] to the heavenly world."

He said, "I would come to you as a pupil. He replied, "Indeed, you deserve this very much, since you have been our Adhvaryu for a year; I shall tell this to you even though you have not yet approached me as a pupil. Then he explained to him that very same taking up of the two offering-spoons which has already been explained. Therefore, one should appoint as Adhvaryu only one who knows this, and not one who does not know it.

Prajāpati, while creating living beings, performed austerities. From him, as he was weary from his austerities, Śrī emerged. She stood there, shining, blazing, and flickering; and the gods longed for her as she was shining, blazing, and flickering.

They said to Prajāpati, "Let us kill her; let us take this [Soma] from her. He said, "This Śrī is indeed a woman; they do not kill a woman. Moreover, you shall take it from her while she is still alive."

From her, Agni took away the consumption of food; Soma, kingship; Varuṇa, sovereign rule; Mitra, the power of the Kṣatriya; Indra, strength; Bṛhaspati, the splendor of sacred knowledge; Savitṛ, the kingdom; Pūṣan, fortune; Sarasvatī, prosperity; and Tvaṣṭṛ, forms.
She said to Prajāpati, "He has indeed eaten this of mine. He replied, "Ask them back by means of the sacrifice."

He saw this sacrifice consisting of ten oblations: a cake on eight potsherds for Agni, a pap for Soma, a cake on ten potsherds for Varuṇa, a pap for Mitra, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra, a pap for Bṛhaspati, a cake on twelve potsherds or on eight potsherds for Savitṛ, a pap for Pūṣan, a pap for Sarasvatī, and a cake on ten potsherds for Tvaṣṭṛ.

He addressed them with this invitatory verse: "Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ who is thousandfold, Pūṣan with his cattle, Sarasvatī with her protection—may Tvaṣṭṛ adorn our forms with sacrifices. They stood before him in response.

With this *yājyā* verse, he returned from beyond in reverse order: "May Sarasvatī, bestowing forms, Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Savitṛ grant to me; may Bṛhaspati grant, and Indra strength to me; may Mitra, Kṣatra, Varuṇa, Soma, and Agni [grant]. Thus they resolved to give back.

He saw the supplementary offerings (anūpa-homa): "May Agni, the eater of food, the lord of food, bestow food upon me at this sacrifice—svāhā! Taking the oblation itself, Agni went forth; he gave food back to her once again.
"May Soma, the king, the lord of kings, bestow sovereignty upon me in this sacrifice, svāhā! Having taken the oblation thus, Soma went forth and restored the sovereignty to her once again.

"May Varuna, the sovereign, the lord of sovereigns, bestow sovereignty upon me at this sacrifice, Svāhā! Having taken up the oblation with these words, Varuna stepped forth and restored sovereignty to her.
"May Mitra, the lord of the kṣatra, bestow the kṣatra upon me at this sacrifice; svāhā! Having taken the oblation, Mitra went forth and restored the kṣatra to her.
"May Indra, the lord of strength, bestow strength upon me at this sacrifice, svāhā!"—having taken up the oblation with these words, Indra went forth and restored strength to her.

"Bṛhaspati is the sacred formulation; may Bṛhaspati bestow upon me at this sacrifice the splendor of sacred formulation, svāhā! Having taken up the oblation itself, Bṛhaspati stepped forward and restored the splendor of sacred formulation to her.
"May Savitṛ, the lord of the kingdom, bestow the kingdom upon me at this sacrifice, Svāhā! Having taken up the oblation with these words, Savitṛ stepped forward and restored the kingdom to her.
"Pūṣan, Bhaga, the Lord of Bhaga, may he bestow Bhaga upon me at this sacrifice, Svāhā!"—having taken up the oblation with these words, Pūṣan stepped forth and restored Bhaga to her.
"May Sarasvatī, the mistress of nourishment, bestow nourishment upon me at this sacrifice; Svāhā! Having taken up the oblation itself, Sarasvatī departed and restored nourishment to her.

"May Tvaṣṭṛ, the maker of forms, the lord of forms, by means of form, bestow cattle upon this sacrifice and upon me—Svāhā! Having taken the oblation, Tvaṣṭṛ stepped forward; he restored the cattle to her by means of form. Ten, tenfold, is the Virāj; the Virāj is prosperity. Ten, tenfold, is the Virāj; the Virāj is prosperity; indeed, one attains prosperity through the Virāj. Ten, tenfold, is the Virāj; the Virāj is prosperity; the Virāj is prosperity; indeed, one attains prosperity through the Virāj.
These, indeed, are ten deities, ten oblations, and ten offerings; he thus becomes established in the Virāj, which consists of food.

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; he sacrifices to the deities in a whisper; there are five *prayāja*s, three *anuyāja*s, and one *samiṣṭayajus*. The two *ājyabhāga*s contain the word "prosperity" (*puṣṭi*): "Through Agni may one obtain wealth and prosperity day by day—glorious, most rich in heroes; increasing the household, driving away disease, finding goods, augmenting prosperity; O Soma, be a good friend to us. The two *saṃyājyā*s contain the word "thousand": "Now grant us, O Agni, thousandfold wealth, accompanied by offspring and prosperity, brilliant, full of heroic strength, most excellent, and undecaying; and protect our prayer, O best invoker of the gods among our hymns; shine auspiciously for us, O Agni, strengthened by the Maruts, most bountiful winner of thousands."

Gotama Rāhūgaṇa discovered this [sacrifice]. It went forth toward Janaka of Videha; he sought it among the Aṅgijits, Brāhmaṇas, and found it in Yājñavalkya. He said, "O Yājñavalkya, I give you a thousand [cows], for in you we have found Mitravindā. He who, knowing thus, performs this sacrifice, or whoever knows this, finds a friend; his kingdom prospers, he conquers renewed death, and he reaches a full lifespan.
Now, therefore, follows the prosperity of the oblation. There are indeed six doors to the Brahman: fire, wind, water, the moon, lightning, and the sun.

He who sacrifices with an oblation that has been scorched enters by means of Agni as the gate of Brahman; having entered by means of Agni as the gate of Brahman, he wins union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman.

Now, he who sacrifices with an oblation that has fallen [from the ladle] enters through Vāyu, the door of Brahman; having entered through Vāyu, the door of Brahman, he wins union with Brahman and residence in the same world as Brahman.

Now, he who sacrifices with unboiled oblation enters by means of the waters, for he enters by means of the waters, the door of Brahman. Having entered by means of the waters, the door of Brahman, he [proceeds].
Now, he who sacrifices with an oblation that has turned red enters by means of the moon, the door of Brahman; having entered by means of the moon, the door of Brahman—
Now, he who sacrifices with the red oblation enters through the door of Brahman by means of lightning; having entered through the door of Brahman by means of lightning—

Now, he who sacrifices with well-cooked oblation enters through the door of Brahman by means of Āditya; having entered through the door of Brahman by means of Āditya, he wins union with Brahman and residence in the same world as him. This is the perfection of the oblation. He who knows this perfection of the oblation—verily, his sacrifice becomes perfected in every respect.

Now, therefore, follows the prosperity of the sacrifice: whatever in the sacrifice is deficient, that is its power of procreation; whatever is redundant, that is its power regarding cattle; whatever is superfluous, that is its power regarding glory; and whatever is perfectly complete, that is its power regarding heaven.
If he should think, "Something deficient has occurred in my sacrifice," he should meditate upon it thus: "This is procreation for me; I shall procreate."
Now, if he should think, "Something has been redundant in my sacrifice," let him meditate upon it thus: "This is conducive to cattle; I shall become possessed of cattle."

Now, if he should think, "A stumbling-block has occurred for me in my sacrifice," he should meditate on it thus: "This [oblation] shall come to me for the sake of prosperity; may prosperity, surrounded by splendor, fame, and the luster of sacred knowledge, come to me. This is how he should meditate upon it.

Now, if he should think, "Success has come to my sacrifice," let him meditate upon this as leading to heaven, thinking, "This shall be for me a world of heaven. This is the prosperity of the sacrifice. He who knows this prosperity of the sacrifice, his sacrifice becomes offered with all-encompassing prosperity.

The Apsaras Urvaśī desired Purūravas Āiḍa. Having found him, she said to him: "Strike me three times a day with a cane; do not lie with me when I am unwilling; do not look at me naked; for this, indeed, is the way of women."

She dwelt with him for a long time; she even became pregnant by him, and she dwelt with him for a very long time. Then the Gandharvas said to one another, "A long time indeed has this Urvaśī dwelt among humans; devise a means so that she may return. A ewe with two lambs was tied to her bed; then the Gandharvas stole one of the lambs.
She said, "Alas, as if my hero were being carried off, as if my son were being carried off! And they carried him away a second time; she spoke exactly as before.

Then he reflected: "How indeed could that [place] be without heroes, how could it be without offspring, where I might be? He sprang up naked; he thought it a long time that he had put on his garment. Then the Gandharvas produced lightning, and they saw him naked as if from the sky. Thereupon she vanished, thinking, "I am going back. While he was wandering along Kurukṣetra, muttering to himself, she became invisible. He went toward her at the edge of the water where there were lotus stalks. Then those Apsarases, having become swallows, flew around him.
Knowing that it was to be abandoned, he said, "This indeed is that man in whom I dwelt. They said to him, "Let us appear to him. "So be it," they replied, and they appeared to him.

Having recognized her, he addressed her: "O wife, O terrible one, stay with me in thought; let us now exchange words together. These unspoken mantras of ours shall not bring us joy even on a future day. "Stay then! Let us speak together!"—this is what he said to her.

The other replied to him: "What shall I do with these words of yours? I have already set out for the dawns like a cow to the stall; O Purūravas, go back to your home! I am as difficult to capture as the wind. He said to her: "You did not do what I told you; indeed, I am now difficult for you to attain. Go back to your home! This is exactly what he said to her.

Then this dejected man said: "Sudeva shall fly away today, never to return; he must go to the furthest distance. Then he shall lie in the lap of Destruction, and there ravenous wolves shall devour him. "Sudeva shall either be bound today or he shall fly away; then wolves or dogs shall devour him"—this is indeed what he said.

The other replied to him: "Purūravas, do not die! Do not flee! Let not the inauspicious wolves devour you. There are no friendships with women; these are but the hearts of hyenas. Do not take this to heart; there is no friendship with women. Go back home! This is what she said to him.

"Whatever of a deformed nature I practiced among mortals for four autumn nights, eating but a single drop of ghee once a day—that very thing I now practice, being fully satisfied. This is the fifteen-verse hymn consisting of questions and answers which the Bahvṛcas recite; he (Yājñavalkya) made it the very heart of that [sacrifice].

She said, "Come on the night of the year's end; you shall lie with me for one night there, and then this son of yours will be born. He came on the night of the year's end, and there were golden pavilions. Then they said to him, "Enter this one," and they led him into that very one.

She said, "The Gandharvas will indeed grant you a boon tomorrow morning; choose it. He replied, "You yourself must choose it for me. She said, "Say, 'May I be one among you alone. In the morning, the Gandharvas granted him a boon, and he said, "May I be one among you alone."

They said, "Indeed, among humans there is no sacrificial body of Agni by which, having sacrificed with it, one might become one of us. So they took some fire, placed it in a pot, and gave it to him, saying, "Having sacrificed with this, you shall become one of us. Taking both that fire and the boy, he departed. Having set down the fire in the forest, he went to the village with the boy alone, thinking, "I will return. But Agni vanished; [he took] the fire from the *aśvattha* tree and the pot from the *śamī* tree. He then went back to the Gandharvas.

They said, "Cook a year's supply of porridge to be eaten by four; then, having anointed three sticks each from this very Aśvattha tree with ghee, he should place them on the fire with verses containing the word 'fuel-stick' (samidh) and the word 'ghee' (ghṛta). That fire which is produced from that shall indeed be that [fire]."

They said, "This is indeed as if indirect; make the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) of aśvattha wood and the lower fire-drill (adharāraṇi) of śamī wood. Whatever fire is produced from that shall be that very [fire]."
They said, "This is indeed somewhat obscure. Make the upper fire-stick of *aśvattha* wood and the lower fire-stick of *aśvattha* wood; whatever fire is produced from that shall be that very [fire]."

He made an upper fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood and a lower fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood. The fire that was produced from that was indeed that very [fire]; having sacrificed with it, he became one of the Gandharvas. Therefore, one should make the upper fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood and the lower fire-drill of *aśvattha* wood. The fire that is born from that becomes that very [fire]; having sacrificed with it, one becomes one of the Gandharvas.

Prajāpati, indeed, fashioned himself by means of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. He made this very right arm the Vaiśvadeva oblation; of that [arm], this thumb became the Āgneya oblation, this [forefinger] the Saumya, and this [middle finger] the Sāvitra.

That sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is indeed the largest; therefore, this [part] of these [limbs] is the largest. This is for Sarasvatī, this is for Pūṣan; then that which is at the joint above the hand is for the Maruts, this is for the Viśve Devās, and this is for Dyāvāpṛthivī. That part, moreover, is undefined (anirukta); therefore it is undefined.

This very right thigh is the Varuṇapraghāsa offerings; its five oblations that are common to all are these five toes. The offering to Indra and Agni is the two ankle-bones; for that belongs to two deities, therefore there are these two ankle-bones. This [part] is for Varuṇa, this for the Maruts, and the backbone is for Ka; for that is undefined, therefore it is undefined.

The Anīkavatī sacrifice is his mouth, for the mouth is the army (*anīka*) of the vital breaths. The Sāṃtapanīya is his chest, for with the chest one is heated (*tapyate*) as it were. The Gṛhamedhīya is his belly; the belly is indeed stability, and it serves for the sake of stability. The Kraiḍina oblation is his sexual organs, for with the sexual organs one plays (*krīḍati*) as it were. This downward vital breath is the Āditya sacrifice.

This very upper thigh is the Mahāhavis; its five oblations that are combined together are these five toes. The Aindrāgna oblation is the two ankle-bones, for it belongs to two deities; therefore these two ankle-bones are [there]. This [other part] is the Māhendra oblation, and this is the Vaiśvakarmana oblation; that indeed is undefined (anirukta), and therefore it is undefined. Now, that which is here within the belly is the Pitṛyajña; that indeed is undefined, and therefore it is undefined.

This very upper arm is the Śunāsīrīya; its five oblations which are combined together are these five fingers. And that joint of the hand which is at the top is the Śunāsīrīya; this [arm] is the Vāyavya, and that is the Saura. Now, that is undefined (anirukta); therefore it is undefined.

These Cāturmāsya sacrifices are three-jointed and two-compounded; therefore, these limbs of a person are three-jointed and two-compounded. Of those four [sacrifices], in two of them there are three-three oblations that are undefined, and in two of them there are two-two.

For them, they churn the fire in four [months]; therefore, he approaches with four limbs. They lead it forward in two [months]; therefore, he returns with two. Thus indeed did Prajāpati fashion himself by means of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; and in the same way, the sacrificer who knows this fashions himself by means of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.

Regarding this they say: "The Vaiśvadeva oblation should be entirely in the *gāyatrī* metre for the sake of attaining heaven; the Varuṇapraghāsas entirely in the *triṣṭubh*; the Mahāhavis entirely in the *jagatī*; and the Śunāsīrīya entirely in the *anuṣṭubh*, so that one may obtain the fourfold Stoma. But one should not do it in that way; for by the very fact that these [oblations] correspond to those [metres], that desire of his is thereby attained.

These Cāturmāsya sacrifices amount to three hundred and sixty-two Bṛhatī verses; by means of these, he obtains both the year and the Mahāvrata. Moreover, this sacrificer is indeed established on two feet; thus he leads the sacrificer himself to the heavenly world and establishes him therein.
Śauceya Prācīnayogya went to Uddālaka Āruṇi, saying, "I wish to understand the Agnihotra through a theological debate."

He said, "Gautama, what is your Agnihotra cow? What is her calf? What is the milk when it is let down? What is the mixture? What is being milked? What is the milk [once drawn]? What is being brought [to the fire]? What is placed upon the fire? What is being illuminated with light? What is it when water has been poured back into it? What is being removed from the fire? What is it once removed? What is being ladled out? What is it once ladled out? What is it when lifted up? What is it being carried away? What is it when it has been set down?"
What kind of fuel did you offer? What was the first oblation? Upon what did you sit? What did you look toward? And what was the final oblation?

"Having become what do you cause [the fire] to tremble? Having wiped the offering-ladle (*sruc*), why did you wipe it on the grass-bunch (*kūrca*)? Having wiped it a second time, why did you sit down with your hand toward the south? Why did you consume the first [portion], and why the second? Why, having stepped aside, did you drink [water]? Having poured water into the ladle, why did you look at it? Why a second time? Why a third time did you sprinkle it toward this direction? Why did you pour water behind the Āhavanīya fire? Why did you bring it to a conclusion? If you have offered the Agnihotra knowing this, then your offering is truly offered; but if you have offered it without knowing this, then it is indeed unoffered."

He said: "My Agnihotra cow is indeed Ida, the daughter of Manu; her calf is Vayu; when she is let loose to join him, it is the Viraj; while being milked, it is for the Ashvins; when milked, it is for the Vishvedevas; while being brought [to the fire], it is for Vayu; when placed on the fire, it is for Agni; while being stirred with the ladle, it is for Indra and Agni; when water is added, it is for Varuna; while being removed from the fire, it is for Vayu; when removed, it is for Heaven and Earth; while being poured out, it is for the Ashvins; when poured out, it is for the Vishvedevas; when raised up, it is for Mahadeva; while being carried, it is for Vayu; and when set down, it is for Vishnu."

Now, that fuel-stick which I place upon the fire is the foundation of the oblations; with that first oblation I reached the gods; when I sat down, I attained the world of Bṛhaspati; and when I looked around, I established both this world and that world; and with that subsequent oblation, I have placed myself in the heavenly world.

"Now, when I offered the oblation and made [the ladle] tremble toward the wind, by that I gratified the plants and trees; when I wiped the *sruva* ladle and wiped it on the grass-bunch, by that I gratified the Fathers; when I wiped it a second time and placed my hand to the south, by that I gratified the Pitṛs; when I first tasted [the remnant], by that I gratified myself; when I tasted a second time, by that I gratified my offspring; then, when I moved away and drank water, by that I gratified the cattle; when I poured water into the *sruk* ladle and sprinkled it out, by that I gratified the serpent-deities; when I sprinkled a second time, by that I gratified the Gandharvas and Apsarases; then, when I sprinkled a third time toward this direction (the north), by that I opened the door to the heavenly world; when I poured out water behind the Āhavanīya fire, by that I gave rain to this world; and when I brought the rite to completion, by that I filled whatever was deficient in the earth. "Venerable sir," he said, "this is common to us both."

Śauceya was informed: "I shall indeed question the Blessed One. "Ask, Prācīnayogya," he said. He (Prācīnayogya) spoke: "At what time, when those fires have been taken out and the vessels have been brought down, and one is about to offer the oblation, if then your Āhavanīya fire were to go out—do you know that danger which exists here for one who is offering? "I know it," he replied. "Before long, the eldest son of him to whom this is unknown would die; however, by means of these sciences, I have crossed over. "What is known? What is the expiation? "The breath has entered the upward-breath (udāna)," [he said]. "One should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire; that itself is the expiation. One should not commit that sin. "This, O Blessed One, is common to us both," he said.

Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I shall indeed question the Blessed One. "Ask, Prācīnayogya," he replied. He said, "If at that very time the Gārhapatya fire were to go out, do you know what fear there is for one who is offering oblations? "I know it," he replied. "Before long, the householder of one who does not know this would die. But by means of knowledge, I have indeed crossed over it. "What is known? What is the expiation? "The Udāna has entered the Prāṇa; one should offer an oblation into the Āhavanīya fire—that is the expiation. Thus one would not commit that offense. "This is common to us both, O Blessed One," he said.

Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I shall indeed question the Blessed One. "Ask then, Prācīnayogya," he replied. He said, "If at that very time the Āhavanīya fire should follow the Gārhapatya fire, do you know the danger that arises for one who offers oblations there? "I know it," he said. "Before long, all the cattle of one for whom this is unknown would perish; however, by means of knowledge, I have indeed crossed over it. "What is known? What is the expiation? "The Vyāna has entered the Udāna," [he replied]. "One should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya; that is the expiation, and one should not commit that offense. "This is common to us both, O Blessed One," he said.

Śauceya, having been instructed, said, "I would indeed ask the Blessed One further. "Ask then, O Prācīnayogya," he replied. He [Prācīnayogya] said: "If at that very time all your fires should go out, do you know what danger there is for one who offers oblations? "I know it," he [Śauceya] replied. "Before long, the lineage of him for whom this remains unknown would become heirless; however, by means of knowledge, I have indeed crossed over. "What is known? What is the expiation? "Having churned the fire before long, in whichever direction the wind blows, I would take up the Āhavanīya fire toward that direction and offer a Vāyavyā oblation. I would know: 'My Agnihotra has become successful, for it belongs to all the deities; indeed, all beings merge into Vāyu and from Vāyu they are released again. That itself is the expiation; I would not commit that offense. "This is common to us both, O Blessed One," he [Śauceya] said.

Śauceya, having been informed, said, "I shall indeed question the Blessed One. "Ask, O Prācīnayogya," he [the teacher] replied. He said, "If at that very time all your fires were to go out when there is no wind, do you know what danger arises for one who offers oblations therein? "I know it," he replied. "One would see only what is unpleasant in this world and what is unpleasant in the next—this is the danger for one for whom this is unknown. But by means of knowledge, I have indeed crossed over it. "What is known? What is the expiation? "Having churned fire after a long while, having drawn out the Āhavanīya fire toward the east, and having sat down behind the Āhavanīya, I myself would drink it. Then I would know: 'My Agnihotra has become complete; it belongs to all the deities. For all beings enter into the Brāhmaṇa and from the Brāhmaṇa they are released again. That is the expiation; I would not commit that sin. "Or rather, I did not know this," he said.

Śauceya was informed: "These pieces of firewood are for the Blessed One. He said, "If you had not spoken thus, your head would have fallen off. Come, approach me. "So be it," he replied. He initiated him. To him he spoke this most secret *vyāhṛti*: "That which is Truth; therefore, one should speak only the truth."

"I have come for the holy life," he says; thereby he offers himself to Brahman. "May I be a student of the holy life," he says; thereby he entrusts himself to Brahman. Then he asks him, "What is your name? Prajāpati is indeed "Ka"; having thus made him belong to Prajāpati, he initiates him.

Then he takes his hand, saying: "Indra is your student; Agni is your teacher; I am your teacher, O so-and-so! These two indeed are the most excellent and most powerful deities; by means of these very most excellent and most powerful deities, he entrusts him. Thus, for one who knows this, his student does not encounter any affliction whatsoever, nor does he himself.

Then he entrusts him to the beings, saying: "I entrust you to Prajāpati; I entrust you to the god Savitṛ. These two indeed are the most excellent and most sublime deities; by means of these two most excellent and most sublime deities he entrusts him. Thus his religious student (brahmacārī) does not suffer any affliction whatsoever, nor does he who knows this.

"Into the waters and the plants I entrust you"—thus he entrusts him to the waters and the plants. "Into heaven and earth I entrust you"—thus he entrusts him to these two, heaven and earth, upon which all this rests. "Into all beings I entrust you for safety"—thus he entrusts him to all beings for safety. In this way, the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) does not suffer any affliction whatsoever; nor does he who knows thus.

"Thou art a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*)," he says; thereby he entrusts him to the Brahman. "Eat water," he says; water is indeed immortality; thus he says to him, "Eat immortality. "Perform thy work," he says; work is indeed vigor; thus he says to him, "Exert thy vigor. "Place fuel on the fire," he says; thereby he says to him, "Enkindle yourself with brilliance and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*). "Do not sleep," he says; this means "Do not die. "Eat water," he says; water is indeed immortality; thus he says to him, "Eat immortality. Thus he encloses him on both sides with immortality. Therefore, the student of sacred knowledge who knows this does not suffer from any affliction whatsoever, nor does he die.

Then he recites the Sāvitrī verse for him. Formerly, they used to recite it for him after a year; [thinking], "Embryos are born measured by a year; thus we place speech into him as soon as he is born."
Then, after six months—there being six seasons in a year, and embryos are indeed born when they have been measured by a year—they place speech in him as soon as he is born.

Now, as for the twenty-four-day rite: there are indeed twenty-four half-months in a year; embryos are born when they have reached the measure of a year. [The thought is: "While he is already born, let us bestow speech upon him."
Then, on the twelfth day; for there are twelve months in a year, and it is a counterpart of the year.
Now, in six days there are six seasons; it is the essence of the year.
Then, after three days; for there are three seasons in a year, and [this] is the essence of the year.

Regarding this, they also sing this verse: "The teacher becomes pregnant by placing his right hand [upon her]; on the third [night] he is born as a Brāhmaṇa together with the Sāvitrī. However, one should indeed recite the Sāvitrī to a Brāhmaṇa immediately; for the Brāhmaṇa belongs to Agni, and Agni is born immediately; therefore, one should recite it to a Brāhmaṇa immediately.

Some recite this Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying, "Speech is indeed the Anuṣṭubh; thus we place speech within him. One should not do so; for if someone were to say of him in that case, "He has swallowed his speech; he will become mute," it would likely come to pass exactly so. Therefore, one should recite this Sāvitrī only as a Gāyatrī.

Now, some say that one should recite for him while he is standing or sitting to the south; but one should not do so. For if someone were to say of him then, "He has indeed produced this [child] as a *bulba* (a swelling or tumor); he will become a *bulba*," it would likely come to pass exactly so. Therefore, one should recite for him while he is standing to the east, looking towards the west.

He recites that [verse] by feet; for there are three vital breaths—prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna—and it is these he thereby places in him. Then he recites by half-verses; for there are these two vital breaths, prāṇa and udāna, and it is prāṇa and udāna he thereby places in him. Then he recites the whole [verse]; for this vital breath is one and whole, and it is the whole vital breath he thereby places in him.

Regarding this they say: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse after having initiated a Brahmin into studentship; for he who enters upon studentship becomes an embryo. [The thought is: 'Lest I should cause this Brahmin to be born from semen that has been spilled.'"

Regarding this, they say: "One may indeed act according to one's desire. For these creatures are of two kinds: divine and human. These human creatures are born from procreation; the divine creatures are the meters, and those he produces from his mouth. From there he produces this [the sacrifice]; therefore, one may indeed act according to one's desire."

Regarding this they say: "A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should not eat honey, for honey is the supreme essence of plants; he should not go to the end of food. Now, Śvetaketu Āruṇeya once said while being a student: "One who eats honey while being a student eats what remains of the threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā). Honey is the essence of that whose remnant is such as this. Just as one would recite a Ṛg-verse, a Yajus-formula, or a Sāman-chant, so is that [the eating of honey]. Therefore, a student who knows this may eat honey at his pleasure.

When the gods were ascending to the heavenly world, the Asuras concealed them with darkness. They said, "There is indeed no way to strike them down other than through a sacrificial session (sattra); come, let us perform a sattra!"

They entered upon a sacrificial session (sattra) consisting of a hundred Agniṣṭomas; as far as one could see while sitting, so far they dispelled the darkness. In the same way, with a hundred Ukthyas, as far as one could see while standing, so far they dispelled the darkness.

They said, "We have indeed dispelled the darkness, but not entirely. Come, let us go back to Prajāpati, our father. Having approached Prajāpati, their father, they said, "O Venerable One, the Asuras have indeed obstructed us with darkness as we were ascending to the heavenly world."

"We entered upon a sacrificial session consisting of a hundred Agniṣṭomas; we dispelled as much darkness as one could see while sitting. In the very same way, with a hundred Ukthyas, we dispelled as much darkness as one could see while standing. Venerable sir, instruct us so that, having dispelled the darkness and having dispelled all evil, we may find the heavenly world, just as you have done for the Asuras."

He said: "Indeed, you have come with two sacrifices that are not complete in their rites; therefore, enter upon the Sattra of a hundred Atirātras, and by means of it, having struck away the darkness of the Asuras and having struck away all evil, you shall find the world of heaven."
