They entered upon the Sattra of a hundred Atirātras; by means of it, they struck away the darkness of the Asuras, struck away all evil, and were born into the heavenly world. Among them, within fifty days, they completed the day-chants for the night-sacrifices and the night-chants for the day-sacrifices.

They said, "We have indeed become bewildered; we do not understand. Come, let us go back to our father Prajāpati. Having approached their father Prajāpati, they said, "The Sāmans of the night belong to the day, and those of the day belong to the night. We are confused regarding the sacrifices; O wise and learned one, instruct us!"
Regarding them, he sang this: "As if a stronger one had followed a great serpent from its lake, [it has been driven] from its own place; therefore, the sacrificial session cannot be extended."

"The *prātaranuvāka* dedicated to the Aśvins, while it is being recited, has indeed driven you from your place; since it has driven you from your place, O wise ones, though being wise, act as if you were unwise—approach that *praśāstṛ* slowly and do not recite against him."

They said, "How then, O Venerable One, is it recited? How is it not recited? He replied: "When the Hotṛ, while reciting the *Aśvina* hymn, reaches the end of the *Āgneya* sacrifice, of the *Gāyatrī* metre, at that moment the Pratiprasthātṛ, having carried around the *vasatīvarī* waters, should cause the Maitrāvaruṇa to begin the *Prātaranuvāka* in the two *havirdhāna* sheds. The Hotṛ recites loudly; the other follows along in a low voice, as if whispering. Thus, he does not meet voice with voice, nor metre with metre."

When the morning litany (prātaranuvāka) has been concluded, having offered the Upāṃśu and Antaryāma cups according to their proper place, he places the filter (pavitra) to be squeezed into the Droṇakalaśa vessel. Having performed the rites with the Tiro'hnya cups and having returned westward, you should consume the Tiro'hnya cups themselves. Then, having completed the "tail of the sacrifice" (yajñapuccha) in due order, having drawn those cups which follow the Antaryāma, having offered the oblation of drops (vipruṣ), and having chanted the Saṃtanī verses with the Bahiṣpavamāna stotra, you should proceed with the day's ritual itself.
Regarding this, there are these verses: "The wise ones, the learned gods who performed the sacrificial session (sattra) for Śatakratu, abandoned darkness by means of four harnessed Saindhava horses."

For here four are engaged: two Hotṛ-priests and two Adhvaryu-priests. Like two smiths fashioning jaws, the wise ones interlace the ends of the days. We do not understand the divine thread they have stretched out; these Dānavas bewilder us. They leave over the work of the preceding day and extend it further with the succeeding day. The wisdom of the deities is difficult to discern. The Soma-pressings, interlaced with other Somas, float along; they sprinkle the steeds that are alike, just as one sprinkles horses carrying wood. "The full jars of flowing liquor at the dwelling of Janamejaya"—with these words, the Asuras and Rākṣasas were driven away.

There are exactly five great sacrifices; these indeed are the great sacrificial sessions: the sacrifice to beings, the sacrifice to humans, the sacrifice to ancestors, the sacrifice to the gods, and the sacrifice to Brahman.

Day after day one should offer an oblation to the beings; thus one completes this sacrifice to the beings (*bhūtayajña*). Day after day one should give [food], even if only a water-pot’s worth; thus one completes this sacrifice to men (*manuṣyayajña*). Day after day one should utter *svadhā*, even if only a water-pot’s worth; thus one completes this sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*). Day after day one should utter *svāhā*, at least as far as a piece of wood [is offered]; thus one completes this sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).

Now follows the sacrifice to Brahman: the private recitation of scripture (*svādhyāya*) is indeed the sacrifice to Brahman. Of this very sacrifice to Brahman, speech is the *juhū* ladle, the mind is the *upabhṛt*, the eye is the *dhruvā*, intelligence is the *sruva* spoon, truth is the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*), and the heavenly world is the conclusion. Indeed, as much of this earth as one might conquer by giving it away filled with wealth, three times that much, and even more—indeed, an inexhaustible world—he conquers who, knowing this, studies his private recitation day after day. Therefore, the private recitation must be studied.

The Ṛgvedic verses are indeed milk-offerings for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the Ṛgveda as his daily private recitation (svādhyāya), satisfies the gods with milk-offerings. Satisfied, they satisfy him with security of possession (yogakṣema), with vital breath, with semen, with his whole self, and with all auspicious prosperities. Streams of ghee and streams of honey flow toward the ancestors as the *svadhā* offering.

The sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) are indeed the oblations of clarified butter for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the sacrificial formulas as his daily private recitation, thereby satisfies the gods with oblations of clarified butter; they, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with security of possession, with vital breath, and with vigor.

The Sāmans are indeed oblations of Soma for the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the Sāmans as his daily private recitation (svādhyāya), satisfies the gods with oblations of Soma. They, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with security of possession (yogakṣema) and with vital breath (prāṇa).

The Atharvāṅgirases are indeed fat-offerings to the gods. He who, knowing this, studies the Atharvāṅgirases as his daily private recitation, satisfies the gods with fat-offerings. They, being satisfied, satisfy him with security of possession and with vital breath. Re! Re! Re!

These instructions, the sciences, the dialogues, the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, the verses, and the *nārāśaṃsīs* are indeed honey-offerings to the gods. He who, knowing this, studies daily as his private recitation these instructions, the sciences, the dialogues, the *itihāsas* and *purāṇas*, the verses, and the *nārāśaṃsīs*, satisfies the gods with honey-offerings. They, being satisfied, satisfy him in turn with security of possession and with vital breath. Thus, O Re!

Now, for this very sacrifice to Brahman, there are four *vaṣaṭ*-calls: when the wind blows, when it lightens, when it thunders, and when it rumbles. Therefore, one who knows this should indeed study while the wind blows, while it lightens, while it thunders, and while it rumbles, so that there may be no failure of the *vaṣaṭ*-calls. Thus he is released from returning death and attains identity with Brahman. Even if he should be unable to do much, he should at least study a single word of the gods; thus he is not deprived of the beings.

Now, therefore, follows the praise of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). When one is devoted to the study and recitation of the Vedas, one becomes focused in mind, independent of others, and accomplishes his goals day by day; he sleeps happily and becomes his own supreme physician. Furthermore, there is restraint of the senses, delight in solitude, the perfection of wisdom, fame, and the ripening of the world. Wisdom, as it increases, brings about four qualities in a Brāhmaṇa: Brāhmaṇahood, worthy conduct, fame, and the ripening of the world. And the world, being ripened, sustains the Brāhmaṇa through four qualities: through honor, through gifts, through invincibility, and through immunity from being slain.

Whatever labors there may be between heaven and earth, the private recitation of the Veda is indeed their highest point and ultimate goal for one who, knowing this, studies his private recitation; therefore, the private recitation must be studied.

Whatever Vedic hymn (chandas) one studies as one's private recitation (svādhyāya), by that very means his sacrificial rite (yajñakratu) becomes performed; for him who, knowing this, studies his private recitation. Therefore, one's private recitation must be studied.

Even if one were anointed, adorned, well-fed, and lying on a comfortable bed, if he recites his own sacred study (svādhyāya), he truly suffers pain even to the tips of his nails—provided he is one who knows this and thus recites his own sacred study. Therefore, one's own sacred study must be recited.
The Ṛg-verses are indeed honey, the Sāman-chants are clarified butter, and the Yajus-formulas are nectar; and when one studies the dialogues (vākovākya), those two are indeed milk-rice and meat-rice.
Verily, he who, knowing this, studies the Rigveda as his daily private recitation, satisfies the gods with honey; and they, being satisfied, satisfy him with all desires and all enjoyments.
Verily, he who, knowing this, studies the Sāmans as his daily private recitation, satisfies the gods with clarified butter; they, being satisfied, [satisfy him].
He who, knowing this, studies the Yajus formulas as his daily private recitation, truly satisfies the gods with nectar; they, being satisfied, [satisfy him].

Verily, he who, knowing this, studies daily as his private recitation the dialogues, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, satisfies the gods with both milk-rice and meat-rice; they, being satisfied, [satisfy him].

The waters go forth, the sun goes forth, the moon goes forth, and the stars go forth. Just as these deities would not exist and would not perform their functions if they did not go forth, even so does a Brāhmaṇa become on that day when he does not study his private recitation (*svādhyāya*). Therefore, one's private recitation must be studied; therefore, one should at least utter a *ṛc*, a *yajus*, a *sāman*, a *gāthā*, or a *kuṃvyā* verse, in order to avoid interrupting the vow.

In the beginning, Prajāpati alone was this universe. He desired, "May I exist; may I procreate. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. From him, thus exerted and having practiced austerity, the three worlds were created: earth, the intermediate space, and heaven.
He heated these three worlds; from them, thus heated, three lights were born: this fire, that which blows (the wind), and the sun.
He heated these three luminaries; from them, thus heated, the three Vedas were born: from Agni the Ṛgveda, from Vāyu the Yajurveda, and from Sūrya the Sāmaveda.

He heated these three Vedas; from them, thus heated, three pure essences were produced: "Bhūḥ" from the Ṛgveda, "Bhuvaḥ" from the Yajurveda, and "Svaḥ" from the Sāmaveda. With the Ṛgveda they performed the office of the Hotṛ, with the Yajurveda that of the Adhvaryu, and with the Sāmaveda that of the Udgātṛ. Whatever was the pure essence of the triple science, with that they performed the office of the Brahman priest. Then it departed.
Those gods said to Prajāpati, "If our sacrifice should falter—whether from the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, or the Sāmaveda—with what shall we heal it?"

He said: "If [the sacrifice] has failed through the Ṛgveda, take four ladlings of clarified butter and offer them in the Gārhapatya fire with 'Bhūḥ'. If through the Yajurveda, take four ladlings of clarified butter and offer them in the Āgnīdhrīya fire—or in the Anvāhāryapacana at a Haviryajña—with 'Bhuvaḥ'. If through the Sāmaveda, take four ladlings of clarified butter and offer them in the Āhavanīya fire with 'Svaḥ'. But if it should be unknown which has failed, recite all three and offer them in the Āhavanīya fire. Thus, by means of the Ṛgveda one heals the Ṛgveda; by the Yajurveda, the Yajurveda; and by the Sāmaveda, the Sāmaveda. Just as one would join joint to joint, even so does he who heals with these [mantras] truly join [the sacrifice]. Now, he who heals it otherwise than this—just as if one were to try to join what is broken with something broken, or as if one were to place poison upon a wound—such is that act. Therefore, one should appoint only one who knows this as the Brahman priest, and not one who does not know this."

Regarding this they say: "Since the office of the Hotṛ is performed with the Ṛgveda, that of the Adhvaryu with the Yajurveda, and the Udgītha with the Sāmaveda, then by what is the office of the Brahman priest performed? One should reply: "By means of this triple knowledge (the three Vedas)."

This Aṃśu cup is indeed Prajāpati; it is his very self, for Prajāpati is this self. And the Ādābhya cup is speech. When, having drawn the Aṃśu, he draws the Ādābhya, he thereby refines his own self and establishes this speech within that self.

Now, the mind is indeed the Aṃśu cup, and speech is the Adābhya; the out-breath is the Aṃśu, and the up-breath is the Adābhya; the eye is the Aṃśu, and the ear is the Adābhya. When they draw these two cups, it is for the sake of completeness and wholeness.
Now, both the gods and the Asuras, being offspring of Prajāpati, contended with one another; they contended over this very sacrifice, [saying], "This shall be ours! This shall be ours!"

Then the gods, praising and toiling, wandered about; they saw this cup, this Adābhya; they drew it. They tore away the pressings; they appropriated the entire sacrifice and excluded the Asuras from the sacrifice.

They said, "We have indeed deceived them," therefore it is called *adābhya*. [Others said,] "They did not deceive us," therefore it is called *adābhya*. Speech, indeed, is the *adābhya*; this speech is undeceivable, and for that reason also it is the *adābhya*. Verily, he who knows this thus appropriates the entire sacrifice of his hateful rival; he excludes the hateful rival from the entire sacrifice and casts him out.
Into that very same cup with which he takes the draught, having poured water from the *nigrābhya* vessels, he takes these stalks.

"You are taken with a support; I take you for Agni, whose metre is the Gāyatrī"—thus he draws the morning pressing, which is in the Gāyatrī metre; he thereby draws out that morning pressing. "I take you for Indra, whose metre is the Triṣṭubh"—thus he draws the midday pressing, which is in the Triṣṭubh metre; he thereby draws out that midday pressing. "I take you for the All-gods, whose metre is the Jagatī"—thus he draws the third pressing, which is in the Jagatī metre; he thereby draws out that third pressing. "The Anuṣṭubh is your song of praise"—whatever indeed is above the pressings, that is in the Anuṣṭubh metre; he thereby draws that out as well. He does not press it [with the stones], for the pressing-stone is a thunderbolt and the Ādābhya is speech; he does so lest he should injure speech with the thunderbolt.

"He shakes them like rays; 'I shake you in the flight of the Vr̥śīs, I shake you in the flight of the Kukūnanas, I shake you in the flight of the Bhandanas, I shake you in the flight of the most intoxicating, I shake you in the flight of the most honey-sweet'—these indeed are the divine waters. Thus, with both those which are divine waters and these which are human, he places sap into him."

"With 'Thee, the bright one, I shake out in the bright one,' for he indeed shakes out this bright one in the bright one; with 'in the form of the day, in the rays of the sun,' he thus shakes it out both in the form of the day and in the rays of the sun."

"The lofty form of the bull shines forth greatly"—this indeed is the lofty form of the bull that shines forth greatly, namely he who burns there, the bright one. "The precursor of the bright [Soma], Soma the precursor of Soma"—he thus makes the bright one the precursor of the bright, and Soma the precursor of Soma. "O Soma, what thy invincible, wakeful name is, for that I take thee"—this indeed is his invincible, wakeful name, namely Speech; he thus takes Speech for Speech.

Then, having gone out, he offers: "To thee, O Soma, for Soma, Svāhā! Thus he offers this very Soma to Soma. In this way, he does not cast his speech into the fire. Then he breathes over the gold; the significance of this is the same as before. Its sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are as many as those of the Aṃśu cup.

Then he gathers the shoots again with the formulas: "O divine Soma, as one who desires, go to the beloved abode of Agni; O divine Soma, as one who has mastery, go to the beloved abode of Indra; O divine Soma, as our friend, go to the beloved abode of all the gods. Indeed, he thereby draws forth those very libations; he causes them to swell again and makes them free from weariness. With those [libations] that are free from weariness, they perform the sacrifice.
Bhṛgu Vāruṇi, indeed, surpassed his father Varuṇa in knowledge; Varuṇa became aware of this, thinking, "He considers himself superior to me in knowledge."

He said, "My son, go toward the east; having seen what you see there, go toward the south; having seen what you see there, go toward the west; having seen what you see there, go toward the north; having seen what you see there, go toward that intermediate direction which lies between these two former ones; and whatever you see there, report it to me."

He set out from there toward the east. He came upon men who, with other men, were cutting up their joints joint by joint and dividing them joint by joint, saying, "This is yours, this is mine. He said, "Alas, O men! Are these men thus cutting up and dividing the joints of these [others] joint by joint? They replied, "Indeed, these [others] attended to us in yonder world; we are now attending to them here in return. He said, "Is there a remedy for this? "There is," they said. "What is it? "Your father knows," they said.

He set out from there toward the south. There he saw men with other men, cutting their joints apart joint by joint and dividing them joint by joint, saying, "This is yours, this is mine. He said, "Alas, O men! Are these men thus cutting up the joints of men joint by joint and dividing them joint by joint? They replied, "In this very way these [ancestors] attended upon us in yonder world; therefore we now attend upon them here in return. He said, "Is there a remedy for this? "There is," they said. "What is it? "Only your father knows."

He turned back from there and went westward. There he saw men being eaten by men who were sitting silently; they were being eaten by those who were sitting silently. He said, "Alas, O sir! Men are indeed eating these men who are sitting silently, by those who are sitting silently. They replied, "In this very way, these [men] attended upon us in yonder world; therefore, we are now attending upon them here in return. He said, "Is there a remedy for this? "There is," they said. "What is it? "Only your father knows," they said.

He departed from there toward the north. He came upon men who were making other men cry out, while those [crying ones] were being devoured. He said, "Alas, O men! Why are these men making these men cry out as they devour them? They replied, "It is because these [men] have treated us in this very way."

He then departed from that very place toward the northern intermediate direction between those two [rivers], the Uttara-manv-antara-deśa. There were two women, Kalyāṇī and Atikalyāṇī; between them stood a dark man with reddish-brown eyes, holding a staff in his hand. Upon seeing him, he was seized with fear. He fled and entered [his father's house]. His father said to him, "Study your private recitation! Why do you not study your private recitation? He replied, "What shall I study? There is nothing. Varuṇa then understood: "He has indeed seen me."

He said: "As for those men whom you saw in the eastern quarter—men who were cutting up men limb by limb and dividing them limb by limb, saying, 'This is yours, this is mine'—they were indeed the trees. In that he places a fuel-stick of wood, he thereby wins the trees; thereby he conquers the world of the trees."

Now, as for those men whom you saw in the southern direction being made by other men to cut their joints apart joint by joint and distribute them, saying, "This is yours, this is mine"—they were indeed cattle. In that he offers with milk, he thereby wins cattle; thereby he conquers the world of cattle.

Now, as for those men whom you saw in the western direction—men sitting silently being eaten by men sitting silently—those were indeed the plants; when he lights it up with grass, by that he wins the plants, and by that he conquers the world of the plants.

Now, as for those men whom you saw in the northern direction being devoured by men who were themselves crying out—those were indeed the waters. In that he brings back the water, he thereby secures the waters; thereby he conquers the world of the waters.

Now, as for those two women you saw—the beautiful one and the exceedingly beautiful one: she who is the beautiful one is Faith (śraddhā). When he offers the first oblation, by that he wins Faith; by that he conquers Faith. And she who is the exceedingly beautiful one is Unfaith (aśraddhā). When he offers the second oblation, by that he wins Unfaith; by that he conquers Unfaith.

Now, as for that man who stands between them—dark-complexioned, with reddish-brown eyes, and holding a staff in his hand—he is indeed Wrath. When he pours water into the offering-ladle and pours it out, by that he secures Wrath; by that he conquers Wrath. He who, knowing this, performs the Agnihotra sacrifice, conquers everything and secures everything through it.

Janaka, the King of Videha, once met with certain Brahmins who were performing their priestly duties: Śvetaketu Āruṇeya, Somaśuṣma Sātyayajñi, and Yājñavalkya. He said to them, "In what manner do you each offer the Agnihotra sacrifice?"

Śvetaketu Āruṇeya said, "O King, I offer two perpetual *gharma* oblations, overflowing with glory, into one another. How is that? The *gharma* is indeed the sun; I offer it into the fire in the evening. The *gharma* is indeed the fire; I offer it into the sun in the morning. "What becomes of him who offers thus? [the king asked]. "He becomes perpetual in prosperity and glory; he wins union with and residence in the same world as these two deities," [Śvetaketu replied].

Then Śomaśuṣma Sātyayajñi said: "O Emperor, I offer only radiance into radiance."—"How is that?"—"The sun, indeed, is radiance; I offer it into the fire in the evening. Fire, indeed, is radiance; I offer it into the sun in the morning."—"What becomes of him who offers thus?"—"He becomes radiant, glorious, and an eater of food; and he wins union with and the same world as these two deities."

Then Yājñavalkya said: "When I take out the fire, I am merely lifting up the Agnihotra itself; for all the gods follow the sun as it sets, and seeing this fire of mine taken out, they turn back toward it. Then, having washed the vessels and set them down, and having caused the Agnihotra cow to be milked, I satisfy those who see me while I see them. "You have examined the Agnihotra most closely, Yājñavalkya," he said. "I give you a hundred cows. "But you have not spoken of its departure, nor its path, nor its foundation, nor its satisfaction, nor its return, nor the one who rises to meet it in the world beyond," [Yājñavalkya] replied. Having said this, he mounted his chariot and drove away.

They said, "This kinsman of a king has indeed spoken over us; come, let us challenge him to a theological debate (*brahmodya*). Yājñavalkya said, "We are indeed Brahmins, while he is a kinsman of a king. If we were to defeat him, what could we say we had conquered? But if he were to defeat us, they would say, 'A kinsman of a king has conquered the Brahmins. Do not take me for granted. They agreed to this with him. Then Yājñavalkya mounted his chariot and drove after him. He came up to him and said, "Yājñavalkya, explain the Agnihotra! "The Agnihotra, O Emperor," [he replied].

When these two oblations have been offered, they rise up; they enter the intermediate space; they make the intermediate space itself their Āhavanīya fire, the wind their fuel, and the rays their bright oblation; they satisfy the intermediate space, and from there they rise up again.
They enter the sky; they make the sky itself the Āhavanīya fire, the sun the fuel, and the moon the bright oblation. They satisfy the sky, and from there they return.

They enter this [earth]; they make this very earth their Āhavanīya fire; they offer fuel to the fire, which is indeed the bright oblation of plants; they satisfy this [earth], and then they depart from it.

They enter the person; they make his mouth the Āhavanīya fire and his tongue the fuel, while food itself is the bright oblation. They satisfy the person. For one who knows this and eats, his Agnihotra has indeed been offered. Then they depart from him.

They enter the woman; they make her womb itself the Āhavanīya fire. The *dhārakā* is the fuel-stick—for this indeed is called *dhārakā*. By means of it, Prajāpati sustained his offspring. The *śukrā* is the oblation; they satisfy the woman with that very semen. He who, knowing this, approaches a woman in union, for him the Agnihotra is truly offered. The son who is born from that is the world to be attained. "This, Yājñavalkya, is the Agnihotra; there is nothing higher than this," he said. To him, Yājñavalkya granted a boon. He said, "Let there be for me the privilege of asking whatever I wish regarding you, O Yājñavalkya. Thereupon, Janaka became a Brahmin.

Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which many sacrificial fees were distributed. While bestowing a thousand cows, he said: "O Brahmins, let him who is the most proficient in sacred knowledge among you drive these away."

Yājñavalkya said, "These [questions] are directed toward the past. They replied, "Are you not perspiring, Yājñavalkya? You are indeed the most proficient in Brahman! He said, "Homage be to the most proficient in Brahman! We are merely seekers of cattle."
They said, "Who will ask this question of us? He replied, "I, Vidagdha Śākalya. Recognizing him, he said, "Cākalya, have the Brahmins indeed made you their fire-drill for extinguishing the embers?"

He said, "Yājñavalkya, how many gods are there? "Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three," he replied. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Thirty-three," he replied. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Three," he replied. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "Two," he replied. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half," he replied. "Yes," he said, "but how many gods are there really, Yājñavalkya? "One," he replied. "Yes," he said, "and who are those three hundred and three, and three thousand and three?"

He said: "These are merely their manifestations; there are indeed only thirty-three gods. "Which are those thirty-three? "The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—that makes thirty-one; Indra and Prajāpati make up the thirty-three."

"Who are the Vasus? "Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, heaven, the moon, and the stars—these are the Vasus; for they cause all this to dwell (vāsayante). Because they cause all this to dwell, they are called the Vasus."

"What are the Rudras? "These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh; when they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep (√rud). Because they cause one to weep, therefore they are called Rudras."
"Who are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year are these Ādityas; for they go along taking up all this [world]. Because they go along taking up all this, therefore they are called Ādityas."
"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed thunder; Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "What is thunder? "It is the lightning bolt. "What is the sacrifice? "It is the sacrificial animals."

"Who are those three gods? "These very three worlds, for all these gods are contained within them. "Who are those two gods? "Food and breath. "Who is the one-and-a-half? "This one who blows [the wind]. "Who is the one god? "Breath."

He said, "You have questioned me about a deity that should not be over-questioned; you will die before reaching home, and not even your bones will reach your house. He died just so, and thinking they were something else, robbers carried off his bones. Therefore, one should not be a reviler, for even one who knows this becomes superior.

One performs the Paśubandha sacrifice; the Paśubandha is indeed cattle. When he performs the Paśubandha, it is with the thought, "May I possess cattle. Therefore, one should perform it in the house, thinking, "I bind cattle in the house"; therefore, one should perform it where there is good pasture, thinking, "I bind cattle where there is good pasture. Indeed, the fires of the sacrificer who offers oblations wear out; as the fires wear out, the sacrificer follows them, and following the sacrificer come both the house and the cattle.

When he performs the animal sacrifice, he thereby makes the fires new again; following the renewal of the fires, the sacrificer, his house, and his cattle are renewed. Indeed, this [animal sacrifice] is a ransom for his own self that bestows long life. For those fires of the sacrificer who offers oblations do indeed crave meat; they meditate upon the sacrificer and set their intention on the sacrificer. Others cook meat at will upon other fires, but for these [fires], there is no desire for meat other than this [sacrifice], provided that they belong to one who possesses them.

When he sacrifices with the animal sacrifice, he thereby ransoms himself by means of a hero for a hero; for the victim is a hero and the sacrificer is a hero. This, indeed, is the supreme food, namely meat; thus he becomes an eater of the supreme food. He should not let a year pass by without sacrificing; for the year is life—thereby he places that immortal life within himself.

Indeed, one form of animal sacrifice follows the model of the *havis*-sacrifices, while another follows the model of the *soma*-sacrifices. That which follows the model of the *havis*-sacrifices is that in which he introduces the vow, in which he leads forward the water, in which he pours out the full vessel, and in which he makes him step the Viṣṇu-steps. Now, that which follows the model of the *soma*-sacrifices is that in which these [rites] are not performed.

Regarding this they say: "Is it an *iṣṭi*, or an animal sacrifice (*paśubandha*), or a great sacrifice (*mahāyajña*)? One should say, "It is a great sacrifice. For at that time, one has performed both the *iṣṭi* and the animal sacrifice; one should say to him, "You have indeed performed this [great sacrifice]."
Its fore-offerings are the morning pressing, its after-offerings are the third pressing, and the sacrificial cake itself is the midday pressing.

Now, some indeed bring the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā) when the omentum has been offered; but one should not do so. For if someone were to say of him at that time, "He has led the sacrificial gifts outside of his vital breaths; he has not strengthened the vital breaths; he will become blind, or crippled, or deaf, or paralyzed on one side"—it is possible that it would indeed happen exactly so.

In this very manner he should act: when the *iḍā* of the cake-offering has been invoked, he should lead forth the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). For this central breath belongs to Indra; thus he strengthens this central breath belonging to Indra with the sacrificial gifts. The midday pressing belongs to Indra, and it is at the midday pressing that the sacrificial gifts are led forth; therefore, he should lead forth the sacrificial gifts only when the *iḍā* of the cake-offering has been invoked.

Regarding this they say: "O Adhvaryu, since for one who has been consecrated (*dīkṣita*) a final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) is not appropriate, where did you consecrate him? They should support him until the *avabhṛtha*. The Adhvaryu, the Pratiprasthātṛ, the Hotṛ, the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Brahman, and the Āgnīdhra—by these he is indeed the Ṣaḍḍhotṛ. Having recited that Ṣaḍḍhotṛ formula, he offers a single oblation with five butter-portions: "The sky is the back, the atmosphere the self, the sacrifice by the limbs, the earth by the bodies; O Lord of Speech, with unimpaired speech, with an unimpaired ladle, he has sent the Hotṛ-offering, which increases the gods, to heaven—Svāhā! That itself is the consecration.

Regarding this they say: "O Adhvaryu, since for one who has been consecrated (dīkṣita) a purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) is not otherwise possible, where will you lead him to that avabhṛtha? When they proceed with the heart-spike (hṛdayaśūla), that indeed is his avabhṛtha.

Madhuka Paiṅgya used to say: "Some perform the animal sacrifice without Soma, while others perform it with Soma. Indeed, Soma was in heaven; Gāyatrī, having become a bird, fetched him. That leaf of his which fell became the *parṇa* (leaf) of the *parṇa* tree—this is the Brāhmaṇa passage that is recited. Some perform the animal sacrifice without Soma, while others perform it with Soma. He who uses a sacrificial post (*yūpa*) other than one made of *pālāśa* wood performs the animal sacrifice without Soma; he who makes the post of *pālāśa* wood performs the animal sacrifice with Soma. Therefore, one should make the sacrificial post of *pālāśa* wood alone."

That which has much sap is indeed unfit for cattle; therefore, one who desires cattle should not make such a sacrificial post. But that which is easily broken is fit for cattle; therefore, one who desires cattle should make such a sacrificial post.

Now, that sacrificial post which, being crooked, has its top like a spike is called "the pigeon. He who makes such a post goes to that world before his full span of life. Therefore, one who desires long life should not make such a post.

Now, that post which is bent at the bottom, straight in the middle, and bent at the top—that is the form of hunger. If one makes such a sacrificial post, his wives will be hungry; therefore, one who desires food should not make such a post. But that which is bent at the bottom, straight at the top, and bent in the middle—that is the form of food. Therefore, one who desires food should make such a post.

When he is about to sacrifice with an animal, if he makes the sacrificial post one cubit long, he thereby wins this very world; and when it is two cubits long, he thereby wins the intermediate region; and when it is three cubits long, he thereby wins the sky; and when it is four cubits long, he thereby wins the quarters. Indeed, this sacrificial post for the animal sacrifice is either three or four cubits long; but whatever is higher than that belongs to the Soma-sacrifice alone.

Regarding this they say: "Should one offer the two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) or not? They say, "One should offer them. For these two butter-portions are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice; what would a man be without his two eyes? As long as they do not exclude a sharer from his own share, he considers himself excluded; but when they exclude him from his own share, then he considers himself excluded. When the Hotṛ recites, "May the Rakṣas be joined with the raw flesh," it is then that he excludes him from his own share.

When the victim is being slaughtered, its heat (śuc) enters the heart, and from the heart it goes to the omentum (ūla). If they were to cook the victim together with the heart, the heat would again spread back into the victim. Therefore, having pierced it into a wooden splinter at the side, one should cook it.

He spreads the clarified butter underneath; that he makes the form of the earth. He places a piece of gold; that he makes the form of Agni. He places the omentum; that he makes the form of the intermediate space. He places a piece of gold; that he makes the form of Āditya. Then, when he pours butter over it from above, that he makes the form of heaven. This omentum indeed consists of five portions: the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year; therefore the omentum consists of five portions.
Just as this chariot wheel or a potter’s wheel would spin without support, even so these worlds were unstable and without support.

Prajāpati reflected: "How indeed might these worlds become firm and established? He made this earth firm with these mountains and rivers; he made the intermediate space firm with birds and rays; and he made the sky firm with clouds and stars.

He uttered "maha. Cattle indeed are *maha*; therefore, he for whom these [cattle] are many is most highly honored in his family. Indeed, these [cattle] become many for him, and he is most highly honored in his family. Therefore, even if they should distress him from his dwelling or drive him away, he should, after offering the *agnihotra*, worship with "maha. He stands firm with offspring and cattle; he does not fall from his dwelling.

There are indeed four fires: the established, the drawn out, the carried forward, and the spread out. This very world is the established fire; the intermediate space is the drawn out; the sky is the carried forward; and the quarters are the spread out. Fire itself is the established; Vāyu is the drawn out; Āditya is the carried forward; and Candramas is the spread out. The Gārhapatya is the established; the Āhavanīya is the drawn out; then that which they lead forth from the Āhavanīya toward the east is the carried forward; and that which they bring northward for the cooking of the sacrificial animal and for the Upayaṅgha cups is the spread out. Therefore, one should perform the animal sacrifice in the fire that has been carried forward.
Regarding this they say: "Of what deity should this animal be? "It should be of Prajāpati," they reply; "for Prajāpati indeed first beheld it; therefore, this animal should be of Prajāpati alone."

Moreover, they also say: "This animal sacrifice should indeed belong to Sūrya. Therefore, when the sun has set, animals are bound for this [sacrifice]; some bind them, while others gather together at their respective pens. For this reason, they say: "This animal sacrifice should indeed belong to Sūrya."

Moreover, they also say: "This animal sacrifice should belong to Indra and Agni alone; for these two deities follow all other gods. If one who is afflicted performs the sacrifice, they carry him across; if one performs it with great splendor, they carry him across. Therefore, this animal sacrifice should belong to Indra and Agni alone."
The animal sacrifice is indeed the vital breath; therefore, as long as one lives, no other has power over his animals, for they remain bound within him.

Prajāpati said to Agni, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to Vāyu," he said. He spoke to Vāyu, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to Puruṣa," he said. He spoke to Puruṣa, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to the Cattle," he said. He spoke to the Cattle, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. They replied, "No. "Then speak to Candramas," he said. He spoke to Candramas, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "No. "Then speak to Āditya," he said. He spoke to Āditya, "Sacrifice with me; let me obtain you. He replied, "So be it. "Those who did not desire this—what indeed shall I have among them? [Prajāpati asked. "Whatever you may desire," [Āditya replied]. "So be it," [Prajāpati said]. He seized him (Āditya). This is that animal of his which was seized and slaughtered. It swelled; he gratified it with these Āprī verses. Because he gratified it with these Āprī verses, they are called *āpriyaḥ*. Therefore, one should say of an animal that has been slaughtered, "Let it lie for a moment. As great a world as one wins by sacrificing with the Aśvamedha, so great a world does one win by this [rite].

The eastern direction breathed over him with "Breathe forth! and thus bestowed the out-breath (*prāṇa*) upon him. The southern direction breathed over him with "Breathe across! and thus bestowed the through-breath (*vyāna*) upon him. The western direction breathed over him with "Breathe away! and thus bestowed the in-breath (*apāna*) upon him. The northern direction breathed over him with "Breathe up! and thus bestowed the up-breath (*udāna*) upon him. The upward direction breathed over him with "Breathe together! and thus bestowed the equalizing breath (*samāna*) upon him. Therefore, when a son is born whose navel-string has not yet been cut, one should say to five Brahmins, "Breathe over him! If, however, he cannot find them, he himself should breathe over him while walking around him; he then reaches a full lifespan and lives until old age.

He took away the breath of the fire; therefore, this [fire] does not burn unless it is blown upon or kindled, for its breath has been taken away. Indeed, he who knows this takes away the breath of his hateful rival.

The wind indeed took away its form; therefore, people hear it as if it were flickering, but they do not see it, for its form has been taken away. Verily, he who knows this takes away the form of his hateful rival.

The mind alone is what a man has taken away; therefore they say, "May the divine mind protect you, not the human mind," for his mind is indeed taken away. He who knows this takes away the mind of his hateful rival.

He took away the sight of cattle; therefore, even when they are looking about as it were, they do not perceive, but only when they smell do they perceive, for their sight has been taken away. Indeed, he who knows this takes away the sight of his hateful rival.

He took away the radiance of the moon; therefore, although these two are similar, the moon does not shine as brightly, for its radiance has been taken away. Indeed, he who knows this takes away the radiance of his hateful rival. Because he took it away (ādatta), he is called Āditya.

A tiger killed the Samrāḍ-dhuk cow of the householder Keśin. He summoned his fellow students and asked, "What is the expiation for this? They said, "There is no expiation here; Khaṇḍika Auddālaki alone knows the expiation for this, but he desires both such wealth as this and even more than that."
He said, "Charioteer, harness my horses; I shall go forth. If he speaks to me, I will complete [the sacrifice]; but if he kills me, the sacrifice will be destroyed along with me."

Having yoked [his chariot], he set out and arrived; seeing him from afar, he said: "Since these very skins are used for wild animals, we shall instead split their ribs and cook them; my black antelope skin has been tied around my neck—do not attack me! Let him come down here!"

"No," he said, "O Venerable One, a tiger has indeed killed my cow that yields milk at will. If you explain it to me, I shall complete [the sacrifice]; but if you kill me, I shall tear apart the sacrifice along with its dismembered parts."

He said, "Let me invite those who are to be invited. Having invited them, he said to them: "If I tell this to him, his offspring will possess this world and not mine; I shall become one who possesses the world of heaven. But if I do not tell this to him, my own offspring will possess this world and not his; he shall become one who possesses the world of heaven. They said, "Do not speak it, O Venerable One; this world indeed belongs to the Kṣatriya. He said, "I shall certainly tell it; for there are more nights beyond these."

Therefore, he said this to him: "Having offered the *spṛti* oblations, say, 'Offer another oblation! and she shall be a cow that milks for you, O Emperor. [He says: "By means of the Moon, I protect your mind, Svāhā! By means of the Sun, I protect your eye, Svāhā! By means of the Wind, I protect your breaths, Svāhā! By means of the Quarters, I protect your hearing, Svāhā! By means of the Waters, I protect your blood, Svāhā! By means of the Earth, I protect your body, Svāhā! Then he should say, "Offer another oblation! and she shall be a cow that milks for you, O Emperor. Thereupon he indeed desisted. Even now these offspring of Kaiśinī are born. He cooks the *brahmaudana*; verily, he thereby bestows seed. With the clarified butter that remains, he anoints the halter and takes it up; clarified butter is indeed brilliance, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati; thus he endows Prajāpati with brilliance. For the horse is indeed impure and unholy.
The girdle is made of darbha grass; darbha grass is indeed purifying. It thus purifies him; he seizes him as one who is purified and fit for sacrifice.
When the horse was sacrificed, its seed flowed out; that became gold. In that he gives gold, he thereby endows the horse with its own seed.

Prajāpati created the sacrifice; its greatness departed from it and entered the great officiating priests (mahartvijas). He sought it through the great officiating priests and found it through the great officiating priests. When the great officiating priests eat the *brahmaudana* (the Brahman’s rice-mess), the sacrificer thereby secures the greatness of the sacrifice. In the *brahmaudana*, he gives gold; for the rice-mess is seed and gold is seed; thus, by means of seed, he places seed within him. It consists of a hundred measures (*śatamāna*); for man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself. In the middle of the day, he takes four kinds of water—the *vasatīvarī* waters; they have been brought together from all the quarters. Since food is in the quarters and water is food, he secures food for him by means of food.

That which is performed without a sacrificial formula (yajuṣ) is indeed a failure of the sacrifice. With the formula, "They have taken this rein of the Order," he takes up the horse's halter; this is for the sake of providing a sacrificial formula and for the success of the sacrifice. It is twelve cubits long; the year has twelve months; thus he attains the year-long sacrifice.

Regarding this they say: "Should the girdle be twelve cubits long, or thirteen cubits? The year, indeed, is the bull among the seasons; its thirteenth month is the hump. This Horse-sacrifice is the bull among sacrifices. Just as there is a hump on a bull, so there is a hump for this [sacrifice]—one should add a thirteenth cubit to the girdle. It is just as the hump of a bull is covered over; such is that.

"Thou art the overlord"—therefore the performer of the horse-sacrifice conquers all the quarters; "thou art the world"—he thereby conquers the world; "thou art the controller, the sustainer"—he thus makes him a controller and a sustainer; "do thou go to Agni Vaiśvānara"—he thus causes him to go to Agni Vaiśvānara; "go with wide extension"—he thus extends him with offspring and cattle; "with the cry of Svāhā"—this is his Vaṣaṭ-call; "go happily to the gods"—he thus makes him go happily to the gods; "to Prajāpati"—the horse belongs to Prajāpati; he thus endows it with its own deity.

Verily, he who binds the horse without having announced it to the Brahman and the gods is liable to meet with misfortune. He addresses the Brahman, saying, "O Brahman, I shall bind the horse for the gods and for Prajāpati; may I prosper thereby. Having thus addressed the Brahman, he binds it after having announced it to the Brahman; he does not meet with misfortune. The Brahman gives the impulse, saying, "Bind it for the gods and for Prajāpati; prosper thereby! Thus he endows it with its own deity. Then he sprinkles it; the significance of this is the same as before.

He sprinkles it, saying, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati. Prajāpati is indeed the most vigorous among the gods; he thus bestows vigor upon this [horse]. Therefore, the horse is the most vigorous of animals.

"I sprinkle you, acceptable to Indra and Agni"—for Indra and Agni are indeed the most powerful among the gods; he thus bestows power upon this [horse], and therefore the horse is the most powerful among animals.

With the words, "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Vāyu," he sprinkles it; for Vāyu is the swiftest among the gods, and thus he bestows speed upon this [horse]. Therefore, the horse is the swiftest among animals.

"I sprinkle thee, acceptable to all the gods," he says; for all the gods are indeed the most glorious among the gods, and thus he bestows glory upon him. Therefore, the horse is the most glorious of animals. "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to all the gods," he says.

Regarding this they say: "Since the horse belongs to Prajāpati, why then does he sprinkle it for other deities? Indeed, all the deities are dependent upon the Aśvamedha. When he says, "I sprinkle thee for all the gods," he causes all the deities to depend upon him; therefore, in the Aśvamedha, all the deities are dependent [upon the sacrificer]. Verily, evil seeks to seize him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The horse is a thunderbolt. Saying, "Away, mortal! Away, dog! he kills a four-eyed dog and washes it under the feet of the horse; thus he tramples him with the thunderbolt, and evil, the rival, does not reach him.

Just as the oblation might spill before it has been offered, so does this animal spill when they release it after it has been washed but not yet sacrificed. When he offers the *stokīyā* oblations, he offers it as a complete offering to prevent spilling; for that which spills from what has already been offered is indeed not spilled. He offers a thousand [oblations], for the heavenly world is commensurate with a thousand; it is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer measured oblations, he would obtain only what is limited"; therefore, he offers unmeasured oblations for the sake of obtaining the unlimited. Prajāpati indeed said: "In the *stokīya* verses, I establish the Aśvamedha; once it is thus established, I proceed from that point onward."

With "Svāhā to Agni," he offers it to Agni; with "Svāhā to Soma," he offers it to Soma; with "Svāhā to the joy of the waters," he offers it to the waters; with "Svāhā to Savitṛ," he offers it to Savitṛ; with "Svāhā to Vāyu," he offers it to Vāyu; with "Svāhā to Viṣṇu," he offers it to Viṣṇu; with "Svāhā to Indra," he offers it to Indra; with "Svāhā to Bṛhaspati," he offers it to Bṛhaspati; with "Svāhā to Mitra," he offers it to Mitra; with "Svāhā to Varuṇa," he offers it to Varuṇa. So many indeed are all the gods; it is to them that he offers it. He offers them consecutively, for the heavenly world is, as it were, turned away; it is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

He who offers oblations directed away is liable to perish away; he turns back again and finds firm support in this very world. He indeed declared this to be the completion of the sacrifice, so that nothing may be spilled—for that which spills of what has been offered is not truly spilled.

Just as if an oblation were to spill before it has been offered, so does this animal spill when they release one that has been sprinkled but not yet sacrificed. When he offers the forms (rūpas), he offers it as a complete offering to prevent spilling; for that which spills from what has been offered is indeed not spilled. With the words, "To the *hiṅ* [sound], svāhā! To the one who has made the *hiṅ*, svāhā!"—these are indeed the forms of the horse; verily, he thereby secures them.

Regarding this they say: "Forms are indeed no oblation; these should not be offered. Yet on the other hand, they also say: "The Aśvamedha is completed here when one offers the forms; they must certainly be offered. For he who offers oblations elsewhere than in the fire, in a place that is not their proper abode, deprives him of his own dwelling-place and brings forth an enemy for him.

Having recited [the verses] prior to the Sāvitrī sacrifice itself, he offers the forms (rūpa) once only into the Āhavanīya fire; thus he offers the oblations in their proper abode. He does not produce a rival for him. He offers at each opening of the sacrifice, for the continuity and non-interruption of the sacrifice.

Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer at every opening of the sacrifice, he would be deprived of cattle and would become worse off; therefore, it should be offered only once, so that he is not deprived of cattle and does not become worse off. He offers forty-eight oblations; the Jagatī meter has forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; thus, by means of the Jagatī, he wins cattle for himself. He offers one additional oblation; therefore, among offspring, there is one who is preeminent.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha; once created, it went away from him and entered the quarters. The gods sought it by means of a quest; they pursued it with Iṣṭis, they sought it with Iṣṭis, and they found it with Iṣṭis. When one sacrifices with Iṣṭis, the sacrificer thereby seeks out the sacrificial horse itself.

They are Sāvitrī verses; for Savitṛ is this earth. Whosoever hides upon her, or whosoever goes elsewhere, it is on her indeed that they find him. No one at all—neither horizontally nor upwards—is able to pass beyond her. In that there are Sāvitrī verses, it is for the very purpose of finding the horse.

Regarding this they say: "The horse is indeed lost when it goes away from us, for they do not bring it back. When he offers the *dhṛti* oblations in the evening—since security (*kṣema*) is the *dhṛti*, and the night is security—he supports it by means of security. Therefore, in the evening, both men and animals become secure. Then, when he sacrifices with the *iṣṭi* offerings in the morning, he truly seeks it; therefore, during the day, one goes out seeking what is lost. Furthermore, when he offers the *dhṛti* oblations in the evening and sacrifices with the *iṣṭis* in the morning, the sacrificer thereby ordains security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*). Therefore, wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, the security and prosperity of the subjects becomes ordained.

Prosperity and the kingdom indeed depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. When a man attains prosperity, the lute is played for him; two Brāhmaṇas, lute-players and singers, sing for a year. The lute is indeed the form of prosperity; they thus bestow prosperity upon him.
Regarding this they say: "If two Brāhmaṇas were to sing [the Saman], the Kṣatra would depart from him; for a Brāhmaṇa is the form of the Brahman, and the Kṣatra does not find rest in the Brahman."

If two Rājanyas were to sing [the Sāman] for him, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) would depart from him; for the Rājanya is the form of the Kṣatra, and spiritual luster does not abide in the Kṣatra. One sings as a Brāhmaṇa, the other as a Rājanya; the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the Brahman (spiritual power), and the Rājanya is the Kṣatra (political power). Thus, his prosperity becomes encompassed on both sides by both the Brahman and the Kṣatra.

Regarding this they say: "If both were to sing by day, prosperity would be liable to fall away from him; for the day is indeed a form of the Brahmin. Indeed, whenever a king desires [to act], he then oppresses the Brahmin, but he becomes more wicked."

"If both were to perform it at night, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) would depart from him; for the night is a form of the Kṣatra, and spiritual luster does not abide in the Kṣatra. Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa sings by day and the Rājanya at night; thus his prosperity is encompassed on both sides by both the Brāhmaṇical power and the Kṣatriya power."

"He sacrificed," "he gave"—thus the Brāhmaṇa sings. Sacrifice and pious works (iṣṭāpūrta) indeed belong to the Brāhmaṇa; by means of sacrifice and pious works he thus endows him. "He fought," "he won that battle"—thus the Rājanya sings. Battle indeed is the heroism of the Rājanya; by means of heroism he thus endows him. One sings three Gāthās, the other sings three; they amount to six. There are six seasons in the year; he thus finds firm support in the seasons, in the year. To these two he gives a hundred. Man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself.

"Vibhū mātrā, prabhū pitrā"—this earth indeed is the mother and yonder sky is the father; by these two he entrusts him. "Thou art a horse, thou art a steed"—he thus instructs him, and therefore offspring are born well-trained. "Thou art a racer, thou art a courser"—he leads him forth, and therefore the horse attains pre-eminence among animals. "Thou art a runner, thou art a swift one, thou art a prize-winner"—this is according to the sacrificial formula itself. "Thou art a bull, thou art manly-minded"—this is for the sake of pairing. "Yayur nāmāsi, śiśur nāmāsi"—this indeed is the dear name of the horse; he addresses him with his own dear name. Therefore, even when two enemies meet and address each other by name, they recognize one another completely.

With the words, "Go along the flight-path of the Ādityas," he causes him to go to the Ādityas themselves. With the words, "O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse consecrated for the sacrifice to the gods," he entrusts him to the hundred princes who are the guardians of the quarters. With the words, "May there be delight here, may there be pleasure here; may there be steadfastness here, may there be self-steadfastness, Svāhā! he offers oblations for a year—sixteen nineties. These indeed are the fetters of the horse; with them he binds him. Therefore, when the horse is released, it returns to its tether. These sixteen nineties are indeed the fetters of the horse; with them he binds him. Therefore, when the horse is released, it does not abandon its tether.

The Aśvamedha is indeed the kingdom; those who guard the horse strive for the kingdom. Of them, those who reach the conclusion (udṛc) become the kingdom by means of the kingdom itself; but those who do not reach the conclusion are cut off from the kingdom. Therefore, one who possesses a kingdom should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. He who, being weak, sacrifices with the Aśvamedha is surely cast away. If enemies should seize his horse, his sacrifice would be cut asunder and he would become worse off. Therefore, they guard it wearing armor, for the continuity of the sacrifice and to prevent its being cut asunder; thus he does not become worse off. Then, having brought another horse, they should sprinkle it; that is the atonement in that case.

Prajāpati desired, "May I sacrifice with the Aśvamedha. He exerted himself and practiced austerity. From him, thus exhausted and heated by penance, seven deities departed from his own self; she became the Dīkṣā (the consecration). He saw these Vaiśvadeva offerings and offered them. By means of them, he indeed obtained the Dīkṣā. In that the sacrificer offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations, he thereby obtains the Dīkṣā. He offers them day after day; verily, day after day he obtains the Dīkṣā. He offers seven; for seven were those deities who departed; through them alone he obtains the Dīkṣā for himself.

The vital breaths indeed depart from those who exceed the period of consecration (*dīkṣā*). They perform the rite for seven days; for there are seven vital breaths in the head, and the consecration is the vital breaths. By means of the vital breaths, he thereby secures the vital breaths and the consecration for himself. Dividing the deity into three parts, he offers the oblation; for the gods are thrice-returned, and these worlds are thrice-returned. Through prosperity and vigor, he becomes firmly established in these worlds.

They amount to twenty-one: twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first. That is the divine kṣatra, that is prosperity, that is sovereignty, that is the summit of the radiant one; he attains self-rule.

He offers thirty *audgrabhaṇa* oblations; the *virāj* consists of thirty syllables, and the *virāj* is all food; it is for the attainment of complete food. He offers four *audgrabhaṇa* oblations and three *vaiśvadeva* ones; they amount to seven. There are indeed seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the head; by means of the vital breaths, he secures the consecration (*dīkṣā*) for him through the vital breaths. He offers the final *pūrṇāhuti* oblation for support and for union.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha; once created, it collapsed forward in its Ṛc and collapsed backward in its Sāman. The Vaiśvadeva hymns raised it up; therefore, when one offers the Vaiśvadeva oblations, it is for the very purpose of raising up the Aśvamedha.
"Kāya svāhā! Kasmai svāhā! Katamasmai svāhā!"—with these words he performs the offering to Prajāpati; by means of the deities whose mouth is Prajāpati, he thus raises him up.
"Svāhā to the one meditated upon! Svāhā to the mind, to Prajāpati! Svāhā to the thought, to the knower!"—whatever was the Brāhmaṇa explanation for the preceding [verses], that applies here as well.
"Aditi, svāhā! Aditi the Great, svāhā! Aditi the Very Gracious, svāhā!"—for this earth is indeed Aditi; it is by means of her that he raises him up.
"To Sarasvatī, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the Purifier, svāhā! To Sarasvatī the Great, svāhā!"—Sarasvatī is indeed speech; verily by means of speech he raises him up.
"To Pūṣan, svāhā! To Pūṣan on the path, svāhā! To Pūṣan the protector of men, svāhā!"—Pūṣan is indeed cattle; verily, by means of cattle he raises him up.
"To Tvaṣṭṛ, Svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ the Turīpa, Svāhā! To Tvaṣṭṛ the Many-formed, Svāhā!"—Tvaṣṭṛ is indeed the fashioner of the forms of paired animals; by means of these forms, he thus raises him up.

"To Viṣṇu, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, the protector of the dwelling, Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, Śipiviṣṭa, Svāhā!"—for Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice; verily by means of the sacrifice he raises him up. With the verse, "All [this belongs] to the god, the leader," he offers the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti). This earth is indeed the full-offering; verily he finds firm support upon her at the end.

"O Brahman, may a Brāhmaṇa endowed with spiritual luster (brahmavarcas) be born!"—thus he bestows spiritual luster upon the Brāhmaṇa himself; therefore, in former times, a Brāhmaṇa was born endowed with spiritual luster.

"May a brave Rājanya, skilled with the bow, a piercer of the foe, and a great chariot-warrior be born in our kingdom!"—thus he bestows bravery and greatness upon the Rājanya himself; therefore, in former times, a Rājanya was born who was brave, skilled with the bow, a piercer of the foe, and a great chariot-warrior.
By saying, "The cow is a milker," he places milk in the cow itself; therefore, in former times, the cow was born as a milker.
"The ox is the bearer"—he thus bestows strength upon the ox; therefore, in former times, the ox was born as a bearer.
With the words, "Swift is the steed," he bestows speed upon the horse; therefore, in ancient times, the horse was born as a runner.
The word *puraṃdhri* (a mature woman) assumes its form only when applied to a female; therefore, a beautiful young woman is naturally beloved.
"Victorious, standing upon the chariot"—thus the Rājanya indeed bestows the majesty of victory; therefore, in former times, a victorious Rājanya was born.
"Fit for the assembly, young"—this indeed refers to one who is in the first stage of life; therefore, a man in the first stage of life is beloved by women.
"May a hero be born to this sacrificer"—thus he bestows vigor upon the progeny of the sacrificer himself; therefore, a hero was born to the one who had sacrificed before.

"May Parjanya rain for us according to our desire"—for indeed, Parjanya rains according to their desire where they sacrifice with this sacrifice; "may our plants ripen fruitfully"—for indeed, the plants ripen fruitfully where they sacrifice with this sacrifice; "may our security and prosperity be established for us"—for indeed, security and prosperity are established where they sacrifice with this sacrifice. Therefore, wherever they sacrifice with this sacrifice, the security and prosperity of the people becomes established.

Prajāpati assigned the sacrifices to the gods; he kept the Aśvamedha for himself. Those gods said to Prajāpati, "The Aśvamedha is indeed the sacrifice; let there also be a share for us here. For them, he prepared these food-oblations (annahoma). In that he offers the food-oblations, he thereby gratifies the gods.

He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance. By means of brilliance he bestows that brilliance upon him. He offers with clarified butter; for clarified butter is the dear abode of the gods. Verily, he prospers them by means of their own dear abode.
He offers with groats; for groats are the form of the gods; verily, he thus gratifies the gods.
He offers with parched grains; for parched grains are the form of days and nights; he thus gratifies the days and nights.

He offers with parched grains; for parched grains are indeed the form of the stars, and thus he gratifies the stars. He offers while pronouncing their names, saying, "Svāhā to out-breathing! Svāhā to in-breathing!"—by pronouncing their names, he truly gratifies them. He offers in successive order, saying, "Svāhā to one! Svāhā to two! Svāhā to a hundred! Svāhā to one hundred and one!"—by offering in successive order, he truly gratifies them in succession. He offers increasing by one each time; for the heavenly world is single-fold, and thus he causes him to go to the heavenly world as a unity. He offers continuously; for the heavenly world is, as it were, continuous, and this is for the conquest of the heavenly world.

He who offers oblations directed away from himself is liable to be burnt away; he must not exceed one hundred and one. If he were to exceed one hundred and one, he would deprive the sacrificer of his life-span. He offers one hundred and one; for man has a life-span of a hundred years and the self is the one hundred and first—he thus establishes himself in life and in the self. With the words, "To the dawning, svāhā! To heaven, svāhā! he offers the two final oblations; for the night is the dawning and the day is heaven—he thereby gratifies both day and night.

Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer both [libations] either by day or by night, he would cause confusion between day and night. Therefore, he offers before the sun has risen with the words, "To the Dawn, Svāhā! and after it has risen with the words, "To Heaven, Svāhā!"—this is to avoid the confusion of day and night.

The Aśvamedha is indeed the king of sacrifices; the sacrificer undertakes the horse-sacrifice as the sacrificer is the sacrifice. When he binds the sacrificial animals to the horse, he places them in the sacrifice itself.

The horse, the hornless goat, and the gayal—these he immolates at the central sacrificial post; by this, he sharpens the very front of his army, and therefore the vanguard of a king’s army is destined to be formidable.
The black-necked [goat] dedicated to Agni is placed on the forehead in front; he thereby establishes the eastern fire, and therefore the eastern fire is auspicious for a king.
He offers a ewe to Sarasvatī below the two buttocks; thereby he makes women the followers of men, and for that reason women are destined to follow after men.
The two Aśvins, dark-red below, [are placed] on the two arms; verily he bestows strength upon the two arms; therefore a king is destined to be strong of arm.
A dark-grey animal dedicated to Soma and Pūṣan he offers at the navel; verily, he thereby establishes that very foundation. Pūṣan is indeed this earth; verily, he finds firm support upon her.
He makes the two Sauryayāma cups, white and black, his two side-armors; therefore, a king, when armored, displays his prowess.
The son of Tvaṣṭṛ placed hairy thighs upon his thighs; he bestowed strength specifically upon the thighs. Therefore, a king is destined to possess strength in his thighs.
A white animal for Vāyu at the tail; he thereby makes it a swelling, therefore offspring resort to a swelling in times of danger.

A cow that miscarries for Indra Svapasya, for the sake of the sacrifice's possession of Indra. A dwarf for Viṣṇu; Viṣṇu is indeed the sacrifice, so he finds firm support in the sacrifice itself at the end.

These, indeed, are the fifteen animals tied to the horse; for the thunderbolt is fifteenfold, and the thunderbolt is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt, by means of that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.

There are fifteen [stotras] for each; likewise for the others, there are fifteen. The thunderbolt (vajra) is indeed fifteenfold, and the thunderbolt is vigor; by means of this thunderbolt, this vigor, the sacrificer repels evil on both sides.
Regarding this they say: "By these [offerings], one has indeed struck away evil," yet he restores Prajāpati incompletely and does not win over this entire world.

One should immolate exactly seventeen animals at the central sacrificial post; for Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati—it is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. There are sixteen on each of the other posts; for this whole world consists of sixteen parts, and thus he secures this entire world.

"How should he propitiate them? they asked. He should propitiate them with the verses of Bṛhaduktha: "Kindled, anointing the heart of prayers. For Bṛhaduktha Vāmadevya, or Aśva Sāmudri, saw these *āprī* verses for the horse; saying, "These are they; with these we shall now propitiate him," one should not do so. One should propitiate them with the verses of Jamadagni. Jamadagni is Prajāpati, and he is the Horse-sacrifice; thus he endows it with its own deity. Therefore, one should propitiate them with the verses of Jamadagni alone.

Now, some perform separate invitatory and offering verses for these animals tied to the horse, saying, "We find [the verses] for these; we do not perform them for the others. One should not do so. The horse is indeed the nobility (*kṣatra*), and the other animals are the common people (*viś*). Those who act thus make the common people a rival and an adversary to the nobility; moreover, they deprive the sacrificer of his life-span. Therefore, the horse belongs to Prajāpati, while the others belong to the gods. Thus he makes the common people submissive and following after the nobility; moreover, he endows the sacrificer with a full life-span.

The goad of the horse is made of gold, those of the animals tied to the horse (paryaṅgyas) are made of copper, and those of the others are made of iron. Gold is indeed light, and the Aśvamedha is sovereignty; thus he bestows light upon the kingdom. Moreover, by means of the light of gold, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world. Furthermore, he makes it a mirror for the attainment of the heavenly world.
Moreover, the horse is indeed the ruling power (kṣatra), and gold is the form of the ruling power; thus he causes the ruling power to prosper by means of the ruling power itself.

Now, as to why they are made of copper for the animals tied to the horse's limbs: just as the king’s own royal servants—the charioteers and the village headmen—are subordinate to the king, so indeed are these animals tied to the limbs subordinate to the horse; and just as copper is to gold, he thus endows them with their own proper form.

Now, as for the fact that the others [the limbs] are made of iron: the other animals are the common people (*viś*), and iron is the form of the common people; he thus makes the common people prosper by means of the common people. They cut off the portions of the horse from a wicker basket on the north side; for the horse is connected with the *ānuṣṭubh* metre, and this northern quarter is connected with the *ānuṣṭubh*; he thus places it in its own quarter. And as to why it is from a wicker basket: the horse has its origin in the waters, and the reed (*vetasa*) is born of the waters; he thus endows it with its own womb.

In the Aśvamedha, the gods did not know the way to the heavenly world; the horse knew it. Therefore, when they glide along with the horse for the sake of the Pavamāna [Soma] in the Aśvamedha, it is for the sake of discerning the heavenly world. They hold onto the tail for the attainment of the heavenly world itself. Indeed, a human does not know the heavenly world directly; the horse, indeed, knows the heavenly world directly.

If the Udgātṛ were to sing the Udgītha, it would be as if one who does not know the terrain were to lead by another path; but when, having excluded the Udgātṛ, he chooses a horse for the Udgītha, it is just as if one who knows the terrain were to lead directly—so indeed does the horse lead the sacrificer directly to the heavenly world. He utters *hiṅ*; he utters that as the Sāman itself, for it is the Udgītha. They tether mares around it; they neigh together, just as the accompanying singers sing along. Gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a hundred-māna piece of refined gold; its Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.

Prajāpati desired, "May I conquer both worlds: the world of the gods and the world of men. He saw these domestic animals and sacrificed them; by means of them, he won these two worlds. By means of the domestic animals, he won this world; by means of the wild ones, he won that world. This world is indeed the world of men, and yonder is the world of the gods. In that he sacrifices with domestic animals, the sacrificer wins this very world by them; in that [he sacrifices] with wild ones, he wins yonder world by them.

If he were to establish [the fires] with village-wood, the roads would be crowded; the boundaries of two villages would be close together, and ṛkṣīkas, man-tigers, robbers, murderers, and thieves would be born in the forests. If he were to establish them with forest-wood, the roads would be desolate; the boundaries of two villages would be far apart, and ṛkṣīkas, man-tigers, robbers, murderers, and thieves would be born in the forests.

Regarding this they say: "This wild animal is indeed without cattle; one must not offer an oblation for it, for if he were to offer, they would soon carry off the sacrificer dead to the forest, since wild animals have the forest as their portion. Yet, if he were not to offer, there would be a desecration of the sacrifice. Therefore, they release them after they have been carried around the fire; thus it is neither offered nor unoffered, they do not carry the sacrificer dead to the forest, and there is no desecration of the sacrifice.

Through the village customs he establishes them; father and son reach an agreement; their paths run together, and the boundaries of the two villages become contiguous. No *ṛkṣīkas*, no man-tigers, no robbers, no murderers, no thieves are born in the forests.

Prajāpati created the Aśvamedha; once created, it went away from him. Having become a *paṅkti*, it entered the year; it became the half-months. He employed it with the fifteen-fold [stomas] and reached it; having reached it, he secured it by means of the fifteen-fold [stomas]. This fifteen-fold [stoma] is indeed the counterpart of the half-months. In that he offers the fifteen-fold [animals], the sacrificer secures the half-months by them.

Regarding this they say: "The year is indeed not secured for him who performs the year-long rite other than with the Cāturmāsya offerings. The Cāturmāsyas are truly the manifest year; when he immolates the animals of the Cāturmāsyas, he secures the year manifestly. "He is deprived of offspring and cattle and fails to reach the heavenly world, he who performs the year-long rite other than with the sets of eleven," so they say. This set of eleven (ekādaśinī) is indeed the heavenly world in its true nature; the set of eleven is offspring and cattle. When he immolates the animals of the set of eleven, he does not fail to reach the heavenly world, nor is he deprived of offspring and cattle.

Prajāpati created the Virāj; once created, she turned away from him and entered the sacrificial horse. He pursued her with the sets of ten [animals] and reached her; having reached her, he secured her by means of the sets of ten. In that he sacrifices the sets of ten, the sacrificer secures the Virāj by them. He sacrifices a hundred; for man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself.

He offers eleven sets of ten animals; for the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is indeed power and vigor. It is for the attainment of power and vigor that he offers eleven sets of ten. There are ten vital breaths in an animal, and the self is the eleventh; it is by means of the vital breaths that he thus makes the animals prosper. They belong to the Viśvedevas, for the horse belongs to the Viśvedevas; this is for the sake of the completeness of the horse. They are of many forms, therefore animals are of many forms; they are of various forms, therefore animals are of various forms.
"They harness the ruddy, bright one as he moves"—the ruddy, bright one is indeed yonder sun; verily, he harnesses yonder sun for him for the attainment of the world of heaven.

Regarding this they say: "The sacrifice indeed turns away from him whose animal, once dedicated, goes elsewhere than to the altar. [He says: "O singer, turn this horse back by this path; do not let it go! Vāyu is indeed the singer; he thus places him (Vāyu) behind him for his sake, so that the horse does not pass beyond.
Verily, brilliance, sensory power, cattle, and prosperity depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

"May the Vasus anoint you with the Gāyatra metre"—with these words the queen anoints him; for clarified butter is brilliance and the Gāyatrī is brilliance: thus she places two forms of brilliance together within him.
"May the Rudras anoint you with the Triṣṭubh metre"—for ghee is brilliance and the Triṣṭubh is power; thus he bestows both brilliance and power upon him in a unified manner.
"May the Ādityas anoint you with the Jagatī metre"—for ghee is brilliance and the Jagatī is cattle; thus he bestows both brilliance and cattle upon him in a harmonious manner.

The wives anoint him; for the wives are indeed the form of prosperity (śrī). Thus they bestow prosperity upon him; from him neither brilliance, nor sensory power, nor cattle, nor prosperity ever departs.

Just as if a portion of the oblation were to spill before it has been offered, so does this part of the animal spill when the hair falls off while it is being washed. When they pierce the glass-beads (kāca), they thereby gather back its hair. They are made of gold; the explanation for that has already been stated. One by one they pierce a hundred and one beads; man indeed has a life-span of a hundred years and the self is the hundred-and-first; thus he establishes himself in life and in the self. With the formulas addressed to Prajāpati—"bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"—they pierce them; the horse belongs to Prajāpati, so they endow it with its own deity. With the words, "O parcher of grain! O eater of raw grain! O you who are in sheep and in cows! he brings down extra food for the horse; he thus makes offspring eaters of food. With the words, "Eat this food, O gods! Eat this food, O Prajāpati! he endows offspring with the eating of food.

Verily, brilliance and spiritual luster depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice. The Hotṛ and the Brahman engage in a theological debate (brahmodya); for the Hotṛ belongs to Agni and the Brahman belongs to Bṛhaspati. Since Bṛhaspati is the Brahman, they together bestow brilliance and spiritual luster upon him in a unified manner. They speak on both sides of the sacrificial post; for the post is indeed the sacrificer. Thus, they enclose the sacrificer himself on both sides with brilliance and spiritual luster.
