"Who, indeed, wanders alone? "Yonder sun, indeed, wanders alone. They bestow upon him that very luster of sacred knowledge (brahmavarcasa); thus they place luster of sacred knowledge in him.
"Who, indeed, is born again? "The moon, indeed, is born again; they bestow life-span upon him."
"What indeed is the remedy for cold? "Fire is the remedy for cold; they thus bestow radiance upon him."
"What is the great sowing-field? "This world, indeed, is the great sowing-field; verily, he finds firm support in this very world."
"What indeed was the first thought?"—the sky is indeed the first thought, rain; verily, he secures the sky and rain.
"What indeed was the great bird?"—the horse is indeed the great bird; verily, he secures long life.
"What was it that was *pilippilā*? "It was *śrī* (prosperity). Verily, he secures prosperity for himself.
"Who was she that was Piśaṅgilā? "Day and night indeed are Piśaṅgilā; verily, he finds firm support in day and night."

When the animals have been assigned, the Adhvaryu takes up the sprinkling waters; intending to sprinkle the horse while the sacrificer maintains contact with him, he recites the formula pertaining to the *adhvara* sacrifice and then proceeds with the formula pertaining to the *Aśvamedha*.

"May Vāyu protect thee with cooked [meats]," he says; thus Vāyu himself cooks it. "And the black-necked one with chāga-meat," he says; for the black-necked one is Agni; thus Agni himself cooks it with chāga-meat.
"Like the Nyagrodha tree with its cups"—for when the gods performed sacrifice with the sacrifice, they turned these cups downward; therefore the Nyagrodha trees grow with their roots turned downward.
With [the verse] "The silk-cotton tree grows," he bestows growth upon the silk-cotton tree; therefore, the silk-cotton tree grows to be the tallest among the trees.
"This one is indeed a chariot-steed, a bull"—with these words he completes the chariot with the horse; therefore, the horse does not draw anything other than a chariot.
"He has come with six and four," so it is said; therefore, a horse stands on three legs, but when harnessed, it moves evenly on all four feet.
"May Brahmākṛṣṇa protect us"—Brahmākṛṣṇa is indeed the moon; verily, he entrusts him to the moon. "Homage to Agni!"—thus he pays homage to Agni.
"With the rein, the chariot is made ready"—by means of the rein alone he completes the chariot; therefore, when it is harnessed, the chariot becomes most beautiful to behold.
"With the rein he is sharpened like a horse"—by means of the rein he thus equips the horse; therefore, when held by the rein, the horse shines most brightly.

"Sharpened in the waters, born of the waters"—for the horse has its origin in the waters; he thus endows it with its own womb. "The Brahman, with Soma as his leader"—he thus causes it to go to the heavenly world with Soma as its leader.

"Fashion thyself a body for the steed"—by this he says to him, "Make for yourself whatever form thou desirest. "Sacrifice for thyself"—he thereby bestows self-sovereignty upon him. "Enjoy for thyself"—by this he says to him, "Cause thy own world to shine as far as thou desirest. "No other can attain to thy greatness"—he thus causes the horse itself to prosper through its own greatness.

"Verily, you do not die here, nor do you suffer harm"—thus he reassures him. "Thou goest indeed to the gods by easy paths"—he thus shows him the very paths leading to the gods. "Where the doers of good deeds sit, where they have gone"—he thus makes him share the same world as those who perform good deeds. "There may the god Savitṛ place thee"—Savitṛ himself places him in the heavenly world. "I sprinkle thee, acceptable to Prajāpati"—this he says in a low voice, and then he holds [the water] up.

"Agni was the victim; with him they sacrificed; he won this world in which Agni is. That shall be your world; you will win it; drink these waters. By this he says to him: "As great as is Agni’s victory, as great as his world, as great as his sovereignty—so great shall be your victory, so great your world, so great your sovereignty."

Vāyu was the victim; they sacrificed with him, and he won this world in which Vāyu dwells. "That shall be your world; you will win it; drink these waters"—as great as is Vāyu’s victory, as great as is his world.

"The sun was the victim; with it they sacrificed, and he won this world in which the sun is. That shall be your world; you will win it; drink these waters. As great as is the victory of the sun, as great as is his world, and as great as is his sovereignty, so great shall be your victory, so great your world, and so great your sovereignty—this is what he thereby says to him. Having satisfied the horse and prepared it again, he sprinkles the other victims with the *prokṣaṇī* waters; from that point on, it proceeds for him.

The gods, indeed, did not know the way upward to the heavenly world; the horse knew it. When they proceed toward the north with the horse, it is for the sake of discerning the heavenly world. They spread out a cloth, an upper covering, and gold for the horse, as they do not do so for any other animal; upon that they quiet the horse, thereby distinguishing it from other animals.

Verily, they kill this animal when they quiet it; while it is being quieted, he offers oblations with the words, "To out-breathing, Svāhā! To in-breathing, Svāhā! To diffused breathing, Svāhā! He thereby bestows the vital breaths upon it; thus, indeed, his sacrifice is performed with an animal that is truly alive.
"O Amba, O Ambika, O Ambalika! No one leads me away!"—with these words he leads up the wives; by this he indeed calls them, and furthermore, he makes them pure for the sacrifice.

With the words, "We invoke thee, the lord of hosts, the leader of hosts," the wives go around him. They thus deny him this [power], and thereby they deny it to him; moreover, they establish him firmly. They go around him three times; for these worlds are three, and by means of these worlds they establish him firmly. Three times again they go around him, making six; for there are six seasons, and by means of the seasons they establish him firmly.

The vital breaths indeed depart from those who perform the shaking (dhuvana) at the sacrifice. They go around nine times; for there are nine vital breaths—they thus place the vital breaths within themselves, so that the vital breaths do not depart from them. With the words, "I have brought forth the one who bears the embryo; you have brought forth the one who bears the embryo,"—for embryos are indeed offspring and cattle—they thereby place offspring and cattle within themselves. Both [the sacrificer and his wife] say, "Let us both stretch out our four feet," for the attainment of the pair. "May you two cover yourselves in the heavenly world," he says; for that where they quiet the animal is indeed the heavenly world; therefore he speaks thus. "May the vigorous stallion, the bestower of seed, bestow seed," he says, for the attainment of the pair.
Prosperity and the kingdom indeed depart from him who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
"Raise her up on high! he says; for the Aśvamedha is royal splendor and the kingdom; verily, he raises royal splendor and the kingdom on high for him.
"As if carrying a burden on a mountain"—for the kingdom is indeed the burden of prosperity; verily, he equips him with prosperity, and thus he places prosperity upon the kingdom within him.
Then he says, "May her middle prosper. Prosperity, indeed, is the middle of the kingdom; verily, he bestows prosperity and food-eating power upon the kingdom from its very center.
With the words, "Purifying as it were in the cold wind," he bestows security upon him; for security is the "cold" of the kingdom; thus he provides security for him.

"The two yakāsakas, the little bird"—the little bird is indeed the people (viś), for it moves crookedly; "it moves crookedly"—for the people move crookedly toward the kingdom (rāṣṭra). "It strikes at the womb, the foot, the snatcher"—the womb is the people, the foot is the kingdom; he thus strikes the kingdom against the people. Therefore, the ruler is one who slays the people.

"Both your mother and your father"—this earth indeed is the mother and yonder sky is the father; by these two he causes him to go to the heavenly world. "Climb to the top of the tree"—the top of the kingdom is indeed prosperity (*śrī*); verily, he causes him to reach the prosperity that is the top of the kingdom. "'Your father, seeking to gain,' in the womb clenched his fist"—the womb is the people (*viś*) and the fists are the kingdom; he strikes the kingdom into the midst of the people. Therefore, the ruler of the kingdom is a slayer of the people.

Because it is said that "the deer eats barley," barley is indeed the common people (*viś*) and the deer is the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*); thus he makes the people food for the kingdom. Therefore, the kingdom eats the people; [as it is said], "he does not consider the cattle to be nourished," therefore the king does not breed cattle. Because it is said, "a Śūdra woman who has a noble lover is neither for nourishment nor for wealth," therefore one does not consecrate the son of a Vaiśya woman.

The vital breaths indeed depart from those who speak impure speech at the sacrifice. Therefore, they recite at the end the fragrant verse, "I have celebrated Dadhikrāvan"; thus they purify their speech, and the vital breaths do not depart from them.
When they fashion the sword-paths, the sacrificer makes that very bridge and passage for the attainment of the heavenly world.

They fashion them with needles; the people are indeed the needles and the horse-sacrifice is the kingdom; thus they place both the people and the kingdom together within him. They are made of gold; the Brāhmaṇa regarding that has already been explained.

There are three kinds of needles: made of copper, silver, and gold. The quarters are indeed made of copper, the intermediate quarters are silver, and the upward direction is gold; it is with these that they fashion him. They are crosswise and upward, and they are of many forms; therefore the quarters are of many forms, and therefore the quarters are of various forms.

Prajāpati desired, "May I become great and more abundant. He saw these two Mahiman cups at the Aśvamedha; he offered them, and thereby he indeed became great and more abundant. Whoever should desire, "May I become great and more abundant," let him offer these two Mahiman cups at the Aśvamedha; he will surely become great and more abundant.

He offers the omentum on both sides; for the Aśvamedha is the sacrificer and the Mahiman cup is the king. Thus, by means of the kingdom, he encloses him on both sides. Some gods have their *svāhā* uttered before [the offering], others have their *svāhā* uttered after; it is these very gods whom he thus gratifies with the words, "Svāhā to the gods! To the gods, svāhā! By means of the king, he completely conquers the omentum. He thus gratifies both the gods who are in this world and those who are in yonder world. These gods, being gratified, carry him to the heavenly world.

The eye of Prajāpati swelled; it fell away, and from that the horse (*aśva*) came into being. Because it swelled (*aśvayat*), that is the "horseness" (*aśvatva*) of the horse. The gods restored it by means of the Horse Sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) alone. He who sacrifices with the Horse Sacrifice indeed makes Prajāpati whole; he becomes everything itself. This is the expiation for everything, the remedy for everything. By means of this, the gods overcame all evil, and they even overcame the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*). He who sacrifices with the Horse Sacrifice overcomes all evil; he overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin.
That northern eye of Prajāpati swelled; therefore, they cut portions from the horse on the left side, but from other animals on the right side.
The mat is made of reeds; the horse has its origin in the waters, and the reed is born from the waters; thus he endows it with its own proper womb.

The Catuṣṭoma Stoma is employed; for the gods, when they tore out the horse's thigh-bone, restored it by means of the Catuṣṭoma Stoma itself. That the Catuṣṭoma Stoma is used is for the sake of the completeness of the horse. The Sarvastoma Atirātra is the final day; for the Sarvastoma Atirātra is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.

Having conquered by means of the supreme Stoma, the Catuṣṭoma, on the next day of the Ayana, he establishes himself upon the twenty-one-fold Stoma as a firm foundation; from that twenty-one-fold foundation, he ascends on the following day to the seasons. For the Pṛṣṭha-stotras are indeed the seasons, and the seasons are the year; thus he establishes himself in the seasons, in the year.

The Śakvarī verses constitute the Pṛṣṭha-stotra; here different metres are used and different animals are sacrificed—both domestic and wild, as it were. That the Śakvarīs are the Pṛṣṭha is for the sake of the horse’s completeness. Other animals are sacrificed, for other and distinct Stomas are performed.

Regarding this they say: "These are not all the animals—namely, goats, sheep, and those of the forest; rather, these are all the animals, namely, those of the cow-pen. Therefore, on the final day he immolates the animals of the cow-pen; for these animals of the cow-pen are indeed all the animals. Thus, he immolates all the animals. They belong to the Viśvedevas, for the horse belongs to the Viśvedevas; it is for the sake of the completeness of the horse. They are of many forms; therefore animals are of many forms. They are of various forms; therefore animals are of various forms.

In that there are three *anuṣṭubh*s, therefore a horse stands standing on three [legs]; in that there are four *gāyatrī*s, therefore a horse runs away, planting all its feet. The *anuṣṭubh* is indeed the highest of meters, the horse is the highest of animals, and the *catuṣṭoma* is the highest of *stomas*; by means of the highest, he causes it to reach the highest state.
The Śakvarī verses constitute the Pṛṣṭha-stotra; for different meters and different Stomas are performed, and in that the Śakvarīs are the Pṛṣṭha, it is for the sake of the horse's completeness.
The twenty-first day is the middle day; yonder sun indeed is the twenty-first, and he is the Ashvamedha. By means of its own Stoma, it establishes it in its own deity.
The Vāmadevya is the Maitrāvaruṇa-sāman; the Vāmadevya is indeed Prajāpati, and the horse belongs to Prajāpati; thus he endows it with its own deity.

The *Pārthuraśma* becomes the *Brahmasāman*. For by means of a rein (*raśmi*), a horse is restrained; and since a horse, if unrestrained, unheld, and unsupported, is liable to go to the furthest distance, the fact that the *Pārthuraśma* becomes the *Brahmasāman* is for the very support of the horse.

The *Saṃkṛtyacāvāka-sāman* is performed; for this Aśvamedha is, as it were, a sacrifice that has fallen into ruin, since one does not know what of it is done or what is not. In that the *Saṃkṛtyacāvāka-sāman* is performed, it is for the sake of the horse’s wholeness. The final day is an Atirātra with all the Stomas; for the Atirātra with all the Stomas is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—it is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.

The fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts, the Stoma is twenty-onefold, and there are twenty-one sacrificial posts. Just as bulls or stallions might gore one another together, so do these Stomas clash when they are twenty-onefold; if he were to bring them into conflict, the sacrificer would meet with ruin and his sacrifice would be destroyed.

The fire-altar should indeed be twelvefold, and there should be eleven sacrificial stakes. In that the fire-altar is twelvefold, the year has twelve months; he thus attains the sacrifice as the year. In that there are eleven stakes—this set of eleven is measured out as the Virāj; its eleventh [stake] is her udder, and by means of it he milks her.

Regarding this they say: "If there were twelve fires and eleven sacrificial posts, it would be as if one were traveling with a single-yoked cart; such would that be. Therefore, the fire-altar consists of twenty-one parts, the Stoma is twenty-onefold, and there are twenty-one sacrificial posts; thus it is as if one were traveling with side-horses.

The twenty-one-fold [stoma] is indeed the head of the sacrifice. He who knows the three heads in the Aśvamedha becomes the head of kings. The fire-altar is twenty-one-fold, the Stoma is twenty-one-fold, and there are twenty-one sacrificial posts; these, indeed, are the three heads in the Aśvamedha. He who knows them thus becomes the head of kings. He who knows the three humps in the Aśvamedha becomes the hump of kings. The fire-altar is twenty-one-fold, the Stoma is twenty-one-fold, and there are twenty-one sacrificial posts; these are the three humps in the Aśvamedha. He who knows them thus becomes the hump of kings.

The horse is indeed sacrificed for all the deities; if one were to make it belong to Prajāpati alone, he would deprive those deities who have no share of their portion. Having made the oblations of clarified butter into portions with the verses, "The horse with its teeth" and "The marshy plant with the roots of its teeth," and having offered them back to the deities, he offers the oblations while excluding [the specific deity]. Thus he satisfies with their respective shares those very deities who have no share. Having offered the Anūcya offerings in the forest, he offers the final oblation to Heaven and Earth. For all the deities are established in Heaven and Earth; it is these he thereby gratifies. The gods and the Asuras were engaged in conflict.

The Sviṣṭakṛt Agnis said, "We shall take for ourselves a special portion (uddhāra) of the horse; by that we shall overcome the Asuras. They took the blood for themselves, for the sake of overcoming their rivals. When one offers the blood to the Sviṣṭakṛts, it serves for the overcoming of his rivals; he prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated. This is true for him who knows thus.

With the neck of a gayal he offers the first oblation; for gayals are cattle and Sviṣṭakṛt is Rudra; thus he interposes the cattle from Rudra. Therefore, wherever this oblation of the Aśvamedha is offered, there Rudra does not harm the cattle.
With a horse's hoof he offers the second oblation; for the one-hoofed animals are indeed Rudra Sviṣṭakṛt, [and thus he protects] the cattle.

With an iron ladle he offers the third oblation; for Rudra Sviṣṭakṛt is indeed made of iron, and thus he interposes the creatures from Rudra. Therefore, wherever this oblation of the Aśvamedha is offered, there Rudra does not harm the creatures.

In all worlds, indeed, deaths are inherent; if one were not to offer oblations to them, death would seize him in every world. Since he offers oblations to the deaths, he conquers death in every world.

Regarding this they say: "If one were to offer oblations while looking about, saying, 'Hail to such-and-such! Hail to such-and-such!', he would make many deaths his enemies and would deliver himself over to death. Therefore, he offers a single oblation to a single [death], saying, "Hail to Death! For indeed, there is only one death in yonder world, namely hunger; it is that very one he conquers in yonder world.

With the words, "To the slaying of a Brahmin, svāhā! he offers the second oblation. Indeed, there is another death that is distinct from the slaying of a Brahmin; for this slaying of a Brahmin is truly death itself. Thus, he directly conquers death.

Muṇḍibha Audanya indeed discovered this expiation for the slaying of a Brahmin: that when one offers the oblation for the slaying of a Brahmin, he satisfies Death itself with that oblation and, having made it a protection, provides a remedy for the slayer of a Brahmin. Therefore, for whomever this oblation is offered in the Aśvamedha—even if he should kill a Brahmin among his future offspring—it provides a remedy for him.
When the horse was sacrificed, its sacrificial essence (medhas) departed; that became the Aśvastomīya. In that he offers the Aśvastomīya, he endows the horse itself with its sacrificial essence.

He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed sacrificial essence (*medhas*), and the *Aśvastomīya* hymn is sacrificial essence; verily, by means of sacrificial essence, he bestows sacrificial essence upon him. He offers with clarified butter; for clarified butter is the dear abode of the gods; verily, he causes them to prosper through their own dear abode.

Having offered the Aśvastomīya, he offers with the Dvipadā verses. The Aśvastomīya is indeed the horse, and the Dvipadā verses are man; for man is two-footed and established on two feet. Thus, he endows him with a firm foundation.

Regarding this they say: "Should the Aśvastomīya be offered first, or the Dvipadā? The Aśvastomīya is indeed cattle, and the Dvipadā is man. Because he offers the Dvipadā after having offered the Aśvastomīya, therefore man stands above the cattle.

He offers sixteen oblations with the *aśvastomīya* verses. Animals indeed consist of sixteen parts; that is the measure of animals. He thus causes him to prosper through the measure of animals. If he were to offer fewer or more than that, he would deprive the animals of their proper measure. He offers sixteen; for animals consist of sixteen parts, and that is the measure of animals. He thus causes the animals themselves to prosper through their own measure. He does not offer any other final oblation; if he were to offer another final oblation, he would fall away from his firm foundation. He offers the final oblation with a *dvipadā* verse; the *dvipadā* is a firm foundation, and thus he finds a firm foundation. With "Svāhā to Jumbaka," he offers the final oblation at the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*). Jumbaka is indeed Varuṇa; he thus directly expiates Varuṇa. He offers it upon the head of a white, bald, moist-skinned man with reddish-brown eyes; for that is the form of Varuṇa, and by means of that very form, he expiates Varuṇa.

Having risen, he offers twelve *brahmaudana* oblations and sacrifices with twelve *iṣṭis*. Regarding this, they say: "The *iṣṭis* are indeed the form of the sacrifice. If one were to sacrifice with the *iṣṭis*, the sacrifice would incline toward him, but he would become worse off. For the meters (*candāṃsi*) of one who has already sacrificed become exhausted; why then should he employ them so soon? Indeed, when the sacrifice is completed, Speech is attained; once attained, it becomes exhausted. For Speech then becomes as if made harsh or as if made bloodless. Since the sacrifice is Speech, therefore he should not employ them."

Having risen, he should offer twelve Brahma-rice oblations. The rice-oblation is indeed Prajāpati; Prajāpati is the year; and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. He thus attains the year and the sacrifice; the sacrifice becomes inclined toward him, and he does not become worse off.
This sacrifice is indeed named Prabhū; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes abundant.
This sacrifice is indeed named Vibhū; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes pervaded.
This sacrifice is indeed named Vyaṣṭi; when they perform this sacrifice, everything becomes individually distinguished.
This sacrifice is indeed called the "Supporter" (vidhṛti); when they sacrifice with this, everything becomes supported.
This indeed is the sacrifice named "Distinction" (vyāvṛtti); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes distinguished.
This sacrifice is indeed named "the vigorous"; wherever they perform this sacrifice, everything becomes vigorous.
This sacrifice is indeed named "The Milky One" (payasvān); when they perform this sacrifice, everything becomes possessed of milk.
This is indeed the sacrifice named "Possessing Spiritual Splendor" (brahmavarcasī); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa is born possessing spiritual splendor.
This indeed is the sacrifice called Ativyādhi; when they perform this sacrifice, a royal warrior (rājanya) is born as an Ativyādhi.
This is indeed the sacrifice called Dīrgha; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, a long stretch of forest arises.
This sacrifice is indeed called Kḷpti; when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes arranged.
This sacrifice is indeed named "Foundation" (Pratiṣṭhā); when they sacrifice with this sacrifice, everything becomes firmly established.

Now, therefore, regarding the expiations: if a stallion should leap upon a mare, one should subsequently offer a milk-oblation to Vāyu. Vāyu is indeed the transformer of seeds; Vāyu is breath, for breath is the transformer of seeds. By means of seed, he thus places seed in him.

Now, if he should become ill, he should subsequently offer a pap to Pūṣan. Pūṣan indeed rules over cattle; thus he gratifies him who owns cattle and who rules over cattle, and he indeed becomes free from disease.

Now, if he should find himself free from disease, he should subsequently offer a Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds, with the earth serving as the potsherd; for this earth is indeed Vaiśvānara, and it is her he thus gratifies; verily, he becomes free from disease.

Now, if he should suffer from an eye disease, he should subsequently offer a pap of cooked rice to Sūrya. For Sūrya is indeed the eye of creatures; for when he rises, then all this world moves. By means of the eye, he thus bestows the eye upon him. As to why it is a pap (caru): by means of the eye, this self moves about.

Now, if he should die in water, he should subsequently offer a sacrificial pap of barley to Varuṇa. For Varuṇa seizes him who dies in the waters; he thus gratifies that very deity who has seized him. Being gratified, she permits him to seize another victim. With her permission, he seizes it. If it is made of barley, it is because barley belongs to Varuṇa.

Now, if it should be lost, one should perform a supplementary sacrifice consisting of three oblations: a cake on one potsherd for Heaven and Earth, milk for Vāyu, and a pap for Sūrya. For whatever is lost, it is as if it has been lost within Heaven and Earth; Vāyu blows over it and the Sun shines upon it, and nothing whatsoever is lost apart from these deities. This is the specific expiation for what is lost. If anything else of his should also be lost, he should sacrifice with this very same offering, and thus he indeed finds it again. Furthermore, if enemies should find the horse, or if it should die, or if they should bring another one and sprinkle it with water—this is the expiation in that case.

Prajāpati desired, "May I obtain all desires; may I attain all forms of distinction. He beheld this three-night sacrificial rite, the Aśvamedha; he took it up and performed it with it. Having sacrificed with it, he obtained all desires and attained all forms of distinction. Indeed, whoever performs the Aśvamedha obtains all desires and attains all forms of distinction.
Regarding this they say: "In which season should one begin? Some say, "One should begin in summer; for summer is the season of the Kṣatriya, and this Aśvamedha is indeed a sacrifice of the Kṣatriya."
One should indeed begin this in spring; for spring is the season of the Brāhmaṇa. And whoever sacrifices, having become as it were a Brāhmaṇa, he sacrifices; therefore, one should begin it in spring.
On the sixth or seventh day before that full moon of Phālguna, the officiating priests—the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ, the Brahman, and the Udgātṛ—assemble; or other priests may follow them.

For them, the Adhvaryu prepares the Brahma-rice porridge for four to eat. The Brāhmaṇa explanation for this has been stated: four bowls, four handfuls, and four pinches—twelvefold; for twelve months are a year, and the year is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.

These four officiating priests (ṛtvij) eat it; their Brāhmaṇa has already been stated. He gives them four thousand [cows]; for a thousand is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything. And he gives four golden śatamāna coins; regarding that, it has indeed been explained.

Then, as the Adhvaryu puts the gold ornament on him, he makes him recite: "Thou art brilliance, pure, immortal. Gold is indeed brilliance, purity, and immortality; thus he bestows brilliance, purity, and immortality upon him. [He says: "Protector of life, protect my life!"—thus he bestows life upon him. Then he says to him, "Restrain thy speech! Speech is indeed the sacrifice; it is for the purpose of commencing the sacrifice.

Four wives are prepared: the chief queen (*mahiṣī*), the favorite (*vāvātā*), the discarded wife (*parivṛktā*), and the daughter of the village headman (*pālāgalī*). All are adorned with golden neck-ornaments (*niṣkin*) and well-decorated for the sake of completeness of the couple. Together with them, he enters the fire-hall; the sacrificer by the eastern door, the wives by the southern door.

When the evening oblation has been offered, he lies down behind the Gārhapatya fire with his wife facing north; the others lie down as well. He lies between her thighs without turning over, thinking: "By this austerity, may I safely reach the end of the year."

When the morning oblation has been offered, the Adhvaryu offers the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti). The full is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. At that offering, he releases his speech by means of a boon, saying, "I give a boon to the Brahman. The boon is indeed everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.
Then, the gold ornament that has been fastened upon him, he gives to the Adhvaryu; by giving it to the Adhvaryu, he places immortal life within himself, for gold is indeed immortal life.

Then he offers the oblation to Agni for the sake of the paths and so that the mouth of the sacrifice may not be spoiled; moreover, since all deities have Agni as their mouth and all desires are centered in the Ashvamedha, [he thinks]: "Having gratified all the gods at the very outset, may I obtain all my desires."

For this sacrifice there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses. The thunderbolt (*vajra*) is indeed fifteenfold; the thunderbolt is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt, by means of that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings are *vārtraghna* (slayers of Vṛtra). Vṛtra is indeed evil; [they serve] for the repelling of evil. "Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of the sacrifice and of the mid-world"—these are the invitatory and offering verses for the oblation, recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). One verse contains the word "head" (*mūrdhan*), the other contains the word "seat" (*sad*). This one who shines yonder is indeed the head; it is for the attainment of him. And as for the one containing "seat," he thereby attains the seat itself. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s. The *virāj* is a meter belonging to all the deities. All desires are contained in the Aśvamedha. Thinking, "Having gratified all the gods, may I obtain all my desires," gold is the sacrificial fee—a hundred-measure piece of refined gold. The explanation for this has already been stated.

Then he offers an oblation to Pūṣan. Pūṣan is indeed the lord of paths; he thus effects a safe journey for the horse. Moreover, Pūṣan is this earth; he thus makes her its guardian. For there is neither affliction nor stumbling for him whom she protects on his way; he thus makes her his guardian.

For this [sacrifice], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati—this is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. The two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "increasing" (*vṛdhant-*) for the sake of the sacrificer’s own increase. The invitatory and offering verses for the oblation are recited in a whisper: "O Pūṣan, in thy service... and "On every path, the guardian of the way, we invoke with speech..."; one contains the word "service" (*vrata-*) and the other contains the word "path" (*pathin-*). Service is indeed vigor; it is for the attainment of vigor and the securing of vigor. Now, as to why there is a verse containing the word "path," it is to provide a safe journey for the horse. The two *saṃyājyā* verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter; the *anuṣṭubh* is speech, and Prajāpati is speech, and the Aśvamedha is Prajāpati—this is for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself. A hundred garments are the sacrificial fee. Clothing is indeed the form of man; therefore, when they see anyone well-dressed, they say, "Who is this? For he is perfected by form; thus he endows him with form itself. There are a hundred [garments]; man has a life-span of a hundred years and a hundred powers; verily, he bestows life, power, and vigor upon himself.

While this [sacrificial cow] is being milked, they bring forward a horse—one in which all forms are present, or one that is preeminent in speed, worthy of a thousand, ancient, and such that there is no other yoke-mate for its position at the pole during the sacrificial gift.

In that he is of all forms—verily, form is everything and the Aśvamedha is everything—it is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything. And in that he is rich in speed—verily, speed is vigor—it is for the attainment of vigor, for the securing of vigor. And in that he is worth a thousand—verily, a thousand is everything and the Aśvamedha is everything—it is for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything. And in that he is preeminent—verily, he who is preeminent increases his vigor beyond measure—it is for the securing of unmeasured vigor. And in that he stands at the right pole, not reaching the yoke—verily, he is he who shines yonder; it is for the securing of him alone.

Regarding this, Bhāllabeya said: "This horse should indeed be of two colors, a black-spotted deer-colored one; for it was produced from the eye of Prajāpati. This eye is indeed twofold—both white and black—and thus he endows it with its own proper form."

Then Sātyayajñi said: "This horse should indeed have three forms: its forepart black, its hindpart white, and it should have a mark like a *kṛttikā* (star-cluster) on its forehead. Now, that which is the black forepart is that black part of his eye; and that which is the white hindpart is that white part of his eye; and that which is the *kṛttikā*-mark on the forehead is the pupil (*kanīnakā*). Thus it is perfect in form. Therefore, whichever one of these may be available—whether many-formed, two-formed, or three-formed, provided it has the *kṛttikā*-mark—one should sacrifice it; but it should be perfect in speed."

For him, these guardians are prepared in front: a hundred armored princes, a hundred armed with quivers, a hundred sons of charioteers and village headmen equipped with arrows and quivers, and a hundred sons of military attendants bearing staffs; and there is a hundred-horse team, worn out and exhausted, upon which they release him and guard him.
Then he performs the Sāvitrī sacrifice: a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ Prasavitṛ; for Savitṛ is indeed the impeller, [thinking] "May Savitṛ impel this sacrifice of mine."

For this [offering], there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are the *vārtraghna* hymns; the invitatory and offering verses for the principal oblation are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), namely, "He who has generated all these beings" and "May the god Savitṛ, rich in jewels, come hither"; the two *saṃyājyā* verses are *virāj*s; the sacrificial fee is gold, specifically a hundred-māna piece of refined gold; the *brāhmaṇa* explanation for this has already been stated.

While the fore-offerings (prayāja) for her are being performed, a Brāhmaṇa lute-player, standing to the south and striking the *uttara-mandrā* lute, sings three self-composed verses: "He sacrificed," and "He gave. The Brāhmaṇa explanation regarding this has already been stated.
Then he offers the second oblation: a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ Āsavitṛ, thinking, "Savitṛ is indeed the impeller; may Savitṛ impel this sacrifice of mine."

For this [offering], there are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* portions contain the word "seat" (*sad*), whereby he wins the seat. "O God Savitṛ, all... and "Truly, that God Savitṛ with power..."—these are the invitatory and offering formulas for the oblation, recited in a whisper; they are both in the *anuṣṭubh* metre, and the *saṃyājyā* verses are likewise. Silver is the sacrificial fee for the sake of variety of form, and also for the sake of ascending and not descending. It is a hundred-measure weight (*śatamāna*); for man has a lifespan of a hundred years and a hundredfold sensory power. Verily, he bestows life, sensory power, and vigor upon himself.
While its fore-sacrifices were being performed, a Brāhmaṇa [played] the lute.

Then he offers the third oblation: a cake on twelve potsherds for Savitṛ of true impulsion. For this indeed is the true impulsion that belongs to Savitṛ; [he offers it] thinking, "May he truly impel this sacrifice for me by means of his true impulsion."

For this [offering], there are exactly seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; the two *ājyabhāga* offerings contain the word "wealth" (*rayimat*), for wealth is indeed vigor—[this is] for the attainment of vigor, for the securing of vigor. The invitatory and offering verses for the oblation are: "To him who is the Lord of all gods, the true master, not to be surpassed," and "That of the divine Savitṛ"—these are recited in a low voice (*upāṃśu*). The two *saṃyājyā* verses are the regular ones, so that he may not stray from the path of the sacrifice; thus, at the very end, he finds firm support in the well-ordered sacrifice. There are two *triṣṭubh* verses, for the *triṣṭubh* is indeed vigor in Indra; [this is] for the securing of power and vigor. The sacrificial fee is gold, a hundred-measure weight of refined gold; regarding this, the Brāhmaṇa has already been explained.
While its fore-offerings were being performed, a Brāhmaṇa [played] the lute.

When she has been established, the Adhvaryu and the sacrificer rise and whisper into the horse’s right ear: “Vibhū by thy mother, Prabhū by thy father. The Brāhmaṇa for this has already been told. Then they let him go northward and eastward; for that which is northward and eastward is the region of both gods and men. Thus they place him in his own region; and indeed, one who is established in his own abode does not come to harm—it is for his safety.

He said: "O gods, guardians of the quarters, protect this horse consecrated for the sacrifice for the gods. Having been thus addressed, the human guardians of the quarters departed, and then these divine ones—the Āpyas, Sādhyas, Anvādhyas, and Maruts—these both gods and men, being in agreement and not turning him back, guard him for a year. As for the reason they do not turn him back: it is he who shines yonder; for who indeed is worthy of turning him back? If they were to turn him back, all this would surely go away; therefore, they guard him without turning him back.

He said: "O guardians of the quarters! Those who shall reach the completion of this [sacrifice] will possess the kingdom; they will become kings worthy of consecration. But those who do not reach its completion will be without a kingdom; they will not be kings, but merely members of the royal clan, commoners unworthy of consecration. Therefore, do not neglect him. After he has bathed, you must keep him away from water, from mares, and from whatever group of Brahmins he may approach. You should ask them: 'O Brahmins, how much of the Ashvamedha do you know? Those who do not know it, you should overcome. For the Ashvamedha is everything; he who does not know this is not a Brahmin. He who, being a Brahmin, does not know the Ashvamedha is no Brahmin at all—he is to be overcome. Prepare drink for him, scatter food for him, and whatever prepared food there is in the country, let all that be yours. Your dwelling shall be in the family of the chariot-maker (rathakāra), for that is the abode of the horse."

Having released the horse, he spreads a golden cushion to the south of the altar; upon it the Hotṛ sits down. To the south of the Hotṛ, the sacrificer sits on a golden mat; to the south [of him] are the Brahman and the Udgātṛ on two golden cushions. In front [of them], facing west, the Adhvaryu sits on a golden mat or on a golden plank.

When they have all sat down, the Adhvaryu gives the direction: "O Hotṛ, recount the beings; seat this sacrificer among the beings. Thus directed, the Hotṛ addresses the Adhvaryu, intending to recite the Pāriplava narrative: "Adhvaryu!"—"Havai Hotṛ! replies the Adhvaryu.

"Manu Vaivasvata is king," he says; "of him the human clans are the subjects; these sit here. Householders who are not learned in the Vedas gather together; he instructs them: "The Rigveda is this Veda; 'This is it,' thus he should recite as if explaining a hymn of the Ṛgveda. Lute-players gather together; the Adhvaryu gives the command: "O lute-players! he says, "sing in harmony with this sacrificer using ancient kings who performed good deeds. They sing in harmony with him accordingly. In that they sing in harmony with him thus, they make him share the same world with those ancient kings who performed good deeds.

Having given the command, the Adhvaryu offers the *prakrama* oblations; or, having traced around the footprint of a horse on the Anvāhāryapacana fire-altar, he performs whichever procedure applies to that case, though the former method is indeed the established rule.

Having recited [the verses] prior to the Sāvitrī sacrifice itself, he offers the forms (rūpāṇi) once only into the Āhavanīya fire. Then, while the Dhṛti offerings are being made in the evening, a Rājanya who is a lute-player, standing to the south, sings three self-composed songs while striking the Uttara-mandrā tone: "He fought," "He conquered that battle. The Brāhmaṇa concerning this has been stated.

Then, on the next day, the second day, when these Sāvitra offerings have been completed in the same manner, this is the procedure: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "King Yama Vaivasvata," he says, "his people are the Fathers; they are sitting here. The elders have assembled there, and to them he points out: "The Yajus-formulas are the Veda; this is it. He should run through a section of the Yajus-formulas as if explaining them. In this very way the Adhvaryu gives the direction; he does not perform the *prakrama* oblations.

Then, on the third day, when these same offerings have been completed, the procedure is exactly as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "Varuṇa Āditya the King," he says, "his subjects are the Gandharvas, and they are sitting here. Young and handsome men have gathered there; he points them out [to the Hotṛ], saying, "The Atharvans are the Veda; this is it. He should recite as if explaining one section of the Atharvans. In this very manner the Adhvaryu gives the summons; he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations.

Then, on the fourth day, when these very offerings have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "King Soma Vaiṣṇava," he says, "his people are the Apsarases; they are sitting here. Young, beautiful women have gathered there, and he points them out [to the King], saying, "The Aṅgirases are the Veda; this is that. Then, as if explaining a single section of the Aṅgirases, he recites from the *Anudravaṇa*.

Then, on the fifth day, when these same offerings have been completed, the procedure is exactly as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "Arbuda Kādraveya, the king," he says, "his subjects are the serpents; they are sitting here. Both the serpents and those who know all things have assembled there, and he instructs them: "The Sarpavidyā is this Veda here. He then recites, as if explaining, one section of the Sarpavidyā.

Then, on the sixth day, when these very offerings have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "Kubera Vaiśravaṇa is the king," he says, "and the Rākṣasas are his subjects; they are staying here. Now, Selagas and Pādakṛts have assembled there; to them he points out: "This is the Veda, the knowledge of the divine folk (devajanavidyā). He then recites, as if explaining, one section of the Devajanavidyā.

Then, on the seventh day, when these very offerings have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "The Asita Dhānva is the king," he says; "the Asuras are his subjects, and they sit here. The usurers have gathered there, and he instructs them: "This is Māyā Veda"; he should perform some kind of magical trick (māyā). In this very way the Adhvaryu gives the summons, but he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations.

Then, on the eighth day, when these same offerings have been completed, the procedure is exactly as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "King Matsya Sāmmada," he says, "his subjects are those who move in the water; they are sitting here. Fishermen and fish gather there, and he points them out, saying, "This is the Itihāsa Veda; this is that one. Thus the Adhvaryu gives the direction; he does not perform the *prakrama* oblations.

Then, on the ninth day, when these same offerings have been completed in this very manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu! says the Hotṛ; "Havai Hotar! replies the Adhvaryu. "Tārkṣya Vaipaśyata, the king," he says, "his subjects are the birds; they are these that sit here. Now, both birds and those who know the science of birds (vāyovidyika) have assembled there; he instructs them. "The Purāṇa is the Veda; this is it," he says, and he should recite some portion of the Purāṇa. In this very way the Adhvaryu gives the summons; he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations.

Then, on the tenth day, when these very offerings have been completed in this same manner, the procedure is as follows: "Adhvaryu!"—"Havai Hotar!"—thus [the Hotṛ calls]; the Adhvaryu says, "Dharma is King Indra; his subjects are the gods; they are seated here. Vedic scholars who do not accept gifts have assembled there; he instructs them: "The Sāmans are the Veda; this is it. He should recite a decade of the Sāmans. In this very way the Adhvaryu gives the summons; he does not offer the *prakrama* oblations.

This *pāriplava* narrative recounts all royal domains, all subjects, all Vedas, all gods, and all beings. Indeed, he who knows this attains union with and residence in the same world as these royal domains; he attains sovereignty and overlordship over all subjects; he masters all the Vedas; having gratified all the gods, he finally finds firm standing among all beings. For whomsoever the Hotṛ priest recites this *pāriplava* narrative when he knows it thus, or for one who himself knows it thus—this very same narrative revolves again and again throughout the year. Because it revolves (*pariplavate*) again and again, it is called the *pāriplava*. He recites it for thirty-six ten-day periods; the *bṛhatī* meter has thirty-six syllables, and cattle are connected to the *bṛhatī*; verily, by means of the *bṛhatī*, he secures cattle for him.

When the year has elapsed, having performed the consecration (dīkṣā) and offered the animal sacrifice to Prajāpati, the Iṣṭis are concluded. "He should perform the sacrifice in the fires of the domestic priest," so say some; but how could one who is consecrated perform a sacrifice? There are twelve days of consecration, twelve days of Upasads, and three Soma-pressings; thus it amounts to the Triṇava Stoma. The Triṇava is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), the horse is the nobility (kṣatra), and the Rājanya is the nobility. Now, the nobility is won by the thunderbolt; thus, by means of the thunderbolt itself, he wins the nobility.

When the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering has been completed and the evening speech has been released, the lute-players assemble; the Adhvaryu gives them the command, saying, "O lute-players, sing together with the gods for this sacrificer! and they sing together for him accordingly.

Day after day, when speech has been released and the Agniṣomīya offerings have been completed at the end, and when the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around—then, when they sing together with the gods, they thereby make him share the same world as the gods.

By Prajāpati [the Soma] is thus carried around day after day during the pressings; and when the Udavasānīyā offering has finally been completed at the end, with the Vasatīvarī waters still present, they sing together with him using the Prajāpati [Stoma]. By means of Prajāpati, they thereby finally make him share the same world as themselves.

There are twenty-one sacrificial posts, all of which are twenty-one cubits long. That which stands at the fire-altar is made of *rājjudāla* wood; on both sides of it are two made of *paitudāru* wood; six are made of *bilva* wood—three in this way and three in that way; six are made of *khadira* wood—three in this way and three in that way; and six are made of *pālāśa* wood—three in this way and three in that way.

Now, as for why these sacrificial posts (yūpas) are thus: when the vital breaths had departed from Prajāpati, his body began to swell. The phlegm that was in it flowed out together and burst forth from the middle of the nose; that became this tree, the Rajjudāla. Therefore it is called *śleṣmaṇaḥ*, for it originated from phlegm (*śleṣman*). By means of that very form, he thereby endows him (Prajāpati). And as to why that one stands nearest the fire: the post nearest the fire is the middle among the posts, and the nostrils are the middle among the vital breaths; he thus places it in its own abode.

Now, when the fiery energy that consisted of water—that which was the fragrance—had coalesced together, it burst forth from the eye; that became this tree, the *pītudāru*. Therefore it is fragrant, for it originated from fragrance; and therefore it is glowing, for it originated from fiery energy. By means of that very form he thus completes it. And because those two [posts] are on both sides of the one standing by the fire-altar (*agniṣṭha*), therefore these two eyes are on both sides of the nose; he thus places them in their own proper abode.

Now, that which was the *kuntāpa* membrane and that which was the marrow flowed together and burst forth from the ear; it became this forest tree, the wood-apple (*bilva*). Therefore, within its fruit, everything is edible. And for that reason it is yellowish, for the marrow is yellowish; thus he endows it with its own proper form. The two [wooden pegs] made of *pitudāru* wood are on the inside, and those of *bilva* wood are on the outside; for the eyes are on the inside and the ears on the outside. Thus he places them each in their own proper abode.

From his very bones the *khadira* tree arose; therefore it is hard and full of pith, for bone is indeed hard. By means of that very form he thus endows him [the sacrificial post]. The posts made of *bilva* wood are inside, and those of *khadira* are outside; for the marrow is inside and the bones are outside. Thus he places them each in its own proper abode.

From his very flesh the Palāśa tree arose; therefore it has many juices and a red juice, for flesh is, as it were, red. By that very form he thus provides him with abundance. The Khadira wood is inside and the Palāśa is outside; for the bones are inside and the flesh is outside. Thus he places them each in its own proper abode.

Now, as to why there are twenty-one: they are twenty-one cubits long, for this one who shines yonder is the twenty-first—twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first; he is the Ashvamedha, he is Prajapati. Having thus prepared this Prajapati-sacrifice in its entirety, he immolates twenty-one Agnishomiya animals upon it; their ritual procedure is the same. This is the ritual of the previous day.

Then, at dawn, there is for Gotama the four-plus-stoma (caturuttara-stoma). For it, the *bahiṣpavamāna* is on four verses; the *ājya* hymns are on eight each; the midday *pavamāna* is on twelve; the *pṛṣṭha* hymns are on sixteen; the *ārbhava-pavamāna* is on twenty; and the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* is on twenty-four.

Regarding this, some perform a four-fold *sāman* for its *agniṣṭoma-sāman*, saying, "It is neither an *agniṣṭoma* nor an *ukthya*. If they should do so, having recited the *stotriya* together, he should recite the *anurūpa* together; the *pṛṣṭha-laud* is the *rathantara*, the *śastra* is the *rathantara*, and the sacrifice is the *agniṣṭoma*. By this, he prospers in this world.

"There are twenty-one Savanīya animals, all dedicated to Agni; their ritual procedure is the same," so say some. However, one should indeed immolate two sets of eleven animals, for the attainment of whatever desire there may be regarding the sets of eleven.

When the Agniṣṭoma has been completed and the Vasatīvarī waters have been carried around, the Adhvaryu offers the food-oblations. The Brāhmaṇa for these has been stated: "To the out-breath, svāhā! To the in-breath, svāhā! with twelve Anuvākas. There are twelve months in a year; the year is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.

The middle day consists of twenty-one [stomas]. Now, yonder sun is the twenty-first; he is the Ashvamedha. By means of its own stoma, he thus establishes it in its own deity. Therefore, it is twenty-one-fold.

Moreover, as to why it is the twenty-first: man indeed consists of twenty-one parts—ten fingers of the hands, ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first. Thus, by means of this twenty-first self, he establishes himself upon that twenty-first foundation; therefore, it is the twenty-first.

Or rather, it is because the twenty-one-fold is the foundation of the Stomas. Indeed, on this day much work of various kinds is performed; thus, when much work of various kinds is performed on this day, he does so thinking, "May it be established upon this foundation, the twenty-one-fold. For this reason also, this day is the twenty-one-fold.

For him, the morning pressing belongs to Agni; the Hotṛ, having recited the fivefold *ājya* hymn beginning with "I think of that Agni who is Vasu," recites the [stotras] of the one-day sacrifice. He recites both the *prauga* hymns—the Bārhata and the Mādhucandasa—in triplets. This serves to fulfill both desires: whatever desire is in the Bārhata *prauga* and whatever desire is in the Mādhucandasa. Thus, the morning pressing is prepared.

Now follows the midday pressing. The *aticandāḥ* verse, "In the *trikadruka*s, the buffalo [drank] the barley-mixture," is the introductory verse for the *marutvatīya* litany. This *aticandāḥ* is indeed the most pre-eminent among the meters; the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is the most pre-eminent among sacrifices. It serves for the attainment of the horse-sacrifice itself. This same verse is recited three times and thus becomes a triplet (*trica*); thereby he obtains that desire which is fulfilled by a triplet. "O Vasu, this pressed juice... is the following verse (*anucara*). This is the constant rule for the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*). Having recited the *paṅkti* and six-footed verses, "For thus, O Soma, in intoxication... and "Thou art the protector of the presser who has spread the sacrificial grass," he places the *nivid* in the one-day portion. Thus ends the *marutvatīya*.

Now, therefore, follows the Niṣkevalya: the Mahānāmnī verses constitute the Pṛṣṭha-stotra; he recites them together with their Anurūpas and the Pragāthas. Indeed, all desires are contained within the Mahānāmnīs, and all desires are contained within the Aśvamedha; it is for the attainment of all desires that he recites: "Indra has grown strong for exhilaration," and "This prayer has been offered for the slaying of Vṛtra. Having recited the Paṅktis and the Ṣaṭpadās, he places the Nivid in the [hymn] belonging to the Ekāha sacrifice; thus the midday pressing is properly arranged.

Now, therefore, follows the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*). The *pratipad* of the Vaiśvadeva [laud] is indeed the *aticandā* verse: "Abhi tvā deva savitāram oṇyoḥ. Its Brāhmaṇa-explanation is the same as that of the previous one. The *anucara* is "Abhi tvā deva savitaḥ," which contains the word "abhi" (towards); this is a form for overcoming. Having recited the Sāvitra [verse], "Ud u ṣya devaḥ savitā damūnāḥ," he places the *nivid* in the [laud] of the one-day sacrifice (*aikāhika*). Having recited the four-verse Dyāvāpṛthivīya hymn, "Mahī dyāvāpṛthivī iha jyeṣṭhe," he places the *nivid* in the [laud] of the one-day sacrifice. Having recited the Ārbhava hymn, "Ṛbhur vibhvā vāja indro no aceti," he places the *nivid* in the [laud] of the one-day sacrifice. Having recited the Vaiśvadeva hymn, "Ko nu vām mitrāvaruṇāv ṛtāyan," he places the *nivid* in the [laud] of the one-day sacrifice. Thus ends the section on the Vaiśvadeva.

Now, therefore, regarding the Āgnimāruta [śastra]: having recited the Vaiśvānara hymn beginning with "The head of heaven, the messenger of earth," he places the *nivid* from the one-day rite (*ekāhika*). Having recited the Māruta hymn beginning with "The Rudras, accompanied by Indra, acting in concert," he places the *nivid* from the one-day rite. Having recited the nine-verse Jātavedas hymn beginning with "This guest of yours, awakening at dawn," he places the *nivid* from the one-day rite. Thus, since these *nivid*-insertions belong to the one-day rites, and the Jyotiṣṭoma is indeed a firm foundation, it serves to prevent falling away from that foundation.

These are his sacrificial animals: a horse, a hornless goat, and a gayal—these fifteen are the animals tied to the sacrificial posts, regarding which the Brāhmaṇa has already been stated. Now, these wild animals: for the spring he immolates francolins, for the summer sparrows, and for the rains partridges; regarding these also, it has already been stated.

Then he immolates twenty-one animals for each of the deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices. [The opponent argues: "There are as many gods as there are deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; all desires are contained in the Aśvamedha. By pleasing all the gods, I shall obtain all desires. One should not do it in that way.

One should immolate seventeen animals at the central sacrificial post; Prajāpati is seventeenfold, the All is seventeenfold, and the Aśvamedha is the All—for the attainment of the All and for the securing of the All. On the other posts, sixteen each; for this All consists of sixteen parts, and the Aśvamedha is the All—for the attainment of the All and for the securing of the All. Thirteen each of the wild animals he immolates in the intermediate spaces; thirteen months are a year, the year is the All, and the Aśvamedha is the All—for the attainment of the All and for the securing of the All.

Now, before the *bahis-pavamāna*, they lead forth the horse after washing it; with it they proceed to the *pāvamāna* chant. The Brāhmaṇa regarding this has been explained. When the *bahis-pavamāna* has been chanted, they make the horse step onto the place for the *āstāva*. If it should smell the barley or should turn about, he should know: "My sacrifice is successful. Having brought it near, the Adhvaryu says: "O Hotṛ, recite the hymn! The Hotṛ recites the hymn for it with eleven verses.

With the verse, "When you first cried out at birth," he recites the first verse three times and the last verse three times; thus they amount to fifteen. The thunderbolt is indeed fifteenfold and is vigor; by means of this thunderbolt, this vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front. Indeed, the thunderbolt is bestowed upon the sacrificer to strike down whoever is to be struck down by him. [He recites: "The steed has come near to the place of slaughter; the racer has come near to the highest dwelling-place."

Having extracted these [verses], he inserts this hymn, "May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, and Aditi not abandon us," into the *adhriqu* [offering]. Some, however, place this verse, "Thirty-four ribs of the horse, the friend of the gods," before the [verses on] the ribs, thinking, "Lest we place the *praṇava* in a place that is not its proper abode," and also, "Lest we separate the singular number from the plural. One should not do so; rather, he should insert the hymn together with it: "The swift steed has gone to the place of sacrifice; the swift steed has gone to the highest dwelling-place."

Having said this, whatever remains of what belongs to the *adhvaryu* he speaks of; they spread out for the horse a garment, an undergarment, and gold, and upon that they quiet it. When the animals have been quieted, the wives come up with the foot-washing waters: four wives, a maiden as the fifth, and four hundred female attendants.

When the water for rinsing the feet has been used, they cause the queen to mount the horse; then they cover them both with a cloth, saying, "May you two clothe yourselves in the heavenly world! For that place where they quiet the animal is indeed the heavenly world. She draws out the horse's penis and places it in the queen's lap, saying, "May the vigorous stallion, the depositor of seed, deposit seed! This is for the sake of the completeness of the couple.

While the two of them are lying down, the sacrificer addresses the horse with the words, "Lift your thighs and place your anus below"; no one else addresses him in response, lest there be someone who acts as a counter-interlocutor against the sacrificer.

Then the Adhvaryu addresses the maiden with a riddle: "O maiden, hey! Hey! O maiden, who is this little bird? The maiden replies to him with a counter-riddle: "O Adhvaryu, hey! Hey! O Adhvaryu, who is that little bird?"

Then Brahmā propositions the queen: "O Queen, hey there, O Queen! Your mother and your father climb to the top of the tree! For her, there are a hundred princesses as attendants; they in turn proposition Brahmā: "O Brahmin, hey there, O Brahmin! Your mother and your father play at the top of the tree!"

Then the Udgātṛ addresses the favorite queen: "O Vāvātā, hey! Hey! O Vāvātā, cause her to rise up! For her, there are a hundred Rājanya attendants; they address the Udgātṛ in return: "O Udgātṛ, hey! Hey! O Udgātṛ, cause him to rise up!"

Then the Hotṛ addresses the discarded wife (Parivṛktī) with the words: "O discarded one! Ho! Ho! O discarded one! Since she is one who breaks through the narrow pass... For her, there are a hundred daughters of charioteers and village headmen as attendants; they address the Hotṛ in return: "O Hotṛ! Ho! Ho! O Hotṛ! Since the gods [have made] the lalāmagu..."

Then the Kṣattṛ addresses Pālāgalī: "O Pālāgalī! Ho there, Pālāgalī! Since the deer eats the barley, it does not consider its own body to be well-nourished. For her, there are a hundred daughters of charioteers (*kṣātra-saṅgrahītṛ*) as attendants; they address the Kṣattṛ in return: "O Kṣattṛ! Ho there, Kṣattṛ! Since the deer eats the barley, it does not think much of its own abundance."

These incitements are indeed the attainment of all speech; all desires are contained in the Aśvamedha. Thinking, "May we obtain all desires by means of all speech," they cause the Mahiṣī to rise. Then they return the way they came. Thereafter, the others recite at the end the verse containing the word *surabhi*: "I have performed the praise of Dadhikrāvan."

Indeed, the life-breaths and the deities depart from those who, at the sacrifice, either speak untruth or speak ill of speech; they purify speech itself for the sake of sacrificing to the gods and so that the deities do not depart. Regarding the omentum (vapā): that which belongs to the *gomṛga* and that which belongs to the hornless goat (*ajetūpara*), they place these two upon the horse and bring them forward, saying, "There is no omentum of the horse. One should not do so; rather, one should explicitly take the fat (*medas*) of the horse itself, while the others are well-known [to be taken].

When the omenta have been cooked, having performed the rites with the *svāhā*-utterances, they turn back toward the west, return to the *sadas*, and engage in the theological debate (*brahmodya*). Having entered by the eastern door, they sit down separately according to their respective hearths (*dhiṣṇya*).
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu, "Who indeed wanders alone? and he replies to him, "The Sun wanders alone."
Then the Adhvaryu asks the Hotṛ: "What indeed is the light equal to the sun? He replies to him: "The Brahman is the light equal to the sun."
Then the Brahman asks the Udgātṛ: "I ask you for the sake of discernment, O friend of the gods. He replies to him: "I am indeed in those three steps."
Then the Udgātṛ asks the Brahman, "Into how many has the Person entered? He replies to him, "Into five has the Person entered."

When this has been recited, the Sadas priests rise and proceed eastward toward the sacrificer; having approached him as he sits in front of the two *havirdhāna* sheds, they sit down around him according to their respective positions.
The Hotṛ asks the Adhvaryu, "What was the first thought? He replies to him, "Heaven was the first thought."
Then the Adhvaryu asks the Hotṛ, "Who is this Piśaṅgilā? He replies to him, "The goat, Piśaṅgilā."
Then the Brahman asks the Udgātṛ: "How many are its stations? How many are its syllables? He replies to him: "Six are its stations; a hundred are its syllables."
Then the Udgātṛ asks the Brahman, "Who knows the navel of this world? He replies to him, "I know the navel of this world."
Then the sacrificer asks the Adhvaryu: "I ask you about the furthest limit of the earth. He should reply to him: "This altar is the furthest limit of the earth."
This theological debate is indeed the attainment of all speech; all desires are contained in the Aśvamedha. [They think: "By means of all speech, may we obtain all desires."

When the *brahmodya* has been uttered, the Adhvaryu, having entered [the Sadas], takes the *mahiman* cup dedicated to Prajāpati with a golden vessel. Its *puroruc* is: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning... Then its *puro'nuvākyā* is: "Subhūḥ, the self-existent, the first... The *praiṣa* is: "Let the Hotṛ worship Prajāpati. The Hotṛ recites the *yajyā*: "O Prajāpati, none other than you... At the *vaṣaṭ*-call, he offers the oblation with: "That greatness of yours which was produced in the day and in the year... He does not pronounce the *anuvaṣaṭ*, for he offers it as a complete oblation (*sarvahuta*). Now follows the offering of the omenta (*vapā*). They should proceed separately up to the omentum of the Vaiśvadeva; once the omentum of the Vaiśvadeva has been offered, they should offer the others following that, so said Satyakāma Jābāla. For all the gods are indeed the Viśve Devāḥ; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities.

"Once the offering for Indra and Agni has been made in the *vadā*, they should offer the others following that," so said Saumapa and Mānutantavya; "for Indra and Agni are indeed all the gods; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities."

"When the omentum of the body has been offered, they should offer the other parts following it," so said Śailāli; "for thus one gratifies them according to their respective deities. "Ka is indeed Prajāpati, and all the gods follow after Prajāpati; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities."

"Having offered to the twenty-one deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices and having divided [the oblation] into twenty-one parts, they should proceed with the offering," so said Bhāllabeya; "for all the gods are as many as there are deities of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities."

"They should proceed separately," says Indrota Śaunaka; "for why should they hasten? In that very way, he gratifies them according to their respective deities. This is their statement, but the established rule is indeed otherwise.

Then Yājñavalkya said: "They should proceed with the offerings to Prajāpati only once, and with those to the individual deities only once; thus he gratifies them according to their respective deities, reaches the completion of the sacrifice directly, and does not stumble."

When the omenta have been offered, the two Adhvaryus enter; with a silver vessel, the Adhvaryu draws the second Mahiman cup for Prajapati. Its introductory verse is "He who by his greatness [rules] over all that breathes and blinks"; the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* are reversed for the sake of avoiding exhaustion. This is the call (*praiṣa*); when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, he offers with the formula, "That greatness of thine which was manifested in the night of the year. He does not perform the secondary *vaṣaṭ* call; the Brahmana explanation for this has already been stated.

They do not cut portions from other animals with the *tedanī* knife; they cut the portion of the horse from the right side, while they cut the portions of the other animals from the left side. They cut the portions of the other animals on branches of the *plakṣa* tree, and those of the horse on branches of the *vetasa* reed.

Regarding this, Sātyayajñi said: "They should do otherwise; they should not exclude the Path from the Āpoda. However, the established rule is that the Ukthya sacrifice wins the intermediate world. The final day is an Atirātra with all the Stomas; for the Atirātra with all the Stomas is everything, and the Aśvamedha is everything. This is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.

Its *bahiṣpavamāna* is the *trivṛt*; the *ājya* stotras are the *pañcadaśa*; the midday *pavamāna* is the *saptadaśa*; the *pṛṣṭha* stotras are the *ekaviṃśa*; the third *pavamāna* is the *triṇava*; the *agniṣṭomasāman* is the *trayastrimśa*; the *uktha* stotras are the *ekaviṃśa*; the *ṣoḍaśin* is the *ekaviṃśa*; the night-stotra is the *pañcadaśa*; the *sandhi* is the *trivṛt*. That which belongs to the second day of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha* is its *chandoma*; it is an *atirātra* sacrifice. By means of that sacrifice, he prospers in yonder world.

There are twenty-one Savanīya animals, all dedicated to Agni; "Their ritual procedure is the same," so some say. However, one should indeed sacrifice these twenty-four bovine animals to twelve deities. There are twelve months in a year, and the year is everything; the Aśvamedha is everything. This is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.

By means of this, Hendruta Daivāpa Śaunaka performed the sacrifice for Janamejaya Pārikṣita; having sacrificed with it, he cast off all evil-doing and all the slaying of a Brahmin. Indeed, whoever sacrifices with the Aśvamedha casts off all evil-doing and all the slaying of a Brahmin.
This very thing was sung in a verse: "At Āsandīvat, Janamejaya bound for the gods a dappled horse that ate grain, was adorned with gold, and wore a green garland."

These same first two days and the *jyotis* *atirātra*—by that [sacrifice] Bhīmasena; these same first two days and the *go* *atirātra*—by that Ugrasena; these same first two days and the *āyus* *atirātra*—by that Śrutasena. These were the sons of Pṛkṣita. This has been celebrated in a verse: "The meritorious sons of Pṛkṣita, sacrificing with horse-sacrifices, one after another, cast off their evil karma through their meritorious deed."

These same two preceding days are followed by an Abhijit Atirātra; with this, Para Āṭṇāra, the Kausalya king, performed the sacrifice. This has been celebrated in a Gāthā concerning Para Āṭṇāra: "Para, the son of Āṭṇāra, the Kausalya Hairaṇyanābha, bound the horse fit for sacrifice and bestowed the full quarters of the earth."

These same two former days and the Viśvajit Atirātra—by means of this, Purukutsa, the son of Ikṣvāku, performed the sacrifice for Durgaha. Regarding this, it was spoken by the seer: "Our fathers were there; they were the seven Ṛṣis when [Purukutsa] was bound in the house of Durgaha."

These same two preceding days [are performed], followed by the Mahāvrata and the Atirātra. With this, Marutta Āvikṣita, the king of the Āyogavas, sacrificed. Then the Maruts became his servers, Agni his steward, and the Viśvedevas his courtiers. This has been celebrated in a Gāthā: "The Maruts were the servers in the house of Marutta Āvikṣita; Agni was the steward, and the Viśvedevas were the courtiers. Indeed, the Maruts become the servers, Agni the steward, and the Viśvedevas the courtiers of him who sacrifices with the Aśvamedha.

These same two preceding days, followed by an Aptoryāma Atirātra—by means of this sacrifice King Kraivya Pañcāla performed a sacrifice. "The Krivis," they say, was the ancient name for the Pañcālas. This has been celebrated in a Gāthā: "The Pañcāla, superior to many men, sacrificed a horse worthy of the Medha at Parivakrā, with a sacrificial fee of a hundred thousand."
Then, by the second [verse], five thousand, twenty-five hundred, and ten thousand Brahmins from the Pañcālas were distributed from every direction.

The Agniṣṭoma is the Trivṛt; the Ukthya is the Pañcadaśa; the third day is the Saptadaśa with its Ukthas; the Ṣoḍaśin is the Ekaviṃśa; the night-chant is the Pañcadaśa; and the Sandhi is the Trivṛt—thus this sacrifice is perfected as the Anuṣṭubh. With this very sacrifice, Dhvasan Dvaitavana, the king of the Matsyas, performed it. Where that lake Dvaitavana now is, that was sung of in a verse: "Fourteen horses did King Dvaitavana, the victor in battle, bind for Indra the slayer of Vṛtra; therefore it is called the lake Dvaitavana."

The Pavamāna stotras are twenty-four-fold, revolving around the nine-fold; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-four-fold, revolving around the twenty-one-fold; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-eight-fold, revolving around the thirty-three-fold. The Uktha-stotras have thirty-two verses each, the Ṣoḍaśin is twenty-one-fold, the night-chant is fifteen-fold, and the Sandhi-stotra is nine-fold. This is the Agniṣṭoma-sāman.

This is Viṣṇu’s stride; with this very [sacrifice], Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, sacrificed. Having sacrificed with it, he attained that pre-eminence which belongs to the Bharatas. This is celebrated in a verse: "Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, bound seventy-eight horses along the Yamunā, and fifty-five at the Gaṅgā for the slayer of Vṛtra."
Then, with the second [verse], Sudyumna bound one hundred and thirty-three royal horses fit for sacrifice and stood over them, saying, "I have surpassed others who are more skilled in magic."
Then, by means of the third [verse], the Apsaras Śakuntalā bore Bharata; he, having conquered the entire earth, brought for Indra more than a thousand sacrificial horses.

Then, on the fourth day, [he said]: "Today Bharata's greatness is such that neither those of old nor those of later times have attained heaven with their two arms, just as mortals cannot reach it; so it was for the five classes of men."

With the Ekaviṃśastoma sacrifice, Ṛṣabha Yājñatura, the king of the Śviknas, performed a sacrifice; this has been celebrated in a verse: "When Yājñatura was sacrificing as the Brahman priest Ṛṣabha, the people, having obtained wealth at the Aśvamedha, were distributing it as sacrificial fees."

With the Trayastriṃśastoma sacrifice, Śoṇa Sātrāsāha, the king of the Pañcālas, performed worship; this has been celebrated in a verse: "While Sātrāsāha was sacrificing with the Aśvamedha, sixty thousand armored men of the Taurvaśas rose up [in support], along with the thirty-three [divinities]."
Then, by the second [verse], six times six thousand six-legged ones are raised up in the sacrifice for you, the father of the world; thirty-three thousand six thousand armored ones [are raised].
Then, when Sātrāsaha, the Pāñcāla king Susrajit, was sacrificing with the third [offering], Indra became exhilarated by the Soma and the Brahmins were satisfied with wealth.

Having taken the horse of Kāśya, Śatānīka Sātrājita performed a sacrifice for Govinata; from that time on, the Kāśis did not establish the sacred fires, saying, "We have already partaken of the Soma-drink."

Its arrangement is as follows: the Pavamāna stotras are twenty-four-fold; they turn back to the nine-fold; the Pavamāna stotras are forty-four-fold; the Ājya stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Uktha stotras are twenty-seven-fold; the Pṛṣṭha stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Pavamāna stotras are thirty-six-fold; they turn back to the thirty-three-fold; the Agniṣṭoma-sāman is [twenty-one-fold]; the Uktha stotras are twenty-one-fold; the Ṣoḍaśin is twenty-one-fold; the night-stotra is fifteen-fold; the Sandhi-stotra is nine-fold.
This very matter has been celebrated in a verse: "Śatānīka Sātrājita took the sacrificial horse from all sides, just as Bharata took the sacrifice of the Kāśīs from the Satvats."

Then, with the second [verse], Śatānīka, having seized Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sacrificial horse—white, moving under his control in every direction, ten-month-old, and powerful—with the *Govinata* hymn, [recited]: "Śatānīka has driven [the horse]."
Now, on the fourth [day], it was said: "Today, among the Bharatas, neither those before nor those after have attained heaven as mortals do with their two wings; neither the seven nor the nine."

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial gifts: from the midst of the kingdom, excluding what belongs to the land, to men, and to the wealth of the Brahmin, the eastern quarter is for the Hotṛ, the southern for the Brahman, the western for the Adhvaryu, and the northern for the Udgātṛ; likewise, the assistant priests (hotṛkas) share in these portions.

When the concluding oblation (udayanīyā) has been completed, he immolates twenty-one barren cows as victims to be bound after the sacrifice (anūbandhyā): those dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa, those to the Viśvedevas, and those to Bṛhaspati; this is for the attainment of these deities. As to why those dedicated to Bṛhaspati are last—Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman—and thus he finally establishes himself in the Brahman.

Now, as to why there are twenty-one: he who shines yonder is indeed the twenty-first—twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun as the twenty-first; it is for the sake of this correspondence.

When the Udavasānīyā offering has been completed, they give as the sacrificial fee four wives, a maiden as the fifth, and four hundred female attendants, according to what has been previously agreed upon.

Then, in the following year, he sacrifices with the seasonal animals (ṛtupaśu): six dedicated to Agni in the spring, six to Indra in the summer, six to Parjanya or the Maruts in the rainy season, six to Mitra-Varuṇa in the autumn, six to Indra-Viṣṇu in the winter, and six to Indra-Bṛhaspati in the cool season. Six seasons constitute a year; thus he becomes firmly established in the seasons, that is, in the year.
