These animals amount to thirty-six; the Bṛhatī metre consists of thirty-six syllables, and upon the Bṛhatī the heavenly world is established. Thus, in the end, by means of the Bṛhatī metre itself, he becomes firmly established in the heavenly world.

The Person, Nārāyaṇa, desired: "May I transcend all beings; may I alone be all this. He beheld this sacrificial rite of the Puruṣamedha, consisting of five nights; he took it up and performed it. Having sacrificed with it, he transcended all beings and became all this. Whoever, knowing thus, performs the Puruṣamedha—or whoever knows this—transcends all beings and becomes all this.

It has twenty-three initiation days, twelve Upasad days, and five Soma-pressing days; thus this is a forty-night rite, including the initiations and Upasads. It consists of forty syllables—the Virāj—and so it attains the state of the Virāj. From that the Virāj was born, and from the Virāj the Puruṣa; this indeed is that Virāj, and from this very Virāj he thus generates the Puruṣa, the sacrifice.

These indeed consist of four decades; and as to why there are these four decades, it is for the attainment of both these worlds and the quarters. By the first decade they attained this very world, by the second the intermediate space, by the third the sky, and by the fourth the quarters. In the same way, the sacrificer attains this very world by the first decade, the intermediate space by the second, the sky by the third, and the quarters by the fourth. For as much as there is here—namely, these worlds and the quarters—the Puruṣamedha is all that; it is for the attainment of all and for the securing of all.

On the day of preparation (upavasatha), there are eleven animals for Agni and Soma; their ritual procedure is the same. There are eleven sacrificial posts. The Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables; the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.

The sacrificial animals at the Soma-pressings consist of sets of eleven; the Triṣṭubh metre has eleven syllables, the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of this thunderbolt and this vigor, the sacrificer repels evil from the front.

Moreover, as to why there are sets of eleven: the set of eleven indeed is this entire universe; for Prajāpati is the set of eleven, and Prajāpati is everything, and the Puruṣamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything and the securing of everything.

This Puruṣamedha is a five-night sacrificial rite; for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and the year consists of five seasons. Whatever is fivefold, whether concerning the deities or concerning the self, all that he obtains by means of this.

For this sacrifice, the first day is an Agniṣṭoma, then an Ukthya, then an Atirātra, then an Ukthya, and then an Agniṣṭoma; thus, this very sacrifice has light on both sides and Ukthyas on both sides.

The five-night sacrifice has the middle [night] like a barley grain (*yavamadhyah*). These worlds indeed are the Puruṣamedha; these worlds have light on both sides—by means of Agni here and by means of Āditya yonder. Therefore, it has light on both sides. Food is the Ukthya, and the self is the Atirātra. Since these two Ukthyas are on both sides of the Atirātra, therefore this body is encompassed by food. And since this Atirātra is the longest of the days and is in the middle, therefore it has the middle like a barley grain. Verily, he who knows this drives away his hateful rival; they say of him, "He exists, and his hateful rival does not exist."

Of this [sacrifice], this very world is its first day; this world of his is the spring season. That which is above this world and below the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is its second day; that of his is the summer season. The intermediate space itself is its middle day; the intermediate space of his is the rainy and autumn seasons. That which is above the intermediate space and below the sky is its fourth day; that of his is the winter season. The sky itself is its fifth day; the sky of his is the cool season. Thus far with respect to the deities.

Now, with respect to the self: his foundation is indeed his first day; the spring season is his foundation. That which is above the foundation and below the middle is his second day; that is his summer season. The middle itself is his middle day; the rainy and autumn seasons are his middle. That which is above the middle and below the head is his fourth day; that is his winter season. The head itself is his fifth day; the dewy season is his head. Thus these worlds, the year, and the self are fully realized in the Puruṣamedha. Indeed, all these worlds are everything; the year is everything; the self is everything; the Puruṣamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything, for the securing of everything.

Now, as to why it is called the Puruṣamedha: these worlds are indeed a city, and this person who blows (the wind) lies within this city; therefore he is a *puruṣa*. Whatever food there is in these worlds is his food, and that which is his food is his sacrificial essence (*medhas*); because this food of his is his sacrificial essence, it is therefore called the Puruṣamedha. Furthermore, it is called the Puruṣamedha because he immolates sacrificial men (*medhya-puruṣa*) within it.

He immolates them on the middle day; for the middle day is the intermediate region (antarikṣa), and the intermediate region is the abode of all beings. Moreover, these animals are food, and the middle day is the belly; thus he places that food within the belly.
He indeed seizes ten of each; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is all food; it is for the attainment of all food.

He offers eleven sets of ten; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is the thunderbolt; the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that very vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle.

He immolates forty-eight animals at the middle sacrificial post; the Jagatī metre consists of forty-eight syllables, and cattle are of the nature of the Jagatī; verily, by means of the Jagatī, he wins cattle for him.

In the others there are eleven each; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables. The Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer repels evil on both sides.

He seizes eight of the best; the Gāyatrī has eight syllables, and the Gāyatrī is the Brahman. Thus he makes that Brahman the highest of this entire universe. Therefore they say: "The Brahman is the highest of this entire universe."
They indeed belong to Prajāpati; for Prajāpati is Brahman, since Prajāpati is of the nature of Brahman; therefore they belong to Prajāpati.

When he is about to immolate the victims, he offers these three oblations to Savitṛ with the verses, "O God Savitṛ," "That most excellent [glory] of Savitṛ," and "All things, O God Savitṛ. He thus gratifies Savitṛ; and he, being gratified, impels these men for him, and being impelled by him, he immolates them.

He immolates a Brāhmaṇa for Brahman; the Brāhmaṇa is indeed Brahman, so he thus causes Brahman to prosper through Brahman. He immolates a Rājanya for Kṣatra; the Rājanya is indeed Kṣatra, so he thus causes Kṣatra to prosper through Kṣatra. He immolates a Vaiśya for the Maruts; the Maruts are indeed the Viś (the people), so he thus causes the Viś to prosper through the Viś. He immolates a Śūdra for Tapas; the Śūdra is indeed Tapas, so he thus causes Tapas to prosper through Tapas. In this way, he causes these deities to prosper through the animals according to their respective forms; they, being thus prospered, cause him to prosper with all his desires.

He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance—by means of brilliance he bestows brilliance upon him. He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is the beloved abode of the gods; verily, he satisfies them with their own beloved abode, and they, being satisfied, satisfy him with all his desires.

Brahmā, having appointed the men, praises him from the south with the Puruṣa hymn, "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet"—with this sixteen-verse hymn. For all this universe consists of sixteen parts, and the Puruṣamedha is everything; [he does this] for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. With the words "Thus you are, thus you are," he thus praises him, magnifies him, and speaks of him just as he truly is. Then the animals were encircled by fire, but they had not yet been immolated.

Then Speech addressed him: "O man, do not let it rest; if you let it rest, man will devour man. He released those [animals] after they had been carried around with fire, and offered oblations to those respective deities. By means of these, he gratified those deities, and they, being gratified, gratified him with all his desires.
He offers with clarified butter; clarified butter is indeed brilliance; verily, by means of brilliance, he bestows brilliance upon him.

He establishes [the sacrifice] with the Ekādaśinī offerings; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables, and the Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt. The Triṣṭubh is vigor; by means of that very thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle.

When the concluding oblation has been completed, he immolates eleven barren cows as the *anūbandhya* victims: those dedicated to Mitra-Varuṇa, those to the Viśvedevas, and those to Bṛhaspati; this is for the attainment of these deities. Now, as to why those dedicated to Bṛhaspati are last: Bṛhaspati is indeed the Brahman; thus, he finally establishes himself in the Brahman.

Now there are eleven [verses]; the Triṣṭubh consists of eleven syllables. The Triṣṭubh is a thunderbolt, and the Triṣṭubh is vigor. By means of that very thunderbolt and that vigor, the sacrificer strikes away evil from the middle. The Traidhātavī is the concluding offering (udavasānīyā); its significance is the same as before.

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*): from the middle of the kingdom, excluding what belongs to the land and the property of the Brahmin, [the gift] is for the virtuous man. The eastern quarter belongs to the *Hotṛ*, the southern to the *Adhvaryu*, the western to the *Brahman*, and the northern to the *Udgātṛ*; likewise, the *Hotṛkā*s are entitled to a share.

Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, he should give away all his possessions (*sarvavedasa*); for the Brāhmaṇa is everything, and all his possessions are everything. The Puruṣamedha is everything; it is for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.

Then, having consigned the two fires into himself and having stood up toward the sun with the Uttara-Nārāyaṇa hymn, he should go toward the forest without looking back; thus he becomes invisible to men. But if he should wish to dwell in a village, he should consign the two fires into the two kindling woods, stand up toward the sun with the same Uttara-Nārāyaṇa hymn, and settle down in his home; then he may perform those sacrificial rites which he might be able to accomplish. Now, this [instruction] should not be imparted to just anyone, for the Puruṣamedha is everything; thinking, "Lest I speak everything to just anyone," he should impart it only to one who is well-known to him, or to one who is learned in the Vedas, or to one who is dear to him—but indeed, never to just anyone.

Brahman, the Self-existent, performed austerity. Then he reflected: "There is indeed no infinity in austerity; come, let me offer myself as a sacrifice in all beings, and all beings in myself. Having offered himself in all beings and all beings in himself, he attained pre-eminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings. In the same way, this sacrificer, having offered all sacrifices in the Sarvamedha, attains pre-eminence, sovereignty, and lordship over all beings.

This very Sarvamedha is a ten-night sacrificial rite; the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the Virāj is all food. It is for the attainment of all food that he performs it. Upon this [altar], he piles the fire-altar as the highest; for the Sarvamedha is the highest of sacrificial rites, and by means of the highest, he causes him to reach the highest state.

For this [sacrifice], the Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma is the first day. Indeed, the Agniṣṭut Agniṣṭoma is Agni; and all the gods have Agni as their mouth. It is for the attainment of all the gods. Its cups belong to Agni, and its *puroruc* verses belong to Agni, so that everything may be dedicated to Agni.

The second day is an *ukthya* sacrifice dedicated to Indra; for Indra indeed is all the gods, and it is for the attainment of all the gods. For him, there are cups for Indra, and the *puroruc* verses are addressed to Indra, so that everything may belong to Indra.

The third day is an Ukthya sacrifice dedicated to Sūrya; for Sūrya is indeed all the gods, and it is for the attainment of all the gods that the draughts (grahas) belong to Sūrya, the Puroruc verses belong to Sūrya, and everything is dedicated to Sūrya.

The fourth day is the Vaiśvadeva; for the Viśvedevas are all the gods, and it serves to obtain all the gods. There are cups for the Viśvedevas, and the *paroruc* verses are addressed to the Viśvedevas, so that everything may be dedicated to the Viśvedevas.
The fifth day is the central Āśvamedhika; on that day he immolates the sacrificial horse for the attainment of the Aśvamedha itself.
The middle sixth day is that of the Puruṣamedha; on it, he immolates men fit for sacrifice, for the sake of attaining the very Puruṣamedha.

The Aptoryāma is the seventh day, for the attainment of all sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*). Upon it, he immolates all animals fit for sacrifice—whatever is animate and whatever is inanimate. He offers the omentum (*vapā*) of those that have one, and the excision of the skin of those without omenta; they scatter the cuttings of herbs and trees, both dry and fresh. He offers food after food for the attainment of every kind of food. He offers everything, he offers to everything, for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything. When the omenta have been offered at the morning pressing, it is exactly the same at the third pressing when the oblations (*havis*) have been offered.
The Triṇava is the eighth day; the Triṇava is indeed a thunderbolt (vajra), and by the thunderbolt, the kṣatra is won; thus, by means of the thunderbolt itself, he wins the kṣatra.
The ninth day is the Trayastriṃśa; the Trayastriṃśa is indeed a firm foundation, for the sake of stability.

The tenth day is the Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas; for the Viśvajit Atirātra with all the Pṛṣṭhas is indeed everything, and the Sarvamedha is everything—for the attainment of everything and for the securing of everything.

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās): from the middle of the kingdom, whatever wealth there is other than that of a Brāhmaṇa—including land and men—the eastern quarter is the fee for the Hotṛ, the southern for the Brahman, the western for the Adhvaryu, and the northern for the Udgātṛ; in that very same way, the assistant priests (hotṛkas) are entitled to a share.

By means of this very sacrifice, Viśvakarman Bhauvana performed the rite; having sacrificed with it, he surpassed all beings and became this entire universe. Whoever, knowing thus, performs the Sarvamedha, or whoever knows this in this way, surpasses all beings and becomes this entire universe.

Kaśyapa officiated as the priest for him; regarding that, the Earth sang this verse: "No mortal whatsoever deserves to give me away. O Viśvakarman Bhauvana, you were foolish; she shall sink into the midst of the waters. This promise of yours to Kaśyapa was in vain."

Then they perform auspicious rites for him; then they prepare a burial mound (śmaśāna) for him, or a house, or a memorial monument. Whosoever dies, he is a corpse (śava); for him they prepare this food, and therefore it is "corpse-food" (śavānna). They call that by the cryptic name "burial mound" (śmaśāna). Indeed, the ancestors (pitṛs) are eaters, and they seize the merit of one who has not prepared a burial mound in that world. For them, he prepares this food, and therefore it is "mound-food" (śmaśānna). They call that by the cryptic name "burial mound" (śmaśāna).

One should not do it too quickly, thinking, "Lest I create fresh evil. One should indeed do it slowly; thus one carries the evil across. Where even those who were together do not remember [the rite], one causes that evil to go into oblivion; but if they should remember it, [it remains].

One should perform it during odd-numbered years, for the ancestors belong to the odd numbers; under a single lunar mansion, for the ancestors belong to a single lunar mansion. On the new moon day there is a single lunar mansion, for the new moon day is indeed a single lunar mansion; because on that night all beings dwell together, one thereby obtains that desire which belongs to all the lunar mansions.

One should perform it in autumn; for autumn is indeed *svadhā*, and *svadhā* is the food of the ancestors; thus he places him in that food, the *svadhā*. Or [he may do so] in Māgha, thinking, "May no evil come to us"; or in the heat of summer, thinking, "May evil be laid low for us."

The four-cornered [burial mounds] were once the gods and the Asuras, both of them offspring of Prajāpati, who contended for the quarters. Those gods drove their rivals, the Asuras, out from the quarters; being deprived of the quarters, they perished. Therefore, those divine offspring make their burial mounds four-cornered. But those that belong to the Asuras are now, on the contrary, circular. For they (the gods) drove them out from the quarters. He places it between the two quarters, the eastern and the southern; for in this quarter lies the door to the world of the Fathers. By means of that very door he causes him to enter the world of the Fathers. With its corners he establishes himself in the quarters, and with its body in the intermediate quarters; thus he establishes him in all the quarters.

Now, therefore, regarding the choosing of the ground: he prepares it on ground sloping toward the north; for the north is the quarter of men—thus he causes him to participate in the world of men. Indeed, the ancestors participate in the world of men when they have offspring; and his offspring becomes more excellent.

"One should build it on ground sloping toward the south," they say, "for the world of the fathers slopes toward the south; thus one causes him to share in the world of the fathers. One should not do so, for that making of a cemetery is indeed called "the disease-bringer"; very quickly another of them follows after [in death].

"One should perform it on ground sloping toward the south," so say some, "for that becomes elevated ground for misfortune. But one should not do it thus; rather, whatever one does on ground sloping toward the north, that itself becomes elevated ground for misfortune.

If, while he is still alive, water should come from the south-east, flow around him, and without striking him, reach this direction so that he might attain inexhaustible waters—then he should do that. For water is indeed food; thus he places food before him, turned towards him. And water is indeed immortality; for this is the direction of living beings, lying between the rising of the Seven Seers and the setting of the sun. He thereby bestows immortality upon the living. This making of a burial mound is called "the warding-off" (*pratimīvan*); it is beneficial for the living, and what is beneficial for the living is beneficial for the fathers.

He should make it pleasant, thinking, "May this be pleasant for me," or he may make it auspicious, thinking, "May this be auspicious for me. He should not make it on a path, nor in the open air, lest he make his sin manifest.

It may be both secret and manifest. That which is secret is indeed evil; he makes that secret. Now, as for that which is manifest: yonder sun is the remover of evil; he himself removes the evil from him. Moreover, he makes him possessed of the light of the sun.
One should not do it where there is such an opening [to view], for that is indeed called "begging"; quickly another among them follows after him.

The variegated should be at the back; for offspring are indeed the variegated, and his offspring will be variegated. If there were no variegated [brick], there should be water either at the back or on the north side, for water is indeed the variegated;
and his offspring will surely be variegated.

He makes it on saline soil; saline soil is indeed seed, it is procreation; thus he causes him to participate in procreation. For the ancestors indeed participate in procreation when they have offspring; and his offspring shall be more prosperous.
For this is the ancestral offering for her ancestors, mixed with *vīriṇa* grass, together with the roots; it is not excessive, yet it binds that very evil upon them.

One should not place a *bhūmipāśa* [trap], nor a *śara*, nor *aśmagandhā*, nor *adhyāṇḍā*, nor *pṛśniparṇī*. One should not perform [any rite] near an *aśvattha* tree, nor a *vibhītaka*, nor a *tilvaka*, nor a *sphūrjaka*, nor a *haridrā*, nor a *nyagrodha*; and as for any others with evil names, one should avoid them by their very names out of a desire for auspiciousness.

Now, therefore, follows the procedure: by means of the rite of the fire-altar, one constructs the burial mound for the builder of the fire-altar. For when the sacrificer builds the fire-altar, he thereby prepares himself for that world by means of the sacrifice; this sacrificial work remains incomplete until the construction of the burial mound. Thus, when one constructs the burial mound for the builder of the fire-altar according to the rite of the fire-altar, he thereby brings the building of the fire-altar to completion.

"One should not let it decay too much, lest one commit a great sin," so they say; "one should let it decay as much as the fire is without wings and tail," some indeed say, "for this body of his is the same as that of the fire."

One should make it only as wide as a man; thus one leaves no room for another. It should be wider at the back; offspring are indeed behind, so he thereby makes the offspring more excellent. It should be broader on the north side; offspring are indeed to the north, so he thereby makes the offspring more prosperous. Having thus measured it, he encloses it with cords twisted counter-clockwise; for the rite of the ancestors is performed counter-clockwise.

Then he says to the excavator: "He should dig as much as he intends to pour; however, he should dig to the height of a man, so that he does not leave room for another. Moreover, the world of the fathers is indeed the world of plants, for they creep toward the roots of the plants. Furthermore, it is so that he may not be separated from this earth."

Some bury [the bones] while they are still hidden. Both the gods and the Asuras, the offspring of Prajāpati, contended for this world. Those gods drove out their rivals, the Asuras, from this world. Therefore, those divine offspring who are not separated [from the earth] make their burial grounds (śmaśāna) unhidden; whereas those who are of the Asura nature are separated—some by this [earth], some by that, some by a bowl (camū), some by this, and some by that.

Then he encloses it with the enclosing-stones (*pariśrit*). Those which are those [enclosing-stones] there, these he encloses with a sacrificial formula; these [here] he encloses silently. Thus he distinguishes between that which belongs to the gods and that which belongs to the fathers. He uses an unlimited number [of stones], for that world is indeed unlimited.

Then he sweeps it away with a Palāśa branch. That which was the sweeping away at the beginning is this very act. With the words, "Let the Paṇis go away, the ill-minded ones who revile the gods," he thus drives away from this world the Paṇis, those ill-minded revilers of the gods, the Asuras and Rakṣasas. With the words, "This is the world of the one who has pressed the Soma," for he who has sacrificed is indeed a "Sutavat" (one who has pressed the Soma); and with the words, "By days, by nights, by the distinct seasons," he makes him share the same world as the seasons and the days and nights.

"May Yama grant us a dwelling," he says; for Yama indeed rules over the dwelling on this earth. He thus asks him for a dwelling on this earth, and casts that [clod] toward the south, while the other toward the north; thereby he distinguishes between what belongs to the gods and what belongs to the fathers.

Then he yokes the plough from the south; some, however, say "from the north," but let him do as he desires. Having given the command, "Yoke! he consecrates it with the formula: "May Savitṛ seek a place on earth for your bodies. It is indeed Savitṛ who seeks this place on earth for his bodies. [He continues: "Let the oxen be yoked for him," for it is for this very rite that the oxen are yoked.

It consists of six oxen; there are six seasons in the year, and thus he establishes him in the seasons, in the year, as a firm foundation. Having turned it to the left, he ploughs the first furrow from the north towards the west with the words, "May Vāyu purify [it]. With the words, "With the brilliance of the southern fire," he ploughs the furrow from the south towards the east along the rear half of the southern fire-altar. With the words, "With the splendor of the Sun," he ploughs the furrow from the front towards the north.

He ploughs four furrows with a Yajus formula; thus he establishes him in that very food which exists in the four quarters. And as for the Yajus formula: the Yajus is indeed the truth, and these quarters are the truth.

Then he draws himself toward [the fire]; whatever food there is in the year, therein he thus establishes him. He does so silently with an unlimited number of [draws], for that world is indeed unlimited.

Then he unyokes it after having performed that rite for which he yoked it, with the words, "May the cows be unyoked," for it is for this very rite that the cows are yoked. He throws out the dung toward the south, and the other [dung] toward the north; thus he distinguishes between what belongs to the gods and what belongs to the fathers.

Then he sows all kinds of herbs. That same all-herb mixture which was there [in the previous case], that he now sows with many verses; this one he sows with a single verse. Thus he distinguishes between what belongs to the gods and what belongs to the fathers. With the words, "In the Ashvattha tree is your seat, on the Parṇa tree is your dwelling," he thereby prays for long life for them; and so, one by one, another of them follows after them in old age.

Then he scatters it on this [ground]. This earth, indeed, is the foundation; he thus establishes him upon this very foundation. Before the rising of the sun—since the fathers are, as it were, hidden, and the night is, as it were, hidden—he does that which is hidden, so that the sun may rise while he is performing it; thus he establishes him during both day and night.

"May Savitṛ cast thy limbs into the lap of the mother," he says; thus Savitṛ himself casts his limbs into the lap of this earth, the mother. "Be auspicious to her, O Earth," he says; he speaks thus so that she may be auspicious to him. "I place thee in the deity Prajāpati, in the world near the water, O [Name]," he says, taking the name; this world is indeed "near the water," and thus he places him in the deity Prajāpati, in the world near the water.

Then he says to someone: "Go in this direction, and having gone without looking back, come back after you have broken the water-jar. There he mutters: "O Death, go along the other path, that which is different from the path of the gods; I speak to you who have eyes and hear: do not harm our offspring, nor our heroes. He thus prays for long life for them; and so, one by one, another of them follows [the deceased] in old age.

Then he arranges it limb by limb: "May the wind be propitious; may the heat be propitious to thee; may the bricks be propitious to thee; may the earthly fires be propitious to thee; let them not consume thee. "May the quarters be fit for thee; may the waters be most auspicious for thee; may the rivers be for thee; may the atmosphere be auspicious for thee; may all the quarters be fit for thee. By this, he makes everything fit for him; by this, he makes it auspicious for him.

Then thirteen foot-measure bricks are made without marks; those very ones which are the fire-altar bricks (agni-īṣṭakā) are these [foot-measure bricks] laid down with a Yajus formula, while these [other] ones are laid down silently. Thus he distinguishes between that which belongs to the gods and that which belongs to the fathers.
There are thirteen; there are thirteen months in a year: he thus establishes him in the seasons, in the year, which is the foundation.

They are a foot in measure; for the foot is a support, and thus he provides support for him. They are unmarked; for the Fathers are, as it were, hidden, and that which is unmarked is, as it were, hidden; thus he makes them hidden by means of what is hidden.

Of these, he places one in the middle facing east; that is the body. Three are placed in front, joined to the head; that is the head. Three are on the south; that is the right wing. Three are on the north; that is the left wing. Three are behind; that is the tail. Thus this body of his possesses wings and a tail, just as it does for Agni.

Then, intending to take the soil from the cleft, he says: "For this is her ancestral [portion], not excessive; moreover, he thereby makes that very evil firmly established. Now, some dig a trench in that intermediate space and bring the soil from there; others plough around it—from the south, then from the west, then from the north—and bring the soil from there. He may do as he wishes.

One should not make it too large, lest one should commit a great sin. It should be as high as a man with arms outstretched for a Kṣatriya; as high as the mouth for a Brāhmaṇa; as high as the pubic region for a woman; as high as the thighs for a Vaiśya; and as high as the knees for a Śūdra, for such is their respective strength.

He should indeed keep it below the knee; thus he leaves no room for another while it is being made. To its north they hold up a splinter of wood; that is offspring, so they thereby hold up offspring to the north. He should not set it down; having either held it or carried it, he should fix it in his house; he thereby fixes offspring in his house.

Having prepared [the ground], he sows barley, thinking, "May it ward off (yavaya) my evil (agha). He covers it with *avakā* plants, thinking, "May there be pleasure (kam) for me. He covers it with *darbha* grass for the sake of smoothness (*arūkṣatā*).

Then they fix it around with pegs: one made of *palāśa* wood in the east; for the *palāśa* is indeed the Brahman, and thus he causes it to go to the heavenly world with the Brahman as its leader. One made of *śamī* wood in the north, thinking, "May there be peace for me. One made of *vāraṇa* wood in the west, thinking, "May it ward off evil from me. A *vṛtra-śaṅku* (Vṛtra-peg) in the south, for the purpose of not allowing evil to pass beyond.

Then, on the south side, they dig two winding channels and fill them with milk and water; these two flow for him toward the two ruddy streams in yonder world. They fill seven more channels with water; for indeed, no one is able to cross over the seven flowing rivers except for the overcoming of evil—for the sake of not being overcome by evil.

They scatter three stones each; they cross over them [with the verses]: "The stony river flows; take hold of one another, arise, cross over, O friends! Here let us leave behind those who were inauspicious; may we, being auspicious, cross over to strengths. As the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

With *apāmārga* plants they wipe away; verily they wipe away evil. "Wipe away sin, wipe away guilt, wipe away sorcery, wipe away blemish—O *apāmārga*, wipe away from us the evil dream," he says; as the sacrificial formula is, so is its significance.

Where there is water, they bathe therein. With the formula, "May the waters and plants be friendly to us," he takes up water with his joined palms. For the waters are indeed a thunderbolt; by means of that thunderbolt, he thus establishes a covenant of friendship. [With the words,] "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate," he causes him whom he pours out against to perish by that very act.

If the waters are still, they cause their evil to stand still; and if they flow, they carry away their evil. Having bathed and put on fresh garments, they walk forward while holding onto the tail of an ox. For the ox belongs to Agni; thus, with Agni at their head, they go from the world of the fathers to the world of the living. Moreover, Agni is the one who carries them across the path; he carries them across.

Reciting this verse, "Up from the darkness," they proceed; thus they advance toward the light of the sun from the world of the fathers, which is darkness. When they have arrived, they offer them collyrium and ointment; for this is human adornment, and by means of it they conceal that death.

Then, having established the fire in the house and having laid down the enclosing sticks made of *vāraṇa* wood, he offers an oblation to the long-lived Agni with a *sruva* ladle made of *vāraṇa* wood, [saying]: "Agni indeed is long-lived; he rules over life. To him alone he begs life for them. The verse "O Agni, you purify lives" (*agna āyūṃṣi pavase*) serves as the portion for the invitatory formula (*puro'nuvākyā*).

Then he offers: "O Agni, long-lived one, increasing by the oblation, with ghee as thy face and ghee as thy womb, having drunk the ghee and the sweet, pleasant [milk] of the cow, protect these here like a father his son—Svāhā! He says this so that he may protect them, so that he may guard them; it is for this very purpose that he speaks thus.

An old ox is its sacrificial fee; old barley, an old stool with a cushion—this indeed is the prescribed sacrificial fee. However, one who has piled the fire-altar may give more, according to his inclination and faith. Thus it is for the piler of the fire-altar.

Now, for one who has not built a fire-altar, this very same selection of the ground applies; the ritual procedure is the same as that of any other rite except for the work pertaining to the fire-altar itself. Regarding this, some say that the pebbles used by one who has maintained the sacred fires are the very same as those used at the establishment of the fires (*agnyādheya*); however, others say one should not do so, for those [pebbles] might scorch one who has not built a fire-altar. Therefore, he may act according to his desire.

Having taken a clod of earth from the very boundary-line, he places it between [the two posts] with the formula: "I set up this enclosure for the living; let no other reach this goal of theirs. May they live a hundred long autumns, placing death within the mountain. Thus he establishes a boundary between the living and the ancestors so that there may be no confusion; therefore, indeed, the living and the ancestors are not seen together. Om! The gods, indeed, sat down for a sacrificial session—Agni, Indra, Soma, Makha, Viṣṇu, and the All-gods—with the exception of the Aśvins.

Kurukṣetra was their place for sacrificing to the gods; therefore they say, "Kurukṣetra is the gods' place for sacrificing to the gods. Therefore, wherever one goes from Kurukṣetra, one thinks, "This is a place for sacrificing to the gods," for that indeed is the gods' place for sacrificing to the gods.

"They sit [in session], thinking: 'May we attain prosperity; may we be glorious; may we be eaters of food. And so indeed these [priests] sit for the sacrificial session (sattra), thinking: 'May we attain prosperity; may we be glorious; may we be eaters of food.'"

They said, "He among us who first reaches the conclusion of the sacrifice through toil, austerity, faith, sacrifice, and oblations—he shall be the best of us; let him belong to all of us together. They replied, "So be it."
Viṣṇu was the first to obtain it; he became the best among the gods. Therefore they say, "Viṣṇu is the best among the gods."
He who is Viṣṇu is the sacrifice; he who is the sacrifice is that Āditya. This glory of Viṣṇu was indeed unable to sustain itself; even now, not everyone is able to sustain this glory.
Taking his three-bowed bow, he departed; he stood propping up his head with the end of the bowstring. The gods, not daring to attack him, sat down all around him.

The ants said to them: "These are indeed ants, namely the termites. If someone were to eat even his bowstring, what would you give him? We would give him food; even if he should reach water in a desert, we would give him all kinds of food. They replied, "So be it."
Approaching him, they bit through his bowstring; when that was severed, the two ends of the bow sprang apart and cut off the head of Viṣṇu.

It fell with the sound "ghṛṅ! Having fallen, it became that Āditya; then the other [portion] was pushed forward. Because it fell with the sound "ghṛṅ," it is therefore called *gharma*; and because it was pushed forward (*prāvṛjyata*), it is therefore called *pravargya*.
Those gods said, "A great hero indeed has been given to us"; therefore he is called Mahāvīra. The essence that flowed from him they rubbed together with their hands; therefore he is called Samrāj.

The gods strove for him as those about to obtain their share. Indra reached him first; Aṅga followed after him; he seized him; having seized him, he became this glory that is here—namely, the glory that is Indra. He who knows this becomes glorious.
He indeed is Makha, he is Viṣṇu; from him Indra became possessed of Makha (Makhavat). For they call him "Maghavan" cryptically; for the gods love the cryptic.
They bestowed food upon those ants; for water is indeed all food, since with it they eat this [world] as if by gnawing, whatever there is here that they speak of.
Then the Vasus divided this Viṣṇu-sacrifice into three parts: the Vasus [took] the morning pressing, the Rudras the midday pressing, and the Ādityas the third pressing.
Agni [presides over] the morning pressing, Indra the midday pressing, and the Viśvedevas the third pressing.
The Gāyatrī is the morning pressing, the Triṣṭubh the midday pressing, and the Jagatī the third pressing; with that headless sacrifice, the gods moved about, praising and toiling.
Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed discovered this bright one, this sacrifice, so that the head of the sacrifice may be restored as it was, and so that this sacrifice becomes complete.
Indra said to him, "If you should teach this to anyone else, I shall cut off your head from that very spot."

Now this had been heard by the Aśvins: "Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed knows this bright [Soma], this sacrifice, how exactly the head of the sacrifice is restored, and how this sacrifice becomes complete."
The two of them said to him, "We would approach you; what shall we recite?"—"This bright one, this sacrifice—how this head of the sacrifice is restored, so that this sacrifice becomes complete."
He said, "Indra has indeed told me: 'If you teach this to anyone else, I shall cut off your head from that very spot. Therefore, I am afraid; lest he should cut off my head, I will not initiate you."

The two of them said, "We two shall protect you from that. He asked, "How will you protect me? They replied, "When they lead you away, we shall then cut off your head and set it aside elsewhere; then, having brought the horse's head, we shall replace yours with it, and with that you will recite for us. When you have recited for us, then they will cut off your [horse] head; then, having brought back your own head, we shall replace yours with it. "So be it," he said.

They brought him [the horse] near; when they had brought him near, they cut off his head and set it aside elsewhere. Then, having brought the head of a horse, they replaced it upon him. With that [horse-head], he recited the Veda for them both. When he had recited for them both, Indra cut off that head of his. Then, having brought his own head, they replaced it upon him.

Therefore, this was declared by the Seer: "When Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, spoke to you two with the horse's head, that he spoke it unhesitatingly"—by this, indeed, it is said that he spoke it without hesitation.

Therefore, one should not recite it for everyone, for that would be a sin; moreover, [one should think], "Lest Indra cut off my head. One should indeed recite it for someone who is well-known, or for one who is learned in the Vedas, or for one who might be dear to him, but certainly not for just anyone.

One should recite for one who has lived for a year; for he who shines yonder is indeed the year, and he is the Pravargya; thus it is him that he thereby gratifies. Therefore, one should recite for one who has lived for a year.

He observes the vow for three nights; for there are three seasons in the year, and he who shines yonder is the year, and he is indeed the Pravargya; thus he thereby gratifies him. Therefore, he observes the vow for three nights.
"The ascetic recites, thinking, 'I am reciting while consuming hot [water]'; the ascetic recites, thinking, 'I am reciting while abstaining from meat.'"
He is one who drinks from a vessel not made of clay; for whatever untruth he speaks in this world is, as it were, mixed with it, therefore he is one who gives what is not made of clay.

One who is not a Śūdra should avoid impurity; for he who shines yonder is indeed Dharma, he is Prosperity, Truth, and Light. A woman, a Śūdra, a dog, and a black bird—these one should not look upon, lest one mingle prosperity with evil, light with darkness, or truth with untruth.

Now, this indeed is glory: he who shines yonder. In that the sun is glory, it is truly the sacrifice that is glory; in that the sacrifice is glory, it is truly the sacrificer that is glory; in that the sacrificer is glory, it is truly the officiating priests that are glory; in that the officiating priests are glory, it is truly the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that is glory. Therefore, when they bring a sacrificial fee to him, he should not immediately assign it to another, thinking, "Lest I should immediately assign to another that glory which has come to me. Rather, on the next day or after two days have passed, having placed that glory within himself, he gives away whatever it may be—gold, a cow, a garment, or a horse.

Now, indeed, he who either teaches this or consumes it enters this life and this light. His rule of conduct is as follows: he should not look at the sun, lest he should be hidden from it; he should not spit while looking at the sun, lest he should spit upon it; he should not urinate while looking at the sun, lest he should urinate upon it. For as great as this [sun] is when it shines, so great is this [man]; [he acts thus] thinking, "Lest I should injure him by these [acts]. Having looked away, he should eat at night; thereby his form is made to correspond to that which shines. Regarding this, Āsuri said: "The gods observe but one vow, namely truth; therefore, one should speak only the truth."

He indeed gathers the materials; and because he gathers them from here and there, that is the reason for their being called "materials" (sambhāra). He gathers them from wherever they are deposited within the sacrifice.

He prepares the black antelope skin; the black antelope skin is indeed the sacrifice, so he thus prepares him within the sacrifice itself. It is with the hair-side up, for the hairs are the meters; he thus prepares him within the meters. To the north, for the north is the direction of men; with the neck toward the east, for that is the way among the gods.
The spade is a thunderbolt, for the spade is indeed vigor; with vigor he thus causes this [altar] to prosper and makes it complete.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed strength and sap. Verily, he thus endows him with strength and sap, and makes him complete.

Moreover, it is of *vaikaṅkata* wood; for when Prajāpati offered the first oblation, that which remained after he had offered it became the *vikaṅkata* tree. The oblation is indeed the sacrifice, and the *vikaṅkata* is the sacrifice; thus he endows this [fire] with the sacrifice and makes it complete.

It is a cubit long; for the cubit is the arm, and by the arm strength is performed. Thus it becomes commensurate with strength; by means of strength he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete.
He takes it up with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a woman. Its significance is the same as before.

Placing her in his left hand and touching her with his right, he recites: "The inspired priests of the great inspired one, the wise, harness their minds and harness their thoughts; he alone, who knows the ways, ordains the priestly functions—the great praise of the god Savitṛ. The significance of this is the same as before.

Then he takes up the lump of clay with the wooden spade on the south side and with his hand on the north side, saying, "O divine Heaven and Earth! When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed away; it went into these two, Heaven and Earth—that which is the clay is this [earth], and that which is the water is yonder [heaven]. From the clay and from the water, the Mahāvīra vessels are made. Thus he endows it with that very sap and makes it complete; therefore he says, "O divine Heaven and Earth! "May I today accomplish the head of Makha for you. Makha is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "May I today accomplish the head of the sacrifice for you. "On the place of sacrifice of the earth. For he gathers them on the place of sacrifice of the earth. "For Makha, thee! For the head of Makha, thee! Makha is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "For the sacrifice, thee! For the head of the sacrifice, thee!"

Then [he takes] the ant-hill; for the divine ants did this very thing, namely, that they restored this head of the sacrifice as it was being cut off. By means of them he now restores this and makes it complete. "The first-born of existence"—for this earth is indeed the first-born of existence; by means of her he thus restores this and makes it complete. "May I today accomplish your head on the earth's place of divine worship! For Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Now, as for "that which was struck by the boar": in the beginning this earth was only this much; it was merely a span in extent. The boar, thinking "this," dug her up. He, Prajāpati, is her lord. By means of that very pair, his own dear abode, he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete. With the words, "May I today accomplish the head of Makha on the earth's place of divine sacrifice; for Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Then he takes the Ādāra plants with the formula, "The vigor of Indra. When Indra encompassed him with his vigor, the sap of that encompassed one flowed out; it lay there as if putrefying. He said, "Alas, this sap of mine has burst forth! It has praised me!"—therefore they are called Ādāras. And because it lay there as if putrefying, therefore they are called Pūtīkas. Therefore they blaze up like an oblation placed upon the fire; therefore they are fragrant, for they were produced from the sap of the sacrifice. And because Indra then encompassed him with his vigor, therefore he says, "The vigor of Indra. With the formula, "May I today accomplish the head of Makha on the earth at the place of divine worship; for Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Now, as for the goat's milk: when the sacrifice had its head cut off, its heat (śuc) departed, and from that the goat was produced. With that very heat he thus endows it and makes it whole. "For Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

He collects these five materials; for the sacrifice is fivefold, the animal is fivefold, and there are five seasons in the year. This one who shines yonder is the year, and he is indeed the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. He touches those collected materials with the words, "For Makha thee! For Makha's head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before.

Then there is an enclosure to the north; approaching it, they mutter: "May Brahmaṇaspati go forth. He who shines yonder is indeed Brahmaṇaspati, and he is also the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "May Brahmaṇaspati go forth. "May Sūnṛtā, the goddess, go forth," for she is indeed the goddess Sūnṛtā. "And [to] the hero, the manly one, whose gifts are fivefold"—thus he praises him and magnifies him. "May the gods lead the sacrifice for us"—thereby he makes all the gods his protectors.

It is enclosed; for the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike this one of ours here"; they therefore enclosed him with this fortress, and in the same way, this [priest] encloses him with this fortress.

Then he places [the clay] on the donkey with the formula, "For Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. Then, having taken a lump of clay, he fashions the Mahāvīra pot with the formula, "For Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before. It is a span high, for the head is, as it were, a span; it is constricted in the middle, for the head is, as it were, constricted in the middle. Then, three finger-breadths from above, he forms a mouth for it; he thereby places a nose in it. When it is finished, he touches it with the formula, "Thou art the head of Makha," for this is indeed the head of the Soma-like Makha. In the same way, he silently fashions the two *pinvana* vessels and the two *rauhiṇa* potsherds.

This sacrifice is indeed Prajāpati. For Prajāpati is both defined and undefined, both limited and unlimited. When he performs an act with a Yajus formula, he thereby perfects that form of his which is defined and limited; and when he acts silently, he thereby perfects that form of his which is undefined and unlimited. He who, knowing this, performs it in this manner, truly perfects this entire and complete Prajāpati. Furthermore, he leaves over a lump of clay for the *upashayā* (the lying-down brick) for the sake of expiations.

Then he impels [the Soma] with *gavedhukā* grass. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed out; from that these plants were born. By means of that very sap, he thus endows it and makes it whole. With the words, "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—this is the same significance as before. In the same way for the other two; silently the two *pinvana* vessels; silently the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds.

Then he fumigates them with: "With the power of the stallion horse, I fumigate thee. For the horse is a stallion, and the stallion is indeed vigor; verily, by means of vigor, he thus endows this [sacrifice] and makes it complete. "On the earth’s place of divine sacrifice, for Makha thee! For Makha’s head thee!"—this is the significance of that very formula. In the same way for the other two; silently the two *pinvana* vessels, and silently the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds.

Then he cooks them; for what has been cooked belongs to the gods. He cooks them with bricks; for the gods did this very thing: by means of those [bricks], they restored that which had been cut off from the head of the sacrifice. He thus completes it and makes it whole. Therefore, he should cook them in such a way that they are well-cooked. Then, having placed the cooking-vessel down, he places the Mahāvīra pot upon it with the formula: "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee! Its significance is the same as before. In the same way, he silently places the two *pinvana* vessels and the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds. He should set them out during the day and take them away during the day, for the day belongs to the gods.

He throws it up with the formula, "For the straight one, thee! This world, indeed, is the straight one, for truth is straight; and he who shines yonder is that straight one, and he is the first Pravargya. It is him, therefore, that he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "For the straight one, thee!"

"To the successful one (sādhave) thee!"—this one who blows here is indeed the successful one, for he blows through these worlds having accomplished his purpose; he is also the second Pravargya. It is him, therefore, that he gratifies by this; therefore he says, "To the successful one thee!"

"For a good dwelling-place, thee!"—this world is indeed the good dwelling-place, for in this world all beings dwell; moreover, Agni is the good dwelling-place, for Agni indeed dwells in this world as all beings. This is the third Pravargya; it is him he thus gratifies. Therefore he says, "For a good dwelling-place, thee! He does so silently at the two milking-pots, and silently at the two Rauhiṇa plates.

Then he binds them with the milk of a she-goat, saying: "For Makha thee! For the head of Makha thee!"—the significance of this is the same as before; in the same way for the other two; silently the two *pinvana* vessels; silently the two *rauhiṇaka* potsherds.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this very life and this very light; his observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the creation.

When he proceeds with this guest-offering (ātithya), and is about to perform the Pravargya rite, he spreads *kuśa* grass pointing eastward in front of the Gārhapatya fire before the Upasad ceremonies. He places the vessels in pairs: the supporting tray (*upayamanī*), the Mahāvīra pot, the two strainers (*parīṣāsau*), the two milking-pails (*pinvane*), the two Rauhiṇa plates (*rauhiṇakapāle*), the two Rauhiṇa offering-spoons (*rauhiṇahavanyau*), and whatever else there may be. These amount to ten; for the Virāj consists of ten syllables, and the sacrifice is the Virāj—thus he brings the sacrifice into correspondence with the Virāj. Furthermore, as to why they are in pairs: power indeed consists of pairs; when two men join together, then they exert power. A pair is a productive union; thus he endows it with that productive union and makes it complete.

Then the Adhvaryu, taking up the sprinkling waters and rising, says: "O Brahman, we shall proceed; O Hotṛ, recite the praises! Now, the Brahman sits to the south of the sacrifice as its protector; it is to him that he thus says, "Sit alert; we shall restore the head of the sacrifice. And when he says, "O Hotṛ, recite the praises," the Hotṛ is indeed the sacrifice; it is to him that he thus says, "Restore the head of the sacrifice. Thereupon the Hotṛ begins his recitation.

"Brahman was born first in the east"—for yonder sun is indeed Brahman, and day after day he is born in the east; and this Pravargya is that very [sun]; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "Brahman was born first in the east. Then he sprinkles [the vessels]; the significance of this is the same as before.

He sprinkles it with the words, "For Yama thee! He who shines yonder is indeed Yama, for he restrains all this; by him all this is restrained. And the Pravargya is that very sun; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "For Yama thee!"
"For Makha thee!"—he who shines yonder is indeed Makha, and he is also the Pravargya; it is him he thus gratifies, and therefore he says, "For Makha thee!"
"By the heat of Sūrya, thee!"—for he who shines yonder is indeed Sūrya, and he is the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "By the heat of Sūrya, thee!"

Having carried out a pillar through the eastern door, they fix it in the south so that the Hotṛ, while reciting his praise, may look beyond it. The Hotṛ is indeed the sacrifice; thus he establishes the sacrifice upon this [pillar], and in this way, this [pillar] causes the Gharma to swell.
Having carried the sovereign's throne-seat around the front of the Āhavanīya fire, he places it to the south facing east, to the north of the king’s throne-seat.
It is made of Udumbara wood; the Udumbara is indeed strength and sap. Thus he endows him with strength and sap, and makes him complete.
It reaches up to the shoulders; for this head is established upon the shoulders, and thus he establishes the head upon the shoulders.

It is woven with cords of balvaja grass; for when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away, and from that these plants were born. By means of that very sap he thus endows it, making it complete.

Now, as to why he places it to the north: Soma is the sacrifice and the Pravargya is the head; since the head is higher, therefore he places it to the north. Moreover, Soma is a king and the Pravargya is an emperor; since imperial rule is higher than kingship, therefore he places it to the north.

When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "Him the sages anoint as they spread him out," then he anoints this Mahāvīra vessel, which is to be used for the performance, with clarified butter, saying, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey. Savitṛ is indeed the impeller of the gods; and all this that exists here is honey. Thus he anoints it with this whole universe. Savitṛ, the impeller, thereby impels it for him; therefore he says, "May the god Savitṛ anoint thee with honey."

Then, sand is strewn on the north side; beneath that he places silver gold with the formula, "Guard against contact with the earth! For the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the *rakṣases* or *nāṣṭrās* should strike this [altar] from below. Silver gold is indeed the seed of Agni; it serves to drive away the *nāṣṭrās* and the *rakṣases*. Moreover, the Earth was afraid of him, thinking, "Lest he, burning and glowing hot, should injure me. He thus places this [silver] between himself and her. It is silver, for this Earth is indeed silver-colored.

When the Hotṛ recites this formula, "Sit down, thou art great, thou art great," then there are tufts of Muñja grass kindled on both sides; having placed them near, he inserts [the splinters] into them. When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed away, and from that these plants were born; by means of that very sap he thus endows it and makes it complete.

Now, when they are kindled on both sides, he thereby drives away the Rakṣases and the destroyers from all directions. While that [fire] is being set forth, the wife covers her head; for it becomes heated and glowing, and she does so lest this heated, glowing [fire] should rob her of her sight.

He applies [the fuel]: "Thou art light; thou art flame; thou art heat. This one who shines yonder is indeed the Gharma; this [sun] is everything, and it is him he thus gratifies. Therefore he says: "Thou art light; thou art flame; thou art heat."
Then he invokes these blessings upon her; for this earth is indeed the sacrifice, and it is upon her that he thus invokes these blessings. She, in turn, fulfills all of them for him.

"Unassailable from the front"—for she is indeed unassailable from the front by the Rakṣases and fiends under the overlordship of Agni; thus he makes Agni her overlord for the warding off of the fiends and Rakṣases. "Give me life"—thus he bestows life upon himself, and so he attains a full span of life.

"Possessing sons on the right"—there is nothing hidden here in this; "under the sovereignty of Indra"—he thus makes Indra her sovereign for the warding off of destructive spirits and Rakṣases. "Grant me offspring"—verily he bestows upon himself offspring and cattle; and thus he becomes possessed of sons and cattle.

"Easy to sit upon from behind,"—there is nothing hidden here; "under the sovereignty of the god Savitṛ"—he thus makes the god Savitṛ its sovereign lord for the warding off of the destructive spirits and the Rākṣasas. "Give me sight," he says; he thus bestows sight upon himself, and so he becomes possessed of sight.

"From the north, O Āśruti!"—by saying this, he means "causing to hear from the north. "By the power of Dhātṛ"—he thereby makes Dhātṛ her overlord for the sake of warding off the destructive Rākṣasas. "Grant me increase of wealth"—he thereby bestows wealth and prosperity upon himself; thus he indeed becomes possessed of wealth and prosperity.

"Supporting from above"—by saying this, he means "supporting from above. "Under the overlordship of Bṛhaspati"—he thus makes Bṛhaspati its overlord for the sake of warding off the destructive spirits and Rākṣasas. "Give me vigor"—he thus bestows vigor upon himself; thus he becomes vigorous and strong.

Then, with his hand turned palm upwards, he makes amends on the south side, saying, "Protect me from all destructive powers. By this he means, "Guard me from all calamities. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Fathers. There are three kinds of Fathers; it is with them that he thus provides for him and makes him whole.

Then, having touched this [earth], he mutters: "Thou art the horse of Manu. For she, indeed, having become a mare, carried Manu; he is her husband, Prajāpati. By means of that very pair, his own dear abode, he thus causes him to prosper and makes him complete.

Then he encloses it with two splinters of *vaikaṅkata* wood facing eastward, saying: "Hail! Be enclosed by the Maruts! He places the exclamation *svāhā* first and the deity last; for this *svāhā* is indeed that which shines yonder, and this is also the *pravargya*. Thus he gratifies that very one; therefore he places the *svāhā* first and the deity last.

"Be thou encompassed by the Maruts!"—the Maruts are indeed the people (viś); thus he makes the nobility (kṣatra) prosper through the people. Thus this nobility is made prosperous on both sides by the people. Silently they go northward; silently eastward; silently northward; silently eastward.

He prepares thirteen; for there are indeed thirteen months in a year, and this one who shines yonder is the year, and he is the Pravargya; thus it is him he thereby gratifies. Therefore he prepares thirteen.

Then he places gold above it, saying, "Protect [it] from touching the sky. For the gods were indeed afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike this [child] from above. Gold is indeed the seed of Agni; thus it serves to drive away the destroyers and the Rakṣases. Moreover, the Sky was afraid of him, thinking, "Lest he, being heated and glowing, should harm me. Therefore, he places this [gold] as an interposition for her. It is green, for the Sky is like a yellowish-green (hariṇī) cow.

Then he fans it with fans, saying "Honey, honey" three times. Honey is indeed breath; he thus bestows breath upon this [fire]. There are three [fans], for there are three breaths: out-breathing, up-breathing, and through-breathing; these he thus bestows upon it.

Then they shake it three times counter-clockwise; for when the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Fathers. There are indeed three kinds of Fathers; it is with them that he thus causes it to flow together.

The vital breaths indeed depart from those who perform the shaking (dhuvana) at the sacrifice. They shake [the ladles] three times toward the right; thus they become six. For there are these six vital breaths in the head; it is these he thereby places in him. They cook the two Rauhiṇa cakes. When the flame arises, then he takes up the gold.

When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "O Aśvins, may our speech be effective," the Adhvaryu, rising up, says, "The Gharma has been relished. If it has indeed been relished, he should know that the sacrificer will become better off; if it has not been relished, he should know that he will become worse off; and if it is neither relished nor unrelished, he should know that he will become neither better nor worse. However, one should fan [the fire] in such a way that it becomes relished.
Now, indeed, he who recites this Anuvāka enters this very light;
his observance of the vow is the same as that at the creation.

When the Adhvaryu, rising up, says, "The Gharma has shone," then they rise and worship with the Avakāśa formulas. The Avakāśas are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Six of them worship, for there are these six vital breaths in the head; he thus bestows those very breaths upon him.

"The embryo of the gods"—this one who shines yonder is indeed the embryo of the gods, for he grasps all this; by him all this is grasped. And he is the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "The embryo of the gods."
"He is the father of thoughts," for he is indeed the father of thoughts; "the lord of creatures," for he is indeed the lord of creatures.
"The god has come together with the god Savitṛ," for indeed the god has come together with the god Savitṛ; "he shines together with Sūrya," for indeed he shines together with Sūrya.

"Agni has come together with Agni," for indeed Agni has come together with Agni; "with the divine Savitṛ," for indeed he has come together with the divine Savitṛ; "he has shone together with Sūrya," for indeed he has shone together with Sūrya.

"Oblation! Agni has come together with fervor"—for Agni has indeed come together with fervor; he utters the exclamation "Svāhā! for the lower deity; this is the same explanation. "Together with the divine Savitṛ"—for he has indeed come together with the divine Savitṛ; "he has shone forth together with Sūrya"—for he has indeed shone forth together with Sūrya.
These indeed are the three spaces; there are three vital breaths—prāṇa, udāna, and vyāna—and it is by means of these that he thus bestows this upon him.

"The upholder of heaven shines forth through the heat of the earth"—for he is indeed the upholder of heaven who shines forth through the heat of the earth; "the upholder, the immortal god among gods, born of heat"—for he is indeed the upholder, the immortal god among gods, born of heat; "bestow upon us speech that yearns for the gods"—speech is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "Bestow upon us the sacrifice by which we may gratify the gods."
"I saw the herdsman, not resting"—this one who shines yonder is indeed the herdsman, for he protects all this; moreover, he never rests. Therefore he says, "I saw the herdsman, not resting."

"Moving hither and thither along the paths"—for he indeed moves hither and thither along the paths with the gods; "clothing himself in those that meet and those that diverge"—for he clothes himself in the quarters that meet and those that diverge, as well as in the rays; "he revolves repeatedly within the worlds"—for he moves about, revolving again and again within these worlds.

"O Lord of all beings, O Lord of every mind, O Lord of every word, O Lord of all speech—this means 'O Lord of all this'"; "O God, hear us, O divine Gharma, as a god protect the gods"—in this there is nothing that is obscure.

"Here you have helped us for the feast of the gods"—this he says specifically regarding the Aśvins; for it was the Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice, and it is them he thus gratifies. Therefore he says, "Here you have helped us for the feast of the gods."

"Honey for the two Mādhvīs, honey for the two Mādhūcīs"—for Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa indeed spoke this Brāhmaṇa named "Honey" (Madhu) to these two; that is their dear abode, and by this he approaches that very abode of theirs. Therefore he says, "Honey for the two Mādhvīs, honey for the two Mādhūcīs."
"For the heart thee, for the mind thee, for the sky thee, for the sun thee; standing upright, place the sacrifice among the gods in heaven"—in this there is nothing, as it were, obscure.

"You are our father; be mindful of us as our father"—for he who shines yonder is indeed the father, and he is the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "You are our father; be mindful of us as our father. "Homage be to you; do not harm me"—thus he invokes this very blessing.

Then, having uncovered the head of his wife, he makes her recite while she gazes at the Mahāvīra: "May we serve thee together with Tvaṣṭṛ. The Pravargya is indeed a male, and the wife is a female; thus a productive union is brought about.

Now, he who either speaks of this [Self] or performs the *abhyañjana* (anointing) rite enters this very life and this light; his rule of conduct (*vratacaryā*) is the same as that at the time of creation.

Then he offers to Rohiṇī: "May Day, with its banner, enjoy [the offering], well-lit with light, Svāhā!"—with this Yajus formula he offers to both at dawn; "May Night, with its banner, enjoy [the offering], well-lit with light, Svāhā!"—with this Yajus formula he offers to both in the evening.
Now, as to why he offers the two Rauhiṇa oblations: Agni and Āditya are indeed the two Rauhiṇas, for by means of these two deities sacrificers ascend to the heavenly world.
Moreover, the two Rauhina cakes are indeed day and night, and the Pravargya is the sun; he thus encompasses that sun with day and night, and therefore it is encompassed by day and night.
Moreover, these two worlds are indeed the *rauhiṇas*, and the Pravargya is the Sun; he thus encloses that Sun within these two worlds, and therefore this Sun is enclosed by these two worlds.
Moreover, the two Rauhiṇa cakes are indeed the eyes, and the Pravargya is the head; thus he places the eye in the head.

Then he takes up the cord with the formula: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I take thee; thou art a girdle. The significance of this is the same as before.

Then he calls the cow from behind the Gārhapatya fire, saying: "O Iḍā, come! O Aditi, come! O Sarasvatī, come! For the cow is indeed Iḍā, the cow is indeed Aditi, and the cow is indeed Sarasvatī. And then he calls her by name three times: "O so-and-so, come! O so-and-so, come!"

When she has arrived, he addresses her: "Thou art the girdle of Aditi, the turban of Indrāṇī. For Indrāṇī is indeed Indra’s beloved wife, and her turban is most multiform; saying "Thou art that," he thereby makes him (the horse) like that very one.

Then he brings up the calf with the formula, "Thou art Pūṣan. He who blows here is indeed Pūṣan, for he nourishes (puṣyati) all this; and he is also the Pravargya. Thus he gratifies him; therefore he says, "Thou art Pūṣan."
Then he says, "Lead [the calf] forward; give milk for the Gharma! For here the Gharma is indeed this sap which she causes to swell; by saying this, he means, "Be gracious toward her."

Then he causes it to swell in the *pinvana* vessel, saying, "Swell for the Aśvins! He thus says this to the two Aśvins; for the two Aśvins restored the head of the sacrifice, and it is them he thereby gratifies. Therefore he says, "Swell for the Aśvins!"
"Swell for Sarasvatī!"—Sarasvatī is indeed speech; by means of speech, the Aśvins restored the head of the sacrifice. It is them he thus gratifies; therefore he says, "Swell for Sarasvatī!"

"Swell for Indra!"—Indra, indeed, is the deity of the sacrifice; by that very deity who is the deity of the sacrifice, the Aśvins thus restored the head of the sacrifice. It is them he thereby gratifies; therefore he says, "Swell for Indra!"

Then he consecrates the drops with the formula: "Svāhā! Like Indra, svāhā! Like Indra! Indra is indeed the deity of the sacrifice; thus he gratifies that very deity who is the deity of the sacrifice. Therefore he says, "Svāhā! Like Indra, svāhā! Like Indra! He says it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold. He makes the utterance of "svāhā" first and the deity last; such is the significance of this.

Then he applies his mouth to her breast with the verse, "That breast of thine which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing... By this he means, "that breast of thine which is placed in secret. "...which bestows jewels, finds wealth, and is easy to give"—by this he means, "she who is the giver of riches, the finder of wealth, and worthy of praise. "...wherewith thou nourishest all desirable things"—by this he means, "wherewith thou supportest all the gods and all beings. "O Sarasvatī, make that [breast] here for suckling"—Sarasvatī is indeed Speech; she is this very milch-cow of the Gharma. "Speech is the sacrifice; grant us the sacrifice wherewith we may gratify the gods"—this is what he says. Then he goes toward the middle of the Gārhapatya fire with the words, "I follow the wide mid-air"; the significance of this is the same as before.

Then he takes up the two shaphas with the formulas, "The Gāyatrī metre art thou; the Triṣṭubh metre art thou. It is indeed by means of the Gāyatrī and the Triṣṭubh metres that he thus takes them up. With the formula, "I enclose thee with heaven and earth," he does so; for these two parīśas are indeed heaven and earth, and the Pravargya is the sun; he thus encloses yonder sun with these two, heaven and earth. Then he wipes it with a bunch of Muñja grass; the significance of this is the same as before.

Then he supports it with the *upayamanī* [ladle], saying, "I support thee with the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Now, the *upayamanī* is indeed the intermediate space; for by means of the intermediate space all this is supported. Or rather, the *upayamanī* is the belly; for by means of the belly all this food is supported. Therefore he says, "I support thee with the intermediate space."
Then he brings goat's milk; for this [fire] becomes heated and glowing, and he thus cools it down; and when that has subsided, he brings cow's milk.

"To Indra and the Aśvins"—Indra, indeed, is the deity of the sacrifice; he thus gratifies whichever deity belongs to the sacrifice. "To the Aśvins"—he thus speaks of the two Aśvins; for the two Aśvins restored the head of this sacrifice, and it is them he thus gratifies. Therefore he says, "To Indra and the Aśvins."

"Of the honey of the bee"—this indeed is the honey of the bee; "drink the heat," he thereby says, "drink the essence. "O Vasus"—these indeed are the Vasus, for they cause all this to dwell; "sacrifice, vaṭ!"—just as when the *vaṣaṭ* has been uttered, so does this become for him as an oblation offered.

" Svāhā to the ray of the sun, the rain-winner! Indeed, one ray of the sun is named "rain-winner," by which he sustains all these creatures; it is that very one he gratifies thereby. Therefore he says, "Svāhā to the ray of the sun, the rain-winner. He makes the utterance of *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light; his rule of conduct is as follows: [during] the creation... [the rest of the text is missing].

When the Hotṛ recites this verse, "May Brahmanaspati go forward; may the goddess Sūnṛtā go forward," then the Adhvaryu, going out toward the east, offers the Vātanāman oblations. For the gods were afraid, thinking, "Lest the Rakṣases, the destroyers, should strike him down here in the interval"; they therefore offered him with the utterance of Svāhā even before the Āhavanīya fire. Since he was already offered, they then offered him into the fire. In the same way, this [Adhvaryu] now offers him with the utterance of Svāhā even before the Āhavanīya; since he is already offered, he then offers him into the fire.

"To the ocean, to thee, the wind, Svāhā!"—this one who blows here is indeed the ocean; from this ocean, indeed, all the gods and all beings surge forth. It is to him that he offers this; therefore he says, "To the ocean, to thee, the wind, Svāhā!"

"To the Sarira, to you, the wind, Svāhā!"—this one who blows here is indeed the Sarira; from this Sarira, all the gods and all beings prevail. It is to him that he offers it; therefore he says, "To the Sarira, to you, the wind, Svāhā!"

"To the invincible wind, svāhā! To the unassailable wind, svāhā!"—for he who blows here is indeed the invincible and the unassailable; it is to him that he offers this. Therefore he says: "To the invincible wind, svāhā! To the unassailable wind, svāhā!"

"To the wind that seeks aid, hail! To the wind that is not harmful, hail!"—for he who blows here is indeed the wind that seeks aid and the one that is not harmful; it is to him that he offers this oblation. Therefore he says: "To the wind that seeks aid, hail! To the wind that is not harmful, hail!"

"To Indra, accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras, Svāhā!"—for he who blows here is indeed Indra; it is to him that he offers this, and therefore he says, "To Indra, thee. By saying "accompanied by the Vasus and the Rudras," he thereby causes Indra to share in the Vasus and the Rudras; furthermore, the form of both the morning pressing and the midday pressing is thus produced.

"To Indra, accompanied by the Ādityas, svāhā!"—for he who purifies here is indeed Indra; it is to him that he offers this, and therefore he says, "To Indra, thee," and "accompanied by the Ādityas. Thus he causes the Ādityas to share in Indra's portion; moreover, this is made as a form of the third pressing.

"To Indra, the slayer of the adversary, thee, Svāhā!"—for he who blows here is indeed Indra; it is to him that he offers this. Therefore he says, "To Indra, thee"; and "the slayer of the adversary"—for the adversary is indeed the rival; thus he says, "To Indra, the slayer of rivals, thee. This is his special portion (uddhāra), just as there is a special portion for a chief; such is his portion, apart from the other gods.

"To Savitṛ, accompanied by the Ṛbhus, accompanied by Vibhvan, accompanied by Vāja, Svāhā!"—for he who blows here is indeed Savitṛ; it is to him that he offers this. Therefore he says, "To Savitṛ, accompanied by the Ṛbhus, accompanied by Vibhvan, accompanied by Vāja. Thus he causes all the gods to share in this [oblation].

"To Bṛhaspati, accompanied by the All-gods, svāhā!"—Bṛhaspati is indeed he who blows here; it is to him that he offers this, and therefore he says, "To Bṛhaspati, thee. By saying "accompanied by the All-gods," he thereby causes all the gods to share in this.

"To Yama, accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs, svāhā!"—Yama is indeed he who blows here (the wind); it is to him that he offers this. Therefore he says, "To Yama," and "accompanied by the Aṅgirases and the Pitṛs. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away and went to the Pitṛs. There are three kinds of Pitṛs; it is to them that he thus grants a share.
These names are twelve; there are indeed twelve months in a year, and this one who shines yonder is the year, and he is the Pravargya; thus he gratifies him. Therefore, there are twelve.

Then he pours from the *upayamanī* into the *mahāvīra* with the words, "Svāhā to the Gharma! This Gharma is indeed that which shines yonder; it is also the Pravargya. Thus he gratifies this very one; therefore he says, "Svāhā to the Gharma! He makes the utterance of *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before.

When it has been brought, he recites: "Svāhā! The Gharma has gone to the Pitṛs. When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its essence flowed away and went to the Pitṛs.
