There are indeed three kinds of Pitṛs; it is these whom he thus gratifies. He places the *svāhā* utterance first for the deity who follows; the significance of this is the same as before.

He does not recite an invitatory formula (anuvākyā), for the ancestors have indeed turned away once and for all; therefore he does not recite an invitatory formula. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer (*yajya*) for the Gharma," and offers it when the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered.

"All regions, seated on the sacrificial fee"—by this he means "all regions, seated on the sacrificial fee. "He has sacrificed here to all the gods"—by this he means "he has sacrificed here to all the gods. "Drink of the honeyed gharma consecrated with Svāhā, O Aśvins"—by this he refers to the two Aśvins, for it was the two Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice; it is them he thus gratifies. He utters the *svāhā* call first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before.

Then, having offered the oblation, he shakes it upwards, saying: "Place this sacrifice in heaven! Place this sacrifice in heaven! For that *gharma* is indeed the sun, and the sacrifice is in heaven; he is placed in heaven and established in heaven. It is him he thus gratifies. Therefore he says: "Place this sacrifice in heaven! Place this sacrifice in heaven! At the second *vaṣaṭ*-call, he offers.

"Oblation to Agni, the worthy of sacrifice!"—this is the portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt, for Agni is indeed the Sviṣṭakṛt. "From the Yajus-formulas"—for he is established in this world by means of the Yajus-formulas; it is these very formulas that he thus gratifies. He makes the utterance of *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before.

Then the Brahman priest pronounces the consecration formula; for the Brahman is the best physician among the officiating priests, and it is by him, as the best physician among the officiating priests, that he heals this sacrifice.
"O Aśvins, drink the gharma!"—by this he means the two Aśvins, for it was the Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice; it is them he thus gratifies.
"With aids that are great by day and great by night"—this is undefined; for Prajāpati is undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he heals this very Prajāpati, the sacrifice.

"Of the weaver (tantrāyin)": he who shines yonder is indeed the weaver, for he moves through these worlds as if along a warp; and he is also the Pravargya. Thus he gratifies him; therefore he says, "of the weaver."
"Adoration to Heaven and Earth"—with these two, Heaven and Earth, he thus pays homage, upon whom this entire universe rests.
Then the sacrificer [approaches]; for the sacrificer is indeed the sacrifice; by means of the sacrifice he thus heals the sacrifice.
"O Aśvins, you drank the Gharma"—by this he speaks to the two Aśvins; for it was the two Aśvins who restored the head of the sacrifice, and it is them he thus gratifies.
"May Heaven and Earth not despise us"—by this he addresses these two, Heaven and Earth, over whom all this exists; "may there be gifts right here"—by this he means, "may our riches be right here."

Then he consecrates the swelling [milk] with the formula: "Swell for food!"—by saying this, he means rain; "Swell for strength!"—by saying this, he means the essence of strength that is produced from rain; "Swell for the Brahman!"—by saying this, he means it for the Brahman; "Swell for the Kṣatra!"—by saying this, he means it for the Kṣatra; "Swell for Heaven and Earth!"—by saying this, he means it for those two, Heaven and Earth, upon whom all this world rests.

In that it swells upwards, it swells for the sacrificer; in that it swells towards the east, it swells for the gods; in that it swells towards the south, it swells for the ancestors; in that it swells towards the west, it swells for the cattle; in that it swells towards the north, it swells for his offspring. Indeed, there is no failure for the sacrificer, for it swells upwards; and furthermore, in whichever direction it swells, it swells for that [quarter]. This occurs when the drops have subsided.

Then he steps out toward the north-east, saying, "Thou art Dharma, O Good Dharma. For that which shines yonder is indeed Dharma; for it sustains all this, and by it all this is supported. And that Pravargya is this very [sun]; thus he gratifies him. Therefore he says, "Thou art Dharma, O Good Dharma."

Then he places it on the donkey with the formula, "O blameless one, bestow manly powers upon us. By this he means, "Without becoming angry, bestow riches upon us. With the words, "Sustain the priesthood, sustain the nobility, sustain the common people," he means, "Sustain all this."
Then he offers with the wood-shavings; the wood-shavings are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon this [person].

" Svāhā to Pūṣan, to the arrow! "—Pūṣan is indeed he who blows here (the wind), for he nourishes all this; and he is also the vital breath (prāṇa). He thus bestows vital breath upon him; therefore he says, "Svāhā to Pūṣan, to the arrow. He makes the utterance of *svāhā* first and the deity last; the significance of this is the same as before. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick.

"Svāhā to the pressing-stones!"—the pressing-stones are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered the oblation, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick.

"Svāhā to the echoes!"—the echoes are indeed the vital breaths, for by the vital breaths all this is echoed; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick.

" Svāhā to the fathers who sit upon the sacrificial grass, who drink the Gharma!"—without having offered this, while looking toward the north, he hides it within the southern half of the sacrificial grass. "When the head of the sacrifice was cut off, its sap flowed away; it went to the fathers. There are indeed three kinds of fathers; it is these whom he thus gratifies. Now, as to why he does not look at it: for the fathers have turned away once and for all.

"Svāhā to Heaven and Earth!"—Heaven and Earth are indeed out-breath and in-breath; he thus bestows out-breath and in-breath upon him. Having offered, he leans [the ladle] against the middle enclosing-stick.
"Svāhā to the All-gods!"—the All-gods are indeed the vital breaths; he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. Having offered, he leans it against the middle enclosing-stick.

Without having offered [the oblation] with the words, "Svāhā to Rudra, invoked by Rudra," he hands it to the Pratiprasthātṛ while looking toward the south. He throws it out toward the north from the north side of the hall; for this is the direction of that god. Thus he gratifies him in his own quarter. And as to why he does not look [at it]: "Lest Rudra should harm me."
These offerings are seven; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, and it is these that he thereby bestows upon him.

Then he pours from the Mahāvīra into the Upayamanī with the formula, "Svāhā! Light with light! Indeed, there is milk as light in the one, and light in the other; for these two lights thus meet together. He makes the *svāhā*-utterance first and the deity last; this is the characteristic mark of that [deity].

Then he offers the Rauhiṇa oblations: "May Day, with its banner, enjoy [the offering], well-lighted by light, Svāhā!"—this is the same explanation; "May Night, with its banner, enjoy [the offering], well-lighted by light, Svāhā!"—this is the same explanation.

Then he hands the remainder of the Gharma to the sacrificer; having sought permission, he consumes it, saying: "The honey has been offered into the most Indra-like Agni. By this he means: "The honey has been offered into the Agni who possesses the most power. "May we partake of thee, O divine Gharma; homage be unto thee; do not harm me"—by this he invokes a blessing.

Then sand is strewn on the south side; they sweep it, and the significance of that is the same as that of the Mārjālīya altar. He throws in the wooden chips; then they perform the Upasad rites. This is the head of the sacrifice that has been restored, just as the Aśvins then restored it.

One should not perform the Pravargya at the first sacrifice, for that would be sinful; moreover, thinking "lest Indra cut off my head," one should do it at the second or the third. For in the beginning, the gods, praising and toiling with a headless sacrifice, proceeded; therefore, [it should be done] at the second or the third. Moreover, this [Pravargya] becomes heated and glowing.

If he were to perform it at the first sacrifice, this [Agni], being heated and glowing, would burn up his offspring and cattle, and furthermore, the sacrificer would be liable to die prematurely; therefore, one should perform it either at the second or the third sacrifice.

One should not perform the Pravargya for just anyone; for the Pravargya is everything, and [one should think], "Lest I do everything for just anyone. One should indeed perform it for one who is known, or for one who is dear to him, or for one who is learned in the Vedas and might reach him through his study.

One should pour it out at a sacrifice involving a thousand; for a thousand is everything, and this [offering] is everything. One should pour it out at a *sarvavedas* sacrifice; for a *sarvavedas* is everything, and this is everything. One should pour it out at the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants; for the *viśvajit* with all the *pṛṣṭha* chants is everything, and this is everything. One should pour it out at the *vājapeya* and the *rājasūya*; for that is everything. One should pour it out at a *sattra* session; for a *sattra* is everything, and this is everything. These are its pourings-out; therefore, it is not elsewhere.

Regarding this they say: "If the sacrifice is headless and lacks the Pravargya rite, then by what does its Agnihotra become possessed of a head? One should reply, "By the Āhavanīya fire. "How then the New and Full Moon sacrifices? One should reply, "By means of the clarified butter and the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa). "How the Cāturmāsya sacrifices? One should reply, "By means of the curd-mixture (payasyā). "How the Animal Sacrifice? One should reply, "By means of the animal and the sacrificial cake. "How the Soma sacrifice? One should reply, "By means of the Havirdhāna shed."

Moreover, they say: when the head of the sacrifice had been cut off, the gods restored its head by means of the Guest-offering (ātithya). Indeed, no one has ever sacrificed with a headless sacrifice who knows this thus.

Regarding this they say: "Since they lead forward the *praṇītā* waters at the sacrifice, why then do they not lead them forward here? Indeed, the *praṇītā* waters are the head of the sacrifice, and the *pravargya* is the head; [they do not lead them forward] lest they should place the head upon the head.

Regarding this they say: "Since the fore-offerings (prayāja) and after-offerings (anuyāja) occur elsewhere, why do they not occur here? The fore-offerings and after-offerings are indeed the vital breaths; the hollows are the vital breaths, and the splinters (śākala) are the vital breaths. [He does this] thinking, "Lest I should cause the vital breaths to mount upon the vital breaths."

Regarding this they say: "Since they offer the two butter-portions elsewhere, why do they not offer them here? These two butter-portions are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice, and these two *rauhiṇa* cakes are the eyes; [they do not offer them here] lest they should place eye upon eye.

Regarding this they say: "Since they offer to the gods with wooden vessels, why then does he offer this one with an earthen one? When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its sap flowed out; it went into these two, heaven and earth—that which is the clay is this [earth], and that which is the water is yonder [heaven]. From that clay and those waters the Mahāvīra vessels are made; by means of that very sap he thus completes it and makes it whole.

If it were made of wood, it would burn up; if it were made of gold, it would melt away; if it were made of copper, it would run over; if it were made of iron, it would consume the pair of tongs. But this very [ladle] stood firm against it; therefore, one offers with that which is made of clay alone.
Now, indeed, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light; his observance of the vow is the same as that at the creation.

On the third day, or the sixth, or the twelfth, having combined the Pravargya and Upasad rites, he sets aside the Pravargya; for this head is, as it were, already set aside. Then, taking all that which is around it, they go together to the front of the hall within the sacrificial altar.

Then the Āgnīdhra prepares three firebrands at the Āhavanīya; having kindled one of them, he offers while holding it at the height of his mouth. When the sacrifice had its head cut off, its heat (śuc) went forth and entered these worlds; with that very heat he thus completes it and makes it whole.

Now, as for that which is at the height of the mouth: that which is at the height of the mouth is, as it were, above; and since yonder world is, as it were, above, he thus endows him with that very heat (śuc) which entered yonder world, and makes him complete.

"O Gharma, that divine heat of thine"—that which is indeed the divine heat; "that which is in the Gāyatrī, in the Havirdhāna"—that which is indeed in the Gāyatrī, in the Havirdhāna; "may it swell for thee, may it expand for thee; to that of thine, Svāhā!"—in this there is nothing at all obscure.

Then, having kindled a second [fire] and holding it at the height of the navel, he offers an oblation; for that which is at the height of the navel is, as it were, the middle, and the intermediate region (antarikṣaloka) is, as it were, the middle; thus, by means of that very heat which entered the intermediate region, he completes him with that heat and makes him whole.

"When the heat has gone to the atmosphere—'the pain which is in the atmosphere'—and to the Triṣṭubh in the Āgnīdhra—'that which is in the Triṣṭubh in the Āgnīdhra,' may that swell for thee, may it heal for thee; 'to that of thine, Svāhā! "—in this there is nothing, as it were, obscure.

Then, having added a third piece of wood, he sits upon it and offers the oblation. For sitting down is, as it were, below; and this world is, as it were, below. Thus, by means of that very pain which entered this world, he endows him with that pain and makes him whole.

"O Gharma, that heat of thine which is on the earth"—that which is the heat on the earth; "that which is in the Jagatī, in the Sadas"—that which is in the Jagatī, in the Sadas; "may that of thine swell, may it expand; to that of thine, Svāhā!"—in this there is nothing, as it were, hidden.

Then he steps out with the words, "For the protection against the enemy of the Kṣatra. That which shines yonder is indeed the divine Kṣatra; thus he says, "For the sake of being the protector against this human Kṣatra. With "Protect the body of the Brahman," he says, "Guard the self of the Brahman. With "We [follow] thee by the law of the Viś," the Viś is indeed the sacrifice; thus he says, "For the safety of the sacrifice. With "We step after thee for new prosperity," he says, "For the safety of the sacrifice, so that we may not stumble."

Then he says, "Sing the Sāman! or "Recite the Sāman!"—but one should rather say, "Sing it," for they sing the Sāman. Now, as to why he sings the Sāman: it is so that these malevolent spirits and Rakṣases may not harm the limbs outside the sacrifice; for the Sāman is the repeller of malevolent spirits and Rakṣases.
He sings in the southeast, for Agni is the repeller of the Rakṣases; he sings in the *aticandas* metre, for this *aticandas* indeed comprises all the metres; therefore, he sings in the *aticandas*.
He sings: "Agni burns, he consumes, he strikes down; ahāva! ahāva!"—for by this he drives away the destructive spirits and the Rākṣasas from there.

They go out toward the north by way of the *jaghanā* (the rear part of the altar) and the *cātvāla* pit, passing in front of the *āgnīdhra* shed; for this is the door of the sacrifice. They proceed in whatever direction the waters may be located.

One should indeed set it down in a pool. For this [fire] becomes heated and glowing; if he were to set it down on this earth, its heat would enter this earth; if he were to set it down in the waters, its heat would enter the waters. But when he sets it down in a pool, he thus harms neither the waters nor this earth. In that he does not throw it into the waters, he thereby does not harm the waters; and in that the waters flow all around it—the waters being a means of pacification—he thereby does not harm this earth. Therefore, one should set it down in a pool.
But he should indeed remove it from the Uttaravedi; for the Uttaravedi is the sacrifice and the Pravargya is the head; thus he restores the head to the sacrifice itself.
He sets aside the first Pravargya vessel while touching it at the northern navel; for the northern navel is speech and the Pravargya is the head: he thus places speech in the head.
"Four-cornered," he says; for he who shines yonder is indeed four-cornered, since the quarters are his corners; therefore he says, "four-cornered."
"The navel of Truth, far-extending"—Truth is indeed Ṛta; thus he says, "the navel of Truth, far-extending. "He who is all-life, far-extending"—thus he says, "he who is whole-life, far-extending."

"Free from hatred, free from crookedness"—there is nothing here that is obscure; "we follow him of another vow," for his vow is one thing and that of human beings is another; therefore he says, "we follow him of another vow. In the same way [he places] the other two [bricks] facing eastward; that is threefold, for this head is indeed threefold.

He places the earth from the front-lying [pit] upon it; verily, he thereby bestows flesh upon him. On both sides of that he places two spits; verily, he thereby bestows two arms upon him. On both sides of those, further out, he places two Rauhiṇa-offering ladles; verily, he thereby bestows two hands upon him.

To the north he places the spade, for that is its proper place; to the south the sovereign's throne-seat, for that is its proper place; to the north the black antelope skin, for that is its proper place. On all sides are the fans; the fans are indeed the vital breaths—verily, he thus bestows the vital breaths upon him. There are three of them, for there are three vital breaths: the out-breath, the up-breath, and the through-breath; it is these he thus bestows upon him.

Then, having placed this rope-fastening on the supporting tray (upayamani), he sets it down behind [the fire] facing east; thus he bestows the belly upon him. On both sides of that, he places the two milking-pails (pinvana); these are the testicles, for he bestows them upon him; for by means of the testicles a bull is made to swell. Behind those, the post-hoop (sthūṇāmayūkha) is the thighs, for he bestows them upon him. Behind that, the two Rauhiṇa potsherds are the knees, for he bestows them upon him; as to why they are single-potsherd ones, it is because these knees are, as it were, single-potsherds. Behind those, the two stirring-sticks (dhr̥ṣṭī) are the feet, for he bestows them upon him; for with the feet one strikes out boldly. To the north are the two pans used for the performance (pracaraṇīya), for that is their proper place. To the south is the Mārjālīya mound, for that is its proper place.

Then he pours milk into this [Gharma], saying, "O Gharma, this is thy soil. Food, indeed, is "soil"; he thus bestows food upon it. "Grow thereby and swell,"—in this there is nothing obscure; "and may we grow and may we swell"—by this he invokes a blessing.

He should not bring all [the food] at once, lest there be no food remaining for the sacrificer; he leaves over either half or more. In the afternoon, having poured out the fast-food for the sacrificer from that remainder, he gives it to him; thus he bestows food upon the sacrificer himself, and so indeed there is no lack of food for the sacrificer.

Then he sprinkles it all around with water; for water is a means of pacification, so he thereby pacifies it. He sprinkles it all around from every side, and thus he pacifies it from every side. He sprinkles it three times, for the sacrifice is threefold.

Then he says: "He sings the Vārṣāhara Sāman. For he who shines yonder is indeed the tawny bull (vṛṣā hariḥ), and he is also the Pravargya; thus it is him that he thereby gratifies. Therefore he says: "He sings the Vārṣāhara Sāman."

Then they purify themselves at the pit (catvāla) with the formula, "May the waters and plants be friendly to us. With his joined palms, he takes up water, for the waters are a thunderbolt; by means of this thunderbolt, he thus establishes a bond of friendship. [He says,] "May they be unfriendly to him who hates us and whom we hate. In whichever direction his enemy may be, he should pour the water out toward that direction; by that very act, he brings about the destruction of that person.

Then he steps out toward the northeast with the verse, "Up from the darkness we have seen the light. Darkness is indeed evil; verily, he thus drives away the darkness that is evil. "Beholding the higher light," for this world is indeed higher than the waters; verily, he establishes himself in this very world. "To the god among gods, to Sūrya, the highest light, we have gone"; for the heavenly world is Sūrya, the highest light; verily, he finally establishes himself in the heavenly world. Without looking back, he approaches and places a fuel-stick on the Āhavanīya fire with the words, "A kindler art thou, brilliance art thou, bestow brilliance upon me!"—verily, he thereby invokes a blessing.

Then, when the Soma has been pressed, they proceed with the curd-mixture (dadhigharma). Soma is indeed the sacrifice, and the Pravargya is the head; thus he restores the head to the sacrifice. This midday pressing belongs exclusively to Indra; since the midday pressing is Indra’s exclusive libation, he gratifies him in his own portion. When the Mādhyandina Pavamāna has been chanted—the Mādhyandina Pavamāna being the vital breath—he thereby places the vital breath into him. With the Agnihotra-ladle [he offers], for the Agnihotra is the mouth of sacrifices; he thus places a mouth upon that which was the head.

As he is being brought forward, he says, "O Hotṛ, speak what is to be spoken by you. For here the Hotṛ speaks. Then, rising up, he says, "The oblation is cooked," for it indeed has been cooked. Having stepped across and called for the *śrauṣaṭ*, he says, "Recite the offering prayer for the Dadhigharma. When the *vaṣaṭ* is uttered, he makes the offering; when the *anuvaṣaṭ* is uttered, he brings the portion and hands it to the sacrificer.

Having invited him to partake, he consumes it with the formula: "In me be that great power (indriya)! For that which shines yonder is indeed the great power; "in me be skill (dakṣa), in me be will (kratu)!"—he thus places will and skill within himself. "The Gharma, three-pointed, shines forth"—for this Gharma indeed shines forth, three-pointed; "with the Virāj, with light"—for he shines with the Virāj and with light; "with the Brahman, with splendor"—for he is with the Brahman and with splendor; "the seed of milk has been brought"—for this seed of milk has indeed been brought; "may we obtain its milking in each succeeding year"—verily, he thereby invokes a blessing. Then they purify themselves at the Cātvāla pit; the significance of this is the same as before.

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial gifts: he gives a hundred-measure weight of gold to the Brahman priest. For the Brahman sits, while gold lies; gold is glory. Therefore, he gives a hundred-measure weight of gold to the Brahman.
Now, that cow which milks the Gharma, he gives to the Adhvaryu; for the Gharma is, as it were, heated, and the Adhvaryu steps out as if heated; therefore he gives her to the Adhvaryu.
Now, that cow which milks the vow for the sacrificer, he gives her to the Hotṛ; for the Hotṛ is the sacrifice and the sacrificer is the sacrifice—therefore he gives her to the Hotṛ.
Now, that cow which provides the fast-milk for the wife, he gives her to the Udgātṛs; for it is indeed the work of the wife that these Udgātṛs perform here, and therefore he gives her to the Udgātṛs.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this very life and this very light; his observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the creation.

The sacrifice is indeed the self of all beings and of all the gods; following its success, the sacrificer prospers with offspring and cattle. But he whose *gharma* vessel breaks is deprived of offspring and cattle; for that case, there is an expiation.
He offers the full-offering (pūrṇāhuti). The full is indeed everything; by means of everything he thus heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.

"Obeisance to the vital breaths together with their overlord!"—the mind, indeed, is the overlord of the vital breaths, for all the vital breaths are established in the mind; thus, by means of the mind itself, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the Earth, Svāhā!"—the Earth, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; thus he heals with all those deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—Agni indeed is the self of all the gods; thus, by means of all the deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"Swāhā to the intermediate space!"—the intermediate space is indeed the abode of all the gods; thus [he offers] to them all.
"To Vāyu, svāhā!"—Vāyu, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus [he offers] to all.
"To the sky, svāhā!"—the sky is indeed the abode of all the gods; thus he offers to all of them.
"To Sūrya, svāhā!"—Sūrya indeed is the self of all the gods; thus [he offers] to all of them.
"To the quarters, svāhā!"—the quarters are indeed the abode of all the gods; thus he offers to all of them.
"To Candra, svāhā!"—Candra indeed is the self of all the gods; thus [he offers] to all of them.
"Oblation to the constellations, svāhā!"—the constellations are indeed the abode of all the gods; thus [he offers] to them all.
"To the waters, svāhā!"—the waters, indeed, are the abode of all the gods; thus he offers to them all.
"To Varuṇa, svāhā!"—Varuṇa indeed is the self of all the gods; thus, it is all [the gods] that he gratifies.
"To the navel, svāhā! To the purified, svāhā!"—this is undefined; for Prajāpati is undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he heals Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
These offerings amount to thirteen; for there are indeed thirteen months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice: thus he heals Prajāpati, the sacrifice.

"To Speech, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the mouth upon him; "To Breath, Svāhā! To Breath, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two nostrils upon him; "To Sight, Svāhā! To Sight, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two eyes upon him; "To Hearing, Svāhā! To Hearing, Svāhā!"—with this he bestows the two ears upon him.

There are these seven oblations; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, and it is these that he thus bestows upon him. He offers the full-offering last; for the full is everything, and by means of everything he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"May [the gods fulfill] the desire and intention of the mind"—for by the mind indeed all this is attained; therefore, by the mind alone he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.

"May I attain the truth of speech"—for by speech indeed all this is attained; by speech he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder. "The form of the cattle, the essence of food, glory, and prosperity—may they rest in me, Svāhā!"—thus he invokes this very blessing.

Then, having ground that [clay] and the secondary clay (upaśayā) together with soft earth, he fashions it according to the prescribed ritual procedure and bakes it according to the prescribed ritual procedure for the purpose of setting it up; now, whichever of the two secondary clays is firm, with that one he should proceed.

The Pravargya is indeed the year; the year is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated, that is spring; when it has become warm, that is summer; when it has swelled, that is the rainy season. Indeed, when the rains swell, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. The rains swell for him who knows this thus.

The Pravargya is indeed these worlds; for these worlds are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated, that is this world; when it has been made radiant, that is the intermediate world; when it has been made to swell, that is yonder world. Indeed, when yonder world swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Yonder world truly swells for one who knows this thus.

These deities indeed are the Pravargya: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya; for these deities are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated, that is Agni; when it has shone forth, that is Vāyu; when it has swelled, that is yonder Āditya. And when yonder Āditya swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon him. Yonder Āditya indeed swells for him who knows this thus.

The Pravargya is indeed the sacrificer; his self, offspring, and cattle are the Pravargya. The sacrificer is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is set forth (*pravṛkta*), that is the self; when it has been heated (*rucita*), that is the offspring; when it has been made to swell (*pinvita*), that is the cattle. For when cattle swell, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. Cattle indeed swell for him who knows this thus.

The Agnihotra is indeed the Pravargya; the Agnihotra is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta* (the heated); when it is ladled out, that is the *rucita* (the radiant); when it is offered, that is the *pinvita* (the overflowing). For when the Agnihotra overflows, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Indeed, the Agnihotra overflows for him who knows this thus.

The New and Full Moon sacrifices are indeed the Pravargya; the New and Full Moon sacrifices are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When [the milk] has been placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *pinvita*. For when the New and Full Moon sacrifices overflow (*pinvete*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. Indeed, the New and Full Moon sacrifices overflow for him who knows this thus.

The *Cāturmāsyas* are indeed the *Pravargya*, and the *Cāturmāsyas* are everything; the *Pravargya* is everything. When [the milk] has been placed on the fire, that is the *Pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *Rukma*; when it has been offered, that is the *Pinvita*. Indeed, when the *Cāturmāsyas* overflow (*pinvante*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. The *Cāturmāsyas* indeed overflow for him who knows this thus.

The Pravargya is indeed the animal sacrifice (paśubandha); the animal sacrifice is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, it is the "Pravṛkta" (the one set forth); when it has been prepared, it is the "Rucita" (the one made radiant); when it has been offered, it is the "Pinvita" (the one that swells). Indeed, when the animal sacrifice swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it; and for him who knows this, the animal sacrifice truly swells.

The Pravargya is indeed Soma; Soma is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is pressed, that is when it is "extracted" (pravṛkta); when it is drawn up, that is when it is "shining" (rucita); when it is offered, that is when it is "swollen" (pinvita). For when Soma swells, then all the gods and all beings enjoy it. Indeed, Soma swells for him who knows this; and for him who knows this, no sacrifice remains unperformed with the Pravargya.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this very life and this very light; his observance of the vow is that which [is prescribed] at the creation.
There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring: the gods and the Asuras. Of these, the gods were fewer, while the Asuras were more numerous; they contended with one another for these worlds.
Those gods said, "Come, let us overcome the Asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha."

They said to Speech, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," she replied, and Speech sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in speech, she procured that for the gods; and whatever is auspicious that one speaks, that she procured for herself. They perceived, "Verily, they will overcome us by means of this singer. Having rushed upon him, they pierced him with evil. That which is evil—namely, that which one speaks here which is improper—that indeed is that evil.

Then they said to the breath, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [said] the breath, and he sang the Udgītha for them. Whatever enjoyment was in the breath, that he procured for the gods by singing; whatever is auspicious that one smells, that he procured for himself. They perceived, "Verily, with this singer they will surpass us," and having rushed upon him, they pierced him with evil. That which is evil, whatever one here smells that is improper—that indeed is that evil.

Then the eye said, "Let me sing the Udgītha for you. "So be it," they replied. The eye sang the Udgītha for them; whatever enjoyment was in the eye, that it secured for the gods, and whatever was beautiful that it saw, that it secured for itself. They perceived, "With this singer, they will surely surpass us. Rushing toward it, they pierced it with evil. That which is evil is precisely that which one sees here as unseemly; that is that very evil.

Then they said to the ear, "Do thou sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," it replied. For them, the ear sang the Udgītha; it sang for the gods whatever enjoyment is in the ear, and for itself whatever is pleasant that it hears. They perceived, "Verily, with this singer they will surpass us," and having rushed upon it, they pierced it with evil. That which is evil—whatever one here hears that is discordant—that indeed is that evil.

Then they said to the mind, "Do you sing for us as the Udgātṛ. "So be it," [it replied]. The mind sang for them; whatever enjoyment was in the mind, that it sang for the gods, and whatever is auspicious that one conceives, that it sang for itself. They perceived: "Verily, with this Udgātṛ they will surpass us. They rushed upon it and pierced it with evil. That which is evil is precisely that which one here conceives that is improper; that is that very evil. In this same way, indeed, they beset these deities with evils, and in this same way they pierced them with evil.

Then they said to the breath in the mouth, "Do thou sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," he replied. For them, this breath sang the Udgītha. They perceived, "Verily, with this singer, they will overcome us. They rushed at him and sought to smite him with evil. Just as a clod of earth would be shattered upon hitting a stone, even so were they shattered and perished in all directions. Thereupon the gods prospered and the Asuras were defeated. He who knows this prospers in himself, and his hateful rival is defeated.
They said, "Where indeed has he gone who thus clung to us? "He is here within the mouth," they replied. He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
This deity is indeed named Dūr; for death is far from her, and death indeed becomes far from him who knows this.

That very deity, having struck away evil—death—from these deities, caused them to go to where the end of these quarters is; there he deposited their evils. Therefore, one should not go to a person, nor should one go to the end [of the quarters], thinking, "Lest I fall into evil and death."
That very deity, having struck away the evil—death—from these deities, then carried them across death.
He indeed carried speech across first; when it was released from death, it became fire. This very fire, having transcended death, shines beyond it.
Then Prāṇa carried him across. When he was released from death, he became Vāyu; this very Vāyu, having passed beyond death, blows.
Then the eye carried it across; when it was released from death, it became the sun. That very sun, having transcended death on the far side, shines.
Then the ear carried it across; when it was released from death, it became these quarters. These quarters have transcended death by passing beyond it.

Then Mind carried him across. When it was released from death, it became the moon. That very moon shines having transcended death beyond. Indeed, this deity carries across death in this same way the one who knows thus.
Then he sang for himself the right to food; for whatever food is eaten here, it is eaten by him alone, and through him one finds firm support in this world.

Those gods said, "All this that exists is only food; you have sung it for yourself. Grant us a share in this food! He replied, "Then enter into me on all sides. They said, "So be it," and they entered around him on every side. Therefore, whatever food one eats with this [breath], by that these [deities] are satisfied. Indeed, those who know this, their own people enter into them in this same way; they become the supporter of their own, the best, the leader, the eater of food, and the sovereign.

And whoever among his own people seeks to be a rival to one who knows this, he is by no means able to support his dependents; but whoever follows him, or whoever desires to support dependents following him, he alone is truly able to support his dependents.

This Āyāsya Āṅgirasa is indeed the essence (rasa) of the limbs; for the vital breath (prāṇa) is the essence of the limbs, since the vital breath is the essence of the limbs, therefore from whichever limb the vital breath departs, that very limb withers, for it is indeed the essence of the limbs.
He indeed is Bṛhaspati; for the Vāc is the Bṛhatī, and he is her lord, therefore he is Bṛhaspati.
He indeed is Brahmaṇaspati; for speech is Brahman, and he is its lord, therefore he is called Brahmaṇaspati.

This very one is indeed the *sāman*. Speech is the *sāman*; he is both "she" (*sā*) and "he" (*ama*), and that is why it is called *sāman*. Furthermore, because he is equal to a louse, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe, he is therefore the *sāman*. He who knows this *sāman* thus attains union with and residence in the same world as the *sāman*.

This, indeed, is the Udgītha: the vital breath (prāṇa) is "ut," for by the vital breath all this is upheld; speech itself is "gīthā," because it is both "ucca" (elevated) and "gīthā" (song); thus it is the Udgītha.

For instance, Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while consuming the King [Soma], said: "May this king have his head split apart, since Ayāsya Āṅgirasa sang the Udgītha by means other than this! For he indeed sang it by means of speech and breath alone.

Now, he who knows the property (*sva*) of this Sāman comes into possession of property. The property of this [Sāman] is indeed its tone (*svara*). Therefore, one intending to perform the priestly office (*ārtvijya*) should desire a good tone in his speech; with that speech, endowed with a good tone, he should perform the priestly office. For this reason, people wish to see one who possesses a good tone at a sacrifice. Moreover, he who possesses property comes into possession of property—he who thus knows the property of this Sāman.
He who knows the gold of this very Sāman obtains gold; indeed, its gold is its tone itself, and he who thus knows the gold of the Sāman obtains gold.

He who knows the support of this very Sāman becomes firmly established. Verily, speech is its support; for it is in speech that this vital breath (prāṇa) is established when it is sung. Some, however, say it is in food.

Now, therefore, follows the ascent of the Pavamāna chants. Indeed, the Prastotṛ priest chants the Sāman; when he begins the Prastāva, at that moment one should mutter these [mantras]: "Lead me from non-existence to existence; lead me from darkness to light; lead me from death to immortality."
When he says, "Lead me from the unreal to the real," the unreal is indeed death and the real is immortality; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality; make me immortal."

"Lead me from darkness to light"—darkness is indeed death and light is immortality; "lead me from death to immortality," he thereby says, "make me immortal. In the phrase "lead me from death to immortality," there is nothing hidden, as it were.

Now, as for those other hymns, he should sing for himself the food and nourishment contained within them; therefore, during those [hymns], he may choose a boon—whatever desire he may wish for. Thus knowing this, the Udgātṛ priest sings forth whatever desire he desires, either for himself or for the sacrificer. This Sāman is indeed a winner of worlds; for one who knows this Sāman in this way, there is no hope of not attaining the world.

In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person. Looking around, he saw nothing other than himself. He first uttered, "I am. From that, the name "I" arose. Therefore, even now, when addressed, one first says, "It is I," and then pronounces whatever other name one may have.
Because he burnt away all evils before all this [universe], therefore he is called *puruṣa*. Indeed, he who knows this burns away anyone who seeks to surpass him.

He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. Then he reflected: "Since there is nothing other than myself, of what am I afraid? Thereupon his fear departed from him, for of what could he have been afraid? Indeed, it is from a second that fear arises.
He indeed did not find delight; therefore, one does not delight when alone. He desired a second. He was of such a size as a man and a woman in close embrace.

He split this very self into two; from that, there came to be a husband and a wife. Therefore, Yājñavalkya used to say, "This body is, as it were, only half of oneself. Consequently, this void is filled by a woman. He united with her, and from that, human beings were born.
He reflected thus: "How indeed can he procreate after having generated himself from his own self? Come now, let me disappear."
She became a cow, and the other became a bull; he united with her, and from that cows were born.
One became a mare and the other a stallion; one became a she-ass and the other a donkey. He united with her, and from that the single-hoofed animal was born.

One became a goat, another a sheep, and another a ram; he ate them all together, and from that goats and sheep were born. In this very way, whatever exists here in pairs, down to the ants, he created all that.
"Therefore, I am indeed the creation, for I have created all this"—from that he became the creation; and he who knows thus participates in this creation of his.
Then he churned; from his mouth as the womb and from his two hands, he emitted fire. Therefore, both of these are hairless on the inside, for the womb is hairless on the inside.
Now, when they say, "Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one," regarding each individual deity, it is indeed the emanation of this very [Self], for he alone is all the gods.
Then, whatever here is moist, that he created from semen; that is Soma. Indeed, this entire world is just this much: food and the eater of food. Soma is the food, and Agni is the eater of food.

This indeed was the over-creation of Brahmā: that he created the gods, who are superior; and since, being himself mortal, he created those who are immortal, it is called the "over-creation. He who knows this comes to possess an over-creation in this very over-creation of his.

In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form alone, as "this has such a name" and "this has such a form. Even now, this is likewise differentiated by name and form alone, as "this has such a name" and "this has such a form."

This very Self has entered here, even to the tips of the fingernails, as a razor might be placed in a razor-case, or as the fire that sustains all things [is contained] in the nest of the sustainer of all; they do not see it, for it is incomplete [when perceived as separate].

Breathing, it becomes what is called breath; speaking, speech; seeing, sight; hearing, hearing; thinking, mind. These are merely its names according to its functions. He who worships any one of these individually does not know [the whole], for this [Self] is incomplete through any one of them alone.

"One should worship [the Self] as 'I am the Self' (ātman), for herein all these become one. This is the track to be followed of all this, namely this Self; for by means of this, one knows all this. Just as one might find [something lost] by means of a footprint, even so does he who knows this find fame and renown."

This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal. If someone were to say to one who declares anything other than the Self to be dear, "He will lose what is dear to him," that would indeed likely come to pass. Therefore, one should worship the Self alone as dear. He who worships the Self alone as dear—verily, what is dear to him does not perish.
Regarding this they say: "What indeed is that Brahman, knowing which men think, 'By the knowledge of Brahman we shall become everything,' and by knowing which it became all this?"

In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman. It knew only itself: "I am Brahman. Therefore, it became all this. Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became that; likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings.

Seeing this very truth, the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu, and I was the Sun. And even now, whoever knows this—"I am Brahman"—he becomes this entire universe. Neither the gods nor anyone else can prevail against his failure to become [Brahman], for he becomes their very Self. But he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know. He is like an animal to the gods; for just as many animals serve a single man, so does each single person serve the gods. When even a single animal is taken away, it is unpleasant; how much more so when many are? Therefore, that is not pleasing to them—that men should know this.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed Brahman, one only. Being alone, it did not flourish. It created from itself a superior form, the Kṣatra—the various ruling powers among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. Therefore, there is nothing higher than the Kṣatra; for this reason, the Brāhmaṇa sits beneath the Kṣatriya at the Rājasūya sacrifice, thereby bestowing glory upon the Kṣatra. This Brahman is the womb of the Kṣatra. Therefore, even if a king attains the highest position, he must ultimately take refuge in the Brahman as his own womb. He who harms him destroys his own womb; he becomes more wretched, just as one who has harmed a superior.
He did not multiply; he created the Viś—the divine races that are enumerated in groups as the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, Viśvedevas, and Maruts.
He did not multiply; he created the Śūdra caste, Pūṣan. This earth is indeed Pūṣan, for she nourishes (puṣyati) everything that exists here, whatever it may be.

He did not flourish at all; he created that form which is superior, namely Dharma. This Dharma is the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) of the sovereign power; therefore there is nothing higher than Dharma. Thus, even one who is weaker asserts himself against one who is stronger by means of Dharma, just as [one does] before a king. That which is Dharma is indeed Truth; therefore, they say of one speaking the truth, "He speaks Dharma," and of one speaking Dharma, "He speaks the truth. For these two are indeed one and the same.

This [Brahman] is the Brahmin, the Kshatriya, the Vaishya, and the Shudra. Among the gods, it became the Brahman through Agni; among men, it became the Brahmin; through the Kshatriya it became the Kshatriya; through the Vaishya it became the Vaishya; and through the Shudra it became the Shudra. Therefore, among the gods they seek their world in Agni alone, and among men in the Brahmin; for by these two forms did the Brahman become manifest.

Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world, it does not protect him, being unknown to him—just as a Veda that has not been studied, or any other work that has not been performed. Even if one who does not know this performs a great meritorious deed, it indeed perishes for him in the end. One should meditate upon the Self alone as the world. He who meditates upon the Self alone as the world—his work does not perish; for from this very Self, whatever he desires, that he creates.

Now, this self indeed is the world of all beings. When he offers oblations and when he sacrifices, by that he wins the world of the gods; when he recites the Veda, by that he wins the world of the seers; when he procreates and when he offers to the ancestors, by that he wins the world of the fathers; when he provides shelter for humans and gives them food, by that he wins the world of humans; when he finds grass and water for animals, by that he wins the world of animals; and whatever creatures in his house—from wild beasts and birds down to the ants—he supports, by that he wins their world. Just as one would desire safety for one's own world, so do all beings always desire safety for one who knows this. This, indeed, has been known and investigated.

In the beginning, this universe was indeed the Self alone, one only. He desired: "May I have a wife, so that I may be born [as offspring]; may I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action. Verily, these are all desires; one cannot find anything beyond these. Therefore, even today, a man living alone desires: "May I have a wife, so that I may be born; may I have wealth, so that I may perform ritual action. As long as he does not obtain even one of these, he considers himself incomplete. This, then, is his completeness.

The mind alone is his self; speech is his wife; breath is his offspring; sight is his human wealth, for by sight one finds it; hearing is his divine wealth, for by hearing one hears it. The self alone is his action, for by the self one performs action. This sacrifice is fivefold; the animal is fivefold; man is fivefold; whatever there is here is fivefold. He who knows this obtains all this, whatever there is.

"When the Father, through wisdom and austerity, produced the seven kinds of food—one he made common to all, two he assigned to the gods, three he kept for himself, and one he bestowed upon animals. Upon that [one] everything is established, both what breathes and what does not. Why is it that these do not perish, even though they are being eaten constantly? He who knows that imperishability eats food with his face; he goes to the gods and lives upon strength. These are the verses.

"That the Father produced the seven kinds of food by means of wisdom and austerity"—for the Father did indeed produce them by means of wisdom and austerity. "One of these is common to all"—this very food which is eaten here is that one which is common to all. He who venerates this [food] does not turn away from evil, for it is mixed.

"He assigned two [portions] to the gods," namely the *huta* and the *prahuta*; therefore, they offer oblations to the gods and offer them repeatedly. Moreover, they say it refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices; therefore, one should not be a frequent performer of animal sacrifices (*iṣṭiyājuka*).

"He gave one [portion] to the cattle"; that was milk, for indeed, at the very beginning, both humans and cattle subsist on milk. Therefore, when a child is born, they first either feed him clarified butter or allow him to suckle at the breast.

Now they say of the calf when it is born, "It is a non-grazer," for everything is established in it—both that which breathes and that which does not; for all this is established in milk, both that which breathes and that which does not.

Regarding this, they say: "One who offers oblations of milk for a year overcomes repeated death. One should not understand it thus; rather, on whatever day he offers the oblation, on that very day he overcomes repeated death. For one who knows this bestows all kinds of food upon the gods. [The question arises: "Why do these foods, though being eaten constantly, never perish?"

"Man indeed is the imperishable, for he generates this food again and again; he who knows that imperishability [is thus praised]. Man indeed is the imperishable, for he generates this food through every act of thought and by means of his works; for were he not to do this, it would surely perish. "He eats the food with his face"—the face is the *pratīka*; "with the mouth," is what is meant. "He goes unto the gods, he lives upon strength"—this is a praise.

"He made three for himself"—namely mind, speech, and breath; these he made for himself. "I was elsewhere in mind, I did not see; I was elsewhere in mind, I did not hear," for it is with the mind alone that one sees, and with the mind that one hears.

Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are indeed the mind. Therefore, even when touched from behind, one discerns it by means of the mind.

Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone; for this [speech] reaches to the end, whereas breath—whether out-breath, in-breath, inter-breath, up-breath, or diffused breath—is not so. All this is indeed breath. This self, moreover, consists of speech, consists of mind, and consists of breath.
These indeed are the three worlds: speech is this world, the mind is the intermediate world, and breath is that world.
These three Vedas are indeed these very [organs]: speech is the Ṛgveda, the mind is the Yajurveda, and the breath is the Sāmaveda.
The gods, the ancestors, and humans—these indeed [are the three]: speech is the gods, mind is the ancestors, and breath is humans.
The father, the mother, and the offspring—mind alone is the father, speech is the mother, and breath is the offspring.
The known, the to-be-known, and the unknown—these are precisely that which is whatever is known. That is the form of speech, for speech is the knower; having become that, speech protects him.
Whatever is to be known through inquiry, that has the nature of the mind; for the mind is indeed that which is to be known through inquiry, and having become that very mind, it protects [the self].
Whatever is unknown is the form of the vital breath, for the vital breath is indeed unknown; having become that very vital breath, it protects him.
Of that speech, the earth is the body and this fire is its form consisting of light; as great as speech is, so great is the earth, and so great is this fire.

Now, of this mind, heaven is the body and the sun is its form of light. As far as the mind extends, so far extends heaven; as great as the sun is, so great is that [heaven]. These two united in sexual union, and from that Prāṇa was born. He is Indra. He is indeed without a rival. For a rival is truly a second; he who knows this has no rival.
Now, water is the body of this vital breath (prāṇa), and that moon is its form of light; as great as the vital breath is, so great are the waters, and so great is that moon.
All these [worlds] are indeed equal and all are infinite. He who worships them as finite wins a finite world; but he who worships them as infinite wins an infinite world.

This very year, Prajāpati, consists of sixteen parts; its fifteen parts are the nights, while its sixteenth part is the constant one. By means of the nights, it waxes and wanes. On the night of the new moon, having entered into all these living beings with this sixteenth part, it is born again in the morning. Therefore, on that night, one should not cut off the breath of any living being, even that of a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity.

That Prajāpati who is the year consists of sixteen parts; he is indeed this very person who knows thus. His wealth constitutes fifteen parts, while his self is his sixteenth part. By means of wealth, he is filled up and by means of wealth he is diminished. This self is the nave, and wealth is the felly; therefore, even if one loses everything, as long as one lives with one's self, they say, "He has lost everything but he has kept the felly."

Now, there are indeed three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods. This world of men is to be won by a son alone, and not by any other rite; the world of the fathers by [the performance of] rites; and the world of the gods by knowledge. Of these worlds, the world of the gods is the best; therefore, they praise knowledge.

Now, therefore, follows the transmission. When he thinks he is about to depart this world, he says to his son: "Thou art the Brahman, thou art the sacrifice, thou art the world. The son replies: "I am the Brahman, I am the sacrifice, I am the world."

Whatever has been spoken, all that is unified in "Brahman"; whatever sacrifices there are, all those are unified in "Sacrifice"; whatever worlds there are, all those are unified in "World. All this that exists is just this much. "May he not enjoy me while I am thus complete," [he thinks]; therefore they say that a son who is instructed is "world-winning" (*lokya*), and for that reason they instruct him. When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters his son together with these very vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Whatever has been done by him in a crooked manner, from all that the son releases him. Therefore he is called "son" (*putra*). By means of the son alone he becomes established in this world; then these divine, immortal vital breaths enter him.
Divine speech enters him from both the earth and the fire; that indeed is divine speech by which whatever one speaks comes to be exactly so.
From the day and from the sun, the divine mind enters him; that indeed is the divine mind by which one becomes truly blissful and does not grieve.

And from the waters and from the moon, the divine breath enters him. That indeed is the divine breath which, whether moving or not moving, neither suffers nor is injured. He who knows this becomes the self of all beings. Just as this deity [is the self of all], so is he; and just as all beings protect this deity, so do all beings protect him who knows this. Whatever these creatures grieve over here, that remains with them alone; only merit goes to him there. Truly, evil does not reach the gods.

Now, therefore, follows the investigation of vows. Prajāpati created the organs of action; once created, they vied with one another. "I shall speak," said speech; "I shall see," said the eye; "I shall hear," said the ear—and so did the other organs, each according to its function.

Death, becoming weariness, took possession of them; having reached them, Death held them captive. Therefore, speech grows weary, the eye grows weary, and the ear grows weary; but he did not reach this very one, which is the central breath.

They resolved to know them, thinking, "This one indeed is the best among us, for whether moving or not moving, he neither stumbles nor suffers harm. Come, let us all assume his very form. They all assumed his form; therefore they are called by this name, "the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*). By this very fact, that family is named after him in whichever family he is born who knows this. And whoever competes with one who knows this, eventually dies of wasting away. This is with reference to the self (*adhyātma*).

Then, with respect to the deities: Fire resolved, "I alone shall blaze"; the Sun, "I shall burn hot"; the Moon, "I shall shine. In this manner, the other deities [resolved] according to their respective domains. Just as the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities; for the other deities set, but Vāyu does not. This deity, namely Vāyu, is the one that never sets.

Now there is this verse: "From whence the sun rises and where it goes to set. It indeed rises from the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and sets in the vital breath. Regarding that, the gods made this law: "That very same [law] holds today and it will hold tomorrow. For whatever these [gods] maintained yesterday, that very same thing they perform today. Therefore, one should observe only a single vow: one should breathe in and one should breathe out, thinking, "Lest the evil, death, should seize me. If one should observe it, and desire to complete it, he who knows thus wins union with and residence in the same world as this deity.

This world consists of three things: name, form, and action. Of these names, speech is their *uktha*; for from it all names arise. It is their *sāman*; for it is equal to all names. It is their *brahman*; for it supports all names.
Now, regarding forms, "the eye" is their *uktha*, for from it all forms arise; this is their *sāman*, for it is equal to all forms; this is their *brahman*, for it sustains all forms.

Now, "the self" is the *uktha* of these ritual acts (*karmāṇi*), for from it all ritual acts arise; this is their *sāman*, for it is equal to all ritual acts; this is their *brahman*, for it sustains all ritual acts. These three, being together, are this one self; and this self, being one, is these three. This is the immortal nourished by the real: breath (*prāṇa*) is the immortal, while name and form are the real; by these two, this breath is nourished.

There was once a learned Gārgya named Dṛptabālāki. He said to Ajātaśatru, the king of Kāśī, "I shall tell you about Brahman. Ajātaśatru replied, "We give a thousand [cows] for such a speech! People run about crying, 'Janaka! Janaka! (meaning, "He is a liberal giver").

Gārgya said: "The person who is yonder in the sun—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as the 'Transcendent,' as the head and king of all beings. He who meditates upon him as such becomes transcendent, the head and king of all beings."

Gārgya said: "The person who is yonder in the moon—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as the Great One, clad in white, King Soma. He who meditates upon him as such has his Soma pressed and poured out day after day; his food does not fail."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the lightning—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him rather as 'the radiant. He who meditates upon him as such becomes radiant, and his offspring becomes radiant."

Gārgya said: "The person who is right here in space—that very one I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I venerate him rather as 'the Full, the Non-active. He who venerates him as such is filled with offspring and cattle; his lineage does not perish from this world."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the wind—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army. He who meditates upon him thus becomes victorious, unconquerable, and a subduer of adversaries."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that very one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the overcomer' (viṣāsahi). He who worships him as such becomes an overcomer, and his offspring become overcomers."

Gārgya said: "This very person who is here in the waters—that is the one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the Counterpart' (Pratirūpa). He who worships him as such, a counterpart indeed approaches him, and never one who is not a counterpart; moreover, a counterpart is born from him."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the mirror—that very one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the Radiant. He who worships him as such becomes radiant himself, and his progeny becomes radiant; moreover, whatever he encounters, he outshines them all."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the quarters—him indeed I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not speak to me of him! I worship him rather as 'The Second who never departs. He who worships him thus becomes possessed of a second; his retinue is never torn away from him."

Gārgya said: "That very sound which follows after one who is walking away—that is what I venerate as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about that! I venerate him rather as 'Life' (asuḥ). He who venerates him thus reaches the full span of life in this world; his vital breath does not leave him before his time."

Gārgya said: "The person who is this very one in the fire—that is the one I meditate upon as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I meditate upon him as Death. He who meditates upon him as such reaches a full lifespan in this world; death does not come to him before his time."

Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the self—that very one I worship as Brahman. Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the embodied one' (ātmanvī). He who worships him thus becomes embodied, and his offspring become embodied. Gārgya then became silent.
Ajātaśatru said: "Is it only that much? "Only that much," he replied. [Ajātaśatru said: "By that much, it is not truly known. Gārgya said: "Let me come to you as a pupil."

Ajātaśatru said: "It would indeed be contrary to the natural order for a Brāhmaṇa to approach a Kṣatriya thinking, 'He will tell me the Brahman. Yet, I shall certainly make it known to you. Taking him by the hand, he rose up. They came to a man who was asleep. He addressed him with these names: "O Great One! O White-Robed One! O Soma! O King! But he did not rise. He woke him by pressing him with his hand; then he rose.
Ajātaśatru said: "When this person, consisting of consciousness, was thus asleep, where did he then abide, and from whence did he return? Gārgya, however, did not know that.

Ajātaśatru said: "When this person consisting of consciousness was thus asleep—having taken the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness—he enters into that space which is within the heart."
When he grasps these, then it is said that the person sleeps; at that time, the breath is indeed grasped, speech is grasped, the eye is grasped, the ear is grasped, and the mind is grasped.
When he moves about in that state of dreaming, those indeed are his worlds; then, as it were, he becomes a great king, or as it were a great Brahmin, or he experiences various high and low states.

Just as a great king, having taken hold of the people of the countryside, moves about his own realm according to his pleasure, even so this [Self], having taken hold of the vital breaths, moves about its own body according to its pleasure.

Now, when one is fast asleep and knows nothing of anything whatsoever, there are the so-called hitā channels—seventy-two thousand in number—which extend from the heart to the pericardium; having slipped down through them, he rests in the pericardium.
Just as a young prince or a great Brahmin, having attained a state of extreme bliss, might lie down, even so do these [breaths] lie down here.

Just as a spider emits its thread, or as tiny sparks fly out from a fire, even so from this Self (ātman) all vital breaths (prāṇas), all worlds, all gods, all beings, and all these selves (ātmanas) emerge. Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "the Truth of truth. The vital breaths are indeed truth, and He is their truth.
Verily, he who knows the child together with its means of accomplishment, its support, its pillar, and its bond, wards off seven hateful rivals.
This very child is this central breath; this is its support, this is its counter-support, the breath is the pillar, and food is the rope. These seven imperishables attend upon it.

Now, those reddish-brown streaks on the axle—Rudra is dependent upon them; those waters on the axle—Parjanya is dependent upon them; that which is the pupil—Āditya is dependent upon it; that which is white—Agni is dependent upon it; that which is black—Indra is dependent upon it; by its lower track the earth is dependent upon it, and by its upper track the sky is dependent upon it. The food of one who knows this does not fail.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "A cup with its mouth below and its bottom above—in it is placed glory of every form. Upon its bank sit the seven seers; Vāk is the eighth, in harmony with Brahman."

"The ladle is downward-opening, with its bottom turned upward"—this refers to this head, for this head is indeed a downward-opening ladle with its bottom turned upward. "In it glory, multiform, is deposited"—glory is indeed the vital breaths (prāṇas); he thus speaks of the vital breaths. "Of it, the seven seers sit upon the rim"—the seers are indeed the vital breaths; he thus speaks of the vital breaths. "Speech is the eighth, attaining union with Brahman"—for speech is the eighth, attaining union with Brahman.

These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja; this one is Gotama and this one is Bharadvāja. These two are indeed Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni; this one is Viśvāmitra and this one is Jamadagni. These two are indeed Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa; this one is Vasiṣṭha and this one is Kaśyapa. Atri is speech, for by speech food is eaten. "Atri" is indeed a name for this [speech]; he becomes the eater of all, and everything becomes his food, who knows thus.
There are indeed two forms of Brahman: the formed and the formless, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and the moving, and that which exists and that which does not exist.
This which is other than the wind and the intermediate space is embodied; it is mortal, it is stationary, and it is existent.
Of this very one who has form, who is mortal, who is stationary, and who is existent—this is the essence: he who shines yonder; for he is indeed the essence of the existent.
Now, that which is formless is air and the intermediate space; this is immortal, this is that which is real.

Of this formless one, of this immortal one, of this unshaken one, of this [Brahman], of this Tyat, this is the essence: namely, this person who is in that orb; for he is indeed the essence of that Tyat. Thus with respect to the deity.
Now, with reference to the self: that which is other than the vital breath and that which is this space within the self—this is the formed, this is mortal, this is stable, this is the existent.
Of this very embodied one, of this mortal one, of this stationary one, of this existent one, the eye is the essence; for it is the essence of the existent.
Now, that which is formless consists of the vital breath and this space within the self; this is the immortal, this is the real.
Of this formless, immortal, and unchanging [Brahman], that person who is here in the right eye is the essence; for he is indeed the essence of that which is unchanging.

The form of this very person is like saffron-dyed cloth, like white wool, like a cochineal insect, like the flame of a fire, like a lotus, and like a flash of lightning; indeed, his splendor becomes like a flash of lightning for one who knows this.

Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this. For there is nothing else higher than this "not this. Furthermore, its name is "the Truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is their truth.
"Maitreyī," said Yājñavalkya, "I am indeed about to depart from this place; come, let me make a final settlement between you and Kātyāyanī."

Maitreyī said: "Venerable sir, if this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal by means of it? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "your life would be just like the life of those who possess worldly means; there is no hope for immortality through wealth."
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which your reverence knows."

Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, you have spoken kindly to us, being dear to us; come, sit down, and I will explain it to you. But while I am explaining, you must meditate upon it. [Maitreyī] said: "Let the Blessed One speak."

Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, O Maitreyī, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear, but it is out of love for the Self (ātman) that the husband is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the sons are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that wealth is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Brahminhood that the Brahminhood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Brahminhood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the Kshatriyahood that the Kshatriyahood is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the Kshatriyahood is dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the worlds that the worlds are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the worlds are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for the gods that the gods are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the gods are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for beings that beings are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that beings are dear. Truly, it is not out of love for everything that everything is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that everything is dear. "The Self, indeed, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. By seeing, hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing the Self, all this is known."

Brahman would desert him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; the Kshatra would desert him who knows the Kshatra as other than the Self; the worlds would desert him who knows the worlds as other than the Self; the gods would desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self; the beings would desert him who knows the beings as other than the Self; everything would desert him who knows everything as other than the Self. This Brahman, this Kshatra, these worlds, these gods, these beings, this all—whatever exists—is this very Self.
Just as when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp the external sounds, but by grasping the drum or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped.
Just as when a lute is being played, one cannot grasp its external sounds; rather, by grasping the lute itself, or the player of the lute, the sound is grasped.
Just as when a conch shell is being blown, one cannot grasp the external sounds; rather, by grasping the conch itself, or the blower of the conch, the sound is grasped.

Just as from a fire kindled with damp fuel various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharva-Aṅgirasas, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret doctrines (Upaniṣads), verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries—all these are the breath of this great Being.

Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters, so the skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations; so the two nostrils are the single point of convergence for all odors; so the tongue is the single point of convergence for all tastes; so the eye is the single point of convergence for all forms; so the ear is the single point of convergence for all sounds; so the mind is the single point of convergence for all volitions; so the heart is the single point of convergence for all the Vedas; so the two hands are the single point of convergence for all actions; so the two feet are the single point of convergence for all paths; so the organ of generation is the single point of convergence for all pleasures; so the anus is the single point of convergence for all excretions; and so speech is the single point of convergence for all branches of knowledge.

"Just as a lump of salt, when thrown into water, dissolves completely into the water itself, so that it would not be possible to take it out again, yet from whichever part one might draw [some], it is salty—exactly so, my dear, this great being, infinite and boundless, is indeed a mass of consciousness alone. Arising from these elements, it vanishes again into them. After death, there is no consciousness," Yājñavalkya said, "so I say, my dear."
Maitreyī said: "Right here, sir, you have bewildered me by saying that there is no consciousness after death."
Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, my dear, I do not speak in delusion; indeed, this is sufficient for understanding."

For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; there one smells another; there one speaks to another; there one hears another; there one thinks of another; there one perceives another.

"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what and whom should he speak? Then by what and whom should he hear? Then by what and whom should he think? Then by what and whom should he know? By what should one know Him by whom all this is known?—O, by what should one know the Knower?"

This earth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this earth. This radiant, immortal person who is in this earth, and this radiant, immortal person who is in the body with respect to the self—he is indeed this Self; he is this Immortal, he is Brahman, he is all this.

These waters are honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for these waters; and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in these waters, and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is within the self in the semen.

This fire is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this fire; and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this fire, and that person consisting of speech, consisting of splendor, and consisting of immortality who is with reference to the self (adhyātma).

This space is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this space; and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this space, and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is here in the self within the space of the heart.

This wind is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this wind; and that person consisting of light and consisting of immortality who is in this wind, and that vital breath consisting of light and consisting of immortality which is with reference to the self—[these are one].
