This Āditya is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this Āditya; and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this Āditya, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is here in the self with respect to the eye.

This moon is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this moon; and this person who is within this moon, consisting of light and consisting of immortality, and this person who is within the self, belonging to the mind, consisting of light and consisting of immortality—[these are one].

These quarters are honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for these quarters. And this person who consists of splendor and consists of immortality, who is in these quarters; and he who, with respect to the self, is the one belonging to the ear, who is present in the hearing, and who consists of splendor and consists of immortality.

This lightning is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this lightning. And that person who is here in this lightning, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, and he who is the internal person corresponding to lightning, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality—[these two are one].

This thunder is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this thunder; and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this thunder, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is within oneself, the one related to sound (*śābda*) and related to the Sāman (*sauvara*).

This Dharma is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this Dharma; and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this Dharma, and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is the one pertaining to the self (adhyātma) in relation to Dharma.

This truth is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this truth; and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this truth, and this person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in the self (adhyātma) with respect to truth—[these are honey].

This human being is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this human being; and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this human being, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is the human being with respect to the self (adhyātma).

This Self is honey for all beings, and all beings are honey for this Self. And that person consisting of light and immortal who is in this Self, and this Self consisting of light and immortal—that is indeed this Self; it is this immortality, it is this Brahman, it is all this.

This very Self is the lord of all beings, the king of all beings. Just as all the spokes are fixed in the nave and the felly of a chariot wheel, even so in this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all gods, and all beings—all these selves are fixed.

This, indeed, is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, the Seer declared: "O Heroes, for the sake of gain, I reveal that terrible deed of yours, even as the thunderbolt reveals rain—namely, how Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa, by means of the horse's head, spoke this honey to you."

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: "O Aśvins, you restored the horse's head to Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; he, seeking the truth, proclaimed the honey to you both—the Tvaṣṭrian [secret], O Dasras, which was hidden in your girth."

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: "He first created the two-footed; he first created the four-footed. Having first become a bird, he, as the Puruṣa, entered into the bodies. Verily, this Puruṣa dwells within all bodies; there is nothing whatsoever that is not covered by him, nothing whatsoever that is not enclosed by him.

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins. Seeing this, a seer declared: "In form after form he has become a counterpart; that is his form for being seen. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyās); for his bay horses are yoked—ten hundred. These bay horses are indeed this [Self]; these ten and thousands are indeed this [Self]—many and infinite. This is Brahman, without prior, without posterior, without exterior. This Self is Brahman, the perceiver of everything. Such is the instruction.

Now, the lineage: This [lineage] is from Śaurpaṇāyya; Śaurpaṇāyya from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from both Vātsya and Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from both Sāṃkṛtya and Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Audavāhi and Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Vaijavāpa and Gautama; Gautama from Vaijavāpāyana and Vaiṣṭapureya; Vaiṣṭapureya from Śāṇḍilya and Rauhiṇāyana; Rauhiṇāyana from Śaunaka, Ātreya, and Raibhya; Raibhya from Pautimāṣyāyaṇa and Kauṇḍinyāyana; Kauṇḍinyāyana from Kauṇḍinya; Kauṇḍinya from Kauṇḍinya; and Kauṇḍinya from both Kauṇḍinya and Āgniveśya.

Āgniveśya from Saitava; Saitava from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Gautama; Gautama from both Bhāradvāja and Āsurāyaṇa; Bhāradvāja from Vaijavāpāyana; Vaijavāpāyana from Kauśikāyani; Kauśikāyani from Ghṛtakauśika; Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa; Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Yāska; Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Āsuri; Āsuri from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Ātreya.

Ātreya from Māṇṭi; Māṇṭi from Gautama; Gautama from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya; Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita; Kumārahārita from Gālava; Gālava from Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya; Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava; Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Pathas Saubhara; Pathas Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa; Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra; Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra; Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins; the two Aśvins from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva; Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana; Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi; Ekarṣi from Viprajitti; Viprajitti from Vyaṣṭi; Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru; Sanāru from Sanātana; Sanātana from Sanaga; Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin; Parameṣṭhin from Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent. Salutation to Brahmā!

Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which many gifts were distributed. There, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas had gathered together. Janaka of Videha desired to know: "Who among these Brahmins is the most learned in the Vedas?"

He enclosed a thousand cows, and ten pādas were tied to the horns of each one. He said to them, "Venerable Brahmins, let him among you who is the most learned in the Veda (brahmiṣṭha) drive these cows away. But those Brahmins did not dare.

Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil: "My dear Sāmaśrava, bring these [cows] here. He brought them, and the Brahmins were incensed, saying, "How can he, the most learned in sacred knowledge among us, speak thus?"

Now, Āśvala was the Hotṛ priest of Janaka of Videha. He questioned him, saying: "Are you indeed, O Yājñavalkya, the most perfect in Brahman among us? He replied: "We pay homage to the one who is most perfect in Brahman; we are merely desirous of cattle. Thereupon, the Hotṛ Āśvala resolved to question him further on that very point.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is overtaken by death, since all is seized by death, by what means does the sacrificer free himself from the reach of death? "By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, and by speech. "Speech indeed is the Hotṛ of the sacrifice; that which is this speech is this fire, and it is the Hotṛ. That is liberation; that is complete liberation."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by day and night, and all this is encompassed by day and night, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of day and night? "By means of the Adhvaryu priest, [who is] the eye, [and] the sun. For the eye is indeed the Adhvaryu of the sacrifice. That which is this eye is yonder sun; that is the Adhvaryu. That is the liberation; that is the complete transcendence.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by the first and second fortnights, and all this is encompassed by the first and second fortnights, by what means does the sacrificer, through the Brahman priest, become released beyond the reach of the first and second fortnights? "By means of the mind, which is the moon. "The mind, indeed, is the Brahman priest of the sacrifice. Now, that which is this mind is yonder moon; he is the Brahman priest. That is the release; that is the release beyond."

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "since this intermediate space is as if without support, by what means does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world? "By the Udgātṛ priest, by Vāyu, by the vital breath (prāṇa). "The Udgātṛ of the sacrifice is indeed the vital breath; that which is this vital breath is Vāyu, that is the Udgātṛ. That is liberation (mukti), that is complete liberation (atimukti). These were the liberations (atimokṣas). "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many ṛg-verses will this Hotṛ priest perform his duties at this sacrifice today? "With three. "Which are those three? "The invitatory verse (puro'nuvākyā), the offering verse (yājyā), and the recitation verse (śasyā) as the third. "What does he win by means of them? "By the invitatory verse he wins the world of the earth; by the offering verse, the world of the intermediate space; and by the recitation verse, the world of heaven."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will this Adhvaryu offer today in this sacrifice? "Three. "Which are those three? "Those which, when offered, blaze up; those which, when offered, overflow; and those which, when offered, lie down. "What does one win by these? "By those which, when offered, blaze up, one wins the world of the gods, for the world of the gods, as it were, blazes up. By those which, when offered, overflow, one wins the world of men, for the world of men, as it were, overflows. By those which, when offered, lie down, one wins the world of the fathers, for the world of the fathers, as it were, lies low."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities will this Brahman protect the sacrifice from the south today? "With one. "Which is that one? "The mind alone. "The mind is indeed infinite, and the All-gods are infinite; by means of that, he wins an infinite world."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *stotriyā* hymns will this Udgātṛ chant today at this sacrifice? "Three," he replied. "Which are those three? "The *puro'nuvākyā*, the *yājyā*, and the *śasyā* as the third—this with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*), which are those that pertain to the self? "The *prāṇa* (out-breath) is the *puro'nuvākyā*, the *apāna* (in-breath) is the *yājyā*, and the *vyāna* (diffused breath) is the *śasyā*. "What does one win by means of these? "Whatever here possesses breath. Thereupon, Aśvala, the Hotṛ, desisted.

Then Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many are the *grahas* (seizers) and how many are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers)? "There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*. "As for those eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*, which are they?"
The out-breath (prāṇa) is indeed the grasper; it is seized by the in-breath (apāna) as the over-grasper, for by means of the in-breath one smells odors.
The tongue, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by taste as the over-grasper, for by means of the tongue one perceives tastes.
Speech, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by the name as the over-grasper, for by speech one utters names.
The eye, indeed, is the grasper; it is seized by form as the over-grasper, for by means of the eye one perceives forms.
The ear is indeed the grasper; it is seized by sound as the over-grasper, for by means of the ear one hears sounds.
The mind, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper, for by means of the mind one desires desires.
The hands, indeed, are the grasper; they are seized by action as the over-grasper, for it is with the hands that one performs action.
The skin, indeed, is a grāha; it is seized by touch as its atigrāha, for by means of the skin one perceives touches. Thus there are eight grāhas and eight atigrāhas.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is food for death, who is that deity for whom death is food? "Fire, indeed, is death; water is its food. [By knowing this] one conquers recurrent death.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him? "His name," [he replied]. "The name is indeed infinite; the Viśvedevas are infinite. By means of that, he wins an infinite world—yes, by means of that, he wins an infinite world."

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do the vital breaths depart from him or not? "No, no," Yājñavalkya replied; "they are simply merged right here. He swells up, he becomes bloated, and bloated, he lies dead."

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when the speech of this dead man merges into fire, his breath into the wind, his sight into the sun, his mind into the moon, his hearing into the quarters, his body into the earth, his self (ātman) into space, his hairs into plants, his head-hairs into trees, and his blood and semen are deposited in the waters—at that time, where does this person come to be? Come, my dear, take my hand."

"O Ārtabhāga," he said, "let us two alone consider this; let us not discuss this among a crowd. So they went out and deliberated. What they spoke of was indeed action; what they praised was indeed action: "One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and evil through evil action. Thereupon, Jāratkārava Ārtabhāga fell silent.

Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were traveling among the Madras as wandering students. We came to the house of Cula Kāpya, whose daughter was possessed by a Gandharva. We asked him, 'Who are you? He replied, 'I am Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, we then asked him, 'Where have the Pārikṣitas gone? Where have the Pārikṣitas gone? That is what I ask you, Yājñavalkya: where have the Pārikṣitas gone?"

He said: "He indeed spoke that; he truly told you where those go who have performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice. "But where do those who have performed the Aśvamedha go? "Thirty-two regions traversed by a divine chariot are this world; the earth extends twice as far around that world; the ocean extends twice as far around that earth. Now, as wide as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly, there is an intervening space; Indra, having become a bird (suparṇa), delivered them to Vāyu; Vāyu, having placed them within himself, caused them to go to where the Pārikṣitas were. "In this way, he indeed praised Vāyu alone. Therefore, Vāyu is the individual manifestation (vyaṣṭi) and Vāyu is the universal manifestation (samaṣṭi). He who knows this conquers recurrent death and attains a full lifespan. Thereupon, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased questioning.

Then Kahoḍa Kauṣītakeya questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. "Tell me, Yājñavalkya, who is this Self within all? "It is that Self within all, O Yājñavalkya, which transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death. Having known this very Self, the Brāhmaṇas rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of a mendicant. For the desire for sons is the same as the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the same as the desire for worlds; both of these are indeed just desires. Therefore, a wise man, having discarded wisdom, should remain in the state of a child; and having discarded both childhood and wisdom, he becomes a sage (muni); and having discarded both non-sagehood and sagehood, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa. By what means would he be such a Brāhmaṇa? He becomes exactly like that by which he would be so—whosoever knows thus. Thereupon, Kahoḍa Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning."

Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. "Tell me, Yājñavalkya, who is this Self within all? "That which breathes with the out-breath (prāṇa) is your Self within all; that which breathes down with the in-breath (apāna) is your Self within all; that which breathes across with the diffused breath (vyāna) is your Self within all; that which breathes up with the upward breath (udāna) is your Self within all; that which breathes evenly with the equalizing breath (samāna) is your Self within all. Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as one might say, 'That is a cow,' or 'That is a horse,' so has this been pointed out. Explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all. "Tell me, Yājñavalkya, who is this Self within all? "You do not see the seer of seeing; you do not hear the hearer of hearing; you do not think the thinker of thinking; you do not discern the discerner of discerning. This is your Self within all. Everything other than this is perishable. Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa fell silent.

Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. She said, "Yājñavalkya," she said, "since all this is woven back and forth upon the waters, upon what are the waters woven back and forth? "On the wind, Gārgī. "On what is the wind woven back and forth? "On space alone, Gārgī. "On what is space woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the intermediate region, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the intermediate region woven back and forth? "On the world of heaven, Gārgī. "On what is the world of heaven woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the sun, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the sun woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the moon, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the moon woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the stars, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the stars woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the gods, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the gods woven back and forth? "On the worlds of the Gandharvas, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of the Gandharvas woven back and forth? "On the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of Prajāpati woven back and forth? "On the worlds of Brahmā, Gārgī. "On what are the worlds of Brahmā woven back and forth? He said, "Gārgī, do not ask beyond this, lest your head shatter apart. These deities are not to be questioned beyond; you are questioning too far, Gārgī. Do not ask beyond this! Thereupon Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased.

Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were living among the Madras in the house of Patañcala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice. His wife was possessed by a Gandharva; we asked him, 'Who are you? and he replied, 'I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa.'"

He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: "Do you know, O Kāpya, that thread by which this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together? Patañcala Kāpya replied: "I do not know it, O Venerable Sir."

He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists, "Do you know, O Kāpya, that inner controller who controls this world and the other world, and all beings from within? Patañcala Kāpya replied, "I do not know him, venerable sir."

He said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists: "O Kāpya, whoever knows that thread and that inner controller—he is a knower of Brahman, a knower of the worlds, a knower of the gods, a knower of the Vedas, a knower of the sacrifice, a knower of the beings, a knower of the Self, and a knower of all. He said this to them: "I know that; yet if you, Yājñavalkya, being ignorant of that thread and that inner controller, drive away the cows that belong to a Brahmin, your head shall shatter apart!"
"O Gautama, I indeed know that thread and that inner controller," [Yājñavalkya said]. "Whoever might say here, 'I know, I know,' let him explain it as he knows it."

"Vāyu, O Gautama, is indeed that thread. By Vāyu, O Gautama, as by a thread, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together. Therefore, O Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart,' for by Vāyu, O Gautama, as by a thread, they are held together. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya; now speak of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin)."
He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, and who controls the earth from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body the waters are, and who controls the waters from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in space, yet is within space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, who controls space from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
He who dwells in the wind, yet is within the wind, whom the wind does not know, whose body is the wind, who controls the wind from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body the sun is, who controls the sun from within—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.

He who dwells in the moon and the stars, yet is within the moon and the stars, whom the moon and the stars do not know, whose body the moon and the stars are, and who controls the moon and the stars from within—he is that.

He who dwells in the quarters, yet is internal to the quarters; whom the quarters do not know, whose body the quarters are, and who is internal to the quarters—He is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
He who dwells in lightning, yet is within lightning, whom lightning does not know, whose body is lightning, and who controls lightning from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who, dwelling in the thunder, is within the thunder, whom the thunder does not know, whose body is the thunder, who controls the thunder from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. This is with respect to the divine; now, with respect to the worlds.

He who, dwelling in all worlds, is internal to all worlds; whom all worlds do not know; whose body all worlds are; who, being internal to all worlds, controls them—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Thus [it is] with respect to the worlds; now, with respect to the Vedas.
"He who, dwelling in all the Vedas, is internal to all the Vedas"—thus indeed is [the Self] with respect to the Vedas; now, with respect to the sacrifice:
"Abiding in all sacrifices, yet internal to all sacrifices"—this indeed is with respect to sacrifice; now, with respect to the elements.

He who, dwelling within all beings, is internal to all beings; whom all beings do not know; whose body all beings are; who controls all beings from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus [it is] with respect to the elements (adhibhūta); now with respect to the self (adhyātma).

He who dwells in the vital breath (prāṇa), yet is within the vital breath, whom the vital breath does not know, whose body the vital breath is, and who controls the vital breath from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
He who, dwelling in speech, is within speech...
He who dwells in the eye, yet is within the eye.
He who, dwelling in the ear, is within the ear.
He who, dwelling in the mind, is within the mind...
He who dwells in the skin, yet is within the skin...
He who dwells in fire, yet is within fire...
He who dwells in darkness, yet is within darkness, beyond darkness.
He who, dwelling in semen, is within semen.
He who, dwelling within the self, is interior to the self...

The unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower—there is no other seer, no other hearer, no other thinker, no other knower. This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal; everything else is subject to suffering. Thereupon, Uddālaka Āruṇi ceased questioning.

Then Vācaknavī said: "Venerable Brahmins, come now, I shall ask this Yājñavalkya two questions. If he answers them for me, none of you will ever defeat him in a debate on Brahman. But if he does not answer them for me, his head shall split apart. "Ask then, Gārgī," [Yājñavalkya replied].

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, just as a Kāśyan or a Vaidehan, the son of a noble family, might rise up having strung his bow and taken two arrow-fitted quivers in his hands to strike down his enemies, even so have I risen up against you with two questions. Answer them for me. "Ask, Gārgī," he said.

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two—the heaven and the earth—and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—upon what is that woven, warp and woof?"

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across all this, [the Unstruck] is woven as the warp and the woof."
She said, "Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya, who has explained this to me; hold yourself back for another [question]. "Ask, Gārgī," he said.

She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what, then, is all that woven to and fro?"

He said: "Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across all this, space alone is woven like warp and woof. [Yājñavalkya asked: "In what, then, is space woven like warp and woof?"

He said: "O Gārgī, this is indeed that syllable which the Brāhmaṇas declare as neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space; it is unattached, intangible, odorless, tasteless, without eyes, without ears, without voice, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, without name, without lineage; it is ageless, deathless, fearless, immortal, stainless, soundless, unopened and unenclosed; it is without before and without after, without inside and without outside; it does not reach anything, nor does anything reach it."

"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, days and nights, half-months, months, seasons, and years stand held apart; under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow toward the east from the white mountains, while others flow toward the west, and toward whichever direction they may go. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, humans praise one who gives, the gods are dependent upon the sacrificer, and the ancestors are dependent upon the giver."

"Or, Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, gives gifts, or performs austerities without knowing this Imperishable—even if for many thousands of years—his world is indeed finite. Or, Gārgī, whoever departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable; but he who departs from this world, Gārgī, having known this Imperishable, is a true Brāhmaṇa."

"Verily, that syllable, O Gārgī, is unseen yet the seer, unheard yet the hearer, unthought yet the thinker, unknown yet the knower; there is no other seer than this, no other hearer than this, no other thinker than this, no other knower than this. This, indeed, O Gārgī, is that syllable in which the ether is woven, both as warp and woof."

She said, "Venerable Brahmins, you should consider yourselves fortunate enough if you can escape from me by merely paying me homage; for surely none of you will ever defeat me in a debate on Brahman. Thereupon, Vācaknavī ceased.

Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He answered with this very *nivid*: "As many as are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva [hymn]—three hundred and three, and three thousand and three. "Yes," he said.

“How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “Thirty-three,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “Six,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “Three,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “Two,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “One and a half,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? “One,” he said. “Yes,” he replied. “Who are those ‘three and three hundred and three and three thousand’?”

He said: "These are merely their manifestations; there are indeed only thirty-three gods."—"Which are those thirty-three?"—"The eight Vasus, the eleven Rudras, and the twelve Ādityas—those are thirty-one; and Indra and Prajāpati make thirty-three."

"Who are the Vasus? "Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, the sky, and the stars—these are the Vasus. For in these all this wealth (vasu) is placed; for they cause all this to dwell (vāsayante). Because they cause all this to dwell, therefore they are called the Vasus."

"What are the Rudras? "These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh; when they depart from this mortal body, they cause one to weep (rodayanti). Because they cause one to weep, therefore they are called Rudras."

"Who are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year; these are the Ādityas, for they go along taking up all this [world]. Because they go along taking up all this, therefore they are called Ādityas."
"Who is Indra? Who is Prajāpati? "Indra is indeed the thunder, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice. "What is the thunder? "It is lightning. "What is the sacrifice? "It is the cattle."
Which are the six? Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, and the sky; for these indeed are all this [universe] as six.
"Who are those three gods? "These very three worlds; for within these all the gods are contained. "Who are the two gods? "Food and breath. "Who is the one and a half? "This wind that blows here."

Regarding this they say: "Since he blows as one alone, how then is he 'one and a half' (adhyardha)? Because everything here has prospered (*adhyardhnot*) within him, therefore he is called "one and a half. "Which one is the single god? They call him Brahman, that which is "yad" (the Beyond).

"He who knows that person whose abode is the earth, whose world is the eye, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self—he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak; it is this very person who is embodied (śārīra). Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Women," he replied.

"He for whom visible forms alone are the sphere, whose world is the eye, and whose light is the mind—he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower, O Yājñavalkya. "I do know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak; it is that very person who is in the sun. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "The eye," he said.
"He whose abode is space itself, whose world is the eye, and whose self is the mind—this person who is in the wind, tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "The vital breath (prāṇa)," he replied.
"He whose abode is desire, whose world is sight, and whose self is the mind—he who is that person in the moon, tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "The mind," he replied.
"He whose abode is fire, whose world is sight, and whose self is mind—this person who is here in the fire, tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Speech," he replied.
"Darkness alone is his abode, the eye his world, and the mind his self; that person who is within this body—he, Śākalya, tell me, what is his deity? "Death," he replied.
"Water indeed is his abode, the eye is his world, and the mind is his [source]. That person who is here in the waters—he is this very one, Śākalya; tell me, who is his deity? "Varuṇa," he said.
"His abode is semen, his world is the eye, and his self is the mind—this person who consists of a son. Tell me, Śākalya, who is his deity? "Prajāpati," he replied.
"Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya, "have these Brahmins indeed made you their charcoal-remover?"

"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya, "since you have spoken over these Brāhmaṇas of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what Brahman do you know? "I know the quarters together with their deities and their foundations. "Since you know the quarters together with their deities and their foundations..."

"Whose deity are you in this eastern direction? "The Sun is my deity. "On what is that Sun established? "On the eye. "On what, then, is the eye established? "On forms (rūpa), for by the eye one sees forms. "On what, then, are forms established? "On the heart (hṛdaya), for by the heart one knows forms; indeed, on the heart alone are forms established. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya."

"What deity is in this southern direction? "Yama is its deity. "In what is Yama established? "In the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). "In what, then, is the sacrificial fee established? "In faith (śraddhā). For when one has faith, then one gives the sacrificial fee; for in faith alone the sacrificial fee is established. "In what, then, is faith established? "In the heart. For with the heart one has faith; for in the heart alone faith is established. "Is it so indeed, O Yājñavalkya? "So it is," said Yājñavalkya.

"Which deity presides over this western quarter? "Varuṇa is its deity. "On what is Varuṇa established? "In the waters. "On what are the waters established? "In semen. "On what is semen established? "In the heart. Therefore, they say of even a well-formed newborn child, "He has slipped as if from the heart; he has been fashioned as if from the heart," for semen is indeed established in the heart. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya."

"What deity are you under in this northern direction? "Soma is my deity. "On what is that Soma established? "On consecration (dīkṣā). "On what is consecration established? "On truth. "Therefore, they say to one who has been consecrated: 'Speak the truth,' for on truth alone is consecration established. "On what is truth established? "On the heart, for by the heart one knows the truth; on the heart alone is truth established. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya."

"Which deity resides in this fixed (dhruvā) quarter? "The deity Agni. "In what is that Agni established? "In speech. "In what, then, is speech established? "In the mind. "In what, then, is the mind established? "In the heart. "In what, then, is the heart established?"
"A fool! said Yājñavalkya. "If you were to think this [the sun] exists elsewhere than in us, or if it were to exist elsewhere than in us, dogs would eat it or birds would tear it to pieces."

"On what, then, are you and the self established? "On the out-breath (prāṇa). "On what, then, is the out-breath established? "On the in-breath (apāna). "On what, then, is the in-breath established? "On the inter-breath (vyāna). "On what, then, is the inter-breath established? "On the up-breath (udāna). "On what, then, is the up-breath established? "On the equalizing breath (samāna)."

"He is this one who is 'Not this, not that. He is ungraspable, for he cannot be grasped; he is undecaying, for he is not subject to decay; he is unattached and unfettered, for he is neither attached nor afflicted. These are the eight abodes, the eight worlds, and the eight persons. Having removed and then replaced those persons, he passed beyond them. "That person of the Upanishads—I ask you about him. If you do not explain him to me, your head shall shatter apart. Śākalya did not know him, and his head indeed shattered. Furthermore, thinking they were merely thieves, robbers carried off his bones.

Then Yājñavalkya said, "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you desires it question me; or let all of you question me. Or let me question whoever among you desires it; or let me question all of you. But those Brahmins did not dare.
He questioned them with these verses: "As a tree is a great forest-plant, so is a person not falsely; his hairs are its leaves, and the outer skin is its bark."
From his skin alone the blood flows; from the skin comes the scab. Therefore, when that [skin] is struck, the sap runs out, as it does from a tree that has been struck.
Its flesh is the sugar-cane, its inner bark is the sinews, its firmness is the bones, and the marrow within is fashioned like marrow.
When a tree is cut down, it grows again from its root, even newer than before; but when a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he sprout forth?

"Do not say, 'From semen. It is born from the living; once born, it is not born again. Who indeed could produce it anew? A tree that grows from a seed, after dying, arises from something else. If they were to uproot the tree along with its roots, it would not come into being again. When a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he sprout? Knowledge, bliss, Brahman—the supreme goal of the giver who bestows [it], for one who stands firm knowing that. Thus [he spoke].

Janaka of Videha was sitting in state when Yājñavalkya arrived. Janaka of Videha said to him, "Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come? Do you seek cattle, or do you seek disputation? He replied, "For both, O Emperor. [Janaka said], "Let us hear what someone may have told you."

Udaṅka Śaulbāyana said to me, "Brahman is indeed breath. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śaulbāyana speak when he said, "Brahman is indeed breath; for what could there be for one without breath? [I asked], "But did he tell you its abode and its support? He replied, "He did not tell me that. [I said], "This [knowledge] is one-footed, O Emperor."

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "Space indeed is its abode; space is its foundation. One should meditate upon it as 'the Dear' (priya). "What is its dearness, Yājñavalkya? "The vital breath (*prāṇa*), O Emperor," he said. "For the sake of the vital breath, O Emperor, one performs sacrifices for which one should not sacrifice, and accepts gifts from those from whom one should not accept them; even there, the threat of death may arise in whatever direction one goes—for the sake of the vital breath, O Emperor. The vital breath, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. The vital breath does not abandon him, and all beings flow toward him."

"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give you a thousand [cows] with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha. Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed his pupil. "Who was it that told you this? [Janaka asked].

Śailina said to me, "Speech indeed is Brahman," just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would say; so did Śailina say, "Speech indeed is Brahman. "If one were to speak thus, what would he have? [I asked]. He replied, "But he told you its abode and its support. "He did not tell me that," I said. "This, O Emperor, is only one-quarter," he said.

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "Speech, indeed, is its abode; space is its foundation. One should meditate upon this as 'Intelligence' (prajñā). "What constitutes intelligence, Yājñavalkya? "Speech itself, O Emperor," he said. "For by speech, O Emperor, one's kin are known; the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvāṅgirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, secret doctrines, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries—by speech alone, O Emperor, these are known. Speech, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. Speech does not desert him; all beings offer him tribute."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus. Thus [ends the section on] the elephant-riders.

Varku Vārṣṇa said to me, "Brahman is indeed sight. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would say, so did that Vārṣṇa say, "Brahman is indeed sight. [I asked: "What could there be for one who does not see? He replied, "But he did not tell you its abode and its support. I said, "O Emperor, this [sight] is indeed one-footed."

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The eye itself is its abode, space is its foundation; one should worship it as 'the True' (satya). "What is its truthfulness, Yājñavalkya? "The eye itself, O Emperor," he said. "For when someone sees with the eye, O Emperor, they ask, 'Did you see? And if he says, 'I saw,' that becomes the truth. The eye, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman; the eye does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, venerates this [breath] as the elephant-herd."

The donkey-drinker Bhāradvāja said to me, "Hearing, indeed, is Brahman. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would say, so did Bhāradvāja say, "Hearing, indeed, is Brahman. [I asked: "What would become of one who does not hear? He replied, "But he told you its abode and its support. [I said: "He did not tell me that. [He replied: "This, O Emperor, is only one-footed."

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The ear indeed is its abode, space is its foundation; one should meditate upon it as 'the Infinite' (Ananta). "What constitutes its infinity, Yājñavalkya? "The quarters of space themselves, O Emperor," he said. "Therefore, O Emperor, whatever quarter of space one goes toward, one never reaches its end, for the quarters of space are infinite. The quarters of space are the ear; the ear, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman. The ear does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it as such. Thus [ends the section on] the elephant's roar.

Satyakāma Jābāla said to me, "Mind, indeed, is Brahman. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might speak, so did Satyakāma speak when he said, "Mind, indeed, is Brahman. [I asked: "For what could there be for one without mind? He replied, "But he did not tell you its abode and its support. I said, "This [Brahman] is but one-footed, O Emperor."

"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya. "The mind alone is its abode, space is its foundation; one should worship it as bliss. "What constitutes its blissfulness, Yājñavalkya? "The mind itself, O Emperor," he said. "For with the mind, O Emperor, one desires a woman. From her a son is born who is like himself; that is bliss. The mind, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman. The mind does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus. [End of the section on] the elephant.

"Vidagdha Śākalya said to me, 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman. Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śākalya speak when he said, 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman. [I asked: 'What could there be for one without a heart? He replied, 'But he did not tell you its abode and support. [I said: 'This, O Emperor, is only one-quarter.'"

"Tell us that, O Yājñavalkya. "The heart itself is its abode, and space is its foundation; one should meditate upon it as 'Stability'. "What is this stability, Yājñavalkya? "The heart itself, O Emperor," he said. "The heart, O Emperor, is indeed the foundation of all beings, for by means of the heart all beings are established. The heart, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman; the heart does not desert him, and all beings flow toward him."

"Having become a god, he goes to the gods—he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give you a thousand [cows] with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha. Yājñavalkya replied, "My father thought that one should not accept a gift without having first instructed [the pupil]."

Then Janaka of Videha, descending from his seat of kusha grass, said: "Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya; instruct me further. He replied: "Just as a king, O Emperor, about to set out on a long journey would prepare a chariot or a ship, even so you have prepared yourself with these secret doctrines (upaniṣads). Thus being honored, wealthy, learned in the Vedas, and instructed in the secret doctrines, where will you go when you are released from this body? "I do not know that, O Venerable One, where I shall go," he said. "Then indeed I shall tell you, where you shall go," [Yājñavalkya] replied. "Let the Venerable One speak," [Janaka] said.

He said: "This person who is here in the right eye is indeed named Indha; though he is Indha, they call him Indra by an indirect name, for the gods prefer the indirect, being as it were averse to the direct."

Now, this person-form in the left eye is his wife, Virāj; their place of union is this space within the heart; their food is this lump of blood within the heart; their covering is this network-like membrane within the heart; and their path for moving about, which exists as a reality, is this channel that rises upward from the heart.

These, indeed, are his channels called the "hitās" (the pierced), which are like a hair split a thousandfold. Through these, he draws up that which flows [from the food]; therefore, this [self] becomes, as it were, more refined in its nourishment than this bodily self.

Of this very person, the eastern direction is his forward vital breaths; the southern direction is his southern vital breaths; the western direction is his backward vital breaths; the northern direction is his upward vital breaths; the zenith is his upward vital breaths; the nadir is his downward vital breaths; all directions are all his vital breaths.

"This very Self is 'not this, not this. It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped; indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed; unattached and unbound, it is neither stained nor afflicted. Indeed, O Janaka, you have attained the fearless. Thus spoke Yājñavalkya. Janaka, the King of Videha, replied: "Salutations to you, Yājñavalkya! May fearlessness come to you from every side, O Blessed One, since you have taught us fearlessness. Here are the people of Videha, and here am I myself."

Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha, thinking, "I shall speak with him on equal terms. Now, when Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya had conversed together regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice, Yājñavalkya granted him a boon. He chose the right to ask any question he desired; Yājñavalkya granted it to him. Then the Emperor himself asked the first question.

"Yājñavalkya," [the King asked], "what is the light of this person? "The light of the sun, O Emperor," he said, "for by the light of the sun alone does this person sit, move about, perform his work, and return. "Just so, Yājñavalkya."

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have? "The moon is his light, O Emperor," he said. "By the moon as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Just so, Yājñavalkya."

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what light does this person have? "Fire is his light, O King," he said. "By fire as his light, indeed, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Just so, Yājñavalkya."

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have? "Speech is his light, O Emperor," he said. "By speech as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns. "Therefore, O Emperor, even where one's own hand cannot be discerned, yet where speech sounds forth, there one goes forward. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya."

"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and speech has been stilled, what light does this person have? "The self is his light, O King," he said. "By the light of the self alone, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns."

"What is the Self? [The answer is: This person consisting of consciousness, who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths—he, being common to both, moves between the two worlds; he meditates, as it were, he stirs, as it were; becoming a dream with his intellect, he transcends this world.
Indeed, this person, when being born and entering a body, becomes united with evils; when departing and dying, he leaves behind the evils, the forms of death.

Now, this very person has indeed two stations: this world and the station of the other world; the third is the intermediate station, the state of dream. Standing in that intermediate station, he beholds both stations—this world and the station of the other world.

Now, as for this progression that occurs in the state of the other world—having ascended that progression, he beholds both evils and joys. When he here sleeps, having taken a measure from this all-encompassing world, having himself struck it down and himself fashioned it, he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light; herein this person becomes self-luminous.

There are no chariots there, no draft animals for chariots, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads. There is no joy, no delight, and no gladness there; yet he creates joy, delight, and gladness. There are no ponds, rivers, or lotus-pools there; yet he creates ponds, rivers, and lotus-pools. For he is the creator.

Regarding this, there are these verses: "Having struck down the body by means of sleep, the Unsleeping One looks on at those who sleep; taking the light, he returns again to his place—the golden, solitary swan, the Person."
Protecting his other nest with his vital breath, having moved outside the nest as the immortal, he goes wherever he desires—the golden, singular swan, the person.
In the midst of sleep, being led along through high and low states, the god creates many forms; as it were, rejoicing with women, as it were, laughing, and even seeing terrors.
They see his pleasure grove, yet no one sees him; therefore they say, "One should not awaken him while he is asleep," for it becomes difficult to treat him whom he does not attend to.

Moreover, they say: "This [state] of his is indeed the very region of waking; for whatever he sees while awake, those same things he sees while asleep. "In this state, this person becomes self-luminous. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One; speak further for the sake of liberation alone."

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that state of dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to his rule and according to his origin, toward the state of waking alone. Whatever he sees there, he does not carry over with him; for this person is unattached. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya," [said Janaka]. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One. Speak further only for the sake of liberation."
Just as a great fish moves back and forth between both banks, the near and the far, even so this person moves back and forth between these two ends: the state of dream and the state of waking.

Just as in this sky a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains poised for its nest, even so this person hastens toward that end where, when asleep, he desires no desire whatsoever and sees no dream whatsoever.

These indeed are his channels called the *hitā* (the "conduits"), which exist with a fineness like that of a hair split a thousandfold; they are filled with white, blue, brown, green, and red [fluids]. Now, when it seems to him as if he were being killed, or as if he were being conquered, or as if an elephant were chasing him, or as if he were falling into a pit—whatever fear he perceives while awake, that he imagines to be fear here through ignorance. But when he thinks, "I am a king," or "I am a god," or "I am all this"—that is his highest world. Then, when he is asleep, he desires no desire at all and sees no dream whatsoever.

This, indeed, is his form in which the self is the object of desire, in which all desires are fulfilled, and which is free from desire. Just as a man embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without nor anything within, even so this embodied self, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña-ātman), knows nothing without nor anything within.

This, indeed, is his form: exceedingly radiant, free from evil, fearless, and without sorrow within. Here, a father becomes no father; a mother, no mother; worlds, no worlds; gods, no gods; Vedas, no Vedas; sacrifices, no sacrifices. Here, a thief becomes no thief; a killer of an embryo, no killer of an embryo; a Paulkasa, no Paulkasa; a Caṇḍāla, no Caṇḍāla; an ascetic, no ascetic; a mendicant, no mendicant. He is untouched by merit and untouched by evil, for he has then transcended all sorrows of the heart.

Indeed, when he does not see that, it is because, though seeing, he does not see the object to be seen; for there is no loss of the vision of the seer, since it is indestructible. But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, which he might see.

Indeed, when he does not smell there, it is because, though smelling, he does not smell that which is to be smelled; for there is no loss of the olfactory power of the smeller, since it is imperishable. Yet, there is no second thing, other than and separate from him, which he might smell.

Indeed, when one does not taste that, it is because, though knowing, one does not taste the taste; for there is no loss of the taster's capacity to taste, owing to its imperishability. Yet, there is nothing second to it, nothing else separate from it, that one might taste.

Indeed, when he does not speak there, it is not that the speech which ought to be spoken fails to be spoken; for there is no loss of the word of the speaker, because of its indestructibility. However, there is no second thing existing there, distinct from him, which he might speak.

Indeed, when he does not hear, it is because, though hearing, he does not hear that which is to be heard; for there is no loss of the hearing of the hearer, owing to its imperishability. But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, that he might hear.

Indeed, when one does not think that [which is to be thought], though he is a thinker, he does not think that which is to be thought; for there is no loss of the thinking of the thinker because of his imperishability. But there is no second thing, nothing else separate from him, that he might think.

Indeed, that does not touch, for although it touches, it does not touch that which is to be touched; for there is no loss of the power of touching on the part of the toucher because of its imperishability. Yet, there exists nothing else, other than and separate from it, which it might touch.

Indeed, that which he does not perceive there, he does not perceive because, though perceiving, he does not perceive that which is to be perceived; for there is no loss of the knower's perception, because of its imperishability. But there is not a second thing existing there, distinct from him, which he might perceive.

"He becomes one with water, a seer, without duality; this, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman. Thus he said to him: "This is his highest world; this is his supreme bliss. All other beings live on but a fraction of this very bliss."
That which is the supreme bliss of humans is when one is prosperous, successful, a lord over others, and most fully endowed with all human desires.
Now, that which is a hundredfold the bliss of human beings is one measure of the bliss of the ancestors who have won the world.
Now, that which is a hundredfold the bliss of the ancestors who have won their worlds is a single bliss of the gods by action, who attain godhood through their ritual acts.

Now, that which is a hundredfold the bliss of the gods by action is one measure of the bliss of the gods by birth; and such is the bliss of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and untouched by desire.
Now, a hundred joys of the Ājānadevas constitute one joy of the world of the gods, as does the joy of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and untouched by desire.

Now, whatever hundred joys there are in the world of the gods, that is equal to a single joy in the world of the Gandharvas—[the joy] of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and untouched by desire.

"Now, a hundredfold the joys in the world of the Gandharvas are equal to a single joy in the world of Prajāpati; and a hundredfold the joys in the world of Prajāpati are equal to a single joy in the world of Brahman—[the joy] of one who is learned in the Vedas, free from blemish, and untouched by desire. This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman. Thus he instructed him. "This is the immortal. I give a thousand [cows] to your honor; now speak further for the sake of liberation alone."

Having indeed enjoyed himself and wandered about in this state of serene confidence (*samprasāda*), and having seen both merit and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, for the sake of waking consciousness alone. Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it, for this person is unattached. "It is even so, Yājñavalkya," [said Janaka]. "I give you a thousand [cows], sir; speak further for the sake of liberation alone."

At this point, Yājñavalkya became afraid, thinking, "The king is wise; he has trapped me from all sides. When one reaches the state of minuteness—either through old age or through illness—and attains a state of extreme attenuation, just as a mango, a fig, or a pipal fruit might be released from its stalk, even so this embodied self, being completely liberated from these limbs, returns again according to the rule, according to its source, for the sake of vital breath alone.
Just as a well-balanced cart, when driven, moves along, even so this bodily self, mounted by the conscious self, moves along while emitting sounds.

Just as when a king approaches, fierce criminals, charioteers, and village headmen prepare for him with food, drink, and lodging, thinking, "He is coming! He is arriving!", even so do all beings prepare for one who knows this, thinking, "Brahman is coming! Brahman is arriving!"

Just as when a king intends to depart, fierce soldiers, magistrates, charioteers, and village headmen gather around him, even so do all the vital breaths gather around one who knows this when his breath becomes directed upwards.

When this embodied self reaches a state of weakness and falls, as it were, into a state of confusion, then these vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around him; taking up these particles of light, he descends into the heart itself.

When this person who is seen in the eye turns away, then he becomes one who is no longer born of form; he becomes unified. "He does not see," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not taste," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not speak," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not hear," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not think," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not touch," they say; "he becomes unified," they say; "he does not know," they say.

The tip of this very heart flashes forth; by that flash, this self departs, either through the eye, or through the head, or through other parts of the body. As it departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after it; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions follow after it. It enters into consciousness alone. Thus, it becomes a knowing self endowed with consciousness. Knowledge and action take hold of it, as does its prior experience.

Just as a caterpillar, having reached the end of a blade of grass, draws itself together [toward the next], even so this person, having struck down this body and caused ignorance to pass away, draws himself together.

Just as a weaver, taking a measure of thread, weaves out another form that is newer and more beautiful, even so this person, having cast off this body and caused ignorance to pass away, weaves out another form—whether that of a father, or a Gandharva, or Brahmā, or Prajāpati, or a deity, or a human, or from other beings.

This very Self, indeed, is Brahman—consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of speech, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of space, consisting of air, consisting of fire, consisting of water, consisting of earth, consisting of anger, consisting of non-anger, consisting of joy, consisting of non-joy, consisting of righteousness, consisting of unrighteousness, and consisting of everything. As it is said, "Consisting of this, consisting of that"—according as one acts and according as one conducts oneself, so does one become: a doer of good becomes good, a doer of evil becomes evil; one becomes holy through holy action and evil through evil action.
Now, moreover, they say: "This person consists of desire alone. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the deed he performs; and whatever deed he performs, that he attains.

Regarding this, there is this verse: "That very being goes forth together with its action; the subtle body (*liṅga*) follows where his mind is attached. Having reached the end of that action which he performs here, from that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action. Thus it is for one who desires. Now, as for one who does not desire—he who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desire is fulfilled—for him the vital breaths do not depart; they are merged right here. Being Brahman, he attains Brahman.
Regarding this, there is this verse: "When all desires that dwell within his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."

"Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill, even so does this body lie. But this bodiless, incorporeal, conscious Self is indeed Brahman, the world itself, O Emperor. Thus spoke Yājñavalkya. "I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One," said Janaka of Videha.

Regarding this, there are these verses: "Subtle is the path, ancient and wide; it has been touched by me and discovered by me alone. By it, the wise who know Brahman, having departed from here and being liberated, go to the heavenly world."
Regarding that, they say it is white or blue, tawny, green, and red; this is the path discovered by Brahmā, and by it go those who know Brahman, the radiant, and the doers of merit.
Into blind darkness enter those who worship the Unmanifest; into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, enter those who delight in the Manifest.
"Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness; to them go after death those ignorant people who lack understanding."
"That indeed we are, and that indeed we become; if we do not know this, there is great ruin. Those who know it become immortal, while others enter only into suffering."
If a person were to know the Self, thinking "I am this," what would he desire, for the sake of what longing, would he continue to wander about following a body?

He whose Self has been discovered and awakened, even though he has entered this dense thicket of doubt—he is the maker of all, he is the creator of everything; his is the world, and he indeed is that very world.
When one clearly perceives this Self as the God who directly rules over the past and the future, then one no longer wavers in doubt.
In whom the five classes of beings and space are established—him alone I consider the Self; knowing him as the immortal Brahman, I am immortal.
Since the year revolves with its days, therefore the gods worship that as the light of lights, for it is life and immortality.

Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, the food of food, and the mind of mind—they have perceived the ancient, supreme Brahman, which is to be attained by the mind alone; herein there is no diversity whatsoever.
He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity; this [Reality] is to be perceived by the mind alone—it is immeasurable and eternal.

"Free from passion, beyond the ether, unborn, the Self, great and firm—having known that very one, the wise Brahmin should practice wisdom; he should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech."

This very Self is the controller of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; it rules over this entire world, whatever exists therein. It does not become greater by good action, nor indeed smaller by evil action. It is the lord of beings, the lord of the world, the protector of the world. It is the bridge and the support so that these worlds may not be confounded.

They desire to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through celibacy, austerity, faith, sacrifice, and fasting; and having known this very Self, one becomes a sage; it is for the sake of this very world that those who have renounced go forth as wanderers.

Indeed, it is said that in former times, learned and wise Brahmins who had studied the Vedas did not desire offspring, saying: "What shall we do with offspring, for us this Self is the world? Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then led the life of mendicants. For the desire for sons is the same as the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the same as the desire for worlds; indeed, both of these are simply desires.

This very Self is "not this, not this" (neti neti). It is ungraspable, for it is not grasped; indestructible, for it is not destroyed; unattached and unbound, for it is neither attached nor afflicted. Therefore, one thinks, "I have done evil," and "I have done good. For he transcends both of these—both the auspicious and the inauspicious—and being immortal, neither what is done nor what is left undone afflicts him. His world is not measured by any action whatsoever.

This has been declared in a Ṛgvedic verse: "This is the eternal greatness of a Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become less. One should know his very state; having known it, one is not stained by evil action. Therefore, one who knows this, being calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and possessing faith as his wealth, should see the Self in the Self alone. He sees this entire world; the whole world becomes his Self, and he becomes the Self of all. He crosses over all evil; evil does not cross over him. He burns away all evil; evil does not burn him. Free from evil, free from old age, free from hunger and thirst, he becomes a Brāhmaṇa—he who knows thus.
Verily, this great, unborn Self is the eater of food and the giver of wealth. He who knows this great, unborn Self as the eater of food and the giver of wealth finds wealth.

"Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, undying, fearless, immortal Brahman. You have indeed attained the fearless, O Janaka," said Yājñavalkya. "I give the Videhas to you, sir, and myself along with them as a slave," [Janaka replied].
Verily, this great unborn Self is undecaying, immortal, fearless, and immortal Brahman. Brahman is indeed fearless; for he who knows thus becomes the fearless Brahman.

Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī; of these two, Maitreyī was a discussant of Brahman, while Kātyāyanī possessed only the wisdom of women. He [Yājñavalkya], being about to adopt another way of life, [prepared to depart].
Yājñavalkya said, "Maitreyī, I am indeed about to depart from this state; come, let me make a final settlement for you with this Kātyāyanī."

Maitreyī said: "If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I thereby become immortal, or not? Yājñavalkya said: "No, no. As is the life of those who possess the means of subsistence, so would your life be; there is no hope for immortality through wealth."
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal? Tell me only that which your reverence knows."

Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, you have spoken what is pleasing to us, even though you are already dear to us. Come now, my dear, I shall tell you that; I shall explain it to you. But meditate deeply on my speech as I explain it. [Maitreyī] said: "Let the Blessed One speak."

Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, O Maitreyī, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. The gods are dear, not out of love for the gods, but rather out of love for the Self that the gods are dear. The Vedas are dear, not out of love for the Vedas, but rather out of love for the Self that the Vedas are dear. The sacrifices are dear, not out of love for the sacrifices, but rather out of love for the Self that the sacrifices are dear. All beings are dear, not out of love for all beings, but rather out of love for the Self that all beings are dear. Everything is dear, not out of love for everything, but rather out of love for the Self that everything is dear. Therefore, the Self, my dear, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. When the Self, my dear, has been seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known."

Brahman would desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self; the Vedas would desert him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self; the sacrifices would desert him who knows the sacrifices as other than the Self; the beings would desert him who knows the beings as other than the Self; everything would desert him who knows everything as other than the Self. This Brahman, this Kshatra, these worlds, these gods, these Vedas, these sacrifices, these beings, this entire universe—all this is what this Self is.
Just as, when a drum is struck...
It is just as in the case of a lute.
It is just as in the case of a conch shell.

Just as from a fire of damp fuel, smoke issues forth, even so from this Great Being have issued forth the Rig-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the expositions, the further expositions, the explanations, what is given, what is sacrificed, what is eaten, what is drunk, this world and the other world, and all beings—all these are his very breaths.
Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters.

"Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of taste, even so, my dear, this great being is infinite, boundless, and entirely a single mass of consciousness. Arising from these elements, it vanishes again into them. After death, there is no consciousness," Yājñavalkya said. "So I say, my dear."
Maitreyī said: "Right here, sir, you have landed me in the midst of utter confusion; indeed, I do not understand this: that after death there is no consciousness."
Yājñavalkya said: "Indeed, I do not speak delusion, my dear; this self is indestructible, for its nature is such that it cannot be perceived. However, it has contact with the material elements."
Verily, when he does not see that.
For indeed, he does not smell that.
For indeed, that which does not taste it [does not perceive it].
For indeed, he does not speak that which is there.
Indeed, when he does not hear that, [he is dead].
For indeed, he does not think that which is there.
For that which does not touch it.
For indeed, he does not perceive that.

Or rather, where there might appear to be something else, there one would see another, smell another, taste another, speak to another, hear another, think of another, touch another, and cognize another.

"But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? By what and whom should he taste? By what and whom should he speak? By what and whom should he hear? By what and whom should he think? By what and whom should he touch? By what and whom should he know that by which one knows all this? By what, my dear Maitreyī, should one know the Knower? Thus far, indeed, goes the instruction for immortality," having said this, Yājñavalkya departed.

Now, the lineage: This [lineage] is from Śaurpaṇāyya; Śaurpaṇāyya from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from both Vātsya and Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from both Sāṃkṛtya and Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Audavāhi and Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Vaijavāpa and Gautama; Gautama from Vaijavāpāyana and Vaiṣṭapureya; Vaiṣṭapureya from Śāṇḍilya and Rauhiṇāyana; Rauhiṇāyana from Rauhiṇāyana; Rauhiṇāyana from Śaunāka and Jaivantāyana; Raibhya from Raibhya; Raibhya from Pautimāṣyāyaṇa and Kauṇḍinyāyana; Kauṇḍinyāyana from the two Kauṇḍinyas; the Kauṇḍinyas from Aurṇavābha; Aurṇavābhas from Kauṇḍinya; Kauṇḍinya from Kauṇḍinya; and Kauṇḍinya from both Kauṇḍinya and Āgniveśya.

Āgniveśya from Saitava; Saitava from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Āsurāyaṇa; Gautama from Gautama and Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Valākākauśika; Valākākauśika from Kāṣāyaṇa; Kāṣāyaṇa from Saukarāyaṇa; Saukarāyaṇa from Traivaṇi; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Sāyakāyana; Sāyakāyana from Kauśikāyani; Kauśikāyani from Ghṛtakauśika; Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśaryāyaṇa; Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Pārāśarya; Pārāśarya from Jātūkarṇya; Jātūkarṇya from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from both Bhāradvāja and Āsurāyaṇa; Āsurāyaṇa from both Traivaṇi and Yāska; Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani; Aupajandhani from Āsuri; Āsuri from Bhāradvāja; Bhāradvāja from Ātreya.

Ātreya from Māṇṭi; Māṇṭi from Gautama; Gautama from Gautama; Gautama from Vātsya; Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya; Śāṇḍilya from Kaiśorya Kāpya; Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumārahārita; Kumārahārita from Gālava; Gālava from Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya; Vidarbhī Kauṇḍinya from Vatsanapāt Bābhrava; Vatsanapāt Bābhrava from Pathas Saubhara; Pathas Saubhara from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa; Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra; Ābhūti Tvāṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra; Viśvarūpa Tvāṣṭra from the two Aśvins; the two Aśvins from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa from Atharvan Daiva; Atharvan Daiva from Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana; Mṛtyu Prādhvaṃsana from Pradhvaṃsana; Pradhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi; Ekarṣi from Viprajitti; Viprajitti from Vyaṣṭi; Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru; Sanāru from Sanātana; Sanātana from Sanaga; Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin; Parameṣṭhin from Brahmā; Brahmā is self-existent. Salutation to Brahmā!

Full is that, full is this; from the full, the full arises. When the full is taken from the full, the full alone remains. Om! Kha is Brahman; Kha is the ancient one. "Vāyuṛaṃ kham," so said Kauravyāyaṇīputra. This is the Veda which the Brāhmaṇas know; by means of this, that which is to be known is known.
Three groups of Prajāpati’s offspring—gods, humans, and asuras—lived as students of sacred knowledge under their father Prajāpati.

Having lived the holy life, the gods said, "May your lordship speak to us. To them he spoke this syllable: "Da. "Have you understood? [he asked]. "We have understood," they replied. "I have told you 'Be self-controlled' (dāmyata)," he said. "Yes," they said, "we have understood."

Then men said to him, "May your honor speak to us. He spoke this very syllable to them: "Da. "Have you understood? he asked. "We have understood," they replied. "What did you understand? he asked. "You told us 'Give' (datta)," they said. "Yes," he said, "you have understood."

Then the Asuras said to him, "May your honor speak to us. He spoke this very syllable to them: "Da. "Have you understood? he asked. "We have understood," they replied. "What have you understood? he asked. "You say to us: 'Be self-controlled (dāmyata), give (datta), and be compassionate (dayadhvam)'—is that what you meant by 'Om'? "Yes," he said, "you have understood. Now, this divine voice, the thunder, repeats that very same thing: "Da-da-da"—meaning, "Be self-controlled, give, be compassionate. Therefore, one should practice these three: self-control, giving, and compassion.

"Vāyu is the breath, the immortal; the body ends in ashes. Oṃ! O Kratu, remember! O Kliba, remember! O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways. Drive away from us the sin that leads astray; we offer you the most abundant word of homage."

This heart is Prajāpati; this is Brahman; this is all. This "heart" consists of three syllables: "hṛ" is one syllable—for him who knows thus, both his own people and others bring gifts; "da" is one syllable—for him who knows thus, both his own people and others give gifts; "yam" is one syllable—he who knows thus goes to the heavenly world.

That indeed was this very thing; it was the Truth alone. He who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as "Brahman is Truth" conquers these worlds; he has indeed already conquered them, even today, who knows this great, first-born Yakṣa as "Brahman is Truth," for Brahman is indeed the Truth.
In the beginning, this world was indeed only water; those waters produced the Real (satya); the Real produced Brahman, Prajāpati; and Prajāpati produced the gods.

Those gods worship it as "Truth" (satya). This [word] consists of three syllables: *sat-yam*. *Sa* is one syllable, *ti* is one syllable, and *am* is one syllable. The first and last syllables are truth, while that which is in the middle is untruth. This untruth, being enclosed on both sides by truth, becomes entirely truth; untruth does not harm one who knows this.

Now, that which is the Truth is yonder sun—the person who is in this orb and the person who is here in the right eye. These two are established in one another: by means of its rays, yonder sun is established in this [person], and by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), this [person] is established in yonder sun. When he is about to depart, he sees this orb as pure; these rays do not return to him.

Of this person who is in that orb, "Bhūḥ" is the head—there is one head and this syllable is one; "Bhuvaḥ" is the two arms—there are two arms and these two syllables; "Svar" is the two feet—there are two feet and these two syllables. Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "Ahaḥ. He who knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind.

Now, as for this person in the right eye: "Bhūḥ" is his head—there is one head, and this syllable is one; "Bhuvaḥ" is his two arms—there are two arms, and these two syllables are two; "Svar" is his two feet—there are two feet, and these two syllables are two. His secret name (*upaniṣad*) is "Aham" (I). He who knows this slays evil and leaves it behind.
They say, "Lightning is Brahman. Because it flashes (*vidāna*), it is lightning; he who knows that "lightning is Brahman" flashes away from all evil. Lightning, indeed, is Brahman.

This person consists of mind, has light for its essence, and is within the heart; like a grain of rice or a grain of barley, so is this person within the inner self. He is the ruler of all, the lord of all, the sovereign of all; he governs all this, whatever exists. Whoever knows thus [attains this].

One should worship speech as a cow. It has four udders: the utterance *svāhā*, the utterance *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *hanta*, and the utterance *svadhā*.
