Two of its udders the gods subsist upon: the *svāhā* and the *vaṣaṭ*. Men subsist upon the *hanta*, and the ancestors upon the *svadhā*. Its bull is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and its calf is the mind (*manas*).

This is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara, who is within the person, by whom this food is cooked—that which is eaten. This is his sound which one hears when one covers the ears; when he is about to depart from this world, he does not hear that sound.

This indeed is the supreme austerity: when one who is ill suffers; he who knows this conquers the supreme world. This indeed is the supreme austerity: when they carry the deceased to the forest; he who knows this conquers the supreme world. This indeed is the supreme austerity: when they place the deceased upon the fire; he who knows this conquers the supreme world.

When a person departs from this world, he goes to Vāyu; for him, Vāyu parts there as much as the hole of a chariot wheel, and through that he ascends upward. He goes to Āditya; for him, Āditya parts there as much as the hole of a drum, and through that he ascends upward. He goes to Candramas; for him, Candramas parts there as much as the hole of a kettle-drum, and through that he ascends upward. He goes to the world that is free from sorrow and free from shadow; in it he dwells for eternal years.

"Food is Brahman," some say; but that is not so, for food putrefies without breath. "Breath is Brahman," some say; but that is not so, for breath withers without food. Indeed, these two deities, having become one, attain the supreme state.

Regarding this, Prātṛda once said to his father: "What indeed could one do that is good for one who knows thus? Or what could one do that is not good for him? He (the father) replied: "Do not touch me with your hand, Prātṛda! For who, having become the unification of these two, can attain the supreme state?"

Therefore, he said this to him: "Vi"—food indeed is "vi," for all these beings have entered (*viṣṭa*) into food; "ram"—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) indeed is "ram," for all these beings delight (*ratāni*) in the vital breath. Indeed, all beings enter into him and all beings delight in him who knows thus.

The Uktha is breath; for the Uktha is indeed breath, since it causes all this to rise up. For him who knows the Uktha, a hero stands ready to rise up. He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Uktha.

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the *yajus*; for by the vital breath all these beings are joined (*yujyante*). All beings are joined for his preeminence; he who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the *yajus*.

The Sāman is indeed breath; for breath holds all these beings together, and all beings strive for preeminence within it. He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman.

The ruling power (*kṣatra*) is indeed breath; for the ruling power is breath, since breath protects him from being harmed. He who knows this attains the full measure of the ruling power and wins union with and residence in the same world as the ruling power.

"Earth, intermediate space, and heaven"—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; this, indeed, is that foot of hers. As great as these worlds are, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers thus.

"The Rig-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants"—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables; this very thing is that foot of hers. As great as this threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā) is, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers thus.

"Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna"—these are eight syllables. Now, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables; this indeed is that [foot] of hers. As far as this living world extends, so much does he conquer who knows this foot of hers in this way.

Now, this very fourth, visible foot of hers is that which shines beyond the dust (parorajā), namely, he who shines as the sun. For what is fourth is the "fourth" (turīya); it is called the "visible foot" because he is, as it were, visible; and it is called "beyond the dust" because he shines high above all the dust. In this very way, he who knows this foot of hers thus shines with prosperity and glory.

This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth, visible foot, beyond the dust of the atmosphere; it is indeed established upon truth. The eye is truth, for the eye is indeed truth. Therefore, if two people should come disputing, one saying "I saw it" and the other "I heard it," one would place more trust in the one who says, "I saw it."

That truth is indeed established in strength; strength, verily, is the vital breath (*prāṇa*), so it is established in the vital breath. Therefore they say, "Strength is more powerful than truth. Thus this Gāyatrī is established with reference to the self (*adhyātma*).

This very [verse] is "gayāṃstatre. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed "gayās"; thus, it protects (tatre) those vital breaths here. Because it protects the vital breaths (gayān), it is called Gāyatrī. That which he recites as "amūm" is this very same [verse]. For whomsoever he recites it, he thereby protects his vital breaths.

Some recite that Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying, "The Anuṣṭubh is speech; thus we utter speech. One should not do so; one should recite it as a Gāyatrī. For even if one accepts a great deal [as a gift], it does not equal even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.

If one were to receive these three worlds filled to capacity, he would obtain only this first foot of her. And if one were to receive as much as this triple knowledge (the three Vedas) extends, he would obtain this second foot of her. And if one were to receive as many living beings as there are here, he would obtain this third foot of her. But this fourth, visible foot of hers, which shines beyond the dust—heaven—cannot be obtained by anyone at all; how then could one receive so much?

The worship of that [Gāyatrī] is as follows: "O Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless, for you have no feet to tread upon. Homage to your fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust of the world! May so-and-so not attain that [goal]!"—or, "May this desire of mine not be fulfilled for him whom I hate! Indeed, the desire does not succeed for the one whom he hates, provided he worships her in this way, saying either, "May I attain that," or "I have attained that."

Janaka of Videha said this to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "Since you claimed to be a knower of the Gāyatrī, why then do you carry [me] having become an elephant? He replied, "O King, it was because I did not know its mouth."

Fire indeed is its mouth; for even if one throws much fuel into the fire, it completely consumes it all. In the very same way, even if one who knows this performs much evil, it entirely melts away, and he becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal.

Śvetaketu Āruṇeya went to the assembly of the Pañcālas. He approached Pravāhaṇa Jaibali while he was being waited upon by his attendants; looking up at him, Śvetaketu addressed him, saying, "O boy! "Yes, sir," he replied. "Have you been instructed by your father? "Yes," he said.

"Do you know how these creatures, when they depart, diverge? "No," he said. "Do you know how they return again to this world? "No indeed," he said. "Do you know how that world is not filled up, even though many go there again and again? "No indeed," he said.

"Do you know at which oblation, when it has been offered, the waters, having become human speech, rise up and speak? "No," he said. "Do you know the entry-point of either the path of the gods or the path of the fathers—that by doing what one enters upon the path of the gods or the path of the fathers?"

"For indeed, I have not heard the word of the seer. I have heard of two paths—the one of the ancestors and the one of the gods and mortals—and by these two everything that moves here comes together, whatever is between the father and the mother. "Not even one of these do I know," he said.

Then he invited him to stay for the night, but disregarding the invitation, the youth ran away. He came to his father and said to him, "Father, you surely told me before that we had been instructed by you. "How so, my dear? [the father asked]. "A kinsman of the royal class questioned me with five questions; I do not know even one of them," he replied. "Which ones were they? [the father asked]. He then recited the beginnings of those questions.

He said, "My dear, you should know us thus: whatever I know, all that I have told you. But come, let us go there and live the life of a religious student (brahmacarya). You yourself go. [The other replied,] "May you yourself go."
Gautama went to where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was; having had a seat brought for him, he had water brought for him, and then he offered him the guest-offering (arghya).
He said, "We shall grant a boon to Master Gautama. He replied, "This boon has already been granted to me; however, tell me that speech which you uttered in the presence of my son."
He said, "Gautama, since those boons belong to the gods, speak for human beings."

He said, "It is indeed known that you have received gold, cattle, horses, female slaves, excellent garments, and clothing; may you not, sir, be a consumer of what is ours—vast, endless, and boundless. "Gautama, I shall approach you by way of the sacred ford," he replied. "I am approaching you as a pupil," [the other said]. Formerly, they used to approach [a teacher] with words alone.

He, whose lineage was renowned for its approach, said: "In this way, O Gautama, neither we nor your ancestors have committed any offense, since this knowledge has not previously dwelt with any Brāhmaṇa. Nevertheless, I shall declare it to you; for who indeed would refuse one who speaks thus?"

That world, O Gautama, is indeed a fire; its fuel is the sun, its smoke is the rays, its flame is the day, its embers are the moon, and its sparks are the stars. Into this very fire, the gods offer faith; from that oblation, King Soma comes into being.

"Or rather, O Gautama, Agni is Parjanya; his fuel is the year, his smoke is the clouds, his flame is lightning, his embers are thunderbolts, and his sparks are hailstones. Into this very fire the gods offer Soma, and from that oblation rain comes into being."

"This world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama; its fuel is the earth, its smoke is the wind, its flame is the night, its embers are the quarters, and its sparks are the intermediate quarters. Into this very fire, the gods offer rain; from that oblation, food comes into being."

"Man, O Gautama, is indeed the fire. His opened mouth is the fuel; his breath is the smoke; his speech is the flame; his eye is the embers; and his ear is the sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer food; from that offering, semen comes into being."

Woman, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama; her lap is the fuel, her hair the smoke, the vulva the flame, what one does within it are the embers, and the pleasures are the sparks. Into this very fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation a person comes into being. He is born; he lives as long as he lives. Then, when he dies, they carry him to the fire.

For him, fire indeed becomes fire; the fuel becomes fuel, the smoke becomes smoke, the flame becomes flame, the embers become embers, and the sparks become sparks. Into this very fire, the gods offer the person as an oblation. From that oblation, a person of radiant complexion comes into being.

Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, venerate truth with faith—they pass into the light; from the light, into the day; from the day, into the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, into the six months during which the sun moves northward; from those months, into the world of the gods; from the world of the gods, into the sun; from the sun, into the lightning. A person consisting of mind comes from the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman. In those worlds of Brahman, they dwell for the highest of high distances; for them, there is no returning again to this world.

Now, those who win a world through sacrifice, through charity, or through austerity, proceed to the smoke; from smoke they go to night; from night to the waning fortnight; from the waning fortnight to those six months during which the sun moves southward; from those months to the world of the fathers; and from the world of the fathers to the moon. Having reached the moon, they become food. There the gods consume them, just as they consume King Soma with the words, "Swell up! Wane away! When that [merit] of theirs is exhausted, they emerge into this very space; from space to air; from air to rain; and from rain to earth. Having reached the earth, they become food. In this very way they return again. But those who do not know these two paths become worms, moths, and whatever is biting.

Verily, he who knows the eldest and the best becomes the eldest and the best among his own people. Breath indeed is the eldest and the best; he who knows this becomes the eldest and the best among his own people, and even among those whom he desires to excel.
He who knows the most excellent becomes the most excellent among his own people; speech indeed is the most excellent, and he who knows this becomes the most excellent among his own people.

He who knows the foundation indeed finds a firm footing; he finds a firm footing on level ground and he finds a firm footing on rough terrain. The eye, indeed, is the foundation, for by means of the eye one finds a firm footing both on level ground and on rough terrain. He who knows thus finds a firm footing on level ground and finds a firm footing on rough terrain.

Verily, he who knows attainment—whatever desire he desires, that is attained for him. The ear, indeed, is attainment; for in the ear all these Vedas are fully contained. Whatever desire he desires, that is attained for him who knows thus.

He who knows the abode indeed becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men; for the mind is the abode—he who knows thus becomes the abode of his own people and the abode of other men.
He who knows procreation is indeed procreated with offspring and cattle; semen is procreation. He who knows this is procreated with offspring and cattle.

These vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahmā, saying, "Who among us is the most excellent? He replied, "He among you, upon whose departure this body is considered the worst off—he is the most excellent of you."

Speech departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the mute live without speaking by means of speech—breathing with the breath, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so have we lived. Then Speech entered back in.

The eye departed. Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the blind, though not seeing with the eye, lived by breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so have we lived. Thereupon, the eye entered back in.

The ear departed. After being away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "As the deaf live—without hearing with the ear, yet breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—even so did we live. Thereupon, the ear entered back in.

The mind departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as the ignorant and deluded live—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and procreating with semen—even so have we lived. Then the mind entered back in.

The semen departed. Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me? They replied, "Just as eunuchs live without procreating—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind—even so have we lived. Thereupon, the semen entered back in.

Then, as the vital breath was about to depart, it tore out these other breaths just as a great Sindh horse from the Indus region might tear up the pegs of its foot-tethers. They cried out, "O Venerable One, do not depart! We shall certainly not be able to live without you. He said, "Then make an offering to me. They replied, "So be it."

Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent; insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation; insofar as I am attainment (*sampat*), you are that attainment; insofar as I am the abode (*āyatana*), you are that abode; insofar as I am procreation (*prajāti*), you are that procreation. "Then what is my food? What is my clothing? [they asked]. "Whatever there is here, even unto dogs, worms, insects, and moths—that is your food; water is your clothing. For one who knows this food of speech, nothing is ever eaten that is not food, nor is anything received that is not food.

Knowing this, learned Vedic scholars sip water before eating and sip water after eating; they consider that they are thereby making this very [breath] non-naked. Therefore, one who knows this should sip water before eating and sip water after eating; he thereby makes this very [breath] non-naked.

He who desires, "May I attain greatness," should, during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight on an auspicious day, having observed the *upasad* vow for twelve days, collect all kinds of herbs and fruits in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood—either a bronze cup or a wooden bowl—and having swept around it, smeared it with cow-dung, and established the fire, he should prepare clarified butter according to the prescribed ritual and, under a male constellation, having mixed the mash, he offers it as an oblation.
O Jātavedas, as many gods as dwell within you who strike down the desires of a person, to them I offer this portion; may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with my desires—svāhā!

"You who lie across, saying 'I am the supporter,' you, the one who brings success, I worship with a stream of ghee—svāhā! O Prajāpati, none other than you possesses these"—with this he offers the third oblation.

Having offered into the fire with the formulas, "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash. [He offers] into the fire with "To the breath, svāhā! To the most excellent, svāhā! into the fire with "To the eye, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā! into the fire with "To the ear, svāhā! To the abode, svāhā! into the fire with "To the mind, svāhā! To procreation, svāhā! into the fire with "To semen, svāhā! into the fire.

"To that which has been, svāhā!"—thus [he offers] into the fire; "To that which is to be, svāhā!"—thus into the fire; "To the All, svāhā!"—thus into the fire; "To the Whole, svāhā!"—thus into the fire.

"To the Earth, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire; "To the Atmosphere, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire; "To the Sky, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire; "To the Quarters, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire; "To the Brahman, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire; "To the Kṣatra, svāhā!"—he offers in the fire.
"Bhūḥ svāhā!"—he offers into the fire; "Bhuvaḥ svāhā!"—he offers into the fire; "Svaḥ svāhā!"—he offers into the fire; "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā!"—he offers into the fire.

Having offered into the fire with "Svāhā to Agni," "Svāhā to Soma," "Svāhā to Splendor," "Svāhā to Śrī," "Svāhā to Lakṣmī," "Svāhā to Savitṛ," "Svāhā to Sarasvatī," "Svāhā to the Viśvedevas," and "Svāhā to Prajāpati," he pours the remnants into the stirred drink (*mantha*).

Then he touches it, saying: "Thou art moving; thou art flaming; thou art full; thou art firm; thou art the unique assembly; thou art the *hiṅ* uttered; thou art the *hiṅ* being uttered; thou art the *udgītha*; thou art the *udgītha* being sung; thou art the *śrāvaṇa*; thou art the *pratyāśrāvaṇa*; thou art moist; thou art kindled; thou art pervasive; thou art abundant; thou art light; thou art food; thou art the finale; thou art the absorber."
Then he lifts it up with: "Unripe art thou; for unripe is it in me. He indeed is the King, the Ruler, the Overlord; may he make me the King, the Ruler, the Overlord."

Then he sips from it with the verse: "The desirable excellence of that Savitṛ; the winds blow honey for the one who follows the Cosmic Order; the rivers flow with honey; may the plants be sweet for us. Bhūḥ! Svāhā!"
We meditate upon the splendor of the divine; may the night be honey-sweet, and the dawn honey-sweet; may the earthly realm be honey-sweet, and may our father, heaven, be honey-sweet—Bhuvaḥ Svāhā!

"May he impel our thoughts. "May the tree be honey-sweet for us; may the sun be honey-sweet; may the cows be honey-sweet for us. Having recited the entire Sāvitrī verse, all the verses containing the word "honey," and all the *vyāhṛtis*, ending with "May I become all this—*bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*! *Svāhā*!"—and having sipped water and washed his mouth, he lies down behind the fire, facing east, with his head toward the east.

In the morning, he worships the sun, saying: "May I become the unique lotus among the quarters; may I become the unique lotus among men. Having returned by the same way he came, sitting behind the fire, he mutters the lineage formula (*vaṃśa*).
Having told this very same thing to his pupil Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi said: "Even if one were to pour this upon a withered stump, shoots would sprout and leaves would grow."
Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya indeed taught this very same [doctrine] to his pupil Madhuka Paiṅgya.
Madhuka Paiṅgya taught this very same [doctrine] to his pupil Cūḍā Bhāgavitti.
Cūḍa Bhāgavitti taught this very same [doctrine] to Jānaki Āyasthūṇa as a pupil.
Jānaki Āyasthūṇa taught this very same [doctrine] to Satyakāma Jābāla, his pupil.

Satyakāma Jābāla, having spoken this very thing to his pupils, said: "Even if one were to pour this upon a withered stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout. One should not speak of this to anyone who is not a son or a pupil.
There are four items made of udumbara wood: a cup of udumbara wood, a dipping-spoon of udumbara wood, a fuel-wood of udumbara wood, and two churning-sticks of udumbara wood.

There are ten kinds of cultivated grains: rice, barley, sesame, beans, small millet, panic seed, wheat, lentils, chickpeas, and vetch; having ground these together, he sprinkles them with curd, honey, and ghee, and offers them as an oblation of clarified butter.
Of these beings, the earth is the essence; of the earth, water; of water, plants; of plants, flowers; of flowers, fruits; of fruits, man; and of man, semen.

Prajāpati reflected: "Come now, I shall provide a support for him. He created a woman; having created her, he worshipped her from below. Therefore, one should worship a woman from below, for she is indeed prosperity (śrī). He brought forth from his own self that pressing-stone facing eastward, and with it he cast her down.

Her altar is the vulva, her hair is the sacrificial grass, her skin is the two pressing-boards, and her ignited fire is the testicles between them. As great as is the world of one who performs the Vājapeya sacrifice, so great is the world of him who, knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse; he takes away the merit of women. But he who, not knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse, his women take away his merit.

Indeed, knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi said; indeed, knowing this, Nāka Maudgalya said; indeed, knowing this, Kumārahārita said: "Many young men of the Brahmin caste, devoid of power and deprived of merit, depart from this world, they who practice this lower laughter without knowing it."

Much indeed is this semen that spills for one who is either asleep or awake; he should touch it or recite over it the mantra: "That semen of mine which today has spilled upon the earth, which has flowed into the plants, and which has entered the waters—this semen I take back up again. May my virility return to me, may my luster return, may my fortune return. May the sacrificial fires return to their places; may they be restored according to their stations. Having taken it with his ring finger and thumb, he should rub it between his breasts or between his eyebrows.
Now, if he should see his own reflection in water, he should consecrate it with the mantra: "In me be splendor, sensory power, fame, wealth, and merit."

This woman who has removed her soiled garment is indeed the Fortune (Śrī) of women; therefore, one should approach and address a renowned woman who has removed her soiled garment. If she does not yield to him, he may, if he wishes, purchase her off. If she still does not yield to him, he may, if he wishes, strike her with a staff or with his hand and pass her by, saying: "I take from you the glory that was in your organ. Thus, she becomes indeed devoid of glory.

If he should desire her and wish for her, having prepared the matter with her, having joined mouth to mouth and touched her private parts, he should mutter: "From the limb you arise, from the heart you are born; you are the essence of the limbs; intoxicate me as if I were pierced by a poisoned arrow."

Now, if one should desire of a woman, "May she not conceive," he should place his member in her, join mouth to mouth, and then breathe in and breathe out, saying: "With my organ, I take away your seed with my seed. Thus she becomes indeed seedless.

Now, if he should desire of a woman, "May she conceive," he should have intercourse with her, having placed his mouth against her mouth, and exhaling and inhaling, he should say, "With my organ, I place seed in your seed. She indeed becomes pregnant.

Now, if one should have a lover for his wife and should hate him, he should kindle a fire in an unbaked earthen vessel, spread out sacrificial grass with its points turned downwards, and into that [fire] he should offer these three reed-shards, smeared with clarified butter and with their points turned downwards, saying: "In my kindled fire thou hast sacrificed; I seize thy hope and expectation, O so-and-so!"—here he pronounces the name. "In my kindled fire thou hast sacrificed; I seize thy sons and cattle, O so-and-so!"—here he pronounces the name. "In my kindled fire thou hast sacrificed; I seize thy out-breath and in-breath, O so-and-so!"—here he pronounces the name. Indeed, he whom a Brahmin who knows this thus curses departs from this world deprived of power and deprived of merit. Therefore, one who knows this should not seek to joke with the wife of a learned Śrotriya, for he who knows this becomes superior.

Now, if a woman should find her menses, she shall not drink from a bronze vessel for three days and must not wear soiled clothes; neither a low-caste man nor a low-caste woman shall touch her. At the end of the three nights, having bathed, she should have rice threshed.

If he should desire, "May a fair-skinned son be born to me who shall recite the Veda and live his full span of life," they should cook rice with milk and eat it with clarified butter, being capable of procreating.
Now, if one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is tawny and reddish-brown, who shall master two Vedas, and who shall live his full span of life," he should have rice cooked with curd.

Now, if one should desire, "May a son be born to me who is dark-complexioned and red-eyed, who shall recite the three Vedas and live his full span of life," he should have boiled rice cooked with meat.
Now, if one should desire, "May a wise daughter be born to me, and may she live her full lifespan," he should have rice cooked with sesame seeds.

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is wise, victorious, capable in assembly, a speaker of words that are to be heeded, who shall study all the Vedas and live his full span of life," then, having cooked meat-rice with clarified butter, the two of them, being capable of procreation, should eat it—either beef or the meat of a bull.

Then, at the very break of dawn, having performed the rites with clarified butter according to the procedure for a *sthālīpāka* (cooked-rice offering), he offers a portion of the *sthālīpāka* with the formula: "To Agni, Svāhā! To Anumati, Svāhā! To the god Savitṛ of true impulsion, Svāhā! Having offered, he takes out [some of the rice] and eats it; he gives the remainder to his wife. Having washed his hands and filled a water-vessel, he sprinkles her with it three times, saying: "Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu, and seek another blooming maiden as your wife."

Then he approaches her, saying: "I am he (Ama), you are she (Sā); you are she, I am he; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc; I am heaven, you are earth. Come, let us two unite; let us two together deposit seed for the sake of obtaining a male son."

Then he causes her thighs to part with the words, "May Heaven and Earth open wide. Having placed his member within her and joined mouth to mouth, he strokes her three times in the direction of the hair with the mantra: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms; may Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you. Place an embryo, O Sinīvālī; place an embryo, O thou of broad locks. May the two Aśvin gods, adorned with lotus-garlands, bestow an embryo upon you."

"The two fire-drills are golden, with which the divine Aśvins churned [the fire]. Into you we place that embryo so that it may be born in the tenth month. As the earth has Agni as its embryo, as the sky is pregnant with Indra, and as Vāyu is the embryo of the quarters—so do I place an embryo in you, O [Name]! At this point, he pronounces her name.

He sprinkles her who is about to give birth with water: "As the wind stirs a lotus pond on every side, so let your embryo stir; let it come forth together with the afterbirth. This stall for Indra has been made, enclosed and walled around; O Indra, drive out [the fetus] from there along with the afterbirth."

When [a son] has been born, having kindled the fire, having placed [the child] on his lap, and having brought speckled butter into a bronze vessel, he offers a portion of the speckled butter with the mantra: "In this [fire] may he thrive for a thousand [years], prospering in his own home; may he not neglect our attendance, [but be blessed] with offspring and cattle, Svāhā! I offer my vital breaths into you with my mind, Svāhā!"
Whatever deed I have overdone by my action, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make that well-offered and well-sacrificed; Svāhā!

Then he performs the rite for longevity: placing [the honey] near the child’s right ear, he says "Speech! Speech! three times. Then he gives him a name, saying, "You are the Veda (Vedaḥ asi). This should indeed be his secret name. Then, having mixed together curds, honey, and ghee, he makes him eat it with a piece of gold held against [his mouth], saying: "Bhūḥ, I place you in me; bhuvaḥ, I place you in me; bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svaḥ, I place everything in you."
Then he touches him, saying: "Be a stone, be an axe, be gold that is not melted; you are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns!"
Then he addresses his mother: "Thou art Iḍā, belonging to Mitra and Varuṇa; thou hast given birth to a hero among heroes; mayest thou be possessed of heroes, she who has made us possessed of heroes."

Then, having handed him over to his mother, she gives him the breast, [saying]: "That breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, which bestows jewels, which finds wealth, which is a good giver, by which you nourish all desirable things—O Sarasvatī, make that available here for him to suck."

Regarding him, they say: "Truly, you have become a father beyond the father; truly, you have become a grandfather beyond the grandfather; you have indeed reached the highest pinnacle in prosperity, fame, and the splendor of sacred knowledge, for a son has been born to a Brahmin who knows thus."

Now, the lineage: This [lineage] we [know] from Bhāradvājīputra; Bhāradvājīputra from Vātsīmāṇḍavīputra; Vātsīmāṇḍavīputra from Pārāśarīputra; Pārāśarīputra from Gārgīputra; Gārgīputra from Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra; Pārāśarīkauṇḍinīputra from Gārgīputra; Gārgīputra from Gārgīputra; Gārgīputra from Bāḍeyīputra; Bāḍeyīputra from Mauṣikīputra; Mauṣikīputra from Hārikarṇīputra; Hārikarṇīputra from Bhāradvājīputra; Bhāradvājīputra from Paiṅgīputra; Paiṅgīputra from Śaunakīputra; and Śaunakīputra [from Kāśyapīputra].

From Kāśyapī Bālākyāmāṭharīputra, [the lineage proceeds] to Kāśyapī Bālākyāmāṭharīputra; from Kautsīputra, to Kautsīputra; from Baudhīputra, to Baudhīputra; from Śālaṅkāyanīputra, to Śālaṅkāyanīputra; from Vārṣagaṇīputra, to Vārṣagaṇīputra; from Gautamīputra, to Gautamīputra; from Ātreyīputra, to Ātreyīputra; from Gautamīputra, to Gautamīputra; from Vātsīputra, to Vātsīputra; from Bhāradvājīputra, to Bhāradvājīputra; from Pārāśarīputra, to Pārāśarīputra; from Vārkāruṇīputra, to Vārkāruṇīputra; from Ārtabhāgīputra, to Ārtabhāgīputra; from Śauṅgīputra, to Śauṅgīputra; and from Sāṃkṛtīputra, to Sāṃkṛtīputra.

From Ālambīputra; Ālambīputra from Ālambāyanīputra; Ālambāyanīputra from Jāyantīputra; Jāyantīputra from Māṇḍūkāyanīputra; Māṇḍūkāyanīputra from Māṇḍūkīputra; Māṇḍūkīputra from Śāṇḍilīputra; Śāṇḍilīputra from Rāthītarīputra; Rāthītarīputra from the two Krauñcikīputras; the two Krauñcikīputras from Vaidabhṛtīputra; Vaidabhṛtīputra from Bhālukīputra; Bhālukīputra from Prācīnayogīputra; Prācīnayogīputra from Sāṃjīvīputra; Sāṃjīvīputra from Kārśakeyīputra; Kārśakeyīputra [from...].

From Prāśnīputra Āsurivāsina; Prāśnīputra from Āsurāyaṇa; Āsurāyaṇa from Āsuri; Āsuri from Yājñavalkya; Yājñavalkya from Uddālaka; Uddālaka from Aruṇa; Aruṇa from Upaveśi; Upaveśi from Kuśri; Kuśri from Vājaśravas; Vājaśravas from Jihvāvat Bādhyoga; Jihvāvat Bādhyoga from Asita Vārṣagaṇa; Asita Vārṣagaṇa from Harita Kaśyapa; Harita Kaśyapa from Śilpa Kaśyapa; Śilpa Kaśyapa from Kaśyapa Naidhruvi; Kaśyapa Naidhruvi from Vāc; Vāc from Ambhiṇī; Ambhiṇī from Āditya. These bright *yajus* formulas are proclaimed by Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya. "For this [seed] has been brought together with brilliance and the essence of milk"—for indeed, this essence of milk has been brought together. "May we obtain its milking year after year"—with this he utters a blessing. Then they purify themselves at the *catvāla* pit; the significance of this is the same as before.

Now, therefore, regarding the sacrificial fees: he gives a hundred-measure weight of gold and bullion to the Brahman priest. For the Brahman sits, while gold lies; gold is glory. Therefore, he gives a hundred-measure weight of gold and bullion to the Brahman.

Now, as for this cow that milks the Gharma, he gives her to the Adhvaryu; for the Gharma is, as it were, heated, and the Adhvaryu goes forth as it were from what is heated; therefore he gives her to the Adhvaryu.
Now, that cow which milks the vow for the sacrificer, he gives her to the Hotṛ; for the Hotṛ is the sacrifice and the sacrificer is the sacrifice; therefore, he gives her to the Hotṛ.
Then, that cow which provides the fast-milk for the wife, he gives to the Udgātṛs; for it is indeed the work of the wife that these Udgātṛs perform here, and therefore he gives her to the Udgātṛs.
Now, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this very life and this very light; his observance of the vow is that which was prescribed at the time of creation.

The sacrifice is indeed the self of all beings and of all the gods; following its success, the sacrificer prospers with offspring and cattle. But he whose *gharma* vessel breaks is deprived of offspring and cattle; in that case, there is an expiation.
He offers the full oblation; for the full is indeed everything, and by means of everything he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.

" Svāhā to the vital breaths together with their overlord!"—the mind, indeed, is the overlord of the vital breaths, for in the mind all the vital breaths are established; thus, by means of the mind itself, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the earth, svāhā!"—the earth, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; thus he heals with all those deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Agni, svāhā!"—Agni indeed is the self of all the gods; thus, by means of all the deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the intermediate space, svāhā!"—the intermediate space is indeed the abode of all the gods; thus he heals by means of all those deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Vāyu, svāhā!"—Vāyu, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the sky, svāhā!"—the sky, indeed, is the abode of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Sūrya, svāhā!"—for Sūrya is indeed the self of all the gods; thus he heals by means of all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the quarters, svāhā!"—the quarters indeed are the abode of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Candra, Svāhā!"—Candra indeed is the self of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the constellations, svāhā!"—the constellations are indeed the abode of all the gods; thus he heals with all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the waters, svāhā!"—the waters indeed are the abode of all the gods; thus he heals by means of all these deities whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To Varuna, Svaha!"—Varuna, indeed, is the self of all the gods; thus, by means of all these deities, he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"To the navel, svāhā! To the purified, svāhā!"—this is undefined; for Prajāpati is undefined, and the sacrifice is Prajāpati; thus he heals Prajāpati, the sacrifice.
These offerings are thirteen; there are indeed thirteen months in a year, and Prajāpati is the year, and Prajāpati is the sacrifice; thus he heals Prajāpati, the sacrifice.

"To Speech, Svāhā!"—thus he places speech itself into him; "To Breath, Svāhā! To Breath, Svāhā!"—thus he places the two nostrils themselves into him; "To Sight, Svāhā! To Sight, Svāhā!"—thus he places the two eyes themselves into him; "To Hearing, Svāhā! To Hearing, Svāhā!"—thus he places the two ears themselves into him.

These offerings are seven; for there are these seven vital breaths in the head, and it is these he thus bestows upon him. He offers the final full-offering (pūrṇāhuti); for the full is indeed everything, and by means of everything he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been torn asunder.
"May [the gods fulfill] the desire and intention of the mind"—for by the mind indeed all this is attained; therefore, by the mind alone he heals whatever in the sacrifice has been injured.

"May I attain the truth of speech"—for by speech indeed all this is attained; he heals with speech whatever of the sacrifice has been torn asunder. "May the form of the cattle, the essence of food, glory, and prosperity rest in me, svāhā!"—thus he invokes this very blessing.

Then, having ground that [main] brick and the *upaśaya* brick together with soft clay, he fashions them according to the prescribed ritual procedure and bakes them according to the prescribed ritual procedure for the purpose of setting them up; then, whichever of the two *upaśayas* is firm, with that one he should proceed.

The Pravargya is indeed the year; the year is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is set forth, that is spring; when it has shone forth, that is summer; when it has swelled, that is the rainy season. Indeed, when the rains swell, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. And the rains swell for him who knows this thus.

These worlds are indeed the Pravargya; these worlds are everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is heated (pravṛkta), that is this world; when it has shone forth (rucita), that is the intermediate world; when it has swelled (pinvita), that is yonder world. Indeed, when yonder world swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Yonder world truly swells for him who knows this thus.

These deities indeed are the Pravargya: Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. All these deities are indeed the Pravargya; all is the Pravargya. When it is heated, that is Agni; when it has shone forth, that is Vāyu; when it has swelled, that is yonder Āditya. And when yonder Āditya swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon him. Yonder Āditya indeed swells for one who knows this thus.

The Pravargya is indeed the sacrificer; his self, offspring, and cattle are it. The sacrificer is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is set forth (*pravṛkta*), that is his self; when it has been heated (*rucita*), that is his offspring; when it has been made to swell (*pinvita*), that is his cattle. Indeed, when cattle swell, then all the gods and all beings live upon them. Cattle indeed swell for him who knows this thus.

The Agnihotra is indeed the Pravargya; the Agnihotra is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it is ladled out, that is the *rucita*; when it is offered, that is the *pinvita*. For when the Agnihotra overflows (*pinvate*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Indeed, the Agnihotra overflows for him who knows this thus.

The *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are indeed the *pravargya*; the *darśapūrṇamāsa* is everything, and the *pravargya* is everything. When [the milk] is placed on the fire, that is the *pravṛkta*; when it is set down, that is the *rucita*; when it is offered, that is the *pinvita*. Indeed, when the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices overflow (*pinvete*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them. For him who knows this, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices overflow.

The *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are indeed the *Pravargya*; the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices are everything, and the *Pravargya* is everything. When [the milk] has been placed on the fire, that is the *Pravṛkta*; when it has been set down, that is the *Rucita*; when it has been offered, that is the *Pinvita*. For when the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices overflow (*pinvante*), then all the gods and all beings subsist upon them; and indeed, the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices overflow for him who knows this thus.

The Pravargya is indeed the Animal Sacrifice (Paśubandha). The Animal Sacrifice is everything; the Pravargya is everything. When it has been placed on the fire, it is "set forth" (pravṛkta); when it has been prepared, it is "shone upon" (rucita); when it has been offered, it is "swollen" (pinvita). For when the Animal Sacrifice swells, then all the gods and all beings subsist upon it. Indeed, the Animal Sacrifice swells for him who knows this.

The Pravargya is indeed Soma; Soma is everything, and the Pravargya is everything. When it is pressed out, that is when it has been "extracted" (pravṛkta); when it is drawn up, that is when it has "shone forth" (rucita); when it is offered, that is when it has "swollen" (pinvita). For when Soma swells, then all the gods and all beings partake of it. Indeed, Soma swells for him who knows this. And for one who knows this, no sacrifice remains unaccompanied by the Pravargya.
Now, indeed, he who either recites this or consumes it enters this life and this light; his observance of the vow is the same as that prescribed for the creation.
